Saudi Arabia has warned that the Houthi militia would face consequences for repeated attacks on the kingdom’s airports, civilian facilities and the holy cities of Mecca and Medina, reaffirming Riyadh’s commitment to protecting its security and freedom of maritime navigation.
In remarks carried by the Saudi Press Agency (SPA), the Saudi cabinet on Tuesday condemned attacks targeting visitors to the Two Holy Mosques, as well as civilian and economic infrastructure.
The group would “face the consequences of its crimes and repeated heinous attacks,” the cabinet said, adding that Saudi Arabia “will not allow threats to its security or freedom of maritime navigation in the Red Sea and the Bab al Mandab Strait.”
Riyadh also thanked countries and international organisations that had condemned the attacks.
Saudi Arabia backs coalition operations in Yemen
The cabinet praised military operations by the coalition supporting Yemen’s internationally recognised government, saying they aimed to neutralise threats posed by the Houthi militias, protect the Yemeni people and safeguard international peace, global trade and supply chains.
The remarks come amid renewed escalation between Saudi Arabia and the Houthi militias, with attacks on airports and civilian facilities reported in recent days.
The latest escalation follows a period of relative calm after a United Nations-brokered truce took effect in April 2022.
Yemen’s conflict began in 2014, when the militia group seized the capital, Sanaa, and other parts of the country, prompting a Saudi-led military intervention in March 2015 in support of the internationally recognised government.
Riyadh welcomes restoration of oil flows
The Cabinet also welcomed the resumption of oil flows through Saudi Arabia’s East-West pipeline, describing the rapid recovery as evidence of the resilience of the kingdom’s energy infrastructure and its ability to respond to emergencies while maintaining supplies to international markets.
The pipeline provides an alternative route for transporting crude oil to the Red Sea, helping Saudi Arabia reduce its reliance on export routes through the Gulf.
The Cabinet’s statement underscored Riyadh’s twin priorities of countering security threats and maintaining the stability of energy supplies and international maritime trade.

Chikli is whitewashing the French far Right - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
18:57:20 UTC
03:57:20 KST

As the head of the far-right party National Rally, Jordan Bardella, expected to become prime minister if Marine Le Pen becomes president in May 2027, faces accusations of antisemitism, he has found an unlikely ally in Diaspora Affairs and Combating Antisemitism Minister Amichai Chikli, whose support reflects a profound shift in his country’s relationship with Europe’s far-right.
In February 2025, newly appointed Foreign Minister Gideon Sa’ar decided to establish closer ties with three far-right parties: Spain’s Vox, the Sweden Democrats, and France’s National Rally (RN).
A month later, Chikli organized a conference on antisemitism attended by far-right parties, including the National Rally, with Bardella in attendance.
For Marine Le Pen, this quasi-official visit to Israel was all the more significant because it focused on antisemitism, representing the culmination of a long journey since she succeeded her father at the helm of the National Front in 2011, before it was renamed the National Rally in 2018.
A dangerous alliance
It was against this backdrop that Israel’s Ambassador to Paris Joshua Zarka welcomed Le Pen in April 2026, describing the RN as a “partner with whom we can talk.”
Le Pen had sought this normalization – and the seal of approval it would confer – from the Representative Council of French Jewish Institutions (CRIF), but had never obtained it, much to the dismay of certain prominent figures in the French Jewish community, such as nazi hunter Serge Klarsfeld.
This alliance between the Israeli government and the RN, and, more broadly, Europe’s far-right, benefits both sides.
For the RN, the “Israeli seal of approval” is an essential element of its strategy to shed its toxic image by dispelling accusations of antisemitism. The aim is less to win over Jewish voters, whose political weight is negligible, than to make voting for the RN “kosher” in the eyes of the French electorate as a whole.
The massive presence of RN elected officials at the November 2023 march against antisemitism, as well as their unequivocally pro-Israel positions, stems at least as much from political calculation as from genuine conviction.
This is why the allegations of antisemitism by the investigative website Mediapart against Bardella, for words he may have uttered when he was 17, are so devastating, and why Chikli’s emphatic support for Bardella and Zarka’s leniency in the matter could play an important role in the RN’s difficult efforts to contain the fallout.
For Israel, which is increasingly isolated on the international stage, the rapprochement championed by Chikli offers the prospect of relying on parties that express sympathy for the country and share a common enemy: Islam and Muslims.
The danger for the Jewish state is that this policy will deepen its isolation among European public opinion, particularly among younger generations. Increasingly unpopular among Democrats in the United States, Israel is now taking a similar risk with Europe’s Left and centrist parties.
In France, this alienation may go far beyond the far-left party with antisemitic overtones, La France Insoumise (France Unbowed), if Israel presents itself as an ideological and political partner of the far-right.
The rapprochement between Israel and the far-right in France, brought into sharp focus by the Bardella affair, reveals a great deal about the Israeli government’s political orientation. It is implementing the goal articulated by its prime minister of turning Israel into a self-sufficient Sparta, embracing and even proclaiming its isolation.
This vision of Israel’s place among the nations will be another major issue in the October 27 election.
Born and raised in France, the writer is the correspondent of French Jewish radio, Radio J, and of the French paper librejournal.fr in the US, where he has been living for 16 years. He also holds US and Israeli citizenships. His opinions are his only.

If You Cannot Say Genocide: Essays on Conscience and Witness
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
18:56:56 UTC
03:56:56 KST

“What task is left to art when words are turned into weapons?” Yahia Lababidi’s If you Cannot Say Genocide: Essays of Conscience and Witness explores the depth of this question impressed upon the reader in the preface. For the author, who is a Muslim of Palestinian descent, the question is pondered from a position of distance as an “inheritor of family dispossession”.
Written between 2023 and 2026, this collection of essays leans upon memory, literature, experiences, observation and reflection, through which disillusion exposes reality. While there is no chronology in Lababidi’s reflections, the preoccupation with words and meaning is persistent. For example, Lababidi writes of his posting as a speechwriter for the UN office in Cairo, where he encounters the politics of language. “I came to see that neutrality, posing as diplomacy, was a form of cowardice that did violence to my nature,” he writes.
Language shapes the rest of Lababidi’s reflections, exposing a world where meaning is determined by the politics of violence. Alongside language, Lababidi shares his own experiences, his awareness of living in the US as the government wields its power elsewhere in the world. But there are other nuances that Lababidi weaves in his essays.
“Memory is still alive, and it asks for responsibility. Distance has a way of laundering conscience. The longer we wait, the easier it becomes to confuse explanation with absolution. We need historians willing to write while the record is still unsettled, while consequences are still unfolding, guided by moral orientation,” Lababidi notes.
Many voices have practiced what Lababidi is insisting upon. The book makes many references to Palestinian writers, from Mahmoud Darwish, Edward Said and Ghassan Kanafani, to contemporary writes such as Omar El Akkad, Munther Isaac and Mohammed El-Kurd. In a way, these voices, particularly Kanafani and El-Kurd, stand in sharp contrast to the rest and even the author’s own reflections at times, who muses about the possibility of sustaining dialogue through cultural endeavours.
As the book continues, however, it becomes clearer that despite an ideal, colonialism is a brutal reality for Palestinians. The author’s distance from Palestine, not having experienced Palestine as Palestinians have experienced it throughout the decades until now, may account for the belief that art transcends. It makes for an uncomfortable read when one keeps in mind the brutality of Israeli colonial violence. But as the book continues, drawing upon Palestinian authors and their struggle from within, or from experience, the author’s voice emerges stronger. Palestinian voices speak through the pages of Lababidi’s essays, bringing a kaleidoscope of memories from artists, poets, writer and revolutionaries. Some stories relating to the Nakba are brought to the helm, and the Palestinian people’s resistance and endurance is shaped through the voices of those who survived the colonial atrocities. In this way, Lababidi’s reflections are accompanying slivers of history, such as when he states, “In our tradition, patience is greater than resignation.”
BOOK REVIEW: Wired to Steal: Zionism and the Shaping of the Western Mind
Written during the genocide, Lababidi’s essays also convey what the media conceals. “Numbers cannot contain this loss; they hide faces and extinguish stories,” he writes. Remaining conscious of language, Lababidi notes the importance of portraying the brutal reality as it is. There is more determination than anger, which suits a book that is dissecting language and what it conveys or seeks to hide. For Lababidi, contrary to the imperialist exploitation, language can convey humanity. It can also view the oppressor, in this case Israel, in its most basic form. “The jailer is never free,” he writes, while noting that colonialism depends upon control. “To normalise such injustice requires ethical numbing, which is another form of imprisonment.” The difference is that Israel has military might on its side.
On the other side of Israel normalising its colonial violence, Lababidi notes that the tools of surveillance and oppression translate into “tools of a structure that systematically erode psychological resilience.” This is a reality which, while acknowledged, is not talked about as much as Palestinian resistance and resilience.
Meanwhile, Lababidi also reflects on how Israel’s genocide in Gaza is managed through language: “The substitution is rarely defended. It happens mid-sentence, as though the speaker felt, in the act of naming, a resistance he could not sustain.” The erasure does not stop there. Lababidi continues, “Reconciliation is invoked before there has been agreement about what has taken place. The conversation advances beyond the wound, as if the wound were already understood.” But genocide has yet to be mentioned, instead of conflict and the multitude of futile synonyms used to conceal what Israel is exposing in plain sight.
And yet, as Lababidi writes, “what we are witnessing in Gaza is the collapse of that illusion.” Language can no longer sustain the deception of the oppressor; the oppression has revealed too much. “To name this genocide is to be honest. To call for Palestinian liberation is to insist that no people should live behind walls, under drones or under occupation,” the author insists. Language fails gradually and eventually the divide is unsurmountable. That space, however, provides opportunity to make language meaningful rather than employ the neutrality of both sides, for example, which the author names as “the purest expression of this invisibility.”
The book proceeds to a graceful conclusion when it gradually moves to criticising imperialism through exposing its own exploitation of language, as well as shedding the author’s own ideals. “Those beliefs lie in ashes,” Lababidi says, when he reflects on an earlier belief that “Israeli leaders sought an end to Palestinian resistance out of existential fear, not imperial ambition.” And yet, there is a bigger realisation – imperialism expects our desensitisation. How does one remain spiritually intact, Lababidi asks. The answer, perhaps, lies in language, in reclaiming its truth when one speaks.

The mathematical secret behind why rose petals curl
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
18:53:35 UTC
03:53:35 KST

This article is from Proof Positive, our friendly newsletter that explores the joys and peculiarities of math. Sign up today for a weekly math essay and puzzle in your email inbox.
While they are undeniably beautiful, roses aren’t among my favorite flowers—too clichéd and romantic. I much prefer an indestructible cactus, a carnivorous plant or a hipster monstera, which, of course, is a must-have in any Japandi-style apartment. But after hearing about the research findings of physicist Eran Sharon’s lab at the Hebrew University of Jerusalem, I’m reconsidering roses. From a mathematical perspective, the flowers are pretty cool—or at least their petals are.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
You can find many videos online explaining that the arrangement of a plant’s petals is related to the golden ratio or the Fibonacci sequence, indicating a deep connection between botany and mathematics. The reason isn’t that nature has a particular affinity for mathematics. Rather the most sunlight reaches the petals when they form an angle with one another that is irrational, meaning its measurements cannot be expressed as the ratio of two integers. The irrationality ensures that no petal is directly above another.
Such insights have fascinated mathematicians and physicists for decades, which is why they have taken a closer look at plant growth. How, for example, can the curly leaf shape of Lollo Rossa lettuce be explained? Why does a carrot bend when it’s cut lengthwise? Questions like these can be answered quite easily with a little math and physics. But the arrangement of rose blossoms has been a long-standing scientific puzzle.
Irregular Growth Leads to Tension
The shape of a leaf is influenced by many different factors, such as the speed of growth, the material and the environment it grows in. For example, if the edge of a leaf grows faster than its center, this can lead to a curled or wavy shape—as with Lollo lettuce. With carrots, on the other hand, the opposite is the case: the inside of the vegetable grows faster than its outside, but because of its firm structure, it usually retains a straight shape. If you quarter the vegetable lengthwise, the structure is weakened, and the insides of the pieces will bend outwards, making visible the pressure that has existed inside the carrot.
Rose petals, however, differ from other flower shapes. They are not simply wavy or curved but have almost triangular tips. Such irregular segments are distinct among flowers. And this raises questions: What distinguishes rose petals from the leaves, petals and shoots of other plants?
To find out, Sharon and his team dissected rose petals, devised theoretical models, created computer simulations and conducted experiments with rubber surfaces. They discovered that the shape of rose petals has a completely different geometric cause than that of other plants.
An Incompatible Geometry
The curling of flower petals can be explained mathematically: because of their differing growth rates, petals “want” to curl, but this is prevented by external factors—such as the tissue not being elastic enough. It’s like trying to flatten the surface of a sphere onto a plane—it’s simply impossible. This “Gauss incompatibility” leads to mechanical stresses that produce virtually all flower shapes.
Gauss incompatibility can only explain smooth and periodic patterns, however, as Sharon and his team were aware. But the shape of rose petals is neither periodic nor smooth: there are isolated locations where a point is formed. To understand this, the researchers first cut the petals into fine strips—once along the horizontal axis and once along the vertical axis. The team’s aim was to visualize the mechanical pressure acting on the petals, similar to cutting carrots to reveal their internal pressure.
The longitudinal strips of the rose petals did indeed curl up, suggesting that the petal preferentially curves in this direction. When cut along the horizontal axis, however, the petal segments remained unchanged. This means a petal possesses a kind of conical structure, which is compatible with a flat geometry and therefore shouldn’t create any internal tension. After all, a flat sheet of paper can easily be rolled into a cone or a cylinder. A rose petal can, in principle, be laid flat on a surface; this confirms that Gauss incompatibility isn’t what causes the unusual shape of the petal. But what causes it then?
Similar questions are addressed in mechanics and industrial manufacturing processes because it’s crucial to know whether a manufactured component exhibits internal stresses and could break. Besides the Gauss equations, which must be considered, there are other equations at play: the Mainardi-Codazzi-Peterson equations. These state, among other things, that the normal vector (the vector perpendicular to the surface) must be uniquely defined. And as Sharon’s team discovered, this isn’t the case with rose petals. They therefore exhibit a geometric incompatibility, albeit a different one than that of other flowers.
Imagine cutting a slice of a pie chart, a shape that roughly corresponds to a flower petal. Now the left side of the slice wants to curl up, and so does the right side—but in different ways. This creates a point in the circular segment where tension accumulates, which in turn leads to the formation of a pointed edge. This can even happen in several places, resulting in multiple points.
Sharon’s research group was able to confirm this mechanism, which had never been observed in nature otherwise, using computer simulations and experiments. Although the team cannot rule out the possibility of other natural processes exhibiting Mainardi-Codazzi-Peterson incompatibility, rose blossoms are currently the only known example.
And that’s what makes roses so unique. I’m still not sure if that’s enough to convince me of their beauty. But I’d never previously considered why flowers look the way they do, so I acknowledge that roses add some new insights into mathematics—and therefore appreciate them a little more.
And as physicist Richard Feynman pointed out in an interview in the early 1980s, looking at a flower with a scientist’s eyes raises “all kinds of interesting questions,” which, in his view, “only adds to the excitement, the mystery and the awe of a flower.”

i24NEWS in Ramallah: West Bank Palestinians see little difference between Israeli election candidates
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
18:51:40 UTC
03:51:40 KST

- i24NEWS
- Middle East
- West Bank & Gaza Strip
- West Bank Palestinians see little difference between Israeli election candidates
West Bank Palestinians see little difference between Israeli election candidates
As Israelis prepare to vote later this month, many Palestinians in the West Bank say they expect little change from the result, despite the election’s potential impact on their lives
Millions of Palestinians will be affected by the outcome of Israel’s election on October 27th, but few have any say in who forms the next government.
For Palestinians living in the West Bank, the prospect of another Israeli government has prompted little expectation of a significant shift in policy. During a visit to Ramallah, i24NEWS found widespread scepticism that a change of leadership in Jerusalem would make much difference to daily life under Israeli military rule.
“There is some engagement, not a great deal. Most Palestinians do not expect the Israeli elections to produce significant change in Israeli policy vis-a-vis the Palestinians," said Dr. Khalil Shikaki, director of the Palestinian Center for Survey and Policy Research.
Palestinians have not held a national election since 2006. Palestinian Authority President Mahmoud Abbas recently postponed a scheduled vote, pushing it back to September 2027, leaving public opinion polls as one of the principal ways of gauging Palestinian political sentiment.
Shikaki, whose research tracks Palestinian public opinion, said many Palestinians believe the outcome of the Israeli election will do little to alter the policies they oppose.
“The overwhelming majority of Israelis, Israelis Jews - this is the perception of the overall majority of Palestinians - support the current policies of Netanyahu, and they will continue to support such policies when pursued by whoever is the next Israeli prime minister.
Little faith in a change of government
Around Ramallah’s Al-Manara Square, the scepticism was easy to find. Asked whether Israel’s election later this month would change anything, one Palestinian resident was unequivocal.
“I don’t think so.”
The same resident was asked whether the election of Yashar leader Gadi Eisenkot in place of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu would make a difference.
“I don’t think so, because they are all from the same direction. There is a little bit of difference between one and another one… the difference is some will make it more easy, some will make it more difficult. But I hope peace comes to everybody.”
Not everyone was quite so dismissive of Eisenkot. Another resident said: “About Eisenkot, he is better than Netanyahu.” A third suggested that removing the most hardline figures from the government could bring some improvement.
“Maybe if they took (Security Minister Itamar) Ben Gvir and (Finance Minister Betzalel) Smotrich out, maybe it’s gonna get a little bit better, but they’re all the same.”
The two issues raised most frequently by Palestinians interviewed in Ramallah were settler violence and the cost of living. Economic pressures have become particularly acute for many West Bank residents since October 7, 2023. The loss of access to jobs inside Israel left many without a source of income that had often paid significantly more than employment available locally. There was some hope that a new Israeli government might ease those pressures, but little confidence that it would.
The far-right stands apart
While many Palestinians view Israel’s mainstream political figures as broadly interchangeable, Shikaki said that distinction does not extend equally to the entire political spectrum.
“They do distinguish and to a large extent they see that Israel has its own crazies, like Ben Gvir and Smotrich.”
Ben Gvir and Smotrich, both prominent figures on Israel’s far right, have become particular sources of concern for Palestinians.
Yet within the centre-right mainstream of Israeli politics, Palestinians see less separation between the current government and its predecessor, led by Naftali Bennett.
“The overwhelming majority of Palestinians do not see a difference between Bennet and Netanyahu. To them these are basically the same people. For some Palestinians, Bennet is even more extreme than Netanyahu.”
The result is a political contest that many Palestinians follow without expecting it to offer a meaningful alternative. Even where individual candidates are regarded as preferable to others, the broader direction of Israeli policy is seen as unlikely to change.
A deep distrust of Israeli media
That scepticism extends beyond politicians to the media reporting on them. West Bank Palestinians, including older residents who often speak Hebrew, tend to be wary of Israeli news outlets and frequently turn to other sources for information about Israeli politics and its implications for Palestinians.
“Al Jazeera remains the single most important source of information for Palestinians regarding almost everything to do with Israeli-Palestinin relations and that includes the Israeli elections,” Shikaki said.
He described a more profound deterioration in trust following the Hamas-led October 7 attacks and the subsequent war.
“October the 7th dramatically changed everything. For most Palestinians information coming out of Israel, any information, was seen as fake news.”
The mutual suspicion reflects a wider divide in how Israelis and Palestinians consume information about one another. Just as many Palestinians distrust Israeli reporting, many Israelis are sceptical of information coming from Palestinian sources.
In 2024, the Israeli government banned Al Jazeera from operating in territory it controls, further complicating an already contested media landscape.
A shared desire for peace
Despite their reservations about Israeli politics and media, the Palestinians interviewed in Ramallah were welcoming to the i24NEWS crew, even knowing they were speaking to a reporter from an Israeli news channel.
Each expressed a desire for peace. That aspiration is not unique to Palestinians. Many Israelis also say they want an end to the conflict, even as the two societies remain deeply divided over responsibility for it and the terms on which it might be resolved.
For the Palestinians who spoke to i24NEWS, however, the immediate question was not simply who would win Israel’s election. It was whether that victory would make any tangible difference to their lives.
Few appeared convinced that it would. The desire for peace was clear. How to achieve it remains the harder question.

Brazil's Flavio Bolsonaro reverses course, backs end to six-day workweek

Brazil's Flavio Bolsonaro reverses course, backs end to six-day workweek
SAO PAULO, Oct 13 - Brazilian Senator Flavio Bolsonaro on Tuesday said he would back a popular labor reform to reduce the country's workweek, reversing his position in a bid to avoid handing a political win to President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva, his leftist opponent in Brazil's presidential elections.
The measure, approved by Brazil's lower house in May as a constitutional amendment, would lower working hours in Latin America's largest economy to 40 hours a week from 44, effectively ending a common practice in some sectors, like retail, of requiring employees to work six days a week.
Bolsonaro, the son of former right-wing President Jair Bolsonaro, defied pollsters at the start of the month to lead President Lula in the first round of Brazil's election by securing 47% of votes cast. The two men will face each other in a runoff on October 25.
Cutting the workweek would mark the biggest overhaul in Brazilian labor rights in decades and a nationwide poll conducted by Quaest in July found nearly 70% of Brazilians support the change.
While the senator and his Liberal Party, PL, had long opposed cutting the workweek, arguing the move was designed to boost Lula's reelection prospects, Bolsonaro changed course on Tuesday, just a day before the Senate was expected to vote on the matter.
"Most Brazilian workers want to see the end of the six-day workweek, so I'm going to vote in favor of ending it," Bolsonaro told journalists, adding that the government would need to offset impacts on business.
Lawmakers aligned with Lula have pushed for a Senate vote before the runoff, hoping to secure approval while the president remains in office.
"It seems to me that, following public pressure and street protests, PL decided to vote in favor of ending the six-day workweek," Lula said during an official event on Tuesday.
The PL has yet to formally announce a change to its position.
"Despite Flavio's lead, the race is still wide open. So it's a smart move by him in avoiding wearing down support on an issue that has broad popular appeal," Leandro Gabiati, director at political consultancy Dominium, said.
While business groups say the measure could increase costs and hurt competitiveness, they will not be left too disappointed by Flavio's decision, Gabiati said.
"The business community still has many ideological and practical reservations about this government," he said. "It will not feel betrayed by Flavio's change." REUTERS

Ukraine allies in Poland after Starlink sabotage, Trump diesel deal
October 13, 2026
The foreign ministers of Germany, Norway, Poland and the UK spoke at the Warsaw Security Forum on Tuesday.
This came as investigators in Germany were chasing down suspects for a fire at a Starlink station in Poland, and as Ukraine's European allies scrambled to deal with US President Donald Trump's latest lurch into Vladimir Putin's lap.
What did the ministers say about Russian diesel and Ukraine?
German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul bemoaned the US decision to lift sanctions on Russian diesel as part of a deal to supply the US — seemingly struck as Trump panics about fuel prices with the Iran war still unresolved and a month to go until midterm elections.
"I would say this is not the time to lower the sanctions regime but to strengthen this," Wadephul said, noting the new package of EU sanctions imposed on Monday.
"We are keeping our course," he said, adding that Europe was asking the authorities in Washington to do the same.
UK Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband arguably found even clearer words.
"Within the bounds of diplomacy we should acknowledge that it's been a very difficult few days," Miliband said in the Polish capital that's just a few hours' drive from Ukraine's western border.
Poland's Foreign Minister Radoslaw Sikorski, meanwhile, said he was counting on "our MAGA president" — a reference to Andrzej Duda of the rival PiS party whom Trump has often praised — to use his "friendship" with Trump to do two things.
"Number one: to secure a permanent US base in Poland. And, number two: to explain to him that Putin is the aggressor, and Zelenskyy is the victim of aggression, and you end the war by convincing the aggressor to limit his level of ambition, not by asking the victim to capitulate," Sikorski said.
Norway's Espen Barth Eide said it was important to focus on the actions of the last four years, also welcoming Monday's latest round of Russian sanctions.
"I feel that what we've done over the last years ... all of this is a very strong signal that Europe, together with Canada and — on most good days — also with the US, we are sending a very clear message to Putin," Eide said.
Facing criticism at home as well, Trump on Tuesday said that the US was still sharing intelligence with Ukraine. He also said that other countries would be buying Russian diesel as part of the deal he announced, without being deemed to breach US sanctions, rather than the US buying it itself. This contradicted or possibly corrected his earlier statements.
Wadephul: Starlink sabotage shows Europe 'in the crosshairs' of Russia
Wadephul also told reporters during his visit that he had spoken with his opposite number Sikorski about the investigations into a fire at a Starlink station in Poland last month.
Two people with Turkish citizenship were arrested in Germany in the southwestern town of Nürtingen, not far from Stuttgart, on Monday. Based on comments from Polish officials, they are suspected of connections with organized criminality but are thought to have been working on behalf of Russia.
Wadephul said that this and other hybrid incidents across the continent showed that "we are in Russia's crosshairs."
The satellite-based Starlink internet service is used extensively by Ukraine's military and so the fire was thought to be targeting accessibility across the border in the warzone.
"We're being attacked and it's not just happening in Ukraine but all across Europe," Wadephul said. "That means we must strengthen our cooperation."
But he also said that the arrests in Germany, which will likely lead to an exatradition process, showed how the security systems were working — both at the policing and intelligence-gathering levels.
He said he did not believe Russia would succeed in "dividing us" with such campaigns, saying that instead he expected they would galvanize European allies.
A private Polish broadcaster meanwhile reported two further arrests in Germany on Tuesday, although German authorities did not immediately comment on them.
Miliband praises Zelenskyy, but says 'let us take seriously' energy ceasefire idea
UK Foreign Secretary Miliband praised Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelenskyy for showing "extraordinary leadership ... in the most difficult of circumstances" since Putin's 2022 full-scale invasion, shortly after Trump's call — mirroring Russian messaging — for presidential elections in war-torn Ukraine.
However, Miliband also said the notion of an "energy ceasefire" raised by Trump — seemingly unilaterally — was nevertheless worthy of consideration given the attacks on Ukrainian energy infrastructure and the onset of winter.
"So let us take up this idea of the full energy ceasefire and let us seek with President Trump to hold Putin to this full energy ceasefire, because that is what we need," Miliband said.
Miliband noted how Zelenskyy had expressed a willingness in theory, even if Russia was yet to do so.
Wadephul added that, if possible, any such efforts to broker a partial ceasefire should also seek to incoporate grain exports and shipments in the Black Sea, particuarly to North Africa.
"This is still necessary. And let us please not forget this and urge Russia also to be ready to enlarge the ceasefire, not only for the energy sector but also for the Black Sea. Because this is needed to stop a lot of people in North Africa from falling into hunger," he said.

Ukraine and the US: What's next after Trump’s diesel deal with Russia?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
18:51:00 UTC
03:51:00 KST

Trump’s diesel deal with Russia and what it means for Ukraine
October 13, 2026
The diesel deal between US President Donald Trump and Russian President Vladimir Putin has sparked anger in Ukraine. Under the agreement, Moscow is allowed to supply Russian diesel fuel to global markets. The US news website Axios reported the move came in response to Kyiv's failure to comply with Washington's demands to stop attacks on oil refineries in Russia.
Trump also declared that it was time "for Ukraine to get a new president."
The agreement to sell diesel was announced while talks between Ukrainian, US and European representatives were taking place in Miami.
"I think our team is simply being used as a cover. That is definitely not fair," Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy told journalists shortly afterwards, describing Trump's decision as "a weak decision by strong partners."
From the Oval Office to Miami
This is hardly Kyiv's first crisis in its relationship with the Trump administration. In February 2025, Trump told Zelenskyy in the Oval Office "you don’t have the cards."
The White House confrontation was followed by a suspension of weapons deliveries and intelligence-sharing agreements. According to media reports, US special envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner threatened to suspend intelligence sharing during the talks in Miami, too, citing Ukraine's attacks on Russian oil refineries as the reason. US officials have denied the reports.
The current tension recalls the dispute in the White House at the time, says Mykhailo Honchar of the Ukrainian Center for Global Studies "Strategy XXI" in an interview with DW. However, he says there is no reason for Ukrainians to panic.
"Last year, too, there were threats and suspensions of intelligence sharing, as well as disruptions in weapons supplies," he said. "Then the Americans realized how much this was hurting them, too, and reluctantly resumed everything."
Is Trump looking for a 'scapegoat?'
All the experts interviewed by DW see a connection between Trump's threats toward Ukraine and the US midterm elections on November 3. In the midterms, all seats in the House of Representatives and roughly one third of Senate seats are up for election.
Ivan Us of the National Institute for Strategic Studies in Kyiv expects a crushing defeat for the Republicans. He says the main reason will be high fuel prices.
"Donald Trump wants desperately to distract attention from the fact that high prices are linked to his war with Iran and the problems in the Strait of Hormuz. He needs a scapegoat for this. And he has decided that Ukraine will be it," the expert said.
Mykhailo Honchar sees Russia as the main beneficiary of Trump's deal with Putin: "This whole diesel deal looks like a disguised request from Putin to Trump to exert influence on Ukraine."
Honchar also links the agreement to a possible sale of the foreign assets of Russian oil company Lukoil. According to The New York Times, potential buyers of these assets include investors with ties to Trump.
How can the crisis be resolved?
Oleksandr Kraiev of the Ukrainian think tank Ukrainian Prism warns against taking drastic action.
"Slamming the door in anger will certainly not help us. In that case, security assistance and intelligence sharing will be off the table. We cannot afford that. It may be difficult, and sometimes even repulsive, but we have to maintain contact with the Americans," the expert said.
At the same time, Ukraine could work with Germany, Denmark, the United Kingdom and France to make deliveries of Russian diesel fuel "simply unrealistic." After all, the tankers would have to pass through these countries' territorial waters on their way to the United States, and the partners have already said they would not allow this.
Ivan Us advises against reading too much into the harsh rhetoric.
"You can say whatever you want in public, as long as you carry on as before," he said of the possible relationship between Kyiv and Washington.
Ukrainian diplomats should work with US Republicans and the MAGA movement. Trump's agreement with Putin is already being criticized in those circles, with some raising concerns that Russia could use the proceeds from the diesel trade to support Iran.
Us also does not rule out a legal challenge to Trump's decision. Republican Senator Tom Tillis told NBC that the president was likely violating a 2022 law prohibiting imports of Russian oil and other energy products.
Ivan Us considers US threats to cut Ukraine off from intelligence or weapons to be little more than "fearmongering" ahead of the elections.
"The US makes such statements not because it intends to take action, but to make the markets believe that it is about to exert pressure and thereby drive prices down," Us said.
What will change after November 3?
The three experts agree that Kyiv should ride out the situation until after the US midterm elections on November 3. Oleksandr Kraiev says he is sure that Trump may back down on this issue after the elections, since abandoning Ukraine would mean showing weakness toward China.
Mykhailo Honchar points out that Trump's deal with Putin is already being criticized by Republicans in both the Senate and the House of Representatives. In addition, Republican Congressman Brian Fitzpatrick has introduced a bipartisan bill named after former US President Ronald Reagan that would block purchases of Russian oil.
"Despite all the threats, and perhaps even some attempts to impose temporary measures against Kyiv, it is unlikely that Trump will go any further. The situation should not be portrayed in apocalyptic terms," Honchar said.
He added that Trump's pressure was also bringing Ukraine and its European partners closer together.

Russia arrests Japanese reporter for alleged espionage
Suspect was arrested on Russia’s far-eastern Sakhalin Island before being transferred to Moscow, says Russia’s FSB.
Russian authorities say they have arrested a Japanese journalist on the far eastern Sakhalin Island, accusing him of espionage.
The Federal Security Service (FSB) announced the arrest on Tuesday, saying the man was believed to have gathered information on Russia’s defence capabilities for Japanese intelligence. The charges carry up to 20 years in prison.
Russia’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs named the journalist as Imai Yuki, who it said worked for Japan’s Hokkaido Shimbun newspaper.
The Japanese government was trying to verify reports of the journalist’s detention, according to an official at Tokyo’s embassy in Moscow cited by Japan’s Kyodo news agency.
The journalist was arrested on Yuzhno-Sakhalinsk, the main city on Sakhalin Island, as he was preparing to leave Russia, said the FSB. He was then flown to Moscow, where a court ordered him to be held behind bars pending the probe, the agency added.
A video shared by Russia’s TASS news agency, attributed to the FSB, shows masked officers appearing to handcuff the suspect in a hotel room, before transporting him to an interrogation room.
The suspect was then shown boarding a plane accompanied by two FSB servicemen, before appearing in a cage on trial in a Moscow court, which authorised his custody for nearly two months.
The Japanese man’s arrest comes amid a spike in tensions between Russia and Japan following Russian President Vladimir Putin’s trip in August to the Kuril Islands, the Moscow-controlled Pacific archipelago that is claimed by both countries.
The Sakhalin region includes Sakhalin Island and the four southernmost islands of the Kuril chain, which Japan calls the Northern Territories.
Russia and Japan never signed a formal World War II peace treaty, with the main obstacle being the unresolved territorial dispute over the Kuril Islands.
Authorities in Russia have arrested numerous foreigners for alleged espionage since it invaded neighbouring Ukraine in 2022.
One of the most prominent cases was the detention of Wall Street Journal reporter Evan Gershkovich in 2023. He was found guilty of espionage by a Russian court, sentenced to 16 years and then freed in a major prisoner swap involving Russia and Western countries in August 2024.

Hungary’s parliament removes Viktor Orbán-era LGBTQ ‘propaganda’ restrictions from 2021 child protection law
Hungary’s parliament has approved amendments to the child protection law adopted in 2021 under Prime Minister Viktor Orbán. AFP called the move the first significant step toward lifting restrictions on the LGBTQ community since pro-European Prime Minister Péter Magyar came to power.
The original law prohibited material accessible to children from “depicting” or “promoting” sexual and gender diversity. The revised law aims to protect minors from content that could “seriously impair the child’s physical, intellectual, emotional or moral development.”
“Fundamentally, our goal was to move away from a flawed paradigm, linking child protection in any way to sexual orientation or gender identities, and shift to a framework that is truly about children and protecting children,” said Szilvia Gyurkó, state secretary at the Ministry of Social and Family Affairs.
Orbán’s Fidesz Party voted against the amendments, but Magyar’s ruling Tisza Party has a two-thirds majority in parliament. The amendments passed without opposition support.
Human rights advocates welcomed the amendments but called for a review of other discriminatory provisions in Hungarian law adopted under Orbán.
Orbán’s government gradually restricted LGBTQ rights under the pretext of protecting children. Among its last such measures were amendments to the constitution and the law on public assembly that banned the LGBTQ community from holding public events.

Sager later called the decision "genuinely disappointing", arguing that "women's sport leagues are strongest when they have dedicated leadership and a staff that wakes up every day solely focused on driving them forward".

"The sport has given me so much," she said.

"It's really exciting, it has become a global game; we have some unreal American imports and then we have the Chinese coming in, it's just so cool to have players from all different areas, and for the game to be developing," she told ABC Sport.

Manuela Puoch has joined the Canberra Capitals, where she will play alongside her older sister, Nyadiew Puoch.
"She said it'll be intense, it'll be fun, she's next door to me," Manuela Puoch said.
And after after having been drafted by the New York Liberty with the 41st pick in the 2026 WNBA draft, her sights are set on the world's top league.
"[My long-term aspirations] are definitely to go to New York, and just keep developing as a player and a person," she said.

Cornell suspends fraternity parties after alleged campus gang rape case

Cornell suspends fraternity parties after alleged campus gang rape case
Chapters face immediate emergency suspensions for violations amid a sweeping ban tackling fraternity parties at the US university.
Cornell University has suspended fraternity parties for the academic year and will give the New York State Police a role in investigating sex crimes on campus.
The Ivy League university announced the major changes on Tuesday, as it sought to reassure the rattled campus community amid the ongoing outrage over its handling of allegations that a female student was sexually assaulted at a fraternity house in 2024.
The accusations came to light after the former student, known as Jane Doe, filed a civil lawsuit last month.
In addition to the blanket suspension of all parties and social events at fraternity houses through the 2026-27 school year, Cornell President Michael I Kotlikoff announced a new “zero-tolerance” policy for violations, noting that any fraternity chapter that breaks the ban will face an immediate freeze.
“These measures will provide time for a thorough review of fraternity life at Cornell to determine whether and how it can safely continue,” Kotlikoff wrote in a letter addressed to the campus community on Tuesday.
The university president pledged to strengthen Cornell’s sexual misconduct response by adding a dedicated case manager to the Office of Civil Rights to guide survivors through the reporting process.
Kotlikoff affirmed that he will be transferring investigative authority from the university police to independent, trauma-informed investigators with the New York State Police in an effort to reform the handling of sexual abuse cases on campus and restore community trust.
Kotlikoff acknowledged that sexual violence extends beyond fraternities, saying Cornell must also confront a campus culture of excessive drinking and drug use and expand education about students’ responsibility to intervene when others are at risk.
Cornell also plans to add victim advocates and expand sexual violence prevention programmes, including education aimed at encouraging bystanders to intervene, he said, calling the various actions announced Tuesday “first steps toward systemic change on our campus”.
“We will take all necessary steps to address the conditions that led to Jane Doe’s experiences, and those of other survivors,” he said.
Doe’s lawsuit was brought against the Chi Phi fraternity at Cornell University and seven of its members, accusing them of drugging and gang raping her during a party on the night of October 19, 2024.
Following her initial allegations in 2024, Cornell shut down the fraternity and temporarily suspended the accused male students, two of whom were later expelled. But critics have said the university’s response was too lenient, prompting it to launch an independent review into its handling of the case, led by a former top US prosecutor.
“We must meet this moment by acknowledging where we have fallen short and taking meaningful action,” Kotlikoff said. “Cornell must be a place where safety is not an open question.”

Saudi-led coalition says it struck resources sustaining Houthi war effort
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
18:45:41 UTC
03:45:41 KST

Rania R.a. Abushamala
13 October 2026•Update: 13 October 2026
 The Saudi-led coalition supporting Yemen’s government said on Tuesday that it carried out a “special military operation” to neutralize vital resources sustaining the Houthi group’s war effort.
The coalition’s joint forces command established that the Houthis “were using civilian facilities and vital resources to support their military activities,” according to a statement by the coalition.
It identified the sites as the central al-Sabaha facility in Sanaa, underground reserve fuel storage sites, fuel tanks and berths used to transport and unload fuel in Al Hudaydah, Sanaa and Dhamar.
The Houthis “were using those resources to directly support their military operations while depriving Yemenis of supplies that should meet their needs,” said the coalition.
It accused the group of using the sites to supply its missile and drone arsenal, which it said threatened Saudi Arabia, airports, ports and commercial vessels in the Red Sea.
The statement added that support had contributed to attacks against civilians and civilian facilities, as well as preparations for imminent attacks on civilian sites in Saudi Arabia and commercial ships in international waterways.
The operation focused on “neutralizing the Houthi militia’s capabilities” used to threaten Saudi Arabia, Yemen, the southern Red Sea and maritime routes, it added.
The coalition said its forces maintained “strict compliance with international humanitarian law” and had taken feasible precautions during the operation’s planning and execution to avoid incidental civilian casualties or damage.
It demanded that the Houthis “immediately” halt attacks targeting civilians and civilian facilities, including airports, ports, oil facilities and infrastructure.
There was no comment from the Houthi group.

Israel’s Yellow Line in Gaza advances, leaving displaced with nowhere to go
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
18:42:52 UTC
03:42:52 KST

Israel’s Yellow Line in Gaza advances, leaving displaced with nowhere to go
As Israel moves Gaza’s Yellow Line westward, displaced families in Shujayea face renewed danger, and nowhere safe to go.
Shujayea, Gaza Strip – Mahmoud Harzeen is pitching a tent about 200 metres from the yellow concrete blocks marking Israel’s so-called Yellow Line, preparing for his sixth move.
Each time the line inches closer, the 35-year-old packs up and moves further back, trying to keep his family away from danger. But every move offers only temporary relief.
“Every time they move forward a little, we move back a little,” Harzeen told Al Jazeera.
The Yellow Line divided Gaza’s territory between Israeli and Palestinian control as part of the October 2025 “ceasefire” agreement.
Israeli forces withdrew behind the line, but have continued to move the demarcation deeper into Gaza. They now control about 65 percent of Gaza, according to the United Nations, up from the 53 percent agreed a year ago.
On October 11, Israeli forces moved the yellow concrete blocks dozens of metres westward in Shujayea, in eastern Gaza City. More of the neighbourhood was brought under Israeli military control and Palestinian families were forced to flee again, with Israel’s shifting boundaries further restricting where they can live and move.
For Harzeen, who supports a family of 10, the latest move is part of a year-long search for somewhere his family can live.
He can’t remember the dates of each displacement. Instead, he recalled the places, one after another: Zeitoun, Sahat al-Shawa, al-Muntazah.
“About six times – every time the line advanced a little – I would feel that it was dangerous, so I would move back a little and try to live there for a while,” he explained.
His most recent move barely lasted one night. After spending time setting up the tent, he slept in it once before Israeli forces moved the Yellow Line forward again, getting too close for Harzeen’s liking.
“I pitched the tent and slept in it for one night,” he said. “The next morning, we took our bedding and our things and left.”
The threat extends beyond the movement of the blocks themselves. Harzeen described living amid drones, helicopters, artillery fire and stray bullets, with shrapnel posing a constant danger to people sheltering nearby.
The nights when the line advances are particularly frightening, he said, recalling tanks, troops and heavy shelling as the blocks were moved.
Israel has continued its attacks despite the “ceasefire”, killing nearly 1,500 Palestinians in the last year. Israel has killed more than 74,000 Palestinians since the war started in October 2023.
“The night they move the line, there are tanks, infantry coming down, and shells being fired,” he said. “All of that happens just so they can move the yellow block a little further forward.”
Most people in Gaza have been displaced multiple times as a result of Israel’s genocidal war and the accompanying large scale destruction of buildings across the enclave. That leaves little space to pitch tents in safer areas and soaring rent that Harzeen can’t afford.
Now he is preparing for the possibility of moving again. “They will probably move it forward again,” he said. “Every time we have to flee, we have to move closer to it. We keep moving.”
Fleeing at night, returning in the morning
For Asma Ali, 32, the Yellow Line’s advance has turned displacement into a cycle of fleeing at night and returning in the morning, never knowing how long her family can stay in one place.
Ali, a mother of three from Shujayea, said her family has been displaced seven or eight times since the ceasefire began.
After staying in central Gaza City, they returned to Shujayea hoping to settle in the al-Mantar area. But then, a month later, renewed shelling and evacuation fears forced them to move again.
The family sought shelter at a school before moving to a house near a bus stop. After a night of heavy shelling, they left in the early hours of the morning and went to stay with family back in the centre of Gaza City. But the advance of the Yellow Line has left Ali uncertain about where her family could go next.
“Every night, we would flee, then come back in the morning,” Ali said. “You spend the night trying to find somewhere to stay, then return the next morning.”
“The night the Yellow Line advances is terrifying,” she said. “The shooting continues from the beginning of the night until dawn. You live in fear.”
Ali said her family lost their belongings – including gold, household items and her children’s clothes – when the dwelling they were staying in was destroyed.
Among the items lost was a brace for her son, who has a disability. She only had the brace for two days.
“It was gone in the blink of an eye,” she said.
The family has been trying to find somewhere safe to stay, but Ali said there is nowhere they can afford to go. Moving south is also difficult, with transport hard to find and little certainty that they will find a safe place there.
Asma’s request is simple: somewhere her children can sleep without the family having to flee again.
“The most important thing is somewhere safe for us,” she said. “Somewhere I can put my children and where we can rest and settle.”

The parents of the victims of paedophile nursery worker Vincent Chan have reacted with fury to the news that he was cleared to return to work after “significant concerns” were raised by the parent of a young girl.
As first revealed in the Guardian, Chan was reported to his employer, the nursery chain Bright Horizons, by a concerned parent in 2021.
After being investigated by Bright Horizons, with the knowledge of Camden council, Chan was cleared to return to work at the nursery on the Finchley Road in north-west London. A year later, in 2022, Chan filmed himself abusing three-year-old girls in his care.
“I feel a level of anger that I can barely put into words,” said one mother. Images of her daughter were found on Chan’s personal devices after his arrest.
She added: “In 2021, around the time serious concerns had been raised about Vincent Chan, he was made my daughter’s key worker. We trusted him with her most intimate care, believing she was safe.
“Knowing there was a chance to stop him before he had such extensive access to her is unbearable. I am heartbroken, but above all furious at Bright Horizons for failing to protect our children.”
The families have called for an immediate “independent examination” of how the 2021 complaint was handled.
In a statement issued by the law firm Leigh Day, which is representing 50 families affected by Chan’s abuse, they called for a “full and independent account of what happened, who knew what, when they knew it and why these decisions were made”.
The parents of Chan’s victims have been promised answers in the form of a repeatedly delayed safeguarding review, led by an independent reviewer appointed by Camden council. But many expressed fury that they only learned the review had been pushed back to 2027 in the Guardian article.
“Expressions of regret are meaningless,” said the parents in a statement. “Families deserve the truth about what happened, accountability for the decisions that were made, and action to make sure this cannot happen again. We cannot wait until 2027 for answers.”
The families also restated their calls for Camden council to consider prosecuting Bright Horizons under health and safety legislation. “The Guardian’s report also strengthens the case for a criminal investigation,” they said.
The row over the decision to clear Chan to return to work has overshadowed the Labour MP Sagal Abdi-Wali’s first week as an MP after her byelection victory in Holborn and St Pancras last week. Before becoming an MP, Abdi-Wali was leader of Camden council, presiding over the delayed review.
Earlier on Tuesday Tulip Siddiq, the Labour MP for Hampstead and Kilburn, wrote to Camden council, asking it to commit to publishing the documentation relating to the 2021 investigation.
“These revelations are causing significant distress to parents in my constituency, particularly the families directly affected by Chan’s crimes,” Siddiq wrote.
“Families should not have to wait any longer for these answers,” she added.
Camden council said: “We know the parents of the children who attended the nursery, and the wider public, will be concerned that a complaint was made about Vincent Chan to Bright Horizons in 2021 – and will want to know how this was responded to.
“In 2021, Camden council’s local authority designated officer (LADO) provided advice to Bright Horizons, after Bright Horizons informed them (the LADO) of a complaint.
“We have shared all relevant documents and information with the independent review team. We want families to get the answers they deserve, in full, through the outcome of the independent review.”
A Bright Horizons spokesperson said: “We remain appalled by Vincent Chan’s crimes, and our thoughts are first and foremost with the children and families affected.
“We strongly encourage parents to share all their concerns with the child safeguarding practice review (CSPR), which is being led by an independent reviewer and will rightly examine this case in full.
“As the review is ongoing, we are unable to comment without the express written authorisation of the committee.”

Five countries allocate €4.1 million to Ukraine to support transport: how the funds will be spent
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
21:39:04 EEST
03:39:04 KST

Five countries allocate €4.1 million to Ukraine to support transport: how the funds will be spent
Kyiv • UNN
Germany has become the fifth donor to the Ukraine Transport Support Fund, increasing its pledged funding to €4.1 million. The funds will go toward infrastructure, locomotives, and equipment.
Germany has joined the Ukraine Transport Support Fund (UTSF), announcing a contribution of €1 million. This was reported on October 13 by Ukraine’s Minister for Restoration, Infrastructure and Transport, Mykola Kalashnyk, according to UNN.
Taking into account the allocations from official Berlin, the total amount of announced funding from the five partner countries has now reached €4.1 million. The funds are to be used to restore damaged transport infrastructure, purchase locomotives and specialized equipment, and modernize road border-crossing points on the border with the European Union.
Details
Germany has become the fifth country to announce funding for the Ukraine Transport Support Fund. Sweden, Norway, Lithuania and Estonia had previously announced contributions. Before Germany joined, the total amount of financial commitments stood at €3.1 million.
Ukraine’s specialized ministry hopes that the funds raised will facilitate the launch of the fund’s first practical projects and test the mechanism for international assistance to Ukraine’s transport sector. This involves the full project implementation cycle: from the Ukrainian side identifying the most urgent needs to conducting procurements, concluding contracts with suppliers and transferring the necessary equipment to transport companies.
At the initial stage, particular attention will be paid to the efficiency of procedures and the speed of aid delivery. The results of the first projects should demonstrate how quickly the fund will be able to respond to damage to transport infrastructure caused by Russian attacks.
What the funding from partner countries will be used for
Ukraine’s priority needs include the purchase of locomotives for the railway sector, specialized equipment to restore damaged transport facilities, and equipment to operate the electronic queue system at 11 road border-crossing points on the border with EU countries.
The need for additional railway rolling stock and repair equipment remains urgent because of systematic Russian strikes on transport infrastructure. They cause material damage and complicate passenger and freight transportation, including the shipment of products from Ukrainian enterprises to foreign markets.
Improving the operation of road border-crossing points will be a separate area of focus. Installing the necessary equipment for the electronic queue system should help streamline traffic and improve the efficiency of border logistics.
How the Ukraine Transport Support Fund will operate
The fund’s main feature is its financing mechanism, which provides international assistance on a grant basis. At the same time, the Ukrainian side will directly determine the priority of projects based on the current state of transport infrastructure and the sector’s most urgent needs. Procurement, in turn, will be carried out by the Central Project Management Agency of Lithuania (CPVA). It will be responsible for concluding contracts with suppliers and directly paying for the necessary machinery and equipment.
This approach is intended to ensure transparency in the use of international funding and create a mechanism for targeted assistance to Ukrainian transport companies.
Why it is planned to expand
According to Mykola Kalashnyk, the need to create an effective mechanism for transport assistance is driven by continuous Russian attacks, which create new infrastructure restoration needs every day.
"Russian attacks create new needs every day. Therefore, our task is to establish a mechanism that will help promptly provide the transport sector with the necessary machinery and equipment. The first projects will lay the foundation for further expanding the Fund and attracting new partners," said the head of the ministry.
The implementation of the initial projects is expected to make it possible to assess the fund’s practical effectiveness, identify potential problems during the procurement and delivery of equipment, and improve international cooperation procedures. In the long term, this should create the conditions for increasing funding volumes and attracting additional donor countries.
Context
The Ukraine Transport Support Fund was established in February 2026 with the participation of international partners and the International Transport Forum (ITF). Its main task is to attract financial resources to restore Ukraine’s transport infrastructure, which suffered significant destruction as a result of Russia’s full-scale invasion.
The first financial commitments from partner countries were announced in June 2026. Germany’s current accession became the next step in expanding international support for Ukraine’s transport sector.

Germany scored the opening two goals, before captain Sam Kerr's had a header on the stroke of half-time to help the visitors close the deficit before the home team's Camilla Kuver scored in the 83rd minute.
Striker Holly McNamara did find a late consolation goal for the Matildas, but Chelsea midfielder Sjoeke Nusken made sure the Europeans dealt the last blow.
After the defeat, Matildas Head Coach Joe Montemurro emphasised the importance of taking on different styles of play.
"Germany was a perfect test for us from that perspective, and we've got a lot of information. Haiti will give us another, different test. We'll look at it from the perspective of what we need in terms of building that toolbox to know that we're prepared for the World Cup," he said to media on Monday.
"They're very difficult to play. They've got some quality players, and they have some very, very good ideas. It's more about our mentality approaching these games. But it's also a good opportunity for me to try some new things."

'Unapologetic Zionism' and the end of Israel's democracy myth
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
18:38:35 UTC
03:38:35 KST

Breadcrumb
'Unapologetic Zionism' and the end of Israel's democracy myth
A Muslim woman on a Tel Aviv beach, a hijab in a crowded street, “Arabs and Jews” sharing public spaces. It is precisely this imagery of everyday coexistence that Israelis often invoke to rebut accusations of apartheid. Yet the country's electoral politics tell a more complicated story.
On 23 September, Israel's Central Elections Committee voted to disqualify Ra'am and the Joint List, seeking to exclude the principal vehicles of Israel’s Palestinian parliamentary representation from the upcoming end-of-October election. The petitions invoked provisions intended to protect Israel's Jewish and democratic character, including prohibitions on supporting armed struggle.
Furthermore, the Balad Party leader, Sami Abu Shehadeh, was banned from the upcoming Knesset elections.
The same elections committee that had issued all these decisions also rejected attempts to disqualify far-right Jewish parties, including Itamar Ben-Gvir's Otzma Yehudit.
Although the Supreme Court overturned the decision, as it has repeatedly done over the past two decades, the irony remains hard to miss.
In 2021, against Arab consensus, Ra'am helped sustain an Israeli governing coalition, breaking a longstanding convention that kept independent Arab parties out of government. Yet five years later, the same party and its controversial leader, Mansour Abbas, found themselves fighting for the right to contest an election.
Exclusion
Today, as Israel swiftly shifts rightward, the boundaries of such participation are narrowing, bringing into sharper focus patterns of exclusion rooted in the state's earliest years, and potentially signalling a reversal in their political status.
Palestinians who remained after the 1948 Nakba, roughly 150,000, were incorporated into the electoral system while much of their population lived under military rule until 1966. They could vote for a parliament whose government restricted their movement, expropriated their land and treated them as a security and demographic threat.
The state wasn’t required to abandon the distinction between individual citizenship and nationality, which was reserved for Jews.
Therefore, Palestinian participation didn’t come with an equal claim to defining what Israel was, or the power to meaningfully improve their status. Nor did Palestinians have the right to return to the villages from which they had been expelled, while a Jew from Warsaw or Brooklyn could immigrate to Israel, acquire citizenship and enjoy preferential access to land and settlement opportunities.
Even in ethnic terms, they were reduced to merely “Arabs”, a generic label devoid of a distinct Palestinian identity, rendering them naturalised citizens in their own land. And simultaneously, or rather ironically, they were cast as an extension of the Arab World, while being severed from the wider cultural and linguistic environment to which they belonged.
Vote but not have a say
For decades, to maintain the state’s democratic image, the system managed this tension through legal restrictions, political bargaining, and institutional accommodation. It worked as long as institutions could absorb political challenges without fundamentally altering Jewish national primacy, while keeping the lid on the underlying conflict. This was, in effect, the achievement of what might be called suits-and-ties Zionism, largely associated with the Labour Party.
The occupation of the West Bank and Gaza in 1967 altered that environment profoundly. Territory that had occupied a central place in religious-nationalist imagination was now under Israeli control.
The impact on Palestinians in the West Bank and Gaza was immediate, through military occupation and land seizures, whilst for Palestinian-Israelis the implications continued to be obscured by the longstanding arrangement that allowed them to “vote but not have a say”. A form of forced social bribe, so to speak.
Nevertheless, Israel has always had the power to withdraw the apparent “privilege” at its discretion. Over the past two decades, exclusionary politics have gradually gained freer rein. What has emerged, especially, is a more “unapologetic Zionism”. The religious-nationalist movements have moved from pressuring governments to exercising authority within them.
For Palestinian-Israelis, this convergence brought together ideological entitlement and the instruments of state power. What religious nationalism advanced as a matter of principle could brazenly be pursued through legislation, backed by the secular language of security and demography. This alignment found expression in electoral campaigns, such as “No loyalty, no citizenship” by the right-wing party Yisrael Beitenu in 2009, or a clip released on election day in 2015, in which Netanyahu warned that “the right-wing government is in danger. Arab voters are heading to the polling stations in droves.”
Protecting the Jewish state
Importantly, these campaigns coincided with, and were followed by, a growing body of discriminatory Israeli legislation, most notably the 2018 Nation-State Law, which reserved national self-determination exclusively for Jews and elevated Jewish settlement to a national value.
When the Arab party Balad submitted a proposed Basic Law entitled A Country of All Its Citizens, challenging the constitutional principle underlying the then-proposed Law, the Knesset Presidium refused to allow it to proceed to parliamentary debate. Supreme Court President Esther Hayut subsequently characterised Balad’s submission as crossing a red line, on the grounds that it negated Israel’s existence as a Jewish state.
Yet the significance of these proposals cannot be measured solely by their legislative success. From the perspective of “discursive institutionalism” and the political psychology of intergroup dynamics, political discourse both reflects and shapes collective attitudes.
Even unsuccessful bills, of which the Knesset has seen many, can signal a growing tolerance for exclusion, weakening social restraints on discriminatory behaviour and making previously contentious measures more politically conceivable. In this sense, the parliamentary arena becomes not merely a site of law-making, but a mechanism for renegotiating intergroup relations.
Such attitudes long predate the war in Gaza, although recent polling suggests they have intensified. A 2014–15 Pew Research Center survey found that 48% of Jewish Israelis supported expelling or “transferring Arabs from Israel”. Meanwhile, the 2025 Israeli Democracy Index found that support for government measures encouraging Arab citizens to emigrate had risen from 36% in 2019 to 53% in 2025. Only 16% of Jewish respondents believed Palestinian national identity was compatible with loyalty to Israel.
The irony is that Palestinian citizens have spent decades seeking to expand their influence within Israeli democracy, while movements determined to restrict that influence have gained power through the same institutions.
This contradiction has sharpened a longstanding Palestinian debate: whether electoral participation offers a way to change the system from within or merely legitimises its inequalities.
Mansour Abbas's entry into the governing coalition in 2021 tested the former proposition and yielded very few results. And today’s attempt to disqualify the principal Arab electoral lists, albeit overturned by the judiciary, marks a further step backwards.
Apartheid does not necessarily require the disappearance of democratic institutions; it can coexist with elections, courts and parliamentary representation when those institutions operate within an entrenched hierarchy of collective rights.
What Israel effectively operates on is a normalised two-tier conception of democracy. It is where political equality is recognised at the level of individual suffrage, however contested in practice, while remaining constrained by the institutional privileging of one national group over another, a principle treated as fixed and non-negotiable.
The legal significance, let alone the everyday implications for Palestinian-Israelis, lies not in individual instances of discrimination, but in whether they form part of an institutionalised system of domination, within which further exclusion can be pursued without fundamentally altering the existing political order. In other words, this version of ethno-democracy becomes the means of administering and perpetuating that hierarchy rather than a mechanism for overcoming it.
The late-October election may reveal just how far that transformation has gone, although the growing vulnerability of Palestinian-Israelis is already more apparent than ever.
Dr Emad Moussa is a Palestinian-British researcher and writer specialising in the political psychology of intergroup and conflict dynamics, focusing on MENA with a special interest in Israel/Palestine. He has a background in human rights and journalism, and is currently a frequent contributor to multiple academic and media outlets, in addition to being a consultant for a US-based think tank.

Moscow court hands blogger Michael Naki a second prison sentence in absentia, bringing his combined term to 14 years
Moscow’s Basmanny District Court sentenced blogger Michael Naki in absentia to five years in a penal colony for publicly calling for activities aimed at undermining Russia’s security (Article 280.4, Part 2, Paragraph “c” of the Criminal Code). It also barred him from administering websites for five years.
The prosecution stemmed from a video posted on Naki’s channel on May 7, 2024. According to Mediazona, the video was titled “Putin can now be eliminated. The day Putin stopped being president.” Prosecutors said the video contained signs of “incitement to overthrow the government in Russia.”
This is Naki’s second sentence in absentia. In 2023, the Basmanny District Court sentenced him to 11 years in a penal colony for spreading “fake news” about the army (Article 207.3, Part 2, Paragraph “d” of the Criminal Code). That case concerned a video in which Naki and Conflict Intelligence Team founder Ruslan Leviev recapped the ninth day of Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
The court combined portions of the sentences in the two cases to impose a total term of 14 years in a penal colony.
