How Are Ukrainians Coping With Russia’s Attacks on Ukraine’s Energy Grid?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
18:37:00 UTC
03:37:00 KST

For Ukrainians, talk of an energy truce doesn’t mean one is coming.
As US President Donald Trump touted an immediate energy ceasefire, blackouts persisted across parts of Ukraine as Moscow continues pounding Ukraine’s energy grid – the rumored deal covers refineries only, while Kyiv insists on a bilateral truce that also protects the grid.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
But for Ukraine, power is only half the problem.
Some luckier than others
While Kyiv residents interviewed by Kyiv Post reported blackouts of varying intensity, people in other regions, from Odesa and Mykolaiv in the south, to Ternopil in the west, said they had yet to experience major disruptions.
In Kharkiv to the east, blackouts appear to be a limited problem.
“In October, the lights were turned off twice: the first time for about an hour, the second time from the morning until exactly 4 p.m.,” Maksym, a 39-year-old PhD student, told Kyiv Post.
But back in the capital, blackouts have been “almost daily” in October for Khrystyna, a 27-year-old head of sales who works remotely.
“Currently, they last up to five hours at a stretch,” she told Kyiv Post.
Kateryna, a 34-year-old data scientist, reported similar problems – which were complicated by Russia’s attacks on bridges spanning the river that cuts through the Ukrainian capital.
“I had initially planned to work from an energy-independent office on Kyiv’s right bank during power outages. However, since I live on the left bank, attacks on the bridges raised concerns about whether I would even be able to get to the office,” she told Kyiv Post.
Russia’s Rassvet Satellites Could Give Drones Space-Based Control, Former HUR Official Warns
                                                                                                                                                                         This photograph shows vehicles with headlights on a non-illuminated road during a power outage in Kyiv on Jan. 20, 2026, following Russian missile and drone attacks on Ukrainian energy infrastructure amid the Russian invasion of Ukraine. (Photo by Roman PILIPEY / AFP)                             
But some in Kyiv are luckier, such as Oleksandr Burdeinyi, a 20-year-old creative marketing manager, who said blackouts haven’t been as severe for him as for his friends, because of nearby critical infrastructure.
“I got lucky living near critical infrastructure – only two power cuts in the last two weeks. Meanwhile, most of my friends and family are dealing with daily blackouts,” he told Kyiv Post.
Ukrainians are no stranger to blackouts due to Russian attacks – in the summer of 2024, as temperatures soared above 30°C (86°F), Russia took out over half of Ukraine’s power-generation capacity.
Then, in the winter of 2025-26, Russia targeted more power plants and heating systems, sending household temperatures to single digits in subzero conditions.
Now, Ukrainians are bracing for similar situations – but worse.
Vadym, a 37-year-old operations director at a company that maintains and oversees boiler rooms and utility systems at 60 buildings and residential complexes in Kyiv, said he has already received numerous requests this month.
“Autumn 2026 has brought many of the same challenges for the utility sector, and we have already received numerous emergency service requests throughout October,” he said.
Water supplies at risk
Almost everyone Kyiv Post interviewed voiced concerns about water supplies in Kyiv and beyond.
“I’m worried about poor mobile coverage and water supply issues. I reckon a complete freeze in the water supply would spell an inevitable disaster,” said Sara, a 24-year-old business analyst in southern Ukraine’s Odesa.
Oleksii Masaltsev, a 44-year-old sound engineer from Khorostkiv in western Ukraine’s Ternopil region, said he is also bracing for water shortages despite experiencing no major blackouts so far.
“I’m preparing for this by stocking up on water, power banks and a charging station,” he told Kyiv Post.
In Kyiv, two months before the cold spell, authorities reported disruptions to water supplies. They urged locals to stock up on food and water on Sunday, Oct. 11, after a Russian attack left over half of Kyiv’s households without running water.
Without power, the water pumps can’t run – meaning there’s no water to flush the toilet, as Kyiv residents told Kyiv Post during the previous winter.
                                                                                                                                                                         People ride the tram along a non-illuminated street during blackout hours in Kyiv on Nov. 21, 2025, following Russian missile and drone attacks on Ukrainian energy infrastructure amid the Russian invasion of Ukraine. (Photo by Tetiana DZHAFAROVA / AFP)                             
“As last year, power outages are causing a range of problems for the buildings we maintain… and in some cases, sewage pumping stations also shut down, disrupting the drainage system,” Operations Director Vadym explained.
Some in Kyiv are bracing for similar conditions.
“I also plan to buy a portable shower, a metal bucket that can be heated on a stove, a portable washbasin, and an electric blanket that can run on power from a portable battery or power bank,” Kateryna said.
A blackout is one thing; not having running water is another.
“We’ve gotten somewhat used to living without electricity – you can buy rechargeable lamps or other light sources. But living without water would be nearly impossible,” Khrystyna said.
Food security threatened
As Kyiv and Moscow go tit-for-tat with strikes on logistics warehouses, Ukraine’s food and medicine supplies have become the latest victims as pharmaceutical warehouses have also been targeted.
And getting enough food for winter is a concern for some.
“What I fear most is food shortages, as the enemy has already started targeting food storage facilities,” 20-year-old Burdeinyi told Kyiv Post.
‘Substantial workforce’ needed for repairs
Vadym, speaking from his experience at a utility service company, said not everything can be fixed at once.
“Once the power comes back on, a technician often has to visit the building in person to restart the equipment. This creates logistical and communication challenges for a company like ours, especially when outages affect multiple buildings simultaneously,” he said.
Then comes the workforce issue, as many Ukrainian men are mobilized to defend the country.
“The average age of our plumbers and electricians is over 60, and training younger specialists takes considerable time,” he continued.
“The vocational schools we have approached have struggled to provide graduates with the practical skills we need. Qualified specialists are increasingly difficult to find, and in some highly specialized roles, there are very few left in the labor market,” he added.
The temporary solution, he said, is training residents to do some of the work.
“To ease the workload on our staff, we ask homeowners’ associations to appoint a technically skilled resident and provide them with additional training,” he said.
“This allows residents to handle minor equipment problems and restart systems after scheduled power outages, reducing the need to call our emergency repair teams.”
How citizens are coping
Almost everyone has some form of backup power to keep the essentials running.
“I’ve had fiber-optic broadband installed, my flat’s on the sunny side, and I’ve got plenty of power banks,” Sara in Odesa said.
“Yes, we have a portable power station to keep the internet running and charge our work devices. We also have several flashlights and a supply of water for household needs,” Khrystyna in Kyiv said.
In Kharkiv, Maksym said the situation is likely better than in Kyiv, though he and his family are prepared nonetheless.
“The situation with light and heat is traditionally better in Kharkiv than in Kyiv. But my family and I are, of course, preparing for the winter as best we can: We bought power banks, and use a stove with a gas cylinder to cook if there is no light for a long time,” he said.
                                                                                                                                                                         This photograph shows a power generator outside a restaurant during blackout hours in the center of Kyiv on Jan. 18, 2026, amid the Russian invasion of Ukraine. (Photo by Sergei SUPINSKY / AFP)                             
But portable power stations can be costly. A Chinese-made Marstek Venus E, with enough capacity to keep a house running for over 24 hours under normal use, costs over Hr. 61,990 ($1,376) – with prices sure to rise as demands surge in winter.
Kateryna in Kyiv said she has resorted to installments to get a smaller power station.
“I… had to find a way to secure a reliable power supply at home as quickly as possible. I ordered a BLUETTI Elite 200 V2 portable power station with a 2,600-watt output and a 2,073 watt-hour capacity,” she said.
“Like many Ukrainians, I couldn’t afford such a major purchase upfront, so I had to buy it on an installment plan.”
Some are considering leaving Kyiv.
“My winter and blackout prep is basically just planning to move out of Kyiv next month. I honestly think living and working here under these conditions is going to be extremely tough,” Burdeinyi said.
But elsewhere in Ukraine, some are also playing a game of wait and see.
“It will be possible to assess the situation once it happens, but the outlook is troubling. What worries me most is a possible energy collapse,” Yurii, a 63-year-old geologist in southern Ukraine’s Pervomaysk, Mykolaiv region, told Kyiv Post.
How the government can help
This question has taken on new urgency after President Volodymyr Zelensky said Kyiv was lagging behind other regions – including frontline areas – in implementing its resilience plan. He warned that even a single Shahed strike can leave a significant part of the capital without power and water, and said decisions were being prepared on protecting critical infrastructure and changing how Kyiv is managed.
Asked about how they think the authorities could help brace their cities for the unforgiving winter, many interviewed by Kyiv Post mentioned Ukraine’s “Points of Invincibility” – tents erected nationwide that provide shelter, power and warm drinks to locals.
“Increase the number of resilience points, rather than shifting this responsibility onto businesses, such as the situation where everyone goes to the Nova Poshta post office to dry their hair,” Sara said, recalling previous blackouts.
                                                                                                                                                                         People come and go at a tent of Point of Invincibility in Kyiv on Jan. 11, 2026, where they can charge devices and warm themself, following Russian missile and drone attacks on Ukrainian energy infrastructure amid the Russian invasion in Ukraine. (Photo by Tetiana DZHAFAROVA / AFP)                             
“Develop resilience centers with electricity supplies, backup internet and stocks of drinking water. Implement anti-corruption reforms, despite the war,” Masaltsev in western Ukraine’s Ternopil region said.
Others emphasized the need to provide water supplies when the pumps fail.
“If water stops flowing to homes, I believe local authorities should ensure access to it in every district or neighborhood,” Khrystyna in Kyiv said.
“For instance, they should equip public water kiosks with backup power, as they currently rely on electric pumps… People need water for basic household needs, even if it isn’t potable.”
Khrystyna said water supplies should be provided via the “Points of Invincibility” as well.
Some also called for the government to decentralize the energy and heating system – an ongoing discussion since 2024 – while ensuring backup power at critical facilities.
“Perhaps it would be wise to set up small, autonomous boiler houses – each serving a few buildings – and equip them with backup power,” Khrystyna said, adding that it would ensure a single attack can’t cut off supplies to entire districts.
“It would probably be a good idea to look into alternative power sources, ensuring generators for boiler rooms and backup power for the water supply,” Sara added.
“Local authorities could be doing much more to develop decentralized energy systems, install cogeneration units, and provide backup power for critical infrastructure,” Kateryna in Kyiv said.
But Vadym noted that households can also help prepare buildings for cold spells, as Kyiv Post covered during the past winter.
                                                                                                                                                                         New valves and pumps inside a restored heating unit in a Kyiv residential building in January 2026. (Photo by Sergii Kostezh / Kyiv Post)                             
“Some associations in Kyiv have also installed rooftop solar panels through grant programs and municipal co-financing schemes, helping their buildings become more energy-independent,” he said.
“Combined with other upgrades to building utility systems, these measures can significantly improve a building’s resilience and help it get through the winter, even if the city’s power grid suffers a complete collapse.”
And older buildings, Vadym said, can sometimes function when the grid fails – if local authorities do their job.
“Older residential buildings can sometimes continue operating without electricity, provided that the district pumping stations supplying them with cold water and central heating have backup power,” he said.
“Ensuring these facilities have reliable backup power is the responsibility of municipal authorities.”

The Australian housing challenge not being solved
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
18:36:18 UTC
03:36:18 KST

In brief
- Millions of spare bedrooms sit empty as downsizing stalls.
- The costs of moving may be reshaping Australia's housing crunch.
Australia's rapidly growing older population has more wealth than ever and millions of spare bedrooms, yet financial incentives are pulling many away from downsizing, new research suggests.
Almost nine in ten older households (aged over 55) have at least one spare bedroom, and 60 per cent have two or more, twice the rate of households aged 25 to 54, new research published in the GemLife Downsizing Australia Report found.
The most popular homes among the 2,100 buyers over 50 looking to downsize surveyed were two and three-bedroom properties, offering low-maintenance living, good security, and proximity to amenities. But separate research indicates there is not enough of this housing being built.
There are about 13 million empty bedrooms across the country, but older people rely on spare rooms for grandchildren, visiting family, home offices or hobby rooms, Australian Housing and Urban Research Institute (AHURI) Managing Director Tom Alves told SBS News.
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
He said their research has found 60 per cent of homeowners aged between 65 and 74 in 2001 were living in the same property 15 years later. And among those aged over 75, fewer than 15 per cent downsized.
AHURI has called for developer incentives to build medium-density housing designed for ageing.
Independent Kooyong MP Monique Ryan told SBS News that making better use of existing housing is one of the few short-term levers that can address the housing crisis.
"Downsizing can help younger families get into larger homes, unlock capital for older Australians, and limits urban sprawl," Ryan said.
Reasons to stay
The family home is a primary store of wealth for many older households, so releasing its equity can mean a loss of the age pension or other benefits, and more retirees are now carrying mortgage debt, Alves said.
"Other financial barriers to downsizing include upfront costs such as stamp duty incurred when purchasing a new home and agent fees incurred during the sales process," Alves said.
"Older households are also unlikely to be eligible for a traditional mortgage, which can create a blockage to moving."
Reasons to go
Changing the age pension assets test and building new senior housing within federally funded developments would help, Ryan said.
"Most important though is that the federal government should support the states in phasing in the replacement of stamp duty with a broad-based land tax, as has been suggested by the Productivity Commission and a number of other Treasury and Senate inquiries."
Stamp duty policy has shifted in South Australia, with exemptions for seniors purchasing some new homes, while concessions also exist in Victoria and the ACT.
A family home is generally exempt from the age pension assets test, but money unlocked through the sale of a house can become taxable if it is not used to purchase another principal home.
From January 2023, money from a home sale intended to buy a replacement can be exempt from an assets test for up to two years, with a conditional one-year extension. But any surplus profit can be taxed.
The federal government also lowered the age from 65 to 55 for downsizers to put up to $600,000 from their home sale into superannuation in January 2023.
The scheme was used by 15,800 people to contribute $4.165 billion in 2024–25, compared with 16,900 contributing $4.491 billion the previous year.
The wealth gap and transfer
As Australians retire with unprecedented levels of wealth, government spending on social safety nets for older Australians continues to grow.
In 1971, just 17 per cent of Australians were over 55, while almost half the population was under 25. By 2028, these groups will be roughly even and by 2069 older people are projected to be the largest age group, and realestate.com.au senior economist Anne Flaherty says this is "going to be a big problem".
"Often the people who are you know living paycheck to paycheck are the ones who actually don't have access to a lot of the concessions that older Australians who who may be more cashed up have access to."
More reasons to stay
Another challenge is that the kinds of properties with the most capital growth are often larger houses, with more land in well-established suburbs, Flaherty said.
"So that's another incentive that people have not to leave their home, but to stay in that property and increase the capital gains they're going to see. (And) adult children can inherit that property, so it might be a way of keeping wealth in the family, which is inefficient because that home could have been used by someone who did need extra space."
Swapping stamp duty to a universal land tax is a "win-win for everyone over the long term", Flaherty said.
"The challenge, of course, is weaning state governments off stamp duty revenue over the short term is very difficult.
"This year is a good example of the problems with stamp duty, given the reduction in overall properties that have been selling. We're going to see a lot of state governments see their revenues take a big hit."
AHURI modelled the potential impact on house prices and rents of replacing stamp duty with a broad-based land tax, finding more affordable housing for both owner-occupiers and renters.

Pope Leo XIV undergoes successful lung surgery, Vatican says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
18:36:00 UTC
03:36:00 KST

Pope Leo XIV, 71, underwent a successful operation Tuesday to remove a lung nodule, with the Vatican saying the procedure was completed as planned and the pontiff had returned to his room afterward.
The 71-year-old Leo returned to his room after the surgery at Rome’s Gemelli hospital, according to a statement from the Vatican spokesman, who promised further information at a later time.
Leo had walked into Rome's Gemelli hospital through the main entrance earlier in the day and waved to dozens of well-wishers who had gathered to greet him. The Vatican said the surgery would be performed by a team led by Gemelli’s chief thoracic surgeon, Dr. Stefano Margaritora.
The operation got under way as medical staff recited the Rosary prayer in the hospital chapel Tuesday evening. "Let us join together in prayer, asking the Lord to sustain our bishop, Pope Leo, and to comfort all those who are hospitalized here,” said the Vicar of Rome, Cardinal Baldassare Reina, at the start of the prayer.
The American pontiff has offered a rare level of transparency about the first publicly disclosed major health problem of his 17-month papacy . He revealed the discovery of the small, localized nodule during his Sunday noon prayer and announced that he would have it removed.
Oncologists say even if the nodule turns out to be cancerous, Leo’s prognosis is "excellent” since it will have been removed at an early stage.
The surgery, which is usually performed under general anesthesia, will require a weeklong hospital stay and the Vatican on Monday canceled all Leo’s audiences through Oct. 20.
"These are things that can be treated very well, if the words he used reflect the clinical situation,” said Dr. Lorenzo Spaggiari, director of thoracic surgery at the European Institute of Oncology, or EIO, in Milan, who is not involved in the pope’s care but knows the team at Gemelli.
But the decision clearly came as a surprise: While Gemelli has a specific papal apartment that past popes have used, complete with a private chapel on the 10th floor, Leo will actually be staying in a nearby room since the papal apartment is currently undergoing renovations, according to the Vatican press office.
Spaggiari said he expected the team at Gemelli would perform a biopsy to determine whether Leo has lung cancer followed by the removal of a section or lobe of the lung where the nodule is located.
Both could be done using robotic techniques, and could be performed consecutively, under the same anesthesia, with different specialist teams, Spaggiari said.
A sophisticated robotic bronchoscopy technology called ION allows a biopsy on nodules as small as 3 millimeters (1/10 inch), Spaggiari said. Both the Gemelli and the EIO have the technology, which has been available in Italy for just two years.
Gemelli also has robotic surgical technology, allowing the operation to remove the nodule to proceed "using a minimally invasive technique,” he said.
The technique involves the surgeon making four small incisions in the chest through which the instruments of the so-called da Vinci robot are inserted, he said. The surgeon then controls the robotic arms looking at a screen providing high-definition, 3D views of the surgical site.
"It’s a very well-established technology. This is something we have been doing for 20 years,” he said.
It wasn't known for certain what technique would be used on Leo. Gemelli has documented using both robotic procedures to diagnose and operate in under four hours.
The biopsy risk is "virtually zero,” while the surgical risk is very small, carrying a 0.6% to 0.8% mortality rate for patients in otherwise good health with good heart and lung function, Spaggiari said.
During the surgery, doctors would also remove lymph nodes that drain the segment or lobe. "If all those lymph nodes turn out to be negative, so stage one, then the outlook is very good,” he said, adding that no other treatment would be necessary.
The nodule was discovered during regular checks, the Vatican has said.
"I think he has had a bit of luck. They found something that was asymptomatic - a lung nodule, possibly a tumor. He might call it something else; we call it luck,” he said.
EIO advises patients not to fly for three weeks after surgery - which would give the pope just the interval needed to make his planned Nov. 6-17 trip to Uruguay, Argentina and Peru, depending on his recovery. The current itinerary for the trip is ambitious and the longest of his papacy to date, calling for Leo to clock just over 31,000 kilometers (19,000 miles) on a dozen flights and two helicopter rides, and a significant altitude change in Peru.
"He has decided to undergo surgery soon in order to not change his plans for future overseas trips, so there is no need to worry, as it is not an emergency,” said Tokyo Cardinal Kikuchi Tsutomu, who saw Leo on Monday.
A lung nodule is a small abnormal area measuring less than 3 centimeters (1.2 inches) that sometimes appears on a CT scan of the chest or abdomen. Often, the scans are done to investigate trauma or a lung infection, unrelated to a lung cancer screening. A nodule can be benign or malignant, and oftentimes surgical removal is recommended both to establish whether it is cancer and to treat a malignancy while it is still localized.
This is believed to be the second hospitalization for Leo, who is known to be sporty and in good shape, with weekly tennis games and swimming.
As a young missionary priest, he came down with typhoid fever in 1985, soon after arriving in Chulucanas, Peru. The illness and hospitalization were a cathartic moment for him to decide to stay in the poverty and discomfort of Peru after living in relative comfort in Rome - a decision that ultimately paved the way to his papacy, according to an interview Leo gave to Elise Ann Allen in 2025 for "Pope Leo XIV: The Biography.”
According to the book, Leo said he prayed to God to let him die rather than suffer the "horrible” pain of the fever. "I was hooked up to an IV, and I said, ‘If this is your sense of humor, Lord, I think you could do a little better.’
"Obviously, I survived; I recovered, but it turned out to be a very significant moment for me, because it was like, ’Well, you’ve already dealt with the illness; you already see what the needs are here - the order, the Augustinians, the church are telling you, ‘We need you here; go for it.’ I never looked back.”
___
Barry reported from Milan.

$1m price tag for an aged care room — but TV, phone, wi-fi cost extra
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
18:33:36 UTC
03:33:36 KST

Aged care residents face bills for TVs, hot breakfasts and soft drinks under new fees
Patricia Massa has lived in her inner-west Sydney nursing home for the past nine years.
The 88-year-old has advanced dementia, but there's one thing that still brings her joy: settling into her room to watch old movies.
In August, it looked like that simple joy would end, after her provider, Uniting, handed out a glossy brochure about its new "Higher Everyday Living Fees" (HELF).
HELF was introduced by the federal government last year under its "once in a generation" reforms.
Although rooms at Uniting's The Marion can cost up to $1.3 million as a deposit, and residents can pay tens of thousands in fees every year, families were told they would have to pay $8.80 a day, or $3,200 a year, if they wanted a free-to-air TV in their room.
"A prisoner gets a television in their cell," said Patricia's daughter, Elizabeth Tosti.
"Surely to goodness, an aged care resident suffering from dementia has a right to free-to-air television in their room."
In March, Aged Care Minister Sam Rae criticised providers for charging high fees for TVs in trials being conducted, saying having access to a TV was a "basic human right".
However, under the government's own policy, the right to a free TV only applies to those who were receiving one while in aged care before November 1, 2025, when the policy changed.
Under the current rules, providers are only required to provide a TV in a communal area, not in new residents' rooms.
It means that Patricia will keep her TV for free, but everyone who comes after will be charged — and not just for TV.
Residents to be charged thousands for telephone, wi-fi and activities
A phone, wi-fi, soft drinks and having mail delivered to your room will also attract a fee for new residents.
Under Uniting's offered "Elevate Plus" package, residents could pay $132 for an extra fortnightly activity, $66 for a one-hour session once a month with a carer to "talk about whatever's on your mind", and $220 for a music concert in the nursing home.
Uniting's brochure said residents could get better value by purchasing a bundle of services for "just $44 a day".
Ms Tosti said the fees would create a two-tiered system that would disadvantage those who could not afford to pay.
"People who have got the money, the capacity to pay these hefty fees, can enter the communal room and listen to someone playing music and the poor residents who can't will have to walk past or be shooed away and told, you can't come in here because you're not paying the package," she said.
Uniting said it was reviewing its "Elevate Plus" package and intended to make changes "as we work towards a model that is fair, affordable and sustainable".
It said residents could choose which services they wanted to pay for and that "televisions in residents' rooms are considered an additional service under the government's funding system".
Nation's largest provider rolling out fees in all its homes
HELF replaces additional and extra services that some providers used to offer to residents as a package that could include things like alcohol at meals and a choice of meals.
It is unknown how many of Australia's 700 residential aged care providers will choose to charge the fees, but Opal, the nation's largest provider, says it is rolling out the scheme to all its 148 facilities.
Opal trialled the scheme earlier this year and later had to refund $190,000 to residents who were charged for services they had already been receiving at no cost.
During the trial, Opal offered a bundled package at one Sydney facility priced at $55 a day, or more than $20,000 per year.
In another trial for residents at Opal's Carine Parkside facility in Perth, residents were charged $12.50 a day, or $4,562 per year, for a hot breakfast.
Under that scheme, those who wanted soft drinks or juice paid $7 a day, or $2,555 per year and anyone wanting wine or beer with their meal paid $15 a day or $5,475 per year.
Opal said fees across its homes would vary according to what residents wished to purchase and it had also introduced "discounted bundles" at a small number of facilities.
Advocates accuse providers of price gouging
Craig Gear, from Older Persons Advocacy Network, wants the government to make sure basics like TV, phone and wi-fi are free for all across the country with all providers.
He said the network had heard reports of gouging by providers under HELF.
"Older people have been coming to advocates about things like margarine being the option on the menu but if you want butter, you're going to have to pay an extra $1.70 per day.
"If you want your meal in your room, you're having to pay $4.50 for that delivery."
The ABC contacted Aged Care Minister Sam Rae for comment but did not receive a response.

Ukraine's Rada backs preliminary bill limiting court access to National Bank banking secrecy
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
21:31:05 EEST
03:31:05 KST

Ukraine's Verkhovna Rada has adopted at first reading bill No. 15555, which would restrict civil and commercial courts' access to information constituting bank secrecy and obtained by the National Bank of Ukraine (NBU) from foreign banking supervisory authorities.
A total of 284 members of parliament voted in favor of the decision on Tuesday, October 13.
The bill provides for amendments to the Civil Procedure Code and the Commercial Procedure Code stipulating that courts will not be able to compel the disclosure of information constituting bank secrecy that the NBU has obtained from banking supervisory authorities in other countries. Courts will be required to reject motions or applications seeking the production or preservation of such evidence.
In addition, the bill proposes supplementing the Law on Banks and Banking with a provision under which the National Bank may disclose information obtained from a foreign banking supervisory authority only with that authority's consent and exclusively for the purposes specified in the relevant agreements.
According to the explanatory note, the bill was developed to fulfill the conditions for closing negotiating Chapter 9, "Financial Services," in Ukraine's EU accession process, implement the provisions of Directive 2013/36/EU, and take into account the Memorandum of Economic and Financial Policies with the International Monetary Fund (IMF).
The proposed amendments are expected to enable the NBU to receive a positive assessment from the European Banking Authority (EBA) regarding the equivalence of its confidentiality regime and remove obstacles to the full exchange of information with central banks and regulators in EU member states.
As reported, bill No. 15555 was registered with the Verkhovna Rada on August 24, 2026, and on September 10, the parliament's Committee on Finance, Taxation and Customs Policy recommended that it be adopted at first reading.

Egg-timer test use growing despite evidence it can't predict fertility
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
18:30:00 UTC
03:30:00 KST

Egg-timer test use growing despite evidence it can't predict fertility
When Clementine Bastos was trying for a baby, her GP recommended the AMH test, also known as the "egg-timer test".
It measures the level of anti-Müllerian hormone (AMH) in a woman's blood to estimate her ovarian reserve.
"It came back low. That stressed me out," the 42-year-old from Sydney/Gadigal Country says.
Clementine's GP recommended she and her husband see a fertility specialist. While starting investigations with that clinic, the then 35-year-old got a surprise.
"I got sent off to do my bloods and turns out I was pregnant, three weeks."
New research led by Flinders University has found nearly one in five women who took the AMH test received a result classified as low.
However, among those who repeated the test after a low result, about one-third later received a result in the normal range.
Despite the test's unreliability, co-author of this new study, Tessa Copp, a senior research fellow in the school of public health at the University of Sydney, says there has been "massive growth" in testing.
"Which is particularly concerning given the number of women receiving a low result and potentially altering their family planning on the basis of that result," Dr Copp says.
Growing evidence AMH test can't predict ability to get pregnant
Analysing health records from almost 1.4 million Australian women, the researchers found AMH testing increased more than 13-fold between 2011 and 2021.
Women aged 30 to 34 experienced the sharpest rise, with test rates increasing almost 20-fold.
AMH testing is not covered by Medicare and can cost more than $100.
"The AMH test is useful for when undergoing IVF, because it can give an indication of how many eggs might be retrieved from a cycle," explains Dr Copp.
"[In that context] it's useful for expectation, and also if a woman has high AMH she might be at risk of hyper-stimulation.
"That's where the benefit stops."
Sign up to the ABC Lifestyle newsletter
She says despite "evidence consistently showing" AMH level is not associated with the chance of conceiving, or how long it will take to get pregnant, the rise in testing is likely linked to women delaying having their first child and a growing awareness of fertility issues.
Dr Copp says "false and misleading information" via social media and commercial promotion is also to blame.
Test causing panic and anxiety
Clementine says she feels the AMH test and discussions she had with a fertility clinic were "fearmongering".
"I was crying at home that we're never going to get a kid. The whole thing was a f***ing nightmare.
"The test [supposedly] tells you something is wrong, you get sent to a clinic … while [I was] sitting there already pregnant."
Dr Copp says it might be "hard for people to see how the AMH test can be harmful", but for some women it has the potential to cause "anxiety and distress" that they may be running out of time to have a baby. Or a "high result" might provide false reassurance they can delay pregnancy.
Karin Hammarberg is an adjunct senior research fellow at Monash University with 20 years' experience as a clinical coordinator of IVF programs.
She says the AMH test can have a "snowball effect", triggering women to have costly treatments such as egg freezing or IVF when they don't need medical intervention.
"It's a cascade of events we really need to make women more aware of.
"This test makes you more confused than insightful and has real-life consequences."
Trying for a baby, age only reliable way to gauge fertility
Luke Grzeskowiak, a pharmacist and researcher at the Flinders Health and Medical Research Institute, led the recent study of AMH testing and says the findings highlight the need for better education of both clinicians and the public.
"AMH testing can be useful in some specialist fertility settings, but it should not be mistaken for a test that predicts whether a woman will be able to have a baby," Dr Grzeskowiak says.
"The best way to support women is with accurate, evidence-based information, so they can make informed decisions about their reproductive health and future family plans."
Dr Copp says the only real test of fertility is "trying to get pregnant when you're ready".
"It's a really frustrating answer that you're not going to know until you try."
Dr Hammarberg says age is the most important factor when understanding fertility.
She says if you want children, it's important to understand the biology of reproduction. Fertility declines with age, but doesn't "fall off a cliff" at 35, she says.
"You only need one egg for conception.
"Trying now is the only way to know if you are fertile [but] people don't always have a choice … You might not have a partner or the financial resources.
"But if you want to leave [having a baby] until later, but have a plan, just get yourself as well informed as possible and make the best decision you can."
Where to get evidence-based information
Dr Copp recommends women curious about their fertility chat to their GP.
She says there is also a lot of evidence-based information that women can access for free and recommends the government website Your Fertility as a starting point.
For those trying to boost their fertility, she says "all the boring stuff" such as having good knowledge of your menstrual cycle, eating well, exercising, not smoking and avoiding too much alcohol may help.
Before undertaking any test or treatment, Dr Hammarberg suggests looking at these "5 questions to ask your doctor or other healthcare provider".
She says while we should expect our questions to be answered honestly, women need to be "self-aware and more demanding of the information".
"Women are capable of making good decisions, but they need the correct information."

Evidence of Western components in Russian Shahed drones presented at Warsaw Security Forum
NAKO representative Yulia Behletsova spoke about this in a comment to Ukrinform.

In addition to its exhibition display, NAKO served as a program partner for a panel discussion at the forum dedicated to strategies for combating sanctions evasion.
“Such forums are extremely effective because they allow us to convey the truth to influential representatives of other countries. Trump fires ambassador after alleged coup threats against Greece
US President Donald Trump has sacked his ambassador to Greece, Kimberley Guilfoyle, after she solicited pay-to-play donations from a Republican donor and allegedly threatened to topple the Greek government.
Guilfoyle’s departure was announced on Tuesday by White House Press Secretary Katie Zacharia, who told reporters that “we have asked Ambassador Guilfoyle to resign.”
“She was doing a good job, but we didn’t like what we were reading,” Trump told reporters shortly afterwards.
Guilfoyle, who was previously engaged to Trump’s eldest son, Donald Jr., was sworn in as ambassador to Greece last September. Less than a year later, the Wall Street Journal claimed that she was using her position to lobby for Greek energy tycoon Alexandros Exarchou. Guilfoyle allegedly pressured several Balkan governments to purchase American liquefied natural gas (LNG) from Exarchou’s firm, Aktor Group, and traveled to Davos aboard his private jet.
At a meeting with Greek officials in March, Guilfoyle allegedly threatened to topple Prime Minister Kyriakos Mitsotakis’ government if the Greek leader refused to purchase US LNG. Guilfoyle reportedly took credit for ousting Romanian Prime Minister Ilie Bolojan, who supported the US-backed Vertical Gas Corridor project, but refused to purchase more American LNG when Romania already possessed adequate domestic reserves.
“We can do that to any country we want. We can do that here,” she reportedly warned Greek Energy Minister Stavros Papastavrou. Papastavrou later denied that Guilfoyle had made any “pressure or threat against our country,” but did not address the Wall Street Journal’s claim that the ambassador played a part in ousting Bolojan.
The newspaper then released a leaked recording in which Guilfoyle told an American businessman that she could make him “a lot of f**king money” if he gifted her an invitation to a dinner in Davos in January. The final straw came last week when Trump donor Eric Deters told MS Now that Guilfoyle asked him for $100,000 to pay off her credit card bill in 2024, promising him access to the Trump administration if he did. 
“It absolutely was a quid pro quo,” Deters said, calling Guilfoyle “a grifter.”
In a social media post addressing her dismissal, Guilfoyle described “the recent allegations” against her as “false.”
“I intend to vigorously defend my name, my reputation, and my integrity,” she added, concluding “I will not allow false accusations to define my decades of public service.”

Consumers say regulators must 'lift their game' after solar battery delays

Lux Solar investigated by watchdog as consumers claim they were ripped off
In short:
Consumers are raising concerns about the conduct of some companies selling and installing batteries under the federal government's Cheaper Home Batteries Program.
There has also been a spike in complaints to federal and state watchdogs.
What's next?
A government spokesperson said it had empowered the Clean Energy Regulator to monitor the industry closely.
After waiting a year for a battery system that never showed up, Bob Emery's frustration boiled over.
He claims the installer, Lux Solar, "can't be trusted".
Mr Emery paid a $1,000 deposit last October for a 48kwh system which he hoped would slash his power bills at his Perth home.
After lengthy delays, he unsuccessfully requested a refund.
The retired electrician also pursued his case with a consumer protection body and industry groups without resolution.
"There are cowboys out there that are ripping people off and it is just not good enough,"
Mr Emery said.
He joins a growing number of customers raising concerns about the conduct of some companies selling and installing batteries under the federal government's Cheaper Home Batteries Program.
The program has sparked unprecedented demand, with more than 530,000 batteries installed since July 2025. Over four years, the scheme has covered estimated costs of more than $7.2 billion.
There has also been a spike in complaints to federal and state watchdogs with the NSW energy and water ombudsman saying complaints in that jurisdiction had doubled since last year.
The Australian Competition and Consumer Commission (ACCC) has several investigations underway and South Australia has announced a crackdown on "dodgy solar companies".
Queensland's Office of Fair Trading confirmed Lux Solar is under investigation.
It is the second solar company in as many months being probed for allegedly charging customers for deposits to install battery systems under the federal scheme that were never delivered.
In June, Lux Solar was kicked out of the voluntary industry-run consumer protection scheme, the New Energy Tech Consumer Code (NETCC) for "major failures," including continuing to take payments without showing it could deliver the systems.
The company has continued to advertise itself as an "approved seller" on its website, despite the Clean Energy Council requesting that wording be removed.
Consumer advocate and CEO of the Consumer Policy Research Centre, Erin Turner, has called for the ad to be investigated.
"That's really potentially misleading and I hope a regulator looks at it because that's a part of the consumer law where we can see really significant court actions with fines of up to $100 million," Ms Turner said.
'I don't have any trust in anyone installing it'
In November 2025, Mr Emery was told the installation of his battery system was two to four weeks away.
Two months later there was still no progress, so he emailed the salesman and asked for a refund.
Again, he was told the "install team" would make contact within a week or two.
Mr Emery grew alarmed when the salesman stopped answering his calls and voice messages with Lux Solar weren't returned.
"I realised I've blown my thousand dollars, so I started looking at government agencies that might be able to help."
Lux Solar is based in Western Australia but also operates in Queensland and New South Wales.
Mr Emery made a complaint to Consumer Protection WA but the watchdog said it was up to him to take the matter to court.
"The government bodies need to lift their game," he said.
"It's put me off the whole (federal battery) program, I don't have any trust in anyone installing it," he said.
His frustration is shared by Brisbane man Justin Albin and his Queensland work colleague who both waited about a year after paying deposits to Lux Solar last October.
In January, a salesman told Mr Albin there had been "some installer issues" but he would get his system as promised.
He received an email which said Lux Solar had more installation teams "ramping back up" and confirmation would come soon.
He sent a legal letter demanding Lux Solar install the system or he would start court proceedings.
Lux Solar offered him a refund which he rejected. If he chose another battery installer now it would be at a reduced rebate.
He also said it failed to account for his lost power bill savings and money he could have made selling power back to the grid.
The company sent him a revised proposal last week.
It wants to put in five batteries instead of three requiring Mr Albin to change timber boards on the front of his home to bear the extra weight.
"They're trying to make best endeavours, but given the communication in the past … I'm still not 100 per cent sure that they'll actually deliver."
There has been growing pressure to expand access to dispute resolution for solar and battery customers by allowing them access to ombudsman schemes.
Ms Turner said she was concerned the Cheaper Home Batteries Program was appealing to businesses attracted to the "honey-pot".
She said consumer protection agencies don't have sufficient powers to force a business to act or punish them.
"There's no penalties for when companies don't deliver on these promises," she said.
"It leaves people stuck.
"We've got a law without any backup, without any teeth, so it's inevitable that you'll see companies continue to do the wrong thing."
Under Australian consumer law, products like solar batteries must be supplied within a reasonable time or customers can seek a refund.
Individuals who fail to supply them can be fined a maximum of $2.5 million, while for a company, the penalties can be significantly higher.
Consumer Protection WA said impacted customers should contact them and this year it had conciliated cases and investigated matters involving solar and battery companies.
Lux Solar was also fined $25,000 after a Workcover WA investigation found it had failed to insure and did not comply with an inspector.
The New South Wales watchdog, the Building Commission, said it had previously taken action against Lux Solar after the company engaged in unlicensed activity and Home Building Compensation Fund insurance.
Lux Solar and the company director were fined a total of $6,750.
The federal watchdog, the Clean Energy Regulator, said it received four referrals about Lux Solar but none related to the creation of small-scale technology certificates which was its primary responsibility.
The taxpayer rebate can only be claimed after providing photos of the installation at the customer's home.
The ABC requested an interview with Lux Solar and sent the company written questions but did not receive a response.
In a statement Energy Minister Chris Bowen said the Clean Energy Regulator has been empowered to monitor the industry closely and the number of battery installations were much higher than the associated rise in complaints.

Pope Leo's lung nodule surgery completed successfully, Vatican says

Pope Leo's lung nodule surgery was completed successfully, Vatican says
Pope Leo XIV underwent a successful surgery Tuesday to remove a lung nodule, according to the Vatican.
"The procedure was completed successfully, within the expected timeframe and as planned, and the Holy Father has returned to his room," the Holy See Press Office said. The office promised further information at a later time.
The 71-year-old Leo had walked into Rome's Gemelli hospital through the main entrance earlier Tuesday and waved to dozens of well-wishers who had gathered to greet him. The Vatican said the surgery would be performed by a team led by Gemelli's chief thoracic surgeon, Dr. Stefano Margaritora.
The operation got underway as medical staff recited the Rosary prayer in the hospital chapel Tuesday evening. "Let us join together in prayer, asking the Lord to sustain our bishop, Pope Leo, and to comfort all those who are hospitalized here," said the Vicar of Rome, Cardinal Baldassare Reina, at the start of the prayer.
The American pontiff has offered a rare level of transparency about the first publicly disclosed major health problem of his 17-month papacy. He revealed the discovery of the small, localized nodule during his Sunday noon prayer and announced that he would have it removed.
The nodule was discovered during regular checks, the Vatican has said. It is not known if it is cancerous. In most cases, this kind of lung nodule is benign, doctors say.
Oncologists say even if the nodule turns out to be cancerous, Leo's prognosis is "excellent" since it will have been removed at an early stage.
The surgery, which is fairly low risk and usually performed under general anesthesia, will require a weeklong hospital stay and the Vatican on Monday canceled all Leo's audiences through Oct. 20.
"These are things that can be treated very well, if the words he used reflect the clinical situation," said Dr. Lorenzo Spaggiari, director of thoracic surgery at the European Institute of Oncology, or EIO, in Milan, who is not involved in the pope's care but knows the team at Gemelli.
The procedure comes just weeks before Leo is scheduled to take a trip to Uruguay, Argentina and Peru at the beginning of November. Doctors typically suggest about three weeks to recover without any flying.
The current itinerary for the trip is ambitious and the longest of his papacy to date, calling for Leo to clock just over 19,000 miles on a dozen flights and two helicopter rides, and a significant altitude change in Peru.
"He has decided to undergo surgery soon in order to not change his plans for future overseas trips, so there is no need to worry, as it is not an emergency," said Tokyo Cardinal Kikuchi Tsutomu, who saw Leo on Monday.
A lung nodule is a small abnormal area measuring less than 1.2 inches that sometimes appears on a CT scan of the chest or abdomen. Often, the scans are done to investigate trauma or a lung infection, unrelated to a lung cancer screening. A nodule can be benign or malignant, and often surgical removal is recommended both to establish whether it is cancer and to treat a malignancy while it is still localized.

New potatoes have tripled in price over a week: what is happening to prices and does Ukraine face a shortage
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
21:28:02 EEST
03:28:02 KST

New potatoes have tripled in price over a week: what is happening to prices and does Ukraine face a shortage
Kyiv • UNN
At the Stolychyi market, the price of new potatoes rose from UAH 20 to UAH 60 per kilogram in six days. Nationwide monitoring recorded an increase of only 2%.
At Kyiv’s Stolichnyi market, young potatoes rose in price from 20 to 60 hryvnias per kilogram in one week. By contrast, mature potatoes cost several times less. In addition, nationwide monitoring by the Ministry of Agrarian Policy showed that the price of this staple root vegetable for Ukrainians increased by just 2%.
What explains such a significant price gap, whether it is related to a reduced harvest, and what buyers should expect in the coming months was examined by UNN.
Where potatoes cost 60 hryvnias
According to data from monitoring of the Stolichnyi market, cited by Ukrainian economic publications, on October 7 a kilogram of young potatoes cost an average of 20 hryvnias, while by October 13 it had already reached 60 hryvnias. In six days, the price had risen by 40 hryvnias (that is, by 200%). Sellers’ price tags for this product range from 50 to 80 hryvnias per kilogram.
By contrast, regular potatoes at Stolichnyi cost approximately 12 hryvnias per kilogram, while on October 12 offers ranged from 10 to 13 hryvnias.
What nationwide statistics show
According to the weekly monitoring conducted by the Ministry of Agrarian Policy and Food, as of October 13, potato prices in Ukraine had increased by 2%. This is a moderate change compared with the surge in young potato prices at one marketplace.
A different picture is provided by supermarket monitoring published by the Minfin portal. According to its data, in the first half of October, the price of regular potatoes rose from approximately 16 to 18.6 hryvnias per kilogram. However, it should immediately be noted that this indicator is based on a limited sample of supermarkets and hypermarkets, so it cannot be considered the average price for the entire country.
Economists explain that such discrepancies in statistics from several sources may arise because of different observation methods: wholesale and retail offers, regular and young potatoes, an individual market and nationwide monitoring are not interchangeable indicators. To assess actual price dynamics, it is important to compare the same product, through the same sales channel, and over a comparable period.
Will Ukraine have enough of a potato harvest
The current price situation does not provide grounds to speak of a nationwide potato shortage. On September 14, Minister of Agrarian Policy and Food Taras Vysotskyi forecast production of approximately 12.5 million tonnes in 2026. According to him, this is enough to meet domestic needs, although the overall harvest estimate is lower than last year’s.
The ministry estimated the amount of potatoes consumed by the population as food at 2–2.5 million tonnes per year. The remainder is used mainly as seed material and feed. Around 400 specialized enterprises are engaged in industrial cultivation on approximately 60,000 hectares. A significant portion of the harvest is grown by households.
Why potato prices can differ so much
A sharp increase in a particular segment does not necessarily indicate a crisis across the entire market. Young potatoes and potatoes intended for long-term storage have different levels of supply and demand. At the end of the young-potato season, even a slight reduction in batches can have a stronger impact on their price tags than on the prices of mass-market produce.
In addition, the final cost of vegetables includes sorting, packaging, logistics, retail expenses, and possible storage losses. During wartime, additional risks include power supply disruptions and rising transportation costs. All of this can affect the final price seen by a homemaker who has gone to a market or supermarket to buy potatoes for her family.
The situation with potatoes in Ukraine: what buyers should expect before winter
The nearest price dynamics will depend on the arrival of produce from the new harvest on the market and on how many potatoes producers place in storage facilities. During the mass sale of the harvested crop, an increase in supply may restrain prices. Later, as the volume of available produce declines, the costs of storing and transporting it will become more significant.
We remind you
As UNN wrote, global food prices reached their highest level since the end of 2022. And one of the reasons is the war in Ukraine.

Russian banks fear massive fines after unprecedented surge in court bailiff inquiries

Russian banks fear massive fines after unprecedented surge in court bailiff inquiries
Russian banks received millions of requests for information about debtors from the Federal Bailiff Service (FSSP) over three days between September 18 and 21, an unprecedented volume, the National Financial Market Council reported.
One regional bank received 12.8 million requests on September 19 alone — as many as it normally receives in a month.
The council’s head, Andrey Yemelin, said the volume of FSSP requests over those three days was at least 10 to 12 times the usual level, and up to 30 times at some banks. More than 90% of the requests concerned people who were not customers of the banks that received them, said Yelena Samokhina, director of the banking development department at the Association of Banks of Russia.
Experts believe technical errors may account for the volume of requests, which the FSSP generates automatically. “The service has previously acknowledged that it resends requests if a bank hasn’t confirmed receipt. If those confirmations were lost, the automated system could have sent banks the entire backlog, along with duplicate requests,” said Mikhail Bryukhanov, chairman of Pervouralskbank’s board of directors.
Banks are legally required to provide the requested information within three days or face fines of 50,000 to 100,000 rubles for each request. Given the volume, Yemelin said “the fines could add up to amounts that pose a real threat to the financial stability of some banks.”
The council asked the Central Bank to look into the situation. The Central Bank said it had “received the inquiry and will review it according to established procedures.”

French lawmakers unanimously back bill to protect sexual violence victims
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
18:23:17 UTC
03:23:17 KST

Şeyma Erkul Dayanç
13 October 2026•Update: 13 October 2026
France’s National Assembly on Tuesday unanimously approved a bill to strengthen protection for victims of sexual and gender-based violence.
The bill passed its first reading in a 503 – 0 vote, following six days of debate. It will now go to the Senate and is not yet in force.
The legislation would require investigators to interview victims and suspects, preserve evidence and look for other potential victims within one year.
It also provides for specialized police units and courts dealing with sexual and domestic violence.
Victims would be entitled to 10 days of leave to attend medical appointments or take legal steps.
The bill would require schools to hold regular interviews with students to help identify violence, with full implementation planned by 2032.
Other measures include expanded incest-related offenses, medical care for child victims and stronger consent requirements for invasive medical procedures.
The bill would also strengthen penalties for sharing sexual content without consent and sending unsolicited sexual images.
Lawmakers rejected several provisions intended to protect foreign victims, including a ban on issuing deportation orders against sexual violence victims who have filed complaints.
The reform gained momentum after the death of an 11-year-old girl, Lyhanna, who was found dead after being raped in southwestern France in June.
The suspect had previously faced several complaints alleging sexual violence against minors.
The government has pledged to assess the cost of the measures and present a budget plan after the Senate examines the bill.

Finland calls for EU tourist visa ban on Russians until Moscow ends war against Ukraine as bloc weighs tougher restrictions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
18:22:40 UTC
03:22:40 KST

Finland’s Foreign Minister Elina Valtonen has called on the European Union to stop issuing tourist visas to Russian citizens until Russia ends its war against Ukraine, urging the bloc to adopt a unified policy. Her call comes as the EU discusses broader restrictions on Russian diplomats, tourists, and former combatants.
Russia has intensified its hybrid campaign across Europe in recent months, with suspected sabotage, arson attacks, and other covert operations targeting infrastructure and undermining security. European officials have increasingly called for a coordinated response, arguing that tighter controls on Russian diplomats, travel, and former combatants could help reduce security risks and limit opportunities for Russian intelligence operations.
In a statement published on 12 October, Finland’s Ministry for Foreign Affairs said Valtonen was calling on the European Commission to introduce stricter guidelines for processing Russian visa applications and propose changes to EU legislation needed to implement a complete ban on tourist visas.
“As long as Russia continues its invasion, Russian citizens should not be issued tourist visas,” Valtonen said. “It is not right that Russians can travel to Europe to enjoy the way of life and freedoms here while their country bombs the homes of Ukrainians.”
Finland banned visas for non-essential travel by Russian citizens in 2022. Valtonen said the same restriction should now be adopted at the EU level.
The Finnish minister has invited other EU member states to join a joint letter to the European Commission. Beyond a complete ban on tourist visas, the letter proposes barring Schengen visas for people in Russian President Vladimir Putin’s inner circle, restricting visas for Russian athletes, and enforcing an EU-agreed visa ban on former Russian combatants.
EU considers wider restrictions on Russians
The proposal comes as EU foreign ministers discuss additional measures to counter Russian hybrid threats. EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said after a meeting of the bloc’s foreign ministers in Luxembourg on 12 October that the EU was considering reducing the number of tourist visas issued to Russians, restricting Russian diplomats’ movements within the bloc, and accelerating entry bans for former Russian combatants, Radio Svoboda reported.
Kallas said the EU needed a comprehensive response to Russian hybrid threats, including new sanctions, stronger enforcement of existing restrictions, action against Russia’s shadow fleet, accountability for hybrid attacks, and improved intelligence sharing.
One proposal would require Russian diplomats to obtain advance permission before traveling to other EU member states, rather than simply notifying authorities of their trips.
Polish Deputy Foreign Minister Marcin Bosacki said tighter rules were necessary because some acts of sabotage and subversion were coordinated, at least in part, through Russian diplomatic missions.
Kallas said the European External Action Service and European Commission would also prepare proposals for further isolating Russia in international sport. She argued that sport and culture should not be used to whitewash Russian aggression.
EU divided over tourist visa restrictions
Several EU countries have pushed to reduce tourist visas for Russian citizens. In June, a group of member states jointly called for fewer visas, according to DW. The Finnish ministry said Schengen countries issued nearly 500,000 tourist visas to Russian citizens in 2025.
Estonia has also proposed measures to bar former Russian military personnel who fought against Ukraine from entering the EU. Estonian Foreign Minister Margus Tsahkna warned that large numbers of Russian veterans could try to enter Europe after the war, potentially with support from Russian intelligence services.
The European Commission has supported including a mechanism targeting former combatants in the EU’s 21st sanctions package, and officials are working on how to implement it.
However, EU countries remain divided over the scope of visa restrictions. France and Italy have previously opposed a blanket isolation of Russian tourists. Member states are also debating how to prevent former Russian combatants from entering the bloc without restricting entry for military deserters or opponents of the war.
No timeline has been announced for the proposed restrictions on Russian tourists and diplomats. The measures remain under discussion and have not been adopted as a bloc-wide ban.

The student movement sprang up last month, with teenagers at France's lycees – high schools for those aged 15 to 18 – blocking the entrances to many schools to demand better classroom conditions.

Perceived heavy-handed reactions from police against the students drove many to join Tuesday's demonstrations.
One teen lost his hand when he picked up a police stun grenade during the protests, while another lost an eye, and another teeth when an officer fired a teargas canister in his face.
Police have opened internal investigations into 34 allegations of violence against demonstrators.
Some 147 teaching staff have been injured in the protests, the education ministry said.
'Not budging'
"We're not giving up the fight, whether it's for the high school students who were hit with a harsh crackdown, or for denouncing police violence," said Patricia, a 20-year-old university student in Paris who did not give her last name.
Some Indian tourists who wandered into the Paris demonstration said they were unnerved.
"Initially we were terrified," said Snehil Jain, a 45-year-old visiting Paris for a week with his wife.
"We had seen the media images of violence around these protests. But then we saw it was a peaceful protest, so we were OK then."
France's education ministry said 214 schools, mostly high schools, were closed Tuesday.

University student union l'Union Etudiante reported 90 percent of universities had closed nationwide to show support.
French students say they are determined to press their demands over absent teachers, dilapidated buildings, overcrowded schedules and other grievances.
They have dismissed a government pledge – made after last week's demonstrations – to send 3,000 substitute teachers to the 114 worst-affected schools.
"We are continuing the blockades. We are not budging," said Naouel, a high school student in Brest. She said she hoped the protests would continue after the half-term holidays, in late October.
Mariolino, a 16-year-old in Nantes, concurred. "Those who think the anger will disappear with the holidays just don't get it," he said.
On Monday, Macron had urged restraint from protesters, saying the issues "deserve time, consultations, discussion and respect".

US Supreme Court agrees to hear watchdog case on Elon Musk’s DOGE records
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
18:21:18 UTC
03:21:18 KST

US Supreme Court agrees to hear watchdog case on Elon Musk’s DOGE records
The Trump administration argues that DOGE is exempt from freedom of information requirements.
The United States Supreme Court has agreed to hear arguments in a watchdog’s lawsuit seeking public records about trillionaire Elon Musk’s Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE).
The high court is intervening on Tuesday for a second time in Citizens for Responsibility and Ethics (CREW) in Washington’s case, which seeks access to DOGE records from its operations in the early days of US President Donald Trump’s second term. The Trump administration asked the court to hear the case.
Last year, the high court reined in a district court’s order for the government to produce DOGE-related records to CREW. The high court’s conservative majority concluded in June 2025 that US District Judge Christopher Cooper ruled too broadly in ordering documents to be turned over to the group.
CREW claims DOGE is a federal agency and therefore is subject to the Freedom of Information Act (FOIA).
The Trump administration argues that DOGE is exempt from FOIA’s requirements as a presidential advisory body.
Cooper ruled in CREW’s favour and ordered expedited processing of the group’s records request. An appeals court panel also sided with CREW.
The Trump administration claims the panel ignored the Supreme Court’s direction to consider separation-of-powers concerns and intruded on the “autonomy and confidentiality” of presidential advisers.
“Subjecting advisory bodies to intrusive discovery triggers the very concerns that Congress sought to avoid by excluding presidential advisory bodies from FOIA’s reach,” US Department of Justice lawyers wrote.
The administration also says the appeals court impermissibly authorised the plaintiffs to take a sworn deposition of DOGE acting administrator Amy Gleason.
CREW says the appeals court fully complied with the Supreme Court’s previous order. The group also asserts that the public has a right to know how DOGE helped the administration carry out a sweeping overhaul of government operations in 2025.
“Undisputed facts in the public record — including the President’s statements — confirmed that (DOGE) was wielding enormous independent authority across the federal government,” CREW lawyers wrote.
In a statement Tuesday, CREW lawyer Nikhel Sus said the lower courts have uniformly ruled that it is entitled to records that could help the court determine whether DOGE wields the type of authority that would make it subject to the Freedom of Information Act.
“We will continue to pursue transparency for the American people, who deserve to know the details of the Trump Administration’s efforts to unilaterally remake the federal government,” Sus said in the statement.
DOGE said it had slashed tens of billions of dollars in expenditures, but its claims were difficult for outside financial experts to verify.
Federal auditors found that some of DOGE’s reported savings across contract, grant and lease terminations were incorrect, lacked supporting evidence or included terminations that were already under way when DOGE was established, according to a report by the Government Accountability Office.

How the Yandex ‘Russian bots’ lie fell apart
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
18:18:55 UTC
03:18:55 KST

How the Yandex ‘Russian bots’ lie fell apart
Did Ukraine’s strikes on Russian data centers destroy the Kremlin’s pro-MAGA bot army? Or are Vladimir Zelensky and his European patrons insulting their citizens with remedial-grade propaganda? RT takes a trip down the rabbit hole.
Ukrainian forces hit three Yandex (Russia’s equivalent to Google) data centers with long-range drones between October 8 and 11. Yandex confirmed that operations were “completely halted” at the facility struck on October 8, and temporarily halted at the center struck on October 11. This much is true, but the story that followed veers into NAFO fiction.
How did the ‘Russian bots’ story begin?
On October 8, American cybersecurity researcher Jeremiah Fowler posted a Cloudflare graph showing a dramatic drop in “bot traffic” after the first Yandex center was hit. As Yandex is primarily a search company, its bots crawl the internet indexing content for users. All search engines function in this way, but Fowler – either through malice or ignorance – conflated this search bot activity with social media bot activity, claiming that the drop in traffic could “disrupt the midterm elections in the US.”
The story spread, hitting the mainstream media on October 11 when Tom’s Hardware published an article claiming that “Russian disinformation bot traffic” had been “nearly eliminated” after the strikes. The word “disinformation” was later pulled from the headline, but the tale had already taken on a life of its own.
That same day, an AI-created graph began circulating, claiming that “Russian bots” were making 56% fewer posts in support of Germany’s right-wing AfD party in the aftermath of the strikes. The graph, which was unsourced and had one axis unlabeled, measured the “decline in activity of Russian bots” up to October 15, four days in the future at the time it appeared online.
Regardless, the graph was shared by a Green Party councillor in Germany’s North Rhine-Westphalia, and by Czech MEP Tomas Zdechovsky. “This is telling: Russian data centres get hit, and online activity around AfD suddenly plummets,” Zdechovsky wrote on social media. “So much talk about German patriotism… then the connection from Russia goes down.”
Who spread the lie?
By October 12, the story had been reported by Germany’s Der Standard and Focus. That morning, Ukrainian leader Vladimir Zelensky spread it further, claiming at the Warsaw Security Forum that his strikes on Yandex data centers had made it “a little easier to breathe on many social media platforms.”
“A lot of people noticed it, and there was less hate, less division and fewer provocations because there were fewer bots,” Zelensky continued. “And it’s pretty clear where those bots were coming from. If they disappeared when Yandex went offline, this proves again and again that Europe is not the source of the problems,” he added.
Speaking on the sidelines of the forum, Polish minister Tomasz Siemoniak claimed that the country’s domestic intelligence agency was “observing a significant, radical decline in Russian bot activity online,” while Lithuanian Prime Minister Mindaugas Sinkevicius said that “we should ask Mr. Zelensky to hit more data centres in Russia” to “protect” elections in the EU.
Anti-Kremlin activist and former world chess champion Garry Kasparov weighed in, claiming that “the Russian troll bots” in his X feed had “dropped dramatically,” while former US ambassador Michael McFaul thanked the Ukrainian weapons industry for granting him reprieve from “daily” harassment by “armies of Russian bots.”
The Russian troll bots in my own feed have dropped dramatically already. MAGA's online support may soon reflect Trump's approval rating!
— Garry Kasparov (@Kasparov63) October 11, 2026
The only problem was none of this was true, and based on the replies to McFaul’s tweet, nobody was buying it.
How was the bots story debunked?
The story didn’t take long to fall apart. Common Consultancy, a Scandinavian NGO that has previously accused Russia of orchestrating social media influence campaigns, concluded that there was “no visible effect” on pro-MAGA or pro-AfD social media posts after the Yandex strikes. Leonid Volkov, an anti-Kremlin activist associated with deceased opposition figure Alexey Navalny, slammed Zdechovsky for spreading “nonsense and falsehood.”
CeMAS, a liberal German think tank, stated that it was “not seeing a drop in the number of posts that could be explained by an attack on data centers.” The Hasso Plattner Institute and Polisphere, two tech nonprofits, concurred, and German newspapers began quietly editing their articles on Monday night.
Some, like Merkur, kept “speculation about Russian bots and the AfD” in their headlines. Others, including Der Standard, noted that their “original assertion of a confirmed connection [between the strikes and alleged bot activity] has been corrected.” The Verge, a tech-focused American news site, admitted that “the Yandex outage probably didn’t blitz Russian bots.”
Is this hybrid war?
By the time the story was debunked and corrected, the damage was done. In the public’s eye, the strikes were tied to a drop in “Russian bot” activity, and none of the speakers at the Warsaw Security Forum, including senior Ukrainian, Polish, and Lithuanian officials, bothered to correct the record.
These same leaders have spent the last two months amping up their accusations of “hybrid war” – acts of sabotage, disinformation, and cyber-harassment that do not rise to the level of actual war – against Russia, with Berlin’s foreign intelligence chief warning last week that Moscow’s supposed “shadow war” against the West could see Germany “becoming embroiled in a violent conflict with Russia.”
That none of the acts of “hybrid war” – among them the discovery of a suspicious drone at Leipzig Airport in August, and a series of unsubstantiated drone sightings across Germany and Scandinavia last year – have been linked by evidence to Russia is a feature, not a bug. “Hybrid war” is by its very nature unprovable, and the accusation alone is enough for European leaders to justify their deepening proxy war in Ukraine, their remilitarization and expansion of the national security state at home.
Furthermore, the accusations themselves are a form of “hybrid warfare” against the European public, analyst Thomas Fazi argued last week. “Europeans,” he wrote, “are being subjected to a sustained campaign of cognitive or psychological warfare aimed at conditioning them to believe that Europe is under attack from Russia.”
Who stands to gain?
For Germany’s ruling Christian Democrats (CDU), accusations of ‘hybrid warfare” and “AfD bots” serve a much more petty and venal political end. Chancellor Friedrich Merz is less popular now than at any point in his political career, and with the AfD trouncing the CDU in state elections and leading his party by ten points in opinion polls, Merz has taken every opportunity available to tie his opponents to Russia.
“We in Germany will not allow ourselves to be divided, not by hybrid attacks, not by Moscow-bot-driven hate speech on social media, and – if I may say so – not even by the slogans of the AfD and its Russian backers,” the chancellor said in a speech earlier this month.
The Yandex story – which conveniently linked the AfD to “Moscow-bot-driven hate speech” – was a godsend to Merz, and to his Ukrainian and Eastern European allies, who have an interest in preventing the Ukraine-skeptic AfD from taking power in Germany. Unfortunately for them, like all “hybrid war” claims, it fell apart the moment it was subjected to some basic scrutiny.

The International Monetary Fund has lowered its forecast for Russia’s economic growth to 0.9% in both 2026 and 2027. The updated forecast, released on October 13, is down from its July projection of 1.1% for each year.
The IMF report says high global energy prices are supporting Russia’s economy despite a decline in supplies caused by Ukrainian strikes that damaged oil infrastructure.
The report says the overall outlook is weak for energy-intensive economies and those dependent on oil and gas imports. Russia, however, benefits from “favorable factors associated with increased defense spending” that partially offset this weakness.
In late September, Russia’s Economic Development Ministry raised its growth forecast for 2026 from 0.4% to 0.6%. The ministry expects growth to accelerate from 1.4% in 2027 to 2.4% in 2029. Russia’s central bank forecasts growth of 0 to 1% in 2026 and 1.5 to 2.5% in 2027.
In early October, the World Bank kept its forecast for Russian GDP growth in 2026 at 0.8%. It expects Russia’s economy to grow by 0.7% in both 2027 and 2028.

Give Riyadh a mirror
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
18:17:08 UTC
