Give Riyadh a mirror
TEHRAN - In an article published on Monday, the editor-in-chief of the Saudi daily Asharq Al-Awsat used the Ansarullah strike on Riyadh airport as a pretext to level a series of sweeping — and at times bizarre — accusations.
The strangest claim comes where he writes of the attack: “Rarely in the history of warfare has a civilian airport crowded with passengers been the target of an attack.” One has to ask: Is Mr. Charbel suffering from memory loss, or is he deliberately seeking to conceal and distort the facts?
It would be possible to compile an extremely long list of Saudi airstrikes on civilian targets in Yemen since Riyadh launched its invasion of its southern neighbor in 2015. Even mourning ceremonies and wedding celebrations of the oppressed people of Yemen were not spared from bombardment, time and again turned into bloodbaths — in some cases with up to 150 victims killed in a single strike.
Let us examine just one case in greater detail. At midday on August 9, 2018, a bus full of schoolchildren stopped at the local market in Dahyan, in Saada province. The students were returning from a picnic — likely experiencing the happiest day of their lives.
Your country’s fighter jets had been circling in the sky above the area for nearly an hour. They were armed with MK-82 laser-guided bombs — bombs you had purchased from the United States just a year earlier. The missiles were fired, and moments later, the happiest day in the lives of 40 children became the last day of their lives. Most of them were under the age of 10.
Have you ever considered that almost everything about the war you unleashed on Yemen bears a striking resemblance to America’s wars? You named your operation “Decisive Storm”; America had “Desert Storm” on its record. The war launched in partnership with Israel against Iran was dubbed “Epic Fury.” You struck Yemeni civilians again and again — and America has never fought a war without repeated attacks on civilian targets. Does the chilling parallel between the Dahyan atrocity and the Minab school not give you pause? And there is one final, telling similarity: Riyadh, too, tried to manufacture a veneer of legitimacy for its aggression by assembling a nominal coalition — precisely what Washington does in most of its military adventures.
Have you ever asked yourselves why, despite possessing such modern and advanced weaponry, you have been unable to defeat Ansarullah? Your problem from the very beginning was that you never properly understood Yemen and its faithful, resilient people. You branded them an “Iranian proxy” — and you continue to do so. Strangely, you insist on denying the reality that Yemenis are independent, and that on matters of both war and peace, they decide for themselves. Until you accept that reality, you will never escape this self-made quagmire, and no mediator will be able to help you.
We, as Iranians — your Muslim brothers and your neighbors — want you to stand with dignity. We take no pleasure in seeing America treat you as a “cash cow,” plundering your wealth through colossal arms and security contracts. How can an America incapable of protecting its own bases and troops in the region possibly protect you and bring you security? Do you remember what Trump said in 2018? He declared openly that without us, Saudi Arabia would not survive two weeks. A year later, he boasted that with a single phone call, he took 500 million dollars from them.
In today’s world, money may solve many problems, but it certainly does not buy authority or respect. You have surely not forgotten what Trump said about your Crown Prince at the summit hosted by Saudi Arabia’s Public Investment Fund (PIF) in Miami this March, before some 1,500 prominent businessmen and investors: “He didn’t think he would be kissing my ass. He really didn’t. He thought it’d be just another American president that was a loser where the country was going downhill. But now he has to be nice to me. You tell him he’d better be nice to me.”
Have you ever wondered why Trump feels entitled to insult your leaders so brazenly?
Whatever the solution to Saudi Arabia’s problems today may be, it does not lie in Washington or Tel Aviv. They harbor a civilizational and existential hostility toward Muslims — a hostility that will not be resolved with bribes worth hundreds of billions.
And finally, I suggest that when you suffer a painful retaliatory blow on the battlefield in Yemen, instead of pointing the finger of blame at others, you take a good look in the mirror first.

The Cabinet of Ministers adopted a resolution On certain issues concerning the organization of reservations for conscripts during mobilization and wartime, MP Yaroslav Zhelezniak (from the Holos faction) said; a government source also confirmed this information to Interfax-Ukraine.
"The document was adopted after one day of revisions, and regarding the reservation percentage – after five days. However, my sources say that they apparently managed to remove this provision regarding the 50% calculation basis," Zhelezniak said on social media.

According to him, it was proposed that the Coordination Center consist of 17 members, including representatives of the Security Service of Ukraine (SBU), the Main Intelligence Agency of Ukraine, the Foreign Intelligence Service of Ukraine, and the National Police. Without a positive recommendation from this body, companies will not be able to obtain "critically important" status or a reservation quota exceeding 50%; moreover, the center will also have the authority to recommend revoking such status, while the document lacks clear deadlines, criteria, and appeal mechanisms.
Interfax-Ukraine reached out to the Cabinet of Ministers for comment.
As previously reported, relevant defense associations – including NAUDI, the Technological Forces of Ukraine, and the Council of Arms Manufacturers – have called on the government to maintain a 100% procurement quota for defense industry enterprises, emphasizing the risks to the fulfillment of defense contracts. The European Business Association (EBA) also expressed concern over possible changes to the procedure for reserving employees subject to military service and called on the government to ensure an open dialogue with the business community before making any decisions.
Regarding the creation of the Coordination Center, Yulia Svyrydenko's government had already adopted a similar decision in July, shortly before her resignation, but it never took effect. At that time, it was envisaged that the Coordination Center would function as a temporary consultative and advisory body to the government, and its tasks would include: coordinating government agencies and finding solutions to problematic situations regarding conscription; reviewing proposals from government agencies regarding the designation of enterprises, institutions, and organizations as critical to the economy and the public's livelihood.

Cornell University has announced that it is suspending parties and other social gatherings at fraternity houses for the rest of the academic year amid intensifying backlash over its handling of allegations that a female student was sexually assaulted at a fraternity house in 2024.
The university has also said that Cornell will involve New York state police in investigating sex crimes on campus.
Michael Kotlikoff, Cornell’s president, announced the measures on Tuesday.
The suspension of all parties and social gatherings at houses governed by Cornell’s interfraternity council is meant to be in effect through the end of the academic year ending in the spring of 2027 – and it is subject to a “zero tolerance” policy that would lead to the immediate emergency suspension of any chapter found to be in violation, Kotlikoff said.
“These measures will provide time for a thorough review of fraternity life at Cornell to determine whether and how it can safely continue,” Kotlikoff wrote in a letter to the campus community.
Kotlikoff also committed to adding a case manager to Cornell’s office of civil rights to help those who report sexual misconduct at the Ivy League institution navigate the processes. Kotlikoff also pledged to work with the New York state police to allow their trauma-informed criminal investigators – who are independent of Cornell University – to investigate allegations.
Such allegations otherwise have been handled by Cornell’s campus police force.
A civil lawsuit filed in September by a woman identified by the pseudonym of Jane Doe alleges that several men assaulted her at Cornell’s Chi Phi fraternity house after she went there in an intoxicated state looking for a friend.
Two of the accused men were subsequently expelled after an internal investigation by Cornell – while others were allowed to resume their studies after writing an essay, attending a workshop or serving a short suspension.
None were ever arrested or charged by local authorities, and disgust over the treatment of the alleged offenders grew when the woman’s lawsuit was made public.
Kathy Hochul, New York’s governor, on 2 October announced that she was appointing Letitia James, the state’s attorney general, to take over Jane Doe’s case as a special prosecutor.
If warranted, James would present evidence to a grand jury that could lead to criminal charges, Hochul said.
Two of the men named in Jane Doe’s lawsuit have challenged James’s appointment. Hochul said James’s appointment is necessary because local police and prosecutors who were obligated to protect Jane Doe “failed” her.

The military operation against the Houthis will continue until their coup is ended and state institutions are restored, said the head of Yemen’s Presidential Leadership Council on Tuesday.
In an address marking the 63rd anniversary of the Oct. 14, 1963 revolution, which led to Yemeni independence, Rashad al-Alimi said the “Dawn of Yemen” operation was advancing toward its ultimate objective of “ending the coup” by Iranian-backed Houthis, restoring state institutions, and placing weapons and decisions on war and peace exclusively in the hands of constitutional institutions.
“This decision is now in effect, and there is no turning back, whatever the sacrifices,” he said.
He said the operation was launched “after exhausting opportunities for de-escalation,” accusing the group of insisting on continuing the war and expanding attacks on cities, villages, neighboring countries, and international waterways.
The operation’s purpose, he said, is to restore state institutions, protect citizens, and ensure that no armed group can override the popular will or threaten neighboring countries and international shipping routes.
Addressing developments in the province of Taiz, al-Alimi pledged that the state would continue working “with all its capabilities” to protect the province, reopen its roads, and ease residents’ suffering.
He said he had instructed the government, local authorities, and relevant agencies to mobilize available resources to meet urgent humanitarian needs, provide food and medicine, assist displaced people and affected families, and secure supplies and vital roads.
He added that protecting the south’s security and stability, and safeguarding its residents’ rights and aspirations, are an integral part of the state’s national responsibility. 
Message to residents of Houthi-controlled areas
Al-Alimi told residents of Houthi-controlled areas that they are “not a target” of the operation, saying their security, rights, and dignity are among its principal motivations.
He urged them to protect their children from recruitment campaigns, avoid sending them into the group’s wars, and avoid military sites and combat zones.
He also called on them to take advantage of announced safe-return and amnesty measures, subject to their legal conditions.
Al-Alimi reaffirmed the council’s commitment to the “justness of the southern cause” and its support for the outcome of dialogue among southern parties under Saudi sponsorship.
He called for “a just and comprehensive solution that addresses past grievances, respects the popular will, and guarantees rights, partnership, and a secure future for all.” 
Condemnation of attacks on Saudi Arabia
Al-Alimi condemned Houthi attacks on neighboring Saudi Arabia, particularly the strike on King Khalid International Airport, which he said killed and injured civilians and Umrah pilgrims of several nationalities.
He also condemned attacks on civilian and vital facilities and threats to the security of holy sites.
Saudi Arabia’s security and stability are “closely linked to Yemen’s security and the interests of its citizens,” he said, adding that attacks on the kingdom’s security and civilian facilities constitute attacks on the Yemeni people’s vital interests and the stability of the entire region.
He thanked Saudi King Salman and Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman for supporting Yemen’s state institutions, armed forces, and security agencies.
Al-Alimi also praised Saudi assistance to Yemen’s economy and public budget, support for services and salaries, humanitarian relief, mine clearance, reconstruction, and development projects.
The statement came as a part of a military escalation that began in July, the most extensive since the relative calm that followed a UN-brokered truce that began in 2022.
Yemen has been engulfed in war since the Houthis seized Sanaa and several of the country’s 22 provinces in 2014, prompting an Arab coalition led by neighboring Saudi Arabia to intervene in 2015 in support of the internationally recognized government.

US sanctions Mexican cartel CDN's horse-racing, business network
MEXICO CITY, Oct 13 - The US Treasury Department on Tuesday sanctioned four people and 11 entities tied to the Cartel del Noreste (CDN), targeting a business network spanning horse racing, construction, trucking and the energy sector that Washington says helped finance the Mexican criminal group.
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent called it the agency's largest action to date against CDN's financial machinery, highlighting the cartel's persistence in using horse racing to launder money.
• Designated individuals include Pablo Cesar Guajardo Alvarez, alias "Takia," the accused CDN plaza boss in Nuevo Laredo and a former leader of the cartel's sicarios.
• Nuevo Laredo businessman Gamaliel Garza Garcia, involved in horse racing in both the US and Mexico, and his son were sanctioned alongside nine companies, including a quarter-horse racing stable, construction firms and fuel and gas businesses that Treasury said operated in support of the cartel.
• The action comes as US officials have raised concerns about cartel-linked horse smuggling across the US-Mexico border. Reuters reported last month that trafficked horses, which are often destined for racing in the US, continue moving through illegal crossing routes also used for drugs and migrants.
• Also targeted was Club La Molienda, a horse racetrack, restaurant and bar in Mexico's Tamaulipas state, that Treasury said is controlled by CDN and serves as a hub for the group's horse-racing activities.
• Tamex, a Nuevo Laredo-based trucking company, was sanctioned after authorities seized two cocaine shipments totaling 52 kg hidden in trailer brake drums linked to the firm.
• Treasury said cartel-linked front companies spent $16 million on US quarter-horse racing operations and laundered more than $22 million between 2008 and 2012, leading to the seizure of 455 horses.
• CDN was founded by brothers Miguel Angel and Oscar Omar Trevino Morales, who were transferred to the US in 2025 to face drug trafficking, racketeering and money-laundering charges. The group is a successor to Los Zetas. REUTERS

====================================================================================================

These Infections Are Linked to 12% of New Cancer Cases
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
18:07:34 UTC
03:07:34 KST

Cancer can seem random. It’s often the result of many factors, including genetic mutations that build up over a lifetime of exposure to sun, pollution, and other sources of DNA damage, combined with a person’s genetic predisposition. DNA damage accumulated over time can weaken the body’s ability to suppress out-of-control cell growth, which is how tumors form.
But infections are another significant cause of cancer. Uncovering the links between certain infections and cancers raises the hope that by preventing infection, one could prevent certain malignancies. A recent report from the World Health Organization’s International Agency for Research on Cancer (IARC) published in the Lancet Oncology found that 12% of new cancer cases in 2024—the most recent year for which data were available—were caused by 12 infections.
Which infections are associated with cancer?
Certain human papillomaviruses, or HPV, are behind the majority of cervical cancers and a number of head and neck cancers as well, says Harriet Rumgay, an epidemiologist at IARC who is an author of the new report. About 4% of new cancer diagnoses in 2024 could be attributed to HPV infection.
Doctors and researchers have known for decades that hepatitis B and hepatitis C infections also drive many cases of liver cancer, linked to 2% and less than 1% of new diagnoses respectively, according to the report.
There is also strong evidence linking Helicobacter pylori, a bacterium that infects the stomach and small intestine, with gastric cancers. This infection was calculated to be behind about 4% of new diagnoses. And Epstein-Barr Virus (EBV), which causes mononucleosis and affects more than 90% of the world’s population, was involved in around 1% of new diagnoses, including lymphomas, nasopharyngeal cancers, and gastric cancers. Seven other infections, including HIV, were also flagged as carcinogens in the study.
Most people who have these infections will not develop cancer. It’s not also immediate—there may be a years-long delay. And infection is often only one of a number of factors contributing to a given cancer. For instance, when it comes to the relatively high rates of EBV-driven nasopharyngeal cancers in China, researchers believe that some genetic predisposition and environmental factors are also involved.
Why do some infections cause cancer?
It depends on the infection. In the case of HIV, the virus suppresses the immune system, making it easier for other carcinogenic viruses to replicate. H. pylori causes tissue damage and produces toxins that destabilize the body’s natural control of cellular growth and division, which can lead to cancer.
With EBV, says Claire Shannon-Lowe, a virologist at the University of Birmingham in the U.K. who studies EBV and cancer but was not involved in the research, it has to do with how the virus hides within immune cells called B cells. “It's a whole host of things that the virus itself is doing to the B cell to make it continually grow,” she says. That includes blocking normal cellular housecleaning procedures that would both root the virus out and arrest cancer development.
How can these cancers be prevented?
Some of these infections have treatments. H. pylori can be cleared with antibiotics, for example, reducing the risk of gastric cancer, and treating HIV reduces cancer risk from the infection as well. Some other infections on the list have vaccines.
In fact, for some of these vaccines, cancer prevention was a major goal driving their development. “The hepatitis B virus vaccine was the first vaccine that was developed against cancer,” says Rumgay. Likewise, the HPV vaccine, which was approved 20 years ago, is intended to prevent cervical cancer. Cancer epidemiologists may start seeing the effects of widespread HPV vaccination in future analyses, Rumgay says. “More and more people who have been vaccinated are starting to reach the age where we would potentially see the impact on cervical cancer rates or other cancer rates,” she says.
However, these vaccines aren’t making it to everyone who might benefit from them. In the U.S., hepatitis B vaccination rates in newborns have declined steeply over the last two years.
For other infections, no vaccines are available. For EBV, a nearly ubiquitous virus with a long, clearly documented history of contributing to cancer, “we don't have an effective vaccine yet, or an effective way of preventing it,” says Rumgay. “This is something that we want to highlight with our study.”
Historically, it was difficult to interest pharmaceutical companies in vaccines for viruses like EBV that are common and nonlethal, says Lawrence Young, a virologist and emeritus professor of molecular oncology at University of Warwick in the U.K. who has spent his career studying cancer and EBV. (Young was not involved in the IARC research.)
But thanks in part to research suggesting EBV might be involved in multiple sclerosis, an autoimmune disorder, “they've all become very interested,” he says. A number of vaccine candidates are now being studied, with some in clinical trials.
For some of the infections implicated by the latest study—the Kaposi-sarcoma associated herpes virus, in particular—there’s need for much more research into prevention, says Rumgay. The hope is that “these new findings might stimulate more development in that area,” she says.

Ukraine, EU open second, third clusters of membership negotiations
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
21:06:55 EEST
03:06:55 KST

Ukraine and the European Union have opened the second and third negotiation clusters regarding membership.
The announcement was made Tuesday in Luxembourg at the conclusion of an intergovernmental conference by Thomas Byrne, Minister of State for European Affairs and Defense of Ireland, which currently holds the EU presidency.
Byrne said Ukraine's future lay within the European Union family and that, as part of the fourth intergovernmental conference on Ukraine's accession, the Council had opened Cluster 2, covering the internal market, and Cluster 3, covering competitiveness and inclusive growth. He said he was pleased to announce this important milestone in Ukraine's accession process together with Vsevolod Chentsov, Ukraine's Deputy Prime Minister for European and Euro-Atlantic Integration, and European Commissioner for Enlargement Marta Kos.
Byrne said these were the third and fourth clusters opened by the EU in negotiations with Ukraine, following the opening of Cluster 1, Fundamentals, in June and Cluster 6, External Relations, in July. He welcomed the continued momentum towards Ukraine's EU membership and said that, after a long period of stagnation, most clusters had now been opened.
The minister said that, despite Russia's ongoing war against Ukraine, its civilian population and civilian infrastructure, Ukraine continued to implement the reforms needed to bring its national legislation into line with EU standards in key areas.
He also said that Ireland, as the country holding the EU presidency, would do everything possible to support Ukraine on its path towards EU accession. Byrne described the day as positive for Ukraine's accession process and said all EU member states recognised Ukraine's progress in implementing key reforms in two important policy areas.
The minister explained that Cluster 2, the internal market, constituted the economic foundation of the accession process and covered nine technical chapters governing a candidate country's integration into the EU single market.
He said Cluster 3, competitiveness and inclusive growth, concerned the driving forces behind socioeconomic development in the EU accession process and comprised eight chapters aimed at bringing the candidate country's economy into line with EU standards.
Byrne added that the progress achieved sent an important signal to Ukrainians who were fighting for the European values of freedom, democracy and equality.
He said the EU would continue working in the near future to advance Ukraine's candidacy in accordance with the current enlargement methodology by opening the remaining clusters. At the same time, he urged Ukraine to continue implementing the necessary reforms, particularly in the area of fundamental principles.
Byrne said Ukraine was part of the European family by virtue of geography and added that the EU looked forward to the moment when Ukraine and its citizens could be welcomed into the European Union family.

The world’s distorted view of Israel is built on persistent myths - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
18:03:41 UTC
03:03:41 KST

If one had to choose a single word that characterizes the prism through which the world sees Israel and internalizes its feelings about us these days, that word would be “canard.” The prism is the vehicle that makes it possible for the viewer to see the truth bent to one’s own liking, while the canard provides the basis that attempts to propagate the lie.
The dictionary states that a canard primarily refers to an unfounded rumor, a false story, or a deliberate hoax. The word is derived from the French canard (meaning “duck”), tracing back to the old French expression “vendre un canard à moitié” (“to half-sell a duck”), meaning to trick or cheat someone.
Of course, some would say that given France’s frequent negativism about Israel, it should not be surprising that the word that describes the world’s preference for internalizing lies about Israel has its source in French.
Examples abound as to how this plays out in real life.
Last week, in a debate between US senatorial candidates in Michigan, Democrat Abdul El-Sayed was asked multiple times by a debate moderator which country he considers a bigger threat to the US: Iran or Israel? Each time, he parried.
“That’s a ridiculous hypothetical because here’s what’s happening right now: Our ostensible ally in Israel has lobbied us to go to war with Iran. I don’t consider an ally a country that takes us to wars we don’t need to fight, and I don’t want to be fighting wars we don’t need to fight,” he said, describing both as “kind of dangerous.”
The canard that Israel is responsible for America’s decision to attack Iran has surfaced so often since the start of the war on February 28 that it is regularly stated as fact. It reminds one of the words commonly attributed to Joseph Goebbels, the propaganda minister of Nazi Germany, though there is no evidence he ever actually said or wrote those exact words.
'Illusion of truth effect'
While the formulation is a paraphrase rather than a direct historical citation, psychologists study this concept as the “illusion of truth effect,” which shows that people are more likely to believe information is true simply because they have heard it before.
The fact is that Israel has urged every American president for the last 40-plus years to take the Iranian nuclear threat seriously and do something about it. No US president prior to the current one has ever chosen to authorize military action against Iran to neutralize their nuclear capability.
However, it was the current US president who chose to invite Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu to the White House briefing room to hear his pitch, but it was US President Donald Trump who decided to launch military action against Iran.
Regardless of how it turns out, it is a canard to blame Israel for taking the US to war against Iran, even if the Netanyahu government was in favor of such action.
However, a canard can be manipulated for other purposes as well. Last week, a decision was made by the Nobel Prize Committee to award this year’s peace prize to South African Jurist Navanethem “Navi” Pillay. Among other anti-Israel positions in her history, she is famous for believing the canard that Israel has committed genocide in Gaza.
While she has done worthwhile work in helping advance a more comprehensive international legal order and, as the Committee noted, “played a central role in ensuring that issues such as war crimes, crimes against humanity, and genocide are brought to justice,” her activities regarding the supposed genocide by Israel in Gaza dramatically tarnish her reputation.
Elisha Wiesel, in an op-ed in The Free Press, wrote: “My father, Elie Wiesel, received the Nobel Peace Prize for ensuring the Holocaust wouldn’t be forgotten. By honoring Navi Pillay, who accused Israel of genocide, the committee has betrayed his legacy.”
Yet the canard is that Israel, which vaccinated over one million residents of Gaza against polio, enabled millions of kilograms of food to enter the strip during the war (most of which was stolen by Hamas and then resold at inflated prices), put its own troops at risk by having them enter buildings to ensure only combatants were attacked, not civilians, and notified the Gazan population of every significant military operation to come with instructions for moving to safer zones, is somehow guilty of genocide.
A truthful look at the facts will show that it is actually Hamas that was engaged in genocide against Israel given their attack on October 7, intent on killing as many Jews as possible. This, in keeping with their original 1988 founding charter explicitly calling for the killing of Jews, which draws on religious texts to justify violence against Jewish people globally.
While a revised document released in 2017 removed this specific language, Hamas did not formally revoke or repudiate the original charter. Organizations like Genocide Watch and various genocide scholars have stated that Hamas’s October 7, 2023, attacks against Israeli civilians and statements by its leadership reflected genocidal intent and acts.
Yet the canard that Israel is guilty of genocide continues, with large portions of the world’s diplomatic corps agreeing with or remaining silent about this blatant misstatement of facts.
Former US president John F Kennedy said: “The great enemy of the truth is very often not the lie, deliberate, contrived, and dishonest, but the myth, persistent, persuasive, and unrealistic.”
When it comes to Israel, the world too easily accepts the myth rather than seek the truth. Our job, the job for all of us, is to shatter the prism that enables the myths to fester and do so at every opportunity. That is our obligation as a community.
The writer, a 42-year resident of Jerusalem, is a former national president of the Association of Americans and Canadians in Israel, a past chairperson of the board of the Pardes Institute of Jewish Studies, and a Board Member of the Israel-America Chamber of Commerce (AMCHAM).

The aliyah plan focuses on support for olim by calling to cut bureaucracy and help them find homes and jobs, while it calls to ensure they find their place as “integral members of Israeli society.”
Some aspects of the plan include reducing bureaucracy by creating a single office for every new immigrant to attend to receive benefits and services, rather than needing to deal with many different agencies.
The plan also demands streamlining the recognition of foreign higher education accreditation to make it easier for olim to work within their professions.
Bennett added that another aim of the B’Yachad plan is to expand support for young olim by easing their transition into education, the workforce, and Israeli society as a whole, thus reducing the rate of departures.
B’Yachad said it would work to “bring home the over 250,000 Israelis who have left the country in recent years.”
The party said additionally that it would work to strengthen support for lone soldiers, giving them increased benefits and advance living stipends for discharged lone soldiers who require them.
B’Yachad also called to work toward helping older citizens by advancing expanded employment, volunteering, and recreational opportunities to help combat loneliness among the senior population.
Bennett’s party called for Israel to be a “Jewish, democratic, liberal, and prosperous country that offers a promising future for both their careers and families.”

How partisan hatred shapes American views of the Black Lives Matter protests and January 6
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
18:00:51 UTC
03:00:51 KST

Americans interpret major political events through a deeply polarized lens, where hostility toward the opposing political party shapes whether they view protests as legitimate or dangerous. A new study published in Political Research Quarterly reveals that this divide is driven not just by party labels, but by intense dislike of political opponents, loyalty to specific party factions, and differing beliefs about what threatens democracy.
The research was conducted by Rongbo Jin at The Chinese University of Hong Kong, Shenzhen, and Spencer Lindsay at the University of Arizona. They set out to investigate how preexisting political attitudes structure the way Americans evaluate two highly contentious events in recent history. Specifically, they looked at the 2020 Black Lives Matter protests and the January 6 attack on the United States Capitol.
The researchers emphasize that comparing public reactions to these two events does not mean the events are morally or qualitatively equivalent. One was a decentralized protest movement seeking racial equality, while the other was a violent attempt to halt the certification of a presidential election. Instead, the comparison serves to illustrate how the American public cognitively processes moments of intense political conflict.
In modern American politics, identifying with a political party is a deeply held social identity. This dynamic has led to a rise in affective polarization, a term describing the phenomenon where Democrats and Republicans not only disagree on policy but actively distrust and dislike each other.
People rarely analyze political information like objective scientists. Instead, they rely on mental shortcuts called heuristics to quickly judge new information. This reliance feeds into motivated reasoning, a psychological process where people readily accept information that flatters their political group while finding reasons to reject facts that make their side look bad.
These cognitive shortcuts are heavily influenced by a person’s core values. The researchers point out that Republicans often prioritize social order and conformity, meaning they might view protests that disrupt the social order as inherently threatening. Democrats, on the other hand, tend to place a higher value on individual rights and inclusion, meaning they are more likely to view protests by marginalized groups as a necessary democratic function.
To understand how these psychological forces shaped views of the recent protests and riots, the researchers first analyzed an original survey of 1,000 adult participants. Conducted in late 2023, the survey asked respondents to evaluate the Black Lives Matter protests and the January 6 event on several dimensions, such as whether they were legal, empowering, or dangerous.
The researchers measured affective polarization by asking respondents to rate their feelings toward both major political parties on a scale from zero to one hundred, with zero being the coldest possible feeling. They also asked participants to place themselves within party factions, such as identifying as a MAGA Republican or a progressive Democrat.
The survey results demonstrated severe partisan splits, with Democrats viewing the Black Lives Matter protests favorably and January 6 negatively, while Republicans exhibited the opposite pattern. Affective polarization amplified these views, as participants who expressed the coldest feelings toward the opposing party held the most extreme evaluations of both events.
The researchers even looked at pure independents, individuals who do not formally align with either party. They found that independents who simply expressed warmer feelings toward the Democratic Party still viewed the Black Lives Matter protests more favorably. This suggests that emotional attachments shape political views even in the absence of a strict party label.
Differences also emerged within the parties themselves. Progressive Democrats evaluated the Black Lives Matter protests much more positively than establishment Democrats. On the political right, MAGA Republicans viewed January 6 much more positively and the Black Lives Matter protests much more negatively than establishment Republicans.
The survey also asked whether participants believed American democracy was currently under threat. Both Democrats and Republicans who perceived a high threat to democracy held more polarized views of these events, but they did so in opposite directions.
For Democrats, believing democracy was threatened was linked to supporting the Black Lives Matter protests and condemning January 6. For Republicans, perceiving a threat to democracy was linked to condemning the Black Lives Matter protests and viewing January 6 more favorably.
The researchers describe this as a “saving democracy” frame. When citizens believe the political system is in danger, they use that belief to justify their evaluations of controversial political actions. Depending on a person’s preexisting political loyalties, the exact same event can be interpreted as either a defense of democracy or a direct attack on it.
Next, the researchers examined data from the American National Election Studies, looking at large surveys from 2016, 2020, and 2024. This included panel data, which tracks the exact same individuals over several years to see how their attitudes shift over time. Because this secondary data set did not include questions about January 6, the researchers focused solely on evaluations of the Black Lives Matter movement.
The panel data revealed that as Republicans grew warmer toward the Democratic Party between 2016 and 2020, they also developed warmer feelings toward the Black Lives Matter movement. Conversely, when Democrats grew warmer toward Republicans, they tended to view the movement less favorably.
The researchers suggest this indicates a shift toward more moderate political positions. When individuals soften their stance toward political opponents, they may also moderate their views on highly polarizing social movements associated with the political left.
The authors note that the study relies on observational data, meaning it can only identify associations rather than establish direct cause and effect. It is possible that evaluating these historical events in a certain way actually causes people to dislike the opposing party more, rather than the other way around.
Additionally, participants were asked in 2023 to evaluate events that took place in 2020 and 2021. Their memories and interpretations may have been shaped by years of political messaging and media coverage in the interim.
Future studies might use experimental designs to better understand the exact sequence of how political identity shapes the immediate processing of breaking news. Tracking public reactions in real time could help researchers map how competing narratives take hold before partisan lines fully solidify.
The study, “Inhabiting Different Worlds: How Partisan Attitudes Shape Americans’ Evaluation of the Black Lives Matter Protests and the January 6th Insurrection,” was authored by Rongbo Jin and Spencer Lindsay.

Trump sees equally tough fight for Republicans to retain Senate and House in midterms

Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
18:00:21 UTC
03:00:21 KST

US President Donald Trump has said that Republicans face an equally difficult fight to retain control of the House of Representatives and the Senate in November's midterm elections, despite forecasts showing a considerably tougher contest in the House.
"I would say equal," Trump told reporters on Tuesday at the White House when asked which chamber would be harder for Republicans to defend in the November 3 vote.
Trump acknowledged the historical disadvantage facing the party of a sitting president, although he insisted that enthusiasm among Republican voters was surging.
"When you have a sitting president... no matter how good they seem to be, they're at a big disadvantage, tremendous disadvantage," he said.
"But I'm doing a tour right now, and I'm doing rallies. The level of enthusiasm for the Republican Party is way up."
Trump's assessment was striking because Republicans have been widely seen as particularly vulnerable in the House, while the Senate's electoral map had initially offered them greater hopes of retaining control.
Election forecaster Decision Desk HQ gives Democrats a 77 percent chance of winning the 435-seat House, projecting that they will take 235 seats to the Republicans' 200.
It also narrowly favours Democrats to capture the 100-seat Senate, giving them a 56 percent probability of victory and projecting a 51-49 majority.
Trump on campaign blitz
Losing either chamber on November 3 would complicate Trump's ability to push his agenda through Congress during the final two years of his presidency, while handing Democrats greater power to investigate his administration.
Trump has embarked on a campaign blitz in the closing weeks of the election, including rallies in traditionally Republican states where his party faces unexpectedly competitive Senate races.
History offers little comfort to the president.
The party holding the White House has almost invariably lost seats in midterm elections, with just three exceptions in the House since 1934, according to figures compiled by the American Presidency Project.
Franklin D. Roosevelt's Democrats gained nine House seats in 1934, while Bill Clinton's party picked up four in 1998 and George W. Bush's Republicans gained eight in 2002.
The worst modern midterm drubbing came in 1938, when Roosevelt's Democrats lost 72 House seats, followed by Barack Obama's Democrats losing 63 in 2010.
Trump himself presided over a split verdict in his first midterms in 2018, when Republicans lost 41 House seats but gained two in the Senate.

====================================================================================================

Browse fields is our last great gas reserve, yet report says we don't need it
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
18:00:00 UTC
03:00:00 KST

analysis
Woodside, activists face off again as heat rises in latest Browse gas fields bid
For more than 50 years, it has sat as a prize just beyond the reach of major Australian and international oil and gas players.
The Browse gas fields, off the coast of Western Australia's spectacular, wild Kimberley region, are the biggest untapped gas resource in the country.
Together, they hold almost 14 trillion cubic feet of gas, or enough to meet Victoria's entire demand for seven decades.
They are also, according to the WA government and oil and gas giant Woodside, the only viable way to head off a looming supply crunch.
"If you're not going to do Browse, but you're going to meet that shortfall, where is that shortfall going to come from?" said WA Premier Roger Cook earlier this year.
Arguments in favour of Browse have been heating up once again in the west.
More than a decade after Woodside and its partners walked away from plans to bring the gas onshore, they are mounting what some say is a last-ditch bid to get the project over the line.
Whereas once their plans focused on building a huge plant in the Kimberley to process the gas into a liquid form, or LNG, they are now looking much further afield.
The project partners want to send it to the North West Shelf, an aging LNG facility in the Pilbara, via a colossal 900-kilometre subsea pipeline.
Most of the gas would be shipped off as exports.
But Woodside, its partners and the state are stressing Browse would also be a critical source of domestic gas for a WA economy that runs heavily on the fuel.
Their position is based on a report from the Australian Energy Market Operator (AEMO) that last year warned WA faced a shortfall of domestic gas from 2030.
"Without Browse … there will be no new significant domestic gas to meet the AEMO-forecast shortfall from 2030," a Woodside spokesman told the ABC.
New research, however, seeks to cast doubt on those claims.
Browse need illusory?
The Australasian Centre for Corporate Responsibility (ACCR), an activist shareholder group that lobbies against fossil fuel developments, argues in a new report that WA does not face a gas supply shortage.
The state, it says, is facing an unwillingness by gas producers to supply anything more than the bare minimum to local users.
"We've had a look at the West Australian gas balance," said Alex Hillman, a gas analyst at the ACCR.
"We found that there's enough gas to supply domestic needs as long as we don't export too much of it."
Under a policy introduced 20 years ago, gas projects in WA are supposed to set aside 15 per cent of their reserves for the domestic market.
Hillman, a former carbon analyst at Woodside, says the warnings about a supply deficit are based on a strict interpretation of the market under that policy.
But he says such forecasts ignore the fact that gas exporters could choose to sell more of their supplies to domestic consumers.
That they don't, he says, is a commercial preference that puts a lie to the notion that Browse is essential to keeping gas flowing in WA.
"A lot of the public discourse around Browse and why it could be approved is around a perceived need for Western Australia," he says.
"If that's the key reason this project is going to be built, our analysis shows that … it's not needed."
According to Hillman, a more immediate problem confronting WA is a lack of processing capacity that could turn raw, field gas into something fit for use in the local market.
Beyond that constraint, he says existing projects in the state, including the Gorgon, Wheatstone, and soon, Scarborough, had more than enough gas to meet local needs.
"The 15 per cent reservation policy … it's not a maximum and they actually could choose to provide more gas from their existing projects if they wanted to," Hillman says.
'Not reasonable or practical'
It's an argument that has been given short shrift by Steve Lewis, the director of BrightSource Consulting.
Lewis, a former Woodside marketing agent who has worked in every part of Australia's gas industry, says the ACCR's conclusions ignore practical and commercial realities.
He says LNG ventures are so large and complex that companies only take the risk of developing them if they can sell to more lucrative export markets.
It was just such an arrangement that founded Australia's LNG industry at the North West Shelf 40 years ago, he notes, and it is no different today.
By recent estimates, the cost of developing the Browse project is likely to add up to $50 billion.
"It appears to me the report is saying the government should renegotiate its existing arrangements instead of allowing the market to operate the way that it normally would," Lewis said.
"On that basis I wouldn't agree with the analysis that it's practical or reasonable.
"It's unlikely that a large project such as a Gorgon, Wheatstone or the North West Shelf would ever have been commercially viable on domestic gas sales.
"The [domestic] market is not big enough."
For Lewis, accepting that WA could bank only on the supplies agreed with LNG projects under the state's gas reservation policy means a shortfall is indeed looming.
He acknowledges demand for gas, in WA as in other states, is declining, noting many of his clients in the mining industry are turning towards renewable energy.
But he says the rate of reduction is far slower than the predicted fall in supplies.
"You are starting to see a decline in overall gas demand in WA as part of that commitment to greener energy," he said.
"But there will always be a place for gas in that mix and so there will always be some demand for gas for the foreseeable future."
Crunch coming: Woodside
Woodside would not comment on ACCR's research.
But a spokesman for the company said that, without Browse, the North West Shelf would be wound down and retired.
Loading
As a consequence, he said, the Karratha gas plant, by far WA's biggest domestic gas plant, would also leave the system.
"This risks keeping coal in the system for longer while increasing energy costs for households and businesses," the spokesman said in a statement.
"In Woodside's view, Browse is the most credible large backfill opportunity to fill long-term unused capacity at Karratha Gas Plant because of the quantity and compatibility of the natural gas resource."
A spokesman for Mr Cook said the government had "not been given a copy" of the ACCR's report, but suggested its conclusions were "inconsistent" with the state's advice.
The spokesman said the report "does not acknowledge how investment certainty" was the key to project development.
He said diverting gas that was "technically" available to the local market would "mean tearing up existing export contracts", putting projects, jobs and energy supplies at risk.
"The government will not make any changes that put future investment — and future sources of domestic gas and jobs for Western Australians — at risk," the spokesman said in a statement.
A 'bad, expensive solution'
Hillman says, even if WA were facing a domestic gas shortage, Browse is, in his words, a "poor solution".
He says the project is remote, expensive and "operationally complex, involving six companies that have consistently failed to reach a final investment decision".
On a global comparison, he says, Browse is expected to be "more expensive than 70 per cent of competing gas resources".
What's more, Hillman says, the fields have huge volumes of carbon, even by the standards of oil and gas projects internationally.
And he says plans to offset carbon in the field itself, by storing it underground, would do nothing to deal with the emissions released by burning the gas in Australia or overseas.
"It would capture a bit less than half of the emissions that happen from this project in Australia," Hillman says.
"And that is only a few per cent of the emissions of this project overall, because most of the emissions … will be associated with the gas that's mostly sent overseas."

====================================================================================================

Housing is the great Australian talking point for good reason
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
18:00:00 UTC
03:00:00 KST

analysis
Australia's housing market obsession is fuelled by necessity
Reserve Bank chief economist Sarah Hunter, born in the UK but now an Australian citizen, was asked on a podcast a few weeks ago if she noticed anything quirky about her new country when she moved here.
Her response? Our unbridled obsession with housing:
"Yes, I think there are a number of quirks about the country here, but I think the one that probably strikes most people when they come here and they live here for a while is housing and how much we all talk about housing and the housing market.
"You get a lot about the housing market in British newspapers and on British media too, but it's heightened over here. So that definitely took some getting used to.
"Like the auction clearance rates being reported on a Monday morning. I'd never known anything like that before."
Why are Australians obsessed with property? Because we have to be. And there are big reasons why it's always on our minds.
Why are we obsessed with property?
The main reasons come down to it being our highest cost.
Firstly, Australia's retail banking sector is an "established oligopoly," as the competition regulator says.
It is one of the most concentrated and profitable banking sectors in the world, and it has been for years.
Our banks mostly offer home loan customers short-term loans on variable interest rates, and they face little competitive pressure to do much differently.
Secondly, Australia has a central bank that moves interest rates up and down to control inflation.
Those two things mean millions of Australian households with a mortgage are hostage to frequent changes in their mortgage interest payments.
It's why we all gather around the TV when the RBA governor holds a press conference like we're watching a grand final.
We're waiting impatiently to see what's going to happen to interest rates (again) so we know what major financial adjustments we'll have to make to our household budgets (again) after having another painful family conversation (again).
Do we enjoy living this way?
The RBA often talks about how disruptive high inflation is to people's lives.
But its interest rate movements are extremely disruptive for millions of households with mortgages too, those who are also dealing with the disruption of high inflation, because it can change their household budgets by hundreds of dollars a month.
Other countries do things differently
In other countries, where banks commonly offer 20-year and 30-year home loans on fixed rates, households barely notice when their central banks move rates around.
But that doesn't mean that those countries are less effective at managing inflation.
It just means the burden of higher interest rates is spread across their communities differently.
Last week, the Sydney Morning Herald's economics editor Ross Gittins noted that Australia's strange way of doing things meant that young home owners were hit particularly hard by the way we manage inflation.
"Our use of interest rates to control inflation is yet another respect in which our economic system is biased against the young," he argued.
"In other countries, mortgages tend to charge a fixed rate of interest for the length of the loan. This means that changes in the central bank's official interest rate still flow through to home buyers but take a lot longer to be felt.
"So changes in the official rate don't cause the great stir they do in Oz. But that doesn't mean other countries' use of interest rates to control inflation is any less effective than ours is.
"Even so, this doesn't seem to have prompted our Reserve Bank to have given any thought to encouraging or requiring a move to long-term mortgage rates."
Is housing shelter or an asset?
There are other big reasons why Australians are obsessed with housing.
For decades now there has been a deliberate political effort in Australia to stop people thinking of housing as "shelter" and to start thinking of it as an "asset class".
After we cut trade tariffs, sent our manufacturing industries offshore, floated our dollar, and opened our financial system to foreign competition, property investing was heavily promoted as one of the surest ways to build wealth in Australia.
Voters were encouraged to become property investors and landlords.
It's why property investors also gather around the TV when the RBA governor holds a press conference these days.
It also explains why our media outlets have so many property-related stories, whether about interest rates, property prices, auction clearance rates, high growth areas for rental yields, and more.
In April, the chief executive of AustralianSuper, Paul Schroder, said Australia now spends way too much on housing and "not anywhere near enough" on productive investment.
He said modern Australia operated on a "myth" that we can keep generating wealth by constantly inflating housing prices. The "whole show" was built on housing, Schroder said, and it couldn't continue this way.
And there's another big reason that may be contributing to our national housing obsession.
Housing isn't considered a human right in Australia.
Loading
Since we don't want to lose our homes or rentals, we have to know what interest rates are doing every six weeks, and what rentals are available in which parts of our cities, so we can all keep a roof over our heads.
Nobody wants to become homeless. And we have very few services available to help us if we do.
People's Bank to break the oligopoly
Are we happy with our national housing obsession?
Many Australians would probably prefer not to have to talk about property all the time.
But so many things are linked to housing. If we start talking about schools and the abysmal state of funding for public schools compared to private schools, which leads to discussions about school catchment areas, that often leads back to discussions about housing affordability, house prices, and interest rates.
It's relentless.
Back in 2009, six well-known economists — Dr Nicholas Gruen, Christopher Joye, Professor Joshua Gans, Professor John Quiggin, Professor Stephen King, and Dr Sam Wylie — caused a stir when they asked a question about Australia's economy:
"Is there a role for a publicly-owned entity, akin to KiwiBank in New Zealand, to offer essential services in Australia's finance sector that leverage off unique government infrastructure (e.g., Australia Post, the tax system, and the government bond market)?"
The media described their idea as a "People's Bank", and there was a lot of interest in it.
It clearly tapped into a deep desire, in elements of Australian society, to break free from the banking oligopoly and its links with inflation management.
Australia's media outlets do publish a lot of property-related stories, but there are complicated reasons why.
Despite the desire, the reality is Australians remain largely hostage to the housing market, and until that changes, we'll see many more headlines on the topic since it's so central to our lives.

Greens warn of private school fees loophole in Labor's trust tax
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
18:00:00 UTC
03:00:00 KST

Greens concerned private school fees paid out of trusts could escape Labor's 30pc tax
In short:
The Greens say a "loophole" for private school fees is a sticking point in Labor's proposed trust laws.
Jim Chalmers will introduce legislation for the 30 per cent minimum tax on discretionary trusts on Wednesday, amid stiff business opposition.
What's next?
Labor requires the support of the Greens in the Senate to pass the tax hike, given that the Coalition is opposed.
Parents who pay private school fees from their trust funds could escape Labor's proposed trust tax, in what the Greens say is a "loophole" that must be closed.
Treasurer Jim Chalmers will today unveil a bill to impose the 30 per cent minimum tax on some trusts. The budget proposal has enraged the business lobby and unnerved Labor backbenchers anxious about small business hostility.
The Greens, whose votes are required in the Senate, have the opposite concern. On Tuesday, the party called for a Senate inquiry into the bill, saying an early draft was "watered down" and the proposal would not get a "free pass".
The ABC can reveal the Greens' main concern is an exemption for money paid from trusts to charities, non-profits and other tax-exempt entities, including private schools.
"People who are wealthy enough to set up trusts should not get a tax break to pay for private school fees when this option is denied to people who can't afford expensive accountants," Greens economic spokesperson Nick McKim told the ABC.
"The treasurer needs to knock this out of the legislation."
In a draft proposal last month, the government indicated it would cap the amount of exempt money each year, but that cap has not yet been set.
The proposal does not change the tax treatment of private schools, since this avenue already exists. But by carving charitable payments out from the new higher rate of tax, the Greens will argue this makes the avenue more attractive.
"There is far too much leniency," Senator McKim said. "Labor is just trying to funnel ever-increasing revenues into the private education system when public schools are being starved of funds."
Chalmers beleaguered on two fronts
Mr Chalmers says the proposal is a crackdown on those who use trust funds as a vehicle to reduce their tax bills.
The 30 per cent minimum tax applies only to so-called "discretionary" trusts, a term the tax office uses to identify trust structures that give their owners the flexibility to shift their money into the names of family members, holding companies, or others.
Tax experts say these complicated structures allow a minority of very wealthy, highly motivated people to achieve dramatic reductions in the tax they pay. The government expects to raise $4.5 billion from the tax in its first year of operation.
But business lobbies and the opposition have argued discretionary trusts are used for a range of legitimate purposes, including by small business owners.
The government has outlined several exemptions, including for family farms that are placed within trusts, charities that operate as trusts, and trusts that are set up to manage deceased estates.
But Andrew McKellar, chief executive of the Australian Chamber of Commerce and Industry, said the tax still sent "the wrong message" and targeted business unfairly.
"We urge all members of parliament to … listen to the views of those small businesses who will be affected: small and medium-sized home builders, family pharmacies, newsagents, small retailers, restaurants and cafes," he said on Tuesday.
The government estimates that 350,000 active small businesses — roughly one in six — used discretionary trusts in 2022-23, the last year of available data. Treasury analysis suggests 140,000 of those would not need to pay the new tax.
Others will get government assistance to restructure their affairs, although there remains concern that those who restructure their businesses as companies would have to pay state and territory stamp duties in the process.
The concerns have been echoed by some Labor backbenchers, with several questions put to Mr Chalmers about the bill's consequences in a Tuesday Labor caucus meeting.
Summarising the angst, one Labor backbencher told the ABC they were "not happy about these compounding attacks on small business".
From little holes, big holes grow
The government is wary about business hostility and has added further exemptions since May to address its concerns. The exemption for trust money given to charities, schools and sports clubs was one such concession.
But Dale Boccabella, an associate professor of accounting and tax at the University of New South Wales, warned that every concession risked creating unintended loopholes, especially given trust laws are notoriously complex.
"The reality is that a small minority of downtown lawyers and accountants sniff a little opening and they will make it into a big opening. That's the way it is. Whether we like it or not, that's the history in this area."
Mr Boccabella said it was possible the law could be drafted with so-called "integrity provisions" to stamp out payments such as school fees if the parliament considers that they are not in the spirit of the law, adding that the Greens' concern was worth probing.
"I know why people would be concerned. We've got a long history in Australia, going back to the 1970s, where people were making donations to church-run schools, and it was well known that the quid pro quo was a reduction in your school fees," he said.
The High Court has tried to clamp down on that practice in the past, ruling that "gifts" to charities for tax purposes cannot come with strings attached. But even where these precedents exist, Mr Boccabella said enforcing them was a challenge for the ATO.
"It's great having a rule, but you've got to enforce it on a case-by-case basis, and the ATO doesn't have the resources to administer even our current rules for trusts on a meaningful scale. They just cannot do it," he said.
Mr Boccabella said his biggest concern with the draft laws was that people who choose to restructure from a trust into a company could still achieve much of the same discretion and could still substantially reduce their tax.
"I think there's a case to be really blunt and really prescriptive … People exploit any break in the system, and the history tells us that this will get exploited," he said.

Far-right and Iran add to mix of terror threats UK faces – not to mention AI
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
17:58:40 UTC
02:58:40 KST

MI5’s annual threat update covers so much ground it is easy to feel anxious. The terror threat has become more diverse, with far-right anti-migrant threats on the rise; while Iran has now firmly emerged alongside Russia as a country seeking to undertake violent and deadly plots in the UK.
“There is no law of physics dictating that rising state threats will be accompanied by diminishing terrorist threats,” MI5’s director general, Ken McCallum, said, although one of his core messages was that people and the country at large needed to focus on being more resilient. “In this new world, we should expect to be tested.”
A key issue highlighted by McCallum was that years of anti-migrant, anti-Muslim hostility had now led to an increase in cases where people were “tipping into terrorist intent” – that is crossing the line from rhetoric to violence. It is a complex area, but one certainly fuelled by political hate narratives and online subcultures.
It is also fuelled by toxic rhetoric from abroad. Authoritarian regimes, McCallum said, were investing heavily “in trying to distort and divide our society” – although he was too polite to mention that there is plenty of evidence that voices from the US led by X owner Elon Musk are keen to sow division in the UK too, as they post about flashpoint events such as the June rioting in Belfast and Southampton.
A second trend is that seemingly far-off conflicts, such as the wars the UK did not start in Ukraine or Iran, have a habit of rippling back home.
It is less than eight months since the US and Israel attacked Iran, subsequently with a little help from Britain, but already Iran is trying to direct terror plots in the UK.
Both MI5 and the counter-terror police may have to do a little better to explain precisely what five men from London were doing in a village next to RAF Fairford in three white vans shortly after midnight on 27 September, given that nothing of significance was found in the vans and nobody has been charged.
But McCallum warned that Iran had “ambitions to come at harder targets, like military sites” – a likely reference to Fairford. That came a day after the British prime minister, Andy Burnham, said Iran’s Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) was “almost certainly” behind the episode. It would be surprising if both were wrong.
That is not the only possible example. At the beginning of October, two Iranians from Liverpool and Salford were charged, accused of trying to make a chlorine powder bomb to target Jewish sites in Manchester. Prosecutors alleged they were directed by a third party, believed to be in Iran. The two have not yet pleaded to the charges; a trial at the Old Bailey is scheduled.
Yet, if these fast-emerging threats were not enough, the normally sober McCallum decided to reference AI.
He warned that AI could refine terror plots, supercharge hackers, produce individually targeted propaganda – and even help develop a novel bioweapon. This, he added, with emphasis, was a subject on which they were “particularly focused”, as if it was episode one of a TV thriller.
While concerns were recently raised about scientists who have used AI to design viruses, as Anthropic warned of five examples of scientists who had used Claude for researching novel pathogens, both instances provoked a scientific debate as to what is actually possible. And what McCallum did not mention was that AI is also an extraordinary and potentially intrusive tool for MI5 to seek out threats.
There is already enough for the intelligence agencies to think about, as the MI5 review makes clear: a country made more dangerous by blowback from strongmen starting what they think will be short wars; a rising tide of hatred that may start online but is morphing into violent intent in real life; a complex cocktail of external and internal threats that could have real-life consequences.
As McCallum himself recognised: “The protection of democracy – its institutions, its representatives, its principles – has never felt more vital.”

Who is behind ‘Black Rus,’ the mysterious group claiming responsibility for an armed incursion into Latvia from Belarus?
A group calling itself “Black Rus” (Chyornye Rusy) has claimed responsibility for an incident on the Latvia-Belarus border in which armed, masked men threatened Latvian soldiers overnight on October 6.
The men, who were accompanying a group of migrants, later crossed from Belarus into Latvia, damaged an electrical distribution panel, stole surveillance cameras, and returned to Belarus.
LSM reported on October 12 that a video statement on the group’s behalf had been posted on a Telegram channel. In it, a man with his face covered and his voice altered says:
This was just a test, and Latvia failed it. Soon you’ll see something similar elsewhere along our border. The European Union and NATO are a colossus with feet of clay that will collapse after our first strike.
Experts interviewed by Latvian journalists called Black Rus “a project of the intelligence services.” Among other things, they said such a group could not exist in either Russia or Belarus without the authorities’ knowledge.
Belarusian leader Alexander Lukashenko said Latvia itself had orchestrated the border incident to “get money from the European Union.” He said the Belarusian authorities had nothing to do with it.
“Operations like this, involving entry into a neighboring country, are impossible without the president’s approval. Nothing like this was cleared with me. That means no such operations took place. I know that for a fact,” Lukashenko said, according to Belarus’ state news agency BelTA.
Latvia and other European countries bordering Belarus have repeatedly blamed Minsk for the migration crisis. They believe the Belarusian authorities are behind attempts by groups of migrants to cross the border illegally and enter the EU. Minsk denies this.
Latvian Interior Minister Janis Dombrava said about 12,000 people attempting to cross illegally from Belarus had been prevented from entering Latvia since the start of 2026 under Operation Werewolf (Vilkatis). He also said several incidents involving damage to surveillance equipment on the Latvian side of the border had been recorded, Delfi reported. Dombrava suggested that Russian or Belarusian intelligence services were responsible but emphasized that this was only a theory and that there was no evidence yet.

Kyiv came under missile attack shortly after 10 p.m. local time on Oct. 12, with powerful explosions reported before an air raid alert was issued in the Ukrainian capital, according to Kyiv Independent journalists on the ground.
Kyiv Independent staff reported powerful blasts in central Kyiv, with air raid sirens and mobile notifications sounding only afterward.

French Navy intercepts Russian shadow fleet tanker in Indian Ocean
The French Navy intercepted and boarded a tanker suspected of flying under a false flag as part of Russia's shadow fleet on Oct. 12, French President Emmanuel Macron announced.
The tanker, DF Peak, was allegedly transporting sanctioned Russian fuel and was halted by the French Navy 450 nautical miles (833 kilometers) south of the French territory of Reunion in the Indian Ocean.
"France is determined to combat the ghost fleet, wherever it may be in the world," Macron wrote on X. "This action, carried out in accordance with international maritime law, demonstrates our determination to uphold the rule of law and combat all illicit trafficking, wherever it occurs."
The tanker DF Peak, previously named Kaliningrad, has falsely sailed under the flag of Benin, according to the Ukrainian Defense Intelligence's War and Sanctions portal. The crude oil tanker is sanctioned by the U.S, EU, Switzerland, Canada, and Japan.
The vessel is currently under escort by the French Navy, France's Armed Forces Minister Catherine Vautrin said on X.
"International law is not optional," wrote Vautrin. "Our armed forces are fully mobilized to enforce it and combat illicit activities at sea."
Russian state media TASS said the Russian embassy in Paris told them that "France is violating international law by detaining merchant vessels on the high seas and is attempting to cover up piracy by invoking the provisions of the UN Convention."
The DF Peak is just one tanker of Russia's "shadow fleet" — a group of aging, poorly insured tankers used by Moscow to ship out its oil in violation of international sanctions. Western governments have also accused Moscow of using the fleet to support its hybrid war against Europe.

Photos: French protests over school conditions swell
Mass rallies continue across France backing high school protests, piling pressure on President Emmanuel Macron.
Tens of thousands of people have joined rallies across France in support of protesting high school students, boosting a movement that is posing a major challenge to President Emmanuel Macron as his term in office winds down.
Some 161,500 people turned out on Tuesday according to the Interior Ministry, more than double the 71,500 it reported for Thursday’s nationwide demonstrations.

The student movement sprang up last month, with students blocking the entrances to many schools to demand better classroom conditions.
What many see as a heavy-handed police response to the students prompted more people to join Tuesday’s demonstrations.
Police have opened investigations into 34 allegations of violence against demonstrators.
Some 147 teaching staff have been injured in the protests, the Education Ministry said.
On Monday, Macron urged restraint from protesters, saying the issues “deserve time, consultations, discussion and respect”.

From no cards to many: Europe warns Trump not to waste Ukraine’s leverage
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
17:56:33 UTC
02:56:33 KST

Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky (L) and Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha (R) listen to US President Donald Trump address the 81st United Nations General Assembly at United Nations headquarters in New York, USA on September 22, 2026. | Angela Weiss/AFP via Getty Images
WARSAW — Ukraine has more leverage than a year ago — and European leaders warn Donald Trump not to squander it by pressuring Kyiv to ease up on Russia.
"In less than two years we went from the stage of no cards to the stage of don't play your cards," Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha told an audience at the Warsaw Security Conference. "That's a true achievement."
Last year, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy was ambushed in the Oval Office by Trump, who ridiculed him for having "no cards" to play against Russia.
Advertisement
Trump’s recent demand that Zelenskyy “better damn well stop” Ukraine’s refinery attacks, and his call for Ukraine to install a new leader, amount to a recognition that Kyiv does indeed have significant leverage in the fight.
Kyiv’s refinery campaign is helping create a growing fuel shortage across Russia and is also harming the Kremlin's ability to finance the war. But European leaders fear that Trump's desperation to lower fuel prices ahead of next month's U.S. midterm elections by pressuring Kyiv to stop its attacks could weaken Ukraine’s hand without persuading Russia to end the war.
Sybiha’s comments drew loud applause at the Warsaw conference and underscored growing tensions among Kyiv, Washington and Ukraine's European allies after Trump said the U.S. had agreed with Vladimir Putin to buy Russian diesel.
The dispute between Washington and Kyiv overshadowed a Warsaw event that is normally strongly pro-American, given Poland's status as a key U.S. ally.
"Ministers and heads of state won’t say so outright what they think about the Americans, but they certainly think a lot of things — the negotiations with Putin are yet another stab in the back for the Ukrainians," said a French lawmaker, speaking on condition of being granted anonymity.
"You end the war by persuading the aggressor to limit his level of ambition, not by asking the victim to capitulate," said Polish Foreign Minister Radosław Sikorski.
Advertisement
His German counterpart Johann Wadephul underlined that Berlin is pushing the Trump administration to fully impose energy sanctions approved by the U.S. Congress.
On Sep. 18, Trump signed the Lindsey O. Graham Russia and Iran Sanctions Act of 2026, codifying existing US sanctions against Russia and expanding the scope for applying secondary sanctions, tariffs and restrictions, including against the energy sector.
"This is not the time to lower the sanctions regime, but to strengthen it," Wadephul said.
U.K. Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband echoed that call, saying Trump should exert pressure on Russia to agree to an energy ceasefire under which both warring nations would stop hitting each other's oil, gas, electricity and other assets.
Russia has so far refused to take such a step.
"Let us take seriously this issue of the energy ceasefire that President Trump has talked about, not simply a refinery ceasefire but a broad energy ceasefire, because in the last week alone we've seen 200 Russian attacks on Ukrainian energy infrastructure," Miliband said.
Advertisement
Trump pressures Ukraine
The U.S. president said on Monday that Putin is keener to end the fighting than Zelenskyy — despite the Kremlin not agreeing to any ceasefire.
"I think actually Putin wants to make a deal more than Zelenskyy," Trump said.
Since Trump announced an energy ceasefire — blindsiding both Kyiv and Moscow — Ukraine has paused bombing Russian refineries even as Russian attacks continue.
While Trump wants the attacks to stop, Ukraine's European allies are keen to cripple Russia's war effort.
"Ukraine is attacking refineries, which is having an effect, and data centers, which is also having an effect," Sikorski said. He also called on Poland's MAGA-aligned President Karol Nawrocki to use his influence with Trump "to explain to him that Putin is the aggressor and Zelenskyy is the victim of aggression."
Wadephul added that he had talked to Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov during the U.N. General Assembly in New York last month, and saw no interest from him in ending the war.
Advertisement
"A lot of people in Europe and especially in Germany were asking us and me, 'Why don't you talk to the Russians?' So now I had that conversation, and you saw the result," he said. "It's a very dire result. And it shows that Russia right now is not ready for ceasefire."
During the same Warsaw event, Sybiha was forced to deny rumors that Washington may have stopped sharing intelligence with Kyiv in retaliation for its campaign of deep strikes against Russian oil refineries.
"You are asking me if we are getting intelligence data from the American side. Yes, we continue this cooperation," he said.
Concerns about a potential cut-off in U.S. intelligence grew on Tuesday after Ukraine's threat detection system failed to detect ballistic missiles that battered Kyiv overnight. Sybiha said the failure was due to a "special type of weaponry which was used by the Russian side."
Zelenskyy also underlined the need for continued intelligence sharing. "There was also a rather treacherous ballistic missile strike on Kyiv — five missiles that hit civilian infrastructure. Unfortunately, there was no warning from our partners regarding this strike. Intelligence on Russian ballistic missile launches helps save lives."
Sybiha stressed that Kyiv needs to continue strengthening its ability to fend off Russia's constant air attacks while Ukraine's troops push back against Russian forces on the front lines.

François Picard is pleased to welcome Alban Guyomarc'h, Researcher in Space Geopolitics at Paris's École Normale Supérieure School of Higher Learning. As a new era of space rivalry unfolds, the International Space Station remains one of the last bastions of cooperation between geopolitical adversaries. For Guyomarc'h, the latest ISS mission is more than a remarkable technological achievement. "It's one of the rare collaboration spaces we still have today in a very conflictual era".
