Guyomarc'h examines the emotional experience of returning from orbit, the geopolitical implications of the ISS's planned retirement, and the intensifying competition to establish a permanent presence on the Moon. From nuclear-powered lunar infrastructure to the growing strategic importance of space, his analysis reveals a central paradox: as humanity acquires unprecedented capabilities to explore beyond Earth, the political foundations of cooperation in space appear increasingly fragile.

EU advances Ukraine accession as Hungary lifts veto, paving way for Zelenskyy-Magyar meeting
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
17:51:14 UTC
02:51:14 KST

EU governments agreed to open two additional accession clusters with Ukraine after Hungary dropped its veto following an agreement on the rights of the ethnic Hungarian minority. Zelenskyy and Magyar may meet in Brussels later this week.
The EU Council has agreed to open two additional accession clusters with Ukraine after Hungary lifted its veto, bringing the total number of opened clusters to four out of six.
The decision follows an agreement on the rights of Hungary’s ethnic minority in Ukraine, a long-standing demand from Budapest.
The breakthrough, alongside the opening of two additional accession clusters, could pave the way for a first bilateral meeting between Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy and Hungarian Prime Minister Péter Magyar in Brussels this week, potentially marking a turning point in relations between the two neighbouring countries.
Hungarian and Ukrainian diplomats are working to arrange the meeting, which could take place on the sidelines of the EU summit, sources told Euronews. However, no date has been set and the meeting has yet to be officially confirmed.
Magyar also raised the possibility of meeting Zelenskyy in a media interview last weekend.
Hungary has criticised Ukraine’s education and language laws since they were adopted in 2015 and 2017, respectively, as those restricted the use of minority languages in schools. The dispute triggered repeated diplomatic tensions, with Budapest under Viktor Orbán blocking Ukraine’s EU accession progress.
Since Magyar’s election victory in April, the new Hungarian government has taken a more pragmatic approach, seeking concrete guarantees for the Hungarian minority while signalling its willingness to let Ukraine’s European integration move forward.
Budapest agreed in June to open the first two accession clusters but made further progress conditional on Kyiv strengthening legal protections for Ukraine’s ethnic Hungarian minority.
Following talks with Hungarian Foreign Minister Anita Orbán in Luxembourg on Monday, Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said the two sides had agreed on the next steps and welcomed progress in implementing their bilateral commitments.
What changes under the new minority law?
One of the key provisions establishes a special legal status for schools where more than half of pupils are taught in a minority language that is also an official EU language. Schools that qualified for this status when the law entered into force can retain it as long as at least 20% of their pupils continue to study in that language.
The law also expands the use of eligible minority languages in school activities and communication, and adds safeguards for native-language education when schools are reorganised or closed.
Pupils taught in eligible minority or indigenous languages will also be able to request translated questions in external examinations, except in language and literature subjects.
Crucially for Kyiv, Ukrainian remains the language of state education. The new provisions strengthen minority-language education without reversing Ukraine’s broader policy of promoting the state language.
The changes build on reforms introduced in 2023, extending protections to minorities whose languages are official languages of the EU. Russian remains outside the scope of the new safeguards.
Beyond the accession talks
Opening the next two clusters is another step in Ukraine’s lengthy accession process, but it does not guarantee membership. Kyiv must still complete extensive reforms, and closing each cluster requires unanimous agreement among EU member states.
Even though Hungary’s objections appear to have been resolved, other EU countries could still obstruct progress.
Agriculture is expected to be one of the most contentious issues in Ukraine’s accession negotiations. Some member states fear that integrating Ukraine’s large agricultural sector into the EU’s Common Agricultural Policy could put pressure on European farmers, subsidies and market competition.
For now, the agreement between Kyiv and Budapest is a significant diplomatic achievement and ends a long-running feud between the two neighbours.

The BASE baseload electricity price index on the Day-Ahead Market (DAM) for the first 10 days of October 2026 stood at UAH 4,197.36 per MWh, 27% below the price for the same period in September (UAH 5,748.97 per MWh).
Thus, according to data from JSC Market Operator, the indicator continued its sharp downward trend for the second consecutive month, as the BASE index fell by 22.1% in the first 10 days of September compared with the same period in August.
Meanwhile, the weighted average electricity trading price on the DAM during the first 10 days of October was recorded at UAH 4,502.75 per MWh, down 21.1% from the first 10 days of the previous month (UAH 5,705.94 per MWh).
At the same time, on the Intraday Market (IDM), the weighted average price of electricity accepted for trading during the first 10 days of October was UAH 3,956.13 per MWh, 37% below the weighted average price recorded in the first 10 days of September, at UAH 6,277.75 per MWh.
"Electricity trading volume on the DAM for the first 10 days of October 2026 totaled 560,723.50 MWh, while 84,472.90 MWh was accepted for trading on the IDM," Market Operator reported.
Compared with the first 10 days of September 2026, trading volumes declined in the first 10 days of October by 26.71% on the DAM and by 24.63% on the IDM.
At the same time, according to former Ukrainian Energy Minister Olha Buslavets, electricity prices at Ukraine's western border increased by an average of 28% on weekdays last week compared with the previous week's figures.
The largest increase was recorded in Hungary, where the average price reached EUR 230 per MWh, 42% above the weekly figure. In other countries, weekday baseload prices ranged from EUR 139 per MWh in Poland to EUR 225 per MWh in Romania.
According to ENTSO-E, during the first 10 days of October, as well as in September and August, Ukraine did not rank first in terms of the highest daily average BASE price index on the DAM when compared with 26 European countries.
Moreover, on October 8, Ukraine recorded the lowest DAM price in Europe.
At the same time, Ukraine topped the European BASE index rankings once in July this year, three times in June, four times in May, 11 times in April, 15 times in March, 21 times in February and 14 times in January.
As reported, the BASE index on the DAM for the first 10 days of September 2026 stood at UAH 5,748.97 per MWh, 22.1% below the price for the same period in August (UAH 7,377.22 per MWh).
Based on its 2025 BASE index on the DAM, calculated using a unified Central European Time (CET) basis, Ukraine ranked second among 27 European countries, with an index of UAH 5,292.62 per MWh.

Iran focused on attacking "harder targets," U.K. spy chief warns
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
17:46:02 UTC
02:46:02 KST

Iran shifts focus to "harder targets, like military sites" with mounting sabotage attacks, U.K. spy chief warns
London — Iran has made a "major shift" in its efforts to attack the United Kingdom, including going after harder targets such as military bases, the head of Britain's domestic spy agency MI5 warned Tuesday.
In his annual threat update at MI5 headquarters in London, Sir Ken McCallum outlined the growing challenges facing the country, from hostile foreign governments and terrorism to the potential misuse of AI. Iran, he said, has demonstrated that it is "keen on subcontracting its U.K. violence … using criminal proxies to try to intimidate oppositionists, Iranian media organizations, and Israeli sites."
"Sadly, much of this aggression has been aimed at British Jewish communities, with whom I want to express solidarity," he said.
"The other major shift this year has been Iranian ambitions to come at harder targets, like military sites," he added.
All of these alleged activities led to more than 50 Iran-linked arrests in the U.K. over the past year alone, McCallum said.
His comments come after a series of arson and sabotage incidents targeting Jewish communities and other sites in the U.K. and across Europe, which McCallum described as "sickening acts."
He declined to provide details about the military installations targeted, including the alleged plot against the U.K. air base RAF Fairford that was thwarted in late September, citing "ongoing investigations."
The U.S. moved all of its long-range bombers off the base in the wake of the incident.
U.K. Prime Minister Andy Burnham said Monday that the incident near the base, which was used by U.S. bombers to target Iran, was "almost certainly" directed by Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps.
But as McCallum noted Tuesday with his reference to "subcontracting" and "criminal proxies," not all of Iran's suspected nefarious activities are easy to attribute to the regime in Tehran.
"Knowingly or unknowingly" working for Iran?
Britain's counterterrorism police unit said it was possible that the RAF Fairford incident "may be activity committed by proxies, or individuals either knowingly or unknowingly, working on behalf of a foreign state."
Iran, like Russia, has been accused repeatedly of using individuals who may be unaware they are even working for a foreign state to conduct sabotage attacks across Western Europe.
The Iran-aligned group Harakat Ashab al-Yamin al-Islamia — or The Islamic Movement of the Companions of the Righteous (IMCR) — claimed responsibility for a string of incidents earlier this year, including attacks on synagogues in the Netherlands and Belgium, and multiple attacks on north London's Jewish community.
A representative for the group told CBS News in March that it would "keep threatening U.S. and Israeli interests worldwide until we've avenged every child in Gaza, Iran, Lebanon, and the resistance nations," and it urged people "to stay away from Zionist and American interests."
Russia is "aggressor number one"
In his wide-ranging address, McCallum said the number of state-threat cases being handled by MI5 had quadrupled over the past decade.
"Since I started in this role in 2020, there has been another generational shift. We have again entered a new era of national security – requiring a new response," he said.
MI5 is devoting more resources to countering state threats in 2026 than it did during the Cold War, he said, highlighting the scale of the challenge posed by hostile foreign actors, and he said among those actors, Russia remains "aggressor number one."
McCallum said Moscow has escalated its attempts to wage "hybrid warfare" against Britain and its allies. That can include a wide range of cyberattacks, sabotage and other hostile activities that fall short of conventional military action, he said.
The intelligence chief suggested Russia's increasingly aggressive approach was linked to its difficulties on the battlefield in Ukraine, arguing that Moscow was seeking to unsettle other European countries "at a time when its military progress in Ukraine remained limited and came at a high cost."
He acknowledged longstanding conventional threats still exist, but were being "sort of well managed by military or other colleagues," while Russia, Iran "and others are seeking to do things beneath the level of conventional armed conflict."
Artificial Intelligence
Artificial intelligence was also a central theme of McCallum's address. He warned of the technology's rapid development amid the equally rapid changes in the security landscape, crediting AI with "supercharging the cybersecurity contest between attackers and defenders."
He said AI could be used to generate propaganda and radicalization material tailored to individuals, potentially making it easier for hostile actors to manipulate people and spread extremist ideologies.
Among the greatest concerns McCallum voiced was the possibility that AI could help people make existing biological weapons more dangerous, or help malicious actors develop entirely new ones.

The EU has officially opened two clusters in the negotiations on Ukraine's accession
Kyiv • UNN
The EU and Ukraine have begun negotiations on the internal market and competitiveness clusters. This continues Ukraine's accession process to the EU.
The European Union has officially opened clusters 2 and 3 in the negotiations on Ukraine’s accession to the EU. This was reported by the EU press service, according to UNN.
Details
Today, the EU and Ukraine took another important step in the accession process by launching negotiations on the so-called "Internal Market" and "Competitiveness and Inclusive Growth" clusters.
The "Internal Market" cluster covers EU policies related to the free movement of goods, services, workers and capital, as well as common rules on competition, financial services, company law and consumer protection.
The "Competitiveness and Inclusive Growth" cluster covers EU policies related to economic competitiveness and growth, including taxation, economic and monetary policy, industry, digital transformation, employment, education, research and customs.
"Today we reached another important milestone on Ukraine’s path to EU membership. The Irish Presidency is committed to advancing Ukraine’s EU accession process. Today’s decision demonstrates Ukraine’s resilience and determination to move forward with reforms amid exceptionally difficult circumstances," said Ireland’s Minister of State for European Affairs Thomas Byrne.
The EU added that today’s decision followed the opening of negotiations on the External Relations cluster in July 2026.

Spain's royals visit Ceuta enclave amid friction with Morocco after border surge
CEUTA, Spain, Oct 13 - Spain's King Felipe and Queen Letizia visited Ceuta's Muslim cemetery on Tuesday where most of more than 100 migrants who died in July's mass crossing into the North African enclave from Morocco were buried.
The visit, the first by Spain's head of state since 2007 and in Felipe's 12-year reign, followed rising friction between Madrid and Rabat, which claims the tiny territory of Ceuta and Spain's other North African enclave, Melilla, as its own.
The streets of the 84,000-person territory, which covers less than 20 square km, were packed with thousands of Ceutans waving Spanish flags to greet the royal couple.
"I am a Spaniard, Spaniard, Spaniard," they chanted.
The Moroccan government has historically opposed Spanish royal visits to the two cities, which Madrid considers part of its territory since the 17th and 15th centuries, respectively.
The two kingdoms have traded barbs over border management following the crossing by more than 72,000 migrants from Morocco.
Addressing civilians in Ceuta, the king said Morocco's relationship to Spain and the EU must be grounded in respect, "while always adhering to the principle that Ceuta is Spain; Ceuta is Europe."
In a speech to parliament last Friday, Morocco's King Mohammed did not mention the royals' planned visit but said the current migration cooperation model with Spain had reached its limits.
While most of the migrants who managed to get into Ceuta later returned, at least 10,000 remain, straining local resources and fuelling some Spaniards' criticism of the central government ahead of a November 29 general election.
The leftist government has sought to present the royal visit as a gesture of support for Ceuta and its residents but right-wing opposition parties accuse Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez of failing to defend Spanish sovereignty over the enclave.
“It’s a real treat that they’re coming to Ceuta for the first time, and they really ought to come more often, because Ceuta is part of Spain and His Majesty the King doesn’t need to ask permission to visit any city in Spain," said Ceuta resident Isabel Bermejo, 57.
At the cemetery, the royal couple stood solemnly in front of the graves, most of which were marked only with numbers as the victims were never identified.
The couple were accompanied by Jewish, Hindu, Muslim and Christian religious leaders, representing the four religions present in Ceuta.
On Wednesday, the royal couple will visit Melilla, 370 km (230 miles) southeast of Ceuta. REUTERS

Swedish activist Greta Thunberg joined protesters outside a high school in a working-class Paris suburb on Tuesday as French pupils took to the streets for another day of demonstrations over poor learning conditions.
Now in its fourth week, the nationwide protest movement over teacher shortages, classroom overcrowding and crumbling school buildings has involved marches, blockades of hundreds of schools and, in some cases, clashes with police.
Pupils clustered outside several schools in Paris and other cities on Tuesday morning, brandishing placards and megaphones.
"We are inspired by the young people who are demanding their basic rights," Thunberg told reporters outside Lycée Paul Eluard in Saint-Denis, north of Paris, one of the schools where the protest movement first gained traction.

Large crowds marched peacefully through Nantes in the west, Strasbourg in the east and Marseille in the south, holding hand-made signs with slogans such as "Tear gas doesn't make us cry as much as the state of the national education system." Marchers were also mustering in Paris.
Footage from BFM TV showed clashes between people dressed in black and riot police in Strasbourg and Nantes, with clouds of tear gas in some streets.
Authorities push for demonstration to be called off following pre-march vandalism
In Lyon, the local authorities asked organizers to call off a march after a group of "hostile individuals" preceding the main procession vandalized shops and a petrol station and clashed with police.
While there was no immediate information on who was involved, it is not uncommon in France for street protests to attract so-called "casseurs," a fringe of rioters who seek to confront police and destroy property.
The scene was calmer in front of Paris city hall, where a youth orchestra played Antonin Dvorak's "New World Symphony." Some musicians had protest stickers on their cellos and violins.

The cash-strapped government has promised to act to address the pupils' concerns, but has little room for maneuver at a time when concerns over the national debt and the budget deficit are pushing up borrowing costs to the highest level in years.
It has expressed sympathy with the students' grievances, but has deployed riot police to quell the protests, leading to confrontations in which hundreds of people have been injured and thousands arrested.
Political polarization ahead of Fench election
The government suspended the use of stun grenades last week after one teenager lost a hand.
Six months ahead of a presidential election, the protest movement and the police response have elicited polarized responses from leading contenders to replace Emmanuel Macron.
"The police are losing their breath running after young people to beat them up and injure them," said hard-left candidate Jean-Luc Mélenchon, who has a chance of making the runoff according to opinion polls, in a post on X/Twitter on Tuesday.
"The only ones not losing their breath are the young people bravely protesting," he added, accusing the media of failing to show the extent of police brutality and renewing his call for adults to stand with the students to protect them.
Far-right leader Marine Le Pen, the frontrunner in the presidential race according to polls, has denounced violence by protesters and called for those who have damaged schools – or their parents if they are minors – to pay for repairs.
The government has already introduced a bill that would allow precisely that. It is going through parliament.

Far-right National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir acknowledged on Monday that Israel’s international diplomacy was relevant to the country’s national security, but he asserted that it shouldn’t take precedence over the nation’s soldiers.
The minister, whose views are often characterized as extreme and who has been criticized for contributing, through his rhetoric, to the deterioration of Israel’s international image, delivered remarks at an English-speaking election campaign event for his Otzma Yehudit party at the Tel Aviv International Salon.
He was joined by Yishai Fleisher, the international spokesman for the Jewish community of Hebron. Early last month, Fleisher was tapped for the number 12 spot on the Otzma Yehudit list.
“I think there’s a great importance to our diplomatic relations and connections,” Ben-Gvir said in response to a question submitted by The Jerusalem Post. “It’s important that we look good on the world stage. But not at the expense of our fighters and our soldiers.”
Ben-Gvir has been a key partner in Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s coalition. Recent polling has projected Otzma Yehudit to win approximately eight seats in the next Knesset. The minister, however, admitted that he viewed things differently from Netanyahu regarding dealing with Israel’s public diplomacy.
Ben-Gvir: A soft approach doesn't help Israel's security or international standing
He pointed to the Gaza-bound flotillas that attempted to break Israel’s maritime blockade of the Gaza Strip, arguing that taking a softer approach doesn’t help Israel’s security or move the needle in bolstering Israel’s acceptance internationally.
“The first time [the flotilla activists] came, Bibi [Netanyahu] said, ‘Let’s make a good impression on the world. Let’s give them big sandwiches,’” Ben-Gvir said.
“Female soldiers were brought in. They were told to wear civilian clothes, and they [the activists] were given a Pilates lesson,” he added.
“That was because the government wanted to make a good impression and wanted us to look good internationally. Do you think that helped us?” Ben-Gvir asked.
He claimed that, on the contrary, the response to the flotilla incident only caused further international condemnation and resulted in additional flotillas attempting to break the blockade.
“They came again because they said, ‘This is great. The Israelis treat us well; give us sandwiches and exercise classes. Israel is fun,’” Ben-Gvir said.
Subsequently, when an additional flotilla arrived in Israel, he had decided to handle the activists in the same manner that terrorist supporters are treated in the United States.
Rough approach deterred more activists from joining future flotillas, says Ben-Gvir
“They were arrested. They were put in a prison for terrorists,” he said.
According to Ben-Gvir, the different approach deterred some activists from returning, with some saying they would only participate in another flotilla once he was no longer in his role as national security minister.
“There are people who want to see us weak. Anyone who is a true friend of Israel wants to see us strong,” he said. “I genuinely prefer to see Israel strong, even if some people, particularly in Europe, don’t like it very much.”
As national security minister, he has also led reforms in Israel’s prison service, significantly worsening conditions for Palestinian inmates, arguing that both the death penalty and harsher prison conditions create deterrence.
Fleisher, who translated for Ben-Gvir on stage after delivering the opening remarks, also spoke to the Post ahead of the event.
Referencing the English-language format of the event, Fleisher confirmed that Otzma Yehudit was looking to reach out to the English-speaking community in Israel ahead of the October 27 election.
“Certainly, we’re reaching out to anybody who wants a safe and free Israel, and that’s English speakers who understand the policies of strength,” Fleisher said. “It’s Russian speakers. It’s folks around the periphery. The ultra-Orthodox. There's a lot of people that we’re reaching out to. We’re not embarrassed about that; we are excited about strong policies, and that’s what people want right now.”
Regarding Israel’s public diplomacy, Fleisher told the Post that Israel must “forge new alliances around the world of people who are like-minded.
“We have to join a conservative alliance around the world, and we have to keep holding strong, not be afraid,” he added.
“We clearly don’t want to see Palestine here. Once [the international community sees] that we’re sure of ourselves, sure of our Jewish identity, they’ll respect us. That’s the language of the Middle East,” Fleisher said.

English football faces major financial risks, regulator warns
Unknown

Efe Özkan
13 October 2026•Update: 13 October 2026
nglish football’s finances are “dangerously exposed,” with most clubs operating close to financial collapse, according to a landmark report by the Independent Football Regulator (IFR) that was released on Tuesday.
The State of the Game report found that 94% of clubs in England’s top five leagues had losses in the 2025-26 season, while more than 60% of clubs in the English Football League (EFL) and National League were technically insolvent.
The IFR warned that a “dangerous cocktail” of rising debt and increasing reliance on owners to provide funding is putting clubs and their supporters at risk.
The report found that 66% of clubs could not survive for more than 90 days without new funding from their owners, while 29% said they could not survive beyond 30 days. It also found that 60% of clubs had no business plan.
“Seventeen clubs are now trading in such a way that if their players played for free, their non-playing costs would mean they would go bust,” IFR chairman David Kogan told BBC Sport. “Thirty-two clubs are operating on only 30 days’ cash. If the owner chooses not to pay cash at the end of the month, those clubs go bust.”
He said the findings showed that reform was needed before clubs faced an even greater financial crisis.
The report also highlighted widening financial disparities in the English football pyramid. The average Premier League club now earns more than eight times the average Championship club.
The IFR said the existing parachute-payment system for relegated Premier League clubs creates incentives for Championship teams to overspend and contributes to rising player wages.
It also warned that increasing net transfer debt, deferred transfer payments and transfer financing were creating financial links between clubs, owners and lenders, increasing the risk that financial problems could spread across the game.
“Nobody in football for 100 years has believed that football was trading in a solvent and effective state,” said Kogan. “But I think now where there’s so much more money involved, the extremes get more extreme.”
The IFR said the foundations of the English football pyramid were under “intense strain” and required urgent reform

Some of the UK’s biggest retailers and hospitality businesses, including Tesco, Costa Coffee and the Co-op, have met John Healey to urge him to cut the cost of employing young people in his first budget.
At the No 11 event on Tuesday morning, the chancellor heard from sector leaders – including the boss of Marks & Spencer, Stuart Machin, and Sainsbury’s chief executive, Simon Roberts – about the impact of the rise in employers’ national insurance contributions (Nics).
Businesses want a partial reversal of the surprise move by Healey’s predecessor, Rachel Reeves, who lowered the earnings threshold at which they start to pay Nics from £9,100 to £5,000 a year. They argue the change contributed to the plunge in the number of high street jobs for young people and part-time workers and a rise in youth unemployment.
They want the Nics threshold raised to £6,000, arguing this would help create jobs and ease inflation pressures on high streets.
Retail and hospitality firms also hope Healey will ease the burden of business rates, and one source close to the meeting said they were optimistic on both fronts. “It felt like they were listening,” the source said.
Healey has vowed to ease the cost of doing business amid mounting pressures on firms from rising energy bills.
Another attender, Helen Dickinson, the chief executive of the British Retail Consortium trade body which represents most big retailers, said: “Retail is a major driver of growth, supporting jobs, investment and communities across the country, and providing vital first jobs and career opportunities for young people.

In her first budget in 2024, Reeves increased the rate of CGT from 10% to 18% for basic-rate taxpayers, and from 20% to 24% for higher-rate taxpayers. That compares with a 20% basic rate of income tax, a 40% higher rate and 45% additional rate for top earners.
Economists have suggested an equalisation of the rates could raise £11.3bn a year for the exchequer. However, according to the Financial Times, Healey has dismissed such calls because of fears it could deter inward investment, but may yet opt for a smaller increase in CGT short of equalisation.
It comes after senior Labour figures floated CGT increases among options to repair the government finances while funding priorities ranging from public services, support for households and long-term infrastructure projects.
The defence secretary, Wes Streeting, suggested the idea of equalisation during his ill-fated May pitch to be the party leader as a “wealth tax that works”.
And the first secretary, Louise Haigh, a close ally of Andy Burnham, argued in an article in the journal Renewal in May – while on the backbenches before her return to cabinet – that CGT rates should be “brought closer to income tax rates”.
A Treasury spokesperson said: “As has always been the case, decisions on tax are a matter for the chancellor to set out at fiscal events rather than routinely commenting on rumour, speculation or proposals.”

====================================================================================================

Wes Streeting might be an unlikely defence secretary – but he’s still a better bet than Penny Mordaunt
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
17:42:24 UTC
02:42:24 KST

When Andy Burnham announced his first cabinet in July, few would have had Wes Streeting marked down as a likely defence secretary. Not even Wes. And no one is more bullish about Wes’s life chances than Wes. It just didn’t seem a natural fit. Defence secretaries tend to be more the unsmiling types who operate in the shadows. Politicians like John Healey, with the pallor of someone who has spent too long in underground bunkers with military chief of staffs. People who slide in and out of rooms without making a fuss.
Wes has always been someone who likes to be noticed. Enjoys the theatre of Westminster. The first to arrive at a party and the last to leave. A natural gossip. “Psst – you’ll never guess what Zelenskyy just said to Trump.”
But in the past few months, Wes has had something of a personality change. At the recent Labour party conference, he kept his appearances distinctly low key. No longer the life and soul of Liverpool, out till 2am before getting up to do the media round just four hours later. It can’t be long before we see him driving a tank somewhere near the Russian border. Wes is gonna be Wes.
He also has the distinct advantage of not being Penny Mordaunt, the former Tory minister who has done more to terrify a nation than any living defence secretary. A few weeks ago, Sky broadcast The War Game, a reality show for superannuated politicians in which Michael Gove was cast as the prime minister and Penny as defence secretary. The set up was that Russia had torpedoed a ship off Scotland, with the politicians and the military placed in a mock-up Cobra meeting and left to come up with responses as the situation developed.
This could have been the moment to restore faith in our democratic institutions. To admire the insight and clarity with which our leaders handle a crisis. To see how they repay the trust and power which we bestow on them. In which case, you should think again. What actually emerged is that politicians are no brighter than the rest of us. They just have egos which make them believe they are the right people in the right place at the right time. And that we are lucky to have them.
To put it bluntly, The War Game was a total shitshow. Just one bad decision after another. For the first two episodes, The Govester was like a rabbit in the headlights. Completely clueless as the UK came under increasing levels of attack. The best he could offer was to repeat back the last thing that was said to him and bark “ASAP!”
Penny, though, was a total menace to herself and the country from the word go. If this is really how defence secretaries behave, we should all be out digging bunkers in open land and stocking up on tinned food. Not that it would do much good. From the outset, Penny was hell-bent on escalating the conflict despite being told Britain’s military defences were totally threadbare and that the UK was only a middle-ranking global power. She couldn’t wait to use up the UK’s arsenal of weapons, and by the end two nuclear warheads were 20 minutes away from annihilating two major cities. Bye bye Britain. Still, at least she would go down as our last ever defence secretary.
So Streeting’s first appearance before the defence select committee was, first and foremost, a moment to give thanks he wasn’t Penny and that we are all – more or less – still here. And Wes looked as if he was now thoroughly bedded in at the MoD. He now talks mainly in letters – SDR, DIP and NAD – and jargon that is designed to be unintelligible to most mortals. Mostly, he wanted to get through the entire session by saying as little as possible and to send any stray reporters who had wandered into the committee room by mistake to sleep. He’d have liked to be more open, he said. But if he was, he’d have to kill us. For the first time in his life, Wes is enjoying keeping secrets. If not exactly his happiest place, then still a happy one.
Wes began by telling the committee that the UK and its Nato allies were facing their gravest threat since the cold war. Given that, you could understand why he wan’t particularly keen on telling us just how unprepared we were for some kind of an attack as our enemies might be listening. When Streeting had taken on the defence job he had spent most of the first week telling the media that he would – like his predecessor – resign if he thought the money being allocated was inadequate.
Three months on and he was rather dancing on the head of a pin. He couldn’t say how, when or even if the commitment to reach 3% of GDP by 2030 would be met. We just had to keep the faith that somehow it would all work out OK. John Healey said it would all end up OK, and if John Healey said so then we ought to believe him. After all, it wasn’t just a question of spending more money – it was also about spending the money he did have better.
It also turned out that some of our defence capacity was largely illusory. Both because it took six years for most military contracts to be delivered, by which time there was a fair chance the hardware would be obsolete, and because much of the increased spending had been backloaded until after the next election. Politicians never tire of passing on costs to future governments.
The MoD’s permanent secretary, Jeremy Pocklington, spent at least five minutes trying to persuade the committee that backloading wasn’t really backloading even if it looked like backloading. For that kind of mind-numbing bullshit, Jezza has been awarded the Companion of the Most Honourable Order of the Bath. Still, Wes did say at one point that he “wasn’t keen on fighting a war”, which I suppose is a start. Gives him the edge over Penny at the very least.

Can Saudi Arabia find a viable path out of Yemen?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
17:41:51 UTC
02:41:51 KST

Can Saudi Arabia find a viable path out of Yemen?
TEHRAN – Saudi Arabia is once again testing its options for dealing with Ansarallah, hoping that what failed the first time might succeed the next.
It tried a war in March 2015 under the banner of the “Arab Coalition,” and the result was a brutal conflict that devastated everything in its path. The war dragged on for eight years before the guns fell silent, without achieving its objectives. Today, it seems decision-makers in Riyadh have fallen prey to the belief that whatever force fails to achieve can be accomplished by using even more force. The war is being reignited, this time with greater intensity and ferocity.
For more than a decade, Saudi Arabia tried blockade, isolation, and sanctions. When these measures failed to break Ansarallah’s resolve, it went a step further on July 13, bombing the runway at Sanaa International Airport to prevent an Iranian aircraft from landing.
On board was a Yemeni delegation returning from Tehran, where it had paid its respects following the martyrdom of the Leader of Iran’s Revolution, Ayatollah Sayyed Ali Khamenei.
The attack was intended as a reminder that the airport remained under blockade. Instead, it became the spark that reignited an unprecedented confrontation between the two sides, with hostilities now unfolding on land, in the air, and at sea, striking deep into both Saudi and Yemeni territories.
The option the Kingdom has refrained from trying is sustained negotiations and genuine dialogue with Ansarallah, whether face-to-face or through trusted intermediaries aimed at a lasting solution. By its very nature, a truce is temporary. It does not address the roots of a crisis or produce the necessary settlements between the conflicting demands and interests of the parties involved.
The collapse of de-escalation
The second extension of the truce agreement expired on October 2, 2022, without an agreement on a third extension, as the parties remained too far apart in their positions. Nevertheless, the ceasefire largely held, and the past four years saw a reduction in hostilities that was disrupted only by isolated incidents, none of which amounted to a significant breach or escalation, until the attack on Sanaa airport three months ago.
In April 2023, a Saudi delegation visited Sanaa. The trip lasted six days. In September 2023, an Ansarallah delegation visited Riyadh to explore the possibility of advancing a political process that could produce lasting solutions. That trip lasted five days.
However, three factors left everything unresolved: first, the widening gap between the two sides; second, Riyadh’s insistence that it was a “sponsor and mediator” rather than a party to the Yemeni crisis; and third, the outbreak of the Al-Aqsa Storm operation, which reshaped regional maps, balances of power, and priorities. As a result, matters remained unresolved, leaving both the intra-Yemeni and Yemeni-Saudi crises open to any number of possibilities and scenarios.
Ansarallah became preoccupied with its military campaign in support of Gaza, achieving tangible results that worked in its favor rather than against it. It subsequently evolved from a local actor into a regional player, particularly after reaching an understanding with the Trump administration under which the U.S. would halt its attacks on Yemen in exchange for ending attacks on American vessels and assets in the Red Sea and the Bab al-Mandab Strait. Meanwhile, relations with Riyadh appeared to have been pushed to the back burner.
Some Ansarallah officials say the war now raging should have erupted two years ago, given the deadlock in efforts to find a solution and the worsening consequences of the blockade. However, the Gaza genocide postponed the entire matter.
There is also a reductive and misleading narrative that portrays the renewed war and confrontation as a response by Ansarallah to an Iranian order. Beyond being false and superficial, this narrative harms those who genuinely believe it, rather than those who repeat it out of spite or to demonize their adversaries.
Misjudging Ansarallah’s position and standing leads to some of the most erroneous and damaging conclusions. Ansarallah indeed makes no secret of its close ties to Iran and its regional axis. It is also true that the Sanaa government did not hesitate to support Gaza in the past and may not hesitate in the future to join a campaign in support of Hezbollah and Iran.
But above all, Ansarallah is an integral part of Yemen’s social and political fabric and one of the country’s fundamental constituencies. All of Yemen may not be governed by Ansarallah alone, but it cannot be governed without it.
Following the July attack on Sanaa airport, it became clear that a fundamental shift had taken place in Ansarallah’s language and preparations. Its leader announced a new equation: “blockade for blockade, ports for ports, and airports for airports.”
Few took these threats seriously until the confrontation on the ground escalated, with Ansarallah extending its control along the coast toward Taiz and the Bab al-Mandab Strait, while reciprocal strikes intensified in the heart of both Saudi and Yemeni territory.
The Kingdom has sought to absolve itself of accusations that it is directly involved in military operations, maintaining its position under the theory that it is a “sponsor and mediator, not a party” to the war.
The path Saudi Arabia has yet to try
The eight-year war failed to achieve its objectives, while Ansarallah emerged stronger and is now expanding its reach.
Nor can Saudi Arabia continue to deny the damage and consequences of its blockade on Yemen, which affects three-quarters of the population. It cannot credibly claim that the limited and restricted flights available, or the reduced flow of goods are sufficient to compensate the Yemeni people for shortages of food and medicine. Neither can it maintain that its measures target only Ansarallah and are directed exclusively at arms supplies.
The realities of Yemeni life and the daily experiences of ordinary Yemenis tell a different story. Reports by international organizations document poverty, deprivation, shortages of medicine and food, and the interruption of salary payments. Such conditions might be endured for another year or two, but allowing them to persist much longer seems untenable.
The option Saudi Arabia has yet to try, with the seriousness it demands, is to open the door to dialogue and negotiations, either directly or through a trusted mediator, such as Oman, in pursuit of solutions and settlements to all outstanding disputes.
Such a dialogue would begin between Sanaa and Riyadh, but it would not end with them. Instead, it would bring all Yemeni parties to the negotiating table, based on the principle that Yemen cannot be governed by a single Yemeni faction. The talks should not be tactical, intermittent, and ceasefire-focused. Dialogue must be a sustained, strategic commitment to a comprehensive negotiated settlement that addresses the root causes of the conflict, the blockade, the humanitarian crisis, and Yemen’s political future. The Kingdom has not genuinely embraced negotiation as a primary strategy, instead treating it as a pause between rounds of military pressure.
Experts believe the time has come to try this approach. It would not be costly and offers the shortest and least expensive path forward for all parties, especially Saudi Arabia, which has much to lose. Has the time finally come to stop repeating failed experiments and take a new path, one that might, at last, lead to a different ending?

‘Our enemies are thinking of testing us’: Netanyahu issues warning two weeks before election
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
17:41:38 UTC
02:41:38 KST

Exactly two weeks before Israel's elections, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu visited the security barrier separating Israel from the West Bank on Tuesday and once again warned of a possible scenario in which Palestinian Authority security forces turn their weapons against Israeli targets.
Netanyahu said there were security alerts in the area and suggested that Israel's enemies were considering taking action in the run-up to the October 27 election. "Our enemies are thinking of testing us in these days leading up to the elections," Netanyahu said. "I warn them that we are prepared for every scenario, including what is known as 'turning the guns around.'"
The possibility of Palestinian security forces turning their weapons against Israel has featured increasingly prominently in Israeli political and security discussions over the past month and a half.
The issue first emerged during a briefing at the IDF's Central Command, when Netanyahu confronted IDF Chief of Staff Lt. Gen. Eyal Zamir with a question about what would happen if Palestinian security personnel turned their guns on Israel. At the time, Central Command officers were presenting an assessment of the situation in the West Bank, including riots involving extremist settlers, the damage caused by their actions and the resulting need to divert military forces.
Netanyahu subsequently raised the issue in an interview, echoing warnings he and members of his government had made previously.
The IDF clarified at the time that the scenario was familiar to the military and had already been included in exercises, but that it had no intelligence indicating the existence of an actual Palestinian plan to carry it out.
At the same time, senior military officers warned that the situation in the West Bank was "getting out of control," while security officials cautioned political leaders that the territory was "on the verge of exploding" because of the growing number of incidents of nationalist violence committed by extremist settlers.
Netanyahu toured the security barrier Tuesday alongside Defense Minister Israel Katz, the head of the National Security Council and the commander of the IDF's Central Command.
According to the Prime Minister's Office, commanders from the IDF, Shin Bet and Border Police briefed Netanyahu on efforts to protect Israeli communities along the barrier, as well as extensive operations in nearby Palestinian villages. The Prime Minister's Office said the operations included efforts carried out day and night to arrest terrorists, confiscate weapons and address potential threats originating from those areas.
Speaking near Tulkarm, Netanyahu said the military had presented him and Katz with a forceful operational plan. "The IDF has presented me and the defense minister with a powerful, robust plan," Netanyahu said. "In such a scenario, I wouldn't advise our enemies to test us. You will encounter a level of force here that you never imagined."
He added: "We will continue to safeguard Israel's security here, along the security barrier and everywhere. We are establishing communities here, more than 104 of them, and many farms. We are safeguarding the security of the State of Israel."
The scenario Netanyahu referred to as "turning the guns around" involves members of the Palestinian Authority's security forces using their weapons against Israeli communities or IDF soldiers.
The Palestinian security services legally possess thousands of firearms in the West Bank, with Israel's approval. Under the scenario discussed by Netanyahu, those weapons would instead be directed against Israeli targets. However, the IDF is not aware of any intelligence indicating that the Palestinian Authority is on the verge of carrying out such a dramatic shift.
Nevertheless, as Zamir explained in response to Netanyahu during the Central Command briefing approximately six weeks ago, the military is unwilling to take chances. Even without intelligence pointing to an imminent move by Palestinian security forces, the IDF is preparing for the most extreme scenario.

China sentences three people to death for running Myanmar scam centres
Dozens more were imprisoned for their involvement in crimes including telecommunications fraud, trafficking and murder.
A court in eastern China has sentenced three members of a criminal gang to death for operating a network of scam centres in Myanmar.
In a statement released on Tuesday, Quanzhou Intermediate People’s Court, a high court in southeastern Fujian province, said it had sentenced Wei Huairen, Chen Dawei and Liao Jingfang for their involvement in the “Wei family criminal gang”.
The syndicate was involved in crimes including drug trafficking, organised prostitution, illegal casino operations, telecommunications fraud and the murder of at least two Chinese nationals.
The court said Wei was one of the group’s leaders and was found guilty of several crimes, including murder.
Three other members were jailed for life, while 55 others were handed sentences ranging from three years and three months to 24 years in prison.
The court said the gang’s operations netted more than $1.8bn.
Chinese state broadcaster CCTV on Tuesday described the gang as operating 14 “large-scale” compounds and having lured “thousands” of Chinese nationals with promises of high wages to Myanmar.
The verdict comes as Beijing intensified its crackdown on cross-border scam networks operating in southeast Asia, where scam parks have become an industrial-scale business.
The International Organization for Migration in July warned that scam centres in southeast Asia employ as many as 300,000 workers and use online schemes to defraud people in the West, many of them elderly.
Many of those conducting the online scams are trafficked foreign nationals forced to work in prison-like compounds.

François Picard is pleased to welcome Valdemar Osted, partner and head of technology at Danish digital consultancy Common Consultancy. Can the fear of disinformation become as dangerous to democracy as disinformation itself? Osted challenges widely circulated claims that attacks on Russian data centres have triggered a sudden collapse in online engagement among supporters of Donald Trump and Germany's far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD). Drawing on social media monitoring and research into inauthentic behaviour, Osted reports finding no unusual decline in Facebook interactions following the attacks.

His analysis raises a broader question for contemporary democracies: when allegations of manipulation become pervasive, can widespread fear of deception lead to democratic destabilisation?

Russia’s Rassvet Satellites Could Give Drones Space-Based Control, Former HUR Official Warns
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
17:38:28 UTC
02:38:28 KST

Russia’s growing Rassvet satellite network could eventually allow its forces to control long-range drones over Ukraine in real time, a former senior Ukrainian intelligence official warned on Tuesday, Oct. 13.
Major General Ilya Pavlenko, who served as deputy chief of the Defense Ministry’s Main Intelligence Directorate (HUR) from 2015 to 2020, made the remarks in an interview with Interfax-Ukraine.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
He cautioned against writing off the project because of problems with its first satellites, arguing that the real question is whether Moscow can make the system reliable enough to support regular military communications over Ukraine. The network, he said, could also be used as another tool for hybrid warfare against NATO countries.
“For Europeans, this is a direct threat,” Pavlenko said, explaining that Russia is moving its jet drone factories underground. This could further limit Ukraine’s ability to break manufacturing cycles or destroy the drones – already hard to intercept due to their speed – before they can even be deployed.
“Fitted with a compact Rassvet terminal, such a drone, launched from a civilian vessel in the English Channel or from a rented trailer in Europe, will be able to strike targets in London or Paris unhindered, controlled directly from the Kremlin,” Pavlenko continued, arguing that Europe simply does not have enough Patriot interceptors to repel Russia’s large-scale attacks conducted by cheap satellite drones.
Ukrainian Startup Zvook Secures Investment From Czech DEPO Ventures
Rassvet – Russia’s domestic attempt of Starlink
Built by the Russian company Bureau 1440, Rassvet is a low-orbit satellite broadband service that users can connect to through dedicated terminals that relay data to satellites overhead.
As such satellites sit far closer to Earth than geostationary ones, the signal’s travel time is significantly shorter, which could improve performance. According to Pavlenko, a satellite at about 500 kilometers (approximately 311 miles) could offer delays of roughly 30 milliseconds, compared with close to 70 at the planned 800 (roughly 497 miles).
The only trade-off is that each satellite passes quickly over any given spot, so continuous coverage of a large area requires hundreds of them. Higher orbit, although with possible delays in speed, could allow each satellite to cover more ground.
Bureau 1440 says the finished system will operate at an altitude of about 800 kilometers (497 miles), deliver speeds of up to 1 Gbps with delays of up to 70 milliseconds, and use 5G non-terrestrial network standards and laser links between satellites.
Actual speeds in combat would also depend on network load, routing, ground stations and the number of users sharing a channel, Pavlenko noted, so the advertised 1 Gbps should not be read as what each terminal will receive.
Kyiv Post could not independently verify these figures.
Russia carried out two launches of 16 Rassvet-3 satellites each in 2026, both on Soyuz-2.1b rockets from the Plesetsk cosmodrome. However, not all of the roughly 32 spacecraft are working as intended, Pavlenko said; one dropped out of its orbit, while others failed to climb to their planned altitude.
Moscow aims to launch 292 satellites in 2027 and 924 by 2035, according to The Moscow Times.
What this means for Ukraine
Russia’s push for its own satellite system sped up after it launched its full-scale invasion against Ukraine in February 2022, particularly because Starlink proved its value to Ukrainian Defense Forces on the battlefield.
For the Russian military, a secure satellite link would mean sharing data between units, streaming video and reaching platforms operating beyond ground networks.
A small constellation can still be military useful, Pavlenko said. Even without constant coverage, a satellite passing over the right area at the right time opens a short “access window” that may be enough to send a video feed, issue a command or adjust a drone’s mission.
That scenario has already been tested, according to Ukrainian intelligence sources cited by Janes in August 2026, who said Russia used its first batch of Rassvet satellites to communicate over Ukraine for several hours.
The biggest concern is drones. Most Russian long-range drones today fly preset routes or rely on civilian mobile networks via a SIM card. With a satellite link, an operator could watch live footage and change a drone’s course or target mid-flight.
Pavlenko said large strike drones, particularly jet-powered models, are the most likely candidates since they can carry the necessary terminals.
Russia began using jet-powered drones extensively in recent months, as they can reach speeds of up to 400-600 kilometers per hour (roughly 250-370 miles per hour), making them significantly harder to intercept.
He identified three main risks for Ukraine: drones gaining a communication channel independent of ground networks, better coordination between dispersed units, and smaller future terminals that could fit on more types of weapons.
There are limits, however. Each drone would need a compatible terminal, antenna, power supply and software, and a satellite link alone would not improve navigation or protect a drone from electronic warfare or air defenses.
Countering the system
Jamming Rassvet will not be so simple, Pavlenko said, noting that effective countermeasures require detailed knowledge of its frequencies, protocols and terminal design – much of which is not public.
Terminals with electronically steered antennas can track satellites quickly and hold a steadier connection, while reprogrammable chips let engineers update satellites with new software after launch.
And shooting down satellites is not much easier. A large constellation can absorb the loss of a few spacecraft, and destroying them creates debris that endangers other objects in orbit, Pavlenko said.
On Aug. 28, Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha announced that Kyiv has petitioned the International Telecommunication Union (ITU) to exclude Ukraine’s territory from the service areas of Rassvet, arguing that the system is used solely to support Russia’s war effort.
“The purpose for Russia to use such satellites over the territory of Ukraine is absolutely clear and it has nothing to do with civilian purposes,” Sybiha said, adding that Moscow intends to use the system to support its war effort and commit “genocidal crimes.”
The following day, the Digital Transformation Ministry, the Foreign Ministry and the Ukrainian State Center of Radio Frequencies filed objections to the Rassvet-1 and Rassvet-3 systems.
Nonetheless, Pavlenko acknowledged that the ITU cannot enforce its decisions. But, if Rassvet’s registration were to be revoked, the system would effectively operate illegally, strengthening the case for jamming it and striking its ground infrastructure.
Risks beyond Ukraine’s front line
Rassvet’s reach could extend well beyond Ukraine’s frontline, Pavlenko said, warning that Russia is planning to sell the system’s access in 70 countries across the Global South.
This could essentially put the service in the hands of criminal groups, including Somali pirates using unmanned boats against merchant ships and Latin American cartels trying to evade US surveillance.
Ukrainian intelligence also believes Russia deliberately registered Rassvet on frequencies that overlap with Iridium, a satellite system used by the Pentagon. If so, any Western attempt to jam Rassvet could disrupt allied military communications as well.
China’s growing role
Amid sweeping sanctions imposed by the EU, Russia has already shifted from Western components obtained through grey-market channels to primarily Chinese electronics.
That is a demanding switch for space hardware, which must withstand radiation and extreme temperatures and cannot be repaired after launch. New components would also mean reworking software and testing equipment, Pavlenko said.
Beyond sales, Beijing gains much from the arrangement as Russia’s war offers a live testing ground for Chinese technology and imposes a steady demand for electronics, optics and communications gear.
Pavlenko singled out Shanghai Fudan Microelectronics, a Chinese chipmaker the US Commerce Department added to its Entity List in September 2025 for supplying technology to Russian military end users. There is no evidence, however, that its components are used in Rassvet satellites.
He also linked the acceleration of Russia’s defense industry to Andrei Belousov, who became defense minister in May 2024.
According to Pavlenko, Belousov was given authority over the wider defense industry and reoriented it toward Chinese chips, optics, thermal imagers and carbon fiber.
He claimed that 90% of the Russian defense sector’s financial settlements now run through the yuan and Chinese banks, although the figure could not be independently verified.
President Volodymyr Zelensky separately warned on Monday, Oct. 12, that Beijing is assisting Russia’s efforts in building Rassvet.
“We know that China works on satellites, works on the possibility of helping Russia with a system similar to Starlink,” he told the Financial Times, adding that “they are getting closer, and they are passing it on to Russia.”
A delegation of bipartisan US lawmakers has backed expanding Ukraine’s access to SpaceX’s Starlink satellite network and urged an effort to win over the company’s owner, Elon Musk, during their visit to Kyiv on Oct. 9.
Musk has repeatedly refused to allow its use inside Russia over fears of nuclear escalation.
Currently, SpaceX allows Ukraine to use Starlink on Ukrainian-controlled territory, including Russian-occupied areas such as Crimea. However, the service inside Russia is completely blocked.

Russian telecom giant Rostelecom offers smaller internet providers relief from surveillance costs. In exchange, it wants their customers — and most of their revenue.
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
17:38:21 UTC
02:38:21 KST

Russian telecom giant Rostelecom offers smaller internet providers relief from surveillance costs. In exchange, it wants their customers — and most of their revenue.
Russia’s largest nationwide telecommunications operators, Rostelecom and TransTeleCom, have begun offering small regional providers service agreements under which the providers would hand over their infrastructure and subscriber bases, Kommersant reported after reviewing the presentations.
Under Rostelecom’s proposal, regional operators would transfer their subscribers, communications lines, and technical support to the company. In return, they would keep 30–40% of revenue and no longer have to cover SORM costs (up to 15 million rubles a year), payroll (up to 16 million rubles a year), or contributions to the universal service fund (at least 1 million rubles a year). The proposal also promises to reduce their exposure to regulatory risk.
TransTeleCom’s proposal outlines fixed virtual network operator (FVNO) models. Under these models, regional operators would no longer need a license or have regulatory obligations. In return, they would receive a share of revenue and retain the “last mile.”
A source told Kommersant that the proposals involve “strictly commercial and voluntary” cooperation.
Representatives of small providers say that under these terms, operators would “effectively become installers.” Rostelecom used to “at least buy companies,” but now it is effectively offering terms under which it “takes 60% of the business” without investing anything, said Yaroslav Dubovikov, executive director of the Association of Telecommunications Companies.
In April 2026, reports emerged that the Ministry of Digital Development was discussing stricter requirements for telecommunications operators with industry representatives. Among other measures, the ministry proposed introducing three types of licenses that could cost between 1 million and 50 million rubles, depending on the category. The Association of Telecommunications Operators warned that the proposal could leave 27 regions without local internet providers.

NEW DELHI: Former election commissioner Ashok Lavasa on Tuesday said the Election Commission of India (ECI) was facing an unprecedented level of controversy and urged the poll body to regain public trust amid protests over alleged irregularities in the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls.Drawing a parallel with cricket, Lavasa said the credibility of an election depended on people believing that the poll panel was impartial.“If people feel that the umpire is not neutral, they will question the winning team's victory as well,” he said while addressing a citizens' convention in Kolkata virtually, according to news agency PTI.Lavasa's remarks came as opposition parties intensified their protests against alleged “vote chori”, demanding the resignation of chief election commissioner (CEC) Gyanesh Kumar over the SIR exercise.Opposition leaders have taken to the streets in recent days and clashed with police in New Delhi.“The EC should regain its credibility and people's trust. Questions over dissent within Election Commission
The former election commissioner referred to an Indian Express report that election commissioners Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi had objected on record at least 14 times over the past 10 months to decisions and orders they said had been issued without their knowledge.
The objections reportedly came even as the nationwide SIR exercise was being overseen by the full commission.Lavasa questioned the lack of publicly available meeting minutes, saying it was difficult to establish whether decisions had been taken unanimously or by a majority.“This casts a doubt in the minds of the people whether the decisions of the Election Commission, including on the SIR, were unanimous or taken by majority,” he said.He also said the Election Commission had not provided an authentic clarification on the reported differences between its members.“Some press statements have been issued, but those create more questions and generate more doubts than they answer,” Lavasa said.The poll panel has maintained that differing views and observations are a normal part of deliberations in any institution. Lavasa flags concerns over SIR

Possibly the priority is to exclude people from the voter list on the suspicion that they are not Indian citizens and not on evidence,” he said.Referring to West Bengal, Lavasa said nearly 60 lakh people's voting rights had gone under adjudication during the SIR, apart from those excluded from the draft electoral rolls. He said the EC had not adequately considered the proximity of the Assembly elections and the difficulty of adjudicating such a large number of cases in time.Lavasa added that around 33 lakh names had been restored to the voter list after adjudication.

He said opposition parties had come to believe they were contesting “fixed” elections.
The convention was organised by CPI(M) leader Bikash Ranjan Bhattacharya and retired bureaucrat Jawhar Sircar.The protests over the SIR have also prompted a wider political confrontation between the opposition and the ruling BJP.Congress leader Rahul Gandhi has vowed to continue the INDIA bloc's campaign against alleged electoral irregularities, while Union home minister Amit Shah has accused the Congress of trying to shield infiltrators by opposing the exercise.

Kyiv backs a mutual truce, but Moscow has not confirmed it, and Russian strikes on Ukraine’s grid have continued.
The paper named three such ties: satellite intelligence, Patriot interceptors, and American weapons bought with European money. A pause in any of them would hit just as Russia’s winter campaign begins. Ukraine says an intercepted document reportedly lays out up to 1,000 Russian missiles, drones, and bombs for 60 critical sites this winter, so any pause in US intelligence, interceptors, or PURL deliveries would land as that campaign gets under way.

Trump briefly suspended that flow in March 2025 to pressure Zelenskyy. A Ukrainian official told Axios that Trump envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner threatened during 9 October talks in Miami to cut off US intelligence.
Russian ballistic missiles hit Kyiv before sirens, gap that lands hard amid fears that Washington could cut data that warns of launches
Patriot interceptors: no quick substitute
The Telegraph called interceptor missiles the second and probably sharpest dependency. Only American Patriot systems can down Russia’s most powerful missiles, which strike Ukrainian cities daily, the paper wrote. Kyiv’s PAC-3 stocks ran dry mainly because US reserves were diverted to the Middle East after America’s war against Iran, the paper added. Five European defense firms—Destinus, MBDA Deutschland, Safran, Airbus, and Thales—signed a letter of intent in July to develop a joint interceptor, but a testable prototype is not expected before next year, the paper wrote. Ukraine is also building its own interceptor with European allies under the FREYJA program.
The night Trump announced a diesel deal with Putin, drones knocked out more than half the tanks at a Russian fuel-export terminal
US arms bought with European money
The third is buying American arms with European money through the Prioritized Ukraine Requirements List (PURL), a NATO-run purchasing scheme. US officials have reportedly warned Europe that Trump may halt those supplies if Ukraine keeps striking Russian oil refineries.

Zelensky’s bullying worked on Europe. But Trump has the backbone to turn the screws back
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
17:36:21 UTC
02:36:21 KST

Zelensky thinks he can bully Trump like he does EU leaders
Vladimir Zelensky has a pattern in dealing with Western partners who disappoint him: raise the disagreement in public, question the partner’s judgment and explain why the decision benefits Russia and Vladimir Putin.
Former German Chancellor Olaf Scholz heard variations of that argument for years, and now US President Donald Trump is hearing them again. The question is whether Zelensky can keep increasing the political cost of refusing Kiev without increasing the cost to Ukraine.
On October 9, Zelensky described Washington’s decision to ease restrictions on Russian diesel as a “weak decision by strong partners.” The announcement came while Ukrainian officials were discussing an end to the Russia-Ukraine conflict with their American counterparts in Miami. Zelensky argued that the arrangement would give Moscow additional resources to continue fighting. His criticism challenged the judgment of the government on which he still depends.
Kiev has an obvious interest in opposing measures that improve Russia’s economic position. But when a partner makes a decision Zelensky doesn’t like, he repeatedly turns a policy disagreement into a public test of that partner’s resolve and overall capabilities as a politician.
German leaders have been the target of this manipulation for years now.
In March 2022, addressing the Bundestag, Zelensky used the country’s own historical memory to indict its policy toward Russia. Invoking Ronald Reagan’s famous appeal in Berlin, he called on Scholz to tear down the new wall he saw dividing Europe – that is, to cut off economic ties with Russia, which had benefitted Germany for decades before.
By June, the demand was more explicit. In an interview with ZDF, Zelensky said Scholz and his government had to decide where they stood. Berlin, he argued, could not balance support for Ukraine against its relationship with Russia. He also criticized Germany’s delay in supplying weapons.
Germany’s government had to consider its own security, resources and voters. Zelensky’s tirades made that look like a choice between the ‘right’ and the ‘wrong’ side.
In November 2024, with Nord Stream already sabotaged and German industry in decline for a second consecutive year, even just talking to Putin earned Scholz another reprimand from Zelensky. The Russian and German leaders held a phone conversation, which Zelensky promptly called a “Pandora’s box,” because apparently it would help Russia escape international ‘isolation.’ That’s despite the fact that Scholz’s message for Putin was a demand for the withdrawal of Russian troops and a reaffirmation of German support for Ukraine. You can denounce Moscow and supply arms to Kiev, but even the most rudimentary attempt at keeping diplomatic channels open is a no-no.
The same approach extended beyond Berlin.
In May 2024, Zelensky warned that Putin would personally applaud Joe Biden’s absence from a planned ‘peace summit’ in Switzerland. Biden’s attendance was framed as a test with an audience in the Kremlin.
Poland received a similar message during a grain dispute in September 2023. Speaking at the UN, Zelensky accused some European partners of performing solidarity in a “political theater” that helped Moscow. He named no country, but Warsaw understood the implication, summoned Ukraine’s ambassador and protested. Polish Prime Minister Mateusz Morawiecki subsequently told him never to insult Poles again.
With Slovak Prime Minister Robert Fico, Zelensky made it personal. In January 2025, amid a confrontation over Russian gas transit, he mocked Fico’s reported vacation in Vietnam and accused him of pursuing shadowy arrangements with Moscow.
Zelensky seems to assume that Ukraine’s supposed cause of being a barrier to Putin’s phantom Europe invasion plans gives him the authority to judge how other governments exercise their responsibilities. A leader who refuses Kiev’s nagging demands must then answer accusations of weakness, misplaced priorities or assistance to Russia.
Trump had already encountered this treatment even before returning to office in 2025.
In an interview published in September 2024, Zelensky questioned whether Trump understood how to end the conflict. He also described his running mate JD Vance as too radical and urged him to study the history of the Second World War. These were public judgments about the competence of men who might soon determine American policy.
In February 2025, responding to Trump’s statements about the conflict and his approval rating, Zelensky claimed the American president lived in a space of disinformation. Later that month, the Oval Office meeting turned into an argument in front of the cameras. Zelensky challenged Vance’s understanding of Ukraine and warned that Americans would eventually feel the consequences of the war despite their distance from it. Trump angrily rejected the suggestion that his guest could dictate what Americans would feel.
One would think Zelensky would take the hint: unlike the meek Europeans, the American president has the willpower to resist political blackmail, and is not liable to take personal insults and turn the other cheek. One would also think that with crucial wartime assets like weapon supplies and intelligence sharing in the balance, Zelensky would cool off and rethink his negotiation tactics. One would be wrong.
After Zelensky criticized the diesel arrangement, Trump suggested that Ukraine get a new leader capable of making a deal. That statement is not a formal policy to remove him, but it does raise the question whether Zelensky himself is the obstacle that prevents a settlement.
Zelensky may believe that confrontation will rally European support, improve his own optics at home or force Washington to offer better terms. Public pressure could be a viable last resort for a leader out of option, allowing him to appeal over the heads of foreign governments to their voters, lawmakers and media.
But that approach depends on those governments accepting the terms of the argument. They must feel that refusing Kiev carries a greater political cost than accommodating it. And some leaders, as misguided as that seems, may truly believe that – or may have painted themselves into a corner by submitting to Zelensky’s earlier bullying, sacrificing their own economies and losing their voters’ trust.
Trump is not one of those leaders. Instead of accepting Zelensky’s accusation of weakness, he has accused the Ukrainian leader of obstructing an agreement. It’s unclear if Zelensky understands that the potential consequences of their quarrel are much worse for Ukraine than for the US.
For Trump, lowering American fuel costs and pursuing an agreement with Moscow are stated objectives. Zelensky cannot assume that he can bully those objectives away. What he might achieve instead is an end to crucial lifelines propping up his crumbling military – like intelligence sharing.
Zelensky has repeatedly tried to make Western leaders pay a political price for saying no to Kiev. Except some of those leaders may have the backbone to turn that price right back on him.

West increasingly vulnerable to energy shocks – IMF
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
17:35:55 UTC
02:35:55 KST

West increasingly vulnerable to energy shocks – IMF
Western economies are becoming increasingly vulnerable to further energy shocks as the Middle East conflict strains global supplies and mounting public debt limits governments’ ability to cushion the impact, the International Monetary Fund has warned.
In its latest World Economic Outlook, released on Tuesday, the IMF warned that the prolonged Middle East conflict was putting further pressure on energy markets, with European gas inventories near 15-year lows. 
“Inventories in energy markets are dwindling and additional geopolitical shocks could still transmit rapidly through prices and supply disruptions,” the report said.
Refined petroleum products remain 70% to 95% more expensive than before the war, with diesel and gasoline facing the greatest pressure. Global oil inventories are being depleted by around 2.7 million barrels a day, according to the IMF.
The report also cited Ukrainian attacks on Russian oil infrastructure, including onshore facilities and sites in the Black Sea, as an additional source of pressure on global crude and refined petroleum markets.
Europe faces additional risks ahead of winter. The IMF cited repeated summer heatwaves and damage to Qatar’s energy infrastructure as factors contributing to gas price volatility. The US-Israeli war on Iran has also severely disrupted shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, a route that normally carries around a fifth of global oil and LNG shipments. Iranian strikes on Qatar’s Ras Laffan complex in March damaged key export facilities, further tightening global supplies.
The EU has committed to ending its reliance on Russian fossil fuels by 2027, having sharply reduced oil and gas imports since the escalation of the Ukraine conflict in February 2022. Moscow has described Europe’s energy problems as “self-made,” with Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov accusing the bloc of committing “harakiri” by abandoning Russian supplies. Lavrov said Russian exporters had shifted to more reliable buyers, particularly in Asia.
Renewed fighting between Saudi Arabia and Yemen’s Houthis has also threatened shipping through the Bab el-Mandeb Strait in the Red Sea, a key route linking the Indian Ocean to the Suez Canal and European markets.
The energy crisis has also prompted Washington to ease restrictions on Russian diesel. Following a phone call on Friday between US President Donald Trump and Russian President Vladimir Putin, the US Treasury authorized certain transactions with Russian diesel until April 7, 2027. Trump has repeatedly blamed Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries for driving up fuel prices.
Despite the mounting risks, the IMF projects global growth of 3.1% in 2026 and 3.4% in 2027, compared with just 1.1% and 1.2%, respectively, for the Eurozone. Global inflation is expected to reach 4.7% this year before easing to 4.1% next year.
