The Cabinet of Ministers has changed the employee reservation quotas for critical enterprises
Kyiv • UNN
In the defense industry and energy sector, it is proposed to reserve 85% of employees, while in utilities - 60%. The criteria will be reviewed by October 20.
The Cabinet of Ministers of Ukraine has approved new rules for reserving employees at critically important enterprises. This is reported by Forbes Ukraine, according to UNN.
Details
From now on, in the defense industry and energy sector, instead of 100% of employees, they propose allowing only 85% to be reserved.
At the same time, for enterprises providing heating, water supply, and waste removal services, they want to lower the limit from 75% to 60%. Where a 50% limit applies, everything will remain unchanged.
The document no longer contains the provision on excluding from the calculation employees who have a deferment (students, parents of many children, and others). In addition, a Coordination Center will be established with the participation of the Security Service of Ukraine, the Main Directorate of Intelligence, the Foreign Intelligence Service, and the National Police.
The criteria for determining the critical importance of enterprises in all sectors are to be reviewed by October 20. One day was allocated for clarifying the document, and five days for final approval of the reservation percentages.
Context
The government prepared amendments to the procedure for reserving conscript-liable employees. For Ukrainians, this will mean the abolition of 100% reservation, particularly in the defense and energy sectors.
According to the amendments proposed by officials from the Ministry of Economy, even enterprises whose operations are essential to the country’s defense capability or the functioning of vital infrastructure may lose the ability to reserve their entire staff.

The sites listed in the Houthi announcement were Aramco's headquarters in Dammam, Saudi Arabia; King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh, which recently suffered a devastating strike; and Aramco's refinery in Riyadh. A map accompanied the warning.
The exchange of threats comes as Saudi Arabia investigates how its air defense systems failed to prevent Saturday's unprecedented deadly strike on King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh, which killed at least 13 people and injured more than 300.
The Houthi missile attacks on Saudi airports mark a dramatic turning point in the long-running conflict between the two sides. The Houthis' ability to enforce an air blockade on Saudi Arabia has been a major humiliation for the kingdom's authorities, with no end to the situation currently in sight.
The disruptions are placing additional pressure on the aviation industry, which has already been struggling in recent years with the consequences of wars across the Middle East and soaring fuel prices.
Saudi Arabia had expected the United States to intervene more directly in Riyadh's war against the Houthis. For now, however, the Americans have limited their involvement to providing intelligence, identifying targets and assisting in the planning of Saudi attacks, without carrying out their own direct strikes in Yemen.
On Saturday, Trump signaled that he might change that position and take a more active role in supporting Saudi Arabia's military campaign.

No, Ukraine's strikes on Yandex data centers didn't cripple Russian influence ops
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
17:31:46 UTC
02:31:46 KST

No, Ukraine's strikes on Yandex data centers didn't cripple Russian influence ops
Ukrainian drone strikes against Russian data centers sparked viral claims about a sudden drop in Russian influence operations on social media — even as experts see no evidence to support this.
Kyiv struck data centers run by Yandex — Russia's "answer to Google" — in three different regions between Oct. 9 and 11, a response to Russian strikes against similar facilities in Ukraine.
Yandex acknowledged the attacks, noting that its data center in Vladimir Oblast had to be shut down due to damage and reported disruptions to various online services within Russia.
Soon after, commentators on social media began reporting an alleged decrease in activity by "Russian bots" online, linking this to Ukrainian strikes on Yandex.
President Volodymyr Zelensky even alluded to this in his address to the Warsaw Security Forum, saying it is "a little easier to breathe on many social media platforms."
Yet beyond anecdotal examples circulating online, there is no data showing that the attacks on Yandex disrupted Moscow-backed disinformation and influence operations.
At least some of the claims appear to stem from a simple confusion of terms.
The bot confusion
The source of this confusion is a chart from the internet company Cloudflare showing that bot activity from Yandex's network dropped to 54.7% after a Ukrainian strike on a data center in Ryazan Oblast.
The rate then plummeted to 0.3% after the third data center was hit in Vladimir Oblast.
But the chart simply shows automated web page requests from Yandex's own infrastructure, primarily its search crawlers — bots that browse and index web content.
It has nothing to do with activity by what is commonly referred to as Russian bots or trolls on social media.
"No reliable graph can consolidate bot and troll activity across multiple social media platforms without their internal data that measures telemetry, traffic, and behavior," Roman Osadchuk, the director of Threat Intelligence at the LetsData tech company, tells the Kyiv Independent.
Osadchuk acknowledges a moderate dip in social media comments and posts, both by bots and real users, over the weekend, but regards it as a coincidence.
This decrease "could be explained by tech complications on the side of companies that run influence operations like SDA or Structura, or it could simply be lower output from the weekend shift on the troll/bot farm, or a general fluctuation in comments."
No major fact-checking or disinformation-monitoring organizations reported a radical drop in Russian disinformation activity on social media, though some European officials echoed the claims.
In Poland, Tomasz Siemoniak, a minister coordinating the work of special services, claimed he had received exclusive information from the country's internal security service, the ABW, about a "radical decline in Russian bot activity online" due to the strikes.
But no such data has been published, and local disinformation monitors report no drop in Moscow-backed influence operations.
The Disinformation Analysis Center at Poland's state-run Research and Academic Computer Network (NASK) recorded no significant decrease in activity by disinformation accounts between Sept. 30 and Oct. 11.
"Only isolated cases of individual accounts becoming inactive were observed, but there is no basis for conclusively linking these instances to the attacks in question," the center's Daria Tomczuk told the Kyiv Independent.
Nor is there convincing evidence in other European countries.
Czech Member of the European Parliament Tomas Zdechovsky shared a graph purportedly linking the Ukrainian attacks to a drop in online activity around the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party.
But the German technology website Rohtext disputed this, noting that the graph does not list a source or explain a methodology. Rohtext reported no links between AfD activity and Yandex centers.
Why striking Russian servers won't silence trolls
Another theory that appeared online is that damage to Yandex data centers may have disrupted the infrastructure supporting Moscow's influence operations.
However, Russian disinformation is believed to heavily rely on decentralized networks of proxies abroad, which would not be disrupted by strikes against Russian data centers.
"There's a lot of documented evidence that these troll operations operate in other countries like North Macedonia or the Philippines," Dave Troy, a disinformation researcher and investigative journalist, told the Kyiv Independent.
Given the blockade on the Russian internet imposed by the outside world and heavy domestic restrictions, it simply makes more sense to run disinformation operations from abroad, he adds.
This proxy strategy also makes it hard to pinpoint a drop in activity that is decisively Russian.
One commentator pointed to a drop in impressions under posts linked to Storm-1516, a Kremlin-backed disinformation group.
But Bot Blocker, a group monitoring Russian disinformation, countered that the bot network used by Storm-1516 is most likely a neutral commercial engagement-for-hire provider, not affiliated with a particular state.
"This engagement amplifying network is quite unlikely to be run from Yandex data centers," Bot Blocker told the Kyiv Independent.
Troy warns that misstating the impact of Ukrainian strikes on Russian data centers could pose a strategic risk by itself.
"The danger is thinking a specific victory has been achieved, but in reality the threat lies elsewhere and must still be assessed and fought," he adds.

The Guardian view on Burnham’s Brexit reset: overdue, but proceed with care | Editorial
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
17:30:25 UTC
02:30:25 KST

The German philosopher GWF Hegel famously evoked the owl of Minerva when discussing the historical wisdom that comes through hindsight. This autumn, she has flown tirelessly over the landscape of British politics. Party conference season was dominated by conflicting Labour and Conservative accounts of the 1970s and 80s. And a decade after the United Kingdom voted to leave the European Union, Andy Burnham this week abandoned all equivocation over the damage – economic but also strategic – that resulted from that decision.
Having declared that it is time to “face up to the reality that Brexit has done more harm than good”, Mr Burnham told the House of Commons on Monday that it would be a “dereliction of duty” not to explore all options for closer relations with Brussels. Though he confirmed that in this parliament he will honour the red lines in Sir Keir Starmer’s Labour manifesto, all bets will subsequently be off.
A long-delayed reset summit, Mr Burnham also announced, will take place next month with deals on food and drink and youth mobility to be negotiated. The former Labour leader Neil Kinnock asserted to an Italian newspaper on Tuesday that the prime minister’s “obvious” eventual objective was to rejoin.
That might well be contested in Downing Street. But as has become the norm in this overture phase of Mr Burnham’s premiership, his Commons statement was bracingly expansive and forthright. It also had the signal virtue of being correct in its diagnosis and prescription. Nevertheless, the reality of reopening the most divisive debate of recent British history will be drawn out, obstacle-strewn and fraught with political risk.
Labour’s hyper-caution over revisiting the EU relationship has increasingly been at odds with polls indicating a substantial majority of the public supports closer ties. But the devil will be in the detail. In the red wall, in particular, much will depend on the prime minister’s undoubted persuasive powers. The need to undo the economic self-harm of Brexit was not something that Mr Burnham chose to emphasise while campaigning for his seat in the leave-voting constituency of Makerfield.
For its part, the EU itself is in flux and may have new red lines of its own. Responding to a more menacing geopolitical environment, Brussels is contemplating deeper coordination in areas such as defence and economic policy. The direction of travel is already evident in the “Made in Europe” strategy, which threatens to leave British-based car manufacturers out in the cold.
As that risk illustrates, it is overwhelmingly in Britain’s interests to be acting in concert with the EU, rather than flailing in sorry isolation on the sidelines. Following the visceral mutual distrust of the Tory Brexit years, Sir Keir restored a basic if circumscribed civility to relations between the UK and the EU. Mr Burnham’s boldness can now open up new possibilities down the line for “a real reset”, to use the formulation of one EU diplomat.
It will not have escaped Mr Burnham’s notice that such a prospect would unite progressive Britain behind it, and could significantly boost Labour’s percentage vote share. His overriding early theme has been the need to rectify the political “wrong turns” of past decades. Beginning the long task of doing so on Brexit is brave, but it promises significant dividends for his premiership and, much more importantly, the country.

The Guardian view on probation: overcrowded prisons need an outlet | Editorial
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
17:29:03 UTC
02:29:03 KST

The early release of thousands of prisoners was bound to be awkward for a new prime minister. Politically speaking, Andy Burnham’s decision to exclude those convicted of manslaughter and some other offences made sense. But with about 2,000 offenders being freed this month, the risk is that by cutting the numbers, he has added to overcrowding problems inside. With the prison and probation services under huge pressure, and a ballot on industrial action expected, there is an urgent need for moves from the government to strengthen both.
Shielded from view as prisons are, and despite the efforts of campaigners and writers such as Jimmy McGovern to draw attention to them, conditions have been allowed to deteriorate to a shocking extent. The latest annual report from the prisons watchdog drew a dismal picture of rampant drug use, organised crime and governors wasting time on form-filling. It warned that the Prison Service’s managers appear to favour crisis management over improvement.
Criticisms of the probation service of England and Wales contained in the latest report by the Institute for Government’s (IfG) appear measured, by comparison. Probation’s problems are less attention-grabbing, and senior leaders are not singled out for blame. But analysis of the impact of sentencing reforms, combined with ongoing staff shortages and tagging failures, are cause for very serious concern all the same. This is a vital public service that was already facing serious difficulties before its caseload was massively enlarged.
Problems date back to the failed part-privatisation of the service. The IfG highlights the toll of “near-constant organisational change”. One result has been de-skilling, with staff increasingly reliant on risk-management protocols rather than judgment. The number of recalls to prison due to breached conditions, rather than new offences, undermines rehabilitation and worsens overcrowding. But an overstretched workforce seems unable to break this cycle. There is simply not enough time to build relationships.
The failure to fit 45% of tags on time is obviously unacceptable; ministers need to get a grip and explain what is happening. The IfG also recommends further sentencing reforms aimed at making the system clearer. Rightly, it points out that the growing gap between jail sentences imposed in court and time actually served risks undermining trust and angering victims. Similarly, licence periods should end at the point where supervision ceases. Currently, there is a pretence that more people are serving community sentences than is actually the case. This places the probation service in a false position.
The pay dispute is the immediate challenge. As part of a settlement, ministers should pledge to rebuild capacity and fill vacancies. Looking further ahead, probation needs closer links to the local services that can help offenders to get back on their feet. The merger with the Prison Service has failed to deliver promised gains.
Managing risks to the public must remain a priority. But Enver Solomon, who leads Nacro, the criminal justice charity, is right to argue for a more “person-centred” style of probation work. No one who knows anything about prisons thinks that they are fulfilling their rehabilitation remit. A renewed focus on purposeful activity inside jails is needed. But as increased numbers of prisoners are diverted towards probation, the service needs resources to deliver what is asked of it.

UN adopts Durban resolution despite antisemitic legacy of anti-Zionist declaration
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
17:28:27 UTC
02:28:27 KST

The UN adopted a resolution calling for the full implementation of the 2001 Durban Declaration, despite arguments that it platforms antisemitism and hatred of Israel.
On Monday, the UN General Assembly formally adopted the new political declaration and draft resolution (A/81/L.4) with 95 countries voting in favor, five against, and 37 abstaining. Argentina, Australia, Canada, Micronesia, and Israel voted against. The United Kingdom, Austria, Germany, Italy, New Zealand, Japan, South Korea, and various members of the European Union abstained.
The draft calls for the comprehensive implementation of and follow-up to the Durban Declaration and Programme of Action (DDPA). The core focus is on “reparatory justice,” “national anti-racism policies,” and “protections against racial profiling and structural bias embedded within contemporary technologies.”
During the debate, Israel’s ambassador to the United Nations, Danny Danon, condemned the attempt to grant further legitimacy to the Durban Conference, 25 years after it took place.
Danon recalled that images of Hitler were circulated during the conference, Zionism was equated with racism, and Jewish participants were physically assaulted. He also noted that during this year’s gathering, Iran’s representative described Zionism as a “doctrine of supremacy.”
Durban Conference became a platform for antisemitism, hatred of Israel
“The Durban Conference was supposed to combat racism, but instead became a platform for antisemitism and hatred of Israel,” said Danon. “25 years later, the United Nations continues to celebrate this disgrace and attempts to rewrite history.”
“Israel will not support a resolution that legitimizes antisemitism under the guise of fighting racism. Durban’s legacy deserves no further recognition, no further celebration, and no further legitimacy. It is time to remove this stain from the United Nations once and for all.”
This follows recent 25th anniversary celebrations of the 2001 Durban Conference at the United Nations.
As a result of campaigning by Danon and Israel’s Foreign Ministry, a record number of 46 countries boycotted the 25th-anniversary events.
According to Mike Waltz, US ambassador to the UN, the US walked out “in protest, as we did at the original conference in 2001.”
Original South African conference boycotted by Israel, US
The original World Conference Against Racism in Durban, South Africa, was famously boycotted midway through by both Israel and the United States.
During the 2001 events, Jewish attendees faced physical harassment, and thousands of copies of the conspiracy theory antisemitic text The Protocols of the Elders of Zion were distributed. Images of Adolf Hitler were also circulated.
The conference has since become synonymous with anti-Zionist discrimination, and is considered by many the birthplace of modern anti-Israel rhetoric.
Preceding the conference was the NGO Forum, which had over 7,000 participants gather to create a pre-planned and coordinated anti-Israel strategy. It was here that the intentional use of words such as “genocide,” “war crimes,” and “apartheid” entered the scene.
While Israel is not explicitly cited or mentioned by name in the newly updated text of the resolution, it continues to object due to the text’s explicit mandate to “reaffirm” the original 2001 Durban Declaration and Programme of Action (DDPA) in its entirety.
Israel argues that it is the only country or geopolitical conflict implicitly criticized within the DDPA.

RAF Bases Test Resilience During Exercise Agile Owl
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
18:26:21 BST
02:26:21 KST

Royal Air Force personnel have successfully completed Exercise Agile Owl, a week long exercise designed to test resilience, operational effectiveness and the ability to generate combat air power from multiple locations.
The exercise saw both RAF Coningsby and RAF Lossiemouth challenged through a series of realistic operational scenarios aimed at testing continuity of operations during periods of disruption.
Alongside the station-focused activity, the Typhoon Air Wing exercised its ability to deploy aircraft and personnel away from their main operating bases, including Kinloss Barracks which is no longer an active airfield. This demonstrates the flexibility and agility required to sustain air operations from dispersed locations.
The ability to disperse aircraft and personnel to protect operational capability is pivotal in maintaining national security.
"Exercise Agile Owl has provided an excellent opportunity to test our ability and capacity to operate away from the home base. The current operational climate requires us to react and deploy at short notice, and it is essential that we demonstrate our ability to support both our aircraft and, more importantly, our people."
Group Captain Paul Hanson
Typhoon Air Wing Commander
Recent conflicts have highlighted the importance of maintaining the ability to operate effectively from challenging and unfamiliar environments. The ongoing war in Ukraine, alongside recent tensions in the Middle East, has reinforced the need for armed forces to remain agile, adaptable and ready to respond in rapidly changing circumstances.
"The exercise gave us the opportunity to explore our capacity to react to threat scenarios while simultaneously supporting both operations at RAF Coningsby and deployed locations. I'm proud of the way our people attacked the problems, fully engaging with the scenarios and confidently resolving a range of challenges as they arose. Lessons identified during the exercise will be used to further strengthen procedures, enhance resilience and ensure the continued ability of both Coningsby and our sister station at RAF Lossiemouth to support UK and NATO defence commitments.”
Group Captain Andy Hampshire
Station Commander RAF Coningsby
Dispersed operations also complicate an adversary's ability to identify, target and disrupt critical military capabilities, helping to ensure that combat air power can continue to be generated when and where it is needed to maintain national security.
“This exercise has been a truly collaborative exercise, incorporating multiple platforms, units, and personnel from across the Air Wings, Air Bases, and the Civilian Agencies.
This exercise has demonstrated our ability to successfully disperse our aircraft, enable dispersed locations, sustain our aircraft and personnel whilst maintaining operations, and finally recover in good order back to our home bases. It has also provided a great learning environment to allow us to refine our plans and shape our training, so that we are fully prepared for whatever the future may hold.”
Wing Commander Sharon
Exercise Coordinator at RAF Lossiemouth
By demonstrating our ability to maintain operational effectiveness in challenging environments, the Royal Air Force reassures the British public and international partners that it remains ready to fly, fight and win, protecting the UK, its interests and its allies whenever called upon to do so.

Saudi Arabia strikes strategic oil depots near Yemen capital
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
17:26:08 UTC
02:26:08 KST

Saudi Arabia has launched a series of strikes on a strategic oil depot on the outskirts of Yemen’s capital, Sana’a, while later on Tuesday it said it had intercepted missiles launched toward Dharan, location of the headquarters of the national energy behemoth Saudi Aramco.
The attacks on both sides were a fresh escalation of the conflict between Riyadh and the Iran-backed Houthi forces. Before its offensive on Tuesday, a Saudi spokesperson warned civilians to leave the target area, in an apparent attempt to strike fear into the local population before the biggest attack so far on Houthi energy infrastructure.
The Central Sabaha Station oil depot on the western side of the city contains large tanks that often hold substantial quantities of fuel derivatives, although the Yemeni Oil Company said its storage facilities were empty at the time of the attack.
Houthi oil depots at the Ras Isa port in Hodeidah, the subject of Israeli attacks in 2024, were also struck in 10 waves of attacks apparently aimed at immobilising the Houthi army as it continues its push south, including towards the city of Taiz.
Earlier the Saudis also struck what they believe to be a Houthi leadership hide-out in the Bani Mu’in area in the Razih border district, west of Saada governorate, northern Yemen.
The strike on the oil depot appeared to be the Saudi response to a Houthi attack on King Khalid international airport in Riyadh on Saturday that killed 13 people and left 300 injured. The airport is closed until Saturday at the earliest, a blow to an economy that is trying to show its security makes the country a safe place to invest.
A Houthi spokesperson responded to the attack on its oil storage by warning “all employees and citizens present near any facility affiliated with Aramco Petroleum in Riyadh to evacuate it and stay away from it, as it is a legitimate target for our forces”.
Later in the day, the Saudi-led coalition said it had intercepted a missile fired at Dharan, the location of the headquarters of Saudi Aramco. It said fragments from the interception fell on a residential area. Witnesses reported hearing loud booms. There was no official comment or confirmation from Aramco.
The incident underlined how Saudi Arabia has complete air dominance over Yemen while the Houthis have to reply using drones and missiles which can be intercepted.
Baraa Shiban, a Yemen specialist at the defence thinktank Royal United Services Institute (Rusi), warned “Saudi Arabia is struggling to respond to the Houthi’s improved arms technology. Until relatively recently Houthi missiles and drones fell in desert areas or if they got through were intercepted. They have learned how to deploy drones that fly lower and are smaller, and are less easy to detect. They are cheap and it does not take many to get through to be effective”.
But the two sides’ dramatic threats to set ablaze the enemy energy infrastructure symbolised how the conflict is escalating rather than blowing itself out.
Donald Trump complained that the Houthis were “behaving very badly” and said he would “never forget” their attacks, which he suggested were an attempt to influence the US midterm elections next month. But he stopped short of announcing any new military action.
The latest phase of the conflict between the Saudis and the Houthis began last month after the rebels seized key areas along the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, a critical waterway for the transportation of Gulf oil and other goods at the southern end of the Red Sea off Yemen.
This week, the Houthis have come closer to throttling the southern city of Taiz, drawing close enough to the city edges to fire rockets into residential areas. City leaders have made repeated appeals to the Yemeni government for military equipment while public health professionals warned of a shortage of medicines for patients in intensive care.
Government-aligned forces sent reinforcements to the south-western district of Al-Mudarabba in Lahij governorate as well as the mountain district of Al-Waz’iyya.
But anti-Houthi forces inside Yemen are not themselves united: a group known as the Southern Transitional Council has been taking a more prominent role in the fight against the Houthis – even though its main objective is to secede from the country’s north.
On Tuesday, Aidarous al Zubaidi, the exiled STC leader, gave a rare address declaring “a popular mobilisation in defence of the south, and its national liberation project” – including by repelling the invading Houthi militia.
Al Zubaidi, now based in Abu Dhabi, made clear he still supported a plan to eventually hold a referendum on the independence of South Yemen.
Zubaidi’s organisation remains banned in Yemen and he has been charged with treason, but there are incremental behind-the-scenes talks under way testing whether the Saudi crown prince Mohammed bin Salman is prepared to legitimise the STC and even permit Zubaidi to return. Reinstatement of the STC would be seen as a betrayal by the current Yemen president, Rashad al-Alimi, but his usefulness to Saudi Arabia is reduced if he does not have the same military forces at his disposal as Zubaidi.

Air raid alerts sound in Kyiv only after blasts are heard
Air alerts sounded in Kyiv on the night of Oct 12 only after several explosions had already ripped through the city.

FUZHOU, Oct. 13 (Xinhua) -- China on Tuesday handed out death sentences to three leading members of a criminal gang led by the Wei family, which carried out criminal activities, including telecom fraud and gambling, in Myanmar.
Three others were sentenced to life imprisonment, while another 55 face jail terms ranging from three years and three months to 24 years, according to rulings made by the Intermediate People's Court of Quanzhou and People's Court of Nan'an, both in Fujian Province in east China.
The courts also correspondingly imposed supplementary punishments including fines, confiscation of property and deportation.
The courts found that the criminal gang led by the Wei family used its influence and set up multiple scam compounds in Kokang, Myanmar, where it exercised armed control and carried out various crimes starting from 2019, including telecom fraud, gambling, blackmailing, organized prostitution, drug trafficking and illegal border crossings.
Their gambling and fraud crimes involved 12.2 billion yuan (around 1.81 billion U.S. dollars), according to the court rulings.
Two Chinese nationals were killed as a result of the criminal gang led by the Wei family during its handling of disobedient personnel involved in telecom fraud, in collaboration with other scam rings, the courts said.
A member of the Wei family gang abused the militia force it controlled in wanton killings, causing the deaths of two Chinese nationals, the courts added.
The defendants were convicted of seven charges including murder and fraud, according to the court rulings. Lawmakers, political advisors, and family members of those involved, among others, watched from the public gallery as the verdicts were announced. ■

BEIJING, Oct. 13 (Xinhua) -- During their talks in Beijing on Tuesday, Chinese President Xi Jinping and Botswana's President Duma Gideon Boko announced the elevation of bilateral relations to a comprehensive strategic cooperative partnership.
Noting that this year marks the 105th anniversary of the founding of the Communist Party of China and the 60th anniversary of Botswana's independence, Xi said the two countries' ruling parties should strengthen cooperation and deepen exchanges on governance experience.
China supports Botswana in pursuing a development path suited to its national conditions, Xi said. He called on both sides to further improve the framework for economic and trade cooperation, and tap into new opportunities created by China's zero-tariff policy for African countries that have diplomatic ties with China.
China is ready to strengthen cooperation with Botswana in the digital economy, agriculture, animal husbandry and other sectors, and to carry out the smart education project, Xi added.
On promoting China-Botswana and China-Africa mining cooperation, Xi said Africa's resources belong to Africa, and this is the premise for cooperation.
China is willing to share its own experience and help African countries formulate mining development plans tailored to their national conditions, and China will encourage Chinese enterprises to transfer green technologies suited to African conditions, Xi said.
He said China will continue to promote China-Africa mining cooperation to move up the value chain and explore affordable, sustainable and innovative financing models.
Noting that Africa's resources should not become a tool for geopolitical rivalry, Xi said China welcomes all parties' genuine contributions to Africa's development and stands ready to work with Africa to create a more enabling environment for investment and business operations.
China has lifted all its poor population out of poverty and forged a successful development path with Chinese characteristics, from which Botswana has much to learn, Boko noted.
He said that Botswana highly values its ties with China, and will firmly adhere to the one-China principle and oppose any separatist moves toward "Taiwan independence" and any external interference in China's internal affairs.
Botswana is willing to strengthen development strategy alignment with China and welcomes more Chinese enterprises to invest and do business in Botswana, said Boko.
He added that the country stands ready to maintain close coordination and cooperation with China, uphold multilateralism, strengthen the solidarity of developing countries, promote Africa-China solidarity and cooperation, and make the global governance system more inclusive and representative.
After their talks, the two heads of state jointly witnessed the signing of multiple cooperation documents covering such areas as implementing the Global Security Initiative, Belt and Road cooperation, green minerals, health, and human resources.
During Boko's state visit to China, the two sides issued a joint statement on establishing a China-Botswana comprehensive strategic cooperative partnership.
Prior to the talks, Xi and his wife Peng Liyuan held a welcome ceremony for Boko and his wife Kaone Boko in the Great Hall of the People. Xi and Peng also held a welcome banquet for them in the evening. ■

Unknown Publisher

02:23:30 KST

LOS ANGELES, Oct. 13 (Xinhua) -- NASA and SpaceX launched a new commercial resupply mission to the International Space Station (ISS) on Tuesday, carrying scientific equipment and supplies to the orbiting laboratory.
A SpaceX Dragon spacecraft carrying about 2,860 kilograms of cargo lifted off at 6:33 a.m. Eastern Time (1033 GMT) from Cape Canaveral Space Force Station in the U.S. state of Florida.
After stage separation, the Falcon 9 rocket's first-stage booster returned to Earth and landed at the Space Force station.
The Dragon spacecraft is expected to dock autonomously with the ISS at about 11 a.m. Eastern Time (1500 GMT) on Thursday, according to NASA.
The spacecraft is delivering supplies for the station's crew and a range of scientific investigations, including the final set of ISS Roll-Out Solar Arrays, hardware for manufacturing artificial retinas in microgravity, and three-dimensional heart tissue models to advance large-scale drug testing, according to NASA.
The spacecraft is scheduled to remain at the space station until mid-November before departing the orbiting laboratory and returning to Earth with time-sensitive research and cargo, splashing down off the coast of California.
The mission marks SpaceX's 35th commercial resupply services mission to the ISS for NASA. ■

15 states elected as members of UN Human Rights Council

Unknown Publisher

01:23:23 CST

UNITED NATIONS, Oct. 13 (Xinhua) -- The General Assembly on Tuesday elected 15 states as members of the UN Human Rights Council.
Through secret ballot, Burundi, Ghana, Nigeria, Zambia (for Africa); Japan, Jordan, Kuwait, Nepal (for Asia-Pacific); Moldova, Ukraine (for Eastern Europe); Brazil, the Dominican Republic, Uruguay (for Latin America and the Caribbean); Germany, Ireland (for Western Europe and other states) were elected.
The 15 states will serve three-year terms starting Jan. 1, 2027.
All 15 candidates were running unchallenged this year.
Burundi, Ghana, Japan, Kuwait, Brazil, and the Dominican Republic were re-elected.
The Geneva-based Human Rights Council is an intergovernmental body responsible for promoting and protecting all human rights around the world. It comprises 47 member states, with about one-third of its membership replaced each year through staggered three-year terms to ensure continuity.
To ensure equitable geographical representation, the council's seats are allocated among five regional groups: 13 for African States, 13 for Asia-Pacific States, six for Eastern European States, eight for Latin American and Caribbean States, and seven for Western European and other States. ■

Xi pointed out that the traditional China-Togo friendship was personally forged by leaders of an older generation of both countries, enjoying a solid foundation and growing ever stronger with the passage of time. China and Togo share aligned visions for friendly cooperation and enjoy broad prospects ahead, Xi said.
Xi called on the two sides to further enhance exchanges at all levels between the two parties and the two countries, deepen the sharing of experiences in governance, and firmly support each other on issues concerning core interests and major concerns.
China welcomes Togo to effectively utilize measures such as China's zero-tariff policy and the "green channel" for products exported to China, further enhance its role as a regional hub for trade and logistics, and facilitate the entry of more distinctive local and regional products into the Chinese market, Xi added.

Xi put forward four principles for the constructive participation of all parties in the settlement of hotspot issues in Africa.
First, adhering to the principle of "Africa-led." The African people are the true masters of Africa and should play a central role in regional affairs, Xi said.
Second, upholding fairness and justice. All participating parties should abide by the purposes and principles of the United Nations Charter and respect the sovereignty and territorial integrity of the countries concerned, he noted.
Third, promoting ceasing hostilities for peace. Wars and unilateral sanctions cannot fundamentally resolve conflicts between countries. It is imperative to uphold mutual respect, conduct extensive consultations, seek common ground while shelving differences, and practice mutual understanding and accommodation.
Fourth, addressing both symptoms and root causes. Efforts should focus on immediate security while planning for long-term development, Xi said.

Noting that next year marks the 55th anniversary of the establishment of diplomatic relations between the two countries, he said Togo is willing to enhance mutual trust with China, strengthen dialogue and communication, deepen enduring and mutually beneficial cooperation to jointly build a Togo-China community with a shared future for the new era, and better benefit the two peoples.
The Togolese side fully agrees with the important principles proposed by President Xi for the constructive participation of all parties in the settlement of hotspot issues in Africa, Faure said.
He expressed Togolese appreciation for China on its significant role in maintaining world peace and stability and jointly addressing global challenges, as well as the willingness to strengthen multilateral cooperation with China, jointly uphold multilateralism, and safeguard the interests of developing countries. ■

The decision was approved by Defense Minister Israel Katz and Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu in the security cabinet, a statement by Katz's office said.
The statement said the move was prompted by "specific intelligence and growing threats from enemies from within and outside," including drone attacks, attempted attacks on senior officials, intelligence gathering and smuggling.
The directive is set to take effect on Sunday and remain in force for six months, providing a temporary security measure while additional solutions are developed, it added.
The ban includes specific exemptions for drones operated by security agencies or on their behalf, as well as ground-tethered fiber-optic drones and SIM-controlled drones that have received the necessary authorization from Israel's Civil Aviation Authority.
The move is part of a broader series of Israeli measures aimed at countering drone-related threats, including import restrictions and regulatory measures. ■

Iran seeking 'harder targets' for attacks abroad, UK warns
October 13, 2026
The leader of the UK's MI5 domestic security service on Tuesday said that Iran is expanding the scope of the hybrid attacks that it coordinates in the UK and elsewhere.
In an annual address outlining his assessment of threats to the UK, MI5 chief Ken McCallum said a "major shift this year has been Iranian ambitions to come at harder targets, like military sites."
The remarks come after the US removed about a dozen long-range bombers from Fairford air base in the southern UK last week following an incident on September 27 during which several men were arrested on "suspicion of terrorism offenses." An investigation is ongoing.
Uptick in 'Iran-linked operations'
McCallum said these kinds of incidents were "not unique," warning that Tehran is seeking targets beyond Iranian diaspora living abroad who oppose the regime.
These include Iranian media organizations, Israeli interests in the UK, and arson attacks on Jewish sites that British authorities say were carried out by Iranian proxies.
The spy chief warned of an "unflinching response" to "those who seek to cause mayhem on British streets – whether hired thugs here or their paymasters overseas."
He added that more than 50 people have been arrested in "Iran-linked operations" in the UK over the past year.
However, McCallum said Iran's ability to carry out more severe and complex attacks using explosive drones remains limited by the sophistication of the proxies and criminals it has used for operations in the UK.
UK says Fairford air base incident likely coordinated by Iran
On Monday, UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham said the suspected plot at Fairford air base was coordinated in Iran and was "almost certainly" directed by Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard (IRGC).
The degree of competence exhibited and the threat posed by the group of young British nationals from London is not entirely clear but seems potentially limited. Seven suspects are currently released on bail under strict conditions pending the investigation
Preliminary reports suggest that despite a widespread security alert and bomb squad deployment the day of the incident, investigators ultimately did not find viable explosives in the "suspicious vehicles" that were reported near the base. They did, however, find accelerants like petroleum.
"We will crack down on Iran's use of criminal networks, using our full range of powers to target them and their funding streams, and we will bring further sanctions to restrict the capacity of Iran and the IRGC to do us harm," Burnham said.
Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband said on Monday that his department had summoned Iran's ambassador to "reiterate" the message that Britain "will not tolerate attacks on our soil."
He named Ruhollah Bazghandi, head of counterespionage operations in the IRGC and Shahram Ali Reza Tamarzadeh Jakki, an alleged facilitator for the Zindashti criminal network.
Miliband said they were being sanctioned for "their role in facilitating or engaging in hostile activity on behalf of the Iranian regime, with the clear intent of threatening, planning or conducting attacks overseas."
Tehran has accusations of involvement in the Fairford incident, along with other accusations of coordinating attacks in the UK.
RAF Fairford is a major military air field fairly close to the south coast of England. It's a rare European base from which the US operates heavy bombers, with the range to reach Iran amid the current conflict in the Gulf.

"Awkward and terrible" — the White House criticized Trump's new press secretary's first briefing
Kyiv • UNN
Trump's advisers criticized Katie Zachariah's first 15-minute briefing. The US president, however, said that she had done very well.
Some White House officials are questioning how long Katie Zachariah will remain press secretary after her first briefing on Tuesday, noting that her performance was unlikely to have satisfied U.S. President Donald Trump, UNN reports, citing CNN.
Details
Several advisers and officials gave negative assessments of the new White House spokesperson's performance in comments to CNN. One of them called her "terrible." Others described the performance as unusual, awkward, unnatural, and at times uncomfortable. Zachariah spent only about 15 minutes at the lectern, devoting most of that time to an opening speech in which she praised Trump's achievements. She called on only three reporters for questions before ending the briefing.
Some White House officials and Trump advisers expressed surprise at why the administration rushed Zachariah to the lectern.
"She should have spent two weeks undergoing intensive training on how to prepare answers to difficult questions before going out there," one of Trump's advisers told CNN before criticizing Zachariah's performance. "The best thing she did was announce the news about (Kimberly Guilfoyle's appointment as ambassador to Greece); at least that takes attention away from her performance."
"Why did they rush her out there?" a White House official asked in surprise. "There was literally no reason to put her out there on her second day on the job, especially unprepared."
After the briefing, Trump spoke favorably about Zachariah, telling reporters shortly afterward: "I thought she did very well."
We would add
The publication notes that the briefing was noticeably shorter than those that have become the norm recently. Briefings by former White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt lasted about 45 minutes on average. During her first briefing, she called on two representatives of the "new media," followed by an Associated Press correspondent. She also took questions from reporters standing in the aisles. Zachariah, meanwhile, called on reporters from the conservative outlet Breitbart (which occupied the "new media" seat), as well as Fox News and the Daily Mail. It appears that their names had been written down in advance.
Another adviser told CNN that although Zachariah's performance "was not brilliant," it was only her first press briefing. He expressed hope that Trump would be understanding toward her and give her a chance to prove herself.
According to CNN sources, Trump had been somewhat impressed by Zachariah's appearances on Fox News before ultimately hiring her. However, one adviser noted that participating in television discussions and speaking before the entire world from the official lectern are completely different things.
"Without a doubt, we all miss Karoline," one of the advisers said.
Zachariah said she was ending the briefing early because Trump would likely be answering reporters' questions shortly on the South Lawn of the White House before departing for Alaska.
"I am ending the briefing because President Trump is heading to the Marine One helicopter for our historic trip to Alaska, and we will be able to ask him all our questions there," she said.
It is currently unknown how frequently Zachariah will hold briefings for reporters. An analysis of the White House video archive conducted by CNN's "Reliable Sources" program showed that Leavitt (who left the position in August) held official briefings about once a week on average before the birth of her second child. During the four months before going on maternity leave at the end of April, she held 14 briefings.
Throughout the rest of 2025, she held another 49 briefings, including several in an unconventional format.

Russia accuses France of ‘piracy’ over tanker seizure
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13

Russia accuses France of ‘piracy’ over tanker seizure
The Russian Embassy in Paris has accused France of “piracy” after its naval forces seized an oil tanker in international waters near Madagascar, rejecting claims that the operation complied with international maritime law.
French President Emmanuel Macron announced the detention of the DF Peak on Monday, saying the vessel was suspected of sailing under a false flag and involvement in illegal fuel transportation.
The tanker was intercepted 450 nautical miles south of Reunion, a French island territory east of Madagascar, Macron said.
According to MarineTraffic, the DF Peak sails under Benin’s flag. Macron did not identify the owner but described the seizure as part of France’s campaign to “fight the ghost fleet wherever it may be in the world.”
The Russian Embassy called the operation a “flagrant violation of international law,” dismissing France’s references to maritime regulations and “international sanctions” as a “fig leaf” concealing “outright piracy and robbery.”
The embassy denounced the sanctions as illegitimate unilateral measures and said the French authorities failed to notify Russian diplomats of the seizure. It added that officials are checking whether any Russian nationals were aboard.
Western governments have used the term ‘shadow fleet’ to describe vessels that allegedly help Russia circumvent sanctions on oil exports. Moscow rejects the designation, arguing that it has no basis in international maritime law.
France previously detained the Tagor tanker in the Atlantic in June, and British forces seized the Smyrtos in the English Channel later that month. Moscow condemned both operations as piracy.
In July, the EU adopted a mechanism allowing member states to sell oil and other cargo confiscated from sanctioned vessels. President Vladimir Putin subsequently warned that Russia could retaliate against ships carrying Western cargo.
The latest seizure comes days after Putin and US President Donald Trump agreed to expand Russian diesel supplies to American and global markets in an effort to ease soaring fuel prices.
Washington subsequently issued a temporary sanctions waiver covering Russian diesel trade until April 7, 2027. Trump announced initial deliveries of more than 300,000 tons, followed by another 500,000 tons in November, and 1 million tons thereafter.

Cholera cases surge in Yemen as conflict intensifies, WHO says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
17:18:45 UTC
02:18:45 KST

Cholera cases surge in Yemen as conflict intensifies, WHO says
Yemen has reported 8,034 suspected cases and 27 deaths this year, with a quarter of cases from the last four weeks.
Suspected cholera cases in Yemen have tripled in the past three weeks, the World Health Organization (WHO) warns, as civilians continue to escape renewed fighting and seek safety in unsanitary camps.
Ramped up combat, which has pushed more than 200,000 people to flee their homes, the WHO said in a report on Tuesday, driving suspected cases from 217 in the week of September 6-12 to 647 in the week of September 27 to October 3.
“Families fleeing conflict are now facing another threat from diseases that can be prevented and treated,” said Annette Heinzelmann, the UN agency’s emergency director for the region.
“Without urgent funding and unimpeded access to safe water, vaccination and essential health services, outbreaks could spread rapidly among already vulnerable communities.”
This year, the global health watchdog said, Yemen had reported 8,034 suspected cases and 27 deaths, with a quarter of the suspected cases occurring in the last four weeks.
Five governorates hosting large numbers of displaced people in the southwest – Abyan, Lahij, al-Dhalea, Taiz and Aden – account for 92 percent of reported cases, they reported. The disease has also reached remote displacement camps in Hadramout in the country’s east that are particularly difficult for medical teams to access.
Emergency response underfunded
Cholera has ebbed and flowed for years as the conflict in Yemen has continued. In 2024, the WHO warned that the country was facing the “highest burden” of a global cholera outbreak. In 2017, a wave of the disease infected hundreds of thousands and killed at least 2,000.
Yemen was already suffering one of the “world’s worst humanitarian crises” and has seen an escalation of food insecurity and disease since fighting reignited between the Houthis and the government in July, shattering four years of fragile calm.
Cholera is an acute intestinal infection that spreads through food and water contaminated with the bacterium Vibrio cholerae, often from faeces. It causes severe diarrhoea, vomiting and muscle cramps.
Contracting the illness can be deadly when not treated with oral rehydration or antibiotics for more severe cases.
The Geneva-based WHO said it had only secured $3.78m of the $31m needed for its 90-day emergency response in Yemen.
The funding is intended to help expand disease surveillance in displacement sites, deploy rapid response teams, strengthen cholera treatment and improve infection prevention in health facilities and cholera treatment sites.

Greta Thunberg joins French student protests amid police clashes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
17:18:00 UTC
02:18:00 KST

Swedish activist Greta Thunberg joined French high school students protesting poor learning conditions Tuesday, as largely peaceful demonstrations were disrupted by clashes with police, who used tear gas to disperse crowds amid reports of thrown projectiles.
Four weeks into nationwide protests over teacher shortages, classroom overcrowding and dilapidated school buildings, more than 161,000 people took to the streets of major cities, according to interior ministry figures. That was down from 266,000 on a similar day of action a week ago.
The government has pledged to address the protesters' grievances, but with public finances already strained and borrowing costs at decades-high levels, it has limited options to invest in public services despite pressure from the streets.
The day started with pupils clustered outside schools with placards and megaphones. In Saint-Denis, a working-class suburb north of Paris, Thunberg joined one of the gatherings.
"We are inspired by the young people who are demanding their basic rights," she told reporters outside Lycee Paul Eluard, one of the schools where the protest movement first gained traction.
"Whether it's not funding schools enough, or the climate crisis, or social injustice crises ... it's about time that young people are stepping up and reclaiming that future."
In front of Paris City Hall, a youth orchestra played Antonin Dvorak's "New World Symphony." Some musicians had protest stickers on their cellos and violins.
The education ministry said 214 schools were closed, down from 800 on a similar protest day a week ago. It said 94.2% of high schools were open.
Six months out from a presidential election that polls suggest could usher in the first far-right government since World War Two, the youth protests, which have been supported by the left, have added to a sense of uncertainty and polarisation.
While most demonstrators marched peacefully on Tuesday, riot police charged and fired tear gas in locations in Paris, Lyon, Strasbourg and Nantes, while a fringe of protesters lit fires, vandalised property and hurled objects at police.
In central Paris, at least one car was set on fire during running confrontations between police and protesters down a central, tree-lined avenue.
In Lyon, the local authorities asked organisers to call off a march after a group of "hostile individuals" preceding the main procession vandalised shops and a petrol station and clashed with police.
While there was no immediate information on who was involved, it is not uncommon in France for street protests to attract so-called "casseurs", a fringe of rioters who seek to confront police and destroy property.
The protest movement and the police response have elicited polarised responses from leading contenders to replace Emmanuel Macron in next year's election.
Hard-left leader Jean-Luc Melenchon, who has a chance of reaching the runoff according to polls, joined one of the marches in Paris, where young protesters chanted his name.
"The police are losing their breath running after young people to beat them up and injure them," he said in a post on X.
"The only ones not losing their breath are the young people bravely protesting," he added, accusing the media of failing to show the extent of police brutality.
Far-right leader Marine Le Pen, the frontrunner in the presidential race according to polls, has denounced violence by protesters and called for those who have damaged schools - or their parents if they are minors - to pay for repairs.
The government has already introduced a bill that would allow precisely that. It is going through parliament.

Tens of thousands of demonstrators took to the streets across France on Tuesday in solidarity with high school students demanding better learning conditions, intensifying pressure on President Emmanuel Macron as he approaches the end of his term.
Some 161,500 people turned out, according to the interior ministry – more than double the 71,500 it gave for the last nationwide demonstrations on Thursday last week.
Unions helping organize Tuesday's rallies put the countrywide turnout at 480,000.
The numbers suggested snowballing street opposition to the government just six months before France votes for a successor to Macron, who is completing his maximum second mandate.
On Saturday, national demonstrations against the spiralling cost of living are to take place, and unions and student groups see the two protest currents fusing together.
The agitation comes as Macron's centrist government struggles to get a cost-cutting budget through parliament, in the teeth of worsening debt that has spooked the bond market.
Although most of Tuesday's demonstrations were peaceful, violence occurred on the sidelines of one of two marches in Paris, where the interior ministry said 41,500 people participated.
AFP journalists saw some cars set on fire and police fired tear gas as masked youths tried to erect barricades across roads and threw objects. Tear gas was also fired during a demonstration in Lyon.
Among those taking part in a demonstration in the Paris suburb of Saint-Denis was Swedish activist Greta Thunberg. She said she was there because "our future is being robbed".
University students were prominent in Tuesday's demonstrations, alongside teachers and union leaders.
They were also backed by far-left opposition France Unbowed (LFI) party, whose chief, presidential hopeful Jean-Luc Melenchon, was seen among crowds in Paris.
Thousands also marched in the cities of Nantes, Lyon, Lens, Strasbourg, Toulouse, Bordeaux and Marseille, according to police and AFP reporters.
"We stand in solidarity with the high schools that are worse off. We need real measures and proper dialogue, not repression," said 16-year-old Emeline, outside a Marseille school.
"We're here because we really feel we're not being heard by the government," said Nina, 17.
The student movement sprang up last month, with teenagers at France's lycees – high schools for those aged 15 to 18 – blocking the entrances to many schools to demand better classroom conditions.
Perceived heavy-handed reactions from police against the students drove many to join Tuesday's demonstrations.
One teen lost his hand when he picked up a police stun grenade during the protests, while another lost an eye, and another teeth when an officer fired a tear gas canister in his face.
Police have opened internal investigations into 34 allegations of violence against demonstrators.
Some 147 teaching staff have been injured in the protests, the education ministry said.
"We're not giving up the fight, whether it's for the high school students who were hit with a harsh crackdown, or for denouncing police violence," said Patricia, a 20-year-old university student in Paris who did not give her last name.
Some Indian tourists who wandered into the Paris demonstration said they were unnerved.
"Initially we were terrified," said Snehil Jain, a 45-year-old visiting Paris for a week with his wife.
"We had seen the media images of violence around these protests. But then we saw it was a peaceful protest, so we were OK then."
France's education ministry said 214 schools, mostly high schools, were closed Tuesday.
University student union l'Union Etudiante reported 90% of universities had closed nationwide to show support.
French students say they are determined to press their demands over absent teachers, dilapidated buildings, overcrowded schedules and other grievances.
They have dismissed a government pledge – made after last week's demonstrations – to send 3,000 substitute teachers to the 114 worst-affected schools.
"We are continuing the blockades. We are not budging," said Naouel, a high school student in Brest. She said she hoped the protests would continue after the half-term holidays, in late October.
Mariolino, a 16-year-old in Nantes, concurred. "Those who think the anger will disappear with the holidays just don't get it," he said.
On Monday, Macron had urged restraint from protesters, saying the issues "deserve time, consultations, discussion and respect".

An independent Premier League commission found Manchester City guilty of serious financial rule breaches between the 2009-10 and 2017-18 seasons, including arranging "sham" contracts with commercial partners to artificially inflate revenue.
The club appealed the ruling, rejecting the allegations and maintaining innocence. Sanctions have yet to be determined.

02:13:50 KST

Elon Musk has become the biggest political donor of the 2026 US midterm elections cycle, funneling about $366m into political groups and campaigns as he backs conservative candidates and rightwing causes. The world’s richest person has poured more than $276m into politics since July alone, some of the most rapid political spending in US history. He’s targeting key races that will determine which party controls the US Senate.
The New York Times first reported the spending numbers, which will be released in a federal filing on Thursday. Musk’s spending outpaces his 2024 presidential election contributions, in which he sunk nearly $300m into Donald Trump’s re-election campaign.
Musk’s political spending reasserts the SpaceX and Tesla CEO as the top Republican mega-donor and furthers his rightwing political influence. Musk, who led the Trump administration’s efforts to gut federal agencies last year, has become an international linchpin for far-right political movements in recent years as he aligns himself with anti-immigrant, conservative leaders.
The tech mogul’s spending spree is also a reversal from a period in the middle of last year when Musk claimed he would step back from making such large-scale political donations. The failures of his so-called “department of government efficiency” (Doge) and costly public backlash to his political influence, as well as a dramatic falling out with Trump, appeared to have dampened his interest in Washington politics.
Musk’s spending is spread throughout a series of political action committees, according to Reuters and the New York Times, including his own America Pac. His largest single spend was a $158m contribution to the Senate Leadership Fund, a Super Pac working to help Republicans retain control of the Senate. Musk has also given $10m to a Pac supporting Ken Paxton, the Texas Republican Senate candidate who is facing Democratic nominee James Talarico in a closely watched and intense race.
Other blockbuster Musk contributions include $76m for America Pac, $20m for the Congressional Leadership Fund Republican Super Pac and $10m for the Republican Governors Association. Musk also gave $10m in January to Nate Morris, a Kentucky Republican Senate candidate who withdrew from the race in May after accepting an offer to become the US ambassador to Colombia.
Some of Musk’s money is going to advertising and messaging campaigns that focus on anti-transgender rhetoric and accuse Democratic candidates of being radical socialists. Musk has long used X, the social media platform he owns, to target his political opponents, push election misinformation and attack trans rights. Over the weekend, he reposted a video from America Pac that showed Talarico’s previous statements on gender, calling it “madness”.
Musk’s immense spending involves some of the largest political donations in US history, but is still only a tiny fraction of his nearly $1tn wealth. The $366m in midterms spending represents about less than 0.04% of his net worth.

Votes without power: What future for Palestinians in Israel?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
17:11:56 UTC
02:11:56 KST

Breadcrumb
Votes without power: What future for Palestinian citizens in Israel?
East Jerusalem - Israel's general election on 27 October, which will fill all 120 seats in the Knesset, is widely seen as a referendum on Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.
But it is also a contest over the political standing of Palestinian citizens of Israel, who make up about a fifth of the population, the descendants of those who stayed on their land during the 1948 Nakba.
Their votes may decide which coalition bloc eventually governs, yet nearly every major Israeli party is working to keep them out of any future government.
“In the dominant political discourse, Israelis often address Arab citizens as subjects, not as equal citizens,” Raafat al-Jawabra, a researcher on Israeli affairs, tells The New Arab.
Most Israeli parties, he argues, do not see Palestinian citizens as a natural political partner, instead using them in their campaigns as a subject for fear and mobilisation.
Ahmad al-Safadi, a Jerusalem-based analyst of Israeli politics, says the problem goes beyond the Israeli right and far-right parties and their electoral campaigns.
Israeli parties, including those on the left, treat the Palestinian vote as a way to strengthen their own electoral base rather than as the voice of a community whose crises of crime, poverty, unemployment, and discrimination need clear policy answers.
The numbers explain why their vote matters. A recent poll by local Channel 12 puts the bloc led by former army chief Gadi Eisenkot and Netanyahu's coalition level at 52 seats each, with Palestinian parties on 12.
Salim Brik, a political scientist who researches Israeli parliamentary and party politics, argues that if Palestinian turnout rises above 65 percent, it could reshape the distribution of seats, possibly to the point where a list allied with Netanyahu fails to cross the electoral threshold.
That arithmetic has shaped the campaign. Netanyahu's Likud and Bezalel Smotrich's Religious Zionism have largely dropped conventional persuasion on the economy, the cost of living, and post-war reconstruction.
They are instead campaigning on the fear of Palestinian citizens and a promise of territorial "Judaisation" in the Galilee and the Negev (Naqab).
If Palestinian participation could decide the outcome, then delegitimising Palestinian citizens and casting any government that relies on them as a security risk serve the same goal.
An election built on exclusion
The clearest expression of this logic was the attempt to remove Palestinian parties from the ballot. In September, the Central Elections Committee, made up of lawmakers, voted to disqualify the United Arab List (Ra'am) and the Joint List.
Likud and its far-right allies backed the move, accusing both parties of supporting armed struggle and rejecting Israel's status as a Jewish state.
Last week, the Supreme Court unanimously reversed the decision, as it has done with similar disqualifications before. But the campaign still produced a result.
Sami Abu Shehadeh, leader of Balad, withdrew his candidacy after justices signalled they were ready to disqualify him over an article he wrote on 8 October 2023. He denied supporting Hamas or the attack.
Itamar Ben-Gvir, who led the case against him, called the withdrawal a victory. Adalah, the legal centre for Palestinian citizens, called the whole effort an attempt to delegitimise Palestinian citizens and their representatives.
According to al-Safadi, the attempts by Netanyahu and his religious right allies to push Palestinian parties out of politics have failed. He also sees a risk for the right. Continuing this rhetoric may lead Palestinian citizens to see the election as a direct confrontation with policies aimed at their political presence.
“Anti-Arab rhetoric could end up increasing turnout among people who now believe their exclusion will affect their daily lives and their place in their own towns,” he argues.
This would reverse a recent trend. Al-Safadi says the racism that followed 7 October, the war on Gaza and military operations in the West Bank depressed Palestinian participation in earlier votes. The same pressures, now accumulated, may push voters the other way.
This is where the right's strategy becomes risky. Recent polling has shown Smotrich's party struggling to clear the threshold, and he has moved further to the fringe by announcing a joint slate with Zehut (Identity) chairman Moshe Feiglin. Netanyahu has warned that a divided right in 1992 led to "the Oslo disaster", Yasser Arafat, and Hamas.
Brik's analysis shows why these warnings matter. In a race this close, a far-right list falling just below the threshold would remove a block of seats from Netanyahu's camp. Higher Palestinian turnout is one of the few factors that could cause that.
“Influencing which lists survive,” Brik says, “is one of the main electoral tools available to Arab parties”.
Al-Safadi adds in this regard that “Arab parties have also strengthened their position through joint electoral frameworks and surplus-vote agreements, which can give them more weight when seats are allocated”.
The fear campaign is therefore aimed at two audiences. To Jewish-Israeli voters, it presents Palestinian citizens as a threat to be contained. Its effect on Palestinian voters is less certain: it could discourage them from voting, or it could mobilise them.
The demographic battle for land inside Israel
The second pillar of the campaign turns long-standing state policy into a campaign pledge. Judaisation programmes, land allocation to Jewish communities, and demolitions in unrecognised villages have a long institutional history, and since 7 October they have been recast as security measures.
With Smotrich in control of settlement-related portfolios, the line between ministerial policy and campaign promise has largely disappeared. The rhetoric of settling "inside the Green Line" brings the logic of West Bank settlement into Israel proper.
The Green Line refers to the 1949 armistice demarcation line drawn after the Arab-Israeli War.
Brik places these issues at the centre of Palestinian citizens' concerns, especially in the Negev, where unrecognised Bedouin villages face problems of planning, land, and demolitions.
He points to the positions of Smotrich and Ben-Gvir, tensions in Palestinian towns such as Majd al-Kurum, and rhetoric about strengthening the Jewish presence in the Galilee and taking control of land owned or used by Palestinian citizens.
These issues, he says, will be on the agenda of any government that includes Netanyahu, Smotrich, and Ben-Gvir.
Al-Safadi ranks land as “the issue gaining the most importance among Arab voters”. Many Palestinians, he says, see what is happening inside Israel, in Jerusalem and in the West Bank as part of the same struggle over land, presence and control.
He argues that the targeting of Palestinian homes and continued planning restrictions and demolitions may strengthen collective action within the community to hold on to the land.
In this framing, land stops being a matter of planning and becomes a question about the limits of citizenship.
How different is Israel's opposition?
The Israeli opposition offers no real alternative. Ra'am made history in 2021 as the first independent Palestinian party to join an Israeli governing coalition, in the government that briefly removed Netanyahu.
Al-Jawabra's reading of the current field suggests the alternative is narrow. Most Jewish-Israeli parties, he says, still reject a government that depends on Palestinian parties, and 7 October marked a turning point in rhetoric that delegitimises Palestinian political participation.
Netanyahu's camp is the most hostile, but al-Jawabra sees no fundamental difference between Avigdor Lieberman and Netanyahu, Smotrich or Ben-Gvir on alliances with Palestinian parties.
Eisenkot has said he does not want such an alliance, though his tone is softer. He has also not ruled out working with Ra'am, while denying reports that he promised it a place in government.
Al-Jawabra names only Yair Golan, leader of the Democrats, as a prominent Israeli politician openly willing to cooperate and ally with Palestinian parties.
The result is that one camp campaigns against Palestinian citizens, and the other campaigns around them.
Votes without power
Even a strong Palestinian result may not translate into power. Brik argues that Palestinian parties have so far failed to turn their parliamentary weight into real bargaining power on land, settlements, and civil rights.
With most Jewish parties refusing to rely on them as direct coalition partners, they may end up as "a partner from outside" rather than a central part of government.
Al-Safadi warns of a return to marginalisation if competing Jewish parties can build coalitions that do not need Arab support, however many seats Palestinian parties win.
That is the central contradiction of this election. Palestinian votes may be needed to block one camp from reaching 61, while the government that forms keeps Palestinian parties at a distance.
Higher Arab turnout increases the community's potential influence, but it does not ensure that Jewish parties will treat it as a coalition partner.
For Palestinian citizens, the vote is a test of their position inside Israel's political system: whether their electoral weight becomes political influence, or whether their votes remain a number in the calculations of Jewish parties.
For residents of the Galilee, the Negev, and Jerusalem, the answer will depend less on the results than on what the next government does about land, demolitions, and planning, and on whether issues of rights and equality reach its agenda or are again postponed behind security and demography.

OpenAI’s blockbuster math proof isn’t what you think it is
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
17:11:03 UTC
02:11:03 KST

Mathematicians are finally making sense of the biggest event in decades for their field—and it’s stranger than anyone thought.
In early September OpenAI posted an inscrutable 166-page solution to the Navier-Stokes problem, one of math’s famed “million-dollar problems.” Initial accounts—including from the company itself—suggested that the proof, produced by an internal large language model (LLM), followed an approach devised by two Spanish mathematicians, Diego Córdoba and Luis Martínez-Zoroa.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
The model’s purported reliance on this “Spanish program” sparked a very public conflict between the company and Tristan Buckmaster, a mathematician at New York University. Buckmaster had spent much of the past year using LLMs to carry out that program alongside Levent Alpöge, an employee of OpenAI’s archrival, Anthropic. The pair cried foul after OpenAI—whose public models Buckmaster and Alpöge had been using—announced a Navier-Stokes proof that seemed to build upon and then leapfrog over their hard-won progress. But the resemblance between the two groups’ methods now seems merely skin-deep.
“When you go to the details, it is a different approach,” says Gonzalo Cao-Labora, a mathematician at EPFL, the Swiss Federal Institute of Technology in Lausanne. Scientific American spoke with several groups of experts working through the OpenAI paper. All said that it’s increasingly clear that the company’s proof does not follow the Spanish program.
The Navier-Stokes equations are the math behind every fluid. OpenAI solved the million-dollar problem by uncovering a flaw in the equations. The company’s artificial intelligence concocted a situation in which the equations declared that the speed of a fluid’s flow should be infinite—a so-called blowup that can’t happen in real life.
OpenAI solved the problem with an “agent swarm,” some 10,000 copies of its new, math-adept LLM, which spent about 88 hours of computing time and 130 billion tokens collectively constructing a blowup. The company’s math team threw all its resources at the problem after learning of significant progress made by Buckmaster and Alpöge. Buckmaster has alleged that OpenAI then attempted to bribe and threaten him to prevent him going public with insinuations of malfeasance, which he ultimately did.
Even top experts have found OpenAI’s proof of blowup to be completely impenetrable. But the agents coded their arguments into Lean, a programming language used to automatically verify that the logical steps toward a conclusion in a given sequence are all valid. Several prominent research groups are now using both the Lean code and the paper, with the help of other LLMs, to get a simplified, bird’s-eye view of the math involved.
The proof does somewhat resemble the Spanish program in that both exploit the same “loophole” in the official framing of the Navier-Stokes problem that was given by the Clay Mathematics Institute. It permits a mathematician to coax the equations into blowing up by constructing a weird, unphysical force that “stirs” the fluid just right. But closer examination reveals that OpenAI’s proof builds its unnatural force in a totally distinct way. The proof’s similarities to Buckmaster and Alpöge’s progress are superficial.
Of course, the OpenAI result’s novelty doesn’t mean it wasn’t influenced by the Spanish program. In fact, OpenAI initially used a smaller team of agents to prove an intermediate result, and some experts say that this more modest squad did follow the program. But the 10,000-agent swarm apparently realized a different path was required to finish the job. Of course, regardless of OpenAI’s insistence that its model couldn’t have seen Buckmaster’s specific user data, the “black box” nature of LLMs means we’ll likely never know the swarm’s exact chain of reasoning.
“I honestly don’t see a factual resolution of this,” says Camillo De Lellis, a mathematician at the Institute for Advanced Study in Princeton, N.J. “It’s not anymore a matter of clearly verifiable mathematical facts.”
What’s important, and perhaps a harbinger of math’s future, is how long it took experts to realize all this. When OpenAI revealed its landmark achievement on September 8, company officials clearly and repeatedly stated that their proof followed the Spanish program. Their combative exchange with Buckmaster before the release seems to suggest that they believed as much. And they weren’t initially certain whether his work had been incorporated in their model’s training data.
That is, OpenAI didn’t understand its own model’s proof. And still, more than a month later, no one fully does.
Last week the company dumped some 400 more results on the community. In the pre-AI era, at least a dozen of those results could have merited any human mathematician a Fields Medal—math’s Nobel Prize. There already aren’t enough experts on Earth to keep pace with the onslaught, and there’s no sign that it’s slowing down.

Trump says US Senate as hard to defend as House in midterms
