Trump says US Senate as hard to defend as House in midterms
WASHINGTON - US President Donald Trump said on Oct 13 Republicans face an equally difficult fight to retain control of the House of Representatives and the Senate in November’s midterm elections, despite forecasts showing a considerably tougher contest in the House.
“I would say equal,” Trump told reporters at the White House when asked which chamber would be harder for Republicans to defend in the Nov 3 vote.
Trump acknowledged the historical disadvantage facing the party of a sitting president, although he insisted that enthusiasm among Republican voters was surging.
“When you have a sitting president... no matter how good they seem to be, they’re at a big disadvantage, tremendous disadvantage,” he said.
“But I’m doing a tour right now, and I’m doing rallies. The level of enthusiasm for the Republican Party is way up.”
Trump’s assessment was striking because Republicans have been widely seen as particularly vulnerable in the House, while the Senate’s electoral map had initially offered them greater hopes of retaining control.
Election forecaster Decision Desk HQ gives Democrats a 77% chance of winning the 435-seat House, projecting that they will take 235 seats to the Republicans’ 200.
It also narrowly favours Democrats to capture the 100-seat Senate, giving them a 56% probability of victory and projecting a 51-49 majority.
Losing either chamber on Nov 3 would complicate Trump’s ability to push his agenda through Congress during the final two years of his presidency, while handing Democrats greater power to investigate his administration.
Trump has embarked on a campaign blitz in the closing weeks of the election, including rallies in traditionally Republican states where his party faces unexpectedly competitive Senate races.
History offers little comfort to the president.
The party holding the White House has almost invariably lost seats in midterm elections, with just three exceptions in the House since 1934, according to figures compiled by the American Presidency Project.
Franklin D. Roosevelt’s Democrats gained nine House seats in 1934, while Bill Clinton’s party picked up four in 1998 and George W. Bush’s Republicans gained eight in 2002.
The worst modern midterm drubbing came in 1938, when Roosevelt’s Democrats lost 72 House seats, followed by Barack Obama’s Democrats losing 63 in 2010.
Trump himself presided over a split verdict in his first midterms in 2018, when Republicans lost 41 House seats but gained two in the Senate. AFP

Who is Yuki Imai, the Japanese journalist Russia has arrested on espionage charges?
A Japanese journalist has been detained on suspicion of espionage on Sakhalin, Russia’s Federal Security Service (FSB) said. The agency identified him as a Japanese national and a correspondent for the newspaper Hokkaido Shimbun but did not release his name. He was detained in Yuzhno-Sakhalinsk shortly before he planned to leave Russia and taken to Moscow.
The FSB released footage of the operation with the detainee’s face blurred. Officers appear to have seized him at a hotel. The footage shows officers forcing him to unlock his devices, and he appears surprised when they accuse him of espionage.
The FSB said the journalist was gathering information about Russian military personnel on instructions from Japanese intelligence. According to the agency, he was collecting data on the number of Kuril Islands residents mobilized for the war in Ukraine and on residents who volunteered to fight.
The detainee is 34-year-old Yuki Imai, according to the case record from Moscow’s Lefortovsky District Court. On October 13, the court ordered him held in custody in an espionage case under Article 276 of Russia’s Criminal Code. He faces up to 20 years in prison.
Imai had been visiting Russia since 2014. His most recent visit began in the summer of 2026, according to the news outlet Ostorozhno, Novosti (1, 2). He studied at St. Petersburg State University and posted photographs from his trips around Moscow and St. Petersburg. He said he had “a bit of an interest in Soviet military equipment,” as well as Russian culture — classical music, ballet, and Soviet cinema. The footage of his detention showed a book by Ivan Bunin in his suitcase.
According to Ostorozhno, Novosti, Imai had recently published articles about the State Duma elections and the unveiling of a monument in Khabarovsk commemorating the Soviet Union’s victory over Japan. He also wrote about Russia’s strengthening ties with North Korea.
During his most recent trip, Imai visited Primorsky Krai, with stops in Vladivostok and Nakhodka and a visit to a children’s arts center there. He interviewed Russian-speaking residents of Japan and took an interest in life in the Russian Far East, the Soviet-Japanese War, and friendship between Russia and Japan.
Imai’s most recent article, published on October 5, is a report from Yuzhno-Sakhalinsk about the presence of North Korean nationals in the region.
News of Imai’s detention came amid reports that Tokyo had extradited a member of the Russian group Qilin to Germany, according to the news outlet Agentstvo. Japanese authorities detained the 28-year-old Russian national in May on suspicion of involvement in a September 2024 cyberattack on a logistics company in Germany. Qilin is ransomware used by hackers, including those linked to North Korea.
The last time a Japanese journalist was detained in Russia on espionage allegations was in 2019. He was accused of trying to obtain classified materials about Russia’s military capabilities in the Far East and was expelled from the country.
Russian authorities use detained foreigners in exchanges for Russians facing prosecution abroad. For example, in 2023, Russia charged Wall Street Journal correspondent Evan Gershkovich with espionage. A court sentenced him to 16 years in a penal colony. Gershkovich was freed in a prisoner exchange with Western countries in 2024.
Relations between Russia and Japan deteriorated after Putin made his first trip to the Kuril Islands in August, visiting Iturup. In response, Japan summoned the Russian ambassador and lodged a “strong protest.”

Baku arrests dozens as hijab ban empties schools
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
17:06:41 UTC

Baku arrests dozens as hijab ban empties schools
TEHRAN — “I don’t have a single B on my report card. Is this the respect I get?” The girl standing at the school gate was crying, and the officials in front of her did not move. “Have I ever done anything wrong? And now you’re telling me I can’t enter the school. Why should I have to give up my religion?”
Video of the exchange spread across Azerbaijan within hours. Then Instagram and TikTok began failing for many users.
On September 21, the Cabinet of Ministers adopted Resolution No. 309, which bans school clothing that breaks uniformity or conflicts with the “principle of secularism.”
The text never mentions the hijab. On October 6, the same standard was extended to teachers, and by the second week of the month, principals in Baku and the provinces were stopping girls at the gate.
About 96 percent of Azerbaijanis identify as Muslim. For a girl who covers her hair, the decree offers two options: remove the scarf or stay home.
Classrooms empty, parents at the gates
Many families refused both. At School No. 69 in Baku’s Balakhani district, students walked out after classmates were barred and unfurled a banner saying the hijab is no obstacle to education. Students at School No. 322 in the capital did the same.
The pattern repeated in Masally, Jalilabad and the township of Hokmali. Boys joined the boycotts. In one Baku neighborhood, parents said they would keep their sons at home until the girls were readmitted. Footage showed students hugging teachers and sobbing outside locked doors.
Women on the staff have been given the same ultimatum. Zahra Hasanova, a teacher, was ordered to remove her scarf at work. “I am hurt,” she told Al Jazeera. “The hijab is a personal choice, and if one day I want to take it off, that should be my choice too.”
Arrests and a feed that would not refresh
Baku sent police. On October 12, the Interior Ministry reported 37 arrests in the capital, accusing the detainees of confronting school staff, damaging property and disturbing public order.
Criminal cases were opened under Article 233, which carries up to three years in prison. Local activists put the number of people taken into custody above 200.
The ministry has also cited violence: a school director’s car set on fire in the Garadagh district and an attempt to burn a school building, with no injuries. It has not shown who was responsible, and nothing connects the organizers of the school protests to either incident.
The online outage followed the same timeline. Instagram and TikTok stopped refreshing for most users, and X also degraded.
Many people could reach the platforms only through VPNs. Officials have not acknowledged a block, and independent monitors have stopped short of confirming one.
The sudden network throttling coincided with viral footage of barred students and empty classrooms, suppressing real-time organizing and obscuring state crackdown. By cutting off digital channels, Baku aims to curb outrage and enforce compliance.
The precedent and those who benefit
The so-called constitution guarantees freedom of religion in Azerbaijan. Practice has long run the other way.
Headscarf restrictions in schools in 2010 and 2012 produced street protests that police broke up with arrests.
In November 2015, the Baku government’s armed forces stormed the historically devout Shia town of Nardaran, launching a deadly assault that left several local believers martyred.
Following the crackdown, Taleh Bagirzade, head of the Muslim Unity Movement, was subjected to severe torture and handed a politically motivated 20-year prison sentence for organizing civil resistance against state anti-Islamic decrees.
Unsanctioned gatherings are violently dispersed, and independent media operate under constant pressure.
This time the dissent has reached the prisons. Polad Aslanov, a journalist already serving a long sentence on “treason” charges, began a hunger strike on October 8. A statement released through his family says he is using the only tool he has left to defend the constitutional rights of girls and teachers.
Demonstrators have also gathered outside the Azerbaijani consulate in Istanbul. President Ilham Aliyev, speaking at a party conference, told critics not to “interfere with our lifestyle.” Some observers read the remark as aimed at Turkey.
Observers note that the crackdown aligns with Baku’s foreign policy priorities as well as its domestic goals.
Aliyev has spent two decades building a controversial partnership with Israel, which buys a large share of its oil from Azerbaijan and sells Baku drones and other weapons, and he keeps a working relationship with Washington.
Baku has long treated its devout Shia population as a security risk. Enforcing the headscarf ban in the language of secularism lets the government act on that suspicion in terms its partners welcome, and neither capital has shown interest in objecting.
The bill is paid by Muslim families in a Muslim-majority country, who are being told that a girl’s education now depends on what she wears.

Trump targets anti-war Muslim congresswoman three weeks before midterms
TEHRAN — U.S. federal agents with Homeland Security Investigations executed a search warrant early Monday morning at the Washington residence of Representative Ilhan Omar. Law enforcement personnel blocked off the surrounding street and removed multiple boxes labeled as “seized evidence” from the premises.
CBS News cited sources familiar with the case indicating that the Justice Department operation centers on decades-old immigration forms filed by Omar’s late father when her family arrived in the United States as refugees from Somalia.
The search took place 22 days before the U.S. midterm elections, violating longstanding Department of Justice guidelines that strictly discourage overt investigative steps against political figures within 60 days of a vote.
Critics argue the action demonstrates a direct weaponization of federal security institutions designed to influence the upcoming election and intimidate political opposition.
Minnesota Governor Tim Walz condemned the raid, stating that Donald Trump is openly misusing executive power to target political adversaries.
Addressing the raid on social media, Omar confirmed her safety while confronting the administration’s actions directly.
She characterized the search as a calculated effort to target political enemies and weaponize law enforcement, noting that Trump has subjected her to baseless hostility for a decade.
She declared that state intimidation would not silence her. Her office formally labeled the operation an outrageous abuse of authority, reaffirming that the congresswoman has committed no legal violations.
Speaking to reporters before traveling to Ohio, Trump denied directing the search while launching sharp personal attacks against Omar.
He described her as “a terrible person” and asserted that her country of origin, Somalia, which he labelled a “non-country,” was plagued by crime and squalor.
These attacks form part of a documented, long-standing pattern of hostility, as Trump has spent months fixating on Omar in what she has described as “an unhealthy obsession,” from suggesting in February that she should be “institutionalized” to repeatedly demanding her deportation at political rallies.
Weeks prior to the search, Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin publicly telegraphed the operation by declaring on television that an investigation was underway and warning that something was going to happen regarding her family background.
House Democratic leaders Hakeem Jeffries, Katherine Clark, and Pete Aguilar issued a joint statement calling the raid deeply disturbing and describing it as a rogue abuse of power.
Representative Rashida Tlaib publicly characterized the operation as a tactic typical of an authoritarian police state.
Meanwhile, the Council on American-Islamic Relations (CAIR) condemned the search as blatant political persecution, pointing out the stark double standard in how federal agencies choose to allocate investigative resources.
This operation underscores a broader context of systemic Islamophobia and xenophobia within the U.S. political structure, where Muslim officials and anti-war advocates routinely face targeted hostility, as well as the growing use of state power to suppress dissent across the country.
As an outspoken critic of Washington’s foreign policy and military support for Israel, Omar has long been a central focus of attacks from the conservative political establishment and the pro-Israel lobby.

Sophocles’ “Antigone” on stage in Mahallat
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
17:03:04 UTC
02:03:04 KST

Sophocles’ “Antigone” on stage in Mahallat
TEHRAN – The play “Antigone” by Sophocles is being performed at the Artists Forum in Mahallat, Markazi Province.
Directed by Rouhollah Soroush, the play will remain on stage through October 27. The cast includes Nasim Ostadhashem, Ali Baratali, Parham Parvaresh, Parastoo Rafati, Panisa Rezaei, Danial Sajadinejad, Amirsaleh Soleymani, Mehdi Azimi, and Mahdis Firouzi.
In Greek mythology, Antigone was a Theban princess and a character in several ancient Greek tragedies. She was the daughter of Oedipus, king of Thebes.
Antigone appears in three 5th-century BC tragic plays written by Sophocles, known collectively as the three Theban plays, with her being the protagonist of the eponymous tragedy “Antigone”.
In her eponymous play, Antigone attempts to secure a respectable burial for her brother Polynices. Oedipus's sons, Eteocles and Polynices, had shared rule jointly until they quarreled, and Eteocles expelled his brother. In Sophocles' account, the two brothers agreed to alternate rule each year, but Eteocles decided not to share power with his brother after his tenure expired. Polynices left the kingdom, gathered an army, and attacked the city of Thebes in the war of the Seven Against Thebes. Both brothers were killed in the battle.
King Creon, who has ascended to the throne of Thebes after the death of the brothers, decrees that Polynices is not to be buried or even mourned, on pain of death by stoning. Antigone, Polynices' sister, defies the king's order and is caught.
Antigone is brought before Creon, confessing her crime and foreknowledge of the king’s edict that Polynices neither be buried nor mourned, claiming the superiority of divine law to human law.
Antigone’s self-defense in defiance of Creon is passionate, courageous, and determined. Creon orders Antigone buried alive in a tomb. Although Creon finally has a change of heart—due to a visit from the soothsayer Tiresias—and tries to release Antigone, he finds she has hanged herself. Creon's son Haemon, who was engaged to Antigone, kills himself with a sword (after an unsuccessful attempt to kill Creon), and his mother, Queen Eurydice, also kills herself in despair over her sons’ deaths (Haemon and Megareus), which she attributes to Creon’s misrule and misjudgment. By her death, Antigone ends up destroying the household of her adversary, Creon.

Tehran Symphony Orchestra to perform “In the Italian Style” concert
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
17:02:29 UTC

Tehran Symphony Orchestra to perform “In the Italian Style” concert
TEHRAN- The Tehran Symphony Orchestra, conducted by Nasir Heidarian and featuring cellist Majid Esmaeili as soloist, will present a concert titled “In the Italian Style” at Tehran’s Vahdat Hall on October 20.
The performance is part of the orchestra’s autumn program and will feature works by Austrian composer Franz Schubert and Soviet-Armenian composer Aram Khachaturian.
The concert will open with Schubert’s Overture “In the Italian Style”, followed by Khachaturian’s “Rhapsody-Concerto”, featuring Esmaeili on cello. The program will conclude with Schubert’s “Symphony No. 2”, bringing together three orchestral works in a performance led by Heidarian.
Austrian composer Franz Schubert (1797–1828) was a central figure of the transition from the Classical to the Romantic era, celebrated for his melodies, expressive harmonies and contributions to symphonic and chamber music. His “Overture in the Italian Style” reflects the influence of Italian opera, particularly the lively, melodic style associated with Gioachino Rossini, whose popularity swept through Europe during Schubert’s lifetime. The work combines energetic rhythms, bright orchestral colors and a theatrical character.
Schubert’s “Symphony No. 2” in B-flat major, composed in 1814–1815. Written when the composer was still a teenager, the symphony reveals his engagement with the Classical traditions of Haydn and Mozart while offering glimpses of the melodic inventiveness that would distinguish his later music.
Aram Khachaturian (1903–1978), an Armenian composer born in Tbilisi, Georgia, became one of the leading figures in Soviet classical music, drawing on Armenian and other Caucasian folk traditions to create works known for their rhythmic energy, vivid orchestration and expressive melodies.
His “Concerto-Rhapsody for Cello and Orchestra”, composed in 1963 and dedicated to renowned cellist Mstislav Rostropovich, combines the structure of a concerto with the freer, episodic character of a rhapsody. The composition places considerable technical and expressive demands on the soloist, moving between lyrical passages and powerful orchestral exchanges.
The Tehran Symphony Orchestra regularly presents works by Iranian and international composers as part of its efforts to expand public engagement with classical music and enrich the country’s musical scene.

Restored “Bashu, the Little Stranger” to go on screen in Montreal
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
17:02:04 UTC
02:02:04 KST

Restored “Bashu, the Little Stranger” to go on screen in Montreal
TEHRAN- A restored 4K version of the late Iranian filmmaker Bahram Beyzaie’s acclaimed film “Bashu, the Little Stranger” will be screened at Cinéma Moderne in Montreal, Canada, on Wednesday evening.
The screening is scheduled for 8:30 p.m. local time, with English subtitles, offering audiences an opportunity to revisit one of Iranian cinema’s notable works exploring the human consequences of war, displacement and cultural differences.
According to the Public Relations and International Affairs Department of the Institute for the Intellectual Development of Children and Young Adults (Kanoon), the film’s restored version was prepared with the institute’s support at Roshana Studio to present the work to audiences in improved visual quality.
Released in 1989, “Bashu, the Little Stranger” follows a young boy from southern Iran who loses his home and family during the Iran-Iraq war. Fleeing the bombing, he takes refuge in a village in northern Iran, where he finds himself in an unfamiliar environment with a different language and cultural traditions.
There, he encounters Naii, a rural woman who gradually forms an emotional bond with the displaced child despite the barriers separating them. Their relationship becomes the heart of the film, illustrating how compassion and human connection can bridge differences in language, background and experience.
The touching acclaimed drama, however, carries subtle undertones about human emotions like love, acceptance, loneliness, and unfamiliarity.
Through Bashu’s journey, Beyzaie examines the effects of war on children and civilians, while addressing broader themes of displacement, identity, mutual understanding and the acceptance of others. The film portrays a child’s struggle to find security and belonging in the aftermath of violence, placing human relationships at the center of its narrative.
Widely regarded as a landmark in Iranian cinema, “Bashu, the Little Stranger” is also an important work in the country’s cinema for children and young adults. Its focus on the experiences of a war-affected child gives the film a perspective that extends beyond the battlefield, highlighting the lasting personal and social consequences of conflict.
In 1999, “Bashu, the Little Stranger” was voted the best Iranian movie of all time by a poll of 150 movie experts.
Born in Tehran in 1938, Bahram Beyzaie was a celebrated Iranian playwright, filmmaker and scholar whose work blended Persian mythology, epic literature, particularly Ferdowsi’s Shahnameh, and contemporary social issues.
Before turning to cinema in the 1970s, he had established himself as a leading playwright and historian. Often called the Shakespeare of Iran, he was admired for his mastery of Persian and his exploration of Iranian history and cultural identity through drama.
His notable works include “Ballad of Tara” (1979), “Death of Yazdgerd” (1982), and “Killing Mad Dogs” (2001).
After moving to the United States in 2010, Beyzaie continued his cultural and academic activities at Stanford University, teaching and researching Persian theater, cinema and mythology. His enduring creative commitment was also reflected in the manuscript “Dash Akol According to Marjan,” completed five years before his passing.
The Montreal screening forms part of efforts to introduce Iranian cinematic works to international audiences and bring restored versions of significant films to a new generation of viewers. The 4K presentation is expected to offer audiences an opportunity to experience Beyzaie’s work in enhanced image quality decades after its original production.
The screening also renews attention to a film whose themes of forced migration, cultural diversity and solidarity remain relevant to contemporary discussions about the human cost of war.

IMF lowers Bulgaria’s growth forecast and raises inflation outlook
Tuesday 13 October 2026 19:18
Tuesday, 13 October 2026, 19:18
PHOTO IMF
Font size
The International Monetary Fund (IMF) has lowered its forecast for Bulgaria’s economic growth this year from 2.8% to 2.6% and revised its average annual inflation projection upwards from 3.8% to 4.9% compared with its spring assessment.
The Fund expects Bulgaria’s economic growth to accelerate to 2.7% next year, up from the 2.5% projected in April. At the same time, its forecast for average annual inflation has been raised from 3.7% to 4.8%.
The outlook for the current account has also deteriorated significantly. The deficit is now expected to reach 8% of gross domestic product (GDP) this year, compared with the 4% projected in April. For 2027, the IMF forecasts a deficit of 6.6% of GDP, up from its previous estimate of 3.2%.
The labour market outlook remains unchanged. Unemployment is expected to fall from 3.6% in 2025 to 3.4% this year and 3.3% next year.

MIchael Reusch, Chief Executive Officer of Fraport Bulgaria

Font size
There is currently no immediate threat to the airports in Varna and Burgas following today’s drone attacks on commercial vessels in the Black Sea. This is what Michael Reusch, Chief Executive Officer of Fraport Bulgaria, which operates the country’s two Black Sea airports, told Radio Bulgaria on the sidelines of the 11th Hotel and Tourism Investment Forum (HTIF) in Sofia. He said the company had already stepped up security measures and was closely monitoring developments.
“Of course, we have raised our security levels, as we are part of the public infrastructure and the national security programme. As far as I know, the country’s official authorities are keeping a very close eye on the situation in communication with NATO and EU partners,” Reusch said.
He stressed that the situation should neither be underestimated nor exaggerated. In his view, the drone attacks in the Black Sea will have no impact on next year’s tourist season or on the Eurovision Song Contest being held in Burgas.
Reusch made the comments just hours after a second consecutive drone attack targeted commercial vessels in the Black Sea, near Bulgarian territorial waters.

Trump's credibility under question
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
17:00:36 UTC
02:00:36 KST

Trump's credibility under question
Khorasan argued that Trump's contradictory behavior has weakened his credibility. Pro-Israel circles in Washington portray Trump's unpredictability as a sign of strength, claiming that Iran should always remain uncertain about his next move.
However, this approach comes at a cost. When a president's statements are seen as unreliable, even promises of agreements or conflict resolution lose their ability to inspire confidence. For Iran, the political lesson is straightforward. Strategic decisions should be based on measurable actions, verifiable commitments, and the preservation of leverage. Regional developments have created conditions in which Iran sees resistance to pressure from Trump as necessary for protecting its security and interests. The country is currently working to rebuild its military capabilities, a process that should be accompanied by active diplomacy. Stronger deterrence would increase the cost of military action for the United States, while diplomatic efforts should raise the political costs associated with Washington's perceived lack of credibility.
Jam-e-Jam: Marco Rubio's efforts are ineffective
Jam-e-Jam discussed recent remarks by US Secretary of State Marco Rubio in Athens, describing them as unconvincing and lacking both scientific and moral foundations. Rubio is attempting to justify what it views as an unjustified war allegedly launched by the United States, with Israeli support, against Iran. More than a year has passed since the conflict began, and Rubio's comments represent a delayed attempt to provide a historical rationale for it. Struggles for power inside the United States often impose costs on the wider world, with Iran currently bearing a significant portion of those burdens. The speech was designed to legitimize the use of military force and to provide Republicans with historical and ideological backing. In the paper's view, such arguments are intended to compensate for political weaknesses and help Republicans avoid setbacks in competition with Democrats.
Resalat: Direct US involvement in Yemen would escalate tensions
Resalat examined recent developments in Yemen and placed them within the broader framework of regional tensions. The paper argued that direct US involvement in the conflict could expand the scope of hostilities beyond a regional dispute and transform it into a broader confrontation. A key aspect of the crisis is the tendency to interpret events in Yemen solely through the lens of rivalry between Tehran and Washington. Such a view minimizes the role of Yemeni political actors and overlooks the domestic and historical roots of the conflict. The newspaper noted that the growing connection between developments in Yemen and the larger confrontation between Iran and the United States has increased the strategic importance of the country. Greater foreign military intervention would make it more likely that the crisis evolves into a component of wider regional competition rather than remaining focused on Yemen's internal political disputes.
Donya-e-Eqtesad: Elections will not change Washington's policy
Donya-e-Eqtesad analyzed Tehran's perspective on its ongoing confrontation with Washington. According to the paper, Iran's main concern is not only military pressure but also a deep distrust of US commitments. Iranian policymakers believe they can withstand pressure and impose additional costs on both the United States and the global economy. Tehran remains skeptical about Washington's willingness to honor agreements, including those signed by Trump himself. From this perspective, US elections do not guarantee a change in policy because, according to some Iranian analysts, Democrats and Republicans differ more in their methods of dealing with Iran than in their overall approach. The paper noted that indirect negotiations between the two countries continue, but disagreements over the sequence of implementing commitments remain a major obstacle. Iran is reportedly seeking a return to the framework of the short-term June agreement while also obtaining economic benefits that, in its view, were not fully realized under previous arrangements.
Arman-e-Emrooz: Successful economic diplomacy in Africa requires institutional support
Arman-e-Emrooz argued that Africa is no longer a peripheral region in international politics but an increasingly important part of the emerging global order. For Iran, one of the most significant developments is the growing geopolitical importance of the Red Sea and the Horn of Africa. Recent events in the Red Sea and the Bab al-Mandab Strait have demonstrated close links between the security of that region and the security of the Persian Gulf, the Indian Ocean, and major trade routes connecting Asia and Europe. As a result, developments there have direct and indirect implications for Iran's strategic environment. The newspaper emphasized that Iran's primary challenge is transforming potential opportunities into sustainable economic partnerships. Past experience, it argued, has shown that economic relations with African countries have often been limited by inadequate financial mechanisms, weak transportation links, insufficient market knowledge, and a lack of consistent private-sector engagement. Consequently, the article concluded that successful economic diplomacy in Africa requires institutional support and infrastructure development. Political agreements alone, without practical economic foundations, are unlikely to produce lasting and meaningful cooperation.

Poland urges Europe to switch to 'war-mode' defense production
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
16:59:23 UTC
01:59:23 KST

Jo Harper
13 October 2026•Update: 13 October 2026
Poland’s Defense Minister Wladyslaw Kosiniak-Kamysz on Tuesday urged Europe to put weapons and ammunition production on a wartime footing to counter Russia's military build-up, Polish state news agency PAP reported.
He also urged the EU to allow urgent defense purchases from NATO allies outside the bloc.
Speaking in Warsaw following talks with European Commissioner for Defense and Space Andrius Kubilius on strengthening European military capabilities, accelerating arms production and securing defense supply chains, Kosiniak-Kamysz said, "I personally favor switching to wartime mode in the production of weapons and ammunition throughout Europe.”
He argued that Russia was already operating in that way, without waiting for others, while Europe could no longer afford to remain complacent.
Kosiniak-Kamysz identified three priority areas for European defense investment: affordable long-range precision-strike capabilities, drones and counter-drone systems, and artificial intelligence.
He urged greater flexibility in European defense procurement, arguing that urgent purchases should be opened to NATO allies outside the EU when European manufacturers could not supply the necessary equipment quickly enough.
"We also propose that, in the case of critical purchases requiring rapid delivery, when it is not possible to obtain this equipment in the European Union, we should open up to our NATO allies who will be able to help us," he said.
The proposal highlights tension in European defense policy between efforts to strengthen the EU's domestic arms industry and the immediate need to acquire military capabilities in response to Russia's war against Ukraine.
It could also have implications for defense manufacturers in non-EU NATO countries, including Türkiye, Britain and the US, although the Polish minister did not identify specific countries or suppliers in his remarks.

Saudi Arabia strikes Yemen capital as Houthis vow to retaliate
RIYADH - Yemen’s Iran-allied Houthis said Saudi Arabia was attacking the Yemeni capital Sanaa on Oct 13 after a Saudi-led coalition warned civilians to stay away from an oil depot on the city outskirts, part of a rapidly escalating war between the sides.
The Houthis have for a week been targeting Saudi airports, including a strike on Riyadh on Oct 10 that killed 13 people, in retaliation for the kingdom’s backing of government forces against the Houthis in Yemen’s reignited civil war.
Houthi-run Al-Masirah television reported that the Saudi-led coalition had targeted the Yemen Petroleum Company’s (YPC) Sabah central station, a fuel depot on the outskirts of Sanaa.
The coalition said in a statement on Oct 13 evening that it attacked the station and other sites in an operation aimed at “neutralising the capabilities of Houthis” to threaten the kingdom, Yemen and international waterways.
It said the Iran-aligned group was using the sites in Sanaa, Hodeidah and Dhamar to “supply its arsenal of missiles and drones” to attack Saudi Arabia and commercial vessels in the Red Sea.
YPC said the facility did not currently hold any stocks of petroleum products and that targeting it did not affect oil reserves or supply chains.
However, the Houthis had earlier threatened a “harsh and painful” response to any strikes on Sanaa, with spokesperson Yahya Saree saying targets could include the Saudi Aramco headquarters in Dhahran and an oil refinery in Riyadh.
The group renewed earlier warnings it had issued to oil workers in Saudi Arabia, telling them to stay away from sites that could be potential targets.
The Saudi Cabinet, chaired by de facto ruler Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, issued a statement saying the Houthis would face consequences for their repeated attacks on the kingdom.
The Oct 10 ballistic missile strike on Riyadh airport was the deadliest in Saudi Arabia for a decade, with further attacks grounding flights across the country even as it hosts a major energy conference.
Reignited Yemen war
Saudi Arabia resumed its military campaign in Yemen in support of the internationally recognised government in a bid to reverse the Houthis’ sudden gains in September when they swept down the Red Sea coast to the critical Bab el-Mandeb Strait.
The strait, the southern gateway to the Red Sea, has become a more vital route for Saudi and other global energy supplies since the start of the Iran war in February when Tehran closed the Hormuz Strait leading from the Gulf to the Indian Ocean.
While a government offensive aimed at driving back the Houthis beginning a week ago pushed them off the area closest to the strait, the group remains embedded nearby and has made gains of its own around the city of Taiz in October.
Saudi Arabia has been seeking wider support from allies for its campaign against the Houthis and to help it ward off their missile and drone attacks.
Turkish President Tayyip Erdogan told Mohammed bin Salman on Oct 13 that Ankara would stand by the kingdom, the Turkish presidency said, but without giving details on any specific new line of support.
Turkey and Pakistan signed a mutual defence pact with Saudi Arabia this summer, though Turkey still needs to ratify the treaty in Parliament.
US President Donald Trump also spoke to Mohammed bin Salman on Oct 13, he told reporters, adding that the Houthis were “behaving very badly”.
He said he may ask Erdogan to intervene in support of Saudi interests.
Washington, Saudi Arabia’s strongest ally and longtime security guarantor, has so far rebuffed Saudi efforts to bring it directly into the war against the Houthis.
The Yemen conflict has resumed as a spillover from the wider US-Iran war that began with the US-Israeli attack on the Islamic Republic starting on Feb 28.
Iran, Riyadh’s longtime arch regional rival, has offered to mediate between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis, its foreign minister Abbas Araghchi said on Oct 11 in statements reiterated by the ministry on Oct 12. REUTERS

Ethiopian troops enter town on border with Eritrea, stoking war fears

Witnesses and a conflict monitor said Eritrean troops had crossed last week into Zalambessa, near Ethiopia's northernmost point, in support of the rebels, but it was unclear if the Eritrean troops or rebels were still present on Tuesday.
Asmara has denied any incursion into Ethiopia and asked the UN to take deterrent measures against Ethiopia. It argues that Addis Ababa's accusations of an invasion by Eritrean forces amounted to a "declaration of war".
Fighting broke out in Ethiopia last month as a rebel alliance led by the Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF) went on the offensive, reigniting a war that killed hundreds of thousands between 2020-22.
With Addis Ababa and Asmara now on opposing sides again, conflicts raging elsewhere in the region and tensions high across the Red Sea, there are fears of broader contagion of violence this time around.
The Ethiopian government's counter-offensive has driven rebels from a string of towns, forcing them to retreat north.
By Tuesday, the army had reached Zalambessa, a town with a population of around 15,000 on the Ethiopian side of the border with Eritrea, according to six sources. The sources included four people in touch with residents, a diplomat and an expert on the conflict in touch with the warring parties.
A spokesperson for a pro-government militia did not confirm the military taking control of the town.
Spokespeople for Ethiopia's military and Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
Having been locked in conflict for years, Ethiopia and Eritrea made peace in 2018 and Eritrea fought in support of Ethiopia’s federal government during a 2020-2022 civil war in Tigray, but relations have since soured again.
Ethiopia has accused Eritrea of backing the rebels and wrote to Security Council members, stating that Eritrean troops had advanced up to 60 km (37 miles) inside Ethiopia.
Eritrea's Foreign Minister Osman Saleh has asked the Security Council to take action against Addis Ababa in a letter seen by Reuters, invoking Chapter VII of the UN Charter, which allows for measures ranging from sanctions to military action.
On Tuesday, Security Council members were due to hold a closed-door meeting on the situation in the Horn of Africa, the Greek presidency of the Security Council said.
The issue of sea access has also roiled relations.
Ethiopia had access to a coastline for decades until Eritrea gained independence from Addis Ababa in 1993. Ethiopia argues that restoring sea access is an existential issue but has said it would be restored through peace and dialogue.

North Korea Revives Russia’s Forgotten Missile Project—and Gives It a Deadlier Upgrade
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
16:53:01 UTC
01:53:01 KST

- Category
- World
North Korea Revives Russia’s Forgotten Missile Project—and Gives It a Deadlier Upgrade
North Korea has unveiled a new missile system capable of striking targets up to 100 kilometers (62 miles) away, combining a rocket booster with a glide bomb in a design resembling Russia’s long-delayed Hermes missile project.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to Defense Express on October 13, the previously unnamed system was displayed during a North Korean exhibition highlighting the country’s technological developments. Military equipment researcher Andrii Tarasenko drew attention to the weapon, which appears to incorporate several significant changes compared with its Russian counterpart.
One of the most notable differences is its ammunition. Unlike the Russian Hermes design, North Korea’s system reportedly uses a glide bomb as the second stage of its rocket, potentially allowing the weapon to travel toward its target after separating from the initial booster.
The launcher configuration also differs substantially. The North Korean system features 22 launch tubes, compared with six on the Russian Hermes launcher. Its reported range is 100 kilometers, while the Russian project was designed with longer-range configurations in mind.
The weapon is not entirely new. North Korea conducted its first publicly reported test launches of a similar system in May 2026, although its official designation and detailed technical specifications have not been disclosed.
Defense Express noted that the combination of a rocket booster and glide bomb resembles the concept behind the US-developed Ground-Launched Small Diameter Bomb (GLSDB), previously supplied to Ukraine.
The GLSDB uses a rocket motor to launch a precision-guided glide bomb from the ground, extending its reach beyond that of conventional air-dropped munitions. However, the system has faced operational challenges, and Defense Express reported that questions remain about whether its technical problems have been fully resolved.
The Russian Hermes project dates back to the 1990s and was intended to provide precision strikes against targets at extended ranges. Despite years of development and testing, the system has not entered widespread operational service, with the latest significant public updates dating to 2023.
According to Defense Express, North Korea’s newly displayed weapon may represent a further development of the original Russian concept rather than a direct copy. The outlet also noted that Moscow’s apparent decision not to pursue Hermes remains unexplained.
Earlier, in March 2025, North Korea unveiled its first airborne early warning and control aircraft, based on the Soviet-designed Il-76 and closely resembling Russia’s A-50 radar plane.
Pyongyang also showcased its Saetbyol-4 drone, which bears a striking resemblance to the US-made RQ-4 Global Hawk, raising questions about North Korea’s use of foreign military designs in developing its own weapons systems.

Russia’s Starlink Rival May Be in Trouble as Two Satellites Fall Toward Earth
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
16:52:54 UTC
01:52:54 KST

- Category
- World
Russia’s Starlink Rival May Be in Trouble as Two Satellites Fall Toward Earth
Two Russian Rassvet-3 broadband satellites intended for a Starlink-style network are rapidly losing altitude and could reenter Earth’s atmosphere within weeks, according to orbital tracking data updated October 13.
SONIKS, a Russian open-source satellite tracking and ground station network that calculates decay forecasts from current two-line element data, lists RASSVET-3 23, NORAD 100089, with an apogee of 250 kilometers and a perigee of 232 kilometers. RASSVET-3 17, NORAD 100083, is at roughly 256 by 236 kilometers.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The service currently projects RASSVET-3 23 to reenter around October 29, and RASSVET-3 17 to reenter around November 1. SONIKS warns that its estimates change as new orbital data arrive and become less accurate farther from the calculation date.
The two spacecraft are clear outliers among the 16 Rassvet-3 satellites launched from Plesetsk on July 19. Most members of the same batch have climbed to roughly 480-512 kilometers, while RASSVET-3 17 and 23 remain near 250 kilometers.
ComNews added that the satellites initially entered an approximately 300-kilometer deployment orbit and were expected to use their own plasma propulsion systems to climb afterward. Following the July launch, Bureau 1440 stated that the spacecraft would begin moving toward their target orbit after completing checks and commissioning. ComNews
The orbital behavior does not by itself establish why the two satellites are descending or prove that their propulsion systems have failed. Bureau 1440 has not publicly announced the loss of either spacecraft.
Rassvet is being developed by the Russian aerospace company Bureau 1440 as a low Earth orbit broadband network often presented as Russia’s answer to SpaceX’s Starlink. The company describes its satellites as orbital 5G base stations connected through laser links, with planned speeds of up to 1 Gbps and latency below 70 milliseconds.
The program has already faced uncertainty over its intended operating altitude. Bureau 1440 continues to list an 800-kilometer target, while Russian telecom publication ComNews found that most satellites from the first operational batch had instead clustered near 500-540 kilometers.
Experts interviewed by ComNews suggested that Bureau 1440 may have lowered the constellation’s working altitude to around 514 kilometers. A lower orbit can reduce latency but also shrinks each satellite’s coverage area and requires more spacecraft to maintain continuous service.
The potential loss of RASSVET-3 17 and 23 would not be the constellation’s first atmospheric reentry. RASSVET-3 4, launched with the first 16-satellite batch on March 23, reentered on June 6 after spending about 75 days in orbit.

According to the foundation’s press release, the interception took place on October 8 in Ukraine’s Chernihiv region, where the brigade’s Spalakh crew destroyed the Russian drone traveling at approximately 430 kilometers per hour at an altitude of 780 meters.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The Serhiy Prytula Charity Foundation released footage of the interception, highlighting the continued development and battlefield testing of jet-powered interceptors designed to counter high-speed Russian aerial threats.
According to the 1020th Anti-Aircraft Missile and Artillery Brigade, the technology remains relatively new to Ukrainian air defense crews, requiring continuous testing and coordination with manufacturers to improve its effectiveness under different operational conditions.

We have limited time to react, so it is important to improve the effectiveness of intercepting such targets each time. A lot also depends on the crew: its experience, a well-trained navigator, and knowledge of fixed-wing UAVs. So we continue working and improving,” the brigade stated.

Kyrylo Liukov, head of the Unmanned Technologies Department at the Serhiy Prytula Charity Foundation, emphasized that successful individual interceptions represent an important stage in developing a broader defense capability.

That is why every successful deployment is important to us. At the same time, we understand that isolated successes are not enough to counter the scale of this threat” Liukov said.
He emphasized the need to move beyond individual successful interceptions toward a systematic approach to countering jet-powered drones by working with manufacturers to improve the systems’ technical and tactical capabilities, gaining further combat experience, and eventually expanding their supply to military units.
The latest interception follows another successful engagement in late September, when the same brigade’s Yastrub crew shot down a Russian Geran-5 attack drone in the Chernihiv region.
During that operation, the Russian drone was traveling at approximately 425 kilometers per hour at an altitude exceeding three kilometers, marking the brigade’s first successful interception of a Geran-5.

Iran develops countermeasures against Starlink
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
16:52:05 UTC
01:52:05 KST

Iran develops countermeasures against Starlink
TEHRAN — Iran has developed technical capabilities to identify and disrupt unauthorized Starlink satellite internet terminals, while intensifying its efforts through international regulatory channels to compel the service to comply with telecommunications rules governing its operations inside Iranian territory.
Mohammad Amin Aghamiri, secretary of Iran’s Supreme Council of Cyberspace, said Iranian specialists had developed and tested several systems to identify and manage satellite communications, adding that one of these technologies had been deployed during unrest in December.
 
Aghamiri said approximately 80% of Starlink communication packets in Iran had been disrupted during that period, while much of the remaining traffic had become largely ineffective. 
He stressed that Iran’s countermeasures extended beyond interference with the Global Positioning System (GPS), saying domestic specialists had developed other technologies to identify satellite user terminals and interfere with communications between transmitters and receivers.
 
Identifying unauthorized Starlink terminals remains a priority for Iranian authorities, he added, arguing that the technology could be countered through a range of technical measures.
Beyond GPS interference: identifying and disabling terminals
Starlink, operated by SpaceX, delivers broadband internet through a constellation of satellites in low Earth orbit. Users connect through specialized ground-based equipment known as user terminals, which communicate with satellites passing overhead.
The system's architecture enables terminals to switch between satellites as their positions change, helping maintain connectivity. This network design also presents challenges for authorities seeking to identify individual terminals operating without authorization across a large territory.
Technical interference with satellite communications and the remote deactivation of user terminals are distinct approaches. The former seeks to degrade or interrupt the communications link, while the latter involves the satellite operator identifying a terminal's location and disabling its access to the network.
Iran's Supreme Council of Cyberspace secretary said the country's countermeasures were not limited to GPS disruption and that Iranian specialists had developed additional capabilities to address satellite communications. His remarks point to a broader focus on terminal identification and communications interference rather than reliance on a single technical method.
The International Telecommunication Union (ITU) has separately confirmed that Starlink has the technical capability to geolocate user terminals and disable them remotely. At its 100th Radio Regulations Board meeting, the ITU noted that Starlink had identified and disabled more than 2,500 terminals operating illegally in a particular area, demonstrating the system's capacity to restrict access geographically.
The ITU's findings are significant to Iran's argument that the operator can take more direct action against terminals operating in territories where its services have not been authorized.
Iran takes Starlink dispute to international regulators
Iran's objections to Starlink's operations are not confined to technical and security concerns. Tehran has pursued the issue through the ITU for several years, arguing that terminals transmitting from within Iranian territory must comply with the country's national telecommunications regulations and applicable international rules.
Aghamiri said Iran's Ministry of Communications had submitted multiple complaints and supporting documents to the ITU over the past two to three years. Tehran has also raised the matter with the relevant Norwegian regulatory authority and the US side, while Iran's Foreign Ministry has issued a formal warning to Norway.
The dispute centers on the authorization of satellite transmissions and the responsibilities of the administrations associated with Starlink's satellite-system filings. Under the ITU framework, satellite transmissions from within a country's territory must comply with applicable regulatory requirements, including provisions governing authorization to operate transmitting earth stations.
In October, Iran formally protested to Norway over the ‘continued failure’ to take effective action against unauthorized Starlink operations. The Foreign Ministry summoned Norwegian Ambassador to Tehran Paul Bjornstad and called for immediate measures to halt transmissions from terminals operating without authorization.
Iranian officials have also raised security concerns, believeing that the United States and Israel have used satellite communications infrastructure to support activities directed against the Islamic Republic. Tehran maintains that the operation of foreign communications equipment without its authorization raises questions of national sovereignty as well as national security.
What the ITU has decided
The ITU's Radio Regulations Board has examined the dispute since March 2023. Its decisions have repeatedly called on Norway and the United States to take appropriate measures to ensure that Starlink transmissions from unauthorized terminals inside Iran are stopped.
At its 101st meeting in March 2026, the Board concluded that Norway's actions were not compliant with obligations under relevant ITU resolutions and Article 18 of the Radio Regulations. It urged Norway and the United States to take all appropriate measures available to them to have Starlink immediately disable unauthorized transmissions within Iranian territory.
The Board also noted that Starlink had the technical capacity to locate terminals and deactivate them remotely. At the same time, it asked Iran to continue its own efforts, to the extent possible, to identify and deactivate unauthorized terminals.
At its 102nd meeting, held from June 29 to July 3, 2026, the Board reiterated its position. It noted that the dispute had remained unresolved since 2023 and that no response had been received from the Norwegian or US administrations on the latest submissions under consideration.
The Board again urged Norway and the United States to comply with the relevant provisions and called for immediate action by the operator to disable unauthorized transmissions inside Iran. However, it also reiterated that it lacked the authority to suspend satellite-system frequency assignments solely because the notifying administration had failed to comply with the relevant resolution.
The distinction is important: the ITU has pressed for enforcement of existing rules but has not ordered a blanket shutdown of Starlink's satellite network or suspended its frequency assignments.
A wider debate over satellite internet and national sovereignty
The dispute highlights a growing challenge in international telecommunications governance: how to regulate global satellite broadband systems whose signals can reach across national borders and whose user terminals can be transported into countries where the service is not authorized.
For Iran, the central issue is not simply access to satellite internet technology. Tehran argues that the operation of transmitting terminals within its territory must respect national authorization requirements and that the service provider and the relevant administrations have a responsibility to prevent unauthorized transmissions.
Aghamiri also pointed to Starlink's use in military conflicts, particularly Ukraine, arguing that satellite communications can support functions extending beyond ordinary civilian connectivity, including military command and control, drone operations, intelligence gathering and espionage networks.
His comments reflect Iran's position that satellite communications infrastructure must be assessed in light of its potential dual-use applications, particularly when deployed in a conflict environment. Such concerns have become increasingly prominent as commercial satellite networks play a growing role in military communications and battlefield connectivity.
The Iranian official also referred to statements by US officials and SpaceX chief executive Elon Musk concerning Starlink's wartime use, arguing that the technology should not be regarded exclusively as a civilian communications service.
For Tehran, the combination of technical countermeasures and international legal action represents a two-track response: developing domestic capabilities to address unauthorized satellite communications while seeking enforcement of international telecommunications regulations.
The unresolved ITU proceedings suggest that the dispute will continue to test the balance between the global reach of commercial satellite networks, the responsibilities of their operators and the regulatory authority of states over communications transmitted from within their territory.

Yes, obesity is a problem – but a greater one is the food industry and its greed | Letters
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
16:50:55 UTC
01:50:55 KST

Your editorial on cancers in under-50s (8 October) rightly names food among the culprits. But the confrontation it calls for should be aimed less at obesity than at what produces it. Obesity is the intermediary; the exposure is a food system engineered for profit.
The Lancet’s series on ultra-processed foods showed these products displacing traditional diets worldwide and driving chronic disease, and documented more than 200 interconnected lobby groups through which the industry organises its influence to block regulation.
I was diagnosed with bowel cancer at 51, narrowly escaping these statistics; the generations below me have eaten ultra-processed diets from birth.
Governments know what works: marketing restrictions, warning labels, fiscal measures, schools and hospitals free from ultra-processed food, and policymaking protected from industry interference.
Yvette Cooper should treat the companies that shaped our diets in the same way that her predecessors eventually treated tobacco: not as partners to consult, but as an industry to regulate.
Prof Kent Buse
Chair, policy and prevention committee, World Obesity Federation
The worrying rise in early-onset cancers underlines the urgency of government intervention on obesity. Our food system is broken when high-fat, -salt and -sugar options are consistently the most accessible and affordable.
Advances in cancer research and weight-loss drugs will play a key role in managing diet-related illness, but treatment alone cannot solve a public health crisis. We must fix the food environment driving obesity in the first place. That requires changing the incentives for large food businesses that make and market the food we eat.
The government’s proposed healthy food standard sets out the most ambitious action for reforming the food environment to date, but progress has stalled since its announcement. It has the potential to reduce national obesity rates by about one fifth in adults and a quarter in children. Nothing else on the table comes remotely close to that.
The first step is establishing mandatory health reporting so that companies can no longer mark their own homework. Then we need clear targets for major food businesses to improve the health of what they actually sell. Ultimately, we cannot protect future generations from preventable diet-related disease until healthier food is the easiest and most affordable option. We cannot let our strategy be “wait for people to get sick and then put them on the drugs”.
Hugo Harper
Director, Nesta
Cancer has become the greatest cause of death among people with type 2 diabetes in England and the problem of metabolic risk and cancer is one of the great threats to health. However, this is not known by health professionals or the 4 million patients with this condition.
Cancer screening programmes work effectively with informed participation. GPs and their practices can use the annual diabetes check to highlight the cancer prevention. Screening programmes and primary care can work together to prevent cancer, if resources are targeted in the best way. The World Cancer Research Fund report has added urgency – let’s use it effectively.
Dr Pawan Randev
Former Cancer Research UK GP
I read with interest Anna Bawden’s article (Cancer rates rising more quickly among younger people, international research finds, 6 October. It seems that “lifestyle choices” are largely responsible for this, but I wonder just how much of a choice is open to us nowadays. We can choose to drink less alcohol, not smoke, exercise more and eat more healthily, but our choice of healthy food is limited, as products become increasingly industrialised with the addition of chemical additives, and we have little or no control over environmental or agricultural pollutants. To all this we might add the stress of the increasing cost of living and difficulty in finding jobs.
I believe it is perhaps not so much a question of poor lifestyle choices, but a lack of lifestyle choices.
Patricia Hampton
Milan, Italy

Jewish writer barred from London group over Zionist beliefs, UKLFI warns of Equality Act breach
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
16:50:53 UTC
01:50:53 KST

UK Lawyers for Israel (UKLFI) intervened after a Jewish comedian and writer was barred from a North London writers group on October 6 due to his Zionist beliefs.
Harry Deansway, whose real name is Joshua Rinkoff, had participated in the Offbeat Writers Group for six months without issues before group organizer Ruby Sullivan messaged him in response to an online comment about antisemitism in late September.
Sullivan stated that she was “very strongly pro-Palestine (NOT antisemitic)” and that “if our opinions on this don’t align it will affect our working together as it’s very important for me that the offbeat space and where I share my work is pro-Palestine.”
Deansway responded that he was “Jewish and a Zionist,” that he was “totally up for having a discussion about it,” and that he had “no issue with someone being pro-Palestine.” He further explained his viewpoint, stating, “I can be a Zionist, which at its core is to believe in the right to Jewish self-determination in their ancestral land and still be against the government of the country and anyone’s actions that make that a possibility at the expense of the suffering of another people.”
Sullivan replied, “I really can’t align with your beliefs as they support the massacre of an entire population. You also feigned an interest in women’s and gay rights to promote this belief, which I also can’t stand behind. [...] I don’t think there is a place in the Offbeat Writers’ Group for you because of this.”
Ideological declaration prepped for prospective members
Sullivan added that she was preparing an ideological declaration for prospective members, noting, “I am looking for a London-based anti-apartheid free zone commitment to sign for the group and am creating a document so when people want to enter the group, they understand our ideologies.”
UKLFI subsequently sent a formal warning letter to Sullivan on October 6, arguing that the exclusion potentially violated the Equality Act 2010. The organization noted that Deansway received protection under the statute based on his Jewish ethnic background, religious practices, and philosophical beliefs surrounding Jewish self-determination.
Furthermore, UKLFI criticized remarks made by Sullivan, specifically her statement that “because of the horrific past the Jewish people have endured, they should not want to inflict the same suffering on others,” pointing out that attributing the conduct of the State of Israel to the Jewish people as a whole constitutes holding Jews collectively responsible for state actions. UKLFI noted that this conduct is identified as an example of antisemitism under the International Holocaust Remembrance Alliance (IHRA) working definition.
Venue management canceled booking
The fallout also impacted a scheduled literary showcase that Deansway organized for October 13 at Bar Gemist. Following Sullivan’s withdrawal and the exit of other performers, venue management canceled the booking by October 2, noting that the event was originally agreed upon due to its connection with Sullivan and her group.
Although UKLFI warned the venue directors that canceling the event could also constitute unlawful discrimination, directors Marion Zoelle and Uros Dezutelj rejected the accusations in a response issued on October 10. They maintained that their choice stemmed from alterations to the event program and communication breakdowns rather than Deansway’s identity or political views.
While affirming that Deansway remained welcome to visit the establishment, the directors declined to reinstate the showcase and stated they would contest any legal claims.
A spokesperson for UKLFI said, “This is McCarthyism dressed up as progressive politics. A Jewish writer has been subjected to an ideological loyalty test and excluded because he believes in Jewish self-determination. People are entitled to oppose Zionism, but they cannot lawfully exclude Jews from cultural activities because they refuse to renounce their beliefs. Jewish artists should not have to pass a political purity test to participate in London’s cultural life.”
The Offbeat Writers Group did not respond to a request for comment by publication time.

Navi Pillay’s Nobel Peace Prize is an insult to Jewish communities - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
16:50:43 UTC
01:50:43 KST

The decision to award the 2026 Nobel Peace Prize to Navi Pillay demeans a prestigious institution and sends a troubling message to Jews around the world: our human rights are negotiable, our suffering is ignored, and those who dismiss our concerns can receive the highest international honors.
A prize intended to advance peace has instead deepened the alienation of a people who know the consequences of hatred that is left unchallenged.
The Nobel Peace Prize carries an extraordinary responsibility. It should reward moral courage, encourage reconciliation, and honor those who reject violence without qualification. Its authority rests on the conviction that human dignity is universal.
Yet in this case, the Nobel committee celebrates someone whose record includes defending a colleague’s rabid antisemitic rhetoric. By doing so, it undermines that conviction and insults previous recipients who pursued peace through an uncompromising commitment to the humanity of others.
When Pillay defended Miloon Kothari, her colleague on the three-person United Nations commission investigating Israel, that alone should have disqualified her from even being considered for this award.
Kothari claimed that the “Jewish lobby” controlled social media and questioned whether Israel should belong to the United Nations. Rather than treating these remarks as an affront to the commission’s integrity, Pillay defended him.
Jews recognize this language immediately. Claims about Jewish control, Jewish money and hidden Jewish influence have accompanied centuries of persecution. Dressing them in the vocabulary of international diplomacy makes them no less dangerous.
That same question hangs over the commission’s accusation that Israel committed genocide in Gaza. Its approach resembled a kangaroo court – the appearance of legal authority without the confidence that comes from demonstrable and meaningful impartiality.
Lack of legal impartiality
The gravest accusation in international law is that of genocide, and it requires the highest standards of evidence and fairness. The commission’s report didn’t even come close. We reject an approach that invents legal definitions to deliver a predetermined condemnation of Israel while expecting Jewish communities to accept the result as unquestionable truth.
Furthermore, Jewish objections were dismissed as attempts to weaponize antisemitism, as Pillay has done before.
Jews have every right to identify prejudice, challenge biased institutions, and demand scrutiny of those who sit in judgment. We are not obliged to remain silent when familiar conspiracies emerge from officials claiming to speak for humanity.
Pillay is similarly not new to waving through anti-Jewish rhetoric. She served as secretary-general of the Durban Review Conference in 2009, when Iranian president Mahmoud Ahmadinejad used an international conference against racism to deliver a tirade of Holocaust denial and rabid antisemitism.
She remained silent throughout the hatred spewed by a man who was responsible for massacring and suppressing his own people, running proxies and allies responsible for the deaths of hundreds of thousands around the region.
Once again, this alone should have ensured Pillay’s name was nowhere near a Nobel Peace Prize.
The announcement of this honor just two days after the anniversary of October 7 deepens the wound. Families had been mourning murdered loved ones, remembering survivors of rape and brutality, and honoring lives shattered by Hamas.
Formal condemnations alone cannot answer these concerns. Jewish victims require our suffering acknowledged, our security treated seriously, and the terrorist nature of Hamas confronted without evasion.
The murder of families, the abuse of hostages, and the deliberate targeting of civilians demand moral clarity. An institution that claims to uphold universal justice must show that crimes against Jews receive its sustained attention, rather than becoming a preliminary footnote to accusations against Israel.
For Jewish communities, these questions have immediate consequences. Children pass security barriers to enter schools. Synagogues require protection. Families consider whether displaying their identity will expose them to hostility.
Peace requires the courage to confront hatred even when it comes from respected colleagues or fashionable causes – even more so when it comes from such a defining and prestigious institution as the Nobel committee. Human rights must remain indivisible and without exempting Jews, and no Nobel medal must be allowed to erase them.
This award is a stain on the committee’s judgment and a profound failure of moral leadership. The Jewish people will continue to demand the equality that international institutions promise.
Our humanity needs no committee’s permission, but any institution that diminishes it forfeits its claim to speak for universal peace.
The writer is the president of the European Jewish Congress, the representative organization of European Jewish communities.

The anti-Zionist rampage through liberal institutions and basic decency is exhausting. We’re in perma-shock. The outrages keep coming, demonizing Israel, undermining the West.
It’s worrying, too. This constant condemnation, the ostracism, needing to stand against the haters, demoralizes many young Diaspora Jews. They’ve been raised to fit in – and to worship many establishments, movements, and professionals now abusing them.
But there they go again. Anti-Zionists hijacked the UN. They poisoned the universities. They muddied feminism’s fight against gendered violence. They’ve seduced doctors, nurses, therapists, and teachers into breaking professional vows of objectivity to target Jews. And now, they’ve profaned the Nobel Peace Prize to validate the Hamas-pleasing genocide libel.
In my Essential Guide to Zionism, Anti-Zionism, Antisemitism and Jew-hatred, I call it the antisemites’ triple double-cross. They betray the Jews, basic liberal-democratic values, and their defining mission, from protecting women to pursuing peace to respecting international law.
Others have scrutinized Navi Pillay’s characterization of Israel as an “apartheid state” in 2017, and the bias that led her to help redefine “genocide” to mean: “a campaign of intentionally, systematically destroying a nation on a mass scale – or anything Israel does in self-defense.”
Instead, I want to reassure my students that the world’s gone mad – not them. The triple double-cross offers them character-building opportunities to think independently, maintain moral clarity, view fads skeptically, and resist the mob courageously.
Sheep don’t make history; greatness doesn’t emerge from following the herd. And if you keep looking over your shoulder, wondering what others say about you, all you get is a sore neck.
In Numbers 23:9, Balaam views the Jews from above the rocky cliffs and the hills, finding them “am levadad yishkon, u’vagoyim lo yitchashav” – a people that dwells alone, refusing to define itself like the others.
In 11th-century France, the commentator Rashi read the rocky reference as evoking Israel’s forefathers and foremothers, starting with Abraham and Sarah, who were iconoclasts, trailblazers. Eight hundred years later, in the Pale of Settlement, Belarus today, the Netziv (Rabbi Naftali Zvi Yehudah Berlin) emphasized that reflexive verb “yitchashav,” to celebrate Jews’ distinct identity. Our enemies don’t define us. We define ourselves differently, in unique terms.
'Do not follow the crowd to do evil'
Judaism celebrates our glorious distinctness. Reinforcing the message, Exodus 23:2 warns: “Do not follow the crowd to do evil, nor should you follow the majority to pervert justice when bearing witness.” That indicts the 61% of American Jewry finding Israel guilty of war crimes, and the 39% swallowing the genocide lie.
More affirmatively, Ethics of the Fathers 5:20 exhorts: “Be bold like leopards, majestic like eagles, swift as deer, and brave as lions when pursuing God’s will.”
Alas, in history, as in the schoolyard – and sadly some frat houses – those who stand tall are often shunned. For older viewers, Gary Cooper’s lonely, brave marshal abandoned by the cowardly townspeople in High Noon (1952), epitomizes the glorious loneliness that Jews and Israel-supporters feel today.
For younger readers, it’s the Ministry of Magic, the media, and his schoolmates shunning Harry Potter when he dares warn of Voldemort’s return. Then, in Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (2003), Harry does what Jews have always done and must do now. Proudly, defiantly, he launches Dumbledore’s Army, knowing he’s on the right side of history.
Admittedly, loneliness can also be a prison, locking people into echo chambers of self-righteousness.
Historically, American Jews and Zionists rejected Eastern Europe’s utter, paralyzing isolation. American Jews built an impressive Empire of Acceptance, shattering one glass ceiling after another. True, in pursuing success – and normalcy – many sacrificed their Judaism, or overly Americanized it.
But history constrained the mass desertion. Hitler’s rise rebalanced Reform Judaism. The movement Zion-ized, learning to appreciate peoplehood power, after decades of trying to renounce Jews’ enveloping solidarity and Israel orientation.
More positively, Israel’s growth and the crisis of Soviet Jewry invited many assimilating Jews into a broad, welcoming, Left-to-Right, religious and secular, blue-and-white tent.
Zionism’s relationship to Jewish apartness was more complex. Zionists believed that ending the exile and returning home would normalize their lives, making Jews less hated. But when I edited The Zionist Ideas, I couldn’t find one thinker who truly sought normalcy.
Judaism’s ideas and values are too catalytic, too counter-cultural. Even Theodor Herzl called Zionism first “a return to Jewishness.”
More recently, the high priest of Israeli “normaliyut,” normalcy, A.B. Yehoshua, actually celebrated being a “total Jew,” using “our texts, our past, our identity in such a way that will imbue us with greatness, hope, and consolation, now that we are home after a painful national journey.” That’s not a recipe for normalcy – or global popularity.
Beyond that internal ideological dynamism are the obsessive anti-Zionists who keep trying to isolate Israel, even as it has flourished. Even now, Israel has ties with 165 other countries.
Forty years ago, when Jew-baiting and Zio-bashing were hibernating in Europe, Norway’s Nobel Committee awarded the 1986 Peace Prize to Elie Wiesel. “Wiesel’s commitment, which originated in the sufferings of the Jewish people, has been widened to embrace all repressed peoples and races,” the committee proclaimed.
Back then, the Nobel committee could hail this unapologetic Jew and Israel lover, while validating the enduring Jewish formula that Wiesel embodied. By leaning into his particularism, into Jewish texts, into our glorious distinctness and distinctiveness, he taught the world enduring lessons about memory, hope, justice, and genuine peace.
We can also balance universalism and particularism, Western normalcy and Jewish singularity, while remembering Wiesel’s reassurance that hatikvah, “hope, is possible beyond despair.”
The writer is a Distinguished Scholar of North American History at McGill University and a Senior Research Fellow at the Jewish People Policy Institute. A former Harvard University finance administrator has filed a federal lawsuit against the institution, alleging religious discrimination after taking paid time off to observe Rosh Hashanah.
