According to the filing, Lilienthal worked remotely from New York as the associate director of the Finance and Grants Administration at the Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health’s Center for Biostatistics in AIDS Research (CBAR).
Lilienthal, who previously worked for Harvard for eight years before returning in September 2024, alleged that his direct supervisor, Jackie Blake, approved his request for paid time off on October 3 and 4, 2024, to observe the Jewish High Holy Day.
However, the lawsuit claims that immediately following his disclosure and observance of the day, he faced sudden heightened scrutiny and manufactured performance concerns. According to the complaint, Blake contacted human resources on the first day of his holiday leave to voice concerns, despite providing no prior negative feedback during his initial business days.
Increased scrutiny after returning from Rosh Hashanah holiday
Upon returning to work, Blake confronted Lilienthal over uncompleted training modules that carried no prior deadlines and allegedly told him, “I don’t want you thinking you can just take off time whenever you want.”
On October 16, 2024, just the 15th business day of his tenure, Lilienthal was terminated via a Zoom call.
When he asked if he was being fired for performance or wrongdoing, Blake allegedly responded, “No.” A day later, HR provided a termination letter citing a lack of “skills or aptitudes,” which the lawsuit calls a pretextual justification.
Lilienthal is suing under Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964, the New York State Human Rights Law, and the New York City Human Rights Law, seeking damages for financial loss, emotional distress, and career damage, alongside a jury trial. Harvard has faced mounting public scrutiny and litigation regarding allegations of antisemitism and campus climate issues since early 2024.

Speaking to reporters on the White House lawn shortly before boarding Marine One for Joint Base Andrews, where he was scheduled to depart for Alaska, Trump was asked whether he intended to endorse a candidate in the Israeli election.
"We haven't even thought about it," the president initially replied.
When a reporter pointed out that he had endorsed political candidates in the past, Trump appeared to leave the door open. "Well, we may be. I may be doing something," he said, before repeating: "I may be. I may be doing something."
The exchange came exactly two weeks before Israel's October 27 election, amid Trump's close political and personal relationship with Netanyahu. Trump did not mention Netanyahu by name in his response, nor did he identify any other Israeli political figure he might consider supporting.
His remarks nevertheless left open the question of whether he intends to play a role in the final stages of Israel's election campaign, at a time when an endorsement from the American president could carry significant political weight.
Trump confirms US continuing to share intelligence with Ukraine
On the Russia-Ukraine war, Trump offered an important clarification after newly appointed White House press secretary Katie Zacharia was unable to answer a question earlier Tuesday about whether Washington had stopped sharing intelligence with Kyiv.
Asked directly whether the United States had suspended intelligence sharing, Trump responded unequivocally. "No, we haven't. We help them, but we're really helping them get to a final answer. We want the war ended, Peter."
He went on to confirm that American assistance, including intelligence cooperation, was continuing as Washington worked with both sides to negotiate an end to the conflict.
"We want the war to end, so we're working with them and with Russia on getting the war to end," he said.
Asked why he believed Russian President Vladimir Putin was interested in ending the war, Trump pointed to his experience in negotiations. "That's what I've done my whole life: is deals," the president said.
"I think they both want it to end," he continued, referring to Putin and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky. "You know, honestly, they both wanted to end, and they don't know how to get to that point."
Trump added: "They don't know how to get there. We're going to get them there."
The president also faced questions about Russian attacks and alleged violations of a ceasefire.
He responded by pointing to Ukrainian strikes on Russian targets, saying, "Ukraine hit many sites the day before."They're hitting each other. But it'll all come to an end," he added.
Trump defends controversial Russian diesel deal
Trump also defended his administration's controversial decision to facilitate additional Russian diesel supplies to international markets, despite concerns that the resulting revenues could help Moscow finance its war against Ukraine.
Asked whether anyone had assured him that Russia would not use proceeds from the arrangement to purchase weapons, Trump replied: "Nobody told me anything."
He insisted that the decision was intended to address global energy shortages rather than provide a direct benefit to the United States.
"That's a diesel deal, not for us. That's being released into the world. That's not being released to us," he said.
"That's a diesel deal that's going to be released into the world for the world market because the world market suffered with high prices, and when you knock out diesel refineries, that's not a great thing."
Later in the exchange, Trump returned to the subject.
"It's a deal for the world. It's not a deal for us. It's a way of getting a lot of oil out to the world," he argued.
He maintained that the arrangement had contributed to lower energy prices, while rejecting suggestions that it was primarily a bilateral commercial agreement benefiting Washington.
Trump on Guilfoyle's removal: 'I didn't speak to her, but she will not be there'
Trump also commented publicly on his administration's decision to seek the resignation of Kimberly Guilfoyle, the US ambassador to Greece, shortly after Zacharia confirmed the move during her first White House press briefing.
Asked about Guilfoyle, who was previously engaged to his eldest son, Donald Trump Jr., the president sought to distance her from his family.
"No, she wasn't a member of my family. She, I guess, dated my son a long time ago," Trump said.
Although he acknowledged that Guilfoyle had performed well in her diplomatic role, he expressed dissatisfaction with recent reports about her conduct.
"She was doing a good job, but we didn't like what we were reading," Trump said.
Asked whether he had personally spoken to Guilfoyle about her departure, he replied: "I didn't speak to her. No, but she will not be there. I didn't like what I read."
The comments followed a series of reports alleging misconduct involving Guilfoyle's dealings with donors and business figures.
Guilfoyle's attorneys have denied the allegations against her. The outgoing ambassador has also rejected the claims and said she intends to defend her reputation.
Earlier Tuesday, Zacharia announced during her debut briefing that the administration had formally requested Guilfoyle's resignation.
"We have asked Ambassador Guilfoyle to resign," Zacharia said. "She has been a wonderful asset to the team, and we wish her well."
Trump also offered a favorable assessment of his new press secretary's first appearance, describing her performance as "very good."
Trump heads to Alaska as midterm campaign intensifies
The remarks came as Trump continued an intensive campaign tour ahead of the November midterm elections, during which Republicans are seeking to retain control of Congress.
Asked whether it would be more difficult for his party to hold the House or the Senate, Trump suggested the challenges were comparable.
"I would say equal," he replied.
He argued that the party of a sitting president traditionally faces a significant disadvantage in midterm elections, regardless of the administration's record.
Nevertheless, Trump maintained that his campaign appearances were generating increased enthusiasm for Republican candidates.
"The level of enthusiasm for the Republican Party is way up, not just where I'm doing them," he said.
The president said he was traveling to Alaska to campaign for Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan, part of a packed schedule of rallies in several states.
"I'm right now going to Alaska to try and help Dan Sullivan, that's a long way away, and I would only do it if I thought he was good, and he's very good," Trump told reporters.
He added that he was holding, on average, one rally every day. "You think that's easy? It's not," Trump said before departing for his next campaign stop.

Iran warns US against renewed military action, stresses readiness for diplomacy and defense
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
16:47:25 UTC
01:47:25 KST

Iran warns US against renewed military action, stresses readiness for diplomacy and defense
TEHRAN — Iran has warned the United States against any renewed military action, saying the consequences would extend beyond the region, while reaffirming its readiness to pursue diplomacy on the basis of realistic proposals and mutual respect for commitments.
Kazem Gharibabadi, Iran’s deputy foreign minister for legal and international affairs, made the remarks in separate interviews with Russia’s RIA Novosti news agency and Al Araby television network, stressing that Washington must adapt to regional realities and abandon military threats in favor of a diplomatic solution.
“If the United States once again chooses the military option, the consequences will not be confined to the region,” Gharibabadi warned, according to his remarks to RIA Novosti. He said Washington must learn from past mistakes and decide whether to continue pursuing confrontation or engage in diplomacy.
The Iranian diplomat emphasized that Tehran had consistently maintained a constructive approach to negotiations and remained prepared for all possible scenarios. He stressed, however, that a diplomatic settlement required realistic proposals and a willingness by the US side to meet its commitments.
Iran finalizing response to US comments
In his interview with Al Araby, Gharibabadi said Iran was finalizing its response to US comments and concerns regarding the proposal Tehran had submitted in New York. Once consultations are complete, Iran will convey its final position through mediators, he added.
Gharibabadi said Iran continued to welcome diplomatic initiatives and had spared no effort to facilitate dialogue with relevant parties. Tehran’s continued engagement in the diplomatic process, he noted, reflected its political flexibility and commitment to finding a solution.
He nevertheless underscored that Iran’s preparedness to defend itself was no less firm than its readiness to negotiate, making clear that diplomatic engagement should not be mistaken for a lack of defensive resolve.
The deputy foreign minister also stressed that the United States must fulfill its own obligations if it expects progress in negotiations. Iran, he said, had not violated its commitments, while Washington had failed to honor its obligations under the Islamabad memorandum of understanding.
Tehran calls for US compliance with commitments
Gharibabadi argued that Iran could not reasonably be expected to demonstrate further flexibility while the United States continued to disregard its commitments. He said Washington needed to take corrective steps to restore the conditions necessary for diplomatic progress.
He added that the US side was already aware of Iran’s demands and conditions for normalizing the situation surrounding the conflict that began in late February. If Washington met those requirements, Tehran would be prepared to take the necessary reciprocal measures.
The Iranian diplomat’s remarks underline Tehran’s position that the path to de-escalation depends on practical steps, reciprocal commitments and an end to reliance on military pressure.
For Iran, diplomacy remains an available avenue for resolving the crisis, but it must be grounded in 'realistic proposals and the implementation of existing commitments.' Tehran has also made clear that its willingness to negotiate does not diminish its determination to defend the country against any renewed military aggression.

Breadcrumb
Palestine Action Canada targets Elbit-owned firm in Ontario
Pro-Palestine activists affiliated with Palestine Action Canada have targeted an Ontario-based subsidiary of Israeli arms manufacturer Elbit Systems, citing the company's role in supplying military equipment amid Israel's military offensives in Gaza and Lebanon.
In a statement sent to The New Arab on Tuesday, the group said it had targeted GeoSpectrum Technologies in Peterborough, Ontario, in the early hours of Monday.
Video footage provided to The New Arab showed activists taking responsibility for damage to the premises.
The footage appeared to show red paint sprayed across the building, writing on its exterior and damage to an outdoor communications box.
It also showed a masked individual apparently tampering with unidentified equipment, while another masked person threatened to smash a window with a hammer.
The activists defended the action, describing Elbit as "the largest profiteer of the genocide of Palestinians."
"Dozens of Canadian companies across the country have been found to supply essential parts and components used in the tanks, drones, and munitions deployed to murder the Palestinian people, with full support of the Canadian state," Palestine Action Canada said.
"GeoSpectrum Technologies, Elbit's Canadian subsidiary, manufactures maritime surveillance and exploration technologies, regularly conducting performance trials with the Royal Canadian Navy and the Department of National Defense," the group added.
Palestine Action Canada has called on the Canadian government to end all trade and ties with Elbit Systems, demanding a full arms embargo and sanctions against Israel.
Local police have confirmed that they are investigating the incident.
They said footage of the incident, which has also circulated on social media, forms part of the investigation.
Police have also classified the incident as a hate- or bias-related crime, adding: "Hate has no place in our community."
According to its website, GeoSpectrum Technologies develops and manufactures marine acoustic systems, including sonar, underwater communications technology, submarine targets and surveillance systems for defence and other applications.
Palestine Action Canada's ongoing Arms Embargo Now campaign has identified several Canadian companies it alleges are involved in supplying components to Israel's defence industry.
The campaign has listed GeoSpectrum Technologies' Peterborough premises among the sites it has identified in connection with Elbit Systems.
The group has previously cited the International Court of Justice's July 2024 advisory opinion that Israel's occupation of Palestinian territiores is unlawful and a subsequent paper by a UN commission in its calls for Canada to comply with international law.
It argues that ending relations with Israel would demonstrate that the Canadian government is not contributing to the continuation of Israel's decades-long occupation or the commission of war crimes and genocide.
The latest development follows discussions at Montreal City Council last month over a motion calling on the Canadian city to suspend all institutional ties with the Israeli government.
However, Montreal ultimately only passed a motion expressing solidarity with Palestinians, removing a clause that called for the severing of institutional and diplomatic ties with Israel.

Secret lies in hospitality: Porto named Europe's most welcoming city, Lisbon close behind
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
16:44:04 UTC
01:44:04 KST

Portuguese hospitality has once again won over international travellers: Porto was voted Europe's most welcoming city, with Lisbon second in Condé Nast Traveller readers' ranking.
Portugal is often considered one of the most welcoming and hospitable countries in the world, with international studies and surveys repeatedly placing the Portuguese people at the top of tourists’ favourites. It is therefore no surprise that Porto has been awarded the title of "Europe's friendliest city".
The distinction comes from readers of Condé Nast Traveller in the Readers’ Choice Awards 2026 (source in Portuguese), which also place the city of Lisbon in second position in this category.
The vote aims to identify cities where "hospitality is at its warmest" and "you find locals eager to help, whether you’re trying to make sense of a neighbourhood restaurant’s menu or looking confused on the metro".
The recognition now given to the Invicta, as Porto is known, "reflects the significant rise in Porto’s popularity as the ideal city-break refuge, both for lovers of good food and for culture enthusiasts", the magazine explains, also highlighting the city’s authenticity and relaxed atmosphere.
"Unwind in a stunning square lined with azulejo tiles or share petiscos – small portions of local delicacies – with residents in a neighbourhood restaurant", Condé Nast encourages, "and you will quickly realise how generous hospitality has made Porto a destination many of us end up returning to time and time again".
Lisbon appears in the next spot. "Few European cities are as picturesque as the sun-drenched Portuguese capital, famous for being built on the seven hills that punctuate the banks of the River Tagus", the magazine notes, describing it as "a wonderful city of winding alleys, soulful fado and creamy pastéis de nata".
"But what really ties it all together is the people. A youthful, inclusive atmosphere pulses through its steep neighbourhoods, and there are plenty of opportunities for travellers to get involved too. Experiencing the vibrant café culture is unmissable, where groups gather to savour their ritual morning espressos, or visiting during the Festival of Saint Anthony to see the cobbled streets fill with open-air parties", the publication recommends.
In the European ranking, the top five is completed by mentions of Amsterdam in the Netherlands, Stockholm in Sweden and Valletta in Malta.

Formycon holds the global rights to FYB206 and will participate in the gross profits of its commercialization partners.With the USFDA’s acceptance of the BLA for review, Formycon has reached a regulatory milestone under the agreement that entitles it to a milestone payment from Zydus, the statement adds.

Ukraine advances EU membership bid with 4 of 6 integration to-do lists unlocked
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
16:41:18 UTC
01:41:18 KST

Editor's note: this article was updated with comments made at a press conference following the opening of the two enlargement clusters.
LUXEMBOURG — Ukraine celebrated the opening of two more EU enlargement clusters at a ceremony in Luxembourg on Oct. 13, a key milestone in the process to eventually become a member state.
Ukraine and Moldova have been advancing their EU membership bids in tandem and are currently trying to open all six of the bloc's enlargement clusters — to-do lists of reforms that must be completed to join the bloc.
"We welcome the continued momentum on Ukraine's candidacy, now the majority of clusters are open, following a prolonged period without movement," said Thomas Byrne, Ireland's Europe Minister, who is chairing enlargement discussions until the end of 2026
On Oct. 13, Ukraine and Moldova unlocked clusters 2 and 3, titled "internal market" and "competitiveness" respectively. They are the two largest clusters by number of policy files.
"Behind these technical names will be real benefits for Ukrainians," said the EU's Enlargement Commissioner Marta Kos.
Among the benefits Kos mentioned: more support for businesses, better working conditions, better consumer protection, and more investments and jobs.
"Ukraine is fully committed to the reforms required for membership and intends to move through this work as quickly as possible," said Deputy Prime Minister for European Integration Vsevolod Chentsov.
The move was made possible the day after the Verkhovna Rada, Ukraine's parliament, passed a law bolstering the rights of the country's Hungarian-speaking minority — a demand that Hungary had said must be fulfilled before it would allow further progress.
In June, Kyiv and Chisinau opened the first cluster, on the rule of law, followed by another on external relations in July.
That leaves only two clusters remaining to be opened, which the European Commission and the Irish Council Presidency of the EU hope to be done with by the end of 2026.
The two remaining clusters risk being harder to get through, as they encompass sectors of the economy such as agriculture and transport, where Ukraine has a competitive edge, and some EU countries fear losing out.
However, two potential opponents, France and Poland, reiterated their support on Oct. 13 for opening all six clusters.
On Oct. 6, the European Commission issued a set of proposals on the future of EU enlargement, which also suggested that Ukraine's agricultural sector would require special treatment, to be handled during the enlargement process rather than used as a block on progress.
Kos told the Kyiv Independent ahead of the opening of the clusters that "once Ukraine will be so far that we will think of what will go in the accession treaty, we will put down the solutions for both sides."
Kos was clear that the process needs to both protect European farmers and help Ukraine export to feed the world, all while Kyiv adopts EU standards.
But Kos' mention of the accession treaty, which is only being drafted near the very end of the EU enlargement process, indicates that she does not expect the strength of Ukraine's agricultural sector to be used as a reason to block progress at this stage.

In Yemen's Taiz, shelling worsens and prices spiral

In Yemen's Taiz, shelling worsens and prices spiral
Oct 13 - With their city encircled by Houthi fighters, residents of Taiz say they face intensifying bombardment and dwindling supplies as the Iran-aligned group tightens its grip on surrounding areas.
Taiz, Yemen's third-largest city, has emerged as a major theatre of the conflict between the Houthis and the Saudi-backed government, after their war was reignited last month by the U.S.-Iran confrontation in the Gulf.
The Houthis cut off a main road from Taiz to Aden last week, leaving government forces encircled.
The International Organization for Migration (IOM) said the situation in Taiz had significantly deteriorated in recent days, and that people, basic supplies and humanitarian goods could not enter the city, driving up prices.
Yemen's internationally recognised government launched a campaign last week to recapture areas controlled by the Houthis, recovering ground near the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, a global shipping artery.
But the Houthis have kept up the pressure near Taiz, seizing the town of Mudiriyat al-Misrakh some 25 km (15 miles) south of the city on Monday, military sources said.
Residents reported heavy shelling of Taiz city on Monday night.
Government sources said the Houthis were to blame.
A spokesperson for the Houthis did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
"We lived a night of terror because of the continuous bombardment," said Ahmed Mahmoud, a resident reached by phone. "This morning there is calm and worry. The streets are empty."
Yassine Muqbil, another Taiz resident contacted by phone, said there had been widespread shelling and his child was too afraid to go outside.
Taiz city had an estimated population of almost 600,000, Katja Juric, IOM's Aden-based Head of Programmes, told Reuters. Government sources said 80,000 had fled in the latest fighting.
INCREASING PRESSURE
Military sources reported fighting in al-Dabab, 10 km (6 miles) from Taiz, and on Sabar Mountain, which overlooks the city to the south, saying government forces who had withdrawn from surrounding areas had regrouped in the city.
Yemeni government warplanes targeted Houthi fighters and equipment in Dabab and Misrakh, government forces said in a statement on Tuesday.
For the Houthis, seizing Taiz city would be a big boost 12 years since the war first erupted. It would leave oil-rich Marib as the last city under government control in northern Yemen.
Mohammed Al-Qadhi, a political and conflict analyst, said Monday evening's heavy shelling and the “tight siege” imposed by Houthi fighters indicated increasing pressure on the city.
"The Houthis know the value of Taiz governorate," he said, noting that its countryside overlooks the coastline and Bab el-Mandeb and that it had served as a bastion of "resistance against the Houthis and their ideology".
The Yemen war erupted in 2014 when the Houthis seized the capital Sanaa, driving the government south.
Fearful of growing Iranian influence and chaos on its borders, Saudi Arabia led a military intervention against the Houthis in early 2015 to restore the government.
The resulting civil war triggered one of the world's biggest humanitarian crises and led to years of fighting and devastating airstrikes by the Saudi-led coalition.
The UN brokered a 2022 truce between the warring sides in Yemen that maintained peace until this year.
'CANNOT FIND FOOD'
In Taiz city, prices of basic goods have shot up.
"By God, we know families who cannot find their daily food," resident Nashwan Saad said on Sunday, adding that a sack of wheat had gone up by as much as some 40%.
IOM's Juric said access to Taiz city had been "significantly constrained", noting that a small bottle of water now cost up to $4. "The prices of basic commodities that are still available in the city have gone up significantly," she said.
"People are rushing to purchase and to stockpile basic commodities as they're anticipating a prolonged conflict and also further supply disruptions in the city."
Abdulrahman al-Qulaia, director general of the Ministry of Industry and Trade Office in Taiz, cautioned against panic.
"We appeal to the entire international community concerned with this matter, to humanitarian organisations and civil society organisations, to work seriously to provide these needs ... and lift the siege on the province." REUTERS

The journalists’ revolt against AI scraping
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
16:39:24 UTC
01:39:24 KST

In just a few short years, artificial intelligence (AI) tools such as ChatGPT and Claude have become mainstream technologies. The companies behind these innovative products tout their immense potential benefit for humanity, but this narrative, while not necessarily wrong, brushes aside that these models are built on the wholesale theft of copyrighted work and threaten to weaken further an already-fragile pillar of democracy: journalism.
That is why Editorial Perfil, a major Latin American publisher headquartered in Argentina (and the owner of Perfil, the newspaper where I am digital director), recently sued ChatGPT’s owner, OpenAI, and the company’s largest external shareholder, Microsoft, for the improper use of Editorial Perfil’s journalistic content in their AI products. In the damages suit brought before the Argentine Federal Civil and Commercial Court, we also accused these companies of “unfair competition” — in other words, abusing their oligopolistic position to our detriment.
While Editorial Perfil is the first Spanish-language publisher to file a copyright-infringement suit against an AI firm, it follows in the footsteps of the New York Times, which sued OpenAI and Microsoft over the same issue in late 2023. The Brazilian newspaper Folha de Sao Paulo brought a similar case last year, resulting in a content-licensing agreement earlier this year (an approach that OpenAI has taken with other publishers, including PRISA, the Spanish conglomerate behind El Pais).
We have been here before: Dominant search and social-media platforms also benefited from copyrighted news content without always sharing in the spoils. Search engines — such as Google’s “free” model — made news articles immensely more accessible by featuring them on their results pages. However, despite relying heavily on this copyrighted content to boost ad revenue, Google was not required to provide adequate compensation to the media companies that might employ hundreds of journalists to produce it. True, these distribution systems drove traffic to publishers’ Web sites, but the playing field was never level and increasingly tilted toward tech firms as they consolidated their power.
In the AI age, OpenAI and Anthropic (which owns Claude), as well as the entrenched tech giants such as Google and Meta (which owns Instagram and Facebook), have supercharged this dynamic. The chatbots and other AI enterprise products they have built on the back of increasingly sophisticated large language models answer Internet users’ questions directly, depriving news outlets of traffic and the chance to serve ads or sell subscriptions to potential readers.
These models required huge amounts of training data, much of which was copyrighted material illegally scraped from the Internet. Anthropic recently settled a class-action lawsuit in California by agreeing to pay US$1.5 billion to book authors who argued that the company had downloaded pirated copies of their works to train Claude. The models constantly thirst for more, particularly up-to-date information on current events.
At Editorial Perfil, we have identified multiple instances in which ChatGPT can replicate content from our historical archive in detail. It does the same with real-time news and would even prompt users to request a daily news recap so that they can avoid wasting time visiting multiple sites. It easily bypasses paywalls; for articles that it cannot find within Editorial Perfil’s own sites, it would use copycat Web sites that illegally reprinted them. Historical server data show that multiple bots are consistently crawling our content — not just from OpenAI, but from all the AI firms as well.
These flagrant abuses are self-evident to anyone with common sense. AI firms are not only stealing content, but also encouraging users to stay within their closed ecosystems, turning the Internet into an oligopolistic market. Yet they still try to argue that they are engaging in “fair use” of “publicly available” content. Unfortunately for OpenAI, it has already acknowledged the value of journalism through its many licensing deals. By contrast, Anthropic has avoided content-licensing agreements with news organizations.
The news industry has been in crisis ever since the digital revolution upended its business model more than two decades ago. A new, more sustainable model never emerged. While those of us in media failed to anticipate how the rise of the Internet would change everything, we tried to reinvent ourselves after the fact. However, the oligopolistic dominance of “big tech” has prevented us from making any real progress, and AI is exacerbating the crisis.
A decimated news industry is a bad outcome for everyone. It would not only result in a less informed public; it would also harm the parasitical AI firms themselves, cutting off an important source of training data. If they cannot be bothered to act in the public’s interest, they should at least look out for their own.
Agustino Fontevecchia is digital director at Perfil in Argentina.

Qantas has been forced to ground a plane in Rome after bedbugs were discovered on the aircraft on its way from Perth, a source with knowledge of the incident said yesterday.
The parasitic insects were found in the front of the economy section of the Boeing 787 Dreamliner as it made its way from Perth to Rome for the QF5 flight on Friday last week, the source said.
Bedbugs are small insects that feed on the blood of some mammals, including humans, which can be hard to eradicate.
Photo: Reuters
As first reported by the Sydney Morning Herald, the aircraft had to be taken out of service for cleaning after its arrival in the Italian capital, resulting in the cancelation of the Qantas Rome to Perth service on Saturday.
A Qantas spokesperson said the flight was canceled to allow its engineers and maintenance teams to carry out a deep clean of the aircraft after “an issue identified on a small number of economy seats.”
The airline wanted to “sincerely apologize” to customers for the disruption, they said.
Affected passengers were given accommodation and rebooked on alternative flights within 48 hours of their original departure, Qantas said.
Its aircraft cabins were cleaned regularly and to an extremely high standard and treated with disinfectant every 50 days as a standard precautionary cleaning measure, the airline said.
Macquarie University parasitologist Michelle Power said the bedbugs had “more than likely” been brought on to the plane in someone’s luggage or on a passenger’s clothes and then escaped into the cabin.
“They’re associated with travel. People may go to a hotel that’s infested and because they like dark spaces and are attracted to the smell of human clothes, they make their way into someone’s luggage,” she said.
“They’re a flightless insect, without planes,” she said.
Bedbugs are not dangerous, even though their bites could be itchy and irritating, but they are difficult to get rid of and could hide in bedsheets and crevices for a long time without needing to feed, Power said.

====================================================================================================

The next AI race brings to light the limits of large language models
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
16:39:21 UTC
01:39:21 KST

More than 50 years after her death, Helen Keller still turns up in artificial intelligence (AI) debates. The communication breakthroughs of the US writer, who was deaf and blind, are often cited as evidence that language is the best path to creating machines that are as intelligent as humans.
Despite loud early doubters, large language models (LLMs) — the technology underpinning the vast majority of today’s AI investment — have proven far more grounded than critics expected. A computer cannot dip its toes in the ocean, but it can recognize enough patterns in the writings of the entire Internet to mimic an understanding of what it means to get your feet wet. Our obsession with LLMs follows a long tradition of affiliating language with intelligence.
Yet Keller’s own retelling of the famous “w-a-t-e-r” milestone was about more than words. As her teacher, Anne Sullivan, spelled out the letters on her palm, Keller also felt a “wonderful cool something” flowing over her hand. She was not simply relating one word to another, she was connecting language to a physical sensation.
That distinction matters as everyone from Nvidia chief executive officer Jensen Huang (黃仁勳) to Chinese President Xi Jinping (習近平) heralds the physical AI era. In the next phase of this tech revolution, marked by AI-powered robots navigating the real world, the limits of LLMs are becoming harder to dismiss. Knowing every sentence ever written about using chopsticks or tying shoelaces is different from being able to feed yourself or get out the door.
I have written before that the two biggest barriers to useful humanoid robots are the hands (dexterity) and the “brains” (AI models that can power real-world actions). Solving both could unlock what Morgan Stanley forecasts would become a US$5 trillion market by 2050. However what if those problems are more interconnected than we thought?
Biologists studying hominin fossils found that primate dexterity and brain development evolved hand-in-hand over generations, suggesting intelligence was shaped not just by observing the world, but by physically acting in it, said a Nature paper published last year.
Achieving so-called artificial general intelligence (AGI) in machines might not be all that different, said Junghee Ryu, the chief executive officer of RLWRLD, a physical AI start-up with offices in Seoul, San Francisco and Tokyo. His company is developing foundation models for robots that can crack five-finger dexterity, and he argues that the hardware and software for robot brains and hands must co-evolve. Earlier this year, RLWRLD announced a collaboration with Nvidia to develop a new benchmark for dexterous manipulation.
LLMs are very good at understanding their circumstances and planning actions, Ryu said, but they still cannot perform any jobs requiring dexterity, making them useless across vast swaths of the labor market. To him, that should throw cold water on recent claims that we have reached AGI, the mythical goalpost marking systems that is as economically viable as humans.
He is not alone. Human-like dexterity, particularly with robotic hands, is the “final component making AGI possible,” analysts at the Korea Investment & Securities wrote in an industry report earlier this year. Hands are connected to 25 percent of the brain motor cortex and 30 percent of the sensory cortex, making them crucial to how humans perceive and act on external information, they said.
Yet even as experts continuously forecast that we are inching closer to AGI, they tend to think we are getting further from machines completing basic physical tasks. In a long-running survey of hundreds of AI researchers, respondents in 2016 thought machines that could fold laundry or assemble any Lego set better than humans would arrive by about 2022 and 2025, respectively. In the latest 2024 iteration, those milestones slipped back to 2030 and 2031.
It makes sense given that the benchmarks that still prove hardest for AI involve acting in the real world, marked by unpredictable environments and where mistakes have physical consequences, Stanford’s latest AI Index report noted. Comparing robot performance in controlled labs versus simulated households, the researchers found a vast gap. It is a sobering reality check, and one that researchers like Ryu think comes down to a lack of dexterity.
It is also a wake-up call for China. Aware of demographic shifts, Beijing has made physical AI a policy priority. The nation seems to have a leg up in humanoids, with Chinese companies accounting for more than 97 percent of global shipments in the first half of this year, US-based Smart Analytics Global said. However, beneath the flashy demos, the illusion of capability breaks down.
This provides an opening for others to tackle the most difficult parts of making robots useful. Doing so would likely continue to reveal the limits of just building bigger language models. The investor mania for LLMs also heightens the risk that the money is piling in faster than the science is advancing. About 76 percent of AI researchers polled last year assert that “scaling up current AI approaches” is unlikely or very unlikely to achieve AGI.
Nowhere are the limits of language and our ability to manipulate it more apparent than in our collective efforts to even find the words to define AGI. The route toward human-like intelligence in the real world might end up looking more like Keller’s, requiring not just words, but touch.
Catherine Thorbecke is a Bloomberg Opinion columnist covering Asia tech. Previously she was a tech reporter at CNN and ABC News. This column reflects the personal views of the author and does not necessarily reflect the opinion of the editorial board or Bloomberg LP and its owners.

EDITORIAL: Price to pay
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
16:39:19 UTC
01:39:19 KST

Kevin Tsai (蔡康永), former host of the variety show Here Comes Kangxi (康熙來了), on Sunday last week attended a campaign event of Legislator Puma Shen (沈伯洋), the Democratic Progressive Party’s (DPP) candidate for Taipei mayor. Chinese on social media expressed outrage.
Tsai, who was born in Taipei and is a second-generation waishengren (Mainlander) whose parents were from Shanghai, like some other Taiwanese entertainers, has a substantial following in China.
Given his background, people on the other side of the Taiwan Strait were under the impression that he was pan-blue, although Tsai had not explicitly identified himself with either political camp.
One thing about him that Chinese might not be aware of is that during the Martial Law era, Tsai was the editor of a school magazine. He received two demerits and nearly got expelled for encouraging his classmates to write about the 228 Incident. In an interview with TVBS in 2005, he said that as a child of the privileged class, he felt guilty toward those who had suffered and wanted more people to know the truth.
Chinese audiences feel betrayed by Tsai’s attendance at Shen’s event because the lawmaker was named on Beijing’s list of “die-hard Taiwan independence separatists” in October 2024.
While Tsai said he wanted to hear all sides and that he did not speak, his attendance alone was interpreted by Chinese critics as supporting independence.
Chinese government-linked social media accounts began mobilizing a boycott of Tsai. Without naming him, they warned that entertainers who profit from the Chinese market while “flirting with Taiwan independence” would “pay a price too heavy to bear.” A commentary published by the Chinese-language United Daily News, which was later removed, described one of the Chinese accounts as having “drawn a blade.”
Several Chinese businesses have distanced themselves from Tsai, while the Chinese propaganda machine pressed on with the attacks, with a social media commentary platform affiliated with the People’s Daily overseas edition naming Tsai, and saying he had failed to admit wrongdoing or distance himself from Taiwanese independence advocates.
While Taipei Mayor Chiang Wan-an (蔣萬安), who is seeking re-election as the Chinese Nationalist Party’s (KMT) candidate, was not concerned that Tsai attended the Shen event, KMT Chairwoman Cheng Li-wun (鄭麗文) was stunned by it. She asked whether he is ready to give up his “massive commercial interests” in China.
Chiang said he respects Tsai’s decision to endorse whoever he feels like and invited Tsai to attend one of his own campaign events. He said that everyone is free to make their own choices and their freedom should not be interfered with in any form.
By contrast, Cheng distanced herself from Tsai, saying they were not friends and that she had no idea why he attended Shen’s event or whether he supported the DPP candidate. She added that Shen is no ordinary DPP politician, but someone with “a very clearly defined political stance.”
By associating with Shen, Tsai runs a great risk of being boycotted, she said.
While Chiang knows the right things to say as an election looms, Cheng, as leader of the KMT, seems to believe that political ideals are tradable items and that only a fool would give up their own interests.
Are national interests and sovereignty also up for sale in her mind?
Mainland Affairs Council Deputy Minister and spokesman Liang Wen-chieh (梁文傑), using a Chinese idiom, said he was shocked by Cheng’s willingness to meekly accept humiliation.
The shamelessness of the KMT is plain to see.
For all of its bluster, the Chinese propaganda machine got one thing correct: National sovereignty is a matter of principle with “no room for ambiguity.” Those who “sit on the fence and go wherever the wind blows” would eventually pay an “unbearable price.”
Next month’s nine-in-one elections are fewer than 50 days away. The opportunists who think they are betting on the winning side while flirting with the Chinese Communist Party might be the ones to face a “price too heavy to bear.”

Infantino could hold presidency

Gianni Infantino could survive weeks of criticism and secure re-election as FIFA president in the absence of a heavy hitter to challenge him, observers have said.
The 56-year-old Swiss has lost the support of many associations in his bid to be re-elected to a fourth and final term since he launched and then hastily walked back his plan to allow private investment into the World Cup.
Infantino does crucially retain his core support in Africa and South America.
Photo: Reuters
His FIFA Forward Enterprise (FFE) plan, which came to light in July just after the hugely successful World Cup, would have created a commercial subsidiary to run FIFA’s biggest events, such as the World Cup.
However, with two of his reported fiercest critics, Aleksander Ceferin and Victor Montagliani opting to run for re-election as heads of European governing body UEFA and North American grouping CONCACAF respectively, the opposition to Infantino is seeking a viable candidate to challenge him in the election next March.
Candidates have to declare by Nov. 18.
Terrence Burns, who was marketing strategist for two successful World Cup hosting bids, said Infantino was always in the box seat.
“He holds all the cards and always has,” he said in an interview. “Any prospective challenger at this point feels either performative or strategic to cut deals.”
Former International Olympic Committee (IOC) marketing chief Michael Payne said “everyone is surprised” that no serious candidate has come forward to challenge Infantino.
“If he is re-elected, which is looking increasingly likely, it will redefine the term Houdini,” Payne said in an interview.
Long-time Infantino critic Lise Klaveness, the head of the Norwegian Football Federation (NFF), has impressed many but has ruled out running.
However, even if Klaveness changed her mind she would face a large challenge in becoming the first woman to run world soccer and emulate Kirsty Coventry, who last year became the first woman elected as IOC president.
“People within the IOC administration were working toward the goal of Coventry being elected, as [her predecessor] Thomas Bach’s wish was for her to be president,” a source close to the world of soccer governance, who asked not to be identified, said in an interview. “Lise faces exactly the opposite. FIFA staff would be working to stop her being elected.”
Infantino is not safe yet, as the opposition have mounted legal challenges in the US and filed official complaints with FIFA committees.
Klaveness and the Norwegian federation have raised three issues, with the common thread being Infantino’s friendship with US President Donald Trump.
The venture capital firm of Josh Kushner, the brother of Trump’s son-in-law Jared, was to be the major investor in FFE.
However, the same source said “there is no certainty that the complaints will be looked into. Even if they were to consider them they would take their time.”
“The fear in the Infantino camp is the Norwegians could take them to CAS [Court of Arbitration for Sport] if dissatisfied with the decision,” the source said.
Burns believes the greatest risk to Infantino comes from the legal challenges launched by UEFA in the US courts to gain access to the papers pertaining to FFE. FIFA are strongly contesting the case.
“This point is a fly in the ointment,” Burns said. “If the FFE was just a case of misguided process and communications strategy, why hide its specifics?”
“That lack of transparency is a rock in Infantino’s shoe that will not fade away,” he added,
Payne believes the lack of support for Infantino from leading soccer nations such as Spain, France and England could be damaging. “Running a global sports federation requires unity — FIFA will be on the brink of civil war, and this is totally new territory for a sports governing body,” he said.
Burns thinks the opposition would reluctantly make peace with Infantino.
He said soccer’s governing bodies would rather avoid division “unless of course there is overwhelming criminal activity to justify it — which there is not.”
The other point that could tip the balance is if there is a “financial upside” for the federations by removing Infantino. On that point, he said, “again, there isn’t.”
Burns said that the process is likely to “result in even greater consolidation of power and influence for Infantino when it is all over.”

Houthi attacks leave Trump with "a difficult dilemma"
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
16:39:18 UTC
01:39:18 KST

Iran's Houthi allies' deadly attacks on Saudi Arabia create "a difficult dilemma for President Trump"
London — Yemen's Iran-backed Houthi rebels have dramatically upped the stakes in the complex Middle East war, killing at least 20 people — including an American — and wounding hundreds more with strikes on Saudi Arabia's airports over the last week.
The question is whether President Trump will order U.S. military action in support of Saudi Arabia, which has been at war with the rebels in Yemen for more than a decade.
Mr. Trump campaigned on ending wars, and he is likely aware, less than a month before the U.S. midterm elections, that opening a new U.S. front in the wider conflict sparked by the Feb. 28 joint U.S.-Israeli attack on Iran could be politically perilous.
If he did, he could argue that it is both to protect the Saudis, as a key U.S. ally, and to stop the Iranian proxy group from threatening global shipping in the vital trade routes of the Red Sea.
Mr. Trump rejected a request last month by Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman to join in the kingdom's strikes on the Houthis, two sources familiar with the matter told CBS News. He came close to ordering airstrikes against the group a week later, but again declined.
Asked Sunday if the U.S. would join Saudi strikes, however, the president replied: "We may. We're gonna look at it … We'll make a decision. We move very quickly."
So, what has changed, and will it be enough to force Mr. Trump's hand?
An American death
Little information has come out about the U.S. citizen killed in the Saturday attack on Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport, but the killing of an American may increase pressure on Mr. Trump to retaliate.
According to Nadwa al-Dawsari, associate fellow at the Middle East Institute, it may not be enough in itself, however, to spur the president to further entrench the U.S. in the wider regional conflict.
"I don't think that the killing of an American will trigger a military response," she told CBS News on Monday. "The Houthis have killed American civilians before, including detainees who died after being tortured by the Houthis in Sanaa, and that did not provoke a response from the U.S., militarily or otherwise. Trump's decision will likely depend on his broader assessment of the risks of further escalation."
Oil prices
Oil prices may be one of the biggest factors in the president's calculus. He has vowed repeatedly to bring down prices at the pump, which have soared as a result of the war with Iran impeding exports from major Persian Gulf energy producers.
The Trump administration insists Iran has no control over the Strait of Hormuz, and more oil has been getting out of the Middle East from the Persian Gulf in recent weeks.
But the Houthis hold significant territory along Yemen's Red Sea coast, which has enabled them to threaten vessels there and in the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, the southern gateway to the Red Sea and another key chokepoint for global energy supplies.
If the Houthis are able to control Yemen's coastline, or enough of it to maintain their threat to shipping via the Bab el-Mandeb, it would put more pressure on energy flows, increasing the leverage Iran and its proxy groups have over global fuel prices.
Thomas Juneau, associate fellow at the Chatham House think tank's Middle East and North Africa Program, told CBS News that this creates "a difficult dilemma for President Trump."
"Direct U.S. involvement would likely lead to greater tension in the Red Sea, and therefore create more upward pressure on oil prices," he said. "Should the U.S. refuse to become directly engaged, however, it will cause growing resentment and anger in Saudi Arabia, where feelings of abandonment caused by a widespread perception that the U.S. is failing to support its partner at a time of need are already acute."
Helping an ally
Despite long-running U.S. accusations that some members of the Saudi leadership supported the al Qaeda Sept. 11 hijackers, and the fallout from the brutal murder of journalist Jamal Khashoggi in 2018, Saudi Arabia has managed to maneuver itself into a position of relative international respectability over the last few years, pursuing a raft of economic reforms to attract foreign investment and building on its status as the world's top oil exporter.
The foreign money and visitors could dry up, however, if the Saudis prove incapable of defending themselves from Houthi attacks.
Saudi authorities regularly report intercepting Houthi weapons. But the death toll over the last week has exposed gaping holes in Saudi defenses. The Reuters news agency reported Tuesday that the Saudi system to warn civilians of a military attack went silent days before the latest series of deadly Houthi strikes.
The Trump administration has fostered close business and defense ties with the Saudis, and failing to come to the aid of an ally in need — especially one that hosts five U.S. military bases — could make Washington appear to be an unreliable ally.
What do the Saudis want, and would it be effective?
Of all the military options at Mr. Trump's disposal, airstrikes on Houthi targets "would make the greatest difference," al-Dawsari told CBS News. The U.S. has, so far, only acknowledged offering intelligence and targeting support to Saudi Arabia.
"The United States can also strengthen air and missile defense cooperation and help identify Houthi launch sites, weapons facilities, and command-and-control infrastructure," al-Dawsari said.
While the aim of U.S. strikes would likely be "to degrade the Houthis' ability to launch missiles and drones against Saudi Arabia and threaten shipping in the Red Sea," al-Dawsari said "airstrikes alone will not eliminate the Houthi threat."
"The real question is whether American military action would be part of a broader effort to weaken the Houthis, or simply another round of limited strikes that they can absorb and recover from," she said.
"The risk is that the United States becomes drawn into a prolonged military campaign against the Houthis while already fighting Iran. But there is also a risk in allowing the Houthis to continue operating as an Iranian military asset and a threat in their own right at Bab el-Mandeb and in the Red Sea," she added.
"The United States has a significant interest in keeping the Bab el-Mandeb open, and in protecting the Saudi economy — in particular, the kingdom's ability to export energy products," said CBS News national security analyst Aaron MacLean. "A world in which the Houthis are regularly scoring spectacular hits in Saudi Arabia … is not a world in which America's interests are secure."
MacLean cautioned, however, that in addition to the risk of making energy markets even more nervous and driving prices up further, "President Trump has to consider that American military action targeting the Houthis will almost certainly be indecisive."
While U.S. strikes could help push the Houthis back and reduce their attack capabilities for a time, "the most Washington can reasonably hope for from a major military operation — adding American airpower to existing capabilities on the ground — is a 'mowing of the lawn,'" said MacLean, and "participating in a protracted conflict with no clear theory of how to end it is a tough sell when you are a president who campaigned on ending so-called 'endless wars.'"
The U.S. has targeted the Houthis before, with strikes between March and May 2025 to prevent the group from attacking commercial ships in the Red Sea. The group claimed those attacks were in support of Palestinians, amid Israel's blockade of the Gaza Strip.
The U.S. strikes did "cause significant pain to the Houthis … much more than what Saudi Arabia has been able to do," said Juneau, at Chatham House in London.
But even those American strikes "were not sufficient to fully deter the Houthis from continuing their attacks in the Red Sea, let alone to defeat them," he said.
"The bar for President Trump to authorize strikes now is seemingly pretty high," according to Mona Yacoubian, director of the Middle East Program at the Center for Strategic and International Studies. "The U.S. is only likely to intercede now in the event of a Houthi attack that results in several U.S. casualties."
Asked about the Houthis, President Trump said Monday that the rebels were "misbehaving very badly." He repeated that in a Truth Social post Tuesday, adding that he thought the group "learned their lesson a year ago when we bombed the HELL out of them."
"Now they've emerged again, probably at the behest of Iran," Mr. Trump said in the post, adding that the rebels were "in a very nasty way, hitting Saudi Arabia, and purposefully trying to drive up Oil Prices, probably prior to the U.S. Elections — NOT NICE. Somebody should explain to them that I'm not running in the Elections, I've already won, IN A MASSIVE LANDSLIDE, but I'll be there after the Elections, and I will never forget!"
In an interview with the French news agency AFP, meanwhile, Houthi political bureau member Mohammed al-Bukhaiti warned Tuesday that if the U.S. chooses to get "involved in the aggression against Yemen, we will not deliberate over the decision to respond, rather, there will be a swift and painful response targeting the U.S. and all its interests in the region."
Given the Pentagon's recent acknowledgment of U.S. munitions shortages caused by the war with Iran, Mr. Trump will have to consider carefully the American military's ability to defend against and respond to potential Houthi retaliatory attacks if he does wade into Yemen's civil war.

Energy security a question of time
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
16:39:16 UTC
01:39:16 KST

On Oct. 5, Saudi Aramco chief executive officer Amin Nasser warned that the world’s oil stocks were “scarily thin.”
For most countries, that means higher prices. For Taiwan, which imports almost all of its fuel, it raises a more basic question: How long can it keep its power on if supplies are cut?
Taiwan holds more than 140 days of crude oil, but its natural gas, which generated 47.8 percent of its electricity last year, would last about 11 days. Japan, by comparison, holds roughly two months of gas.
After the US-Israeli strikes on Iran on Feb. 28, shipping through the Strait of Hormuz collapsed and Qatar, Taiwan’s second-largest gas supplier, stopped production. In April and May, no gas cargoes reached Taiwan from Qatar or the United Arab Emirates. Refiners rerouted oil through Saudi Arabia’s Red Sea ports and bought more from the US.
To keep the power on, Taiwan bought gas on the spot market, where single cargoes are sold to the highest bidder. Spot purchases rose from about 30 percent of supply to between 60 and 65 percent, and the price Taiwan paid rose by about 70 percent. Electricity prices for large industrial users rose 41.58 percent, while the government absorbed three-quarters of fuel cost increases for households.
It worked, at a high cost to industry and public finances, but it might be harder to repeat.
For one thing, a tight oil market also makes gas more expensive. That might seem odd, as oil and gas are different fuels, but most of the long-term contracts that supply gas to Asia, including those from Qatar and Australia, do not fix a price in advance. Instead, the price of each gas shipment is set by a formula tied to the price of crude oil: When oil rises, gas bought under those contracts rises with it. Taiwan is no exception. CPC Corp, Taiwan, the state-run importer, has said its gas import price formulas are “traditionally linked to crude oil prices,” using Brent crude or the average price of crude imported into Japan as the benchmark.
Australia and Qatar, which together supplied two-thirds of Taiwan’s gas last year, sell mainly on such oil-linked terms.
Aramco estimates that refilling the world’s oil stocks will add about 2 million barrels a day to demand for at least 18 months, keeping oil prices high. Taken together, that means Taiwan will pay more even for gas it has already secured under contract, adding to costs that CPC cannot pass on to consumers.
The Hormuz crisis is not over. Qatar has extended its suspension into early December and its main export plant at Ras Laffan, damaged in March, is still running at reduced capacity. Even when the strait reopens, supply will take time to recover.
Taiwan is entering winter without the supplier that provided one-third of its gas last year.
The short gas buffer matters for Taiwan in three ways:
The first is economic. Gas generates nearly half of Taiwan’s electricity, so a shortage would quickly become a power problem for industry, including the chipmakers at the heart of its economy. Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co (TSMC) alone uses about 9 percent of Taiwan’s electricity.
The second is fiscal. This year’s shortfall was covered by paying more, and the bill has landed on CPC and the treasury: a projected NT$56 billion (US$1.75 billion) loss for CPC this year and a request for supplementary public funding.
The third is political. The 11-day figure has already been used against Taiwan. In March, posts on Chinese social media claimed that Taiwan was about to run out of gas and officials replied with general assurances rather than figures.
A thin buffer is a vulnerability that others can exploit, even when supply holds.
The government knows the problem. It set a target of 14 days of gas reserves in 2018 and Qatar’s share of CPC’s gas supply has fallen to 11 percent this year.
However, three obstacles have slowed efforts to build a larger gas buffer.
The first is storage. Gas tanks need a port terminal, land, distance from homes, local consent and environmental approval. Planners moved the third terminal, at Guantang Industrial Port (觀塘工業港) in Taoyuan’s Guanyin District (觀音), offshore to protect the Datan algal reef, and it began commercial operations only last year. The fourth faces land contamination problems and the fifth is behind schedule.
Because Taiwan can store so little, it needs about 30 gas carriers to arrive every month, so any delay at sea quickly eats into its reserves.
The second is money. CPC must hold down domestic prices and secure fuel abroad. It expects its seventh straight annual loss this year, with debts above 90 percent of its assets. That makes cheaper, more secure long-term contracts harder to sign.
The third is competition from neighbors. In March, Minister of Economic Affairs Kung Ming-hsin (龔明鑫) said gas swaps with Japan and South Korea were difficult because “everyone is scrambling for cargoes.” Japan and South Korea have since expanded swaps with each other. The Energy Administration has said that Taiwan is open to holding gas reserves in Japan or South Korea, provided the gas can still reach Taiwan when needed.
Three steps could help. The first would be to explore whether CPC’s two roles can be separated. It means funding household price support openly from the budget, as the supplementary funding CPC has requested would partly do, so that the company can focus on securing supply.
The second would be to give storage projects a clear timetable. Environmental and local concerns are legitimate, but regulators could review terminal projects within a fixed time limit, reducing costs and delays.
The third would be to publish the gas reserve regularly. A regularly published figure for days of gas held would make claims like those in March easier to answer and let the public follow progress toward the 14-day target.
Mihir Shete is an academic at National Chengchi University.

Nangang Station leading source of emissions: TRC
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
16:39:14 UTC
01:39:14 KST

Taipei Railway Corp (TRC) has disclosed its latest greenhouse gas emissions report, with Nangang Station — not Taipei Railway Station as many assumed — listed as its largest source of emissions.
TRC launched its sustainability program in 2024, establishing a greenhouse gas inventory as the first step toward achieving net zero emissions, it said on Tuesday last week.
The company conducted an initial inventory of 32 major stations, established an emissions management system and obtained carbon-footprint labels for three of its passenger services: the Tze-Chiang Limited Express, the Chu-Kuang Express and local trains.
Photo: CNA
Last year, TRC expanded the inventory to cover all 613 operating sites, maintenance facilities, offices and ancillary facilities.
Train operations accounted for 75.1 percent of its total carbon emissions, while station operations contributed 15.6 percent, Sustainability Development Section chief Peng Hsien-fu (彭賢富) said.
TRC’s emissions reached 428,400 tonnes of carbon dioxide equivalent (tCO2e) last year, with train and station operations accounting for about 90 percent of the total, he said.
All five stations with the highest emissions are in the six special municipalities.
Nangang Station ranked first with 6,923.95tCO2e, followed by Taipei Station ranked second with 6,859.48tCO2e, Kaohsiung Station with 5,793.22tCO2e, Banqiao Station with 5,362.84tCO2e and Songshan Station with 4,268.61tCO2e.
Among maintenance facilities, Fugang Maintenance Depot in Taoyuan had the highest emissions at 3,474.97tCO2e, followed by Hsinchu Maintenance Depot at 2,491.51tCO2e, Qidu Maintenance Depot in Keelung at 2,473.9tCO2e, Taipei Maintenance Depot at 1,986.78tCO2e and Kaohsiung Maintenance Depot at 1,814.75tCO2e.
TRC is introducing more energy-efficient trains, regenerative braking systems, smart maintenance and digital management to reduce emissions, Peng said.
The company is also integrating operating and equipment data through its SOPHIA cloud platform to improve energy and equipment management, he said.
From 2019 to last year, TRC issued 55.36 million mobile tickets, reducing emissions by a cumulative 341tCO2e and saving NT$55.36 million (US$1.73 million) in printing costs, Peng said.
TRC has also installed solar power facilities at its stations, maintenance depots and rolling-stock bases. It has leased out 73 sites for solar installations, with a combined capacity of 40.6 megawatts.
The facilities generate about 60.44 million kilowatt-hours of electricity annually, enough to supply about 16,200 households, it said.
The company has set a target of reducing its carbon emissions by 3 percent by 2028.

Reject the merger of Grab and Foodpanda
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
16:39:12 UTC
01:39:12 KST

Southeast Asian food delivery platform Grab Holdings Ltd in March applied to acquire Delivery Hero SE’s Foodpanda operations in Taiwan, with the Fair Trade Commission (FTC) scheduled to announce its decision on Oct. 27.
On the surface, the deal is a business merger — but in substance, it involves personal data, national geospatial information and digital sovereignty. It cannot be assessed solely in terms of market share and price competition.
Grab has extensive and long-standing connections to Chinese capital. In 2015, Chinese ride-hailing firm Didi Chuxing and China Investment Corp, a sovereign wealth fund, invested in Grab. Grab invested in Chinese autonomous-driving firms WeRide and Momenta, and formed a joint venture with Ping An Good Doctor in 2018, integrating artificial intelligence (AI), identity, medical and payment data.
Grab signed a memorandum of cooperation with Huawei Technologies Co’s Petal Maps last year, and integrated electric vehicle systems with BYD Co and Guangzhou Automobile Group Co. It has worked with Ant Group Co on cross-border payments since 2016, deepening the partnership in 2023 through travel assistant Alipay+ Voyager.
Map data have national security implications. Through delivery workers’ GPS locations and images, Grab accumulates detailed, real-time local data that are far more valuable than static maps. Articles 7 and 14 of China’s National Intelligence Law require organizations and citizens to support and assist intelligence work. Even if Grab claims that its partnership with Huawei does not cover Taiwan, the nation has no way to verify whether data could be fully isolated from China following the acquisition.
Storing data overseas could render oversight ineffective. Grab claims that Taiwanese user data are stored in Singapore, but once data leave Taiwan, the government’s inspection powers under Article 22 of the Personal Data Protection Act (個人資料保護法) become difficult to enforce.
The government cannot verify whether data have been transferred to a third country, leaked or reused. Grab has suffered data breaches in Singapore involving account balances, license plates and home addresses. If the acquisition proceeds, the security of approximately 6 million consumers’ spending and mobility records, as well as transaction data, would be at stake.
Digital sovereignty is the foundation of a nation in the AI era. South Korea has restricted the export of high-precision map data on national security grounds since 2007, only beginning to ease the restrictions under some conditions in the past few years. Europe and the US have also strengthened controls on cross-border data flows. Those developments show that data sovereignty has become the core of national governance.
As a major tech power, Taiwan should do more to support domestic businesses rather than allow critical data to flow to overseas platforms with complex ties.
The acquisition poses risks to personal data, national geospatial information and digital sovereignty, outweighing any possible economic benefits. Article 13 of the Fair Trade Act (公平交易法) stipulates that “the competent authority may not prohibit any of mergers filed if the overall economic benefit of the merger outweighs the disadvantages resulted from competition restraint.”
The provision applies when a merger’s overall economic benefits outweigh the harm caused by reduced competition — a condition this case fails to meet.
The FTC should carefully weigh the risks and reject the acquisition.
Hsueh Hua-yuan is a professor in National Chengchi University’s Department of History and chairman of the Taiwan Association of University Professors.

The government yesterday condemned a series of attacks last week targeting King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh that resulted in deaths and civilian casualties, adding that one Taiwanese was injured in one of the attacks and hospitalized in Saudi Arabia.
The Ministry of Foreign Affairs did not disclose when or where the Taiwanese was injured or their identity, citing privacy concerns.
Officials from Taiwan’s representative office in Saudi Arabia visited the person at the hospital, the ministry said.
Photo: Taipei Times

The ministry on Monday raised its travel alert for Saudi Arabian border regions, with Yemen on the highest level of “red,” urging people to leave the country immediately.
On Sunday, it raised the travel alert for the rest of Saudi Arabia to the second-highest level — “orange” — advising Taiwanese to avoid unnecessary travel to the country.
Taiwan’s representative office in Saudi Arabia on social media urged Taiwanese in the country to avoid travel to King Khalid International Airport.
It also urged Taiwanese to remain vigilant in the event of further attacks, follow safety instructions issued by local media and Saudi Arabian authorities, and maintain open lines of communication so the office can contact them when necessary.
In an emergency, Taiwanese in Saudi Arabia can call the representative office for assistance at +966-505-223-725, or ask family members in Taiwan to contact the ministry’s all-hours emergency hotline at 0800-085-095, the ministry said.
A missile strike by the Houthis in Yemen hit the airport on Saturday, killing 13 people and wounding hundreds. Ministry expanding preschools
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
16:39:11 UTC
01:39:11 KST

The Ministry of Education is allocating more than NT$500 million (US$15.58 million) this year to expand public preschool capacity amid growing demand for affordable childcare among dual-income families.
The measure is part of government efforts to alleviate the burden of parents with young children and boost the nation’s birthrate.
As of last month, Taiwan’s population had declined for 33 consecutive months, official statistics showed.
Photo: Lee Wen-te, Taipei Times
In the past, kindergartens in Taiwan accepted only children aged three or older. After the government changed the preschool system by integrating kindergartens and daycare centers in 2012, children can attend preschools from age two until they start elementary school.
However, a preschool must have a dedicated class for two-year-olds to enroll children of that age.
The Early Childhood Education and Care Act (幼兒教育及照顧法) stipulates that each preschool class for children aged two to under three may enroll no more than 16 children.
Classes with eight or fewer children must have at least one childcare and education services personnel, while those with nine or more must have at least two.
The law also stipulates that two-year-olds should not be placed in the same class as those in other age groups.
The curriculum should focus on daily care, developing self-care skills, and learning through play and exploration, while reading, writing and arithmetic instruction aimed at achieving proficiency is prohibited.
The enrollment of two-year-olds in preschool classes rose from 14.7 percent in 2016 to 64.1 percent last year, ministry data showed.
The ministry has established 600 public and quasi-public preschool classes for two-year-olds, three times its original target of adding 200 classes from 2024 to this year.
Since 2017, the government has subsidized more than 4,100 preschool classes nationwide, while the number of preschool teachers has reached 270,000, the education ministry said.
The ministry added that it is investing more than NT$500 million to increase the availability of preschools and preschool classes this year.
Wang Hui-chiu (王慧秋), a section chief of the ministry’s K-12 Education Administration, said that local governments are in charge of assessing and planning how to increase the number of preschools or preschool classes based on the number of children and teachers in each district, as well as actual enrollment, while the ministry offers subsidies to fund the increases.
“We are not asking all preschools to offer a dedicated class for two-year-olds or change the classes for children aged three to five to accommodate them. Local governments should make adjustments based on parents’ requests and other factors and consider offering classes for two-year-olds at elementary schools that have childcare facilities first,” Wang said.
Monthly fees at public preschools are capped at NT$1,000 for the first child, with second children and subsequent siblings attending for free.
At nonprofit preschools, the monthly cap is NT$2,000 for the first child, NT$1,000 for the second and free for subsequent children.
At quasi-public preschools, the caps are NT$3,000, NT$2,000 and NT$1,000 respectively, while children from low- and lower-middle-income families are exempt from fees.
Eligible families whose children do not attend public or quasi-public preschools can instead receive monthly childcare subsidies of NT$5,000 for the first child, NT$6,000 for the second and NT$7,000 for subsequent children.
Public preschools also offer extended care on weekdays and additional childcare services during winter and summer vacations, with 95 percent currently offering extended care.
Since 2021, the government has also encouraged government agencies and state-owned enterprises to set up childcare facilities for employees, with about 166 such facilities established as of this year.

INTERVIEW: Techman positive about robots’ long-term prospects
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
16:39:08 UTC
01:39:08 KST

Techman Robot Inc (達明機器人) remains positive about humanoid robots over the long term, despite near-term hurdles that lie in technological maturity and real-world application capability, company vice president William Wang (王偉霖) said in an interview with the Taipei Times last week.
“I believe the long-term prospects for humanoid robots are very good, but there are still many challenges that need to be overcome at this stage,” Wang said at the company’s headquarters in Taoyuan’s Guishan District (龜山) on Wednesday last week.
The challenges include safety, precision, stability, cycle time, quality and payload capacity, while costs remain significantly higher than those of conventional robotic arms, he said.
Photo courtesy of Techman Robot Inc
Humanoid robots also need to be integrated with higher-level factory systems, such as manufacturing execution systems or warehouse control systems, to receive instructions on where to go and what tasks to perform, Wang said.
The company’s TM Xplore I humanoid robot, first showcased last year, can perform material handling and picking tasks, he said.
Techman plans to provide its second-generation model to some research institutions by the end of this year, Wang said.
The company looks to begin on-site trials with partners as early as the first quarter of next year, while also testing the robot at its own factories, he said.
Several semiconductor, automotive components, consumer electronics and logistics companies have expressed interest in the robot, he added.
For Techman, a robotic arm partner of Nvidia Corp, technologies developed for humanoid robots can be applied to and enhance its existing single-arm and dual-arm robotic systems, Wang said.
The company aims to use learning-based technologies to enable humanoid robots to adjust their grasping methods and trajectories according to changing environments, he said.
“After we build up these technological capabilities, we will look back and consider whether they can also be applied to certain single-arm collaborative robot applications to make them perform better,” he said.
Techman expects its collaborative robot business to grow by at least 20 percent this year from last year, supported by rising automation demand and solid market momentum, Wang said.
With continued collaborative robot demand from the semiconductor, electronics manufacturing, automotive and warehousing sectors, Techman expects revenue this year to exceed last year’s NT$1.82 billion (US$56.7 million) and is targeting double-digit growth next year, he said.
Besides strong interest from the semiconductor sector, the company is also targeting growing robot demand for artificial intelligence (AI) server assembly and inspection, Wang said.
Robot applications in AI servers include loading and unloading for surface-mount technology processes, back-end assembly and inspection, Wang said.
The company plans to start deliveries of its TM45S heavy-payload dual-arm collaborative robot unveiled in August for AI server assembly and semiconductor handling in the first quarter of next year, he said.
As the number of inspection items and quality requirements in AI server assembly processes increases, the company expects more opportunities to deploy its machine vision and AI recognition technologies, he said.
The company’s robot and vision inspection solutions are already deployed at Quanta Computer Inc’s (廣達) factories, Wang said.
It also supplies solutions to Kinpo Electronics Inc (金寶) for rack-related operations and Accton Technology Corp (智邦) for assembly, inspection and surface-mount technology-related production processes, he said.
China accounts for about 30 percent of Techman’s total sales, followed by Taiwan and Europe at about 20 percent each, while Japan and Southeast Asia each account for about 10 percent, Wang said.
Beyond robot sales, Techman is also upbeat about the growth prospects of its in-house system integration business over the next few years, as the business provides production-line and factory-wide automation solutions, he said.
