Another source familiar with the discussions said Netanyahu hoped joint military action against the Houthis would strengthen relations between Israel and Saudi Arabia and potentially pave the way for a normalisation agreement.
Saudi authorities have not publicly commented on the reported proposal.
The revelation comes as Saudi Arabia faces escalating Houthi missile and drone attacks, including deadly strikes on King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh.
An attack on Saturday killed 13 people and wounded more than 300, while another strike on Sunday killed a Pakistani resident and injured 11 others, according to Saudi authorities.
Netanyahu condemned Saturday's attack and offered condolences to the victims' families, despite Israel and Saudi Arabia having no formal diplomatic relations.
The Israeli leader has long regarded normalisation with Saudi Arabia as a major diplomatic objective, building on the Abraham Accords through which Israel established formal relations with several Arab states.
However, negotiations between Israel and Saudi Arabia, which had advanced before October 2023, were derailed by Israel's war and genocide in Gaza.
Riyadh has repeatedly insisted that normalisation must be linked to the establishment of an independent Palestinian state, a position at odds with Netanyahu's opposition to Palestinian statehood.
The reported Israeli overture suggests Netanyahu is attempting to use Saudi Arabia's confrontation with the Houthis to revive prospects for rapprochement, despite the continuing political obstacles presented by the Palestinian question.
Israel has previously conducted its own military strikes against Houthi targets in Yemen, meaning the latest proposal concerns participation in the Saudi-led campaign rather than Israel's first involvement in the conflict.
Saudi Arabia intervened militarily in Yemen in March 2015, leading a coalition that included the UAE in support of the internationally recognised government after the Houthis seized Sanaa.
A UN-brokered truce in April 2022 substantially reduced large-scale hostilities, but renewed fighting erupted in July this year.
The latest escalation has seen Houthi forces make territorial gains along Yemen's Red Sea coast, prompting a Saudi-backed government counteroffensive and renewed attacks across the Saudi-Yemeni border.
Saudi Arabia has sought greater US assistance against the Houthis, while Netanyahu's reported proposal would bring Israel directly into a military campaign that has already strained Riyadh's defences.
For the Saudi leadership, the prospect of openly cooperating with Israel remains politically sensitive, particularly amid continuing anger over the genocide in Gaza and the absence of any progress towards Palestinian statehood.

Europe’s satellite sovereignty push faces funding test as EU space budget cycle ends
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
16:20:55 UTC
01:20:55 KST

Regulators, EU officials and Spanish satellite operator Sateliot gathered at the European Parliament on Tuesday to debate how spectrum and investment will shape Europe’s networks in orbit, with the EU’s 2021-2027 space funding cycle ending next year.
National telecoms authorities, EU policymakers and Barcelona-based satellite company Sateliot met at the European Parliament in Brussels on Tuesday to discuss how radio frequencies and fresh money will decide who controls the communications Europe relies on from orbit, with the bloc’s current seven-year space budget expiring in 2027.
Euronews was at the event, organised by Sateliot, whose spacecraft act as mobile phone masts in space, connecting Internet of Things (IoT) devices such as sensors and trackers where ground networks don’t reach.
The EU’s €14.8 billion space programme for 2021-2027, which funds Galileo, the bloc’s satellite navigation system, and Copernicus, its Earth observation service, ends next year along with the Multiannual Financial Framework (MFF), the EU’s seven-year budget.
For 2028-2034, the European Commission wants space funded from a new European Competitiveness Fund, a single pot for strategic industries that would set aside €131 billion for defence and space.
EU leaders are due to discuss the next budget at the European Council meeting on Thursday and Friday.
The Commission’s defence industry and space department, DG DEFIS, closed bids on 29 September for a four-year, €55 million framework contract for management and legal support on three fronts: IRIS², the EU’s planned secure satellite constellation, space surveillance and tracking, which monitors objects in orbit, as well as analysis of the space economy.
More calls under Horizon Europe, the EU’s research and innovation programme, follow in 2027, while EUSPA, the EU Agency for the Space Programme, and the European Space Agency (ESA), an intergovernmental body separate from the EU, keep running tenders.
Spectrum and sovereignty
Much of the debate centred on spectrum, the radio frequencies that satellites and mobile networks need to transmit.
In May, the Commission proposed a single EU-wide licence for mobile satellite services, which link satellites directly to phones and other devices, in the 2 GHz band, whose current rights expire in May 2027. It would specifically reserve part of the band for European operators and a secure system linked to IRIS².
European Parliament Vice-President Javier López hosted the meeting and the Commission’s digital department, DG CONNECT, was represented by Gerasimos Sofianatos, head of the radio spectrum policy unit.
"This discussion could not come at a better moment considering the current geopolitical tensions and the debate surrounding technological competition", said López in his opening statement.
"A Europe that controls its own network and data is a Europe that can act independently and make its own decisions [...] satellite connectivity is a perfect example of an area where we must achieve strategic control", López added.
Speaking to Euronews after the event, the CEO and co-founder of Sateliot Jaume Sanpera stated that "we have to build and support European champions that can compete globally in the space sector," adding that "today half the world wants to work with European companies in defence and space because we are more predictable."
In September, the ESA selected Sateliot to contribute to IRIS²’s Low-LEO layer, a testing ground in low orbit where new government services are tried out before any are added to the main system. The ESA plans in-orbit test missions from 2027 to 2029.
Through its RESCUE-NET project, Sateliot will also study how 5G connectivity from space can keep public authorities connected when ground networks fail. The ESA signed 18 contracts worth €20 million in total with nearly 80 companies for this phase.
From SpaceX to PLD Space
For small satellites, reaching orbit still largely means flying American.
On 1 October, Sateliot sent five satellites built by Spanish small-satellite maker Alén Space into orbit on Transporter-18, a rideshare mission by Elon Musk’s rocket company SpaceX that carries spacecraft for many customers, taking its total launched to 11.
The extra satellites double its daily passes over any given point, the company says.
Asked by Euronews whether Europe can expand its fleets without relying on non-European launchers, Sanpera said that he is optimistic and mentioned that there are currently four or five companies in the race to fill that gap.
The CEO of Sanpera also explained that the firm's next launch will be in July 2027, again in collaboration with SpaceX, but the one after that will be with PLD Space, a Spanish launch company based in Elche.
That launch in late 2027 will not only be entirely European, but it will also feature Sateliot's first two Tritó satellites, a larger next generation designed to offer 5G direct-to-device services to ordinary phones.
They will fly on Miura 5, a small orbital rocket built by PLD Space that has yet to fly.
Back in August, PLD won a conditional €158.9 million contract under ESA's European Launcher Challenge, which backs new European rockets, and it plans a debut launch from Europe’s spaceport in French Guiana by the end of this year.
Meanwhile, Sateliot, which is raising €150 million from investors, comprising €100 million in equity and up to €50 million in debt, aims to grow its constellation to more than 500 satellites by 2028 the latest.

The pressure Kyiv wants from the EU

Morocco's biggest party strikes deal to form coalition government
Morocco's largest political party is joining forces with three rivals to form a coalition government, pledging a "shared reformist vision" as it bids to address rising youth anger over economic inequality and corruption.
Prime Minister Fatima Ezzahra El-Mansouri's Authenticity and Modernity Party (PAM) will enter government with the nationalist Istiqlal Party and two small left-wing factions, the Socialist Union of Popular Forces (USFP) and the Party of Progress and Socialism (PPS), the parties said in a joint statement on Monday.
PAM emerged as the kingdom's largest party following the 23 September election, winning 97 of the 395 seats in the lower house. Istiqlal came third with 65 seats.
King Mohammed VI appointed Mansouri as the country's first-ever female prime minister a week after the vote, tasking her to form the next government.
The coalition will have a narrow nine-seat majority in the assembly and will be expected to deliver on electoral pledges to tackle the rising cost of living, boost youth employment, and improve public services.
Her administration will take power amid rising social discontent over deteriorating public services and narrowing job prospects.
It will also oversee preparations for the World Cup, which the North African country will co-host with Spain and Portugal in 2030.
The tournament emerged as a flashpoint in the wave of anti-government demonstrations that rocked Moroccan cities last year, with Gen-Z protesters criticising the billions of dollars being invested in football stadiums at the expense of the country's underfunded healthcare and education systems.
September's election received one of the lowest turnout rates in the country's electoral history, with only 38% of voters turning up to vote. The low turnout means that PAM is forming the next government with the support of fewer than 5% of eligible voters.
PAM is a socially liberal party created in 2008 by an adviser to the king. This is the second time it has been in government after it entered a coalition as a junior partner of the National Rally of Independents and Istiqlal following the 2021 parliamentary election.

Hackers Turn French Supermarket Refrigerators Into Furnaces
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
16:20:00 UTC
01:20:00 KST

Reported by
A massive cyberattack targeted hundreds of French supermarkets overnight on October 11 to 12, remotely hijacking refrigeration systems to trigger intense defrost cycles, spoiling vast quantities of food and sparking fires.
The unprecedented incident has triggered a national criminal investigation. The Paris Prosecutor's Office confirmed to OCCRP Tuesday that its cybercrime section has initiated an investigation, entrusted to the Anti-Cybercrime Office (OFAC). The probe aims to "identify the victims and establish a link between the incident and the damage reported by them, specifically regarding food spoilage and the outbreak of fires."
Hackers gained remote control of the store refrigeration systems by exploiting internet-connected controllers. The attack methodology mirrors vulnerabilities the operational technology security firm Claroty warned the industry about two months prior. In a prescient August report titled "Freeze the Controller, Defrost the Food," the firm's Team82 research division warned about the possibility that hackers could access Danfoss refrigeration systems to bypass security and manipulate temperatures.
Now, hackers have executed exactly that kind of breach, accessing the controllers and remotely manipulating temperature settings to reach 50 degrees Celsius (122 degrees Fahrenheit).
At the DEF CON hacker convention in August, Team82 researchers had demonstrated exactly how attackers could use a hidden "code-of-the-day" authentication mechanism and a command-injection vulnerability to take over Danfoss AK-SM 800A platforms. While Danfoss had issued a firmware update in August 2025 to address the flaws, Claroty noted that public internet-scanning tools recently identified 2,765 exposed Danfoss controllers still online.
The scope of the vulnerabilities extends beyond a single manufacturer. A security bulletin updated Tuesday by CERT-FR—France’s national center for cybersecurity incident response—confirmed compromises of Danfoss AK-SM and AK-SC series controllers, as well as Copeland XWEB and Dixell XWEB monitoring systems. These devices function as the digital nerve centers for commercial refrigeration, allowing operators to remotely monitor temperatures, trigger alarms, and manage energy consumption.
CERT-FR warned that attack campaigns are likely still ongoing and strongly advised against exposing these management interfaces to the public internet. A simple factory reset, the agency noted, is insufficient for unpatched equipment, which will "certainly be compromised again."
The physical and financial toll across France was immediate, forcing stores to discard food stocks and calling the country's food security into question. The Mousquetaires Group, a French multinational retail conglomerate, told OCCRP that 300 of its stores in France were compromised. The group stated that the impact ranged from equipment malfunctions to complete system inoperability, resulting in millions of euros in losses.
"It will take us about a week to return to normal operations for customers, but two to three weeks to fully restore our systems," the Mousquetaires Group’s press office told OCCRP. "Everyone in the industry was aware of the risk of hacking, but this situation is deeply concerning because it appears to involve outside interference; it is essentially an attempt to destabilize operations."
Other impacted retail chains include Carrefour, Monoprix, and E.Leclerc.
Dominique Schelcher, CEO of the supermarket chain Coopérative U, provided a detailed update on X on Tuesday, confirming that 80 of his network's nearly 2,000 stores were targeted. While staff interventions prevented a break in the cold chain in the vast majority of cases, affected products in other locations were immediately withdrawn and destroyed to ensure food safety.
Defending the use of internet-connected refrigerators, Schelcher explained the technology is essential for round-the-clock remote temperature monitoring and rapid response to anomalies.
"Attacking equipment essential to the conservation of fresh products means attacking the food supply chain of the French people," Schelcher wrote. "It is unprecedented, extremely serious, and unacceptable."
Moving forward, Claroty warned that artificial intelligence is reducing the time needed to scan systems for vulnerabilities, allowing attackers to carry out disruptive hacks at scale across commercial enterprises dependent on refrigeration.

British and Irish governments ‘should negotiate paramilitary disbandment in Northern Ireland’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
16:17:54 UTC
01:17:54 KST

The British and Irish governments should engage with paramilitary groups in Northern Ireland to negotiate their disbandment, according to a report.
A “window of opportunity” exists to establish a formal transition mechanism for loyalist and republican groups, provided certain conditions are met, it said.
The Independent Report on Paramilitary Group Transition to Disbandment, commissioned by both governments and published on Tuesday, said groups should not receive financial rewards for engaging in the process.
Fleur Ravensbergen, a Dutch conflict resolution expert who authored the report, said in Belfast: “I have concluded that there is sufficient merit in and support for a formal process of paramilitary group transition.”
Ravensbergen said she found “significant willingness to engage” among paramilitaries during a year-long scoping exercise.
She added: “There was limited support for the term ‘disbandment’ as the endpoint of a transition process. However, objections to disbandment appeared to be less about what transition should achieve and more about the wording.”
Paramilitary groups were expected to fade after the 1998 Good Friday agreement, but some endured and evolved into lucrative enterprises involved in drug dealing, extortion and coercive control.
Agreeing a transition process was more important than the terminology used to describe disbandment, said Ravensbergen, a lecturer in conflict resolution and governance at the University of Amsterdam.
She said: “I believe that the risks of the persistence of paramilitary structures, continued drift and unmanaged fragmentation outweigh the risks associated with attempting a structured and time-bound transition process. Inaction is not a neutral option. My consultations suggest that a window of opportunity exists to pursue further progress, but that this may weaken over time.”
Chris Bryant, the Northern Ireland secretary, thanked Ravensbergen and said the government was committed to ending paramilitarism.
Bryant said: “While these groups may pose as protectors of their communities, they are largely engaged in criminality including drug dealing, extortion and intimidation, blighting the very communities they perversely claim to protect. Their continued influence is a stain on our collective conscience.”
He said the government would consider the report and liaise with authorities in Dublin before responding to the proposed transition mechanism.
He added: “It is evident from the report that the implementation of any process will face challenges and will need the support from across the political community in Northern Ireland.”
Naomi Long, Northern Ireland’s justice minister and a member of the Alliance party, criticised Ravensbergen’s appointment as an interlocutor last year, saying engagement with paramilitaries and criminal gangs risked giving them a veneer of legitimacy.
Long said at the time: “The idea that paramilitary groups can transition into law-abiding entities has long since moved beyond the point of credibility. They cannot continue to be treated as if they are genuinely committed to reform – that moment passed long ago.”
The report did not identify individuals or specific organisations because discussions were held on a confidential basis.
It said: “The nature, extent and impact of paramilitary influence vary considerably between paramilitary groups, communities and geographical areas. However, it is clear that residual paramilitary structures continue to cause harm in some communities.”
Ravensbergen said a transition mechanism would need credible monitoring and verification of progress and robust law enforcement.
She declined to comment on the recent standoff between the Orange Order and nationalist residents at Garvaghy Road in Portadown, saying it was outside the report’s remit. There is speculation that renewed tension over the Drumcree parade may boost paramilitary recruitment.

"I think there are a great many of us in France who remain motivated. It’s a misunderstanding of the movement to think that the anger will disappear once the holidays begin," said Mariolino, a 16-year-old in his final year of secondary school.
Thunberg 'extremely proud of French students'
The Swedish activist, wearing her trademark keffiyeh, has spoken to journalists gathered outside a high school in Saint-Denis, where more than a hundred students gathered early this morning to block the entrance.
"Young people aren’t being included in the discussions. Our future is being stolen from us and, as we’ve seen here, schools aren’t receiving the investment they need," said the 23-year-old.
Greta Thunberg at the Lycée Paul Eluard in Saint-Denis, north of Paris. Credit: Julien de Rosa, AFP
"So, what are we supposed to do? Give up? Of course not. That is precisely what people are saying here: we are not going to give up and we are going to fight for this future that is being stolen from us right before our eyes," she added, saying she was "extremely proud of French students".
(FRANCE 24 with AFP, AP and Reuters)

Iran’s intensifying attacks on ships, threatening oil export recovery: Report
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
16:15:52 UTC
01:15:52 KST

Diyar Güldoğan
13 October 2026•Update: 13 October 2026
Iranian attacks on ships transiting the Strait of Hormuz have intensified, raising concerns that renewed hostilities could disrupt the recovery in Persian Gulf oil exports, Bloomberg reported on Tuesday.
Shipping industry sources have reported signs that cargo movements through the strategic waterway may be slowing after oil flows approached prewar levels earlier this month.
Available data, however, have yet to show a clear decline in oil-loading activity at several major regional export terminals, and some shipowners have reported no significant disruption to vessel movements, said the report.
The latest escalation comes as tensions spread in the Middle East, with Saudi Arabia facing attacks by Yemen’s Houthi group. The deteriorating security situation helped push crude oil prices above $106 a barrel in London on Monday, although prices eased slightly on Tuesday.
Four tankers were struck by unidentified projectiles in separate incidents while transiting the Strait of Hormuz on Oct. 11, according to the UK Maritime Trade Operations agency. That was roughly twice the agency’s average daily number of reported attacks during the previous week, according to Bloomberg.
The increase in attacks appears to be prompting greater caution among ship operators. Bloomberg-compiled tanker-tracking data showed that more than a dozen supertankers and several Suezmax-class vessels had turned around or reversed course while approaching Fujairah in the United Arab Emirates, near the entrance to the strait.
Shipbrokers and some vessel owners operating in the region have also reported signs of reduced activity, particularly longer waiting times for ship-to-ship oil transfers. One shipowner involved in the operations said traffic had not slowed.
Ship-to-ship transfers have been instrumental in sustaining regional exports. The practice allows shuttle tankers to transport oil through the high-risk Strait of Hormuz before transferring their cargo to other vessels for delivery to international buyers.

Loves Trump, lies and conspiracies: Katie Zacharia is the perfect presidential press secretary | Arwa Mahdawi
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
16:14:58 UTC
01:14:58 KST

Poor Donald Trump. His (third) wife seemingly can’t bear to be near him and his (fifth) press secretary recently abandoned him to be with a baby she had only recently met.
“She decided she loved her children more than she loved Donald Trump,” the president lamented in August when Karoline Leavitt decided to step down a few months after giving birth. “I’m very upset about this. She has to go home and spend time with her children. That does happen on occasion with some people – when they love their children.”
Apparently, Leavitt loves her children and Fox News, because, in a highly predictable turn of events, the 29-year-old has got a gig there now. But don’t worry too much about the president: he’s found himself a new woman to attack the press and act as his mouthpiece. On Friday, Trump announced that he’d appointed Katie Zacharia, previously a communications adviser for the Trump Media and Technology Group, as the new press secretary. Unlike some of Trump’s other lackeys, Zacharia has government experience: she was once a Department of Homeland Security spokesperson. Her most important qualification, however, is her fealty to King Trump. “She has an unblemished record of support,” Trump said in his announcement. “She is … a devoted fan and member of Maga!”
While you’ve obviously got to worship the president to get a top comms role with him, there are a few other job requirements. Not least a willingness to embrace what former Trump adviser Kellyanne Conway called“alternative facts”. Zacharia gets full marks in that department. Last year the press secretary, who once worked for an anti-abortion advocacy group, claimed on X that the abortion medication mifepristone “is connected to the manufacturer of the deadly gas Zyklon B, used in the World War II concentration camps”. While there is a tenuous corporate connection which conspiracy theorists have tried to play up, mifepristone was developed in the 1980s by a French company.
The origins of mifepristone aren’t the only alternative facts Zacharia is fond of. She has echoed Trump’s big lie that the 2020 election was “stolen” and used her Truth Social account to promote the QAnon conspiracy theory, which posits that Trump is saving the world from a cabal of satanic paedophiles. She’s also promoted Pizzagate, the baseless theory that Hillary Clinton and her 2016 campaign chief, John Podesta, were operating an underground child sex-trafficking ring from a Washington DC pizza shop.
While Zacharia scores highly when it comes to devotion and unhinged theories, I suspect that she’s going to need to ramp up her public hatred of Joe Biden if she wants to stay on her boss’s good side. Biden is dealing with stage four cancer and mostly staying out of the public eye, but Trump still acts as if he’s running against the man. According to a recent Reuters analysis, Trump has invoked Biden’s name about 900 times this year. And not in a pleasant way.
Beni Rae Harmony, 24, who is Trump’s new assistant press secretary, seems to suffer from the same Biden Derangement Syndrome afflicting the president; indeed, it might be part of the reason she got the job. A Christmas 2021 photo of Harmony wearing a “Fuck Joe Biden” T-shirt while holding a rifle recently did the rounds online. The White House subsequently defended Harmony, calling her “a trusted voice for the Maga movement”.
Beyond bashing Biden, another helpful quality for a Trump spokesperson is a fondness for insults. White House communications director, Steven Cheung, whom Trump reportedly refers to as “my sumo wrestler” probably leads the pack there. He’s forged a shock-jock style comms strategy and endeavours to be as crass as possible. Cheung has told the former secretary of state, Mike Pompeo, to “shut his stupid mouth”, labelled senator Jon Ossoff “the biggest cuck loser in politics”, and described the former FBI head, James Comey, as “one of the dumbest motherfuckers in human history”. He’s also fond of calling people “retards”, recently directing the slur at CNN host Erin Burnett.
Cheung’s rhetoric would get a lot of ordinary people fired. But it has made him a fixture in Trumpworld: he’s been with the president in various capacities for a decade now. That’s rare for Trump, who cycles through staff. If Zacharia lasts even a year in her new role, meanwhile, I’ll be surprised. With a (very likely) disastrous midterm election approaching, she has her work cut out and will need all the alternative facts she can find. Zacharia has also admitted that she is probably not even the best person for the job. “President Trump does not need a spokesperson,” Zacharia gushed on X last month. “He is his own best Press Secretary.”
Arwa Mahdawi is a Guardian columnist

Qatar’s emir vows that country will emerge stronger as he outlines national strategies
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
16:12:42 UTC
01:12:42 KST

Qatar's emir outlined in a speech to the nation how the Gulf nation has managed to overcome the consequences of the Iran war and will emerge stronger and better equipped to adapt to global changes by diversifying its economy and focusing on non-carbon industries in addition to existing LNG exports.
Qatar’s Emir Sheikh Tamim bin Hamad Al Thani said on Tuesday that his country "will emerge from this crisis more resilient and better equipped to adapt to global changes," outlining the country's national strategies which now also focus on diversifying the economy towards the "non-hydrocarbon sectors," in addition to the traditional model of liquefied natural gas global supply which Qatar wants to increase.
In a speech to the nation at the opening of the Shura Council’s annual session in Doha, Sheikh Tamim made it clear that "Qatar was attacked on its territory by Iran, in a blatant violation of its sovereignty, the provisions of international law, and the principles of good-neighborly relations."
“Qatar has always preferred to resolve disputes through negotiation and diplomatic and peaceful means," Sheikh Tamim added.
"Our commitment to dialogue and peaceful solutions does not mean being complacent about defending our country," he said. "Our right to defend our sovereignty does not conflict with our determination to prevent a wider war."
Iran has consistently maintained that it was only targeting US interests among its neighbours during the war.
Against the backdrop of widening conflicts across the region, he stressed the need for the Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) countries to cooperate, stating that "the security of the GCC states and the protection of their sovereignty and stability are non-negotiable."
Sheikh Tamim urged "to redouble our efforts to secure navigation in the Gulf and the Strait of Hormuz, and to protect energy and water facilities, as well as civil infrastructure."
Sheikh Tamim also outlined the country's response during the war and its strategies going forward, based on long-term planning before the crisis and the measures Qatar implemented to adapt to the war's consequences.
He addressed "the extraordinary events" that impacted the country and the region, which "demonstrated (...) our ability to respond to crises efficiently and responsibly" and that "resilience isn't born in the moment of crisis; rather, it is the result of the planning that precedes it."
"In this crisis, Qatar has shouldered three responsibilities simultaneously: protecting its sovereignty, fulfilling its role in energy security and the global economy, and keeping the doors of diplomacy open," Sheikh Tamim said.
Based on these responsibilities, Qatar's Emir outlined "four key elements" that formed the country's strategy in addressing the crisis: "first, defending the homeland firmly without being drawn into war; second, maintaining essential services, supply chains, and economic activity; third, contributing to efforts to secure a ceasefire and reopen waterways; and fourth, urging negotiations and seeking opportunities to return to talks to reach peaceful resolutions to the conflict."
Sheikh Tamim acknowledged Qatar's key role in global energy systems, supplying about one-fifth of the world’s liquefied natural gas (LNG), and said that "any disruption affecting it is quickly reflected in markets and consumers everywhere."
"The closure of the Strait of Hormuz, together with the direct damage inflicted on some energy facilities in Ras Laffan Industrial City, disrupted a significant portion of the country’s exports," the Qatari emir said.
Signalling a key development, Sheikh Tamim said Qatar absorbed the shock by focusing on the "non-hydrocarbon sectors", which "continued to grow with their contribution reaching approximately 80% of real GDP."
He explained that the "non-hydrocarbon sectors" alternative "reflects the resilience of the national economy and its ability to sustain growth under exceptional and complex circumstances", and that "the stock of foreign direct investment continued to grow."
He revealed that "the total revenues declined by 42% during the first half of the year, while public expenditure fell by 14%, without compromising essential services or development priorities," as "the state did not succumb to panic."
"Instead, it continued to look to the future with confidence in the national economy," Sheikh Tamim said.
"We decided not to reduce essential services and opted to maintain our developmental priorities, in order to sustain Qatar’s ongoing economic momentum," Sheikh Tamim said.
"The policies adopted by the state prior to the crisis — including strengthening reserves, reducing public debt, budgeting based on conservative oil price assumptions, and developing non-oil revenues — have enabled us to absorb the repercussions of this crisis thus far."
Moving forward, Sheikh Tamim said the Gulf country's "aim is not to return to the pre-crisis situation, but rather to use the recovery as a springboard to accelerate economic diversification and strengthen national capabilities."
"Our duty is to always strive for the best, but we must also be prepared for the worst-case scenarios, and everyone—institutions and citizens alike—must take responsibility," the emir told the nation.
He outlined the country's plans for the energy sector, which include the expansion of the North Field Gas project to increase LNG production capacity, the progress of the Golden Pass project in the US and QatarEnergy's increased investments and international partnerships, "alongside the development of petrochemical industries, solar energy projects, and efforts to strengthen water security."
He also outlined the country's focus on food security, agriculture, technology, institutional efficiency, investment in education "to face the challenges of our time" and in digital transformation.
Sheikh Tamim said the Palestinian cause remained a priority for Qatar, declaring that "what has happened in the Gaza Strip is undoubtedly a genocide, and those responsible must not escape accountability."
He warned of "the dangers" resulting from Israeli settler attacks on Palestinians in the West Bank, "not to mention the repeated raids on the Al-Aqsa Mosque, and countless violations of the provisions of international law, the UN Charter, and international humanitarian law."
Sheikh Tamim's criticism in his national speech underlined Qatar's ongoing firm position towards Israel's actions in Gaza and Lebanon. Israel's Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has lashed out frequently at Qatar, calling it "a hostile state".
Beyond Gaza and the Gulf, the emir reaffirmed Qatar's continuing role in mediating political agreements to resolve the crises in Sudan, Libya, Yemen and Somalia.

How will emergency rule in Pakistan's KP affect Afghan ties?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
16:11:00 UTC
01:11:00 KST

How will emergency rule in Pakistan's northwest affect Afghan ties?
October 13, 2026
Pakistan on Sunday announced that the northwestern province of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa had been put under emergency rule.
Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif's federal government defended the move, saying the provincial administration — led by imprisoned former Prime Minister Imran Khan's Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI) party — was working "hand in glove" with the Pakistani Taliban, known as Tehrik-e-Taliban Pakistan (TTP).
"The PTI government in the province has not equipped the police and security forces to counter militancy. Instead, they have links with TTP and did not cooperate with the federal government to fight terrorism," Talal Chaudhry, minister of state for interior affairs, told DW.
Information Minister Attaullah Tarar said the government had "solid evidence" to support its allegations, the Associated Press news agency reported.
He said the suspension and imposition of a state of emergency in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa would allow security forces and the new administration to better coordinate efforts to combat terrorism.
The move comes as thousands of Khan supporters continue to stage anti-government protests and demand the former leader be released from jail.
But the federal government has denied that its action was driven by domestic politics.
A stronghold of Imran Khan's PTI
Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, which has suffered an increasing number of militant attacks in recent months, is a political stronghold of former PM Khan.
The cricketer-turned-politician has been in jail since 2023 on corruption and other charges that he and his supporters say are politically motivated.
His PTI party had long governed the volatile province, but Islamabad's decision to impose emergency rule has now effectively removed it from power.
Pakistan's constitution allows the federal government to take over from provincial authorities during an emergency.
Islamabad said Khyber Pakhtunkhwa would now be administered directly by a new governor, assisted by an advisory council. This arrangement will initially be in place for six months, but could be extended for as long as necessary, authorities said.
Is governor rule the solution?
Khan's party has lambasted the suspension of the provincial government.
"This is more a coup disguised as emergency and governor rule," said PTI spokesperson Sayed Zulfikar Bukhari.
It has also sparked questions about provincial autonomy and the future of civilian rule, with critics warning that the abrupt removal of an elected administration risks weakening accountability and deepening political divisions.
"Governor's rule should only be imposed in extreme constitutional crises, not political disputes, and its legality should be reviewed by the Constitutional Court," Osama Malik, a senior constitutional expert, told DW.
"While it may temporarily reduce militant attacks, lasting security requires political engagement and stronger civilian law enforcement."
Raja Qaiser Ahmed, assistant professor of regional security and foreign affairs at Quaid-i-Azam University in Islamabad, echoed this view.
"Federal rule can never be a substitute for an elected political authority. The argument of provincial autonomy would also definitely surface amidst this uncharacteristic measure taken," he told DW.
"It may, though, streamline coordination between the federal government and the province, which was a missing link for quite some time."
Surging militancy poses acute security challenges
Pakistan has seen a surge in militant violence in recent years.
Authorities have recorded more than 2,800 militant attacks since January, which have killed or wounded about 3,000 people, according to the AP news agency.
Islamabad blames Afghan-based elements for the attacks and has accused the ruling Taliban of allowing Afghan territory to be used to harbor militants.
Pakistan wants Kabul to clamp down on the TTP, which is a separate group but closely linked to the Afghan Taliban. The TTP seeks to impose a hard-line interpretation of Islam, particularly in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa.
"We have been asking Kabul to recognize terrorists as terrorists and take action against them. They must do so because their own peace, security, and future are linked to Pakistan," asserted Chaudhry, the deputy interior minister.
The Afghan Taliban deny the allegations and say they cannot be held accountable for security incidents inside Pakistan.
Will it escalate the Afghanistan-Pakistan conflict?
The dispute has fueled growing tensions between the neighbors, which have escalated into armed clashes in recent months, heightening fears of a wider confrontation.
Ahmed believes the suspension of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa's provincial government is likely to aggravate tensions between Pakistan and Afghanistan.
"Security measures taken in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa would further impinge on the Pakistan-Afghan relationship, which is seemingly locked in a protracted cycle of offense and escalation," said Ahmed.
After announcing emergency rule, Islamabad also authorized the deployment of additional army troops and military equipment to the region to support authorities.
Ayesha Siddiqa, an independent military and security analyst, warned that the suspension of the elected provincial government could complicate counterterrorism efforts by deepening resentment among local communities.
"After ending the political government, I don't think the security situation will improve. In fact, there will be less willingness among local communities to support counterterrorism operations," she told DW.

Saudi Arabia's military struggle against Houthi attacks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
16:11:00 UTC
01:11:00 KST

Saudi Arabia's military struggle against Houthi attacks
October 13, 2026
Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthi militia continues to escalate its attacks on Saudi Arabia targeting energy facilities but, above all, airports.
On Saturday, a missile attack on Riyadh's international airport killed 13 people and injured more than 300. In a second attack on Sunday, the militia killed another civilian and injured 11 others.
According to their own statements, the Houthis also attacked Saudi Arabia's airport in Dammam and two oil facilities within the past 24 hours. Saudi Energy Minister Prince Abdulaziz bin Salman Al Saud warned of the consequences for energy security and announced a strong response.
According to a report by the US think tank American Enterprise Institute, Saudi Arabia is targeting Houthi missile launch pads, storage facilities and other military infrastructure in Yemen. The institute quotes Saudi military spokesman Turki al-Maliki in its October 11 report as saying that 136 military targets have already been destroyed.
However, years of Saudi-led military intervention between 2015 and 2022 in Yemen have not succeeded in defeating the Houthi militia. Moreover, the Saudi-led international coalition formed in 2015 has fallen apart and the United Arab Emirates has withdrawn its troops.
The Iran-aligned Houthis not only control large parts of northern Yemen but also increasingly the western coastline from where they disrupt international shipping through the Red Sea and the strategically important Bab el-Mandeb Strait. In early September, drones also severely damaged the Saudi East-West oil pipeline. The temporary shutdown disrupted oil exports and increased risks for the energy markets.
Saudi Arabia calls on Pakistan, Turkey, the United States
For weeks, the Saudi government has been seeking allies in the fight against the Houthi militia. In late September, the United Kingdom and France pledged military support to defend Saudi infrastructure. London offered aerial refueling for Saudi fighter jets, while Paris announced it would provide troops, radar systems and air defense technology to protect the Yanbu oil terminal.
However, while the US recently refused to fight alongside Saudi Arabia against the Houthis, there could now be a change of heart in Washington, writes political analyst Osamah Al-Rawhani in a study by the Yemeni think tank Sanaa Center for Strategic Studies.
He notes that it remains to be seen whether this could actually lead to a successful offensive, as holding on to captured territories and launching counterattacks require significant financial resources, political commitment and the necessary resolve.
In his view, it is questionable whether Saudi Arabia would be able to muster the necessary perseverance. The kingdom could, however, change its current strategy. "If the costs of the war continue to rise, Riyadh might look for a way to withdraw from the conflict," Al-Rawhani says.
Saudi Arabia's asymmetrical war against the Houthis
Marcus Schneider, project manager at the Friedrich Ebert Foundation's Center of Expertise on Peace and Security in the Middle East and North Africa, shares a similar view.
"To eliminate the Houthis, ground troops would be needed but Riyadh has no experience with this type of warfare, especially in a foreign country," Schneider recently told DW. As such, he believes the Saudi leadership is less concerned with achieving a military victory than with reducing its vulnerability, securing the broadest possible coalition of partners and gaining political maneuvering room.
"The Houthis are well-entrenched in Yemen and can withstand considerable blows. Above all, Saudi Arabia needs stability for its Vision 2030 reform set and that is currently further away than ever," Schneider said.
He added that military asymmetry is also a key factor: Saudi Arabia possesses modern weapons and spends enormous sums on its armed forces. The Houthis, on the other hand, do not need to win a conventional war. It is enough for them to deploy missiles and drones, threaten infrastructure and disrupt shipping traffic.
Are the UAE, Pakistan, Turkey changing course?
Saudi Arabia may also be able to turn to another partner in the region: the United Arab Emirates (UAE). According to media reports, Anwar Gargash, a senior diplomatic advisor to the UAE president, spoke out in favor of closer security cooperation among the Gulf states. "We are all targets," he stated on X.
Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia have undermined the security of the entire region, he notes. "It is necessary to revitalize cooperation among the Gulf states, particularly in the areas of security and defense, and to strengthen the collective security system," Gargash added.
Pakistan, which signed the Mecca Joint Defense Agreement in early August along with Saudi Arabia and Turkey, also initially ruled out military intervention.
According to media reports, however, the country is now said to be carrying out airstrikes on Houthi missile and drone positions — a claim that Islamabad denies. Pakistan does not intend to deploy ground troops. Turkey, another member of the Mecca Pact, rules out an offensive military operation but is providing air defense equipment.
Saudi Arabia can thus build on additional military support, according to an analysis by the US think tank Soufan Center. Whether this will result in an effective strategy, however, depends on whether the partners go beyond limited airstrikes and political expressions of solidarity and on whether the fragmented Yemeni government forces can better coordinate their military operations.
Meanwhile, Iran has offered to act as a mediator between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis. However, given Iran's support for the Houthis and the recent attacks on Saudi Arabia, it is questionable whether Saudi Arabia will accept this offer.
Saudi Arabia and the US are allies, whereas Iran and the US have been at war since February. It is also unclear whether Tehran wields sufficient influence over the Yemeni militia to persuade it to halt the attacks.

Kimberly Guilfoyle: US ambassador to Greece resigns amid allegations
October 13, 2026
Kimberly Guilfoyle has stepped down as US ambassador to Greece.
White House Press Secretary Katie Zacharia earlier told reporters that Guilfoyle had been asked to resign, calling her "an incredible asset to the team."
"We wish her well," Zacharia added.
Guilfoyle's position became untenable after the Wall Street Journal (WSJ) reported on her supposed threats against Greece and her acceptance of improper gifts. Most recently, WSJ published an article with screenshots of text messages documenting her attempts to receive cash from a Republican donor in exchange for influence in the Trump administration.
Trump before firing: 'We're not happy'
The past week has seen much speculation as to whether Guilfolyle would have to go, with the Associated Press (AP) revealing that President Donald Trump and Secretary of State Marco Rubio were "extremely pissed off" over the former Fox News host's conduct.
On Monday, Trump said "we're looking at it" when asked if Guilfoyle could be fired, adding, "we're not happy."
Rubio initially defended Guilfoyle and continued to do so in Greece last week, saying, "Our ambassador has been a strong ambassador here."
Ultimately, however, he lashed out at journalists for asking about the allegations against Guilfoyle, accusing them of seeing their own reporting as "gospel" and insisting that he would not comment until he knew the whole story.
There have been mixed reports suggesting that the State Department's investigator general might look into the matter, though this has not yet been confirmed.
Top Democrats in the House of Representatives and the Senate have called for investigations.
Guilfoyle calls posting 'honor of a lifetime,' vows to 'defend reputation'
After news broke of Guilfoyle's fall from grace within the White House, she released a lengthy post on X, lauding her own performance and calling her posting to Athens "the honor of a lifetime" as well as thanking Trump and Rubio for putting their trust in her.
Guilfoyle also said she wanted to, "address the recent allegations against me," writing: "These allegations are false, and I intend to vigorously defend my name, my reputation, and my integrity. I have dedicated my professional life to fighting for justice, standing up for what is right, and defending the values that make America exceptional. I will not allow false accusations to define my decades of public service."
Her most vocal accuser, Eric Deters, has vowed to sue Guilfoyle and her attorneys for defamation over her denials of wrongdoing in dealings with him.
What exactly is Guilfoyle accused of?
Guilfoyle, a TV personality who was formerly married to California Governor Gavin Newsom and later engaged to Trump's eldest son Don Jr., has been accused of numerous improprieties during her tenure in Greece.
Greece is an important NATO ally for the US, especially in the Eastern Mediterranean and in terms of Red Sea shipping security.
Among other things, she is said to have bragged about luxury travel and the perks of chumming with energy company executives before threatening that the US could easily undermine Greek democracy if it did not get what it wanted from the host country.
She also appeared to favor shady deals with individual Greek construction and energy company execs, going so far as to bring their lobbyists to top-level diplomatic meetings.
Guilfoyle was further reported to have alienated embassy staffers with her behavior and reportedly exploded after not being invited to a Greek-themed event at this year's World Economic Forum in Davos, Switzerland, demanding she be allowed to attend.
The straw that broke the camel's back, however, was a media offensive started by Republican Party donor Eric Deters, who grew weary of Guilfoyle's insistence that he pay off her credit card in exchange for influence that she had been unable to deliver.
Deters began doing media interviews with any outlet that would listen after the WSJ story broke, publishing text chains in which Guilfoyle implored him to transfer $100,000 (€89, 400) to her American Express account, writing, "Honey please, I need you to get this done for me today."
Deters, who said he had already paid her $300,000 and gotten nothing in return, told numerous US media outlets the deal was "absolutely a quid pro quo" and that he had warned Guilfoyle that he would go public about their dealings if she could not rectify the situation.

Majority in US say Trump prioritises personal wealth over all else: Poll

Majority in US say Trump prioritises personal wealth over all else: Poll
A majority of US adults say President Trump and his family have inappropriately profited from presidency.
Most US adults believe President Donald Trump has placed his personal financial interests and those of his inner circle ahead of the country’s since returning to the White House in 2025, according to a new nationwide poll.
The poll, conducted by the Associated Press-NORC Center for Public Affairs Research and released on Tuesday, suggests that public perception of the Republican president leans heavily critical: Over half of surveyed adults view Trump’s second term as self-serving by investing in his own business and commercial pursuits “a lot”. Roughly one quarter believe he focuses on national interests, but only 11 percent feel Trump represents regular Americans. Fifty-five percent of Republicans surveyed said that Trump has prioritised his personal business interests “a lot” or “some”.
Half of the respondents report that Trump has placed zero priority on people “like them”.
As Trump’s family business pulls in record funds from new ventures helped by his policies, the poll results suggest that most US adults think growing his own finances has been the north star of Trump’s presidency, at least to some extent.
Trump’s June financial disclosure revealed massive post-election influxes of foreign and corporate capital into his business empire, stemming primarily from over $1bn in cryptocurrency ventures after he loosened regulation on the industry, as well as from international real estate.
During his first year as president, the Trump Organisation – Trump’s multinational family-owned enterprise dedicated to property development and global brand licensing – made eight real estate deals with authoritarian or one-party foreign states. Some speculate these countries were highly motivated to maintain favourable relations with the US to keep Trump happy on fronts like trade tariffs, military protection and private business dealings.
The administration, meanwhile, has repeatedly dismissed concerns over Trump’s business conflicts of interest, maintaining that he acts solely in the interest of Americans.
In late September, a separate Reuters/Ipsos poll found that Trump’s approval rating has fallen to 32 percent – the lowest of his political career – as his fellow Republicans soured on his handling of the cost of living crisis amid the deeply unpopular Iran war.
The dip in performance and approval ratings follows a high point in January 2025, when the newly inaugurated president boasted a 47 percent approval rating right after taking office.
According to the AP-NORC poll, which surveyed more than 2,000 US adults in late September, general sentiment around the administration’s ethical conduct is highly polarised, with far more citizens feeling that the president has neither prioritised the country as a whole nor everyday Americans.
Just over 40 percent of respondents believe Trump has “done something illegal” vis-a-vis allegations of personal enrichment while in office, with another 18 percent viewing his financial dealings as “unethical but not illegal”.
Opinions surrounding the lawfulness of the president’s financial practices split sharply along party lines, with Democrats overwhelmingly viewing the actions as illegal, compared with about three in 10 independents and about one in 10 Republicans, who largely see his behaviour as justified.

UK spy chief says Iran is stepping up targeting of military bases
MI5 chief says operations linked to Iran led to 50 arrests during the past year.
UK PM says RAF base incidents 'likely coordinated' by Iran
The head of the United Kingdom’s domestic spy agency has said Iran is ramping up attempts to strike sensitive military targets after a series of incidents at airbases in Britain, even as Tehran has denied any involvement.
In his annual speech, M15 Director-General Ken McCallum on Tuesday said there had been a major shift in Tehran’s calculus this year and that “Iranian ambitions to come at harder targets, like military sites”.
McCallum’s warning came after UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham said Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) was “almost certainly” behind a suspected plot against Royal Air Force (RAF) Fairford, an airbase used by US bombers to carry out strikes on Iran. The incident prompted the United States to withdraw its military jets from the facility over security concerns earlier this month.
UK airbase incidents
British police declared a major incident after three “suspicious” vans drove close to the RAF Fairford airbase in Gloucestershire on September 27. Five British men in their 20s were arrested “on suspicion of committing offences under the Explosives Act”, but all were released on bail.
Police said they found a supply of petrol in three vans linked to the suspects, but no explosives. The men were later released without charge on police bail “under stringent conditions”.
Two others were arrested later, including a British-Iranian national, but were later released. None of the men have been charged.
Two Latvian men were arrested for trespassing at RAF Molesworth, which is used by the US military and NATO for intelligence operations, on Friday. The men were also released on bail.
UK Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband said on Monday that the government was sanctioning two Iranians for their “role in facilitating or engaging in hostile activity on behalf of the Iranian regime”.
One is Ruhollah Bazghandi, the head of IRGC counterespionage operations, and the other is Shahram Ali Reza Tamarzadeh Jakki, whom British officials described as a facilitator for Iran’s Zindashti criminal network.
‘Not unique’
McCallum said he could not speak about the recent incident at RAF Fairford because it was an ongoing investigation, but added, “The RAF Fairford incident … is not unique. There have been other examples, not just in the UK but around the world.”
The spy chief said UK authorities had carried out 50 arrests over the past year to disrupt Iran-linked operations.
However, he said he doubted Iran’s ability to launch complex attacks, perhaps using explosive drones, due to the limited sophistication of operatives Tehran used in the UK.
“Given what we’ve actually seen in practice in the UK in recent years, that has not been anywhere near [that] level of capability,” McCallum said.
“That said, clearly it is the case that in countries closer to its own homeland, the IRGC has quite deep experience of using more conventional and hybrid technology in a more aggressive and sophisticated way,” the MI5 boss added.
Tehran has rejected accusations of involvement in the Fairford incident or any other accusations of harmful activity in Britain.

Navi Pillay’s Nobel Peace Prize: Restoring moral authority of peace through justice
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
16:05:57 UTC
01:05:57 KST

Navi Pillay’s Nobel Peace Prize: Restoring moral authority of peace through justice
GOA, India - For a world fractured by double standards, the recognition of a lifelong defender of human rights is a reminder that peace cannot be separated from accountability. True peace is not achieved simply when the powerful agree to stop fighting. It is achieved when the vulnerable no longer have to live at their mercy.
The award of the 2026 Nobel Peace Prize to Navanethem “Navi” Pillay, the South African jurist and former United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights, arrives at a moment when the meaning of peace itself is being contested. Wars continue to devastate societies, international institutions struggle to command respect, and the application of international law remains deeply entangled with geopolitical interests. In such circumstances, recognising a woman whose life has been devoted to confronting discrimination, defending victims and strengthening international justice carries significance beyond the honour bestowed upon an individual.
It is also an opportunity for the Nobel Peace Prize to reaffirm its essential purpose. The prize must stand for something greater than diplomatic prestige, political expediency or the celebration of whichever causes happen to enjoy the support of influential governments. Its enduring authority depends on its willingness to recognise those who challenge entrenched power, defend human dignity and insist that no nation, government or individual should stand above the law.
Pillay’s recognition is therefore important not simply because of what she has accomplished, but because of what her career represents: the conviction that peace without justice is an incomplete peace, and that international law loses its meaning when its protection is distributed according to political convenience.
From apartheid to the defence of universal justice
Pillay’s journey began in apartheid South Africa, where racial discrimination was entrenched in law and institutional power. Born into a family of Indian Tamil origin in Durban, she experienced the indignities of a system that denied equal rights and opportunities to the majority of the population. Rather than accepting the structures of exclusion surrounding her, she chose the law as an instrument of resistance.
Her contribution to the anti-apartheid struggle was not incidental to her later international career. As a lawyer, she defended people subjected to political imprisonment, challenged abuses of authority and worked to protect the rights of those whom the apartheid system sought to marginalise. Her professional choices reflected a fundamental understanding: laws do not become just merely because a state enacts them, and governmental authority does not confer moral legitimacy on discrimination.
The struggle against apartheid established a principle with continuing relevance across the world. A system cannot claim legitimacy while denying a section of humanity equal dignity, freedom and protection. Nor can oppression be transformed into justice simply by giving it a legal form.
This is a lesson that extends well beyond South Africa. Across West Asia and elsewhere, communities confronting occupation, displacement, discrimination and prolonged conflict understand the difference between peace proclaimed by political leaders and justice experienced by ordinary people. A settlement that leaves fundamental grievances unresolved may end a phase of violence without creating the conditions for lasting peace.
Pillay’s life offers a powerful reminder that the defence of human rights must begin with the people whose rights are denied, rather than with the political interests of those who exercise power over them.
International justice must not have political favorites
Pillay carried these convictions into the international arena, serving as a judge of the International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda, presiding over that tribunal, and later serving as a judge at the International Criminal Court. Her judicial work contributed to the development of international jurisprudence on genocide and sexual violence. The landmark Akayesu judgment, delivered during her service at the Rwanda tribunal, helped establish that sexual violence can constitute an act of genocide when the necessary legal elements are met.
This was more than a legal advance. It challenged the longstanding tendency to treat the suffering of women during conflict as secondary to the supposedly larger political and military narrative. It affirmed that atrocities committed against vulnerable people deserve the full attention of the law, and that survivors must not be erased from the historical record.
From Rwanda to every other conflict in which allegations of grave international crimes arise, the principle remains the same: victims deserve investigation, recognition and justice, while those accused must be afforded due process and responsibility must be established through lawful procedures.
As United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights from 2008 to 2014, Pillay occupied one of the most demanding positions in the international human rights system. The office required her to defend universal standards in the face of pressure from governments with different political systems, strategic interests and ideological commitments. Human rights could not be defended consistently if criticism depended on whether the government concerned was a friend or an adversary.
That remains one of the central crises confronting the international order. Governments frequently invoke international law when accusing their opponents, yet become defensive when the same standards are applied to their own conduct or that of their allies. Some violations provoke immediate outrage; others encounter diplomatic hesitation, political obstruction or carefully worded expressions of concern.
Such selectivity does not merely damage the reputation of international institutions. It weakens the confidence of ordinary people in the very idea of international justice. When the law appears powerful against the weak but cautious before the powerful, it begins to resemble an instrument of political management rather than a universal safeguard.
For countries across West Asia, this contradiction is especially consequential. The credibility of international law cannot be sustained if its principles are proclaimed universally but applied unevenly in situations involving occupation, civilian casualties, displacement and allegations of serious international crimes. No community should have to wonder whether its suffering will matter less because acknowledging it would inconvenience a powerful state.
Pillay’s legacy does not require the international community to accept every allegation without examination or every institutional decision without criticism. It requires something more rigorous: evidence must be examined, legal standards must be applied consistently, and accountability must not be abandoned because its consequences are politically uncomfortable.
Palestine and the credibility of international system
The question of Palestine brings these contradictions into particularly sharp focus. Decades of occupation, repeated cycles of violence, the dispossession of Palestinians and the catastrophic destruction and human suffering in Gaza have intensified demands for an international order that does more than issue declarations.
Pillay has been associated with efforts to scrutinise alleged violations in the occupied Palestinian territory, including through her work with the United Nations Independent International Commission of Inquiry on the Occupied Palestinian Territory, including East Jerusalem, and Israel. The commission she chaired concluded in 2025 that genocide had been committed in Gaza. That finding has been strongly contested by Israel and must be understood in its proper institutional and legal context. Its existence nevertheless illustrates the significance of independent investigation when allegations concern crimes of the gravest order.
The broader issue cannot be reduced to whether governments welcome or reject a particular finding. The question is whether international institutions can investigate serious allegations independently, whether their findings receive a reasoned response, and whether credible processes of accountability can proceed without political intimidation.
For Palestinians, justice cannot mean simply the temporary cessation of bombardment while the conditions that deny them freedom, security and self-determination remain unaddressed. Nor can the language of peace be used to demand that victims abandon their claims while the structures responsible for their suffering remain intact.
Equally, the defence of Palestinian rights must rest on universal principles that protect civilians and uphold human dignity without exception. International humanitarian law, the prohibition of genocide and the prohibition of torture cannot be selectively invoked. They must apply irrespective of nationality, religion, political affiliation or military power.
This is the significance of Pillay’s career for the wider region. Her work invites governments and peoples alike to insist that international law be judged by its consistent application, not by the identity of those it protects or holds accountable.
The Nobel Peace Prize must recover its moral purpose
The Nobel Peace Prize has historically recognised people and movements whose struggles connected peace with freedom, equality and resistance to oppression. Its recognition of Martin Luther King Jr., Nelson Mandela and other figures demonstrated that peace is not simply the absence of armed confrontation. It is also the pursuit of social conditions in which human beings can live with dignity and without fear of arbitrary power.
Yet the prize is not immune to the political controversies surrounding international life. Its selections can generate legitimate debate over the relationship between peace, democracy, diplomacy and geopolitical alignment. The 2025 award to Venezuelan opposition leader María Corina Machado, which the Nobel Committee justified by reference to her promotion of democratic rights and a peaceful transition from dictatorship, became part of precisely such a debate. Critics questioned the political implications of the choice, while its supporters defended the committee’s stated rationale.
The issue is not that every controversial decision invalidates the prize, or that its recipients must satisfy every political constituency. The greater danger is that repeated perceptions of political selectivity can diminish the moral authority of an institution whose influence depends on public confidence in the principles it represents.
The Nobel Peace Prize cannot settle every international dispute, compel governments to obey the law or substitute for functioning judicial institutions. But it possesses a powerful capacity to direct the world's attention towards struggles that deserve recognition. Its choices help define what the international community celebrates as peace, and what it is prepared to overlook.
Pillay’s recognition offers an opportunity to bring that purpose into sharper focus. Her career has not been built around the promise of an easy diplomatic solution. It has been shaped by the demanding work of defending rights, strengthening legal institutions and confronting the impunity that allows grave abuses to recur.
This is a conception of peace that should resonate across political boundaries. It does not belong exclusively to the West, the Global South, any particular religion or any geopolitical bloc. Nor should international justice be portrayed as the exclusive property of one political tradition. Its legitimacy rests on the proposition that every human being possesses dignity and that every state bears obligations under international law.
For Iran and other countries of the region, the award provides an occasion to engage with that universal proposition while continuing to scrutinise the institutions through which it is implemented. Defending international law requires neither uncritical acceptance of every Western position nor the rejection of international institutions simply because their decisions are disputed. It requires a consistent commitment to legal equality, national sovereignty, human dignity and accountability for serious violations.
The test of principle is whether it survives when its application challenges our own political preferences.
Peace is a responsibility, not a slogan
Pillay’s life brings the meaning of the Nobel Peace Prize back to the human beings whose lives are shaped by war, discrimination and impunity. A displaced family needs more than declarations of concern. A survivor of sexual violence needs more than sympathy. A political prisoner needs more than a diplomatic expression of regret. People whose homes, communities and livelihoods have been destroyed need institutions capable of protecting their rights and securing meaningful remedies.
Justice cannot restore every life or erase every wound. Nor should the pursuit of accountability become an excuse to reject negotiations that can save lives. Ceasefires, diplomacy and political settlements remain essential. But peace becomes durable only when they create a credible path towards freedom, security, recognition and justice.
The Nobel Peace Prize awarded to Navi Pillay should therefore be understood as a recognition of a lifetime spent defending the principles without which peace becomes little more than a temporary arrangement between those who possess power. It honors a woman who confronted apartheid at its foundations and carried that commitment into the international institutions charged with defending humanity against grave abuses.
The true measure of this recognition will not be the ceremony, the medal or the declarations that accompany it. It will be whether the principles associated with Pillay’s work receive renewed support, whether independent institutions are strengthened, and whether the international community becomes more willing to confront violations even when doing so carries political costs.
The Nobel Prize does not become meaningful simply because it honors a distinguished individual. It becomes meaningful when that recognition reminds the world of obligations it would otherwise prefer to evade. In an age when the language of peace is frequently invoked while justice remains elusive, Navi Pillay’s recognition offers a clear and demanding message: no nation should possess a license to violate human dignity, no victim should be considered expendable, and no government should be beyond scrutiny.
Peace requires justice. Justice requires accountability. And accountability must never depend on who holds the power.
*Ranjan Solomon is an author, researcher, and freelance writer focused on global and national justice.
