‘We've been given the chance to live again’: Alon Ohel and Eli Sharabi talk about life after Hamas captivity
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
16:05:45 UTC
01:05:45 KST

A year after Alon Ohel was released from Hamas captivity, he and fellow former hostage Eli Sharabi reunited Tuesday for a joint interview at ynet's "People of the Nation" conference, reflecting on the friendship they formed during a year and two months together in Gaza tunnels, their lives since returning home and the everyday freedoms they no longer take for granted.
Sharabi, a resident of Kibbutz Be'eri, was released in February 2025 after 491 days in captivity. Ohel, a pianist abducted at age 22 from the Nova music festival, was freed in October 2025 alongside the last living hostages, after 738 days.
‘All of Israel was part of it’
Neither man imagined what life would look like after his release from captivity. "We never imagined we'd become such well-known figures," Sharabi said. Following his release after 491 days, he became one of the most prominent voices advocating for the hostages who remained in Gaza. "We couldn't believe that all of Israel was so involved in this," he said.
Sharabi had imagined his wife and daughters running toward him at the border upon his return. Only after his release did he learn that his wife, Lianne, and their daughters, Noiya and Yahel, had been murdered in Be'eri. His brother Yossi had also been abducted and killed in captivity.
"Everything that came afterward was completely unexpected," Sharabi continued. "But ultimately, there are certain realities you wake up to in the morning, and you have to figure out what to do with them. And that's it. The rest is history."
Ohel said he had expected to have to take care of everything himself after returning home. "When I got out, I realized my parents had taken care of me," he said. "Today, I'm mainly focused on my rehabilitation and my music."
Asked whether people they encounter on the street tend to cry or hug them, Ohel answered: "Both together."
"Sometimes you practically have to pick people up off the floor, really. They're so incredibly emotional, and I give all that love back," Sharabi added. "I'm the most approachable person in the world."
He acknowledged that his approach to public attention had changed. "I used to be a private person, but after everything the people of Israel did for us, it's the least I can do."
‘I'm incredibly proud of it’
The friendship the two men developed in captivity has continued since their release. "We talk, we meet. We're both very busy people, and we try to do it as much as possible," Sharabi said.
Asked about the private jokes they share, he explained: "There are things that stayed with us from there. Of course, we laugh about them, remember them and get emotional together."
"We're also very different people," Sharabi said. "There are a lot of similarities, too," Ohel added.
Sharabi pointed to a few unexpected connections between them. "He was born on February 10, and I was born on February 13. I worked 200 meters from his father and simply didn't know it."
More important than those coincidences, Sharabi said, was the fact that they shared similar values. "That was the foundation on which we were able to build this incredibly close and caring friendship, and I'm prouder of it than anything in the world."
The little things that are no longer taken for granted
Asked what ordinary activity they appreciate most after being deprived of it in captivity, Ohel had a simple answer: "Opening the refrigerator."
For Sharabi, it was taking a hot shower. "You don't take it for granted after showering with half a bucket of cold water once every six weeks, sometimes once every two months," he said. "Begging for showers, begging to shave, begging for everything."
Even the frustration of sitting in traffic has returned, although Sharabi said it rarely lasts. "Very quickly, you tell yourself, 'I have all the time in the world.'"
Asked when they had last felt happy, Ohel replied: "All the time, all the time." Sharabi added: "Every day I have my family beside me, my friends and the things I do." 
"We're alive," Ohel said. "We've been given the chance to live again."
‘I'm in an amazing relationship’
Ohel is in a relationship with Goni, a childhood friend who campaigned for his release. Asked whether he had brought her to Sharabi for his approval, Sharabi replied: "Far from it."
Ohel explained what he valued about being in a relationship with someone who knew him before captivity. "She really knows you, not just what people said or told her about you," he said. "I think it's much more open and free, without defenses."
Sharabi revealed that he, too, has been in a relationship for about six months. "I'm in an amazing relationship. I'm happy, and everything is good." When asked to share more about his partner, however, he drew a firm boundary. "That's my private life. Absolutely not."
‘There isn't a day I don't cry’
The two men offered different perspectives on how their time in captivity had changed them. "I haven't changed at all," Sharabi insisted. "The situation changed, but Eli is still Eli."
Ohel saw things differently. "I was kidnapped at 22. Today I'm 25. Without a doubt, what I went through shaped me."
Sharabi said his sense of humor had always been an essential part of his personality. "I'm a joker. I don't know how to get through a day or even an hour without joking around. It's always been part of me."
He said he also finds himself crying frequently. "I think I'm making up for all the days in captivity when I didn't cry. There isn't a day I don't cry," he said. "Most of the time, I cry because I'm moved. But of course, I also cry because of an enormous sense of longing. It exists alongside life. It doesn't stop me from living."
Ohel said he also sees crying as an important emotional release. "I think it's a way of letting things out, and it's important. I don't try to hide it, either."
From diving in Thailand to a stroller and a baby
Asked what moment from before October 7 he would most like to share with Ohel, Sharabi recalled his travels in Thailand. "I would have liked him to go diving with me," he said. "I had incredible days of diving in Thailand, and we talked about it throughout our entire captivity."
When asked where he hoped to see Ohel in three years, Sharabi offered a particularly personal wish. "I'd love to see him with a stroller, with a baby. He'll be an amazing father," he said. "And in those moments when he says, 'Enough, I've had it,' I'll take the baby and look after him. I'll be there for him."
"That will definitely happen," Ohel replied.
Asked what he wished for Sharabi, Ohel said: "That you live your life and travel nonstop, just like we always talked about. Just enjoy yourself."
‘We must stay united, not only when things are hard’
At the end of the interview, three years after October 7, the two men were asked to share a message with the Israeli public. "Every day that passes never comes back. Enjoy yourselves," Sharabi said.
"Don't take your family for granted. Hug them every day. Appreciate the basic things in life, the things that really matter, not material possessions."
Ohel concluded with a call for unity. "We need so much to remain united and together. Not to be united only when things are hard, but also when things are good, and to keep it that way."

Brazilian polls show Lula, Flavio Bolsonaro in technical tie
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
16:03:31 UTC
01:03:31 KST

Mariam Ashalem De Andres
13 October 2026•Update: 13 October 2026
Brazilian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva and Sen. Flavio Bolsonaro are statistically tied ahead of an Oct. 25 presidential runoff, according to polls released Tuesday by PoderData/Aya and BTG/Nexus.
The PoderData/Aya survey put Bolsonaro, of the Liberal Party (PL), at 51% of valid votes, compared to 49% for Lula, of the Workers' Party (PT). The BTG/Nexus poll showed Bolsonaro with 52% and Lula with 48%.
Both results fall within the respective margins of error, indicating a technical tie between the candidates.
PoderData/Aya recorded a narrower gap than in its survey on Oct. 8, when Bolsonaro led Lula by 53% to 47%.
The results represent a 2-percentage-point gain for Lula and a corresponding decline for Bolsonaro.
In voting intentions, PoderData/Aya recorded 48% for Bolsonaro and 46% for Lula, while BTG/Nexus put the candidates at 48% and 45%, respectively.
The remaining respondents were undecided, declined to answer or said they would cast blank or null ballots.
PoderData/Aya interviewed 3,000 voters by telephone between Oct. 10 and 12, with a margin of error of 1.8 percentage points.
BTG/Nexus interviewed 2,002 voters aged 16 and older during the same period, with a margin of error of 2 percentage points.
The BTG/Nexus survey was commissioned by financial institution BTG Pactual. Both polls were registered with Brazil's Superior Electoral Court.
In the first round on Oct. 4, Bolsonaro received 47.03% of valid votes, while Lula secured 45.16%, according to the results.
The candidates will face each other again on Oct. 25, when Brazilians will choose their next president.

Hundreds of early-release prisoners in England and Wales not being tagged, say MPs
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
16:03:20 UTC
01:03:20 KST

Hundreds of prisoners released early across England and Wales, including stalkers and violent offenders, are not being tagged, MPs have said, despite promises of the “toughest supervision in British history”.
As the government begins releasing a second tranche of 650 offenders to relieve prison overcrowding, police and probation officers have said they are struggling to cope with a new influx of offenders who are supposed to be monitored in the community.
Speaking during an urgent question in the Commons on Tuesday, the Labour MP Clive Efford asked why the outsourcing company Serco had failed to tag prisoners as they leave prison. Serco has denied any such failure.
“They are not actually fulfilling their contracts. It can’t be beyond the tech firm’s ability to tag people on release. So what are these companies going to do about it?” he said.
The shadow justice secretary, Nick Timothy, said most prisoners were not being tagged before release, despite assurances from the government that the tagging system would be the “toughest in history”.
“The justice secretary told the country that proper safeguards would be put in place with a presumption that all released prisoners would be tagged. He called it the toughest tagging regime in history, but that was nonsense,” he said.
Jake Richards, the justice minister, replied: “We are working closely with Serco and have seen an improvement in the implementation since March this year. Although there is a presumption of every person being tagged, ultimately it is an operational decision.”
A Serco spokesperson said it is “delivering an excellent service, tagging a record number of people, and consistently meeting all our contractual measures”.
The spokesperson added: “The Ministry of Justice has publicly recognised the quality of our performance and our team has successfully delivered four early release schemes.
“We attempt to fit an electronic monitoring device to every person required to wear one. Where it is not possible to fit a device, or where the person breaches the conditions of their release, the individual is reported to the relevant authorities, who are responsible for considering and taking any further action.”
About 2,000 criminals, including domestic abusers and violent offenders, are being freed this month, with another 3,000 to follow in stages over the next year. The total was reduced from 6,000 after an intervention by Andy Burnham.
Prisoners convicted of manslaughter are excluded, meaning the killers of PC Andrew Harper, who died in the line of duty in 2019, will not be eligible.
Typically, those being released should expect to be electronically tagged and subject to other monitoring conditions for the second third of their sentence.
But the probation service union, Napo, said the releases were putting enormous strain on its members, who monitor offenders in the community.
The union held a pre-ballot meeting on Tuesday concerning taking strike action over pay and workloads.
Pay negotiations ended earlier in October with a “best and final” conditional pay offer worth 5%, which the union’s negotiating committee rejected. Members will be asked to vote for industrial action on pay, along with a question on workloads, in a formal ballot on industrial action to launch on 19 October.
The union says probation officers have been required to take on large amounts of extra work since tens of thousands of prisoners began being released early in 2022.
A senior Prison and Probation Service source said a failure to place tags on released offenders as they left prison meant it could then be up to a month before they were tagged.
“If we do not tag them as they leave prison, there is a good chance that we won’t tag them at all before they reoffend,” they said.
Mark Rowley, the Metropolitan police commissioner, said many of those who breached their tagging conditions – by consuming alcohol or drugs, or by breaching a curfew, for example – were not facing sanctions if arrested.
“We’re seeing 95%-plus of the tagging breaches that we arrest are simply being bailed back into the community on the same condition. So there is zero sanction,” he said.
The number of people in prison has jumped by more than 1,700 in the past three months. The prison population in England and Wales was at 87,499 on Monday, according to Ministry of Justice data, up from 85,761 on 29 June, a rise of 2%.
Alex Norris, the justice secretary, has said released offenders will be monitored under the “toughest supervision in British history”.
New restriction zones designed to control the movements of the highest-risk sexual and violent offenders should confine released prisoners to areas a few miles wide, in an effort to reassure their victims.
However, this month the victims’ commissioner, Claire Waxman, said the government’s confidence in the plan was “not yet matched by the reality on the ground”.

Kyiv and Berlin have also agreed to hold a meeting of national security advisers in the E3 format, with Ukraine participating, according to the statement. The format involves an informal grouping of three leading European countries: the United Kingdom, France and Germany.
Zelenskyy and Merz discuss energy truce and support for Ukraine
During the conversation, the two sides also discussed US President Donald Trump’s proposal for an energy truce and Russia’s subsequent actions. Russian forces continue to attack Ukraine’s energy infrastructure, Zelenskyy noted.
“This is exactly how the Russians behave when pressure eases. It is very important that Europe continue to act on principle,” Zelenskyy stressed.
Germany is coordinating preparations for a meeting of the Coalition of the Willing, the Ukrainian president noted. The two sides also discussed support for Ukraine’s financial stability. Further steps are to be coordinated in greater detail during a meeting scheduled for this week, Zelenskyy said.
The Coalition of the Willing seeks additional support for Ukraine
The Coalition of the Willing was initiated by the United Kingdom and France, which held talks with representatives of 37 countries in March 2025 on supporting Ukraine in the event of a peace agreement. The initiative envisaged financial assistance and the deployment of troops, air forces or naval forces to protect Ukraine against renewed Russian aggression, Bloomberg reported.
The latest meeting of the Coalition of the Willing took place on 24 August and was the 16th meeting, according to a statement on the website of the President of Ukraine. Zelenskyy called on partners to strengthen Ukraine’s air defense and provide at least 300 missiles for Patriot systems for the winter, the statement said.
The president also proposed bringing forward part of the European loan financing planned for 2027 so that Ukraine could receive the funds this year. He separately stressed the need to find a mechanism for using frozen Russian assets to defend Ukraine and to unblock the maritime corridor in the Black Sea.
“We value this format—the Coalition of the Willing. It brings together countries that are ready not only to talk about security but also to act. We need this—to act and build real security together,” Zelenskyy stressed.
A ceasefire in words, but fresh attacks on energy infrastructure in practice
Ukraine and Russia had allegedly agreed to an immediate energy ceasefire, US President Donald Trump said on Truth Social on 11 October. However, at the time of publication, neither Kyiv nor Moscow had confirmed such an agreement, Ukrainska Pravda reported.
Ukraine supports the ceasefire and is awaiting details from the US side, Volodymyr Zelenskyy said in a post on X the same day. Russia must also agree to halt the strikes, he stressed.
Ukrainian forces had received the relevant orders, and Kyiv was ready to refrain from striking Russian energy infrastructure provided Russia reciprocated, Zelenskyy said in his evening address on 11 October.
Russia continued attacking Ukraine’s energy infrastructure after the ceasefire was announced, including striking a gas production facility and a petrol station, Zelenskyy said on his official Telegram channel on 12 October. Moscow had shown no willingness to abide by the ceasefire, the president added.

Burnham links airbase incident to Iran amid complex US relations
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
16:00:44 UTC
01:00:44 KST

Breadcrumb
Burnham links RAF Fairford incident to Iran amid delicate relations with US
UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham attributed recent threats to an RAF base in Gloucestershire to Iran on Monday, but this may cause further problems for him in future.
Five men were arrested near RAF Fairford, which hosted long range bombers for the United States, including B1 and B52 bombers, on 27 September, after the police received a call concerning suspicious activity in the area.
The men were arrested on suspicion of offences under the Explosives Act, and on suspicion of preparing an act of terrorism. Two other men were subsequently arrested in connection to the incident. The men have all been released on bail.
Rob Geist Pinfold, a lecturer in Defence Studies at King's College London, told The New Arab that linking the incident to Iran could end up putting Burnham in a "tough spot".
"There was this hyping up that this was an imminent terror threat. The residents were evacuated. They were hosted at a local leisure centre, and then we went from that to the suspects being released on bail," Geist Pinfold said.
The US responded to the attacks by removing their planes from the base. Shortly after the US and Israel's attacks on Iran in February, the UK granted permission for the US to use RAF Fairford for operations against Iran. The base is strategically important because it has a long runway from which long-range bombers, including B-1 and B-52 bombers, can take-off.
"The UK government has to walk a very, very strange tightrope here of not being part of the war effort but the same time, unlike other European countries, allowing the US to use the bases in its territory as part of that war effort, which is why Iran painted a target on Fairford," said Geist Pinfold.
Support for the war on Iran is low in the UK. In April, 65% of Brits disapproved of US military strikes against Iran, according to a poll by Ipsos.
The US President is also unpopular among Brits. In September, a YouGov poll found that just 10% of people in the UK have a favourable opinion of Donald Trump. By comparison, 85% have an unfavourable opinion of him.
"This is a tough spot for Andy Burnham," Geist Pinfold said, "[He] might find himself doing the same thing as [former Prime Minister] Kier Starmer, trying to pretend the special relationship is still alive and well when there are very clear cracks in the surface."
"[The UK] certainly doesn't think the war was a good idea now but at the same time it doesn't want to alienate the US and at the same time it does see Iran as a national security threat," Geist Pinfold told The New Arab.
When asked if the UK might become more involved in the Iran war, Geist Pinfold said, "I would suggest it depends on what happens with our Gulf partners because at the end of the day, the UK like other European countries sees the Iran conflict as a threat to national security, but also potential opportunity simply because Gulf states are looking to diversify the security partnerships."
"For a country like the UK with a strong defence industry that also is looking for a quick fix, or at least a boost to its economy ASAP, that's a very, very attractive potential."

A large trial of genotype-guided antidepressant prescribing finds no early benefit but higher remission later
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
16:00:38 UTC
01:00:38 KST

A randomized clinical trial found that using genetic test results to guide the prescription of selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) for depression did not improve symptoms after 3 months compared with usual care. However, among patients whose genetic profiles called for a different medication or dose, 48% of those in the genotype-guided group reached remission at 6 months, compared with 39% of those receiving usual care. The paper was published in JAMA Network Open.
Depression is a common mental health disorder marked by persistent low mood, loss of interest or pleasure, and other symptoms that can substantially disrupt everyday life. Its prevalence has risen over the past decade among adults, adolescents, and school-aged children. Uncontrolled depression is closely linked to suicide, which is now the second leading cause of death among adolescents and young adults.
One of the most widely used treatments for depression is a class of antidepressants called selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors, or SSRIs. These medications increase the availability of the neurotransmitter serotonin in the brain by reducing its reuptake into nerve cells. Although SSRIs are commonly prescribed, they do not work equally well for everyone. They can also take six weeks or longer to produce a response, and can cause adverse effects that lead some patients to stop treatment.
Part of this variability may be related to genetic differences in the liver enzymes that break down SSRIs, particularly CYP2D6 and CYP2C19. Variants in the genes for these enzymes can make a person a poor, intermediate, normal, rapid, or ultrarapid metabolizer, changing how much of an SSRI remains in the body. Some other medications can also slow CYP2D6 activity, producing a similar effect. Genotype-guided prescribing uses genetic test results to help clinicians choose a medication or dose suited to how a person processes it.
The Clinical Pharmacogenetics Implementation Consortium has published guidelines for adjusting SSRI prescriptions based on these genes, but most psychiatry experts and practice guidelines have not endorsed routine genetic testing, citing insufficient evidence. Earlier trials have been criticized for relying on proprietary commercial algorithms, using small samples, or failing to meet their main goals.
Study author Kathryn V. Blake of Nemours Children’s Health in Jacksonville, Florida, and her colleagues conducted a large randomized clinical trial to test whether genotype-guided SSRI prescribing improves depression in routine clinical care. The trial focused on CYP2D6 and CYP2C19 and used publicly available guidelines rather than a commercial algorithm to generate recommendations.
Study participants were 1,460 people with depression treated at primary care, psychiatry, and family medicine clinics in nine U.S. health systems between 2021 and 2024. Participants were aged 8 years or older, had experienced depression for 3 months or longer, and were about to start or adjust SSRI treatment. They included 1,239 adults, with an average age of 41, and 221 children and adolescents, with an average age of 15; 75% were female.
Participants were randomly assigned either to a genotype-guided group or to usual care. All provided DNA samples, which were analyzed for variants in the genes for CYP2D6 and CYP2C19, but only the genotype-guided group’s results were returned during the study; the usual care group’s samples were analyzed after it ended.
For the genotype-guided group, clinicians received recommendations about which SSRI to prescribe and at what dose through electronic health record alerts, consult notes, or pharmacist consultations, based on established guidelines and drug labels. The recommendations also accounted for other medications that can slow CYP2D6 activity. Clinicians were not required to follow the recommendations. The SSRIs covered were sertraline, escitalopram, citalopram, fluvoxamine, and paroxetine.
The main analyses focused on the 692 participants (about 47%) whose genetic results were “actionable,” meaning guidelines recommended a different medication or dose for them. Depression symptoms were measured with Patient-Reported Outcomes Measurement Information System (PROMIS) questionnaires for adults and children, and with the Patient Health Questionnaire-8 as a secondary measure.
At 3 months, depression symptoms had decreased modestly in both groups, but the decrease was nearly identical, and side effects were similar as well. At 6 months, however, 48% of patients in the genotype-guided group had reached remission on the PROMIS measure, compared with 39% in the usual care group. Using the second questionnaire, remission rates were 30% and 21%, respectively.
The genetic guidance did change prescribing: at 3 months, 85% of patients in the genotype-guided group were taking a medication and dose consistent with their genetic profile, compared with 74% in the usual care group. Among patients whose results did not call for any change, the two groups did not differ.
“In this randomized clinical trial, genotype-guided prescribing of SSRIs did not improve control of depression symptoms at 3 months compared with usual care but was associated with higher depression remission rates at 6 months. These findings suggest a possible longer-term clinical benefit and indicate that future studies should focus on the durability and long-term impact of genotype-guided prescribing in the management of depressive symptoms,” study authors concluded.
The study contributes to the development of new ways to treat depression. However, the trial did not meet its primary goal of improving symptoms at 3 months, and the 6-month remission rates were secondary outcomes. Clinicians and patients also knew which group they were in, and patients could see their genetic results in their health records, which may have influenced how they reported their symptoms.
The authors also note that the study design did not include a formal diagnosis of major depression, so the sample may have included patients with milder forms of depression. About 15% of patients in the genotype-guided group with actionable results were still not receiving a gene-matched prescription at 3 months, and delays in treatment changes, which were not tracked, may help explain why differences did not appear until later.
The paper, “Genotype-Guided Antidepressant Prescribing for Patients With Depression: A Randomized Clinical Trial,” was authored by Kathryn V. Blake, Lindsay J. Hines, Michelle Liu, Rachel A. Myers, Jordan F. Baye, Kerri L. Cavanaugh, Benjamin Q. Duong, Leslie A. Hulvershorn, Carol A. Mathews, James W. Murrough, Lori A. Orlando, Natasha J. Petry, Emma M. Tillman, Azita Sadeghpour, Deepak Voora, Sara L. Block, Emily J. Cicali, Sabrina Clermont, Erica N. Elwood, Elizabeth C. Harris, Khoa A. Nguyen, Michelle A. Ramos, Marc B. Rosenman, Nandini Shroff, Saskia Shuman, Christina Wyatt, Carol R. Horowitz, Simona Volpi, Rajbir Singh, Renee A. Rider, Hrishikesh Chakraborty, Paul R. Dexter, Julie A. Johnson, Todd C. Skaar, Larisa H. Cavallari, and Josh F. Peterson.

Trump says US still sharing intel with Ukraine, defends Russian diesel deal

"We are helping them, and we are sharing intel," Trump told reporters. "We want the war to end, so we're working with them and Russia on getting the war to end."

A nervous and brief debut: Katie Zacharia limits White House briefing to 15 minutes, 3 questions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
16:00:33 UTC
01:00:33 KST

Washington DC — She was visibly nervous. She relied heavily on notes. She took deep breaths. And veteran White House reporters found themselves witnessing a "briefest briefing" ever.
However, when Katie Zacharia delivered her first White House press briefing on Tuesday, she conveyed the US administration's key points and broke significant news during a high-pressure debut.
Taking the custom podium in the James S. Brady Press Briefing Room — a small theater in the West Wing of the White House — for roughly 14–15 minutes, including an eight-minute prepared opening statement, Zacharia began her briefing by stating that she was "honoured to work for" US President Donald Trump "and the American people", thanking the US president "for the trust that he has placed in me."
She highlighted Trump's recent Ohio rally, his "America First" priorities of "lower taxes, higher wages, and one of my favourites, secure borders."
Zacharia said Trump is planning to hold rallies in Alaska, Arizona, Montana and Georgia, "building off of the incredible momentum generated over the last several days from his stops in Tennessee, New York, Texas, and Nebraska."
"He is an energetic president. Attendance is at record highs as enthusiastic, hard-working Americans are lining up and packing arenas to support President Trump and Republicans," she added.
Zacharia, tapped by Trump to replace Karoline Leavitt, who resigned in August to spend more time with her two young children, claimed that US real wages rose by up to 2 percent under Trump administeration, but fell nearly 4 per cent under former president Joe Biden.
President Trump is the first president in modern history to actually lower prescription drug prices, delivering the biggest drop in 63 years, she added.
"Trump has created more than 1 million private sector jobs in his second term, including nearly 112,000 factory construction jobs and 72,000 manufacturing jobs this year alone," she added.
Zacharia highlighted US energy expansion, major investments, and security initiatives under Trump administration, saying "this is a president, an administration that is looking out for you, the American people, and I’m thrilled to officially be part of this incredible journey together."
Guilfoyle resignation
Zacharia, a conservative commentator, a lawyer and former communications adviser to Trump's media company, however, gave reporters a big news on Kimberly Guilfoyle, the US ambassador to Greece.
"We have asked Ambassador Guilfoyle to resign," Trump's new press secretary told reporters. "She has been a wonderful asset to the team, and we wish her well."
The announcement came a day after Trump confirmed he was considering dismissing Guilfoyle, a former television host and the ex-fiancee of Donald Trump Jr.
Guilfoyle has come under scrutiny following media reports regarding her financial dealings and ties with wealthy business figures.
According to US media reports, she asked a prominent Trump supporter Eric Deters to settle $100,000 in credit card debt ahead of her July 2025 Senate hearing.
Reports citing messages and recordings reveal Guilfoyle boasted of luxury trips and hotel stays funded by wealthy Greek business figures.
The State Department is reportedly investigating whether Guilfoyle received improper gifts.
Zacharia's disclosure regarding Guilfoyle's status was one of only three questions she addressed from reporters – Nick Gilbertson of Breitbart, Peter Doocy of Fox News, and Alina Shirazi of the Daily Mail.
She said her job was to amplify and expand Trump's agenda, describing the US leader as "his own best spokesperson." She also did not answer whether US will stop intelligence sharing with Ukraine.
During remarks concerning her family, the California mother of four momentarily misspoke, stating, "my president — excuse me, my husband… That’s a good one", which drew laughter from the room before she regained her composure and continued.
Comparisons with Karoline Leavitt
Audible gasps were heard as she ended the briefing, citing Trump's departure on Marine One to Alaska to take no further questions.
"I've now been covering the White House for nearly four years — and that was without a doubt the shortest briefing I've ever attended. By a wide, wide margin," noted journalist Bernd Debusmann Jr.
A White House official interviewed by MS NOW's Jake Traylor immediately stated that Zacharia better improve — and quickly.
"Getting behind the podium is tough, but she got off on the wrong foot. She needs to get much better, fast, otherwise she’ll break Scaramucci’s record,” the unnamed official told Traylor.
Former White House communications director Anthony Scaramucci served for just 10 days during Trump's first term in 2017.
Zacharia's first press briefing lasted roughly 15 minutes, taking questions from just three reporters for five minutes, noted NBC News' White House correspondent Monica Alba.
"By comparison, Karoline Leavitt’s first briefing lasted around 47 minutes and she took questions from 20 different reporters."
Zacharia's supervisor, however, described her debut briefing as a "tremendous start".
"A tremendous start for the new White House press secretary," said Steven Cheung, White House director of communications.
"She commanded the room and effectively reminded the American people of all the great work President Trump and his Administration has done thus far."
Debut briefings are rarely easy, and the litmus test will come in subsequent briefings. Meanwhile, Zacharia must now build rapport with a White House press corps accustomed to combative exchanges, fast-paced political shifts, and a president who, she herself described, as "his own best spokesperson."

Philippe, Glucksmann, Retailleau : les temps forts du Sommet sur la compétitivité économique de POLITICO
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
16:00:25 UTC
01:00:25 KST

Philippe, Glucksmann, Retailleau : les temps forts du Sommet sur la compétitivité économique de POLITICO
Les trois candidats à la présidentielle ont répondu aux questions de nos journalistes sur l’Europe, l’intelligence artificielle ou l’énergie. Thèmes sur lesquels les clivages ont été nombreux.
Edouard Philippe, Raphaël Glucksmann et Bruno Retailleau participent lors du Sommet POLITICO sur la Compétitivité Économique à Paris, le 13 octobre 2026. | François le Guen/POLITICO
PARIS — Un peu plus de deux semaines après le Playbook Paris Live, où Gabriel Attal, Marine Le Pen et Jean-Luc Mélenchon étaient reçus, trois autres candidats à la présidentielle étaient invités à s’exprimer ce mardi sur les enjeux économiques du moment lors du Sommet sur la compétitivité économique de POLITICO.
Voitures thermiques et droits de douane
Avec l’ouverture du Salon de l’Auto, c’est l’un des sujets d’actu du jour : l’interdiction de la vente des voitures à moteur thermique dans l’Union européenne à partir de 2035 — un accord pour assouplir cette mesure est sur le point d’être conclu entre la France et l’Allemagne. Sans surprise, Edouard Philippe, Raphaël Glucksmann et Bruno Retailleau ne partagent pas le même avis sur la question.
Le candidat Horizons considère que cette décision est une erreur. “Une stratégie, ça doit s’appuyer sur une analyse précise des moyens qu’on est capable de mettre en œuvre. Et de fait, on n’a pas été capable de mettre en œuvre ce qui aurait permis de rendre cette stratégie possible, pour autant qu’elle ait été adaptée”, a-t-il estimé lors de notre sommet. L’ancien Premier ministre plaide pour une meilleure protection du marché européen via la mise en place de droits de douane élevés sur l’importation de véhicules chinois. Une question de “réciprocité”, a-t-il martelé pendant l’entretien.
Advertisement
Une vision rejetée quelques instants plus tard par Raphaël Glucksmann. “Je ne vois pas du tout en quoi cet objectif [de 2035] était une erreur”, a rétorqué le tout nouveau candidat du PS et de Place publique. L’eurodéputé plaide pour que les constructeurs automobiles se concentrent sur le développement de l’électrique. “C’est ça l’avenir”, a-t-il insisté, jugeant que l’Europe a “un énorme sujet de naïveté vis-à-vis de la Chine”.
Deux positions renvoyées dos à dos par Bruno Retailleau, qui a rappelé que le groupe du Parti populaire européen, dans lequel siègent les eurodéputés LR, s’était opposé à l’instauration de cette règle lorsqu’elle a été votée au Parlement européen. “Ma position, elle est très nette, elle n’a pas changé, ça fait des années que je le demande, je dénonce cet accord”, a insisté le candidat des Républicains. Il aurait préféré voir “imposer le principe de la neutralité technologique”, via un “cadre très exigeant”, mais progressif pour les constructeurs.
Sur la question des échanges commerciaux avec Pékin, le Vendéen rejoint la position d’Edouard Philippe en s’affichant en faveur de “vrais droits de douane” sur les importations chinoises. “A partir du moment où les règles ne sont pas loyales, on doit pouvoir les compenser”, a défendu Bruno Retailleau.
Energies
Autre dissonance entre les candidats : l’énergie. Pronucléaire, Edouard Philippe a insisté sur la nécessité de “défendre” et “favoriser” l’atome, tout en ajoutant que le “risque associé à [son] exploitation” est “réel”. Si, par mesure de sécurité, il fallait interrompre la production des centrales nucléaires françaises, il faudrait que d’autres technologies puissent prendre le relai et produire de l’électricité, a-t-il exposé, mentionnant les énergies renouvelables. Sinon, la France pourrait se retrouver dans une “situation qui peut-être terrible”, a-t-il prévenu. Le candidat Horizons est par ailleurs favorable à la construction de tous les réacteurs EPR2 envisagés par l'exécutif.
Du côté de Bruno Retailleau, le discours est beaucoup plus mesuré sur les renouvelables. Le candidat LR a confirmé vouloir couper leurs subventions s’il était élu, tout comme il compte abandonner la programmation pluriannuelle de l'énergie (la PPE3), définie par le gouvernement Lecornu. Prudent, Bruno Retailleau l’est aussi sur le développement des EPR2. Alors que la construction de six nouveaux réacteurs a déjà été décidée, “on verra” pour les huit autres prévus, a-t-il temporisé.
Vision de l’Europe
Face aux menaces en matière de défense, sécurité ou IA, Raphaël Glucksmann a répondu qu’il fallait “sortir de l’intergouvernemental” et que l’Union européenne devait assumer sa puissance dans le rapport de force avec la Chine ou les Etats-Unis.
Advertisement
“Il faut un instrument pour les financements européens. Si vous avez des financements européens, oui, vous allez voir que subitement les projets européens fonctionnent”, a-t-il plaidé. Pour le candidat PS-Place publique, la France a tout intérêt à diversifier ses alliances en ne regardant pas seulement vers l’Allemagne, mais en se tournant vers la Pologne ou les pays baltes. “La puissance française, elle se construira dans sa capacité à construire une coalition en Europe”, a-t-il martelé.
Pour Edouard Philippe, la relation franco-allemande est “absolument déterminante dans l’ensemble européen”, même s’il ne faut “pas réduire la politique européenne” uniquement à ce duo. Selon le candidat Horizons, la France aurait tout intérêt à “être plus crédible” et à “régler [ses] sujets” (comprenez : ses sujets budgétaires et le redressement des comptes publics), si elle veut retrouver du poids politique en Europe. “Nous sommes les seuls à ne pas savoir respecter des règles communes qui ont été respectées par tous les autres. Et ça, ça nous plante”, a-t-il déploré.
La question budgétaire, c’est par cet angle que Bruno Retailleau a abordé le thème de l’UE. Selon lui, la France doit “absolument” réduire sa contribution au budget de l’Union européenne, a-t-il estimé. Le candidat des Républicains a par ailleurs apporté son soutien aux Etats membres dits “frugaux”, partisans d’un budget de l’UE réduit. “Si la France ne fait pas partie de ces pays frugaux, ça veut dire qu’on a totalement perdu contact avec la réalité”, a jugé l’ancien ministre de l’Intérieur.
Mouvement lycéen
Interrogé sur son soutien au mouvement lycéen, dont c’était "l’acte V" aujourd’hui, Raphaël Glucksmann considère que son rôle n’est pas de manifester, mais “de répondre aux revendications des lycéens et de répondre à une angoisse qui est une angoisse existentielle”. Favorable à la suppression de Parcoursup, il souhaite remplacer la plateforme par “un procédé qui est transparent, mais qui ne peut pas être le retour à ce qu’on faisait avant”, car “ce n’était pas non plus fonctionnel”, a-t-il jugé, sans donner plus de précisions.
Pour Bruno Retailleau, il ne faut pas considérer que les lycéens qui expriment des revendications dans les médias “représentent tous les lycéens”. S’il reconnaît que certaines préoccupations sont “justes”, comme “sur Parcoursup ou sur une angoisse pour l’avenir”, il oppose par exemple les revendications des lycéens ruraux aux citadins. Et note que la situation est moins bouillonnante dans une grande partie du pays.
Le candidat LR a aussi critiqué la présence de la militante écologiste suédoise Greta Thunberg devant un lycée de Seine-Saint-Denis ce matin, jugeant qu’elle incarne une “écologie dévoyée” se résumant souvent à “une forme de gauchisme”.

Centre asks states to go into ‘mission mode’ to curb stubble burning as farm fires rise in MP, Rajasthan
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
16:00:10 UTC
01:00:10 KST

Centre steps up anti-stubble burning drive ahead of peak crop residue season (representative image)
NEW DELHI: The Centre on Tuesday asked Madhya Pradesh, Rajasthan, Punjab, Haryana and Delhi-NCR authorities to work in “mission mode” to prevent stubble burning ahead of the peak crop residue burning season, flagging a sharp rise in farm fires in Madhya Pradesh and Rajasthan.Union agriculture minister Shivraj Singh Chouhan and environment minister Bhupender Yadav chaired a high-level inter-ministerial meeting with state agriculture ministers and officials to review crop residue management and measures to control farm fires.“Very little time remains between the harvesting of the current crop and the sowing of the rabi crop. Therefore, the administrative machinery must step away from paperwork and work directly on the ground on a war footing,” the two ministers said, according to a statement from the agriculture ministry.States have been directed to hold immediate meetings with district magistrates to ensure strict monitoring and implement practical solutions, the ministry said.
Farm fires surge in Madhya Pradesh, Rajasthan
Reviewing data from September 15 to October 12, Chouhan noted that stubble-burning incidents had declined by 53.3% in Haryana and around 32% in Uttar Pradesh compared with the corresponding period last year. Punjab had also recorded a fall.However, the rise in Madhya Pradesh and Rajasthan prompted concern.
Madhya Pradesh's farm-fire count increased from 55 to 277, a jump of 452%, while Rajasthan's tally rose from 20 to 60, an increase of 200%.Chouhan directed the two states to identify affected districts and villages and immediately prepare special action plans. He also cautioned states reporting fewer incidents against becoming complacent, as a substantial portion of the harvest was still pending.The latest figures reflect the uneven spread of farm fires across northern and central India.Madhya Pradesh recorded 277 incidents by October 11, followed by Uttar Pradesh with 121 and Punjab with 118. Rajasthan reported 45 cases, Haryana seven, Uttarakhand three and Delhi one, taking the total across the seven states to 572.Stubble burning had been detected in 87 districts by October 11, with Amritsar recording 60 incidents, the highest among the seven states covered.
Farmers need affordable alternatives, says Centre
Chouhan said farmers had only 20-25 days between paddy harvesting and wheat sowing, making burning a quick and inexpensive way to clear fields despite its impact on soil nutrients, soil organisms and air quality in Delhi-NCR.“Simply telling farmers not to burn stubble is insufficient; we must provide them with easy, accessible and affordable alternatives,” he said.He said crop residue could be incorporated into the soil to serve as organic manure or removed for use in bio-CNG, bio-ethanol, electricity generation and fodder production.The government also aims to develop a system in which farmers can benefit from environmentally friendly practices, including through carbon credits.Chouhan urged states to promote short-duration crop varieties, including Pusa 2090 and PR126, instead of longer-duration varieties such as Pusa-44, to give farmers sufficient time to clear fields before the next sowing season.
Centre flags idle crop residue machines
The Centre has supplied more than 3.54 lakh crop residue management machines to states, including 26,109 during the current financial year. However, a central survey found that around 40% of older machines in Punjab and 48% in Haryana were idle or non-functional, news agency PTI reported.Chouhan directed states to repair existing machines alongside distributing new ones. He also called for the activation of Custom Hiring Centres to ensure that small and marginal farmers could access machinery at affordable rates.Between 2018-19 and 2025-26, the Centre released Rs 4,266.47 crore to states under the Crop Residue Management scheme. Punjab received Rs 2,056.50 crore, Haryana Rs 1,171.71 crore, Uttar Pradesh Rs 868.67 crore and Madhya Pradesh Rs 59 crore.For 2026-27, Rs 592.57 crore has been allocated, of which Rs 430.87 crore has been released.Chouhan expressed concern over slow utilisation of funds and urged Punjab to submit utilisation certificates for earlier releases so that the next instalment could be cleared without delay.
Monitoring to intensify after 3 pm
Yadav called for stronger enforcement and ground-level monitoring, identifying key districts in Punjab and Haryana for closer scrutiny.In Punjab, these include Sangrur, Tarn Taran, Amritsar, Patiala and Gurdaspur. In Haryana, the focus districts are Kaithal, Karnal, Kurukshetra, Ambala and Fatehabad.He stressed the need to integrate stubble-burning data with the Commission for Air Quality Management and the Central Pollution Control Board, while tracking harvesting schedules and weather conditions that affect air quality in the National Capital Region.
Yadav said monitoring should not rely on satellite data alone. District collectors should conduct ground assessments, while enforcement measures should include patrolling and flying squads, particularly after 3 pm, when satellites do not pass over the region.Chouhan also called for direct supply chains connecting farmers with thermal power plants that use stubble pellets for co-firing, compressed bio-gas plants and second-generation bio-ethanol facilities. He urged states to implement approved supply projects without delay and asked drought-hit regions to store crop residue safely for use as livestock fodder.The ministers said state governments would remain responsible for implementation, with the Centre providing technical, administrative and financial support.

Hezbollah announces aid for displaced in Lebanon, despite pressures
Hezbollah announced on Tuesday an aid programme for Lebanese who lost their homes in the war with Israel, with benefits capped at $14,000 per household, despite US and Lebanese sanctions on the militant group.
The announcement also comes despite US sanctions on Iran, which backs Hezbollah with weapons and resources, and tighter controls by the Lebanese authorities on Hezbollah's funding and supply routes, after the group emerged significantly weakened from two wars with Israel since October 2023.
At a press conference in Beirut's southern suburbs, the head of Hezbollah's Executive Council, Ali Daamouch, announced assistance of up to $14,000 per household for residents of Beirut and its southern suburbs, and $12,000 for other regions.
The assistance will go to displaced people whose homes have been destroyed or made uninhabitable, and to residents of areas in the south occupied by Israel, on the condition that beneficiaries do not have a second home, Daamouch said.
“The aim of the project is to support those directly affected who have been displaced from homes that have been destroyed or damaged and who do not have alternative accommodation,” he said.
Hezbollah will pay the assistance in four instalments over the course of a year, he added, without specifying the source of the funds or the number of beneficiaries the Shia movement can cover.
The aid announcement was the first from Hezbollah since it drew Lebanon deeper into war with Israel on 2 March in support of Iran, which the US and Israel began attacking on 28 February. Israel had already been striking southern Lebanon before that.
In December 2024, after an earlier war with Israel in support of Gaza, Hezbollah announced similar assistance worth $77 million to the displaced, describing it as a "a gift from the Iranian people and Hezbollah".
During the press conference, Daamoush said that "reconstruction and providing shelter for displaced people are the responsibility of the state," adding that the issue "must be kept out of political calculations". Hezbollah's critics say the state must not bear the burden for a war it did not choose.
Israeli attacks since 2023 have destroyed or damaged more than 290,000 homes, according to provisional figures from Lebanese authorities, particularly in the south of the country and in Beirut's southern suburbs, strongholds of Hezbollah.
The total cost of the two wars could exceed $27 billion, Prime Minister Nawaf Salam said in September, citing World Bank estimates.
He said the state, already reeling under a crushing financial crisis for the past seven years, does not have the means to rebuild southern regions destroyed by the war.
Despite a US-backed framework agreement signed between Lebanon and Israel in late June, Israeli strikes and demolitions have continued in southern Lebanon.

2026-10-13

Mücahithan Avcıoğlu
13 October 2026•Update: 13 October 2026
Turkish business leaders called for a renewed approach to Türkiye's EU accession process in an open letter to Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni, saying closer integration would strengthen Europe's economic and strategic position.
The letter, published in Italian daily Corriere della Sera, said it is time to reconsider the approach holding back Türkiye's membership process and provide the country with a clear accession perspective.
Signatories included Foreign Economic Relations Board (DEIK) President Nail Olpak, Türkiye-Europe Business Councils Chair Mehmet Ali Yalcindag, and Türkiye-Italy Business Council Chairwoman Lale Cander.
"Europe will be stronger on the global stage if it fully harnesses the economic, technological, and strategic potential that Türkiye brings to a shared European future," the letter said.
The chairs of 26 business councils between Türkiye and EU member states said Europe had entered an era in which economic competitiveness, technological strength, and security are inseparable.
Geopolitical instability, rapid developments in artificial intelligence and advanced technologies, the energy transition, and the changing global economic order are reshaping Europe's interests, vulnerabilities, and ability to act, they said.
The letter reaffirmed the Turkish business community's commitment to European values and its determination to contribute to Europe's economic strength and global competitiveness.
Turkish companies and entrepreneurs have been integral parts of European value chains, industrial ecosystems, and innovation networks for decades, it noted.
The signatories said growing social concerns, demographic changes, and persistent geopolitical instability are shaping Europe's security environment, making deeper integration with Türkiye an important element of the EU's response.
While acknowledging challenges that both sides must address, they said global turbulence had made breaking the stagnation in Türkiye's accession process increasingly urgent.
"It is time to reassess the current approach that is hampering Türkiye's accession process," the letter said.
Providing Türkiye with a clear and unequivocal EU membership perspective would reaffirm the deeply interconnected futures of Türkiye and the bloc, helping restore strategic clarity and mutual trust, it added.
The business leaders called for a stronger roadmap, saying the dynamism of Turkish society and the EU's transformative power could help address existing challenges and move the accession process forward.
The letter also highlighted the potential for Türkiye's full integration into the EU's emerging economic security and defense architecture.
A modernized EU-Türkiye Customs Union would help strengthen Europe's competitiveness in a geopolitically fragmented world, it said.

US insists "no change" to arms supplies to Ukraine via PURL
The US says it is continuing to supply weapons to Ukraine through the Prioritised Ukraine Requirements List (PURL).
Source: US Ambassador to NATO Matthew Whitaker in comments to AFP, as reported by European Pravda
Details: Whitaker said he did not want to comment directly on "unconfirmed reports" that the Trump administration has threatened to halt arms supplies if Kyiv continues its strikes on Russian energy infrastructure.
Quote: "I don't think that's consistent with what I know today, which is that the United States continues to sell our equipment and munitions to our European and Canadian allies that then provide it to Ukraine. I know of no change to that programme."
Details: Whitaker acknowledged, however, that equipment deliveries under the PURL programme are currently being delayed, particularly when it comes to air defence systems.
"Air defence largely is in high demand, and the availability is probably not as good as we would like," he explained.
He noted that companies are developing new approaches to intercepting incoming projectiles and expressed confidence that the problem can be resolved.
"I think it's a short-term challenge," the ambassador added.
He also warned that timing is critical as Ukraine approaches winter.
"Ukraine is facing a winter where, if there is not an energy ceasefire ... their electricity and heating infrastructure could be under a lot of pressure," he said.
Whitaker reported that Washington is working with allies that possess air defence systems to get them to Ukraine as quickly as possible.
"We'll continue to every day work on it, try to find available inventory, and then increase production on both sides of the Atlantic," he added.
Background:
- The Financial Times previously reported that the Trump administration is threatening to halt arms supplies through the PURL mechanism if Ukraine does not stop striking Russian oil refineries. Under the PURL programme, Ukraine receives US-made equipment purchased by NATO allies.
- NATO subsequently stated that deliveries of US weapons to Ukraine are continuing.

According to him, since the suspect’s actions bear all the hallmarks of espionage, a criminal case has been opened against him under Article 276 of the Criminal Code of the Russian Federation (espionage), followed by his detention.

Yemen has been engulfed in conflict since the Houthis seized the national capital, Sanaa, and several provinces in September 2014, prompting a Saudi-led coalition to intervene in March 2015 in support of the internationally recognized Yemeni government.

New 2,000-hryvnia banknote: how many of these notes are already in circulation and why there are so few of them
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
18:55:14 EEST
00:55:14 KST

New 2,000-hryvnia banknote: how many of these notes are already in circulation and why there are so few of them
Kyiv • UNN
The NBU has put around 400,000 2,000-hryvnia banknotes featuring Vasyl Stus into circulation. They account for only 0.01%.
In Ukraine, approximately 400,000 banknotes with a denomination of 2,000 hryvnias featuring Ukrainian poet and dissident Vasyl Stus were put into cash circulation on September 4, 2026. UNN reports this, citing the data of the National Bank of Ukraine.
Details
The new banknote is currently the rarest among all banknotes of the national currency. It accounts for just 0.01% of the total number of banknotes in circulation.
According to the NBU, as of October 1, 2026, the total amount of cash in circulation in Ukraine stood at 973 billion hryvnias. This is 46.7 billion hryvnias, or 5%, more than at the beginning of the year, when the corresponding figure was 926.3 billion hryvnias. In total, 2.6 billion banknotes worth 962.5 billion hryvnias are in cash circulation, along with 15.4 billion coins worth 10.4 billion hryvnias.
Banknotes with a denomination of 500 hryvnias remain the most widespread, accounting for 25.3% of the total number of banknotes. Banknotes with a denomination of 1,000 hryvnias rank second, with a share of 20.5%.
At the same time, the new 2,000-hryvnia banknotes account for the smallest share, just 0.01%. According to the regulator, since the new denomination was introduced, approximately 0.4 million such banknotes have entered circulation, with their total value estimated by the NBU at 0.7 billion hryvnias.
Why a 2,000-hryvnia banknote appeared in Ukraine
The National Bank introduced the new denomination on September 4, 2026. It is the highest-denomination banknote in the history of independent Ukraine. The national financial regulator explained the need for the new denomination by the growth of wages, consumer prices, and the overall amount of cash. The previous highest denomination, 1,000 hryvnias, was introduced back in 2019. At the same time, the NBU emphasized that introducing a 2,000-hryvnia banknote would not, in itself, increase the money supply or create additional inflationary pressure. The new banknotes enter circulation in exchange for noncash funds or banknotes of other denominations.
The introduction date was chosen symbolically. On September 4, 1965, Stus, together with Viacheslav Chornovil and Ivan Dziuba, spoke out against political repression of the Ukrainian intelligentsia during the premiere of the film "Shadows of Forgotten Ancestors" in Kyiv. September 4, 1985, was also the date when the poet died in a Soviet labor camp.
What the 2,000-hryvnia banknote looks like
Vasyl Stus is depicted on the front of the banknote, while the reverse features the building of the Faculty of Philology at Donetsk National University, where the poet studied. The banknote is made predominantly in blue colors and contains more than 20 security features.
Why the amount of cash is increasing in Ukraine
According to the National Bank, the amount of cash in circulation decreased during the first quarter of 2026, but demand for it picked up again in the second and third quarters. Among the main reasons, the regulator cites seasonal factors, as well as intensified Russian attacks on critical infrastructure facilities, including energy, logistics, and telecommunications infrastructure.
Despite the increase in the amount of cash, its growth rate has slowed. While cash increased by 8.2% over the first nine months of 2025, the increase fell to 5% over the same period in 2026. According to NBU calculations, as of the beginning of October, there were an average of 64 banknotes and 199 coins per resident of Ukraine. Against this backdrop, the 2,000-hryvnia banknote remains relatively uncommon for now.

Rubio’s understanding of thymos is very deficient: Francis Fukuyama
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
15:53:22 UTC
00:53:22 KST

Rubio’s understanding of thymos is very deficient: Francis Fukuyama
‘Rubio celebrates the agreement over Greenland, without mentioning his desire to grab it away from Denmark’
TEHRAN – The political scientist Francis Fukuyama says U.S. Secretary of State understanding of of thymos -- pride, spiritedness, the desire for recognition -- is very deficient.
Speaking at Athens on October 7, Rubio talked about thymos as the core value of Western civilization. But, Fukuyama says, Rubio has a very attenuated understanding of thymos, and does not understand how it is a double-edged sword.
Writing in the Persuasion website on October 12, Fukuyama says Rubio’s boss Donald Trump “is a perfect example of unconstrained megalothymia,” which by contrast means “Janus-faced.”
Fukuyama, the senior Fellow at Stanford University, says Bubio’s boss “wants his face to be carved into Mount Rushmore as one of the greatest of American presidents, but also seeks pettier acclaim like the Nobel Peace Prize or his name on the Kennedy Center."
The author of The Realm of the Last Man adds, “He (Trump) recently showed Maggie Haberman a list of history’s most powerful rulers, whom he clearly admired and wished to equal. The list included Genghis Khan, Attila the Hun, Napoleon, Mao, and Stalin, and not a single democratic statesman.”
Fukuyama’s article titled “Thymos and American Foreign Policy” is as follows:
Secretary of State Marco Rubio gave a speech at the Pnyx in Athens on October 7, a place just below the Parthenon that I spoke at a few years ago. It sounds as if one of his speechwriters has been reading my books, because at the heart of his address he talks about thymos (he transliterates it as thumos) as the core value of Western civilization. This is correct in some fashion, but Rubio’s understanding of the idea is very deficient.
The Secretary of States says the following:
For the Greeks of antiquity, the pursuit of excellence was the very principle of man’s existence. They organized all of civic life around contest, ambition, competition: in philosophy and poetry, in sculpture and drama, in athletics and art, in war and statecraft. The classical Greek city was an arena for great men to test and prove themselves, to hone their potential through perpetual struggle—to be the best, the strongest, the most beautiful, straining to inch ever closer to perfection.
Now I know that to modern ears, what I just described, this way of life, may sound odd; it may even sound cruel. The ideal of many ideologies in our time has, frankly, become a world of perfect safety, devoid of risk or failure, with neither the glory of victory nor the shame of defeat …
The ancient Greek city-states were filled … with intense passion and rivalry and faction and conflict. But from that constant struggle for distinction—from that came the great flowering of art and philosophy and political and intellectual energy that would transform a collective of Mediterranean cities into the birthplace of the greatest civilization in the world.
The thumos, as the ancient Greeks called it—the fire of passion, strength, courage, pride—is the heart of great civilization. And without it? Without it, nations lose their will to fight, the will to strive, the will to survive.
I spoke of thymos at some length back in 1992 in The End of History and the Last Man, and have returned to it in In the Realm of the Last Man, my new memoir. Thymos—pride, spiritedness, the desire for recognition—is indeed important for Western civilization. But Rubio has a very attenuated understanding of it, and does not understand how it is a double-edged sword.
Thymos is at the core not just of Western civilization, but, as Hegel and his interpreter Alexandre Kojève noted, of politics as a whole. The first bloody battle between early human beings was driven by the desire for dominance and recognition, by the willingness to risk one’s life. This struggle for dominance leads to a society of masters and slaves, in which neither party is fully satisfied—the slave for obvious reasons, but the master as well because he is recognized by someone who is only a slave. The solution to this problem unfolds over historical time, with the emergence of a society based on mutual and equal recognition of all human beings. Such a society was articulated for the first time in the Declaration of the Rights of Man and Citizen in the French Revolution, as well as the U.S. Constitution’s Bill of Rights. Both rest on a fundamental Christian idea, the universal equality of all human beings under God. Liberal societies recognize equality of dignity by granting and protecting basic human rights.
In The End of History and the Last Man, I created two neologisms, isothymia and megalothymia. Isothymia is the desire for equal recognition, which is fundamentally at the base of any modern democracy. Human beings universally feel resentful and angry when they are disrespected, when their fundamental dignity is held to be lower than that of another group or individual. Today’s polarized politics is driven by isothymia: left-wing identity politics by the demand of marginalized groups for equal recognition, and an emerging right-wing version based on a narrative of white or Christian victimization.
Megalothymia, by contrast, is Janus-faced. It can be the source either of human progress, or of the greatest crimes and tyrannies human societies have had to endure. Secretary Rubio is correct that the striving to be better than other people is the source of all human excellences, in the arts, in sports, in the economy, or in politics. But the will to be better than other people can lead to domination, tyranny, and unspeakable crimes. George Washington, Abraham Lincoln, and Winston Churchill were clearly driven by megalothymia—but so were Hitler, Stalin, and Pol Pot.
Thymos thus presents a conundrum for democracies. The equal rights protected by a liberal state rest on isothymia, the demand for the equal recognition of human dignity. But a successful society also needs megalothymia for all the reasons Rubio outlines: it needs risk-takers, innovators, and brave citizens willing to fight on behalf of their fellows. The problem is, first, distinguishing between the good and bad forms of megalothymia, and second, channeling this passion into activities that benefit the broader society.
I wrote about Donald Trump back in 1992 in The End of History and the Last Man. I was looking for positive outlets for megalothymia, and argued that a capitalist economy would bleed off the desire for dominance and channel it into business. Little did I realize that, some decades later, Donald Trump would not be content with being rich, but would want political power as well.
Trump is a perfect example of unconstrained megalothymia. He cannot distinguish between good and bad attributes that deserve recognition, nor does he care about the quality of judgment of those recognizing him. He wants his face to be carved into Mount Rushmore as one of the greatest of American presidents, but also seeks pettier acclaim like the Nobel Peace Prize or his name on the Kennedy Center. He recently showed Maggie Haberman a list of history’s most powerful rulers, whom he clearly admired and wished to equal. The list included Genghis Khan, Attila the Hun, Napoleon, Mao, and Stalin, and not a single democratic statesman.
Secretary Rubio’s desire to stay on his boss’ good side leads him to twist reality like a pretzel. He speaks about an alliance between the United States and Europe based on shared values, gliding over a president who clearly admires autocrats far more than those of other democratic countries. He talks about the wonders of science and technology created by Western civilization, even as his administration is cutting funding for scientific research across the board. He celebrates the agreement over Greenland, without mentioning his desire to grab it away from Denmark.
Secretary Rubio praises thymos without regard to the ends to which it is directed. He would do well to remember that it was an excess of megalothymia that led Alcibiades and the Athenians into the disastrous Sicilian Expedition, which Thucydides explains was the beginning of their defeat in the Peloponnesian War. The Secretary should also focus a bit on the lines from the Declaration of Independence: “We hold these truths to be self-evident, that all Men are created equal.” It is this principle of human equality, and not the celebration of great individuals, that has underlined a lot of American foreign policy over the decades.
It is to this principle that the Founding Fathers, as well as many subsequent generations of Americans, vowed to sacrifice their lives, their fortunes, and their sacred honor.

Russian state TV showed a man lying on a floor and handcuffed by three masked men in black uniform. A voice behind the scene tells him he is suspected of spying.

‘Act five’: National Assembly opens budget debate amid ongoing student protests in France
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
15:48:55 UTC
00:48:55 KST

The French government's budget proposal includes a €1.2 billion increase in funding for the National Education Ministry, as France grapples with one of the highest public deficits in the eurozone.
Another major day of demonstrations took place across France on Tuesday, with students and trade unions taking to the streets to protest education conditions and funding as the National Assembly began its debate on the government's budget proposals for 2027.
Teaching unions told Euronews that they were dissatisfied with the government's response to concerns over long school days, overcrowded classrooms, run down facilities, and teacher absences.
"It is clear that the responses that have been provided are inadequate and do not meet the needs set out," Elisabeth Allain-Moreno, secretary-general of SE UNSA, a teachers' union, said.
France's Education Minister Édouard Geffray announced on 8 October that 3,000 available supply teachers would be deployed across more than 500 priority schools by Tuesday in a bid to solve teacher absences.
On Tuesday, he announced that just 35% of the target had been achieved.
"We have a generation that is articulating demands that we identified years ago, which we have been advocating for and were never heard," Morgane Verviers, secretary-general of UNSA Education, told Euronews.
"It's clear that the responses provided are inadequate and don't meet the needs set out," Moreno added.
Budget proposal under fire
The government's budget proposal includes a €1.2 billion increase in funding for the National Education Ministry, as France grapples with one of the highest public deficits in the eurozone.
However, critics say this measure is insufficient, arguing that a 1.6% increase in funding falls short of inflation, which is forecast at 1.8%.
Sabrine Kharbach, a spokesperson for l'Union Etudiante, France's biggest student union, said she felt the government had underestimated students' ability to understand budget matters.
"They believe that students and young people are not aware of the economy and don't understand what's happening. But we truly understand, when we see that there's an additional $400 billion being allocated to the military," Kharbach told Euronews. France's government has allocated a total budget of €413.3 billion to its armed forces for 2024 to 2030 under its Military Programming Law (LPM).
"We have to ask ourselves if they want to invest in death or in the future," she added.
One secondary school student said she felt her generation was not being taken seriously, despite being the "future of France."
"We can't turn a blind eye to issues, especially in secondary schools in the suburbs, which really lack funding," she said.
Swedish activist Greta Thunberg also joined Tuesday's protests, telling the AFP news agency that "young people are not being included in the conversation."
"Our future is being robbed away from us," she added.
Thunberg's visit to France comes after French students' grievance struck a chord with young people across Europe, leading students in Belgium and Italy to stage their own demonstrations over the past week.
Jean-Luc Mélenchon, the leader of the hard-left France Unbowed party, was also among those who joined the protests.
Taking to X on 8 October, he declared that the Bastille had been "retaken" after a mass protest on Paris' Place de la Bastille captured audiences worldwide.
Police violence sparks outrage
France's protests and school blockades began in Paris’s suburbs in mid-September, before rapidly spreading nationwide.
While many demonstrations have been peaceful, others have been marred by sideline riots and clashes with police.
Rights groups have accused officers of exercising disproportionate force whilst dealing with protesters following a wave of injuries to students.
According to figures shared by France's Ministry of Justice on Friday, there have been 6,877 arrests since the beginning of the movement, mostly involving minors.
More than 215 students and nearly 800 police officers have also been injured.

IsDB chief in Jakarta: A US$2.56 billion plan with a missing climate pillar
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
15:47:15 UTC
00:47:15 KST

Dr Muhammad Al Jasser, chairman of the Islamic Development Bank (IsDB) Group, spent four days in Jakarta, from 7 to 10 October 2026. The IsDB is a development bank owned by 57 mostly Muslim countries. It pays for roads, hospitals and farms using Islamic finance rules, which avoid interest.
He left behind a five-year plan worth billions of dollars. It is a useful plan with one large hole. In a country that is among the most exposed to climate change, the plan has no climate pillar.
On 8 October, Finance Minister Suahasil Nazara launched the partnership strategy for 2026 to 2030, the fourth of its kind. The bank attached an “indicative” figure of about US$2.56 billion. Indicative means a target, not a cheque. Money flows only when each project is approved and signed.
The plan has two pillars. Al Jasser outlined the first as infrastructure: transport, food and farming, fisheries, and energy security and transition. The second is people: health, schools and job skills. Climate appears only in that one phrase, “energy transition”. There is no climate goal, no share of the money set aside for it, and no plan for adapting to floods, rising seas and drought.
This gap matters because Indonesia’s risks are real. The country still depends heavily on coal for electricity. Jakarta and many coastal cities face rising seas, and farmers face longer dry seasons. Every port, road and rice field the plan pays for will have to survive that climate.
The gap is also hard to explain from the bank’s side. Research group E3G found that climate projects made up 46 per cent of IsDB operations in 2023, beating the bank’s own target. Yet from 2019 to 2022 it lent far more for fossil fuels than for clean energy. Indonesia’s plan follows the old habit, not the new target.
Each pillar can still turn green. Roads and ports can be built to resist floods. Food projects can favour crops that survive drought, without clearing forests for new farmland. Fisheries support can protect mangroves, which shelter coasts and store carbon. A bridge washed away in its tenth year is a loan repaid for nothing.
READ: Indonesian, Egyptian presidents condemn Israeli settlement expansion in Jakarta talks
The people pillar fits too. Heat and floods spread diseases such as dengue, so stronger clinics are a form of climate protection. Vocational schools can train workers for solar power, electric transport and energy-saving buildings.
Scale makes this choice urgent. Over five decades the IsDB Group has approved about US$7.2 billion for some 350 projects in Indonesia. The new plan equals more than a third of that history in five years. Still, about half a billion dollars a year is small for a country of more than 280 million people, so every dollar should serve two goals: growth and climate safety.
Islamic finance offers the tool. The bank offered project loans, trade finance, support for private companies and insurance. Indonesia pioneered green sukuk, Islamic bonds for climate projects. Pairing the bank’s money with green sukuk would bring in Gulf investors who want clean, faith-based assets.
Delivery is the next test. Six IsDB projects worth about US$1.8 billion are already running in Indonesia. Al Jasser added that the US$2.56 billion could grow if projects move well. That opens a door: if Indonesian ministries prepare strong green projects, the bank has room to fund more. The risk is familiar: slow land clearing, weak studies and shifting priorities have delayed foreign-funded projects before, and green projects need even better preparation.
Indonesia also has the power to ask. Al Jasser called it one of the bank’s most important partners, a founding member and its fifth-largest shareholder. In 2024, then Finance Minister Sri Mulyani Indrawati pressed the bank to hire more Indonesians in senior posts. The bank is now preparing a new climate action plan for the same five years. Jakarta should use its votes to shape it.
National goals point the same way. Al Jasser also met Coordinating Minister for Economic Affairs Airlangga Hartarto to discuss connectivity, health, education, food security and energy. President Prabowo Subianto wants food self-sufficiency. In a hotter climate, food security and climate safety are the same goal.
Indonesia can also give, not only borrow. Deputy Planning Minister Febrian Ruddyard argued that Indonesia can share its solutions with other developing countries. Its experience with disasters, mangroves and green sukuk is valuable to IsDB members facing the same storms and heat.
The test is simple. By 2030, what share of the US$2.56 billion went to clean energy and climate protection? Were the new ports, roads and farms built to survive floods and drought? Did Jakarta help write the bank’s climate plan, and do more Indonesians sit in the bank’s top jobs? Those answers will show whether this plan filled its missing pillar.
