Eastern Mediterranean hardest hit by attacks on healthcare, funding cuts: WHO chief
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
15:46:59 UTC
00:46:59 KST

Beyza Binnur Dönmez
13 October 2026•Update: 13 October 2026
The Eastern Mediterranean faces mounting threats to healthcare from widespread attacks and severe funding cuts affecting nearly 2,000 facilities, the World Health Organization (WHO) chief warned on Tuesday.
Addressing the 73rd session of the WHO Regional Committee for the Eastern Mediterranean in Cairo, Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus said: "This region has recorded more attacks on health facilities, health workers, and patients than any other."
He stressed that hospitals, ambulances and health workers are protected under international humanitarian law and "must never be a target."
He praised WHO teams operating in Gaza, Sudan, Yemen, Lebanon and Afghanistan, often at considerable personal risk.
"The best medicine is peace," he said, urging an end to regional conflicts.
Tedros also warned that sudden and severe funding cuts have affected nearly 2,000 health facilities across the region, and called for greater domestic investment in healthcare to reduce dependence on international aid.
Despite financial pressures, Tedros said the WHO secured 95% of the resources needed for its current two-year budget period, "with some pockets of poverty."
He said the organization reached a point of stability after reducing its budget and workforce, including cutting the number of assistant directors-general by half and directors by almost half.
Tedros added that the WHO's reserves were now double their level when he took office, while its budget 23% larger.
The two increases in member states' assessed contributions helped cushion the impact of funding cuts and the US withdrawal, he said, urging governments to approve another increase in May 2027 to strengthen WHO's long-term financial stability.
Tedros also highlighted ongoing efforts to reform the global health architecture, saying a task force had been established following a mandate from member states at the World Health Assembly in May.
The task force is expected to report later this year, he said, stressing that the Eastern Mediterranean region, which accounts for a significant share of global humanitarian needs, must have a "strong voice" in shaping the reforms.

DR Congo: Kabila’s move towards M23 raises questions over peace
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
15:46:00 UTC
00:46:00 KST

What Kabila's new armed coalition means for the DRC conflict
October 13, 2026
Joseph Kabila's decision to lead a new political-military movement, the Front for the Refoundation of the Nation (FRN), puts the former president of the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) in more direct confrontation with President Felix Tshisekedi's government. Kabila announced the FRN on October 12 in Goma, eastern DRC, at his residence, where leaders of the AFC/M23 rebel movements joined him.
FRN coalition adviser, Claude Ibalanky, said the group would unite opposition forces, including figures associated with the AFC/M23 movement. The new structure succeeds the Congo River Alliance (AFC), which had been allied with the M23 rebellion. Its leadership includes former AFC leader Corneille Nangaa and M23 political leader Bertrand Bisimwa. Sultani Makenga, a senior M23 military commander, was also assigned a senior role in the new organization.
The announcement comes as diplomatic initiatives seek to end fighting between Congolese government forces and the rebellion.
Congolese authorities have accused Kabila of supporting the insurgency, allegations he has denied. On September 30, 2025, a military court sentenced him to death in absentia after convicting him of treason, war crimes and other offenses linked to the conflict in eastern DRC. Kabila has rejected the case as politically motivated.
Adolph Amisi Makutano, an official of the ruling Union for Democracy and Social Progress (UDPS), criticized the former president for taking a more public role.
"It was a lack of courage that made this gentleman drag his feet. They held several meetings and today he is being pushed to step out into the open. But it is a disgrace for the DRC," Makutano said.
Why is eastern Congo at war?
Eastern DRC has experienced decades of conflict involving armed groups, competition over territory andmineral resources, and tensions with neighboring countries.
The aftermath of Rwanda's 1994 genocide against the Tutsicontributed to successive regional conflicts, as armed groups and refugees crossed borders and neighboring states became involved in Congo's civil wars.
M23 takes its name from a March 23, 2009, peace agreement. The movement says the Congolese government failed to honor commitments to integrate its fighters and protect minority Congolese Tutsis.
Kinshasa, the United Nations (UN) and Western governments haveaccused Rwanda of supporting M23 and exercising influence over its operations. Rwanda denies backing the rebellion and cites security threats posed by armed groups operating in Congo. In 2025, M23 captured Goma and Bukavu, two major cities in eastern Congo. Its territorial gains weakened government control across parts of the region, displaced civilians and intensified an already severe humanitarian crisis.
Kabila's leadership of the new front raises questions about whether he intends to consolidate opposition to Tshisekedi, strengthen the rebellion's political leadership, or pursue both.
Political implications of Kabila's move
Alex Vines, Africa program director at the European Council on Foreign Relations, sees the move as evidence that Kabila remains politically ambitious. "It shows Kabila's political ambition is alive and kicking and he is prepared to challenge Tshisekedi," Vines told DW.
Timo Roujean, head of the Konrad Adenauer Foundation's office in Kinshasa, cautioned against assessing Kabila's potential support based on ethnic identity alone. He told DW that economic performance and political dynamics in Kabila's home region of Katanga are also relevant.
The new front could give the movement more explicitly political leadership, but it remains unclear whether the reorganization will broaden its domestic support or alter its negotiating position. Conflict analyst Cliffton Chifuwe told DW the alliance does not rule out a negotiated settlement, but could make a durable agreement harder to achieve.
"The Kabila alliance with M23 does not make peace impossible. However, it raises the threshold for achieving that settlement and its ability to hold," Chifuwe told DW.
For Chifuwe, lasting peace requires more than a cessation of hostilities. It also depends on credible security arrangements, the restoration of state authority, humanitarian access, and conditions that allow displaced people to return safely. The new FRN coalition also raises questions for mediators about whether existing peace frameworks can accommodate the political realignment and whether the parties involved can ensure compliance with any agreement.
As this new development plays out, the central issue for civilians in eastern Congo remains whether the leadership change will open a path to settlement or make an already complex conflict harder to resolve.
Wendy Bashi, Saleh Mwanamilongo and Jean Noel Ba Mweze contributed to this article
Edited by: Chrispin Mwakideu

garden divides perkins&will’s são paulo office tower into two stacked volumes

garden divides perkins&will’s são paulo office tower into two stacked volumes
jeronimo faria lima combines a screen-printed glass facade, two stacked volumes, and an elevated garden, using patterned glazing and planted terraces to shape the tower’s appearance and connect it with the surrounding urban fabric.
[FEATURED]
sunken plaza likns corporate tower with São Paulo’s public realm
Jeronimo Faria Lima by Perkins&Will rethinks the corporate tower through its relationship with São Paulo’s public realm. Located at the intersection of Brigadeiro Faria Lima Avenue and Jeronimo da Veiga Street, the project uses a sunken plaza, pedestrian bridge, and elevated garden to connect the building with the surrounding streets.
The first basement level contains a sunken plaza with cafés, social areas, and collaborative spaces, extending public activity into the building. From here, a pedestrian bridge leads to the main lobby, creating a gradual transition between the street and the tower. Transparent enclosures, continuous finishes, and aligned sightlines maintain visual connections between interior and exterior spaces.
Layered volumes and planted terraces shape Jeronimo Faria Lima
The tower is divided into two stacked volumes, separated by a garden level that breaks up the building’s vertical mass and introduces vegetation into the dense urban setting. Planting continues from the entrance to the terraces, linking different levels and creating areas for pause.
On the facade, screen-printed patterns form a graphic layer across the glass, reinforcing the tower’s vertical lines while changing in appearance with shifting daylight. The detailing also required precise craftsmanship, including hand-cutting and assembly at the junctions between ceiling planes along the building’s edges to preserve the geometry of the volumes.
Through its sequence of public spaces, planted terraces, and carefully detailed facade, Jeronimo Faria Lima by Studio Perkins&Will integrates circulation, social areas, and landscape into the design of a corporate building.

Palestinian mufti bans buying olives stolen by Jewish settlers

Breadcrumb
Palestinian mufti bans buying olives stolen by Jewish settlers
Palestine's grand mufti has issued a religious ruling prohibiting Palestinians from buying olive oil or olives stolen from Palestinian farmers and sold by Israeli settlers.
Sheikh Mohammed Ahmad Hussein, the Grand Mufti of Jerusalem and the Palestinian Territories, said purchasing stolen produce was forbidden because those selling it did not legally own it.
He said buying the goods would also encourage the seizure of Palestinian land, the theft of its resources and the displacement of its residents.
The ruling follows reports that Israeli settlers established an olive press inside an outpost built on land belonging to al-Lubban al-Gharbi, north-west of Ramallah.
The facility could allow settlers to process olives taken from Palestinian-owned land in the occupied West Bank and sell the resulting oil.
According to the report, settlers have promoted the press as capable of processing both small and large harvests and have encouraged the sale of the oil at prices competing with those in Palestinian markets.
The mufti said Palestinian institutions and the public should reject the trade in produce obtained through theft or the seizure of land.
The ruling comes during an olive harvest season marked by growing settler attacks on Palestinian farmers and agricultural land across the West Bank.
Recent incidents have included the theft of harvested olives and equipment, the destruction of trees and attempts to prevent farmers from reaching their land.
The attacks have intensified during a season in which settlers have also organised campaigns to prevent Palestinians from reaching their olive groves.
The olive harvest is an important source of income for thousands of Palestinian families and has increasingly become a focus of settler violence and restrictions on Palestinian access to farmland.
Palestinian farmers have described a pattern of settler attacks, land seizures and destruction of olive groves that they say is intended to force them away from their land.

Less than half of EU citizens support Ukraine's quick accession, poll shows
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
15:41:16 UTC
00:41:16 KST

A survey published by eupinions on Oct. 13 found a significant gap between Ukrainians and EU citizens in support for Ukraine’s accelerated EU accession and their views on Kyiv’s role in defending Europe against Russian aggression.
The survey, conducted by Nira Data across all 27 EU member states and Ukrainian government-controlled territories and published by the Bertelsmann Stiftung’s eupinions project, found that 47% of EU citizens believe Ukraine should join the bloc in the coming years, compared with 83% of Ukrainian respondents.
Support for Ukraine's EU accession varied across the bloc, reaching 69% in Sweden, the highest share among the countries surveyed. Romania recorded the lowest level of support, at 40%.
Economic costs of Ukraine's accession appeared to be a key driver among respondents in most EU countries.
"Ukraine's precarious financial situation poses a challenge to the EU as a whole, as stability in our large European neighbor is a matter of shared interest. The estimated financing needs for reconstruction alone now exceed 500 billion euros ($560 billion)," said Miriam Kosmehl, the organization's expert on Eastern Europe.
Twenty-eight percent of EU respondents consider increased financial burden as the main challenge if Ukraine joins the Union.
The question of security was also raised in the report.
Over half, or 58% of Ukrainians, believe that their country is making a greater contribution to protecting the EU from possible Russian aggression. On the other hand, only 16% of EU citizens agree with the statement.
Besides Ukraine, Germany, France, and the Netherlands had the highest percentage of citizens who believe Ukraine does more to protect Europe from Russia.
However, a mere 14% of EU citizens believe that Ukraine's membership has the possibility of making the Union "stronger and more influential on the global stage."
Kosmehl noted that Ukraine's defense of its sovereignty and independence directly impacts the future of democracy and security in Europe.
“Russia seeks to exploit internal divisions to weaken EU consensus and solidarity. Open societies face particular challenges in addressing targeted influence operations,” she adds.

IMF forecasts that Gulf economies will shrink amid conflict
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
15:40:56 UTC
00:40:56 KST

Breadcrumb
IMF forecasts that Gulf economies will shrink amid ongoing US-Iran conflict
The Middle East and Central Asia is the only region in the world set to see negative economic growth in the final few months of 2026, according to the International Monetary Fund's latest forecast.
The overall drop in gross domestic product (GDP) is forecast to be 0.3% across the Middle East and Central Asia.
The countries in the region with the highest level of economic contraction are Gulf states that rely on oil exports, which have been severely affected by ongoing conflicts in the region.
Kuwait, Iraq and Qatar are forecast to have the largest economic slump, with GDP in these countries set to fall by 16.7%, 16% and 15.6% respectively.
The Strait of Hormuz has been closed by Iran in retaliation for the US and Israel lauching a war against the country. Both the US and Iran are now claiming control of the waterway, which is a key export sites for goods, particularly oil, to and from the Gulf.
This has made it difficult for Gulf states to export oil outside the region, leading to a worldwide increase in prices and a severe recession in the Gulf.
Kuwait, Iraq and Qatar have less diverse economies than their Gulf neighbours Saudi Arabia and the UAE, whose economies are forecast to drop by 3.3% and 3.9% respectively.
"Qatar and Kuwait depend wholeheartedly on the wholesale of energy," Fawaz A Gerges, Professor of International Relations at the London School of Economics, told The New Arab, "their economy is very much narrower, limited to basically energy. While Iran, Dubai and Abu Dhabi have succeeded in diversifying their economies to a certain extent."
The forecasts are based on economic figures from a few months ago, prior to Saudi Arabia's recent involvement in Yemen's war. Last month the Houthis bombed Saudi Arabia's East-West pipeline, which became a key piece of infrastructure for oil exports after the closure of the Strait of Hormuz.
This has further disrupted Saudi oil exports, which could mean that Saudi Arabia's economic contraction will be higher than the recent forecasts show.
However, after the pipeline was damaged, Saudi Arabia increased their exports via the Strait of Hormuz.
"After the pipeline was hit, the Saudis noticed that it was now kind of feasible to get oil out through the Strait of Hormuz," David Butter, economic analyst and associate fellow of Chatham House's MENA programme told The New Arab, "so strangely enough, probably production and exports have actually increased since the Houthis started to target Saudi Arabia."
Iran, which has been a centre point of the regional war since the US and Israel launched their invasion last February, is set to see slightly lower economic contraction than some other countries in the Gulf at 7.6%.
The difference in contraction between Iran and countries like Kuwait and Iraq is in part due to Iran's economic diversity. However, the war has also provided an opportunity for economic growth.
"The military economy actually feeds into the GDP," Butter said, "there will be a big step up in the production of weapons, and maybe payments to soldiers."
Though they expect the Gulf's economy to shrink in the final quarter of 2026, the IMF are predicted that the economies of various countries will recover in 2027.
"The assumption there is that a lot of things will return to normal in 2027," Butter said.
"Of course. that's not necessarily going to be the case."

How to prepare your body for winter: a dietitian explains what to change in your diet in autumn
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
18:39:14 EEST
00:39:14 KST

How to prepare your body for winter: a dietitian explains what to change in your diet in autumn
Kyiv • UNN
In winter, it is recommended to diversify your diet with protein, complex carbohydrates, fish, and seaweed. Vitamin D and supplements should be discussed with a doctor.
In autumn, it is worth reviewing one’s diet to support the body during the cold season and provide it with the necessary nutrients. A dietitian, Oleksandr Kushch, told a UNN journalist more about which foods should be added to the menu, why it is important to monitor protein intake, and how to control cravings for sweets in winter.
Details
Oleksandr Kushch explains that, along with the shortening of daylight hours and the drop in temperature, people may notice changes in their appetite and weight. Therefore, according to the doctor, when planning one’s diet, it is important to take physical activity and the amount of energy a person expends throughout the day into account. In particular, people with predominantly sedentary jobs should pay close attention to the amount of fatty food they consume.
We have an evolutionary mechanism that switches our metabolism from summer metabolism to winter metabolism. Therefore, in winter, our body spends approximately 300–400 calories per day on warming itself, because people used to live, in principle, in cold and hunger, and only over approximately the last 200 years have people more or less begun living in comfortable conditions. That is why our body switches to storing fat
That is why, according to the dietitian, cases when people notice that they begin gaining weight in winter are an absolutely normal situation,
So, if we want to maintain our weight, we naturally need to take these 300–400 calories into account. For example, if a person exercises and is often outdoors, these calories are used; however, if a person sits in an office, then, if unused, they will be deposited under the skin. In other words, the first thing to do is adjust one’s diet to the conditions of one’s own life
The dietitian advises against making fatty meat, full-fat dairy products, butter, and hard cheeses with a high fat content the basis of one’s diet. At the same time, it is not necessary to give up such products completely. What matters is taking one’s lifestyle and overall dietary balance into account. According to the doctor, in autumn and winter, particular attention should be paid to the variety of foods and providing the body with the necessary vitamins and micronutrients.
You can consume treats in small amounts, but you should not make them the basis of your diet. And to support the immune system, the diet should be enriched with vitamins and micronutrients. I believe that the only absolutely civilized way is to consume vitamins, micronutrients, and antioxidants in capsules or tablets. This is an entirely normal practice
Which foods should be added to the winter menu
Oleksandr Kushch explains that during the cold season, it is worth paying attention to offal, which contains various vitamins and micronutrients. It is also important to consume protein regularly, as it is needed not only to maintain muscles but also for the functioning of the immune system. In addition, the dietitian names complex carbohydrates, which provide the body with energy, as one of the important components of the diet.
During winter, we must support our muscular system. Let me remind you that proteins are not only about muscles; they are also part of the immune system, because proteins are used in the synthesis of immune complexes in our body and perform an important transport function in the blood. Therefore, in a balanced, varied diet, it is desirable to have between three and five sources of protein. This is also very important. Instead, in winter, carbohydrates should nevertheless be obtained from complex carbohydrates, for example, whole-grain cereals. Of course, you should not overindulge in sweets or in overtly fatty products containing saturated fats
Oleksandr Kushch also advises adding eggs, unsweetened fermented dairy products, such as Bulgarian or Greek yogurt, as well as fatty ocean fish and even seaweed to the menu. For dressing dishes, the dietitian recommends using a blend of different oils, including olive, pumpkin seed, and walnut oil. At the same time, he noted that the specific selection of foods depends on a person’s means and nutritional needs.
It is very good, of course, when your diet includes fatty varieties of ocean fish in winter. This is a very good source. Seaweed, by the way, is a very interesting product. It is a good source of iodine, zinc and selenium as well. There are no particular foods that are, so to speak, completely prohibited during the winter period, but the emphasis should be shifted appropriately
Should you take additional vitamins in winter, and how can you control your craving for sweets?
In autumn and winter, the issue of taking additional vitamins should also be considered with the body's needs in mind, the doctor says. At the same time, the expert draws particular attention to vitamin D, as well as omega-3 fatty acids. Oleksandr Kushch emphasizes that before taking supplements, it is advisable to consult a doctor in order to determine the need for them and the appropriate dosage.
There are recommendations from the Ministry of Health to take additional vitamin D, for example, from September to May — 2,000 [IU] for adults who do not have a vitamin deficiency. For children and adolescents, it is 1,000–1,500 international units. Because, for example, vitamin D3, which everyone likes to discuss so much now, is a powerful immunomodulator and protective agent. Again, I will say that all beneficial substances, vitamins, trace elements and antioxidants are essentially immunomodulators. Our immune system should be flexible. Because if a person with a virus sneezes on you, then, of course, you will get sick, both with and without immunomodulators; however, it will of course be easier to endure the illness if the person is nevertheless protected
Which foods help maintain normal potassium levels in the body26.05.26, 12:09 • 65359 views
During the cold season, the desire to eat sweets and calorie-dense foods may also intensify. According to the dietitian, sweets can be part of the diet, but they should not become the main source of energy. Instead, it is worth choosing more often foods that provide a longer-lasting feeling of satiety.
We are looking for a cheap source of quick energy. But this is the wrong approach, because we cannot constantly depend on sweets as a source of energy. We need a long-term source of energy, which we obtain primarily from complex carbohydrates
Thus, preparing for winter involves a varied diet, sufficient amounts of protein, complex carbohydrates and other nutrients. It is also important to take physical activity levels into account and not rely solely on individual foods or vitamin supplements to support the immune system.

OPINION - The words have changed, the occupation continues: The reality of the Gaza ceasefire
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
15:39:02 UTC
00:39:02 KST

Let’s make something clear from the outset: the so-called Trump Gaza plan, announced on Sept. 29, 2025, which led to the Oct. 10 ceasefire [1], created widespread hope that international diplomacy had finally prevailed to halt the violence.
Today, however, the reality on the ground tells a different story. Despite the overwhelming global support the plan received to end the violence, the evidence suggests that Israel utilized the agreement to navigate its military challenges in Gaza while preserving much of its control over the besieged territory.
The plan did not return Gaza to the days before the genocide. The intermittent Israeli violence of the past has become daily killing, while the pre-genocide siege has tightened into a suffocating blockade imposed on a population barely surviving amid the ruins of its cities and refugee camps. 
Genocide under the guise of a ceasefire
Since the ceasefire began on Oct. 10, 2025, Israeli forces have killed [2] at least 1,471 Palestinians and wounded another 5,189, according to Gaza’s Health Ministry. These figures exclude those who have died from disease, lack of adequate medical care, and other consequences of the ongoing humanitarian catastrophe. In almost any other conflict, such numbers would be described as evidence of a continuing war. Yet in Gaza, they are recorded under the reassuring language of a ceasefire. Even more heartbreaking is that the victims include at least 327 killed and 547 wounded children.
Not a single hospital [3] in Gaza is fully functional, according to a joint statement issued by more than 100 humanitarian and human rights groups. The morgues continue receiving new fatalities, alongside hundreds of bodies recovered from the rubble. An estimated 10,000 Palestinians remain buried [4] beneath destroyed buildings. What kind of ceasefire forces Gaza’s Health Ministry to maintain separate records for those killed during the genocide and those killed since the supposed cessation of hostilities? What kind of ceasefire allows bombing to resume without warning, vehicles carrying civilians to be struck, homes to collapse upon their inhabitants, and families to continue burying their children? 
Unfulfilled promises and shrinking spaces
Even the humanitarian provisions of the agreement have remained largely unfulfilled. The plan envisaged [5] aid deliveries on a scale of approximately 600 trucks daily. Yet a UN assessment found that UN-coordinated humanitarian shipments averaged [6] fewer than 100 trucks per day during the agreement’s first 172 days. Where is the heavy machinery needed to remove the rubble, recover the dead, and begin rebuilding what Israel has destroyed?
Speaking of rubble, Gaza now contains [7] approximately 61 million tons of it—around 20 times the debris generated by all wars worldwide over the preceding 18 years, according to figures cited by humanitarian organizations. Even the ruins are closing in on Palestinians. Last month, 21 people, including 12 children, were killed [8] when a damaged building collapsed in Gaza City.
Meanwhile, the space available for Palestinian life continues to shrink. Since the ceasefire began, Israeli military control has expanded [9] from approximately 53 to 63% of Gaza (some estimates put the number at 70%), according to the UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs. Despite the overwhelming international backing the plan received, its supposed guarantors have utterly failed to halt Israel’s ongoing oppression or enforce compliance with the agreement’s central provisions. Instead, much of the political discussion has focused on disarming Palestinian resistance, as though resistance itself were the original cause of colonialism, military occupation, siege, apartheid, and genocide.
While championed by the Trump administration and its allies as a definitive solution for peace, in practice, Israel used the ceasefire to regroup and achieve objectives it had previously struggled to reach. Under this arrangement, Palestinians are expected to refrain from armed actions, even as Israeli military operations, territorial expansion, and restrictions on essential supplies continue. 
The danger of a new status quo
Without meaningful resistance to Israel's policies—whether by Palestinians or through sustained international political and legal pressure—the danger is that Israel will escalate its push for the ethnic cleansing of Palestinians from Gaza. This is why Gaza must remain at the center of international attention. Public mobilization, political pressure, legal accountability, and solidarity cannot be suspended simply because an agreement has been labeled a “ceasefire.”
The international community must challenge the premise that the genocide has ended merely because the language used to describe Israel’s actions has changed. A ceasefire without enforcement, accountability, or an end to occupation cannot become a substitute for Palestinian freedom.

11 sailors missing off Bulgaria in ship attacks, as Trump tries to ‘soften’ Putin with diesel deal
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
15:37:58 UTC
00:37:58 KST

Two merchant ships were struck by drones Tuesday in the Black Sea off Bulgaria, sinking one vessel and leaving 11 sailors missing, as the NATO member suggested Russia could be responsible but stopped short of directly accusing Moscow.
The attacks came exactly one week after another cargo ship was sunk by drones off the Bulgarian coast, raising concerns about the growing threat to commercial shipping near NATO territory. They also coincided with fresh diplomatic tensions over President Donald Trump's efforts to bring Russian President Vladimir Putin back to peace negotiations, including a controversial agreement allowing Russian diesel exports.
Bulgarian officials said the two vessels were attacked roughly 30 kilometers (19 miles) from the country's coast. The ship that sank, the Guinea-Bissau-flagged HS Dignity, went down off the village of Krapets. Five crew members were rescued, while 11 remained missing.
The second vessel, the Maltese-flagged Chelsea 3, was struck by three drones overnight. All 15 crew members, seven Ukrainians and eight Azerbaijanis, were rescued, with five suffering minor injuries.
Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev convened an emergency security meeting Tuesday morning and described the attacks, which occurred close to his country's territorial waters, as "absolutely unacceptable."
Radev said Bulgaria was seeking greater assistance from NATO and the European Union to strengthen maritime and airspace surveillance. Although he did not directly accuse Russia, he suggested Moscow stood to benefit from the attacks.
"We have no clear evidence to accuse any of the parties," he said, adding that logic suggested the outcome served Russia's interests.
Bulgaria subsequently summoned Russian Ambassador Eleonora Mitrofanova, who said after meeting Radev that she had received no information from the Russian Defense Ministry about the attacks. She also suggested they could have been a provocation by a third party. Moscow did not immediately comment on the incidents. Ukraine, however, explicitly blamed Russia.
"Russia's latest attack on commercial vessels near Bulgaria's territorial waters, which injured Ukrainian and Azerbaijani citizens, once again demonstrates Moscow's deliberate disregard for civilian lives and maritime security in the Black Sea," Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said.
Sybiha urged Ukraine's international partners to increase pressure on Moscow, accusing Russia of attempting to disrupt global food supplies by targeting commercial vessels in one of the world's most important grain-export corridors.
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen also condemned the attacks, saying the Black Sea had become another front of escalation in Russia's war against Ukraine.
Tuesday's attacks followed a series of similar incidents that have heightened concerns about the security of shipping routes near Bulgaria and Romania, both NATO members.
On October 6, two cargo vessels came under drone attack off Bulgaria. The Togo-flagged Alfa Watan sustained catastrophic damage and sank, leaving its 10 crew members, nine Syrians and one Egyptian, missing. Bulgarian authorities subsequently suspended the search without establishing their fate.
The second vessel, the Palau-flagged Able, caught fire following the attack. All 18 crew members were rescued, including two who suffered serious injuries. Both vessels were operated by Turkish companies.
A day earlier, the Turkish-owned cargo ship Royad Mammadov, which was carrying grain, was struck off Romania's coast and later sank. Romanian authorities reported two deaths and 11 survivors. Ukraine accused Russia of launching the drone attack.
Russia and Ukraine are among the world's largest grain exporters, and the war has repeatedly threatened international food supplies by disrupting Black Sea shipping.
Russia has intensified its bombardment of Ukrainian Black Sea ports, forcing Kyiv to rely increasingly on Danube River facilities and shipping routes running close to the Bulgarian and Romanian coasts. Ukraine, meanwhile, has stepped up attacks on Russian vessels involved in grain exports elsewhere in the Black Sea and in the Sea of Azov, near the mouth of the Don River.
The maritime escalation has added another dimension to the economic confrontation between Moscow and Kyiv, with both countries seeking to disrupt the other's trade and sources of revenue. The latest attacks unfolded as Trump sought to revive stalled negotiations aimed at ending the war, while increasing pressure on Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky to halt drone strikes against Russian oil refineries.
Trump has blamed Ukraine's attacks on Russian energy infrastructure for contributing to rising global diesel prices, although energy experts say the war involving Iran has been the principal driver of the increases. On Sunday, Trump unexpectedly announced what he described as an energy ceasefire under which Russia and Ukraine would stop attacking each other's energy facilities.
Neither Moscow nor Kyiv confirmed that a formal agreement had been reached, and Ukraine subsequently accused Russia of continuing its attacks.
On Tuesday, Zelensky said Ukraine had refrained from striking Russian refineries and other energy facilities for the two days following Trump's announcement, but Moscow had not reciprocated.
"Ukraine has not carried out strikes on Russian oil refineries or the energy sector in general for the two days since the American president announced an energy ceasefire," Zelensky said. "However, Russia did not heed the American president," he added, accusing Moscow of attacking Ukrainian energy facilities and critical infrastructure. He said 19 Ukrainian regions had come under attack during the two-day period.
Zelensky said the strikes demonstrated that Moscow had no intention of exercising similar restraint. He insisted Ukraine remained prepared to take reciprocal steps toward de-escalation, but argued that meaningful progress required stronger international pressure on Russia. "Wars end when the aggressor realizes that it cannot prolong the war," he said.
Zelensky also warned that easing pressure on Moscow, delaying military assistance to Ukraine or making it harder to defend civilians against ballistic missiles would not advance peace.
His comments came amid reports that Washington was threatening to suspend the mechanism through which European countries purchase American weapons for delivery to Ukraine unless Kyiv stopped targeting Russian refineries.
The dispute has intensified following Trump's agreement with Putin to permit Russian diesel exports to international markets despite existing sanctions. The arrangement, intended to ease fuel shortages and slow rising diesel prices, has drawn sharp criticism from Ukraine and several European countries, which fear it will provide Moscow with additional revenue to finance its war.
Zelensky previously described the agreement as "a weak decision by strong partners." The deal would release more than 2.25 million barrels of Russian diesel onto U.S. and international markets. Some energy experts have questioned whether the relatively limited volume would have a meaningful effect on global prices.
According to a Reuters report, the diesel agreement was not merely intended to address fuel prices but was also part of an American attempt to persuade Putin to resume negotiations over ending the war.
Three people familiar with discussions between American and Ukrainian officials said Trump's envoys, Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, explained the strategy during a meeting in Miami on Friday.
Two of the sources said Witkoff and Kushner told Ukrainian representatives that Putin was currently unwilling to negotiate an end to the war and that the diesel deal could help restart three-way talks involving Washington, Moscow and Kyiv.
A third source said the United States believed the agreement could help "soften" Moscow's position by signaling Trump's willingness to pursue cooperation with Russia.
The strategy was intended to demonstrate that Washington was prepared to offer Moscow economic incentives while encouraging Kyiv to suspend its attacks on Russian energy infrastructure, potentially creating conditions for renewed negotiations.
The Ukrainian delegation left the Miami meeting without formally agreeing to the proposals, according to Reuters, although officials indicated they were open to an energy ceasefire if Russia also observed it.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov did not explicitly deny the Reuters report Tuesday but said he saw no "direct connection" between the diesel agreement and Moscow's willingness to participate in peace negotiations.
He described the arrangement as mutually beneficial cooperation between Russia and the United States that served the interests of both countries and international energy markets.
Against this backdrop, Ukrainian Foreign Minister Sybiha delivered a pointed remark about Washington's changing demands on Kyiv during a security conference in Warsaw on Tuesday. "In less than two years, we have gone from 'You don't have the cards' to 'Don't play your cards.' This is an achievement," he said.
The remark referred to Trump's confrontation with Zelensky in the Oval Office in February 2025, when the American president told his Ukrainian counterpart that he lacked leverage in negotiations with Russia.
Now, as Washington urges Ukraine to stop attacking Russian oil infrastructure, Sybiha suggested the administration was effectively acknowledging that Kyiv possessed strategic leverage, but was asking it not to use it.

Sweden’s centre-left leader fails in second bid to form government
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
15:37:18 UTC
00:37:18 KST

Sweden’s centre-left leader fails in second bid to form government
Social Democratic leader Magdalena Andersson says ‘conditions not in place’ to form government, prolonging deadlock.
The leader of Sweden’s left-wing Social Democratic Party, Magdalena Andersson, has said her efforts to form a government have failed, prolonging a political deadlock a month after parliamentary elections.
Speaking at a news conference Tuesday, Andersson said talks with the three other parties in the country’s left-wing bloc had hit an impasse.
Despite progress, she said she did not believe conditions were in place to “form a government that can be tolerated by parliament”.
It is her second time failing to form a government after Sweden’s parliamentary vote on September 13.
Shortly after the announcement, the country’s parliament speaker, Andreas Norlen, who had tasked Andersson with gauging conditions to form a government, said a vote on whether to make Andersson prime minister would proceed in parliament on Thursday. He conceded that Andersson would likely fail to pass the vote.
Under the Swedish system, a prime minister can secure office so long as a parliamentary majority does not vote against them.
Sweden’s centre-left opposition bloc narrowly defeated outgoing Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson’s right-wing bloc in last month’s election, winning 176 seats to the right-wing bloc’s 173. However, Andersson’s bloc has struggled to form a government due to competing terms from several of its members. The Centre Party has said it will oppose a government that includes cabinet posts for the Left Party, which has in turn insisted it will only support a left-wing government of which it is a member.
If Andersson fails in Thursday’s vote, Norlen is expected to ask Kristersson, who currently leads a caretaker government, to hold negotiations with other parties.
Speaking to reporters, Norlen said he considered Kristersson a potential next candidate, but the speaker did not wish to commit to that too soon and would “respect the process”.
To succeed, Kristersson would need to convince an opposition party to support him or at least not vote against him.
The speaker of parliament has four attempts at proposing a prime minister for parliament to vote on. If the fourth attempt fails, a snap election must be called.
After Sweden’s 2022 election, negotiations to form a government took more than a month, and those following the 2018 election lasted more than four months.

====================================================================================================

Saudi Arabia's strategic deadlock against Ansarullah
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
15:36:47 UTC
00:36:47 KST

After more than a decade of military intervention in Yemen, Saudi Arabia now faces a crisis whose consequences have gone beyond the battlefields and affected the security of vital infrastructure, international credibility, and Mohammed bin Salman's economic programs. The recent attacks on King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh and the expansion of clashes on Yemen's fronts show that the security costs of Riyadh's regional policy continue to rise. These developments once again highlight a strategic reality: purchasing advanced weapons and relying on the support of foreign powers alone cannot create lasting security.
According to published reports, the attack on Saturday, October 10 on Riyadh International Airport left at least 12 dead and more than 300 wounded. Another attack on Sunday also left one dead and 11 wounded. Following these incidents, the airport's operations were disrupted and airlines canceled their flights. These Ansarullah attacks have raised questions about Saudi Arabia's defensive capability against missile and drone attacks.
The importance of these developments is not limited to the number of casualties or material damage. Riyadh Airport is one of Saudi Arabia's important communication hubs and the gateway for investors, international company executives, and foreign tourists into the country. Disruption in the operations of such a center can have consequences beyond the security domain and affect economic actors' confidence in the stability of the investment environment. This issue is doubly important for a country that, through the implementation of Vision 2030, seeks to reduce its dependence on oil revenues and become a regional hub for tourism, technology, and investment.
In recent years, Mohammed bin Salman has pursued major projects, including NEOM, with the aim of transforming Saudi Arabia's economic structure. However, the realization of such programs requires a stable environment, secure infrastructure, and investor confidence. When the capital's airport is targeted by attacks and airlines are forced to cancel their flights, the issue is not just the ability to counter a military attack; rather, the international credibility of a country that wants to present itself as a safe destination for business and tourism is also put to the test.
Foreign Support; Security Guarantee or Strategic Dependence?
One of the most important dimensions of Saudi Arabia's current crisis is the limitation of this country's reliance on foreign allies. Over the past decades, Riyadh has spent enormous sums on purchasing advanced weapons, air defense systems, and Western fighter jets. Despite this, recent attacks have shown that possessing advanced military equipment does not necessarily mean immunity against attacks. Defending a country's extensive infrastructure against combined missile and drone attacks requires operational readiness, sufficient stocks of interceptor missiles, an early warning network, and sustained counter-capability.
Under such circumstances, requesting help from allies to strengthen air defense can cover part of Saudi Arabia's immediate needs, but it will not be a substitute for a sustainable security strategy. There is a fundamental difference between selling weapons, exchanging intelligence, providing technical support, and direct entry into a military conflict. Western governments may support Saudi Arabia within the framework of their own interests, but this support does not necessarily mean accepting the costs of a long and high-risk confrontation with Ansarullah.
Washington's behavior also demonstrates the importance of this limitation. In 2025, after about 52 days of airstrikes against Ansarullah, the United States halted its operations with an agreement mediated by Oman. This agreement did not mean the destruction of Ansarullah's military capability, and the group's threats against shipping were not completely eliminated. Nevertheless, this experience showed that air superiority and firepower, without achieving specific political objectives, do not necessarily lead to a desirable strategic result.
Now, too, America's direct entry into the Saudi-Ansarullah conflicts can create new costs. The expansion of military operations, the consumption of interceptor missile stockpiles, and the possibility of intensified threats against shipping routes complicate Washington's calculations. Especially since regional developments and the continuation of the crisis between Iran and America have imposed additional pressure on Washington's military resources and strategic decision-making. Therefore, Riyadh cannot consider foreign support as a definitive guarantee for preventing attacks or winning a long confrontation.
The Return of the Costs of Intervention in Yemen
The root of Saudi Arabia's current deadlock must be sought in a policy that was pursued from 2015 with the aim of changing the balance of power in Yemen. The military intervention of the Saudi-led coalition and the participation of the UAE not only did not lead to the removal of Ansarullah from Yemen's political and military equations, but over the years created extensive human, economic, and security costs. Airstrikes, restrictions on the entry of goods, and the difficulty of people's access to food, medicine, and medical services have imposed heavy pressure on Yemeni society.
Now, with the renewed intensification of clashes, part of the consequences of this policy has returned inside Saudi Arabia. Developments on various Yemeni fronts, including around Taiz and the Red Sea coasts, have gained greater strategic importance. At the same time, the situation in the coastal areas and the vicinity of Bab al-Mandab can complicate Riyadh's security calculations. Of course, the control status of these areas on the battlefield is variable, and an accurate assessment requires reliable and up-to-date information.
Bab al-Mandab is one of the important passages of global trade and energy transfer. Any intensification of conflict in this region can increase maritime transportation costs and affect the security of trade routes. From this perspective, the Yemen crisis is no longer merely an internal matter or a dispute between Riyadh and Ansarullah, but has become linked to the security of the Red Sea, international trade, and the interests of regional and transregional powers.
From a political perspective as well, current developments show that military pressure alone cannot eliminate the will of an actor with deep roots in Yemen's internal equations. Over the past years, Ansarullah has been able to maintain its political and military structure despite extensive attacks and economic and military pressures, and to impose costs on its regional rivals. This reality does not necessarily mean the absolute superiority of this group or the end of Saudi Arabia's military capability; rather, it shows that achieving political objectives through the military path faces serious limitations.
The Way Out of the Deadlock
Saudi Arabia now faces two simultaneous pressures: on the one hand, the necessity of defending vital infrastructure and reducing vulnerability to attacks; on the other hand, the increasing costs of continuing intervention in Yemen and the difficulty of achieving a sustainable political result. The continuation of the cycle of attack and response may expand the scope of damages, threaten the security of maritime routes, and spend more resources on military costs instead of economic development.
The way out of this situation is not merely increasing weapons purchases or pinning hopes on the direct entry of foreign powers. Riyadh must accept that sustainable security on its southern borders will not be achievable without taking into account Yemen's political and social realities. Stopping attacks, reducing humanitarian restrictions, moving toward an inclusive political agreement, and accepting the determining role of Yemenis in determining their country's future can provide the ground for reducing tension.
The experience of more than a decade of intervention in Yemen has a strategic lesson for Saudi Arabia and other countries in the region: military power and foreign support cannot substitute for understanding the realities on the ground and a political settlement of differences. If Riyadh continues to tie its security to weapons purchases and the promises of foreign allies and refrains from reviewing its regional policy, the possibility of repeating costly crises will remain. Ultimately, relying on foreign powers without creating sustainable mechanisms for resolving regional disputes is, more than a guarantee of security, a kind of leaning on the wind.
MNA

Feature: Chinese books bring German readers closer to China
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
23:36:03 CST
00:36:03 KST

FRANKFURT, Oct. 13 (Xinhua) -- For some German readers, discovering China begins with the turn of a page.
At the 2026 Frankfurt Book Fair that concluded on Sunday, a bookseller from Hannover who gave his name as Axel stopped at the joint Chinese pavilion when a poster of Chinese science fiction writer Liu Cixin caught his eye. He recalled that when he first read Liu's "The Dark Forest," he could barely sleep that night.
"I was completely captivated by that universe," he told Xinhua. Since then, he has kept Liu's trilogy on the shelves of his small bookstore, and his fascination with the works has also prompted him to seek out more Chinese science fiction writers.
For German translator and sinologist Karin Betz, Chinese science fiction is one field that has attracted particularly strong interest in Germany in recent years. Betz translated the latter two volumes of Liu Cixin's Remembrance of Earth's Past trilogy and has long followed and translated Chinese science fiction.
She believed one important reason for its appeal is the quality of the writing itself. Liu, she said, writes in the tradition of classic hard science fiction while bringing new perspectives on science and distinctly Chinese elements to the genre.
During the book fair, Betz spoke with Xinhua about her more than four decades of work with Chinese literature. From wuxia -- Chinese martial arts fiction centered on ideals such as loyalty, honor and justice -- and realist fiction to contemporary science fiction and stories of modern life, she said the growing range of themes and styles is giving German readers a broader view of Chinese literature.
"Literature and art are among the best ambassadors for a country," she said. "By crossing linguistic boundaries, literary works can open up new possibilities for understanding and dialogue between societies."
Mohamad El Khatib, CEO of the Lebanese publishing company Digital Future, told Xinhua that his company has brought in a large number of books from Chinese publishers, focusing on children's books and literature.
"I find that Chinese books are becoming more advanced compared with the last few years. I believe we can find a lot of titles that can become bestsellers in the global market, which is what made me come to see what new things they have and what new works they create," he said.
Christina Werum-Wang, German director of the Frankfurt Confucius Institute, has extensive experience in teaching Chinese in Germany.
German readers used to be more interested in classical philosophy and literary classics when they thought about Chinese books. More and more people are now becoming curious about, and paying attention to, works that reflect China's social development, technological innovation and contemporary life, Werum-Wang observed.
"At the Confucius Institute in Frankfurt, German students and readers often ask me: If we want to understand China, where should we start? I always tell them: Start by reading books." ■

BANGKOK, Oct. 13 (Xinhua) -- Thailand plans to cap fares on Greater Bangkok's urban rail network at 17 to 45 baht (about 0.50 to 1.35 U.S. dollars) per trip from January, aiming to cut commuting costs for passengers who switch between lines run by different operators, the government said on Tuesday.
Passengers will initially continue to pay full fares when traveling and receive the difference back later through "Paotang," a state-backed mobile payment app, said deputy government spokesperson Lalida Periswiwatana.
Only Thai nationals who register and meet eligibility criteria will qualify, Lalida said, noting that the scheme is a post-trip refund system, not an immediate reduction of fares charged at station gates.
She said Jan. 1, 2027, remains a target date and the actual effective date depends on system readiness and the necessary approvals. The Ministry of Transport will announce official details on registration, eligible card types, and refund conditions.
Rail lines in Bangkok and surrounding provinces are run by several operators under separate concessions, so commuters who change routes often pay a new entry fee each time, pushing up the cost of longer journeys.
Deputy Transport Minister Siripong Angkasakulkiat said the ministry is preparing to ask the cabinet for budget funds to cover the fare difference. Existing concession agreements will stay in place during the transition, allowing the scheme to proceed without first restructuring operators' contracts. ■

Feature: China-trained Somali doctors return to rebuild healthcare system
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
23:35:37 CST
00:35:37 KST

MOGADISHU, Oct. 13 (Xinhua) -- When Hilal Mohamed Nur first arrived in China to pursue postgraduate medical studies, he felt a mix of excitement, curiosity, and nervousness.
Thousands of kilometers from home, he was unsure what to expect from the language, culture, and people. "I didn't know the language or the people, but I was ready to learn," Nur told Xinhua.
Years later, Nur is applying the knowledge and experience he gained in the Asian country to help strengthen Somalia's healthcare sector.
Supported by a Chinese Government Scholarship under the China Scholarship Council (CSC), he earned a Master of Medicine from Xi'an Jiaotong University in Shaanxi Province.
Today, he serves as head of the education and research department at Mogadishu's Madina Hospital, a key public healthcare facility.
Reflecting on his time in China, Nur recalled how the warmth and hospitality he encountered helped him adapt to an unfamiliar environment.
Welcomed by staff and peers at Xi'an Jiaotong University, Nur became the first Somali student in the medical department to pursue a master's degree, joining a small group of Somali undergraduates studying medicine and surgery.
Despite language and cultural barriers, they bonded over shared passions like football, creating lasting connections that enriched his understanding of Chinese society far beyond the classroom.
The partnership dates back to 1978, when the two countries signed a cultural and educational agreement to establish Chinese scholarships for Somali students.
Today, these exchanges continue to open doors for Somali scholars and professionals.
In August 2025, the Chinese Embassy in Somalia hosted a reception for nearly 70 local scholarship recipients under the CSC and the Ministry of Commerce programs.
For Nur, the value of his education became immediately clear upon his return to Somalia during the height of the COVID-19 pandemic.
Specializing in emergency and general care, his expertise directly matched the urgent needs of the healthcare sector.
The Ministry of Health appointed him as a health data analyst at the national hospital, where he provided daily analytical updates to guide the government's pandemic response. Meanwhile, Nur also contributes to medical education as a lecturer at SIMAD University in Mogadishu.
Through his combined efforts in hospital administration, research and teaching, he continues to strengthen health service delivery while mentoring Somalia's next generation of medical professionals.
Mohamed Abdi Bafo, another Somali physician educated in China, followed a similar path.
After graduating with a Bachelor of Medicine and Bachelor of Surgery from Southeast University in Nanjing, Jiangsu Province, he returned home to serve as a surgeon at Madina Hospital.
Bafo noted that when the newly renovated Digfeer Hospital, now known as the Recep Tayyip Erdogan Training and Research Hospital, began recruiting staff, many of the successful candidates were China-trained graduates.
He attributed their readiness for clinical practice to the rigorous hands-on training received at Chinese universities, where access to advanced laboratories, modern medical equipment, and structured clinical workflows helped them build strong practical skills.
In a health system undergoing major reconstruction, such hands-on experience is invaluable, he added. ■

BANGKOK, Oct. 13 (Xinhua) -- The heads of the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and World Bank warned here on Tuesday that deepening geopolitical and economic fragmentation could hinder global economic growth, urging nations to balance national security priorities with open trade and multilateral cooperation.
Speaking at a panel discussion during the Annual Meetings of the IMF and the World Bank, IMF Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva cautioned that while the global economy has demonstrated surprising resilience against compounding shocks, rising protectionism and the breakdown of international cooperation carry severe long-term costs.
Georgieva emphasized that while early estimates warned fragmentation could cost up to 7 percent of global gross domestic product, the opportunity cost of foregone cooperation is even more concerning, as it highlights the hidden toll of duplicate investments, slowed scientific breakthroughs, and the erosion of cross-border trust.
She warned policymakers against sliding into complacency or retreating into total self-sufficiency, reminding them that sound macroeconomic and financial stability remains the "first line of defense" and that current resilience must not be taken for granted.
World Bank Group President Ajay Banga pointed out that global trade dynamics are undergoing a structural transformation. Over the past two decades, developing economies' share of global trade has doubled from 20 percent to 40 percent, with half of that volume now taking place directly between developing nations rather than flowing strictly to advanced economies.
Banga highlighted that addressing demographic shifts, including 1.2 billion young people entering adulthood across emerging markets over the next 15 years, requires scaling private capital mobilization.
"Public financial circumstances everywhere ... are all stressed," Banga said, noting that governments cannot fund sustainable growth alone.
He called for concerted reforms to de-risk private capital flows through physical and digital infrastructure investments, predictable regulatory frameworks, and robust support for micro-, small-, and medium-sized enterprises, which generate roughly 75 percent of employment globally. ■

Unexploded Israeli ordnance threatens Lebanon's olive harvest
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
15:31:40 UTC
00:31:40 KST

Breadcrumb
Unexploded Israeli ordnance threatens Lebanon's olive harvest
Unexploded ordnance left behind by Israeli attacks is threatening lives and livelihoods in southern Lebanon, where two people have been killed in recent days as residents attempt to return to their land during the olive harvest.
On Sunday, engineer Hussein Ali Ramadan was killed when an explosive device detonated while he was harvesting olives in his orchard in Froun, in the Bint Jbeil district.
A day later, Edgar Gillo, a warrant officer in Lebanon's Internal Security Forces, was killed by another explosion while working on agricultural land in the border town of Ain Ebel.
The deaths have prompted local municipalities, including Froun and Yater, to warn residents against entering olive groves without consulting the relevant authorities, amid fears of unexploded munitions, cluster bombs and landmines.
Hassan Bazzi, mayor of Froun, told The New Arab that the danger persists even in areas where residents have resumed their normal lives.
"What happened two days ago in our town, when a young engineer from Froun was killed while attempting to harvest olives, is painful evidence of the scale of this danger," he said.
"It confirms that war does not truly end simply because military operations have stopped, as long as these remnants continue to threaten people's lives."
For southern Lebanon's farming communities, avoiding potentially contaminated land can mean sacrificing an already precarious livelihood.
A Froun resident told The New Arab that agriculture remains the principal source of income for many families, who have already suffered enormous losses during Israel's attacks.
"Today, they are trying to return to their land to recover whatever they can, but the risks are considerable," the resident said, citing cluster munitions, continuing Israeli attacks and possible contamination from white phosphorus.
Andrew Moore, the HALO Trust's regional director for the Middle East, North Africa, told The New Arab that extensive bombardment inevitably leaves behind munitions that fail to detonate.
"Any area that has been subject to extensive fighting and bombardment there will always be a certain proportion of the ordnance that fails to function as designed," he said.
Such weapons can include artillery shells, mortar rounds, grenades and tank ammunition. Moore explained that unexploded ordnance generally poses the greatest danger when disturbed, including during agricultural work or reconstruction.
Although the HALO Trust does not currently operate in Lebanon, Moore said its experience in other conflict zones demonstrates the difficult choices facing returning farmers.
"The reality is people will always take risks if their livelihoods depend on them," he said.
"If it's a choice between taking a risk of moving an item of ordnance or not harvesting your crops or planting your crops or whatever it involves, obviously harvesting at this time of year, then too many people do make the choice to harvest the crops."
The Lebanese army has been conducting surveys and controlled detonations of unexploded ordnance in areas affected by Israeli attacks, including Mayfadoun, Shaqra and Baraachit.
However, Lebanese military sources told The New Arab that continuing Israeli attacks have repeatedly obstructed clearance operations, sometimes striking soldiers directly or nearby while they accompanied residents to agricultural land.
The sources said comprehensive assessments remain difficult because of ongoing attacks and Israel's continued presence in parts of southern Lebanon.
Bazzi similarly warned that Froun's eastern outskirts, facing the area known as the Yellow Zone, remain too dangerous for comprehensive surveys.
"Areas that have not undergone field surveys cannot be considered definitively safe," he said, urging residents not to approach or handle suspicious objects.
Moore identified access as the principal obstacle to clearance, followed by the sheer scale of contamination.
"The biggest issue in southern Lebanon is access," he said, adding that the extent of the danger may only become apparent as more residents return.
Hisham Younes, president of the Green Southerners Association environmental NGO said the situation recalled Israel's 2006 war on Lebanon, when cluster munitions severely obstructed the return of displaced communities.
He warned that unexploded weapons also threaten ecosystems and agricultural recovery, alongside potential longer-term contamination from heavy metals and white phosphorus.
Lebanese Prime Minister Nawaf Salam said southerners had the right to harvest their olives without fearing for their lives, pledging to prioritise clearance and safe returns.
But with Israeli attacks continuing and large areas still unsurveyed, farmers face the prospect of another harvest overshadowed by the deadly remnants of war.

====================================================================================================

Friday the 13th Series Crystal Lake Is Everything Wrong With Film-to-TV Adaptations
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
15:30:04 UTC
00:30:04 KST

Friday the 13th is proof that a movie need not be a cinematic masterpiece to become a franchise-fueling horror classic. Sean S. Cunningham’s low-budget 1980 film brought the teen-slasher thrills of Halloween to a summer camp preparing to reopen years after two counselors were murdered there. Its plot was skeletal and its performances workmanlike. The attitude it implied toward sex and drugs was as hysterical as any “Just Say No”-era afterschool special. Yet the movie was also viscerally effective, cycling through the sensations of suspense, titillation, and terror so quickly that, for its hormone-addled young audience in particular, it was impossible to look away. Say what you will about Friday the 13th; it’s not boring.
So it’s extra disappointing that Crystal Lake, an eight-episode Peacock horror series that reboots the franchise around the mother of victim turned bogeyman Jason Voorhees, is such a slog. Four years in the making, it emerges from a development morass involving the departure of original showrunner Bryan Fuller (who had previously reinvented The Silence of the Lambs franchise in his stylish cult crime drama Hannibal) over creative differences with production company A24. Brad Caleb Kane, whose credits include quality shows like Lodge 49 and Tokyo Vice along with It: Welcome to Derry, replaced Fuller, who retains a story credit, in 2024. This might help to explain why the series, premiering Oct. 15, turned out to be such a convoluted, dull, incoherent, ultimately pointless mess. Whatever the reason, it epitomizes everything wrong with the TV adaptations of horror touchstones that IP-crazed streamers keep churning out.
Jason’s mom, Pamela, is the villain of the original movie, where she’s played by Betsy Palmer, though at that point in the franchise she’s identified only as “Mrs. Voorhees.” The boy’s death by drowning in 1957, due to the negligence of the same horny counselors who would be killed the following year, unhinged his mother—to the extent that, in the film, she carries on both sides of conversations she imagines she’s having with him, in a reverse-Norman-Bates type scenario. Mrs. Voorhees enters almost 80% of the way through Friday the 13th and is dead a little over 10 minutes later, her head macheted off in lurid slow motion by final girl Alice (Adrienne King).
The series’ version of Pam is a single mother in early-’70s Crystal Lake, NJ, the small town where the eponymous camp is located. Played by Linda Cardellini, whose casting as a woman who’s equal parts loving and driven by repressed rage is Crystal Lake’s one stroke of genius, she cooks at the camp and the local school by day and cares for Jason by night. Her boy is a sweet preteen who has physical differences (his head is large, bald, and lumpy) and is prone to seizures. Fiercely protective, she enrolls him in Camp Crystal Lake in order to keep him close by, even though the cruel campers ostracize him. But Pam’s helicopter parenting backfires when he disappears in the lake as the two counselors who are supposed to be supervising, Claudette (Danielle Kotch) and Barry (Phoenix Parnevik), sneak off to snog. Jason’s only friend, an empathetic fellow outcast named Grace (Gwendolyn Sundstrom), stumbles upon the couple and freezes, transfixed. By the time Pam realizes something is wrong, Jason has vanished.
But a body is never found, and so she’s convinced her son isn’t dead. In part because of that apparently irrational belief and in part because she’s hurt to see her neighbors moving on so quickly after the death of a child they treated like a freak, she can’t abide the camp reopening the very next year. This is where the plot gets unwieldy. A pair of thugs disguised as state troopers arrive to drag Pam back to some dark past that is only hinted at throughout the first six episodes of the season. She kills them, kicking off a cat-and-mouse homicide investigation led by the local police chief, Levon, a.k.a. Lee (William Catlett), a Black cop whose race underlines his outsider status in a town full of white yokels, and who carries some unspecified baggage from a past stint in Newark. A tentative romance takes root between Lee and the woman he doesn’t realize is on a mini murder spree. He also, conveniently, has a newspaper-reporter sister (Devin Kessler) to help him investigate what brought the victims to Crystal Lake.
The series plods forward from there, punctuated by some mild scares and semi-inventive kills, generating lots of clutter but negligible momentum. Kane dutifully remixes memorable aspects of the franchise—the snake in the cabin, the sex and drug panic, the trap-door endings. The ‘70s setting is exploited for side plots, from the trendy encounter group to which Pam accompanies liberated diner denizen Rita (a fun but underused Joy Suprano) to an itinerant band of Central Casting hippies, that mostly serve as time wasters. Clichés are nested within clichés; a prototypical penultimate flashback episode takes us back to the ’50s, where every nightmare of suburban womanhood is on display. Crystal Lake invokes various themes, some latent in the movies and some not: small-town racism, fear of difference, corporate cruelty, the strain of sexism that underestimates the anger of a woman like Pam at everyone’s peril. Yet its engagement with these societal ills rarely goes deeper than the acknowledgment that they exist.
Maybe there’s a better show buried under all this. A24 has a reputation for aesthetics, and while this isn’t its most visually inventive work, the retro-VHS flourishes are well done. As she did in Dead to Me, Cardellini makes us feel the love and pain behind Pam’s violence. Grace could’ve been a fascinating character, but she fades away in the final third of the season, before her precociousness and confusion can develop into anything worth exploring. The most intriguing plot twist happens in the flashback episode, yet it’s no sooner introduced than abandoned.
There’s no context in which Crystal Lake would’ve been satisfying. Like too many horror series (Something Very Bad Is Going to Happen, Hemlock Grove), it stretches a feature’s share of plot into a season that feels interminable. And like too many horror series adapted movie franchises (I Know What You Did Last Summer, The Purge, Scream), it tries to extend a premise that was never especially rich in its original incarnation and has since been exhausted by endless sequels. But Crystal Lake suffers especially from its poor timing, premiering just a few months after Jane Schoenbrun’s Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma, a brilliant meditation on how the sex and violence of Friday the 13th and its ilk shoot straight to the subconsciouses of fans who encounter them while still young enough to be figuring out who they are, what turns them on, and what scares them senseless. Schoenbrun understands something crucial that seems to have eluded Kane: It isn’t the characters or the setting or even the creativity of the bludgeonings that make a slasher movie indelible. It’s the way they make us all into Grace, forever changed by a voyeuristic spectacle we may not understand but can never un-see.
