a warning splashed across large campaign billboards hanging over bridges and roads across Israel ahead of the Oct. 27 election. The slogan urges Israelis to vote for right-wing parties by portraying an opposition victory as opening the way for the establishment of a Palestinian state, Anadolu reports.
Yet, the Palestinian state that Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and his right-wing allies repeatedly invoke as an election threat is largely absent from the political programs of the main opposition parties in Israel.
Those parties broadly agree that a political settlement with the Palestinians is currently unattainable, although their positions range from maintaining the status quo while providing Palestinians with certain measures of relief to restoring relations with the Palestinian Authority (PA).
The right-wing Yisrael Beiteinu party, led by opposition leader Avigdor Lieberman, has gone further by advocating the dissolution of the PA.
Netanyahu and his allies are betting that warnings that an opposition government could lead to Palestinian statehood will mobilize right-wing voters to turn out on Oct. 27.
Opinion polls indicate that neither Netanyahu’s bloc nor the opposition is currently able on its own to reach the 61 seats needed for a majority in the 120-member Knesset to form a government.
Although most opposition leaders have repeatedly said they will not seek support from Arab parties to secure a governing majority, Netanyahu and his partners claim they will ultimately resort to seeking Arab support.
Arab citizens make up more than 20% of Israel’s population of more than 10 million.
If neither bloc succeeds in forming a government, Israelis could face another election several months later, with the current government remaining in a caretaker capacity until a new coalition is formed.
‘We are in no one’s pocket’
Yousef Jabareen, chairman of the Joint List, an alliance of three Arab parties, said Tuesday that any support for an opposition candidate seeking to form a government will come with conditions.
“Our top priority is to bring down the bloodshed government that has made our lives miserable over recent years,” Jabareen told a conference organized by the Yedioth Ahronoth newspaper.
He said the Joint List will be prepared to provide a parliamentary “safety net” for a “real and substantive alternative” to Netanyahu’s government.
“A strong and large Joint List can be a decisive factor,” he said.
Jabareen added that he is not currently holding talks with the so-called “change bloc,” referring to the opposition parties.
“We do not give anyone a blank check, and we are in no one’s pocket,” he said. “When they realize there are no other options but to cooperate with us, we will begin negotiations and present our demands.”
READ: Hamas urges national dialogue after Palestinian elections postponed to next year
Asked about those demands, Jabareen said: “We are part of the Palestinian people.”
“The entire world supports the establishment of a Palestinian state alongside Israel on the 1967 borders, with both states living in peace,” he added.
He called for a “political horizon that brings hope, peace and economic prosperity.”
Of the UN’s 193 member states, 160 recognize the State of Palestine, according to the Palestinian Foreign Ministry. Palestine is also a member of more than 100 international organizations and treaties.
Palestine has held UN non-member observer state status since 2012, while the US has repeatedly used its veto at the Security Council to block full UN membership.
Netanyahu’s incitement
Netanyahu and his coalition partners quickly portrayed Jabareen’s comments as proof that Palestinian parties will demand the establishment of a Palestinian state in return for supporting the Israeli opposition.
Referring to Jabareen, Netanyahu wrote Tuesday on US social media platform X: “Eisenkot and Lieberman’s partner: We will establish a Palestinian state.”
Gadi Eisenkot leads the opposition Yashar party, while Lieberman heads the Yisrael Beiteinu party.
Seeking to rally right-wing voters, Netanyahu said: “If we do not go out and vote, we will get a left-wing government led by Eisenkot and Lieberman that will establish a Palestinian state.”
He said voting for his Likud party is “the only way to prevent it.”
Netanyahu is standing trial on corruption charges, which he denies. He also faces an International Criminal Court arrest warrant issued in November 2024 over war crimes and crimes against humanity in Gaza.
Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich, leader of the far-right Religious Zionism party, also attacked Jabareen’s comments Tuesday.
“Just two days after announcing his intention to provide a safety net for a government headed by Eisenkot, the chairman of the Joint List reveals his dangerous plan to establish a terrorist state in the heart of Israel,” Smotrich wrote on X.
“Lieberman will ask him to remain silent, and Eisenkot will rush to deny it, but the truth remains: This is what Israel will look like if the left comes to power,” he added.
Eisenkot opposes 2-state formula
Eisenkot himself, however, rejects the two-state formula.
“My position on the Palestinian issue has remained consistent: The principle of two states for two peoples is a mistake,” he told Israel’s Channel 7 podcast Sunday.
He also strongly rejected the idea of a binational state that would incorporate millions of Palestinians as Israeli citizens.
“I believe annexing 2.8 million Palestinians in Judea and Samaria (West Bank) and another 2 million Palestinians in the Gaza Strip will be a disaster for Israel. I do not want that.”
A binational state entails the establishment of a single state for Jews and Palestinians in the region extending between the Jordan River and the Mediterranean Sea — that is, historic Palestine.
“I want a state that is the homeland of the Jewish people, with a strong Jewish majority — a strong state that is confident in itself,” he added.
Eisenkot also rejected Lieberman’s proposal to dissolve the PA, establish an Israeli-Jordanian confederation across roughly half of the occupied West Bank and annex the remainder to Israel.
“I strongly oppose it,” Eisenkot said. “I oppose any Jordanian deployment or involvement in Judea and Samaria. Responsibility rests solely with the Israeli army.”
READ: Eisenkot attacks Netanyahu: Those who evade responsibility cannot prevent the next disaster
He said he will not object to a Palestinian police force handling civilian affairs as long as overall security control remained in Israeli hands.
“There is no other military force between the river and the sea,” he said.
Eisenkot did not offer an alternative political solution to the Palestinian issue.
On Gaza, he said Israel should focus on dismantling Hamas’ military and governing capabilities, creating a different governing authority in the enclave and conducting a long-term process aimed at preventing a repeat of the Oct. 7, 2023 events.
Eisenkot also criticized Netanyahu’s government, saying the US had effectively taken responsibility for arrangements involving Iran, Gaza and Lebanon.
He nevertheless said any agreement concluded by the Israeli government with Washington will also bind him and that he would insist on implementing it.
Netanyahu has headed the current government since late December 2022, a coalition widely described as the most right-wing in Israel’s history.
Conditions for joining government
Asked how he would form a government if the opposition failed to win at least 61 Knesset seats, and whether he would rely on Arab parties, Eisenkot laid out four principles that he said would be prerequisites for joining a government he leads.
They include recognizing Israel as “a Jewish, democratic and liberal state.”
He also demanded acceptance of mandatory military, national or civilian service for all citizens — Jews, Arabs and ultra-Orthodox Jews — and support for dismantling Hamas’ military and governing capabilities.
“When I look at the Arab parties, I do not see any Arab party that accepts the four principles,” he said. “That is why it does not matter whether you ask me about this person or that person.”
Asked specifically whether Ra’am leader Mansour Abbas could join his government, Eisenkot said: “Mansour Abbas does not accept the four principles, so he is not part of my government.”
He similarly ruled out the Joint List led by Jabareen as a coalition partner under those conditions.
Asked about accusations that he is a leftist who supports evacuating illegal settlements and establishing a Palestinian state, Eisenkot rejected the characterization.
“I have never defined myself as left-wing,” he said. “I have defined myself as an Israeli patriot and someone who loves the land.”
“I support Jewish settlement under two conditions,” he added. “First, that it is in accordance with Israel’s map of national interests, and second, that it complies with the law.”
Israel has occupied the West Bank, including East Jerusalem, since 1967. Israeli settlements built on occupied Palestinian territory are considered illegal under international law.

Last Seen in Crimea: Kyiv Independent documentary investigates Russia's secret detention system for Ukrainian civilians
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
15:26:22 UTC
00:26:22 KST

Last Seen in Crimea: Kyiv Independent documentary investigates Russia's secret detention system for Ukrainian civilians
The Kyiv Independent's War Crimes Investigations Unit has released Last Seen in Crimea, a new documentary investigating a system of detention in Russian-occupied Crimea where Ukrainian civilians have been held without contact with the outside world, often without formal charges, and subjected to torture and other forms of abuse.
The documentary was released online on Sept. 11, on the Kyiv Independent's YouTube channel and website. An in-person screening was held in Kyiv on the same day at the National Museum of the History of Ukraine in the Second World War, followed by an audience Q&A with the Kyiv Independent team.
The investigation traces how Russia's system of political repression in Crimea, built up since the 2014 occupation, has expanded to include civilians taken from territories occupied after Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
At the center of the film are two detention facilities in Crimea's capital of Simferopol — SIZO No. 2 and the more secretive SIZO No. 8 — as well as the officials and structures behind them.
The Kyiv Independent's reporting found evidence that SIZO No. 2, formally operated by Russia's Federal Penitentiary Service, has been used to hold Ukrainian civilians under conditions that former detainees describe as abusive and coercive, with Federal Security Service (FSB) personnel having particular access to the facility.
SIZO No. 8, meanwhile, was formally transferred under FSB control in 2026 and has remained largely closed to public scrutiny. The investigation also identified Anton Panin, a former FSB investigator involved in the politically motivated case against Crimean Tatar activist Nariman Dzhelyal and his co-defendants, as the apparent head of SIZO No. 8 shortly before the facility came under FSB control.
"For us, one of the key goals of this investigation was to identify the individuals directly responsible for the unlawful detention, ill-treatment, and torture of Ukrainian civilian detainees in the occupied territories," says film author Olesia Bida.
"Systems like this do not operate on their own — they depend on those who run them and those who carry out their orders."
One of the survivors featured in the film, Anatolii, a businessman from Kherson Oblast,, was abducted from his home after helping wounded Ukrainian soldiers escape Russian-occupied territory. He spent years being moved between makeshift detention sites and prisons before being taken to SIZO No. 2 in Simferopol, where he was tortured and held in abusive conditions. His family did not know whether he was alive for months.
The documentary also follows Dzhelyal, a Crimean Tatar activist who spent five months in SIZO No. 2 after being detained in 2021 and accused of sabotage. He was later sentenced to 17 years in prison before being released in a prisoner exchange and is now Ukraine's ambassador to Turkey.
A third story follows Tetiana Zelena, whose brother Serhii Lykhomanov was detained in Crimea in December 2023. His family spent two months trying to establish where he was being held before learning that he was in SIZO No. 8. His lawyer was denied access to him even after a court authorized a visit.
Together, the stories show how the system operates across different stages of detention: people can disappear without their families knowing where they are, be held without meaningful access to legal representation, and in some cases remain outside any formal legal process altogether.
Human rights experts interviewed for the film describe this status as incommunicado detention — people held without charges, court decisions, or contact with the outside world.
For the investigation, the Kyiv Independent interviewed 13 former detainees of SIZO No. 2 and obtained testimony from three additional former detainees through their lawyers. The team also spoke with around two dozen relatives of Ukrainian civilians who remain in detention. Because many of those still held are unable to speak publicly, some relatives requested anonymity for the safety of the detainees.
The investigators also cross-referenced leaked Russian databases, procurement records, court and other documents, and social media activity to identify people involved in the detention system. This reporting helped the team trace the career of Panin, who had previously worked as an FSB investigator and was later linked to the administration of SIZO No. 8.
The scale of the system extends far beyond the people featured in the film. According to Ukraine's Ombudsman Dmytro Lubinets, Russia is holding roughly 16,000 Ukrainian civilians across some 200 detention sites in Russia and occupied Ukrainian territories.
Only around 450 had been returned home at the time of the film's release. Unlike prisoners of war, Ukrainian civilian detainees do not have a functioning exchange mechanism. The U.N. Human Rights Monitoring Mission in Ukraine has also documented deaths of Ukrainian civilians in Russian captivity.
The documentary can be watched on the Kyiv Independent's YouTube channel and website, alongside the full written investigation, Inside Russia's FSB prison system in occupied Crimea, by Bida, a War Crimes Investigations Unit reporter and the film''s author.
Last Seen in Crimea is the latest documentary from the Kyiv Independent's War Crimes Investigations Unit, founded in 2023 to document Russian atrocities against Ukrainian civilians. Over three years, the unit has produced more than a dozen documentaries, held more than 90 screenings worldwide, and received multiple journalism awards, including an IRE Award.
Readers who want to support further investigations like this one can join the Kyiv Independent community.
The team behind Last Seen in Crimea:
Author Olesia Bida
Director Maksym Yakobchuk
Video Editor Dmytro Chaika
Journalist & Researcher Myroslava Chaiun
Cinematographers Oleh Halaidych, Liza Pyrozhkova, Nikita Petrenko, Mykola Lebediev, Max Salii
Executive Producer Anastasiia Mozghova
Line Producer Lera Zaherst

Do women hit a biological ‘cliff’ at menopause?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
15:26:07 UTC
00:26:07 KST

Menopause, despite being a fact of life for most women, is something of a scientific enigma. We know it occurs when the ovaries stop releasing new eggs and estrogen production drops. But the biological consequences of this change beyond reproduction are murky at best. Now new research raises questions about a “physiological cliff” at menopause.
In a recent study published in Nature Medicine, researchers analyzed health data from more than one million women in the U.S. and Israel and found certain “jumps” in physiological traits such as bone density, liver health and other markers at the onset of menopause.
“Menopause is not a slow part of aging. It’s an abrupt, body-wide transition across bone, liver, kidney, blood chemistry, fats, and more,” says Uri Alon, the study’s senior author and a professor at the Weizmann Institute of Science in Rehovot, Israel. “That makes sense since estrogen has receptors in almost every cell in the body.”
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
The study analyzed trends in menopause using a population-wide analysis that averaged hundreds of millions of health tests.
Alon and his colleagues pinpointed certain “jumps” in health markers: in the case of bone health, they found a “jump in the direction of bone loss,” Alon says. They also observed sudden changes in tests related to kidney function, liver health, and more. Some of these leaps were positive—such as for iron and hemoglobin levels, likely because monthly bleeding stops, Alon says.
The results were surprising, he says: previous work had suggested menopause’s physiological changes were more gradual. When Alon and his team saw the “cliff” in the data, “the hair on the back of our necks stood up,” he says. “So we tested it hard.”
“We ran it on men with the same age distribution and saw no jumps,” he says. Location also didn’t seem to matter—medical records from women in the U.S. and in Israel revealed similar “jumps” across health tests.
Women who were on hormone therapy tended to see smaller jumps in some tests, “especially in bone, liver and kidney,” Alon says. The findings suggest some women might benefit from starting this therapy earlier in life, before menopause—but more research is needed to understand how hormone therapy might help.

PARIS — Conservative presidential candidate Bruno Retailleau said France should seek a rebate on its contribution to the EU budget ahead of a key European summit in Brussels this week.

Advertisement
European leaders are meeting in Brussels on Thursday and Friday to discuss the bloc’s long-term budget, the Multiannual Financial Framework, which is pitting the so-called frugal countries against those who want a bigger EU budget. France sits in neither camp.

Retailleau said he would seek “a negotiation,” rather than unilaterally impose a lower contribution, as Le Pen says she would do.
“I’m not going to behave like Marine Le Pen, I’m pro-European,” said Retailleau.
Retailleau argued that France’s defense and nuclear deterrence investments should also be included in the country’s contribution calculation, because the concept of forward deterrence benefits France’s European neighbors.

MI5 chief lists Iran, Russia, AI and terrorists among threats to UK

MI5 chief lists Iran, Russia, AI and terrorists among threats to UK
LONDON, Oct 13 - MI5 spy chief Ken McCallum delivered his annual speech on Tuesday outlining his view of the threats to Britain, from hostile states such as Iran and Russia to the development of artificial intelligence.
Here is a summary of the main threats and issues he detailed in his speech and subsequent questions from media:
RUSSIA
McCallum called Russia, which denies involvement in hostile acts in Britain and other Western countries, "aggressor number one". He said it was escalating "hybrid" warfare, staying below the threshold that would trigger a direct NATO response.
He said Russia's capabilities had been reduced by the expulsion of 1,000 officials from embassies since the invasion of Ukraine, which meant it had to rely on native volunteers and criminal proxies.
IRAN
Tehran is also using criminal proxies - to target opponents, Iranian media organisations and Israeli interests in Britain - and has expanded its hybrid campaign in the last year, McCallum said.
He said operations connected to Iran had yielded more than 50 arrests in the UK, and that many had been aimed at Jewish communities.
The other shift had been "Iranian ambitions to come at harder targets, like military sites", he said.
Tehran also rejects accusations of malign activity in Britain.
ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE
McCallum said AI was "supercharging the cybersecurity contest between attackers and defenders", producing tailored propaganda and material for individuals.
MI5 has caught potential attackers using it to try to improve reconnaissance and attack methodologies. AI-enabled drones added a new challenge, he said.
McCallum said the greatest concern about the misuse of AI was terrorists developing bioweapons or even creating new pathogens.
AI also presented a risk in itself.
"Put at its simplest, human history has given us no experience of facing an actor which is smarter than we are, is capable of out-thinking us. This is genuinely novel and deserves the serious attention it is getting."
TERRORISM
Britain in April raised its national terrorism threat level to "severe", meaning an attack within the next six months is highly likely.
McCallum said Al Qaeda and Islamic State continued to inspire plots, and MI5 was still having to respond to attempts to carry out mass-casualty attacks.
He said the most marked trend of the last year had been the increase in cases where extreme anti-immigration and anti-Muslim grievances were tipping over into terrorist intent.
An investigation into one 13-year-old who had been radicalised by extreme right-wing ideology had led to an unnamed foreign partner thwarting a lethal attack on its soil, he said.
BREXIT
On Sunday, Prime Minister Andy Burnham said Russia had interfered in Britain's 2016 referendum vote to leave the European Union, something Moscow has denied.
Asked about such interference, McCallum said it was public knowledge that Russian media such as Russia Today "came in pretty strongly around the time of the referendum", and there had been a certain amount of activity from trolls and bots.
But he said Russian online trolling had been comparatively unimpressive. REUTERS

Broken children: France confronts crisis of sexual violence against minors
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
15:24:00 UTC
00:24:00 KST

Broken children: France confronts crisis of sexual violence against minors
To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.
Issued on:
In France, a new "comprehensive law" aims to strengthen preventative measures, the judicial process and support for child victims of sexual violence. Yet advocacy groups, lawyers, and healthcare professionals point out that the legislation has numerous shortcomings. We take a closer look in this edition of France in Focus. Warning: viewers may find parts of this report disturbing.
In France, one child is reportedly raped or sexually assaulted every three minutes.
CIIVISE, the independent commission on incest and sexual violence involving minors, estimates that 160,000 children are victims of these crimes every year.
The murder and rape of 11-year-old Lyhanna in May shocked the country and accelerated the creation of a "comprehensive law". Its aim is to intervene at every level, from preventative measures to the judicial response, including the protection and support of victims.
Silence
Mié Kohiyama was five years old when she was raped by her cousin. She says she lived with traumatic amnesia for 32 years before her memories of the incident returned.
Now a co-founder of the Be Brave France charity, she advocates for the elimination of statutes of limitations.
She explained to the National Assembly in April: "When these victims face a wall of refusal from the justice system, it is an absolutely devastating form of violence. You have to be incredibly strong not to give up and kill yourself."
Her story illustrates one of the challenges of childhood sexual abuse: it can take some victims decades to speak out and file a complaint.
Since 2018 in France, the statute of limitations for rapes committed against minors has been 30 years from the age of majority, meaning up to age 48. But for victims who were raped before 2018, the law is different.
In the rest of the European Union, half of its member states have abolished statutes of limitations for the most serious sexual crimes.
Carine Durrieu-Diebolt is a lawyer who specialises in defending these victims; she believes the law is too complex. "In France now, a victim who was raped as a minor has 30 years from the time they reach adulthood to take legal action. So, until the age of 48. But that's not the case for every victim, because the law changes and it doesn't apply in the same way to everyone. So abolishing the statute of limitations would simplify the law and give everyone the same legal framework."
The issue is all the more sensitive because DNA evidence diminishes and becomes unusable over time. But Durrieu-Diebolt believes investigators should devote more resources to the preliminary investigation: "Very often, in cases of sexual assault, not everything is done that could be. For example, there isn't always a search of the perpetrator's home. Wiretaps are very rarely used in these cases, whereas in drug cases, all these measures are employed. There is no need for physical evidence of rape on the victim's body to prove that a rape occurred."
Ordinary citizens-turned-cyber vigilantes
Sexual violence against children is rising on the Internet.
"Punisher," a volunteer with Les Enfants d'Argus association, has been tracking child sex offenders on social media for six years. The association says he has helped identify more than 200 individuals.
Volunteers often create fake profiles of children to monitor the requests that they receive and compile files that are then forwarded to the authorities.
But these police forces are facing a huge volume of cases.
In 2025, the Office for Minors (OFMIN) reported receiving approximately 200,000 reports – that's nearly 500 every day. Its director, Division Commissioner Aurélie Besançon, says the office has only about 60 agents.
The investigators' work is complicated further by artificial intelligence. Offenders can now create or modify images and videos in a highly realistic manner using the face of a child or teenager, easily fooling their prey, and making it harder for investigators to track them down.
For AI specialist Ninon Bajard, young internet users must remain cautious. "The rule in 2026 is simple: don't believe anything you see online. If there's even the slightest doubt, don't send anything, so you can't be blackmailed."
Preventative measures
Sexual Violence Resource Centres (CRIAVS) conduct research, compile information, and train professionals on how to deal with perpetrators.
There are 27 of these centres across France. Most have set up a free, confidential helpline for people who are sexually attracted to children.
For healthcare professionals at the CRIAVS Rhône-Alpes, in east-central France, the goal is to intervene before the offence is committed.
Contrary to popular belief, not all perpetrators of sexual violence against minors can be classed as paedophiles, notes Mathias Poiteau, a psychologist at Le Vinatier Hospital in Lyon. "The vast majority of people who commit sexual acts against minors don't have a paedophilic attraction. We're often dealing with either extreme immaturity, or issues of control, aggression and a desire for power and domination because a minor is more vulnerable."
The STOP helpline received more than 4,500 calls in 2025 – triple the number of calls as the year it was launched, 2021.
Laure Vivier, medical secretary at CRIAVS Rhône-Alpes, explains: "Paedophilia is a disorder. That can be difficult to hear, of course. But some people who have these fantasies didn't choose to have them. Without in any way condoning what these people are experiencing, we have to recognise that instead of leaving them on their own, we need to talk to them so that the fantasy remains just a fantasy."
But the programme has its limits: calling the helpline does not mean that the person will subsequently agree to medical or psychological treatment.

Britons travelling to EU countries told not to apply for delayed Etias visa waiver
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
15:21:04 UTC
00:21:04 KST

Britons travelling to EU countries have been told not to apply for an Etias visa waiver, with more than 150 websites touting the service despite its introduction being delayed.
Non-EU citizens, including UK travellers and those from other visa-exempt countries including the US, Australia and Canada, will soon need to pay €20 (£17) for an electronic waiver to enter the Schengen zone under the European travel information and authorisation system (Etias).
The system was scheduled to be come into effect soon after the rollout of the EU’s parallel border scheme, the entry-exit system (EES). Both, however, have been repeatedly postponed, and the persistent problems after the introduction of EES, including the software at French entry points, have meant Etias remains suspended.
The director of public affairs at the travel association Abta, Luke Petherbridge, said: “While Etias was due to come into force this year, it is now back on hold. Abta believes it shouldn’t be brought in until EES is fully operational and working properly.
“This is particularly important when you consider that European authorities believe over 150 websites offering Etias already exist, but there is only one official site people should apply through when live.”
Abta research found awareness was growing of the impending border requirements – up from 41% in 2024 to 56% now. The price to apply has risen from €7 to €20 – over-70s and under-18s do not need to pay – but no date has been set for launch.
The pan-European border agency, Frontex, warned about the existence of scam websites long before Etias was to have been introduced. Commercial sites can legitimately apply for the waivers on behalf of clients, but the agency said the risk posed by third parties ranged from data protection and identity theft to extortionate fees.
It found that some unofficial websites were also providing inaccurate information over who needed an Etias while mimicking the layout of the official website and using convincing domain names.
“If you use one of these sites, not only will you lose money, you are also putting your personal data at risk as well,” Petherbridge said. “What I can’t stress is enough that you can’t – and shouldn’t - apply for an Etias now.”
EES is in full operation, but border authorities have been told the EU will not enforce penalties if they continue to suspend the system at entry points when queues escalate.
That flexibility has meant the worst fears of the travel industry have largely been avoided this summer. Abta surveys found only 46% of visitors to Europe reporting having full checks, with half of those people waiting less than 30 minutes, and only 13% queuing for an hour.

====================================================================================================

Brexiters can’t cope with the fact that Putin was cheering them on | Rafael Behr
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
15:21:02 UTC
00:21:02 KST

Russian territorial aggression against Ukraine didn’t feature much in the Brexit referendum campaign. It made headlines briefly when Boris Johnson blamed Moscow’s 2014 annexation of Crimea on the European Union.
According to the Vote Leave frontman, Vladimir Putin’s land grab was a consequence of Brussels making foreign policy “on the hoof” and having “pretensions to running a defence policy”.
The logic of that position was that Kyiv had no right to choose its own allies and that European democracies should never have supported Ukrainian aspirations to escape submission to Moscow. It is the appeasement fallacy: if only the west acquiesced to Putin’s conviction that Kyiv is a Russian city and that Ukraine is not a proper country, he would not want to suffocate his neighbour’s independence.
That notion is refuted by all the evidence of campaigns to coerce countries deemed by the Kremlin to be errant possessions since the collapse of the Soviet Union.
When Nigel Farage repeated the EU-provocation theory of the Ukraine war during the 2024 general election campaign, one prominent defender of Ukrainian sovereignty described the Reform UK leader’s assertions as “ahistorical drivel” and “Kremlin propaganda”. That stalwart friend of Kyiv was one Boris Johnson.
There is nothing unusual about Johnson contradicting himself. His talent as a political communicator came from the ability to hold whichever view was expedient to him in the moment and, for the duration of that moment, appear to hold it sincerely. In a more generous reading, he rose to the occasion of Putin’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, understanding events in their proper geopolitical perspective (and with access to classified intelligence reports), which afforded a different reading of Putin’s motives.
In 2016, his focus had been wilfully myopic. The goal of maximising Eurosceptic votes meant reaching for any argument that presented Brussels in a negative light. If that involved narrating the cause of a conflict on the other side of the continent in warped terms that matched the Kremlin story, so be it.
Putin despised the EU for his reasons; the leave campaign despised it for theirs. Johnson was not minded to interrogate whether that alignment of enmities discredited his cause.
This is the context in which Andy Burnham’s recent assertion that Russia meddled in the referendum needs to be understood. The prime minister said it was inconceivable, given all the evidence of Kremlin interference in elections around the world, that the toolkit of subversion would not have been deployed in support of Brexit.
That is not a controversial claim to anyone with a glancing awareness of Russian foreign policy and the means by which it is pursued – the swarms of bot accounts flooding social media with falsehoods; dirty money channelled to extremists; industrial dissemination of conspiracy theories and stoking of intercommunal tensions to undermine social coherence, deplete trust in democracy and make it less functional.
No candidate who was knowingly complicit in that process will admit as much. But even those who were unaware that their cause was boosted by Kremlin troll farms have incentives to deny it. No one wants their heroic victory recast as useful idiocy in service of a hostile power.
Conservatives have called Burnham’s intervention “dangerous and divisive”, which could be interpreted as a denial that interference happened or just as a preference that it not be mentioned to protect delicate pro-Brexit sensibilities.
Farage’s feelings were certainly hurt. He called the prime minister a liar and described the whole thing as a “Russia hoax” – the formula Donald Trump applied to well-substantiated allegations that his 2016 presidential campaign got a helping hand from Moscow. The Reform leader can’t be too surprised by the idea of Kremlin influence in British politics. His party’s former leader in Wales is serving a jail term for taking bribes from Russian spies.
The backlash forced Downing Street to clarify that the prime minister didn’t mean to cast aspersions on the legitimacy of the referendum result. That is the right position when there is no way of knowing what impact, if any, foreign meddling might have had. The views that interference happened and also that the leave campaign would have prevailed anyway are compatible.
Some remainers might seek comfort in the idea that Britain’s democracy was hijacked and diverted through clouds of Russian-induced false consciousness to the wrong destination. The banal truth is that the Eurosceptic side won enough arguments and voters made their choice freely.
Brexiters didn’t need any outside help to turn latent anti-immigration sentiment into active hostility to free movement across European borders.
The Russia dimension is more relevant when it comes to a geopolitical argument that the pro-European side failed to land. In June 2016 it was hard to make the peril of strategic isolation for Britain, self-exiled from the club of European democracies, no longer confident in the transatlantic relationship, seem vivid or imminent.
Trump’s first presidential election was five months away. The full extent of his scorn for the US’s allies and his admiration for authoritarians would not be clear for years. His propensity to behave like a private client of the Putin regime can still shock, even if it no longer surprises, as with the sanctions-busting deal he struck last week to import billions of dollars of Russian diesel.
The hope, entirely vain, is to depress pump prices and assuage voter frustration ahead of midterm elections in November.
On top of the cash infusion for the Kremlin’s war effort, Trump added a bonus of rhetorical venom for Volodymyr Zelenskyy, calling for regime change in Kyiv. He blames Ukrainian targeting of Russian refining capacity for rising global energy costs because his narcissistic ego resists the truth – that his war in Iran has been a disaster for the US and a boon for its enemies. The fact that Russia is an Iranian ally, providing Tehran with intelligence support to resist US military pressure, is no impediment to Trump’s commercial collaborations with the Kremlin.
The exact character and motive involved in that relationship may never be elucidated. But there is no need to seek out hidden levers of influence that may not even exist when publicly available data paints a full enough picture.
Trump and Putin are two greedy despots who recognise no boundary between national interest and self-enrichment. They see law not as a restraint on government but as an instrument to be wielded by powerful leaders against perceived enemies. Their approach to domestic politics is gangsterish, based on networks of patronage and tribute. Their view of foreign affairs is imperial, based on the belief that strong states have natural title to territory in their immediate vicinity, and that big countries can trade in the fate of smaller ones like casino chips.
It is as obvious to Trump that Moscow has a seigneurial right over Ukraine as it is that he should be allowed to decide who governs Venezuela and who sells its oil.
That ethos leads inevitably to competition for resources where rival spheres of influence meet and, if there is no international framework for resolving that competition, to war. This is the lesson, learned the hard way in the 20th century, that became the foundational idea of the European project – the principle of swapping nationalistic rivalry for mutually beneficial cooperation within a common framework of law. That is why Putin and Trump cannot understand the EU and why they hate it.
And that is why the error of Brexit is more pronounced today than it was when the question was put in a plebiscite, and why Burnham is right to draw attention to the fact that Russia had a preferred side. The prime minister is also right when he says that rejecting the possibility of restoring closer ties with the EU would be “a dereliction of duty”.
Many falsehoods were propagated in the referendum campaign, but none greater than the leavers’ boasts of patriotism, when their agenda was certain to make Britain poorer and weaker. A decade into the error, there is no patriotism in pretending that Brexit has worked or in crying betrayal when anyone suggests a reversal. Isolation from the rest of Europe is the result that Britain’s enemies wanted in 2016. Sticking to that path is the route they would choose for Britain again today if they had a vote.
- Rafael Behr is a Guardian columnist

IMF warns AI market correction could threaten global financial stability
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
15:20:54 UTC
00:20:54 KST

Mücahithan Avcıoğlu
13 October 2026•Update: 13 October 2026
The International Monetary Fund warned on Tuesday that a correction in artificial intelligence-related markets could threaten global financial stability if investment and profit expectations disappoint, with existing financial vulnerabilities potentially amplifying the shock.
Presenting its October Global Financial Stability Report during the IMF-World Bank Annual Meetings in Bangkok, the fund said financial stability risks remain elevated despite the resilience of markets to repeated shocks and heightened uncertainty.
Athanasios Vamvakidis, an official in the IMF’s Monetary and Capital Markets Department, said stronger-than-expected economic growth, robust corporate earnings and optimism about AI had helped support global markets.
That resilience, however, should not be interpreted as evidence that the financial system is safe, he cautioned.
The IMF identified an AI-related market correction as one of three major risks that could spark financial stress, alongside rising sovereign bond yields and cyber incidents capable of disrupting financial services or undermining confidence.
An AI correction could emerge if expectations for investment or profitability are not met. Meanwhile, inflation pressures, fiscal imbalances and large volumes of government and private-sector borrowing are contributing to risks in sovereign bond markets.
Although the threats could be manageable individually, weaknesses already present in the financial system could magnify their effects, the fund warned.
The IMF said its banking-sector stress test, incorporating severe shocks related to AI, bond markets and energy, showed that banks remained broadly resilient.
Nevertheless, a group of weaker banks would face insufficient capital under that scenario, and the share of vulnerable institutions has been increasing.
The fund also highlighted risks in nonbank financial institutions, including insurers, pension funds, private credit providers and hedge funds.
Insurers and pension funds hold more illiquid assets, which could expose them to greater difficulties during a downturn. Private credit faces rising borrower leverage and liquidity pressures that could constrain lending.
Hedge funds can help support markets, but their borrowing and concentration in similar trades could amplify stress when conditions deteriorate.
Emerging markets have also demonstrated resilience, although weaker policy buffers in some economies and less transparent alternative financing sources in certain frontier markets remain concerns.
The IMF urged policymakers to strengthen financial resilience before further shocks materialize, noting that high public debt and limited policy space could complicate their response.
Its recommendations included placing public debt on a sustainable path, preserving central bank independence, maintaining a commitment to inflation targets and communicating policy clearly.
The fund also urged stronger cyber resilience and close monitoring of risks across banks and nonbank financial institutions.

India: Can 'cockroaches' threaten Modi's political grip?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
15:20:00 UTC
00:20:00 KST

India: Can 'cockroaches' threaten Modi's political grip?
October 13, 2026
India's Cockroach Janata Party (CJP) may have anticipated pushback from the government after its first round of protests in July, but the scale of barricading and detentions that greeted its leaders in a fortress-like New Delhi on October 10 was unlike anything they had anticipated.
The CJP began as a satirical online movement after the chief justice of India, Surya Kant, referred to unemployed young people as "cockroaches" in an offhand remark. The name is an ironic riff on the name of Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi's ruling Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP).
In its latest round of agitation, they are demanding the resignation of the country's controversy-hit Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar, after more than 130 million names were reportedly removed from electoral rolls nationwide.
What happened over the weekend?
CJP founder Abhijeet Dipke, accompanied by co-conveners Ashutosh Ranka and Saurav Das, was detained from the plane in which he landed in the national capital on Saturday.
Meanwhile, police were stationed outside the homes of several other faces associated with the movement, including social media personality Dhruv Rathee, who has nearly 20 million followers on Instagram.
In central Delhi, buses were loaded with protesters, many of whom were taken to far-flung centers, where they were kept for hours. According to local media, at least 3,000 people were detained across the city.
How the government is handling the protests
The protests come as Modi marks 25 uninterrupted years leading elected governments, first in Gujarat state as chief minister and then as prime minister of India.
Ironically, "this celebration has happened at the time when he's politically at his weakest," Delhi-based writer Nilanjan Mukhopadhyay told DW. Mukhopadhyay is the author of Modi's 2013 biography "Narendra Modi: The Man, The Times."
He contrasted the government's current response with its approach in July, when thousands of young protesters took to the streets to demand the resignation of Modi's education minister over repeated exam paper leaks.
At the time, authorities had used batons, detentions and pellets to disperse the crowds gathered in central Delhi, which had been on the streets for days.
This time, authorities shifted to mass security deployments and preemptive action on a large scale. This included notices to those associated with earlier protests, transport cuts, the internet cutoff and airport arrests.
"The government has learned from its previous experience. They didn't allow people to sit at Jantar Mantar for any length of time, so it couldn't balloon," Pearl Pandya, senior analyst for Asia at global monitor ACLED, told DW.
"What's worrying is whether this becomes a playbook for the future — that you are not allowed to protest in the first place," she added, referring to the government's decision to remove the 18th-century observatory Jantar Mantar in central Delhi from the list of designated protest sites.
Authorities, however, have announced three new designated protest sites in the national capital.
Mukhopadhyay had a different reading of the situation. "The scale of this deployment is actually a defeat for Mr. Modi," he said.
Mukhopadhyay argued that it was already a setback for the government if it was forced to deploy security forces on such a scale in response to protests from a completely new socio-political movement.
Why October hasn't matched July
Despite the momentum, the CJP has not been able to replicate its success from July, with the protests against Kumar being led primarily by opposition leaders and student organizations.
"Education was far more of a cross-cutting issue... the right to vote is still seen as an intrinsically political one, where it's the opposition versus the BJP," Pandya said.
The CJP, however, has long maintained that it is non-political. This is often cited as the reason for them amassing such a large following of young followers.
Mukhopadhyay criticized that stance, saying: "You cannot raise issues about electoral neutrality... without saying that these are political issues."
Despite the differences between the previous round of CJP protests in July and the current wave of demonstrations, sociologist Surinder Singh Jodhka emphasized continuity.
"I don't think they're qualitatively different. Once again, young people are the ones who are mobilized, and they are much more encouraged because the earlier round of protests was successful," he told DW. "And it's also asking similar questions about institutions, about democracy, about transparency and accountability."
"There is a new hope for those who had earlier given up on India, and felt like the right wing was in complete control," Jodhka added.
Abrupt change of government unlikely
Dismissing comparisons with volatile protests in neighboring Nepal and Bangladesh, which brought down their governments, the analysts pointed to India's strong institutions as a safeguard against a dramatic change of government.
"India has had a very strong state system and state institutions," Jodhka explained, highlighting that even the opposition parties were asking for "the revival of institutions, rather than an overthrow of the state."
Pandya also stated that faith in the judiciary "would prevent these protests from tipping over into a popular revolution which unseats the government."
Nevertheless, she said, sustained discontent "might come to bite the government in 2029... or before that in the state elections."
It could also erode Modi's popularity, which has been a defining feature of Indian politics over the past decade, the expert indicated.
For Mukhopadhyay, the most troubling aspect of the current protests is the erosion of the electoral body's credibility.
Recalling the pride he felt when he registered to vote at 21, he drew comparisons with young Indian voters today. "The youngsters are now fighting for their vote."

Yemeni government forces launched the “Dawn of Yemen” operation earlier this month, aiming to recapture Houthi-held areas and restore government control.
The Houthis have controlled the capital Sanaa and several other provinces since 2014. A Saudi-led coalition intervened in Yemen in March 2015 in support of the internationally recognized government. The current escalation began in July as the 2022 truce broke down.

Iranian attacks on vessels in and around the Strait of Hormuz have reached their highest pace since the war with the US began on Feb. 28, with six ships targeted in a single day, according to data from the UK Maritime Trade Operations agency (UKMTO) and international maritime security sources, Anadolu reports.
Data from UKMTO and maritime security sources showed that more than 18 commercial vessels were targeted by Iran during the first 12 days of October, including six on Monday.
Between Oct. 5 and 12 alone, at least 14 attacks, attempted attacks and interceptions involving vessels were recorded in and around the strait, according to the same sources.
UKMTO data and statements by Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) indicated a marked rise in attacks on commercial shipping since clashes between Tehran and Washington resumed in July.
At least 12 attacks on oil tankers and cargo ships were recorded in July, while at least 10 vessels were targeted in August, including oil and liquefied natural gas tankers off the UAE port of Fujairah and Oman’s Sohar.
The number rose to 18 vessels in September as the US and Gulf countries increasingly resorted to ship-to-ship transfers, using smaller vessels to transport oil before loading it onto larger tankers in safer areas.
READ: Iran says LPG carrier struck, catches fire while crossing Strait of Hormuz via ‘illegal’ route
The IRGC claimed that the operations were “illegal oil smuggling and an attempt to break the Hormuz blockade” and expanded its operations to include supply vessels, tugboats and small tankers in the Gulf.
The IRGC also claimed that some targeted vessels were damaged by explosions after striking naval mines while sailing “illegally” through routes it considered “unsafe.”
Tehran says the escalation in its operations against shipping is a response to a “US naval blockade,” while warning vessels against using routes it has not approved or crossing the area after switching off navigation and identification systems.
Since April, Iran has imposed restrictions on maritime traffic through the Strait of Hormuz, including designated transit routes and a requirement for prior coordination with the IRGC Navy.
On May 30, Tehran announced that vessels passing through the strait would be required to obtain prior authorization from the IRGC Navy, warning that transit without permission would constitute a “security threat.”
The developments come amid continued tensions between Iran and the US over navigation through the Strait of Hormuz, one of the world’s most important strategic routes for energy and commodity supplies and a key issue in negotiations between the two sides.
The war began with US and Israeli attacks on Iran on Feb. 28, before a ceasefire was reached in April. Clashes between Washington and Tehran later resumed as negotiations stalled despite the two sides signing a memorandum of understanding in June.

Greta Thunberg joins French school protests as Paris warns of Israeli influence campaign
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
15:17:11 UTC
00:17:11 KST

Swedish activist Greta Thunberg, who rose to prominence as an environmental campaigner before expanding her activism to other causes associated with Europe's political left, including strongly anti-Israel positions, joined student protesters in France on Tuesday as demonstrations that began in mid-September entered their fourth week. Dozens of schools have been set on fire during the unrest, and more than 6,800 people, most of them teenagers, have been arrested.
Wearing a Palestinian keffiyeh, as she frequently does, Thunberg joined demonstrators outside a high school in a working-class suburb of Paris ahead of another day of protests over what students describe as deteriorating conditions in French schools.
The nationwide protest movement is led primarily by students from working-class and immigrant neighborhoods, who accuse the government of neglecting their schools, leaving them with overcrowded classrooms, teacher shortages and poor sanitation.
Over the past two weeks, students have repeatedly blocked school entrances, frequently clashing with police. Officers have used stun grenades and tear gas, while protesters have thrown stones, bottles and other objects.
More than 1,000 police officers, educators and students have been injured in the unrest. Several protesters have suffered serious injuries, including a teenager who lost sight in one eye after being struck by a rubber bullet and another whose hand was amputated after he picked up a police stun grenade.
Protesters, their parents and supporters have accused police of using disproportionate force. Opponents of the demonstrations, however, argue that the unrest is not a genuine protest over school conditions but a political show of force by the left, particularly given the explicit support protesters have received from Jean-Luc Mélenchon's radical-left party, La France Insoumise (LFI), or France Unbowed.
Some critics portray the protesters as immigrants and members of minority communities, including Muslims, challenging public order and the French state. They accuse Mélenchon and his allies of deliberately fomenting chaos ahead of next year's presidential election, in which polls suggest he will reach the decisive second round before losing to far-right leader Marine Le Pen.
Students gathered again Tuesday morning outside several schools in Paris and other French cities, carrying placards and megaphones.
Thunberg arrived at Lycée Paul Éluard in Saint-Denis, a suburb north of Paris and one of the schools where the protest movement initially gained momentum. "We are inspired by young people demanding their fundamental rights," she told reporters outside the school. "Whether it is inadequate funding for schools, the climate crisis or crises of social injustice, it is time for young people to take the initiative and reclaim their future."
Large crowds also marched Tuesday in Nantes in western France, Strasbourg in the east and Marseille in the south. Some demonstrators carried signs reading, "Tear gas doesn't make us cry as much as the state of the national education system." French broadcaster BFM TV aired footage showing clashes between black-clad individuals and police in Strasbourg and Nantes, with clouds of tear gas filling some streets.
In the Paris area, teenagers blocked entrances to several schools before dawn. In Marseille, students slowly pushed large wheeled garbage containers into position outside their high school, blocking access.
In Lyon, local authorities asked organizers to cancel a march after a group of what they described as "hostile individuals" moved ahead of the main procession, vandalized shops and a gas station, and clashed with police.
Authorities did not identify those involved. However, French street demonstrations are often joined by individuals known as "casseurs," rioters who seek confrontations with police and engage in property destruction.
France's Education Ministry said 214 schools remained closed Tuesday because of the protests, down from 800 during last Tuesday's main day of demonstrations. According to the ministry, 94.2% of high schools were open.
The cash-strapped French government has promised to address students' concerns, but its room for maneuver is limited as worries over the national debt and budget deficit have driven government borrowing costs to their highest level in years.
In response to allegations of excessive police force, the government suspended police use of stun grenades last week. The move, however, did little to calm the political dispute.
"Police officers are running out of breath chasing young people to beat and injure them," Mélenchon wrote Tuesday in a social media post. "The only ones who are not running out of breath are the young people protesting courageously."
Mélenchon accused the media of failing to fulfill its responsibilities by allegedly not showing the true extent of police violence. He again called on adults to stand alongside the students and protect them.
Le Pen, who leads the presidential race according to polls, condemned violence by protesters and called for those responsible for vandalizing schools, or their parents if they are minors, to pay for repairs. The government has already introduced legislation that would allow such payments to be required, and the bill is currently making its way through parliament.
Meanwhile, French Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot warned Tuesday that foreign actors were attempting to interfere in France's presidential election, scheduled for April and May next year, specifically mentioning billionaire Elon Musk and an "Israeli company."
Barrot warned that foreign actors were "exploiting our divisions" and cynically using immigration, secularism and the Israeli-Palestinian conflict as weapons to inflame hatred and tensions. He specifically cited an Israeli company that he said had created fake French social media accounts "to stage artificial confrontations around the Palestinian issue."
Barrot appeared to be referring to the Israeli company BlackCore, which French authorities accused in June of operating fake accounts to conduct a smear campaign against candidates from Mélenchon's party during municipal elections held in March. France also sought Israel's assistance at the time in investigating the matter.
Barrot additionally denounced what he described as "extensive online harassment campaigns by Elon Musk against European leaders," aimed at influencing national debates by exploiting the viral reach of his social media platform.
Musk has publicly supported far-right political forces in Europe, including Germany's Alternative for Germany (AfD) party, and has sharply criticized European governments over their permissive immigration policies.
In his warning Tuesday, Barrot also condemned what he described as the exploitation of France's student protests by "hostile narratives originating in Russia and China, as well as Iran and the MAGA movement."
His reference to President Donald Trump's MAGA movement appeared to be an indirect criticism of the U.S. president, who commented on the French student demonstrations last week on his Truth Social platform.
"What is happening in France is nothing but mass immigration that has gotten completely out of control," Trump wrote. "This has nothing to do with schools. It is about Islam trying to take over a country that was once great!"
Addressing the alleged attempts at foreign interference, Barrot said: "We see them, we denounce them, and we stop them with zero tolerance." "We will not tolerate any foreign interference, no matter where it comes from. This is a matter of sovereignty."

King Felipe VI says Ceuta is ‘inalienable’ part of Spain in landmark visit
King Felipe VI and Queen Letizia visited Ceuta on Tuesday for the first time in 14 years, with the monarch reaffirming Spain’s sovereignty over the North African enclaves claimed by Morocco. The landmark visit comes amid strained relations with Rabat and the aftermath of a mass migrant influx that saw makeshift camps cleared ahead of the royals’ arrival.
Cheering crowds waving Spanish flags filled Ceuta on Tuesday as King Felipe VI and Queen Letizia made a diplomatically sensitive visit to the city following July's migrant influx from Morocco.
Their trip is the first royal visit since 2007, when a diplomatic crisis erupted with neighbouring Morocco, which claims sovereignty over Ceuta and Spain's other North African territory of Melilla.
Addressing civilians in Ceuta, the king said Morocco's relationship to Spain and the EU must be grounded in respect, "while always adhering to the principle that Ceuta is Spain; Ceuta is Europe."
"Ceuta and Melilla are an inalienable part of the political and national reality that is Spain. The sovereignty and territorial integrity of our country are not negotiable," Felipe said.
To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.
More than 70,000 migrants streamed into the small city of around 80,000 inhabitants in an unprecedented surge on July 30-31. Scores died.
Most returned to Morocco in the following hours, but thousands have remained for weeks in often dire conditions, sleeping rough in the streets or on the beach.
The crisis has angered locals and damaged Socialist Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez before a November 29 general election in which migration will feature prominently.
Felipe and Letizia greeted the well-wishers who thronged the streets, stopping to shake hands and exchange words with them en route to the city hall to meet local authorities.
Read more‘We won’t go back’: Young Moroccan migrants in Ceuta refuse to abandon their European dream
People raised their phones to take pictures of the royal couple, while some wore T-shirts bearing the slogan "Ceuta is not for sale. Ceuta must be defended".
Cristina Carrasco, a 50-year-old civil servant who waited all morning to see the royals, told AFP "it was a pleasure and a source of pride" to have shaken hands with Felipe.
"We all told him, 'don't forget us,' and he said, 'no, we won't forget you,'" recounted Carrasco, who felt "grateful and proud" about a visit that "we deserved".
Retiree Silvia Salmeron, 71, said the visit "was a breath of fresh air. I got goosebumps".
'Pressure cooker'
At the city hall, Ceuta's leader Juan Jesus Vivas thanked Felipe and Letizia for coming in "the most difficult moment of our recent history".
Ceuta is "a pressure cooker that could explode at any time", he said.
The authorities have set up thousands of places in temporary shelters and cleared the main camps on the beaches, but some migrants continue to live on the surrounding hills and the streets.
Read moreLast Ceuta migrant camp removed ahead of Spanish king's visit
Ana Maria Diaz, a 69-year-old pensioner, said the king should have come earlier to see the makeshift migrant encampments and visit the outlying areas of Ceuta where they concentrate.
"You don't see it here but if you go to the outlying neighbourhoods... it's terrible," Diaz, who was holding a Spanish flag, told AFP.
The government insists it must respect international law by assessing whether the migrants are entitled to asylum, while hundreds of unaccompanied children cannot be summarily deported.
The royals will visit a cemetery where they will pay tribute to the migrants who died – most by drowning as they tried to swim around a border barrier.
Felipe is also due to make a speech during a meeting with members of Ceuta's civil society before the monarchs travel to Melilla on Wednesday.
Diplomatic risks
The visit comes at a particularly sensitive time for Spain's historically delicate relations with Morocco, as rumours swirl over the potential role Rabat may have played in the July rush.
Read more'No facts': Morocco denies involvement in deadly Ceuta migrant rush
The Spanish right has accused Morocco of orchestrating it for political motives, which Rabat and Sanchez have denied.
Moroccan King Mohammed VI broke his silence on Friday, condemning "the irresponsible statements made by certain political and media circles and their blatant instrumentalisation of the situation", in apparent reference to Spanish criticism.
On Monday, newspaper El Pais reported that Moroccan warships repeatedly entered Ceuta's waters during and after the rush in a rare violation of Spanish sovereignty.
Spanish government spokeswoman Elma Saiz confirmed but played down the report on Tuesday, speaking of "a one-off incident that was resolved in a completely normal manner".

Omair Ahmad on Love, Loss and the Lingering Spirit of Lucknow
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
15:14:46 UTC
00:14:46 KST

Omair Ahmad is the author of ‘Encounters’, ‘The Storyteller's Tale’, ‘Tall Tales by a Small Dog’, ‘The Kingdom at the Centre of the World: Journeys Into Bhutan’ and ‘Jimmy, The Terrorist’, which won the Crossword Award for Fiction and was shortlisted for the Man Asian Literary Prize. He is also a prominent columnist and a political and social commentator. In this conversation, he discusses his latest novel, ‘Homecoming’. Excerpts:Q: How did this book come about? A: The genesis of this was when I was in DC. I just finished my second master's and I was missing home. Being a brown guy with a Muslim name in America, just when the war on terror was at its apogee leaves you a little off the place. And I hadn't been able to travel home since I’d gone, which was in 2001. So I met this person, a friend, and she invited me to a book club and everyone was writing little bits and they asked me to write something. And so I wrote the beginning of this novella, which is no longer the beginning. Much has changed, everything has changed. But there is a strong emotion behind it and I think that has carried through even now... My wife says it's about love, loss and Lucknow. I've gone very much for mood and the feel of a place.
So there's a bit of history, there's. But it's largely about people. So there's characters I've known, characters I've imagined, bits of stories that I've heard about Lucknow. Q: It is a form of storytelling which is disappearing as we are moving more and more into very nuclear and urban families. A: This was one of those things that I really struggled with. The novel as a form is very much a product of the European enlightenment pathway. It has the individual at the centre... If you pick up most novels, it's a very narrow thing of who they are. But for me, as a product of this country, of this culture, I always wanted to know what's behind them. Because we always understand people as being part of this family, this mahalla, this web of relationships. No person just is a person standing on their own... They are so much more than a person. They're also part of the past. They're also part of the relationship in their environments... The idea of the novel as a European construct and the way that we communicate is sometimes different, and we think that that's wrong. But I think one of the things which I have improved on is I'm no longer very apologetic about that. This is who I am. This is who we are. This is how we tell our stories... We are multilingual people. We talk in lots of languages. Even like, say, the Urdu or Hindi that I use at home and on the street and with elders versus young. These are all almost different languages. The way we use them, trying to transpose that into any language.. you're really struggling, because the forms aren't there. There's no correct way to go about it... I know that while I'm writing in English, I'm not necessarily thinking in English when I'm writing. And I'm writing about people who will be only partially thinking in English, if at all, or speaking in it. And so it's guesswork. It's just trying to bully my way through somehow to make this language work like that.
Q: There's a sentence you use: Memories are such flimsy things. A: Things are clearer in our memories than they were in real life. And if you ever had an argument with anybody, you know this true. Because in your memory, your argument is very clear. And in their memory, the argument is very clear. The reality is it was never clear. It was always messy.
But there is truth there. And memory is important for us, especially as a country where so much of our history is actually oral history. And so much of our history has been badly reinterpreted by colonial administrators for their own design, and that we have swallowed wholesale. And then we spend our whole time... like how you take fish bones out once you've taken a bite... But I struggle with this because I don't know what is true in all of this. And I wanted to register that little thing that, yes, we think our memories are clearer than what is recorded, but should we be that trusting of our own memories or other people's memories as well?

US ambassador to Greece resigns amid misconduct allegations
Kimberly Guilfoyle has faced mounting allegations, including offering access to Trump officials in exchange for money.
United States President Donald Trump’s Ambassador to Greece, Kimberley Guilfoyle, has resigned following a series of allegations of misconduct, including claims that she offered a political donor access to senior administration officials in exchange for money.
“We have asked ambassador Guilfoyle to resign,” White House press secretary Katie Zacharia told reporters earlier on Tuesday. “She has been a wonderful asset to the team, and we wish her well.”
The announcement comes after weeks of damaging reports about Guilfoyle’s conduct.
Shortly after Zacharia’s comments, Guilfoyle posted on social media that she was resigning.
“While my time as Ambassador may be coming to an end, my commitment to President Trump, the America First movement, and the country I love will never end,” she wrote.
She also denied the allegations against her.
“These allegations are false, and I intend to vigorously defend my name, my reputation, and my integrity,” she said.
According to The Wall Street Journal, Guilfoyle asked a Trump donor to cover a $100,000 credit card bill shortly before her congressional confirmation hearing, promising him access to administration officials in return.
The newspaper also reported that she told guests at a reception that she could use US influence to undermine the Greek government, promoted the interests of a Greek construction and energy company, and allowed one of its lobbyists to attend private diplomatic meetings.
Guilfoyle’s lawyers have said the money she sought was payment for previous speaking engagements and public appearances that she had not received.
Trump had signalled on Monday that he was considering removing her from the post.
“Well, we’re looking at it,” he told reporters. “We’re not happy.”
Secretary of State Marco Rubio initially defended Guilfoyle, calling her a “strong ambassador,” but later declined to comment on the allegations and criticised reporters for asking about them.
Guilfoyle is a former Fox News host and California prosecutor. She is the former wife of California Governor Gavin Newsom and was previously engaged to Trump’s eldest son, Donald Trump Jr.

Did Ukrainian strikes on Russian datacentres reduce online disinformation?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
15:13:26 UTC
00:13:26 KST

Did Ukrainian strikes on Russian datacentres reduce online disinformation?
While some viral online graphs suggest less bot activity, Zelenskyy’s claims of improved social media discourse do not entirely pass muster
Over the weekend, Ukraine carried out at least three airstrikes on datacentres belonging to the Russian search engine company Yandex. Reports suggest at least two of these datacentres took significant damage, with Telegram footage appearing to show one on fire. Yandex acknowledged the strikes, and Russian media reported that several websites appeared affected by the downed datacentres.
On Monday, Volodymyr Zelenskyy suggested the strikes had dampened Russia’s massive disinformation operation, saying: “It suddenly became a little easier to breathe on many social platforms. There was less hate, less division and fewer provocations.”
It is a commendable hope, but experts say the Ukrainian president may have overstated his case.
Did Ukraine’s strikes lead to a decline in Russian disinformation?
Probably not. While a few graphs went viral on social media suggesting there had been a big decline in activity from Yandex bots, those graphs are unrelated to Russian disinformation.
“Our platforms are still monitoring Russian social networks across the world and there is no discernible change in their posting patterns,” said Amil Khan, the chief executive of Valent, a tech startup that tracks disinformation.
Khan and his team track about 40 disinformation networks around the world, from the UK to Australia to Syria, and monitor what narratives they put out and how publics respond to them. They have seen no drop in the volume of posts from these networks, saying: “Yandex datacentres have no practical connection to social media bot farms.”
So what exactly did happen?
Yandex is a search engine which also hosts websites and bots. Data from Cloudflare, which monitors worldwide internet traffic, shows a marked decline in activity from bots associated with the Yandex network on 8 October and 11 October, corresponding to the dates of two of the strikes.
The independent Russian news outlet Meduza reports that a number of websites in Russia are down: major banks, retailers, sports apps and Yandex’s services such as Yandex Go and Yandex Eats. It suggests the damage took out a large part of Yandex’s operation and could take months to fully repair.
Some online commentators have mistaken the Cloudflare data to mean that the decline in bot activity has led to a major drop in disinformation on social media. But this is not what experts have noticed.
What are these different kinds of bots?
“The term ‘bot’ can mean many different things,” said Michał ‘Rysiek’ Woźniak, an internet infrastructure expert. “When Cloudflare data shows a precipitous drop in ‘bot’ traffic, that does not mean ‘automated social media troll accounts’, it means ‘software that makes automated web requests on a large scale.’” What Cloudflare picked up was a decline in activity from Yandex’s web crawlers. These are used by search engines to index websites and help users to find them, said Khan.
State-sponsored disinformation networks – the kind of “bots” a lot of people misinterpreted this as – could still be affected by the strikes, said Woźniak. “But those effects are going to be much more indirect.”
Those networks are far more distributed, and more resilient, said Ned Mendez, the head of research at Alliance4Europe. “Platforms will routinely flag traffic from datacentres as likely automated, so serious bot operations run more through distributed methods, such as residential connections and phone farms, that airstrikes can’t really knock out.”
So how could Ukraine disrupt Russian disinformation in Europe?
“We can’t simply bomb the bots out of existence, however appealing that might sound,” said Mendez. “They aren’t really a single set of buildings that can be switched off.”
Khan said the Ukrainians could consider taking action against companies such as the Internet Research Agency, Yevgeny Prigozhin’s Wagner-linked troll farm that was engaged in influence operations until 2023. But another tactic could be to work with Europe to disrupt the supply chain and recruitment pipeline of private sector contractors used by the Kremlin.
Another tactic could be to pressure big social media companies to moderate disinformation on their platforms. Khan’s team has successfully worked with Meta to tamp down on inflammatory content in Sudan.
But, said Khan, the Trump administration would probably push back on this, hard. “I can see why blowing up datacentres is an easier option.”

Lassa fever kills 268, spreads to 119 local governments in 24 Nigerian states
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
15:10:38 UTC
00:10:38 KST

Kabir Adeniyi
13 October 2026•Update: 13 October 2026
Nigeria has recorded 268 deaths from Lassa fever, with 1,138 confirmed cases reported in 24 states and 119 local government areas in 2026, according to the Nigeria Centre for Disease Control and Prevention (NCDC) on Tuesday.
The figures were contained in the agency’s latest situation report covering Sept. 28 to Oct. 4, corresponding to epidemiological week 40. The case fatality rate stood at 23.6%, compared to 18.6% during the corresponding period in 2025.
The NCDC said confirmed cases increased from 924 during the same period in 2025 to 1,138 in 2026, while deaths rose from 172 to 268.
Nigeria recorded 8,414 suspected cases during the first 40 weeks of the year, compared to 8,041 in the corresponding period last year.
Despite the rise in cumulative infections and deaths, new confirmed cases declined to three in week 40, down from 13 in the preceding week. The latest cases were reported in Bauchi and Benue states, with one death recorded during the week.
Five states: Ondo, Bauchi, Taraba, Edo and Benue accounted for 88% of confirmed cases recorded in 2026. Ondo had the largest share, at 36%, followed by Bauchi with 23%, Taraba with 12%, Edo with 11% and Benue with 6%, according to the NCDC.
The agency attributed the high fatality rate partly to late presentation at health facilities, high treatment costs and poor health-seeking behavior in affected communities.
Lassa fever is an acute viral illness primarily transmitted to humans through contact with food or household items contaminated by infected rodents. Human-to-human transmission can also occur through contact with infected bodily fluids, particularly in health care settings without adequate infection-prevention measures.
The NCDC has urged residents to keep their surroundings clean, store food in covered containers and dispose of waste properly to reduce contact with rodents. It also advises those experiencing symptoms such as fever, weakness or headache to seek medical attention promptly.
