Karnataka sets 2030 goal to strengthen disaster prevention and resilience
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
15:09:51 UTC
00:09:51 KST

Karnataka deputy chief minister G Parameshwara announced a 2030 target for the state to emerge as a national leader in disaster prevention and preparedness.
Karnataka deputy chief minister G Parameshwara on Tuesday announced a 2030 target for the state to emerge as a national leader in disaster prevention and preparedness, stressing the need to make risk reduction an integral part of governance and development planning.Speaking at the inaugural meeting of the state platform for disaster risk reduction, held on the International day for disaster risk reduction, he said preventing disasters, safeguarding livelihoods and building long-term resilience must be key priorities for the state.Parameshwara said development should not be judged merely by investment, infrastructure creation or economic growth, but also by the extent to which people's lives and livelihoods are protected. Floods, droughts and landslides can wipe out homes, agricultural produce and livelihoods built over many years, he pointed out.“For a government, a disaster may be an administrative emergency. For an affected family, it can mean a lifetime of hardship,” he said, calling for a shift from post-disaster relief and rehabilitation towards preventing avoidable damage and loss.
Focus on risk assessment and resilient infrastructure
Referring to the United Nations' sendai framework for disaster risk reduction 2015-2030, Parameshwara said Karnataka must improve risk assessment, early warning mechanisms, disaster preparedness and investment in resilient infrastructure.
He noted that the state faces multiple hazards, including droughts, floods, landslides across the Western Ghats and threats to coastal communities. Rapid urbanisation, changing land-use patterns and growing pressure on natural drainage systems have further heightened disaster risks, he added.The deputy chief minister called for comprehensive disaster risk assessments of major public infrastructure projects. He urged government departments to identify vulnerable assets and incorporate risk-reduction measures into their annual plans and budgets.He said the revenue department, working through the Karnataka state disaster management authority and district administrations, should strengthen disaster planning, vulnerability assessments, coordination of early warnings and measures to protect livelihoods.
Departments urged to strengthen coordination
Emphasising the need for coordinated action across departments, Parameshwara said the urban development department should prioritise flood prevention and drainage management, while the rural development department must improve disaster preparedness at the village level.The agriculture, education and health departments, he said, should focus on protecting farmers, schools, hospitals and essential services during emergencies.He also called for wider adoption of technology, including satellite imagery, geospatial data, artificial intelligence and predictive analytics, to strengthen risk assessment and improve early warning systems.Merely issuing alerts would not be enough, he said, emphasising that warnings must reach vulnerable communities in time for people to take appropriate protective measures.Parameshwara advocated a people-centred disaster preparedness network linking scientific institutions, district administrations, gram panchayats and households.He stressed the importance of developing local preparedness plans, building community volunteer networks, identifying safe shelters and evacuation routes, and conducting regular mock drills, particularly in areas prone to disasters.
Children, senior citizens, persons with disabilities and economically vulnerable households must receive special attention in disaster planning, he added.
Livelihood protection to remain a priority
Highlighting the economic consequences of disasters, Parameshwara said disaster management efforts must account for the losses suffered by farmers, fishermen, small traders and daily-wage workers, rather than focusing only on damage to physical infrastructure.He said the Karnataka state disaster risk reduction roadmap 2025-2030 must be implemented through measurable targets, time-bound action plans, clearly assigned responsibilities for departments and regular monitoring.The state platform for disaster risk reduction, he added, should concentrate on tangible improvements, including stronger infrastructure, uninterrupted essential services and timely assistance for families affected by disasters.

Ukraine Trains With SeaFox Underwater Drones for the Black Sea Mine-Clearing Mission Ahead
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
15:09:20 UTC
00:09:20 KST

- Category
- War in Ukraine
Ukraine Trains With SeaFox Underwater Drones for the Black Sea Mine-Clearing Mission Ahead
Ukrainian naval crews have practiced locating and destroying sea mines with SeaFox underwater drones during training in the United Kingdom, preparing for the enormous mine-clearing effort that could continue in the Black Sea for years after active fighting ends, BFBS Forces News reported on October 12.
The drills took place under Operation Interflex Maritime, with British mine-warfare specialists evaluating crews from Ukraine’s Sandown-class mine countermeasure vessels. Forces News journalists observed the training aboard the Ukrainian minehunter Cherkasy.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
During the exercise, sailors first deployed the reconnaissance version of SeaFox, equipped with a camera and sonar. The remotely operated vehicle searched the seabed and located a training mine roughly the size of a barrel that had been placed by British personnel.
After confirming the target’s position, the crew used a training version of the drone to rehearse the destruction procedure without explosives.
In the final phase, sailors launched the combat SeaFox C, which carries an explosive charge of about 1.5 kilograms. The drone was remotely guided toward the practice mine and detonated alongside it.
SeaFox is a family of remotely operated underwater vehicles developed by Germany’s Atlas Elektronik for detecting, identifying, and neutralizing naval mines.
The system uses sonar and a video camera to inspect underwater objects, while operators control it through a fiber-optic cable.
The vehicle is roughly 1.3 meters long, weighs about 40 kilograms, and can operate at depths of up to 300 meters.
The SeaFox I reconnaissance version is reusable, allowing crews to inspect and classify suspected mines, while the SeaFox C is an expendable system that destroys both itself and the target when its explosive charge detonates.
The training is part of a broader effort to prepare Ukraine’s Navy for postwar Black Sea mine clearance. Russian and Ukrainian mine warfare, drifting mines, and unexploded ordnance have created a threat to commercial shipping and coastal waters that is expected to persist well beyond the end of active hostilities.
Earlier, the Ukrainian Navy earned NATO-certified authority to command multinational mine countermeasure forces for the first time in its history, marking a major step in its operational integration with the Alliance.

Türkiye and the European Union must act with a shared understanding of competitiveness and economic security amid global trade turbulence, Turkish Trade Minister Omer Bolat said Tuesday. 
In a post on Turkish social media platform NSosyal following a Türkiye-EU Business Summit in Brussels, Bolat said he addressed business leaders alongside EU Commissioner for Trade and Economic Security Maros Sefcovic at the event, which drew broad participation from Turkish and EU business circles. 
Bolat said bilateral trade exceeding $233 billion and European capital accounting for approximately 70% of foreign direct investment in Türkiye showed the depth of their economic partnership and mutual interdependence. 
He said Sefcovic stressed the strategic importance of Türkiye-EU economic and trade relations and highlighted the key role of the High-Level Trade Dialogue mechanism in advancing those ties. 
Bolat stressed that the EU's new industrial and competitiveness policies should take into account the strong production and supply chains established through the Customs Union. 
"Türkiye is not only an important trading partner for Europe; it is also a strong production base, a reliable supply chain partner, and a strategic partner in global competition," he said. 
Türkiye's potential to strengthen Europe's industrial capacity, supply security, and competitiveness in global markets is becoming increasingly important, Bolat added. 
Deepening economic relations on the basis of existing achievements would therefore serve both sides' long-term interests, he said. 
Bolat reaffirmed their determination to strengthen cooperation in the green and digital transitions, make more effective use of the opportunities offered by the Customs Union, and reinforce ties between their business communities to boost joint competitiveness and bilateral trade. 
He also said the Century of Türkiye vision, pursued under President Recep Tayyip Erdogan's leadership, aims to expand the country's production, export, investment, and technological capabilities while strengthening its position in the global economy. 
Türkiye will continue working to advance its role in international trade by drawing on its strategic location, industrial infrastructure, skilled workforce, and manufacturing capabilities, he added. 
'Solution should not be to exclude trusted partners' 
In his speech at the Türkiye-EU Business Summit, Bolat called on the European Union to include Türkiye as a trusted partner in its proposed "Made in EU" initiative, warning that excluding the country from the bloc's industrial framework would undermine decades of economic integration and established supply chains. 
"We respect the (EU’s) ideal Industrial Accelerator Act, which is normal, and we suffer from the same grave concerns about huge imports from third countries. But the solution should not be to exclude trusted partners or Customs Union," he said. 
"The solution which we strongly request and expect from our member countries, European Parliament and European Commission and EU Council of Ministers, is that Türkiye should be a trusted partner with the 'Made with Europe' project," Bolat said, adding that Türkiye is working closely with its European counterparts on the issue.
He stressed that Türkiye's inclusion would serve the interests of both sides, particularly their auto, ye industries and wider manufacturing sectors, given the deep integration of their economies. 
Bolat added that high-level trade dialogue last year had already helped reduce the number of outstanding trade-related issues within the Customs Union from 29 to 14, with further progress expected. 
Visa difficulties 
Bolat also said Turkish citizens continue to face difficulties obtaining visas despite Türkiye's status as an EU candidate country and its longstanding institutional ties with the bloc. 
He acknowledged that recent European Commission measures had eased visa procedures somewhat, but said significant obstacles remain.
Procedures were eased, “but not enough," he said, referring to the difficulties faced by Turkish businesspeople, academics, transport operators, and students.
He stressed that visa-related barriers are incompatible with the objective of strengthening ties between Türkiye and the EU, while welcoming what he described as the constructive and sincere approach of European counterparts.

Poland Uncovers Suspected Foreign Intelligence Operation Behind Attack on Starlink Station
Polish and German authorities have detained two additional suspects over the September arson attack on a Starlink ground station in central Poland that helps provide internet connectivity to Ukraine.
RMF24 reported the arrests on October 13, citing its investigative reporter Krzysztof Zasada. One suspect is a woman detained in Berlin during a separate counterterrorism operation, while the fourth suspect is a man also held by German authorities.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Investigators suspect the woman provided logistical support for the sabotage operation and may have driven two Turkish nationals previously accused of carrying out the attack. Polish prosecutors are assessing her exact role before deciding whether to seek her extradition.

Polish authorities previously identified two Turkish citizens as the suspected perpetrators of the arson. German officers detained them at Poland's request, and they are awaiting extradition proceedings. Investigators believe the two acted on behalf of a foreign intelligence service in Germany.
The September 23 fire struck a Starlink ground station in Wola Krobowska in Poland's Mazovia region. Two days later, prosecutors opened an investigation into suspected sabotage and a terrorism-related offense committed on behalf of a foreign intelligence service.
The facility is operated by the state-owned telecommunications company Exatel and forms part of the infrastructure that carries internet traffic through Poland to Ukraine.
The latest arrests expand the investigation beyond the suspected arsonists to the logistical network that may have supported the operation. Polish authorities were also expected on October 13 to decide further steps concerning the extradition of the two Turkish suspects already detained in Germany.
Polish prosecutors suspect the Starlink station arson was orchestrated by Russian intelligence services as part of an operation targeting satellite communications infrastructure supporting Ukraine.
In a statement issued on September 25, Poland's National Prosecutor's Office confirmed there were reasonable grounds to suspect that the perpetrators had acted on orders from Russian intelligence agencies.
Investigators believe the operation was intended to disrupt Starlink internet traffic and communications in Poland and other Central and Eastern European countries. The investigation involves Poland's Internal Security Agency and Central Bureau of Investigation. The suspected Russian involvement remains under investigation.
The arson came amid mounting concern over suspected Russian sabotage and other hybrid threats targeting critical infrastructure across Europe.
Investigators suspect the perpetrators acted on orders from Russian special services, aiming to disrupt Starlink connectivity in Poland and other Central and Eastern European countries.
A week before the attack, on September 16, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen proposed a NATO-style counter-hybrid mechanism for the EU. Under the plan, any member state facing sabotage, drone incursions or other non-military aggression could request emergency talks to coordinate a joint response.

‘Shocking and sobering’: UK bird populations fall to lowest level on record
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
15:08:25 UTC
00:08:25 KST

Wild bird populations in the UK have fallen to their lowest level since records began, figures show, with nearly half of species in decline.
Figures produced by leading nature conservation bodies for the government show that average populations across 132 native breeding species fell by 19% between 1970 and 2025, with farmland birds and seabirds the worst hit in recent years.
Prof Richard Gregory, the head of monitoring at the RSPB, called the overall findings “shocking and sobering”.
“Birds are indicators of the way we’re looking after the countryside and the world around us,” he said. “We’re losing the birds that people are so emotionally connected to and want to protect.”
Average populations of turtle doves have fallen by more than half in five years, showing no sign of the bird recovering from the brink of extinction. Tree sparrows, wood warblers and capercaillie were among the birds with the next biggest average annual decreases between 2019 and 2024.
Swifts, whose arrival for many marks the beginning of summer, have declined by about 25% in five years, an average of nearly 6% a year across the UK. Bullfinches fell at a similar rate nationally, and by an average of 11% a year in England.
Of the 132 native breeding species tracked, 45% have declined over the past five years, while just 27% have increased. In England, 55% of monitored species have declined.
Seabirds are the worst hit group, down by more than a fifth over the past five years. Dr Ailidh Barnes, who helps build the index at the British Trust for Ornithology, said avian flu had “decimated” species such as Arctic skuas and terns.
The disease spread quickly, she said, because seabirds nested shoulder to shoulder, and each year a different species appeared to suffer. “There’s a lag of data collection and then data analysis, and now we’re actually seeing that effect coming through,” she said.
Farmland bird populations have decreased by 63% since 1970 and 12% since 2020. Defra attributes the long-term decline to changes in farming since the 1950s, including the loss of mixed farming (crops and livestock), increased pesticide and fertiliser use, and the removal of hedgerows.
Gregory said if the trend continued, the songs of farm birds such as skylarks and yellowhammers would become only “memories” of what the countryside used to be like.
“It’s a familiar story of declining farmland [birds],” he added. “That’s not showing any upturn. We need to do more there to get nature-friendly farming right and help support farmers.”
Despite the general decline, some populations are booming. Red kite populations have risen by 48% since 2019, and firecrests are up 300% over the same period. Gregory also highlighted the number of cranes “really coming back from extinction in the UK”, rising to 87 pairs nationally.
Gregory said these examples proved concerted efforts to save species worked. “We know the main drivers of change and we can bring about recovery, but we need to massively scale up our conservation intervention,” he said. “We need more funding to support these conservation measures and they need to be at a larger spatial scale.”
A Defra spokesperson said: “We are committed to the recovery and protection of our native birds. There are multiple pressures on wild bird populations, including avian flu. We are acting to protect them, from supporting farmers to manage their land in a way that benefits farmland birds, to working with fishers to prevent the accidental catch of seabirds.”

Russia funnels nearly half its budget into defence, cutting social spending
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
15:05:02 UTC
00:05:02 KST

Russia’s 2027 draft budget allocates a record share to defence and security, as regions quietly divert funds for foster children and orphans to war payments and “coffin money” for soldiers’ families is cut by up to 95% in some areas.
Russia's parliament will vote later this month on a budget that allocates a record 44% of federal spending to defence and security — double the share for social programmes — as the Kremlin presses ahead with a fifth year of all-out war in Ukraine.
The State Duma, Russia's lower house of parliament, is due to begin examining the 2027–2029 draft on 22 October.
President Vladimir Putin's United Russia party won an absolute constitutional majority in September's parliamentary elections, making major amendments unlikely before it passes.
Military expenditure this year has reached 17 trillion roubles (€181 billion) against the 12.1 trillion (€129 billion) originally budgeted, showing the escalating cost of the full-scale invasion Russia launched against Ukraine in February 2022. Defence and security's 44% share of the 2027 budget is the highest on record.
The Finance Ministry's draft lists "fulfilling social obligations to citizens" as its top priority. The figures tell a different story. Social policy spending will fall 7% in 2027, from 7.1 trillion roubles (€76 billion) to 6.65 trillion (€71 billion), covering pensions, payments to veterans, maternity benefits and other support.
The government has pledged to index these payments against inflation. Russia's official inflation rate has exceeded 8% for much of the past two years, and independent economists put the real figure higher.
The Kremlin has announced a 10 trillion rouble (€107 billion) "children's budget" over the next three years, covering maternity payments, child benefits, and housing programmes. The ratio of those funds to defence spending is one to five.
Federal payments to servicemen and their families fall under the "national defence" section, whose spending will rise by roughly a quarter next year.
War at the expense of orphans and the poor
The federal budget is not the only source of pressure on social spending. Russia's regions partly fund war-related payments, many of which are already running deficits, forcing local authorities to cut civilian budgets.
In late September the Arkhangelsk region redirected more than 63 million roubles originally earmarked for social support — two-thirds from payments to foster parents, the rest from support for large families — to one-off war payments and death compensation.
A few days earlier the Tula region cut 54 million roubles from spending on foster children, low-income households, families with disabled children, housing repairs for orphans and support for labour veterans, redirecting the sum to servicemen's pay and compensation for the dead.
In St Petersburg, authorities have prepared a bill reducing spending on education, transport repairs and medical projects while increasing payments to servicemen.
'Coffin money' being cut
Regional lump-sum death payments — known informally as "coffin money" — have been cut across Russia since autumn of last year.
The payments are regional supplements to the federal one-time compensation paid to families of troops killed in action, and regions sharply raised them in 2022–2023 as they competed to attract recruits.
In Ulyanovsk region the payment stood at 1 million roubles (€10,700). By February it had been halved, then cut again to 50,000 roubles (€533).
In Bashkortostan, the initial 2 million roubles (€21,300) payment has fallen to no more than 100,000 (€1,100).
Kirov and Omsk regions have halved payments from 1 million to 500,000 roubles (€5,300). In Kemerovo the payment went down from 3 million to 1 million. In Saratov, families who received 1 million roubles until late September now receive a tenth of that.
The sums attracted fraud. In Primorsky Krai, a warrant officer was alleged to have arranged marriages between contract soldiers heading to the front and local women, with the compensation shared among participants if the men were killed.
In Khabarovsk, authorities detained six people in February on suspicion of orchestrating similar arrangements, using notarised powers of attorney to access soldiers’ bank accounts, with alleged damages reaching 2.4 million roubles (€25,600).
Some families receive nothing at all. Soldiers classified by the military as missing or as deserters rather than confirmed dead are ineligible for the one-time payment. Relatives of those killed say the designation is used to withhold compensation.
Healthcare insignificant
Healthcare spending will fall to 7 trillion roubles (€75 billion) next year, a 6.8% reduction according to calculations by independent Russian media, though the Finance Ministry disputes the figure.
Over the three-year period, healthcare will receive 28.6 trillion roubles (€305 billion) against 50 trillion roubles (€533 billion) for the military.
Funding for ambulance services has been cut by more than a quarter. The programme to build and repair outpatient clinics in the regions has been halved.
The national cancer programme will receive 3.9 billion roubles in 2027, down from 44.9 billion this year.

China builds a lighter cousin of the U.S. HIMARS
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
15:04:45 UTC
00:04:45 KST

- China has developed a light rocket launcher on an upgraded Dongfeng Mengshi MV3 truck with a modular 20-round pod for 122 mm rockets.
- The launcher can fire guided or unguided rockets out to a maximum range of 40 km.
China has developed a new light, highly mobile rocket launcher built on an upgraded version of the Dongfeng Mengshi MV3 tactical truck, carrying a 20-round launch pod that can fire guided or unguided 122 mm rockets out to 40 km (25 miles), according to images and details shared by Chinese military commentator DS北风 on X.
The launcher uses a modular, box-shaped launch pod mounted on the rear of the truck, a design that lets crews swap out a spent pod for a fresh one instead of reloading individual tubes.
The 20 rockets in each pod can be a mix of guided and unguided types, and the maximum range of 40 km puts it in the same class as the 122 mm rocket launchers that make up much of China’s tactical rocket artillery.
The Mengshi, built by Dongfeng Motor, is China’s equivalent of the Humvee, a four-wheel-drive tactical vehicle used across the People’s Liberation Army, and the MV3 is the third generation of the family. Putting a rocket launcher on a light truck lets airborne, air assault and light infantry units take their own rocket artillery into terrain where heavier trucks cannot go, and lets crews fire and move away quickly before enemy counterfire arrives.
The concept is similar to the U.S.-made HIMARS, which mounts a pod of six 227 mm GMLRS guided rockets on a five-ton truck and has been widely used in Ukraine. China’s new launcher carries more but smaller rockets with a shorter range, trading reach for volume of fire at shorter distances. The PLA already fields 122 mm rocket launchers on larger trucks and tracked vehicles, as well as the PHL-16, a long-range modular system that fires heavier rockets and missiles from interchangeable pods.

Despite being wounded by shrapnel, Yair Frankenthal used his first-aid training to help fellow students after an unexploded munition detonated near Israel's northern border. "I immediately began checking who needed medical attention," he recalled.
Frankenthal, 15, a youth volunteer with Magen David Adom (MDA), was among the students injured when an unexploded munition  detonated during a school hike on Ramim Ridge in northern Israel. Despite his own injuries, he continued helping his wounded classmates.
"I instructed my younger brother's friend, who was also on the trip and was injured by shrapnel, on how to treat himself so I could go and help those who were more seriously wounded," Frankenthal recalled.
"After I heard the loud explosion, I realized I had been injured too, but I immediately began checking who needed medical attention so I could use the knowledge I'd gained from the first-aid course I took as an MDA youth volunteer," he continued.
"The other boys called MDA's emergency hotline, and I began providing medical treatment to one of the boys who was very seriously injured. I noticed he had no pulse and wasn't breathing, so I performed CPR until the MDA first responder arrived."
Frankenthal said he sustained relatively minor injuries. "I was lightly injured by two pieces of shrapnel that penetrated my leg and shoulder. I'm feeling well, and I'm happy to be going home from the hospital today."
David Radko, a volunteer EMT with MDA's motorcycle response unit who also works as a teacher, described the events of Monday's deadly incident, in which ninth-grade student Yair Wilensky was killed.
"I immediately began triaging the casualties and stopping their bleeding. Despite the horrific scenes and the distress they were experiencing, the boys cooperated with me in an extraordinary way," he said. "Everyone tried to help their friends as much as they could. Some even applied tourniquets to their friends to stop the bleeding."
Radko, 29, a resident of Kiryat Shmona, was the first emergency responder to arrive at the scene. "I was returning from work when MDA's emergency dispatch center alerted me to the incident, and I immediately headed in that direction," he recalled.
"Reaching the injured was complicated because of the terrain, but I did everything I could to get there quickly. From the first glance, it was clear that this was a very serious scene. The injured were scattered along the route, some holding their wounded friends and trying to help them. Further along, I saw those who were more seriously injured."
For Radko, who teaches 10th grade, the incident was particularly difficult.
"This incident hits a very sensitive spot for me," he said. "I'm a 10th-grade homeroom teacher myself, and arriving at a scene like this makes you think of the injured boys as though they were your own students. And, of course, without even realizing it, I immediately put myself in the shoes of the teachers who were on that trip."
Throughout the incident, Radko remained in contact with MDA's emergency dispatch center, helping additional medical teams reach the location while continuing to treat the injured students.
He also praised the students who assisted him and their wounded friends. "I gave them instructions on how to help, and they listened and followed them," he said. "It was an extremely difficult and complex scene, and seeing injured children in that condition is never easy. We did everything we could to provide them with the best possible care."

New White House Press Secretary Katie Zacharia debuts in her first press conference - analysis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
15:01:59 UTC
00:01:59 KST

It took Katie Zacharia approximately 13 minutes to offer a first glimpse of how she intends to handle one of the most visible jobs in Washington.
Making her debut as White House press secretary on Tuesday morning, Zacharia praised President Donald Trump, called on just three reporters, delivered a significant announcement about the future of the US ambassador to Greece, and offered a brief, unexpectedly amusing glimpse of her nerves when she accidentally referred to her husband as "my president."
The new press secretary, who succeeded Karoline Leavitt, appeared visibly excited as she stepped up to the podium in the James S. Brady Press Briefing Room. Her voice occasionally sounded tense, with audible breaths between sentences, but she maintained a smile and made her central message unmistakable: She had long wanted to work for Donald Trump.
"I have wanted to work for him for a very long time," Zacharia said, thanking the president for placing his trust in her.
Anyone expecting a lengthy introductory exchange between the new spokesperson and the White House press corps, however, was in for a short encounter.
Much of the briefing was devoted to prepared remarks highlighting what Zacharia described as the administration's accomplishments, from wages and prescription drug prices to energy production, foreign investment, manufacturing and border security.
"President Trump is fighting and delivering for American workers every minute of every day," she declared.
With just three weeks remaining until the midterm elections, Zacharia also devoted considerable attention to Trump's campaign rallies, describing record attendance and growing enthusiasm among Republican voters.
Three reporters, and little room for improvisation
When Zacharia finally opened the floor to questions, only three reporters were called upon: Nick Gilbertson of the conservative Breitbart News, Fox News correspondent Peter Doocy, and Elina Shirazi of the Daily Mail.
The selection was notable not only because of the outlets represented, but also because of the way the briefing unfolded. Zacharia called on the reporters directly, by name, rather than inviting questions from the room more broadly.
There was no indication that the exchanges had been arranged in advance, but the carefully managed format left little room for spontaneous participation by the rest of the press corps.
The first question came from Gilbertson, occupying the White House's designated new media seat.
After praising Leavitt for opening the briefing room to voices beyond traditional news organizations, Gilbertson asked whether Zacharia intended to continue that approach.
"My predecessor Karoline Leavitt did an incredible job," she replied. "We are absolutely going to keep it, and we're going to expand on it to the extent possible. We love new media, and we want to be able to embrace it."
Asked whether Trump's campaign schedule would intensify ahead of the elections, she answered without hesitation.
"Absolutely, you can expect more of the midterm blitz."
She added that Kentucky had been included in the president's upcoming travel schedule, alongside stops in Georgia and Florida.
Where does White House messaging end and campaigning begin?
The most substantive question about Zacharia's new role came from Doocy, the Fox News correspondent.
He pointed out that she was taking office just three weeks before midterm elections that Trump himself had described as challenging for Republicans.
"Is your job just to speak about White House matters, or is it to make things less tough for Republicans in the midterms?" Doocy asked.
Zacharia did not draw a clear distinction between the two responsibilities.
"Well, but Peter, I get to do what I was doing on the outside already, which was hoping to amplify, multiply, and expand upon President Trump's incredible agenda for the American people," she replied.
She said her aim was to communicate the administration's achievements more effectively, working closely with a president who, in her words, "is his own best spokesperson."
Her answer suggested that, at least in her understanding of the role, promoting the president's agenda and helping communicate his political successes are closely intertwined.
Doocy then switched to a more direct foreign policy question: Had the United States stopped sharing intelligence with Ukraine?
"I'll have to get back to you on that," Zacharia replied.
A major announcement: Guilfoyle asked to resign
The briefing's most significant news came in response to a question from Shirazi, who asked about Kimberly Guilfoyle, the US ambassador to Greece.
Trump had said the previous day that he was considering firing Guilfoyle amid reports raising questions about her conduct.
Shirazi asked whether the administration had established a timeline for a potential dismissal and whether possible replacements were already being considered.
Zacharia's response was brief but consequential.
"We have asked Ambassador Guilfoyle to resign," she announced. "She has been a wonderful asset to the team, and we wish her well."
The statement marked a significant development in the controversy surrounding Guilfoyle, a former Fox News personality who was previously engaged to Donald Trump Jr.
Reports had raised questions about her conduct in the role and her dealings with donors and business figures. Her attorneys have denied the allegations against her.
For Zacharia, it was an unusually consequential announcement to deliver during a first appearance that otherwise focused heavily on celebrating the administration's achievements.
My president, excuse me, my husband
Then the questions turned personal.
Shirazi noted that Zacharia is the mother of four children and that her family had been living in California. She asked how the new press secretary intended to manage the demands of her White House position while raising a young family.
She also asked whether Leavitt, who left her role to spend more time with her own family, had offered any advice.
Zacharia became noticeably more animated.
"Well, first of all, I want to give my husband an amazing shout-out," she began.
She explained that she has four children, aged 12, 10, 8 and 6, including three boys.
"I adore my family. I love them. They are my priority," she said, stressing that spending evenings with her children remained extremely important to her.
Then came the moment that briefly interrupted the seriousness of the briefing.
"So my president, excuse me, my husband," Zacharia said, immediately correcting herself.
"That's a, that's a good one," she added.
The slip was a small but revealing moment in an otherwise controlled debut, with the new press secretary apparently having her boss on her mind even while discussing her husband.
Regaining her composure, Zacharia explained that her husband had brought all four children to Washington for the week because the family was celebrating two birthdays.
"We are very, very protective of celebrating birthdays as a family," she said.
The family, she added, plans to relocate to Washington.
Zacharia also spoke about stepping away from her professional career between 2014 and 2020 while raising her children, and how she later tried to incorporate family life into her work.
She recalled bringing her children to the Fox News bureau, where they would sometimes sit beside her as she prepared for television appearances.
Regarding her predecessor, Zacharia said Leavitt had been an important source of support and had offered advice on navigating the demands of the position.
Still, she acknowledged that the job might not lend itself to a conventional work-life balance.
"I think this job is not one you necessarily balance," she said.
She then found another opportunity to praise the president.
"President Trump is the most family-friendly president we've ever had," Zacharia declared.
She argued that Trump's willingness to appoint her, knowing she had four children and that the role would be demanding, demonstrated his confidence in her ability to meet those responsibilities.
Trump is heading to Alaska - and the briefing is over
Just as the exchange became more personal, Zacharia brought the proceedings to an abrupt end.
"In fact, I am going to end it because President Trump is heading out to Marine One for our historic trip to Alaska, and we can ask him all of the questions out there," she said.
The president was preparing to depart the White House for Joint Base Andrews, where Air Force One would take him to Alaska for another campaign rally.
As Zacharia prepared to leave, reporters could still be heard attempting to ask additional questions, including whether Trump had personally spoken with Guilfoyle about her departure.
But the new spokesperson was already wrapping up.
And with that, her first White House briefing was over almost as quickly as it had begun.
Zacharia, an attorney and conservative political commentator who served as a communications adviser to Trump Media & Technology Group before her appointment, enters the role at a particularly sensitive moment for the administration.
Her predecessor, Leavitt, became one of the administration's most recognizable public faces before leaving to focus on her family. Zacharia now faces the task of establishing her own relationship with a press corps accustomed to frequent confrontations, rapid political developments and a president who regularly prefers to speak for himself.
Whether Tuesday's tightly controlled, approximately 13-minute briefing represents a lasting approach or merely the caution of a first appearance remains to be seen.
What was clear from the outset was Zacharia's determination to defend the president enthusiastically, emphasize his achievements, and leave the central stage to him whenever possible.
And judging by that first slip of the tongue, Trump was rarely far from her thoughts - even when she was talking about her husband.

South Africa releases state land to black farmers
South Africa is releasing about 2.5 million hectares of state-owned land to black farmers and providing title deeds to expand their role in commercial agriculture, President Cyril Ramaphosa has said.
In his weekly letter to the nation, Ramaphosa said expanding access to land, financing and agricultural training was essential to transforming the sector, creating jobs and strengthening South Africa’s food security.
”The first step in building a new generation of South African farmers is providing them with titled access to land,” he said. Through the Proactive Land Acquisition Strategy, the government is releasing the land in various parts of the country to black farmers, Ramaphosa added.
The president stressed, however, that access to land needed to be accompanied by funding, skills development, mentorship and technology to help emerging farmers establish commercially successful businesses. ”Far too often, emerging farmers are kept trapped at subsistence level because they cannot get the financing they need for farming inputs, infrastructure and additional land,” he said.
Ramaphosa cited Redlands Farm, a commercial dairy farm in Stutterheim in the Eastern Cape owned and run by young black farmers, as an example of how financial support could help farmers expand their operations. “Redlands’ success shows that with effective partnerships, a transformed agricultural and agribusiness sector can boost the rural economy and create jobs.”
The farm has grown its operations with assistance from the Land Bank and is a beneficiary of its Blended Finance Scheme, which combines government grant funding with loan finance. The president encouraged more lenders and agribusinesses to participate and develop additional funding instruments for farmers.
Ramaphosa noted that South Africa’s agricultural sector had more than doubled since 1994, with record exports of R270 billion in 2025, making the country the world’s 32nd-largest agricultural exporter. The country exports products including table grapes, maize, beef, wine, citrus, sugar and wool. Nearly half of its agricultural exports go to other African countries, while the remainder reaches markets in the European Union, Asia, the Middle East and the Americas.
However, the sector’s growth had not benefited all communities equally. ”We still have what has been called ‘two agricultures’. Predominantly white-owned commercial farms account for the bulk of the country’s commercial farming output, while black farmers only account for around 10%,” Ramaphosa said.
The president warned that relying on a relatively small segment of the population to meet the country’s food needs was unsustainable as the population grew and demand for food increased. Ramaphosa added that transformation was necessary both to address historical inequalities and to ensure the country could meet future food demand.
Agriculture employs around 944,000 people, with a further 200,000 working across the broader value chain. The president cited a 2025 University of Pretoria study that found a strong correlation between investment in agriculture and poverty reduction. According to him, land ownership alone would not guarantee success, as farmers also needed practical experience and knowledge of crops, weather conditions and animal diseases.
Pamaphosa highlighted the work of commodity organisations, including the Citrus Growers’ Association, Grain South Africa, the National Wool Growers’ Association, Potatoes South Africa, Red Meat Industry Services, the Milk Producers’ Organisation and Fruit South Africa, in supporting a more inclusive agricultural economy. ”As government, we are on a concerted drive to expand and diversify export markets for our agricultural products. We are engaging with agribusinesses and farmers around issues such as new breeding techniques and advances in agricultural biotechnology,” said Ramaphosa.
Stronger partnerships between government, farmers, businesses, lenders, traditional leaders and communities would help grow the sector and create jobs. ”We can bring more land under cultivation, create a new generation of black commercial farmers and ensure that we grow enough not only to feed all our people, but to sell to markets across the world,” the president concluded.

A duo goes against the tide to explain an origin of human endurance
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
15:00:00 UTC
00:00:00 KST

A duo goes against the tide to explain an origin of human endurance
Perhaps it was diving, not just chasing prey on the African savanna, that made us marathoners
Two researchers may have opened floodgates on the debate over why humans can run marathons, swim the English Channel or dive a hundred meters and back on a single breath and their ape cousins can’t.
Humans evolved endurance for feats like these not just by running down prey on the African savanna, but also by diving for food in lakes or coastal waters, the duo propose September 17 in PaleoAnthropology. The hypothesis adds complexity to a decades-old theory that puts the drivers for evolution exclusively on land. But it coexists with a history of pushback for any water-related ideas.
The work is causing ripples among anthropologists. “I could not work out [at first] if this was groundbreaking or dumb,” says Christian Tryon, a paleoanthropologist at the University of Connecticut in Storrs.
In 1960, researchers came up with what’s been called the aquatic ape or waterside hypothesis, which suggested that our ancestors evolved longer legs and other adaptations from swimming for their suppers in watery habitats. Popularized in media accounts but not adequately vetted in peer-reviewed journals, the idea was shunned by the scientific community as additional fossils pointed away from a life in water. More recently, the dominant theory has been that it was landlocked human ancestors who gradually developed our remarkable endurance. “There’s been this reluctance to really think about anything sort of water-related as important in human evolution,” Tryon says.
Yet evolutionary anthropologist Josephine Joordens, a self-professed “water person” who trained as a marine biologist, had long wondered whether coastal life was vital to the evolutionary process, because it provides easy access to both water and land resources. Joordens combined forces with Erika Schagatay, a physiologist at Mid-Sweden University in Östersund, to formulate what they call the “dive first, run later” hypothesis.
Schagatay — herself a freediver — has spent decades observing and monitoring modern sea foraging people such as the Ama in Japan and the Sama-Bajau in Southeast Asia. Joordens studied fossil evidence and combed the literature about aquatic activities. Our evolution “was likely a very complex and very dynamic process,” says Joordens, of the Max Planck Institute for Evolutionary Anthropology in Leipzig, Germany.
They propose some Homo species wound up shallow-water diving repeatedly about 2 million to 3 million years ago, much the way the Sama-Bajau do today. These people spend four to six hours per day repeatedly diving several meters deep to catch fish and collect shellfish and other food. They evolved bigger spleens than their non-diving counterparts and, it seems, enhanced respiratory and cardiovascular capacity. They have the ability to “pace” breathing periods and breath-holding to avoid fatigue. In our ancestors, that could have paved the way for the cardiorespiratory stamina needed in modern endurance running, Schagatay says.
These Homo divers evolved heavy bones to help stay underwater and downward facing noses to keep water out, the two suggest. They eventually passed those endurance-boosting traits on to other populations with lighter bones and a more terrestrial lifestyle.
The study “shows there is a lot of evidence” for forage diving as an early evolutionary driver, says Leslea Hlusko, a paleobiologist at the Centro Nacional de Investigación sobre la Evolución Humana in Burgos, Spain.
This idea is not a retread of the aquatic ape theory, says Christopher Ruff, a biological anthropologist at Johns Hopkins School of Medicine. “Occasional aquatic foraging is quite a different proposal“ from the discredited theory’s primarily aquatic existence and should be taken seriously, Ruff says.
Not everyone thinks the dive first idea holds water.
Multiple factors work against the idea that diving could have helped humans become better endurance runners, says Daniel Lieberman, a paleoanthropologist at Harvard University. He argues that endurance diving does not require an enhanced aerobic capacity: It slows the heart rate, whereas running speeds it up. He disputes how and why heavy bones arose; they could have developed in people who used their bodies for heavy work and not because such bones helped divers with buoyancy issues. Nor is the downward pointed nose meaningful given that many diving mammals have forward facing noses. Other reasons, such as keeping the air in nostrils moist, were probably more important in selecting for this feature, he says.
What’s more, many people around the world have long relied on running down game for food, says archaeologist Eugène Morin of Trent University in Peterborough, Canada. “Diving is costly and the [caloric] returns are low,” so early humans would not choose to dive if other foraging opportunities existed, he argues.
Critiques aside, “the simple ‘ape walked out from forest to savanna’ story clearly does not cut it anymore,” says Pascal Gagneux, a biological anthropologist at the University of California, San Diego. Coastal routes around Africa, along Africa’s lakeshores and out of Africa “must have played a huge role” in human evolution, Gagneux says.
The pair knows they risk the ire of their peers in presenting this “dive first”  hypothesis, but Joordens says, “we are both in our early 60s and we both have beautiful careers, so we thought ‘whatever happens, happens.’”
And Tryon ultimately found the paper worth the read. “If nothing else, it gets people thinking and it gets people looking.”

Companies rushed in on AI. Now some are pulling back
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
15:00:00 UTC
00:00:00 KST

Employers around the globe are grappling with the fallout from rushing to adopt fast-changing artificial intelligence tools.

And after thinning its workforce, especially middle managers, in a 2023 efficiency push, the company is expanding its managerial ranks again, LinkedIn posts from workers show.

After receiving “what was clearly an AI-generated doc” from a co-worker, he used his AI to summarize it and came away with no new thinking about the idea, he said. He warned his followers against falling into this potential “doom loop”, where AI does the reading and writing and leaves behind an “ocean of sameness”.
Meanwhile, Walmart store and warehouse employees are being plagued by unreasonable expectations, errors and false alerts from AI tools that assign tasks, schedules and monitor performance, Business Insider reported.
Employers are navigating a flood of errors and low-quality work that are sapping employee time, raising privacy and security risks and pushing up costs. Now, some businesses that started off fast and furious on AI are pumping the brakes, implementing restrictions where experimentation was once encouraged, bringing back experienced workers and upping training efforts.
C-suite leaders say when it comes to AI, there’s a sense that “we’re driving the truck and building it at the same time, and that’s a problem,” said Johnny C Taylor Jr, president and CEO of the Society for Human Resource Management. “If we could all rewind … we would have introduced [this] in a more thoughtful, slow way.”
Despite billions of dollars that firms around the globe have invested in AI over the past few years, major returns remain to be seen: 90% of executives say AI efforts have yet to translate to productivity gains at their companies, according to an Atlanta Federal Reserve working paper. And an Ernst & Young survey published last month found that 36% of senior AI executives at companies with at least $1bn in annual revenue reported an AI incident that led to issues including data loss, financial damage, brand damage or operational disruptions.
Firms from Microsoft to McKinsey are limiting usage for employees, as the flood of new tools and rapacious consumption weighs on bottom lines. Others, such as Palantir, Booz Allen Hamilton and Nvidia, are restricting employee use over growing concerns about the security of their organizations’ data with AI companies, Reuters reported.
Microsoft and Walmart declined to comment. Meta, Palantir, Nvidia and Booz Allen Hamilton did not respond to requests for comment.
“We initially treated AI like a traditional technology rollout: deploy the tools, provide training, drive adoption,” Kathleen Hogan, Microsoft’s chief strategy and transformation officer, said in a recent blogpost about the company’s AI adoption journey. “We learned that access and usage do not equal transformation.”
Expertise gaps and errors
AI remains a mixed bag for managers and employees alike: more than half of employees said they “aren’t getting the AI training they need”, while most managers said they were outskilled in AI by their staff, according to an Indeed survey published in July. Just 45% of managers said they felt “equipped to effectively lead AI natives”.
Many workers feel “like they’re being asked to make use of these tools without any guidance about how they best could be deployed”, said Zack Mabel, director of research at the Georgetown University Center on Education and the Workforce. Meanwhile, managers are balancing orders to “roll this out, find productivity gains and don’t compromise on quality”, he added.
Companies are trying to address these perceived gaps by moving away from one-off webinars for broad swaths of staff and toward “sustained, role-specific training”, Taylor said.
Microsoft found that “adding agents to a broken process still leaves a broken process” and “speeding up one step just creates a longer queue at the next”, Hogan’s blogpost reads. The company found that focusing on employee training, particularly pairing up early-career engineers with more seasoned employees, boosted productivity.
One barrier to bigger AI-induced gains is the technology’s tendency to produce “plausible-looking output” with weaknesses or mistakes that are not immediately apparent, explained Jessica Reif, assistant professor of management at the Wharton School of the University of Pennsylvania.
“This makes it more likely that an error propagates through a workflow instead of being immediately corrected,” which can cause problems to snowball, said Reif.
Meanwhile, AI’s limited ability to assess human workers is still limited, which is creating tension at some companies. At Walmart, frustration is mounting among some rank-and-file store employees over inconsistent and inaccurate AI tools, Business Insider reported.
Employees described bots that set unreasonable standards for human workers while introducing a host of their own inefficiencies and errors. AI tools plotted nonsensical routes for fulfilment workers that made it harder to fill orders quickly, pumped out useless safety alerts and set unrealistic schedules that left store employees cutting corners to keep up.
These bots assume that workers are “going to be perfect every single time”, one manager told Business Insider. “We’re not going to hold people to these impossible standards.”
Walmart declined to comment.
Rising risks
Neil Elan, attorney at Stubbs Alderton & Markiles LLP, said he had observed “a growing gap” between how his corporate clients think AI is being used and how it is actually being used, which is creating issues with confidentiality, intellectual property, efficiency and employee conduct.
It’s also creating headaches for companies when workers’ use of ChatGPT spills into public view.
The night before Will Moye was set to face 3M in court over a 2020 gas explosion at a Houston manufacturing plant that killed three and damaged hundreds of homes and businesses, the attorney received a report from the company’s independent expert witness.
Skimming on his iPad, Moye noticed telltale signs of AI: strange formatting and fonts and time stamps showing that 14,500 pages were assembled in a matter of hours. Moye suspected that the author, Josh Autenrieth of Knighthawk Engineering, lacked expertise and had relied on ChatGPT, despite billing 3M $90,000 for a report arguing the company was not liable.
Autenrieth’s chat logs, which Moye requested and shared in court, show he prompted ChatGPT, “What am I looking at?” after uploading a picture of the gas detector at the heart of the case.
The jury found that 3M had failed to properly inspect the gas detection system and ordered the company to pay $61.5m to 24 homeowners. Moye said after the verdict, the jury “expressed a profound disbelief” that the company would hire an expert who would make claims “without any foundation”.
“[3M] were trying to reset the narrative,” Moye said. “And they hired an expert who’d never touched the machine.”
A 3M spokesperson said that “after independently reviewing the facts and reaching his own conclusions”, Autenrieth “used AI as a tool in preparing his report”.
Autenrieth’s legal counsel Janina Wojtkowski said ChatGPT didn’t produce his opinions or replace his “professional judgment” but assisted in formatting, structuring and drafting amid “severe deadline constraints”.
Performance boost? Not so much
As companies and workers muddle through the unknowns of early AI adoption, costs are still coming into focus, while broad productivity gains remain elusive.
In a study published in May, University of Pittsburgh researchers concluded that productivity didn’t rise after companies invested in AI and cut staff. Although executives have been overwhelmingly optimistic about AI’s potential impacts for years, “management optimism does not effectively translate into … better performance,” the paper states.
More than 112,000 job cut announcements in the US so far in 2026 have mentioned AI, making it a top reason for layoffs, according to Challenger, Gray & Christmas.
Earlier this year, Meta paused its practice of tracking employees’ computer activity to train its AI, according to Reuters. Meta also recently told employees that their adoption and usage of AI tools would no longer be part of performance reviews, the Information reported.
Meta did not respond to a request for comment.
Mark Ma, University of Pittsburgh professor and researcher on the AI layoff study, said leaders are focused on short-term performance, “which is why they tried to rush ahead by investing in AI and laying off workers”.
But companies’ share prices tend to dip after they announce AI-related layoffs, he noted, suggesting that “the stock market also does not think these will work out.”
“A lot of these mistakes could have been avoided,” Ma said. “Now I feel some managers have learned their lesson.”

The Russian Rassvet satellite network is being developed not only for the war against Ukraine, but also as a tool for carrying out provocations, illegal schemes, and hybrid aggression against NATO countries and the international community, Deputy Chief of the Main Intelligence Agency of the Ukrainian Ministry of Defense from 2015 to 2020, Major General Illia Pavlenko said in an interview with Interfax-Ukraine.
According to Pavlenko, the creation of an autonomous satellite infrastructure will allow Russia to covertly carry out sabotage operations anywhere in the world.
"This is a direct threat to Europeans. The enemy is moving its jet-powered UAV production facilities underground. Equipped with a compact Rassvet terminal, such a drone, launched from a civilian vessel in the English Channel or from a rented trailer in Europe, will be able to strike targets in London or Paris unhindered, guided directly from the Kremlin. Europe simply won't have enough expensive PAC-3 missiles for the Patriot system to repel massive attacks by cheap satellite-guided drones," the major general said.
Pavlenko identifies Russia's plans to sell network access in 70 countries of the Global South as a separate risk. "Somali pirates will undoubtedly use this connection to guide unmanned boats toward civilian vessels, and drug cartels in Latin America will use it to circumvent U.S. surveillance systems. Giving them such a tool is effectively like giving an enemy nuclear weapons," he said.
In addition, the general noted that the Russian developers of Rassvet have chosen an operating frequency band that completely overlaps with the frequencies of the American Iridium satellite system used by the Pentagon, creating a risk of interference and complicating the use of electronic warfare (EW) capabilities.
"This is a major threat to the Americans and NATO countries. By jamming Rassvet's frequencies in the event of a hybrid conflict or the fight against smuggling, they risk completely crippling their own communications and the command and control of their warships or units," a former high-ranking military intelligence official said.

AI-assisted icon of ‘cyber-apostle’ blessed in Belarus (VIDEO)
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

AI-assisted icon of ‘cyber-apostle’ blessed in Belarus (VIDEO)
An AI-generated icon depicting a teenage Catholic saint has been blessed in Belarus, in what could be the first such ceremony worldwide, according to local media and footage of the sermon. The artwork depicts Carlo Acutis, an Italian teenager and devout Catholic who used the internet to spread faith and was canonized by the Pope last year.
The image was blessed by Archbishop Emeritus Tadeusz Kondrusiewicz during Sunday Mass at the Church of St. Mary Magdalene in the town of Novolukoml, in the northeastern part of the country. 
“Today we enter the world through the internet. What are we looking for there? Holiness? Far from always,” Kondrusiewicz told the congregation during the sermon, adding he hoped that the icon would help believers to find religious truth online.
The archbishop went on to praise Acutis as an example of how young people can embrace modern technology while living a devout Catholic life.
The image shows the saint holding a laptop and a rosary, with a golden sun on his chest and a spiral staircase turning into a road leading to heaven. It was created using AI and other digital tools – although not completely – by prompt engineer Dmitry Kulpanovich, photographer Viktor Veden, and designer Andrey Kabanov. The church placed the icon in a side altar as a movable cover for its existing image of Mary Magdalene.
Born in London in 1991 and raised in Milan, Acutis became known as the “cyber-apostle” and “God’s influencer.” He built websites promoting Catholicism, including a catalogue of alleged Eucharistic miracles, and is credited with converting several people. He died of leukemia in 2006, aged 15, and became the first millennial saint when Pope Leo XIV canonized him in September 2025.
However, the ceremony sparked criticism from some believers on social media who argued that an AI-generated image cannot be considered an icon and used for prayer.
While Pope Leo XIV has not explicitly opposed AI-generated art, he warned earlier this month that it should not be equated with human creativity. “Algorithms lack the spark of the human,” he said.

Cost of insuring warehouses skyrockets in Russia following drone strikes
Insurers have hiked the prices of insurance policies due to massive Ukrainian strikes on large warehouse facilities in Russia, which have caused multi-billion-rouble losses for major online marketplaces.
Source: The Moscow Times, as reported by Ukrainska Pravda
Details: According to the services Polis.online and Rental Pro, the average rate for warehouse insurance in Q3 2026 has increased 13-20 times year-on-year and nearly 7 times compared to Q2 (reaching 2% of the property value).
Market participants told Russian media outlet Vedomosti that the cost of policies for large warehouses has risen even more steeply.
For instance, at Renaissance Insurance, the cost of a policy for a Class A dry warehouse went up 37.5 times between June and September, rising from 0.08-0.15% of the insured sum to 3-5%. The broker Mains estimated that insuring a warehouse containing inventory worth 10 billion roubles (about US$100 million) would cost up to 500 million roubles (US$5 million). A year ago it cost 20-25 million roubles (US$200,000-250,000).
The Moscow Times notes that Ukrainian forces began striking large Wildberries warehouses in mid-July, and Ozon facilities late August.
According to the report, Data Insight estimates the losses suffered by Wildberries due to the destruction of warehouses and infrastructure at between 147 and 280 billion roubles (about US$1.47-2.8 billion), and Ozon's losses at approximately 100 billion roubles (US$1 billion).
Background:
- The Russian company Yandex announced the shutdown of a data centre in Vladimir following a drone attack. Prior to that, a Yandex data centre in Sasovo, Ryazan Oblast, completely ceased operations after a drone attack.
- Following a series of Ukrainian attacks on Wildberries logistics centres, the company announced a tender for the supply of 478,000 sq m of galvanised metal mesh for the eight Russian regions where it has logistics hubs.
- Ozon's share price plunged 12.7% to 2,600 roubles (about US$26) on the Moscow Exchange after Ozon warehouses in various regions of Russia were attacked by drones for three days in a row.
- In August, Kremlin leader Vladimir Putin instructed the Russian government to adopt a programme to rebuild logistics and warehouse facilities damaged by Ukrainian strikes, which he described as "terrorist attacks".

EU spent $320 bn on Russian energy since 2022
The EU has spent more than $320 billion on Russian energy since the escalation of the Ukraine conflict in 2022 despite sweeping sanctions, Russian Deputy Prime Minister Aleksandr Novak has said.
The EU drastically reduced Russian oil and gas imports and pledged to phase out Russian fossil fuels entirely by 2027.
Energy costs have surged across much of the bloc in recent years, with the crisis exacerbated by the US-Israeli war against Iran.
In August, Chancellor Friedrich Merz acknowledged that the German embargo on Russian energy contributed to the “ongoing energy crisis” and undermined German industry. French President Emmanuel Macron has warned of soaring costs from replacing Russian pipeline gas with more expensive liquefied natural gas (LNG).
In an interview with Russian broadcaster Vesti on Monday, Novak said the value of Russian energy supplies to the EU have reached $320.7 billion, exceeding the $250 billion figure previously cited by Washington.
“Despite sanctions, our energy resources continue to flow through specific routes that remain exempt,” Novak said, noting that deliveries reached $21.3 billion in the first nine months of 2026 alone.
He stressed that Russia continues to honor its contracts, insisting that it is not Russia’s “fault that the share of exports to the European Union has changed significantly,” adding: “We are supplying what our European counterparts want.”
Novak also said Russian and American companies have begun talks on diesel deliveries following an agreement between US President Donald Trump and Russian President Vladimir Putin. According to him, Russia could boost diesel exports to global markets to 3.5 million tons a month by the end of the year.
The remarks come as Brussels rolls out new sanctions targeting over 1,600 individuals and entities. Polish Foreign Minister Radoslaw Sikorski welcomed the measures, calling them the “harshest so far.”
Despite pledges to phase out Russian energy, France, Spain, and Belgium remain major buyers of Russian LNG, while Hungary and Slovakia continue importing Russian pipeline oil and gas through sanctions exemptions.
Russian presidential envoy Kirill Dmitriev accused Brussels of hypocrisy, arguing that the EU and “legacy media” are concealing its energy purchases while criticizing America’s diesel agreement with Russia, which he said will benefit “US farmers, consumers, the energy market, and the world.”

How Iran made the Houthis into such a problem
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
14:55:47 UTC
23:55:47 KST

How Iran made the Houthis into such a problem for the U.S. and its allies
Yemen's Houthi rebels have morphed over the last decade from being a little-known group in northwest Yemen, to Iran's most potent ally in the region and a central opponent of the United States and its allies across the Middle East.
While Iran's other proxy forces have been depleted in recent years, the Houthis have taken center stage in the Middle East, offering yet another example of how a smaller, guerrilla-style force that's dug in on the ground can cause asymmetric damage through hard-to-repel aerial attacks.
In support of their Iranian benefactors, the Houthis launched initial attacks on Israel not long after the U.S. joined the Jewish state in strikes across Iran on Feb. 28, sparking the ongoing conflict in the Middle East.
Saudi Arabia, one of the world's richest nations and a key American ally, is now bearing the brunt of the Houthis' attacks, which have killed at least 20 people at Saudi airports over the last week. Along with other allied groups, the militants have also attacked Saudi oil infrastructure, helping drive up global energy prices by threatening the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, which, like the Strait of Hormuz, is a key maritime chokepoint for oil and gas shipments.
The Saudis have asked the U.S. to join its military operations against the Houthis, and President Trump, who initially rejected the request, said over the weekend that he's considering it.
Iran's "most powerful proxy"
The Houthis are backed financially and militarily by Iran, officials from the U.S. and Israel, as well as many regional analysts, have said for years.
They were once a relatively marginal group within what Iran calls its Axis of Resistance — a loose alliance of anti-Israel, anti-U.S. militant groups that includes Hamas in Gaza and Hezbollah in Lebanon. Both of those U.S.-designated terrorist organizations have been severely weakened by Israeli operations launched in the wake of the Hamas-led attack on Oct. 7, 2023.
The Houthis joined Hamas and Hezbollah's attacks on Israel and became the target of an Israeli counteroffensive, as well as military operations by the Biden and Trump administrations. But unlike Hamas and Hezbollah, the group has rebounded and emerged better armed, battle-hardened and confident.
"The Houthis are the most powerful proxy within the Iranian network, hands down," said Mohammed Al-Basha, founder of the Basha Report, a U.S.-based risk advisory group. "Any U.S. military strategy planning a campaign on Iran will have to take into consideration what the Houthis will do next."
After the 2023 attack on Israel, with help from Iran, the group really started gaining capacity and momentum.
"Before Oct. 7, we didn't see them getting the newest equipment from Iran. After Oct. 7, they got the best," al-Basha told CBS News, adding that Tehran not only armed the Houthis, but also helped the group hone its skills in penetrating air defenses.
The Houthis started adopting new tactics, including targeting Israel with layered attacks using drones, cruise missiles and then ballistic missiles to overwhelm the country's significant defenses.
Now the Houthis are using the same tactics against Saudi Arabia.
In the age of asymmetric warfare, the group has also used Yemen's ranking as one of the poorest countries in the world as something of a strategic advantage: They rely on a strongly ideological support base willing to suffer economic pain and isolation if the tradeoff is inflicting great damage to the Saudis and the global economy, said Yoel Guzansky, a senior research fellow focused on Persian Gulf politics and security at the Institute for National Security Studies.
"All you need is a not very sophisticated surface-to-surface missile to strike Riyadh airport. They can assemble those in small factories in the mountains," Guzansky said.
What do the Houthis want?
Houthi military spokesman Brig. Gen. Yahya Saree said recently that the group's attacks on Saudi Arabia are in response to a "brutal Saudi aggression against our country and our people."
But al-Basha said the Houthis' real objectives are not retaliation, but power and recognition.
They want to seize control of all of Yemen, and to get the Saudis to both recognize their legitimacy, and help bankroll their expansion, he said, which is why he believes they have coupled their campaign inside Yemen with the attacks on Saudi Arabia.
The Houthis' Iran-powered evolution
The Houthi movement grew out of the Zaydi Shiite Muslim sect, which has roots that date back centuries in northern Yemen. They are a minority in the country, which is predominantly Sunni Muslim, but the number of Zaydis is significant, representing as much as a third of Yemen's overall population.
The Houthi movement originally emerged as an effort to protect Zaydi culture within Yemen, but it evolved into a group that has as its slogan: "Allah is the Greatest; Death to America; Death to Israel; A Curse upon the Jews; Victory to Islam."
Analysts estimate that the armed Houthi force consists of hundreds of thousands of combat-ready fighters. The group itself claims to have trained more than a million militants.
Their march to real power began in 2012, when the then-much-smaller group, consisting of thousands of fighters, capitalized on unrest in Yemen following the Arab Spring ouster of longtime authoritarian President Ali Abdullah Saleh to build a loyal following in the north of the country.
In 2014, they seized the capital Sanaa, sparking a civil war with the Western- and Saudi-backed government. The government was forced to relocate to the southern port city of Aden, where it is still based, and it has also retained control of the less-populated eastern portion of the country.
The Houthis quickly took control of key state military and civilian powers, including missile brigades and special forces, and the ability to levy taxes, explained al-Basha.
The group survived a first round of fighting with the Saudi-led military coalition from 2015 until 2022. During that time, military advisers from Hezbollah and Iran helped train Houthi commanders and combatants — and built up the group's ability to manufacture its own weapons, including drones and missiles, according to analysts.
The Houthis may also be using AI software to fine-tune their weapons. U.S. tech firm Anthropic released a report in September saying it had identified "threat actors" based in northern Yemen using their Claude Code software "in place of human software engineers to develop the guidance, navigation, and control (GNC) software that steers and stabilizes a flying vehicle."
The weapons the unnamed actors were attempting to develop included guided rockets and multi-stage ballistic missiles, according to Anthropic, which said it did not have evidence of the actors successfully fielding an operational device.
While they can produce some of their own weapons, however, Fabian Hinz, a weapons analyst with the International Institute for Strategic Studies, wrote last year that the Houthis "remain dependent on Iran for key technologies and advanced capabilities. While Tehran's support has, in some areas, evolved from the direct provision of complete systems to enabling localized manufacturing, it remains a critical enabler of Houthi military activity."
But it is not a one-sided relationship.
"With Hamas and Hezbollah severely weakened, the Houthis have become an increasingly indispensable pillar of Iran's regional strategy, providing Tehran with a relatively resilient and cost-effective means of threatening Saudi Arabia, Israel, and international shipping while projecting power far beyond Yemen," Guzansky told CBS News. "Their strategic value to Iran has arguably never been greater, even if the Houthis retain considerable autonomy in their decision-making."
Yemen's devastating war
Situated at the southern end of the Arabian Peninsula, the Houthis are geographically isolated from any outside ground force, with the exception of the Saudis, who don't have the manpower to take on such a well-entrenched enemy, analysts say.
Domestically, in Yemen's vicious civil war, the well-coordinated group faces opposing forces that, while largely aligned with the Saudi-backed government, are themselves divided and operating under separate command structures.
Since Yemen descended into war in 2015, the United Nations estimates that some 377,000 people have died, more than half due to indirect causes such as starvation and disease amid the fighting.
More than 201,210 people have fled from their homes, according to data from the United Nations' International Organization for Migration, including more than 3,700 who have fled by sea to Djibouti.
According to figures published by the World Health Organization last week, Yemen's Ministry of Health and Population had reported 959 deaths and 4,207 injuries attributed directly to the fighting across 10 provinces between the beginning of September and Oct. 2.
The Houthi-run Ministry of Health said Tuesday the death toll from the recent escalation of fighting, during the same period, stood at 107, with 278 more wounded.

Women with autoimmune diseases face longer waits and more misdiagnoses than men
Unknown
