14:38:13 UTC
23:38:13 KST

Archaeological Survey of India (ASI) has found the missing head of an 11th-century Vishnu idol at Khajuraho, whose restoration became the subject of a recent controversy involving the Supreme Court, and plans to reattach it after expert examination.ASI has also introduced a three-year deadline for archaeological excavations to curb delays in research and cut approval times for most conservation projects to 15-20 days, director general Yadubir Singh Rawat told TOI in an exclusive interview. He also revealed plans for a preliminary excavation at Ujjain's Vaishya Tekri, where a Buddhist stupa could be larger than Sanchi's, although its actual scale and significance remain to be established.Controversy over the beheaded Vishnu idol at Khajuraho's Javari temple reached the Supreme Court last year when advocate Rakesh Dalal sought restoration, replacement or reconstruction of the seven-foot statue.While dismissing the petition, then CJI BR Gavai had remarked, “Go and ask the deity itself to do something now.”Though Gavai later clarified his remark in court and said he respects all religions and that his statement was taken out of context, his words drew criticism, and a lawyer subsequently attempted to throw a shoe at him inside the courtroom.
Rawat said the missing head had been found in an ASI store. “During a visit to Bhopal for the BRICS summit, I learnt that the statue's head—which had been kept in our store—had been found. The person in charge informed me that someone likely tried to break off the head to steal it but failed to do so. We are having experts examine it and will soon reattach it to the statue.”On delays in archaeological research, Rawat said ASI had introduced a three-year timeframe for completing excavation projects, with permissions continuing automatically across financial years. He acknowledged that some researchers showed enthusiasm during fieldwork but delayed finalising reports, holding up publication of findings.ASI had also granted circle officers financial powers ranging from Rs 50 lakh to Rs 1 crore, reducing the need for approvals from HQ. Rawat said most annual conservation programmes now received clearance within 15-20 days, except those requiring expert consultation.At Vaishya Tekri in Ujjain, a recent survey identified a cluster of Buddhist stupas and a water reservoir. Rawat said the structures differed from Sanchi because they were built using unbaked bricks. The last excavation there took place in 1973.ASI plans to begin with a limited vertical excavation to establish the site's significance before committing to a larger project estimated to cost Rs 60 crore. “The true picture will only emerge after excavation. We will proceed only after confirming its significance, although the site already falls within a protected area,” Rawat said.He said acquiring and excavating the entire site would require substantial resources, making preliminary investigation necessary to determine whether a full-scale project was justified.On encroachments at protected monuments, Rawat questioned the continued reliance on a colonial-era list prepared under the Ancient Monuments Preservation Act of 1904.“The root of this problem lies in the list prepared by British rulers in 1904 under the ‘Ancient Monuments Preservation Act’—a list that the then-central govt adopted post-independence without any review. The British had included cemeteries and graves of their obscure soldiers, horses, mules, and pets—which they deemed highly significant—among the monuments protected by the ASI. Before adopting that list, a review should have been conducted to determine what was truly important in the national interest,” he said.Rawat said a review in 1953 incorporated state monuments into a definitive list, but the central list remained unchanged. The resulting difficulties eventually led to 17 monuments being removed from it.Explaining disparities in funding, he said allocations depended on visitor numbers, maintenance requirements, security expenses and public facilities. Taj Mahal and Red Fort, he said, served as showcases for ASI, while Taj Mahal's maintenance required substantial expenditure because of its delicate structure and heavy tourist footfall. ASI paid around Rs 3 crore monthly for more than 200 CISF personnel deployed there.Rawat acknowledged that lesser-known monuments, including the pyramid-like Bhim ki Gada structure in Bareilly, had received inadequate attention. He said ASI circles had been instructed to prepare conservation and tourism development proposals for such sites.On skeletal remains excavated at Rakhigarhi in Haryana, Rawat said ASI had signed an MoU with Anthropological Survey of India and Birbal Sahni Institute of Palaeosciences. ASI would lead the project, while the two institutes would examine the remains to determine physical characteristics, age, diet, diseases, sex and other details. A one-year deadline had been set for submitting the report.For Uttarakhand, Rawat outlined plans to trace the historic walking route from Rishikesh to Badrinath and Kedarnath along the left bank of Alaknanda river.
He said references in Gita Press archives pointed to several temples and traditional halting places used by local and tribal communities that had not been adequately documented. Ancient markers or surviving remains could provide information about travel and settlement patterns.“There is also a need to trace the ‘Swargarohana Path’ taken by the Pandavas to Kedarnath, as described in the Mahabharata. It is my personal wish that this project be pursued with full dedication and in ‘mission mode’ by the concerned circle,” he said.

North Khorasan, the province I almost missed
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
14:37:18 UTC
23:37:18 KST

North Khorasan, the province I almost missed
TEHRAN - A friend’s suggestion was all it took to set me on the road to North Khorasan, one of the few Iranian provinces I had never visited and, until then, had rarely considered as a travel destination.
We set out to explore the province over three days, keeping costs low and relying on local guides and the knowledge of people familiar with the region. What followed was a journey through mountain strongholds, traditional homestays, Turkmen hospitality, living musical traditions, local festivals and a secluded valley where a man had spent years building a world of his own. By the end, I had discovered how easily a place can remain off one’s travel map until the moment one finally gives it a chance.
A train to the edge of the desert
We boarded the train from Tehran around midday, heading towards Jajarm, one of the southernmost cities of North Khorasan province. We would not be getting off in the city itself, however, but at Jajarm railway station, roughly 30 kilometers away. From there, our tightly scheduled exploration of the province would begin.
By the time we arrived, it was around 8 p.m. The long train ride had carried us away from the bustle of the capital and towards a landscape where the desert and mountains seemed to set a different pace for life.
Our first night’s accommodation was a modest traditional homestay near the railway line, tucked behind a small pistachio orchard. Built largely of mud brick and earth, the property consisted of perhaps six or seven rooms. It was not the sort of place that would appear in a glossy hotel brochure. That, as I would discover, was part of its appeal.
Our hosts, a middle-aged couple known affectionately as Uncle Ghorban and Aunt Zeynab, welcomed us with a warmth that made the long journey feel worthwhile.
Dinner was a traditional meal accompanied by local music. There were no polished dining tables or carefully staged decorations. Instead, the setting had the unpretentious charm of a family home where visitors were treated less like customers than guests.
We ate, listened to music and gradually settled into the rhythm of a place that seemed far removed from the hurried world we had left behind.
The accommodation was basic. We slept on simple mattresses laid on the floor, and nothing about the rooms could be described as luxurious. The walls were made of earth, the surroundings were quiet, and above us stretched a night sky scattered with stars.
I began to understand that comfort does not always come from the things we buy or the services we expect. Sometimes it comes from the absence of things that have come to dominate our daily lives: traffic, noise, constant notifications, crowded schedules and the persistent feeling that we should always be doing something.
The following morning brought some of the most memorable moments of the entire trip. Aunt Zeynab had prepared two kinds of local bread. One was plain, while the other was enriched with aromatic herbs, sesame seeds and black seeds.
The smell of freshly baked bread filled the space, making it difficult to think about anything else.
There was also strained yoghurt that had been stored in a sheep’s skin, along with fresh eggs and vegetables from the family’s own garden.
Then came the butter.
Our hosts used a simple traditional arrangement involving a sheep’s skin and wooden poles to make butter from milk. The process was a reminder of how everyday necessities were once produced through household labor and local knowledge, long before industrial food production made such tasks almost invisible to urban consumers.
Nothing was presented as an attraction. These were simply the things our hosts did, and had perhaps done for much of their lives. Yet for us, they offered a glimpse into a way of living that is becoming increasingly unfamiliar to people in large cities. Under that simple roof, I felt an unusual sense of calm.
Before leaving, we thanked Uncle Ghorban and Aunt Zeynab for their hospitality. It was a brief encounter, but it left a lasting impression.
Through the mountains of Raz and Jargalan
After breakfast, we set off towards the northern part of the province. Our destination was Raz and Jargalan, a district close to the border with Turkmenistan, where mountains, valleys and remote settlements preserve traces of a past that is not always easy to read from the landscape.
The drive took around four hours. It was a long journey, but the scenery gave us plenty of reasons to look away from the road and towards the surrounding countryside.
Among the most striking sights were ancient juniper trees, some of which were said to be hundreds of years old, with some estimated to be as much as 2,000 years old. Their twisted trunks and weathered branches seemed to embody the endurance of life in a landscape shaped by harsh weather and the passage of time.
North Khorasan has many such reminders of time’s passage, although visitors who hurry towards more famous destinations may never encounter them.
The region’s historical attractions were no less compelling.
At one point, we came across a large defensive structure perched high on a mountain. Our guide explained that it had served as a refuge during periods of invasion. When danger approached, people could retreat to the elevated stronghold and pull up the ladders used to reach it, making access difficult for attackers.
The location was striking, but the first question that came to my mind was not how the structure had been built. It was how people had managed to reach it.
Imagine a community suddenly threatened by an invading force. Families would have to abandon their homes, gather whatever possessions they could carry and make their way up a steep mountain path. Children, elderly people and those carrying food or other necessities would all have to negotiate the same difficult ascent.
Then, once inside, they would have to wait, uncertain about what was happening below and whether they would ever return to their homes.
The defensive advantages of such a place become obvious when viewed from a distance. But imagining the people who depended on it makes the history far more immediate.
A little farther along our route, we encountered another remarkable sight: a series of man-made caves cut into a mountainside, arranged in three levels.
According to our local guide, the lowest level had been used to keep animals, while the upper levels served other purposes associated with refuge and shelter.
Iran’s history is often presented through the grandeur of its palaces, mosques, monumental tombs and celebrated ancient cities. Yet the country’s past also survives in less conspicuous places: a refuge on a mountain, a room cut into rock, a mud-brick house or a path worn smooth by generations of footsteps.
These are places where history is not always written in inscriptions. Sometimes it is recorded in the landscape itself.
The mountain refuges also brought to mind the long history of insecurity experienced by communities across this part of Asia. Trade routes connected distant regions, but those same routes could bring armies, raiders and political upheaval. For people living in exposed settlements, the ability to seek shelter was not an abstract architectural concern. It could determine whether a family survived.
We eventually left that mountains behind and continued towards a different kind of encounter, one that would reveal another dimension of North Khorasan’s character.
A Turkmen welcome, with an unexpected pizza
By midday, we had reached a traditional accommodation run by a Turkmen couple and their two sons.
The atmosphere was different from that of our previous night’s homestay, but the same spirit of hospitality was immediately apparent.
Our hosts wore traditional Turkmen clothing and distinctive hats. Their appearance, manner and surroundings offered a glimpse of a cultural identity that has been preserved across generations in this borderland region.
North Khorasan is home to a diverse population, including Kurdish Kurmanji speakers, Turkmens, Persians and Turkic-speaking communities. The province’s cultural richness is not simply a matter of different ethnic groups living within the same administrative boundaries. It is visible in its music, languages, food, handicrafts, clothing and everyday social customs.
Here, cultural identities have developed through centuries of coexistence, exchange and adaptation.
Turkmen communities, in particular, have maintained distinctive traditions in carpet weaving, textiles, music and horsemanship, while their cuisine reflects both local resources and wider cultural connections across Central Asia.
Lunch at the guesthouse brought some of those culinary traditions to the table. The food combined Iranian and Turkmen influences, giving us an opportunity to sample flavors that felt familiar in some respects and different in others.
Then came the surprise: a pizza that our hosts described as their own creation. It was delicious.
I had not expected to encounter a distinctive house pizza in a traditional guesthouse near the border with Turkmenistan. Yet that small detail seemed to capture something important about the character of the place. Cultural traditions do not necessarily survive by remaining frozen in time. They often continue through the ability to absorb new influences while retaining a recognizable identity.
Once again, the welcome was informal and sincere. We were travelling on a limited budget, and our hosts made us feel that this was no obstacle to receiving generous hospitality.
After lunch, we headed towards a reservoir behind a dam for a short boat ride. The water offered a welcome change after hours of mountain roads and dry landscapes. The surrounding hills formed a quiet backdrop, and for a while we could simply enjoy the view without having to think about the next destination.
Before long, we were back on the road, leaving Raz and Jargalan behind and heading towards Shirvan.
After approximately three hours on the road, we reached Shirvan, where one of the most memorable encounters of the journey was waiting for us.
Our first stop was a traditional dutar workshop run by master instrument-maker Khosrow Haddad and his sons.
The dutar is a long-necked, two-stringed lute found in Iran and across Central Asia. Its name comes from the Persian words do, meaning two, and tar, meaning string.
Although the instrument looks relatively simple, its cultural significance is considerable. In parts of northeastern Iran, particularly among Kurdish and Turkmen communities, the dutar is closely associated with the musical traditions of the Bakhshi, performers who have historically carried songs, stories, poetry and local memory from one generation to the next.
A dutar is not merely a musical instrument. In the hands of a skilled performer, it can become a means of preserving a community’s sense of itself.
The workshop was also a shop where instruments were displayed and sold. Yet it felt much more like a place devoted to a lifelong passion than a commercial enterprise.
Master Haddad had spent more than five decades making dutars and teaching others to play them. His students shared his enthusiasm, and the atmosphere suggested that the craft was being sustained not only through technical instruction but also through personal commitment.
Master Haddad and his students took turns performing several local pieces, first individually and then together. The music filled the workshop, turning an ordinary room into a space where the outside world seemed to recede.
The sound was distinctive: sometimes gentle and reflective, sometimes energetic and rhythmic. The musicians’ movements were unforced, and their concentration was evident. They did not seem to be performing merely to entertain a group of visitors. They were sharing something they knew intimately and cared deeply about.
As the music continued, conversation gave way to listening.
In this workshop, the dutar seemed to connect the present with a much longer cultural past. The instrument’s two strings carried melodies shaped by local experience, while the musicians’ knowledge ensured that the tradition remained alive.
The performers were known as Bakhshis, a title associated with traditional musicians and storytellers in parts of northeastern Iran and Central Asia. Their role has historically extended beyond entertainment. Depending on the local tradition, a Bakhshi may preserve epic narratives, recount historical events, perform poetry and transmit the songs through which a community remembers its past.
We had planned to make a relatively short visit. But the evening continued, one performance leading to another, and the prospect of leaving became increasingly unappealing.
It was close to midnight when we finally departed.
That night, I realized that some of the most valuable places in a destination may be workshops like this one, where cultural heritage is not simply preserved behind glass but practiced, discussed and passed on.
We went to another traditional guesthouse late that night, tired from the journey but reluctant to let the experience fade.
The next morning, we were back on the road.
Farhangestan-e Kanimal: A lifetime collected under one roof
The following day’s itinerary included a private collection known as Farhangestan-e Kanimal, a two-storey building filled with objects that offered a different perspective on the province’s history.
The collection had been assembled by its elderly owner, a man of about 90 who had devoted considerable effort to bringing together materials from different periods of Iran’s past.
The ground floor contained books, historical documents, newspapers and magazines. Their range suggested an interest extending well beyond a single subject or period. The collection offered a glimpse into the changing ways Iranians had recorded events, circulated ideas and understood the world around them.
Upstairs, the focus shifted from the written record to the material culture of rural and nomadic life. There were objects associated with traditional households, village work and pastoral communities. Together, they evoked a way of life in which many everyday tasks depended on practical knowledge, locally available materials and tools that were often made to serve more than one purpose.
What made the visit especially rewarding was hearing the collection’s owner talk about it.
The owner guided us through the collection, sharing his knowledge and memories. At his age, he had witnessed an extraordinary span of social change, even if not every object in the museum belonged to his own lifetime.
The contrast between the two floors was especially striking. Downstairs, newspapers and documents recorded public events, political developments and changing ideas. Upstairs, household objects revealed the quieter history of how people lived.
Both are necessary to understand the past.
In a province such as North Khorasan, where rural and nomadic traditions have helped shape local identity, preserving these objects is particularly valuable.
Farhangestan-e Kanimal left me with a warm impression precisely because it was so personal. It was not simply a display assembled to attract visitors. It reflected the sustained curiosity of an individual who had spent much of his life gathering pieces of the past.
Beside the private museum was an apple orchard. With the owner’s permission, I picked two apples directly from the trees and ate them.
They were exceptionally crisp and fragrant, with a freshness and flavor that seemed entirely different from the apples I usually bought in Tehran.
I later learned that North Khorasan is known for its apple production. The province’s agricultural diversity is one of the less celebrated aspects of its identity, alongside its cultural heritage and natural attractions.
Wrestling, apples and the festive spirit of Shirvan
After lunch at a cozy traditional restaurant, we headed to a local event featuring koshti ba chokheh, a form of traditional wrestling associated with the Khorasan region.
The atmosphere was lively. People had gathered to watch the matches, and the event offered a glimpse into a sporting tradition that has long occupied a special place in the region’s social life.
Koshti ba chokheh is generally associated with local celebrations and communal gatherings, including Nowruz festivities and, historically, weddings. It has also been an important setting for demonstrating strength, skill and the qualities expected of a pahlavan, or champion.
The sport is rooted in a wider culture of wrestling across Iran, where physical strength has traditionally been linked to ideas of courage, honor, generosity and community standing.
In Khorasan, the local form has developed its own identity, with characteristic clothing, techniques and customs.
The wrestling event was also a reminder that cultural heritage is not confined to architecture, museums and handicrafts. It can be embodied in movement, physical skill, competition and collective emotion.
A short distance away, another celebration was taking place: the Shirvan Apple Festival.
The event featured apples and a range of apple-based products, including apple vinegar. Modest stalls displayed local produce, offering visitors an opportunity to see the agricultural side of the province’s identity.
The festival was particularly interesting because it brought together two different dimensions of local life. On one side was a traditional sport rooted in community gatherings. On the other was an agricultural celebration centered on a crop associated with the region.
Both were expressions of local identity, but in different ways.
In a stall that was in fact a vast tribal tent, some women were preparing different kinds of bread, and the sight of them working around the ovens gave the festival a warm, informal atmosphere.
At the festival, the women were not just selling food. They were demonstrating a skill and sharing something of the cultural world from which it came.
I bought several pieces, thinking that they would be a pleasant reminder of the journey when I returned home.
By then, North Khorasan had already offered us much more than I had expected: mountain history, living musical traditions, an elderly collector’s personal museum, exceptionally fresh apples and a traditional sporting event.
Yet the most extraordinary experience of the trip was still ahead.
The hidden valley of Estarkhi
It was early in the evening that we left the apple festival and continued towards Esfarayen.
It was during this drive that we reached the historical Estarkhi village, where I encountered a bizarre house that would become one of the defining memories of the journey.
To reach it, we first had to walk for about ten minutes down a dirt track on a steep slope. The path was quite narrow and, as far as I can remember, there was a precipice alongside it. By the time we arrived in the area, however, it was already dark. Still, we felt it would be a shame to leave without seeing the house.
After about ten minutes of walking downhill, we reached a small river, whose flowing water stood out in the silence of the night. We then followed an uphill dirt path for another two or three minutes before finally reaching the house.
The owner, a man named Ali, warmly welcomed us. He was middle-aged, with long, graying hair and a long gray beard. After serving us tea, he showed us the different parts of the house, which he had built with his own hands over many years, with very little in the way of resources.
The owner had created the place brick by brick, drawing on the materials and possibilities of his surroundings. The complex offered views of the wooded valley and mountains, while the nearby river and waterfall gave it a setting that felt almost separate from the outside world.
There were also treehouse-style rooms built around the sturdy trunks and branches of two walnut trees said to be about a century old.
I spent some time talking to the owner.
He explained that, during a period when he had very little money, he had gradually carved into the rocks using a pickaxe and a sieve, working slowly over the years to shape the site.
His account suggested a long process of trial, labor and patience rather than a project completed according to a conventional timetable.
What struck me most, however, was not only the physical work he had undertaken. It was the way he spoke.
He talked quietly, without any apparent need to impress his visitors. There was a remarkable calmness in his face and manner, and it seemed to extend into every sentence.
I had met many people during my years of travelling and reporting, but his presence affected me in a way I found difficult to explain.
Perhaps it was the contrast between the stillness of the valley and the relentless pace of Tehran. Or perhaps it was the sight of someone who had devoted years to creating a place according to his own vision, without rushing towards a quick result.
In an age when projects are often measured by how quickly they can be completed and how soon they can generate a return, there was something unusual about encountering a place that appeared to have grown at the pace of its maker.
I imagined him working through different seasons, returning to the same rocks, gradually changing the contours of the site and finding ways to make the buildings fit the terrain.
Such a project requires more than technical ability. It demands persistence, a willingness to live with uncertainty and a clear enough idea of the desired result to keep working when progress is slow.
The luxury of having nowhere to hurry
The longer I remained there, the more I thought about the meaning of travel.
There was something deeply appealing about the idea of staying in the historical village of Estarkhi to see its other gems and spending a morning without checking the time.
We eventually had to leave. The journey was not over yet. We still had to reach Esfarayen before midnight to spend the night.
One last night in Esfarayen
After leaving Estarkhi, we continued to Esfarayen, where we spent the night in another traditional guesthouse.
By then, the pace of the trip had begun to catch up with us. We had covered long distances, visited a wide variety of places and met people whose stories had added unexpected depth to the journey.
Our accommodation was modest, in keeping with the spirit of the trip. We were not looking for luxury, and the simple guesthouses had allowed us to experience something closer to local life than we might have encountered in standard hotels.
The next morning, we rose early and headed back towards Jajarm to catch our train to Tehran.
There was one important place we had hoped to visit but could not fit into the schedule: the historic city of Belqeys.
I was disappointed not to see Belqeys, but the omission also gave me a reason to return.
For a traveler, an unfinished itinerary is not always a failure. Sometimes it is an invitation.
The train arrived at Jajarm station about half an hour late.
As we waited and then settled into our seats for the return journey, I began to think about everything that had happened over the previous three days.
The trip had started with a simple suggestion from a friend. I had accepted because North Khorasan was a province I had never visited, without expecting that the experience would leave such a strong impression.

Farage vows to shut down UK ‘asylum scam’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
14:37:15 UTC
23:37:15 KST

Farage vows to shut down UK ‘asylum scam’
Reform UK leader Nigel Farage has unveiled a sweeping immigration crackdown plan that would suspend Britain’s asylum system for up to five years, deport tens of thousands of migrants and scrap key legal protections for asylum seekers.
Speaking at a press conference on Monday, Farage called illegal immigration a “national security emergency,” accusing successive Conservative and Labour governments of losing control of Britain’s borders.
“We’re in the most terrible mess as a country. We literally have no idea who is here,” Farage said. “There are too many people here who frankly should not be here. We need time to sort out the mess.”
The proposals, outlined in a policy document titled “Ending the Asylum Scam,” would immediately void around 90,000 pending asylum applications if Farage’s party comes to power, with claimants facing deportation to their home countries or safe third countries.
Refugees granted asylum in the past five years would also have their cases reviewed, while new asylum claims and most refugee resettlement routes would be suspended.
The plan would also see Britain withdraw from the European Convention on Human Rights (ECHR), repeal the Human Rights Act, pass mass deportation legislation and suspend the application of the 1951 Refugee Convention pending its reform. Countries refusing to accept deported nationals would face visa bans, flight restrictions, asset-related measures and potentially tariffs.
“We just want this to be a normal country. A country that detains and deports people that come illegally, as virtually every other country in the world does… A country that does everything it can to protect its own citizens,” Farage said. “We have to end this asylum scam.”
He also renewed his pledge to stop illegal English Channel crossings within the first 100 days of a Reform government and portrayed the next election as crucial to restoring public trust.
Farage has long accused the British government of favoring migrants and minorities over the white working class, citing asylum policies as an example of what he calls a “two-tier system” in which “anti-white racism” is embedded in the state. His latest plan comes amid mounting tensions over immigration and crimes involving foreign nationals.
Non-British nationals accounted for 13.1% of cautions and convictions in 2024 and 12.1% of the prison population in 2025, according to official data. Last week, an Afghan refugee was ordered indefinitely detained in a psychiatric hospital over a fatal stabbing in west London. This summer, a stabbing involving a Sudanese asylum seeker in Belfast sparked anti-immigration protests and counterdemonstrations, underscoring growing divisions.
Britain has also faced years of outrage over the notorious “grooming gangs” scandal, which exposed organized sexual abuse of minors by gangs predominantly comprising men of Pakistani origin. Longstanding failures by police and local authorities prompted a nationwide inquiry earlier this year, but public anger intensified after a Pakistani national convicted of leading a Rochdale grooming gang could not be deported under existing immigration laws.
Home Office figures show 93,525 people claimed asylum in the year ending March 2026, down 12% from the previous year, but still well above pre-2021 levels.
The next UK general election is due in 2029. Reform, which previously led opinion polls, has lately slipped behind Labour amid scrutiny of its funding and a change in Labour leadership. A recent Ipsos poll put Labour at 27% and Reform at 23%, with immigration remaining a leading concern among voters.

Lights, bells and liability: Europe’s privacy regulators crack down on smart glasses
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
14:34:37 UTC
23:34:37 KST

BRUSSELS — Privacy regulators want people wearing smart glasses in public to look and sound like a truck backing down a road.
Europe's powerful data regulators have made stringent new recommendations on how smart glasses should alert people that the wearable devices are filming, including a combination of flashing lights, audio alerts and notifications sent to the phones of people nearby.
The statement is not legally binding but will guide how privacy regulators in Europe assess whether smart glasses users and manufacturers are complying with EU privacy rules like the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR).
The regulators said smart glasses manufacturers should implement a combination of transparency measures to make other people aware that they are being recorded.
The measures may include lights or sounds when users are recording, requiring smart glasses users to activate them with an audible voice command, sending notifications to the smartphones of people nearby and other design "clues" to help people spot smart glasses.
The group of privacy regulators said that not only should users of smart glasses respect other people's privacy but that the devices' manufacturers and people providing connected apps or services may also be responsible for making sure they comply with privacy rules.
The GDPR applies to companies and organizations, and doesn't apply when people process personal data in a household context. The regulators said this household exemption should be "narrowly interpreted" when it comes to smart glasses, and would not apply when someone shares photos or videos of others "to an indefinite number of persons on a public social media account."
Advertisement
Tech firms like Meta have pitched their smart glasses to consumers on the basis that they are sleek and discreet. Meta has included an LED light in its smart glasses, which activates while recording, which it has said is a key privacy safeguard.
Samsung and Google have also recently announced that they're collaborating on a new line of "intelligent eyewear" set to launch later this year, and Apple is reportedly aiming to hit the market with its own smart glasses by the end of 2027.
The regulators' statement could now force smart glasses manufacturers to reassess whether and how they sell smart glasses to European consumers. The EDPB called for industry-wide standards to be developed to make sure people are able to spot smart glasses and understand how they process data.
The European group of privacy regulators also commissioned a study into the social acceptability of smart glasses, published today.

The unthinkable becomes thinkable: Ukraine’s politicians begin discussing compromise
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
14:33:58 UTC
23:33:58 KST

The unthinkable becomes thinkable: Ukraine’s politicians begin discussing compromise
Russia’s campaign of large-scale strikes against Ukraine’s economic infrastructure, underway since August, appears to be producing political consequences as, in Kiev, the possibility of peace is once again being discussed, and not simply in terms of negotiations from a position of strength.
For perhaps the first time since the conflict began in 2022, some Ukrainian politicians are openly considering serious compromises with Moscow, including concessions previously regarded as politically unthinkable.
Remarkably, one of the most prominent voices in this emerging debate belongs to Alexei Goncharenko, a Ukrainian MP long associated with the most uncompromising wing of the country’s political establishment.
Until recently, Goncharenko treated virtually any compromise with Moscow as treason and his position was effectively that Ukraine should continue fighting regardless of the human cost.
On October 2, however, he published what amounted to a political manifesto acknowledging that Ukraine was losing and insisting that negotiations with Russia should begin wherever possible.
Nothing, he suggested, should be excluded from discussion, including neutrality, the removal of sanctions against Russia, the status of the Russian language, and other contentious issues because sacrificing an entire nation for the increasingly remote prospect of NATO membership was, in his view, unacceptable.
The reaction was immediate. Goncharenko was branded a Kremlin sympathizer, expelled from Petro Poroshenko’s European Solidarity party and added to the ‘kill list’ database maintained by the controversial Ukrainian website Myrotvorets.
Yet he wasn’t entirely isolated because other political figures, including parliamentary committee chairman Daniil Getmantsev and Kharkov Mayor Igor Terekhov, have expressed positions suggesting a growing willingness to reconsider Ukraine’s approach and MP Anna Skorokhod also introduced legislation proposing neutrality.
For now, these politicians represent only a small minority of the Ukrainian establishment, therefore they possess neither the influence nor the institutional resources necessary to alter government policy.
Nevertheless, their emergence is significant as for the first time in years, an identifiable group within Ukrainian politics is openly challenging the prevailing assumption that the conflict must continue until Kiev achieves its stated objectives.
Previously, there was little meaningful political alternative, given how Zelensky’s principal rivals, including Poroshenko and former military commander Valery Zaluzhny, have offered different personalities and political styles, but little fundamental disagreement over the conflict itself.
The notable exception was Alexey Arestovich, the former presidential adviser who resigned in early 2023 and subsequently left Ukraine after he became an outspoken critic of Zelensky and advocated a different future for Ukraine, including some form of peaceful coexistence with Russia.
His proposals initially attracted limited support, while speculation about his presidential ambitions gradually faded.
Three years later, however, the political environment has changed considerably as successive Ukrainian counteroffensives, peace initiatives, and victory plans have failed to produce the results promised by Kiev. Meanwhile, forced mobilization, corruption scandals, and declining foreign military assistance have increased public frustration.
Dissatisfaction was accumulating, but largely remained private because for many Ukrainians living far from the eastern front, the war’s consequences, although serious, were still less immediate than those experienced in frontline regions.
Russia’s intensified air campaign against Ukraine’s energy and economic infrastructure since August has changed that calculation as disruptions to electricity, transport, and economic activity have brought the consequences of the conflict more directly into everyday life. It would be surprising if this had no effect on public attitudes.
In this respect, Goncharenko may simply have articulated concerns that were already becoming more widespread and the nervous reaction of Ukraine’s political hawks is particularly revealing. Rather than acknowledge that their own policies may have contributed to growing dissatisfaction, they have sought explanations involving Russian influence and political betrayal.
The fact that Goncharenko himself was previously among the most uncompromising supporters of the war makes his change of position especially uncomfortable for them and this presents a potential danger for Zelensky.
His continued hold on power rests partly on the argument that political leadership shouldn’t change during wartime, even as the prolonged suspension of normal electoral politics raises increasingly difficult constitutional questions.
But if discussion of peace becomes more widespread, it may eventually lead Ukrainians to question whether the present leadership is capable of delivering it.
The familiar argument against changing horses in midstream loses some of its force when people begin to suspect that the horse can’t reach the opposite bank, but for the moment, however, any suggestion of an imminent political transformation would be premature.
Ukraine’s emerging peace camp remains politically weak and far from achieving the influence necessary to challenge the government, also is there no guarantee that public frustration will translate into an organized political movement.
As long as the existing leadership retains control of the principal state institutions, the security apparatus, and much of the political agenda, fundamental changes in Kiev’s approach remain unlikely.
Nevertheless, something important has happened because arguments that were once confined largely to private conversations are beginning to appear in public political debate.
Whether this develops into a genuine challenge to Zelensky remains uncertain, but the political monopoly enjoyed by advocates of continuing the conflict is, at least, beginning to face open dissent.

Novelist Thelyson Orelien denies AI use, admits plagiarism 'mistakes'

Novelist Thélyson Orélien rejects AI claims after bestseller pulled from French prize list
Thélyson Orélien, the Haitian-Canadian writer whose best-selling debut novel was pulled from the prestigious Goncourt prize list amid an AI uproar, said Tuesday "not a single sentence" had been written by a machine. He did, however, admit to "unacceptable mistakes" regarding accusations of plagiarism involving earlier works.
A top-selling Haitian-Canadian writer who was accused of using AI to write his breakthrough debut novel denied the allegations Tuesday in his first detailed response to the scandal, while acknowledging past plagiarism "mistakes".
Thélyson Orélien, 38, was accused of using artificial intelligence to write his French-language novel about migration "C'était ça ou mourir" ("It Was Either That Or Die"), which was set to be translated in more than 20 countries.
The book has become shrouded in suspicion and been withdrawn from the shortlist for France's top book prize, the Goncourt, after tests with AI detector Pangram indicated a 100-percent probability it contained computer-generated text.
Read morePrix Goncourt drops Canadian-Haitian writer from top French literary prize list over AI claims
"They say that 'C’était ça ou mourir' was written by an artificial intelligence. That's slander and heresy," Orélien wrote in a statement sent exclusively to AFP.
"Here and there I did use tools for research, particularly for foreign idioms. But not a single sentence in this book was created by a machine, nor the meaning or the structure of a story that comes from my gut."
At the height of the media storm around his book last month, Orélien had vowed to talk when "things calm down" and promised to provide "proof" that the book had been written without recourse to AI.
In his statement, he said he had started writing the book in late 2017 "on the corner of a table" and he completed a first draft in 2019 of more than 300 pages – several years before the advent of AI-enabled text generating services such as ChatGPT.
He has not made early drafts available, however, and his Canadian publisher Boreal has said it is unable to categorically confirm or deny the allegations of AI use.
'Apology'
The AI scandal surrounding Orélien is one of the biggest in the literary world, focusing attention on whether AI use is acceptable for novelists and leading to questions about the reliability of apps that claim to be able to detect text written by services such as ChatGPT or Claude.
Pangram is considered one of the most reliable and testing by AFP on an excerpt of "It Was Either That or Die" indicated a 100-percent probability that Orélien had used AI to produce it.
AFP ran excerpts through other AI detection tools and came up with a variety of results – from it being "very likely" to have been written by a human to "100 percent" AI-generated.
Watch moreWill AI write our books? Row over bestseller fuels fear over future of literature
Orélien also addressed evidence of plagiarism which emerged in media reports in the weeks after the AI claims, in particular over a newspaper column and a short story he wrote before the publication of his novel.
He admitted to "unacceptable mistakes" without mentioning any specific cases.
"I was just over 20, I was probably a little too impatient, without really understanding how much I still had to learn. I wanted to write, I was reading a lot... But admiring someone does not give you the right to take, to claim as mine texts that are not my own," he wrote.
"I deeply regret it and offer my heartfelt apologies without reservation."
Orélien fled his native Haiti following a 2010 earthquake that struck the Caribbean island, already ravaged by poverty and unrest.

Russia builds giant bomber shelters at Engels air base
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
14:32:25 UTC
23:32:25 KST

- Satellite imagery shows Russia nearly finishing frames for the first three of 16 large aircraft shelters at Engels-2 bomber base.
- Each shelter measures about 63 by 63 meters, large enough to cover Tu-160 and Tu-95MS strategic bombers.
Russia has nearly finished the steel frames for the first three of 16 large aircraft shelters it is building at Engels-2, the main base for its strategic bomber fleet, satellite imagery published by open-source analysis group AviVector shows.
An Airbus Defence and Space image dated Oct. 12 shows three side-by-side shelter frames standing on new concrete pads at the base in Russia’s Saratov region, each linked to the airfield by a freshly paved taxiway. AviVector first spotted ground being broken in early September, reporting in a Sept. 6 post, based on imagery taken on Sept. 5, that work had started on the first of 16 planned shelters.
Each shelter measures roughly 63 by 63 meters (207 by 207 feet), with 7-meter (23-foot) side walls and a peak height of about 17 meters (56 feet), according to AviVector’s estimates. That footprint is large enough to cover a Tu-160 supersonic bomber, which is about 54 meters long with a wingspan of nearly 56 meters when its wings are fully spread, as well as the smaller Tu-95MS turboprop bomber. Behind the frames, workers have built earth berms that deflect jet blast upward when aircraft run their engines, a sign the shelters are meant for aircraft to start up and taxi from directly.
Engels-2 sits about 600 km (370 miles) from the front line in Ukraine and is home to the bulk of Russia’s long-range bombers, which fire cruise missiles at Ukrainian cities from inside Russian airspace. Ukraine has repeatedly sent long-range drones against the base since December 2022, hitting fuel and ammunition storage and, in the past few months, parked aircraft. In July, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said the SBU had destroyed a Tu-95 at Engels, and a satellite image taken days later appeared to show the wrecked bomber. A second Tu-95 was damaged in an SBU Alpha drone strike on the base on Aug. 28.
Until now, Russia’s bombers at Engels have been parked in the open, where commercial satellites can photograph them and drones can find them. Covered shelters would hide which aircraft are present and give them some protection against drone warheads and debris, and Russian crews have also painted outlines of Tu-95 bombers on the tarmac at Engels to confuse drone operators and imagery analysts. Russia can no longer build new Tu-95s, so every airframe lost to a strike permanently shrinks its long-range fleet.
The structures visible in the imagery are steel frames that have yet to be clad, and it is not yet clear what materials will be used for their walls and roofs. AviVector has not given a timeline for completing all 16 shelters, and the Russian Ministry of Defense has not commented on the construction.

Poland and Norway have signed a declaration on deepening security cooperation, including joint defence production, strengthening NATO’s northern and eastern flanks, and continuing to support Ukraine.
“In a world where the international order, laws and principles are being violated by the world’s biggest players, Poland and Norway show how partnership can be built on shared values and interests,” said Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk, alongside his Norwegian counterpart, Jonas Gahr Støre.

The two leaders signed a declaration on strategic partnership during a visit by a Norwegian delegation to the Warsaw Security Forum, where Norway is this year’s partner country. The agreement sets out a framework for closer long-term cooperation between the two countries.
Among the commitments made by the two countries are “deeper operational cooperation” and expanding joint procurement and production between their respective defence industries.
Warsaw and Oslo also pledged to work together on strengthening NATO’s eastern and northern flanks, as well as to coordinate responses to cyberattacks, hybrid operations and foreign information manipulation.
“The point is that Europe should take on greater responsibility for security,” said Støre. “We must invest in it more coherently and consistently, so as to avoid duplication, but invest in such a way that regional defence systems are stronger.”
The declaration also promises continued support for Ukraine in its defence against Russia, as well as efforts to ensure a just and lasting peace and to “hold Russia accountable for its war of aggression”.
Although security issues dominate the declaration, the two countries also pledged to deepen economic ties, including in the energy and maritime sectors.
Robin Allers, a scholar at the Norwegian Institute for Defence Studies, told the Polish Press Agency (PAP) that the move to sign the declaration with Poland was part of a broader Norwegian strategy to deepen mutual commitments with key NATO partners amid uncertainty over US engagement in Europe.
“Today’s agreement demonstrates your country’s increasingly important role in Europe,” said Allers, pointing to Poland’s growing economic and military strength, as well as its role in supporting Ukraine.

Last year, Norway opened a facility in Poland, Camp Jomsborg, for training Ukrainian military personnel. In January, it was announced that Poland will manufacture missiles for rocket artillery systems that Norway is purchasing from South Korea. The two countries also have close energy ties. In 2022, the Baltic Pipe began delivering Norwegian gas to Poland, helping the country reduce its reliance on Russian supplies. Norway’s Equinor is also involved in developing one of Poland’s first offshore wind farms in the Baltic.

Hurricane Simon weakens to Category 1 off Mexico's Pacific coast
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13

23:31:10 KST

Mariam Ashalem De Andres
13 October 2026•Update: 13 October 2026
Hurricane Simon weakened to Category 1 off Mexico's Pacific coast on Tuesday, as authorities warned of continued heavy rainfall, strong winds and dangerous waves in western states.
The National Civil Protection Coordination (CNPC) reported the weakening in a post on US social media company X, urging residents in affected areas to remain alert as hazardous weather conditions persist.
Simon had maximum sustained winds of 150 kilometers per hour (93 miles per hour), with gusts reaching 185 kph, according to authorities.
The hurricane's center was located off the Pacific coast of Mexico, west of Cabo Corrientes in Jalisco and south-southwest of Mazatlan in Sinaloa.
Authorities warned that the storm could continue to generate heavy rainfall, strong winds and high waves along parts of Mexico's western coastline, despite its downgrade in intensity.
The National Meteorological Service (SMN) forecast heavy to very heavy rainfall in western Mexico, including areas of Jalisco, Nayarit, Colima and Sinaloa, raising concerns about possible flooding and landslides.
Jalisco, located along Mexico's central Pacific coast, and neighboring Colima could experience hazardous coastal conditions, while Nayarit, north of Jalisco, could also be affected by the storm's rain bands.
Sinaloa, further north along the Pacific coast, remained under close monitoring as Simon continued a northwestward trajectory.
The weakening does not necessarily mean the threat has ended, as heavy rainfall and dangerous waves can persist even after a hurricane loses intensity.
Simon strengthened earlier in its development, prompting authorities to monitor its trajectory and warn communities along Mexico's Pacific coast.
Authorities continue to track the hurricane as it moves over the Pacific, with its future path and the extent of its effects depending on changes in its intensity and movement.
Residents were advised to follow guidance from civil protection officials and remain alert to warnings as weather conditions evolve.

13 October 2026•Update: 13 October 2026
US existing-home sales increased 1.5% in September, beating expectations of a 0.8% decline, according to National Association of Realtors (NAR) data released on Tuesday.
Sales rose on a monthly basis in the South and West, remained unchanged in the Midwest and fell in the Northeast. All four regions recorded declines compared to last September.
Despite the seasonally adjusted monthly increase, August and September were the two weakest months for home sales this year, said NAR Chief Economist Lawrence Yun.
Recent increases in mortgage rates have reduced the number of buyers able to qualify for a home purchase, he added.
Rising housing inventory and longer selling times, meanwhile, are giving buyers greater negotiating power, according to Yun.
He said sellers need to set realistic expectations based on local market conditions and may need to offer price reductions or other incentives to attract buyers.
The existing-home sales report covers completed transactions involving single-family homes, condominiums and cooperatives.

Swiss Re estimates CHF1.7 billion hailstone damage

Swiss Re estimates CHF1.7 billion hailstone damage
The extreme weather that hit Switzerland at the end of August caused insured losses of around CHF1.7 billion, according to an estimate by Swiss Re.
The reinsurance company notes that the weather is increasingly becoming a driving force behind catastrophic events in Europe as well.
The hailstorm that struck Switzerland occurred in a relatively densely populated area, said Leopold Camara, a senior executive at the company, during a press conference at the reinsurance industry meeting in Baden-Baden, Germany.
More
Is it raining harder and harder? Yes, it’s not just your imagination
It could have been even worse: “The same event in Zurich would probably have caused much greater losses.” The unusual storm on August 28 brought not only strong gusts of wind but also large quantities of hail, with hailstones locally reaching a diameter of up to five centimetres. The regions hardest hit were Bern, Solothurn, Aargau, Zurich and Thurgau.
Cars were particularly hard hit. According to Swiss Re, damage to vehicles is in fact becoming an increasingly significant aspect of extreme weather events. A single event can affect many thousands of vehicles. As for the hailstorm at the end of August, damage to motor vehicles alone amounted to around CHF 800 million.
This was not an isolated incident: in northern Italy, too, hailstorms in July and August caused extensive damage to cars. Prevention is also becoming increasingly important. Measures include issuing warnings about such events as early as possible and providing access to covered parking facilities.
According to Swiss Re, the current year has also shown how forest fires caused by extreme heat and prolonged drought are becoming increasingly significant for the insurance sector.
Over the last few decades, the associated losses have risen by 8–11% annually. However, for the sector, heatwaves represent an interconnected risk affecting various areas of insurance. Extreme weather conditions can, in fact, jeopardise energy supplies, infrastructure and the entire economy.

MOSCOW, October 13. /TASS/. The number of people who sympathize with Russia in Germany has not decreased following the closure of the Russian House in Berlin; on the contrary, these people have become more active, Russian Foreign Ministry Spokeswoman Maria Zakharova said at the 3rd International Catherine Forum.
She also noted that by seizing tankers, the West is trying to revive maritime piracy, but the world apparently sees how destructive such actions are.
TASS has compiled the spokeswoman’s key statements.
Further humanitarian work in Germany
Russia continues its humanitarian work in Germany after the closure of the Russian House in Berlin, now in an online format: "The Russian House in Friedrichstrasse, which had been operating since 1984, has been closed. Germany has denounced the intergovernment agreement. Another consulate general, in Bonn, has been closed. But our work has not stopped. It has simply shifted to the online format. At this point. As for the future, we will be looking for other formats. Not because that is how the task has been framed within our country, but because we see a positive response, and even urgent calls, for Russia not to withdraw from there and continue maintaining its humanitarian and cultural presence."
The audience in Germany that sympathizes with Russia has not shrunk but has become more active after the closure of the Russian House in Berlin: After all, despite the reduction in these venues, which was carried out by the German authorities, the audience is not shrinking; on the contrary, it is only growing. And this is despite the direct pressure, blackmail, and threats from the German authorities."
German residents who have no Russian roots but who "want to develop themselves and their children, to give them the opportunity to learn foreign languages, marched with picket signs around the building of the Russian House in Berlin, demanding that their own government not do this": "They are not foreign agents or influence agents. They are people who understand the contribution of Russia and Russian culture to the world’s heritage, who understand that the world would never have been as it is today, in the very best sense of the word, without Russian scientists, people of education, culture, and arts, and who simply want to develop on their own. They don’t demand any money from their country’s government, they simply want it to make a decision in their favor, in favor of German citizens."
The West’s piracy
The West is seeking to revive maritime piracy by seizing tankers in international waters: "Maritime piracy the West is seeking to revive adds to the destabilization of the situation around the world."
Western countries have "broken free from the constraints of international law and immediately tried to destroy it and do away with the law of the sea as well."
There is no doubt that the world sees how destructive such actions are: "The West was constrained by [legal frameworks], and this prevented them from carrying out their expansionist policies. I think that, in time, everyone will come to understand just how utterly destructive their actions are."
Russia’s openness to the mass media
Russia is open to absolutely all mass media outlets: "We never shut out any correspondents, nor do we close our country off to them."
"We are open to all media outlets because that is how people receive information. We understand that if we are not represented there, that place will be taken by those who disseminate Russophobic and anti-Russian information."
Foreigners and returnees in Russia
The number of repatriates in Russia is expected to increase by the end of 2026: "As of today, 14,967 people have registered with Russia’s Migration Service under the state program during the first nine months of 2026. Of these, 6,025 are repatriates. By the end of the year, their number is expected to rise further compared to 2025."
Consulates have issued nearly 2,000 visas to foreign nationals seeking temporary residence permits in Russia who share traditional values: "According to the consular department, as of October 4, 2026, Russian consular offices have issued 1,989 visas under Decree No. 702 [‘On Providing Humanitarian Support to Persons Who Share Traditional Russian Spiritual and Moral Values’]."
The situation in the Balkans
Russia will never abandon its stance that Kosovo is part of Serbia and will continue to support the UN Security Council’s relevant Resolution 1244: "We often hear people say: "Nowadays, we often hear: how long are you going to keep fighting for this UN Security Council Resolution 1244, which states that Kosovo is part of Serbia?" We will stand firm for it and there is no other choice for us."

Dutch-born panda cub Lang Yue to move to China this month
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
Lang Yue, the giant panda cub born at Ouwehands Dierenpark in Rhenen, Utrecht, two years ago, will leave for China at the end of October, the zoo has said.
The zoo agreed with the China Wildlife Conservation Association that giant pandas born outside China must move there before their fourth birthday, the zoo said in a statement.
Lang Yue, who was born on July 12, 2024, no longer depends on her mother for food. In the wild, giant panda cubs stay with their mother for about two years before living alone.
In China she will join the national breeding programme for the species, and the zoo hopes she will eventually have cubs of her own. Ouwehands zoo is also planning a farewell ceremony.
Her parents, Wu Wen and Xing Ya, will stay in Rhenen. They arrived from China in 2017 as part of a conservation partnership between the zoo and China, broadcaster NOS reported. The zoo is hoping the pair will breed again.
Lang Yue is the second panda born in the Netherlands. Her older sister Fan Xing, born in May 2020, was sent to China in September 2023.

The Pacific Ocean broke records for the duration and intensity of hurricanes due to El Niño
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
17:25:30 EEST
23:25:30 KST

The Pacific Ocean broke records for the duration and intensity of hurricanes due to El Niño
Kyiv • UNN
A series of powerful hurricanes in the Pacific Ocean broke records for duration and intensity. Scientists link this to El Niño, warm water and climate change.
According to scientists, a series of extremely powerful hurricanes in the Pacific Ocean has broken the record for the intensity and duration of storms east of the International Date Line. This is being fueled by an especially strong natural phenomenon known as El Niño. CBS News reports, UNN writes.
Details
According to Colorado State University researcher Phil Klotzbach, storm activity remains high. Hurricane Simon is currently raging in the region, and conditions also exist for the formation of another powerful storm. On Tuesday, the Pacific Ocean is expected to tie the record for the number of days with a hurricane, a record that will likely be surpassed soon.
Hurricane Simon off Mexico’s west-central coast. Satellite image from the morning of October 13, 2026. NOAA / National Hurricane Center.
Scientists explain this activity by several factors, the main one being El Niño. This phenomenon weakens vertical wind shear, which usually inhibits storm development. In the Pacific Ocean, winds are predominantly moving in the same direction as the hurricanes, contributing to their intensification.
Water temperature also plays an important role. In the area of the Pacific Ocean where the storms are forming, it is several degrees Fahrenheit above normal. According to University at Albany Professor Kristen Corbosiero, the warming is linked to El Niño. Researcher Kim Wood also noted that water temperatures are affected by climate change caused by the burning of coal, oil, and gas.
At the same time, weather conditions in the Atlantic Ocean have hindered hurricane development. The accumulated cyclone energy index there is less than 18% of normal for this time of year. This year, the Atlantic basin recorded a record-long period without the formation of any hurricanes. The first was Isaias, which formed on October 7.
The last five hurricanes in the Pacific Ocean—Nolo, Odalys, Polo, Rachel, and Simon—reached major hurricane status, with wind speeds of at least 111 miles per hour. Nolo, Odalys, and Simon reached Category 4, while Polo set a record for the longest time spent as a Category 5 hurricane—two and a half days.
According to scientists, exceptional activity has affected both the eastern and central Pacific. Usually, one of these regions is more active than the other, but in 2026 both are showing high activity due to weaker wind shear, warmer water, and increased humidity.
Meanwhile, an atmospheric disturbance is being observed off the coast of Mexico that, according to the U.S. National Hurricane Center, has a 90% chance of developing into Tropical Storm Trudy. It may strengthen later.
Scientists believe that, under the favorable conditions being observed due to El Niño, the formation of new storms in the Pacific Ocean may continue.
Hurricane Simon off Mexico’s west-central coast. Satellite image from the morning of October 13, 2026. NOAA / National Hurricane Center.

PM promises EUR 1 million to film industry starting in 2028  - The Baltic Times
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
14:23:52 UTC
23:23:52 KST

RIGA - Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs (United List) has promised the Latvian film industry EUR 1 million starting in 2028, although there is still no clarity about the source of this funding.
The prime minister, who met with film industry representatives on Tuesday, told reporters that this issue is scheduled to be addressed next year as part of a review of funding that is allocated without a competitive bidding process. Kulbergs stressed that things will not continue this way.
He noted that an agreement has now been reached to offer the film industry funding that the industry can count on, and that the rules will be further developed later. Kulbergs emphasized that plans are in place to develop a model for financing the film industry.
As reported, Kulbergs had previously expressed the view that the government should consider abandoning the proposed tax on streaming platforms and instead focus more on supporting the development of the film industry. The prime minister noted that it is necessary to assess whether the benefits of such a tax outweigh the potential risks to Latvia’s relations with its strategic partners.
Kulbergs believes that the potential revenue from the tax would be relatively small, whereas the interest of foreign film producers in filming in Latvia could yield more significant benefits for the country. He noted that during his visit to the U.S., the president met with representatives of the film industry, including Warner Bros., who expressed interest in potential opportunities for cooperation.
Representatives of the Latvian film industry have raised objections to Kulbergs’ remarks, arguing that the new tax should be implemented.
Currently, the amendments approved by the Saeima in the second reading stipulate that an electronic media outlet providing on-demand audiovisual services must submit a report on revenue earned in Latvia from on-demand audiovisual services in the previous year for the first time by May 31, 2028, for the period from January 1, 2027, to December 31, 2027. However, if investments totaling at least EUR 300,000 are made in 2027 and 2028, the revenue earned in 2026 and 2027 would not need to be reported.
The aim of the draft law is to promote the creation of high-quality audiovisual content in the Latvian language and to ensure its wider availability to viewers, as stated by the Ministry of Culture in its explanatory notes. The ministry says that consumption of international streaming platforms has increased significantly in recent years, yet their products include relatively little content produced in Latvia, and furthermore, they have not yet invested in the production of Latvian films and series.
The requirements are expected to apply both to service providers registered in Latvia and to streaming platforms registered in other European Union (EU) member states whose target audience is in Latvia.
Under the proposal, service providers will be required to invest at least 3.5 percent of the revenue they generated in Latvia during the previous year. Investments may be made by funding the production of Latvian films and TV series, acquiring distribution rights to them, or making contributions to the budget of the National Film Center. These requirements will not apply to service providers with low revenue or a limited audience.
NKC Director Dita Rietuma previously told committee members that once the changes take effect, the film industry could receive an estimated EUR 600,000 to EUR 1 million per year.
The ministry notes that in Latvia, on-demand audiovisual services are provided by 26 electronic media outlets registered in Latvia, including Tet and Latvijas Mobilais Telefons (LMT), while approximately 80 service providers registered in other EU countries also operate in the Latvian market, including Netflix, Disney+, Amazon Prime Video, Apple TV+, and others.

Swiss government rejects further change to married couples' tax

Swiss government rejects further change to married couples’ tax
The Swiss government has launched its referendum campaign against the initiative ‘Yes to fair federal taxes for spouses too – Stop discrimination against marriage!”, which will be put to a vote by the people and the cantons on November 29.
Tax discrimination against marriage is now a thing of the past, thanks to the public’s endorsement of individual taxation in March.
+ Individual taxation receives massive support from Swiss Abroad
The Federal Council and parliament reject the proposed constitutional amendment put forward by the Centre Party, which provides that, for direct federal tax purposes, married couples should continue to be taxed jointly as a single economic unit.
At the same time, it calls for the Constitution to stipulate that they must not be treated less favourably than cohabiting couples.
To this end, the initiative’s promoters propose an alternative method of calculating tax, under which the tax authorities would automatically apply the tax rate most favourable to the couple. In the Federal Council’s view, the initiative is obsolete, as the electorate already approved the switch to an individual taxation system by a large majority in March 2026.
More
Swiss parliament rejects return to joint taxation of spouses
According to the Federal Council, the initiative’s approval would lead to administrative chaos with conflicting tax systems. The Confederation would have to continue to tax married couples jointly, whilst the already approved individual taxation system would apply to cantonal and municipal taxes.
Furthermore, the initiative would favour married couples and penalise unmarried people.
Joint taxation also creates obstacles for those with a second income – in most cases women – and undermines their financial independence. Depending on how the initiative is implemented, the Confederation also warns of a fall in tax revenue that could amount to as much as CHF3 billion a year.

Kimberly Guilfoyle asked to resign as ambassador after reports she asked Trump donor to pay bill
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
14:23:41 UTC
23:23:41 KST

Kimberly Guilfoyle is stepping down as US ambassador to Greece after weeks of reports that she sought payment from a Trump donor in exchange for access to administration officials.
The decision, announced by the White House on Tuesday morning, ends the diplomatic career of one of Donald Trump’s longest-standing political allies. It came after the US president and Marco Rubio, the secretary of state, were reported to have grown furious over the allegations.
“We have asked Ambassador Guilfyole to resign, she has been a wonderful asset to the team and we wish her well,” said Katie Zacharia, the new White House press secretary, during her first briefing on Tuesday.
Guilfoyle – the former fiancee of Trump’s eldest son, Donald Trump Jr – later confirmed her departure from the post, which she described as the “honor of a lifetime”, and denied what she described as “false” allegations.
Pledging to “vigorously defend my name, my reputation, and my integrity” in a post on social media, she wrote: “While my time as Ambassador may be coming to an end, my commitment to President Trump, the America First movement, and the country I love will never end.”
The most serious claim, first reported by the Wall Street Journal on 8 October, centers on the donor Eric Deters.
Citing Signal messages, the paper reported that in July 2025, days before her Senate confirmation hearing, Guilfoyle pressed Deters to pay off a $100,000 American Express bill, assuring him the transfer would not show up anywhere. “Honey please I need you to get this done for me today,” she wrote, according to the report.
Guilfoyle offered to use her influence on his tax and legal problems in return and told him she had contacted the IRS commissioner and the justice department on his behalf.
He has also said he paid Guilfoyle about $300,000 over the years without receiving “one favor”, and told MS Now the request “absolutely was a quid pro quo”.
Guilfoyle also expressed concern about the exchanges becoming public, according to the Wall Street Journal. “Eric, I really wish you would stop papering all these things,” she wrote in one message. In another, she told him: “What a nightmare you’ll literally cost me my ambassadorship stop writing.” She urged him to call her on Signal instead.
The Journal has also reported that Guilfoyle accepted improper gifts and services, made an alleged threat to a host-country official, and promoted the interests of a Greek company, Aktor, during official engagements. A lawyer for Guilfoyle, Jesse Binnall, said she disputes the authenticity of the messages.
Guilfoyle, 57, a former San Francisco prosecutor who was married until 2006 to Gavin Newsom, California’s governor, became a fixture of Trump’s political orbit after leaving Fox News in 2018 as she began dating Trump Jr. The couple became engaged in late 2020, and she was a prominent speaker at Trump’s campaign events, including the 2024 Republican national convention, before breaking up soon after in September 2024.
Trump, as president-elect, then named her for the Athens post in December 2024, weeks after his election win, calling her “a close friend and ally”. That month, Trump Jr had been photographed holding hands with Bettina Anderson, a Palm Beach socialite, and Guilfoyle was absent from the family’s post-election portrait, which did include Trump Jr’s ex-wife and their children. Trump Jr married Anderson in May.
The nomination stalled for months in the Senate until Republicans used the “nuclear option” in September 2025 to overcome a Democratic filibuster and confirm her by simple majority. She was sworn in as the first woman to represent the US in Greece, succeeding the Biden appointee George Tsunis, and arrived in Athens in late October 2025.
It ends a tenure that lasted less than a year. Hours before Tuesday’s announcement, the Greek government had denied any suggestion the ambassador was on her way out. “There has been no relevant request, nor has it been discussed with Greek authorities,” said Pavlos Marinakis, a government spokesman, when asked if she would resign.
But speculation had been rife. The allegations of misconduct engulfing the envoy were not only embarrassing for Guilfoyle. The Greek media had begun to speak of the US embassy being “headless” and dysfunctional only days after Rubio’s high-profile visit to the country. “If truth be told, she is not respected in Athens,” one well-placed insider confided.
Alec Mally, a former senior US diplomat who had handled Greek affairs at the US state department, told the Guardian the US embassy in Athens had been put “in an impossible situation because the ambassador had increasingly come across almost as if she were representing an old-style Balkan country”.
“With allegations multiplying daily, the question was whether her Trump family Teflon was anywhere near sufficient to keep her in the job,” Mally said. “It would not surprise me if the Greek public reacts with joy to the news of her resignation.”
Although there were some who argued the direct access to Trump “outweighed all the negatives” there were many who thought her appointment had been “an insult to the country’s reputation”, he added.
In recent weeks Guilfoyle had done what she had rarely done in the whirlwind 11 months since she assumed the post: remained out of sight. But reported claims she had told Greece’s energy minister that Washington was capable of toppling any government – including the center-right administration in Athens – if they didn’t toe the line had stirred outrage. On the left where many have still not forgotten Washington’s support of the 1967-74 military dictatorship, Guilfoyle’s comments had caused widespread consternation.
On 9 October in a stormy debate in parliament, Giorgos Gerapetritis, Greece’s foreign minister, was forced to deny the claim – one of several surrounding the US envoy’s alleged improper behavior reported by the Wall Street Journal – beforeSia Anagnostopoulos, the prominent leftwing politician and former deputy foreign minister, who had said it was “a question of national dignity that the American ambassador is called to give an explanation”.
Within hours of arriving in Greece, Guilfoyle was seen at a bouzouki music club, attending a party thrown by a popular singer who would go on to be one of her closest friends in Athens. “I think we can safely say she was like no ambassador Greece has ever seen before,” said one official, speaking on condition of anonymity. “I don’t think that in these uncertain times many will be shedding tears at the news of her departure.”

"There is no doubt that the Saeima has the right to decide contrary to the responsible committee, which has worked on the bill and prepared specific amendments for consideration. This is a matter of the Saeima’s conceptual decision-making.
