As previously reported, a new legal institution - partnership - has been effect in Latvia since July 1, 2024.
To ensure the legal, economic, and social protection of these relationships, provisions governing partnerships are also included in other laws, including the Law on Administrative Liability.
The Law on Administrative Liability provides for the right of the victim and witness not to testify against themselves and their fiance, spouse, parents, grandparents, children, grandchildren, siblings, and the person with whom the natural person lives and with whom they have a common household.
The amendments provide for the right of a witness and a victim not to testify against their partner, as well as restrictions on the partner to undertake defense or representation in certain cases.
Although the rights and restrictions are currently established as a result of the application of the relevant provisions, the Law on Administrative Liability contains explicit references to partnership relationships. This not only complies with the approach to regulating the issues concerned established by the Law on Administrative Liability, but also ensures more effective protection of individuals in partnership relationships.

A property may offer enough room for a distinctive home, yet the surrounding setting still shapes every practical design choice. In Quebec, urban sites require careful use of available land, while rural parcels can support broad layouts with connected work or storage areas. Early decisions about the footprint, roof profile, openings, and interior zones help create a residence suited to its location.
A barndominium Quebec can combine comfortable residential rooms with a garage, workshop, barn, or open storage area beneath one pre-engineered roof. Custom structural plans allow the building dimensions and exterior details to reflect the site, intended use, and applicable codes. This approach gives property owners control over usable space without relying on a standard prepackaged layout.
Urban Barndominium Design Choices
Urban properties in Quebec usually have defined lot boundaries, neighbouring structures, and established streetscapes that influence the building form. A compact rectangular footprint can organize the residence and garage without creating awkward leftover areas around the site. Simple exterior lines also help the structure maintain a clean residential appearance.
Plan A Practical Interior Layout
Open living areas can reduce unnecessary partitions and place the kitchen, dining room, and lounge within one connected zone. Bedrooms and private rooms can occupy a quieter section away from garage doors or workshop activities. A mezzanine may provide space for an office, guest room, or additional storage when the building design includes sufficient height.
Useful urban layout choices include:
- An attached garage with direct residential access
- Large windows placed for daylight and privacy
- A defined entrance facing the street
- Interior storage near frequently used rooms
Rural Barndominium Design Choices
Rural properties can accommodate wider buildings that connect residential areas with substantial garages, workshops, or agricultural storage. The building orientation can account for driveway access, surrounding views, prevailing weather, and the movement of equipment across the property. Wide overhead doors may suit vehicles, machinery, trailers, or recreational equipment stored beside the living quarters.
Create Defined Residential And Work Zones
A rural barndominium in Quebec needs clear separation between quiet living spaces and active work areas. Interior walls, insulation, and carefully positioned doors can limit sound transfer between the two zones. Separate exterior entrances also allow workshop or storage access without directing traffic through the home.
Practical rural design details may include:
- High ceilings for large equipment clearance
- Covered entrances for seasonal weather protection
- Open bays for vehicles or machinery
- Dedicated storage beside the work area
Match Exterior Details To The Property
Exterior finishes can give the building a residential character that suits an urban neighborhood or a rural landscape. Coordinated wall panels, roofing, trim, windows, and doors create a consistent architectural appearance. Cathedral ceilings and varied exterior features can add visual interest while remaining compatible with the engineered steel structure.
Insulation should form part of the original design because it affects residential comfort, energy performance, and indoor sound levels. The chosen package must suit Quebec’s seasonal temperature changes and the intended use of each interior zone. A carefully planned envelope supports dependable year-round use across living, garage, workshop, and storage areas.
Select A Barndominium Supplier in Quebec That Offers Custom Building Configurations
A supplier that offers custom building configurations can provide engineered designs that match the property's dimensions, intended use, and layout requirements. Flexible building options allow residential spaces, garages, workshops, and storage areas to fit within one coordinated structure. Engineered plans also help support code compliance and efficient project planning before construction begins.
Careful design decisions create a barndominium that remains practical as property needs change over time. A layout that reflects the site and intended use can improve functionality without unnecessary structural modifications later. Thoughtful planning from the beginning supports a durable and well-organized building for years of residential use.

Kazakhstan cuts oil production shortfall by 4 mln tons
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
14:23:30 UTC
23:23:30 KST

Kazakhstan cuts oil production shortfall by 4 mln tons
Kazakhstan produced 69.4 million tons of oil in January–September 2026, down 8.3% from the same period last year, while petroleum product output increased by 2.4%, Qazinform News Agency reports.
Vice Minister of Energy Yerlan Akbarov presented the latest production figures during a Government's meeting.
“Oil production totaled 69.4 million tons during the reporting period, equivalent to 91.7% of the volume recorded in the same period last year,” he said.
Oil production fell at Kazakhstan’s three largest oil fields. In the first nine months of 2026, Tengiz produced 26.7 million tons (88% of last year’s level), Kashagan 12.8 million tons (94%), and Karachaganak 7.5 million tons (82%).
Overall, the country’s oil output declined by 8.3% year-on-year. To help offset the shortfall, authorities decided to postpone scheduled maintenance at the Tengiz and Kashagan oil fields.
The Ministry of Energy is currently holding talks with field operators to increase production volumes.
“We have managed to reduce the country's overall production shortfall from 5.9 million tons to 1.9 million tons. Oil production is projected to reach 96 million tons in 2026,” Akbarov said.
Meanwhile, Kazakhstan produced 11.9 million tons of petroleum products in the first nine months of 2026, marking a 2.4% increase compared with the same period last year.
Gasoline output rose by 3.9% to 4.6 million tons, while diesel production increased by 3.3% to 4.8 million tons. Jet fuel production climbed by 21.8% to 700,000 tons, whereas fuel oil output dropped by 31.8% to 800,000 tons.
The Ministry of Energy expects petroleum product output to reach 15.45 million tons by the end of 2026, unchanged from the previous year.
Earlier, Qazinform reported Kazakhstan’s Energy Ministry had outlined the timeline for the launch of new gas infrastructure and processing projects.

Getty Images to go private in restructuring deal
Getty Images has secured backing from its major investors and lenders for a restructuring that will reduce debt, bring in fresh capital and take the company private, reports a Qazinform News Agency correspondent.
Under the agreement, affiliates of the Getty family and Koch Equity Development have committed up to $533 million in new equity. They will own the reorganized company upon completion.
Bondholders representing 83.5% of unsecured bonds have agreed to retire $270 million in senior unsecured notes. Most secured creditors and all revolving credit lenders support lower interest obligations and extended debt maturities.
“This transformational transaction is underpinned by the strength of the business and the significant growth potential we see ahead,” chairman Mark Getty said.
The company plans to implement the agreement through a prepackaged Chapter 11 bankruptcy reorganisation involving certain U.S. entities. The process is intended to address legal liabilities unrelated to its operations and is expected to finish by year-end.
Koch Equity Development will provide up to $143 million in financing to support the restructuring, alongside cash generated by ongoing operations.
Getty Images said business would continue normally, with no anticipated impact on employees, contributors, partners or customers. Vendors are expected to be paid in full in the ordinary course of business.

Source: a senior EU official involved in drafting the document for the EU leaders' summit, who spoke to European Pravda's correspondent on condition of anonymity
Details: EU leaders may approve a document expressing their regret over the Trump-Putin deal.
"Regarding the deal that has been announced, we consider it unfortunate, so we regret that this deal has been reached. I believe this position is shared by the leaders," the European Pravda source said.
"I think that following the discussion on Ukraine at the European Council, we will have an expression of regret regarding this decision," the official added.
The senior EU official pointed out that this is not the first time the US has made deals with Russia that run counter to previous agreements among Western nations that support Ukraine.
"Trump's decision contradicts the strategy we have adhered to over the past four and a half years, namely not only to put pressure on Russia, but also to decouple our energy, our fossil fuel energy, from Russian sources. And we have been quite successful in doing this," the European Pravda source stressed.
The official recalled that "with the full implementation of the REPowerEU strategy, the idea is to completely sever this link [with Russia]".
"We will continue with this strategy, because we know that this is also a way not only to stop Russia's financing for its war machine, but also to put pressure on Russia to end this war," the senior official emphasised.
"This isn't the first time we have had disagreements with the US about the war in Ukraine... Since President Trump took office, dialogue with the US has not always led to full agreement on how the EU and the US see things. But dialogue is always better than no dialogue at all," the source concluded.
The source also noted that "we have seen many cases where this dialogue has led the US to change its position, or essentially to bring the two positions closer together".
Background:
- As European Pravda previously reported, between March 2022 and July 2026, EU member states paid Russia around €197 billion (approximately US$209 billion) for fossil fuels.

From Dreyfus to David Milstein: The enduring accusation of Jewish dual loyalty - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
14:22:34 UTC
23:22:34 KST

On October 7, as Jews around the world mourned the largest massacre of our people since the Holocaust, New York’s Mayor Zohran Mamdani could not bring himself to give us even that one day.
Mamdani, who has accused Israel of genocide and campaigned on arresting its prime minister, marked the anniversary with a statement reminding New Yorkers that the suffering neither began nor ended on October 7.
The word “Israel” did not appear in it. He attended a vigil, made some hollow statements, then went on to his next meeting. For parts of his own base, even that brief appearance at a memorial was too much, and they protested against his attendance.
The next morning, October 8, The New York Times published a long investigation into David Milstein, senior adviser to US Ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee. I have watched many hit jobs over the years, and this one is among the most disturbing.
The Times said it interviewed 15 American officials. Every one of them is anonymous. Nine former diplomats were consulted for context, also anonymous. The few people who speak on the record are a former ambassador and a Democratic senator, and neither describes anything he personally saw Milstein do.
In a government the size of ours, a reporter can always find unnamed people willing to say unflattering things about someone. Those sources might sit on the Left. They might sit on the Right. Anyone who has followed the strange alliance of people who loathe Israel knows they can be found on both sides.
The core accusation is that David reviewed and revised embassy reports before they went to Washington. The article itself admits that reviewing and amending those reports is part of his job, and that political advisers to previous ambassadors did the same. So the charge comes down to this: he did his job with a point of view the Times dislikes.
The charge of dual loyalty
The article mentions that he left Washington to study in a Jerusalem yeshiva. It mentions his family. It describes him as a familiar figure in circles that support Israel. The message is that this man is too Jewish, too devoted, too close to Israel to be trusted with American interests. We have a name for that accusation. It is the oldest charge against Jews in public life: dual loyalty.
Huckabee has said he has absolute confidence in David and calls him a man of impeccable integrity. In response to the Times, he categorically rejected the story. I know David’s reputation, and I agree with the ambassador.
Here is a young man who served on Capitol Hill, who served two administrations, who has given his career to strengthening the alliance between America and its closest friend in the Middle East. He is a proud American patriot. He was preparing for his wedding when the Times decided he would make a useful target.
In 1894, Alfred Dreyfus, a Jewish captain in the French army, was convicted of treason on forged evidence. He was publicly stripped of his rank while crowds outside shouted for death to the Jews. His real crime, as all of France would eventually learn, was being a Jew in a position of trust.
A young journalist from Vienna named Theodor Herzl watched that spectacle. What he saw convinced him that Jews would remain vulnerable until they had a land of their own to defend them. Two years later, he published the book that launched modern Zionism.
The tactics have changed very little since then. Today the weapon is a newspaper story stitched together from unnamed accusers rather than a forged letter. The goal is the same: to push Jews out of positions of influence, and eventually out of public life altogether, by suggesting their loyalty lies elsewhere.
The difference is that now we have Israel. That fact infuriates those who would prefer we had nowhere to go. Israel is the answer Herzl found in Paris, and it remains the reason so much hatred is aimed at any Jew who stands with it openly.
This is a message for my fellow Jews in New York who believe they can keep their Judaism while holding Israel at arm’s length. I understand the instinct. History offers no example of it working.
If Israel did not exist, the people who hate us would find another excuse, as they always have. Recently I watched a prominent voice in one hassidic community publicly side with Mamdani over Israel’s prime minister. That path will not protect anyone. When they come for the Jew who supports Israel, they will not stop to check how strongly the next Jew feels about it.
Jews have always been the canary in the coal mine. This fight concerns the West itself: democracy, freedom, the idea that people can build better societies through faith, family and responsibility.
The movements now rising on the far Left, many with roots in socialist and communist ideology, have brought ruin wherever they have taken power. Jews stand in their way, and so does Israel. That is why the attacks come first for us.
Mamdani showed us on October 7 exactly how much our grief is worth to him: a few hollow words, quickly followed by the same accusations he has hurled at Israel for years.
The Times showed us on October 8 what comes next, when a dedicated public servant is dragged through the mud by faceless accusers for the crime of loving Israel while serving America. Anyone fooled by a single day of sympathy has not been paying attention.
The men and women who stand with the Jewish people, as Milstein has done his entire career, deserve our loudest and most public defense.
Milstein deserves our support. The Times owes its readers names, evidence, and context. The rest of us owe ourselves the clarity Herzl found in Paris more than a century ago: our safety depends on standing together, with Israel, and without apology.

For AP, Oct. 7 is a monument to mark Palestinian suffering - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
14:22:04 UTC
23:22:04 KST

Deganit Bar Hay, an Israeli survivor of the Hamas-led October 7 massacre, cannot barbecue because the smell of burnt flesh is still a trigger three years later, she told the Associated Press. Let that horrific thought sink in for a moment.
Hundreds of thousands of survivors of Hamas’s rampage of murder, maiming, rape, torture, kidnapping, burning, and destruction share her enduring trauma.
In Israel, three years afterward, one in five Israelis are still “struggling to function” due to mental health disabilities, a new study found.
But for the leading wire service, Deganit’s ongoing trauma is merely a footnote to what the news agency considers the real story: that is, the “tragedy in Gaza.”
On the eve of October 7, 2026, the third anniversary of the deadliest day for Jews since the Holocaust, Deganit’s heartbreaking pain is buried in the seventh paragraph. The article’s focus, as the headline puts it, is “Much of the world sees tragedy in Gaza. Many Israelis, scarred by October 7, see only a threat.”
Deganit’s trauma serves as a mere vehicle to probe what the news agency sees as the real story on the anniversary of this horrific massacre of Israelis: “tragedy in Gaza.”
Thus, as Israelis gathered to mark the Palestinian mass murder of their own people in their homes and at a music festival, the AP perversely highlights Palestinian victimhood.
Even more perversely, on the anniversary of Hamas’s unprecedented slaughter of Israeli civilians, the AP faults Israeli victims for not seeing beyond their own self-absorbing pain to share concern for Palestinian hardships.
“There is little discussion of Palestinian civilians,” a subheading complains.
Indeed, in the opening paragraphs describing Israelis peering through binoculars towards “the shattered Gaza town of Beit Hanun,” AP falsely frames the scene as Israelis exhibiting cruel callousness towards Palestinian civilians.
“The lookout is a rare place where they can confront the Palestinian territory firsthand, and some celebrate its devastation,” AP’s Cara Anna opines, completely erasing Hamas from the equation.
She then cites one onlooker quoted in an Israeli documentary: “Wow, destroyed beautifully.”
In her fallacious telling, Israelis rejoice in the pain of civilians, not in the destruction of the terror infrastructure that enabled the unspeakable horrors their own communities suffered on October 7 and still torment to this day.
The news agency’s unfortunate photo choice reinforces the distorted narrative in which ghoulish Israelis supposedly rejoice in the suffering of neighboring civilians.
Of the five photos and one video illustrating the October 7 story, the first image viewers encounter is not of Israelis mourning their dead or visiting their still savaged homes, but of Israelis peering through the binoculars towards the Gaza Strip.
“Three years on, a visit to the communities attacked that day made clear: it’s too soon for many residents to see the Palestinians next door as anything other than a threat,” AP reports, implying that their fears are unfounded and unjustified.
AP's double standards
Alleging that the “vast majority of [Gaza’s] 2 million residents live in rat-infested camps or among the debris,” AP charged: “But empathy for them is still unthinkable for many in Israel, with memories raw.”
Under what moral or journalistic compass does a leading news outlet mark the anniversary of a massacre by highlighting the victims’ ostensible failure to empathize with the plight of the other side?
At the time when Israelis commemorate their dead, and their living dead – those who have been completely unable to pick up the pieces of the wreckage of their lives in the wake of the trauma, loss, devastation, and physical injuries – why in the world would their thoughts be turned to their brutalizers’ population?
Is there any precedent in human history or psychology in which the victims spend the anniversary of the horrific day in which their lives and communities were destroyed pondering the ensuing hardships of the side responsible for the unspeakable horrors they endured?
Last March, when AP covered the fourth anniversary of the Russian massacre of Ukrainians in Bucha near Kyiv, its reporters did not question the victims’ failure to identify with Russian suffering endured due to the war they themselves started by invading Ukraine.
On the contrary, the story rightly noted the atrocities which Russian perpetrators inflicted on their Ukrainian victims, including the Bucha slaughter of at least 400: “Authorities say that many of the victims were gunned down in the street. Some had their hands tied behind their backs, and others showed signs of torture or rape.”
Many Israeli victims – shot or burned – had their hands tied behind their backs. Some were tied together, parents and children. Sometimes naked. They were tortured and raped.
And yet, in its October 7 anniversary story, AP didn’t note the bodies found with their hands tied behind their backs or those that showed signs of torture or rape.
Instead, it laments that Israelis show signs of insensitivity towards Palestinian suffering.
“Many Israelis are still turned inward,” said Anna, an editor on AP’s Global Desk who has reported from Ukraine.
“Empathy is biased and parochial; it focuses you on certain people at the expense of others; and it is innumerate, so it distorts our moral and policy decisions in ways that cause suffering instead of relieving it,” psychology professor Paul Bloom wrote in Against Empathy: The Case for Rational Compassion.
It turns out that empathy also distorts journalistic decisions. In AP’s entrenched empathy bias, even October 7 is a moment to mark Palestinian suffering.
According to this orthodoxy, not even the still-suffering victims of October 7 are exempt from bowing their heads at the immutable altar of Palestinian victimhood.

Under the plan presented by Hezbollah Executive Council chairman Ali Damoush, eligible families in Beirut and its southern suburbs will reportedly receive $14,000, including $8,000 for furniture and $6,000 for rent. Families elsewhere in Lebanon will reportedly receive $12,000, comprising $8,000 for furniture and $4,000 for rent, maintaining the same rates as in 2024.
Damoush claimed the assistance would cover families whose homes were destroyed, deemed uninhabitable following technical assessments, or severely damaged, as well as those displaced from Israeli-occupied areas or nearby locations.
The aid will be restricted to families who used the affected properties as their primary residences and do not own a second home, excluding summer homes and abandoned properties, according to the terror group.
Payments will be made in four installments over one year, starting with $3,500 for families in Beirut and its southern suburbs and $3,000 elsewhere.
Damoush said that eligibility and the type of assistance would be determined based on a set of criteria assessing the extent of damage to each property.
US economic pressure on Iran is boosting difficulty in transferring funds to terror proxy Hezbollah
Hezbollah received the cash last month despite tightening US economic pressure on Iran and increasing difficulties in getting funds to Tehran's Lebanese ally, according to the two people who spoke to Reuters.
At the time, a Hezbollah official said an amount had been secured and that a plan for distributing it would be announced in the coming days, without elaborating on the source of the funds.
The United States disputed the Reuters report, saying the money was "not there." Iran has not commented.
Damoush on Tuesday declined to comment on either the Reuters report or the US reaction, and declined to provide a figure for the total amount Hezbollah would dedicate to shelter support.

France Explores Nuclear Microreactors to Power Military Bases and Field Operations

France Explores Nuclear Microreactors to Power Military Bases and Field Operations
France’s army is considering the use of compact nuclear reactors to supply electricity to military installations, command centers, and field hospitals as part of a broader effort to modernize its battlefield energy infrastructure.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to the French Army’s Déclinaison capacitaire d’Action Aéroterrestre Future (DCF) document, published by its Future Combat Command (CCF), nuclear microreactors are among several technologies being examined to improve energy independence and operational capabilities.
The official document identifies energy production and storage as priorities for future ground operations, with containerized nuclear reactors emerging as one potential solution for supplying electricity to military facilities.
These compact installations could provide power to command posts, logistics centers, and deployed medical facilities, potentially reducing dependence on conventional fuel deliveries and external electricity networks. French military planners have identified three areas of energy development.
The first focuses on compact, high-energy-density batteries for individual soldiers and robotic systems, intended to increase available power without significantly increasing equipment weight.
The second involves hybrid propulsion and the electrification of armored vehicles. These technologies could reduce vehicle detectability while supplying additional electricity to onboard systems.
The third focuses on evaluating containerized nuclear reactors as an alternative source of electricity for military operations.
However, France has not announced a procurement program or selected a manufacturer. It remains unclear whether the army would adapt existing commercial reactor technology or pursue a system developed specifically for military applications.
The proposal remains at the research and capability-planning stage, with no confirmed deployment timeline.
Separately, France has been expanding its nuclear defense capabilities. On March 2, President Emmanuel Macron announced plans to increase the country’s nuclear warhead stockpile and stop publicly disclosing its size, citing a deteriorating global security environment.
He also confirmed that France’s next-generation nuclear-powered ballistic missile submarine, Invincible, is scheduled to enter service in 2036.

Wall Street's biggest banks reported another strong quarter on Tuesday, but they warned that higher rates and inflation could bite.
Higher profits at four of the biggest US banks offered fresh signs of economic resilience, as consumers continued repaying their debts and businesses kept investing heavily in AI.
But even as JPMorgan Chase, Citigroup, Wells Fargo and Goldman Sachs reported higher profits than a year ago, they warned about the long-term impact of higher interest rates and the pressure rising prices could put on consumers if inflation is not brought under control.
JPMorgan Chase, the largest US bank by assets, posted a $15.3 billion profit in the third quarter, or $5.57 a share, up from $14.4 billion, or $5.07 a share, in the same period a year earlier. The results missed analysts' expectations, with Wall Street expecting the bank to earn $5.93 a share.
It was a rare earnings miss for JPMorgan and its CEO, Jamie Dimon. The last time the bank missed analysts' expectations was nearly three years ago. The bank reported $658 million in investment securities losses and a 12% rise in expenses. Fixed income markets revenue fell 4% from a year earlier, although overall markets revenue rose 15%.
"The US economy continued to be fueled by strong business investment and ongoing consumer spending," Dimon said in a statement. "However, large fiscal deficits, sticky inflation, elevated asset prices, rising interest rates and geopolitical conditions continue to shift under the surface."
The big banks typically open the quarterly earnings season, and this is a key one for the stock market given that strong corporate profits have helped push the S&P 500 to record levels.
Analysts expect companies in the S&P 500 to deliver overall growth of nearly 30% in earnings per share from a year earlier, according to data provider FactSet. If they're correct, it would be the third consecutive quarter of growth above 25%.
Goldman Sachs, whose third-quarter profits rose sharply as revenue from its equities business jumped 72% from a year earlier, also reported that its fixed income, currencies and commodities revenue fell 24% from the second quarter. The bank posted a profit of $5.29 billion, or $17.01 a share, compared with $4.1 billion, or $12.25 a share, a year earlier.
The bond market saw significant volatility this summer, as investors became increasingly worried about government spending and inflation. Yields on 10-year and 30-year US Treasury bonds rose to levels not seen in years. Higher diesel, technology and food prices gave the Federal Reserve reason to raise interest rates last month, despite pressure from the White House against a rise.
Citigroup said its third-quarter profits jumped 40% from a year ago, beating Wall Street expectations. The bank posted higher revenue from investment banking and wealth management, while profits in its credit card division were flat.
Wells Fargo posted a profit of $5.95 billion, or $1.87 a share, beating Wall Street forecasts. The San Francisco-based bank has seen its profits climb steadily in recent quarters after federal bank regulators removed the asset cap imposed following its sales practices scandal nearly a decade ago.

Today, at the Starodorozhsky training range in the Republic of Belarus, servicemen of the CSTO joint NBC protection and medical support formation began practical operations as part of the “Barrier-2026” special exercise.
At this stage of the exercise, the participants are practicing occupying the designated area, engineering preparations for the assembly area, camouflage, organizing comprehensive support, and preparing the forces and assets of the joint formation to carry out tasks in support of the CSTO Collective Peacekeeping Forces.
As part of NBC reconnaissance, the crew of an RKhM-8 reconnaissance chemical vehicle collected a sample from a suspected contaminated area and delivered it to a field chemical laboratory to test for the presence of hazardous or particularly dangerous infectious agents.
The field chemical laboratory complex consists of two modules. The first detects toxic or radioactive substances in samples, while the second detects biological warfare agents and pathogens of dangerous infectious diseases.
During the exercise, laboratory personnel conducted real-time polymerase chain reaction (PCR) testing of a soil sample taken from an area potentially contaminated with biological warfare agents. The analysis was performed using an ANK-32 nucleic acid analyzer capable of processing 32 samples simultaneously.
The exercise involves practicing joint actions to conduct biological reconnaissance, collect and analyze samples, and carry out full decontamination.
The Republic of Belarus is hosting the command-and-staff exercise with the CSTO Peacekeeping Forces “Indestructible Brotherhood-2026” and the special exercise with the CSTO joint NBC protection and medical support formation “Barrier-2026”.
At the Starodorozhsky training range, the “Barrier-2026” special exercise focuses on practicing the elimination of sources of biological threats in the area of responsibility of the CSTO Collective Peacekeeping Forces.
The exercises involve contingents of the CSTO Troops (Collective Forces) from the Republic of Belarus, the Republic of Kazakhstan, the Kyrgyz Republic, the Russian Federation and the Republic of Tajikistan. These include military contingents, units of internal affairs bodies (police) and the National Guard, as well as operational groups from the CSTO Joint Staff and Secretariat. The Russian military contingent is primarily composed of units of the Combined Arms Army of the Central Military District.
In total, more than 1,500 servicemen and over 300 items of weapons, military and special equipment are involved, including approximately 80 different types of unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs).

CSTO Collective Peacekeeping Forces Commander approves the concept for a peacekeeping operation as part of the “Indestructible Brotherhood-2026” exercise

Colonel Alexey Yelfimov, Commander of the CSTO Collective Peacekeeping Forces and a representative of the Armed Forces of the Republic of Belarus, organized the work of officials of the Joint Command of the Collective Peacekeeping Forces to assess the situation and develop the concept for the upcoming joint actions. In the afternoon, the concept for the peacekeeping operation was approved.
The concept defines the areas where the main efforts are to be concentrated, the tasks assigned to peacekeeping units, and matters related to coordination, comprehensive support and command and control.
While presenting the concept, Colonel Alexey Yelfimov said, in particular:
“Based on an analysis of the current situation and the mandate received, I have decided to focus the main efforts on creating conditions for a just and peaceful settlement of the conflict.
The peacekeeping tasks are to be carried out in three stages.
At the first stage, the Collective Peacekeeping Forces will occupy their area of responsibility, separate the opposing sides, ensure a safe environment in the crisis area and isolate the area of responsibility.
At the second stage, the CSTO Collective Peacekeeping Forces will monitor the area and the activities of the population, guard and defend critical infrastructure facilities, establish comprehensive protection zones, and ensure the safe transit of all types of transport and the functioning of communications.
At the third stage, the main focus will be on transferring critical infrastructure facilities and the area of responsibility to the local authorities.”
At the same time, units at the training range began tactical training sessions focused on their forthcoming actions as part of the CSTO Collective Peacekeeping Forces.

Russian forces use group of civilians as 'human shields' near Kupiansk, fire at them afterwards, Ukraine's military says

Russian forces use group of civilians as 'human shields' near Kupiansk, fire at them afterwards, Ukraine's military says
Russian forces led a group of civilians toward a gas pipeline, using them as human shields, and afterwards opened fire at them near the front-line city of Kupiansk in Ukraine's Kharkiv Oblast on Oct. 13, the Ukrainian military said, providing alleged drone footage of the incident.
The group included two women, a child, and several men who were being led toward the Shebelinka–Ostrogozhsk gas pipeline, according to Ukraine's 13th Khartia Corps. The group came under repeated mortar and artillery fire as it moved.
Drone footage recorded by Ukrainian reconnaissance units showed casualties among the civilians, Khartia said, adding that Ukrainian troops had not opened fire. Based on the impact patterns, the strike originated from the eastern bank of the Oskil River, where Russian forces are positioned, the corps said.
Khartia called the strike a "deliberate provocation" and warned that Russian media could use footage from the incident to falsely accuse Ukraine of attacking civilians. The corps said it would hand over the materials for a war crimes investigation.
"Civilians are used as human shields by the Russians, and then become their target for disinformation campaigns," Khartia wrote.
Ukraine's Joint Forces grouping separately said on Oct. 13 that Russian forces had struck a column of civilians leaving Kupiansk during what it described as a forced evacuation. The military said it was still establishing the number of casualties.
According to the Joint Forces grouping, Russian troops had conducted similar operations in recent weeks, using civilians as human shields to cover the withdrawal of some of their soldiers.
The Kyiv Independent could not independently verify the claim.
Throughout the full-scale war, the Russian military has regularly breached international warfare conventions, including through indiscriminate attacks on civilian areas and the abduction of civilians from occupied territories.
On Sept. 29, Khartiia Corps said Russian troops use civilians, including children and elderly people, as human shields to flee via a gas pipeline in northeastern Kharkiv Oblast amid the Ukrainian push in the Kupiansk sector.
Khartiia Corps said the group of civilians would have to walk more than 10 kilometers (about six miles) through the pipeline before exiting into a forest, where they would likely be transported to Russian-occupied territory.

In Warsaw, Albares defends role of Europe, multilateralism and international law in the face of challenges to world order
Spain
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
16:20:03 CEST
23:20:03 KST

PRESS RELEASE 154
In Warsaw, Albares defends role of Europe, multilateralism and international law in the face of challenges to world order
- More than 3,000 participants from over 90 countries have gathered at the Warsaw Security Forum to discuss security in Europe and transatlantic relations
- During the event, the minister held a bilateral meeting with his Polish counterpart, Radosław Sikorski
The Minister for Foreign Affairs, European Union and Cooperation, José Manuel Albares, took part on Tuesday in the Warsaw Security Forum, where he defended Spain’s position of preserving, strengthening and reforming the multilateral system – with international law at its core – in the face of the profound transformation of the international system, as well as the fundamental role that a more sovereign European Union must play in all of this. On the fringes of the Forum, the Minister held a bilateral meeting with the Polish Minister for Foreign Affairs, Radosław Sikorski.
“The real question is not whether change is on the horizon. Change is already underway. The real question is whether that transformation will be governed by international law and cooperation, or by coercion and spheres of influence,” the minister stated in his address to the panel ‘What will come after the liberal international order?’.
A leading forum
Joining the minister on the panel to share their views were the Foreign Ministers of Ukraine, Andrii Sybiha, and of Estonia, Margus Tsahkna; Republican Senator Roger Wicker; and the former Foreign Minister of Iceland and current Council of Europe Special Envoy for the situation of Ukrainian children, Þórdís Kolbrún Gylfadóttir.
The Warsaw Security Forum, which has established itself as a leading platform for debate on security issues, seeks to promote high-level institutional dialogue to coordinate defence policies, strengthen deterrence, enhance democratic resilience and anticipate hybrid threats, ranging from the war in Ukraine to cyber security and energy security. This year’s event features over 3,000 participants from more than 90 countries, including five Heads of Government and over 30 ministers.
Ukraine
In his speech, Albares emphasised the need to preserve at all costs the principles and norms that restrict the use of war, such as sovereign equality, territorial integrity, the prohibition on the use or threat of force, human rights and the peaceful settlement of disputes. In this regard, he added, Russia’s aggression against Ukraine is testing whether the borders and political decisions of sovereign States can be altered through the use of force.
The minister called for a just and lasting peace for Ukraine, with credible guarantees, which does not reward aggression and which respects its sovereignty and territorial integrity.
He also advocated for Europe to take a more decisive role in its own defence, with a decisive step towards EU Common Defence as a pillar contributing to a stronger NATO, and with more integrated military capabilities, a more robust European defence industrial base, and a genuine 360-degree approach to security, which recognises that Europe’s security challenges come from the east and the south, and include hybrid and cyber threats, as well as other threats to economic security and environmental challenges.
Bilateral meeting
On the sidelines of the Forum, the minister met with his Polish counterpart, Radosław Sikorski, at the Polish Ministry of Foreign Affairs to discuss and strengthen bilateral relations, as well as to review the EU agenda and key issues on the international stage.

Motorsport as a bridge between Italy and Japan. To mark Japan’s National Sports Day, celebrated on October 12, the Italian Embassy in Tokyo brought together over 200 guests for an event dedicated to the sporting and industrial excellence of “Made in Italy” in two- and four-wheeled competitions.

According to the diplomat, the evening serves as confirmation of this: “Italian creativity and design engage with Japanese industry, giving rise to successful collaborations.” High-quality cars, motorcycles, and components, he added, bring to Tokyo “a testament to one of the most competitive ‘Made in Italy’ ecosystems in the world, both on the racetrack and in international markets.” The event is part of the sports diplomacy initiatives promoted by the Italian Ministry of Foreign Affairs. There was also a focus on esports, thanks to a collaboration with Polyphony Digital, the development team behind the Gran Turismo video game series for PlayStation. Finally, during the evening, the 1000 Miglia announced a special event scheduled for April 2027 between Nara and Kyoto, to mark the centennial of the historic Italian race.

Pentagon awards $8.3M for 10-minute blood clotting test
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
14:18:25 UTC
23:18:25 KST

- DARPA awarded Abram Scientific up to $8.3 million to develop CoagCare, a handheld clotting test that delivers results in under 10 minutes.
- The work supports DARPA’s RAPIID program, which aims to field an FDA-authorized shelf-stable blood substitute kit as early as fiscal 2029.
DARPA, the Pentagon’s research agency, has awarded Abram Scientific a contract worth up to $8.3 million to develop CoagCare, a handheld device that shows how well a wounded person’s blood is clotting in under 10 minutes from a single drop, so medics can decide on transfusions far from a hospital.
The Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency funds high-risk technology for the U.S. Department of War, and over the past few years it has put a growing share of its medical work into one problem: keeping badly wounded troops alive until they reach surgery. Abram Scientific, based in Menlo Park, California, announced the award on Oct. 13, a year after DARPA gave it $2 million in October 2025 to shrink the device to a size that can travel with medics.
Uncontrolled bleeding is one of the leading causes of preventable death after severe injury, on the battlefield and in civilian emergencies, and the best treatment is whole blood given as soon as possible. Donated blood has to be kept refrigerated and expires within weeks, which makes it hard to stock at small outposts, aboard ships or with units that may wait days for evacuation in a large war. Military medics often fall back on “walking blood banks,” drawing fresh blood from fellow soldiers on the spot, but that only works when donors are close by and screened.
DARPA is trying to solve that with a program called RAPIID, short for Resuscitation and Prevention of Ischemia-Induced Dysfunction, launched in May. The 36-month effort aims to turn lab-made blood components, such as oxygen-carrying substitutes and dried plasma, into a shelf-stable kit medics can carry, with the goal of FDA authorization as early as fiscal 2029. It builds on an earlier DARPA program, FSHARP, in which a team led by the University of Maryland, Baltimore showed that synthetic parts could perform key functions of whole blood. RAPIID also needs fast bedside tests, because a medic has to know what a casualty’s blood is doing before deciding which substitute to give and how much.
CoagCare is meant to be that test. It pairs a compact meter with a single-use card and measures how thick and dense a drop of blood becomes as it clots, tracking the process from the moment a clot forms until it breaks down. Hospital machines that do the same job, known as thromboelastography and thromboelastometry, can take 30 to 60 minutes per test and need laboratory conditions, while CoagCare is designed to work despite the vibration inside ambulances and MEDEVAC helicopters.
“Rapid access to actionable coagulation information can be critical for saving lives in trauma care, when every minute matters,” said Abhishek Ramkumar, founder and CEO of Abram Scientific.
Under the new contract, Abram Scientific will tune CoagCare to guide doses of the blood substitutes being developed under RAPIID and set up production lines for the meter and its test cards. The company will also design a military version for frontline use, and because the military and civilian models take the same disposable card, one factory line can serve both.
Swiss plasma products maker Octapharma led a Series A funding round in Abram Scientific in February to speed up development and help the company apply for FDA 510(k) clearance, which would allow CoagCare to be sold for managing transfusions in civilian trauma and surgery. Abram Scientific holds 17 granted patents on the technology and is working toward that FDA filing while it builds the military version for DARPA.

Todd Haynes at Lumière Festival: 'It is a time to remember how important it is to protect our freedoms'
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
14:17:37 UTC
23:17:37 KST

"It is a time to remember how important it is to protect our freedoms, and our ability to speak freely." Euronews Culture sits down with celebrated filmmaker Todd Haynes during this year's Lumière Film Festival.
One of the guests of honour this year at Lyon’s Lumière Film Festival is none other than Todd Haynes, one of the most important and singular voices in contemporary American cinema.
The celebrated director and screenwriter of Far From Heaven, I’m Not There, Carol, and May December is known for his pioneering work associated with the New Queer Cinema movement of the early 90s. He then gained acclaim for his films exploring the emotional repercussions of social repression and the unspoken desires revealed by marginalized experiences.
He attends the Lumière Film Festival to present the restored versions of his directorial debut Poison (1991), a provocative exploration of AIDS-era perceptions. He also presents the Julianne Moore-starring psychological drama Safe (1995), marking the first time that these two films have screened in French cinemas since their initial releases.
Euronews Culture sat down with Todd Haynes during the festival to discuss the enduring timeliness of Poison and Safe, his thoughts on the evolving Hollywood ecosystem, as well as his upcoming film De Noche.
Euronews Culture: How does it feel to be at the Lumière Film Festival in Lyon, the birthplace of cinema?
Todd Haynes: Pretty thrillingly natal! No, really, it's a festival I've been hearing so much about for so long. And it really is such a celebration of movies of all kinds, of every genre, of every era. Restorations are presented, artists are attributed, and it's a really remarkable place and atmosphere, and it's so much about just the filmmaking and the films.
There's a retrospective of your films, including two newly restored versions of Poison and Safe. How do you look back on these films, and how do you feel about the fact that there are going to be audiences at this festival who are seeing these two films for the very first time?
I was there for the introduction of Poison. People were asked in the theater who were seeing it for the first time and almost every hand went up! And it was a completely full theatre, so that just demonstrates a kind of interest and curiosity about what's being shown in Lyon, and an audience that is very enthusiastic about it.
So, it's incredibly meaningful. These are my first two features. They are very, very different. Poison came out in the height of the AIDS era and it was among the first couple of films that would join other films in being categorised as the New Queer Cinema. None of which, I don't think, would have been possible outside of that political and socio-economic crisis - the public health crisis of AIDS. In certain times, those kinds of conditions make creating film and documentary, and protest and organised resistance, essential. They drive a kind of urgency that we don't always feel in our medium or our market. That was absolutely true for Poison. And then I made a film [Safe] that also is, in my mind, inconceivable without the AIDS era as a framework. It's a film that takes the place about as far away from the battlefield, if you will, but still engaged. A lot of the themes and issues deal with illness, and the body, and feeling alienated from the world around you...
I had the pleasure of re-watching both films, and that sense of isolation in Safe still feels incredibly prescient.
That’s always surprising and encouraging to hear. I understand how that might be what people could say about Safe. The film was watched again during Covid. There was a lot of discussion about the film and articles that came out were sent to me. And sadly, these issues remain relevant when we're hit by things that are overwhelming and that challenge every single aspect of the way we lead our lives, and the assumptions about how to live our lives that we take for granted.
Both explicitly and implicitly about the AIDS crisis, do you find it heartening or disheartening that Poison and Safe still feel timely? After all, Poison was made at a specific time, and there are many members of the gay, trans, queer communities who continue to feel threatened and continue to express fears...
Absolutely. One does feel at times like we’re in a replay, if not crashing backwards in battles we’ve fought. Battles around reproductive rights, around tolerance and acceptance over queer communities and trans communities. Poison in particular addressed very much that sense of vulnerability that the community was feeling under the siege of AIDS and HIV.
Jean Genet, who's a writer and thinker and poet and playwright who I've always loved - but also derived a certain energy from his attitude about how important it is to remember that being defined marginal... The goal to that is not necessarily to find your way back to the table and become just like everybody else. For him, his queerness, it came out of a criminal background. He liked that homosexuality had this criminal aspect to it. He used that as a way of weaponising his critique of dominant culture. Poison was made at the very end of the 80s and we needed a voice like that.
I'm heartened to see that some of Jean Genet’s books are displayed next to DVDs of your films at the Lumière marketplace...
Oh, I didn’t see that. That’s awesome!
From a European perspective, when you look at present day Hollywood, it’s hard not to see a sense of regression. For instance, to take a recent example, the Paramount-Warner merger feels like it threatens the financing of films from a plurality of voices. What are your thoughts on the evolution of the studio system and Hollywood at the moment?
It's distressing when you see the conglomeration of huge media organizations that one might imagine would provide enough revenue and foundation for risk-taking to still occur. But sadly, that is rarely what you end up seeing. I don't feel it, particularly in the moment, among some of the big streaming companies. There's a sense of wanting to repeat what worked the last time, and keep replicating what the audiences seem to crave. And that's tough.
For my last couple films, we've really gone elsewhere. I mean, we did sell May December, my last feature, to Netflix - and they were a fantastic company, full of incredibly smart people who really believed in the film. But the way we made the film was through the limited amount of investment that we absolutely had to have to get it done so we could all retain our creative freedom and identity. That's how we put together the financing for my current film that I'm finishing now, De Noche. And in that case, I really do want a company fully committed to theatrical release.
Discourse around film and the creation of film feels in jeopardy at the moment. For example, we saw it this year at the Berlinale with the controversy surrounding Tricia Tuttle and the pro-Palestinian speeches made by invited filmmakers. Do you fear or foresee that cultural institutions will become increasingly threatened by political pressure, like in Berlin?
Sure. I think Germany has a unique, specific, and at times contradictory attitudes or laws around how we discuss Israel, for instance. There's this happening on the one hand where speech is kind of being watchdogged and limited, and people have a hard time of just saying that it doesn't have to be about Jewish people to have problems with the policies of Netanyahu, or whoever it may be.
But at the same time, the AfD is rising in Germany... So you have that complete sort of disconnect between these two forces - one trying to make remedy after an incredibly horrific past in history, and then all of a sudden, wanting such extreme change to come into place from completely the opposite direction.
So, Germany is a unique case, but I think we're feeling similar things about a crackdown on content and what is called ideology or point of view in the United States. It's targeted at the media, it's targeted at the news industries, and it's targeted at universities... So it is a time to remember how important it is to protect our freedoms, and our ability to speak freely.
To temporarily move away from the doom and gloom, I wanted to share with you that the first film of yours that I saw was Velvet Goldmine (1998), which had a profound impact on me. I remember seeing the trailer for the first time, watching Brian Slade in his feather outfit on stage, hearing the gunshot followed by the needle drop of T. Rex’s '20th Century Boy', and... it still gives me goosebumps.
(Laughs) Awww....
The film turns 30 very soon... How do you look back on Velvet Goldmine and please tell me there’ll be a resotration?
Oh, it's another film that sort of realised or completed a phase of my creative life that was very profound and deep in that whole era of music and the early 70s. And the very interesting relationship between the UK and the US in how that music came to be. Criterion Collection is working on the release of Poison that will coincide with that 30th anniversary. I'm very, very excited about that.
Music plays a big part in your filmography – whether it’s Karen Carpenter, Bob Dylan, The Velvet Underground... I read somewhere that you’re working on a documentary about The Cure...
You know, that was news to me! (Laughs) Somebody brought it up... I mean, I love The Cure and they were formative in my life. Their music and evolution as a band from record to record... But no, it's not something I'm doing, and I'm not exactly sure where that came from! (Laughs)
Can you blame people for trying to manifest this project into existence?
(Laughs) Exactly!
Well, glad we got that cleared up! You mentioned your upcoming film, De Noche... You’ve wrapped, right?
We've wrapped the film and we're in post-production. We're moving from the picture cut to the sound. The whole production was based in Mexico. And this film was a particular struggle to get to this place, so I'm very proud of it.
You mention struggles...
Oh well, it began with the relationship with an actor [Joaquin Phoenix] who came to me for it and we moved forward. We got very close to production two years ago, and then he had a very abrupt or unexpected change of heart and walked away. And so De Noche 1 fell apart. But it was remarkable how the financiers and the investors who were there for that version came back, and demonstrated loyalty to the project and a film that means so much to all of us.
I’m glad De Noche 2 happened, with Danny Ramirez and Pedro Pascal starring. You also worked with Jon Raymond, who you’d previously collaborated with on the miniseries Mildred Pierce. I’m a huge fan of his work with Kelly Reichardt, especially on Old Joy and First Cow, which is a masterpiece in my book.
I couldn't agree more. Jon is a novelist first and has become a screenwriter. I’m so proud to have played even the smallest part in introducing Jon to Kelly when I moved to Portland, Oregon. They met each other, and they really hit it off. Many of his short stories were the first places that she went to in order to resuscitate a career in feature filmmaking that she had kind of put aside. And amazingly, well before she ended up even settling down in the Pacific Northwest, she and Jon really became the chroniclers of that region, its history, of Portland and beyond. So that unexpected move in my life to Portland from New York City... There have been so many rewards from it. And Jon is one of my dearest, closest friends. He's the most fabulous human being.
I can't wait to see De Noche. Is there anything else you can tell us about the film?
I don't know if I've ever quite seen anything like it before as a concept. It sort of begins as a detective story in the late 30s in a very corrupt Los Angeles, and through circumstances and the corruption that these two characters have become embroiled in, they're forced to leave Los Angeles and flee to Mexico. A very inexplicable, unexpected relationship begins to form between the two of them. To get to that point, a lot of dynamics of divisions between them in terms of power and race are overcome bit by bit, step by step, through the exploration of each other as lovers. It ultimately becomes a love story that that leaves you, I hope, longing and wondering what will happen between these two men.
To wrap up, at the opening ceremony of the Lumière Festival, you shared with me that the first film that had a profound impact on you was Mary Poppins. What was it about that film that marked you?
For one thing, it was the sort crown jewel of the Disney experiment, in terms of the films that came out of Disney at that time. The score is so exquisite, the two actors who take the leads are just perfection, it's so beautifully produced... I think for a three-year-old's imagination, there’s something about a maternal subject who comes with unique powers, and also discipline. Just a curious combination of various aspects of that character. I think seeing a movie on the big screen for the first time can't be overstated. The sheer power of that... I think all of those things conjoined to make it a sort of escapable moment of introduction to this medium.
This year has been a very good one in terms of cinema attendance and that being mirrored at the box office. Still, there are cinemas struggling and many fears expressed about the threat that artificial intelligence represents for the creative arts. As broad a question as this is, are you optimistic about the future of cinema?
I have to be optimistic. Because it's a medium I just love. I wasn't able to shoot De Noche on film, as we couldn't afford it, but it will always be my starting point on any film that I make. And what you are seeing among young people is an incredible desire to go out of their houses and leave their home screens and their phones behind and join in the experience of watching a movie on the screen.
You know how we all thought vinyl was going to go away with the introduction of CDs and MP3 and there was a sort of counter movement that was like ‘No, I want to hold it in my hand'... The desire to actually experience it and the warm resonance of hearing vinyl play with a needle on... Sometimes the simplest technology remains the best and the most profound. I hope that continues and I hope we can see that still being played out. It is about younger people and exposing them to what that experience means, and what that's like to share communally in a theatre in the dark.
On that note, Mr Haynes, thank you very much for your time.
The Lumière Film Festival takes place until 18 October in Lyon, France. The restored versions of Todd Haynes' Poison and Safe are being screened, as well as Far From Heaven and I'm Not There. Safe is out now on Criterion 4K UHD Blu-ray.
Todd Haynes' new film, De Noche, finished shooting in April 2026. No release date has yet been announced.

Ken McCallum said the ramp up in alleged Russian hybrid attacks across Europe had come as Russia's military progress in Ukraine was "minimal and horrifically costly."
The director general of Britain's MI5 domestic intelligence service warned on Tuesday that Russia remained "aggressor number one" amid increasing threats from foreign states.
Delivering an annual speech from Thames House in London, Ken McCallum told attendees that MI5 was currently "devoting more resources to countering state threats than during the Cold War."
"The Russian military and intelligence services are once again escalating their attempts at hybrid warfare, being careful to stay below the NATO Article 5 threshold, which would be foolish for them to cross," he added.
A number of states have accused Moscow of being behind hybrid attacks on European territory in recent months, including Germany and Estonia. Berlin blamed Russia for a drone attack at Leipzig/Halle airport in August, while Tallinn said that Russian special services had ordered an arson attack targeting defence firm Milrem Robotics, also in August.
According to McCallum, such incidents are part of a Russian plan to "unsettle" European nations as it continues to wage its all-out war in Ukraine, which began in February 2022 after Moscow launched its full-scale invasion of the country.
McCallum said the ramp up in alleged Russian hybrid threats had come as Russia's military progress in Ukraine was "minimal and horrifically costly," adding that it was turning to proxies to carry out attacks.
"With its traditional covert footprint eviscerated by almost 1,000 expulsions since the invasion, the Kremlin's global toolkit is weak. So, we see them scrambling to pay criminals to do their bidding," he told the audience.
British Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said the UK would continue to support Ukraine "100%" despite warnings of "consequences" from Russia. Last week, Burnham again reiterated his "complete solidarity" with Kyiv and stressed that his government would go further with sanctions on Russia.
Iran
McCallum also addressed Iran in his speech, calling it another state "keen on subcontracting its UK violence" and saying it was looking to "expand" its hybrid campaign.
"Today, we continue to see familiar Iranian intent, using criminal proxies to try to intimidate oppositionists, Iranian media organisations, and Israeli sites," he said.
Over the last year, McCallum said Iran-linked operations had led to more than 50 arrests.
He added that much of the aggression had targeted British Jewish communities, but that Iran was also looking to go after "harder targets, like military sites."
His comments come after Burnham told parliament on Monday that an incident at a UK airbase that houses part of the US Air Force was "almost certainly directed" by Iran's Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC).
On 27 September, five men were arrested near RAF Fairford in Gloucestershire, southwest England, on suspicion of explosives offensives, before being further arrested on suspicion of preparing a terrorist act. They were later released on police bail.
Police later arrested another man, a 25-year-old dual UK-Iranian national, in London on suspicion of preparation of terrorist acts related to the incident. A 22-year-old British man was then arrested on 6 October, also in London and on suspicion of preparation of terrorist acts. Both were released on police bail.
According to UK Counter Terrorism Policing, all seven men remain on police bail as specialist teams "continue to pursue all lines of enquiry."

Bangladesh’s Russian-built nuclear reactor reaches key milestone

Unknown Publisher

Bangladesh’s Russian-built nuclear reactor reaches key milestone
The first unit of Bangladesh’s Russian-backed Rooppur power plant, the country’s first nuclear reactor, has achieved criticality, sustaining a controlled nuclear chain reaction for the first time.
Criticality – where a self-sustaining chain reaction occurs – is a major step toward electricity generation and keeps the plant on track to be connected to the power grid by the end of November. The unit reached the milestone at 3:34 PM local time on Sunday, three days after receiving clearance from the Bangladesh Atomic Energy Regulatory Authority.
It followed commissioning delays from technical problems with safety valves. Russian specialists helped resolve the issues, and the reactor underwent further tests before the regulator authorized the controlled reaction.
The reactor successfully initiated nuclear fission, with operating parameters performing according to design, the Daily Star cited Bangladeshi Science and Technology Secretary Md. Anwar Hossain as saying. Further regulatory approvals will be required before electricity generation begins.
Russian state nuclear corporation Rosatom expects the unit to connect to Bangladesh’s grid by the end of the month, CEO Aleksey Likhachev said in Dhaka on Friday.
The Rooppur plant, located about 160 km from Dhaka, comprises two Russian-designed reactors with a combined capacity of 2,400 megawatts. Moscow is financing $11.9 billion in state loans for the project, which is estimated to cost up to $12.8 billion.
The project is expected to diversify Bangladesh’s electricity supplies as the country faces pressure from high energy import costs and disruptions linked to the Middle East conflict.

OPEC+ countries increase oil production by 956,000 bpd in September — report

MOSCOW, October 13. /TASS/. OPEC+ nations participating in the oil output cut agreement increased their crude production by 956,000 barrels per day (bpd) month-on-month in September, according to data from the latest OPEC monthly report.
Excluding Iran, Libya, and Venezuela - which are exempt from the deal - as well as the UAE, which withdrew from OPEC and OPEC+ effective May 1, the alliance's output stood at 30.753 million bpd.
OPEC+ previously extended the deadline for members to compensate for earlier overproduction through the end of 2026, though an updated schedule has not yet been released. The previous timeline envisaged the compensation period ending in June 2026. Consequently, the alliance's baseline September quota stood at 36.206 million bpd, meaning actual production fell short of the target allocation by 5.453 million bpd.
Among the OPEC+ nations, Saudi Arabia recorded the largest increase in oil production in September, scaling up output by 744,000 bpd to 8.001 million bpd. Other producers also boosted output: Iraq ramped up production by 386,000 bpd to 3.920 million bpd, Kazakhstan by 22,000 bpd to 1.851 million bpd, and Algeria by 3,000 bpd to 1.003 million bpd. Meanwhile, Kuwait’s oil production dropped by 140,000 bpd to 1.766 million bpd, and Russia pared output by 38,000 bpd to 8.643 million bpd, while Oman’s production remained virtually flat month-on-month at 939,000 bpd.
Among OPEC members exempt from the alliance's production curbs, Libya saw its output drop by 59,000 bpd to 1.291 million bpd in September, while Iran’s production fell by 99,000 bpd to 1.957 million bpd. Venezuela, however, marginally increased production by 18,000 bpd to 1.150 million bpd. Meanwhile, the UAE, which recently withdrew from OPEC and OPEC+, boosted its oil output by 86,000 bpd to 3.917 million bpd.

Netflix has decided to broadcast the FIFA World Cup in Europe — where it will show the matches
Kyiv • UNN
Netflix will exclusively broadcast all 104 matches of the 2030 World Cup in Spain and Andorra. One match per day will be available for free.
Netflix has taken a major step in the field of live sports broadcasting in Europe by acquiring from FIFA all rights to the 2030 FIFA World Cup in Spain and Andorra. UNN reports this, citing The Hollywood Reporter.
Details
The deal, announced on Tuesday, October 13, will give Netflix exclusive rights to all 104 matches of the tournament in these territories. The streaming service plans to do everything possible to provide full live coverage of the matches, pre-match, half-time and post-match shows, as well as a daily match review. Netflix also announced plans to create a major pre-tournament program to build interest in the event.
Not all matches will be available with a paid Netflix subscription. Under the agreement, Netflix will provide one match per day free of charge in Spain and sublicense a package of matches, including every Spain match, both semi-finals and the final, to the national free-to-air broadcaster.
Spain, the reigning FIFA World Cup champion, will also host the 2030 World Cup together with Morocco and Portugal. The year 2030 will mark the event’s 100th anniversary, and celebratory matches will also be played in Argentina, Paraguay and Uruguay.
This is not Netflix’s first major football deal. The streaming service holds the rights to broadcast the 2027 and 2031 FIFA Women’s World Cups, and earlier this year announced a four-year agreement with the Confederation of North, Central America and Caribbean Association Football (CONCACAF) to broadcast, starting in 2027, the Nations League final and CONCACAF Gold Cup tournaments in Mexico.
But acquiring the rights to broadcast the World Cup in the very heart of Europe, in one of the world’s most football-oriented countries, is a significant step forward for Netflix and a clear signal of the company’s ambitions regarding live sports broadcasting at the international level, the publication notes.
In the United States, Netflix already broadcasts NFL and MLB games, as well as selected boxing, MMA and WME events.

The Germany Enabling Office (GEO) is the United Kingdom’s military mission in Germany and the responsible authority for enabling, monitoring and assuring the conduct of United Kingdom defence in Germany under the United Kingdom’s obligations to the NATO Status of Forces Agreement (NATO SOFA) and the Supplementary Agreement (SA) in Germany.

Ben-Gvir won't have a surplus-vote agreement after refusing to sign with Winter
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
14:12:05 UTC
23:12:05 KST

Otzma Yehudit chairman Itamar Ben-Gvir announced Tuesday afternoon that he would not sign a surplus-vote agreement with Ofer Winter, leaving his party as the only one in Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's bloc without such an agreement. The arrangement is valid only if both parties pass the electoral threshold. Yoaz Hendel, whose Reservists Party joined forces with Yaron Zelekha, has already announced that he will not sign an agreement with Ben-Gvir.
Surplus-vote agreements can be signed until Friday, 11 days before the election. In a post published Tuesday afternoon, Ben-Gvir echoed the message of Likud's campaign against Winter, accusing him of being "Bennett 2.0."
Winter's Amcha Israel party responded to the post: "Itamar, grow up. People are fed up with the gimmicks, the rhetoric and this way of doing things. Just a moment ago, you said these elections were fateful, and now you're announcing that you'll throw votes in the trash. The dishonest campaign isn't working and won't help the right-wing camp. Instead of defeating enemies, you're busy with an unsuccessful attempt to destroy your own brothers. It's no wonder so many right-wing voters are disgusted by this approach."
In recent days, Likud has focused much of its attention on Amcha Israel voters, launching an aggressive paid campaign against Winter's party across social media platforms. Using targeted advertising to reach relevant audiences, the campaign has featured dozens of videos and statements by candidates on Winter's list, including remarks made several years ago, all in an effort to drive voters away and ensure the party fails to cross the electoral threshold.
Winter himself accused Netanyahu on Monday during an interview at the "People of the State" conference organized by Ynet and Yedioth Ahronoth, saying he would hold the prime minister responsible if his party failed to pass the electoral threshold.
"I will say that the person responsible for the right's downfall is Benjamin Netanyahu, who won't stop, won't let up and keeps shooting us in the back even though we are a right-wing party. Someone who shoots himself in the foot shouldn't be surprised when he starts limping afterward. That's the story," Winter said.
How do surplus-vote agreements work?
A surplus-vote agreement is an arrangement signed before an election between two Knesset lists, under which they agree to cooperate in the allocation of remaining seats.
The idea is that votes insufficient to give one party an additional full seat will not go to waste but may help the party with which it signed the agreement secure another seat.
After the votes are counted and the initial allocation of seats is completed, the total number of valid votes cast for parties that passed the electoral threshold is divided by 120 to establish the initial number of votes required per seat.
Each party initially receives the number of full seats corresponding to its vote total. Because this calculation generally does not allocate exactly 120 seats, several remain to be distributed.
This is where surplus-vote agreements come into play. Two parties that have signed such an agreement are treated as a single list for the calculation. Their combined vote total is divided by the number of seats they have already received together, plus one.
For example, if two parties receive a combined 400,000 votes and initially win 11 seats, their quotient would be 400,000 divided by 12, or approximately 33,333 votes. That figure is compared with the quotients of the other parties or pairs of parties, and the list or pair with the highest quotient receives the next seat. The calculation is then repeated for each remaining seat, with the number of seats already allocated adjusted accordingly.
Finally, when a pair of parties wins an additional seat, it is allocated between them through an internal calculation using the Bader-Ofer method.
A surplus-vote agreement therefore does not physically transfer ballots or votes from one party to another. Instead, it gives the two lists an advantage in the allocation of the final seats by allowing them to be treated as a single list for that calculation.
The surplus-vote agreements and their impact on the election
About a month ago, four parties opposing Netanyahu's continued tenure as prime minister announced surplus-vote agreements.
The first to announce an agreement were former Prime Minister Naftali Bennett of the Beyachad party and Avigdor Liberman and his Yisrael Beyteinu party.
Yashar! chairman Gadi Eisenkot had preferred to sign an agreement with another party in the bloc but was ultimately "forced" to partner with the Democrats and Yair Golan. Subsequently, the Joint List and Ra'am signed a surplus-vote agreement aimed at preventing votes from going to waste in the election.
The next parties to sign were Likud and Religious Zionism. The agreement between Netanyahu and Minister Bezalel Smotrich left Ben-Gvir's Otzma Yehudit with the choice of signing an agreement with Winter's Amcha Israel or remaining without a partner, against the backdrop of Likud's intensifying campaign against Winter.
Hendel and Zelekha's party also proposed a surplus-vote agreement to Winter, but he did not respond.
The last parties to sign such an agreement were the ultra-Orthodox parties Shas and United Torah Judaism, which emphasized that the arrangement reflected the "continuation of cooperation between the factions, in accordance with the instructions of the sages and elders of the generation."
The parties of Aryeh Deri and Yaakov Asher said: "In the next Knesset as well, they will continue to cooperate fully on the core issues concerning the preservation of the Torah world and the status of yeshiva students."

Ex-mayor of China’s Chongqing under investigation for ‘serious’ violations of party discipline, national laws

Amir Latif Arain
13 October 2026•Update: 13 October 2026
A former mayor of China’s Chongqing municipality is under investigation for suspected “serious” violations of party discipline and national laws, state media reported Tuesday.
Huang Qifan, 74, a native of Zhejiang province, held several key positions, including mayor and deputy secretary of the Communist Party of China (CPC) Chongqing municipal committee, Beijing-based Xinhua News reported.
The announcement was published online by the Communist Party of China Central Commission for Discipline Inspection and the National Commission of Supervision, without providing further details about the allegations against him.
Huang began his career as a worker at a coking plant in September 1968 and joined the CPC in March 1976. He spent decades working in Shanghai before moving to Chongqing in 2001.
From February 2017 to March 2018, he worked for the Financial and Economic Affairs Committee of the National People’s Congress, China’s top legislature.
The latest investigation comes amid President Xi Jinping’s years-long anti-corruption campaign, which has seen many top generals and senior officials investigated and removed.
Overall, roughly 52% of senior People’s Liberation Army positions have seen officials investigated or removed in recent years, reflecting an unprecedented shake-up under Xi.
