Europe certifies AMPS missile protection on VIP business jet
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
14:11:00 UTC
23:11:00 KST

- BIRD Aerosystems installed its AMPS missile protection suite with DIRCM on a Bombardier Global 7500 and received EASA certification for the installation.
- The system detects and confirms infrared missile launches and uses a directional infrared countermeasure to divert shoulder-fired missiles.
BIRD Aerosystems has installed its Airborne Missile Protection System on a Bombardier Global 7500 business jet and received European Union Aviation Safety Agency certification for the installation, giving the long-range VIP aircraft protection against shoulder-fired, heat-seeking missiles.
The Israeli company, part of U.S.-listed Ondas Holdings, announced the milestone on Oct. 12. EASA approval means the missile protection suite is now part of the aircraft’s certified configuration and meets European airworthiness rules for the Global 7500. BIRD did not name the aircraft’s owner or operator.
Known as AMPS, the suite is built to defeat man-portable air defense systems, the shoulder-launched infrared missiles that pose the main threat to aircraft during takeoff and landing. Sensors on the jet watch for a missile launch and confirm that it is a real threat before the system starts tracking the incoming missile. A directional infrared countermeasure then points an infrared beam at the missile’s seeker to throw it off course, and BIRD says the confirmation step keeps false alarms close to zero.
“The Global 7500 is another aircraft now protected by BIRD Aerosystems, joining a growing number of high-value platforms equipped with our airborne missile protection suite. This program reflects the continued expansion of our activity in the market and the growing demand for advanced protection against MANPADS and other missile threats,” said Ronen Factor, co-CEO and founder of BIRD Aerosystems.
Bombardier’s flagship business jet can fly about 14,260 km (7,700 nautical miles) without refueling, enough to link Europe with Asia or the United States nonstop, and several governments use it to carry heads of state and senior officials. Fitting a missile protection system to a civil-certified jet requires changes to the airframe, wiring and power supply that must be approved by aviation regulators, and BIRD handled design, installation and certification for this aircraft as a single program.
The Global 7500 joins the list of VIP and head-of-state aircraft that already carry AMPS. BIRD’s systems also protect military helicopters and transport planes, and the company says its customers include U.S. government agencies, United Nations air operations and NATO forces. Alongside missile protection, BIRD builds an airborne surveillance package called ASIO for maritime patrol and search-and-rescue aircraft.
BIRD says AMPS can be adapted to a wide range of aircraft and that it provides support for the system after installation, and the newly certified Global 7500 configuration is now available to other operators of the jet.

Albert Heijn begins restocking as hack traced to foreign servers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
14:07:40 UTC
23:07:40 KST

Albert Heijn begins restocking as hack traced to foreign servers
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
Albert Heijn has started restocking its supermarkets and restarting some IT systems, two days after a “cyber incident” took down many of its supply chains.
Parent company Ahold Delhaize said on Tuesday it was carrying out a “controlled restart of certain systems” and had so far found no indication that customer data had been stolen. It has not said which systems are back up.
Sources in the security sector told broadcaster NOS that Albert Heijn had identified suspicious attack traffic on its systems. According to NOS, the chain’s security staff appear to have switched systems off as the traffic came in, preventing the hackers from getting deeper into the network.
Foreign servers
The company knows that several servers were used in the attack, in the US, Poland, Moldova and Turkey, the sources said. The location of a server doesn’t mean that that is where the attacks are coming from, as traffic can be routed through other countries.
Albert Heijn’s investigation also suggests that servers belonging to Ahold Delhaize’s US arm may be involved. “That could mean the hackers broke into those servers and used them to attack Dutch systems,” cybersecurity expert Pim Takkenberg told NOS.
Another expert, Joey Fennis, said hackers were clearly involved, but it was not yet possible to say what, if any, damage it had caused. “It may also be that Albert Heijn detected them in time,” he said.
Albert Heijn said in a written statement that it was taking the incident “very seriously”, but could not go into technical details at this point.
Shop impacts 
Work at some of Albert Heijn’s six distribution centres in the Netherlands stopped completely on Monday, leaving gaps on shelves. The chain now says several centres are operating, and it is laying on extra deliveries.
Albert Heijn says some shelves may stay empty, like fruit, vegetables and other fresh produce. Online ordering and deliveries are still not possible, and customer service is still unreachable. Chemist chain Etos and off-licence chain Gall & Gall are also affected.
Other countries 
Belgian supermarket chain Delhaize, also owned by Ahold Delhaize, reported IT problems on Monday. Albert Heijn’s stores in Belgium are supplied from the Tilburg distribution centre, and the chain told broadcaster VRT the impact there was limited.
The incident came on the same weekend as a separate cyberattack on hundreds of supermarkets in France. There, hackers remotely forced refrigeration systems to defrost, and chains including Intermarché and Coopérative U had to throw away fresh and frozen food.
An Ahold Delhaize spokesperson told news agency Reuters there was no evidence of a link between the two attacks.

Leonardo DRS wins $63M U.S. Army thermal sight order
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
14:07:18 UTC
23:07:18 KST

- The U.S. Army placed a $63 million production order with Leonardo DRS for FWS-I thermal weapon sights under an existing IDIQ contract.
- FWS-I sends its thermal image wirelessly to ENVG-B goggles and the IVAS headset, letting soldiers aim without shouldering the weapon.
Leonardo DRS has won a $63 million U.S. Army production order for its Family of Weapon Sights–Individual, a clip-on thermal sight that sends its image wirelessly to a soldier’s night vision goggles so a target can be found and aimed at without raising the rifle to the eye.
DRS announced the order on Oct. 13, saying the U.S. Army placed it under an existing indefinite-delivery, indefinite-quantity contract for thermal weapon sights used by dismounted troops. How many sights the order covers and when they will be delivered were not disclosed.
Known as FWS-I, the sight links to the Enhanced Night Vision Goggle–Binocular, or ENVG-B, and to the U.S. Army’s Integrated Visual Augmentation System headset. Once connected, the heat image from the weapon appears in the helmet display with an aiming point, so a soldier can see where the rifle is pointed while still watching the surrounding area.
“Modernization at the tactical edge depends on giving soldiers the information they need without adding unnecessary complexity,” said John Baylouny, president and CEO of Leonardo DRS.
Because it uses an uncooled thermal detector, FWS-I needs no cryogenic cooling, which keeps it light and quick to switch on. Picking up body heat lets troops spot people and vehicles at night or through smoke when camouflage would otherwise hide them, and its clip-on mount allows the same unit to move between different weapons.
“FWS-I combines advanced uncooled thermal imaging with soldier-worn display integration to help improve target acquisition and situational awareness for dismounted soldiers,” said Jerry Hathaway, senior vice president and general manager of Leonardo DRS Electro-Optical Infrared Systems.
For several years the U.S. Army has fielded FWS-I alongside ENVG-B to close-combat units, and the pairing forms its rapid target acquisition capability, which puts the rifle sight’s picture into the goggle. Management of the IVAS headset, which can also show the sight image, moved to Anduril in 2025 as the U.S. Army reworked that program.
Electro-optical and infrared gear for the U.S. Army is a long-running business for DRS, which also supplies sensors for combat vehicles and aircraft, and the company expects to keep producing FWS-I under the same contract as further orders arrive.

Israel elections: Palestinian state caught between Netanyahu’s incitement, Eisenkot’s rejection
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
14:07:17 UTC
23:07:17 KST

“Right or Palestine” -- a warning splashed across large campaign billboards hanging over bridges and roads across Israel ahead of the Oct. 27 election. The slogan urges Israelis to vote for right-wing parties by portraying an opposition victory as opening the way for the establishment of a Palestinian state.
Yet, the Palestinian state that Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and his right-wing allies repeatedly invoke as an election threat is largely absent from the political programs of the main opposition parties in Israel.
Those parties broadly agree that a political settlement with the Palestinians is currently unattainable, although their positions range from maintaining the status quo while providing Palestinians with certain measures of relief to restoring relations with the Palestinian Authority (PA).
The right-wing Yisrael Beiteinu party, led by opposition leader Avigdor Lieberman, has gone further by advocating the dissolution of the PA.
Netanyahu and his allies are betting that warnings that an opposition government could lead to Palestinian statehood will mobilize right-wing voters to turn out on Oct. 27.
Opinion polls indicate that neither Netanyahu’s bloc nor the opposition is currently able on its own to reach the 61 seats needed for a majority in the 120-member Knesset to form a government.
Although most opposition leaders have repeatedly said they will not seek support from Arab parties to secure a governing majority, Netanyahu and his partners claim they will ultimately resort to seeking Arab support.
Arab citizens make up more than 20% of Israel’s population of more than 10 million.
If neither bloc succeeds in forming a government, Israelis could face another election several months later, with the current government remaining in a caretaker capacity until a new coalition is formed.
Yousef Jabareen, chairman of the Joint List, an alliance of three Arab parties, said Tuesday that any support for an opposition candidate seeking to form a government will come with conditions.
“Our top priority is to bring down the bloodshed government that has made our lives miserable over recent years,” Jabareen told a conference organized by the Yedioth Ahronoth newspaper.
He said the Joint List will be prepared to provide a parliamentary “safety net” for a “real and substantive alternative” to Netanyahu’s government.
“A strong and large Joint List can be a decisive factor,” he said.
Jabareen added that he is not currently holding talks with the so-called “change bloc,” referring to the opposition parties.
“We do not give anyone a blank check, and we are in no one’s pocket,” he said. “When they realize there are no other options but to cooperate with us, we will begin negotiations and present our demands.”
Asked about those demands, Jabareen said: “We are part of the Palestinian people.”
“The entire world supports the establishment of a Palestinian state alongside Israel on the 1967 borders, with both states living in peace,” he added.
He called for a “political horizon that brings hope, peace and economic prosperity.”
Of the UN’s 193 member states, 160 recognize the State of Palestine, according to the Palestinian Foreign Ministry. Palestine is also a member of more than 100 international organizations and treaties.
Palestine has held UN non-member observer state status since 2012, while the US has repeatedly used its veto at the Security Council to block full UN membership.
Netanyahu and his coalition partners quickly portrayed Jabareen’s comments as proof that Palestinian parties will demand the establishment of a Palestinian state in return for supporting the Israeli opposition.
Referring to Jabareen, Netanyahu wrote Tuesday on US social media platform X: “Eisenkot and Lieberman’s partner: We will establish a Palestinian state.”
Gadi Eisenkot leads the opposition Yashar party, while Lieberman heads the Yisrael Beiteinu party.
Seeking to rally right-wing voters, Netanyahu said: “If we do not go out and vote, we will get a left-wing government led by Eisenkot and Lieberman that will establish a Palestinian state.”
He said voting for his Likud party is “the only way to prevent it.”
Netanyahu is standing trial on corruption charges, which he denies. He also faces an International Criminal Court arrest warrant issued in November 2024 over war crimes and crimes against humanity in Gaza.
Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich, leader of the far-right Religious Zionism party, also attacked Jabareen’s comments Tuesday.
“Just two days after announcing his intention to provide a safety net for a government headed by Eisenkot, the chairman of the Joint List reveals his dangerous plan to establish a terrorist state in the heart of Israel,” Smotrich wrote on X.
“Lieberman will ask him to remain silent, and Eisenkot will rush to deny it, but the truth remains: This is what Israel will look like if the left comes to power,” he added.
Eisenkot himself, however, rejects the two-state formula.
“My position on the Palestinian issue has remained consistent: The principle of two states for two peoples is a mistake,” he told Israel’s Channel 7 podcast Sunday.
He also strongly rejected the idea of a binational state that would incorporate millions of Palestinians as Israeli citizens.
“I believe annexing 2.8 million Palestinians in Judea and Samaria (West Bank) and another 2 million Palestinians in the Gaza Strip will be a disaster for Israel. I do not want that.”
A binational state entails the establishment of a single state for Jews and Palestinians in the region extending between the Jordan River and the Mediterranean Sea -- that is, historic Palestine.
“I want a state that is the homeland of the Jewish people, with a strong Jewish majority -- a strong state that is confident in itself,” he added.
Eisenkot also rejected Lieberman’s proposal to dissolve the PA, establish an Israeli-Jordanian confederation across roughly half of the occupied West Bank and annex the remainder to Israel.
“I strongly oppose it,” Eisenkot said. “I oppose any Jordanian deployment or involvement in Judea and Samaria. Responsibility rests solely with the Israeli army.”
He said he will not object to a Palestinian police force handling civilian affairs as long as overall security control remained in Israeli hands.
“There is no other military force between the river and the sea,” he said.
Eisenkot did not offer an alternative political solution to the Palestinian issue.
On Gaza, he said Israel should focus on dismantling Hamas’ military and governing capabilities, creating a different governing authority in the enclave and conducting a long-term process aimed at preventing a repeat of the Oct. 7, 2023 events.
Eisenkot also criticized Netanyahu’s government, saying the US had effectively taken responsibility for arrangements involving Iran, Gaza and Lebanon.
He nevertheless said any agreement concluded by the Israeli government with Washington will also bind him and that he would insist on implementing it.
Netanyahu has headed the current government since late December 2022, a coalition widely described as the most right-wing in Israel’s history.
Asked how he would form a government if the opposition failed to win at least 61 Knesset seats, and whether he would rely on Arab parties, Eisenkot laid out four principles that he said would be prerequisites for joining a government he leads.
They include recognizing Israel as “a Jewish, democratic and liberal state.”
He also demanded acceptance of mandatory military, national or civilian service for all citizens -- Jews, Arabs and ultra-Orthodox Jews -- and support for dismantling Hamas’ military and governing capabilities.
“When I look at the Arab parties, I do not see any Arab party that accepts the four principles,” he said. “That is why it does not matter whether you ask me about this person or that person.”
Asked specifically whether Ra’am leader Mansour Abbas could join his government, Eisenkot said: “Mansour Abbas does not accept the four principles, so he is not part of my government.”
He similarly ruled out the Joint List led by Jabareen as a coalition partner under those conditions.
Asked about accusations that he is a leftist who supports evacuating illegal settlements and establishing a Palestinian state, Eisenkot rejected the characterization.
“I have never defined myself as left-wing,” he said. “I have defined myself as an Israeli patriot and someone who loves the land.”
“I support Jewish settlement under two conditions,” he added. “First, that it is in accordance with Israel’s map of national interests, and second, that it complies with the law.”
Israel has occupied the West Bank, including East Jerusalem, since 1967. Israeli settlements built on occupied Palestinian territory are considered illegal under international law.

Isamaa rakes in €229k in 3rd quarter as party donations surge ahead of election
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
14:07:00 UTC
23:07:00 KST

Isamaa rakes in €229k in 3rd quarter as party donations surge ahead of election
Opposition party Isamaa collected by far the most donations among parliamentary parties in the third quarter of 2026 (Q3 2026), taking in €229,301.
The non-parliamentary Parempoolsed raised more than two major parties, the coalition Reform Party and the opposition Centre Party. Reform reported the highest overall revenue in the quarter, at over half a million euros.
Parties' main sources of revenue are donations and state support, the latter issued to all parties who polled above 2 percent at the preceding election, in proportion to votes received. Membership dues make up a smaller proportion of revenue.
According to the Political Parties Financing Surveillance Committee (ERJK), Isamaa's largest donors in Q3 2026 were Bigbank owner Parvel Pruunsild (€100,000), energy and real estate entrepreneur Janek Veeber (€50,000), transport entrepreneur Hugo Osula (€25,000), and Postimees owner Margus Linnamäe (€15,000). Membership fees brought in €3,360. With state funding included, Isamaa's Q3 2026 revenue totaled €326,090.
Reform collected €70,179 in donations and €1,700 in membership fees. Its total revenue was €505,562, the highest of any party. Its largest donors were casino magnate Armin Karu (€25,000), real estate businessman Marek Mägi (€15,000) and wind farm entrepreneur Andres Sõnajalg (€15,000).
Centre took in €64,112 in donations and €14,727 in membership fees. Total revenue came to €266,015. Its largest donation, €3,977, came from Jaak Madison, one of the party's two MEPs.
The opposition Conservative People's Party of Estonia (EKRE) raised €5,791 in donations and €1,103 in membership fees in Q3 2026. Total revenue came to €207,627 once state support is included. Its largest single donation, €1,500, came from Evelin Poolamets, one of the party's MPs.
The other coalition party, Estonia 200, collected €167,633 in total, almost all of it from state funding (€163,383). Donations amounted to €2,132, with the largest, €600, from MP Diana Ingerainen. Membership fees brought in €1,665.
The Social Democrats (SDE), in opposition since spring 2025, received €44,250 in donations and €6,439 in membership fees. Total revenue was €155,722. Their largest single donation, €5,000, came from entrepreneur and local politician Pille-Riin Raidsepp.
The non-parliamentary Parempoolsed does not collect membership dues. It reported €138,043 in donations in Q3 2026, and total revenue of €145,568. Businessmen Rain Lõhmus and Raul Kirjanen each provided €30,000.
The Riigikogu elections take place March 7, 2027, meaning parties will be spending on campaigning in the intervening months.

Russian leader Vladimir Putin and UAE President Sheikh Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan discussed the Middle East crisis and Russia's diesel supply deal with the United States, the Kremlin has said.
The Kremlin said on Tuesday that the two presidents discussed further development of bilateral cooperation "against the backdrop of the 55th anniversary of the establishment of diplomatic relations between Russia and the UAE."

The US-Israeli war on Iran has continued for more than seven months, driving up global energy prices as commercial oil traffic through the strategic waterway has effectively halted.
Separately, the UAE’s state news agency WAM reported that the two leaders also exchanged views on several regional and international issues of common concern, particularly developments in the Middle East and ongoing efforts to address them.
Both leaders stressed the importance of strengthening regional security and stability for the benefit of countries and peoples across the region.

Italian Archaeological Discovery: Monumental Building Unearthed in Pakistan
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
16:06:24 CEST
23:06:24 KST

An imposing ancient monumental building has been unearthed in Taxila, in Pakistan, as part of the KhyberPath project, funded by the Italian Agency for Development Cooperation (AICS) and carried out by the Italian Archaeological Mission of Ca’ Foscari University of Venice, in collaboration with the archaeological authorities of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa and with the support of ISCOS.
                                    
The excavations, which began in mid-August in the Jandial area, have revealed a structure nearly 100 meters long and over 50 meters wide, located near the famous Ionic temple, outside the walls of the ancient city of Sirkap. The building’s function—likely public or religious—remains to be determined. The site, first identified in 1864 by the British archaeologist Alexander Cunningham, had never been thoroughly explored.
                                    
The discovery is part of the KhyberPath project, which is active at eight archaeological sites between Taxila and the Swat Valley, including Sirsukh and Barikot.  The findings confirm the contribution of Italian cooperation to the preservation of Pakistan’s archaeological heritage and highlight the need to protect the historic sites of Taxila—a UNESCO World Heritage Site—which are threatened by increasing urban expansion.

23:05:50 KST

Leader of opposition in the Lok Sabha Rahul Gandhi, Congress President Mallikarjun Kharge, party leaders Priyanka Gandhi Vadra, KC Venugopal, and other leaders of the INDIA bloc address a joint press conference, in New Delhi. (PTI Photo)
NEW DELHI: “It is our commitment to you that the people who have done this, Mr. Modi, Mr. Shah, Mr. Gyanesh Kumar, the lady who's hiding right now in Dehradun, and others are going to be brought to justice," Rahul Gandhi said announcing a united INDIA bloc's resolve to continue its agitation against alleged SIR irregularities.A day after the INDIA bloc's high-voltage protest march against Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar over alleged electoral irregularities, leader of opposition in Lok Sabha Rahul Gandhi hosted a high tea for opposition leaders at his residence. Following the meeting, INDIA bloc leaders addressed a press conference."Yesterday, you saw an expression not of the political party standing here, but an expression of the people of India...We would like to thank the people of Delhi, the people of India, who stood with us against what is being done. This is not about us. This is about the people of India," Rahul said.
But then who was the 'lady hiding right now in Dehradun' whom the leader of opposition in Lok Sabha was referring to in his statement?Rahul Gandhi and other opposition leaders have been relentless in their attacks on the Prime Minister and the Union home minister, but it was his reference to a 'lady hiding in Dehradun' that added an element of mystery to the press conference.
Was the Congress leader referring to Seema Khanna, the Election Commission's Director General (IT), whose name has figured in opposition allegations of 'vote theft'?There is no confirmation that Khanna is the woman Rahul was referring to. The Congress leader did not identify her, and there is no independently verified information linking her to Dehradun. However, her name has repeatedly surfaced in allegations raised by opposition leaders against CEC Gyanesh Kumar.
Why is Seema Khanna's name in the controversy?
Khanna's name came into focus following a report by The Indian Express, which said Election Commissioners Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi had raised objections at least 14 times over 10 months to decisions related to the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls.Among the concerns raised was the growing centralisation of control over electoral-roll software and restrictions on the powers of Electoral Registration Officers (EROs), who are legally responsible for maintaining voter lists.The controversy centred on the Election Commission's digital systems, including ERONet and ECINet, which are used to manage electoral rolls and election-related services. ECINet is a unified digital platform developed by the Election Commission to streamline electoral processes and improve transparency and accessibility.The investigation raised questions about whether local election officials had adequate access to make corrections, restore voters' names and exercise their statutory powers, or whether some of these functions had become concentrated within the Commission's IT department headed by Khanna.Rahul Gandhi did not name Seema Khanna, but AICC media coordinator Harmeet Kaur appeared to draw a connection between his remark and the EC official in a post on X."Where is Seema Khanna? Is she hiding in Dehradun? And who is shielding her? Remember EC data still under her control! Who is protecting her, and what are they trying to hide?" Kaur wrote, sharing a video of Rahul's remarks at the press conference.
Last month, Trinamool Congress MP Mahua Moitra filed a police complaint against CEC Gyanesh Kumar at Delhi's Parliament Street Police Station, alleging procedural violations, unilateral decision-making and manipulation of electoral rolls.Speaking to ANI, Moitra directly named Khanna while accusing the Election Commission of manipulating voter lists through its software."Very important things like the crores of new voters were not being allowed to come on the list because of the addition of a new question on Form 6, the new voters list. And we now find that the two other election commissioners had said this is completely illegal; still, the question linking parentage was put in," Mahua Moitra had said."We find how the EROs and the BLOs and the ground-level officials were not kept in the loop and denied access to the software, and Seema Khanna, who was DGIT, along with Gyanesh Kumar, played with the software from the back end to manipulate voter lists while keeping EROs and block-level officials in the dark. This is a very serious charge," she alleged.
She also questioned changes to Form 6, used for registering new voters, and alleged that 33 lakh valid voters in West Bengal had been kept off the electoral rolls through questionable appeals.Moitra argued that decisions taken without the consent of the other two Election Commissioners could not be treated as decisions of the full Commission. These allegations have not been established.The Election Commission, however, has maintained that differing views among its commissioners are part of the decision-making process and that its decisions were unanimous. It has also described ECINet as a unified platform intended to improve electoral services.While Khanna's name has repeatedly figured in the wider controversy, there is still no confirmation that she was the woman Rahul Gandhi referred to during Tuesday's press conference.

The Israeli witch hunt of Sami Abu Shehadeh exposes the lie of the ‘Jewish and democratic’ state
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
14:05:06 UTC
23:05:06 KST

On Thursday, October 8, Palestinian lawmaker and citizen of Israel Sami Abu Shehadeh, chairman of the Balad/Tajammu’ party, which seeks a democratic state for all its citizens, was effectively barred by the Israeli Supreme Court from running in the coming Israeli elections on October 27.
I say “effectively” because the court faced him with an ultimatum: resign, or we will confirm your disqualification [by the Knesset Elections Committee] the next day.
The story shows the limits of discourse for Palestinians in Israel, even when they seek to be incorporated into the country’s fictitious “democracy.” In fact, Abu Shehadeh’s case shows how this illusion can be completely erased over nearly anything that questions or challenges the state.
The article
The disqualification case against Abu Shehadeh rests on a single article published on October 8, 2023, that appraised the logic of the Hamas-led attack dubbed “Operation Al-Aqsa Flood.” As Adalah, a Palestinian-run legal center in Israel, makes clear, the article “sought to examine their political context and contains no call for violence.”
The head of the centrist Yashar party, Gadi Eisenkot (who currently appears to be Netanyahu’s and Likud’s best-polling rival), was most influential in inciting against Abu Shehadeh. The devil is in the details.
In backing the effort to disqualify Abu Shehadeh, the Yashar party accused the article of describing the Hamas attack as “an important historic event militarily, politically, and strategically,” and as saying that “if small, besieged Gaza managed to do this, and on this scale, others can do so more effectively and easily.”
Yashar summarized: “Support for the armed struggle of a terrorist organization against Israel is grounds for disqualifying a candidate. In our view, Abu Shehadeh crossed that line.”
But if one reads Abu Shehadeh’s article through, it becomes clear that this is a major distortion (I have provided the full text in English, translated from the original Arabic, here).
The event was historic militarily, politically, and strategically, and that is indisputable. But as to the last quote, it comes from another section altogether, and here it is important to get the context:
“The third observation concerns the comparison with the October 1973 War; what has transpired is vastly different from that conflict in every sense and dimension. While the element of surprise is indeed a shared factor—underscoring the crucial point that Israel and its intelligence agencies are merely human and do not know everything—it is also possible to prevent them from infiltrating our states, parties, and political movements. This is achievable provided the will exists and we organize ourselves correctly. Moreover, if tiny, besieged Gaza could accomplish this—and on such a scale—then others can certainly do so even more effectively and simply.”
This speaks simply of an element of surprise. Shehadeh is clearly extrapolating this element to the larger paradigm of “states, parties and political movements,” where prevention of Israeli infiltration is certainly always a major issue.
Yashar’s conclusion that this constitutes “support for the armed struggle of a terrorist organization against Israel” is completely a political opinion.
Abu Shehadeh claimed in his defense that he “never called for violence, did not support the events of October 7 and [does] not justify them,” but to no avail.
It is worth noting that Gadi Eisenkot’s own Dahiya Doctrine is a doctrine of massive state terror which has been operationalized in repeated Gaza onslaughts and the current genocide – and I think he should be disqualified and actually sent to The Hague for trial. But that’s how it works in the apartheid state.
The disqualification of Abu Shehadeh had an unusually wide backing – including from the State attorney, from the judge leading the committee, and from the furthest left on the Zionist spectrum – The Democrats.
The kangaroo court
Even more egregious than the disqualification itself was the Supreme Court discussion on October 1. Here, Shehadeh was being taunted and the campaign against him was blatantly clear.
Here is one exchange from those proceedings:
Judge Alex Stein: “You have many publications in English. Maybe you can show me one article in which you wrote that Hamas is a terror organization.”
Abu Shehadeh: “There is no such article.”
Stein: “What Abu Shehadeh is saying is cheap talk. A person, when they have no more to lose – will say anything. Show me once where Abu-Shehadeh said, when he had something to lose – something else. Show me one article in English, where he called Hamas “a terror organization”, show me once where he claimed that acts are ‘terror’. He has tens of articles. Is there such an article?”
In Israel’s highest court, Abu Shehadeh is being mocked and derided for not using the political term “terror organization” to describe Hamas. It cannot be required that a serious person like Sami Abu Shehadeh apply the political term “terror organization”, which has no legal meaning in the international laws of war. He could just as well call Israel a “terror state”, and I would personally be fine with that, but it becomes a question of whether one would engage in hyperbole.
So the judge is actually inciting against Abu Shehadeh with hyperbole and, in my view, should resign immediately, but that’s obviously not going to happen. On the other hand, this is precisely what the panel of judges eventually proposed Shehadeh do.
Abu Shehadeh’s pleas for the court to recognize his impeccable record as a lawmaker were to no avail. Abu Shehadeh:
“I have promoted in the Knesset matters and laws regarding the handicapped. All my life, I have dealt with human rights, also with Jewish lawmakers. I request of you [the ability] to continue.”
In the afternoon, court President Yitzhak Amit confirmed that the panel of nine judges reached a consensus that Abu Shehadeh’s article is “outrageous and abhorrent”. He said they were poised to accept the disqualification, so they gave Abu Shehadeh an ultimatum: resign, or be disqualified.
A court-ordered disqualification would have set a precedent for a Palestinian lawmaker since the disqualification law (Knesset law, amendment 7A) was established. Abu Shehadeh thus opted to withdraw his candidacy, “to avoid a Supreme Court ruling that could set a dangerous legal precedent with grave consequences for the already limited space for Palestinian political participation in the Knesset,” as his legal defense from Adalah stated.
This is the state of affairs. Israeli ministers who have incited genocide, actually commanded it in real time, sadistically bragged about their systemic torture of Palestinian hostages, even Democrat leaders who called for the starvation of the whole of Gaza (like the mentioned Democrats leader Yair Golan) – they go free and stand for office. But just utter a word about resistance to that – and you’re a terror supporter.
Smotrich and Ben-Gvir charge at the weak judge
Minister Bezalel Smotrich of Religious Zionism, who serves as de facto governor of the occupied West Bank, who just recently called for a “war” on the West Bank and “to do there what we did in Gaza”, charged the court, and particularly its President, for going soft on Abu Shehadeh (since they didn’t confirm the disqualification outright). Smotrich said,
“Yitzhak Amit doesn’t want, and is unable to, write a simple verdict which tells terror-supporters, who support armed struggle against the state of Israel, like the despicable Abu Shehadeh, who supported the worst massacre that happened to the Jewish people since the Holocaust, that they are disqualified from running for the Knesset, and instead pleads to him that he would resign.”
National Security Minister Itamar Ben Gvir of Jewish Power intoned likewise:
“We promised, we fulfilled! I am pleased that our struggle led to the resignation from the Knesset of Sami Abu Shehadeh, after the things he wrote and his support of Hamas a day after October 7. Nonetheless, I regret that the Supreme Court has allowed him to resign without a verdict being handed down.”
Sami Abu Shehadeh’s political fate was sealed, at least as far as coming elections are concerned. He had to decide whether to let the court do it, or do it for the court, and he opted for the latter, out of a calculation that involved future consideration of others.
Abu Shehadeh is clearly one of the most morally courageous politicians in Israel – light years away in stature from those genocidal monsters across the Zionist spectrum. But they were looking for political blood, and Sami Abu Shehadeh is their symbolic lamb of terror.

OPEC again revises downward global oil demand growth outlook in 2026

Unknown Publisher

MOSCOW, October 13. /TASS/. The Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries (OPEC) has revised downward its international oil demand growth forecast for 2026.
The figure is expected to grow by 0.2 mln barrels per day (bpd) and the demand will stand at 105.72 mln bpd, OPEC said in its October report. The organization expected one month earlier that the global demand will grow by 0.4 mln bpd in 2026.
The decline by about 0.2 mln bpd is expected in OECD countries, while non-OECD nations are expected to show growth by 0.4 mln bpd.
OPEC at the same time increased its outlook for 2027. The organization now expects the global oil demand to grow by 2.6 mln bpd annually. The increase by 0.5 mln bpd is projected in OECD countries, and by about 2 mln bpd in non-OECD countries.

NASA’s Perseverance rover sets extraterrestrial driving record on Mars
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
14:03:41 UTC
23:03:41 KST

Efe Özkan
13 October 2026•Update: 13 October 2026
NASA’s Perseverance rover has set a new record for the longest distance traveled by a vehicle on another planet, surpassing the previous mark held by the agency’s Opportunity rover, NASA said in a press release Tuesday.
Perseverance had traveled 28.1 miles (45.2 kilometers) on Mars as of Sunday, exceeding Opportunity’s 28.06-mile (45.16-kilometer) record set during its 15-year mission from 2004 to 2018.
The rover reached the milestone while exploring the western rim of Jezero Crater, where scientists are searching for evidence of ancient hydrothermal systems and possible signs of past microbial life.
Perseverance landed on Mars in February 2021 and has since helped scientists reconstruct the history of Jezero Crater, which once contained water. NASA said in 2023 that the area could have supported microbial life billions of years ago.
The rover has covered the distance relatively quickly thanks to its autonomous navigation system, AutoNav, which allows it to analyze images of the terrain, identify hazards and plan routes while driving.
Perseverance can travel up to 1,351 feet (412 meters) during a single Martian day, or sol.
NASA has extended the rover’s mission through the end of 2028, allowing it to continue exploring the Jezero Crater rim and potentially add to its driving record.

Flying machine gun: IAI and Sig Sauer test Fire Storm 250
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
14:03:27 UTC
23:03:27 KST

- IAI and SIG SAUER completed a live-fire test of FIRE STORM 250, a VTOL drone armed with an M250 machine gun on a MICROLIGHT weapon station.
- The drone flies up to three hours with 200 rounds, and a human operator must authorize every shot.
Israel Aerospace Industries and SIG SAUER have completed a live-fire test of FIRE STORM 250, a vertical-takeoff drone armed with SIG SAUER’s M250 machine gun, in which the aircraft hovered over a simulated battlefield, picked out targets with its onboard camera and hit them in single-shot and semi-automatic modes.
The companies announced the result on Oct. 13 at the Association of the U.S. Army’s annual meeting in Washington, where the drone made its debut a year ago. During the trial it fired from several distances and altitudes, and IAI says the shots confirmed the system’s accuracy and built-in safety features. The aircraft is meant to give small tactical units an armed aircraft of their own for close air support and border security.
Endurance is up to three hours with 200 rounds on board. Because the drone takes off and lands vertically, crews can launch it from forward positions with no runway. The gun rides in SIG SAUER’s MICROLIGHT remote-controlled weapon station, which the company calls the lightest airborne weapon station in the world, and the station, gun and ammunition together weigh 53 pounds (24 kg). Stabilization keeps the gun steady while the drone hovers, and the operator sees sensor and fire-control data merged into one targeting picture.
The M250 is the belt-fed light machine gun the company built for the U.S. Army’s Next Generation Squad Weapon program, in which it is replacing the M249 Squad Automatic Weapon. The U.S. Army type-classified it in May 2025, and the airborne version can fire 6.8×51 mm rounds or standard 7.62×51 mm NATO ammunition.
“We’re proud of the new SIG SAUER M250, which is combat-proven technology,” said Sali Okanin, Israel general manager for SIG SAUER.
The operator gets live video, target tracks and engagement options from the drone and must authorize each use of the weapon before it fires.
A multi-fuel internal combustion engine powers the aircraft, so units can refuel it in the field with the fuel they already carry instead of waiting for batteries to recharge. IAI and SIG SAUER designed it to travel with small units that have few people to spare, flying overwatch for troops on the move or guarding borders and key sites. Several drones can also work in relays to keep a round-the-clock watch over an area and scout ahead along a unit’s route.

Palestinians dream of returning home after Israel raids West Bank camps
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
14:02:25 UTC
23:02:25 KST

Palestinians dream of returning home after Israel raids West Bank camps
Palestinians have been displaced from their homes in Tulkarem refugee camp and dream of returning home.
Ramallah, occupied West Bank – Every day, Fuad Abu Salam sips his morning coffee outside his rented home in the Thinnabeh suburb, gazing at every detail of the sprawling Tulkarem refugee camp in front of him. This West Bank camp he can see in the distance once housed a two-storey building comprising four apartments, each measuring 300 square metres (3,229sq feet), in which he and his extended family lived.
After he was displaced from the camp, he, his wife, his four children, and his mother were confined to a small, rented apartment no bigger than 100sq metres (1,076sq feet) in Thinnabeh. His home in Tulkarem was partially destroyed when he left the camp.
Everything changed for Fuad and his family on January 21, 2025, when Israel launched a military assault in the occupied West Bank dubbed “Iron Wall”, initially targeting the Jenin refugee camp. A week later, the operation expanded to include the Tulkarem and Nur Shams camps in the city of Tulkarem.
Israeli forces forcibly displaced the entire populations of the three camps during January and February 2025 and continue to prevent their return, the United Nations has said.
Mass displacement
Data from UNRWA cited in a report titled, Destruction of Palestinian Refugee Camps in the Northern West Bank, stated that 33,362 Palestinians remain forcibly displaced from the three camps. By October 2025, 52 percent of structures in the Jenin camp, 48 percent in the Nur Shams camp, and 36 percent in the Tulkarem camp had been destroyed or damaged.
The Israeli operation has affected hundreds of homes, roads, and infrastructure, including water and electricity networks, while humanitarian aid to the camps has been cut off.
Israeli forces killed 102 Palestinians, including 21 children, during the period covered, according to the report. This represents 46 percent of the total number of Palestinians killed by Israeli forces in the West Bank during this period.
On Sunday, the Israeli Supreme Court ordered the government to provide a timeline for the return of displaced people to the three camps, setting November 23 as a deadline for a response.
Israel’s far-right Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich rejected the ruling, warning that the return of residents could allow for the reconstruction of what he termed “terror infrastructure”. He called on the government not to implement the decision.
Meanwhile, Israeli Defence Minister Israel Katz opposed the court’s intervention, asserting that the army’s continued presence in the camps was a security decision and stating his intention to maintain a military presence there.
Fuad, 42, a greenhouse installer, found himself forced to flee with all the camp’s other residents and more than 40 family members. But he and his neighbours carried with them the hope of returning home.
They moved between the homes of relatives, enduring harsh living conditions, until he finally settled in the Thinnabeh suburb of Tulkarem.
The neighbourhood, which overlooks the camp, has “restored his spirit” because he can see his home even if it’s from afar. Although he is unable to reach the building, he can gaze at it and imagine a time when he can return.
“If a decision were issued right now allowing us to return, I would go back immediately without a moment’s hesitation,” he said.
But his home is no longer what it used to be. It was partially demolished and set on fire by Israeli soldiers, rendering more than 80 percent of the apartment block uninhabitable. Fuad plans to use the rubble to rebuild his home.
“I will never waver in my resolve to return, even if it means pitching a tent over the ruins and living there,” he declared.
Mohamad Ararawi, 18, from the Jenin refugee camp, also saw his home razed to the ground with a wide road replacing it.
He told Al Jazeera that his family of 40, who had lived in a five-story building in the al-Damaj neighbourhood, all fled the camp when the Israeli military operation began, seeking shelter in homes belonging to other relatives.
“My mother, father, five sisters, and I took refuge in my brother’s unfinished apartment. We endured harsh conditions, suffering through biting cold and scorching heat, before gradually completing the construction until it became somewhat habitable,” he added.
Returning is all that matters to them, and they refuse to live anywhere but the camp, even if it lacks basic amenities.
A near-impossible return
Returning the displaced back to their homes is not merely an issue of clearing roads for residents. Returning would mean living in a camp in which infrastructure has been damaged and hundreds of homes destroyed, all amid a lack of necessities.
Nihad Shawish, a member of the Nur Shams Camp Popular Services Committee, told Al Jazeera that the scale of destruction makes the residents’ return fraught with immense difficulties, despite their will to go back to their homes.
Approximately 400 homes, most of them three to four stories high, were destroyed, he said, while about 100 homes were burned down during the Israeli army’s presence in the camp.
Even the ones that survived are not necessarily habitable; they sustained severe damage affecting doors, windows, and interior facilities. The collapse of some buildings has also damaged neighbouring homes.
Approximately 10,900 camp residents remain displaced, including families staying in private homes and others at a school in the Thinnabeh suburb.
Faisal Salameh, an official with the Tulkarem Camp Popular Committee, told Al Jazeera that more than 2,000 housing units were completely destroyed, while approximately 90 per cent of the camp’s homes sustained partial damage, rendering them uninhabitable.
“Israel has turned the camp into an environment that drives residents away, given the widespread destruction and the ban on reconstruction in certain areas that have been converted into roads,” he noted.
Despite these conditions, Salameh said that displaced residents are eager to return to the camp as soon as a decision by the Israeli government permits them to.
The camp was home to approximately 15,000 people. The majority of the displaced currently live in rented homes or with relatives, while others have sought shelter in schools, mosques, or makeshift tin shacks.
Israeli rejection
While the Israeli Supreme Court’s ruling opens the door to discussing the return of displaced persons to camps in the northern West Bank, its rejection by Israeli government ministers raises questions about whether it will be implemented. Until then, the lives of the displaced families remain in limbo.
Mohamad Halaseh, an expert on Israeli affairs, told Al Jazeera that the Israeli right-wing isn’t just trying to alter the structure of the judicial system, but also seeking to undermine its legitimacy and exert pressure on judges.
He explained that the effect of political stances is evident in the disregard for Supreme Court rulings. He cites the issue of Palestinian prisoner visitations, a case in which the state failed to comply with the court’s decisions, as one example of this.
“The continued disregard for court rulings undermines the judiciary’s ability to compel the government to act when judicial decisions conflict with the stance of the political leadership,” he said.
Several precedents make the implementation of court rulings on the camps unlikely, he said. This is particularly distressing for residents who also face strong Israeli political opposition to the return of Palestinians to the three camps.
“Declared political stances set a limit on the extent to which executive institutions comply with judicial rulings,” he said.

Ministry of Defence Police: misconduct hearings
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
15:01:46 BST
23:01:46 KST

Ministry of Defence Police: misconduct hearings
Find out about misconduct hearings involving Ministry of Defence Police (MDP) officers and how to attend these public hearings.
Misconduct hearings
To increase openness and transparency in the MDP (and the police service in general), misconduct hearings, special case hearings and police appeals tribunals, involving Police Officers, are held in public.
Misconduct hearings deal with allegations of gross misconduct committed by MDP officers on or off duty. Gross misconduct is defined as ‘a breach of the police standards of professional behaviour (PSPB)’ that is so serious as to justify dismissal’. Misconduct hearings form part of the disciplinary process and are not criminal proceedings.
Accelerated Misconduct Hearings
Accelerated Misconduct Hearings take place when the investigation of allegations of Gross Misconduct, committed by MDP officers on or off duty, identifies that special conditions, such as the following are satisfied:
- that there is sufficient evidence, in the form of written statements or other documents, to establish on the balance of probabilities that the conduct of the officer concerned constitutes Gross Misconduct
- it is in the public interest for the officer concerned to cease to be a member of the MDP without delay
Police Appeals Tribunals
Police Appeals Tribunals deal with appeals submitted by MDP officers, against the findings and/or the outcomes of misconduct hearings (including accelerated misconduct hearings), under the MDP Conduct Regulations, or stage 3 meetings under the Performance Regulations.
The decision to hold misconduct hearings and police appeals tribunals in public was announced by the Home Secretary in 2015. The Ministry of Defence Police followed suit in March 2017 by amendments to the Ministry of Defence Police conduct (2015) and performance (2012) regulations, and by subsequent revision of those Regulations into the new Ministry of Defence Police (Conduct, Performance and Appeals Tribunals) Regulations 2020, which came into effect for all cases assessed as Gross Misconduct after 2 November 2020.
This change of legislation does not affect misconduct meetings, where a breach of PSPB does not amount to gross misconduct. These proceedings will be held in private and the public have no right to observe (except in the case of a complainant or the commission^, where appropriate).
^Director General (IOPC) or Ombudsman (NI) if they conducted or directed the investigation.
What happens at a misconduct hearing
At a misconduct hearing the facts are heard by a panel, often with the help of witnesses, to enable a finding to be made. If an officer is found to have committed misconduct or gross misconduct, depending on the circumstances, the available outcomes are:
- written warning (only if misconduct only found)
- final written warning
- reduction in rank
- dismissal without notice
What happens at an Accelerated Misconduct Hearing
An accelerated hearing is heard by the Chief Constable. Due to the evidence being incontrovertible there is no requirement for any witness attendance. If an officer is found to have committed gross misconduct, the available outcomes are:
- final written warning
- reduction in rank
- dismissal without notice
What happens at a Police Appeals Tribunal
Police appeals tribunals are heard by a panel chaired by a person nominated by the Lord Chancellor who satisfies the judicial appointment criteria. The tribunal determines whether the ‘grounds of appeal’ on which the appellant relies, have been made out. On the determination of an appeal, a tribunal may make an order dealing with the appellant in any way in which they could have been dealt with at the original hearing.

Any member of the public or press can request to attend a misconduct hearing, provided that they are aged 18 or over.
When the date of a misconduct hearing is confirmed, the details will be published below. Due to the MDP being a national force the location of the misconduct hearing may vary (dependent upon the case).

Anthropic warns AI will soon self-replicate and spread beyond data centres
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
14:01:43 UTC
23:01:43 KST

The company says AI models may be mere months away from being able to copy and spread themselves onto internet-of-things devices such as smart ovens and TVs, making them difficult to stop should they decide to carry out cyberattacks.
Anthropic announced this week that small AI models are just months away from being able to self-replicate themselves on internet-of-things devices such as smart ovens and TVs.
That matters because today’s AI models operate in data centres, where the companies that own them can pull the plug if something goes wrong.
A model scattered across thousands of poorly secured gadgets in homes and offices would have no such off switch. Stopping it would mean tracking down and cleaning every infected device, making it extremely hard to halt if it turned to cyberattacks.
The latest announcement comes in a year that has seen the world’s leading AI models and their agents repeatedly bypass their safety nets or guardrails, mounting attacks on competing companies and government agencies around the world.
While this is one way a rogue AI could spread, Anthropic warned that a self-replicating AI could also be a “powerful cyber model that breaches data centres at high pace, or a model that scams people for compute credits”.
The company says it cannot say for certain what form exactly autonomous AI replication will take.
Models with 30 billion parameters or fewer can already complete many of the steps needed to replicate, though they make mistakes when stringing them together end to end, according to Anthropic.
But if small models keep improving at their current historical rate, they will be able to match this capability by the end of the year.
Anthropic says the cyberthreat posed by self-replicating AI is an unintended consequence of progress elsewhere.
“The capabilities that make AI models generally powerful coding agents also generalize to cyber tasks, including autonomous replication,” the company said in a statement.
Code that copies itself from one computer to another is nothing new. Some of the most damaging cyberattacks in history have relied on this kind of self-spreading program, known as a worm.
The 2010 Stuxnet attack used a sophisticated worm, widely believed to have been built by the US and Israel, to sabotage centrifuges at Iran’s Natanz uranium enrichment plant.
In 2017, the WannaCry ransomware attack locked users around the world out of their files and demanded ransoms in Bitcoin.
Unlike these worms, however, AI models and agents will be able to work out unfamiliar devices on their own. That would let them spread not only from computer to computer, but also from computers to other devices.
Anthropic predicts a future “awash with agents running on all types of hardware, including some that aren’t under human control”.

Russia’s Starlink alternative is losing satellites: two &quot;Rassvet&quot; spacecraft could burn up in the atmosphere in the coming weeks
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
17:01:22 EEST
23:01:22 KST

Russia’s Starlink alternative is losing satellites: two "Rassvet" spacecraft could burn up in the atmosphere in the coming weeks
Kyiv • UNN
"Rassvet" satellites No. 17 and No. 23 failed to reach their operational orbit and are rapidly losing altitude. Their atmospheric reentry is forecast for October 29 and November 1.
Two Russian “Rassvet” satellites, which were intended to become part of an alternative to the American Starlink system, are rapidly losing altitude and could burn up in the atmosphere as early as late October or early November. This was reported by UNN, citing Clash Report, data from the SONIKS satellite-monitoring system, and the specialized publication RussianSpaceWeb.
The spacecraft failed to reach the required orbit after being launched in July 2026. Earlier, Russia had already lost one satellite from this system because of similar problems.
Details
According to Clash Report, problems affected the “Rassvet” No. 17 and No. 23 satellites, which were part of the second batch of spacecraft launched by Russia on July 19, 2026. After being placed into an initial orbit, both satellites were supposed to independently reach their operational altitude using their own engines. However, they failed to perform the necessary maneuvers and consequently began gradually approaching Earth.
In particular, satellite No. 17 is at an altitude of about 245 kilometers and, according to Clash Report, loses approximately 1.7 kilometers every day. A similar situation is being observed with spacecraft No. 23. Information about the critical decline in altitude is also confirmed by open data from the SONIKS space-object monitoring system. As of October 13, the minimum orbital altitude of satellite No. 17 was 235.66 kilometers, while the maximum was 255.75 kilometers. For spacecraft No. 23, the corresponding figures were 232.20 and 250.05 kilometers.
According to the system’s forecasts, satellite No. 23 could enter the dense layers of the atmosphere as early as October 29, while No. 17 could do so on November 1, 2026. At the same time, these dates are preliminary and may change if the spacecraft perform corrective maneuvers. At such low orbits, the satellites are affected by atmospheric drag, which gradually reduces their speed. Without their engines operating, the spacecraft continue to lose altitude until they enter the dense layers of the atmosphere, where they usually break apart and burn up.
How Russia has already lost one “Rassvet” satellite
The current incident is not the first case of problems with Russia’s satellite system. On March 23, 2026, Russia launched the first production batch of 16 “Rassvet” spacecraft. However, one of them, satellite No. 4, was never able to begin the necessary maneuvers to raise its orbit and burned up in the atmosphere around June 6.
Later, on July 19, a second batch of 16 satellites was launched. However, as early as late August, the specialized publication RussianSpaceWeb reported that some satellites from the second batch were not demonstrating any noticeable maneuvers to raise their orbits. Two spacecraft gradually descended below 300 kilometers, creating a risk of their prematurely leaving orbit.
Overall, during 2026, Russia placed 32 production spacecraft into orbit, and together with six experimental satellites from previous years, the total number of launched spacecraft in the project reached 38.
According to the Russian industry publication ComNews, as of October 7, among the 31 production satellites that remained in orbit, 17 spacecraft had reached an altitude of about 510 kilometers. Another nine were at altitudes ranging from 446 to 498 kilometers, while five were between 253 and 375 kilometers. Thus, some Russian satellites continue to operate, but technical problems affecting individual spacecraft are complicating the deployment of a fully operational network.
What is known about Russia’s Starlink analogue
The “Rassvet” satellite system is being developed by the Russian company “Bureau 1440,” which is part of the “ICS Holding” structure. The project envisages creating a low-Earth-orbit network of broadband satellite internet intended to provide communications in remote regions and potentially be used for military purposes.
Development of the system began before Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, but its military significance increased after Russian forces’ access to terminals of the American Starlink system was restricted.
Russia expects that its own satellite network will reduce dependence on foreign communications technologies, particularly during combat operations. According to the published plans, Moscow aims to deploy a constellation of 292 satellites by 2027 and increase their number to 924 by 2035. The system is scheduled to begin commercial operations in 2027.
Despite the difficulties, the developer continues testing satellite communications. In particular, on October 7, the company conducted a public video call between Adygea and Moscow via the "Rassvet" system. It lasted about five minutes. However, as industry experts note, such tests do not yet indicate that a fully operational network capable of providing uninterrupted coverage over large areas is ready.
How Russia's satellite system threatens Ukraine
Despite the technical problems, Ukrainian intelligence considers the development of the "Rassvet" system a potential threat. In August 2026, Vadym Skibitskyi, Deputy Head of the Main Directorate of Intelligence of the Ministry of Defense of Ukraine, reported that Russia was deploying its own satellite system faster than anticipated in previous plans.
According to Ukrainian military intelligence, the Russian military has already used the first group of "Rassvet" satellites to provide communications over Ukrainian territory for several hours. In the future, such a network could be used to transmit intelligence, coordinate military units, and control unmanned aerial vehicles. But there is a nuance: to ensure uninterrupted satellite communications, the enemy needs to deploy significantly more spacecraft than it currently has.
Recall
At the end of September, Ukraine called on the United States to impose sanctions on several Russian organizations that, according to Ukraine, are helping develop Moscow's "Rassvet" satellite network, a national alternative to SpaceX's Starlink.

Six days of diesel for America, and billions for Putin
Mark Cary, United States member
U.S. President Donald Trump's MAGA Republican Party is projected to lose the midterm elections in a few weeks, and much of his power and support within the government could evaporate.
Trump needs a scapegoat for the crippling rise in diesel prices in the United States. He has now decided that scapegoat will be Ukraine and President Volodymyr Zelensky.
The diesel "deal" Trump announced a few days ago is nothing but a calculated act of gaslighting aimed at Americans and a wholesale admission that he has always been on Team Russia.

read also
The US-Russia sanctions bill is not a sanctions bill
Karl Frost, United States / Germany member
The Lindsey Graham bill in the US, passed by Congress on Sept. 16, was celebrated internationally as a landmark Russian sanctions bill. Ukraine supporters who cheered this seem not to have fully appreciated that most Democrats voted against it.
Despite appearances, legally, the bill does not mandate Russia-related sanctions. The legally consequential aspect of the bill is authorizing discretionary tariff powers for the president with no meaningful oversight.
The bill identifies two categories of tariff targets: the top five importers of Russian oil and the top five facilitators of Russian sanctions evasion.
There is language in the bill "mandating" these tariffs. However, the bill gives the president arbitrary, discretionary powers to make exceptions. In other words, the president is not actually mandated to impose these tariffs.
Trump already had the power to sanction Russia, which he was not using, so there is no reason to think this further permission to tariff Russian oil consumers will be used, especially in light of his announcement that the U.S. would buy diesel fuel from Russia to offset fuel price increases caused by his war with Iran.
Unlike the "importer" tariffs, which do have relatively objective criteria, the "facilitator" tariffs are based on presidential interpretation. The Supreme Court has repeatedly affirmed, for example in Dalton v. Specter, that where a statute grants such pure executive discretion as spelled out in the bill, courts will decline to review the factual basis behind the president's determination. The president could theoretically designate any nation currently locked in a trade dispute with the U.S., including allies of Ukraine, as a "facilitator of sanction evasions," slap them with 100% tariffs, and face zero judicial review.
This is the central concern raised by Democrats. As U.S. Representative Don Beyer stated, "This bill would do more harm than good for America and for Ukraine. Giving (Trump) this power when he has shown us over and over again what he will do with it would be an incredible mistake."
Is there anything to do about this?
Mostly no, at least not directly, except for dropping illusions. This matters because the bill is being presented as a tool to pressure Russia and support Ukraine. Trump already declines to use his existing sanctions powers, so there is little reason to expect this one to pressure Russia, and it could actually backfire on Ukraine.
read also

The stronger the evidence, the weaker the link between prenatal acetaminophen and autism or ADHD
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
14:00:31 UTC
23:00:31 KST

A new analysis of research on acetaminophen use during pregnancy finds little evidence that the common pain reliever causes autism or attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder in children. Earlier reviews had reported small increases in risk, but these associations shrank when the researchers focused on the highest-quality evidence, though small associations remained in some analyses. The study was published in Developmental Medicine & Child Neurology.
Acetaminophen, also known as paracetamol and sold under brand names such as Tylenol, is a widely available medication used to treat pain and reduce fever. Because it does not carry the same risks of birth defects as many other pain relievers, it has become the standard first-line treatment for pain and fever during pregnancy. Estimates suggest that more than half of pregnant women globally use the medication at some point during gestation.
Over the past decade, conflicting studies have fueled a debate about the safety of prenatal acetaminophen exposure. A 2019 meta-analysis, for instance, pooled early observational research and found that prenatal exposure to the drug was associated with higher rates of ADHD in children. Regulatory bodies and medical professionals debated whether this risk was genuine or the result of flawed research methods.
Soon after, scientists began to question whether these risks were actually caused by the drug itself. A 2021 study comparing brothers and sisters suggested that family background and genetics, rather than acetaminophen use, likely explained the apparent link to ADHD.
Further support came from a 2024 study of nearly 2.5 million Swedish children. When its authors compared siblings, taking acetaminophen during pregnancy was not linked to a higher risk of autism or ADHD.
The debate took a political turn in September 2025, when U.S. President Donald Trump advised against acetaminophen use during pregnancy, citing a possible autism risk, and the Food and Drug Administration began updating the drug’s label to note a possible association. The next day, the European Medicines Agency said it had found no evidence that the drug causes autism, a position echoed by regulators in the U.K. and Australia. The conflicting nature of these past studies and public health messages created confusion for both expectant mothers and healthcare providers.
The new study, led by Hoda Tayebi-Hillali of the University of Santiago de Compostela in Spain, set out to determine whether the reported risks hold up once methodologically weaker studies are set aside. “Previous systematic reviews had reached discordant conclusions, and many counted the same primary studies several times without acknowledging it,” Tayebi-Hillali told PsyPost.
“We set out to settle this debate rigorously: we quantified the overlap between reviews, appraised their quality, and reanalyzed the underlying primary studies according to their risk of bias,” she said. “Our goal was to give clinicians, pregnant women, and health authorities an answer grounded in the best available evidence, not in headlines.”
The researchers conducted an umbrella review, which is a large-scale analysis that gathers and synthesizes data from previously published meta-analyses. They searched six major scientific databases for studies published up to November 2025. In total, they included seven meta-analyses that together encompassed more than three million participants.
Initially, the researchers pooled the results of all the meta-analyses regardless of quality (three examined autism, and all seven examined ADHD). In this unrestricted analysis, they found small positive associations. The pooled risk ratio was 1.17 for autism and 1.29 for ADHD, meaning children exposed before birth had about a 17 percent and 29 percent higher relative risk of a diagnosis than unexposed children.
Next, the team rated the quality of each meta-analysis using a standard checklist. Most were judged to be of low quality, often because they did not report how much acetaminophen women took or did not list the studies they had excluded. Dropping only the weakest reviews barely changed the results (1.17 for autism and 1.28 for ADHD). Only one meta-analysis, published in 2025, earned a high-confidence rating, and it reported smaller risk ratios of 1.10 for autism, a result that was not statistically significant, and 1.16 for ADHD.
Because many of the meta-analyses relied on the same primary studies, the researchers went a step further and analyzed the individual primary studies themselves. They rated each for risk of bias using a standard tool that weighs problems such as unaccounted-for confounding factors, how exposure was measured, and how participants were selected.
When the analysis was limited to primary studies with a low risk of bias, the risk ratios fell to 1.05 for autism, based on two large studies from Sweden and Japan, and 1.17 for ADHD, based on three studies. Both estimates remained slightly above 1, meaning a small association persisted, and the results of the ADHD studies varied considerably.
“One of the most striking findings was how much the estimates changed once we took the quality of the evidence into account,” Tayebi-Hillali explained. “Associations that initially appeared consistent were substantially attenuated when we excluded lower-quality reviews and primary studies at higher risk of bias. It was also particularly telling that some sibling-comparison studies, which help control for the genetic and environmental factors shared within a family, did not find the associations originally reported. This underscores the importance of distinguishing between a statistical signal and a possible causal relationship.”
Given the baseline global prevalence of autism (about 1 in 117 children) and ADHD (about 1 in 60 children), the actual absolute increase in risk would be expected to be modest even if the remaining association were genuine. “Even taking the figures at face value, the impact would be very small,” Tayebi-Hillali noted. “Moreover, in observational studies, a risk ratio this small can readily be explained by bias, without the drug playing any role at all. The size of the effect, therefore, does not justify alarm.”
The findings are in line with research covered by PsyPost in 2026, which found that prenatal exposure to acetaminophen was not tied to autism or ADHD in sibling-matched analyses. Both suggest that previously observed links largely reflect confounding and other biases rather than the medication itself.
The findings stand in tension with a 2025 review covered by PsyPost, which reported that the associations were strongest in the more rigorous studies, particularly those that measured the drug in biological samples. The authors of the new review, by contrast, regarded biomarker measurements taken from umbilical cord blood, meconium, or maternal blood as being of uncertain validity.
The findings also contrast with a 2022 study and a 2016 study previously covered by PsyPost, which linked prenatal acetaminophen to attention and behavior problems in children. Those studies measured parent-reported symptoms rather than formal diagnoses, and although both were among the primary studies the new review examined, neither met its strictest risk-of-bias standards.
As with all research, there are a few things to keep in mind. “The main misinterpretation to avoid is the claim that our study proves paracetamol causes autism or ADHD; equally, it would be wrong to conclude that we have shown any exposure, regardless of dose or duration, to be entirely free of risk,” Tayebi-Hillali cautioned. “Our work is a synthesis of observational studies and therefore cannot establish causality on its own.”
A major consideration is “confounding by indication.” Pregnant women usually take acetaminophen to treat fevers, infections, pain, or inflammation. These underlying health issues can sometimes influence fetal brain development, making it difficult for scientists to separate the effects of the drug from the effects of the illness it was being used to treat. In addition, many studies relied on self-reported questionnaires, which can mislabel who was actually exposed, as people may not accurately recall exactly when or how often they took an over-the-counter medication.
The most rigorous estimates also rest on a small number of studies: a single high-quality meta-analysis and two or three primary studies. The researchers did not formally assess publication bias, the tendency for studies with positive results to be more likely to get published. The review also could not evaluate how much acetaminophen women took, for how long, or when in pregnancy; some earlier studies reported higher risks with use lasting more than 28 days, but most did not report timing at all.
“The next step should be to improve the quality of the observational studies available, with a more precise characterization of the dose, frequency, duration, and timing in pregnancy of paracetamol use, as well as of the clinical indication that prompts it,” Tayebi-Hillali added. “Designs that better control for familial, genetic, and environmental factors, such as sibling-comparison studies, are especially important, together with rigorous assessments of risk of bias.”
Animal studies have suggested that acetaminophen might interfere with hormones involved in development, but the authors note that this experimental evidence is not enough to show the drug alters human fetal brain development. Given the well-documented harms of untreated fever and pain during pregnancy, they conclude that acetaminophen remains an appropriate first-line treatment when medically needed, at the lowest effective dose and for the shortest necessary time.
“Headlines that present an association as if it were proven causation can convey an alarm that the evidence does not warrant. At the same time, it is essential to acknowledge uncertainty and to keep investigating,” Tayebi-Hillali said. “We should also remember that untreated fever and pain during pregnancy can have consequences, so avoiding a clinically necessary medication without consulting a healthcare professional is not a risk-free decision either.”
The study, “Prenatal exposure to paracetamol and the risk of autism and attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder: An umbrella review and meta-meta-analysis,” was authored by Hoda Tayebi-Hillali, María Blanco-Suárez, Berta Rivas-Mundiña, Jacobo Limeres-Posse, Márcio Diniz-Freitas, and Pedro Diz-Dios.

Lukashenko explains why Belarus holds military inspections
