14:00:11 UTC
23:00:11 KST

MINSK, October 13. /TASS/. Belarusian President Alexander Lukashenko, at a meeting with law enforcement and security officials, explained why regular inspections of military personnel and training are necessary – especially for those who, in the event of wartime, will be called up from the reserve.
"I won’t hide this from my potential adversaries in a future conflict – God forbid, of course – but I constantly remind the defense minister that today the country must have designated points where armed forces will be deployed instantly, within 24 hours – and our logistics allow us to do this in Belarus – and these points will be occupied. Fortified areas, as we used to call them. There are a certain number of them on the western border," his press service quoted him as saying.
Lukashenko said that every military serviceman must know every point, especially those who will be called up from the reserve.
"I remember this from my own military service in the army. We were taught back then: if something happens, you must be in that trench with that weapon. We are doing the same today so that our military personnel know which direction to act in. We’ve been there more than once, we’ve visited this fortified area, and we know what weapons they’ll use to defend our country," he explained.
"And our foes should know: we know our Belarus well. We know whether tanks can pass through the wooded and swampy terrain somewhere or not. If they can’t, we know where they’ll go. We clearly understand where we need to deploy our armed forces."
Lukashenko noted that under the current conditions, it will not be possible to build roads through the swamps, as it was done at the beginning of Operation Bagration in 1944. According to him, modern weapons, in particular drones, will not allow this to be done.
Thus, there is a clear understanding of where a potential adversary might cross the border, the head of state pointed out.
"That’s where we must block everything. It’s simple and clear; no grand strategy is needed from the Defense Ministry. I say it again: this is very important for those whom we will call up from the reserve, so that they know where they are," he said. "Because [Deputy Interior Minister, Commander of Interior Troops Nikolay] Karpenkov will transfer its flying detachments to the right place within a few hours. But when they are fully equipped, having conducted combat coordination from conscripts, they should know which trench they will be in.
"I’m saying this so that the Defense Ministry and the minister understand what I expect from you. This isn’t even about the experience of the special military operation in Ukraine – it’s just ordinary experience in the armed forces. We’re working through it, and we need to work through it carefully, without haste."

Could I make six figures from my couch? Influencers said yes – so I tried
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
14:00:04 UTC
23:00:04 KST

A very specific kind of content began taking over my social media feeds at the end of last year.
I had just finished a short-term contract and returned, with some reluctance, to the financial masochism of freelancing. As I mourned the end of steady paychecks and paid days off – as well as finally having enough money for regular haircuts – I couldn’t tear my eyes away from the glow of the screen.
A typical video starts with an ordinary-looking woman doing ordinary things: typing on a laptop, sipping coffee, perhaps doing some light cleaning. Bright, optimistic music blares in the background.
Then text stretches across the frame: she has made thousands of extra dollars each month, working just a few hours a day from the comfort of her home.
Sometimes the woman – and it’s almost always a woman – speaks directly into the camera. She was able to quit her job and spend more time with her family thanks to her side hustle! It allowed her to pay off debt, cover her mortgage and travel, all while setting her own hours! And with her tips and tutorials, you too can begin making money like her.
Across the screen come promises like:
“How to make passive income online …”
“How to earn daily with your phone …”
“Side hustles for women …”
“Lazy girl side hustles that have made me over $100K …”
The gospel of making money on the side, answering to no one but yourself and with no prior training or special skills, has gone global. As of October, Instagram alone had 8.5m posts tagged #sidehustle and 25.6m tagged #passiveincome, with content creators posting from kitchens in the midwest, beaches in New Zealand, country rambles in the UK and hammocks in Bali.
“It’s the perfect hybrid of labor and leisure, where the money comes in as you are going about your day,” said Brooke Erin Duffy, a communications professor at Cornell University who studies the impact of social media on creative work and labor. “The term ‘passive income’ puts an especially seductive spin on this. You don’t have to do anything and you just reap all of the benefits.”
These women were offering ways to make money that seemed doable: designing and selling stationery, earning commission on goods I already use, creating products with little to no overhead. The “passive” part would come in after a few hours of upfront work: you set up your hustle once, then sit pretty as the profits pour into your bank account.
With my financial future looking a lot more uncertain, I decided to put some of their hustles to the test. I went in with cautious optimism: I wanted to know how realistic these schemes really were, and whether I could actually make money from any of them.
What I found instead was what I believe to be the new face of multilevel marketing – and the future of scamming and getting scammed.
It’s easy to understand the allure of side-hustle content.
Plainly put, things are looking grim. In 2026, amid an affordability crisis, a few extra hundred dollars a month can be life-changing. It can mean paying down debt, being able to take a sick day or ordering a pizza when you’re too tired to cook.
But influencers rarely present side hustles as a response to global financial insecurity. They sell them as easy freedom, attainable without even getting out of bed. It’s easy to see why people buy in.
“On TikTok, I see reels that go insanely viral of just girls of all ages, being like, ‘how can I make money from home?’” said Erin McGoff, a career advice content creator who has more than 7m followers across different platforms.
I had a few rules for what I was and wasn’t willing to do. I didn’t want to put my face on any social media, and I didn’t want to use AI to create any products or videos.
Making and selling digital templates – probably the hustle that resurfaced the most during my nightly doomscrolling – checked all these boxes. The idea is simple: use the graphic design platform Canva to create invitations, planners or ebooks, then sell them on marketplaces such as Etsy. And according to the influencers, the earning potential is enormous:
“Use Canva to pay off your debt in under 45 seconds …”
“Canva is basically a money printer …”
“How Canva can pay your rent …”
I like pretty stationery and enjoy putting together E-vites centered on ridiculous party themes, so I decided to try it out and go all in with a boozy bachelorette aesthetic, heavy with bright colors and graphics of alcoholic beverages. I named my store GirlyGirlStationery and focused on putting together invitation templates that looked like a Barbie fever dream after a night of drinking pink prosecco.
But a professional graphic designer, I am not. I got overwhelmed quickly, second-guessing every design decision. I felt myself clenching my jaw trying to align my images and format my borders. In one instance, I had a listing up for several weeks before I realized that I had placed the goose illustration comically off center.
To make things worse, a quick Etsy search turned up thousands of templates that looked better than mine, many clearly using the same Canva artwork and styling. Some shops had more than 2,200 templates for sale; it had taken me eight hours to make eight and another five to fix them after realizing I had used Canva Pro elements that buyers would have to pay to download.
I made my first sale 12 days after I officially launched my Etsy store – an addictively giddy feeling that was undercut by the fact that I didn’t really make any profit.
I had kept the prices of my products low to drive upfront sales, with each template going for $2. Not taking into consideration the one-time $19 fee I paid to set up the shop, but adding in the processing fee, the transaction fee and the listing fee of $0.20 per listing, I made about $1.25 on that one sale.
In total for my first month on Etsy – about 23 and half hours of work – my net profit was negative 32 cents.
I grew up in the type of middle-class Massachusetts suburb where multilevel marketing (MLM) schemes had a foothold.
I remember listening to my mother complain each time she returned from what was supposed to be a casual social gathering but had turned out to be an acquaintance’s sales pitch for tupperware or cubic zirconia jewellery. After graduation, I watched from afar as a number of my former schoolmates began guilting their Facebook friends into buying “buttery soft leggings” and sisterhood-empowering mascara.
So when I started watching side-hustle influencers, some of the language felt immediately familiar, particularly in the way they present something nonsensical in a sensical way, making the aspirational seem easily achievable.
Take this Instagram video: “Instead of watching Netflix tonight, take 30 minutes, open Canva and create a digital product that you can sell 1,000 times a month for $17. That’s $17,000 each month.”
Yeah, OK – the math checks out. And I do watch a lot of Netflix. But wait, will I actually sell this product 1,000 times a month?
Most audaciously, some had found another way to monetize the hustle itself. If at first you don’t succeed, buy my masterclass, pdf, ebook or training program, they told their followers. Many of those products traced back to the same small ecosystem, with influencers spawning new micro-influencers who repeat the same scripts.
“There are thousands of accounts that are like ‘make money with Katie’, ‘make money with Marie’, ‘make money with Stephanie’, and they all are selling $7 courses,” said McGoff, the career advice content creator. “It’s a digital marketing or digital products course, but what the course does is it upsells you to a more expensive course and then that course just incentivizes people to sell the course.”
These courses immediately sent up a red flag for me. And yet, I reasoned, these women weren’t just trying to get me to buy questionable courses, nor were they dangling the prospect of private jets or luxury beach vacations before me. These weren’t get-rich-quick schemes, but a chance to make some extra cash without putting on a bra or changing out of my sweatpants. They boasted flexible hours that work around nap times and school pickups for mothers and homemakers who already feel exhausted. The upfront costs were minimal: all you needed was an internet connection.
I contacted Stacie Bosley, an economics professor at Hamline University who specializes in the MLM industry. She confirmed that, at face value, these side hustles did not meet the definition of an MLM.
In an MLM scheme, Bosley said, “you’re contractually buying the right to sell a company’s products but you’re also getting compensated for recruiting people and that compensation is not really tied to legitimate sales.” She continued: “It’s just sort of dressing around a pyramid scheme in that it’s really not about retail sales, but about recruitment.”
These side hustles don’t have one big bad overlord at the top of the pyramid. Each is supposed to be an independent venture: you make a product and sell it. Yet influencers promote them with the cultish zeal of Mary Kay saleswomen. With digital templates, that enthusiasm defies basic economics: if everyone follows their advice and starts selling Canva templates on Etsy, the market becomes flooded, making it harder for anyone to stand out.
“It’s a deceptive offer, that somehow you can just do this and that it can work for everybody without any acknowledgment of demand,” Bosley said. 
***
I decided to branch out.
Next up was affiliate marketing, another popular hustle that met my personal rules. This one has you promoting a brand’s products through a personalized link that earn you commission whenever someone makes a purchase through it. It’s like a referral code, except you get paid instead of getting a discount.
The side hustlers kept telling me that I didn’t need to have a huge follower count or social media presence to become an affiliate marketer, with companies such as ShopMy, LTK and Amazon Associates making it easy.
But like the digital template scheme, it just didn’t make sense. Why would anyone bother to buy a product through me, with my hyperlink, if they didn’t know me?
I didn’t want to use my personal social media accounts, but influencers had a workaround: create a new account dedicated to affiliate marketing. Several recommended Pinterest, where you can post images linking directly to products, and DigiStore24 as the affiliate network that provides links to products you can earn commissions on.
Sadly, most of the products on DigiStore24 are the sort of garbage you would send to your spam folder: shady supplements, weird energy pendants and online courses on how to be a better lover. I decided to try my luck with a light therapy mask – the only product I do use on a frequent basis. I made three pins that all together got 79 impressions in their first six weeks – and no sales.
After a few weeks of nothing, I decided to try another affiliate marketing site, FlexOffers.com – and I was almost immediately rejected. The email told me I should get back in touch with them should I “later have more traffic sources”.
So I went directly to brands I knew. Sephora’s affiliate program directed me to Rakuten Advertising, where I applied to promote Wet ‘N Wild and Dr Brandt, this time using my actual Instagram account. Both applications were rejected the same day for failing the company’s social media network policy, with no explanation of what that meant.
That was when the logic of the side hustle economy began to come into focus.
Influencers had insisted that anyone could do this: no following, business experience or digital expertise required. But almost every hustle I tried seemed to demand precisely those things. “Affiliate marketing is a real way to make money, but it is far from a get-rich-quick secret and it is definitely not passive,” said McGoff.
What was much more reliable was the attention generated by talking about side hustles. Creators boosted engagement by asking viewers to comment words like “content” or “begin” to receive free prompts and tutorials, turning would-be entrepreneurs into hopeful followers. I watched one woman start a new Instagram account in May devoted entirely to side hustles. Six months later, she had more than 27,000 followers.
The hustle, increasingly, seemed to be selling the idea of the hustle. It’s the influencer as a possibility: if you work hard enough and follow their instructions, you too can quit your office job, be your own boss and make six figures for just a few hours of work a day.
The pyramid may look different, but by borrowing the tactics, psychology and promises of MLMs, it feels like a pyramid scheme all the same.
“What they’re selling, it’s the same as MLMs,” said Mara Einstein, a media studies professor at Cuny Queens College and author of Hoodwinked: How Marketers Use the Same Tactics As Cults.
“They’re selling a dream.”
And yet, not everyone in this space is a scammer.
On one end, there are grifters and creators who aren’t fully honest about their earnings and partnerships. Waleed Khan, a 24-year-old financial consultant in Calgary who is reviewing various side hustles, said he discovered that one person promoting the “clipping” side hustle – when you make money by breaking down popular videos into clips and posting them on to YouTube shorts – was actually the founder behind the clipping website he was instructing viewers to use for the scheme.
And on the other end, there are people who really do make these hustles work.
After giving birth to her son, Tricia Orme, a 38-year-old mother of two in Washington state, started exploring print-on-demand. And she was “really bad at it” at first, Orme said. “My designs were terrible.”
But as she kept going, she found a hole in the market. She needed a way to show customers what her designs would look like on clothing without having to photograph models wearing each product herself. So she began using AI to generate stock images of people in blank clothing, then placing her designs on to them.
Thus, she became the @mockupmama. The digital products she sells are the stock images she created on AI, so that others pursuing a print-on-demand side hustle have ready-made mockups on which to display their products.
After making $146,578.22 in Etsy sales over the course of three years, she has turned her focus toward mentorship and teaching how to sell and market digital products.
“I am such a firm believer that if you have more than you need, build a longer table, not a higher fence,” she said. She has had about 300 people buy a $150-250 course from her and has about 155 active students who pay $19 a month to be in her private coaching group.
She is, by all accounts, successful – and that shouldn’t be a surprise. Success stories will happen because once you take away the social media, these hustles are basically a combination of sales and marketing – trades as old as time itself. Digital products, be they print-on-demand T-shirts or silly stationery, is just art you make on a graphic design platform.
But not everyone is an artist, or talented at sales or marketing. Orme, for example, had worked in corporate retail and had an understanding of the marketplace before beginning her venture.
“It’s like dating apps,” Einstein said. “Almost everybody knows at least one or two people who met through a dating app. So you keep pointing to them like, ‘keep trying, you can do this too.’”
“Part of their job is making it look easy,” said Duffy, the Cornell communications professor. But in reality, success in these spaces is a combination of “pluck, luck and the algorithm”, she said.
Over six months, I tried to launch five different side hustles. I made just two sales and spent more than $200 on Etsy fees, a Canva subscription and eRank, a tool Orme recommended for identifying popular search terms and boosting sales.
Khan, the Calgary content creator, also didn’t make much from digital templates. The only big profit he’s made so far is the C$600 he got for using AI to create websites for small businesses – and that only happened when he got off the internet and put in real world effort.
“The claim was you can make $15,000 a month doing this,” he said. “I made these websites. I called 20 or 25 local businesses and calling didn’t work. Eventually I went in physically to these businesses, to 10 or 15, and only two of them said yes.”
I had difficulty finding others struggling with their side-hustle journey, as this is not a space with a big audience for failure – but it’s very clear that Khan and I are not the only ones out there.
And then there’s the question of what all these hustles are putting out into the world.
Every day, new accounts pop up, promising new ways to make money: using AI to copy bestselling coloring books, or churning out slop videos for YouTube views. Etsy, once a haven for handmade crafts and original work, is now awash with generic templates and AI-generated goods.
I thought I had escaped the MLM trap: no boxes of garbage to store, no friends to guilt into buying it. But the garbage is still there. We’ve just moved it out of our homes and garages and on to the internet.

AI godfathers Hinton, Bengio including 400 scientists call for global body to monitor advanced AI
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
14:00:03 UTC
23:00:03 KST

Around 400 scientists, including AI pioneers Geoffrey Hinton and Yoshua Bengio, have called for an international body to oversee containment standards and incident reporting for advanced cyber-capable AI systems.
Both Hinton and Bengio are widely recognised as among "godfathers of artificial intelligence (AI)" and have consistently warned of the risks posed by unregulated technology.
"We, the undersigned scientists, contend that both more AI safety research and more emphasis on containment technologies and procedures are needed," said the researchers in an open letter.
The proposed body would set industry-wide containment standards and maintain a registry of significant security incidents, which the scientists said should eventually be made public.
In the letter, the researchers said frontier AI models should initially be air-gapped from external networks and subject to independent oversight, arguing that voluntary industry commitments are not enough.
"Without immediate changes in AI development and deployment practices, such incidents will continue to occur, and future incidents will be far more damaging to our exposed critical infrastructure," they warned.
The proposal comes a month after Anthropic, OpenAI, Google , Meta, xAI and Nvidia signed a White House accord committing to voluntary safety measures without any formal enforcement mechanism.
In the United States, the Trump administration opposes any binding regulation that could hinder innovation, amid fierce competition with China, and instead promoted a voluntary code of conduct.
No federal law specifically governs these models in the United States.
Series of incidents
The letter also follows a series of incidents that researchers say exposed weaknesses in how advanced AI systems are tested and contained, including cases where AI models bypassed insufficiently sandboxed environments and compromised external systems.
The signatories from 34 countries said organisations developing or testing cyber-capable models should immediately adopt high-assurance containment standards while governments work towards a more formal oversight regime.
Policymakers are increasingly debating how advanced AI systems should be supervised. EU tech chief Henna Virkkunen told Reuters news agency on Friday that the bloc's AI Act is sufficient to address risks from rogue AI systems.
On Sunday, the Trump administration lifted its block on US labs giving Britain's AI Security Institute early access to models for safety testing.
Nobel laureate Hinton and Bengio shared the 2018 Turing Award with Meta's Yann LeCun, another leading AI researcher.
LeCun did not sign the letter and has argued that recent security incidents primarily reflect engineering failures rather than existential AI risks.
Hinton recently warned US lawmakers that they may have only a year to establish safeguards before artificial intelligence moves beyond human control.
Intelligence explosion
Hinton and top researchers have also warned in a paper that self-improving AI could spark an "intelligence explosion", urging governments to establish oversight before rapid development begins.
"We might rapidly obtain superintelligent AI systems that transform many sectors of society, bringing unprecedented breakthroughs in science and industry. At the same time, these developments could arrive much faster than society can adapt to the resulting risks, such as AI-enabled pandemics, cyber attacks on critical infrastructure, and large-scale labour disruption," the paper warned.
Humans may have little to no oversight over automated AI R&D, raising the risk that superintelligent systems irreversibly escape human control and act to marginalise humanity, read the the paper, which was also authored by Jakub Pachocki, OpenAI's chief scientist, Jack Clark, a co-founder of Anthropic, and Eric Horvitz, Microsoft's chief scientific officer.
"Finally, an intelligence explosion could transform modest AI capability leads into decisive ones: even the prospect of a decisive lead could provoke international conflict, and an actual one could severely erode checks and balances within and between states, companies, and branches of government," it warned.
Meanwhile, on Tuesday, AI giant Anthropic said that small artificial intelligence models may be only months away from being able to behave like a computer worm, copying themselves from one internet-connected gadget to the next without human help.
The finding potentially opens a new front in the cybersecurity threats emerging from AI, which have rattled governments and the companies rushing to adopt the technology.

World Tennis extends suspension of Russian and Belarusian tennis federations
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
16:59:00 EEST
22:59:00 KST

World Tennis extends suspension of Russian and Belarusian tennis federations
The International Tennis Federation (World Tennis) has voted against the return of Russia and Belarus to team competitions and refused to reinstate the membership rights of the national federations of these countries.
Source: Ukrainian Tennis Federation
Details: A vote on the potential return of Russia and Belarus to international tennis took place during the World Tennis (WT) Conference and General Assembly in Almaty in Kazakhstan on 13 October.
Resolutions were submitted to the delegates regarding the resumption of participation by the Russian and Belarusian national teams in international team competitions, as well as the reinstatement of the membership rights of those countries' tennis federations within WT.
Following the vote, none of the proposed resolutions received the necessary support from the delegates.
The current restrictions remain in force. The national teams of Russia and Belarus will not be allowed to participate in international team competitions under the auspices of WT, and their respective national federations will not regain their membership rights.
Background:
- In May, the International Olympic Committee (IOC) lifted the ban on Belarusians competing in international events under their own flag, and in July, it reinstated the rights of the Russian Olympic Committee.
- Following the release of the IOC's recommendations, the International Tennis Federation did not support their initiative and refused to allow representatives of Belarus to return to competitions under their national flag.

“Russia’s aggression is not a war film that simply ends because we have grown tired of it and want something different. The war will end only if we support Ukraine and put strong pressure on the aggressor. It is time for Europe to implement measures that have been postponed so far, whether that means using frozen assets or restricting the issuance of visas to Russian citizens,” Tsahkna said.
“Ukraine is fighting for our freedom and security too. Russian forces that were previously stationed near our borders have suffered heavy losses in Ukraine, and Ukrainian resistance is keeping Russia’s military forces tied down there,” Tsahkna said. “Russia is trying to use fear to influence both Estonia and the wider Western world, including by carrying out acts of sabotage within our societies. It is important that we remain united, attribute Russia’s acts of sabotage and cyberattacks, and hold those responsible to account,” Tsahkna stressed.

“The Coalition of the Willing must also regain momentum, as it is extremely important to develop security guarantees for Ukraine that will ensure Russia’s aggression against Ukraine never happens again,” Tsahkna said. “At the same time, we must remember that Ukraine, with its wartime experience and combat-ready army, also has a role to play in ensuring Europe’s future security.”
The discussion also featured Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha, Spanish Foreign Minister José Manuel Albares and US Senator Roger Wicker. It was moderated by former Icelandic Foreign Minister Thórdís Kolbrún Reykfjörd Gylfadóttir.

Rare earths investor hires carrier admiral, opens D.C. base
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
13:57:42 UTC
22:57:42 KST

- Mining investor Appian hired former EXIM banker Brian Greeley and added retired Rear Adm. John Meier and ex-Ford executive Christopher Smith as advisors.
- Appian opened a Washington, D.C., base as it advances a critical minerals portfolio with about $2.5 billion in planned development spending.
Retired Rear Adm. John Meier, the first commanding officer of the aircraft carrier USS Gerald R. Ford (CVN 78), has joined mining investor Appian Capital Advisory as a senior advisor on defense supply chains.
Appian announced the hire on Oct. 13 together with two other appointments. Brian Greeley, who was chief banking officer at the Export-Import Bank of the United States, becomes chief financial officer for the firm’s critical minerals business, while Christopher Smith, the former head of government affairs at Ford Motor Company, joins Meier as a senior advisor. The firm, which advises private funds investing in mining, has also opened a base in Washington, D.C., and plans to spend about $2.5 billion over the next five years developing mines and plants for minerals including rare earths, graphite and lithium.
Meier spent 37 years in the U.S. Navy and last served as commander of Naval Air Force Atlantic, which runs the service’s East Coast carriers and aviation squadrons; at Appian he will focus on which minerals U.S. and allied defense supply chains need, for current projects and future deals. Greeley’s job is the money side, financing the portfolio, lining up long-term buyers and making sure new acquisitions can meet industrial and defense specifications. Smith, who earlier ran policy and government affairs at LNG exporter Cheniere Energy and served as assistant secretary for fossil energy at the U.S. Department of Energy, will work on fitting projects to what manufacturers need to buy.
“These appointments reflect the growing complexity of sourcing, financing and delivering critical minerals projects at the pace industrial and government customers now require,” said Michael W. Scherb, founder and CEO of Appian.
Several of Appian’s assets produce materials that end up in military hardware. Atlantic Strategic Minerals in Virginia runs a producing mineral sands operation and the largest minerals separation plant in North America, and is adding rare earth processing. Gippsland Critical Minerals in Victoria, Australia, owns the advanced-stage Fingerboards Project, which Appian says could supply 7.1% of the world’s dysprosium and terbium, two heavy rare earths used in the heat-resistant magnets inside missile fin actuators, fighter jet systems and electric motors. Appian also owns Graphcoa in Brazil and Allied Graphite in the United States, which together mine graphite and turn it into battery anode material, and U.S. Strategic Metals, which is building a U.S. plant to recycle and produce battery metals.
China refines most of the world’s rare earths, and its 2025 export controls on dysprosium, terbium and other heavy rare earths sent Western defense contractors and governments looking for supplies from outside the country.
“In my experience structuring financing for critical minerals projects at EXIM, I saw firsthand how aligning private capital with policy goals can accelerate projects to completion and meaningful production,” said Brian Greeley, chief financial officer for critical minerals at Appian.
Appian manages about $5 billion and has a technical staff of around 100 geologists, engineers and metallurgists. Since 2016 it has brought 12 mining projects into production, and its operations now employ more than 13,000 workers, with the new Washington office set up to handle its growing U.S. holdings and its work with defense companies and government agencies.

====================================================================================================

Calls for more humanitarian assistance for Syria at UNSC session
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
13:54:33 UTC
22:54:33 KST

Breadcrumb
Calls for more humanitarian assistance for Syria at UN Security Council session
The UN Security Council held a session discussing the humanitarian situation in Syria Monday evening, focusing on supporting the country’s transitional phase, strengthening stability, and accelerating recovery and reconstruction efforts.
The meeting took place amid the continuing hardship facing millions of Syrians, particularly displaced people returning to their areas of origin, as winter approaches.
After more than 14 years of a devastating civil war, around 90% of Syrians live in poverty, and tens of thousands of people are still internally displaced, unable to return to their destroyed homes.
Muhammad Yahya, the UN Assistant Secretary-General for Humanitarian Affairs, said that four million internally displaced people had returned to their areas of origin in Syria since last December.
But, he also noted that these returns continued to face significant challenges, including damaged homes and shortages of essential services in areas of return.
Yahya warned that the humanitarian situation facing displaced people could deteriorate amid the approach of winter. He called for the needs of the most vulnerable families and individuals to remain a priority alongside ongoing recovery and return efforts.
Call for ‘genuine partnership’
The Syrian government has called on the international community to move beyond political support towards a genuine partnership that would help rebuild the country.
During the session, Syria’s ambassador to the United Nations, Ibrahim Olabi, said Syria was continuing its efforts to build a stable state based on institutions and the rule of law.
He called on the international community fulfil its commitments to Syria and help address the challenges facing recovery and reconstruction efforts.
Olabi called for the provision of equipment and technical expertise needed to clear landmines, unexploded ordnance and other remnants of war.
He said that Syria’s recovery would benefit not only the country itself but would also represent an investment in regional security and stability.
UN Assistant Secretary General Yahya said Syria had a genuine opportunity to achieve recovery, but warned that this opportunity could be lost if the investment needed to support stabilisation and reconstruction was not provided.
Humanitarian success dependent on ‘stability’
Claudio Cordone, the UN Deputy Special Envoy for Syria, said the success of the transitional period depended on ensuring stability and improving living conditions for Syrians.
He mentioned the European Union’s announcement last January that it would provide 620 million euros (US$691 million) in support for Syria, as well as the World Bank’s approval of US$175 million to fund agricultural projects in the country.
Cordone called for funding and technical assistance, alongside projects that would deliver tangible benefits to Syrian communities.
He revealed that the United Nations was holding discussions with the Syrian government about the possibility of convening a conference on reconstruction and recovery, based on priorities identified by Syria itself.
The UN official noted that approximately one million Syrian children were still deprived of schooling because of damage to the education sector, teacher shortages and the economic difficulties facing families.
At the same time, he welcomed the Syrian government’s initiative to develop a national action plan to combat sectarian hate speech.
Cordone added that the UN office remained in contact with the Syrian authorities concerning upcoming elections and the possibility of providing UN support for the electoral process.
After Syrian rebels overthrew the Assad regime in December 2024, current President Ahmed Al-Sharaa controversially said that it would take at least four years to organise democratic elections in Syria.
The current Syrian parliament was chosen by a mixture of specially formed committees and direct appointments by Sharaa.
Representatives of the US and France as well as former Assad allies Russia and China all made statements supportive of the current Syrian government during the session.

As Russian missiles slip through Kyiv's air defenses without warning, officials say US intelligence sharing remains intact. For now
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
13:52:03 UTC
22:52:03 KST

As Russian missiles slip through Kyiv's air defenses without warning, officials say US intelligence sharing remains intact. For now
A police officer photographs the engine of a Shahed drone in front of a multistory residential building damaged in a Russian drone strike in Kyiv, Ukraine, on Oct. 12, 2026. (Evgeniy Maloletka / AP)
Despite the recent failure of Kyiv's early warning system and threats to halt U.S. intelligence sharing with Ukraine, Washington made no such decision, Ukrainian and American sources told the Kyiv Independent.
Five Russian S-400 missiles struck the Ukrainian capital shortly after 10 p.m. local time on Oct. 12, causing "massive explosions," Kyiv Independent journalists reported. Air raid sirens and mobile alerts sounded only after the attack.
The attack came as Washington had threatened to suspend intelligence sharing unless Kyiv stopped striking Russian energy infrastructure, the Kyiv Independent has learned.
Ukraine receives intelligence from the U.S. to help detect and track Russian missile launches and other aerial threats.
Zelensky described the strike as "particularly vile," saying Kyiv "received no early warning from our partners about this strike." His remarks raised questions about whether Washington had suspended intelligence assistance to Ukraine.
Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha, in turn, publicly said that intelligence sharing with the Americans continued, saying on Oct. 13, "Yes, we continue this cooperation."
Multiple sources told the Kyiv Independent that there was no decision to cut intelligence sharing. The incident instead appears to have involved a failure to detect or communicate the missile launch in time to warn Kyiv.
"They say they didn't cut it off, but they didn't warn us (about the attack) either."
The S-400 is a Russian air defense system with secondary ground-attack capabilities. Since 2022, Russia has repeatedly used the system, as well as its older version, the S-300, to strike Ukrainian cities.
One senior Ukrainian official familiar with the matter said Ukraine's military leadership contacted its U.S. counterparts after the strike to clarify what had happened.
"They say they didn't cut it off, but they didn't warn us (about the attack) either," the official said.
"The Americans said they just didn't see (the launch)... That's a weak excuse."
The official alleged that the incident might have been "a game" to test Ukraine's reaction. Ukraine's military leadership also warned senior officials that if similar incidents became a pattern, they could indicate that Washington was using intelligence assistance to pressure Kyiv.
There is, however, no evidence in the information provided that the incident resulted from a deliberate decision to withhold intelligence.
Detection of ballistic missile launches is largely carried out by a network of sophisticated infrared detecting spy satellites, which identify the thermal spikes caused by the launch of ballistic missiles, Fabian Hoffmann, a senior research fellow at the Norwegian Institute for Defence Studies, told the Kyiv Independent.
The system is generally extremely reliable but not infallible, Hoffmann said, explaining that certain environmental conditions, such as dense, unusually high cloud coverage, could impair its functioning.
Like any system, Hoffmann said, it was susceptible to "human or technical failure" or "extraordinary circumstances" that could impair its functioning.
Missile attacks on Kyiv, which precede air raid warnings, are uncommon but have occurred several times since 2022. In almost all cases, it was the ballistic missiles, which fly at extremely high speeds, that escaped detection by radar.
"Friends, this is not the first time that the intelligence services of our partners have not recorded the launch of the S-400," Zelensky's advisor, Sergey Beskrestnov, said on Oct. 12. "You should not draw conclusions prematurely."

Allies did not warn Kyiv of Russian ballistic missile strikes, says Zelenskyy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
13:51:50 UTC
22:51:50 KST

Ukraine received no early warning from its partners about a Russian ballistic missile strike on Kyiv in which five missiles hit civilian infrastructure, Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on Tuesday.
The Ukrainian president described the attack on Monday as “particularly vile”. He emphasised that receiving intelligence from Ukraine’s western allies “helps saves lives, and this is one of the most critical issues”.
“This is precisely what helps prevent people from being killed – when there is an early warning about ballistic missiles,” he wrote on social media. He did not apportion blame for the lack of warning, calling it unfortunate.
US officials made explicit threats over the weekend to their Ukrainian counterparts that the Trump administration was on the brink of halting intelligence sharing with Kyiv.
On Tuesday, however, Trump denied intelligence sharing had stopped. He told reporters: “We are helping them, and we are sharing intel. We want the war to end, so we’re working with them and Russia on getting the war to end.”
Trump has demanded that Ukraine stop attacking Russian oil refineries and has blamed Zelenskyy for the rise in fuel prices in the US. On Friday the US president announced a deal with Vladimir Putin to import diesel from Russia, dropping previous US sanctions.
Asked on Tuesday whether Russia could use proceeds from the sale to purchase more bombs, Trump sidestepped the question. “That’s a diesel deal, not for us. That’s being released into the world. That’s not being released to us,” he said.
Earlier the president claimed Moscow and Kyiv had agreed an “energy ceasefire”, something Zelenskyy described as “news to me”. Ukraine’s leader said his military had not struck Russian oil refineries or energy facilities in the two days following Trump’s Sunday announcement.
The Kremlin, however, had ignored the “ceasefire” and continued to bomb Ukraine’s energy infrastructure as before, with multiple attacks, he said.
“Russia did not heed the president … the Russians sent absolutely clear signals that they have no intention of refraining from strikes,” he noted on Tuesday.
Ukrainian commanders say American intelligence is not needed to identify targets for deep strikes on Russia, with oil refineries marked on Google Maps. But they say it plays a crucial role in warning of Russian ballistic missile launches, and the takeoff of long-range bomber aircraft.
In recent months Russia has dramatically stepped up its bombardment of Ukrainian towns and cities. Ukraine has struggled to shoot down incoming missiles and jet-powered drones and has appealed to partners to boost its dwindling supplies of US-made Patriot missiles.
According to the Financial Times, the Trump administration has also threatened to suspend the procurement scheme under which Ukraine’s European allies buy advanced US systems, which are then sent to Kyiv, including badly needed Patriots.
The Kremlin’s systematic campaign against Ukraine’s power grid has led to widespread blackouts in Kyiv and other cities. Putin’s apparent goal is to shut off heating and electricity for millions of civilians this winter, and to trigger a new wave of refugees into neighbouring EU states.
Speaking in Warsaw, Ukraine’s foreign minister, Andrii Sybiha, indicated that cooperation with the US was continuing and said the lack of warning about the Kyiv attack was due to a “special type” of Russian weaponry.
On Monday, Russia also bombarded the city of Kharkiv, destroying a residential building. Sharing footage from the scene, Zelenskyy said four people had been killed and 41 injured. Rescuers spent the entire night searching for people trapped under the rubble, he added.
Meanwhile, 11 sailors were missing after their ship was sunk by a drone attack off the coast of Bulgaria. The incident prompted Bulgaria to summon Russia’s ambassador.
Two cargo ships were hit by drones overnight and one was sunk, Bulgarian officials said. Bulgaria stopped short of explicitly accusing Russia of carrying out the attacks but the prime minister, Rumen Radev, said their outcome “benefits the Russian Federation”.
The row between Washington and Kyiv is the most serious since last year, when Trump threw Zelenskyy out of the White House.
Ukraine’s president has said he is willing to stop hitting Russian oil refineries – but only on a reciprocal basis and with “real guarantees” that Moscow will cease its attacks on Ukraine’s own energy sites.
“Direct or indirect support for Russia, delaying aid to Ukraine and complicating protection of lives from ballistics – this is what will definitely not work for peace. A strong America, a strong Europe, strong partners are needed,” he said on Tuesday.

Ukrainian arrested for plotting mass stabbing in Poland

Ukrainian arrested for plotting mass stabbing in Poland
A Ukrainian student has been arrested in Poland on suspicion of plotting a mass stabbing, prosecutors announced on Monday.
The alleged plot came to light at the John Paul II Catholic University of Lublin, where the 21-year-old suspect, identified as Yaroslav F., was studying criminology.
Fellow students reportedly raised the alarm after becoming concerned about his aggressive and extremist statements, fascination with violent crime, and attempts to recruit like-minded individuals.
According to the Lublin prosecutor’s office, the suspect was preparing to carry out racially motivated killings as part of a gruesome online challenge known as “Bloody Friday.” A court ordered him held in pretrial detention for three months at the prosecutors’ request.
Investigators said that the student had purchased three knives, including two throwing knives, and viewed graphic online material depicting torture. He also allegedly attempted to recruit an accomplice to commit murder.
Yaroslav F. has pleaded not guilty and faces up to 15 years in prison if convicted.
University spokesman Wojciech Andrusiewicz confirmed to the Polish Press Agency that the suspect was studying criminology, describing him as “lost in life.”
“We urge everyone to refrain from making accusations or inflaming tensions,” he said. “Let us consider together how to solve the problems of young people.”
The case comes amid growing tensions between Warsaw and Kiev over historical grievances and the Ukrainian government’s glorification of nationalist figures implicated in atrocities against Poles during World War II.
Polish politicians have condemned Ukrainian leader Vladimir Zelensky’s decision in May to name an elite commando unit “Heroes of the UPA,” after the Ukrainian Insurgent Army, a Nazi-allied nationalist militia responsible for massacres of Polish civilians.
Zelensky further angered Warsaw by selecting senior UPA figures for reburial at a planned national pantheon.

All trains between Odense and Fredericia replaced by buses after cable fault
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
13:51:32 UTC
22:51:32 KST

The Danish government has presented a proposed budget for 2027 that prioritizes national security, with more money allocated to defence amid an increasingly tense international security situation.
The proposal, titled “A stronger defence of Denmark – a strengthened Denmark to defend”, was presented by Finance Minister Peter Hummelgaard of the Social Democrats (S) at the Ministry of Finance on Friday morning.
The government wants to ensure that defence spending reaches 3.5 percent of gross domestic product (GDP) by 2030.
Hummelgaard said the proposal reflected the need to make “hard priorities” in response to the current security situation. He also described the Danish economy as being “in top shape”.
“The government’s proposal for the finance bill shows that we take responsibility upon ourselves, and that we lead the way in working for a greener, freer, and more equal Denmark,” Hummelgaard said.
Pia Olsen Dyhr of the Socialist People’s Party (SF), the minister for economic and interior affairs, also highlighted the security situation.
“We do not solve all the challenges we have in Denmark with this finance bill. But we are well on our way,” she said at the press conference.
“I also think everyone must remember that we are in an escalated security policy situation,” Olsen Dyhr said.
Much of the proposed budget had already been announced, either in the government’s policy platform or through statements by ministers in recent weeks.
The proposal allocates 1.2 billion DKK to children’s services and education in 2027, including Denmark’s public primary and lower secondary schools, known as folkeskole.
It also sets aside a total of 10.1 billion DKK in 2030 for tax cuts. These include abolishing the intermediate income tax and the top-top tax, as well as reducing corporation tax.
“We are simplifying the tax system,” said Taxation and Growth Minister Jakob Engel-Schmidt of the Moderates (M).
The tax measures will be negotiated separately as part of a tax reform. While the budget proposal includes tax cuts, the government also plans to freeze several tax thresholds, which would increase the tax burden for some taxpayers as incomes rise.
The liberal think tank Cepos estimates that the government’s various plans will result in a net tax cut of 2.2 billion DKK in 2030.
Business and Competitiveness Minister Martin Lidegaard of the Danish Social Liberal Party (R) highlighted investment in young people and education.
“We are significantly strengthening knowledge, general education, and formal education in Denmark, from ABC to PhD. It is good for the individual young person, but it is also good for Denmark’s future,” Lidegaard said.
Unlike in recent years, when the government’s fiscal room for manoeuvre helped fund much of its budget plans, this proposal includes several measures to find additional savings.
These include cuts to the Danish student grant (SU), savings on senior pension payments, a proposed tax on cruise ships and further reductions in state administration costs.
The government must now negotiate with other parties in the Danish Parliament, the Folketing, to secure a majority for the 2027 budget.
The proposal includes a negotiating reserve of 500 million DKK annually from 2027 to 2030, which other parties can seek to use to fund their own priorities.

French embassy in Riyadh tells citizens to avoid Saudi airports targeted by Houthis
France's embassy in Saudi Arabia told its citizens to avoid the airports in Riyadh, Jeddah and Dammam on Tuesday as fighting escalates between a Saudi-led coalition and Yemen's Iran-backed Houthi rebels, who have been attacking Saudi airports and oil facilities since last week.
The French embassy in Saudi Arabia told its citizens to avoid the airports in Riyadh, Jeddah and Dammam on Tuesday and advised against travelling to those cities following a series of Houthi attacks.
"Given the security situation, French nationals are strictly advised against travelling to or transiting through King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh, King Abdulaziz Airport in Jeddah, and King Fahd Airport in Dammam," the embassy said in a statement.
"It is also not advised to travel to Riyadh, Jeddah, and Dammam unless necessary," it added.
Read moreWhy Yemen’s war is escalating
Fighting has escalated between the Saudi-led coalition and the Iran-backed Houthis, who have been attacking Saudi airports and oil facilities since last week in a spillover from the wider regional conflagration between the US and Iran.
Saudi Arabia has in recent weeks launched strikes against the Houthis and is backing a Yemeni government counteroffensive after the group seized strategic territory along the Red Sea coast last month.
The conflict has disrupted air travel in Saudi Arabia, with Riyadh airport remaining closed after a deadly missile strike on Saturday claimed by the Houthis.

Business and Competitiveness Minister Martin Lidegaard of the Danish Social Liberal Party (R) highlighted investment in young people and education.
“We are significantly strengthening knowledge, general education, and formal education in Denmark, from ABC to PhD. It is good for the individual young person, but it is also good for Denmark’s future,” Lidegaard said.
Unlike in recent years, when the government’s fiscal room for manoeuvre helped fund much of its budget plans, this proposal includes several measures to find additional savings.
These include cuts to the Danish student grant (SU), savings on senior pension payments, a proposed tax on cruise ships and further reductions in state administration costs.
The government must now negotiate with other parties in the Danish Parliament, the Folketing, to secure a majority for the 2027 budget.
The proposal includes a negotiating reserve of 500 million DKK annually from 2027 to 2030, which other parties can seek to use to fund their own priorities.

China Focus: China builds nationwide green hydrogen hubs for low-carbon shift
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
21:50:48 CST
22:50:48 KST

HOHHOT, Oct. 13 (Xinhua) -- For decades, Inner Mongolia's windswept steppes fueled China's heavy industry with coal. Now this same land generates green hydrogen from wind and solar -- a sharp shift as China's hydrogen sector moves from pilot demos to commercial scale, with hubs spanning Baotou's mining belt to Shenzhen's tech coast for the global low-carbon transition.
This push has received significant policy backing since late 2025, when the National Energy Administration released the first batch of hydrogen pilots in the energy sector, covering nine regions and 41 projects. Among them, Baotou in north China's Inner Mongolia Autonomous Region is one of the key pilot sites.
Supported by abundant wind and solar resources and a strong industrial base, the city is building an integrated hydrogen value chain that spans green hydrogen production, storage, transport and diversified applications.
Nearly 20 leading industry players have established a presence in Baotou, helping to develop several benchmark projects in the hydrogen sector. Among them, a 200,000-kW renewable hydrogen demonstration project operated by a hydrogen subsidiary of China Huadian is producing 7,800 tonnes of green hydrogen annually. Construction of a 195-kilometer hydrogen pipeline linking Bayan Obo to downtown Baotou is also underway.
On the application side, hydrogen heavy-duty trucks are already operating in mining areas, while hydrogen buses have entered urban routes in Baotou.
In May, a hydrogen-powered two-wheeler developed by a local company was launched for public use in the city, with an initial batch of 1,000 units intended for public-use and convenience services. The project aims to expand the application of solid-state hydrogen storage in civilian transport.
Baotou's drive reflects a wider effort in Inner Mongolia to use hydrogen as a lever for energy transition. In 2025, the region's green hydrogen output reached 12,694 tonnes, a 3.6-fold year-on-year increase. To date, eight green hydrogen projects have been completed, giving the region an annual production capacity of 80,000 tonnes, among the highest in China.
Similar momentum is visible in other parts of the country. In north China's Shanxi Province, the city of Lyuliang is building a full hydrogen value chain ranging from production to end use. The city has achieved an annual hydrogen production capacity of 135,000 tonnes, built 14 refueling stations with a daily capacity of more than 30 tonnes, and deployed 1,315 fuel-cell vehicles.
Shenzhen, in south China, meanwhile, is a national pioneer in this sector and is home to nearly 200 companies active across the hydrogen and fuel-cell industry. Covering hydrogen production, storage and transport, refueling, fuel cells, system integration and end-use applications, the local industry has surpassed 50 billion yuan (about 7.4 billion U.S. dollars) in scale, with fuel-cell vehicles holding the largest market share among Chinese cities.
These regional developments reflect a broader national expansion. According to a report from the National Energy Administration, China's hydrogen output topped 39 million tonnes in 2025, marking continued industry expansion and keeping the country a global leader in both production and consumption.
Demonstrations across multiple scenarios are also speeding up. In transport, long-haul heavy-duty applications and low-altitude operations are being actively tested. In 2025, almost 8,000 fuel-cell vehicles were deployed, more than 10 hydrogen-fueled vessels entered service, and over 30 hydrogen-powered drones were released or test-flown.
China has also approved five city clusters for comprehensive hydrogen applications, spanning multiple regions -- a move aligned with the 15th Five-Year Plan for building a new energy system, which calls for coordinated development across the entire hydrogen value chain.
"China's green hydrogen capacity now accounts for more than half of the global total, and the hydrogen industry is moving from demonstration applications to scaled-up development," said Zhang Lin, a senior official at the China Electricity Council.
Zhang added that the next five years would be a critical period for China's hydrogen sector to shift toward market-driven growth, with the rise of a full value chain covering production, storage, transport and use, creating significant opportunities for the country's green transition and a market worth trillions of yuan. ■

Chinese President Xi Jinping meets with President of the Council of Ministers of Togo Faure Essozimna Gnassingbé, who is on an official visit to China, at the Great Hall of the People in Beijing, capital of China, Oct. 13, 2026. (Xinhua/Li Xiang)
BEIJING, Oct. 13 (Xinhua) -- Chinese President Xi Jinping on Tuesday put forward four principles for the constructive participation of all parties in the settlement of hotspot issues in Africa, during his meeting with President of the Council of Ministers of Togo Faure Essozimna Gnassingbé, who is on an official visit to China.
First, adhering to the principle of "Africa-led." The African people are the true masters of Africa and should play a central role in regional affairs, Xi said.
Second, upholding fairness and justice. All participating parties should abide by the purposes and principles of the United Nations Charter and respect the sovereignty and territorial integrity of the countries concerned, he noted.
Third, promoting ceasing hostilities for peace. Wars and unilateral sanctions cannot fundamentally resolve conflicts between countries. It is imperative to uphold mutual respect, conduct extensive consultations, seek common ground while shelving differences, and practice mutual understanding and accommodation.
Fourth, addressing both symptoms and root causes. Efforts should focus on immediate security while planning for long-term development, Xi said. ■

Feature: Chinese Wu Opera bridges cultures in Zimbabwe
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
21:50:06 CST
22:50:06 KST

HARARE, Oct. 13 (Xinhua) -- Wu Opera performers in vibrant costumes brought centuries-old Chinese operatic traditions to life in Harare, the capital of Zimbabwe, on Monday, captivating the audience with expressive gestures, soaring vocals and martial arts.
The showcase featured a vibrant selection of classic Wu Opera repertoire, including the elegant "The Goddess of Heaven Scatters Flowers," the witty and expressive "The Sedan Ride," and the action-packed "Three Fights Against the White Bone Demon," a beloved narrative from the Chinese literary classic "Journey to the West."
Originating in east China's Zhejiang Province, Wu Opera, also known as Jinhua Opera, is a traditional performing art that seamlessly weaves together singing, acrobatics, and stylized movements to convey timeless stories rooted in Chinese history and folklore.
Beyond its striking attire and intricate choreography, the art form explores universal human themes of love, courage, justice, and devotion, offering local audiences a vivid window into China's rich cultural tapestry.
The "Wu Opera in Africa" showcase, presented by the Zhejiang Wu Opera Research Center, was hosted by the Chinese Embassy in Zimbabwe, the Zhejiang Provincial Department of Culture, Radio, Television and Tourism, and the municipal government of Jinhua.
The performance forms part of a series of cultural events taking place across Zimbabwe this year to celebrate the China-Africa Year of People-to-People Exchanges, designed to deepen cultural ties and foster mutual understanding between the two sides.
Tang Xiaoping, minister counselor and charge d'affaires ad interim of the Chinese Embassy in Zimbabwe, described the show as a highlight of bilateral exchanges.
"Through closer people-to-people and cultural exchanges, we can deepen mutual understanding, build more consensus, and inject new momentum into global peace and development," Tang said. "Tonight's Wu Opera performance is undoubtedly one of the most remarkable highlights of this year's people-to-people exchanges."
Tsitsi Gezi, deputy speaker of the National Assembly of Zimbabwe, echoed Tang's sentiments. "A performance can express what words sometimes cannot, allowing deeper connections between our peoples," Gezi said. "Though governments may formalize relations, it is events like this that make friendships personal and enduring."
Gong Jianjun, director of the Management Center at the Wu Opera Theater of China, said he was proud to share Chinese cultural heritage with local audiences.
"Through the bridge of Wu Opera, we hope to leave our finest artistry in Zimbabwe and allow local audiences to feel the profound charm of traditional Chinese culture," Gong said. "We use opera as a medium to foster mutual learning among civilizations."
Experiencing Chinese opera for the first time, audience member Inaty Sibanda noted how the performers' elaborate costumes and evocative movements conveyed profound emotions, bringing the narrative unfolding on stage vividly to life.
"I found it very amazing. I love the colors and the attire. To me, it was more like a fairy tale story that they were telling us about their culture. And it was beautiful and lovely," she said.
Sibanda added that witnessing the opera offered a unique opportunity to learn about China's heritage, expressing hope that similar cultural events could be held regularly to enhance local awareness.
Another viewer, Vheneka Roy, said he was impressed by the artists' dedication and skill, as well as the richness of Chinese cultural heritage. He said the showcase deepened his appreciation of the common ways Zimbabweans and Chinese express themselves.
"What caught my attention was that the performers were truly enjoying themselves. They didn't look rigid at all," Roy observed. "They were very much in flow, allowing themselves to become the piece and naturally convey its meaning."
For Roy, the immersive experience highlighted the powerful potential of cultural diplomacy in cementing genuine people-to-people bonds between China and Zimbabwe.
"If there is one takeaway today, it is to be proud of where we are from while appreciating others for where they are from," Roy said. "We can appreciate each other in all aspects without superseding each other." ■

Feature: Kenyan youth explore climate finance to promote green agriculture
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
21:49:57 CST
22:49:57 KST

NAIROBI, Oct. 13 (Xinhua) -- Coffee plants grow among taller trees on a farm in Murang'a County, central Kenya, where the leafy canopy provides shade and helps retain soil moisture. In the fields, farmers are replacing some synthetic fertilizers with organic alternatives to improve soil health and reduce production costs.
These practices are part of efforts by local smallholder farmers to adapt to changing climatic conditions and rising agricultural costs.
Kenyan entrepreneur Godfrey Noel is exploring how digital technology and climate finance can help make such changes more accessible to farmers.
In September, Noel and his team won gold at the final of the Global AgriInno Challenge 2026 in Hangzhou, east China's Zhejiang Province, with their AgriKonnekt project, which seeks to connect smallholder farmers in East Africa through digital agricultural services.
The project provides measurement, reporting and verification services to cooperatives, farmer organizations and financial institutions. By collecting and verifying data on farming practices, the team aims to assess their environmental benefits and help link those benefits to climate finance.
For Noel, the challenge is not simply encouraging farmers to adopt more sustainable practices, but also ensuring they have the resources to do so.
Noel noted that smallholder farmers face mounting pressure from unpredictable rainfall, extreme weather events, rising input costs and deteriorating soil conditions, all of which can undermine agricultural productivity and household incomes.
"Climate finance has a lot of money, but to get that money into agriculture, you have to demonstrate the environmental benefits of these practices and show that the data is credible and verifiable," Noel said.
His team has developed a digital platform to collect and analyze farm-level information and generate reports. Internet of Things (IoT) devices installed on farms gather basic data, including soil pH and moisture levels, while satellite data provides an additional means of monitoring and verification.
By combining ground-based measurements with satellite observations, the system seeks to establish a more reliable picture of farming practices and their environmental impact.
The verified data is then submitted to climate finance providers for assessment. Once approved, funding is channeled to provide farmers with inputs such as organic fertilizers, seedlings and seeds at no cost to them, according to Noel.
The arrangement is intended to ease farmers' financial burden while encouraging practices that can improve soil conditions and support more resilient agricultural production, Noel added.
The project currently covers about 2,000 farmers in Kenya. Noel said the team works with cooperatives and community-based organizations to reach more farmers and strengthen local accountability. It aims to expand its reach to at least 12,000 farmers across Kenya, Uganda and other areas over the next 12 months.
For Irene Kabochi, chief executive officer of Murang'a Farmers Cooperative Union, helping farmers adapt to changing weather patterns has become an increasingly important priority.
"We want to proactively help farmers prepare for changing climatic conditions and take measures to mitigate the effects of climate change," she said.
Kabochi said the team's data services and agricultural technology support could help cooperatives collect and analyze farm information, laying the groundwork for accessing climate finance.
The cooperative is working with Noel's team to diversify agricultural production beyond coffee by introducing crops such as macadamia and avocado. It is providing seedlings to farmers and plans to establish a demonstration farm to explore farming methods better suited to local climatic conditions.
For Simon Macharia, a farmer who has grown coffee for more than a decade, access to quality seedlings has offered a practical incentive to improve production.
The coffee seedlings he received free of charge through the project have encouraged him to consider how better planting materials and improved cultivation methods could raise yields.
He added that farmers participating in the project had begun trying more scientific and environmentally friendly cultivation practices, seeking to reduce chemical use, improve farm ecology, and lower production costs.
"For us farmers, we need to protect the land while also making farming more profitable," he said.
During Noel's visit to Hangzhou for the competition, Noel toured agricultural technology exhibitions and visited institutions including Zhejiang University.
A visit to a greenhouse particularly caught his attention. He saw a specialized growing medium containing multiple nutrients to support plant growth, which led him to think about the challenges facing Kenya's arid and semi-arid regions.
Large areas of northern Kenya, including Turkana, face difficult conditions for crop production, Noel said.
He believes that exploring suitable protected-farming systems and cultivation technologies could offer additional options for food production, provided they are adapted to local environments.
His team is also following developments in Chinese agricultural IoT technology, with an eye toward solutions that can function in remote Kenyan areas where electricity supplies and network connectivity are unreliable.
Noel added that linking environmental protection with tangible economic benefits for farmers is key to encouraging the wider adoption of sustainable agricultural practices and ensuring their long-term viability. ■

Feature: Chinese training opens new doors for South African women entrepreneurs
China

Climate campaigners staged a demonstration outside the UK Department for Energy Security and Net Zero (DESNZ) in London on Tuesday, calling on the government to halt development of the controversial Rosebank oil and gas field in the North Sea.
Organized by activists from groups including Fossil Free London, the protest called on the UK government to reject new oil and gas licenses and accelerate the transition to renewable energy.
A public consultation on the Rosebank project concluded in August 2026, following a landmark legal challenge that found the previous approval of the development unlawful.
The Court of Session in Edinburgh ruled that the previous Conservative government had failed to fully consider the project’s downstream emissions when approving the development.
Rosebank, estimated to contain more than 480 million barrels of oil, is the UK’s largest undeveloped oil and gas field.
The project is primarily owned by Norwegian state-backed energy company Equinor and Ithaca Energy through a joint venture.
Opponents, including the #StopRosebank campaign, argue that developing the field would prolong the UK’s dependence on fossil fuels and undermine international climate targets.
Supporters of the project, meanwhile, have argued that domestic oil and gas production is necessary to safeguard the country’s energy security during the transition to cleaner energy sources.
The UK government is considering whether to approve the Rosebank and Jackdaw oil and gas projects, which were initially approved by the previous Conservative administration.
Although Labour pledged to ban new drilling in the North Sea in its 2024 election manifesto, Prime Minister Andy Burnham has vowed to take a “pragmatic” approach to decisions on new developments.

Yemeni government launches air strikes on Houthi positions
Yemeni rights group accuses the Houthis of killing five civilians and injuring more than a dozen others.
Forces loyal to Yemen’s internationally recognised government say they have carried out a series of air strikes on Houthi positions and military equipment in the country’s southwest.
A total of nine air strikes were conducted in Taiz governorate on Tuesday, including five in Dhubab district and four in al-Masrakh district, the government said.
According to the Taiz Military Axis Media Center, affiliated with the Ministry of Defence, fighting is ongoing between government forces and the Houthis in al-Shaqab, south of Taiz.
The Yemeni Network for Rights and Freedom said on Tuesday that the Houthis had killed at least five civilians, including a five-year-old girl in Taiz during the previous 24 hours and injured 17 others.
The organisation accused the Houthis of shelling residential neighbourhoods, damaging at least seven homes. It also alleged that the group had fired more than 180 projectiles across Taiz during the previous 24 hours.
The war in Yemen erupted in 2014 when the Houthis, an armed group also known as Ansar Allah (Arabic for Supporters of God), seized the capital Sanaa and forced the government to flee.
An international military coalition led by Saudi Arabia intervened in support of the internationally recognised government in 2015, leading to years of fighting between the warring sides.
A 2022 UN-backed truce halted most fighting, but tensions have been high in Yemen since the Iran-aligned Houthis declared a naval blockade of Saudi Arabian ports and shipping passing through the Bab al-Mandeb strait in July.
In September, the Houthis carried out a lightning ground offensive on Mocha, pushing back forces loyal to Yemen’s government from the strategic port city. The same month, the group’s forces again swept through and seized territory along the western coast and the Bab al-Mandeb strait, including the strategically located Mayyun Island in the strait.
As the fighting in Yemen continues to rage, the president of the International Committee of the Red Cross, Mirjana Spoljaric, warned that civilians across the Middle East are bearing the brunt of escalating hostilities and has called for all parties to de-escalate.
“Civilians are paying an unacceptable price as a result of military operations in the Middle East,” Spoljaric said in a statement.
“In Yemen, the scale of death, displacement and damage to civilian infrastructure, including in Aden and Sanaa, is mounting at an alarming rate. Across the Middle East, civilian infrastructure has repeatedly been hit and lives have been lost,” she said.
At least 46 civilians have been killed and more than 130 others injured in Yemen since August, many of them children, according to the United Nations.
More than 200,000 people have been displaced in Yemen since September, according to the UN’s migration agency (IOM).
As the fighting in Yemen has escalated, the Houthis have carried out a series of attacks on Saudi Arabia’s airports and oil facilities. At least 14 people were killed in separate Houthi missile attacks on King Khalid airport in Riyadh over the weekend, drawing widespread international condemnation.
Saudi Arabia’s energy minister promised the kingdom would carry out a “serious response” to the attacks.
Several airlines have cancelled flights to Saudi Arabia and neighbouring countries in response to Houthi attacks. These carriers include Qatar Airways and Emirates, the United Arab Emirates’ flagship carrier.
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz spoke to Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman (MBS) on Tuesday about regional issues. Merz told MBS that Iran must engage in serious negotiations and accused Tehran of destabilising the region.
Meanwhile, Egyptian Foreign Minister Badr Abdelatty has met Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) Secretary-General Jasem Mohamed AlBudaiwi. Abdelatty said in a post on X that “Gulf security is integral to Egypt’s national security”.
Abdelatty also spoke to his Iranian counterpart, Abbas Araghchi, and urged an immediate halt to Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia. Although Tehran provides the Houthis with crucial financial and military support, several analysts suggest that Iran holds little sway over the group.
