====================================================================================================

Beyond resilience: Israel's traumatized families need support, not just admiration - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
13:46:31 UTC
22:46:31 KST

As a mother of four, when I heard about yesterday’s school-trip explosion in the north, I thought first about the parents. They had sent their children off for a day with classmates and teachers. Then came the calls no parent ever wants to receive.
A teenager was killed, and over 20 students and teachers were injured when unexploded ordnance detonated during a hike near the Lebanese border. The students came from Ma’alot-Tarshiha, a community that has experienced rocket fire, drone alerts, and direct impacts from the war in the last three years.
And then, because of my work in mental health, I thought about what happened yesterday in the context of everything these children and their families are already carrying.
There will be investigations and questions about how this happened. Those questions deserve answers. But alongside them, we need to ask another question: What does another devastating event mean for children, families and communities who have already lived through years of threat?
Our phones are still buzzing with flydubai memes. Passengers and crew helped save an Israel-bound flight after the co-pilot attacked the captain and tried to crash the plane. Israelis became superheroes: the people you want sitting beside you when everything goes wrong.
While public story is about courage, background holds unbearable loss
But I know of a father and daughter who were traveling together on that plane. They had already lost their son and brother during the war. In WhatsApp groups I belong to, trauma experts were discussing who could help them find the right therapists. While the public story was about extraordinary courage, another conversation was about finding care for a family facing another terrifying experience on top of an unbearable loss.
We can celebrate courage and still leave room for what comes afterward. Surviving does not tell us how someone is sleeping, whether they feel safe boarding another plane, or what the experience means alongside an earlier loss.
And we should be careful about turning extraordinary responses into ordinary expectations. Must Israelis always be Superman? Must children keep adapting? Must bereaved families keep finding reserves of strength?
We tend to organize trauma around events: October 7, a rocket attack, a death, a flight, an explosion. Services, funding, and public attention often follow the same logic. Something happens; an emergency response is mobilized.
But people live through these events in sequence, carrying what came before. The next experience does not arrive on an empty page.
There is also a dimension of trauma that receives less attention than fear: what happens to trust.
“Moral injury” is a term used in mental-health research and clinical practice. It describes the psychological wound that can occur when an experience violates deeply held beliefs or values. The word “moral” refers to what has been wounded, not a judgment that anyone is immoral. It can involve guilt, shame, anger, or a sense of betrayal, and can occur with or without PTSD.
It is not another name for disappointment, or a diagnosis we can assign to people from afar. But it gives us language for questions that may surface after a tragedy.
We accept that life contains risk, while relying on others to help us navigate
I trusted that my child could go on this trip because someone had checked the route, assessed the dangers left by the fighting, and approved it. I trusted that the children knew what not to touch. I trusted the aircraft manufacturer, the airline, and the people and procedures responsible for deciding who could enter the cockpit.
We organize our lives around trust. We accept that life contains risk, while relying on others to help us navigate it. October 7 already shook that belief. An invasion from Gaza, entire communities overrun, so many hostages; all things many of us considered unfathomable.
New tragedies can touch that earlier wound. The question becomes bigger than “Was this trip safe?” or “Can I board another plane?” It becomes: “Can I still trust the things I rely on to live my life?”
Responding to all of this requires room for different needs, different reactions, and different timelines.
Someone may want to talk; someone else may need time. Courage, humor, grief and fear can all have a place. A person who acted heroically may still need help afterward.
A diagnosis should not be the price of admission to compassion.
We can acknowledge a sense of betrayal without prejudging responsibility, and help people rebuild a sense of safety while answers are still emerging.
That flexibility needs to be built into the support system. The injured need care. The bereaved need sustained support. Classmates, siblings, parents, and teachers need opportunities to ask questions and receive clear, age-appropriate information. Some will need practical guidance and support from people they trust. Others will need specialized treatment.
This is what a population-health approach looks like in practice: support across the affected community, with levels of care that adjust as people’s needs change. Neither sending everyone to therapy nor waiting for a diagnosis is enough.
The search for therapists in those WhatsApp groups reminds us how much knowledge and generosity exists here. The task is to turn that capacity into accessible pathways, so finding appropriate help does not depend on knowing the right person.
That means building a system that provides support beyond the first days, makes it easy to find the right level of care, and checks back rather than assuming that silence means recovery. It means funding the coordination and follow-up that rarely make headlines but belong in any serious response.
Admiration for Israeli resilience comes easily. But yesterday’s event is a reminder that we owe these children, families, and communities more than admiration for how much they can endure.
We owe them a lasting commitment to their recovery.
Gila Tolub is a co-founder and executive director of ICAR Collective, Israel’s Collective Action for Resilience, which is dedicated to accelerating trauma healing and advancing mental health resilience through coordinated collaboration across Israel’s public health, NGO, academic, and research communities.

====================================================================================================

Eisenkot wants a new direction. His Palestinian policy has a problem - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
13:46:25 UTC
22:46:25 KST

Gadi Eisenkot’s significance lies not only in the possibility that he may become Israel’s next prime minister, but also in the nature of the political alternative he offers. He opposes the full annexation of the West Bank and criticizes settler violence and the policies of the far Right, yet remains opposed to a fully sovereign Palestinian state and insists on overriding Israeli security control. In one interview, he raised the possibility of Palestinian self-government or what he described as a “minus state,” without a Palestinian army and without a large-scale evacuation of existing settlements.
This vision raises a question that goes beyond the differences between Eisenkot and Benjamin Netanyahu: Can Eisenkot offer a political alternative that opens the way to a lasting settlement, or would his proposals simply manage the conflict more efficiently without changing its underlying causes?
Improvements in security and economic management, however necessary, do not guarantee a political settlement unless accompanied by tangible progress on settlements, Palestinian sovereignty, rights, and mutual security. Nevertheless, some of his proposals could open a different political path if translated into clear and implementable commitments.
The real test of Eisenkot’s vision, therefore, is not how moderate his rhetoric appears compared with Netanyahu’s, but whether it can bring about meaningful changes in political, geographic, and economic realities while expanding the options available to Palestinians and Israelis. The issue is not simply how to manage the existing situation more effectively, but whether his policies would address the conditions that perpetuate the conflict or merely make its continuation easier to manage.
Constrained politics: Can Eisenkot change the direction or merely manage the constraints?
On August 27, 2026, Eisenkot argued that implementing the two-state solution after the October 7, 2023 attacks was unrealistic. At the same time, he opposed the settlement project known as E1, which threatens geographic continuity between Palestinian communities. In further statements in September, he reiterated his opposition to the establishment of a Palestinian state.
These positions illustrate the limits of the political approach he represents. He recognizes the dangers of annexation and uncontrolled settlement expansion, yet does not explain how the possibility of political separation can be preserved without a clear vision for Palestinian sovereignty.
Eisenkot therefore needs to answer a fundamental question: If the two-state solution is currently unacceptable to him, what viable political alternative does he propose? Does he regard existing security arrangements as a transitional phase or as a permanent model for relations with the Palestinians?
Postponing difficult decisions may appear to reduce immediate risks, but it can also narrow future options until a political settlement becomes even harder to achieve.
After the Israeli elections: Will the government change, or will policy change?
A change of government in Israel should not automatically be taken as a change in policy toward the Palestinians. Heightened security concerns since October 7, 2023, may continue to limit prospects for a settlement, even if Israeli leaders differ in their approaches to security, settlements, and relations with the Palestinian Authority.
Findings published by the Jewish People Policy Institute in August 2026 illustrate this political environment. Among Israeli Jewish respondents, 38% selected scenarios involving the annexation of the entire West Bank, while 35% chose scenarios based on partition. Another 22% selected a scenario involving annexation accompanied by the relocation of the Arab population to other countries. These were long-term strategic options presented in a survey, not direct measures of immediate support for annexation or population transfer.
In this context, Eisenkot rejects annexing millions of Palestinians and governing them directly, while also opposing a fully sovereign Palestinian state. His challenge, therefore, is not simply to change the way the conflict is managed, but to clarify whether the self-government he proposes is a transitional arrangement leading toward a settlement or a permanent condition of limited sovereignty. The real test for any future Israeli leadership is whether its policies create new, verifiable political possibilities or simply manage the status quo differently.
Settlements: Where does confronting violence end and addressing the underlying problem begin?
In an interview with The Jerusalem Post on September 24, 2026, Eisenkot pledged to reorganize the Civil Administration and policing in the West Bank under military coordination and restore enforcement measures against settlers who engage in violence. In another interview, he reaffirmed his support for settlements he considers consistent with Israeli law and Israel’s security interests, while rejecting a large-scale evacuation of existing settlements.
Confronting settler violence, however, is not the same as addressing settlement expansion itself. Nor does the classification of settlements under Israeli law determine their legality under international law.
Eisenkot needs to clarify whether he is prepared to halt projects that undermine Palestinian geographic continuity, rather than merely remove outposts that Israel itself considers illegal. A practical measure of his policy would be whether Palestinians can remain in their homes, access their land, and work safely, alongside effective protection of Israeli civilians from attacks.
Protecting civilians is essential for both peoples, but that responsibility does not relieve political leaders of the need to address the conditions that allow violence and control over land to remain enduring features of the conflict.
Palestinian sovereignty: Could a “minus state” become a permanent solution?
Eisenkot wants Palestinians to continue managing their own affairs, but opposes a Palestinian army or foreign military forces between the Jordan River and the Mediterranean Sea, while insisting on Israeli security superiority. His approach raises a question that goes beyond political terminology: How much independence can an entity exercise if it lacks ultimate control over its security, borders, and resources?
The Palestinian experience since the Oslo Accords has shown that self-administration does not automatically develop into political sovereignty. Eisenkot therefore needs to specify the powers he would be willing to grant Palestinians, the limits of Israeli intervention, and the guarantees that would prevent a transitional arrangement from becoming permanent.
Without a clear path toward addressing rights and self-determination, his proposed model could become a more orderly means of maintaining control rather than ending it.
The Palestinian Authority: Preserving it for what purpose?
Eisenkot opposes dismantling the Palestinian Authority or replacing it with a direct Jordanian role. He has also made clear that he does not want Israel to govern millions of Palestinians. This distinguishes his approach from those calling for the Authority’s dissolution or a reduction in its role.
But preserving an institution does not necessarily mean empowering it. Does Eisenkot envisage a Palestinian Authority capable of exercising meaningful political and economic powers, or an administrative body whose responsibilities remain limited to public services and security coordination?
At the same time, the Palestinian leadership faces responsibilities that cannot be postponed, including renewing political legitimacy, holding elections, strengthening accountability, and reforming institutions. Yet successful reform also requires political conditions in which Palestinian institutions can exercise their powers.
Eisenkot therefore needs to create room for the Palestinian Authority to develop into a genuine political partner, rather than merely preserve it to avoid an administrative and security vacuum.
The economy: Between work permits and the ability to build a future
Eisenkot advocates improving Palestinian living conditions by allowing certain groups to work in Israel, subject to strict security approvals, while encouraging foreign investment, including investment from Arab countries.
Such measures may provide important income and opportunities, but they do not, on their own, address the structural problems facing the Palestinian economy, including clearance revenues, banking relations, freedom of movement, trade, and access through crossings.
A survey conducted by the Palestinian Center for Public Opinion between June 24 and July 5, 2026, among 503 respondents in the West Bank, including east Jerusalem, and the Gaza Strip, found that 92.6% reported weakened purchasing power, while 90.7% believed poverty and unemployment had increased.
These findings reflect the economic pressures as perceived by respondents, without independently establishing their causes. They raise an important question for Eisenkot: Is his objective to ease immediate economic hardship, or to enable Palestinians to develop an economy capable of producing, investing, and planning for the future?
Economic stability depends not only on increasing the number of work permits, but also on creating conditions in which businesses and households can make economic decisions with greater stability and independence.
Gaza: The limits of a security-based Solution
In his October 6, 2026 interview, Eisenkot expressed his commitment to advancing US President Donald Trump’s 20-point plan for Gaza, while insisting on the complete disarmament of Hamas before the restoration of civilian governance, the deployment of an international force, and the start of reconstruction.
This approach reflects the priority he gives to security, but it raises questions about whether lasting stability can be achieved if rebuilding institutions and restoring essential services are delayed until all security conditions have been fulfilled.
The long experience since 1967 has demonstrated that military superiority alone has not brought the conflict to an end. Eisenkot needs to present a vision that links security arrangements with civilian governance, reconstruction, and Palestinian participation in determining the future, while preventing the political separation of Gaza from the West Bank from becoming permanent.
Rebuilding homes and infrastructure is a humanitarian necessity, but it cannot be sufficient if Gaza’s political future remains unresolved.
Palestinian public opinion: Is there still an opportunity?
Palestinian public opinion reveals a dimension that may receive insufficient attention in Israel’s security debate. A telephone survey conducted by the Palestinian Center for Public Opinion between July 5 and 18, 2026, among 309 respondents in the West Bank and Gaza Strip, found that 92.9% selected non-military means as the most effective way to gain international support for Palestinian rights, compared with 3.2% who chose military action.
The survey also found that 68.9% believed coexistence could be possible if based on justice and equal rights, while 77.7% regarded the lack of trust as an obstacle to peace.
These findings do not indicate support for Eisenkot’s vision or acceptance of a “minus state.” They do, however, suggest a conditional openness that could provide a basis for political progress. Eisenkot needs to recognize that addressing security concerns alone will not build trust if political rights remain without a credible future.
In this context, Prof. Raphael Cohen-Almagor’s 2026 book, Resolving the Israeli–Palestinian Conflict, published by Cambridge University Press, offers an important perspective grounded in trust, fairness, political courage, and mutual recognition. The book goes beyond these principles to discuss practical arrangements, beginning with the restoration of civilian and economic cooperation and moving toward a settlement in which the two-state solution remains central.
The comparison is revealing: If an Israeli scholar sees a way to combine security guarantees with a political settlement, the question facing Eisenkot is why overriding Israeli security control should remain an open-ended substitute for resolving Palestinian sovereignty.
Regional normalization: Can peace be achieved without the Palestinians?
Eisenkot sees opportunities to expand regional cooperation through US mediation, strengthen relations with Egypt, Jordan, and countries already participating in normalization agreements, and potentially extend those relationships to additional Arab states. He has acknowledged that these countries seek changes in the West Bank and in Israel’s treatment of Palestinians, while emphasizing that his decisions would be guided by Israeli interests.
This raises a fundamental question: Can Eisenkot use regional cooperation to open a path toward a political settlement, or does his approach aim to strengthen Israel’s regional position without substantially changing its relationship with the Palestinians?
Normalization may create economic, security, and diplomatic opportunities, but it cannot replace the need to address Palestinian rights. Nor are Arab positions identical: Saudi Arabia’s position on Palestinian statehood reflects considerations that differ from Jordan’s more immediate interests in the West Bank and Jerusalem.
Eisenkot needs to clarify whether he is prepared to turn regional cooperation into an incentive to halt settlement expansion, strengthen Palestinian institutions, provide mutual security guarantees, and establish a political process with clearly defined objectives.
Conclusion: The real test of Eisenkot’s vision
Eisenkot should not be treated as identical to Netanyahu. There are differences in their approaches to institutional management, confronting settler violence, relations with the Palestinian Authority, and engagement with the international community. Yet differences in governance do not necessarily translate into differences over the nature of a political solution.
His vision should therefore be assessed through observable outcomes: Will settlement expansion that undermines geographic continuity stop? Will Palestinian powers be expanded? Will the Palestinian economy become more capable of sustaining itself? Will civilian protection become more effective? And will a political process emerge that addresses sovereignty, rights, and mutual security?
Security without a political horizon may develop into a permanent system for managing the conflict, while justice without capable institutions and credible security arrangements may remain a difficult goal to achieve. Nevertheless, some of Eisenkot’s proposals could mark the beginning of a political shift if accompanied by clear, verifiable commitments that move the relationship from managing the conflict toward addressing its causes.
The real test for Eisenkot is not whether he can manage the conflict more efficiently than Netanyahu, but whether he is prepared to make decisions that bring a political settlement within reach. The question is not simply how the existing situation is managed, but whether the proposed policies change the conditions that keep it in place.
Dr. Nabil Kukali is the founder and president of the Palestinian Center for Public Opinion (PCPO) and a specialist in public opinion research and survey methodology. He has more than three decades of experience in social, political, and economic research and has supervised numerous national and international studies throughout Palestine and the Middle East.

Ukraine says it hit 12 Russian refineries in September. No refinery strikes reported since Trump’s “energy ceasefire”
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
13:45:35 UTC
22:45:35 KST

Ukrainian forces hit 12 large Russian refineries in September, Ukraine’s Ministry of Defense said, according to ArmyInform on 12 October. The farthest on the ministry’s list, Lukoil’s refinery in Perm, lies about 1,500 kilometers from Ukraine’s border. Since Trump's 11 October announcement, Euromaidan Press has found no reports of new Ukrainian refinery strikes in the official and unofficial Ukrainian and Russian sources it monitors.
A refinery-for-refinery pause would limit Ukraine’s ability to disrupt Russia’s oil industry while leaving Moscow free to keep attacking Ukraine’s energy system, giving Russia an advantage in a war where both sides use energy infrastructure as a target. The issue has become urgent since Trump announced an “energy ceasefire” on 11 October, after which Ukraine reported holding off strikes on Russian energy facilities while Zelenskyy said Russia attacked several Ukrainian energy sites.
The campaign continued into October. Ukraine’s General Staff said Ukrainian forces struck the Samara oil pumping station overnight into 10 October, the third attack on the station that month, according to Radio Svoboda.
Ukraine held off, Russia hit six energy sites
Zelenskyy said Ukraine had refrained from striking Russian energy facilities overnight on 11–12 October following Trump's announcement. Monitoring channels and official Russian sources did not report any new refinery strikes on 13 October.
“Last night, we did not attack any energy facilities on the territory of Russia because President Trump said that there would be an energy ceasefire,” Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said.
He added that Ukraine does not announce its next operational steps. Zelenskyy said Russia attacked six Ukrainian energy facilities on 12 October alone, according to Radio Svoboda.
Refineries first, power plants possibly later
A White House official told Axios that the proposal would begin with both sides halting attacks on oil refineries, with a possible agreement covering power plants to follow. Axios reported that Russia had not accepted a ceasefire.
The Institute for the Study of War (ISW) said the proposal, as described, would give Russia a major concession without offering Ukraine anything in return: Russia has scores of operating refineries, while Ukraine has one. ISW also said the proposal would allow Russia to continue its winter strikes on Ukrainian power stations.

EXPLAINER - What to know about Nord Stream sabotage trial
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
13:44:10 UTC
22:44:10 KST

Kanyshai Butun
13 October 2026•Update: 13 October 2026
- Incident triggered competing accusations over who was responsible, with several countries rejecting allegations of involvement
Germany is preparing to put a Ukrainian national on trial over the September 2022 explosions that damaged the Nord Stream gas pipelines in the Baltic Sea, with prosecutors alleging that Ukrainian state authorities ordered the operation.
The suspect, identified as Serhii K., is accused of helping lead a group that carried out the sabotage. His indictment marks the first time German prosecutors have formally brought the Nord Stream sabotage case before a court.
Another suspect, identified by Germany as Vladimir Z., is in custody in Croatia and is fighting extradition. He was earlier detained in Poland.
What happened to Nord Stream?
Nord Stream is a network of offshore natural gas pipelines connecting Russia and Germany beneath the Baltic Sea. The four lines of Nord Stream and Nord Stream 2 had a combined annual capacity of 110 billion cubic meters.
Construction of the first Nord Stream pipeline was completed in 2011, and it began operating in 2012. Nord Stream 2 was completed in September 2021 but never entered service.
In September 2022, Nord Stream AG, the operator of the pipelines, confirmed damage to both systems as Danish and Swedish authorities reported explosions and gas leaks in sections passing through their respective waters.
Pipeline pressure stabilized, and the gas leaks stopped several weeks after the incident, with Russia opening a criminal case on charges of international terrorism.
Russian President Vladimir Putin later described the US and countries with alternative energy supply routes to Europe, including Ukraine and Poland, as “beneficiaries” of the disruption.
Which countries have been accused of involvement?
While Western officials initially suspected Russia, German investigators later focused on possible Ukrainian involvement. The US, Poland and the UK have also faced allegations, but have denied involvement.
Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov dismissed claims of Russian involvement as “quite predictable and also predictably stupid,” stressing Moscow lost a route for gas supplies to Europe.
The US rejected the allegations as “Russia's disinformation,” while Poland called the claims “completely groundless insinuations.” 
In August, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said Germany should not prosecute suspects accused of blowing up the Nord Stream pipeline, adding that those who built the project “should be ashamed, not those who disabled them.”
The UK also rejected allegations, saying Russia was “resorting to peddling false claims of an epic scale.”
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy denied Kyiv's involvement, saying the government has officially never taken part in any operation related to the Nord Stream blast.
He said Ukraine held high-level talks with Germany on the issue, and that German officials knew Kyiv was not involved in planning or carrying out the operation.
What do German prosecutors say?
Serhii K. was detained in Italy near Rimini in August 2025 on suspicion of involvement in the sabotage. He was extradited to Germany three months later and has remained in pretrial detention in Hamburg.
The suspect is charged with causing an explosion, damaging property, disrupting public services and being an “accomplice to war crimes” for targeting civilian objects, prosecutors said.
German prosecutors allege that Serhii K. was an officer in the Ukrainian army at the time, and helped plan the operation with other military personnel “acting on behalf of state bodies in Ukraine.”
Prosecutors allege the objective was to destroy both pipelines, permanently halt Russian gas deliveries and prevent Moscow from using energy revenues to finance its war against Ukraine.
Investigators claim the suspects traveled to Germany using forged Ukrainian passports and hired a yacht, the Andromeda. Traces of the explosives HMX and RDX were found aboard the vessel.
According to prosecutors, the explosives were attached to the pipelines near Denmark’s Bornholm island using timers by Sept. 22, 2022. They detonated four days later, causing extensive damage and rendering the pipelines inoperable.
Serhii K. denies the allegations.
The high-profile trial opens in a Hamburg court on Wednesday.

Court orders government to enforce rules on docking pigs’ tails
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
13:44:08 UTC
22:44:08 KST

Court orders government to enforce rules on docking pigs’ tails
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
A court has ordered the Dutch government to enforce the rules banning pig farmers from docking their animals’ tails in a case brought by animal rights campaigners.
Junior agriculture minister Silvio Erkens has been told to assess three pig farms that have been accused of breaking the rules, which only allow tail docking in exceptional circumstances.
Erkens had rejected a demand from pig welfare group Varkens in Nood to rule whether the three farms were breaking the law, arguing that the rules were too vague to enforce.
But the Dutch Trade and Industry Appeals Tribunal (CBb) said the law required farmers who docked pigs’ tails to show that they met the conditions for being exempted from the ban, enabling the junior minister to make a ruling.
Varkens in Nood said the ban on docking had existed for 30 years but 99% of pigs still have their tails docked. Farmers claim that the practice is necessary to prevent pigs from biting each other’s tails, but campaigners say better living conditions for pigs on farms would solve the problem.
Docking tails is only permitted if the pigs are less than four days old and in situations where wounds have been caused by biting and the farmers have tried other remedies without success.
Food standards
Erkens must now direct the food standards agency NVWA to decide within six months if the three farmers in the case have complied with the law and whether enforcement measures are needed.
The petitioners hope it will lead to the end of the so-called “tolerance” of tail docking, which has been banned across the EU since 1991 but is still widely practised in the Netherlands.
Varkens in Nood says the tails are usually amputated without anaesthetic, a painful procedure that inhibits the pigs’ ability to communicate and allows farmers to keep them in cramped, basic stalls.
Hanneke Wellenberg, of Amsterdam law firm Soeverein Advocaten, said the decision was “a crucial ruling for the millions of pigs in this country”.
“Now that pig farmers will have to end the routine docking of pigs’ tails, they will have to make big improvements to their animals’ living conditions to prevent tail biting.”
Varkens in Nood also asked the court to impose a conditional fine on the farmers until they complied with the rules. But the court said it did not have enough information to make a judgment on whether the law had been broken.

Man killed by tiger at Yorkshire Wildlife Park named
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
13:44:01 UTC
22:44:01 KST

A man killed by a tiger at a zoo in South Yorkshire has been named locally as William Chapman.
Chapman scaled the fence and entered the enclosure at Yorkshire Wildlife Park near Doncaster on Saturday afternoon. Witnesses described seeing Chapman, who has not been officially named by police, walking up to a 200kg male Siberian tiger, named Altai, which attacked him.
The incident lasted only a couple of minutes and Chapman, who is believed to have been in his 20s, was pronounced dead at the scene shortly after.
Videos in which onlookers urged him not to approach the tiger and to “play dead” during the attack were shared online in the aftermath, as well as a number of AI-generated fakes. Police advised members of the public to avoid sharing them. They said the man’s family was being supported by specialist officers.
Yorkshire Wildlife Park was evacuated on Saturday and remained closed for a fourth day on Tuesday.
Dan Swaine, the executive director of place at Doncaster council, said: “As the relevant licensing authority for the Yorkshire Wildlife Park, I can confirm that, in line with our statutory duties, the council has launched a health and safety investigation.
“We are also working with multiple agencies, including the police and health agencies, and are supporting the Yorkshire Wildlife Park in response to the incident. At this time, we won’t be commenting further on the individual or the investigation and we ask that the privacy of those involved is respected at this difficult time.”
The park said staff were receiving specialist support and that Altai, an endangered tiger, would not be euthanised.
Wildlife and zoo experts told the Guardian it was unlikely the wildlife park would have been able to prevent the incident.
Amy Dickman, a professor of wildlife conservation and the director of WildCRU at the University of Oxford, said: “I would not conclude that there was a major issue with zoo safety – the harsh reality is that it is virtually impossible for zoos to stop people who are very determined to breach safety measures.”
Campbell Murn, a lecturer in conservation science at the University of Reading, who until recently sat on the Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs’ zoos expert committee, said: “It’s simply not possible … at an attraction like Yorkshire Wildlife Park that gets hundreds of thousands – if not over a million – visitors a year to keep an eye on everybody all the time.”
He added: “If a determined thief wants to get in your house, they’re going to get in your house. You can mitigate risk to a certain point but there’s sometimes no stopping events from happening, unfortunately.”
A spokesperson for the Born Free Foundation, which campaigns to phase out zoos, called for an “urgent review” into “how the man managed to enter the enclosure and what happened next”.

EU expresses regret over Trump-Putin 'diesel deal,' but dialogue will continue – European diplomat
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
16:43:15 EEST
22:43:15 KST

The European Union expresses regret over the so-called "diesel deal" between US President Donald Trump and Kremlin leader Vladimir Putin, noting that this is not the first time differences have arisen between Europe and the United States regarding the war Russia is waging against Ukraine. Dialogue will continue.
A European diplomat informed journalists in Brussels on Tuesday on the eve of the European Council meeting scheduled for October 15-16 in Brussels—where continued support for Ukraine in standing against Russian aggression will be among the agenda items—answering a question on whether European Council President António Costa intends to raise this issue for discussion among EU leaders.
"Regarding the announced deal: we consider it regrettable, we regret its conclusion. It contradicts the strategy we have followed over the past four and a half years, which involves not only pressure on Russia, but also rejection of Russian energy sources—and not just fossil fuels," he said.
Demonstrating the dynamics of phasing out Russian fuel, the source noted that in 2021 Russia's share in imports of fossil fuels—both oil and gas—dropped sharply. "Regarding oil, we went from a level of around 45% of imports to 12% today, so the reduction is obvious. And thanks to full implementation of the REPowerEU strategy, we plan to completely sever this connection. Regarding gas, the figure dropped from 26% to, I believe, 2%. So I repeat: this is a European strategy," he stated.
The diplomat noted that such measures are "not only a way to stop Russia from funding its war machine, but also a means of pressure on Russia to stop this war."
At the same time, he drew attention to the fact that the agreement announced by US President Donald Trump with Russia is "not the first time we have had differences with the US regarding the war in Ukraine." "The experience of recent years—and certainly the period following President Trump's taking office—shows that dialogue with the US does not always lead to full agreement on the vision of the situation between the European Union and the United States, but such dialogue is in any case better than its absence. We have also seen many cases where, thanks to this dialogue, the US changed its position or the positions of the parties moved closer together. Therefore, in my opinion, such practice should continue; it is a completely natural and necessary process," he expressed confidence.
The diplomat emphasized that all EU leaders "share a common position regarding the situation in Ukraine." For this reason, according to him, it makes no sense for European Council President Costa to "singling out this specific moment." "I think the European Council will express regret over this [Trump-Putin deal] decision," the journalists' interlocutor added.

Iraq faces six-month air defence gap after US-led coalition exit
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
13:41:36 UTC
22:41:36 KST

Breadcrumb
Iraq faces six-month air defence gap after US-led coalition exit
Iraq faces a potential six-month gap in its air defences following the withdrawal of US-led coalition forces, with new systems not expected to arrive until early next year.
The coalition completed its military withdrawal at the end of September, removing air defence systems that had helped protect parts of the country, including the Kurdistan Region.
Baghdad says agreements have been reached to purchase new equipment, but the first systems could take up to six months to arrive.
The transition has taken on added urgency after two drones targeted a camp for Iranian Kurdish refugees near Erbil last week.
Sabah al-Numan, spokesman for the commander-in-chief of Iraq's armed forces, said Baghdad had made "tangible progress" in acquiring new air defence systems.
He said the first batch would arrive within six months and be deployed across the country.
The package would include advanced radar systems, interceptor weapons and aircraft, he said, as part of a wider plan to strengthen Iraq's control over its airspace.
Numan said the country's security situation remained relatively stable and that Iraqi forces were maintaining a high level of readiness.
However, the announcement leaves questions over Iraq's ability to detect and intercept aerial threats before the new systems become operational.
Iraq has long struggled with limited and ageing air defence capabilities, while drones and missiles have become an increasingly prominent security threat.
A Defence Ministry official nevertheless played down the prospect of an immediate security vacuum.
"The available Iraqi air capabilities are not at a high level, and there is no denying that, but the security situation in the country is relatively calm," the official told The New Arab on condition of anonymity.
The official said Iraq retained "reasonably good capabilities" and that there were currently no expectations of major security breaches.
Concerns are particularly acute in the Kurdistan Region.
Kurdistan Region President Nechirvan Barzani said on Monday that both federal Iraq and the autonomous region required effective air defence coverage.
"Let us be realistic. The Kurdistan Region and Iraq as a whole need an air defence system," he told the MERI Forum in Erbil.
Barzani said an earlier agreement negotiated under former prime minister Mohammed Shia al-Sudani with the United States had included plans to provide air defence capabilities covering Kurdistan.
"Air defence is not only a need for the Iraqi state. The Kurdistan Region also needs it," he said.
He also stressed that weapons should remain under state control.
Military expert Aqil al-Shammari warned that the process could take longer than the six months announced by the government.
He said another three months could be required to integrate the equipment, establish command-and-control systems, train personnel, arrange maintenance and complete deployment.
"Owning the system does not mean providing complete air coverage," the former brigadier general told The New Arab.
Shammari said the transition period would be a major test of Baghdad's ability to protect Iraqi airspace.
Kurdish officials had warned before the coalition withdrawal that removing foreign forces and their air defence systems without an immediate replacement could leave the region vulnerable.
The withdrawal forms part of a wider transition towards a new security relationship between Baghdad and Washington focused on training, technology and military co-operation without a direct US combat presence.
They have argued that protecting Kurdistan's airspace is ultimately the responsibility of the federal government because it forms part of Iraq's national airspace.
Those concerns intensified after two explosive-laden drones targeted a camp housing Iranian Kurdish refugees near Erbil last week.
No casualties were reported, but the attack renewed fears that gaps in Iraq's air defences could leave the Kurdistan Region vulnerable to further drone strikes.
The withdrawal has also raised wider questions over whether Baghdad can manage its security without the coalition's military presence.

Miriam González Durántez launches new centrist party in Spain
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
13:41:05 UTC
22:41:05 KST

The Spanish lawyer Miriam González Durántez has launched a new liberal, centrist party, vowing to clean up politics and give voters an alternative to the dominant socialist and conservative parties as the country gears up for next month’s snap general election.
González Durántez, an ex-EU adviser who is married to the former British deputy prime minister Nick Clegg, says her new party, Democracia21, will offer a modern, transparent kind of politics that “doesn’t feed on fear, insults or nostalgia”.
Democracia21’s manifesto accuses both the ruling Spanish Socialist Workers’ party (PSOE) and the rightwing People’s party (PP) of squandering decades of government for short-term political ends.
“In the meantime: housing became unaffordable, young people left, bureaucracy grew like a religion, and bickering took the place of governing,” it says. “Old-school politics turned every problem into a narrative – and every solution into an electoral threat.”
Mindful of the corruption scandals that eventually toppled the last PP government – and the graft allegations enveloping the administration and inner circle of the socialist prime minister, Pedro Sánchez – the new party is promising “a radical political cleanup”, including far greater transparency for parties.
González Durántez, who announced that Democracia21 will run in Madrid and Barcelona in the election on 29 November, has also positioned herself on two of the biggest issues facing voters: the housing crisis and immigration.
The eviction last month of an 87-year-old woman in Madrid unleashed waves of demonstrations across Spain, led to the setting up of a protest camp in the centre of the capital and prompted Sánchez’s minority government to propose emergency measures to try to make the rental market more equitable. When those measures were voted down by rightwing and far-right parties at the beginning of October, the prime minister announced a snap general election.
Speaking at her party’s launch over the weekend, González Durántez accused both the PSOE and the PP of ignoring the housing crisis.
“One lot has been in government for eight years and the other controls 80% of Spain’s regional governments,” she said. “What’s going on here is that they only remember about housing when an election comes around and all the people are on the streets.”
González Durántez proposed scrapping housing taxes for people under 35, and argued that a young person earning €1,300 (£1,098) a month should not be paying more than €350 a month in rent.
She also defended the benefits of controlled immigration and of Spain’s place within the European project, which she described as “absolutely existential” for the country.
“Immigration is an asset and an essential competitive advantage for Spain right now,” she said. “We need to get rid of all the xenophobic talk but the state needs to be in control of immigration. We need to decide who comes in; how they come in; when they come in and, if they have to leave, we will also decide when they leave. None of this is contradictory. We need to do all that while ensuring that Europe doesn’t fall into the traps of those political forces that haven’t come to reform Europe, but to break it.”
Democracia21 is not the first centrist party to have tried to shake up the traditional socialist and conservative duopoly. The liberal Ciudadanos party, founded in 2006, briefly looked set to push past both the PSOE and the PP, but its decision to lurch to the right and its refusal to back the no-confidence motion that turfed the conservatives out of office in 2018 proved fatal. Ciudadanos’s support was so depleted by the last general election in July 2023 that it chose not to take part in the poll.
Sánchez’s decision to call the snap election is another gamble from Spain’s pragmatic and unpredictable prime minister. Polls suggest the PP will comfortably beat the PSOE to win first place, but is unlikely to secure an absolute majority, forcing it to rely on Vox’s support to govern.
Sánchez, meanwhile, will be hoping that the PP’s decision to side with Vox and the rightwing Catalan pro-independence Junts party to torpedo the housing proposals will mobilise leftwing and moderate voters.
The prime minister, however, is already facing an electoral setback after Spain’s supreme court decided to maintain its suspension of the voting rights of tens of thousands of overseas voters who benefited from a law his government introduced in 2022 offering Spanish citizenship to the descendants of those exiled during the civil war and subsequent Franco dictatorship.
The move has angered the PP and Vox, who have accused Sánchez of seeking to create more socialist voters beyond Spain’s borders. Although the suspension looks set to remain in place for the election, the court has said its ruling will not affect those who can prove that their parents or grandparents “suffered exile for political or ideological reasons, or for reasons of belief or sexual orientation”.
The PSOE has denounced the political pressure behind the decision as an affront to democracy.
“The grandchildren of the Franco regime will be able to vote, but not those of the exiles, just as the PP and Vox wanted,” the party’s organisational secretary, Rebeca Torró, posted on X. “Their fascist agenda has struck at the cornerstone of democracy: the right to vote. We will not stop denouncing this outrage.”

Tallinn says no to motorcycles, e-scooters in bus lanes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

22:41:00 KST

Tallinn says no to motorcycles, e-scooters in bus lanes
Tallinn is pushing back against plans to let motorcycles and e-scooters use bus lanes, warning they could slow public transport and increase crash risks.
In a submission to the Riigikogu's Economic Affairs Committee, the city reiterated its opposition to a bill allowing motorcycles to use public transport lanes. It also rejects a separate proposal to allow light electric vehicles, including e-scooters, in the lanes.
Deputy Mayor Joel Jesse (Center Party) said adding more traffic would make it harder for buses to stay on schedule and increase the risk of crashes.
E-scooters, he said, pose particular concerns due to the sheer difference in size and mass, and large vehicles' blind spots also increase both the likelihood and severity of collisions.
"In spots where buses share the lanes with rams, there's the added risk of getting caught in the tracks," the deputy mayor continued, adding that wet and icy roads can worsen conditions from fall through spring in particular as well.
EV explosion
Tallinn also wants to revoke the existing right under the Public Transport Act for taxis and electric vehicles (EVs) to use public transport lanes, saying fewer vehicles would help public transport run faster and more reliably.
Traffic in public transport lanes has increased significantly, the city said, with the number of registered EVs rising from 1,649 in 2020 to more than 13,000 this year, about two-thirds of them in Harju County.
This rapid increase in EVs has already slowed public transport in the dedicated lanes, making it harder for them to remain on schedule. "This shows that access to public transport lanes should be narrowed rather than expanded," the city added.

Russia denied interfering in the vote.

US Supreme Court to hear asylum fight involving Nigerian cook
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
13:40:35 UTC
22:40:35 KST

US Supreme Court to hear asylum fight involving Nigerian cook
Oct 13 - The US Supreme Court agreed on Tuesday to hear a bid by President Donald Trump's administration to deny asylum to a man who was forced to prepare meals for an apparent separatist group in Nigeria, in a case that could expand what officials may deem terrorist activity under American immigration law.
The justices took up the Justice Department's appeal of a lower court's ruling in favor of Nigerian citizen Izuchukwu Ozurumba, who was denied US asylum due to his work cooking for a group known as the Unknown Gunmen that US officials considered to be a terrorist organization. The lower court ruled that cooking did not qualify as "material support" for terrorism under the immigration statute.
The Supreme Court is expected to hear arguments and rule in the case by the end of June.
The administration, in appealing the case to the Supreme Court, said that if the lower court's ruling were allowed to stand, it would "substantially increase the burden on the government in excluding aliens with links to terrorism."
The case centers on whether Ozurumba's work for the group fell under provisions of US immigration law that bar the entry of non-US citizens who have "engaged in a terrorist activity," including actions that provide "material support" for such activity or "to a terrorist organization."
"At stake in this case is whether the government can use an overly broad reading of the law to shut the door on people seeking asylum," said Aimee Mayer-Salins, an attorney with the Amica Center for Immigrant Rights, which is helping to represent Ozurumba.
The lower court "correctly recognized that asylum should not be denied to immigrants who provided no meaningful support to a terrorist group," Mayer-Salins added.
Following a job tip in 2022, Ozurumba took a van to a remote camp outside of Lagos, according to court papers. After he was hired, he eventually learned the camp was run by the Unknown Gunmen, a group likely associated with Nigerian separatists, according to court papers.
Ozurumba soon "observed that the young men's movements from the camp coincided with news reports of murder and arson," his lawyers said in a court filing. Ozurumba sought to leave but was forced to stay without pay, they added.
After six months he escaped while on an outing for supplies, eventually making his way back to Lagos, they said.
Ozurumba then faced beatings and threats of death, prompting him to flee to Venezuela, where the threats continued, his lawyers said. Ozurumba then traveled to the southern US border and entered the country illegally in July 2023. Ozurumba eventually applied for asylum and other protections from deportation.
'BASIC HUMAN NEEDS'
During Democratic former President Joe Biden's administration, an immigration judge deemed the Unknown Gunmen a terrorist organization and found that Ozurumba's cooking for the group rendered him inadmissible, and denied him any protections from deportation.
The judge concluded that the cooking helped the group accomplish its goals by satisfying their "basic human needs," and that it was irrelevant that he had worked under duress.
Ozurumba was deported back to Nigeria last year while his case was on appeal.
The Richmond, Virginia-based 4th US Circuit Court of Appeals sided with Ozurumba in September 2025, ruling that he was a captive laborer and his cooking did not constitute material support.
Ozurumba's work "provided nothing that the organization could use or readily divert to plan or carry out its terrorist activities," the 4th Circuit ruled, but declined to order the government to return him to the US while the case proceeds.
"Providing meals to a terrorist organization's members is no less a material form of support than providing gasoline for its vehicles," the Justice Department told the Supreme Court in its appeal. REUTERS

Brussels Public Prosecutor, Julien Moinil (pictured right), has given details of the killing of a police officer on Monday night during a police operation in the Brussels borough of Jette. At the press conference in Brussels today Moinil was flanked by Chief of Police Michel Goovaerts and Chief Public Prosecutor Frédéric Van Leeuw (pictured left).
Moinil said that several suspects have been arrested in connection with the shooting that led to the death of the police officer.
Walloon Brabant police were called out to a robbery in Tubize, the prosecutor explains. The number plate of the suspects’ vehicle had been passed on, and the Brussels anti-robbery squad was able to locate the vehicle.
“Two teams were deployed for surveillance. A member of the team, an experienced police officer in plain clothes, went to the scene on foot to carry out a reconnaissance in preparation for an intervention.”
Shortly afterwards, the officer, who had been shot in the head, was found near the vehicle. Several weapons were found at the scene. An investigating judge has been appointed to investigate the murder.
Moinil said that several suspects have since been arrested but was unable to provide further details on this matter, in the interests of the investigation.
The Prosecutor expressed his condolences to the family of the victim and continued:
"Police officers take risks in increasingly difficult circumstances. They are human beings. Behind every police officer there is a mother, a son, a brother, a sister. People who are worried."
"We live in a time when police officers are often criticised. But my view is that the police deserve respect and support. My thanks go to them."
Officer named as 41-year-old Nordine
Police chief Michel Goovaerts paid tribute to his officer, who had been killed.
“Nordine, aged 41, joined the police force in 2009, initially as an inspector. Ten years later, in 2019, he realised his dream: to join the anti-robbery squad. He did so with great dedication and professionalism.”
“What I can guarantee is that we will keep the memory of Nordine alive”.
More details emerge
In response to questions Prosecutor Moinil said revolvers were used, not military grade weapons. He also confirmed that the victim was hit by one bullet.
The Prosecutor did not want to comment on the quantity of drugs that was found. His response to other questions was also that the investigation is still ongoing.
He did, however, say that three weapons were found near the vehicle.
Earlier shooting in Elsene
The shooting in Jette was not the first of the evening. Brussels Public Prosecutor Julien Moinil also provided details of the first fatal shooting of the night in the Brussels borough of Elsene. A man was shot dead, but the incident is not believed to be related to the slaying of the police officer in a second Brussels municipality, Jette.
“The victim in Elsene was shot dead on Monday shortly before 6 pm, in the entrance hall of a block of flats. The victim was hit by several shots and died shortly afterwards in hospital.”
“The perpetrators have not yet been identified. An investigating judge has been appointed to look into the murder. That investigation is in full swing” Moinil noted.

It was not clear whether Moscow had deliberately avoided targeting power plants.
Russia hit no Ukrainian energy targets on Tuesday for the first time since US President Donald Trump's weekend announcement of an "energy ceasefire", while hammering cities' transport and logistics overnight with ballistic missiles and drones.
Russia's defence ministry, in its daily summary of overnight strikes, made no mention of Ukrainian energy facilities. A Kremlin spokesman, asked about the energy ceasefire, would only say that contacts were ongoing, but declined to provide any further details. However, one missile came down just over a kilometre from a plant providing heating to much of the city of Lviv, in the west.
Trump's ceasefire announcement on Sunday came two days after his declaration of a deal that lifted US sanctions on Russian diesel exports to allow Russia to supply almost 2 million metric tons of diesel, a bid to lower US fuel prices.
Reuters and other media outlets have reported that US officials have threatened to cut off intelligence sharing and weapons sales to Ukraine unless it halts its strikes on Russian oil refineries.

Trump wants cheaper diesel for Midterms

MOSCOW, October 13. /TASS/. Russia was again the largest supplier of oil to India (accounting for 45% of the country's oil imports) and to China (30% of the country's oil imports) in August 2026, the Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries (OPEC) said in its report.
In particular, Russia provided 45% of India's oil imports in August, while another 12% came from the UAE, and 9% from Venezuela, the OPEC reported, citing data from Kpler analytical firm.
India's total oil imports in August 2026 decreased relative to July, averaging 4.5 million barrels per day (bpd) compared to 5.05 million bpd the month before.
In the meantime, China's oil imports continued to recover in August, increasing from 8.38 million bpd to 8.89 million bpd, which is 6% more than the previous month. Russia remained the largest supplier of oil to China, with its share of supplies during the reporting period standing at 30%, while Brazil provided another 10% of supplies, and Saudi Arabia accounted for 8% of supplies.

The expanded network is intended to meet the fuel needs of both Lithuanian forces and NATO allies while creating a flexible and resilient supply system.
The ministry said it was also working with other state institutions to make the best use of existing fuel storage facilities and related infrastructure.

Wheat prices post sharpest drop in over 2 years amid easing geopolitical risks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
13:37:37 UTC
22:37:37 KST

Burhan Sansarlioglu and Emir Yildirim
13 October 2026•Update: 13 October 2026
Wheat prices plummeted by 12.7% in September to $6.75 per bushel, the sharpest monthly decline since June 2024, after reaching an intramonth peak of $7.95, as a potential peace deal between Russia and Ukraine, favorable weather conditions, and declining demand came to the fore.
Climate and geopolitical developments influenced wheat's supply and demand, but the commodity still ended the month around 35% above its initial value at the start of the year, having concluded January at the $5-a-bushel level.
Zafer Ergezen, a futures and commodity markets expert, told Anadolu that earlier price rallies were supported by supply risks affecting Black Sea grain exports, but recent market dynamics shifted downward as US-Russia relations developed positively.
“Along with the El Nino effect being weaker than expected, a short-term weakening of US wheat exports and concerns over a global economic growth slowdown are among the main drivers pulling wheat prices down,” he said.
With the prices of Russian and Ukrainian wheat falling, US wheat remained expensive relative to European wheat, decreasing demand for wheat produced in the US.
“American wheat was expensive due to the stronger dollar, driving up the dollar cost of wheat, which is among the factors that made European wheat more attractive,” he added.

In telephone conversations with European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen and NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte, Prime Minister Rumen Radev called for joint efforts to halt attacks on commercial vessels in the Black Sea, the press service of the Council of Ministers reported.
Both expressed their appreciation for Bulgaria’s swift response in rescuing the sailors in distress, as well as their solidarity with the country following the attacks on merchant vessels near its territorial waters. They also expressed their readiness to provide allied support in clarifying the circumstances surrounding the incidents. For his part, the prime minister once again called for assistance to strengthen Bulgaria’s maritime and airspace surveillance and monitoring capabilities.
European Council President António Costa also issued a statement expressing the European Council’s solidarity with Bulgaria following last night’s strikes. He added that Russia’s growing hybrid activities would be discussed at the upcoming EU meeting in Brussels.

Israel approves 15-storey UAE embassy complex near Tel Aviv
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
13:36:08 UTC
22:36:08 KST

Breadcrumb
Israel approves 15-storey UAE embassy complex near Tel Aviv
Israeli authorities have approved plans to build a permanent 15-storey embassy complex for the United Arab Emirates in Herzliya, near Tel Aviv, amid reports of recent tensions between the two countries.
The project, approved on Tuesday by the Tel Aviv District Planning and Building Committee, will include diplomatic offices and accommodation for the Emirati ambassador and embassy staff, according to Israeli real estate publication Magdilim.
The approval comes nearly a year after the plans were first submitted in October 2025, with Israeli authorities describing the development as a step towards strengthening diplomatic relations with Abu Dhabi.
The new embassy will be built at 9 Sapir Street in the commercial district of Herzliya Pituach, on a plot measuring approximately 2,500 square metres.
The project will have a maximum of 15 floors, with a total permitted construction area of 15,000 square metres.
Under the approved plans, up to 20% of the permitted floor space will be allocated to residential accommodation for the Emirati ambassador and diplomatic personnel, located on the upper floors.
The development will also include a separate entrance to an underground car park, an expanded access road and improvements to surrounding public facilities and pedestrian walkways.
According to Israeli media reports, the land is currently owned by Herzliya municipality, with arrangements underway to transfer ownership to the Israeli state through coordination with the Israel Land Authority before leasing it to the UAE.
In exchange, the municipality will receive another plot of land in Herzliya's marina district as part of a land-swap agreement.
Erez Ben Eliezer, the Tel Aviv district planner at Israel's Planning Administration, described the project as significant for both the city and Israel, saying it would strengthen international relations and pave the way for future cooperation.
He said the embassy's location near international companies and advanced technology firms would make it a prominent landmark in Herzliya's commercial district.
The UAE embassy currently operates from temporary offices in Tel Aviv and Herzliya, with the new complex intended to become its permanent diplomatic headquarters.
No date has been announced for the start of construction or the building's opening.
Approval comes amid reported diplomatic tensions
The approval comes at a sensitive time in UAE-Israel relations, following reported disagreements over an attempted hijacking involving a Flydubai flight last month.
Israeli economic news website Ice linked the timing of the approval to recent tensions between Abu Dhabi and Tel Aviv following the incident, which saw a Flydubai aircraft make an emergency landing at Saudi Arabia's Tabuk airport in late September.
The website cited reports of disagreements between the two countries over their handling of the incident and its consequences for passenger travel.
The attempted hijacking took place on 30 September, when an Omani co-pilot allegedly tried to seize control of a Flydubai flight travelling from Dubai to Tel Aviv and crash it into Ben Gurion Airport.
Passengers and crew thwarted the attempt, and the aircraft landed safely in Saudi Arabia.
The embassy project comes six years after the UAE normalised relations with Israel in September 2020 under the US-brokered Abraham Accords.
The agreement led to the exchange of ambassadors, the opening of diplomatic missions and a series of economic and trade cooperation agreements between the two countries.

Ukraine Holds Fire on Russian Energy Sites for 48 Hours, but Moscow Keeps Targeting Ukraine’s Energy Grid
Unknown

2026-10-13
13:34:10 UTC
22:34:10 KST

- Category
- War in Ukraine
Ukraine Holds Fire on Russian Energy Sites for 48 Hours, but Moscow Keeps Targeting Ukraine’s Energy Grid
Ukraine has refrained from striking Russian oil refineries and other energy facilities for two consecutive days following US President Donald Trump’s announcement of an energy ceasefire, while Russia has continued attacking Ukrainian energy infrastructure, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said.
According to Zelenskyy on October 13, Ukraine has observed the proposed pause in energy-related strikes despite continued Russian attacks on civilian and critical infrastructure across the country.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
“Ukraine has not carried out strikes on Russian oil refineries or the energy sector in general for the two days since the American President announced an energy ceasefire. But Russia did not heed the American President,” Zelenskyy stated.
The Ukrainian president emphasized that Russian forces had continued targeting Ukraine’s energy facilities and other critical infrastructure during the same period, with attacks reported across 19 regions in just two days.
“During this time, the Russians have attacked both our energy facilities and our critical infrastructure, sending absolutely clear signals that they have no intention of refraining from strikes on Ukraine,” he said.
Zelenskyy reiterated that Ukraine remains prepared to take reciprocal steps toward de-escalation but stressed that international pressure on Moscow is necessary to secure meaningful progress.
The statement follows another wave of Russian attacks on Ukraine, during which Moscow deployed more than 100 weapons, including jet-powered drones, loitering munitions, and ballistic missiles, from the previous evening into the following day.
Kyiv also came under a ballistic missile attack, with five missiles striking civilian infrastructure, according to the Ukrainian president.
Zelenskyy expressed concern that Ukraine had received no advance warning from its international partners about the missile launches, emphasizing the importance of timely intelligence sharing in protecting civilians.
The Ukrainian president stressed that advance notification of ballistic missile launches remains essential for reducing casualties and improving the effectiveness of civilian protection measures.
“Global pressure on Russia contributes to exactly that—bringing peace closer. But direct or indirect support for Russia, slowing down assistance to Ukraine, and making it harder to protect lives against ballistic missiles will certainly not help bring peace,” Zelenskyy said.
The latest wave of attacks also affected western Ukraine, where a Russian drone struck an educational institution in central Rivne, injuring at least 14 people. According to Oleksandr Koval, head of the Rivne Regional Military Administration, one person was seriously injured, while three others sustained injuries of moderate severity.
