On the universality of Gazan resistance: A century-long struggle for human rights
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
13:33:58 UTC
22:33:58 KST

The struggle of Gaza’s people is frequently interpreted through the competing languages of security, nationalism, religion and geopolitics. Each illuminates part of the conflict, yet each can obscure its most fundamental question: are Palestinians entitled to the rights every human being possesses simply by being human? Viewed through the history of human rights, Gazan resistance acquires a significance extending beyond one people or territory. It exposes the distance between humanity’s proclaimed commitment to universal dignity and its willingness to protect those whose rights are repeatedly denied.
The Universal Declaration of Human Rights, adopted in 1948, rejects hierarchies of human worth. Rights belong to people regardless of nationality, religion, political allegiance or recognition by a sovereign state. Palestinians therefore need no special justification for claiming life, liberty, education, property and security. Their entitlement precedes the political arrangements through which these rights should be protected.
Gazan resistance, understood as the broader struggle against dispossession and for individual and collective freedom, makes this principle concrete. It encompasses political mobilisation, civic action, cultural continuity and the work of sustaining society under destructive conditions. Its universal significance arises from the rights being defended and the insistence that Palestinians must be able to exercise them.
A Century of Dispossession and Resistance
Beginning this history on 7 October 2023 reduces an extended struggle over rights to the aftermath of one event. It obscures the experiences shaping successive Palestinian generations: dispossession, displacement, occupation and the frustration of political freedom.
The century-long dimension emerges from the imperial arrangements preceding Israel’s establishment. The 1917 Balfour Declaration supported a Jewish national home in Palestine while describing the existing non-Jewish population through safeguards for civil and religious rights. Incorporated into the British Mandate, this formulation recognised one population’s national aspirations without equivalent recognition of the other’s.
The violence surrounding Israel’s establishment transformed political exclusion into mass dispossession. The April 1948 attack on Deir Yassin by Irgun and Lehi became an enduring expression of Palestinian civilian vulnerability.
During the Nakba, approximately 750,000 Palestinians were uprooted. Gaza became a major refuge for people separated from their homes, livelihoods and communities.
The coincidence of the Nakba and the Universal Declaration in 1948 reveals a profound historical dissonance. As the international community articulated universal dignity, Palestinians lost essential conditions for exercising their rights. Their subsequent struggle has continually exposed the gap between recognition and protection.
Israel’s occupation of Gaza in 1967 added further layers of control. Its withdrawal of settlements and permanent ground forces in 2005 did not establish Palestinian sovereignty. The International Committee of the Red Cross continued to regard Gaza as occupied because Israel retained effective control over key dimensions of access and movement. The Israeli blockade imposed in 2007 further constrained economic and social life.
Recurring violence intensified these conditions. The United Nations recorded 2,251 Palestinian deaths during the 2014 hostilities, including 1,462 civilians. A UN commission investigating the 2018 Great March of Return found that Israeli forces killed 183 demonstrators with live ammunition. Gaza’s insecurity thus long preceded October 2023.
The three generations of human rights illuminate this experience. Civil and political rights protect against violence and arbitrary power; socioeconomic rights sustain dignified life; collective rights concern a people’s future. In Gaza, their interdependence is unavoidable.
READ: UN verifies 1,076 Palestinian deaths in Gaza since ceasefire, warns of possible war crimes
First-Generation Rights: Life, Liberty and Security
The right to life is fundamental. By October 2026, Gaza’s health authorities reported over 74,000 Palestinian deaths since October 2023, according to Reuters.
Genocide directly concerns this right.
In September 2025, the UN Independent International Commission of Inquiry on the Occupied Palestinian Territory, including East Jerusalem, and Israel concluded that Israel had committed genocide in Gaza.
It identified four genocidal acts, including killing, serious bodily or mental harm, destructive living conditions and measures intended to prevent births, alongside genocidal intent. Separately, in January 2024, the International Court of Justice ordered binding provisional measures requiring Israel to prevent acts prohibited by the Genocide Convention and enable urgently needed humanitarian assistance.
Liberty and security also require protection against arbitrary detention and torture. A July 2024 UN report documented detention without charge or trial and accounts of ill-treatment. Freedom of association likewise matters: UN experts condemned Israel’s 2021 designation of six Palestinian civil society organisations as terrorist organisations. These findings connect physical survival with safeguards against arbitrary power and the defence of dignity.
Property Rights: The Foundations of Freedom
Property connects individual protection to the history of dispossession. Article 17 of the Universal Declaration recognises ownership and prohibits arbitrary deprivation of property. A Palestinian home or agricultural plot also sustains family continuity, independence and attachment to place.
OCHA’s September 2025 humanitarian snapshot reported that 92 per cent of Gaza’s housing units were destroyed or damaged. Such devastation simultaneously removes shelter, accumulated savings and the physical foundations of community life. Rebuilding therefore concerns the restoration of social continuity as well as material assets.
Settlement policies elsewhere in the occupied Palestinian territory reveal a related connection between property and political exclusion. In its July 2024 advisory opinion, the International Court of Justice found Israel’s continued presence unlawful and identified obligations concerning settlement cessation, evacuation and reparation. Its findings connected Israeli policies to the denial of Palestinian self-determination.
Property links individual rights to collective freedom: people cannot meaningfully control their future while repeatedly losing the material foundations of their existence.
Second-Generation Rights: Education, Health and Livelihoods
Economic and social rights deepen this understanding. People may survive bombardment while losing everything needed for a viable future. Education, healthcare, food and employment give dignity practical substance. Their destruction produces injuries that outlast immediate violence.
In August 2025, famine was formally confirmed in Gaza Governorate. The joint announcement by UN agencies linked starvation to conflict, repeated displacement, severe restrictions on humanitarian access and the collapse of essential systems. Hunger thus exposes how the destruction of social infrastructure can threaten life as directly as armed violence.
Healthcare illustrates the same interdependence. In September 2026, OCHA documented shortages of cancer medicines, dialysis supplies and insulin, linking disruption to underfunding and obstacles to the entry of available medicines. Interrupted treatment can cause irreversible harm even after supplies resume.
Education reveals the consequences across generations. A November 2025 assessment presented by UNESCO found that 95 per cent of Gaza’s higher education campuses were damaged or destroyed, with 22 of 38 completely destroyed. OCHA reported approximately 200,000 children without structured learning in September 2026. These losses threaten the knowledge and professional capacity essential to future recovery.
Yet the defence of education continues.
UNESCO reported providing temporary learning spaces for 10,000 university students. Such efforts embody resistance through the preservation of learning: students and educators sustain capacities on which rebuilding their society depends.
Livelihoods connect these examples. UNRWA has documented how restrictions on fishing constrain families’ incomes. Under blockade, access to the sea becomes a question of economic survival. Restoring rights therefore requires opportunities to work and produce alongside emergency assistance.
Humanitarian relief is indispensable, but a durable response must restore the ability to sustain an independent life. Otherwise, assistance risks becoming the permanent means of supporting people whose freedom remains unresolved.
OPINION: Gaza’s displaced face a deadly choice: collapsing buildings or flooded tents
Third-Generation Rights: Self-Determination and Cultural Continuity
Self-determination brings these dimensions together. Frequently discussed alongside collective or third-generation rights, it is expressly recognised in the common first article of the two principal international human-rights covenants. It encompasses peoples’ ability to determine their political status, pursue development and control their natural wealth and resources.
For Palestinians, this reaches into daily life. Who determines access to land and water? Who decides whether people can move, rebuild or establish economic connections? Self-determination concerns the capacity to influence these conditions instead of remaining permanently subject to decisions made elsewhere.
Restrictions on fishing demonstrate how collective and socioeconomic rights overlap. Access to natural resources supports livelihoods, food security and development. Control over those resources therefore affects both individual welfare and a people’s capacity to shape its future.
Cultural continuity belongs within the same struggle. By 24 March 2026, UNESCO had verified damage to 164 cultural sites in Gaza, including religious buildings, monuments, museums and archaeological sites. These losses affect the places through which communities locate themselves in history and transmit belonging. They diminish Palestinian collective life and humanity’s shared inheritance.
Maintaining family records, preserving cultural knowledge and documenting violations consequently carry political significance. These practices defend claims that displacement and impunity might erase. They assert that Palestinians possess a history and the authority to help determine their future.
Gaza and the Universal History of Emancipation
The significance of this assertion becomes clearer within the broader history of emancipation. The American struggle for independence advanced government by consent. The French Revolution gave enduring force to liberty and equality. South Africa’s anti-apartheid movement challenged institutionalised racial inequality. Their importance lies partly in how particular struggles expanded the reach of principles presented as universal.
These histories also expose a persistent tension. Movements and states can proclaim universal rights while excluding people from their enjoyment. Progress depends on those excluded demanding that the principles apply to them. Universality gains practical meaning through resistance to the claim that some people must indefinitely await protection.
Gazan resistance belongs within this history through its assertion of rights whose validity extends to everyone. National character and universal significance are compatible: Palestinians seek to exercise freedoms that cannot coherently be reserved for others. Their struggle demands that human rights apply even when protection challenges powerful interests.
This places responsibility on institutions and governments invoking universal principles. Recognising Palestinian suffering must translate into protection, accountability and the restoration of conditions necessary for freedom. Palestinian voices and choices must inform reconstruction and political arrangements; treating people solely as aid recipients overlooks their agency.
If protection depends on geopolitical importance or diplomatic alliances, rights become privileges distributed through political favour. Defending Palestinian rights therefore also defends the equal application of standards that governments claim to accept as universal.
Gaza therefore tests whether human dignity generates obligations when fulfilling them carries political costs. Sympathy alone cannot resolve that question. Universal rights acquire credibility through consistent protection, especially where power makes their enforcement difficult and inconvenient.
The rights Palestinians defend emerge from their particular history, but their validity does not stop at Palestine’s borders. Life, liberty, a home, education, healthcare and the freedom to shape a collective future belong to the common substance of human dignity.
The universality of Gazan resistance lies in its insistence that Palestinians must be able to exercise the rights humanity has already declared to be universal.

Formula 1 returning to Africa after decades
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
13:32:58 UTC
22:32:58 KST

Formula 1 returning to Africa after decades
Formula 1 will return to Africa for the first time in more than three decades after signing a 10-year agreement to host a Grand Prix in Rwanda, the racing championship announced on Tuesday.
The first race is expected to take place in the early 2030s, once a new circuit has been completed. The purpose-built track will be located in Bugesera, around 40 km south of the capital, Kigali, near the new international airport. Developed under the Rwanda Development Board, the circuit will meet the FIA’s safety and technical standards.
South Africa hosted Formula 1 races from 1962 to 1985. The championship returned to the country for two more races in 1992 and 1993. Morocco is the only other African country to have hosted a Formula 1 World Championship race, held in Casablanca in 1958.
The championship estimates that it now has more than 100 million fans across the continent, with nearly 60% of followers in key sub-Saharan African markets under the age of 35.
“Today belongs to Africa. For more than three decades, the world’s premier motorsport championship has raced without this continent, and that changes with this agreement,” Rwandan President Paul Kagame said.
FIA President Mohammed Ben Sulayem described the return as “a historic moment” for the sport and “an important step in the continued global growth of motorsport.”
Formula 1 CEO Stefano Domenicali said Rwanda’s inclusion will bring the championship to every inhabited continent. The date of the inaugural Grand Prix has yet to be announced.
Africa already hosts major motorsport competitions, including Kenya’s Safari Rally, part of the World Rally Championship, and the African Rally Championship, which features events in Rwanda, Uganda, and Tanzania. The continent was also home to the Dakar Rally before the event moved to South America in 2009 and has been held in Saudi Arabia since 2020.
Other major sporting events are also coming to Africa. Kenya will become the first African country to host the World Athletics Championships in 2029, Morocco will co-host the 2030 FIFA World Cup, and Senegal will stage the 2026 Youth Olympic Games – the first Olympic event on the continent.

France's national Anti Terrorism Prosecutor’s Office (PNAT) has taken over the investigation into the Aubagne school shooting after initial findings suggested a possible link between the 14-year-old suspect and the “True Crime Community” movement, Franceinfo reported.
The suspect is accused of firing several shots at his middle school on Monday, injuring the principal and a teacher.
Initial investigations, including an examination of the minor’s digital devices, point to “probable adherence to the True Crime Community (TCC) movement, as well as the framing of the criminal act carried out at his school within this ideology,” said the PNAT.
The Marseille prosecutor’s office initially opened an investigation into attempted murder following the shooting at the Joseph Lakanal middle school.
The student fired once or twice in a common area on the first floor shortly after 9 am local time (0700GMT), injuring the principal and a teacher who were in the corridor, according to Marseille prosecutor Nicolas Bessone.
Both victims were hit in the lower limbs and taken to hospital.
Their injuries were not life-threatening, according to media reports.
The student then went to the second floor and fired twice more, including once inside an occupied classroom, where the shot hit the blackboard. No students were injured, said Aubagne Mayor Jean-Pierre Squillari.
A suspect student was arrested on suspicion of carrying out the shooting.
French President Emmanuel Macron expressed solidarity with the injured principal and teacher, as well as with students and parents left in shock, praising the school staff’s response.
The shooting was reported to be unrelated to student protests taking place elsewhere in France.

NASA&apos;s Perseverance rover breaks record for off-world driving distance
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
16:32:37 EEST
22:32:37 KST

NASA's Perseverance rover breaks record for off-world driving distance
Kyiv • UNN
NASA's Perseverance rover covered 45.22 km on Mars, surpassing Opportunity's record. It drove more than 90% of the route autonomously.
NASA’s Perseverance rover has broken the record for the distance traveled among all vehicles on another planet, the U.S. space agency reported. UNN writes about this with reference to Engadget.
Details
The six-wheeled buggy with a nuclear-powered engine had covered 45.22 km by October 11, surpassing NASA’s Opportunity rover, which traveled 45.16 km across the surface of the Red Planet. Perseverance covered this distance in just five and a half years, while Opportunity took nearly 15 years.
Although the 45.22 km it has covered to date may not seem like a particularly great distance, it is quite impressive considering that the vehicle’s maximum speed is only 0.16 km/h. It is also impressive given the difficult terrain it had to navigate, as NASA showed in a video.
The 1,025-kg rover reached this milestone after heading into a region called Idube to study an object called "Lac de Charm" (Lake Charm), featuring one of the oldest landscapes ever explored in our Solar System. "The rocks and terrain of Lac de Charm are so ancient that their terrestrial analogues were eroded away long ago by erosion and plate tectonics (there are no tectonic plates on Mars), and it is in Idube that the science team hopes to find traces of ancient hydrothermal systems," NASA explained.
Perseverance’s longevity is partly explained by the thoughtful navigation decisions made by its AutoNav autonomous system. Using it, the rover can capture images of the terrain and detect hazards in real time, automatically moving between waypoints selected by mission planners. Processing 600,000 measurement points with each view, it has been able to cover more than 90 percent of its total distance autonomously.
Thanks to a recent software update, Perseverance can now lean more and turn less to reduce wear on its components, while simultaneously checking its position against orbital maps as it moves. Next, the team wants to overcome problems with glare from sunlight that obstructs the camera’s view, so that the rover can operate for longer.
Perseverance may have surpassed Opportunity, but the Curiosity rover is also still exploring Mars and has covered 38.15 km to date. Next in terms of distance traveled among U.S. spacecraft are the crewed rovers from the Apollo 16, 17, and 18 missions—with the Apollo 17 rover having covered the greatest distance, 35.74 km.

French school shooting suspect linked to online group that glorifies mass killers
A 14-year-old pupil suspected of shooting and wounding a headmaster and teacher near Marseille may have been involved in an online network associated with the glorification of mass killers known as the True Crime Community, prompting France’s anti-terror prosecutor to take over the case.
The French anti-terrorism prosecutor has taken over an investigation into a school shooting after an initial probe found the 14-year-old suspect appeared to belong to a group called the True Crime Community.
A pupil at a school near the southern city of Marseille shot and wounded two teachers on Monday with a hunting rifle that had been hidden in a guitar case, causing panic as children ran for cover, officials said.
Read moreTeen wounds headmaster and teacher after opening fire at French school
The anti-terrorism prosecutor’s office said on Tuesday the Marseille Prosecutor’s Office had decided to relinquish jurisdiction for the case.
“Initial investigations, including an analysis of the minor’s digital devices, indicate probable affiliation with the True Crime Community (TCC) movement and suggest that the criminal act committed at his school was motivated by this ideology,” the prosecutor said in a statement on Tuesday.
“The TCC is an ecosystem of online communities that glorifies perpetrators of mass killings and, in certain ways, incites the use of extreme violence,” it added.
It said it had opened investigations into charges of “attempted murder in connection with a terrorist enterprise, participation in a terrorist criminal conspiracy with the intent to commit crimes against persons, and violations of weapons laws in connection with a terrorist enterprise.”

The ‘Godzilla Minus Zero’ Filmmakers Terrified Bystanders With Their Monster Sounds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
13:30:00 UTC
22:30:00 KST

Actor Seth Green—yes, that one—has seen Godzilla Minus Zero and says it’s awesome.
While introducing the New York Comic Con panel for the 39th film in the Godzilla franchise, Green stressed that the filmmakers behind the movie “have created kaiju that feel physically real and, trust me, emotionally terrifying.”
While a lot of that terror came from the work of Oscar-winning visual effects artist Tatsuji Nojima, some it came from the shrieking of Godzilla and his three-headed nemesis, King Ghidorah. Those roars were the work of sound designer Natsuko Inoue and her team, who created the monsters’ outsize vocalizations by rolling speakers to the top of an outdoor dam—much to the horror of people nearby.
“There were people having a picnic, maybe people just taking a stroll,” Hisafumi Takeuchi, who also worked on sound for the film, said during the panel. “The person walking their dog, though—they had the worst time, because the dog was freaking out and barking back at us.”
Since the creatures are imaginary, getting their screams to sound realistic is essential to making them seem believable—and genuinely scary—onscreen. At first, Inoue wasn’t sure if the idea of recording at the dam would work. Those fears were quickly put to rest.
“The first time we sent that roar out on the speakers, I could see the relief and confidence in everyone's eyes,” Inoue said. “By using speakers and projecting it into the real world, capturing the reverb, the echo, the reflection of the sound back with the mic, it manifests it in our world.”
For other kaiju sound effects, Inoue’s team took an analog foley approach. To simulate Ghidorah’s dragon-like wings, for example, they flapped a rubber fisherman’s suit and mixed that noise with the sounds of an accordion-like air duct.
Getting two of Toho’s most famous monsters right was a huge undertaking, especially after the success of Zero’s predecessor, Godzilla Minus One, which brought home $114 million worldwide at the box office. Following that 2023 film’s harrowing mix of post–World War II malaise and bracing kaiju destruction will be tough, but a new trailer shown during the film’s panel at NYCC promised a sequel full of aerial dogfights and a punch-’em-up for the ages between Godzilla and Ghidorah.
Like the previous film, Godzilla Minus Zero is directed by Takashi Yamazaki and features visual effects from Tatsuji Nojima, whom Green called “the first Gen Z Oscar-winner” for his work on One.
Nojima began doing visual effects as a hobby while he was still a teenager before joining animation house Shirogumi as a compositor. After Yamazaki noticed a crude animation of waves that Nojima was working on, the director tasked the budding animator with developing the idea. Nojima turned around a fully rendered shot of ocean water over rocks that looked indistinguishable from reality. After that, Nojima recalled, Yamazaki said, “OK, I think you’re ready to animate and do VFX for Godzilla now.”
During the panel, Nojima broke down how he created a shot from the trailer showing Godzilla bursting out of the ocean while chasing a seaplane. “I simulated 200 million particles to get the whitewater effect correct in Godzilla Minus One,” he said. “With this shot in Godzilla Minus Zero, the scale is absolutely different with the new Imax aspect ratio, plus there was no live-action plate, so we're dealing with a lot of CG on screen. We required 2 billion particles.”
Godzilla Minus Zero is set to hit US theaters on November 6 and Japanese theaters on November 3, which has become known as Godzilla’s birthday since it marks the date in 1954 that Ishirō Honda’s original film was released in Japan.

Kyiv Calls WP’s 4-Point Peace Plan ‘American PR’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
13:29:56 UTC
22:29:56 KST

Ukraine has rejected the characterization of a reported four-point peace proposal as a joint US-European plan, saying the ideas reflect the position of only part of the American administration’s negotiating team.
Dmytro Lytvyn, communications advisor to Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, responded on Tuesday, Oct. 13, to an opinion column in The Washington Post by columnist David Ignatius.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“It is not ‘the US and European countries,’” Lytvyn told journalists.
“This is an outline of the vision of some members of the US team at the meeting in Florida, which was attended by Americans, Ukrainians and Europeans. Good PR by the Americans,” he added.
Lytvyn did not say that Ukraine had accepted or formally rejected the individual proposals outlined in the column.
What The Washington Post described
Citing an unnamed US official familiar with the negotiations, Ignatius wrote that American officials were attempting to develop a broad package offering postwar economic and security benefits to both Ukraine and Russia in exchange for territorial compromises.
“We need to make the problem and the solution bigger to help both sides see what the postwar situation would be – and then make concessions,” the official said.
The ideas were discussed during a six-hour meeting in Florida on Friday, Oct. 9, hosted by Trump’s presidential envoys, son-in-law Jared Kushner and personal friend and golf partner Steve Witkoff.
US Intelligence Still Flows to Ukraine, Sybiha Says
The talks included Ukrainian officials and representatives of the UK, France and Germany. The meeting was held at the Shell Bay Golf Club in Hallandale Beach, a development personally owned by Witkoff.
The newspaper described four proposed components.
Reconstruction funding for Ukraine
The first component would establish a framework for financing Ukraine’s postwar reconstruction, reportedly involving the World Bank and investment company BlackRock.
The funds would be used to rebuild destroyed regions, restore the Ukrainian economy and support the families of soldiers who were killed or wounded.
According to the US official cited by the newspaper, negotiators asked Kyiv to provide detailed estimates of its financial needs and assurances that reconstruction funds would be protected from corruption and postwar profiteering.
The column said Ukraine had not yet supplied the requested figures but was expected to do so within days if the negotiations continued.
Article 5-style security guarantees
The second component would provide Ukraine with security commitments from the US and European countries.
The unnamed official described the proposed guarantees as equivalent to NATO’s Article 5 collective-defense clause, with Western countries pledging to respond militarily if Russia attacked Ukraine again.
Russia would separately negotiate agreements with European states addressing its claimed security concerns. The column did not explain what concessions or restrictions those agreements could involve.
Russian energy returns to Europe
The third component would seek to integrate the Ukrainian, Russian and European economies through an energy agreement.
One option reportedly discussed was a pipeline carrying Russian oil and gas to Europe, with Ukraine and Russia sharing the profits.
Such an arrangement would provide Moscow with long-term access to the European energy market while potentially lowering energy prices in Europe, according to the White House official.
The proposed agreement would also establish conditions and a timetable for lifting existing economic sanctions against Russia.
No details were provided about which pipeline might be used, who would operate it or how revenues would be divided.
Ceasefire along the current front line
The fourth and most politically difficult component would involve a ceasefire along the existing front line, described by negotiators as the “line of control.”
Russia would abandon its original objective of conquering all of Ukraine but retain control of the Ukrainian territory it occupies when the ceasefire begins, including parts of the Donbas.
For Ukraine, this would mean tolerating continued Russian control without necessarily granting legal recognition to Moscow’s annexation claims.
The column noted that establishing such a line would be complicated by daily battlefield movements.
White House pressure over Russian refineries
The discussion also covered Ukrainian attacks on Russian oil refineries, although this was not presented as one of the plan’s four components.
Kushner and Witkoff reportedly asked Ukraine to halt those attacks and warned Kyiv that Trump intended to conclude his diesel arrangement with Russia.
The Trump administration had previously pressed the Ukrainian delegation to stop striking Russian refineries, arguing that the attacks were contributing to higher fuel prices.
Zelensky later proposed a reciprocal “diesel deal” under which Ukraine would stop targeting Russian energy infrastructure if the US guaranteed protection for Ukraine’s electricity system.
The four-point proposal has not been published as an official document, approved by the participating governments or presented as an agreement accepted by Russia.

The European Commission president has urged EU leaders to adopt tougher measures against irregular migration, including an emergency response framework and expanded powers for the bloc’s border agency, Politico reported Tuesday.
In a letter to the leaders of all 27 member states ahead of this week’s European Council summit in Brussels, Ursula von der Leyen called for measures to respond when migration is used as a tool to destabilize the bloc.
“We must prevent such threats and make clear that we will never compromise the protection of our external borders: no state or non-state actor will be allowed to exploit our rules or our values to destabilise the Union,” she wrote.
Her proposals include establishing an emergency response framework for cases in which migration has been weaponized, expanding the powers of European Border and Coast Guard Agency Frontex, and boosting the EU’s deportation rate.
The letter follows a migration crisis in Spain’s North African exclave of Ceuta over the summer, when around 70,000 migrants arrived from Morocco, according to the report.
Von der Leyen’s letter will inform discussions on migration scheduled for Friday, day two of the summit.

'Absence from draft SIR doesn't mean deletion': EC to Bombay HC
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
13:28:59 UTC
22:28:59 KST

The Election Commission of India clarified that missing names from the draft electoral roll during the Special Intensive Revision do not imply their deletion.
The Election Commission of India (ECI) on Tuesday told the Bombay high court that a voter's name missing from the draft electoral roll prepared during the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) does not automatically imply deletion. The court reserved its judgment on a writ petition filed by a Goa resident.Senior Advocate Ashutosh Kumbhakoni, appearing for the ECI, told the Goa bench that the SIR involves preparing the electoral roll afresh, unlike a Special Summary Revision (SSR), which focuses on updating an existing list.The bench, comprising Justices Valmiki Menezes and Amit Jamsandekar, reserved its verdict after hearing arguments in the matter. The hearing took place amid an ongoing controversy over the SIR exercise and the functioning of the ECI.Paresh Salgaonkar and five members of his family, who live in the St Cruz constituency of North Goa district, had approached the court alleging that their names were removed from the electoral roll during the revision process.
ECI clarifies the nature of the SIR exercise
Kumbhakoni submitted that an SIR is a comprehensive, de novo exercise in which the electoral roll is prepared from scratch.
In contrast, a summary revision updates the existing electoral roll on the basis of information received through the prescribed procedure.“Absence from the draft SIR roll does not automatically amount to deletion,” the ECI lawyer said, maintaining that a name missing from a draft list being prepared afresh could not technically be described as deleted.The lawyer further argued that the petitioner had allegedly not lived at the address recorded in the electoral rolls before the SIR for eight to 10 years. He also contended that the petitioner had not applied for an address change before the revision exercise began.“In fact, my lord, this is a classical case which shows the effectiveness of SIR,” Kumbhakoni told the court.According to the news agency PTI, the judges observed that they had made it clear from the outset that the petition did not challenge the SIR process itself.
Petitioner’s lawyer recounts timeline of events
Advocate Vivek Rodrigues, representing the petitioner, detailed the events surrounding the enumeration exercise and the subsequent absence of the petitioner's name from the draft electoral roll.Rodrigues said the enumeration process began on November 4, 2025. The Booth Level Officer (BLO) visited both the petitioner's former and current addresses on November 8.On November 12, the petitioner contacted the BLO to request an enumeration form. However, the officer declined, saying the form had to be delivered to the address listed in the electoral roll, which was the petitioner's previous residence.The petitioner later submitted Form 8 to seek a change of address. The ECI acknowledged receipt of the application on December 8, 2025. However, the petitioner's name was absent when the draft electoral roll was published on December 16, Rodrigues told the court.The BLO subsequently informed the petitioner that the Form 8 application was still being processed and had not been rejected.
Rodrigues said the petitioner received a letter from the ECI on January 17, 2026, informing him that his address-change application had been forwarded to the Electoral Registration Officer (ERO).The final date for submitting objections to the draft electoral roll was January 19. However, the petitioner's application was rejected on January 21, after the deadline had passed.“On January 21, my application is rejected. So I am neither in the boat nor in the canoe, left in the sea,” Rodrigues argued before the bench.

Ex-Congolese president launches rebel front
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
13:28:44 UTC
22:28:44 KST

Ex-Congolese president launches rebel front
Former Democratic Republic of the Congo (DR Congo) President Joseph Kabila has launched a political and military front with rebel leaders, including those of M23, which has captured large parts of the country’s east in its war against the government.
The Front for the Refoundation of the Nation (FRN) was announced on Monday at Kabila’s residence in Goma, the rebel-held capital of North Kivu province. Coalition adviser Claude Ibalanky said it would unite resistance forces to end what it calls “tyranny” through “any means necessary, including the use of force.”
The FRN replaces the Congo River Alliance (AFC), according to the declaration. Kabila heads it, with AFC leader Corneille Nangaa and M23 political chief Bertrand Bisimwa as vice presidents. M23 military commander Sultani Makenga will lead its armed forces.
On Friday, Kabila accused President Felix Tshisekedi’s government of corruption, poor governance, and military failures, and criticized its critical minerals agreement with the US.
Kabila took office in 2001 following the assassination of his father, President Laurent-Desire Kabila, and governed until Tshisekedi succeeded him in 2019. The 55-year-old returned to rebel-held Goma last year after living abroad, mostly in South Africa, since late 2023.
On September 30 last year, the High Military Court sentenced him to death in absentia for treason, war crimes, and crimes against humanity over alleged support for M23. The verdict came about five months after Kinshasa suspended his party’s activities and ordered his assets seized. He denied the charges and called the proceedings politically motivated.
Washington imposed sanctions on him in April, accusing him of financing the AFC and encouraging Congolese troops to defect.
Eastern DR Congo has endured more than three decades of conflict, with dozens of armed groups competing for territory and mineral wealth. The AFC/M23 rebel coalition captured Goma and Bukavu during an offensive in early 2025. DR Congo, UN experts, and Western governments accuse Rwanda of backing it, which Kigali denies. The violence has killed thousands and deepened a humanitarian crisis, with 18.5 million people needing assistance this year, according to UN agencies.
Fighting has continued despite a US-brokered peace accord with Rwanda and Qatar-mediated talks with the rebels. Congolese news outlet Actualite.cd reported renewed clashes between AFC/M23 and pro-government Wazalendo militias near Bukavu on Sunday and Monday, with at least one child wounded by gunfire and residents fleeing.

Oli London on October 7: 'If you are silent, you are complicit'
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
13:28:24 UTC
22:28:24 KST

Oli London, the British author of Gender Madness and a news commentator with a large following on Twitter/X, says the events of October 7 left him no choice but to speak out.
In an interview with The Jerusalem Post during his eighth visit to Israel in three years, London said he watched footage of the Hamas massacre as it emerged in real time, describing it as "the worst thing I've ever witnessed." He said he was equally troubled by the speed with which pro-Palestinian demonstrations appeared in London and other Western cities, which he alleged were organized and funded in advance, noting that protesters were waving flags and placards before Israel had launched any military response.
London argued that much of the hostility toward Israel is "nothing to do really with Palestine or Israel," but rather reflects a resurgent antisemitism that has entered the mainstream. Drawing comparisons with 1930s Germany, he warned that those who remain silent as Jews are attacked in Europe "are complicit."
London's switch to Christianity
London, who became a Christian four years ago, linked his support for Israel to a broader personal transformation. He told the Post that during the COVID-19 pandemic he spent much of his time on TikTok, where, he said, changing one's gender identity was presented as trendy and met with widespread praise. As someone who had long felt like an outsider, he said that affirmation was powerful, but it did not make him happy. He described turning to church, and later to faith, as a turning point that reversed nearly all of his earlier views.
That experience, he said, helps him understand why young people, including members of the LGBTQ community, have embraced the pro-Palestinian cause, which he attributed to a desire for acceptance rather than conviction. He pointed out that Tel Aviv hosts the only Pride celebration in the Middle East and questioned why activists are largely silent on anti-gay laws in Uganda and executions in Iran.
London said his advocacy has come at a price, including lost relationships, the loss of fashion brand partnerships, and accusations online that he is a paid propagandist, particularly after he became one of the first influencers to visit the Gaza border communities in the weeks after the attack. To critics who point to his past, he responded that "everyone has the ability to change."
London was also sharply critical of Western media, accusing outlets including the BBC and Sky News of chasing clicks with misleading coverage of the Israel-Hamas war, and urged young people to compare multiple sources and, where possible, visit a place before forming an opinion. He described the United Nations as "morally bankrupt," faulting it for its treatment of Israel while, in his view, neglecting the plight of women in Afghanistan, persecuted Christians in Nigeria, and victims of the regime in Iran.
He also weighed in on Ed Sheeran's recent effort to address both sides of the conflict, saying public figures should "never try to appease the mob." London spoke during a visit to Israel with a summit of some 1,000 Christian pastors, which included prayer at the Garden Tomb, a visit to the Church of the Holy Sepulchre and a boat trip on the Sea of Galilee, an experience he said left his faith "strengthened tenfold." His message to Israelis, he said, is that they are not alone: "The internet is not the real world."

Most recently, a 19-year-old resident of the northern Israeli village of Shibli was indicted for membership in a terrorist organization on September 7.
Investigators alleged that the 19-year-old had expressed support for ISIS, watched material about the terrorist organization, and pledged allegiance to it.

The Warsaw Security Forum is dangerously deluded
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
13:28:23 UTC
22:28:23 KST

The Warsaw Security Forum is dangerously deluded
The Warsaw Security Forum has long been a soapbox for Eastern Europe’s most belligerent elites to air their fantasies of inflicting a military defeat upon Russia. This year, with nuclear weapons on the table, the forum has taken on a dangerous new dimension.
Running from Monday to Tuesday in the Polish capital, this year’s WSF takes place at a critical juncture for Europe. With Vladimir Zelensky’s Ukraine taking nightly punishment from Russian missiles and drones, his British and EU backers have spent months ramping up their war rhetoric, in a seemingly coordinated attempt to telegraph their intent to join the conflict.
The UK’s Labour and Conservative parties have spoken of the need to prepare for a high-casualty war on the continent; Germany’s foreign intelligence chief has warned that the country “is in danger of becoming embroiled in a violent conflict with Russia;” France has fired a nuclear-capable ballistic missile in a demonstration that President Emmanuel Macron described as an explicit “message” to Moscow. Meanwhile, politicians and military brass in multiple countries have accused Russia of waging an invisible – and unprovable – “hybrid war” against the West.
Amid this gyre of escalation, the WSF should serve as a stage for Eastern Europe’s political leaders and military strategists to share their rational assessments of the situation. However, realpolitik is not on the agenda in Warsaw.
Warsaw’s demands
Several weeks before the forum kicked off on Monday, the WSF’s annual report offered a preview of what was in store. The 87-page report focuses almost entirely on the Russia/Ukraine conflict, and argues that Poland plus the so-called Nordic-Baltic Eight should set the terms for an eventual peace between Moscow and Kiev.
Their demands read like terms of surrender. Russia, they argue, should be subjected to permanent sanctions; dialogue with Russia may not be allowed to “evolve into political normalization;” Russia must be forced to pay reparations to Ukraine; Russian assets must be seized to finance Ukraine’s bid for EU membership; and Ukraine must be offered NATO and EU membership as a prerequisite to a peace deal.
That these demands are identical to Kiev’s own maximalist goals is not a coincidence. The report was authored by WSF Chair Katarzyna Pisarska, founder of the International Center for Ukrainian Victory (ICUV). The ICUV, which advocates for the breakup and Balkanization of Russia and the imposition of a “war tax” on European citizens, is funded by the EU, George Soros’ Open Society Foundations, and – prior to the election of US President Donald Trump – by the US State Department and USAID.
Among the report’s contributors are anti-Russia hardliners like former Lithuanian Foreign Minister Gabrielius Landsbergis, former Estonian President Toomas Hendrik Ilves, and Estonian Foreign Minister Margus Tsahkna. The latter claimed last week that NATO possesses the ability to close the Baltic Sea “within hours,” strangling Russia’s economic “lifeline” and creating an “existential” crisis for the country.
The Kaliningrad gambit
The report goes far beyond Ukraine’s immediate wartime demands. NATO, it recommends, should treat sustained “hybrid attacks” as “an Article 5 contingency,” even “if no single incident” justifies activating the bloc’s common-defense clause. After arguing that invisible – and often nonexistent – attacks should constitute grounds for war between nuclear powers, the report then makes its single most escalatory statement:
Any peace deal, it argues, should include “the demilitarization of Kaliningrad,” a Russian exclave that the report describes as “a hostage within range” of European missiles.
NATO forces have held three separate military exercises on the borders of Kaliningrad this year. Last month, Polish Foreign Minister Radoslaw Sikorski suggested that NATO “exercise so aggressively” on the borders of the exclave, to keep Moscow “uncertain of what we will do.”
The consequences of miscalculation or overreach by the West are huge. In a statement released by three of its embassies this month, Moscow’s Foreign Ministry warned that Russia is “ready to use all its arsenal, including nuclear weapons, to defend its territory if NATO countries try to isolate Kaliningrad.”
Warsaw doubles down
Presenting his so-called ‘Theory of Victory’ at the WSF on Monday, NATO Supreme Allied Commander Europe General Alexus Grynkewich brushed off Moscow’s warning. Should Russia respond to an attack on Kaliningrad in any way, “we will stop the attack and deny them the ability to achieve their objectives, whatever those might be. We will, in short, ensure any attack, against any ally, proves utterly futile,” he said.
“This includes not just the attacking force itself, but anything and everything that supports, sustains, and controls that force,” he added, in a statement seemingly endorsing countervalue strikes on Russia.
Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk, who drew criticism for describing the Russia-Ukraine conflict as “our war” at last year’s WSF, said that Poland has already “prepared for various scenarios” involving open war with Russia. Portraying the Russia/Ukraine conflict as “a confrontation between good and evil,”Tusk called on “every patriot in Poland, in Europe” to commit more money, weapons, and support to Kiev.
Speaking on Tuesday, Lithuanian Prime Minister Mindaugas Sinkevicius called on Zelensky to “strike more data centers in Russia” – something that Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov noted last week cannot be done without “the drones and missiles that Britain and continental Europe supply to Ukraine.”
In short, there were no de-escalatory voices at Warsaw. The full list of speakers – described by the WSF as “brightest minds in defense and diplomacy” – includes:
- Ukrainian leader Vladimir Zelensky and five of his ministers
- Tusk and 17 senior Polish officials
- Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Store
- Lithuanian Prime Minister Mindaugas Sinkevicius
- Estonian Foreign Minister Margus Tsahkna
- German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul
- Anti-Kremlin activists Garry Kasparov and Vladimir Kara-Murza
- Russian oligarch and wanted criminal Mikhail Khodorkovsky
- Self-declared Belarusian leader Svetlana Tikhanovskaya
- Palantir, Anduril, Northrop Grumman, Lockheed Martin, and Raytheon executives
Washington’s ambassador to NATO, Matthew Whittaker, is the only senior US official attending the forum. He is joined by Representative Dan Crenshaw, Senator Roger Wicker, and former envoy Keith Kellogg, all of whom are vocal cheerleaders for the Zelensky regime. Reportedly branded an “idiot” by Trump over his public support for Zelensky, Kellogg was sacked by the US president in January.

Who is sponsoring this circus?
The Warsaw Security Forum may fill its panels exclusively with anti-Russia hardliners and publicly advocate for the “demilitarization” of Russian territory, but it does not take place on the West’s diplomatic fringes. The WSF is held in partnership with NATO, the Council of Europe, Soros’ Open Society Foundations, the Munich Security Conference, and 21 major defense companies, including the aforementioned Palantir, Anduril, and Northrop Grumman.
Every forum is the same
The WSF’s partnerships, with NATO in particular, confer legitimacy upon an organization openly threatening Russian territory, and tie the entire Western order to the hostile rhetoric of Poland and the Baltics – at a time when Moscow has given clear warnings of the consequences, should this rhetoric be followed by action.
However, while the WSF was once a clearing house for the most bellicose anti-Russia policies, the ideas aired in Warsaw are now common fodder on the security conference circuit. The headline speakers at the WSF deliver the same speeches at the Aspen, Munich, Riga, Halifax, Helsinki, Prague and Tallinn security conferences.
Zelensky has headlined Helsinki, Munich, and the World Economic Forum’s Davos conferences this year. Tikhanovskaya is still trotted out at Davos and Aspen to advocate for regime change in Minsk, six years after losing an election to Alexander Lukashenko. Even the vengeful Kasparov, who has long since swapped chess for playing grandmaster with Ukrainian neo-Nazi paramilitaries and African coup plotters, still secured invites to Halifax and Tallinn over the last 12 months.
All of these conferences have become anti-Russian slop factories, each indistinguishable from the last, serving attendees the same blend of panic, hostility, and fantasies of defeating the world’s largest nuclear power. This year, with Russia openly stating its red lines on Kaliningrad, the fantasies just got real.

Iranian matchmaking app removed by Google after allowing girls as young as 12 to register
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
13:28:05 UTC
22:28:05 KST

Major platforms have removed the Iranian matchmaking app “Adam and Eve” after an investigation found that girls as young as 12 could register, according to announcements from Google, Meta, and the US-based Human Rights Activists News Agency (HRANA).
Although the app has maintained that it is only available to adults over the age of 18, HRANA found in its investigative report, Child Marriage in the Digital Age, that children as young as 12 could register. The platform’s search system also allowed users to filter prospective spouses by age, including girls as young as 13.
The app has also publicly posted about the marriage of a 16-year-old bride to a 23-year-old man, who met through the platform.
The Jerusalem Post also accessed the app’s website and reviewed profiles advertising girls as young as 15 for marriage. However, a closer examination of one profile revealed that the girl was in eighth grade, indicating that she was likely 13 or 14. The profile also displayed a green notice, indicating parental approval.
Although Google and Meta confirmed this week that they would remove the app, Iranian digital rights organization Filterbaan had warned in July last year that "Adam and Eve," alongside several Telegram channels, was facilitating child marriages.
An investigation published by Filterbaan at the time found that nearly 17% of the profiles posted on Adam and Eve in the six months before the report’s publication belonged to individuals under the age of 18.
A whistleblower within the app’s administration also told Filterbaan that, beginning in July 2023, the app’s director, Hossein Asghari, had directly ordered that minors’ profiles be published and presented as part of an “Islamic marriage and an Islamic-Iranian lifestyle.”
The youngest child known to have married through the app at the time of Filterbaan’s investigation was just 11 years old.
Under Article 1041 of Iran’s Civil Code, the minimum marriage age is 13 for girls and 15 for boys. However, marriage below those ages is permitted with a guardian’s consent and “consideration of the child’s best interests, as determined by the competent court.”
“The exploitation of children is a horrific crime, and we work aggressively to fight it on and off our platforms,” a Meta spokesperson told HRANA. “We investigated the information provided by HRANA and identified external links to underage marriage services. We have removed these entities from Meta platforms.”
Google removed the app for 'violating policies'
Google separately told the organization that “the app was removed from Google Play on October 9 for violating our policies.”
Despite global efforts to combat child marriage, the practice remains widespread. UNICEF’s child marriage data portal reports that one in five young women worldwide married before their 18th birthday. Meanwhile, Iran’s Statistical Center recorded approximately 25,900 marriages involving girls under the age of 15 in 2022.
Licensed by the Iranian regime, "Adam and Eve" is part of a broader expansion of matchmaking services operating with government authorization. HRANA reported that Iran had only one licensed matchmaking platform in 2020, but that number had risen to more than 200 by early 2025.
Efforts to raise Iran’s minimum marriage age gained momentum throughout the 2010s, with proposals to set the minimum age at 16 for girls and 18 for boys and require court permission for marriages involving children over 13. However, government policy shifted in 2021, following Ebrahim Raisi’s appointment as president, toward enabling and encouraging child marriage.
The proposed Prohibition of Child Marriage Bill was subsequently removed from the government’s agenda, despite efforts by the then-vice president for Women and Family Affairs to secure its approval by the executive branch of the Islamic Republic.

UK government raises concerns over autonomous AI agents
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
13:27:51 UTC
22:27:51 KST

UK government raises concerns over autonomous AI agents
Britain will expand its use of artificial intelligence to protect government systems from cyberattacks and develop measures to respond to incidents involving autonomous AI agents, Qazinform News Agency reports.
According to the UK government, two pilot projects have already helped identify and fix more than 1,000 potential vulnerabilities in government IT systems. The program will now be expanded to strengthen the security of services people rely on every day.
The government will also consider strengthening the Cyber Security and Resilience Bill and the associated regulatory framework. The aim is to protect hospitals, utilities and other essential services from emerging risks, including situations in which autonomous AI systems evade human oversight.
Particular attention will be paid to AI agents capable of performing complex tasks with minimal human supervision. According to the government, serious incidents involving these systems could unfold faster and have a wider impact than the emergencies existing response mechanisms are designed to handle. The National Cyber Security Centre and the AI Security Institute are helping develop approaches to responding to such incidents.
AI Minister Kanishka Narayan said Britain should become one of the hardest countries in the world to attack using artificial intelligence. He also urged developers to take warnings from their own scientists seriously.
“Listen when your scientists warn of serious dangers. Investigate unexpected behaviour. And if you cannot adequately control the risks, do not release the system,” the minister said.
The government will also examine how to identify and report both serious incidents and near misses, using the lessons learned to reduce the risk of future harm.
Earlier, Qazinform News Agency reported that an OpenAI agent had bypassed restrictions and gained unauthorized access to Australia’s government-run Medicare statistics portal.

Hackers heat supermarket fridges across France in ‘unprecedented’ cyberattack (VIDEO)

Hackers corrupt supermarket fridges across France (VIDEO)
Hackers remotely overheated refrigerators at hundreds of supermarkets across France, destroying tons of fresh and frozen food, according to local media reports and industry executives. The massive cyberattack has left retailers facing millions of euros in losses, with some stores forced to close temporarily.
According to Le Monde, the attack struck overnight into Monday, affecting around 300 Intermarche and Netto stores, 100 Cooperative U outlets, 80 Carrefour supermarkets, 30 Monoprix locations, and several E.Leclerc stores, bringing the estimated total to more than 500.
Apart from supermarkets, the cyberattack affected wholesaler Metro, members of the French meat industry association Culture Viande, and independent butchers may also have been hit.
According to BFM-TV, hackers targeted refrigeration controllers supplied by Danish manufacturer Danfoss, which allow technicians to adjust temperatures remotely. The culprits activated automatic defrosting systems, forcing refrigeration units to heat up in some cases to 50C instead of keeping food cold.
🚨🇫🇷 HACKER seize CONTROL of SUPERMARKET refrigerators in France, HITTING 500 stores. Intermarché, Super U and Carrefour are affected, with the cold chain broken and tons of food destroyed. This is no accident, it's an artificial strike on the food supply chain! https://t.co/Slh8opyH1P
— Global Dissident (@GlobalDiss) October 13, 2026
As a result, supermarket employees arrived for work to discover overheated refrigeration units and shelves of food that could no longer be sold. In some cases, hackers extended the defrost cycle from one hour to eight hours so that alarms would go off later, allowing them to maximize the damage.
The exact scale of losses is unclear, but an Intermarche in Haguenau, eastern France, lost around €50,000 ($56,000) worth of frozen food. An E.Leclerc store in nearby Wasselonne had to discard fresh and frozen products valued at €220,000.
Cooperative U CEO Dominique Schelcher described the attack as unprecedented and unacceptable. Intermarche chief Thierry Cotillard estimated that nationwide losses could reach tens of millions of euros.
The attackers remain unidentified, and no ransom demand has been reported. The intrusion method also remains unclear, although Intermarche spokesperson told BleepingComputer that the attack affected a service provider that manages refrigeration equipment.
Cybersecurity researcher Kevin Beaumont suggested that thousands of Danfoss controllers are directly accessible over the internet, with the username set to ‘admin’ and the password automatically changing every day to the current date.
Danfoss said the most affected systems were obsolete products, including the AK-SM 800 and AK-SC 355 models, which no longer receive security updates. France’s cybersecurity agency, ANSSI, has urged operators to disconnect vulnerable management interfaces from the internet or restrict access to trusted connections.
Danfoss equipment has already been implicated in major cyberattacks. The company reported that 16 Russian supermarkets using AK-SM 800 controllers were targeted in 2022, around the time of the escalation of the Ukraine conflict. That year, 40 Israeli stores were hacked. The company cited inadequate firewall or VPN protection.

Russia cuts oil production by 38,000 bpd in September, OPEC says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
13:24:32 UTC
22:24:32 KST

MOSCOW, October 13. /TASS/. Russia reduced its crude oil production by 38,000 barrels per day (bpd) month-on-month in September to 8.643 million bpd, according to the latest report by the Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries (OPEC).
In September, Russia's production quota under the OPEC+ agreement stood at 9.949 million bpd, factoring in voluntary output caps. Consequently, Russia's oil production for the month was 1.306 million bpd below its targeted allocation, excluding the compensation schedule.
Currently, oil production in Russia is capped under the OPEC+ agreement. From early 2024 through March 2025, Russia's baseline production quota - including voluntary restrictions -stood at 8.978 million bpd. This figure did not account for obligations to compensate for past overproduction during the voluntary restriction window.
In April 2025, Russia began gradually scaling up its output month-on-month in accordance with the OPEC+ roadmap. In September 2025--a year ahead of schedule--OPEC+ nations completed the phase-out of voluntary cuts totaling 2.2 million bpd and began unwinding another 1.65 million bpd in supply curbs to return the curtailed volumes to the market. By September 2026, these countries had completed the restoration of this volume to the market. For the remainder of the year, previously approved baseline quotas will apply to all OPEC+ countries without additional restrictions, fixing Russia's quota at 9.949 million bpd.

Hungarian MPs scrap Orbán's anti-LGBTQ measures
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
14:23:45 BST
22:23:45 KST

Hungarian MPs scrap Orbán's anti-LGBTQ measures
- Published
The Hungarian parliament has voted to amend child protection laws, scrapping measures that stigmatise gay and transgender people. LGBTQ and human rights activists warmly welcomed the move, but called for changes to other Orbán-era laws.
The 2021 Child Protection Law, passed by the large Fidesz majority of then-Prime Minister Viktor Orbán, banned the "portrayal or promotion of homosexuality or transgenderism".
Since Orbán's April election defeat, the Tisza government of Péter Magyar has been working to dismantle the previous government's legacy.
Minutes after Tuesday's vote, Budapest said the EU had agreed to release €4.2bn (£3.5bn) of funds frozen in the last years of the Fidesz government.
The European Commission said last month that the Magyar government had addressed a number of "rule of law breaches affecting the EU budget", and urged EU leaders to unlock the funds , externaland readmit Hungary to two key EU programmes - Erasmus+ and Horizon Europe.
Hungary's 2021 law had affected a wide range of other laws, including education and the right of assembly.
Magyar's Tisza party commands the same two-thirds majority that Orbán's party used to have, and the measures passed on Tuesday were bundled together by the new government in a package of laws designed to unravel the Fidesz legislation.
"We are very happy that this got adopted," Tamás Dombos of civil rights group the Háttér Society told the BBC. "We've been fighting this so-called child protection law for five years. There have been problems with the bill submitted to parliament, but most of those problems have been fixed."
Both the Fidesz and Tisza governments made child protection central to their image.
But while Fidesz under Viktor Orbán appealed to the conservative electorate by identifying gay and transgender people as a threat to public morals, Tisza under Prime Minister Péter Magyar is trying to remove or soften legislation, without actually identifying as a liberal-minded government in favour of full equality.
In June 2025, the Gay Pride march through Budapest drew an estimated quarter of a million people, despite a promise by then-Prime Minister Viktor Orbán to his supporters that he would prevent it happening.
Police stood aside despite an official ban, and proceedings against the city mayor and others for organising the festival were later dropped. This year's event went ahead without restrictions.
The child protection issue turned from being a strong card in Orbán's hand to become his Achilles heel, when the public found out that his government had supported the pardon of the deputy head of a children's home who had been found guilty of covering up the paedophile crimes of his boss.
In his own election campaign, Péter Magyar presented his party as a champion of the rights of children in state care, while painstakingly avoiding the issues of gay and transgender rights, for fear of alienating right-wing voters.
"We are still knocking on a closed door," Dombos told the BBC, "but at least they are listening on the other side."
This marked a major improvement on the Orbán years, he said, where his community felt constantly targeted. Other issues he wanted addressed include the full recognition of same-sex marriage, same-sex couples' rights to adopt children, and the restoration of the right of transgender people to change their names in official documents.
"I'm very cautious," Magyar said in an interview published in Finnish daily Helsingin Sanomat on Saturday. "As prime minister, it's my duty to represent all Hungarians, and we have sensitive issues, such as the situation of sexual minorities."
Fidesz and its sister party, the Christian Democrats, voted against the new amendments to the law on Tuesday.
"There is no place for the promotion of LGBTQ content in schools or the media," the Christian Democrats said in a statement on their website.

Kyiv • UNN
The Ukrainian vessel "Noosphere" has departed from Cape Town for Antarctica. As part of this mission, scientists plan to expand research and international cooperation.
The sixth Antarctic season of the Ukrainian research vessel "Noosphere" has begun. As reported by the National Antarctic Scientific Center, this mission plans to expand the area and types of research במסגרת international cooperation, UNN reports.
The "Noosphere" is currently sailing from Cape Town (South Africa), where it is forced to be based because of russia’s full-scale invasion, to Antarctica. The vessel’s captain is Andrii Starish.
First stop, research, and international cooperation
The first stop is the Polish Antarctic station "Arctowski," to which the "Noosphere" is providing logistical support for the construction of new buildings. After that, the icebreaker will head to Punta Arenas (Chile). There, it will pick up the first group of Ukrainian seasonal expedition members and cargo and head to "Vernadsky." Arrival at our station is expected in early December.
Many studies are planned this season as part of international cooperation:
-  the first Indonesian expedition will work aboard the "Noosphere" and at the station, implementing new geological, biological, and oceanographic projects together with our scientists; 
-  cooperation with Mexico, the United States, and the Czech Republic will continue; 
-  two studies will be conducted as part of the EU’s POLARIN project. One focuses on the distribution of microbial communities in the air of polar regions, while the other concerns carbon monitoring in the Southern Ocean; 
-  the main event will be a large-scale Ukrainian-Swedish study of the Weddell Sea. It lies east of the Antarctic Peninsula, and this is the first such significant expansion of the research area for Ukrainian polar science. During the expedition, researchers plan to study extremophile organisms that live in “black smokers” — underwater geysers with temperatures of up to 400°C. Scientists will also search for cold-water corals and even a sunken vessel. In addition, research into atmospheric rivers and ocean currents will continue. 
As usual, the "Noosphere" will provide rotation of the annual expeditions at "Vernadsky."
The NANC also added that all joint research is funded by foreign partners and grants. Thus, the expansion of the types and area of research has become possible without funding from the state budget.
Reminder
From January 2022 to May 2026, the "Noosphere" successfully completed five Antarctic seasons.

One of the officials said the investigation also aims to find out why air defense systems did not provide earlier warning of the attack in which the Houthi missiles and drones flew over 1,000 kilometers (620 miles) to reach Riyadh.

Hungary: Lawmakers scrap Orban-era anti-LGBTQ+ provisions
October 13, 2026
Hungary's parliament on Tuesday passed a bill amending a 2021 law targeting the LGBTQ+ community that was passed under nationalist ex-leader Viktor Orban.
The 2021 "child protection" law introduced restrictions on the "portrayal" or "promotion" of sexual and gender diversity in content accessible to children. In reality, this meant that even books addressing these topics in an age-appropriate manner could only be sold in black plastic packaging with warnings.
Critics argued that the law promoted the bigoted view automatically linking homosexuality and child abuse. The European Court of Justice had also ruled in April that it violated EU treaties.
Tuesday's amendment repeals most of the statute, except the provision protecting under-18s from sexually explicit or violent material. It passed with the support of the governining majorty, with 139 lawmakers voting for in favor and 51 against.
What brought about this change?
Hungary's longtime Prime Minister Viktor Orban was voted out of office in April. While his successor Peter Magyar is also a conservative and an immigration hardliner, he promised to break with Orban's repressive policies on media, the judiciary, and other issues.
Magyar has promised to dismantle what he calls the rampant corruption and authoritarian structures put in place under Orban's government.
"We welcome this important signal of commitment for our common values," EU commissioners Michael McGrath and Hadja Lahbib said in a joint statement. The bloc then unfroze €4.2 billion ($4.7 billion) in funding to Hungary following the vote.

EU expands migration cooperation with eastern Libya through new funding
BRUSSELS, Oct 13 - The European Union has signed an additional €25 million ($29 million) in funding to expand migration cooperation into eastern Libya, according to a letter from European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen to EU leaders seen by Reuters.
The funding will support border management, search-and-rescue and anti-smuggling activities in eastern Libya. It is a further sign of deepening EU engagement with the region controlled by military commander Khalifa Haftar as Brussels seeks to curb irregular migration across the Mediterranean.
Libya, where control is split between rival western and eastern administrations, has been a major transit route for migrants attempting the dangerous sea crossing to Europe since the 2011 NATO-backed uprising that toppled Muammar Gaddafi.
The EU and its member states have long supported and trained the Libyan coastguard, which intercepts migrants at sea. While the EU formally recognises only the Tripoli-based government, it has stepped up contacts with authorities in eastern Libya since last year as migrant departures from areas controlled by Haftar in eastern Libya have risen.
The move follows the July announcement by the EU that it would establish a Maritime Rescue Coordination Centre in the eastern Libyan city of Benghazi, further expanding cooperation with authorities in the east.
"Libya remains the top country of departure for illegal crossings to the EU," von der Leyen wrote, describing an upcoming EU-Libya meeting as a way to keep cooperation going.
She said the EU and the International Organization for Migration were supporting voluntary returns from Libya to countries of origin.
"We are equally focused on reducing the number of migrants arriving to Libya with the sole intention to cross illegally into the EU," she added. REUTERS

‘No regret’: The EEA’s six steps to make Europe more competitive without sacrificing sustainability
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
13:20:00 UTC
22:20:00 KST

From resource efficiency to education, these six sustainable steps could make Europe more competitive in the long term.
Geopolitical instability, technological disruption and climate change are casting a shadow over Europe’s future.
Could investing in sustainability make the continent more resilient?
A new report by the European Environment Agency (EEA) reveals how Europe could strengthen its long-term competitiveness by nurturing both the economy and nature.
Rather than promoting short-term productivity and economic growth based on resource depletion and environmental degradation, the EEA urges a more holistic approach that treats nature restoration and social capital as integral to long-term stability.
The report, titled ‘Competitive by nature: Europe’s long-term competitiveness through the lens of sustainability’, released on 13 October, identifies six ‘no-regret’ options that could boost the economy while sustaining life on Earth.
6. Investing in climate adaptation and resilience
Europe is warming faster than any other continent, with flooding, heatwaves, droughts and wildfires growing increasingly extreme as a result of climate change.
Adapting to this new reality and mitigating its effects is no longer just an environmental necessity but an economic one too, the EEA argues.
This includes investing in nature-based solutions, like restoring wetlands and floodplains or adding green space to cities, which can help soak up floodwater and cool urban areas.
5. Using resources more efficiently
Europe imports a huge share of its raw materials and energy, and recent supply shocks have shown how risky that is.
Disruptions to shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, triggered by the war on Iran, have put immense pressure on fuel supplies, prompting an accelerated shift to homegrown renewable energy.
But the technology behind wind turbines, solar panels and batteries relies on critical minerals, and the grids to carry all that clean power still have to be built.
Circularity – repairing, reusing and recycling products – “can reduce demand for primary materials and energy, preserve the value embodied in products and infrastructure, and limit exposure to volatile commodity and energy markets,” the EEA says.
Sometimes there are trade-offs, however: for example, while keeping old buildings and infrastructure in use is good for circularity, it can lock in assets that are inefficient or vulnerable to climate impacts.
4. Leveraging next-gen tech
AI can be leveraged to help Europe use its resources more wisely, the EEA says. Digital tools can track materials through supply chains, manage variable renewable energy on the power grid, and monitor environmental damage in real time.
Building these capabilities at home also reduces Europe’s reliance on technology developed elsewhere.
The EU is already utilising these tools to strengthen accountability: its Digital Product Passport launched in July and will first be a requirement for batteries from February 2027. Consumers will be able to access information, for example through a QR code, on the origin of a product’s materials, its environmental performance, and how it can be repaired or recycled.
But the energy- and water-hungry data centres needed to fuel AI are a growing concern in their own right.
The EEA also encourages the development of next-gen biotechnology – making materials and fuels from plants and other biological sources, rather than oil and gas. While this can cut fossil fuel use, it also comes with its own footprint: growing biomass takes land and water and can put nature under strain.
3. Investing in skills and education
Spreading and developing these new technologies is key to developing a low-carbon economy that sacrifices neither wages nor the environment. While a recent EEA analysis found that clean energy is creating jobs across the EU, it faces major bottlenecks in workforce availability and training.
That’s why the agency’s latest report urges investment in skills, education and lifelong learning that will create a resilient workforce capable of adapting to a rapidly changing world.
Ensuring these skills are spread across different demographics would foster social cohesion and fairness.
2. Building public trust
In several EU countries, climate policy has become politically divisive, with fierce debate over costs, farming rules and red tape.
Ensuring the green transition leaves no one behind would also help to build public trust in and support for it. Without this, even well-designed policies risk being watered down, delayed or scrapped.
The EEA argues that clear, predictable regulation and effective institutions are integral to this. Companies are more likely to invest in clean technologies if they can rely on clear, stable rules, and the public is more likely to back the transition if it trusts those rules are applied fairly.
1. Leading on sustainable standard-setting
The EU’s single market has the power to shape global rules on everything from chemicals to carbon emissions. The EEA says it should keep playing an active role in setting environmental and social standards, including through international institutions.
Cooperating with other countries through democratic, international forums like the UN’s COP can help create common rules, diversify trade relationships and make supply chains more resilient.
But the system is under strain. Nearly 200 nations pledged to transition away from fossil fuels at COP28 in 2023, yet a new agreement on fossil fuels is considered unlikely at COP31 in Türkiye next month. Meanwhile, fossil fuel-reliant nations are pushing to delay the UN climate science panel’s next major report until after the global climate summit, with the IPCC meeting this week to try to resolve the deadlock.
At home, the EU is also under pressure to simplify its own green rules in the name of competitiveness. The EEA maintains that sustainability can reinforce competitiveness.

Argentina asked the International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea to intervene Tuesday and block the UK from developing offshore oil fields around the Falkland Islands, known in Argentina as the Islas Malvinas.
"The request submitted to the Tribunal seeks to preserve Argentina's sovereign rights over its continental shelf and to prevent activities unilaterally and illegally authorized by the United Kingdom from aggravating the dispute recognized by the United Nations," President Javier Milei's office said in a statement.
