The UK and the Falkland Islands Government, an archipelago 483 kilometers (300 miles) east of Argentina's coast, maintain that the exploration licenses are fully lawful, arguing that islanders possess the right to self-determination and the development of their natural resources.
Argentina reiterated its "legitimate and imprescriptible sovereign rights" over the Falkland Islands, South Georgia, the South Sandwich Islands and surrounding maritime areas.

'We're not giving up': Activist Greta Thunberg joins France student protests
Thousands of student protesters marched through central Paris on Tuesday as part of nationwide demonstrations supporting high school pupils who have been protesting for better classroom conditions, with Swedish activist Greta Thunberg taking part.
With just six months to go before elections to replace President Emmanuel Macron, French authorities had been hoping that the protests were easing ahead of half-term holidays starting at the end of this week.
But teenagers at high schools called lycees—backed by university students, teachers, unions and the far-left opposition party France Unbowed (LFI)—have said their demands have not been met.
French presidential candidate Jean-Luc Melenchon was seen among the crowd of demonstrators in Paris.
Outside the Paris city hall, demonstrators—mostly university students—gathered in the early afternoon to the tune of an orchestra playing the The Rebel Fanfare from the Star Wars movies.
"I'm expecting a surge of solidarity," said 20-year-old Patricia, not wishing to give her surname.
"We're not giving up the fight, whether it's for the high school students who were hit with a harsh crackdown, or for denouncing police violence," she added, referencing multiple allegations of police brutality against protesters in recent weeks.
The education ministry said 214 schools were closed on Tuesday. Most of these were high schools out of the country's 3,700.
University student union l'Union Etudiante reported that 90 percent of universities had closed nationwide to show support.
Thunberg, who became famous as a teen for school strikes to demand action on climate change, stood among pupils demonstrating outside a school in the capital's largest suburb, Saint-Denis.
"Young people are not being included in the conversation. Our future is being robbed away from us," the 23-year-old told reporters outside the Paul Eluard high school.
'Country without a future'
French students say they are determined to press their demands for solutions to too many absent teachers, dilapidated buildings, overcrowded class schedules and other grievances.
The protests, launched late last month, have seen teenagers pile up dumpsters and security barriers outside hundreds of lycees.
Rallies were also underway in other cities on Tuesday.
In the western city of Nantes, thousands marched behind a banner reading "Schools without money, a country without a future".
"I think there are a lot of us in France who are still motivated," 16-year-old Mariolino said. "Those who think the anger will disappear with the holidays just don't get it."
In the northeastern city of Strasbourg, Adeline Ferier, 42, a middle school French teacher, said she was demonstrating to support her 16-year-old daughter.
"I think it's great that young people are aware of inequalities and are getting involved," she said.
More than 70,000 people took to the streets last Thursday in the last major event of the movement.
'Issues that deserve time'
The demonstrations in recent weeks have mostly been peaceful, but clashes have occasionally broken out due to attacks by the police.
More than 6,800 people—largely children—have been taken into police custody over the course of the protests, according to the justice ministry.
Police have opened internal investigations into 24 allegations of brutality against demonstrators.
Some 147 teaching staff members have been injured in the protests, the education ministry said.
Authorities said fireworks fired through tubes on Monday injured two school workers in Reims, one school worker in a Paris suburb and a police officer outside a school in Marseille.
Tuesday's demonstrations supporting the students were to be followed on Saturday by wider public rallies against the rising cost of living.
Macron, speaking to reporters at a car show on Monday, urged restraint from protesters.
"These are issues that deserve time, consultations, discussion and respect," Macron said just months before elections to replace him.
After last week's nationwide demonstrations, the government promised that some 3,000 substitute teachers would be deployed in the coming days to replace absent staff at the 114 worst-affected high schools.
The education minister said on Tuesday that 35 percent had already been assigned.
High school students are demanding a 10 billion-euro ($11 billion) boost for lycees.

Gazan families fight to protect slain journalists' legacies
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
13:16:18 UTC
22:16:18 KST

Breadcrumb
'Killed twice': Gaza families fight to clear the names of journalists branded militants by Israel
"Publishing my son’s name on that list is a second assassination," begins 70-year-old Bakr al-Louh. "The first time, they killed his body. Now they are killing his legacy and his career as a journalist. They are killing him in his grave."
His son, Ahmed al-Louh, was a photojournalist working for Al Jazeera. He was 39 when an Israeli strike hit a civil defence post in Nuseirat refugee camp, in central Gaza, on 15 December 2024. He had returned there shortly before, after filming ambulances carrying the bodies of people killed in an earlier Israeli strike nearby.
On 1 October, the family found Ahmed’s name and photograph in The Press Files, an online database published by the Israeli occupation. It names 170 Palestinian journalists and media workers killed in Gaza and claims they were members or fighters of armed factions.
"This news destroyed us," his father says. He says the allegations against Ahmed are "lies, with no basis in truth."
Ahmed’s page on the site lists him as a military operative in Hamas’s armed wing. When The New Arab viewed it on 11 October, it contained no supporting evidence. Its only image linked to an internal address and did not load.
The Israeli army claims the database is the product of an in-depth investigation, drawing on open-source information, documents seized in Gaza, interrogations of alleged militants and intelligence gathered during military operations.
But the evidence it presents varies widely, from cropped documents to old photographs.
In 49 cases, the main evidence is an obituary published by an armed group. An analysis by +972 Magazine found that 59 of the pages contain no evidence at all, only a line saying the claim is based on intelligence sources.
For Bakr al-Louh, the list is an extension of the war on Gaza’s journalists. Targeting them, he says, is "an attempt to silence the free word and the truth, because the occupation doesn’t want any voice or image to come out of Gaza that exposes its massacres."
The fear does not stop with the dead. "We have a real fear that these accusations will reach the rest of the family," he tells The New Arab. If any of them needs urgent medical treatment outside Gaza, he worries Israel could reject them on security grounds.
‘He moved in the open’
Ahmed Khaireddine, 30, was a cameraman for Al-Quds Al-Youm. He was killed on 27 December 2023, when an Israeli strike hit his home in Beit Lahia, in northern Gaza. His uncle Mohammed Khaireddine, a journalist with Al-Aqsa TV, died with him, along with 23 other members of the family.
The Press Files describes Ahmed as an Islamic Jihad commander and lists his employer as Al-Aqsa TV, the channel his uncle worked for. His brother Basel, 36, a journalist himself, says the photograph on the page is fabricated. He says he had never seen it in his life. He believes the way his brother died is the clearest proof the allegations are false.
"Before he was killed, Ahmed spent more than 80 days moving around with his camera and his blue vest, covering al-Shifa and the Indonesian hospitals," he tells The New Arab.
"If he had really been a military target, they would have picked him off in the streets and public squares, where he moved openly. But he was killed with his family, in a massacre that destroyed three adjoining houses at once and killed more than 30 civilians."
Many of the names on the list, he says, belong to colleagues he saw every day. "We saw them all the time where journalists gathered at hospitals and out in the field, and we never once saw them among gunmen or fighters. They were doing their work in the open, and the drones above them knew very well they were civilians doing their jobs," Basel says.
He says Israel is deliberately confusing political affiliation with combat. "A Palestinian is born with a political affiliation. That is nothing shameful, and it does not take a journalist out of the civilian work protected under international law."
'A ready-made warrant'
Photojournalist Bilal Abu Samak says the database’s real purpose is to justify the killing of journalists who covered the war. He and Mohammed both describe the accusations as a ready-made warrant, one that could be used against journalists who are still alive and still reporting.
Gaza’s journalists, Abu Samak says, are civilians who wear protective vests and carry no weapons.
"Through this list, they are trying to terrify us and force us to abandon journalism, especially as they keep barring international journalists from entering Gaza to document their violations," he says.
"We demand real protection for press crews, and that the professional legacy of our colleagues who were killed be preserved."
Israel has barred foreign reporters from Gaza since the start of the war, apart from brief visits escorted by the army, and denies deliberately targeting journalists.
The Committee to Protect Journalists (CPJ) told The New Arab it was still reviewing all the claims in the database. When new information emerges about the killing of a journalist anywhere in the world, it said, it reviews each case independently and updates its records.
CPJ published the database a week after completing its own review.
On 24 September, the New York-based group removed 22 people from its list of journalists killed in Israel and the Occupied Palestinian Territory. It found that 19 of them had been militants or had taken part in combat, and that three could not be confirmed as journalists.
CPJ now counts 191 Palestinian journalists and media workers killed by Israeli forces. It said Israeli forces remain responsible for the large majority of journalist killings worldwide since 2023, and that each case in its review required interviews with at least two independent, credible sources as well as desk research.
The Palestinian Journalists Syndicate puts the toll higher, at more than 260. Its secretary-general, Ahed Farawneh, says the timing of the Israeli database is no accident.
"The occupation is trying to get around the huge numbers of journalists killed by levelling these false accusations of links to armed groups," he says, "to justify targeting them after a global outcry and strong condemnation from journalists’ unions and international organisations."
When the syndicate looks at the lives of those killed, he says, it finds that "they were working under the sun," in plain sight and far from any armed faction.
The syndicate says it applies criteria matching those of the International Federation of Journalists before recognising anyone as a journalist killed in the line of duty.
It is also building a case file of killings, injuries, arrests, destroyed offices and homes, and families wiped out and documenting the ban on foreign press and on bringing cameras and equipment into Gaza.
"We have obtained power of attorney from the families of those killed, and from injured journalists and former detainees, to file cases at the International Criminal Court," Ahed says.
"Unfortunately, the court is still stalling on opening this file. But together with the International Federation of Journalists, we insist on it, and on the families’ right to take the occupation to court."
He points to earlier legal efforts over the killings of journalists Shireen Abu Akleh, Ahmed Abu Hussein and Yaser Murtaja. The syndicate is also working with rights groups and legal experts to bring cases in countries whose laws allow prosecution of war crimes committed abroad.
'In case of doubt'
Hussein Hammad, a specialist in media and human rights, says the database deliberately blurs the line between political or institutional affiliation and taking a direct part in hostilities.
Working for a media outlet linked to a political faction, or sympathising with one, does not strip a journalist of civilian protection, he says.
International humanitarian law is clear on this. Article 79 of Additional Protocol I to the Geneva Conventions states that journalists on dangerous professional missions in armed conflict are civilians and must be protected as such.
Under Article 51, civilians lose that protection only "for such time as they take a direct part in hostilities." Article 50 adds that "in case of doubt whether a person is a civilian, that person shall be considered to be a civilian."
Accusing journalists after they have been killed, with no chance to answer the charges, has no legal value, Hammad says, and amounts to a cover for extrajudicial killing.
International justice, he adds, does not accept military verdicts based on evidence the victim or their lawyer can never see or challenge. He says the response must be to document every violation, gather physical evidence and build cases for court.
For Bakr al-Louh, the fight is also about memory. His son’s last assignment was to document the dead of Nuseirat being carried to hospital. Shortly afterwards, he was among them.
Ismail Nofal is a Gaza-based journalist specialising in human interest stories

Over 70 unexploded aerial bombs uncovered in Jõgeva nature reserve
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
13:16:00 UTC
22:16:00 KST

Over 70 unexploded aerial bombs uncovered in Jõgeva nature reserve
Dozens of Soviet-era aerial bombs, many of them live, have been excavated and safely disposed of in Jõgeva County, Maaleht reported.
The safety work was planned and covered a known danger zone at a former Soviet military facility.
On the penultimate weekend of September, Rescue Board and Defense League bomb disposal teams removed dozens of explosives from the former Utsali training ground in Jõgeva County.
They recovered more than 70 items from the area over the three days, including explosive devices and their components.
Most of the finds were aerial bombs, including both training and live versions.
The site was selected because the Soviet Air Force had once used it extensively for bombing exercises. Bomb disposal specialists had previously been called to the area, so it was a known danger zone.
Over 30 bomb disposal specialists and assistant specialists, along with more than 50 members of the Estonian Defense League and other support personnel, took part in the search operation.
Hazardous items were transported to a demolition site.
Marti Mereäär, head of the Southern Estonia bomb disposal unit, noted that explosive devices can remain dangerous for many years, and under no circumstances should they be handled. Members of the public should call 112 in such cases.
This is even the case with items of war memorabilia in the home, if there is reason to fear they are explosives. "Calling out bomb disposal specialists is free of charge, and there is no penalty for reporting an artillery shell found at home," Mereäär added.
What should you do if you find suspected explosives?
- Under no circumstances should you touch the object
- Move to a safe distance immediately
- After moving a safe distance away, call the emergency number 112 as soon as you can
- Note the location of the found object

Schools urged not to make pupils with special educational needs repeat grades
‘Repeating a grade will only aggravate their social and emotional adjustment difficulties and increase mental health risks,’ updated guide says
Hong Kong schools should not require students with special educational needs (SEN) or severe mental illness to repeat a grade, under revised education authorities’ guidance that warns the practice could worsen their adjustment difficulties.
The latest version of the Education Bureau’s School Administration Guide requires subsidised schools considering grade retention for pupils with special educational needs (SEN) to consult parents through a team of professionals, including an educational psychologist.
“Repeating a grade will only aggravate their social and emotional adjustment difficulties and increase mental health risks,” according to the guide, which was updated in August and came to the attention of the media on Tuesday.
The team should also include the school’s student support team and teachers, as well as psychiatrists when necessary, it said.

Iranian attacks target 6 ships near Strait of Hormuz in 1 day, highest since war with US began
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
13:13:18 UTC
22:13:18 KST

Ahmet Dursun, Mohammad Kara Maryam, and Lina Altawell
13 October 2026•Update: 13 October 2026
Iranian attacks on vessels in and around the Strait of Hormuz have reached their highest pace since the war with the US began on Feb. 28, with six ships targeted in a single day, according to data from the UK Maritime Trade Operations agency (UKMTO) and international maritime security sources.
Data from UKMTO and maritime security sources showed that more than 18 commercial vessels were targeted by Iran during the first 12 days of October, including six on Monday.
Between Oct. 5 and 12 alone, at least 14 attacks, attempted attacks and interceptions involving vessels were recorded in and around the strait, according to the same sources.
UKMTO data and statements by Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) indicated a marked rise in attacks on commercial shipping since clashes between Tehran and Washington resumed in July.
At least 12 attacks on oil tankers and cargo ships were recorded in July, while at least 10 vessels were targeted in August, including oil and liquefied natural gas tankers off the UAE port of Fujairah and Oman’s Sohar.
The number rose to 18 vessels in September as the US and Gulf countries increasingly resorted to ship-to-ship transfers, using smaller vessels to transport oil before loading it onto larger tankers in safer areas.
The IRGC claimed that the operations were “illegal oil smuggling and an attempt to break the Hormuz blockade” and expanded its operations to include supply vessels, tugboats and small tankers in the Gulf.
The IRGC also claimed that some targeted vessels were damaged by explosions after striking naval mines while sailing “illegally” through routes it considered “unsafe.”
Tehran says the escalation in its operations against shipping is a response to a “US naval blockade,” while warning vessels against using routes it has not approved or crossing the area after switching off navigation and identification systems.
Since April, Iran has imposed restrictions on maritime traffic through the Strait of Hormuz, including designated transit routes and a requirement for prior coordination with the IRGC Navy.
On May 30, Tehran announced that vessels passing through the strait would be required to obtain prior authorization from the IRGC Navy, warning that transit without permission would constitute a “security threat.”
The developments come amid continued tensions between Iran and the US over navigation through the Strait of Hormuz, one of the world’s most important strategic routes for energy and commodity supplies and a key issue in negotiations between the two sides.
The war began with US and Israeli attacks on Iran on Feb. 28, before a ceasefire was reached in April. Clashes between Washington and Tehran later resumed as negotiations stalled despite the two sides signing a memorandum of understanding in June.

====================================================================================================

Annual dementia cases worldwide projected to more than double by 2050: Study
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
13:12:30 UTC
22:12:30 KST

Dilara Hamit
13 October 2026•Update: 13 October 2026
The number of people developing dementia worldwide each year could more than double from 11.4 million in 2023 to 24.7 million by 2050, according to a major international study.
The research, published Monday in JAMA Neurology, analyzed individual data from 38,418 participants across 22 population-based studies in 18 countries and territories on six continents.
Across more than 287,000 person-years of monitoring, 3,001 participants developed dementia. The researchers calculated a global age- and sex-standardized incidence rate of 9.7 new cases per 1,000 person-years.
Incidence measures how frequently new cases develop, rather than prevalence, which refers to the total number of people already living with a condition.
After researchers accounted for differences in age, the incidence rate among women was 10.6 cases per 1,000 person-years, compared to 8.6 among men.
The difference between countries at different income levels was greater. Low- and middle-income countries recorded 13.6 cases per 1,000 person-years, compared with 8.3 in high-income countries.
“For the first time, we can compare dementia incidence across a geographically diverse group of populations using the same statistical approach, giving us a clearer picture of where and among whom new cases are occurring,” said lead author Ashleigh Vella of the University of New South Wales’ Centre for Healthy Brain Ageing.
“What stands out is that dementia incidence is not evenly distributed. We see higher rates among women and in low- and middle-income countries,” she added.
The projection of 24.7 million annual cases in 2050 was calculated by applying the study’s age- and sex-specific incidence rates to expected population figures. It assumes that incidence rates remain constant, meaning the projected rise is driven largely by population growth and aging.
Researchers said the findings could help governments anticipate future demand for diagnosis, treatment, long-term care, and support services, particularly in lower-resource countries that have historically been underrepresented in dementia studies.
Dementia currently affects more than 57 million people worldwide, while previous research has projected that the number living with the condition could approach 150 million by 2050.
Study co-author Henry Brodaty said 24 million new cases each year would place “enormous pressure on individuals, families, health systems, and economies around the world.”
“Population ageing means we cannot simply wait for people to develop dementia and then respond,” he said, calling for action to reduce modifiable risk factors, identify people at risk earlier and improve diagnosis, treatment and care.

The EU is preparing to demand tougher sanctions against Russia in defiance of Trump&apos;s policy - Politico
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
16:12:26 EEST
22:12:26 KST

The EU is preparing to demand tougher sanctions against Russia in defiance of Trump's policy - Politico
Kyiv • UNN
EU leaders plan to demand tougher sanctions against Russia and limit Moscow's oil revenues. This comes in defiance of Trump's deal with Putin on diesel fuel exports.
European leaders are preparing to demand tougher sanctions against Russia at a summit on Thursday, October 15. This will put them at odds with U.S. President Donald Trump just days after he struck a deal with Kremlin leader Vladimir Putin to ease restrictions on Russian diesel fuel exports. Politico reports, writes UNN.
Details
EU leaders plan to call for "further sanctions and measures targeting Moscow’s oil revenues" at a European Council meeting, according to a recent draft of a joint statement, as EU governments reject Trump’s claim that he has secured an "energy truce" between Russia and Ukraine.
The disagreement, the outlet notes, "lays bare the growing divide over how to bring Moscow to the negotiating table." While Trump seeks to lower fuel prices in the United States by allowing more Russian diesel fuel to reach global markets, European leaders argue that restricting the Kremlin’s energy revenues remains essential to forcing Putin to end the war.
"Russia is not interested in de-escalation, a ceasefire, or peace," Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said at a security conference in Warsaw on October 12. "That is why I will go to Brussels to ask my partners to seriously consider tightening sanctions against Russia."
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz also called for further restrictions, pointing to Moscow’s ongoing attacks on Ukraine’s energy infrastructure despite Trump’s announcement of a truce.
"Russia will negotiate in good faith only under pressure," Merz said on October 12. "After Moscow’s reckless attacks on Ukraine’s civilian energy supplies, we must further strengthen [the sanctions]."
The push, the outlet writes, came after EU foreign ministers on October 12 approved the largest expansion in the bloc’s history of its sanctions list against Russia, covering more than 1,600 individuals and organizations.
"The European Commission is also preparing its 23rd package of sectoral sanctions, which Kyiv expects will be circulated among EU governments by the end of the year," according to a senior Ukrainian official.
Other European countries hold a similar position. The United Kingdom and Norway have also pledged to increase pressure on Moscow, the outlet writes.
"It is important to impose sanctions against Russia so that it does not finance the war," Norwegian Defense Minister Tore O. Sandvik said, calling for loopholes in the existing restrictions to be closed.
Trump’s Election Calculation
Behind closed doors, many European diplomats believe that Trump’s abrupt shift toward easing restrictions on Russian energy is driven mainly by domestic political concerns ahead of next month’s midterm elections in the United States.
This is a "widely held view" among EU officials, according to one senior official.
The U.S. president, it is noted, is facing growing pressure over fuel prices, which have risen sharply since the start of the U.S.-Israeli war with Iran. After promising during his 2024 campaign to bring gasoline prices below $2 per gallon, Trump now faces an electorate paying more than twice that amount, while Republicans risk losing control of Congress.
His deal with Putin is intended to release an additional 4.8 million tonnes of Russian diesel fuel onto global markets over the coming months, with the aim of easing pressure on fuel supplies and prices.
But European and Ukrainian officials question whether the additional supply will have a significant impact, saying that the total promised volume amounts to only about 10 days of U.S. demand. They believe the deal risks undermining efforts to deprive Moscow of the revenues financing its invasion.
The "reality" is that the additional fuel will have a "minimal" impact on prices in the United States, an EU senior official said.
"This is about midterm elections," said a second EU official. "He said he would lower prices, but then decided to start a war with Iran."
Officials also doubt whether putin intends to abide by the allegedly Trump-brokered "energy truce."
For now, the publication writes, most European officials are reluctant to publicly criticize Trump, despite any doubts about the agreement. The EU and Ukraine should maintain their position over the coming weeks, when the administration's long-term intentions toward Ukraine may become clearer, one diplomat said, adding that Trump could even change course again if putin does not deliver the promised diesel fuel.
Pressure on Washington
The dispute has also revived calls for Europe to urge Washington to impose its own sanctions on moscow.
Tusk called on Europe and the United States to act together to show russia that they are ready to impose tougher measures, while EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas urged Washington to coordinate its approach with Brussels.
Kallas pointed to sweeping legislation on sanctions against russia backed by the late Republican Senator Lindsey Graham, which Trump signed last month but has not yet fully implemented.
Some Republicans are also calling for tougher action. "I think we need to enact the sanctions bill against Russia," Republican Representative Dan Crenshaw said at a conference in Warsaw.
This, the publication writes, raises broader questions in Europe about its dependence on Washington, particularly amid reports that U.S. officials threatened to restrict Ukraine's access to American weapons if Kyiv did not stop attacking Russian oil refineries.
For now, there are "no signs" that Washington is carrying out these threats, a NATO official told the publication, arguing that restricting sales would also harm American arms manufacturers.
"PURL is a good deal for Americans," the official said, referring to the NATO initiative under which European allies finance purchases of American weapons for Ukraine.
EU Defense Commissioner Andrius Kubilius, while not commenting directly on these reports, said Europe urgently needs to assume "primary responsibility" for its own defense, as Washington reduces its military presence on the continent.
"However, the immediate test will come on Thursday, when EU leaders will try to maintain pressure on moscow, even as their most powerful ally moves in the opposite direction," the publication says.

Fingerprints, DNA, and a route out
The men were held under European arrest warrants and now await transfer to Poland. Interior Minister Marcin Kierwiński wrote that the suspects would face charges of “subversion, sabotage on behalf of a foreign intelligence service” after their transfer to Poland. Polish authorities issued European arrest warrants for the suspects, who were subsequently detained in Germany.
Police chief Marek Boroń said investigators reconstructed how the suspects prepared the attack and fled. “We have secured recordings pointing to this specific action. We have fingerprints, the perpetrators’ DNA, how they moved, when they came to Poland, and when they were evacuated from our country,” he said. One suspect lives in Germany, and the other had been ordered to leave the country, he added.
Warsaw points at Moscow
Prime Minister Donald Tusk called the fire another act of Russia's hybrid war and promised the saboteurs will answer to Polish justice.
“We have no doubt that Russian intelligence services are behind this act of sabotage,” said Tomasz Siemoniak, the minister coordinating Poland’s special services.
Those services increasingly turn to people tied to the criminal world, he added.
Two more possible links
German counterterrorism officers detained a woman in Berlin, and a man is also in German custody, Polish radio RMF FM reported, citing its reporter. Both may be linked to the arson. The woman allegedly picked up the Turkish men near Łódź after they entered Poland from Germany, then drove them to Wola Krobowska. The man’s role is still being examined.

Black Sea shipping drawn into war
Bulgarian officials said five crew members had been rescued but 11 were still listed as missing from the ship which sank off the coast of the village of Krapets. President Iliana Iotova identified the vessel as the Guinea-Bissau-flagged cargo ship HS Dignity and said a search and rescue operation was ongoing.
Another ship, the Chelsea 3 sailing under a Maltese flag, was also hit by three drones overnight, Bulgarian officials said. All crew from that ship — seven Ukrainians and eight Azerbaijanis — were rescued and none seriously injured.
A week ago nine Syrian sailors and one Egyptian were lost at sea from a ship that sank when hit by drones in Bulgaria's Black Sea exclusive economic zone. Another ship was also hit that night but the crew was rescued.
After meeting Radev in Sofia, Russian Ambassador Eleonora Mitrofanova said she had no information from the Russian Defense Ministry about attacks on commercial vessels in the Black Sea but did not rule out they could be a provocation by a third party, the Bulgarian government said.
More than four and a half years into the war that Moscow launched with its full-scale invasion in 2022, Black Sea shipping has increasingly been drawn into a prolonged battle of economic endurance.
Ukraine and Russia are both among the world's largest exporters of grain.
Russia has been bombing Ukraine's Black Sea ports, forcing Ukraine to rely increasingly on river ports on the Danube and shipping routes close to the coasts of NATO members Bulgaria and Romania.
Ukraine, for its part, has increasingly targeted Russian grain-exporting ships in other parts of the Black Sea and the Azov Sea at the mouth of the Don River.

French fridge fright: Why supermarkets have become target for hackers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
13:08:46 UTC
22:08:46 KST

French fridge fright: Why supermarkets have become target for hackers
More than 500 shops across France were hit in a major cyberattack targeting freezers, which caused tonnes of food to perish.
Hundreds of French supermarkets have suffered unprecedented cyberattacks resulting in tonnes of food perishing and raising fears about the vulnerabilities of food systems to advanced technology.
The attacks, which appeared to target internet-linked refrigeration systems manufactured by a Danish company, raised the temperature of fridges and freezers to as high as 50 degrees Celsius (122F) at more than 500 shops and supermarkets across the country. Supermarkets confirmed the attacks on Monday.
France’s cybersecurity agency has advised companies operating affected freezer models to immediately disconnect them from the internet – or restrict access to them – and to perform software updates.
It is unclear who may have been behind the attacks, but authorities say they have now launched an investigation.
Here’s what we know:
What happened?
Hackers gained internet access to the refrigeration systems and remotely cranked up temperatures in freezers and fridges to 50C during the night when shops were closed. Millions of euros worth of food was spoiled, according to retailers. In some cases, the raised temperatures sparked fires or melted equipment.
French supermarket groups E-Leclerc, Intermarche, Carrefour, Monoprix and Cooperative U were all hit.
At least 300 of Intermarche’s stores and its Netto brand were affected. Cooperative U said more than 100 of its supermarkets were targeted, while Carrefour said 80 supermarkets were affected and Monoprix reported that about 5 percent of its roughly 490 stores were hit.
Officials are still investigating who launched the attack and how it was carried out. French TV channel BFM reported that the attackers appeared to have remotely triggered a forced defrosting option in the refrigeration systems.
The systems targeted are built by Danish manufacturer Danfoss, according to France’s government cybersecurity agency. The refrigeration models attacked included the AK-SM800 and AK-SC355.
Danfoss told the AFP news agency that most of the affected control systems were “legacy” products that had “outdated firmware”. The company said it had previously advised supermarkets to update them.
AFP also reported that officials are liaising with other European countries which may have been affected.
It is unclear exactly how much food has been lost. The attacks come after President Emmanuel Macron ordered last month that the country’s critical infrastructure be protected from Russian “hybrid attacks”.
Have supermarkets been hit by cyberattacks before?
Yes. Attacks like these have been reported in other parts of Europe and in the United States.
In April 2025, British retailer and supermarket chain Marks and Spencer suffered a sophisticated ransomware attack that the company said cost it approximately 300 million pounds ($397m) after it was forced to suspend online and app orders. The attack was orchestrated by a hacker group called Scattered Spider, using ransomware from DragonForce, another criminal group. Ransomware attacks involve using malicious software to hide essential data unless a ransom is paid.
According to UK media, the same hackers also tried to attack Co-op and the iconic Knightsbridge store, Harrods.
Similar reports have also emerged from the US. In June 2025, United Natural Foods, a frozen food company which supplies big supermarket brands such as Whole Foods, said it had discovered a cyberattack that forced it to take its systems offline. The company did not reveal the nature of the attack.
In November last year, Ahold Delhaize USA said it was the victim of a cyberattack that disrupted operations at more than 2,000 stores, including Hannaford, Food Lion and Stop and Shop.
Why target supermarkets?
They are an easy target and the consequences can be widespread.
As food and agricultural systems increasingly digitise, analysts say supermarkets selling perishable foods are increasingly vulnerable to attacks due to the nature of their stocks.
The rising sophistication of cyberattacks now means that common people and local, third-party companies relying on big chains for business are also falling victim as attacks disrupt supply chains, experts say.
Speaking to Al Jazeera, tech and cybersecurity analyst Steven Lachance said smart appliances connected to the internet will always be vulnerable as hackers seize on security lapses to log in to the systems remotely and trigger malicious features.
“It’s the new reality of having these connected equipment,” Lachance said, pointing out that attacks could evolve to target medical or energy systems.
“This should come as a global wake-up call … Throughout society, we have connected infrastructure that is live on the internet, and that can be hacked. It’s a new reality, and we absolutely need national and international measures to prevent those attacks; otherwise, it’s just going to keep happening,” he warned.

Trump’s diesel deal opens a new rift with Europe over Ukraine
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
13:06:42 UTC
22:06:42 KST

Trump’s diesel deal opens a new rift with Europe over Ukraine
Trump calls for Zelenskyy to be replaced, while Europe devotes summit to funding Ukraine.
Russia has claimed it can supply even more diesel to the global market than the quantities agreed with United States President Donald Trump.
“By the end of the year, we could reach supply volumes of 3.5 million tonnes per month to global markets, just as was the case before the crisis,” Alexander Novak, Russian deputy prime minister, told the news programme Vesti on Monday.
President Vladimir Putin and Trump spoke on Friday on an agreement expected to bring 300,000 tonnes of diesel to global markets in October, half a million tonnes in November, and a million tonnes in December.
“Diesel Prices for Americans and, indeed, the World, will be COMING DOWN, IN RECORD NUMBERS, AND FAST!” Trump posted.
But experts are sceptical, and the move has opened a rift between the US and Europe on the Ukraine war.
Kostis Stambolis, executive director of the Institute of Energy for South-East Europe (IENE), described the US move as “purely political” and designed to put Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy in a corner.
Trump wants to signal that the US has “no problem with Russia”, unlike Europe, he said.
“Russia produces 5.8 million tonnes of diesel a month. Two million are likely to be available for export,” he added.
Europe has reacted to the diesel deal by backing Ukraine, whose war funding will be “front and centre” of this week’s European Council summit, European Commission President Ursula Von Der Leyen said on Sunday.
Finnish Foreign Minister Elina Valtonen on Monday called on Europeans to ban all tourist visas to Russians.
Stambolis believes Trump was leveraging European weakness to shift its position on Ukraine.
“About 30 European refineries have closed in the past 15 years for environmental reasons, because they have to pay to emit greenhouse gases,” he said, referring to Europe’s Emissions Trading Scheme, “so now Europe is not self-sufficient in products”.
Trump is showing the Europeans “he doesn’t want to deal with Europe and to hell with them … This is opening the rift between the US and the EU further,” said Stambolis.
Ukraine says it has destroyed roughly half of Russia’s refining capacity, forcing Moscow to stop exporting lucrative petroleum products which help it to finance its war.
It has also bombed Russian tankers carrying crude oil to global markets.
Zelenskyy said the strategy was effective, and Trump’s deal, which would suspend sanctions on Russian oil products until April 2027, undermined it.
“Gifts to Putin will not lead to peace,” Zelenskyy said Saturday. “Any weakening of sanctions against Russia without a clear and lasting de-escalation agreement with Russia is an obvious sign of weakness.”
Although Trump announced an energy ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine on Sunday, leading Ukraine to suspend its attacks on refineries, Russian strikes pounded Kyiv’s energy grid and killed 12 people in Dnipropetrovsk.
“I do not think he has earned a respite,” Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov said of Zelenskyy.
Europe supports Ukraine’s economic strategy against Russia’s war machine, but Trump has blamed it for raising petrol prices at the pump for Americans as he heads into Congressional midterm elections in early November.
“[Zelenskyy] wants to make problems for our farmers, our ranchers, with diesel fuel because Russia supplies a large portion of the diesel fuel throughout the world,” Trump told reporters in the White House after Zelenskyy’s reaction.
“I think it’s time for Ukraine to get a new president,” he said.
Politics over economics
Trump has followed a seemingly self-contradictory policy towards Russia.
He cut US military aid to Ukraine when he assumed power in January 2025, but agreed to sell Europe weapons to help Ukraine.
He had a public dispute with Zelenskyy in the Oval Office in February 2025, saying “You don’t have the cards,” but at the NATO summit this year said Zelenskyy had “done an amazing job” and “been very effective”.
Last month, Trump signed the Lindsey Graham Act, which would allow him to punish countries buying Russian oil. Eleven days later, he reversed policy.
“The moment the pendulum comes to one side, Trump tries to balance it with a completely different and opposite tool,” said Victoria Vdovychenko, an expert on European security at Cambridge University’s Centre for Geopolitics.
“In this way he sees how he controls the narrative, but also negotiations of any kind,” she told Al Jazeera. “So this pendulum will continue to prevail.”
How expensive is diesel in the US?
According to the US Energy Information Agency (EIA), average US diesel and petrol prices briefly spiked but ultimately changed little on account of the Ukraine war, yet they have risen a great deal on account of the US-Israel war on Iran.
US diesel was priced at $4.10 a gallon on the day of Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, February 24, 2022. It had fallen to $3.81 on the eve of Trump’s Gulf war, February 28, 2026.
It has since risen by 78 percent, to $6.19 in early October.
It is a similar story for US regular unleaded gasoline, priced at $3.48 a gallon before the Russian invasion. It stood at $2.79 before Trump’s Gulf war, but has since risen by half, to $4.15 a gallon.
The US government has little room to reduce taxes, which constitute just 11 or 12 percent of retail price, so it can only manipulate prices through supply.
Will the diesel deal bring down prices?
“If the market knows that there will be much more diesel in the coming weeks, it factors this into today’s prices and discounts it now,” Stambolis told Al Jazeera.
But much more important in bringing down oil prices than the Trump-Putin deal will be an October 2 announcement by the G7 to release 100 million barrels of oil from strategic reserves, he said.
A remainder of 80 million barrels from a previous, 400-million-tonne release in March will also be released.
“This release will start happening in the next two weeks,” Stambolis said. “The world is 5 million barrels a day short of crude compared to before the Gulf war. It’s a very significant percentage on 100 million. All prices vary on this margin.”

Trump either ‘a useful idiot’ or purposefully weakening Europe, says MEP Glucksmann
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
13:06:01 UTC
22:06:01 KST

PARIS — Fresh off his dominant victory in a center-left primary over the weekend, French presidential candidate Raphaël Glucksmann slammed U.S. President Donald Trump’s decision to ease restrictions on Russian diesel exports as a move that benefits the Kremlin at Europe’s expense.
“There is, at the head of the United States, someone who is either a useful idiot or an agent of the destruction of European strength and freedom,” Glucksmann said at POLITICO’s Competitiveness Summit in Paris. “[Russia’s war against Ukraine] targets us directly, us Europeans, and we are alone.”
The MEP also insisted that sending his far-right rival Marine Le Pen to the Elysée Palace in 2027 would be a victory for Russian leader Vladimir Putin and a step toward “the defeat of the European continent.”
Advertisement
Le Pen has previously expressed “a form of admiration” for Putin, and her party, the National Rally, received a loan from a Russian-linked bank in 2014. Le Pen said her party borrowed money overseas because French banks refused loans and that the loan had no impact on her political stances. The party has since paid back the funds.
Though Le Pen condemned Russia’s all-out war in Ukraine, some elected officials within her party remain strongly opposed to helping Ukraine and favor a stronger relationship with Russia.
At a POLITICO event last month, Le Pen said she believed France could provide Ukraine with military training and assistance but could no longer afford financial support given France’s budgetary constraints.
Le Pen currently boasts a double-digit lead over her competitors for the first round of next year’s presidential election, according to POLITICO’s Poll of Polls. Glucksmann is in fourth, trailing former Prime Minister Edouard Philippe and far-left candidate Jean-Luc Mélenchon. France’s presidential election will go to a runoff if neither of the top two candidates gets more than 50% of the vote in the first round.
In his interview with POLITICO, Glucksmann, one of the race’s strongest pro-European voices, doubled down on his support for a European Sky Shield for Ukraine and the need for a more robust, sovereign European defense industry — a push also endorsed by French President Emmanuel Macron and widely shared across the French political spectrum.
“For decades,” Glucksmann said, “we have delegated our sovereignty and our security to Washington, and we are now realizing what a mistake that was.”
Advertisement
In practical terms, however, Europe remains split over whether non-EU countries should be allowed to tap its defense money. France is leading the push to limit the outsiders’ access to the European Competitiveness Fund.
Glucksmann also said Europe should take on joint debt to fund defense projects — a proposal Germany and other fiscally conservative EU members have been loath to consider — instead of attempting member-state-to-member-state projects like the failed Franco-German next-generation fighter jet.
Without joint investment, he said, “no European countries, including Germany, will be able to face, in the short term, the war of the future” against powers like China, Russia and the U.S.
“It’s a life or death question,” Glucksmann said.
Wars abroad, protests at home
In a sweeping interview, Glucksmann outlined how his foreign policy, if elected president in April 2027, would involve strengthening ties with countries in central and eastern Europe instead of courting leaders like Putin or China’s Xi Jinping.
The next president, he said, “should go to Warsaw; should go to Tallinn,” rather than Beijing or Moscow. The MEP has frequently criticized Macron for hosting Putin at a lavish ceremony in the Versailles Palace in 2017 and offering Xi a tour of his grandmother’s village in southwest France in 2024.
Advertisement
The center-left candidate said Europe needed to “leverage its position of strength” when it comes to negotiations with China, with whom the bloc is trying to reduce its €1 billion-a-day trade deficit. He also said that the EU should stick by its goal of phasing out combustion engine vehicles by 2035 and invest in electric vehicles so as not to “abdicate” the sector to the Chinese.
Glucksmann is pitching himself to voters as a French president who will confront what he considers to be strongmen at the head of global powers like Xi, Putin and Trump.
With the presidential campaign under way, Glucksmann is also looking to strengthen his credentials on the domestic front. He said recent protests by high school students — which center, among other grievances, on the lack of substitute teachers in France, overcrowded classrooms and the run-down state of several schools — are “perfectly legitimate and justified.” He also argued that teachers are underpaid.

Rada proposed to legalize veterans' right to wear military uniform after discharge without special permits
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
16:05:55 EEST
22:05:55 KST

Members of Parliament propose that the Verkhovna Rada of Ukraine grant veterans the right to wear military uniforms after discharge from service without separate permits or additional approvals.
According to draft law No. 16130 dated October 7, the right will arise from the day of discharge from military service or, if the relevant status is granted later, from the day it is granted, taking into account the transitional provisions of the law.
Persons who already hold the relevant status on the day the law enters into force and have been discharged from military service will acquire this right automatically on the day it enters into force.
Information regarding this right is expected to be displayed in the veteran's electronic ID, including in the Diia application.
The Ministry of Veterans Affairs noted that male and female veterans will be able to wear the uniform of the military formation or state body where they served, or, if it no longer exists, the uniform of its successor.
At the same time, certain restrictions are provided: military uniforms and insignia cannot be used to impersonate an active-duty service member or to create a false impression of one's position or official authority.
"The fundamental approach of the draft law is to give veterans the opportunity to wear military uniforms without unnecessary bureaucracy while simultaneously preventing its use for deception," the ministry added.
The document was developed by a group of MPs with the participation of experts from the Ministry of Veterans Affairs.

Ukraine hits Yandex data centers; Zelensky claims fewer bots, hate speech online, but no evidence of a link
Users pointed to a drop in posts containing phrases like “Free Palestine” and “Genocide” on X after the strikes, but researchers said some of the graphs covered an unfinished day
Ukrainian drones hit three data centers belonging to Russian tech giant Yandex between October 8 and 11. As a result, President Volodymyr Zelensky now claims the strikes made social media a calmer place by knocking out bots.
The facilities were in the Ryazan, Kaluga and Vladimir regions. Yandex, often called “Russia’s Google,” said operations at its Vladimir data center, east of Moscow, were completely suspended after Sunday’s strike, and that it was working to restore connectivity. No one was hurt.
The earlier strikes disrupted payment services, websites, trading platforms, the company’s AI chatbot and smart home devices, and Yandex said it was “very difficult to predict” when they would be back online. The Ryazan site houses two of Yandex’s three supercomputers used to develop artificial intelligence.
Cloudflare Radar data showed automated traffic from Yandex’s network fell about 94% on Sunday compared with the second half of September. NetBlocks put the company’s cloud network connectivity at about 30% of normal levels and its main network at about 63%.
Kyiv said it was targeting sites that provide revenue for Moscow’s war machine and that repairs could force Russia to divert resources. Sunday’s strike came hours after US President Donald Trump warned Ukraine to “damn well stop” attacking Russia’s oil refineries so Moscow could release more diesel to the global market.

- Bipartisan senators demand Trump reverse Russian diesel deal, citing 2022 import ban | i24NEWS
Users on X pointed to graphs showing fewer posts containing phrases such as “Free Palestine” and “Genocide” after the strikes, along with more mentions of Zelensky and fewer posts backing Germany’s AfD party. Some read it as proof that Russian bot farms were behind part of the anti-Israeli discourse online.
There is no independent evidence of that.
Some of the graphs covered a day that had not yet ended, so the drop may partly reflect fewer hours of data. Much of Yandex’s automated traffic also comes from web crawlers, which count as bot traffic but don’t spread political messages.
The strikes come as both sides step up attacks on infrastructure in a war now in its fifth year. Russia has also hit Ukrainian data centers, causing internet outages and prompting some firms to move their servers abroad.

Iran sees ‘false flag’ operations after UK blames IRGC for airbase incident

Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
13:03:56 UTC

Iran sees ‘false flag’ operations after UK blames IRGC for airbase incident
Iran has been accused of being behind a plot against an airbase in the UK.
Tehran, Iran – Iran’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs has condemned the United Kingdom’s attribution of an alleged plot near a military airbase in the town of Fairford to the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), which it views as part of a greater Western effort.
British Prime Minister Andy Burnham told Parliament on Monday that the suspected plot last month against the Royal Air Force base was “highly likely to have been coordinated in Iran” and “almost certainly directed by Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard”.
Burnham promised action against what he described as Iran-linked “criminal networks” and their financing networks.
The UK announced sanctions against two Iranian nationals over alleged “hostile activity” at RAF Fairford in southern England.
It follows an incident around the base, which hosted US military aircraft, in the early hours of September 27, when five British men in their 20s suspected of “terrorism” and explosives offences were arrested. The men were not charged and were released on police bail. Another two men were also arrested and later released.
Information about a suspected security threat to RAF Fairford and the events remains opaque.
In a statement late Monday, the Iranian ministry described the UK’s claims of an Iranian role as “an ugly plot” that would also serve to “evade accountability for Britain’s participation” in the ongoing war against Iran on February 28.
It said the UK had failed to provide sufficient evidence to back its claims and rejected the accusations of Iranian involvement as a “clumsy false flag operation”.
“Britain’s track record of fabricating security claims against other countries, which have in some cases led to damaging tensions and conflicts in West Asia, is well known,” the ministry said, without elaborating.
British Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood said investigators assessed the coordinator to be a known individual based in Iran, although she did not name that person or disclose the supporting communications, financial records or other intelligence.
RAF Fairford is a prominent base for United States aircraft that have participated in the war on Iran, which began on February 28 following US and Israeli strikes that killed several Iranian leaders and officials, including Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei.
After news of the incident, the US withdrew approximately a dozen B-1 bombers from the Fairford base.
US media cited unnamed sources as alleging there was intelligence suggesting the bombers could run the risk of being hit by small drone attacks.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu publicly claimed at the start of October that his administration warned the UK about a plot.
“We gave the Brits the intel that there was going to be an attack, and it’s an Iranian-sponsored attack, and pretty much the next day they slapped sanctions on us,” he said during an interview with US broadcaster Fox News.
Netanyahu was criticising UK measures in response to the illegal expansion of Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank amid a diplomatic dispute.
Earlier this month, Tehran grouped the Fairford incident with allegations surrounding the Flydubai cockpit attack – which authorities in the United Arab Emirates claimed was a “suicide” mission to crash the plane at Israel’s Ben Gurion airport in Tel Aviv.
“I think even a schoolchild recognised how amateurishly it was designed,” Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baghaei said about the aircraft incident.
He also argued that such incidents were being manufactured to assign blame and justify a war facing public opposition in the US and elsewhere.
IRNA, the official news website of the Iranian government, argued in an analysis last week that the Western-led vote at the board of governors of the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) to refer the case of Iran’s nuclear programme to the United Nations Security Council could be classified as another attempt to pressure Iran to capitulate to US demands.
It said increasing reports over recent weeks attributing a major role and responsibility to Tehran for the considerable battlefield advances gained by the Houthis in Yemen pointed to a “plan to identify Iran as the main reason for insecurity” on the regional and global stage.
“The series of suspicious incidents recently, which have been attributed to Iran by the US president and senior officials without offering any evidence, appear to be a coordinated wave to smear Iran,” IRNA said.
But UK officials have advanced undeterred with measures against Iran in reaction to the Fairford incident.
Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband summoned Iran’s ambassador and sanctioned one person identified as an IRGC counterespionage chief, and another described as a facilitator for a criminal network. Measures included asset freezes and travel bans. But the two named men were not explicitly identified as Fairford’s organisers.
The UK government in July designated the IRGC as a “terrorist” organisation.
On Friday, the UK was among 32 countries, including Australia, Canada, France, Germany, and the US, to “condemn in the strongest terms Iran’s use of violent attacks, including the acts of lethal plotting, arson, sabotage, cyberattacks, and other hybrid activities against us and our partners”.
“We recognise the United Kingdom’s attribution of Iran’s involvement in the incident at RAF Fairford on 27 September. The UK has also concluded this event demonstrates the IRGC’s continued willingness to project hostile activity beyond its borders through covert networks and proxy actors,” they said in a joint statement.

Putin signs off on labor mobility pact with India
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
13:03:47 UTC
22:03:47 KST

Putin signs off on labor mobility pact with India
Russia has completed the ratification of its labor agreement with India, with President Vladimir Putin signing the document on Monday. The pact, which eases the procedures for hiring temporary employees, comes as Moscow seeks more Indian workers to address labor shortages.
The State Duma approved the pact on October 1, followed by the Federation Council a day later.
The agreement covers Indians working in Russia and Russians employed in India under employment or service contracts. It also applies to full-time students taking temporary jobs outside their studies.
“The agreement is clearly significant for Russia as there is a need for manpower, both qualified and unqualified,” a research fellow at the Center of the Indo-Pacific Region, Institute of World Economy and International Relations of the Russian Academy of Sciences, Gleb Makarevich, told RT. “For India, it creates opportunities to export labor, increase remittance inflows, and somewhat ease the social burden on the country’s broader system of governance.” 
“With this agreement we can clearly see the institutionalization of the cooperation on labor mobility between the two countries, and we can expect a further increase in the number of Indian workers going to Russia,” he added.
Russian authorities have estimated an immediate shortage of at least 2.3 million workers in the country. Sberbank, its largest bank, has called for easier entry procedures for Indian workers to help address shortages in the construction industry.
"Russia is facing a labour shortage, which has become the main factor holding back economic development,” researchers at the India Lab at the Moscow School of Management, Igor Gundobin and Lydia Kulik, wrote in a report titled ‘Human Capital in India and Russia: In Search for Complementarity’.
“India sees itself as a talent pool for the global economy for the coming decades and is actively pursuing the opportunities for educational and labour migration with all its key partners.
“The strategies of India and Russia are thus complementary, and their demographic structures are mutually reinforcing,” they added.
Moscow has agreed to accept around 70,000 skilled Indian workers in 2026, Indian Foreign Minister S. Jaishankar told a parliamentary panel earlier this month.
The labor agreement was signed in New Delhi last December during Putin’s visit to India. The two countries also signed a separate accord to combat irregular migration and approved a program to expand economic cooperation through 2030.
Workers will still need employment permits and must work in the jobs for which those permits were issued. The agreement requires foreign employees to receive pay and working conditions no less favorable than those offered to local workers in comparable positions.
Employees laid off because of business closures or staff reductions will be entitled to compensation under local laws. Pension, social security, and medical insurance provisions will also be governed by host-country legislation and applicable bilateral agreements.
The agreement will formally take effect once both governments complete the required domestic procedures and exchange written notifications.

Iran threatens Gulf data centres: How exposed is the region’s internet?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
13:03:33 UTC
22:03:33 KST

Iran threatens Gulf data centres: How exposed is the region’s internet?
Iran has warned that cables and data centres in the region could be attacked, as Houthi allies hold internet chokepoint.
Iran’s security chief, Mohsen Rezaei, has warned that cables, data centres and artificial intelligence (AI) facilities across the region could be attacked if war with the United States erupts again.
The warning comes as the capture of Yemeni territory along the Red Sea coastline last month by the Iran-backed Houthis has raised concerns over the safety of internet cables linking Europe and Asia. Fierce fighting is under way between Yemen’s internationally recognised government and the Houthis at several locations, including Bab al-Mandeb, through which nearly one-fifth of global internet traffic passes.
Data centres and US business interests were hit in Bahrain and the United Arab Emirates during the US-Israel war on Iran. Tehran said these attacks were in response to US attacks on Iranian civilian installations.
Active hostilities have largely ended since the June memorandum of understanding between Iran and the US, but attacks on ships passing through the global oil chokepoint – the Strait of Hormuz – have continued.
So how exposed is the region’s internet? Here’s what you need to know:
Why are data centres and internet cables vulnerable?
Because so much data travels through a few narrow routes.
More than 90 percent of data capacity between Europe and Asia passes through cables under the Red Sea, according to estimates by the research firm TeleGeography.
They enter the sea through Bab al-Mandeb, a strait about 26km (16 miles) wide at its narrowest, one of the busiest maritime routes connecting Europe to Asia.
Cables can be cut by anchors or sabotage, and repairs in a war zone need permits and safety guarantees.
Data centres, which run banking apps and cloud services, are large, fixed targets.
“An attack does not necessarily need to destroy the servers themselves to render an entire facility inoperable,” Andreas Krieg, a senior lecturer in security studies at King’s College London, told Al Jazeera.
Data centres depend on uninterrupted electricity, cooling and telecommunications, he said, while undersea cables “are difficult to protect continuously and disruption can affect several countries simultaneously”.
Has Iran threatened to attack data centres and cables?
Yes, repeatedly since the war began in February.
On March 11, the semi-official Tasnim news agency said Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) has published a list of “Iran’s new targets”, including cloud infrastructure belonging to Google, Microsoft and Oracle in Israel and some Gulf states.
That same month, the IRGC named 17 US firms in a Telegram post, including Google, Meta, and Apple, as well as the Emirati AI company G42 as potential targets.
Krieg said he would take Rezaei’s threat seriously, but drew a distinction between Iran’s ability to cause significant disruption and its ability “to systematically destroy the Gulf’s digital infrastructure”.
“What makes Mohsen Rezaei’s warning particularly significant is that he is not simply threatening another set of targets,” he said. “He is identifying a new category of strategic infrastructure that connects Gulf economic diversification directly to American technological power.”
He described the warning as “fundamentally about deterrence”, aimed “as much at Abu Dhabi, Riyadh and Doha as at Washington”, giving Gulf governments a reason to discourage another US offensive.
Have tech infrastructure and cables been attacked before?
Yes.
In March, Amazon Web Services (AWS) said two of its facilities in the UAE were “directly struck” by drones, while a strike near one in Bahrain “caused physical impact to our infrastructure”.
Abu Dhabi Commercial Bank said its app was unavailable due to a region-wide IT disruption, though it did not directly link this to AWS.
In September, AWS said it could not restore several sites in Bahrain and one in the UAE.
Under the sea, three cables were damaged in February 2024, most likely by the dragging anchor of the Rubymar, a cargo ship disabled by a Houthi missile, according to the industry consensus reported by Data Center Dynamics, with repairs taking months.
In September 2025, two cables were cut near Jeddah, slowing internet access across the Middle East and South Asia. No cause has been confirmed.
The March attacks “exposed the limits of treating commercial infrastructure as something that automatically benefits from national air defence”, Krieg said.
“Gulf militaries can intercept most incoming threats, but even a small number of successful strikes can produce disproportionate economic consequences,” he said, adding that relatively cheap drones can threaten facilities holding billions of dollars’ worth of equipment.
Have the Houthis attacked undersea cables?
Not directly, as far as is known, and the group has denied causing the 2024 damage.
But in mid-September, the Houthis seized the port of Mocha and territory around Bab al-Mandeb.
On September 11, they reached Mayyun Island, which splits the strait in two.
On October 5, Yemen’s internationally recognised government said it had retaken Mocha and positions near the strait. The Houthis denied it.
Are there alternatives to the Red Sea?
Some, but they cost more and are still being built.
On September 10, Iraq signed a contract with Qatar’s Ooredoo to carry data from the Gulf to Europe across its territory, the Ministry of Communications said in a statement.
Minister Mustafa Jabar Sanad told the Iraqi News Agency the underground cable runs from al-Faw to Rabia near Turkiye’s border.
On October 7, Ooredoo’s international arm agreed to buy fibre from Iraq’s iQ Networks to extend the route towards Turkiye, subject to government approval.
Microsoft said in September it would invest more than $400m in subsea and land connectivity across the Middle East by 2030, in a blog post.
The technology news site Rest of World reported on October 7, citing an unnamed source, that Google and Meta had begun sending some traffic through Iraq.
Neither company has responded to Al Jazeera’s request for comment.
Krieg said genuine resilience would require geographical redundancy, “potentially including facilities outside the Gulf”.
“That creates a tension between digital sovereignty and operational security,” he said, as Gulf governments have invested heavily in keeping sensitive data and computing within their own borders.
How will it affect the Gulf’s tech hub ambitions?
Investment continues, but the war has already taken a toll on the sector. Gulf states have staked their post-oil economies on technology.
In Abu Dhabi, the Emirati firm G42 is building Stargate UAE with OpenAI, Nvidia and others.
It sits within a planned 5-gigawatt UAE-US AI campus.
Saudi Arabia’s Public Investment Fund launched Humain, an AI company chaired by Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, in May 2025 to build data centres and an Arabic-language AI model, the Saudi Press Agency reported.
Qatar’s sovereign wealth fund joined the US investor Blue Owl in a $3bn data centre push in September 2025.
In September, Microsoft said it would invest more than $10bn in Kuwait, Qatar, Saudi Arabia and the UAE through 2030, with a new focus on “digital resilience”, in a blog post.
But AWS said it had “exhausted every option” to restore some data hosted in Bahrain.
Krieg said the threats would not “fundamentally reverse” Gulf ambitions, but would “change the economics and geography of AI investment”.
“The Gulf has traditionally sold itself as a stable environment in an unstable region. The war has challenged that proposition,” he said.
The UAE is particularly exposed, he said, because its AI strategy is “deeply integrated with American technology companies”, making Emirati infrastructure “more attractive as a target for Iran”. Qatar, with its diplomatic ties to Tehran, is “somewhat better positioned politically”.
“In many ways, Iran is threatening to do to the Gulf’s emerging digital economy what it has already done to its maritime economy,” Krieg said – to “make reliability itself a geopolitical bargaining chip”.

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz pledged Tuesday to press ahead with social security reforms despite record-low approval ratings and disagreements within his governing coalition.
Speaking at the Employers’ Day conference in Berlin, Merz warned that Germany’s “social security systems are reaching the limits of their financial sustainability.”
He said the reform effort coincided with “multiple crises,” including the war in Ukraine, the Gulf conflict, rising oil prices and US tariffs.
“In this situation, we are trying to implement reforms that have been neglected, in some cases for decades,” he said. “We must look beyond this period of multiple crises. We must identify the structural imbalances, and we must find structural solutions. The long-term growth potential of our economy must increase.”
Merz acknowledged the demands that simultaneous changes to Germany’s social security systems would place on the public.
“Never before have all of our social security systems been reformed at the same time,” he said. “I am grateful that a large majority is at least aware of the need for this modernization and also accepts it. We want to get this done in a way that is equally fair and equally sound for everyone.”
An ARD-DeutschlandTrend poll conducted Sept. 28-30 found that just 10% of eligible voters were satisfied with Merz’s performance, while 88% were dissatisfied. It was the lowest satisfaction rating for a chancellor recorded by the survey.
However, a separate September poll for ZDF found that 85% considered fundamental reforms important, even if they involved financial burdens and cuts.
Despite his center-right Christian Democrats (CDU) witnessing a series of losses in state elections last month, Merz has vowed to push ahead with the plans amid some wavering from his Social Democrat (SPD) coalition partners.
In particular, the centre-left SPD is seeking to negotiate over a new rule banning early retirement without deductions for workers with 45 years of social security contributions – a position that Merz has so far refused to soften.
"I will continue to fight to ensure that, despite occasional differences of opinion within the government, the right course of action and the necessary steps always prevail," Merz said.

Interns paid as little as 500 euros a month, while unpaid placements become more common
Finland
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
16:02:12 EEST
22:02:12 KST

Duunitori analysed more than 14,000 internship advertisements published on its service for Yle, covering the period from 1 January 2023 to 28 September 2026.
In 52 percent of the advertisements, employers did not disclose the salary or state whether the internship was unpaid.
The proportion of advertisements explicitly offering unpaid internships also increased. Between January and September in 2023 and 2024, unpaid positions accounted for 4.5 percent of advertisements. For the same period in 2025 and 2026, the figure rose to 7.3 percent.
Unpaid internships were particularly common in human resources and recruitment, as well as marketing and communications.
Public-sector employers were significantly more likely to disclose internship salaries and offer paid internships.
Among advertisements that disclosed a monthly salary, the most common range was between 1,500 - 2,000 euros.
"We would certainly have a lot of people coming to us even without compensation"
Insurance company Lähi-Tapiola is advertising a full-time internship in debt collection services on Duunitori. The fixed-term position lasts at least three months, is linked to the applicant’s studies and starts in November. The advertised salary is 500 euros a month.
Susa Nikula, Director of People and Culture at Lähi-Tapiola, says the company has paid interns such salary for several years.
"We would certainly have a lot of people coming to us even without compensation, because the internship is part of their studies and young people need it. However, it is good to pay some kind of salary for the internship."
The company has also considered whether the amount is sufficient.
"We have sometimes wondered whether 500 euros is too little. On the other hand, I know companies that take interns on for free," Nikula added.
Lähi-Tapiola takes on around 150 interns across Finland during the winter season.
Applicants want greater transparency
Lotta Viljamaa, a recruitment expert at Duunitori, says the lack of salary information is a broader problem in job advertisements, not just those for internships.
"Of course, not mentioning the salary is a fairly big problem in job advertisements. Applicants then don’t know what they will be paid or what they are applying for," Viljamaa says.
She says this partly reflects the fact that people in Finland do not tend to discuss salaries very openly.
Those looking for internships want greater transparency, Viljamaa says. Advertisements should make clear whether a position is paid and, if so, how much it pays.
In September, Yle reported on a Ukrainian student who had spent a year and a half looking for an internship. Finding placements has become more difficult in some fields, including business.
Nikula says Lähi-Tapiola has also seen increased competition for internships and jobs.
"More people are applying for internships and jobs now than before. It’s always great that there is interest and that we are able to offer internship positions," she says.
