Lake Tuzkan – life and tourism around Jizzakh’s desert lakes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
13:00:55 UTC
22:00:55 KST

Lake Tuzkan brings fishing, tourism and recreation to the dry landscape of Jizzakh, as new transport links are expected to make the area easier to reach.
The landscape of Jizzakh region changes quickly. Dry earth and sandy stretches dominate much of the Mirzachul area, until a large body of water appears on the horizon.
Lake Tuzkan is part of the Aydar-Arnasay lake system, one of the largest inland water areas in Uzbekistan. Its setting, between the Hungry Steppe and the Kyzylkum Desert, gives the lake a distinctive place in the region.
For visitors, the contrast with the surrounding landscape is part of the attraction. For local communities, the lakes have a more practical role, providing livelihoods through fishing, tourism and other activities.
A lake in the middle of the steppe
Tuzkan is one of Uzbekistan’s largest lakes and has long been connected with life in the surrounding communities.
Local residents depend on fishing, while tourism has created another source of income. Visitors come for time by the water, fishing and recreation, while some also seek the mineral-rich waters of Tuzkan for what they describe as health and wellness benefits.
Tourist Ulugbek Musulmonov says the natural environment was one of the main reasons for his visit.
“Our main reason for coming here is the natural environment and the health benefits of Tuzkan lake,” he says, adding that some visitors come with the hope of improving particular health conditions.
The lake is also part of the wider Aydar-Arnasay system, where fishing remains an important economic activity for communities living nearby.
The surrounding area has gradually developed facilities for visitors, creating a tourism economy alongside traditional activities connected with the lakes.
Tourism takes hold by the water
On the shore of neighbouring Lake Aydarkul, Aydarkul resort has developed accommodation and recreation facilities for visitors.
The resort has 225 rooms and can accommodate up to 600 guests. Its facilities include conventional rooms, capsule-style accommodation, restaurants, a beach and shaded outdoor platforms known locally as tapchans, as well as boats and other water activities.
Operations manager Jamshid Qarshiboyev says the resort received large numbers of visitors during the summer season, including tourists from Uzbekistan, Russia and Kazakhstan.
Weekend events, including festivals and concerts, have become part of the resort's programme. Swimming, boating and time on the beach are among the main activities available to guests.
The resort also has a medical centre offering treatments such as massage and hydromassage. Guests staying at the resort can receive one complimentary treatment as part of their accommodation package.
The resort's location beside Aydarkul also gives visitors access to Tuzkan, where the waters are saltier and mineral-rich.
Fishing remains another attraction. It is restricted during certain periods of the year, but resumes after the closed season.
For some guests, a visit that begins as a day trip becomes an overnight stay.
A changing destination
The development of tourism around the lakes is also changing the way visitors reach the area.
A new airport has been developed at Arnasoy, near the lakes, while construction of a railway line from Do‘stlik towards the Aydar-Arnasay lake system began in 2026. The projects are intended to improve access for visitors from Uzbekistan and abroad.
The development could give the lake area a larger role in regional tourism, particularly for visitors already travelling through Uzbekistan's better-known historic destinations.
For Ahmad Jabir Abdullah Mohammed Al Harbi, a visitor from the United Arab Emirates, the new airport could help introduce the area to a wider international audience.
He describes the lakeside as a place for quiet and relaxation and says he would recommend it to people from his home country and elsewhere.
The area is still developing, however, and some planned facilities have yet to be completed.
Keeping visitors safe
As visitor numbers increase, safety has become another part of managing the recreation area.
The Aydar-Arnasoy recreation area has operated since November 2025, with safe tourism officers working around the clock.
Tourism police officer Meyirbek Amirxanov says the area can receive between 6,000 and 7,000 visitors on a Saturday or Sunday.
Surveillance cameras cover the recreation area and are connected to the Ministry of Internal Affairs’ Qalqon security-monitoring system.
The most common requests involve children who become separated from their families and visitors who lose personal belongings. Amirxanov says officers receive around five or six such requests on an average day and deal with them as they arise.
With more visitors expected as transport links improve, managing large crowds will remain an important part of the area's development.
A landscape shaped by water
The history of Tuzkan goes beyond its growing tourism industry.
The lake is a natural feature, but the wider landscape has also been affected by human activity. Irrigation and water-management projects during the 20th century changed the region's hydrology and contributed to the formation of the wider Aydar-Arnasay lake system.
Today, the result is an unusual landscape: large expanses of water surrounded by dry steppe and desert.
Along the shores, recreation areas have introduced another layer of activity. Families gather for weekends, visitors swim and fish, and resorts provide accommodation and organised entertainment.
For local communities, the lakes remain connected to everyday economic life. For visitors, they offer a different experience of Jizzakh, away from the region's more familiar image of open steppe.
The planned transport links are expected to bring more visitors to the lakes once completed.
The landscape itself remains the main attraction: water stretching towards the horizon, with the dry plains and desert beyond it.

Ketamine and psychedelics share a surprising link to the immune system
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
13:00:30 UTC
22:00:30 KST

A recent study found that rapid-acting antidepressants like ketamine and psychedelics may relieve depression by regulating specific immune system pathways in the body and brain. The research suggests that rebalancing a precise set of immune signaling molecules can predict how well a patient will respond to treatment. These findings were published in the journal Molecular Psychiatry.
Standard antidepressants often take weeks to relieve symptoms of major depressive disorder. In contrast, compounds such as ketamine and psilocybin act within hours, providing rapid relief for patients with treatment-resistant depression. Despite their rapid effects, these therapies present unique challenges.
Ketamine’s benefits often fade within a few weeks, requiring repeated treatments. Meanwhile, therapies involving psychedelics require extensive clinical supervision and psychological support. Researchers want to understand the exact biological mechanisms that make these drugs work so quickly, hoping to develop new therapies without these drawbacks.
Ketamine and psychedelics target entirely different receptors in the brain. Ketamine blocks a receptor called NMDA, while classic psychedelics like psilocybin and LSD stimulate a specific serotonin receptor. Because both classes of drugs produce rapid antidepressant effects, researchers suspect they eventually activate the same downstream molecular pathways inside the cells.
Clinical depression is associated with chronic, low-grade inflammation throughout the body. Fast-acting antidepressants also activate a cellular pathway known as mTOR, which controls both structural changes in the brain and immune cell metabolism. A team of scientists led by Gregory H. Jones, a researcher at the National Institute of Mental Health and The University of Texas MD Anderson Cancer Center, set out to identify these shared biological responses.
The researchers first examined lab-grown human brain cells, known as induced pluripotent stem cells. These are adult cells that have been reprogrammed into an embryonic-like state and then coaxed into becoming brain cells. The team treated these specialized cells with either ketamine, a ketamine byproduct called HNK, LSD, or psilocybin.
After treating the cells, the scientists analyzed which genes were turned on or off by each drug. To see if these genetic changes matched biological activity in humans, the researchers compared the cell data with spinal fluid samples. These samples were previously collected from healthy volunteers who had received intravenous ketamine.
By comparing the two datasets, the team found 103 proteins that were altered by ketamine in the spinal fluid and also changed by at least one of the drugs in the lab-grown cells. Very few of these proteins were exclusive to ketamine and its byproduct; 86 percent were also altered by at least one of the psychedelics. When the team mapped how these proteins interact, they discovered two distinct functional modules.
The primary module was a highly connected network centered around immune system signaling. Two immune molecules, interleukin-15 and monocyte chemoattractant protein-1, emerged as central hubs in this network. Interleukin-15 helps regulate the body’s defense cells, while monocyte chemoattractant protein-1 directs immune cells to areas of inflammation.
A secondary module contained proteins related to insulin signaling and the brain’s ability to rewire its connections. This dual structure suggested that immune signaling might direct the broader brain changes caused by these fast-acting drugs.
To test whether these immune signals apply to real-world depression treatment, the researchers analyzed data from a clinical trial. The trial included 39 participants with treatment-resistant depression and 25 healthy volunteers. Each person received a single intravenous dose of ketamine or a placebo.
The research team looked at gene expression in the participants’ blood before and after treatment. Before receiving ketamine, patients who eventually responded well to the drug showed lower interleukin-15 activity than those who did not respond. These responders also showed higher activity in signaling pathways for B-cells, a type of white blood cell that produces antibodies.
Four hours after the ketamine infusion, this pattern reversed in the responders. Their interleukin-15 activity increased, while their B-cell signaling decreased. The researchers used computational tools to estimate changes in specific blood cell types, finding that proportions of natural killer T-cells also shifted after treatment.
Next, the researchers measured the actual levels of immune proteins circulating in the participants’ blood plasma. They focused on a molecule called interleukin-7, which acts as a primary driver of B-cell development. They compared these interleukin-7 levels to brain wave activity measured by magnetoencephalography, a highly sensitive neuroimaging technique.
The team looked specifically at gamma power, a measure of high-frequency brain wave activity that often changes in response to rapid-acting antidepressants. Before treatment, higher levels of circulating interleukin-7 strongly correlated with higher gamma brain wave power in patients with depression. This relationship was particularly strong in deep brain regions like the thalamus and striatum.
Following the ketamine treatment, this relationship inverted. Higher interleukin-7 levels became associated with reduced gamma power in a collection of brain regions called the default mode network. The default mode network is typically active when a person is resting or wandering in thought, and it is often hyperactive in depressed patients.
The team also looked at the ratio of different immune molecules to see if they could predict treatment success. They found that a higher starting ratio of monocyte chemoattractant protein-1 to interleukin-7 predicted a worse response to ketamine. Conversely, a higher ratio of two other immune proteins, interleukin-4 and interferon-gamma, predicted a better antidepressant response.
The researchers noted several limitations to their work. The lab-grown brain cells were derived entirely from female donors, and the spinal fluid samples came exclusively from healthy volunteers. This demographic limitation means the results might not fully represent how these drugs affect the broader population or people with clinical depression.
The data collection in the human trial also featured mismatched timing across different biological measurements. Blood samples were drawn four hours after the ketamine infusion, while brain imaging occurred six to nine hours post-infusion. This difference in timing could complicate how the immune and brain wave changes relate to each other over time.
The findings are primarily exploratory and serve to generate hypotheses for future testing. Larger, independent studies will be necessary to confirm if modulating these specific immune pathways can reliably treat depression. Direct validation in human subjects could eventually lead to therapies that mimic the rapid effects of ketamine without the associated side effects.
The study, “Convergent neuroimmune signaling underlying rapid antidepressant response to ketamine and psychedelics,” was authored by Gregory H. Jones, Jessica R. Gilbert, Jenessa N. Johnston, Nirmala Akula, Anton Schulmann, Miranda Arakelian, Shiyong Peng, Peixiong Yuan, Ewurakua A. Winful, Mani Yavi, Brandi Quintanilla, Abdel Elkahloun, Ruin Moaddel, Ioline D. Henter, Dede Greenstein, Rodrigo Machado-Vieira, Christopher M. Bartley, Bashkim Kadriu, Moran Amit, Katy Rezvani, Mark D. Kvarta, Francis J. McMahon, and Carlos A. Zarate Jr.

Apple Reboots Its Smart-Home Strategy With New Hardware and a ‘Home Collection’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
13:00:00 UTC
22:00:00 KST

Apple has lagged in the smart home race, which Amazon and Google have dominated for a decade with Alexa and Google Assistant (now Gemini), respectively.
But after finally revamping Siri AI this year and turning the butt-of-the-joke voice assistant into a more competitive companion—paired with a more mature Matter-supported ecosystem of smart home gadgets—Apple now has the brains to power the home system it has always envisioned.
That starts with three new devices: the Apple HomeView, the company's first smart display; the HomePod Mini 2 smart speaker; and the fourth-generation Apple TV 4K.
Apple announced the products at a media-only event in New York City, and it also revealed a slew of new smart-home gadgets made in collaboration with LG and Schneider Electric, including a video doorbell, thermostats, and security cameras.
Here's everything you need to know.
The Apple HomeView
The cornerstone of Apple's latest smart-home push is the Apple HomeView, a countertop gadget made up of a 7-inch square display resting on a speaker base. It operates like smart displays we've seen from Amazon and Google, but it’s an entirely new device category for Apple.
It runs what Apple calls “HomeView Software,” so while the interface may resemble an iPhone or iPad, the HomeView runs a stand-alone operating system and lacks access to the App Store. As an alternative, Apple has curated a selection of apps for the system, including Messages, Safari, and FaceTime, alongside select third-party media apps like Spotify. (If an app developer has made an app for the CarPlay standard and it's installed on your iPhone, that app can also populate on the HomeView.)
Siri AI powers the core experience, which Apple revamped this year in iOS 27. Now, Siri can answer broad questions like Gemini or ChatGPT, and it can provide personalized answers; the same personal context Siri has cataloged on your iPhone is accessible to the HomeView. Ask it to open the recipe your friend Alex messaged about, or add a dentist appointment to the family calendar, and it can handle it.
Apple's HomeView supports up to six iCloud profiles, and each person can set up a custom view only visible to them once the device’s camera detects their face. Yes, there’s a camera on the HomeView. The computer vision trick where the HomeView displays a custom view for a specific individual when they approach it only works if the person’s iPhone is on the same Wi-Fi network and was recently unlocked. You need an iPhone with Apple Intelligence support (iPhone 15 Pro or newer) to get the most out of the device; you can't set it up with an iPad.
We have a separate story with more details if you'd like to read more about the HomeView, which is available for preorder now and goes on sale November 13 in the US, UK, Australia, Canada, New Zealand, India, Singapore, and South Africa. It costs $299.
The Apple Home Collection
One of the biggest problems with Apple's smart-home presence is its relatively meager HomeKit device ecosystem, especially compared to the many smart home devices that can be controlled by Amazon and Google’s platforms. The Matter standard—which allows supported devices like smart bulbs, smart switches, and smart shades to interact with any connected home platform—has helped expand HomeKit support. But Apple is also nudging the ecosystem along with the “Apple Home Collection.”
This new selection of smart-home hardware designed in collaboration with LG and Schneider Electric includes the LG Indoor Camera Plug-In ($200), LG Outdoor Cam Plug-In ($300), LG Video Doorbell ($250), LG Smart Deadbolt Lock ($350), LG Smart Thermostat ($200), LG Temperature Sensor ($40), Schneider Home Smart Thermostat ($200), and Schneider Home Room Sensor ($40).
These devices connect to the Apple Home app automatically when you install them, and all of them are controllable through Apple’s products; you don't need separate LG or Schneider accounts or multiple apps.
I got a brief look at some of them in action. The LG Indoor Camera tilts downward when it detects you're home to give you some added privacy, though there's no privacy shutter to block the camera itself. The LG Deadbolt can unlock automatically as you approach by sensing your iPhone or Apple Watch; there's a nice green LED animation that circles the lock to show you when it unlocks. The LG Video Doorbell has two cameras: one to see who is at the door, and one to monitor any packages left at your door.
The LG Outdoor Camera has a floodlight upgrade ($400) that will automatically activate when it detects motion. With the right iCloud+ subscription, you can enable smart video descriptions that send alerts to tell you who is outside (it can recognize faces), that your pet has been spotted in the yard, or that a package has been dropped off.
The products in the Apple Home Collection will be available in December, with the security cameras launching in the UK, US, and Canada. The thermostats and door lock meet North American standards, so Apple is only selling them in the US and Canada.
The HomePod Mini 2
Apple has decided not to launch a successor to the flagship 2023 HomePod 2 smart speaker—maybe it thinks the HomeView, which is essentially a speaker with a screen on it, would cannibalize sales. Instead, it has updated the smaller, cheaper sibling: Say hello to the HomePod Mini 2.
The Mini 2 costs $149, with preorders open now and official sales kicking off October 30. That's a $50 price bump from the original HomePod Mini, though only $30 more if you factor in Apple's recent price hike due to the ongoing memory crisis.
Oddly enough, the HomePod Mini 2 will not have the new Siri AI experience out of the box—that will arrive later on via a software update (and yes, you will need an Apple Intelligence-enabled iPhone to use Siri AI on the HomePod Mini 2). It's otherwise a minor hardware update, resembling the existing HomePod Mini but in new colors: green, white, midnight, pink, and black.
One new feature is Sound Glow—the lights on top of the HomePod Mini 2 will match the album artwork colors of whatever song is playing. It also works with soundscapes, so if you ask Siri to play rain sounds, the lights will display a pitter-patter animation like raindrops falling on a surface.
You can color-match the HomePod Mini 2 to the iMac; pair two of the devices and use them as the default speakers for Apple's all-in-one computer. Apple's S10 chip powers the speaker, the very same processor that debuted on the Apple Watch Series 10.
The Apple TV 4K
Four years since the last Apple TV 4K, Apple finally has a successor. But what may surprise you the most about the fourth-gen streaming box isn't the hardware or features; it's the price: $299.
Apple raised prices on its products earlier this year, but this is a whopping $170 increase for the Apple TV, though this model has Wi-Fi and Ethernet and starts with 128 GB of storage instead of 64 GB on the last version. Preorders are live now, and it ships November 13.
Once again, Siri AI is the star of the show, as Apple touts the ability to ask the assistant for recommendations or play “that show my friend Alinda recommended,” leveraging the personal context from your iPhone. The hardware has three far-field microphones, letting it pick up your voice easily when you're on the couch, even when the TV is playing content. The A19 chip sits inside, which Apple first introduced on the iPhone 17.
If you have ever lost your TV remote, you might be more excited that the new Apple TV 4K remote has built-in Find My support. That means you can ping it in the Find My app or ask Siri for its location, and the familiar AirTag chime will play through the remote's speakers. (It supports ultra-wideband, so you can use Apple's precision-finding mode to locate it between the couch cushions.) The remote is backward compatible, so you don't need the fourth-gen Apple TV 4K if you buy the new remote as a replacement for an older Apple TV.
You can also pair four second-gen HomePod speakers to the new Apple TV 4K, setting two in front of you and two behind you for a surround-sound home theater experience. I heard this in action with two HomePod 2 speakers by the TV and two HomePod Mini 2 models behind the couch—it really does make whatever you’re watching feel more immersive. The speakers calibrate automatically to give you the best sound for your room.
Apple calls this one of the easiest ways to set up a home theater. That four-speaker arrangement would cost you $1,000, but that’s a decent price for a wireless surround-sound system that pairs with all of your Apple products. Just know the surround-sound capability is restricted to specific HomePod models. You're out of luck if you have the original 2017 HomePod or the first-gen HomePod Mini.
The smart-home revamp comes as Amazon and Google both zhuzh their ecosystems by replacing their aging assistants with Alexa+ and Gemini, powered by large language models, which you can think of as a soft reboot. That timing might work in Apple's favor, according to Jitesh Ubrani, director of Consumer Devices Research at IDC.
“Amazon and Google have both reset their platforms with Alexa+ and Gemini, but even their rollouts have been slow,” Ubrani writes in a statement to WIRED. “That means Apple is bringing Siri AI to the home at a point when the competition hasn’t pulled far ahead.”
Apple may finally have the hardware in place, but Siri AI has to prove it belongs in the room.

Why Pakistan Tested an Extended Range Version of the Fatah-IV
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
13:00:00 UTC
22:00:00 KST

On October 6, Pakistan tested an extended range (ER) version of the Fatah-IV ground-launched cruise missile. This was the third launch of the Fatah-IV missile system, the last having been conducted in May 2026. The latest test is unique compared to the first two, because this time the missile had a reported range of more than 750 kilometers.
The Fatah-IV is a byproduct of the 2025 India-Pakistan clashes. The missile was first unveiled publicly during Pakistan’s Independence Day event on August 14, 2025. It features terrain-hugging flight capability intended to reduce radar detection, has a maximum speed of Mach 0.7, and carries a 330 kilogram blast-fragmentation explosive warhead.
The ER version appears to have wings positioned on the underbelly, not in the center of the missile body, as was the case in its earlier version. The ER missile also appears slightly larger to store more fuel, allowing it to cover a longer distance than its reported 750 km range. Based on available imagery, the Fatah-IV ER could have a range of around 1,000 km.
What are the key rationales behind Pakistan testing the ER version of Fatah-IV? There seem to be quite a number of possibilities. First, Pakistan is likely looking to counter the Indian Air Force’s (IAF) future strategy of launching air-launched missiles from standoff ranges. It remains a strong possibility that the IAF will move its assets to rear bases in the next encounter with the Pakistan Air Force (PAF) because the IAF does not want to repeat what happened on the night of May 6-7, 2025, when it lost multiple jets in air-to-air engagement with the PAF. Therefore, the IAF will likely launch payloads from a distance beyond the range of both PAF air-to-air missiles and Pakistan’s long-range land-based missile defenses.
The IAF will be able to conduct such strikes in the future because the Indian government has already sanctioned an increase in range of the BrahMos supersonic cruise missile, with reports estimating the new range to be around 800 km. This posed a serious challenge to Pakistan because the Taimoor air-launched cruise missile and other conventional systems available in the country’s arsenal remained inadequate to threaten IAF installations located deep inside mainland India. The ER Fatah-IV will fill this gap by enabling Pakistan to strike radars and the fighter jet fleet of the IAF deployed at bases far away from Pakistan’s border.
Second, India’s key metropolitan cities and commercial hubs are located in southern and central India, far away from Pakistan’s border. By contrast, Pakistan’s major urban hubs are all located relatively close to India. This previously provided New Delhi an advantage over Islamabad, as India could target Pakistan’s commercial hubs with conventional munitions. However, with the introduction of the Fatah-IV, India’s main business metropolis, Mumbai, from now on will come within range of Pakistan’s conventional strike force, thus posing a credible threat to the Indian business capital.
The ER Fatah-IV will allow Islamabad to dissuade India from launching conventional counter-value strikes against Pakistan’s key cities because New Delhi’s own central commercial hub can be targeted in a similar manner. India is likely to remain dissuaded from approaching such a path in a limited confrontation with Pakistan because missiles striking Mumbai will not only create negative international headlines but also damage the morale of the people and investors in India.
Third, in the post-Operation Sindoor era, the Indian military ordered more air defense systems including the S-400, tested new ones like the Kusha long-range interceptor, and announced the integration of all of them under the aegis of Mission Sudarshan Chakra to formulate an impenetrable missile defense shield. To penetrate such a shield and strike targets at longer range, Pakistan will need systems to avoid radar detection. The Fatah-IV fulfills this requirement, thus posing a credible threat to Indian military installations and dissuading New Delhi from ordering pre-emptive military strikes against Pakistan.
Pakistan’s official policy eschews any arms race. The ultimate objective behind the development of the ER Fatah-IV is to strengthen Pakistan’s conventional deterrence vis-à-vis India. The development of the Fatah-IV did not occur in a vacuum; it became a compulsion after India launched “unprovoked” attacks against multiple locations inside Pakistan in May last year. The episode was the turning point for Pakistan. It led to the introduction of the conventionally armed Fatah-IV cruise missile because Islamabad wants to further reinforce its conventional counterforce strike capabilities.
The development of one system does not guarantee deterrence; however, the intent and posturing matter. By introducing the Fatah-IV and continuously developing it, Islamabad is signaling to New Delhi that the old days are gone now. Indian military installations located deep inside the country are no longer safe from Pakistan’s conventional missile force.
The ER Fatah-IV exists to protect Pakistan’s national security at a time when India believes that territorial victory remains the ultimate goal in modern conflict, as evident from the recent statement of India’s army chief General Dhiraj Seth. In the presence of such a belligerent mindset of the adversary, it becomes a compulsion for the other side to take appropriate defensive measures. The Fatah-IV is one such measure taken by Pakistan to boost the country’s defense and to protect its territorial sovereignty.

Quick hits: Carey's classic starts the rot and Hoff finishes it off
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
12:58:49 UTC
21:58:49 KST

Alex Carey breaks the game open with a spectacular take, Pat Cummins confuses Beau Webster for Muttiah Muralitharan, and Josh Hazlewood's career-best wins it for Australia.
Here are the quick hits from the final day of the first Test between Australia and South Africa.
1. Smith returns to the field
After not taking to the field after Pat Cummins's tea time declaration on day four, there were serious concerns that Australia would have to push for victory without the fielding brilliance of Steve Smith.
The Australia vice-captain was hit in the helmet by an Anrich Nortje bouncer while batting and was held back over fears of a delayed concussion.
But Australian fans would have been delighted to have seen Smith out on the field and warming up ahead of the final day's play, with the slipper supreme right to re-assume his role in the cordon.
Speaking on Fox Cricket, Mitch Starc said Smith appeared to have "the light back in him" and he certainly seemed to as he snared a sharp chance at first slip, his fifth of the match, to get rid Kyle Verreynne in the 67th over.
2. Carey's screamer starts the rot
Australia tried a lot of tricks to break the Aiden Markram-Wiaan Mulder partnership on the final morning of the Test at Kingsmead.
For 154 balls, near misses elicited plenty of "Ooh"s and maybe even the occasional "Aah", but little more despite some sensational bowling.
Then, in the space of four balls, everything changed.
Josh Hazlewood swung one towards the pads of Mulder, facing his 110th delivery, and it kept going down the leg side.
Mulder tried to help it on its way to fine leg as he'd done many times before, but only managed to get a faint tickle on it and that wasn't enough to evade Alex Carey.
Australia's phenomenal wicketkeeper shuffled and leapt to his left, sticking his gloved hand out and plucking the ball out of the air just centimetres off the grass.
The partnership broken, wicket-taking suddenly looked straightforward as Matt Renshaw nicked off Kyle Verreynne just three balls later to allow the Aussies to breathe a little easier.
3. Australia's shocking review
With six overs still remaining between lunch and the new ball, Cummins had time to kill.
The Australia captain decided that cycling through his part-time spinners would be the most efficient way to get the 80th over.
But with the pitch offering some substantial turn and the South African tail exposed, the Australian fielders were an in excitable mood.
And in the first over after the break, that excitement was channelled into one of the most questionable reviews of Cummins's captaincy career.
Beau Webster, who has never been a big spinner of the ball to start with, pitched his off break far enough from the stumps that Jansen felt comfortable kicking it away.
Webster would have had to have transformed into a prime Muttiah Muralitharan to have gotten that one back towards the pegs — and he hadn't. The DRS projected the ball to be missing by a considerable distance.
4. Hazlewood's career-best figures
Jansen and Markram made it to the new ball, but things went downhill pretty quickly after Starc and Hazlewood got their hands on the fresh cherry.
Hazlewood, who had started things off with the first two wickets of the innings on day four, produced a sensational 85th over double strike to all but end the South African resistance.
First, he found some movement off the pitch to castle Jansen, then, he procured some extra bounce to have Simon Harmer caught for a three-ball duck.
Mitch Starc then got in on the act to have the brilliant Aiden Markram caught behind on review, before Hazlewood fittingly ended the Test with the dismissal of Anrich Nortje.
The Proteas had lost their final four wickets for five runs and Hazlewood had career-best figures, with his 6-49 eclipsing the 6-67 from Bengaluru in 2017.
5. Markram in his element
Every time Aiden Markram bats in Tests against Australia, many of us find ourselves perplexed by his Test average in the mid-30s.
But all the ingredients were there to turn him into a modern Graeme Pollock.
Markram averages over 60 against Australia, comfortably highest among any of his Test opponents. His fourth-innings average is in the mid-40s — for reference, Steve Smith's run-chase average is 31.65. And, among grounds he's played more than two Tests on, Kingsmead is his best.
And Markram was almost chanceless as he held South Africa's innings together with a marathon 237-ball 75, before his late dismissal spelled the end for the Proteas.

Who gets to be English in today’s Britain?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
12:58:06 UTC
21:58:06 KST

Breadcrumb
Who gets to be English in today’s Britain?
What better way to highlight the dangerously racist political climate we are living through in Britain than to kick off Black History Month by having the former Home Secretary, Suella Braverman, state live on television that non-white people could not be English?
Braverman, now a Reform UK MP, came under fresh fire after saying (and defending) that she couldn’t be English because she is of “Asian origin” but is British. Even her former Conservative colleagues criticised her for making that assertion.
Now, these comments are hardly out of character for someone who infamously stated that grooming gangs were “almost all British-Pakistani”, called migrants arriving onto UK shores an “invasion”, oversaw increasingly harmful and dehumanising immigration policies, and has pledged to scrap the Equality Act. And this is but a very short list of her political legacy so far.
Whilst we know all too well that the rhetoric Braverman and her ilk are peddling is meant to feed the flames of far-right politics, there is some truth in what she is saying.
In this climate, amidst rising fascist mass mobilisations in Britain and across Europe, where far-right politicians are also gaining ground, brown and black communities, migrants and Muslims are being told loud and clear that they do not belong in the West.
As the daughter of a white British mother and a Muslim, North African father, my own life trajectory has shown me the harsh way that English is, all too often, synonymous with whiteness.
As a child, I innocently never questioned whether I belonged. I was born here, grew up here. All my cultural references, my education, my way of thinking were moulded by this country - one that I believed I was a part of.
However, that facade collapsed around me in what felt like an instant when I decided to wear the hijab as a teenager. Suddenly, I was visibly foreign. People asked me where I was from - no, where I was really from.
People looked at me strangely when I was with my white grandparents, as though I was some sort of brown exchange student visiting them from abroad. I faced racism for the first time in my life in my small white town, where overnight teachers would ask me if I was going to have an arranged marriage instead of going to sixth form, and people would mutter Islamophobic comments in the street.
My Englishness was being rescinded. I had committed the ultimate crime, which was to make myself visibly Muslim, and so whatever place I had in this exclusive club was reversed immediately.
Englishness and being visibly Muslim could not, and would not, go hand in hand.
But I quickly learned that Englishness was an exclusive club with fickle, superficial rules. And ironically, amidst this resurging ‘Englishness’, it is unclear what it actually means to be English. Even the most supposedly proud patriots can’t seem to define it; they rely instead on what for them this identity is not: being non-white, migrant and Muslim.
It feels as though we have passed a tipping point in Britain. Gone are the days of so-called diversity, equality and inclusion, and multiculturalism being seen as aspirational is well and truly over. Instead, we’re offered a dangerous nationalism that feeds a Great Replacement hysteria that means immigration is no longer seen as a productive element of globalisation, but as a hostile act of war designed to bring about the end of true Englishness.
Ultimately, Braverman’s words will have a far more sinister and long-lasting impact than a controversial soundbite dominating the news cycle. Comments like these have serious consequences for already marginalised people facing even more acute discrimination in the wake of this wave of far-right fascism taking over British politics.
Whilst we can argue that no politician can dictate how we define ourselves, and certainly not gatekeep entry to an entire nationality based on skin colour, Braverman’s words shouldn’t be dismissed as marginal personal reflections about identity. We have to take seriously the fact that they are being expressed on a massive national platform that feeds a political agenda seeking to sanction the dehumanisation and criminalisation of anyone who fails to fit into an increasingly narrow definition of what it means to belong in Britain.
As Reform continues to achieve electoral success, and as fear grows that they may even end up at Number 10, charged statements by the likes of Braverman could soon form the foundation of actual policy. This means the very real threat of material harm to thousands whose right to be in this country is suddenly rescinded due to something as fickle as the colour of their skin or their parents’ ethnic origins.
Nadeine Asbali is a freelance writer and secondary school teacher based in London. She is the author of Veiled Threat: On Being Visibly Muslim in Britain.
Follow Nadeine on X: @nadeinewrites

Deadly Houthi attacks in Yemen’s Taiz as government forces advance in Marib
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
12:57:33 UTC
21:57:33 KST

Deadly Houthi attacks in Yemen’s Taiz as government forces advance in Marib
Government troops launch major offensives across multiple fronts, while Houthi bombardments kill civilians in southwestern Yemen.
Yemeni government forces say they have made strategic advances into the Marib governorate in north-central Yemen as they push on with operation “Dawn of Yemen”.
The offensive by the Saudi-backed Yemeni government forces, launched just over a week ago, comes after major gains by the Iran-backed Houthis, an armed group also known as Ansar Allah or Supporters of God, in September, when it swept along the country’s Red Sea coast, capturing the strategic port city of Mocha and territory around the Bab al-Mandeb, one of the world’s most important shipping routes.
Rashad al-Alimi, chairman of Yemen’s Presidential Leadership Council, said operation Dawn of Yemen aimed to retake all remaining Houthi-held territory, including the capital, Sanaa, which the group has controlled since 2014, when the war first started.
Meanwhile, intense clashes and Houthi shelling on residential neighbourhoods in Taiz in the southwest of the country have caused dozens of civilian casualties.
Operation Dawn of Yemen
In the northwest of Marib governorate, a military source told Al Jazeera that government troops have successfully taken control of strategic, commanding heights surrounding the strategic Maas camp facility in the Medghal district. The source noted this followed intensive attacks that had breached the Houthi group’s fortifications.
On the southern front, forces from the Saba and Bayhan axes announced the capture of the al-Muqailat and Jabal Zajjar positions north of the Harib district. Government forces claimed the fierce clashes resulted in the Houthis retreating and suffering human and material losses.
This field progress coincided with continued violent battles along the front lines in the north and south of Marib. Government forces launched concentrated strikes using warplanes, drones, artillery and rocket launchers, targeting Houthi military positions and reinforcements.
The armed forces’ media centre published footage it said documented drone attacks on Houthi military barracks and vehicles within the scope of the third military region’s operations, noting the destruction of multiple combat vehicles and equipment.
Above: Footage from the battles within the operational theatre of the seventh military region north of Marib: Media centre of armed forces.
Military spokesperson Colonel Majid al-Nuzaili announced on Monday that operations have involved 1,879 precise strikes, neutralising 950 Houthi fighters and destroying 380 military vehicles.
Meanwhile, Houthi-affiliated media reported that air strikes targeted Kamaran Island and the al-Qanawis district in the coastal Hodeidah governorate along the Red Sea and the Harf Sufyan district in Amran, western-central Yemen.
Escalation in Taiz
In the southwestern governorate of Taiz, where the Houthis have the city of Taiz under siege, government forces and popular resistance fighters are engaged in fierce battles across multiple major axes amid a wide-scale field escalation.
On the western fronts, heavy fighting has flared in al-Dhabab, Hathran and Jabal Han as government troops have sought to thwart infiltration attempts and repel Houthi attacks. Sources within the government forces told Al Jazeera that troops captured 81 Houthi fighters in al-Dhabab on Monday afternoon.
In the southern and southwestern countryside, battles have intensified in the al-Shaqb, al-Aqroud and al-Misrakh areas. A field military source told Al Jazeera that government forces are involved in fierce clashes from all directions in the al-Shaqb area of Taiz, with confrontations extending to areas the Houthis seized on Monday in Sabir.
Also in the southwest, a field military source from the Southern Giants Brigades told Al Jazeera that Houthi forces had fired a ballistic missile at the highly strategic mountain range of Jabal Kahboub at midnight. The source confirmed there were no human or material casualties, with damage limited to the missile’s distant impact zone.
Civilian toll rises
The military escalation has severely affected civilian populations. Al Jazeera correspondent Abdullah Qatran reported seeing Houthi mortar shelling targeting the al-Ikhwa residential neighbourhood in the centre of Taiz, resulting in an undetermined number of deaths, injuries and property damage, causing widespread panic.
With Taiz under Houthi siege, civilians there are also suffering severe shortages of fuel and other essential supplies. Yemen’s Ministry of Public Health and Population said on Saturday that medicines, intravenous fluids, medical supplies and fuel at the city’s health facilities were “nearing depletion”.
Compounding this, the Yemeni Network for Rights and Freedoms has documented 43 violations by Houthi forces in Taiz over the past 24 hours, which have killed five civilians and wounded 17. According to a report by Yemen’s state-run Saba news agency, casualties included five-year-old Ahlam Abdulsalam, who died when shelling struck her family’s home in the al-Misrakh district.
The rights group stated that Houthi forces have fired more than 180 projectiles at residential areas, including mortar and artillery shells, Katyusha rockets, tank rounds and drones. The bombardment has damaged seven homes, 12 private vehicles and the al-Saeed Mosque in Taiz city.
Saba also reported that a Houthi attack early on Tuesday struck al-Safwa Hospital, shattering windows, injuring at least one person, and triggering panic among patients and medical staff. This followed earlier Houthi shelling in which five people, including three children, were injured in the al-Dhahra residential area and the nearby Beer Basha district.
The Yemeni Network for Rights and Freedoms warned that continuous shelling and restrictions on supplies are worsening humanitarian conditions, calling on the United Nations and the international community to take urgent steps to protect civilians.

Potentially paralysed tourist stranded in Greece after balcony fall
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
13:57:14 BST
21:57:14 KST

Potentially paralysed tourist stranded in Greece after balcony fall
- Published
A Scottish tourist who fell from a balcony in Greece is unable to travel home due to the cost of a specialist flight.
Denby McLaren from Larkhall cannot currently use her legs after the three-storey fall, which happened while she was visiting Rhodes to celebrate her 30th birthday.
She has a broken vertebra and multiple fractures to her foot, with her family now waiting to learn if she has suffered permanent injuries.
An air ambulance offering stretcher and medical assistance is needed to get back to Scotland, but these are not covered by her travel insurance. A fundraiser has now been set up to help.
Denby, who works as cabin crew with an airline, was on holiday with her mum Sharon when the accident happened on 6 October.
She has been in hospital since then, with her partner Craig Anderson travelling to Greece to be with her.
Leeanne Weir, a friend of the family, told BBC Scotland News: "It's absolutely horrific. She can't move her legs, she has a broken vertebra and multiple broken bones.
"The biggest worry is that she can't move her legs and we don't know whether this has affected her spine and if she will be paralysed. But she is also lucky to be alive after a fall like that.
"Denby is a lovely girl, just a really sweet person. It's awful what's happened to her."
Although Denby has medical cover, it does not extend to paying for the specialist repatriation needed.
Leeanne said: "The worry is also that the longer she is there in Greece all the other bills are going up for every extra day they are there.
"Apart from the severity of the injuries they have the language barrier and the added pressure of just trying to get home."
The Go Fund Me page has so far raised about £19,000 of the £28,000 target.
Leeanne said: "It doesn't have to be a huge contribution - we have had a phenomenal response from people so far, whether it's £5 or £50.
"We just want to get her home and start being cared for at home."

Int'l counter-terrorism forum opens in Beijing

21:56:48 KST

BEIJING, Oct. 13 (Xinhua) -- Over 320 representatives from 62 countries and international organizations have gathered in Beijing for the three-day Great Wall-2026 International Forum on Counter-Terrorism.
Hosted by the Chinese People's Armed Police Force, this year's forum provides a platform for representatives to share insights and experience on pragmatic cooperation in the fight against terrorism in four seminar sessions.
Topics such as trends of terrorist activities facilitated by unmanned weapons and intelligent technology, and corresponding counter-terrorism capacity building, are on the agenda for discussion.
Visits to military training demonstrations and viewing of unmanned equipment have also been scheduled for the attendees, the organizer of the forum said.
The armed police form an important force for a country in combating terrorism and safeguarding social stability. The Chinese People's Armed Police Force has hosted five editions of this forum since 2016, with the aim of pooling global strengths to erect an impregnable fortress against terrorism.
An important participant in and contributor to the global fight against terrorism, China has conducted pragmatic cooperation with other countries in terms of intelligence exchanges, border control, case investigations and counter-terrorism financing.
The country has also organized training sessions and seminars to share its experience with the international community and help with capacity building in combating terrorism. ■

Xi Focus: Xi calls for decisive progress in Healthy China advancement
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
20:56:39 CST
21:56:39 KST

Chinese President Xi Jinping, also general secretary of the Communist Party of China Central Committee and chairman of the Central Military Commission, delivers an important speech during a national meeting on health in Beijing, capital of China. The meeting was held in Beijing on Monday and Tuesday. (Xinhua/Xie Huanchi)
BEIJING, Oct. 13 (Xinhua) -- Chinese President Xi Jinping has called for efforts to firmly follow a path with Chinese characteristics in developing the country's health programs, to secure decisive progress in the Healthy China Initiative over the 15th Five-Year Plan period (2026-2030).
Xi, also general secretary of the Communist Party of China (CPC) Central Committee and chairman of the Central Military Commission, made the remarks at a national meeting on health held in Beijing on Monday and Tuesday.
Xi stressed that people's health is a key benchmark of a nation's prosperity and strength.
Since the 18th CPC National Congress in 2012, the Party has made a major decision to launch the Healthy China Initiative, promoting the establishment of the world's largest systems of medical services, traditional medicine, disease prevention and control, and healthcare security, said Xi, noting that the country has achieved historic accomplishments and made all-round progress in healthcare.
In 2025, China's average life expectancy rose to 79.25 years, while its major health indicators remained at the leading position among upper-middle-income countries and countries with a population exceeding 100 million.
Xi said the goal is to build a Healthy China, where health services are ensured in a balanced, inclusive, high-quality and efficient manner.
Xi stressed that people's health should be factored into all policies and reflected in every aspect of work.
Prevention, he said, is the most cost-effective and efficient approach to protecting public health. He called for greater emphasis on foundational health work, addressing risks at their source, and encouraging the public to adopt a sound understanding of health and take an active role in managing their own well-being.
He also called for a stronger disease prevention and control system to guard against large-scale outbreaks.
Xi underscored the need to optimize the functions and structural layout of medical institutions so that people can access medical care close to home and receive effective treatment.
China has supported the development of 125 regional medical centers in areas where high-quality medical resources are relatively scarce.
Notably, more than 90 percent of residents can access nearby medical and healthcare services within 15 minutes, while primary-level medical institutions account for over 50 percent of all medical visits nationwide.
He also urged efforts to improve mechanisms for the preservation and innovative development of traditional Chinese medicine, strengthen basic research and original innovation in the health sector, and enhance the patient experience.
Xi stressed that coordinating the development and regulation of medical services, medical insurance, and pharmaceuticals should be a key priority in reforming China's medical and healthcare systems.
He also called for efforts to train and develop a sufficient number of highly qualified medical professionals.
Efforts will also be made to actively promote the building of a global community of health for all, work with other countries to address major challenges in the health sector, and continuously improve the health and well-being of people around the world, he said.
Other Chinese leaders Li Qiang, Zhao Leji, Wang Huning, Cai Qi, Ding Xuexiang and Li Xi attended the event.
In his concluding remarks, Li Qiang said Xi's important speech provided guidance for advancing China's health sector.
Li called for better coordination between improvements in public health and economic and social development, and urged deeper reform, innovation, opening up and cooperation, stronger prevention and control of major diseases, further development of a tiered diagnosis and treatment system, and greater use of science and technology to improve health services. ■

Turning the clocks back to standard time: benefits, risks, and an unresolved future
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
15:56:38 EEST
21:56:38 KST

Turning the clocks back to standard time: benefits, risks, and an unresolved future
Kyiv • UNN
Ukraine is turning the clocks back to standard time, although the law on permanent standard time has not been signed. The savings are minimal, and adaptation takes up to two weeks.
Every year on the last Sunday of October, Ukraine, like many countries around the world, switches to standard time. At 04:00, the clock hands are moved back one hour. This provides an extra hour of sleep on a day off, but the question of whether this tradition is appropriate in the 21st century remains open to this day. Despite the fact that two years ago the Verkhovna Rada adopted a bill under which Ukraine was to remain on standard time permanently, the president has still not signed it. UNN will explain how to prepare for the clock change and discuss the history of this practice
The history of the tradition
The idea of changing the time emerged long before the advent of modern electrical grids. In 1784, Benjamin Franklin published an essay in which he jokingly suggested getting up earlier to save candles. However, the scientific and economic rationale was provided by British builder William Willett in 1907. He was outraged that in summer people slept through the first hours of sunlight and wasted artificial lighting in the evening. The first country to officially introduce seasonal clock changes at the state level was the German Empire in 1916 — during the First World War, this was a critical measure to save coal. The practice was subsequently adopted by Great Britain, the United States, and most European countries.
In Ukraine, the practice of changing the clock hands was introduced during the Soviet era in 1981 and, after independence, formalized by a resolution of the Cabinet of Ministers in 1996.
Economic rationale: myth or reality
The main purpose of seasonal clock changes is the rational use of daylight and saving electricity. In the 20th century, when most energy was spent specifically on lighting businesses and homes, this was highly noticeable. However, the structure of energy consumption has changed significantly in the modern world. Thanks to energy-efficient LED technologies, lighting accounts for only a small share of total energy consumption. Instead, household appliances, air-conditioning systems, heating, and continuously operating infrastructure have become the main consumers. Modern studies show that the actual electricity savings from changing the clock hands range from 0.2% to 1%, which, on a national scale, is an almost imperceptible figure.
Impact on human health and biorhythms
Although the transition to standard time is considered easier on the body than the spring transition, it is still stressful for human physiology. Disruption of natural circadian rhythms, that is, the internal biological clock, causes what is known as "desynchronosis."
In the first days after the clock change, fluctuations in blood pressure are recorded. Although the risk of heart attacks increases more significantly during the spring transition, in autumn the body responds to the change in the light pattern with increased fatigue. The reduction in evening daylight hours can trigger seasonal affective disorder or autumn depression. The body receives less sunlight, which reduces the production of serotonin and vitamin D. The adaptation of the biological clock to the new schedule takes from several days to two weeks. During this period, people more often complain of insomnia, reduced concentration, and increased irritability.
How can adaptation be made easier?
Three to five days before the clock change, start going to bed and getting up 15–20 minutes later. Try to spend more time outdoors during the first half of the day so that your body receives natural light. Avoid heavy food, alcohol, and excessive coffee consumption in the evening; moderate physical activity will help normalize sleep.
The modern context and the future of time changes
In recent years, an active debate has been underway around the world over abolishing seasonal clock changes. In 2019, the European Parliament supported a decision to abandon the practice, calling on EU member states to determine a permanent time. However, due to bureaucratic coordination and the pandemic, this decision has not yet taken final effect.
In Ukraine, there have also been repeated attempts to abolish the seasonal time change and establish a single standard time. As early as 2024, we were supposed to switch to winter time only; the Verkhovna Rada passed this bill, but the president has still not made a decision. On the one hand, fixing the time is about caring for citizens and their health, as well as the absence of any real economic benefit, while on the other hand, attention is drawn to the convenience of synchronizing time with European partners and the country’s geographical features.

Natural disasters leave 68 dead or missing in Vietnam in 9 months
China
Unknown Publisher

20:56:31 CST
21:56:31 KST

HANOI, Oct. 13 (Xinhua) -- Natural disasters in Vietnam left 68 people dead or missing and caused estimated economic losses of over 3.9 trillion Vietnamese dong (about 150.5 million U.S. dollars) in the first nine months of this year, the Vietnam News Agency reported Tuesday.
The country recorded 20 types of natural disasters during the period. These disasters destroyed 237 houses and damaged or unroofed 24,584 others, according to the Vietnam Disaster and Dyke Management Authority.
The disasters inundated or damaged 127,353 hectares of rice and other crops, while 64.5 kilometers of roads were affected by landslides, the report said.
Deputy Minister of Agriculture and Environment Nguyen Hoang Hiep stressed the need to strengthen local authorities' preparedness for natural disasters. ■

China unveils railway sci-tech innovation plan for 2026-2030
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
20:56:17 CST
21:56:17 KST

BEIJING, Oct. 13 (Xinhua) -- China, which operates the world's largest high-speed rail network, has issued a railway science and technology innovation plan for the 15th Five-Year Plan period (2026-2030).
This innovation plan outlines key tasks in basic research and frontier technologies, engineering construction, technical equipment, transport services, digital and intelligent railways, safety, and green and low-carbon development.
The plan, recently released by the National Railway Administration (NRA), proposes to basically establish a science and technology innovation system that leads railway modernization by 2030.
During the 2026-2030 period, China plans to build about 30 new railway industry science and technology innovation bases under the NRA, achieve breakthroughs in no fewer than 100 key core technologies, and produce no less than 500 major scientific and technological achievements.
It will also plan no fewer than 20 typical application scenarios or demonstration projects in areas such as the 400 km/h high-speed train operating system.
Regarding technical equipment, the plan proposes to steadily and orderly advance research on 600 km/h high-speed maglev technology as well as testing and verification of key technologies for domestic production.
In the case of transport services, the plan will promote upgrading the official 12306 ticketing platform from a single ticket-buying service to whole-journey intelligent services, providing one-stop intermodal travel solutions that precisely match passengers' "personalized, differentiated and diversified" needs.
China will accelerate the building of large models, datasets and computing power infrastructure in the railway industry, and will establish a minimum of 20 high-quality industry datasets and more than 20 typical artificial intelligence application scenarios, according to the plan.
Concerning green and low-carbon development, the plan calls for promoting demonstration operation of low-emission and low-fuel-consumption diesel locomotives as well as locomotives and rolling stock with multi-source power such as battery and hydrogen, establishing and improving a carbon management system, and helping total railway carbon emissions peak by 2030.
In contrast to the railway sci-tech innovation plan for the 14th Five-Year Plan period (2021-2025), the new plan places greater emphasis on basic research and frontier technologies, thereby better advancing high-level scientific and technological self-reliance and strength in the railway sector.
By the end of 2025, the country's total operating railway mileage had reached 165,000 km, including more than 50,000 km of high-speed rail.
On Sept. 28 this year, China opened four high-speed rail sections, connecting Xiong'an in north China's Hebei Province with Shangqiu in Henan Province in central China, Xi'an with Ankang in Shaanxi Province in northwest China, Yichang with Xingshan in central China's Hubei Province, and Harbin with Yichun in Heilongjiang Province in the country's northeast.
During the National Day holiday, which lasted from Oct. 1 to Oct. 7, these new lines made it easier for people to visit relatives and brought new vitality to tourism along the routes.
China's high-speed rail network is projected to hit 70,000 km by 2035, featuring eight north-south vertical lines and eight east-west horizontal lines. Once complete, the network will connect major cities, city clusters and key economic zones across the country. ■

France to miss target for reducing greenhouse gas emissions in 2026: study
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
20:56:15 CST
21:56:15 KST

PARIS, Oct. 13 (Xinhua) -- France's greenhouse gas emissions are projected to fall by 2.8 percent in 2026 from the previous year, but this reduction would remain less than that required to meet the country's climate goals, according to a report released Tuesday.
The Interprofessional Technical Center for Studies on Air Pollution (Citepa), an independent body responsible for monitoring the country's emissions, said in its latest barometer that France's greenhouse gas emissions, excluding carbon sinks, totaled an estimated 179.7 million tons of carbon dioxide equivalent (CO2e) in the first half of 2026. This was down 4.1 percent from the same period in 2025.
The decline was mainly driven by the buildings and transport sectors, where emissions fell by 12.0 percent and 4.5 percent, respectively, according to Citepa.
However, the downward trend is expected to slow in the second half of the year, with emissions projected to fall by 1.3 percent year on year, the report said.
For the whole of 2026, France's greenhouse gas emissions are projected to reach 349.4 million tons of CO2e. This represents a reduction of 2.8 percent, slightly below the 3.1 percent decline envisaged for 2026 under France's third National Low-Carbon Strategy (SNBC 3). It would also remain well below the average annual rate of emission cuts needed to meet the country's climate targets by 2030.
Citepa said France's emissions reductions will need to accelerate in the coming years to comply with its carbon budgets and meet its climate targets for 2030. Under the SNBC 3 roadmap, annual emissions cuts are expected to accelerate to 5.7 percent in 2027 and 6.1 percent in 2028 from the previous year. ■

Researchers develop new X-ray tech mapping elements in 3D with far less data
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
20:56:12 CST
21:56:12 KST

JERUSALEM, Oct. 13 (Xinhua) -- Researchers have developed a new X-ray method to map elements inside a sample in three dimensions without scanning every tiny point, Israel's Bar Ilan University said in a statement on Tuesday.
The technique, called X-ray fluorescence ghost tomography and detailed in the journal Optica, could help scientists study materials, batteries, rocks and biological tissues faster and more efficiently.
X-rays make atoms glow at element-specific energies, or "colors," allowing researchers to identify them.
Instead of copying an image pixel by pixel, the new method projects patterns of X-rays through the sample and collects the combined glowing signals with a detector. Then a computer solves one large mathematical problem to rebuild the 3D element map.
In tests, the researchers mapped nearly 2.8 million 3D pixels using only 400 pattern measurements per angle. Across 276 angles, that totaled about 110,000 measurements, versus 4.75 million for the old point-by-point scanning. That is roughly 97 percent less data, while retaining useful detail.
They explained that the method exploits the fact that most real samples are "sparse," or mostly empty or made of only a few materials.
The researchers caution that denser samples will require corrections, and the computation is heavy. Still, the approach could make 3D chemical imaging faster, cheaper, and practical for large or delicate samples, they said. ■

Chinese study finds global urban land subsidence uneven but generally slowing
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
20:55:54 CST
21:55:54 KST

BEIJING, Oct. 13 (Xinhua) -- Global urban land subsidence varies widely but has generally slowed in recent years, according to a study by a Chinese research team published Oct. 12 in the journal Nature Cities.
Researchers from Peking University, South China Normal University and other institutions systematically assessed land subsidence between 2014 and 2023 in 465 cities worldwide, each with a population of over one million.
Land subsidence is a global issue that poses a major challenge to urban infrastructure safety and sustainable development.
According to the research, subsidence is most severe in Southeast Asia, West-Central Asia and North America, with representative cities including Mexico City and Toluca in Mexico, and Medan and Bandung in Indonesia. Mexico City recorded the most intense localized subsidence, with rates exceeding 0.2 meters per year.
Although land subsidence remains widespread, global urban subsidence has generally slowed in recent years. The research team detected marked deceleration in many cities across Southeast and East Asia.
This indicates that water resource allocation and groundwater management measures in the two regions are effective, said Hu Xie, a researcher of the team at Peking University.
"In China's Beijing-Tianjin-Hebei urban agglomeration in particular, large-scale water diversion projects such as the South-to-North Water Diversion Project and stronger groundwater management have helped replenish groundwater in some areas, significantly easing subsidence," Hu said.
The team also built an open platform for global urban land subsidence, offering the dataset in a searchable and visual format to the public.
As geological and groundwater big data accumulate and artificial intelligence and complex models advance, the analysis of subsidence causes and risk assessment will have a stronger data and methodological foundation, said Tao Shengli, a researcher at Peking University. ■

Lagarde’s book plug raises questions about ECB ethics standards
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
12:54:27 UTC
21:54:27 KST

Christine Lagarde addresses a press conference after a meeting of the Governing Council of the European Central Bank (ECB) in Berlin on September 10, 2026. | John MacDougall/AFP via Getty Images
FRANKFURT — European Central Bank staff want to know whether President Christine Lagarde breached her own ethics standards by plugging her forthcoming book at an ECB press conference last month.
The central bank’s staff committee raised its concerns with the ECB’s chief compliance officer in a letter dated Oct. 9 and seen by POLITICO. Staffers are seeking clarity on whether Lagarde breached the central bank's code of conduct, and have raised concerns about “potential double standards” between the ethics requirements for staff and the ECB’s six executive board members.
Lagarde mentioned her memoir, Lady First, during a monetary policy press conference on Sept. 10, when asked how she would keep the book’s commercial promotion separate from her ECB role. The Frenchwoman told reporters that “any marketing, publishing, commercial operations will happen either at weekends or on a day or two that I will take as a holiday.”
Advertisement
She then added: “I strongly encourage you to buy the book.” The autobiography's English version is expected to hit the shelves on Feb. 4. A spokesperson for the ECB said Lagarde has done nothing wrong.
The podium plug has fueled speculation that Lagarde may leave the ECB by the time the book is published, well before the end of her official term in October next year. Lagarde has declined to commit to staying for the full term, triggering an early race for the EU’s most powerful economic job.
The book plug might’ve been in jest. But staffers want to know whether writing and publishing the book falls within her “occupation” under Article 11.1 of the ECB’s statutes. If not, the union has asked whether the central bank's Governing Council received and granted an exemption. The letter also asked whether the manuscript was vetted for confidential or policy-sensitive material, and whether promoting the book at an official event was consistent with the ECB's code of conduct.
“President Lagarde informed the ECB’s Ethics Committee and the Compliance and Governance Officer about the book project and has received approval," the spokesperson for the central bank said.
The staff committee reminded the ECB's compliance chief that staff rules require employees to seek prior authorization before publishing material outside their work at the central bank. The rules also restrict employees from using ECB resources, or their position, for private activities.
Advertisement
While ECB staff is subject to a different set of rules than the bank’s leadership, the committee said that any differences in treatment should be “objectively justified” and proportionate, the letter said, adding that ethical expectations should become “more — not less — demanding as institutional responsibility increases.”
Similarly, the staff committee wanted to know whether Lagarde had disclosed any contact with the World Economic Forum and if any potential conflicts of interest had been assessed. The ECB president is rumored to be in talks about a leadership role at the global think tank, although this has never been confirmed.
“The book project is a private activity, carried out in the President’s own time, and does not use ECB resources,” the ECB's spokesperson said. The staff committee declined to comment.

Jerusalem court upholds 5-year suspension for gynecologist Guy Rofe over patient exploitation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
12:53:43 UTC
21:53:43 KST

The Jerusalem District Court rejected an appeal by gynecologist Guy Rofe to shorten or cancel the five-year suspension of his medical license, the Health Ministry announced Tuesday.
The court found that Rofe used his position as a treating physician to pursue intimate relationships with two patients, mixing medical advice with sexual messages. It also upheld findings that he withheld medical records from investigators and continued advertising himself as a practicing gynecologist despite his suspended license.
“I will examine you as a gynecologist and as a lover,” he wrote to one patient, according to the judgment. She was a 19-year-old soldier whom he treated while serving as a military doctor in the reserves.
In messages to the second patient, he interspersed discussions of blood tests, pregnancy, and contraception with comments about her appearance and about his sexual fantasies.
During an examination, the judgment said, he told her, “Maybe don’t get dressed, I don’t think there’s any need,” and placed a hand on her knees.
Rofe facing charges of rape, indecent acts
The decision means Rofe remains barred from practicing medicine and cannot present himself to the public as a licensed, practicing physician.
Rofe also faces a separate criminal prosecution on charges of rape by deception and indecent acts by deception against a soldier who came to him for treatment. According to the indictment, he performed sexual acts under the guise of a medical examination. Those charges remain pending; the five-year suspension rests on disciplinary findings concerning different incidents.
The judgment does not specify whether the soldier mentioned in the disciplinary case is the same woman involved in the criminal prosecution.
Rofe’s license was initially suspended on November 29, 2024, in connection with the criminal proceedings.
The disciplinary complaint at the center of the latest ruling was filed on September 4, 2025. It contained four counts: two concerning his conduct toward the patients, identified as “A” and “D”; one concerning his refusal to provide medical records for five patients; and one concerning his continued online advertising.
Retired judge Amnon Straschnov, acting under authority delegated by the health minister, adopted the disciplinary committee’s findings on all four counts, except the allegation concerning Rofe’s refusal to hand over WhatsApp correspondence.
On April 20, Straschnov ordered the five-year suspension. The committee’s majority had recommended three and a half years, while its minority favored at least 10 years or permanent revocation.
Straschnov found the majority’s recommendation insufficient given the harm to public trust, the misleading advertising, and Rofe’s persistent refusal to cooperate with oversight authorities.
Rofe appealed, seeking to have the decision canceled and the case returned to the committee or the suspension reduced to no more than six months.
He argued that he had been denied a fair opportunity to defend himself because hearings proceeded in his absence, despite his having reported illness and a family event.
The court found, however, that Rofe had missed two hearings and failed to submit a written defense. The committee then gave him further opportunities to respond and offered to arrange another hearing around dates he proposed. He did not provide them.
“A doctor who chooses to turn his back on the disciplinary proceedings and deliberately cause prolonged delays cannot now complain that the proceedings were decided in his absence,” Judge Nimrod Flax wrote in the October 8 judgment.
Rofe also challenged the findings concerning the patients. Regarding patient A, he disputed the existence of a special relationship of trust and dependence, citing her withdrawal of a criminal complaint, the closure of that investigation for lack of guilt, and the time elapsed since 2018. That investigation was distinct from the pending criminal prosecution.
Regarding patient D, he argued that she had initiated the sexual conversations, that no physical contact had occurred, and that no emotional harm was proven.
Flax rejected Rofe’s attempt to compare his conduct with less serious disciplinary cases. The judgment described “a continuing and systematic pattern of conduct” involving violations of professional boundaries, refusal to supply medical records, and misleading advertising during suspension.
Accused of withholding medical records
The Health Ministry argued that Rofe’s appeal presented a partial account and concealed his repeated disregard of the committee’s decisions. It said his continued advertising violated both the law and court decisions.
Rofe argued that protection against self-incrimination entitled him to withhold medical records. He also maintained that investigators already possessed most of the information and that his refusal had not harmed their inquiries.
The court rejected that defense.
Medical records, it held, are documents doctors must create and preserve by law, rather than personal material protected against self-incrimination in these disciplinary proceedings. Records for three patients had still not been supplied.
His refusal “directly undermines the Health Ministry’s ability to exercise oversight and obstructs the proper examination of complaints by additional patients,” Flax wrote.
The court also rejected Rofe’s argument that he had not actually treated patients while advertising himself as an active physician. The advertising itself misled the public, it said, regardless of whether treatment took place.
Rofe’s continued conduct despite explicit court decisions, Flax wrote, “casts a heavy shadow over [his] very fitness to work in a professional field governed by ethical rules.”
The Health Ministry described the ruling on medical records and self-incrimination as a first in Israel. It said it would continue monitoring compliance with the suspension and maintain a policy of zero tolerance toward conduct that harms patients or undermines public trust.
The five-year disciplinary suspension remains in place independently of the outcome of the criminal prosecution.
