With defense-tech investment surging, INNOFENSE Cohort 7 opens
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
12:53:00 UTC
21:53:00 KST

Israel’s Defense Ministry and SOSA have opened applications for the seventh cohort of INNOFENSE, a defense‑tech accelerator that has become an important pipeline for start-ups seeking entry into the country’s rapidly expanding defense tech innovation ecosystem.
The program, run jointly by SOSA and the Defense Ministry’s Directorate of Defense Research & Development (MAFAT), invites start-ups to tackle real operational challenges inside Israel’s defense establishment.
Selected companies will work directly with IDF and Defense Ministry teams and get 200,000 NIS in funding to build and test early versions of their technology without giving up any ownership of their company.
The announcement comes during a period of intense growth for Israel’s defense‑tech ecosystem. Start-ups working with the Defense Ministry raised nearly $3 billion in the first half of 2026, triple the total amount raised in all of 2025.
According to figures presented at the Haifa DefenseTech Start-ups and Investors Forum, defense‑tech and dual‑use companies account for almost 30% of private investment in Israeli hi‑tech.
Built around operational validation
INNOFENSE places start-ups directly inside the defense establishment, embedding them with IDF and Defense Ministry teams to work on real operational problems. Each company is matched with a specific Defense Ministry partner and asked to prove its technology in conditions that mirror actual battlefield use. That process is designed to show whether a system works and to pave the way for procurement and longer‑term cooperation.
The program has already built a strong track record. Over six cohorts, INNOFENSE has worked with 92 start-ups, led to 15 commercial agreements, and provided NIS 13 million in non‑dilutive funding for proof‑of‑concept projects.
More than 30% of participating companies have gone on to receive follow-on orders from MAFAT worth NIS 18 million, and alumni have collectively raised more than $500 million.
Start-ups selected for the new cohort receive NIS 200,000 in funding, workspace at SOSA for six months, mentorship from senior defense and industry figures, and access to SOSA’s global innovation network.
What cohort 7 is looking for
Applications for cohort 7 are open to both Israeli and international start-ups that have a presence in Israel. The new cohort is targeting technologies in communications & radio frequency, AI and data, sensing and threat detection, space and satellite technology, robotics and energy, manufacturing and materials, and simulation and training, as well as open innovation for out‑of‑the‑box solutions.
SOSA and MAFAT are encouraging startups with adaptable technologies to apply, meaning that companies do not need to have defense-ready solutions.
Col. (res.) David “Duddy” Rokach, managing partner of SOSA HLS & DEFENSE and co-founder of INNOFENSE, said that it was established to “bridge the gap” between civilian innovation and defense needs.
“What makes the program unique is the direct engagement with operational end users, combined with the ability to validate technologies in a real defense environment and create a pathway toward continued cooperation,” he said.
“With six cohorts behind us, we have demonstrated that this model creates tangible value for both the defense establishment and participating startups. We are now looking for the next generation of companies ready to turn their technologies into operational impact.”
Global expansion
INNOFENSE is part of SOSA’s broader work connecting governments, defense organizations, industry leaders, start-ups, and investors to accelerate the adoption of emerging technologies. 
SOSA has innovation centers in Tel Aviv, New York, New Jersey, São Paulo, and Singapore and works with global partners to move solutions from concept to deployment and deliver operational impact.
The accelerator’s international footprint continues to grow. In Singapore, SOSA’s Hatch innovation center, which is operated with the Home Team Science & Technology Agency (HTX), is also opening applications for the next cohort of Dimension X, a public‑safety program offering up to SGD 100,000 for early‑stage technology pilots.

"You found your place and devoted yourself to it completely. I visited you six months ago – there, in the east. I saw how people listened to you, respected you, how they came to you for decisions.
How that same five-foot-tall girl who was once rejected became a commander whom people trust. I looked at you and thought, 'You are so incredible'. And I am so proud of you," Viktoriia shared.
On 8 October, Yaryna was killed in an FPV drone strike on the Kramatorsk front.
"My Yarynka. My Hetera. 'Yavir', 'Nishtiak' and Madam Commander to her fellow soldiers [...]
I still don't know how to come to terms with this. How to write about you in a way that doesn't sound like a goodbye. Because you – you are all about life. About being constantly on the go, about laughter, about the mountains, about Ukraine, about the strength within you that no one could measure by your 88 pounds.
It feels like only yesterday we were planning to go for a walk after school, and today I was getting ready to see your mother and break the news of your death..." the soldier's friend wrote.
The date and time of Yaryna's funeral will be announced later. A fundraiser has been launched to provide support for her family and help with the funeral expenses.
Background: Valeriia "Demon" Stepanova, an FPV drone operator, was killed in a drone strike at the front.

Israel turns back Ethiopian flight over Indonesian pilot: report
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
12:52:39 UTC
21:52:39 KST

Breadcrumb
Israel orders Ethiopian Airlines flight to turn back over Indonesian pilot: report
Israel ordered an Ethiopian Airlines flight bound for Tel Aviv to turn back because one of its pilots was Indonesian, according to Israeli media reports.
The cargo aircraft was approximately an hour into its journey from Addis Ababa and still in Ethiopian airspace when Israeli authorities ordered it to return, Israeli broadcaster Channel 12 reported on Monday.
According to the broadcaster, the pilot's nationality had been flagged to Israeli intelligence and airport authorities, prompting security officials and the Transportation Ministry to bar the aircraft from landing.
The plane returned to Addis Ababa, where the Indonesian pilot was replaced before it departed again and landed in Tel Aviv.
Ethiopian Airlines reportedly described the incident as a mistake, saying it had been unaware that the pilot was barred from operating flights to Israel.
The New Arab contacted Ethiopian Airlines for comment but had not received a response by the time of publication.
The incident comes as Israel imposes sweeping nationality-based restrictions on foreign airline crews, barring citizens of several countries without diplomatic relations with Israel from operating flights to the country.
According to Channel 12, Israeli authorities instructed foreign airlines not to assign pilots or crew members from designated countries to flights bound for Israel.
The restrictions reportedly cover nationals of Afghanistan, Algeria, Indonesia, Iran, Iraq, Kuwait, Niger, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, Somalia and Venezuela.
Israeli authorities have also notified foreign airlines operating flights to Ben Gurion Airport of additional restrictions affecting crew members with dual nationality, according to aviation news website Paddle Your Own Kanoo (PYOK).
The measures reportedly apply to crew members holding citizenship of any of 29 countries on an Israeli list, although PYOK said the restrictions could extend to as many as 31 countries.
Under the rules, even a crew member holding a US passport could be barred from operating a flight to Israel if they also hold citizenship of a country on the restricted list.

MI5 chief warns of threats to UK from Russia, Iran and AI
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
13:52:12 BST
21:52:12 KST

MI5 chief warns of threats to UK from Russia, Iran and AI
- Published
MI5 is devoting more resource to countering state threats than during the Cold War, the head of the intelligence service has said.
Sir Ken McCallum said threats from foreign adversaries had quadrupled in the last decade, with Russia "aggressor number one" as well as increased Iran-linked aggression against Jewish sites and military bases.
At an annual speech in London, MI5's chief said Russia was waging hybrid warfare at a time when AI was "supercharging the cyber-security contest between attackers and defenders".
He also warned of rising threats from "extreme right-wing terrorism" and said MI5 had "caught terrorists seeking to exploit Al," including by integrating the technology with drones.
He said the biggest threat from the misuse of AI was extremist groups using the technology to harness new and existing bioweapons.
However, he noted that work countering terrorism and state threats was now "pretty much of equal scale" which he described as a "huge shift" in recent years.
Sir Ken said Russia had stopped short of "conventional conflict" against Nato and is instead trying to unsettle European countries while its progress in its full-scale invasion of Ukraine is "minimal and horrifically costly".
Hybrid warfare or hybrid attacks are loose terms which tend to describe non-military methods, for example cyber-attacks, sabotage or misinformation, designed to exert pressure and destabilise an adversary.
These are quite often employed using proxies, but Russia always denies involvement in such attacks despite growing evidence to the contrary.
Sir Ken said MI5 successes in identifying and expelling Russian spies from the UK had left the Kremlin dependent on paying proxies for attempted attacks.
"With its traditional covert footprint eviscerated by almost 1,000 expulsions since the invasion, the Kremlin's global toolkit is weak, he said.
"So we see them scrambling to pay criminals to do their bidding."
He added: "These are not the actions of a great power with the strategic upper hand."
His comments come as a growing number of leaders across Europe have warned Russia may be preparing attacks to test their commitment to supporting Ukraine.
Asked after the speech about Prime Minister Andy Burnham's recent comments that Russia interfered with the Brexit referendum, Sir Ken said it was "not new news" that there had been attempts from Moscow but distinguished between "interference attempted" and "outcome achieved".
He said it was a matter of public record that there were pieces in Russian media and "so-called internet trolls and bot farms" seeking to influence the Brexit debate, but also stressed that the result of the 2016 referendum was "not in dispute".
He added that he was "worried" about the the ongoing debate on Russian interference.
"I am a little bit anxious that we don't play into our adversaries' hands by making these trolls look 10ft tall," he told reporters.
Meanwhile, Sir Ken warned that Iran is also expanding a hybrid campaign in the UK.
The intelligence chief said there had been 50 arrests in the last year over Iran-linked activities.
Much of this Iranian aggression has been aimed at Jewish communities, Sir Ken added, and also at "harder targets, like military sites".
Sir Ken did not mention arrests at RAF Fairford directly during his speech, but told reporters afterwards the incident was "not unique".
He added: "We have seen Iranian interest beyond RAF Fairford in the UK."
The incident at the airbase in Gloucesteshire, where three suspicious vans were seen parked nearby, has seen seven people arrested and bailed by counter-terrorism police.
Burnham has said the incident was "almost certainly directed by Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard".
The MI5 head said in his speech: "What I can say is that those who seek to cause mayhem on British streets - whether hired thugs here or their paymasters overseas - will meet an unflinching response."
Sir Ken added that the National Security Act - a 2023 law designed to target people working against UK interests for foreign powers - is in heavy use, and has been employed to tackle threats from China as well as Iran and Russia.
On the emerging threat posed by AI, Sir Ken said: "It can produce propaganda and radicalising material tailored to the individual.
"We've caught terrorists seeking to exploit Al to improve their reconnaissance and attack methodologies, with Al-enabled drones adding a new twist."
Sir Ken said the bioweapons threat posed by AI was "not yet realised" but warned the technology has the "potential to change the stakes".
"These risks are real. The UK Intelligence Community - MI5, GCHQ, MI6 - is working closely with the UK's globally respected AI Security Institute to take them on."
Sir Ken said AI poses unknown threats, telling Thames House: "Put at its simplest, human history has given us no experience of facing an actor which is smarter than we are".
He announced MI5 had launched an AI Threat Assessment Centre, which he said would assess sources and "separate the bluster from the realities".
In April, the UK's terrorism threat level was raised to severe for the first time in five years, meaning an attack is highly likely.
Sir Ken said Islamist groups like Al Qaeda and so-called Islamic State both continue to direct and inspire attacks, while the increased risk was also driven "in significant part" by extreme right-wing terrorism.
He continued: "Over the last year the most marked trend has been an increase in cases where extremist versions of anti-immigration and anti-Muslim grievance are tipping into terrorist intent."
Sir Ken said extreme right-wing terrorism tended to "skew young", driven by the internet - adding that MI5 had in recent months investigated a "radicalised extreme right-wing 13-year-old here in the UK".
He said: "That investigation generated insight that enabled one of our international partners to prevent a lethal attack on their soil."

Environment Ministry tours Taoyuan water and biomass recycling plant
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
12:51:49 UTC
21:51:49 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — The Ministry of Environment toured an upgraded water treatment facility in Taoyuan on Monday to see how it reuses organic waste, according to a press release.
At the Guishan Water Resources Recycling Center, Deputy Minister Shen Chih-hsiu (沈志修), Circular Taiwan Network Founder Charles Huang (黃育徵), and Taiwan Sugar Corporation Chair Wu Ming-chang (吳明昌) met with Yuen Foong Yu Fun Spring Circutech Chair Yeh Hui-ching (葉惠青) and the center’s team. They saw how the facility’s anaerobic digestion system converts kitchen waste into biogas.
The facility treated wastewater for 30 years before the Taoyuan City Government partnered with Yeh to upgrade it, per Business Today. It reopened on Oct. 15, 2025, and now treats about 23,000 metric tonnes of wastewater and approximately 30 tonnes of kitchen waste each day.
Anaerobic digestion uses microorganisms to break down organic matter, such as kitchen waste, livestock waste, or compost, in sealed, airtight settings. Biogas can generate electricity around the clock, unlike weather-dependent solar and wind power.
Yeh toured the facility and explained its installation maintenance cycle and material management process. Center staff demonstrated how organic matter is converted into biogas.
The center said the biogas is fed into a network of generators with a capacity of up to 800 kWh. It is expected to generate 6.4 million watts by late 2026 while cutting runoff sludge by 40%. Shen said he hopes the ministry will introduce the technology to other industries to help eliminate agricultural and kitchen waste.

Argentina seeks tribunal order against UK oil activity near Falklands
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
12:50:44 UTC
21:50:44 KST

Argentina seeks tribunal order against UK oil activity near Falklands
Oct 13 - Argentina's government said on Tuesday it had filed a request for provisional measures with the International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea seeking to halt British-authorized hydrocarbon activity near the Falkland Islands.
The request aims to prevent the United Kingdom from exploiting hydrocarbon resources on the continental shelf of the Northern Falklands Basin, the government added in a statement.
The filing "seeks to preserve Argentina's sovereign rights over its continental shelf and prevent activities authorized unilaterally and illegally by the United Kingdom," the government added.
Addressing Britain's parliament after Argentina's move, Uma Kumaran, parliamentary under-secretary for the foreign office, said that "legitimate commercial activity in the Falkland Islands remains lawful, and the British government stands behind those engaged in it."
Kumaran added that the UK would engage with the tribunal process but would not provide a running commentary on the proceedings.
"The notification does not constitute a judgment by an international court or tribunal. It does not invalidate licenses issued by the Falkland Islands government, alter the islands' regulatory authority, or require lawful hydrocarbon development activities to cease," Kumaran said. Britain also announced it was taking legal measures to protect businesses from pressure to comply with Argentine domestic measures.
Tensions between Argentina and the UK over the territory that is controlled by Britain but claimed by the South American country have escalated. Last month Milei's government presented legislation to crack down on companies drilling for oil off the Islands.
The government's proposal would toughen penalties on companies and individuals who participate in activities linked to natural resources in the Falklands, and in Argentina's maritime spaces without authorization from Argentine authorities. The new bill, which has yet to be approved by Congress, aims to revamp 2011 legislation with a tougher framework.
Argentine Foreign Minister Pablo Quirno said on X that the latest request aims to prevent the start or continuation of hydrocarbon development on the Sea Lion project.
Oil companies Navitas Petroleum and Rockhopper Exploration, owners of the Sea Lion offshore project north of the Falklands, have previously indicated they do not expect Argentina's actions to derail development.
Navitas Petroleum Chief Executive Ian Ramsey on Tuesday welcomed Britain's support for the project.
"In the face of Argentina's increasingly aggressive efforts to pressure companies associated with the development, we are grateful that the UK Government has made its position clear; that it will robustly defend the Falkland Islands' right to pursue lawful economic development," Ramsey said in a statement to Reuters. Poland called on Europe to switch to a &quot;war footing&quot; due to the pace of weapons production in the russian federation
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
15:50:26 EEST
21:50:26 KST

Poland called on Europe to switch to a "war footing" due to the pace of weapons production in the russian federation
Kyiv • UNN
Poland's Minister of Defence called on Europe to sharply increase the production of weapons and ammunition. russia is outpacing the EU in terms of arms production.
Polish Defence Minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz said that Europe must accelerate the production of ammunition and weapons in order not to fall behind Russia’s pace. He warned that failure to do so would have negative consequences for Europe. Euronews reports, writes UNN.
I am actually in favour of a wartime footing when it comes to production in the defence sector. That is exactly how the Russian Federation is operating now. We cannot ignore this fact
Russia switched to wartime production in the defence sector even before its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. According to forecasts, in 2026 it will spend 7.5% of its gross domestic product on the armed forces.
According to a recent report by Estonian intelligence, in 2025 Russia produced approximately seven million artillery, mortar, tank and missile munitions. Russian forces are currently using approximately 10,000–15,000 munitions daily, continuing their aggression against Ukraine.
By contrast, Europe’s defence industry suffered from insufficient funding and fragmentation for decades.
Russia is outproducing the EU in terms of ammunition production. According to a leaked report on Europe’s defence readiness, the 27 EU member states and Norway are expected to produce only two million 150 mm artillery shells this year.
The efforts of European countries and NATO members to rearm have delivered the largest annual increase in defence spending since the Cold War. Despite this, total defence spending by EU member states in 2025 was estimated at €418 billion, or 2.2% of the European Union’s combined GDP, the report says.
Kosiniak-Kamysz said that it was “time” for Europe to prepare to defend itself independently by significantly increasing production in the defence sector.
He warned that failure to do so would be a “costly” mistake for Europeans, adding: “This is one of the shortcomings, but in the future it will also have a negative impact on us and future generations.”
As the publication notes, Poland is among the countries that spend the largest share of GDP on defence capabilities. According to US representative to NATO Matthew Whitaker, the country allocates 4.7% of its GDP to core defence needs.

More than 20 fintech licences issued in 2026: LIAA’s foreign representatives prepare to bring the next companies to Latvia  - The Baltic Times
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
12:50:02 UTC
21:50:02 KST

The FinTech Latvia Association (FLA) and the Investment and Development Agency of Latvia (LIAA) held a workshop for LIAA’s foreign representatives. They are often the first people a foreign fintech company talks to when choosing its base in the European Union. At the workshop, they received the facts and arguments showing why a Latvian licence is a fast and reliable route into the European market.
The workshop came at the right time, as interest in Latvia as a fintech jurisdiction is growing. Since the beginning of 2026, Latvijas Banka has issued more than 20 licences to fintech companies – payment institutions, crowdfunding platforms, investment brokerage firms and crypto-asset service providers. Many other companies are currently in the licensing process or in pre-licensing consultations.
Tīna Lūse, Director of the FinTech Latvia Association: “We want Latvia’s fintech sector to grow and become stronger. That is why the association works actively to ensure that companies, the regulator and public institutions act in concert and pursue a common goal. A foreign company deciding where to enter the EU often speaks to LIAA’s representatives first. If they can confidently say that a licence in Latvia can be obtained within a few months and that the regulator is open to dialogue, Latvia is seriously considered.”
A sector that earns globally and pays taxes in Latvia
Latvia is home to 127 fintech companies. At the end of 2024, they employed 3,644 people – 9% more than a year earlier. The sector’s total turnover in Latvia reached almost €372 million, with profits of €97 million. The companies paid more than €91 million in taxes to the state budget – 28% more than in 2023.
Latvia is a base from which fintech companies conquer global markets: they obtain their licence and build their teams here, while serving clients across Europe and beyond. More than 800,000 investors from abroad invest through investment platforms licensed in Latvia, with the largest share coming from Germany. In total, more than €13 billion has been invested through these platforms, which serve almost a quarter of Europe’s peer-to-peer lending market.
The largest fintech groups headquartered in Riga also operate in many countries – the largest of them in as many as 17 countries on three continents. In 2025, the combined revenue of the two largest groups exceeded half a billion euros. That is more than the entire sector’s turnover in Latvia, which means that, including operations abroad, the sector’s total turnover could be up to twice as large.
Latvia’s advantages over other EU jurisdictions
- An accessible regulator. Latvijas Banka’s Innovation Hub, regulatory sandbox and free pre-licensing consultations. With well-prepared documents, a licence can be obtained within 2–3 months of submitting a complete application.
- A trusted jurisdiction. Latvia was the first country assessed by MONEYVAL in its new, 6th evaluation round. It received a high or substantial effectiveness rating on 10 of the 11 outcomes.
- Local talent. More than 90 of Latvia’s fintech companies are of Latvian origin, and the sector builds on strong local expertise in finance and technology.
Santa Purgaile, Deputy Governor of Latvijas Banka: “The requirements are the same across the European Union, but Latvijas Banka ensures that the licensing process is clear and smooth and provides all the advisory support companies need. Already in the pre-licensing consultations, companies learn exactly what we expect from them, so we can review a well-prepared application within a few months. A Latvijas Banka licence allows a company to operate throughout the European Union, and its value is further enhanced by Latvia’s internationally highly rated anti-money laundering framework.”
The workshop supports the implementation of Latvia’s Financial Technology Sector Development Strategy 2025–2027. By the end of 2027, the strategy aims to increase the number of fintech companies by 30%, attracted investment by 15% and jobs in the sector by 18%. FLA and LIAA work closely together to promote Latvia internationally and develop the fintech sector at home. Together, they take part in numerous international events – with Latvian stands at industry exhibitions and on trade missions – strengthening the international visibility of Latvia’s fintech ecosystem. Their next joint steps include Money20/20 Europe 2027 in Amsterdam and visits to Germany, Austria and France.
“Latvia has knowledgeable finance and technology professionals and companies that operate successfully in international markets. We want new foreign fintech companies to develop their business here too, creating well-paid jobs and increasing service exports. When choosing where to locate in Europe, companies need to understand how to obtain a licence, find employees and grow their business. Our foreign representatives are often their first point of contact with Latvia. The more specific our answers to these questions, the greater the chance that a company will choose Latvia,” says LIAA Director Ieva Jāgere.
FLA will publish the latest sector data in its annual Fintech Pulse 2026 report, which will be presented on 27 November.
About the FinTech Latvia Association
The FinTech Latvia Association is the industry organisation of Latvia’s financial technology sector, bringing together 39 members: payment and electronic money institutions, lenders, investment and crowdfunding platforms, regulatory technology companies and crypto-asset service providers. The association represents the sector in its relations with public institutions and the regulator, and publishes the annual industry report Fintech Pulse. www.fla.lv

"I would like to remind everyone that attempts are being made to destroy local self-government and remove 300 heads of communities. As head of the Association of Ukrainian Cities, I can say that 300 city mayors are being removed from office for various contrived reasons, made up on the spot, and replaced with heads of military administrations," Klitschko said in the video address.
He emphasized that he had been elected by Kyiv residents and noted that he was doing everything possible to live up to their trust. According to him, voters would be able to assess how well he had succeeded in the next elections.
Klitschko also rejected the accusations against him as groundless and noted that the city authorities regularly provide information about preparations for the heating season. "But, excuse me, given the intensity of the shelling, the power outages, the destruction of the electricity supply system and the ongoing damage to infrastructure, the mayor of the city is not responsible for air defense," he said.
As reported, an Interfax-Ukraine correspondent said that the Verkhovna Rada had supported a motion by MP Mariana Bezuhla to summon Klitschko. A total of 151 MPs voted in favor of the decision at Tuesday's session, while eight voted against.

Estonian court convicts gas station clerk who stole 67,000 liters of fuel
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
12:49:00 UTC
21:49:00 KST

Estonian court convicts gas station clerk who stole 67,000 liters of fuel
A court has convicted a former Olerex employee who, according to the charges, stole a total of 67,000 liters of diesel fuel from storage tanks while working at a gas station in Jüri.
The Ministry of Justice and Digital Affairs announced last week that a court had recently ruled on a case involving the theft of nearly 67,000 liters of diesel fuel from a gas station in dozens of separate incidents.
Toomas Tomberg, a prosecutor with the Northern District Prosecutor's Office who handled the case, told ERR that the thefts took place at the Olerex gas station in Jüri.
Prosecutors accused Igor Sorokin of using his access to the gas station's systems while working as a customer service representative to repeatedly steal diesel fuel from a storage tank.
According to the charges, he committed a total of 51 thefts between December 9, 2022, and January 25, 2024. To conceal the thefts, he switched off the gas station's video surveillance system before pumping diesel fuel into tanks installed in a vehicle he was using. Prosecutors accused him of stealing nearly 67,000 liters of diesel fuel worth almost €108,600.
The court found Sorokin guilty of large-scale, systematic theft and sentenced him to two years and six months in prison, suspended for a three-year probationary period. He was also ordered to compensate Olerex for €108,589 in financial losses. The ruling has not yet entered into force.
"The court proceedings confirmed that this was not an isolated act but a series of systematic thefts committed over an extended period. Although the defendant was caught in the act during one incident in January 2024, work schedules, video surveillance logs, storage tank records, witness testimony and other evidence gathered allowed the court to find that the remaining incidents described in the charges had also been proven," Tomberg said.
He added that the court agreed with prosecutors that the evidence formed a coherent and reliable body of proof establishing the defendant's actions throughout the period covered by the charges.
According to Tomberg, the case is notable both for the amount of fuel stolen and the length of time over which the thefts took place.
"It also demonstrates that prolonged, concealed activity causing financial losses to a company can be proven even when direct evidence relates to only part of the criminal activity, while the remaining incidents are established through a body of mutually corroborating circumstantial evidence," he said.
Recurring fuel theft on the rise
According to statistics from the Ministry of Justice and Digital Affairs, more than 2,000 fuel thefts have been recorded so far this year, nearly 50 percent more than a year ago.
The ministry noted that this does not necessarily mean people across Estonia have suddenly become twice as inclined to steal. Rather, the statistics suggest that thieves have become more systematic in their activities and that some incidents are being classified as criminal offenses because of their repeated nature.
A single theft may constitute a misdemeanor, but when someone repeatedly and knowingly engages in the same behavior, it becomes a criminal offense.
Fuel thefts are largely responsible for the more than 6 percent year-on-year increase in property crimes, the ministry said.

Chinese delegation visits Japan-Russia disputed island to explore joint projects

Saadet Gokce
13 October 2026•Update: 13 October 2026
A Chinese delegation has visited Russian-held islands claimed by Japan to conduct feasibility studies for joint projects, Kyodo News reported Tuesday.
The delegation’s visit followed Russian President Vladimir Putin’s trip to the island of Etorofu in August, his first visit to the Russian-controlled but Japanese-claimed island chain off Hokkaido, which prompted protests from Tokyo.
Russia calls the islands the Southern Kuril Islands, while Japan refers to them collectively as the Northern Territories.
The Chinese delegation from the northeastern province of Heilongjiang, which included businesspeople, visited the largest of the disputed islands, Kyodo reported, citing the government of Sakhalin Oblast, a Russian Far Eastern region that includes the islands.
Sakhalin authorities said the visit focused on international cooperation, with Gov. Valery Limarenko highlighting the area’s potential for tourism and other businesses.
Tokyo maintains that the Northern Territories, consisting of Iturup, Kunashiri, Shikotan and the Habomai islet group, were “illegally” seized by the now-defunct Soviet Union soon after Japan’s surrender in World War II on Aug. 15, 1945.
Russia argues that the seizure was legitimate.
The territorial dispute has prevented the two countries from signing a peace treaty since World War II. Tensions have deepened in recent years amid Japan’s sanctions against Moscow over the Russia-Ukraine war.
The Japanese government summoned Russian Ambassador to Japan Nikolay Nozdrev to lodge a “strong protest” over Putin’s visit, while Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi said the islands were an inherent part of Japanese territory “both historically and under international law.”

====================================================================================================

Scientists wonder: Is my AI stealing my ideas?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
12:48:08 UTC
21:48:08 KST

Recently, controversy and accusations have followed artificial intelligence companies flexing their models’ research capabilities. When OpenAI claimed an internal model had solved one of math’s seven million-dollar problems, a mathematician at New York University insinuated that the company had stolen his progress, which he had shared with one of their chatbots. Weeks later, the New York Times reported a similar story unfolding between Anthropic and a biologist at the University of Copenhagen regarding a group of enzymes.
Despite this, scientists from all disciplines are opting to use these companies’ large language models. Some use them as a soundboard or a tool for literature review, others for cleaning up nearly finished work. And mathematicians and theorists are tapping their new, powerful models to generate entire proofs for their research. But as researchers feed more of their data and ideas into these models, concerns are growing about how that content is getting used.
Both OpenAI and Anthropic stated unequivocally that they did not train their models on the mathematician’s and biologist’s uploaded data, respectively. But the companies—which have not consistently met academic norms—don’t have every scientist’s trust. Some suspect they may not even have the full picture themselves. Their agents could be accessing data in ways the companies don’t even realize. After all, it took three months for the public to learn that OpenAI’s models had breached containment and hacked into foreign government databases.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
With these conspiracy theories swirling, some researchers are now seeing the models more as competitors than tools—and the use of them as a betrayal. “I’m not encouraging it, and I’m not doing it myself,” says Clément Canonne, a theoretical computer scientist at the University of Sydney. “I’m not using them.”
Ahead of taking their companies public, OpenAI and Anthropic are increasingly stepping into math and science to show how capable their products are. But AI has sometimes felt less like a guest over for dinner and more like an unwanted visitor breaking and entering. If scientists feel that these companies are rifling through their every interaction, they may start locking them out entirely.
The lack of transparency invites these sorts of fears. “Right now, these systems infer things about you without telling you that they’re inferring things about you,” says Jennifer King, a fellow at the Stanford University Institute for Human-Centered Artificial Intelligence, who researches data privacy and policy.
King says the only way for researchers to really ensure their safety when using large language models at the present moment is to look at their account settings carefully. According to her, “enterprise” accounts—which represent a special deal worked out between a client company and the AI’s owners—seem to be safe. “But if you are on a personal account, all bets are off,” she warns. She describes how users on personal accounts need to explicitly opt out in many cases to prevent their information being used from training.
Plus, even if a company isn’t intentionally using your data to train their models, one of their many agents could always go rogue, infiltrating company data and hoovering up individual users’ conversations with their chatbots. While there is no evidence this happened in the case of any of the AI companies’ scientific discoveries, rogue events over the summer have left some extra concerned about who they trust with their data.
The trouble is, it’s hard to get much evidence at all out of the tech giants. “The companies are not transparent about these practices, so it’s really hard to pin down,” King says. That means experts can’t speculate about any particular case. But in general, “the companies spy on you and use that information against you,” says Bruce Schneier, a security researcher and activist.
The new AI models are very capable, including for research, and many believe they will help researchers find new results faster. So scientists may feel they face a choice: either use the models and risk leaking a discovery or don’t and risk someone who does publishing it first.
All this has created an uneasy landscape in which many scientists are left feeling they have to give up their privacy and work to keep up. “There is definitely a pressure,” Canonne says. “If you’re not using them, are you going to be irrelevant?”

MI5 to step up on AI threats amid bioweapon risk
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
12:45:58 UTC
21:45:58 KST

Director General of MI5, Sir Ken McCallum speaks at Thames House, the headquarters of the UK's Security Service on October 13, 2026 in London. | WPA pool photo by Jonathan Brady/Getty Images
LONDON — Britain’s spies will have a leading role in Britain’s preparation for AI threats, the head of MI5 announced on Tuesday, after warning the technology could enable terrorists to access bioweapons.
Ken McCallum, director general of the U.K.'s domestic intelligence agency has established the AI Threat Assessment Centre to help determine how the government views potential threats.
Giving his annual threat update from MI5 headquarters in London, McCallum said: “Human history has given us no experience of facing an actor which is smarter than we are, is capable of outthinking us.”
Advertisement
He stressed the “real” risks of AI, saying MI5 has caught terrorists seeking to use AI to “improve their reconnaissance and attack methodologies,” in addition to the danger of AI-enabled drones.
Though it has not yet been “realized,” he said he attaches “the greatest weight” to AI’s potential to “change the stakes on existing or even new bioweapons.”
He said “low-capability” terrorists may get a “capability” uplift if the safety guardrails in AI models don't work as intended.
He added that for a long time “many terrorists would dearly love” access to chemical, biological or radiological weapons, but that it has been hard for them to achieve.
“One risk is that AI could enable dangerous knowledge to get into the hands of people who [...] didn't have that knowledge.”
McCallum added that “sober attention” must be given to the risk that “AI could generate novel pathogens not previously seen.” He noted that the government is taking “additional steps” on bioweapons.
Advertisement
One thing that “does trouble me”, McCallum said, is the pace at which the world is evolving. He noted that the "weird bits inside MI5” that focus on how Britain's adversaries will act in five years from now are seeing those timelines shortening due to AI.
He said it is now his responsibility to “drag my organization forwards at a faster pace than human beings generally want to be dragged.”
Sifting threats from hype
The new threat assessment centre, known as AITAC, will bring together expertise from bodies including Britain’s AI Security Institute, National Crime Agency, and the National Cyber Security Centre to “separate the bluster from the realities” of AI's threat to the British public.
Asked how the agency would work, McCallum said it would look at emerging trends and how the U.K. can best think about and prioritize the various manifestations of AI threats.
Though the government, rather than AITAC, will decide the response to AI, McCallum said it was partly set up to avoid “competitive analysis, slightly conflicting and confusing messages that otherwise might exist, where you have different departments offering their own opinion” on the issue.
Advertisement
He said that it would enable everyone to have “a single version of the truth, a single understanding, a single lexicon, typography.”
McCallum also said MI5 will now give national resilience — such as protecting critical infrastructure, countering cognitive warfare, and addressing technology threats — “front-rank mission status” alongside its twin roles of countering state threats and terrorism.
He noted that MI5 is now devoting more resources to countering state threats than it was during the Cold War, noting an uptick in anti-immigration cases tipping into terrorist intent, while Iran has shifted its ambitions to hit harder targets such as military sites.

Egypt's Baha'i minority is running out of space to bury their dead
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
12:45:47 UTC
21:45:47 KST

Egypt's Baha'i minority is running out of space to bury their dead
CAIRO, Oct 13 - In a Cairo cemetery shaded by palms and tangled shrubs, pale graves are packed so tightly that in some places only narrow strips of sand and broken pavement separate one family’s plot from the next.
This is the last remaining burial place of Egypt's Baha'i community, a religious minority long on the margins of official life, and it is quickly running out of room.
As it fills, the cemetery has become a symbol for the community of the bureaucratic obstacles and restrictions they say complicate everything from school enrollment to pensions and marriage registration.
"God forbid that this area becomes completely full. If that happens, we would have no other places where we can bury," said Joumana Labib, a 25-year-old architect whose extended family is buried there.
The Baha'i faith, whose members are scattered across different continents and believe their 19th century founder Baha'u'llah is a prophet, was brought to Egypt by merchants in the 1860s, not long after it originated in Iran. With current numbers in Egypt estimated in the thousands, they are a tiny minority in a mainly Muslim country of about 110 million.
The Egyptian constitution guarantees religious freedom, though mainstream Islamic scholars view the Baha'i faith as heretical and officials are often reluctant in practice to recognise religions outside the main Abrahamic faiths.
BURIAL REQUIRED WITHIN ONE-HOUR JOURNEY
While Islamic tradition requires burial within a day, Baha'i practices allow a body to be moved no more than one hour from the place of death, creating particular challenges.
Burial grounds once used by Baha'is in the port cities of Alexandria and Port Said have been filled or reassigned over the years, leaving many families to transport bodies to Cairo, according to the Egyptian Initiative for Personal Rights (EIPR), a leading Cairo-based rights group.
Community members say requests for new burial grounds in Alexandria and Port Said — where much of Egypt's Baha'i community lives — have been rejected without clear written explanations, said Marina Samir, who heads EIPR's freedom of religion and belief work.
"Death becomes, instead of a time when people are trying to comprehend their loss, a logistical process," Samir said.
Egypt's government information agency and the governorates of Alexandria and Port Said did not respond to requests for comment.
Last year, in a response to a UN human rights report, Egypt's government said it "does not impose any restrictions on personal belief or religious affiliation, including adherence to the Baha’i faith".
Based on government data, there were "sufficient burial sites to meet the needs of all citizens", it said.
President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi has repeatedly stressed the need for religious coexistence and said the state works tirelessly to fight discrimination and promote tolerance.
MARRIAGE WITHOUT RECOGNITION
A landmark 2009 court ruling allowed those who do not follow Islam, Christianity or Judaism to leave a dash in the religion field on their identity documents.
The change allowed Baha'is to avoid declaring a faith they do not follow, but still left them facing practical difficulties.
One of the biggest is establishing Baha'i marriages in official records. Baha'i couples are often registered as "single" even after decades together, which can complicate child registration, inheritance, pensions, health insurance and family records.
Hanan Kamal El-Din, 65, said her identity card describes her as single, although she married in a Baha'i ceremony 45 years ago and has two children in their 40s.
"What harm would recognising this marriage do to society?" she said.
Like other Baha'is, she won an individual court ruling recognising her marriage in 2020. But that decision was overturned by a higher court in January this year, a ruling other Baha'i couples now fear could affect them as well.
Ahmed Helmy, 49, also won a court ruling allowing his documents to show he was married, but said his wife has already been removed from the family section of his account on the government’s digital services platform.
He worries his status on his identity card will revert to "single" when he next renews it.
"If I do not have proof of marriage, I cannot add my wife to health insurance," he said. "Anything I own, my wife won't be able to inherit. Anything she owns, I won't be able to inherit."
For Labib, the community's shrinking burial space and the bureaucratic hurdles are connected by the same demand: to be treated as an equal citizen.
"I am not asking anyone to accept my religion," she said. "I am asking them to accept me as a person in this country." REUTERS

More
Beyond tariffs: how Switzerland turned trade talks into climate action with Mercosur
It was argued that large-scale soya cultivation and intensive cattle farming are key drivers of rainforest deforestation in the South American Mercosur states.

Government, parliament must reach a common understanding to manage economic conditions: Qalibaf
TEHRAN- Parliament Speaker Mohammad-Baqer Qalibaf, emphasizing the necessity of coordination and consensus between the government and parliament in managing the country's economic conditions, said: "Accurate assessment of the current situation and outlining upcoming scenarios can provide the basis for more effective decision-making to improve people's livelihoods and manage economic challenges in the second half of the year."

In this meeting, which was attended by Ali Nikzad, First Vice Speaker of the Parliament; Gholamreza Tajgardoun, Head of the Budget and Planning Committee; Mohammad-Javad Askari, Head of the Agriculture, Water, Natural Resources and Environment Committee; Shamseddin Hosseini, Head of the Economic Committee; Ali Babaei Karmani, Head of the Social Committee; Seyyed Hamid Pourmohammadi, Head of the Plan and Budget Organization; Ahmad Meidari, Minister of Cooperatives, Labor and Social Welfare; Abdolnaser Hemmati, Governor General of the Central Bank; Gholamreza Nouri Qezeljeh, Minister of Agriculture; Seyyed Ali Madanizadeh, Minister of Economic Affairs and Finance; and Babak Negahdari, Head of the Parliament Research Center, the ministers and government officials and the heads of committees and the head of the Parliament Research Center discussed and exchanged views on various issues including the commodity coupon (Kalabarg) plan, securing the livelihood of the people and the armed forces, the state of agricultural and livestock production, the supply of production inputs, investment and economic growth, compensation for war damages, and other issues related to their areas of responsibility.
The Speaker of the Islamic Parliament in this session, emphasizing the necessity of forming a common understanding between the government and parliament about the country's economic conditions, said: "The most important point that we must pay attention to is the necessity of consensus and having a common understanding of the current situation and upcoming conditions."
He added: "We have passed the first six months of the year, and we now have experience from this period; accordingly, we must plan for the next six months by accurately assessing past events."
Qalibaf added: "Both the government and the parliament and all institutions are trying and managing the conditions, and in this regard, we need to make decisions with a more precise view based on an assessment of the conditions."
The Parliament Speaker, emphasizing that we must determine what the scenario ahead for the next six months is, and if we have consensus on this, we can design better for it, said: "Alongside issues such as compensation for damages, supply of raw materials and matters of the industrial sector, improving the livelihood level of the people and the armed forces are two important priorities that must be seriously considered."
He emphasized: "The decisions we make must be such that the people's table is the last place affected by sanctions and war, and also the first place where a correct managerial decision has a positive effect; in this regard, we must set goals correctly and accurately and direct resources toward the point we want."
The head of the legislative branch added: "As someone who has managed crises from the first days of the revolution until now and has learned management in crisis, I say with all my being that in times of crisis, the greatest opportunities exist for us, and we must not neglect this matter."
Emphasizing that today economic war is more important than cognitive, military and cyber wars, and economic war is the main axis of the war against us, hr stated: "In economic war, our main challenge is the challenge of decision-making, management and stable governance."
Stating that in war conditions we must accept responsibility, make decisions, and courageously defend those who work, he said: "Do not doubt that if we move forward in coordination in this gathering, we can, through synergy, place the parliament and the government on a single axis in the economic field and move forward."
Qalibaf, stating that currently the most important priority in all decision-making is the livelihood of the people and the armed forces, said: "We must act in such a way that the people's livelihood is the last place harmed by the pressure of war and sanctions, and the first positive result of decisions is on the people's table. This view must also exist in economic growth, reconstruction, and providing liquidity to the industrial sector."

The great Indian scam trap: More aware, yet still vulnerable
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
12:45:18 UTC
21:45:18 KST

A 79-year-old woman in Mumbai recently tried to buy dry fruits worth Rs 248 after seeing an advertisement on WhatsApp. Instead, she lost Rs 11.7 lakh after a caller posing as a company representative persuaded her to make 13 UPI transfers. She was warned that her bank account could be closed due to a technical error.Her experience brings together several findings in the GSMA India Consumer Scam Report 2026, based on an online, English-language survey of about 500 Indian adults conducted from July 29 to August 3. Online shopping scams were cited by 33% of Indian victims, more than any other type. Among surveyed victims who lost money, two in three recovered nothing.The survey compares Indian respondents with those in Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand, Indonesia, the Philippines and Vietnam. Three in four Indians surveyed (75%) said they were very concerned about online data privacy, against 48% across those six countries. Yet two in three (66%) were comfortable sharing personal details with “conversational apps” when buying, against 40% across the region. A third (33%) said they were "very comfortable" doing so, against just 7%. The report does not name the apps or establish whether respondents actually shared their details.
Privacy fears high, but Indians willing to share data
Trusting the channels scammers use
Indians also rate everyday communication channels as more trustworthy than respondents in the six Southeast Asian countries. These are also channels regularly used by scammers. Among Indian victims, 42% were scammed through messaging apps, 37% through social media and 33% through email. The email figure is almost double the regional 17%. And 64% of Indian victims were scammed through multiple channels, against 43% across the Southeast Asian countries.
Messaging apps lead scam routes, with 42% exposure
After online shopping, prize, lottery or inheritance scams were cited by 31% of Indian victims (remember the Nigerian prince emails?), and job or income scams by 30%. QR-code or payment-link scams were cited by 27%, against 18% across the region.Scammers also apply psychological pressure. Urgency featured in 39% of Indian victims' experiences, while secrecy or confidentiality featured in 33%, against a regional average of 22% for secrecy. In the Mumbai case, the alleged fraudster created a fear of losing banking access by warning that a technical problem could lead to account closure. Digital-arrest scams often play on the secrecy angle by leveraging potentially sensitive information.Technology adds another layer. Nearly half of Indian respondents (48%) said they had encountered AI-written scam messages, the same share reported fake AI images, and 42% said they had seen deepfake videos of real people.
The changing behaviour pattern
Indians are gradually becoming more guarded against scams. Seventy-two per cent of Indian respondents said their own experience, or that of someone close to them, had changed how they behave. Sixty-one per cent avoided some incoming contacts or online transactions because of scam concerns, and 26% had cut back on or changed how they shop online, up from 20% in 2025.There is healthy scepticism about platforms too. Sixty per cent associated Facebook with scams, up from 51% in 2025, and Instagram's figure rose from 50% to 57%.But only 49% had strengthened their account security, against 58% across the region. Among victims, 93% said that, in hindsight, they had done something they should not have, and 91% felt confident they would not fall for a similar scam again.Indians are relatively willing to let institutions use their data to detect fraud. Of the respondents, 87% were comfortable with banks or financial providers doing so, 82% with the government, 81% with mobile operators and 73% with digital platforms, each higher than the corresponding regional figure.
Recovering losses is difficult
Twelve per cent of Indian respondents said they had been scammed in the previous year, against 8% across the region. Of the 165 Indian respondents who had ever been scammed, 86% approached at least one organisation, against 69% across the region. The share going to the police rose from 37% in the 2025 survey to 49%.However, a third of reported cases remained unresolved, and in 35%, no organisation took primary responsibility in the victim's experience. Among those who lost money, 67% recovered nothing. India's recovery outcome was nevertheless better than the six-country average. Some 33% recovered some or all of their money, against 18% across the region.
India's record is better than countries in Southeast Asia
The home ministry told Parliament that the Citizen Financial Cyber Fraud Reporting and Management System had "saved" more than Rs 11,158 crore across over 32.80 lakh complaints by June 30, 2026, but that figure does not show how much victims got back. In a separate disclosure, the ministry reported more than Rs 206 crore refunded over the three financial years from 2023-24 to 2025-26. The National Crime Records Bureau does not maintain data on money lost or recovered in cyber fraud cases, Rajya Sabha was informed.
Scam, a global menace
GSMA, which represents mobile operators, calls for closer coordination among banks, platforms, telecom companies and authorities after scams are reported, and for greater transparency from government and police.Scams are a global business. The Global Anti-Scam Alliance estimates that consumers across 42 surveyed markets lost about $442 billion to scams in a year. In the US, the FBI recorded $20.877 billion in cybercrime losses in 2025, more than $2.9 billion of it from two forms of call-centre fraud: fake tech support and government impersonation. The FBI's 2025 Internet Crime Report recorded 5,879 complaints from India, the second-highest among countries outside the US, after Canada.
Since 2022, the FBI and CBI have run 27 joint operations against such fraud in India, leading to more than 475 arrests. One of them, Operation Chakra, broke up a Noida-based network in December 2025 accused of duping more than 600 Americans of over $48.7 million.If you are conned, call 1930 immediately. It may help save your money.

World standards day ceremony held in Tehran
TEHRAN- The ceremony commemorating World Standards Day was held on the morning of October 13, under the slogan "Shared Vision for a Better World" and focusing on "Clean and Affordable Energy." The event was organized by the National Standards Organization of Iran and attended by a number of national officials and those active in the quality sector at the Summit Hall.
The ceremony also emphasized the necessity of developing clean energy, increasing productivity, and upgrading standards related to energy consumption in energy-intensive industries. Optimizing production processes, developing renewable energy infrastructure, and reducing environmental pollution are among the areas in which these standards play a role.
The implementation of energy management standards in the agricultural and food industry value chain is also particularly important. The use of clean and low-consumption technologies in sectors such as cold storage, processing industries, and industrial greenhouses, in addition to helping manage production costs, can help maintain product quality after harvest and reduce agricultural waste.
Standardization of energy-intensive equipment and processes in agriculture and the food industry also provides the basis for increasing productivity, optimal use of resources, and strengthening sustainable food security infrastructure. From this perspective, the development and implementation of energy-related standards, in addition to economic effects, are also important in protecting natural resources and reducing the environmental consequences of production activities.
In another part of the ceremony, top production and service units at both national and provincial levels, conformity assessment bodies including inspection companies and partner laboratories, corresponding technical committees, quality control managers, sample drafting secretaries, and pioneers in the field of quality were honored.
This ceremony was held with the aim of explaining the role of standards in improving the quality of products and services, enhancing productivity, and supporting sustainable development.

MOSCOW, October 13. /TASS/. Russia is open to all foreigners who share and respect its values and culture, according to a welcoming address by Russian Historical Society Chairman and Foreign Intelligence Service Director Sergey Naryshkin to participants of the Third International Catherine Forum.

"Today, Russia is open to everyone who shares its spiritual and moral values, respects the culture and traditions of the peoples inhabiting our country, and seeks to build their future here," Naryshkin noted. "I am convinced that the proposals developed here will help continue a centuries-old tradition through which people from different countries have found a new homeland in Russia."

"The ability to unite representatives of a wide variety of peoples while preserving the diversity of their traditions and cultures has been and remains a key foundation of Russian statehood, our civilizational advantage and an integral part of our national character," he added.
"This characteristic was particularly evident during the reign of Catherine II. In response to her call, tens of thousands of people from German lands, Switzerland and the Netherlands moved to Russia. As we approach the 300th anniversary of the empress’s birth, it is encouraging that this year’s Catherine Forum is revisiting this historical experience, which remains relevant to this day," the Russian Foreign Intelligence Service director concluded.
About the forum
The Catherine Forum is an international public and government platform dedicated to Russia’s civilizational development, traditional spiritual and moral values, and international humanitarian cooperation.
The forum is being held for the third time this year. Its agenda focuses on integrating foreign nationals moving to Russia, attracting highly qualified foreign specialists, reducing barriers for people relocating to the country, supporting Russian-speaking communities abroad, public diplomacy and Russia’s image in the international media landscape.
TASS is the informational partner of the forum.

African Union holds Kigali talks as fighting continues in eastern DRC
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
12:40:26 UTC
21:40:26 KST

African Union holds Kigali talks as fighting continues in eastern DRC
Three former African presidents discussed security commitments, refugee protection and regional cooperation.
Kigali, Rwanda – The African Union (AU) has held consultations in Kigali, Rwanda, as part of efforts to advance the peace process in the eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), where fighting continues despite diplomatic initiatives to end the conflict.
The consultations, held on October 6, focused on implementing the Washington Peace Agreement, security arrangements, the disarmament, demobilisation and reintegration of fighters, refugee protection and regional economic cooperation, the AU said in a statement.
The delegation comprised former Ethiopian President Sahle-Work Zewde, former Kenyan President Uhuru Kenyatta and former Botswana President Mokgweetsi Masisi. Zewde is the deputy chairperson of the AU Panel of Facilitators for the eastern DRC peace process.
From Goma to Kigali
The Kigali consultations followed meetings in Goma, eastern DRC, on October 5. According to the AU, the delegation met representatives of the United Nations Organization Stabilization Mission in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (MONUSCO), the UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA), the International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC), the Expanded Joint Verification Mechanism Plus (EJVM+) and the Alliance Fleuve Congo/March 23 Movement (AFC/M23).
Following the Goma meetings, the AU panel called for respect for ceasefire commitments, cooperation with verification mechanisms and restraint from actions that could undermine the peace process. It also stressed the need to protect civilians, ensure safe humanitarian access and prevent sexual and gender-based violence.
In Kigali, the facilitators held separate consultations with Rwandan officials and representatives of regional institutions. The AU said the discussions covered security commitments, the protection of refugees and returnees, and regional economic cooperation, including mineral traceability, cross-border trade, energy and infrastructure.
The facilitators said they would continue their engagements in Kinshasa as part of efforts to support dialogue and advance the peace process.
Two agreements, separate negotiations
The consultations come amid parallel diplomatic efforts to address the conflict. The Washington Peace Agreement, signed by the DRC and Rwanda on June 27, 2025, includes security commitments intended to address concerns over armed groups and the presence of forces in eastern DRC.
Implementation remains a central issue. At a meeting of the agreement’s Joint Oversight Committee in June 2026, the parties expressed concern over escalating fighting and called for the agreement to be fully implemented, including commitments concerning the Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Rwanda (FDLR) and the disengagement of forces.
The Washington agreement is separate from the Doha Framework for a Comprehensive Peace Agreement, signed on November 15, 2025, by representatives of the Congolese government and AFC/M23 under Qatar’s mediation.
The Doha framework provides a basis for negotiations between the two sides on outstanding issues, including security arrangements and ceasefire monitoring. Subsequent discussions have focused on implementing existing commitments and negotiating remaining protocols.
The two processes address different aspects of the conflict: the Washington agreement deals with relations and security commitments between the DRC and Rwanda, while the Doha process addresses negotiations between the Congolese government and AFC/M23.
Kinshasa and Kigali remain at odds
Kinshasa accuses Rwanda of supporting AFC/M23, an allegation Kigali denies. Rwanda, in turn, accuses the Congolese government of supporting and arming the FDLR, which it considers a threat to its national security.
The Washington agreement includes commitments by the DRC to address the FDLR and by Rwanda concerning the disengagement of its forces and the lifting of defensive measures. The parties have continued to discuss how those commitments will be implemented and verified.
The continued diplomatic engagement reflects the challenges facing efforts to resolve the conflict, with security commitments and negotiations involving different parties proceeding on separate tracks.
The AU’s consultations in Goma and Kigali form part of its wider mediation efforts. Whether those efforts contribute to improved security will depend on the implementation of commitments by the parties and continued engagement in the respective peace processes.

Nord Stream: Trial of Ukrainian attack suspect begins in Germany
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
12:40:00 UTC
21:40:00 KST

Nord Stream: Germany puts suspected pipeline saboteur on trial
October 13, 2026
The aerial photos made headlines worldwide: On September 26, 2022, massive quantities of methane gas bubbled on the surface of the Baltic Sea near the island of Bornholm. Unknown people had blown up three of the four sections of the Nord Stream 1 and 2 gas pipelines from Russia to Germany.
The attack, which occurred seven months after Moscow launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine, meant the end of a mega energy project between Germany and Russia in which both sides had invested billions, and which secured affordable Russian gas for Germany. However, the flow of gas via Nord Stream 1 had been restricted or stopped several times by Russia since the Ukraine war began; Nord Stream 2 was not yet operational.
From October 14, Ukrainian citizen Serhii K. is facing trial before a court in the northern German city of Hamburg. He was arrested in Italy in August 2025 on a European arrest warrant and later extradited to Germany. This week he must answer for the attacks before the Hanseatic Higher Regional Court. He is accused of being an accomplice to a war crime by attacking civil energy infrastructure, disruption of public services, causing an explosion and destroying structures.
Ukraine aid criticized
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has repeatedly said that Ukraine was not involved in the 2022 attack on the Nord Stream underwater gas pipelines.
"Ukraine has never officially taken part in any operation related to the blowing up of Nord Stream," Zelenskyy told reporters again in August in response to a question about the ongoing investigation.
The fact that the accused is Ukrainian is especially politically sensitive. Germany continues to support the country after it was attacked by Russia: militarily, financially, with humanitarian aid and by taking in about 1.3 million refugees.
Critics of Germany's support for Ukraine, especially the right-wing extremist Alternative for Germany (AfD) and the left-wing populist Alliance for Social Justice and Economic Reason (BSW) want to improve relations with Moscow, resume energy deliveries from Russia – including via a repaired Nord Stream pipeline — and stop supporting Ukraine. Some of them have practically delivered their verdict on Serhii K., although the trial has not yet begun, and assume that Ukraine's political or military leadership was behind the attack on the pipeline.
Sahra Wagenknecht, former leader of the BSW, told news agency Reuters in 2025 following Serhii K.'s arrest: "It is totally absurd that Germany spends many billions on aid for Ukraine but never demands an explanation from [President Volodymyr] Zelenskyy. Questions should also be raised about possible compensation."
Alice Weidel, co-leader of the AfD, has shared similar sentiments. In early 2026, she asserted that the German government must seek financial repayment from Ukraine. If the AfD came into power, she would demand Kyiv compensate Germany for blowing up the pipeline and pay for its repair. According to her, a country that does such things is "no friend of Germany." She has, however, failed to provide proof that Ukraine was behind the attack.
Who benefited from blowing up the pipeline?
In an interview with public broadcaster Deutschlandfunk in 2023, German naval commander Göran Swistek pointed out that, given the technical, financial, and organizational effort involved, “there is likely a state-run structure behind it.” In his opinion, a group of amateurs could not have carried out the act.
However, he considered it unlikely that this state could be Ukraine, since Ukraine, after all, would not want to jeopardize German support. At the time, Swistek thought a false lead pointing to Russia was possible.
The German-Russian Nord Stream project had many opponents from the beginning, including Poland, the US, the Baltic countries and — especially since Russia's full-scale invasion — Ukraine. That is why investigators always ask: Who benefits from the explosion?
Henning Hoff from the German Council on Foreign Relations (DGAP) thinks it is important to shed light on the background context.
"By halting supplies or using the threat to do so as leverage, Russia exerted immense pressure on Germany at the time, and gas markets went haywire," he told DW. "The explosion thwarted Russian attempts to extort Germany, prices for natural gas sank. I think one could say: The explosion was in German interests."
Berlin's dilemma
But what will happen if the Ukrainian Serhii K. is found guilty and a connection to the military or political leadership of Ukraine is proven? Could the German government still continue its current course regarding Ukraine?
The German government faces a dilemma: On one side, judicial independence must be preserved and consequences for the sabotaging German infrastructure must be pursued. On the other side, the German government wants to prevent Russia from instrumentalizing the case. However, pressure on Germany would increase enormously, also from within the country.
Roderich Kiesewetter, a lawmaker with the ruling center-right Christian Democrats (CDU), said there is no reason to deviate from the current course of support, even in the case of involvement by Kyiv: "Irrespective of the outcome, no consequences at all are appropriate, because our support for Ukraine is carried out in the interest of our own national security and stems from a sense of responsibility for a free Europe."
The debate around support for Ukraine is escalating in Germany, regardless of the court process. Public backing for Ukraine is decreasing, especially for deliveries of weapons.
The AfD gained significant support in three state parliament elections held in eastern Germany during September. The party could potentially supply the state premier in Saxony-Anhalt. The AfD has also led nationwide polls for months, far ahead of the conservative CDU of Chancellor Friedrich Merz.
In addition, the AfD and BSW have drawn a connection between planned government spending cuts on social services and aid to Ukraine.
Wagenknech told a campaign event before the state parliament elections that the federal government was "Sinking billions upon billions into the black hole of Ukraine, while in Germany, in our schools, the children are no longer properly learning reading, writing and arithmetic." Tino Chrupalla, co-leader of the AfD, raised the question of whether citizens were prepared to spend so much money on a non-EU and non-NATO country.
Repair of Nord Stream unlikely
Given very expensive energy costs, it is not only the AfD and BSW who suggest repairing Nord Stream and receiving new deliveries of gas from Russia. Some CDU politicians favor this too, such as Saxony state premier Michael Kretschmer. He views a repaired gas pipeline as a possible bargaining chip for talks with Russia. Kretschmer's position, however, contradicts the federal CDU party line and European Union sanctions policies.
His party colleague Kiesewetter considers it dangerous: "Russia has always used energy as an instrument of geo-economic extortion. It would be extremely dumb if we were to again learn nothing from history and cling to a special path with Russia. That would fuel mistrust among our partners in Europe. I can only advise everyone, including people from the CDU, to keep their distance from such calls, because they are against German interests."
Hoff from the DGAP also rejected positions like Kretschmer's. "That is an illusion. There is no returning to the time before Russia's war. The supposedly cheap Russian gas, which has cost Germany dearly, will never flow again, if only because Putin has no interest in it doing so. It serves only as an instrument of propaganda for polarizing German politics and weakening support for Ukraine."
In any case, the outcome of the trial in Hamburg will undoubtedly influence the public debate about further support for Ukraine.

Nord Stream: Germany puts suspected Ukrainian pipeline saboteur on trial
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13

Nord Stream: Germany puts suspected pipeline saboteur on trial
October 13, 2026
The aerial photos made headlines worldwide: On September 26, 2022, massive quantities of methane gas bubbled on the surface of the Baltic Sea near the island of Bornholm. Unknown people had blown up three of the four sections of the Nord Stream 1 and 2 gas pipelines from Russia to Germany.
The attack, which occurred seven months after Moscow launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine, meant the end of a mega energy project between Germany and Russia in which both sides had invested billions, and which secured affordable Russian gas for Germany. However, the flow of gas via Nord Stream 1 had been restricted or stopped several times by Russia since the Ukraine war began; Nord Stream 2 was not yet operational.
From October 14, Ukrainian citizen Serhii K. is facing trial before a court in the northern German city of Hamburg. He was arrested in Italy in August 2025 on a European arrest warrant and later extradited to Germany. This week he must answer for the attacks before the Hanseatic Higher Regional Court. He is accused of being an accomplice to a war crime by attacking civil energy infrastructure, disruption of public services, causing an explosion and destroying structures.
Ukraine aid criticized
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has repeatedly said that Ukraine was not involved in the 2022 attack on the Nord Stream underwater gas pipelines.
"Ukraine has never officially taken part in any operation related to the blowing up of Nord Stream," Zelenskyy told reporters again in August in response to a question about the ongoing investigation.
The fact that the accused is Ukrainian is especially politically sensitive. Germany continues to support the country after it was attacked by Russia: militarily, financially, with humanitarian aid and by taking in about 1.3 million refugees.
Critics of Germany's support for Ukraine, especially the right-wing extremist Alternative for Germany (AfD) and the left-wing populist Alliance for Social Justice and Economic Reason (BSW) want to improve relations with Moscow, resume energy deliveries from Russia – including via a repaired Nord Stream pipeline — and stop supporting Ukraine. Some of them have practically delivered their verdict on Serhii K., although the trial has not yet begun, and assume that Ukraine's political or military leadership was behind the attack on the pipeline.
Sahra Wagenknecht, former leader of the BSW, told news agency Reuters in 2025 following Serhii K.'s arrest: "It is totally absurd that Germany spends many billions on aid for Ukraine but never demands an explanation from [President Volodymyr] Zelenskyy. Questions should also be raised about possible compensation."
Alice Weidel, co-leader of the AfD, has shared similar sentiments. In early 2026, she asserted that the German government must seek financial repayment from Ukraine. If the AfD came into power, she would demand Kyiv compensate Germany for blowing up the pipeline and pay for its repair. According to her, a country that does such things is "no friend of Germany." She has, however, failed to provide proof that Ukraine was behind the attack.
Who benefited from blowing up the pipeline?
In an interview with public broadcaster Deutschlandfunk in 2023, German naval commander Göran Swistek pointed out that, given the technical, financial, and organizational effort involved, “there is likely a state-run structure behind it.” In his opinion, a group of amateurs could not have carried out the act.
However, he considered it unlikely that this state could be Ukraine, since Ukraine, after all, would not want to jeopardize German support. At the time, Swistek thought a false lead pointing to Russia was possible.
