US Intelligence Still Flows to Ukraine, Sybiha Says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
12:39:32 UTC
21:39:32 KST

Ukraine continues to receive intelligence from the US, Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said on Tuesday, Oct. 13, following concerns that Washington may have suspended the cooperation.
Speaking at the Warsaw Security Forum, Sybiha was asked about the absence of an advance air raid warning before Russia’s overnight ballistic missile attack.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“You are probably asking me if we are receiving intelligence data from the American side. Yes, we continue this cooperation,” Sybiha said, according to The Guardian.
Sybiha did not disclose what types of intelligence Washington continues to provide or whether the scope of the cooperation has changed.
Why Kyiv’s air raid alert was delayed
Sybiha confirmed that the air raid alert during Monday night’s Russian attack was activated late but said this was caused by the weapons Moscow used rather than an interruption in US intelligence sharing.
“It is also true that yesterday’s attack, or nighttime attack, the red alert was launched with a delay, but this was because of the special type of weaponry used by the Russian side,” he said.
Ukraine’s Air Force said it had not received prior information about the launches. The ballistic missiles were detected only after the attack was already underway.
Russia targeted Kyiv with approximately six ballistic missiles at around 10:10 p.m. on Monday, striking transport and warehouse facilities in several districts.
The attack came after a Russian drone struck a residential high-rise earlier in the day. Russian missile and drone attacks across Ukraine from Monday into Tuesday killed two women and injured nine people in Kyiv.
Europe Pushes Back Against Trump’s Russian Diesel Deal, Vows to Keep Sanctions
Ballistic missiles travel at extremely high speeds and follow trajectories that significantly reduce the time available to detect them, activate alerts, and reach shelter.
Reports of US pressure fuel concerns
Questions over intelligence sharing emerged after reports that US officials had threatened to restrict military support unless Ukraine stopped striking Russian oil refineries.
During talks in Miami, US presidential envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner reportedly warned Ukrainian negotiators that Washington could suspend intelligence sharing if Kyiv continued its long-range attacks on Russia’s energy infrastructure.
A person familiar with the discussions also told Reuters that the US had raised the possibility of restricting weapons procurement through the Prioritized Ukraine Requirements List (PURL).
The reported threat followed US President Donald Trump’s calls for Ukraine to halt attacks on Russian refineries amid rising global diesel prices.
An assessment of the possible suspension found that losing US intelligence would particularly affect Ukraine’s early warning against ballistic missiles, although European intelligence and Ukraine’s own surveillance capabilities could replace part of the lost coverage.
Sybiha’s statement indicates that the reported restrictions have not been implemented.
From “no cards” to “don’t play your cards”
Sybiha also argued that Ukraine’s position in relations with its partners had strengthened significantly during the war.
“In less than two years, we have gone from a situation where you have no cards in your hands to a stage where we are told not to play our cards,” he said at the Warsaw Security Forum, according to Ukrinform.
“This is our real achievement and an important lesson that we have learned,” Sybiha added.
He said Ukraine was defending the idea of freedom on the battlefield and paying a high price for it.
According to the foreign minister, the future of Europe, the global security architecture, and the fate of international law are now being decided in Ukraine.
“Ukraine’s front line is Europe’s first line of defense,” he said.

Syrskyi says redeploying troops from Kursk would not have changed situation near Pokrovsk
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
12:39:00 UTC
21:39:00 KST

Syrskyi says redeploying troops from Kursk would not have changed situation near Pokrovsk
According to Ukrinform, Syrskyi made these remarks in an interview with BBC News Ukrainian.
"No, it would not have been better. The point is that in the Kursk sector, the offensive grouping consisted of only three understrength Air Assault Forces brigades and two assault battalions," he said in response to a question about whether the resources should instead have been directed toward defending the eastern front.
According to Syrskyi, only one brigade took part in the offensive at full strength. Two other brigades initially operated with two battalions each, while the 95th Brigade had just emerged from heavy fighting in the Toretsk sector before the operation.
Other units involved in the operation were tasked with consolidating and holding the captured territory. Their personnel strength stood at approximately 60–70% of full capacity.
"So, if they had been deployed in the Pokrovsk sector—and we consider the Pokrovsk sector to include two directions, Dobropillia and Pokrovsk—the Russians had nearly 100,000 troops concentrated there. Those two brigades, and then another brigade, would not have made any difference, given their technical condition," the former commander-in-chief explained.
He said Ukraine's military leadership chose the Kursk direction after assessing the entire front line.
In early summer 2024, Russia was advancing along 13 operational axes, with its forces enjoying a numerical advantage of between 4.5 and six to one in some areas. At the same time, Russian defenses in the Sumy region had weakened after troops were redeployed to the Kharkiv direction.
"But the defenses in the Sumy sector had been significantly weakened, and there were virtually no active troops there. That is precisely why I made the decision to launch the offensive operation, which was approved by the President of Ukraine," Syrskyi said.
According to him, within a month, Ukrainian troops had taken control of 1,273 square kilometers of Russian territory.
Russia redeployed approximately 70,000 troops to the Kursk region, and its offensive operations came to a halt across all operational and strategic directions except Pokrovsk.
"This effectively gave us the opportunity to prepare reserves, give our troops a respite, and restore the combat effectiveness of units that had suffered losses in such intense fighting," Syrskyi said.
He added that Russian defenses in the Kursk sector had been weak. Border-guard units consisted primarily of conscripts and were spread thinly along the front, with individual positions separated by 10–12 kilometers.
After the Ukrainian offensive began, Russian forces redeployed units in a chaotic manner. Those units entered combat almost immediately and suffered significant losses.
According to Russian figures cited by Syrskyi, on some days the casualty ratio in the Kursk sector was one to five, unfavorable to Russian forces.
As previously reported, Ukrainian forces launched an operation in Russia's Kursk region on August 6, 2024, crossing the state border near the towns of Sudzha and Korenevo.

Swiss banks are looking to hire fewer staff
Swiss banks are recruiting fewer staff, according to an analysis of job vacancies published on the websites of the ten leading companies in the sector in Switzerland.
Overall, in September, the number of job adverts fell by 2% (to 515) compared with August, according to a survey conducted by the job portal Indeed on behalf of the agency Awp.
+ Do young Swiss still want to become bankers?
On a year-on-year basis, the decline stands at 14%, and the fall is even more pronounced when compared with September 2024 (-27%) or 2023 (-72%).
All banks are showing lower demand for labour, but this is particularly evident at UBS. For the purposes of this assessment, only job vacancies in Switzerland were taken into account.
+ What it takes to succeed in the new world of Swiss banking
There are also a significant number of unemployed bank employees. According to the latest figures from the State Secretariat for Economic Affairs, 4,638 people who had previously worked in a bank were registered as unemployed across Switzerland in September.
A year earlier, the figure was almost a fifth lower. Compared with August, however, the number of unemployed has fallen slightly (-0.5%).

The Apple HomeView Is Like a Giant Apple Watch for the Home
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
12:38:32 UTC
21:38:32 KST

It’s a big year for Apple firsts. The company launched the first MacBook Neo, unveiled its first folding iPhone in September, and installed a new CEO for the first time in 15 years. Now comes the Apple HomeView, Apple’s first smart display.
Rivals like Google and Amazon have made countless screen-enabled smart speakers since voice assistants invaded the home a decade ago. But Apple stuck with a smaller smart home ecosystem centered on its HomePod speakers, even removing the iPad as a hub device a few years ago, which forced users to buy an Apple TV or HomePod to get started. Maybe that’s why it hasn’t found much success in the home.
Announced Tuesday at an event in New York City, the 7-inch smart display arrives alongside several other new smart home devices as part of Apple’s bid to revitalize its lagging ecosystem. The HomeView costs $299 and comes in two versions—a speaker base and a wall-mounted display—both priced the same. Preorders are live, with sales kicking off on November 13.
A Big Apple Watch
The first thing I thought of after seeing the Apple HomeView in action is that it looks like a blown-up Apple Watch. The 7-inch square screen has multiple “faces” you can swipe through, exactly like the smartwatch. You can even customize the face’s colors and add different complications for more glanceable information.
The faces can range from a clock, your favorite photos of friends, family, or pets (you can even use shared albums) to weather updates and, yes, Snoopy animations. Swipe up for the home screen, which is more like an iPhone or iPad, with apps neatly arranged alongside widgets. Except the HomeView doesn’t run iOS or iPadOS—it runs the generically named HomeView software.
It doesn’t have an App Store. Instead, Apple has a curated selection of apps, including FaceTime, Messages, and Safari. A handful of third-party media apps like Spotify are available, and developers can bring over existing CarPlay apps. If your iPhone already has one of these CarPlay apps installed, it can automatically appear on the HomeView after setup. (There are no video streaming apps like YouTube, Netflix, or Disney+, but if those companies choose to make their apps available on the CarPlay framework, they will show up on the HomeView; for now, you'll have to consume videos by using the Safari browser.)
To get the most out of the HomeView, you need an iPhone with Apple Intelligence support (an iPhone 15 Pro or newer)—you can’t set it up with an iPad. Apple says you can still set it up with an older iPhone and access some of Siri AI's smarts (like broad world knowledge), but smarter app actions and personal context queries require an iPhone with Apple Intelligence.
The aluminum hardware, powered by Apple’s A18 chip, comes in four colors: silver, starlight, rose pink, and space gray (Apple color-matches the woven cable, too). The standard HomeView has a speaker base with a screen that tilts manually up or down for angled viewing, but you can also buy a wall-mountable version. The latter offers three mounts to choose from, one of which is DIY-friendly and has a visible power cord that needs to run to an outlet. The other two are designed for professional installers, either hardwired or connected via Power over Ethernet (PoE).
Technically, the primary speakers—two full-range drivers—are built into the screen. But the standard HomeView has a base that houses a down-firing woofer and two force-canceling passive radiators for stronger bass. It sounds pretty good based on a very limited listening experience, and can fill a large room quite well. The wall-mounted variant won’t have that extra oomph but Apple claims it tunes the audio for wall placement.
The 7-inch Liquid Retina display has familiar elements, like True Tone, which adjusts the screen’s color temperature to match the room’s lighting. The ambient light sensor can also reduce display brightness from 500 nits to 0.3 nits, which is the lowest brightness Apple has ever engineered on a screen. That’ll be helpful if you place the HomeView on the nightstand.
That is, if you're comfortable placing a camera-equipped display in the bedroom. A 12-megapixel Center Stage camera and four-microphone array sit on the front, but they aren’t just for FaceTime calls. The camera handles facial recognition, allowing the software to adapt to whoever is looking at the screen. Apple says all of this data stays on device.
“Trust is becoming increasingly important with rising consumer expectations around privacy and security,” writes Anshika Jain, principal analyst at Counterpoint, in an email to WIRED. “In fact, Apple could actually benefit from its privacy-first approach.”
You can add up to six iCloud accounts, and the user interface will adapt to each person, like Google’s Pixel Tablet. That means your wife can tint every app icon green and have no widgets on her home screen, but if you stand in front of the HomeView, it’ll switch to your setup. You won’t be able to view other household members’ sensitive messages and personal information. For this personal content to show up, you don’t just have to stand in front of the HomeView—your iPhone needs to be on the same Wi-Fi network and must have been recently unlocked.
The HomeView can also recognize voices, which helps if Dad asks Siri AI to “Play music.” It will play from Dad’s music library and his preferred music app, rather than another iCloud user’s music. If you have multiple HomePods or HomeViews, you can manage your speaker groups in the HomeView’s interface.
The HomeView also supports Apple’s Handoff tech, so you can bring your iPhone close to send a Safari recipe to the smart display, or have it continue the podcast you were listening to on your commute. In the middle of a FaceTime or phone call? Put your iPhone near the HomeView, and it’ll transfer it over.
Betting on Siri AI
Like any smart display or smart speaker, Siri AI powers the HomeView. It is, after all, the main way to interact with the device (though yes, there’s a keyboard you can pull up to type). Apple spent a great deal of time revamping Siri this year, finally launching a more capable assistant in iOS 27.
Siri AI on the HomeView understands your personal context from your iPhone, so if you ask it to play a song your friend Eric recommended, it’ll know right away what you mean by looking at your Messages history. You can ask when your brother Jeff will likely arrive at your home from the airport on Thursday, then set a schedule for Siri to turn on the coffee maker 15 minutes before his estimated arrival. All of this can be done with natural language, meaning you don’t have to say specific commands for Siri AI to understand you.
One neat trick is the HomeView’s ability to convert recipe pages from Safari into digestible content. Load a recipe, and it will let you view the ingredients or “Start Cooking,” no need to read three paragraphs of the author’s relationship to the stew. It automatically converts the recipe into step-by-step instructions, even auto-populating timers for relevant steps so you can start individual timers as you progress.
Naturally, the HomeView is also designed to control all of your smart home devices, too. You can create a widget for any device you have added in the Home app to quickly control it on the HomeView. And if you swipe to the left from the home screen, you’ll see the “Camera” face, which shows a live stream of connected security cameras (you can view nine feeds at once).
Much like the upcoming iPhone Duo folding phone, Apple is late to market. The company is betting on tight iPhone integration, glanceable Watch-like software, and a more context-aware Siri to make the HomeView feel more like a screen you’ll actually want on your counter. Everything hinges on whether Siri can hold up its end of the bargain—and the voice assistant doesn’t exactly have the best track record.
“The greater challenge is to make AI useful for everyday interactions,” Jain says. “Apple must provide a more capable Siri experience and ensure seamless control across its entire product range in order to stand out from the competition.”

Asia's fertility hub: Thailand emerges as top destination for IVF treatment

Asia's fertility hub: Thailand emerges as top destination for IVF treatment
To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.
Issued on:
Thailand has become one of Asia's leading fertility hubs. Every year, thousands of foreign patients travel to Bangkok's state-of-the-art private clinics for IVF, egg donation and other fertility treatments. They come from China, South Korea, Europe and across Southeast Asia, looking for what may be harder to find at home: shorter waiting times, lower costs and, in some cases, fewer restrictions.
Bangkok's fertility clinics now cater to an international clientele, offering everything from hotels and interpreters to medical packages, fast-tracked appointments and personalised care. For many of these couples, Thailand is the latest stop on a journey that has already been long, expensive and emotionally draining.
But behind the gleaming, high-tech clinics lies a darker side to the industry. Demand from overseas, particularly from China and South Korea, has spawned a network of middlemen and agencies – and, in some cases, illegal operations. NGOs warn that young Thai and Cambodian women are being recruited as egg donors. Some are approached on social media or messaging apps and offered several thousand euros to undergo invasive medical procedures, sometimes with little information about the potential risks.
FRANCE 24's Theo Collet, Adrien Quilico, Morel Antoine, Adam Hancock and Aruna Popuri report.

Netflix has secured exclusive broadcasting rights for the 2030 FIFA World Cup in Spain and Andorra, with all 104 matches to be streamed live, the company announced on Tuesday.
Under the agreement, one match per matchday will be available free in Spain.
A package of matches, including every Spain match, both semifinals and the final, will also be made available to a national free-to-air broadcaster, Netflix said, adding that further details about the arrangement would be announced closer to the tournament.
The agreement marks Netflix's first acquisition of broadcasting rights for a major men's international football tournament in Spain.
The 2030 World Cup will be jointly hosted by Spain, Morocco and Portugal, with centenary celebration matches also taking place in Argentina, Paraguay and Uruguay to mark the tournament's 100th anniversary.

Russia’s Convict Soldier Allegedly Kills Six of His Own, Including Secret FSB Cyber Specialist
A Russian soldier recruited from prison after seven criminal convictions allegedly shot dead six fellow servicemen, including a former operative of a secretive Russian Federal Security Service (FSB) unit, during a dispute between Russian military units in Ukraine’s Kharkiv region.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to an investigation published by The Insider on October 13, the suspect, Alexey Korolev, was serving an 11-year prison sentence for drug-related offenses involving mephedrone before joining the Russian military. He now faces murder and extortion charges in a military court in temporarily occupied Donetsk.
The shooting reportedly occurred on October 25, 2025, near Lyman Pershyi, during Russia’s offensive operations around Kupiansk.
According to Ukraine’s I Want to Live project, the confrontation began after a Russian FPV drone mistakenly struck an all-terrain vehicle belonging to another Russian unit.
Several soldiers assaulted reconnaissance personnel and seized their drone-control equipment. When the reconnaissance unit attempted to recover it the following morning, another confrontation erupted.
Korolev opened fire after a fellow serviceman referred to his criminal past and threatened him with sexual violence. Six Russian soldiers were killed and two others wounded.
Among the dead was 22-year-old Rodion Kravets, whose banking records identified him as a specialist at military unit 71330, which corresponds to the FSB’s highly classified 16th Center.
According to The Insider, the unit specializes in signals intelligence, including intercepting and decrypting electronic communications, penetrating foreign computer networks, and conducting cyber espionage operations.
The UK government has linked the 16th Center to Russian intelligence cyber activities, while the European Union has also attributed cyberattacks to the unit.
Kravets reportedly began working there in June 2023 before later appearing in military records as a soldier of Russia’s 27th Separate Motorized Rifle Brigade. It remains unclear whether he had permanently left the FSB or was temporarily assigned to combat operations in Ukraine.
Another victim, 28-year-old Vadim Petukhov, was reportedly associated with Russia’s elite Rubikon drone warfare center, although investigators could not independently verify the connection.
Court records reviewed by The Insider show that Korolev had previously been convicted of robbery, theft, fraud, hooliganism, and drug-related crimes.
His case reached the Southern District Military Court in March 2026. His lawyer confirmed that the proceedings are being held behind closed doors but declined to provide further details.
Earlier, in February 2026, a Russian soldier who had twice been released from prison to fight in Ukraine was arrested on suspicion of another murder. The suspect, Viktor Savvinov, had previously been convicted of three killings but was repeatedly allowed to join the Russian military despite his criminal record.

Russia Hit Kyiv With 5 Ballistic Missiles—Ukraine Says Allied Warning Never Came
Ukraine received no advance warning from its partners before five Russian ballistic missiles struck civilian infrastructure in Kyiv, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said, stressing that intelligence on ballistic launches is one of the most critical tools for getting civilians to safety in time.
Russia launched more than 100 aerial weapons against Ukraine from the evening into the following day, including jet-powered drones, loitering munitions, and ballistic missiles, Zelenskyy wrote on X on October 13.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Ukrainian defenses intercepted a significant share of the incoming weapons, but several strikes caused casualties and widespread damage.
“Since last evening and up to now, the Russians have attacked Ukraine with more than a hundred different weapons—jet-powered drones, loitering munitions, and ballistic missiles. A significant portion of these strike assets were shot down. But unfortunately, not all of them,” Zelenskyy said.
Kharkiv was among the hardest-hit cities. A Russian strike destroyed an apartment building, prompting an overnight rescue operation as emergency workers searched through the rubble. Four people were killed and 41 others injured in the city, according to Zelenskyy.
“An ordinary residential building was destroyed in Kharkiv; the rescue operation continued virtually all night as first responders searched for people under the rubble. Four people were killed in this strike on the building in Kharkiv. My condolences to all their families and loved ones,” he said.

“There was also a particularly vile ballistic missile strike on Kyiv—five missiles that hit civilian infrastructure. Unfortunately, we received no early warning from our partners about this strike,” Zelenskyy said.
The Ukrainian leader emphasized that advance intelligence is especially important during ballistic missile attacks because of the extremely short flight time, which leaves civilians and air defense crews only minutes to react.
“Intelligence on Russian ballistic missile launches helps save lives, and this is one of the most critical issues,” Zelenskyy said. “This is precisely what helps prevent people from being killed—when there is an early warning about ballistic missiles.”

We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The confirmed targets included:
- a repair base near Kondrinka in Russia’s Kursk region servicing Iskander-M self-propelled launchers and transporter-loader vehicles;
- a Russian radar station near Skryabine in Russia’s Bryansk region;
- a fuel and lubricants depot near Dovzhansk in the temporarily occupied Luhansk region;
- an ammunition depot near Rubizhne in the temporarily occupied Luhansk region;
- Russian troop concentrations near Selydove, Rozdolne, Suzhenka, and Myrnohrad in the Donetsk region;
- Russian personnel near Naberezhne in the Zaporizhzhia region and Kuzemivka in the Luhansk region.
The Iskander-M is a Russian mobile short-range ballistic missile system designed to strike high-value targets behind the front line. Its launchers and support vehicles allow Russian units to relocate quickly and conduct missile strikes from dispersed positions.
Damage to a repair base can reduce the availability of launchers and support vehicles by disrupting maintenance and the return of damaged equipment to service. The General Staff did not disclose the extent of the damage or Russian losses from the strikes.

US and Europe Draft Peace Framework That Freezes Frontline and Sets Terms for Russia Sanctions Relief
The US and European countries are developing a peace plan for Ukraine that would freeze fighting along the current front line while combining reconstruction funding, security guarantees, and a potential energy arrangement involving Russia, The Washington Post reported on October 12.
The initiative is being shaped by US envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff together with European partners, according to the report. The proposal is built around expanding the settlement beyond a ceasefire to include economic and security incentives for both Ukraine and Russia.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The Kremlin has already recently rejected Zelenskyy’s proposal for a 60-day ceasefire that would allow Ukraine to hold presidential elections. Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov stated that Moscow does not want a temporary ceasefire, even as Zelenskyy accused Russia of already violating the proposed energy arrangement.
One part of the new peace plan would establish a large-scale reconstruction framework for Ukraine. The World Bank and BlackRock are involved in efforts to create a financing structure for rebuilding damaged areas, supporting families of killed and wounded service members, and restoring the Ukrainian economy, The Washington Post noted.
The security component would require the US and European countries to respond militarily if Russia attacked Ukraine again. A US official described the proposed commitment as effectively equivalent to NATO’s Article 5 collective defense guarantee.
The Washington Post reported that another element under discussion concerns energy cooperation. One option involves a pipeline carrying Russian oil and gas to Europe, with revenues potentially shared between Ukraine and Russia, while the plan would also establish conditions and a timetable for lifting sanctions on Moscow.
The ceasefire component would halt fighting along the current front line. Under that arrangement, territories presently occupied by Russia, including parts of the Donetsk and Luhansk regions, would remain under Russian control while negotiations continued.
The outlet also noted that the proposal is complicated by doubts over whether the Russian leader, Vladimir Putin, is prepared to accept a settlement.
US President Donald Trump recently announced a deal with the Russian leader, Vladimir Putin, to release millions of tons of Russian diesel onto US and global markets, while Washington has also pressed Ukraine to halt strikes on Russian refineries. Zelenskyy stated that Kyiv would stop those attacks only if Russia ended its own strikes on Ukraine’s energy infrastructure.

‘Help non-native speakers with Dutch!’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
12:36:17 UTC
21:36:17 KST

Flemish Economy Minister Hilde Crevits (Flemish Christian democrat CD&V) launched the ‘Spreektaal’ or ‘Spoken Language’ campaign at the Albert Heijn supermarket in Rumbeke (West Flanders) today. During Dutch Language Week, she is asking customers to help non-native speakers who ask for explanations in broken Dutch by communicating with them in Dutch. From today, all shop staff will be wearing a badge bearing the words “We’re open to a chat”.
“Today we are making a very special appeal,” says the minister. “If you go shopping and there are people asking for explanations about a product in broken Dutch, please help them in Dutch. Every year, hundreds of thousands of people start taking Dutch lessons. They are looking for places to practise.”
A small corner of the shop has been set aside where people can have a coffee and have a natter. According to Crevits, some people don’t dare to ask for help because they’re afraid of making mistakes. “But if you pluck up the courage, you’re guaranteed always to be helped in Dutch,” she says.
Crevits was initially surprised herself that a department store could play a part in this. Until she heard the story of a woman who, 20 years ago, could barely speak Dutch. She asked another woman where the aubergines were. A friendship grew out of that. “Now, 20 years later, they are best friends.”
Making mistakes is all part of the process
Jean-Paul Fraeyman is the manager of the supermarket on Koestraat. He notices that many non-native speakers apply for jobs when he is looking for new staff. “The better they learn the language, the easier it is for them to integrate, both into the running of the shop and in their personal lives,” he says.
He wants customers to know that making a mistake whilst learning Dutch is all part of the process and “is absolutely not viewed negatively”.
The same goes for the West Flemish dialect!
Carolina Sergant is the shop’s marketing manager and says she often discusses Dutch language courses with staff.
“Our shop has many staff members with an integration background. They started via local social services, via work-based learning or a VDAB training course they’ve completed.”
She believes staff can even learn the idiosyncratic West Flemish dialect - that many Flemings from outside the coastal province struggle to comprehend - on the job too, as customers will speak to them in broad West Flemish.

France seizes another 'shadow fleet' tanker; Russia decries 'piracy'
PARIS/MOSCOW, Oct 13 - France's military was taking a tanker suspected to be part of Russia's "shadow fleet" skirting Western sanctions to Reunion island on Tuesday in what Moscow called another act of "piracy".
Sanctions on Russia for invading Ukraine and aimed at cutting its oil revenue have spawned a fleet of often ageing and unregulated vessels helping Moscow keep its crude exports flowing.
The DF Peak, previously named the Kaliningrad and flagged from Benin, is at least the fifth Russian-linked tanker to be seized by France since 2024.
"We had doubts regarding the flag under which this vessel was sailing, so we carried out an inspection," French army spokesperson Colonel Xavier Rival told a news conference.
"Those doubts remain, and therefore the vessel is currently proceeding to Reunion Island by decision of the public prosecutor, so that we can examine the matter in detail."
The US on Monday temporarily eased sanctions on the sale of Russian diesel as the Middle East war disrupts oil supplies and boosts prices.
Europe has been taking tougher action against tankers using false flag registries to transport Russian oil, including boarding vessels at sea.
Russia's embassy in France was quoted by the state RIA news agency on Tuesday as saying that the seizure of the DF Peak was "piracy" and a blatant violation of international law.
RIA cited the embassy as saying it was trying to determine if any Russian citizens were among the crew. France had also not notified Russia about the tanker's seizure, it said.
DETERMINED TO TACKLE SHADOW FLEET
In a post on X on Monday evening, President Emmanuel Macron showed French military personnel intercepting and boarding the tanker from helicopters in what he said was some 450 nautical miles south of Reunion, a French territory in the Indian Ocean.
"France is determined to combat the shadow fleet, wherever it may be in the world," he said, adding that it was suspected of sailing under a false flag and being involved in illicit fuel transportation activities.
The vessel’s Hong Kong-based manager listed in shipping databases, Zheng Xin Marine, could not be reached for comment.
The vessel has been hit by US, UK and EU sanctions in 2024.
It was partially loaded and last seen off the coast of Madagascar on October 12 at 0429 GMT with its previous port listed as Guanta in Venezuela, LSEG ship tracking data showed.
Russia has used such tankers, which typically lack mainstream insurance or safety certification, to skirt sanctions by sailing under the flags of various nations to obscure their true ownership, cargo and movements. REUTERS

PPA: Migrants more visible in Tallinn's Nõmme, not more numerous
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
12:34:00 UTC
21:34:00 KST

PPA: Migrants more visible in Tallinn's Nõmme, not more numerous
The latest group of illegal migrants apprehended in Tallinn's Nõmme district does not mean that neighborhood has seen more cases than other parts of the city, authorities say.
The Police and Border Guard Board has detained two groups of illegal migrants in recent months, most recently on Sunday evening.
Overall, the PPA has detained 83 migrant groups in Estonia since mid-summer, and 352 individual illegal migrants since July 21, amid heightened migratory pressure on the Belarus-EU border.
In both reported cases in Nõmme, the PPA acted on neighbor tip-offs, as well as in other cases close to the nearby Tallinn University of Technology.
Rainis Sinikas, head of the PPA North Prefecture's border and migration supervision department, noted that the detained migrants are spread across different districts. It is largely Nõmme's character, he said, that makes detentions more likely for those accommodated there.
As a leafy suburb on the southern outskirts of the capital, Nõmme is a place where local residents tend to recognize each other by sight, Sinikas said. Outsiders, still more so those of a different ethnic background from the majority, tend to stand out more than they might in more central areas of Tallinn.
"The point of detention is largely connected to where migrants live. Through a trafficker, they find accommodation somewhere in a Tallinn district. Since Nõmme is a small garden suburb where many neighbors know each other, a number of people of another nationality attracts attention," Sinikas said.
"In the city center, people moving around during rush hour may not be noticed. But in a small garden suburb, far more attention is paid to who is moving around, and so more reports come in," he continued.
Sunday evening's operation in Nõmme began when residents reported what they said were two dark-skinned men outside a building. The men appeared not to be familiar with the area.
PPA officials went to the scene and detained both men. Checks revealed they were Sudanese nationals staying in Estonia illegally. During conversations, it emerged that several other illegal migrants were hiding in the area. Police then launched a search involving patrols, service dogs and the Rescue Board.
This led to eight additional men, also of Sudanese origin, being apprehended. They had been hiding in wooded areas.
"Generally the practice has been that running away and abandoning belongings doesn't happen very often, but this time it did," Sinikas said.
In the July case, it emerged that migrants had congregated at a short-term rental building. The PPA is still establishing the circumstances of Sunday's incident.
"In practically every case we establish whether they have already stayed overnight in Estonia. If they have, we check the accommodation or apartment used as short-term let. We also establish their route in detail: how many came in and where they came from. Through continuous and consistent procedural steps, we establish their background and whether we can apprehend more migrants at that address. Practice has shown that sometimes we do," Sinikas added.
October has so far seen no let-up for the PPA in detaining migrant groups, mainly in Tallinn but also in Pärnu and central Estonia.
On Monday, the PPA detained a group of seven illegal migrants in the city center. Migratory pressure is likely to continue and possibly rise ahead of winter, the PPA said.
The PPA says it receives constant tip-offs about possible illegal migrants. Sinikas denied that tip-offs had been primarily race-based. Actions and behavior stand out, he said — and even dirty clothing in the autumn weather.
"Since the weather is muddy, many of the detained groups get muddy too," Sinikas said.
Not only the PPA but other agencies are coming under heavy pressure. Over 250 people are now in the Tallinn detention center. The courts are overworked too, since detaining people is a legal process, on top of sentencing human traffickers caught in Estonia.
"The situation is difficult and could turn into a crisis situation. Various institutions, including administrative courts and local governments, are overloaded. We order interpretation and our entire network of cooperation partners is under great strain," Sinikas said.
The situation is complicated by the fact that different nationalities are placed in the detention center together, which has led to conflicts.
"It doesn't take much — there have been disagreements and pushing, even over a TV remote. So far we have managed to prevent and avert larger conflicts, but there are still such scuffles and quarrels," Sinikas said.
Sunday's group consisted of Sudanese nationals. The group apprehended Monday in central Tallinn were Somalis. "There are a lot of Bangladeshi, but also Pakistani and Afghan citizens. The circle is quite wide, and people from Ethiopia and Eritrea have also been detained," Sinikas said.
Regardless of country of origin, the migrants mostly arrive in Estonia from Belarus via Latvia, which it borders. They then make their way northwards.
Processing the return of one migrant usually takes over a month, including establishing that they did indeed cross the border illegally from another state. Estonia has so far sent 105 migrants back to Latvia.
The migrants themselves have said during proceedings that their intended destination was a western EU country, for instance Finland, Germany or Spain.
Sinikas said that while some have stated a desire to remain in Estonia, it is not clear whether this is their genuine wish or a script they have been taught.
That "also has to be established during proceedings," Sinikas noted.
Interior Minister Igor Taro (Eesti 200) discussed the Belarus-backed migration pressure on Latvia's border with his Polish counterpart Marcin Kierwiński at the ongoing Warsaw Security Forum. Taro said the migratory pressure should be treated as an attack on the whole EU, and that escalation must carry a cost beyond the existing sanctions on Minsk.
"All our allies are ready to support Latvia, just as we have previously stood alongside Poland and Lithuania. Responsibility lies entirely with the Belarusian regime, which supports and incites illegal border crossings and contributes to damage to Latvia's border infrastructure," Taro said.
Taro is set to take part in a panel discussion on Tuesday about government resilience in the era of hybrid attacks.

Patient’s death during rhinoplasty: court finds anesthesiologist guilty but exempts him from punishment due to the statute of limitations
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
15:33:22 EEST
21:33:22 KST

Patient’s death during rhinoplasty: court finds anesthesiologist guilty but exempts him from punishment due to the statute of limitations
Kyiv • UNN
In Odesa, a court found an anesthesiologist guilty of medical negligence that led to the death of a patient during plastic surgery. However, despite the guilty verdict, the doctor avoided criminal punishment due to the expiration of the statute of limitations. The court also did not revoke his right to practice medicine.
It took the Prymorskyi District Court of Odesa more than eight years to issue a verdict in the case concerning the death of a patient after plastic surgery at a private medical facility, which later changed its name to "Mozart Medical Center for Plastic Aesthetic Surgery and Cosmetology." The court established that the anesthesiologist had improperly performed his professional duties, used a contraindicated drug, and failed to provide the required level of medical care. At the same time, despite finding the doctor guilty, the court spared him criminal punishment because the statute of limitations had expired, UNN reports.
The tragedy occurred on May 4, 2017, at the Odesa private medical center for plastic aesthetic surgery and cosmetology "Mozart." The patient arrived for scheduled nose-correction surgery—rhinoseptoplasty and submucosal vasotomy of the inferior nasal turbinates. At around 10 a.m., the woman was taken to the operating room. The anesthesiologist began administering anesthetic drugs, including the inhalational anesthetic sevoflurane.
The patient's condition soon deteriorated sharply. She developed malignant hyperthermia—a life-threatening reaction of the body to certain anesthetic drugs. Her body temperature rose rapidly, and cardiac arrhythmias developed.
The operation was stopped, and emergency care was initiated. She was later transported to another medical facility, but the woman could not be saved. At 1:35 p.m., doctors pronounced her dead.
As the court established, the immediate cause of death was acute heart failure associated with malignant hyperthermia. The court found that the tragedy could have been prevented. The patient had already experienced a dangerous reaction to anesthesia during one of her previous surgical procedures. The relevant information was contained in her medical records.
In addition, the patient's relatives and close acquaintances testified that they had warned the doctors before the operation about her previous problems with anesthesia. However, as the court established, the anesthesiologist did not take a complete medical history and failed to take into account information about the previous episode of malignant hyperthermia.
The court also established a number of violations during the provision of emergency care. In particular, the necessary monitoring of blood parameters was not carried out, the measures required by the clinical protocol were not fully implemented, and the decision to transport the patient to another medical facility before her condition had stabilized was deemed erroneous by the court.
The accused doctor did not admit his guilt. He claimed that he had taken the patient's medical history, but had not been informed of any contraindications. The anesthesiologist also explained that he had tried to determine whether dantrolene—the drug used to treat malignant hyperthermia—was available, but had been told that it was not.
Several forensic medical examinations were conducted during the proceedings. The experts' conclusions regarding the doctor's liability differed, but the court of first instance found the defense's arguments unconvincing and concluded that the anesthesiologist's guilt had been proven beyond a reasonable doubt.
Guilty, but not punished: how the statute of limitations came into play
The criminal proceedings were initiated as early as May 4, 2017—the day the patient died. In 2019, the case was already being heard by the Prymorskyi District Court of Odesa. It was only on September 22, 2025, that the Prymorskyi District Court of Odesa issued a guilty verdict.
The doctor was found guilty under Part One of Article 140 of the Criminal Code of Ukraine—improper performance by a medical worker of their professional duties, resulting in serious consequences for a patient.
At the same time, the court expressly stated that, given the nature of the offense and its consequences, the doctor should have been sentenced to imprisonment. However, this did not happen.
Under Article 49 of the Criminal Code of Ukraine, a five-year statute of limitations applies to the relevant category of less serious offenses. By the time the verdict was issued, more than eight years had already passed since the patient's death.
As a result, the court applied the provisions of Part Five of Article 74 of the Criminal Code of Ukraine and exempted the defendant from punishment due to the expiration of the statute of limitations. In other words, the court established the doctor’s guilt but did not impose any criminal punishment on him.
Moreover, the verdict does not provide for disqualification from practicing medicine either, although Part One of Article 140 of the Criminal Code of Ukraine provides for this type of punishment for a period of up to five years.
Interestingly, according to a court ruling dated November 11, 2019, after the tragedy, the doctor was officially employed as an anesthesiologist at City Clinical Hospital No. 11. In the 2025 verdict, the court also stated that the defendant works as an anesthesiologist.
Almost UAH 364,000 in compensation for the patient’s death
Separately, as part of the criminal proceedings, the court considered the civil claim filed by the injured party. The deceased’s relatives demanded compensation for expenses related to the patient’s death and the court proceedings. In particular, these included transportation, funeral, monument production, legal assistance, and interpreter services.
The court granted the claim in full and ordered the doctor to pay UAH 363,981.65 in property damage. In addition, the anesthesiologist must reimburse the state UAH 21,464.61 in costs for conducting the examinations.
However, it is important to distinguish between these decisions: compensation for property damage to the injured parties is not a criminal punishment and does not replace one.

As Houthis approach Yemen's Taiz locals flee fear of another siege
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
12:33:00 UTC
21:33:00 KST

As Iran-backed Houthi rebels push to capture the strategic city of Taiz in Yemen's 12-year civil war, fear gripped the locals with many deciding to flee.
Weam Abdullah and her family are among the war-displaced population leaving Yemen’s third largest city. They had survived a yearslong siege by the rebels earlier in their country’s civil war and they didn’t want to endure that again.
They made it out just in time. Shortly after Abdullah, her husband and two young children left, the rebels captured a key town on Oct. 4, largely encircling Taiz and cutting off most supply routes from government-held areas.
"We already feel dead, there was already despair” in the city, Abdullah told The Associated Press by phone from a province farther south. "We feel as if we are cursed. Everyone is conspiring against us even though we’re not affiliated with any party or politics.”
The assault follows a lightning offensive last month in which the rebels seized Yemen’s Red Sea coast, strengthening their ability to attack Saudi oil shipping and plunging global energy prices further into turmoil.
The advance has triggered fear among Taiz's more than 1 million residents, who live in the rugged mountains of southwestern Yemen. On a recent day, crowds mobbed groceries in the city center to buy up food and other essentials, fearing they will soon run out. Diesel fuel and cooking gas supplies are running low, residents said.
Some residents are collecting cardboard and wood to burn for cooking, while merchants are raising food and water prices, said Shaif al-Gabiri, a child protection consultant at the Civic Center for Advocacy and Support, a local nonprofit group.
"If the siege continues, then these stocks will run out," he said.
Explosions from fighting between Houthis and pro-government forces echo from the surrounding mountains. Some strikes have hit the city itself, reminding residents of an ordeal they hoped might be over.
Taiz has been on the front line of Yemen’s civil war since 2014 when Houthi rebels seized the north and much of the country’s west, including the capital, Sanaa. Saudi Arabia later entered the war at the head of a coalition backing the internationally recognized government, which had been forced to flee south.
A strategic gateway to the south, Taiz is also one of Yemen’s most important historical and cultural centers. It once served as the capital of several Islamic dynasties and a major center of religious learning.
Al-Qahira Castle, a monumental fortress more than 800 years old, overlooks the city from a hill. To the south rises Mount Sabir, more than 3,000 meters (9,800 feet) high, its slopes carved into agricultural terraces.
For much of the war, Houthi forces surrounded most of Taiz and blocked its main roads. Bombardments regularly struck the city center, power cuts were frequent, and residents struggled to find food.
The only routes to government-held areas were steep, winding mountain back roads. Bringing in supplies or getting people to hospitals in the southern port city of Aden took hours.
Taiz was "a jungle" at the time, Abdullah said. If people didn’t die "from artillery, then they would die from the siege, malnourished because of lack of food," she said. After nightfall, "many streets were deserted and looked scary."
A truce reached in 2022 eased fighting across Yemen and brought some life back to Taiz. Many who had fled returned, and homes were rebuilt. But prices remained high, and residents struggled to get by, Abdullah said. Houthi forces still controlled areas north, east and west of the city and charged "customs” duties on supplies passing through.
The truce ended in August when the Houthis launched a new assault. Last month, they seized the Red Sea coast, capturing the port city of Mocha and several strategic islands. They then began advancing around Taiz.
Abdullah said her family feared a new siege would be worse than the last. Her children were afraid to go outside to play.
"This is why we left," she said. "The situation was terrible, you couldn’t get essentials, and there’s a shortage in everything ... There is no diesel to work water pumps."
As they fled Taiz, they saw government reinforcements heading toward the city and heard explosions and gunfire, she said. They passed through Turbah, about 40 kilometers (25 miles) south of Taiz, before reaching the government-controlled province of Lahj.
Days later, the Houthis captured Turbah, encircling Taiz and a pocket of government-held territory.
As well as the main roads out of Taiz, some of the alternative mountain routes used in the past are now closed, causing "some confusion and panic," according to Abdelrahman al-Qaliaa, director of the Taiz branch of the Industry and Trade Ministry.
He urged residents crowding stores to only buy what they immediately needed to prevent shortages.
Pro-government forces are fighting Houthis in the mountains southwest of Taiz, trying to break the rebels' hold.
Ahmed Abdel-Jaber said shelling near his house in a mountain village wounded his 7-year-old grandson in his stomach. The boy was taken to a hospital in Taiz.
Abdel-Jaber moved his family of nine to another village farther from the fighting. "If we decide it’s unsafe there, we’ll flee to another area," he told the AP by phone.
Growing numbers of government soldiers, women and children wounded in the fighting have been brought to hospitals in Taiz.
"Hospitals could run out of diesel at any point," said Dr. Fahd Nazary of the Taiz provincial health office. Delivering medical supplies has also become more difficult, he said. "This is a huge catastrophe."
Al-Gabiri, the child protection consultant in Taiz, described fears that the fighting could worsen.
"Here I am sitting in a coffee shop," al-Gabiri said, "knowing that at any moment a shell could fall on me or an explosive could come from any direction, hitting any house and any street."

Ehsan Adouane started interviewing scientists on YouTube at the age of nine. At 13, he beat thousands of entrants worldwide to win one of Dubai's top tech prizes.
His app, Ettan Ehsan turns homework into a game, breaking school subjects into quick, visual challenges. It took the Best Youth-made App award at this year's Create Apps Championship. "I want to now help students just like me to make homework more fun and more fast-paced and more gamified," he says.

The competition was fierce. There were 9,754 entries this year, more than the competition's first two editions combined. Launched in 2023 as a local contest, the championship opened to the world in its second year and has now drawn applications from 153 countries. The winners were honoured on 7 October by Mohammed bin Rashid bin Mohammed bin Rashid Al Maktoum, at Emirates Towers Boulevard.
'A very disconnected world'
For almost 20 years, Agnieszka Kocznur designed retail spaces for beauty brands. Then she walked away to back her own idea. "I left my corporate job; I'm completely full-time on Rush, and I really believe we can create an impact on human disconnection," she says.
RUSH, which matches travellers with group trips built around shared interests, won the Most Impactful App award. "This reward matters because we are living in a very disconnected world with technology, but we found a way for technology to bring us together." Her message to anyone hesitating is simple. "I think you have to be courageous, believe in your ideas, and apply, see what happens."

Alan Villegas spent years teaching entrepreneurship in Mexico City. Then he decided to put his teaching into practice. He quit academia, and after an earlier fintech venture elsewhere, chose Dubai. "Whenever we've asked them for anything or opened a door, they've immediately done it," he says, pointing to "the real open-door policy to regulators and government officials".
Last year's App of the Year, Boom, helps delivery drivers find customers and set their own prices. For co-founder Mariam Mohammed Almarri, the win was the turning point. "Before the championship, the application was still a project in its early stages of ideation and prototyping."
This year's finalists and semi-finalists now head straight into a six-month programme with Oraseya Capital, the venture capital arm of Dubai Integrated Economic Zones Authority, built to get young start-ups ready for investors. For anyone still wondering whether to take the leap, Takeem's advice is blunt. "If you're thinking about getting involved, my advice is just do it."

Sea birds covered with oil were found on Monday dead and dying on Black Sea beaches dozens of kilometers from a tanker attacked and disabled by Ukrainian drones, contradicting official Russian statements the vessel was structurally intact and environmentally-threatening amounts of product had not leaked into local waters.Images published by the Anapa-based regional wildlife protection group Zhemchuzhnaya Reabilitatsionniy Tsenter (Zhemchuzhnaya Rehabilitation Center) on Sunday and Monday showed seagulls, grebes, pigeons and a white swans soiled with oil and needing treatment. Zhora Kavanosyan, a Sochi-based ecologist, in a Monday Telegram report said beach-walkers found some oil-covered birds near the villages of Lazarevsky, Sosnovka and the city of Gedzhelik, all seaside resorts in the heart of the the Black Sea’s “Russian Riveria” region.

The damaging Ukrainian drone strike hit the Fiberia-flagged Aframax Rio 30 km (19 miles) off shore Sochi, setting the vessel ablaze and forcing the crew to abandon ship.

Ukraine has accused Russia of using the Aframax as a shadow tanker to evade international sanctions on Russian crude oil and fuel exports. Russia’s Greenpeace branch in a Friday statement said the Aframax Rio following damaging hits by Ukrainian drones had spilled oil and potentially lost some of its structural integrity, and that the abandoned vessel drifting northwards parallel to the shore posed a serious threat to local wildlife and wetlands.

Ukraine in mid-July 2026 launched a martime drone strike campaign targeting Russian tanker traffic in the Black and Azov Seas, with shadow tankers thought by Kyiv to be assisting Moscow in evading international sanctions top priority targets for drone operators.
According to claims by Ukraine’s Unmanned Systems Forces (USF), since then through September, Ukrainian aircraft had hit or disabled 300+ Russian shadow tankers, of which 134 were hit in the Sea of Azov and 166 in the Black Sea.
Among the most spectacular attacks was a pair of November sea drone strikes that disabled the tankers Kairos and Virat off Turkey’s Black Sea coast, and a December 2025 aerial drone that hit the suspected shadow tanker Quendil in the central Mediterranean.Thanks to high oil prices and pressing Kremlin need for overseas cash earnings, Russian export of crude and petroleum products from its Black Sea ports has continued at reduced volumes. According to open source ship movement tracking platforms, Russian tanker traffic westward into the Black Sea escapes are roughly 1/3 pre-full-scale-war levels.

Why the TTP Remains the Central Fault Line Between Pakistan and Afghanistan
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
12:29:00 UTC
21:29:00 KST

On October 11, Pakistan’s military reported that security forces had killed 12 militants and Afghan Taliban personnel during an attempted crossing from Afghanistan into Pakistan’s Kurram district. A Pakistani soldier was also killed in the exchange of fire. The Inter-Services Public Relations (ISPR), the military’s media wing, said Afghan Taliban border posts had opened fire in support of the attempted crossing.
The incident came 10 days after Pakistani airstrikes in Afghanistan, which Islamabad said targeted militant camps and hideouts. Pakistan reported that the strikes killed 22 militants. At the same time, the United Nations Assistance Mission in Afghanistan (UNAMA) confirmed that at least 10 civilians, most of them children, were killed and nine injured in Kunar and Helmand provinces. The U.N. mission called for de-escalation and greater protection of civilians, underscoring the humanitarian risks of continued cross-border hostilities.
These incidents reflect a wider deterioration in Afghanistan-Pakistan relations, driven in part by Islamabad’s concerns about militant groups operating from Afghan territory.
On September 18, a suicide car bombing at a mosque inside the Kohat Police Lines complex in Pakistan’s Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province, followed by an armed assault, killed at least 31 people, including 16 police personnel, and injured more than 100, according to local police officials. Ittehadul Mujahideen Pakistan (IMP), a militant alliance linked to the Hafiz Gul Bahadur faction, claimed responsibility for the attack. The IMP operates within the broader network of militant groups active along the Afghanistan-Pakistan border and has had links with the Tehreek-e-Taliban Pakistan (TTP), a militant umbrella organization waging an insurgency against the Pakistani state.
The scale of the threat is reflected in the 2026 Global Terrorism Index, which ranked the TTP as the world’s third-deadliest terrorist organization in 2025. The index identified rising violence by both the TTP and the Balochistan Liberation Army (BLA) as contributing to Pakistan’s worsening security environment. Islamabad has maintained that the Afghan Taliban authorities are allowing the militant outfits, including the TTP and the BLA, to maintain sanctuaries in Afghanistan, an allegation Kabul denies.
The Kohat attack was just one manifestation of a broader security dispute that has strained Afghanistan-Pakistan relations for years. In 2022, shortly after the Taliban returned to power in Afghanistan, Pakistan negotiated with the TTP through mediation by Afghanistan’s Taliban authorities. They reached a ceasefire in June 2022, but the agreement collapsed in November, when the TTP announced a resumption of attacks across Pakistan.
A February 2023 U.N. Security Council monitoring report cited assessments by several member states that the Taliban’s return to power in Afghanistan had emboldened the TTP and contributed to an escalation in its attacks against Pakistan. The report also examined links between the TTP and other armed groups. Subsequent U.N. Security Council monitoring reports have provided further support for Pakistan’s security concerns. A July 2024 report noted that the TTP continued to operate from Afghanistan and conduct attacks inside Pakistan, citing member states’ assessments of Taliban tolerance and support for the group. The December 2025 report went further, describing the continued harboring of TTP leaders in Afghanistan and the facilitation of the group’s operations by the Taliban authorities.
As concerns about cross-border militancy persisted, Islamabad pursued a parallel response at home. In June 2024, the government approved Azm-e-Istehkam, a national framework intended to strengthen intelligence-based operations and law enforcement. However, domestic counterterrorism measures have not resolved the cross-border dimension of the threat.
Regional diplomacy has struggled to bridge the divide between Islamabad and Kabul. The eighth Moscow Format Consultations on Afghanistan, held on October 5, offered a recent example of this impasse. The meeting brought together Afghanistan and regional powers, including Pakistan, China, India, Iran and Russia, to discuss security and regional cooperation. It ended without a joint statement after the Pakistani and Afghan delegations struggled to agree on the language concerning terrorism. Pakistan’s Special Representative for Afghanistan, Mohammad Sadiq, emphasized the threat posed by militant groups operating from Afghan territory, while the Afghan Taliban delegation resisted the proposed wording. The disagreement illustrated a fundamental obstacle: the two sides have yet to agree on how to define and address the security problem itself.
The Moscow impasse followed earlier attempts to ease tensions through direct negotiations. After the October 2025 fighting, Qatar and Turkiye hosted talks that produced a ceasefire, followed by further rounds of negotiations in Istanbul, Doha, and Riyadh. These efforts did not resolve the central dispute. Pakistan seeks verifiable action against the TTP, while the Afghan Taliban authorities deny that the group operates from their territory in the manner Islamabad alleges. Without agreement on the underlying security concerns, diplomatic engagement has struggled to produce a durable settlement.
Economic ties have suffered as a result. In January 2026, Pakistani and Afghan traders agreed to establish a joint committee to discuss reopening border crossings. However, commercial negotiations could not overcome the wider security impasse. Since the October 2025 clashes, Pakistan has kept its border crossings with Afghanistan closed to trade – by far the longest closure in recent decades, disrupting a key transit route into Central Asia. The economic burden has fallen on traders and transporters on both sides, while Afghanistan has sought to diversify its trade through Iran, India, and other regional partners.
The costs of confrontation are therefore not confined to the security domain. Prolonged border closures disrupt livelihoods and commercial networks, while airstrikes and armed clashes expose civilians to further harm. The biggest challenge is to prevent the security dispute from becoming a self-reinforcing cycle in which militant violence prompts punitive measures, those measures deepen bilateral hostility, and deteriorating relations make cooperation against militancy even more difficult.
Breaking this cycle requires practical measures rather than competing declarations. First, Pakistan and the Afghan Taliban authorities could establish a verification mechanism, facilitated by a mutually acceptable third party such as Qatar, Turkiye, or China, to investigate specific allegations of militant activity and assess compliance with security commitments. Second, trade routes could be reopened gradually against measurable security benchmarks, linking economic recovery to demonstrable progress. Third, regional powers could support a sustained counterterrorism dialogue focused on information-sharing, specific incidents, and border management. Such targeted cooperation may offer a more realistic starting point than broader diplomatic forums where disagreements over the nature of the threat continue to prevent consensus.

Could the US cut Ukraine off from vital military intelligence again?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
12:28:56 UTC
21:28:56 KST

The United States already showed it could suspend intelligence-sharing with Ukraine when it briefly cut off cooperation in March 2025 during a diplomatic confrontation.
When Russian ballistic missiles struck Kyiv on Monday night, residents were caught off guard. There was no advance air-raid warning, leaving people confused and with no time to seek shelter as explosions rocked the capital.
Such incidents have occurred before, but this time the lack of warning fuelled speculation that Washington might have suspended intelligence-sharing with Kyiv amid escalating diplomatic tensions.
President Volodymyr Zelenskyy confirmed on Tuesday that Ukraine had received no advance warning from its partners about the incoming missiles, stressing that such intelligence was critical to save civilian lives.
Ukraine's Air Force initially reported that Russian forces had launched what appeared to be six ballistic missiles towards the capital at approximately 10pm.
Zelenskyy subsequently said five missiles had struck civilian infrastructure, describing the attack as "particularly vile."
"Intelligence on Russian ballistic missile launches helps save lives and this is one of the most critical issues. This is precisely what helps prevent people from being killed – when there is an early warning about ballistic missiles," Zelenskyy said.
But Ukrainian presidential adviser Serhii Beskrestnov, known as "Flash", cautioned against linking the incident to a possible US intelligence cut-off.
"This is not the first time that an S-400 launch has gone undetected by our partners' intelligence services. There are certain technical nuances involved. We should not jump to conclusions," he wrote in a post on Facebook.
Ukraine's Air Force said its radar systems detected the incoming missiles during the attack, but that it had received no information about their launch from Russian territory. It said it was investigating why the warning had not arrived.
Air Force spokesperson Yurii Ihnat confirmed that the air-raid alert had sounded only once the attack was under way, but stressed that the US was not Ukraine's only intelligence partner, with other NATO countries also providing information on Russian strategic aviation, naval movements and ballistic missile launches.
"There are moments when this information fails to arrive. This is not the first case," Ihnat said.
Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha also dismissed speculation that Washington had deliberately withheld intelligence.
Speaking at the Warsaw Security Forum Sybiha said intelligence cooperation with the US was continuing and attributed the absence of an early warning to a "special type of weaponry" used by Russia.
The European Commission also sought to play down concerns about a possible suspension, saying on Tuesday that, to its knowledge, Washington had not threatened to cut off intelligence-sharing or weapons sales to Ukraine.
Washington's intelligence leverage
The uncertainty comes amid reports that Washington has threatened to suspend intelligence-sharing and weapons sales, including supplies purchased by European allies for Ukraine, unless Kyiv stops targeting Russian oil refineries.
Ukraine considers Russian oil facilities legitimate military targets, arguing that the revenues they generate help Moscow finance its war.
The possibility of a suspension is far from hypothetical.
In March 2025, the Trump administration temporarily halted intelligence-sharing and military assistance to Ukraine amid a diplomatic confrontation with Kyiv. Both were subsequently restored following talks between American and Ukrainian officials in Saudi Arabia.
The episode demonstrated how quickly Washington could use security cooperation as a source of political leverage and how dependent Ukraine remained on American capabilities.
US intelligence remains crucial to Ukraine's ability to anticipate Russian attacks, particularly through satellite-based systems capable of detecting missile launches before incoming weapons appear on ground-based radar.
Other NATO countries also share intelligence with Kyiv, but it remains unclear how far European allies could compensate should another American suspension come into force.
For now Ukrainian officials largely insist cooperation with Washington continues and there is no evidence that Monday's missing warning resulted from a deliberate decision to withhold intelligence.
European military sources told Euronews that intelligence-sharing would likely be the last form of US support to be withdrawn, as cutting it off could also put American diplomats and those of its allies stationed in Ukraine at risk.

Around 650 prisoners to be released early in England, Wales
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
12:28:16 UTC
21:28:16 KST

Aysu Bicer
13 October 2026•Update: 13 October 2026
Around 650 prisoners are set to be released early from jails in England and Wales on Tuesday in the second phase of a government scheme aimed at tackling overcrowding in the prison system.
The scheme allows eligible offenders serving sentences of up to 2 1/2 years to leave prison after serving one-third of their sentence, rather than half, according to the BBC.
The second wave follows the release of around 700 prisoners on Oct. 1, all serving sentences of less than 19 months.
The government plans to release around 5,000 prisoners in stages, with the process extending to June next year for those serving sentences of more than 12 years.
The number of eligible prisoners was reduced from an initial estimate of 6,000 after officials excluded rapists and the most serious child sex offenders. Those convicted of manslaughter are also ineligible, along with offenders convicted of several other offenses, including indecent assault involving members of child grooming gangs.
The scheme has raised concerns among victims’ groups and probation officers over public safety and the capacity to supervise offenders after their release.
Alice Russell-Harris of domestic abuse charity Refuge told the BBC that releasing perpetrators could put survivors at serious risk of harm. She said license conditions, including electronic tagging and exclusion zones, were frequently breached by perpetrators.
Concerns have also been raised about delays in fitting electronic tags, which are used to monitor curfews and other release conditions.
Meanwhile, probation service union Napo said its members were overwhelmed by workloads and the need to provide intensive supervision to released offenders.
Union General Secretary Ian Lawrence warned that the number of prisoners being released was placing significant pressure on the service, calling for additional resources.
The developments come as the government prepares to present plans to overhaul criminal courts to Parliament, while probation officers prepare to vote in a ballot that could lead to strike action over pay and workloads.

Generative AI transforms internet marketing, ushers in ‘citation economy’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
12:28:10 UTC
21:28:10 KST

Enes Ege and Emir Yildirim
13 October 2026•Update: 13 October 2026
Search engines and virtual assistants powered by artificial intelligence (AI) are reshaping digital marketing by replacing click-driven metrics with a “citation economy,” as experts say producing original and verifiable content has become increasingly important for brands to stand out amid the oversaturation of generative AI content.
Digital visibility across AI platforms like ChatGPT, Perplexity and Google AI Overviews hinges on “generative engine optimization,” or “GEO,” according to a report by Princeton University and partner institutions.
Researchers developed a test dataset called “GEO-bench,” which includes over 10,000 different queries to analyze the data processing architecture of generative search engines.
The test showed that digital content with verifiable statistics, credible citations and expert opinions increased its visibility in AI-generated answers by up to 40%.
With more and more users relying on AI-generated summaries rather than clicking through search engine query results, marketing agencies worldwide are reshaping their strategies to adapt to the changing trend.
Experts say this transition will usher in a new era where brands that produce high-quality original content will prevail over those that boast massive ad budgets.
Bunyamin Sarac, co-founder and CEO of Indexa, told Anadolu that brands appearing in AI chatbot answers and AI-generated search engine summaries are more successful as internet traffic shifts away from the simple click-based system.
Sarac stated that AI engines evaluate real-time search results using trust signals like “source authority,” “timeliness” and “extractability.”
“Developers of these models do not fully share the details of their source selection mechanism, so we can’t really say that there’s a definitive formula, but research and observation showed certain signals that these models look for,” he said. “AI responses are trained by two sources: the data set used to train the model and web search inquiries at the moment that the answer is generated to a prompt.”
Sarac noted that click-through rates drop when users receive an AI summary, citing Pew Research Center findings that showed that while 8% of users who read an AI summary on Google clicked on one of the resulting links, this rate was nearly double among those who did not see a summary.
“We expect a decline in web traffic from information-seeking inquiries, as visitors who click on a website will be those who have already read the AI summary or done their research through AI and are closer to making a purchase – the metric for success will shift from the number of clicks to the number of times that a product or brand was recommended for critical search inquiries,” he added.
Erdem Dagdemir, co-founder and CEO of Analythick, told Anadolu that conventional search engine optimization (SEO) focused on technical code and voluminous data, which is no longer sufficient. He urged brands to embrace a newer approach that highlights human context, real-world customer satisfaction and organic digital footprints.
“AI does not look at the volume of data but at its qualitative accuracy and depth, synthesizing information by cross-referencing a brand’s digital footprint and asking if the source is trustworthy and whether customers are satisfied,” he said.
“Brands must plan their operations, establish effective communication, and build trust by prioritizing customer satisfaction,” he added, noting that if these digital footprints do not corroborate a brand’s corporate promises, AI might completely remove the brand from recommendations.
Dagdemir stated that large language models (LLMs) go through online forums and review sites to reveal persistent consumer complaints to decide whether a brand or product can be recommended to users. He added that marketing teams clinging to outdated methods, like oversaturating superficial content, will lose ground to competitors who offer verifiable information.
“The clear and fast responses AI chatbots are made to deliver force people and industries to adapt to this new pace, and Türkiye’s ecosystem stands at this threshold of adaptation – while some brands are still using outdated methods to cling to their prominence, the fundamental rule of the new era is no longer about visibility but about reliability, and amid the clutter of information and scarcity of quality content, I think brands that abandon ad-driven strategies in favor of offering genuine and accurate information will gain a significant edge over competitors in AI-generated search responses,” he added.
