Two ships struck by drones in Black Sea off Bulgaria
Finland
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
15:28:05 EEST
21:28:05 KST

Eleven sailors are missing after drone strikes hit two cargo ships off Bulgaria's Black Sea coast on Tuesday, 13 October, sinking one vessel and damaging another. Bulgaria has summoned Russia's ambassador and requested assistance from NATO and the European Union.
Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev condemned the attacks, which occurred near the country's territorial waters, and convened an emergency meeting with security officials.
Add Helsinki Times as a preferred source on Google (opens Google in a new tab)
The vessel that sank was identified by Bulgarian President Iliana Iotova as the Guinea-Bissau-flagged HS Dignity. It went down approximately 31 kilometres east of the coastal village of Krapets.
Reuters reported that five crew members had been rescued, while 11 remained missing. Other initial reports gave a lower number of survivors. Search and rescue operations continued on Tuesday.
The second vessel, the Ukrainian-owned Chelsea 3, was struck by three drones approximately 33 kilometres off the coastal town of Byala at around 1.30am local time.
The Maltese-flagged cargo ship, registered in Ukraine's Odesa, was travelling from Turkey to Moldova when the attack occurred.
All 15 crew members, comprising seven Ukrainians and eight Azerbaijanis, were rescued by Bulgarian border authorities and transported to Varna. Five received treatment for minor injuries.
"This is absolutely unacceptable — another attack in the immediate vicinity of Bulgarian territorial waters," Radev said in a televised address.
Bulgarian authorities have not established who launched the drones. Radev said there was no conclusive evidence identifying those responsible, although he suggested that the attacks benefited Russia.
Following the incident, Bulgaria summoned Russian Ambassador Eleonora Mitrofanova for discussions in Sofia.
According to Reuters, Mitrofanova said she had received no information from Russia's Defence Ministry concerning attacks on commercial vessels. She also raised the possibility that a third party had staged the incidents as a provocation.
The attacks prompted Bulgaria to seek assistance from NATO and the EU to strengthen maritime monitoring, airspace surveillance and investigations into the strikes.
Radev discussed the situation with NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte and European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen.
Rutte said NATO would continue monitoring security developments in the Black Sea and adjust its military presence along the alliance's eastern flank when necessary.
"The Black Sea has become another front of escalation of the Russian war in Ukraine," von der Leyen wrote on X, condemning the attacks and calling for those responsible to face accountability.
Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha directly accused Moscow of targeting civilian shipping and threatening international food supplies.
"The Black Sea is a lifeline for global food security," Sybiha wrote on X, accusing Russia of using attacks on commercial shipping to disrupt food transportation.
The incidents follow drone attacks against commercial vessels in Bulgaria's exclusive economic zone on 6 October.
One of those ships, the Alfa Watan, sank, leaving 10 sailors, including nine Syrians and one Egyptian, missing and presumed dead. Another vessel sustained damage, but its crew survived.
Russia and Ukraine have increasingly targeted maritime infrastructure and vessels during the war, which began with Russia's full-scale invasion in February 2022.
Russian forces have struck Ukrainian ports and shipping facilities, while Ukraine has attacked Russian vessels and maritime infrastructure in the Black Sea and Sea of Azov.
The attacks have affected commercial routes used to transport grain and other goods, including shipping corridors near Bulgaria and Romania, both NATO members.

From Data Localization to Digital Openness: Uzbekistan’s Regulatory Shift
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
12:28:00 UTC
21:28:00 KST

During a visit to New York in late September, the head of Uzbekistan’s presidential administration, Saida Mirziyoyeva, met with Google Vice President Karan Bhatia to discuss the possibility of launching YouTube monetization in Uzbekistan. Uzbekistan has been actively seeking to expand its partnership with global digital companies in line with the country’s growing digital economy. Tashkent even re-wrote the laws that once made it difficult for international technology platforms to operate in the country.
The 2021 amendment to Uzbekistan’s Law on Personal Data imposed a restriction on the storage and processing of Uzbek citizens’ data abroad, raising the question of how domestic regulation could accommodate services operating across borders. PayPal, Stripe, Netflix, Spotify, and Amazon Web Services refused to enter the Uzbek market while Apple Pay, Google Pay, and Google Cloud limited their functionality.
However, it soon became clear that the regulations introduced to protect personal data got in the way of generating money. Last year, the Center for Economic Research and Reforms (CERR) calculated Uzbekistan’s annual losses without YouTube monetization alone as $50 million annually. Mirziyoyeva’s efforts reflect the country’s wider attempt to re-attract global tech-companies by revising local regulations.
The Economic Cost of Data Sovereignty
In May 2021, Uzkomnazorat, Uzbekistan’s digital and telecommunications regulator, announced that VKontakte (Mail.ru Group), Twitter (Twitter Inc.), and WeChat (Tencent Inc.) were processing Uzbek citizens’ data abroad in violation of the data protection law. On July 2 of that year, Uzkomnazorat blocked access to those social media sites over alleged non-compliance with data-localization requirements.
“If the internet companies are planning to work in Uzbekistan, they have to observe the legislation of Uzbekistan,” noted Temur Akhmedov, then with the Institute for Strategic and Interregional Studies under the President of the Republic of Uzbekistan. In August 2022, just over a year later, Uzkomnazorat walked its enforcement decision back, removing Twitter, VKontakte, and WeChat from its “register of violators of the rights of personal data subjects.” The platforms were unblocked with no explanation given for the change.
By 2024, the data protection law’s cost for Uzbekistan’s economy became more apparent. As the government sought to integrate international payment systems like PayPal, AliPay, UniPay, Apple Pay, and Google Pay into the country’s banking system to attract more tourists, requirements to store citizens’ personal data locally emerged as a major obstacle.
During the negotiations with Apple and Google, the Central Bank of Uzbekistan noted that “in order to connect Visa and Mastercard cards issued by Uzbek banks to the Apple Pay and Google Pay systems, it is necessary to review some requirements of the current legislative documents, in particular, the Law of Uzbekistan ‘On Personal Data.’”
TBC Bank Group PLC’s representative Oliver Hughes, during a December 2024 presidential meeting with entrepreneurs, suggested allowing banks to store their data in the cloud both in Uzbekistan and offshore jurisdictions.
“We are talking about the personal data of citizens,” President Shavkat Mirziyoyev said. “This is a very serious matter. We have no right to make mistakes.” He emphasized the need for a carefully considered solution.
By 2025, the debate on data localization increasingly focused on its economic costs. In July 2025, Kotib AI Research, an AI company, estimated the potential cost of the localization law to Uzbekistan’s economy at $3.2 to $4.5 billion a year. The absence of PayPal alone had cost the country at least $1.8 billion in revenue over the previous five years. Uzbekistan is the only country in Central Asia without access to the service. PayPal’s global payment system is built on a single data infrastructure, and it does not keep each country’s data separate. It is reportedly technically inconsistent to store only Uzbek users’ data on a separate local server, as a single server cannot isolate the national user traffic.
International payment systems have further been affected by the data protection law, increasing the cost of operating digital services and limiting access to the international payment infrastructure. Limited access to international payment systems costs Uzbekistan around $500-800 million annually.
Apart from affecting the e-commerce and fintech sectors, the data localization rules also impact AI development. Since AI technologies rely on cloud servers, APIs, and international platforms, strict localization can increase compliance costs and complicate the entry of international service providers into the Uzbek market. Requiring data to be stored locally conflicts with the objective of the country’s AI Strategy 2030. The strategy aims to strengthen cooperation with international organizations and leading foreign technology companies and encourage the exchange of knowledge through joint research projects.
Article 27 of the Data Protection Law also complicates YouTube monetization. The platform cannot run its ads in the country, which limits the creative economy’s ability to generate jobs and revenue. In 2024, the estimated value of the advertising market in the country reached 2.1 trillion Uzbek soms ($164.3 million), with 29 percent coming from digital ads. According to the CERR, the introduction of YouTube monetization might increase Uzbekistan’s gross domestic product by 0.05-0.1 percent.
What began as an effort to protect citizens’ data was increasingly being questioned on economic and legal grounds. In July 2025, government representatives, lawyers, technology companies, and financial services firms met to further highlight concerns about Article 27 of the Personal Data Law. During the meeting, the experts discussed the ambiguity of the law’s language and the problems with its drafting. To the business experts, the law seemed unclear, which raised the question of the absence of a dedicated body for obtaining authoritative guidance. While some experts suggested the full repeal of the data localization clause, others argued that only government agencies and companies with more than 20 percent state ownership should follow the law’s rules, while those with commercial operations should have more flexible rules, provided user consent is in place for cross-border data transfer.
From Regulatory Uncertainty to Legislative Reform
In January 2026, on the third reading, the Legislative Chamber of the Oliy Majlis passed an amendment allowing certain data to be stored and processed abroad, provided that certain security requirements are met. In March, the proposed amendment to the law on personal data was officially adopted. Biometric and genetic data of individuals, along with data associated with telecommunications operators, must be stored domestically. Other categories of personal data may now be stored and processed abroad if the foreign state provides adequate protection.
In July 2026, the Cabinet of Ministers published a list of 49 countries where the personal and anonymized data of Uzbekistan’s citizens can be transferred automatically without informing the authorized body, these included the United States, Austria, and the United Kingdom.
The amendments to Uzbekistan’s data protection legislation mark a bold step toward the development of the country’s digital economy and integration with global digital services. Central Bank official Jamshid Usmanov said that the regulators, together with the national card payment networks Humo and Uzcard and commercial banks, had begun negotiations on launching Apple Pay and Google Pay following the legislative amendments.
The reforms have not yet brought in the major international services Tashkent hopes to attract. The legal changes reflect the country’s vision to align national legislation with global standards to strengthen its digital economy. While the state might not have abandoned the principle of data sovereignty, this development reflects a shift from rigid, sovereignty-based control to a more pragmatic, economically oriented regulatory model. That said, the liberalization of data localization might bring changes, but the success of the reform will depend on whether international technology and payment services believe Uzbekistan’s regulatory environment is predictable enough to risk entering the market.

Burc Eruygur
13 October 2026•Update: 13 October 2026
The Kremlin said on Tuesday that Russia is continuing contacts with Washington concerning a potential energy ceasefire in Ukraine mentioned by US President Donald Trump last week.
In remarks to journalists at a press briefing, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said the topic was discussed during Monday’s news conference and that he had nothing to add to that conversation.
“Contacts regarding this matter are ongoing,” Peskov said, noting that he does not see a correlation between Russia’s position on Ukraine and a deal -- unveiled by Trump on Friday following a phone call with Russian President Vladimir Putin -- for Moscow to supply diesel to the US and global markets.
Peskov described the diesel agreement as a “highly mutually beneficial” aspect of Russian-American cooperation.
“This serves the interests of the United States, the interests of global energy markets, and the interests of the Russian Federation; that is why it is happening,” Peskov further said, claiming that European countries may attempt to hinder the agreement.
Peskov also said that Russia is a country that offers competitive products on global markets and will continue to do so.
He said Kremlin was unaware of reports that the US would cease intelligence sharing with Kyiv, as well as a US- and European-proposed peace plan for the Ukraine war reported by The Washington Post.
The spokesman also said that it was too early to discuss a compensation mechanism for financial losses suffered by Yandex users as a result of recent Ukrainian attacks against the company’s data centers.
On Sunday, Trump announced on his Truth Social media platform that Russia and Ukraine had agreed to an immediate ceasefire on attacks targeting each other's energy infrastructure.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy told Axios earlier Sunday that Kyiv was prepared to halt strikes on Russian oil refineries if Moscow stopped attacking Ukraine's energy infrastructure, stressing that any de-escalation must be reciprocal and backed by guarantees.
Meanwhile, Peskov said Monday that the Kremlin had no immediate comment on the proposed halt, though contacts with the US concerning the topic were ongoing.

Iran and Russia ramping up hybrid campaigns in Britain, UK spy chief says
Iran is ramping up attempts to hit harder targets such as military sites in Britain while Russia is escalating its hybrid warfare as it lashes out against Ukraine's allies, the UK's domestic spy chief said on Tuesday.
In his annual speech on wide-ranging threats to Britain, MI5's Director General Ken McCallum also said the greatest concern about the misuse of AI was terrorists being able to develop bioweapons or even create new novel pathogens.
McCallum said state threats had quadrupled over the last decade meaning his organisation now devoted more resources to the issue than during the Cold War.

"The RAF Fairfield incident ... is not unique. There have been other examples, not just in the UK but around the world," he said.
On Russia, which likewise denies involvement in hostile acts in Britain, the UK spy chief said it remained the "aggressor number one".
He echoed comments from other European spy agencies that Russia was using tactics just short of conventional conflict, citing the attempted drone attack on a cargo plane at a German airport and a cyber attack on Polish energy infrastructure.
"It's no accident that Russian aggressors are trying to unsettle other European homelands at a time when their military progress in Ukraine is minimal and horrifically costly," he said.

Deputy Minister Artur Harazim opens 17th Warsaw Human Rights Seminar
Poland
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
14:25:20 CEST
21:25:20 KST

Deputy Minister Artur Harazim opens 17th Warsaw Human Rights Seminar
12.10.2026
Impact of artificial intelligence on the administration of justice and the protection of human rights were the topics of the 17th Warsaw Human Rights Seminar. The event attended by MFA Undersecretary of State Artur Harazim was held in Warsaw on 12 October 2026.
Advances in artificial intelligence improve the efficiency of the administration of justice and facilitate access to legal information. At the same time, however, they give rise to significant challenges in terms of algorithmic transparency, data protection, non-discrimination, accountability, and the protection of procedural rights.
During the Seminar, experts sought answers to the question of how to reconcile the use of new technologies with the standards of the European Convention of Human Rights and the principles of the rule of law.
The Seminar was inaugurated by the deputy head of Polish diplomacy, Artur Harazim, who underlined that:
The central question is not whether AI will become part of our justice system. In many respects, that process has already begun. Our objective should be to ensure that innovation serves justice.
The keynote address entitled “Artificial intelligence and the future of human rights protection” was delivered by former President of the European Court of Human Rights Robert Spano. Then, President of the Supreme Administrative Court Jacek Chlebny spoke on the use of emerging technologies in administrative courts.
Later on, Poland’s Commissioner for Human Rights Sylwia Gregorczyk-Abram and a European Court of Human Rights judge Úna Ní Raifeartaigh discussed the future of human rights protection in the digital age. The Court’s role in the protection of human rights in the era of artificial intelligence was also addressed, as well as the impact of technology on legal practice and representation before the courts.
The Seminar was attended by judges and representatives of the European Court of Human Rights, the Council of Europe, and the Court of Justice the European Union, as well as the representatives of national human rights institutions, the judiciary, public administration, the legal profession, and academia.
The event concluded with a session on the future of human rights and justice in the era of artificial intelligence, featuring the Council of Europe Commissioner for Human Rights Michael O'Flaherty.

11 infants treated for suspected food poisoning at West Bank settlement daycare
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
12:25:09 UTC
21:25:09 KST

Eleven Israeli infants at a daycare center in the West Bank settlement of Beitar Illit were treated Tuesday after showing symptoms of suspected food poisoning, police and emergency services said.
Police said the symptoms followed exposure to food, after firefighters and rescue personnel ruled out the presence of hazardous substances at the scene. The daycare center was closed and the incident was reported to the Health Ministry.
According to Magen David Adom, five infants were taken to Hadassah Ein Kerem Hospital in Jerusalem. The hospital said one was in moderate condition, while the other four were undergoing further examinations.
The infants arrived with "flushed faces and showing signs of distress," the hospital said.
Four women who accompanied the infants were also being treated at the hospital, all in mild condition.
In January, two infants died at a private, unlicensed daycare in an ultra-Orthodox neighborhood in Jerusalem. Another 53 infants were evacuated from the building, many suffering from coughing.
Medical examinations indicated that the two infants may have suffered from heatstroke. Emergency responders said they had been inside a stroller in a closed room heated by an air conditioner running at full power. The infants were sweating and had red spots on their skin, symptoms that can indicate heatstroke.
Initial emergency service reports said the infants had been harmed by toxic fumes, but firefighters later ruled out the presence of hazardous substances or toxic gas.
"The findings are that there are no findings," Prof. Yaniv Sherer, director of Hadassah Ein Kerem Hospital, said at the time. "We have not located or isolated any material in the infants' blood that explains what happened."
Sherer said heat or overcrowding may have contributed, but that the hospital could not determine the cause.

Yemeni families’ search for missing loved ones hindered by new fighting
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
12:25:00 UTC
21:25:00 KST

Yemeni families’ search for missing loved ones hindered by new fighting
Hundreds of people have gone missing in Yemen, with families not knowing if they were killed in fighting or detained.
Sanaa, Yemen – In 2020, 18-year-old Munif bid farewell to his family and left his home in Sanaa to fight with the Houthis on the front lines of Yemen’s civil war
After six months, all of his comrades went back to their families, but Munif never returned home.
More than six years have passed, and Munif’s family, who asked to use just his first name for security reasons, are still searching for answers about his fate.
He is one of hundreds of people who have disappeared in Yemen since war broke out in September 2014, when the Houthis – an armed group also known as Ansar Allah (Arabic for Supporters of God) – captured the capital and forced the internationally-recognised government to flee south.
“Ten other men from our village joined the front line on the Saudi-Yemen border. All of them came back. We asked them about my brother’s whereabouts, but none could tell us where he had gone,” said Mohammed, Munif’s brother. “A definite answer about his status would be a relief for the entire family.”
There were hopes that a truce in 2022 between the Saudi-backed Yemeni government and Iran-aligned Houthis could help families begin their search for their missing loved ones.
Since July this year, the International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC) has received more than 1,800 tracing requests from families looking for missing relatives in Yemen.
But the resumption of fighting in July has halted this search for many families, who are trying to find out if loved ones have been detained, injured, killed, or simply lost in records, due to displacement or desertion.
After careful consideration, Mohammed believes there are two possible outcomes for his brother, Munif.
“He might have been hit by an air strike, leaving no trace of his body, or perhaps he was captured, and he remains in captivity,” Mohammed said.
If Munif was killed in an explosion, finding a body part that could be identified would bring the family some relief. But the family is still hoping for the latter scenario, and that Munif is being held captive by government forces.
“We would have accepted his death, adjusted to the loss, and forgotten my brother’s possible return. We just need to know what happened to him,” he said.
“We have heard about some fighters who were believed to be dead, and their families accepted the news of their deaths and mourned them. However, they emerged alive after years of captivity. So, Munif may still be alive.”
Both sides have held many prisoners of war over the decade-long conflict, but the number of captives remains uncertain.
In May, Yemen’s internationally-recognised government and the Houthis signed a United Nations-backed agreement in Jordan to exchange more than 1,600 detainees. However, the implementation of the deal was postponed after both sides accused each other of obstructing the agreement.
Abdulaziz, 24, has been on the front lines in Marib, an energy-rich region in central Yemen, fighting for the Houthis. Before the recent surge in fighting, he used to call his family once every 10 days. But for the past two months, his family has not heard from him.
“We are waiting for a phone call from Abdulaziz, and we do not know if he will ever call us,” said Ahmed, Abdulaziz’s brother.
Fighting has intensified on the front lines in Marib and Al-Jawf since the Houthis seized part of the Yemeni coast in September, and Rashid al-Alimi, the head of the Presidential Leadership Council (PLC), announced a counteroffensive by government forces.
The use of artillery, drones and warplanes to target Houthi positions likely means that many more people will be killed or missing.
Ahmed, 26, assumes that his brother may have been killed in attacks by government forces in recent weeks.
“We have not received any information from his comrades and field leaders about his injury or death. But my parents state that Abdulaziz’s voice or appearance is the only believable proof that he is alive,” he said.
“Abdulaziz is in the battlefield. And people there kill or get killed. So, his [possible] death is not a shock for me. But continued ambiguity is more painful than confirmed news of his death.”
With no word on his whereabouts, Abdulaziz’s mother will not know whether to wait for his safe return or begin to mourn his loss. “Whether he continues to be lost or his dead body returns, my mother’s eyes will never stop filling with tears,” Ahmed added.
Christine Cipolla, the head of the ICRC’s Yemen delegation, said families of the missing had the right to know about the fate of their loved ones.
“Behind every missing person is a family living in anguish. Their pain cannot be ignored, and their wait must not be prolonged,” she said in a statement.
Two months ago, Ali, 23, joined the Houthis’ campaign against government forces on Yemen’s western coast.
His parents objected to Ali leaving home to fight. But because he was unemployed, he insisted on joining the Houthis.
Five days ago, the family received a call informing them of Ali’s death.
“We were told that Ali was killed in the fighting in Mocha. So far, we have not received his body, and we do not know where it is,” Yasser told Al Jazeera. “Recovering his corpse would ease our grief, end our uncertainty, and prove that he is really dead.”
Yazeed Al-Jeddawy, a research manager at the Sanaa Center for Strategic Studies, told Al Jazeera that the ICRC and other qualified humanitarian teams must be allowed safe access to all parts of Yemen to recover bodies, document the missing and preserve identification evidence.
“This is not only about meeting legal obligations. Families may carry the pain and uncertainty of not knowing for decades, and their experiences will become part of how this war is remembered,” Al-Jeddawy said.
Some missing people may have been detained or forcibly disappeared, while others may have been killed in fighting or separated from their families.
The Yemen-based NGO, Mwatana for Human Rights, conducted more than 2,000 interviews with families of victims between September 2014 and July 2025. The study reported at least 1,592 incidents of enforced disappearance involving 2,120 victims.
The Houthi armed group was found responsible for 756 incidents of disappearance involving 897 victims. Forces linked to the internationally-recognised government were connected to 351 incidents involving 449 victims, while the Saudi-led Arab coalition was responsible for 65 incidents involving 91 victims. Forces linked to the Southern Transitional Council (STC) were involved in 387 incidents involving 630 victims.
Al-Jeddawy said the issue of the missing is another stain on both sides of the conflict, which has already killed between 150,000 and 227,000 people and displaced millions.
“History will judge the parties not only by the battles they fought or the territory they gained, but also by whether they showed basic humanity towards the dead, the missing and the families left searching for answers,” he said.

INTERVIEW - 'It's very real, not just words': Palestinian ambassador welcomes UK shift on Israel
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
12:24:33 UTC
21:24:33 KST

INTERVIEW - 'It's very real, not just words': Palestinian ambassador welcomes UK shift on Israel
Husam Zomlot says British measures against illegal Israeli settlements are ‘very good start,’ but enforcement is now priority
Aysu Bicer
13 October 2026•Update: 13 October 2026
LONDON
Ambassador urges sanctions against institutions supporting settlements, rejects Israeli move against UK diplomatic presence in East Jerusalem
‘Israel's response always when the world reacts to its illegality is to double down on the illegality,’ he says
Britain is moving beyond condemnation of Israel’s occupation toward concrete action, Palestinian Ambassador to the UK Husam Zomlot said, welcoming measures against illegal settlements while urging the government to ensure they are fully implemented.
“The UK government policy has improved, and now we see action rather than just words and statements and condemnations, and we see clear definition of the situation,” Zomlot told Anadolu.
“It's a work in progress, but it's a very good start,” he added.
His comments come amid a diplomatic dispute over British plans to ban imports from illegal Israeli settlements and restrict businesses supporting their construction and expansion in the occupied West Bank.
Israel responded by ordering the British consulate general in occupied East Jerusalem to close.
Britain announced on Oct. 8 that the building would remain open as the UK Mission, Jerusalem, although some staff had been withdrawn.
For Zomlot, the UK's policy shift is significant because Britain has committed to measures intended to impose consequences for the occupation. The next test, he said, is whether those commitments translate into effective restrictions.
“It’s very real and not just words,” he said. “The issue now is enforcement, implementation.”
UK ‘resets’ approach to Israel
Since October 2023, British policy toward Israel and Palestine has undergone a significant evolution. Under the Conservative government of Rishi Sunak, Britain strongly backed Israel’s right to defend itself, while Royal Air Force surveillance aircraft were deployed over the eastern Mediterranean.
As civilian casualties mounted in Gaza, humanitarian access deteriorated and concerns over violations of international law intensified, Britain’s position came under growing pressure.
Under Keir Starmer, the government suspended some arms export licenses in 2024, imposed sanctions on two Israeli ministers in 2025 and recognized Palestinian statehood that year.
But Prime Minister Andy Burnham's government has pledged broader action against economic support for settlements, including financial, construction and other services.
At Labour’s recent party conference, Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband acknowledged demands for a change in policy, telling those who had protested against the treatment of Palestinians: “We hear you, you were right.”
“Under Andy's leadership, we have reset our approach. We call out ethnic cleansing by the settler terrorists in the West Bank. We call out the evidence of war crimes in Gaza. We call out Israel's illegal occupation of Palestine. And we match words with actions,” Miliband said.
Enforcing the measures
Zomlot said Britain’s position established common ground on both the goal of ending the occupation and the use of sanctions to achieve it.
“We agree on the mechanism, which is sanctions. You have to sanction illegality. That's not a political demand. That's a legal obligation on the UK government and on all governments worldwide, all states, all nations that are contractors of international law and international legality.”
He described the change as “a big step forward,” but said implementation would require sustained attention.
The government has set a six- to nine-month timetable for the legislation underpinning the new restrictions. Miliband has said the measures target settlements rather than trade with Israel within its pre-1967 boundaries.
Zomlot wants restrictions to encompass financing, promotion and insurance, alongside other business support for settlements.
He also called for sanctions against Israeli state institutions, organizations and agencies that he said supported, protected or financed them.
“We have been saying, while the settlements are the crime, Israel is the criminal,” he said.
“So we cannot just punish the crime, but not the criminal, and that's what we are working with the British government towards.”
Public pressure
Zomlot credited public campaigning with helping drive the shift, saying ministers had responded to demands for stronger action on Palestinian rights.
“We still have some way to go, and we need to continue working with the British people because it was the British people who spoke it,” he said.
“The main force here is the public opinion, the public pressure. The public has spoken.”
An April 2026 poll by YouGov found that over six in 10 of the British public opposed Israel’s ongoing military actions in Gaza and the West Bank, while just 13% said they were in support.
Invoking the anti-apartheid movement, he praised those campaigning against genocide and ethnic cleansing and supporting Palestinian freedom and liberation.
Dispute over Jerusalem mission
The confrontation over Britain’s diplomatic presence in East Jerusalem has brought the consequences of the policy shift into focus.
Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Saar ordered the consulate general to close by Oct. 8, following a 30-day deadline imposed in response to the settlement measures.
Israel also announced restrictions on other British activities, including participation in Gaza aid coordination and training for Palestinian Authority security forces, as well as entry bans targeting British citizens.
Miliband said the consulate building would remain open under a new designation. “The Consulate General building will not be closing, and will be known as the UK Mission, Jerusalem from today,” he said.
Britain maintains that Israel has no legal right to close the mission and that East Jerusalem is occupied territory. The government said it would work to rebuild its diplomatic presence and refrain from reciprocal action while credible discussions continued.
Zomlot rejected Israel’s authority to order the closure.
“Israel has no right, has no jurisdiction over Jerusalem. East Jerusalem is an occupied city,” he said.
He described the mission, which has maintained a British diplomatic presence for nearly 200 years, as an important connection between the two peoples.
“It serves as the address between Britain and the British people and the Palestinian people,” he said.
He called the move against the British diplomatic presence “a very illegal act” and urged London not to accept it.
“Israel's response always when the world reacts to its illegality is to double down on the illegality,” he said.

====================================================================================================

Pacific region sets record for big, long-lasting hurricanes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
12:22:15 UTC
21:22:15 KST

Pacific hurricane region sets record for big, long-lasting storms, due to El Niño
The drumbeat of monster hurricanes in the Pacific has broken a record for nasty, long-lasting storms east of the international date line, turbocharged by nature's supersized El Niño, scientists said.
"Since September 20, when Odalys formed, it's been berserk," said Colorado State University researcher Phil Klotzbach, who forecasts and studies storm activity. "This year, just everything that forms is just lasting a long time and getting really powerful."
One of the key measurements meteorologists use to judge hurricane seasons is called accumulated cyclone energy, or ACE, which includes a storm's wind speed and longevity. On Sunday, a section of the Pacific east of the date line, which brews storms headed for Hawaii, Mexico and the U.S. West Coast, passed the old mark set in 2018. The area is still going strong with Hurricane Simon and appears on the verge of spawning another one that will really ramp up in strength, Klotzbach said.
On Tuesday, the Pacific will tie a record for most days with a hurricane spinning and is likely to break it soon after that, Klotzbach said.
"It feels like almost everything that can spin up does spin up," said University of Arizona atmospheric scientist Kim Wood.
Several meteorological factors have come together to supercharge the Pacific, chief among them the El Niño, Klotzbach and other hurricane researchers said. An El Niño weakens and shifts the high-altitude vertical winds that otherwise can dampen or even decapitate storms. In the Pacific, that wind shear runs east to west, generally with the direction storms travel, so it's like riding a bicycle with a tailwind, Klotzbach said.
Meanwhile, the weather pattern has dampened hurricanes in the Atlantic, where the ACE is less than 18% of what's normal for this time of year. El Niño makes the wind shear in the Atlantic like riding into a headwind, he said.
The Atlantic basin set a record this year for its longest stretch without any hurricanes developing. Isaias was its first, on Oct. 7.
Another factor is warm water, which serves as hurricane fuel. By definition, El Niño is a warming of the equatorial Pacific that changes weather worldwide. In the Pacific storm basin, it's several degrees Fahrenheit warmer than normal, said Kristen Corbosiero, a professor of storm atmospheric sciences at the University at Albany in New York.
Usually in the Pacific, the extra warm storm-friendly water doesn't run as deep as it does in the Atlantic. So when one storm goes over a patch of water, it brings up cold water and makes it hard for a subsequent storm in the same area to stay alive, Wood said. But not this year.
Hurricane Rachel, whose remnants swamped Las Vegas over the weekend, didn't suffer as it went over, churned up by Category 5 Hurricane Polo, Wood said. She said the waters are warm from both El Niño and climate change from the burning of coal, oil and gas.
Another factor in recent storms was a counterclockwise atmospheric spin over Central America - called a gyre - that spits out seeds of stormy weather that can form into hurricanes. It spit out both the Atlantic's Isaias and the Pacific's Simon at about the same time, Corbosiero and Klotzbach said.
The last five Pacific hurricanes — long-lasting Nolo, Odalys, Polo, Rachel and Simon — have all reached major status with winds of at least 111 mph. Nolo, Odalys and Simon hit Category 4, while Polo set the record for time spent at Category 5 at two-and-a-half days.
When Klotzbach made those calculations on the record-breaking activity of the eastern and central Pacific, he looked at all storms east of the date line.
That's a slightly different approach from the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration, which breaks that broad area into two regions. Neither NOAA-defined region is quite at record levels for ACE yet but, put together, they are.
Part of that is because often when one of those subregions is more active, the other isn't quite as crazy, but in 2026 they both are hyperactive, Wood said.
"This is the first year that both sides have been this active together," Wood said. "Usually, it's kind of focused more on one or the other, so that speaks to just the wide extent across this region of where there's been that lower shear, those warmer waters, and that higher moisture."
Off the Mexican coast is a disturbance that the National Hurricane Center gives a 90% chance of becoming Tropical Storm Trudy, which then could power up to something big, Klotzbach and Corbosiero said.
"It seems like that area is just one after another. So I would not be surprised to have another storm," Corbosiero said. "This year, because of the El Niño, we do have very favorable conditions. So as long as there's some sort of the seeds either from the gyre or from remnant ends of cold fronts, it seems like this is going to continue for a bit."

PM Orpo: Finland working on €60m fuel subsidy package
Finland
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
15:19:57 EEST
21:19:57 KST

Finnish Prime Minister Petteri Orpo (NCP) says the government is continuing negotiations on a fuel subsidy for those struggling with high pump prices.
"It's narrowed down to around 60 million euros, which is what's being discussed now."
However, where that sum would come from remains open, according to Orpo. He noted that there's little financial elbow room at the moment.
He said the key priorities are easing commuter travel and supporting professional transport.
Orpo commented on the matter at an event held by the Finnish Association of Political Journalists on Tuesday.
At the end of last month, the PM's National Coalition Party floated a nine-billion-euro savings proposal, among other things it suggested two billion euros in savings by reforming the pension system.
In another savings proposal, finance ministry officials suggested raising the age of retirement to 70. But Orpo has characterised that as unrealistic and reiterated that on Tuesday.
According to Orpo, the National Coalition wants to examine unpaid periods within the pension system — that is, pension accrual during periods when individuals are unemployed or studying, for example.
"Removing those would significantly strengthen the pension system," Orpo said, adding that savings could also be made in pension system administration.
Orpo also said the length of people's working lives should be extended, by enabling young people to begin higher education sooner than they currently do.
Data centre questions
The PM was also asked about suspected illegal logging at Google's Muhos and Kajaani data centre construction sites — and what his role was in that process.
"I haven't been involved in any permit processes whatsoever. I see data centres as a major opportunity for Finland when they're handled properly," Orpo replied.
According to him, not all of the planned data centre projects will move forward, but Google's project has the potential to offer major societal benefits.
Orpo also answered questions about data centre energy demands, and whether there will be enough electricity as more of the power-hungry facilities arrive.
He said the government has taken steps to strengthen the transmission grid so that planned investments in Finland can be accommodated.
According to Orpo, a number of other energy-intensive investments besides data centres are coming to Finland.
As an example, he pointed to a planned aluminium plant in Kokkola.
"There's interest in Finland because we have clean energy," he said, adding that he believes new electricity will be generated as demand for it grows.
Trump's turn against Ukraine
Orpo was also asked about US President Donald Trump positioning himself against Ukraine.
Last Friday, Trump announced that Russia had agreed to supply more than 300,000 tonnes of diesel fuel to US and world markets. To facilitate that move, the US is temporarily lifting sanctions on Russia for the deliveries.
Trump characterised his conversation with Russian President Vladimir Putin as very successful. Trump has also said that Ukraine should not bomb Russian oil refineries.
According to The Financial Times, Trump is also threatening to halt the supply of US weapons to Ukraine.
Orpo was asked what he thinks of Trump's actions and how Europe should respond.
"It really was a huge disappointment. A direct deal with Putin, which goes against everything we've done together—together with the United States. He's making a deal with Putin which is financing Putin's war."
According to Orpo, Europe must forcefully state its position to Trump. He says Europe needs to continue supporting Ukraine, while ensuring that support from the United States continues.

FIFA paid Infantino $1.76M in undisclosed compensation: Report

Halis Sunnetci
13 October 2026•Update: 13 October 2026
FIFA President Gianni Infantino received an additional $1.76 million in compensation in 2024 that was not publicly disclosed by football’s world governing body, potentially violating its own statutes, The Times reported Tuesday.
According to the British newspaper, Infantino received two separate salaries: one from FIFA in Switzerland, disclosed in its annual report, and another from FWC2026 US Inc., the company established to organize the 2026 World Cup.
FIFA’s 2024 annual report listed Infantino’s compensation at 4.274 million Swiss francs ($5.13 million), while a filing with the US Internal Revenue Service showed he received an additional $1.76 million from the organizing company that year.
Miguel Maduro, FIFA’s former governance committee chairman, described the failure to disclose the payments as “a clear violation of FIFA’s statutes” and called for an independent investigation.
“It is a clear contravention of the rules if he is paid other amounts by companies related to FIFA and it is not made public. The FIFA statutes impose an obligation of full transparency,” Maduro told the newspaper.
The Times also reported that $626,229 of Infantino’s additional 2024 compensation was classified as “other reportable compensation.”
FIFA rejected allegations that it had breached its statutes, saying it fully complied with reporting requirements.
A FIFA spokesperson said the president’s compensation and contractual benefits were determined by the organization’s compensation subcommittee.
“These benefits are reported to the US authorities in line with reporting requirements,” the spokesperson said.

====================================================================================================

Global militaries ban foreign electric cars from bases over data security risks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
12:19:42 UTC
21:19:42 KST

Anadolu staff
13 October 2026•Update: 13 October 2026
Critical defense sites are increasingly restricting the presence of foreign electric and smart vehicles on their premises as governments worldwide shield their militaries against espionage and data security risks.
Such measures, adopted across Europe, North America and Asia, have also recently been adopted by major Turkish defense firms, including Aselsan, Roketsan, Havelsan and Turkish Aerospace Industries' (TAI) Engine Industries (TEI) subsidiary.
Experts warn that smart and electric vehicles (EVs) pose threats with their advanced sensors, external cameras, high-gain microphones and live GPS tracking, as these vehicles map their surroundings and transmit data to proprietary servers owned by foreign manufacturers.
For instance, Poland enacted a ban in February 2026, barring Chinese vehicles from entering defense installations due to surveillance risks.
The Polish army also banned defense personnel from pairing their mobile devices with the in-vehicle infotainment systems of Chinese cars, saying these measures were aimed at protecting the defense infrastructure of NATO allies.
In Czechia, authorities restricted Chinese-made cars, including specific Tesla and Volvo models made in China, from accessing military facilities and nearby security zones.
These measures expanded to Czech industrial infrastructure after the ORLEN Group banned Chinese-assembled cars from entering or parking at petrochemical refineries.
Meanwhile, Germany's military and intelligence bodies implemented strict parking bans for Chinese cars, reports show.
Public broadcasters WDR and NDR said the parking lot of the Bundeswehr Operational Command in Schwielowsee, near Potsdam, does not allow Chinese cars to be parked. Owners of such vehicles are allowed to park in designated areas.
Similar restrictions are reportedly in place at German Federal Intelligence Service (BND) facilities.
The German Defense Ministry confirmed bans within designated high-security zones but declined to publish specific restricted models for security reasons.
At the same time, the UK's defense installations expanded local screening procedures, with several bases no longer allowing Chinese-made models, even though the UK Defense Ministry said there was no central regulation banning such vehicles from entering all military facilities.
Switzerland placed targeted restrictions on always-online vehicles around critical electronic installations, including the Zimmerwald Electronic Warfare Center near Bern.
France's counterintelligence agency, DRSD, warned defense installations about potential espionage vulnerabilities involving Chinese BYD-made and Tesla vehicles.
Meanwhile, the US advanced federal legislation to keep foreign always-online vehicles off sensitive military bases.
The National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2027 included provisions banning foreign-linked connected vehicles from entering Defense Department bases starting July 1, 2027.
These measures follow earlier Commerce Department rules phasing out the import and sale of vehicle software and hardware tied to Chinese and Russian firms.
At the same time, China is also among the countries establishing restrictions. In fact, the country set an early precedent in 2021 by banning Tesla vehicles from military facilities and government compounds due to concerns over unauthorized data logging.
Beijing eased some restrictions in 2024 after Tesla complied with China's data standards, but strict bans on foreign software and hardware remain across state organs.
Russia tightened perimeter controls on electronic devices and connected transport at its defense plants.
State agencies and defense firms like Rostec enforced parallel bans on Western technology, such as a ban on Apple hardware for official use due to concerns over espionage.
Similar to the rest of the world, Turkish aerospace and defense campuses also barred foreign EVs due to their numerous sensors and the mapping data they transmit to foreign entities, TEI CEO Mahmut Faruk Aksit said in a recent statement.
The synchronized global crackdown on foreign technology, especially foreign-made EVs, showed how the evolution of civilian EVs turned smart mobility into a frontier of military counterintelligence.

====================================================================================================

Spanish crown returns to Ceuta after 19 years amid lingering migration crisis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
12:18:26 UTC
21:18:26 KST

King Felipe VI visits Ceuta and Melilla today and tomorrow with Queen Letizia, the first royal trip to both cities since 2007, coming two and a half months after a mass influx of migrants into the Spanish autonomous city of Ceuta.
Felipe VI has taken 12 years on the throne to make it to Ceuta, and he is doing so in the same month, intriguingly, as his great-grandfather. The King and Queen Letizia will enter Ceuta's City Hall, in Plaza de África, launching a two-day trip that continues tomorrow in Melilla. It is the first time they have officially set foot in both cities as monarchs.
The last royal visit was by Juan Carlos I and Queen Sofía, in November 2007, after an 80-year gap. This time the backdrop is very different: around 72,000 people crossed over illegally from Morocco to Ceuta on 30 and 31 July, into a city of just over 80,000 residents.
What does Felipe VI's visit to Ceuta and Melilla involve?
In Ceuta, the president of the Autonomous City, Juan Jesús Vivas, will present them with the keys to the city, a gesture also extended to Juan Carlos I and Sofía in 2007. Afterwards they will visit the Vicente Aleixandre school and end at the Muslim cemetery of Sidi Embarek, where an religious ceremony will be held in tribute to those who died trying to swim across the border. Dozens of them are buried there because Morocco refused to take back the bodies.
The big difference compared with 2007 is that the King and Queen will spend the night in Ceuta. Juan Carlos and Sofía did not.
Tomorrow it is Melilla's turn. The royals will arrive at 11:45am CET at the Assembly Palace; in the afternoon they will visit the Pintor Eduardo Morillas school and meet representatives of Melilla's civil society at the Melilla Puerto hotel. The Royal Household has mirrored the schedule in both cities, in order to give them equal weight even though Melilla did not experience anything comparable to Ceuta's influx.
Pedro Sánchez will not travel with them. The prime minister's office, Moncloa, says the premier does not usually accompany the monarchs on their official trips. The minister on duty is likely to be Ángel Víctor Torres, head of Territorial Policy and in charge of the single command for the crisis.
A migration surge still unresolved in Ceuta
According to the Interior Ministry, more than 70,000 people entered Ceuta from Morocco between 30 and 31 July. Sánchez was in the city on the 31st and described it as an attack on Spain's territorial integrity. On 6 August, Felipe VI received Vivas at the Marivent palace, during his holidays in Mallorca, and the Ceuta leader emerged saying the King wanted to travel when the government considered it appropriate. At the end of August, Sánchez announced that the trip would go ahead once the right conditions were in place.
On 29 September, at the gala dinner during France President Emmanuel Macron's state visit, the King called for greater solidarity from European countries and branded the situation in Ceuta "unacceptable".
Since August, 11,026 people have returned to Morocco, according to Torres: 10,513 voluntarily and 513 expelled.
Juan Carlos I in Ceuta and Melilla, November 2007
Juan Carlos I and Queen Sofía visited Ceuta on 5 November, 18 years ago, and Melilla the following day. They spent around five hours in Ceuta, where the King spoke of an "outstanding commitment" to the city. It was the first visit by a monarch in 80 years.
Rabat reacted before the trip even began. It recalled its ambassador in Madrid for consultations and, according to AFP, Mohammed VI viewed the visit as an offence to the patriotic feelings of Moroccans. Hundreds of people protested in Tetouan and at the border, while in Ceuta thousands of residents cheered the King.
Alfonso XIII in Ceuta in October 1927
Alfonso XIII, Felipe VI's great-grandfather, arrived in Ceuta on the morning of 5 October 1927 aboard the battleship Jaime I, accompanied by Queen Victoria Eugenia and General Primo de Rivera, then head of government. At the Puntilla quay he was received by the high commissioner, General Jose Sanjurjo, and Ceuta's commander-in-chief, General Agustin Gómez Morato.
He inspected the troops and visited the Legion barracks in Dar Riffien, already in Protectorate territory, where the Queen presented a standard to the Tercio regiment. In the afternoon he watched a parade, attended a ceremony at Nuestra Señora de África and ended the day with a reception at the Municipal Palace, which the royal couple inaugurated.
The following day they travelled to Tetouan, capital of the Protectorate, and left 1,000 pesetas (around 6 euros at the time, roughly 2,000 euros in today's money) for Ceuta's poor. The King had already visited Melilla in 1904, to lay the foundation stone of the port, and again in 1911 and 1926, according to El Faro de Melilla.
The timing was significant. It had been six years since the disaster of Annual, near Melilla, where thousands of Spanish soldiers were killed, a blow to the monarchy. Alfonso XIII was accused of having encouraged the advance that ended in catastrophe.
Then came Primo de Rivera's coup, which the King backed, and in 1925 the Alhucemas landing, which paved the way for the end of the Rif War.
The Paramount newsreel preserved by the Ministry of Culture shows Spanish and Rifian troops, enemies until recently, marching together before the King. Four years after that trip, on 14 April 1931, his reign came to an end.
Morocco's reaction
Rabat has spent decades claiming sovereignty over the two cities, which have belonged to Spain since the 17th and 15th centuries respectively. So far it has not responded to enquiries about the trip, and successive Moroccan governments avoid mentioning Ceuta and Melilla in their official statements.
Tomorrow, 14 October, a demonstration has been called in Castillejos to protest against the presence of the King and Queen of Spain in Ceuta and Melilla.
On Saturday, in his opening speech to parliament, Mohammed VI insisted that Morocco's sovereignty does not tolerate pressure, threats or blackmail and described relations with Spain as a "sovereign choice", but he did not mention Ceuta at any point.

Sudan’s anti-war coalition calls for immediate humanitarian truce
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
12:17:10 UTC
21:17:10 KST

Sudanese civilian and political groups opposed to the ongoing civil war has called for an immediate, unconditional humanitarian truce and a Sudanese-led peace process after talks Monday with the African Union’s high-level mediation mechanism in Addis Ababa.
The delegation, which included former Prime Minister Abdalla Hamdok, met the Quintet mechanism at the African Union headquarters Monday to discuss efforts to end the conflict and establish a peace process led and owned by Sudanese people.
Participants included U.N. personal envoy Ramtane Lamamra, African Union envoy Mohamed Ibn Chambas, representatives of the Intergovernmental Authority on Development (IGAD), European Union special representative Annette Weber, and observers from Norway and Germany.
In a statement, the groups said an immediate and unconditional humanitarian truce was a priority to protect civilians, ensure aid delivery and pave the way for peace.
Coalition leader Shehab Ibrahim told Sudan Tribune that the delegation presented a framework based on three parallel tracks: a temporary cease-fire, humanitarian assistance and comprehensive political dialogue.
He said the tracks must proceed simultaneously, warning that addressing them separately would complicate efforts to resolve the conflict.
The groups said political dialogue should address the root causes of the crisis and establish the foundations for an inclusive peace and a sustainable democratic civilian transition.
They called for civilian forces to participate in designing and leading the process under fair criteria to prevent any one party from dominating it. The statement also called for the exclusion of the National Congress Party, the Islamic Movement and their affiliated organizations.
Ibrahim said discussions addressed the possible participation of members of the dissolved National Congress Party, which ruled under ousted President Omar al-Bashir.
The coalition outlined its objections to the former ruling party’s inclusion, arguing that dismantling the previous regime’s economic base and safeguarding independent military decision-making remained essential priorities.
The sides agreed to form a joint preparatory committee to set an agenda, determine participants, select venues for future talks and expand engagement with international facilitators.
Discussions also covered future constitutional structures and governance arrangements, which the parties agreed to address in broader political negotiations.
The groups urged regional and international mediators to coordinate their efforts under a unified framework bringing together the Quad, the Quintet and the Troika.
They also called for stronger pressure on the warring parties and those obstructing peace, including extending the arms embargo to cover all of Sudan, halting external support fueling the conflict, cutting off funding for the war and holding those responsible for atrocities accountable.
The statement rejected granting legitimacy to authorities established as a result of the war and stressed the importance of preserving Sudan’s territorial integrity and national unity.
The groups said they would continue engaging with the Quintet, the Quad and other actors seeking a peaceful resolution. They also pledged to broaden support for an independent civilian anti-war movement that does not align with either side.
Their stated goal is to restore Sudanese people’s rights to security, freedom and democratic civilian rule and complete the path of the December Revolution, which led to al-Bashir’s overthrow in April 2019.
Sudan’s war began on April 15, 2023, when fighting erupted between the Sudanese Armed Forces and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces following a power struggle between their leaders. The conflict has displaced millions and triggered a severe humanitarian crisis.

It said the goal was to explore whether "rapid, low-carbon aerial transit" could help local businesses overcome "transport bottlenecks" and speed emergency orders.

Polish retailers remove some Halloween products after school stabbings
WARSAW, Oct 13 - Polish retailers have begun removing some Halloween-themed products such as fake knives from shelves following three recent stabbing attacks at schools, company representatives said on Tuesday.
Thousands of police officers have been deployed to schools since the end of last week after two stabbing incidents involving teenagers on consecutive days.
Politicians have pointed to the negative influence of social media, video games and what Prime Minister Donald Tusk called "a very grim trend of violence".
In response, some major retailers, including Jeronimo Martins' Biedronka, Poland's largest retail chain with about 3,900 stores, said they would scale back their Halloween ranges, removing items such as fake knives and gruesome costumes.
"Guided by concern for the welfare of children and youth, we decided yesterday to withdraw selected Halloween products that may arouse unintended associations," Biedronka category director Małgorzata Polakowska said.
Children's retailer Smyk said it was withdrawing accessories featuring motifs that imitate dangerous tools, such as plastic knives and cleavers, across its store network.
"We believe that in the current circumstances, the presence of such items on the shelves of a store whose offer is directed to families is inappropriate," Smyk said in a statement.
Although Halloween is not a traditional Polish holiday, it is widely celebrated by young people influenced by Western popular culture.
The latest attack occurred on Saturday, when three people were injured at a further education college in Warsaw, Poland's third stabbing attack at an educational institution in four days.
On Thursday, a 15-year-old former pupil wearing a helmet-mounted camera killed a caretaker and injured two other staff members at a primary school in Leszczydol-Nowiny, northeast of Warsaw. On Wednesday, a 19-year-old wounded 10 people including himself at a school in Ostroleka, north of the capital. REUTERS

Rada introduces auctions to attract investment in fisheries, simplifies access to water bodies
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
15:13:06 EEST
21:13:06 KST

The Verkhovna Rada has passed as a whole the law On Stimulating the Economic Development of the Fisheries Industry (draft law No. 12384), aimed at increasing the investment attractiveness of the sector and developing aquaculture and mariculture.
As an Interfax-Ukraine correspondent reports, 275 MPs voted in favor of the decision at a meeting on Tuesday, with the required minimum being 226 votes.
The law establishes the legal framework for attracting investment through transparent auctions for fishery water bodies, internal sea waters, territorial sea, and the exclusive economic zone for the development of aquaculture and mariculture. To use such water areas, the requirement to allocate a land plot of the water fund and mark its boundaries on the ground is eliminated, allowing investors to operate within designated coordinates of the water space.
In addition, the document allows using state- or municipally-owned land plots with an area of up to 0.1 hectares located in coastal protective strips without changing their designated purpose to accommodate necessary equipment and temporary structures.
The law also defines a list of water bodies that cannot be subject to investment attraction: these include objects leased under the Water Code, drinking water intake reservoirs in the first zone of sanitary protection, objects of water users, natural reserve fund sites with prohibited activities, and objects with approved bioresource catch limits (except aquaculture). Such lists will be approved by the specialized authority based on investment proposals from state bodies, local self-government, and business.
A scientific and biological rationale will be developed for each object within the framework of investment attraction, and relations will be formalized through agreements on attracting funds for aquaculture development or fishery operation in specialized commercial fish farms. The document also introduces state control and monitoring over the execution of investment obligations to ensure the rational use of aquatic bioresources.
The document was registered in the Rada on January 8, 2025. It was passed in the first reading on May 13, 2025, after which parliamentarians referred it for a repeat second reading on July 1. The initiators of the document are Head of the Subcommittee on Economic and Financial Policy in the Agro-Industrial Complex of the Rada Committee on Agrarian and Land Policy Artem Chornomorov, Head of the Rada Agrarian Committee Oleksandr Haidu, Head of the Servant of the People David Arakhamia, First Deputy Head of the Servant of the People faction Andriy Motovylovets, and member of the Rada Budget Committee Anatoliy Urbansky (For the Future).

Spanish royals make rare visit to Ceuta after migrant crisis
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
13:12:51 BST
21:12:51 KST

Spanish royals make rare visit to Ceuta after migrant crisis
- Published
King Felipe VI has begun a visit to Ceuta as the Spanish exclave continues to grapple with a migrant crisis triggered by an influx of around 70,000 people from Morocco in July.
It marks the first Spanish royal visit to the city in nearly two decades and comes amid tensions with Morocco, which maintains a longstanding claim to the territory.
The majority of migrants have left since the surge across its border, during which humanitarian organisations estimate at least 141 people died. But thousands have remained, mostly sleeping rough until recently.
The situation has sparked concern locally and criticism of Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez's response ahead of elections next month, with immigration set to be a key issue.
The king and Queen Letizia were greeted by cheering crowds waving Spanish flags as they visited Ceuta's city hall upon their arrival on Tuesday, where they met local officials to hear how the crisis had affected the territory.
The pair said the visit - the first since that taken by King Felipe's father, Juan Carlos I, in 2007 - had been "long awaited and long overdue" in a message in the city's book of honour, broadcaster RTVE reported.
They added they aimed to demonstrate "the commitment of the entire country to the future of the people of Ceuta, which is the future of Spain".
The royal couple will later attend an interfaith ceremony at the Sidi Embarek Muslim cemetery where many of those who died during the summer's crossings were buried.
King Felipe is due to deliver a speech from Ceuta's Parador hotel in the evening, before travelling on Wednesday to Melilla - Spain's other city on the North African coast, which Morocco also claims.
The Spanish government meanwhile said the "historic" visit marked a turning point in the crisis. Asked whether they feared how Morocco might respond, a spokeswoman said it was also "absolutely normal" for the royal family to visit "two Spanish cities".
The king and queen were handed the key to the city by Ceuta's conservative Mayor Juan Jesús Vivas, who said the influx had turned the exclave into "a pressure cooker that could explode at any moment", placing social cohesion, essential services and security at risk.
He had previously described the situation as "the most serious national security crisis of the democratic era" in Spain, and estimated that 15,000 migrants remained in the city.
Central government estimates are much lower, with officials saying 7,400 places were available to house the migrants.
Since the crossing in late July, residents of the 18.5 sq km (7.2 sq miles) territory have expressed concerns about safety and pressure on local infrastructure. Some have destroyed shelters and blocked aid being supplied to the migrants.
The majority of arrivals had been sleeping rough on Ceuta's beaches until the central government erected makeshift shelters last month, as part of its efforts to identify the migrants and determine whether they were eligible to remain in the city.
The crisis thrust Ceuta and immigration to the centre of the national political arena, prompting demonstrations on mainland Spain in support of Ceuta's people and criticism of the Socialist-led government's handling of the situation.
It has also thrown a spotlight on Spain's relationship with Morocco, who many initially blamed for the situation - although Sánchez has maintained there is no proof that Spain's neighbour knowingly allowed or engineered the mass crossing.
Earlier this week, he confirmed a media report that Moroccan military vessels had entered Spanish waters off Ceuta during the crossing, but played down the importance of the incident.
- Shots heard as police start moving migrants from Ceuta beaches 
  - Published18 September
- Spanish intelligence warned of Ceuta mass crossing plans before surge 
  - Published9 September
- Protests in Spain against government's handling of Ceuta migrant crisis 
  - Published2 September
Morocco has meanwhile reiterated its longstanding sovereignty claims to both Ceuta and Melilla amid the crisis.
In August, its Justice Minister Abdellatif Ouahbi spoke of his country's "historical and geographical right" to the exclaves and called for bilateral talks on the issue, which the Spanish government rejected.
The opposition has accused Sánchez of failing to stand up to Rabat. The leader of the conservative People's Party (PP), Alberto Núñez Feijóo, said Sánchez was lying about the causes of the crossing and was guilty of "frivolity" on this issue.
"To Morocco, [we should offer] loyalty and good neighbourliness, but also firmness," he said.

====================================================================================================

What a looming Ethiopia-Eritrea war could mean for Egypt
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
12:11:48 UTC
21:11:48 KST

Breadcrumb
As war looms between Ethiopia and Eritrea, what's at stake for Egypt?
Cairo, Egypt - As fighting in Ethiopia threatens to reignite a full-scale war, Egypt has repeatedly denied accusations that it is backing the rebels.
But Cairo has good geostrategic reasons to watch the crisis closely.
In late September, seven armed groups in northern Ethiopia, several of them former enemies, formed an alliance united by a single aim: to topple the government of Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed.
The alliance has raised fears that the peace deal that ended Ethiopia’s two-year war in 2022 may unravel. That conflict killed an estimated 600,000 people, making it one of the deadliest of the 21st century, and drove tens of thousands from their homes across the country’s borders.
Egypt denies Addis Ababa’s allegations that it is supplying arms to the new alliance. Yet its interest in Ethiopia extends well beyond the latest fighting.
In recent years, Cairo has worked to expand its influence across the Horn of Africa, deepening political, military, and economic ties with Somalia, Eritrea, and Djibouti, while maintaining longstanding relationships with Sudan and South Sudan.
Military-cooperation agreements and mutual-defence pacts have helped cement this presence. Egypt is also preparing to deploy troops to Somalia as part of the African Union’s Support and Stabilisation Mission.
For Cairo, instability in Ethiopia is not simply a neighbouring country’s problem: it is a potential threat to its wider regional interests and national security.
Containing Ethiopia
Egypt’s strategy in the Horn of Africa has centred on strengthening ties with countries surrounding Ethiopia, partly to counter what Cairo perceives as Addis Ababa’s ambitions for regional dominance.
A central source of friction is the Nile, Egypt’s principal source of freshwater. Over the past decade, Ethiopia has built the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam (GERD) on the Blue Nile, giving it greater control over the timing of water flows downstream.
Addis Ababa is also planning at least three further dams that could affect water supplies to Egypt and Sudan.
The Ethiopian government argues that such projects are essential to economic development, electricity generation and lifting tens of millions of people out of poverty.
Egyptian analysts, however, see a broader strategic calculation. They argue that Ethiopia’s growing control over the Nile could give it economic and political leverage over downstream countries.
“My belief is that Ethiopia doesn't need all these dams to economically develop or generate electricity for its people,” Egyptian water resources expert Nader Nour-Eddin told The New Arab.
The GERD stalemate
Egypt is totally dependent on the Nile for the needs of its population of 120 million, as well as its agricultural and industrial activities.
The fallout from the GERD has forced Cairo into an expensive adaptation strategy that has so far cost it billions of dollars, including through the construction of a series of seawater desalination plants and others for sewage treatment.
Egyptian President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi has repeatedly described the Nile as an "existential issue" for his country.
Earlier this month, he described the Nile as his country's "lifeline" and said that Egypt would continue to defend its Nile water rights through all measures enshrined in international law.
The stalemate over the GERD, following a decade of failed negotiations between the Egyptians and the Ethiopians, is also part of an evolving struggle between the two sides over the Red Sea.
Landlocked Ethiopia's Red Sea quest is causing concern in Egypt, where it is viewed as part of Ethiopia's desire to control a crucial maritime chokepoint that leads up to an indispensable economic artery for the Egyptians, namely the Suez Canal.
Ethiopia says that Red Sea access is indispensable for its economic development and trade with the outside world.
The risk of a regional war
A war between Ethiopia and Eritrea might have seemed unlikely only a few months ago. Now, however, the two countries are edging towards confrontation, raising questions about how Egypt might respond.
Tensions between the two countries have been piling up for several months, especially as Ethiopia has escalated its rhetoric on access to the Red Sea, with the Eritrean Port of Assab at the centre of its plans.
Ethiopia talks about this port within the context of its historical right to ownership, with Ethiopian officials and commentators framing Eritrea's 1993 independence from Ethiopia and Ethiopia's loss of sea access as a "conspiracy".
Ethiopian political analyst Jemal Beshir Ahmed said the loss of his country's coastline in 1993 was the result of political decisions, the Eritrean armed struggle, and external geopolitical involvement that left Ethiopia landlocked.
"This is an Ethiopian political interpretation, rather than an undisputed historical fact," he told The New Arab.
Ethiopia views Assab as the "most natural option", he added, given its proximity to the Ethiopian border, its existing infrastructure, and its long history as an important outlet for Ethiopian trade.
The civil war raging in northern Ethiopia is now drawing in multiple outside parties, opening the door for them to settle old scores, achieve geostrategic gains, or vanquish their rivals.
Eritrea, reportedly supporting the Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF), has deployed troops in northern Ethiopia, in what is seen as an attempt by Asmara to create a buffer against Ethiopian National Defense Force (ENDF) advances towards the Eritrean border and consequently into Assab, which is located only a few kilometres away from the Ethiopian border.
It probably views the war as a good chance to create an advance base in this area to prevent – or at least slow down – any attempt by the ENDF to march towards the joint border.
Ethiopia may use the same deployment of Eritrean troops as an excuse to move its forces into the neighbouring country and recapture Assab, thus killing two birds with one stone: regain a territory historically believed to be its own and settle old scores with Eritrean President Isaias Afwerki, a figure loathed by many in Addis Ababa.
In any war between Eritrea and Ethiopia, Egypt may exploit an opportunity to kill Addis Ababa's regional ambitions and undermine the Horn of Africa state for many years to come, preventing it from becoming the potential Red Sea threat or Nile Basin hegemon that Cairo fears.
It can do this by offering support to the Eritrean army in its expected showdown with the ENDF.
Those closely following these serious developments believe a war erupting in the Horn of Africa would become a magnet for all types of external forces.
Independent Eritrean Horn of Africa specialist Azeez Hagos said a war between the two countries would be difficult to contain as a purely bilateral conflict.
"This war would erupt in an already interconnected regional environment," he told The New Arab.
Northern Ethiopia is unstable, Sudan is emerging from a devastating war, in which Addis Ababa has faced accusations of supporting the Rapid Support Forces (RSF), and tensions involving Egypt, Somalia, and the Red Sea are already overlapping.
"If the balance in Sudan continues to shift, some of that political and security pressure could also rebound towards Ethiopia," Hagos said.
He noted that the danger becomes even greater if the conflict reaches southern Eritrea or Assab.
At that point, he said, it would no longer be only a land war between two neighbouring states.
"It would directly involve Red Sea security, ports, maritime routes and the interests of littoral states and other regional powers," Hagos said. "I would not see such a war as simply another Eritrean-Ethiopian confrontation."
A quadrilateral Egyptian-Eritrean-Somali-Sudanese summit in the Egyptian Mediterranean city of Alamein earlier this month offered insights into the anti-Ethiopia alliance forming on the margins of the Ethiopian civil war.
Calls for support for Addis Ababa are also pouring in, including from Israel, whose foreign minister in early October expressed backing for Ethiopia's unity and stability.
A war with Eritrea would complicate Ethiopia's situation, forcing it to fight a foreign enemy, while at the same time battling a host of internal adversaries.
The growing involvement of outside powers, alongside the flow of weapons to competing parties, illustrates how the conflict could become a proxy battleground in a wider struggle over maritime chokepoints and the distribution of political and military influence across the Horn of Africa.
Unless diplomacy prevails, the confrontation risks developing into a prolonged war of attrition, destabilising both the Horn of Africa and the Red Sea region as rival powers compete to shape their future.
Saleh Salem is an Egyptian journalist
Edited by Charlie Hoyle
