Hamas praised the awarding of the 2026 Nobel Peace Prize to South African jurist Navi Pillay in a statement issued on Friday, citing her role in advancing accusations of genocide against Israel and calling for international legal action against Israeli officials.
The terrorist organization welcomed the Norwegian Nobel Committee's decision to honor Pillay, a former UN high commissioner for human rights who chaired a commission of inquiry that concluded Israel had committed genocide in the Gaza Strip.
In its statement, Hamas described the award as "an important step toward international justice," praising Pillay's involvement in investigating Israel's military operations in Gaza and calling for further international legal action against Israeli officials.
The statement followed the announcement of Pillay as the 2026 Nobel Peace Prize laureate, a decision that prompted sharp criticism from Israel's political leadership.
Hamas said the award represented international recognition of what it described as crimes committed by Israel against Palestinians, pointing specifically to the September 2025 findings of the UN Independent International Commission of Inquiry chaired by Pillay.
The commission's report concluded that Israel had committed genocide in Gaza, an allegation rejected by Israel, which has maintained that its military operations targeted Hamas following the terrorist organization's October 7, 2023, massacre.
"The findings of the Independent International Commission of Inquiry, which was chaired by Pillay, concerning the crimes committed in the Gaza Strip, as well as the conclusion of its report issued in September 2025 that the crime of genocide had been committed, underscore the gravity of what our people have endured," Hamas said.
The terrorist organization called on the international community to pursue Israeli officials through international courts, demanding an end to what it characterized as impunity for alleged war crimes.
UN inquiry into Gaza genocide allegations
The controversy surrounding Pillay stems in part from a September 2025 UN commission report, which determined that Israel had committed four of the five acts of genocide defined by the 1948 Genocide Convention. The commission alleged that Israeli actions demonstrated an intent to destroy Palestinians in Gaza.
The commission, established in 2021, was tasked with investigating alleged violations of international law in Israel and the Palestinian territories. Pillay chaired the panel alongside commissioners Chris Sidoti and Miloon Kothari.
Israel rejected the findings, accusing the commission of relying on inaccurate information and failing to adequately account for Hamas's conduct during the war. The Foreign Ministry denounced the report as fabricated and accused its authors of acting as proxies for Hamas.
The war began when Hamas-led terrorists invaded southern Israel on October 7, 2023, killing approximately 1,200 people and abducting more than 250 others into Gaza. The massacre triggered Israel's military campaign against the terrorist organization.
Pillay, who previously served as president of the International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda and as a judge at the International Criminal Court, was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize for her broader career advancing international law and accountability for international crimes.
The Norwegian Nobel Committee said its decision recognized her efforts to promote peace and international legal principles, rather than specifically endorsing the conclusions of her Gaza investigation.
Hamas, however, placed the commission's allegations against Israel at the center of its response, using the Nobel announcement to renew its demands for international legal proceedings against Israeli officials.
In its statement, the terrorist organization also praised Pillay's earlier work defending anti-apartheid activists in South Africa and her service on international tribunals, presenting those roles alongside her involvement in the Gaza inquiry.
Herzog condemns Nobel decision as 'moral erosion'
President Isaac Herzog sharply criticized the awarding of the Nobel Peace Prize to Pillay during a ceremony honoring Israel Bonds on Monday, describing the decision as an "affront to any life-affirming, peace-loving people."
According to remarks covered on Tuesday, Herzog condemned the Nobel Committee for recognizing Pillay, whom he accused of advancing false allegations against Israel.
"Awarding the Nobel Peace Prize to one of the leading proponents of the genocide lie is a cynical decision which celebrates a shameful display of moral erosion," Herzog said.
His remarks came amid broader criticism from Israeli officials, including Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who accused Pillay of spreading false accusations against the Jewish state.
"The Nobel Prize committee has lost its moral compass," the Prime Minister's Office said in response to the announcement.
"It has awarded its highest honor to a bigot who built her career around inventing and propagating blood libels against the only Jewish state."
The contrasting responses highlighted the dispute surrounding Pillay's work, with Hamas explicitly endorsing the UN investigation's findings while Israeli leaders rejected both the report's conclusions and the Nobel Committee's decision to recognize its former chairwoman.
Hamas concluded its statement by renewing its call for international action against Israeli officials accused of crimes in Gaza.

How protests have shaped India: From anti-Hindi agitation to farm laws
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
11:57:51 UTC
20:57:51 KST

How protests have shaped India: From anti-Hindi agitation to farm laws
Activists challenging India’s government over electoral roll controversies have a long legacy of protest to draw on.
New Delhi, India – Central parts of the Indian capital have been flooded in recent days with thousands of armed personnel, chasing down young protesters demanding the resignation of the country’s chief election commissioner (CEC) and struggling to secure a place to stage a sit-in in New Delhi.
Since last week, several student organisations and a wide spectrum of opposition parties have been engaged in a tactical tug-of-war, with tens of thousands turning up on Monday, far outnumbering police personnel.
Protesters are demanding sweeping reforms and the resignation of CEC Gyanesh Kumar after revelations of election irregularities. The agitation marks the latest challenge to Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s grip on power, after his education minister was forced out by the same group of demonstrators less than three months ago.
The Modi government has tried to portray protesters as representing antinational interests, working to slow down India’s growth or even to enable its breakup.
But India, the world’s most populous country, has had a long history of street protests, from its freedom struggle against the British Empire to waves of movements during the 79 years of the Indian republic that have shaped its modern identity.
“Time and again the government [of the day] has opposed these protests, [and] at times engaged with them critically,” Rasheed Kidwai, a political analyst in New Delhi and former journalist, told Al Jazeera. “But protests have run centrally through India’s story all along.”
Here is a look at major street protests in India and how they often forced powerful governments and leaders to yield.
Anti-Hindi agitations (1965)
India’s newly-formed constitution envisaged Hindi replacing English as the central government’s official language after a 15-year transition, ending on January 26, 1965. Many people in southern India, particularly Tamil speakers in the then Madras state (now Tamil Nadu), feared that this would sideline them in government employment, civil service examinations and dealings with the central administration.
For the federal government of a vast and diverse country, the idea of one common official language of communication was attractive as a tool of unification. But for many of the ancient societies that had agreed to come together under the Indian Union, this led to fears of cultural domination by the Hindi-speaking north of the country.
Demonstrations by several student organisations, opposing the imposition of Hindi, broke out, often leading to clashes with the police.
The Dravida Munnetra Kazhagam (DMK), a regional political party advocating Tamil nationalism, led by CN Annadurai and M Karunanidhi, spearheaded the protests. In January 1965, Annadurai was arrested on the eve of an anti-Hindi agitation. Two young supporters immolated themselves, and Hindi books were burned.
Then-Prime Minister Lal Bahadur Shastri assured protesters that English would continue to be used alongside Hindi. The DMK won Tamil Nadu’s state election in 1967, ending the until-then dominant Congress party’s rule in the state.
It was one of the defining moments of Indian federalism and regional identity in a young nation. English has remained one of India’s two official languages — and the Congress party has never returned to power in Tamil Nadu on its own.
The JP Movement (mid-1970s)
The JP Movement — named after its socialist leader, Jayaprakash Narayan — began amid student protests against corruption, inflation and government mismanagement in the states of Gujarat and Bihar in 1973-74.
Soon, it evolved into a nationwide challenge to then-Prime Minister Indira Gandhi and her Congress government’s dominance over Indian politics. Students, civil society groups, trade unions and opposition parties subsequently joined the agitation.
Narayan famously called for “Sampoorn Kranti”, or “Total Revolution”, a slogan that still rings in India.
The movement set the stage for a national emergency, declared by Gandhi on June 25, 1975, suspending civil liberties and censoring the press. After the emergency ended, opposition parties united and defeated Congress in the 1977 general election, ending Gandhi’s uninterrupted reign and giving India its first non-Congress government.
The Total Revolution did not come to pass, as Narayan had envisioned, but the movement fundamentally altered opposition politics — showing no leader was beyond the electoral consequences of mass dissent. Many of the leaders who emerged from this movement went on to become state chief ministers and leading federal ministers.
Mandal Commission protests (early 1990s)
In August 1990, then-Prime Minister Vishwanath Pratap Singh announced that his government would implement recommendations of a panel that had been set up more than a decade earlier under a member of parliament, Bindeshwari Prasad Mandal. The Mandal Commission, as it was known, recommended that 27 percent of central government jobs be reserved for people from Other Backward Classes (OBCs), communities identified as socially and educationally disadvantaged.
The decision triggered nationwide protests against reservation by students of privileged castes, who feared losing out on their dominance over government jobs. At the time, OBCs only held a little over 12 percent of government jobs — though they represented 52 percent of the national population.
Supporters of reservations argued that concrete actions were needed to address entrenched caste discrimination and unequal access to opportunities.
More than 100 students tried to die by suicide by setting themselves alight, and more than 60 succeeded, during those protests.
In 1992, the Supreme Court upheld the 27 percent OBC reservation in central government employment, excluding the relatively financially better-off “creamy layer” within communities. The move marked one of the largest affirmative action initiatives in independent India.
Protests against liberalisation, globalisation (early 1990s)
Rather than a unified campaign, the protests arose from a series of labour protests and strikes against India’s economic reforms, launched in 1991 under then-Prime Minister PV Narasimha Rao and Finance Minister Manmohan Singh, who would go on to become prime minister in 2004.
The reforms reduced restrictions on private enterprise and opened more sectors to foreign investment. Trade unions feared that privatisation and easier business closures would cause job losses, weaken collective bargaining and erode workers’ protections.
Left-aligned political parties supported many of these protests. But the protests could not prevent the reform programme from proceeding.
Successive governments have continued to expand private sector participation, pursue disinvestment in state-owned enterprises, and modify labour regulations.
Anna Hazare’s anticorruption movement (2011)
The movement erupted amid public anger over major corruption scandals involving the Congress-led coalition government, including a controversy around licensing of the country’s 2G spectrum and allegations surrounding preparations for the 2010 Commonwealth Games, held in New Delhi.
Activists demanded a strong law with an independent anticorruption ombudsman empowered to investigate and punish corruption involving public officials.
Social activist Anna Hazare led the movement through hunger strikes, also featuring activists such as Arvind Kejriwal, Kiran Bedi and Prashant Bhushan. Its demonstrations attracted large crowds across the country.
Parliament passed a law in December 2013, establishing a statutory framework for an anticorruption watchdog. But more than a decade later, its impact is minimal.
The movement was divided over whether activists should enter electoral politics. Kejriwal broke away to establish the Aam Aadmi Party (AAP) in 2012 and went on to become a two-time chief minister of Delhi state.
The legacy of the movement remains largely in the shadow of Kejriwal today, who is now in opposition after Modi’s Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) won the Delhi state election last year.
Protests following the ‘Nirbhaya’ gang rape (2012)
On December 16, 2012, a 23-year-old paramedical student was gang-raped and brutally assaulted on a moving bus in New Delhi. She died on December 29 while receiving treatment. Victims of sexual assault cannot be named publicly under Indian law. So she was widely referred to as “Nirbhaya”, meaning fearless in Hindi.
The crime triggered mass demonstrations against sexual violence, unsafe public spaces, inadequate policing and the treatment of women in the country. Protesters demanded justice for the victim and fundamental changes to how authorities handled sexual assault cases.
Students, young people, women’s rights activists, and common residents mobilised in Delhi, including around India Gate and other key locations.
Four adult defendants were convicted and sentenced to death; their executions took place in 2020.
Parliament passed the Criminal Law (Amendment) Act, 2013, broadening the legal recognition of sexual offences, criminalising offences including stalking and voyeurism, and strengthening penalties for several crimes.
Activists continue to argue that stronger laws alone cannot address entrenched misogyny and inadequate policing. And crimes against women, including sexual crimes, remain rampant across most parts of India, including the capital.
Anti-CAA protests (2019-20)
India’s Citizenship Amendment Act (CAA), passed in December 2019, offers an expedited path to Indian citizenship for Hindu, Sikh, Buddhist, Jain, Parsi and Christian migrants from Afghanistan, Bangladesh and Pakistan who arrived before December 31, 2014. Muslims were excluded from this provision.
Critics argued that making religious identity a basis for preferential citizenship undermined India’s secular constitutional principles. Millions feared the law could work alongside a proposed National Register of Citizens (NRC) to place Muslims at greater risk of exclusion and possible expulsion from India.
The movement was decentralised. Students at Jamia Millia Islamia and Aligarh Muslim University led major demonstrations, while women-led sit-ins, especially at Shaheen Bagh in Delhi, became national symbols of resistance against Prime Minister Modi’s Hindu majoritarian politics.
In February 2020, large-scale mob violence primarily targeting Muslims broke out in northeastern Delhi. More than 50 people, mostly Muslims, were killed.
Meanwhile, the sit-in in Shaheen Bagh lasted 101 days before police cleared the site on March 24, 2020, soon after imposing the COVID-19 lockdown. Dozens of Muslim activists were arrested and charged under antiterrorism laws. Student leaders such as Umar Khalid and Sharjeel Imam remain in jail, six years on, with no trial.
The protests could not secure repeal of the law, but delayed its implementation. The government notified its implementation in March 2024, bringing the citizenship process into operation.
Farmers’ protests (2020-21)
In 2020, the Modi government introduced three agricultural laws intended to liberalise farm markets and facilitate direct sales to private buyers.
Many farmers, particularly in northern India, feared that the changes would weaken the government-regulated wholesale markets through which much of their produce was sold. They also worried that the reforms would undermine the minimum support price (MSP), a government-set price for certain crops.
Numerous farmer unions surrounded and shut down roads leading up to Delhi under the Samyukt Kisan Morcha, a coalition formed to coordinate the agitation. Thousands of farmers camped on Delhi’s outskirts for months.
More than 700 farmers died amid extreme weather, road accidents, suicides and clashes.
In November 2021, Modi announced that the government would repeal the laws.
It marked the first such moment when protesters had wrestled a significant concession from Modi, who built his political currency as a leader who does not compromise.
‘Cockroach’ protests (2026)
It was a dig at India’s Chief Justice Surya Kant’s remarks, equating the country’s unemployed youth with “cockroaches” and “parasites”, sparking fury in the backdrop of a decade of sliding in multiple democratic indices.
Student Abhijeet Dipke doubled down on the viral joke, creating a pressure group – the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) – and led protests against irregularities in the national medical school entrance examination. The newbie protesters of the CJP movement were held together by left student organisations, choking Parliament Street and the popular protest site Jantar Mantar in New Delhi.
The Gen Z protests eventually forced out the education minister, Dharmendra Pradhan, in July 2026.
The CJP protesters have again come together, along with opposition parties, this time demanding CEC Kumar’s resignation.

TASS has compiled the key statements by the Kremlin spokesman.
On Putin’s schedule
- Russian President Vladimir Putin will meet with Transport Minister Andrey Nikitin at the Kremlin today.
- The Russian leader will also have an international telephone conversation.
On US-Europe joint "peace plan"
- The Kremlin has seen a report in The Washington Post about the United States and Europe moving toward a joint peace proposal on Ukraine but has received no information about it: "We have seen media reports but we have heard nothing about it."
On the possibility of an "energy ceasefire"
- Moscow continues contacts on a possible "energy ceasefire," but there have been no new developments since yesterday: "We discussed this issue yesterday, and for now I have nothing to add to what we said then. Contacts on this matter are continuing."
On the Russia-US diesel deal
- There is no connection between the diesel agreement with the United States and Russia’s position on Ukraine; rather, it is a mutually beneficial example of Russian-US cooperation: "I don’t see any connection here. - European Union sanctions and other unilateral actions could hamper the implementation of the fuel deal between Russia and the United States: "That it could interfere is beyond doubt."
- European cynicism is a subject of widespread discussion in international media: "The issue of European cynicism, as [US Treasury Secretary Scott] Bessent put it, is being widely discussed in global media."
- European countries themselves remain major purchasers of Russian crude oil and petroleum products: "The fact is that European countries, just like all other nations, are heavy buyers of Russian oil and Russian petroleum products."
- Diesel fuel supply agreements serve the interests of Russia, the United States and global energy markets: "This corresponds to interests of the United States, this corresponds to interests of international energy markets, and is in line with interests of the Russian Federation, and so it takes place."
- Russia is selling and will continue to sell energy resources, its competitive commodity, on international markets: "Russia in this aspect is a country presenting its competitive commodity to global markets. We will continue doing that."
On intelligence sharing with Ukraine
- The Kremlin is not aware of US President Donald Trump’s alleged plans to suspend intelligence sharing with Kiev or disable the Starlink internet service in Ukraine if Kiev continues strikes on Russian refineries: "We know nothing about it."
On a possible Putin-Zelensky meeting
- Moscow’s position regarding a potential meeting between Russian President Vladimir Putin and Ukraine’s Vladimir Zelensky or the need for Ukraine to hold an election is well known and unchanged: "Yesterday, we repeatedly talked about it and I have nothing to add. No changes here. Our position on all these issues is very well known."
On the Yandex situation
- It is too early to discuss a compensation mechanism for financial losses that users of Yandex services may have incurred following Ukrainian attacks on the company: "It is premature to talk about financial losses at this point. You know that the company is strong and powerful. Yes, it is facing difficulties now. Of course, this issue is currently being discussed in the government, but the company is taking emergency measures to deal with the aftermath of this attack."

Indigenous women challenge Islamist oppression, call for cross-community solidarity
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
11:57:35 UTC
20:57:35 KST

The same radical Islamist forces behind the October 7 attacks, in which more than 1,200 people were killed, are also responsible for attacks on the Druze in Syria and the mass murder and oppression of Iranians and Hindus in India and Kashmir, according to six women from Indigenous communities. They spoke at the panel, Asia & the Middle East: Conversations Across Communities, hosted by Indigenous Bridges on Monday night.
Hindu activist and regional analyst Kavya K, known online as “Kavya Speaks”; Israeli Druze activist Rania Dean; Kurdish speaker and educator Schilan Kurdpoor; Iranian human rights activist Honey Montzemi; and Native American and Jewish Indigenous rights activist Lani Anpo shared their experiences of oppression and silencing by Islamist forces with Ateret Shmuel, the Jewish director of Indigenous Bridges.
Despite hailing from different countries, including Iran, the United States, Israel, and India, the women said they shared experiences of gender-based violence, genocide, forced assimilation, silencing, and intimidation.
Each said she had been accused of Islamophobia and subjected to death threats or doxxing for speaking about her community’s experiences.
They also emphasized the need to build alliances among Indigenous communities to overcome their minority status and more effectively confront what they described as the oppressive forces of political Islam.
Both Kurdpoor and Kavya said radical Islamist forces often target women first because attacks on women also threaten families and the transmission of cultural traditions between generations.
Kavya argued that the targeting of women had led Hindu communities to adopt new gender-based restrictions, keeping women out of public life for their own protection. She contrasted these restrictions with what she described as the historically prominent role of women in Hindu communities.
As an example of women’s power and status in Hindu religious tradition, she cited the Hindu goddess Kali, who defeated the demon Mahishasura when the male gods could not.
Shmuel noted how it was the Kurds who were able to weaponize the misogynistic beliefs of Islamic State against the group. The ISIS fighters believed that being killed by a female combatant would prevent them from entering paradise and receiving the rewards promised to martyrs, including the 72 virgins described in popular accounts of the group’s ideology.
Aware of this, Kurdish fighters in Rojava established the Women’s Protection Units (YPJ), an all-female Kurdish military force operating in northern Syria. Kurdpoor recounted how the women used battle cries to signal their presence, sometimes prompting ISIS fighters to flee. She also described the role of women in the broader Kurdish-led military effort and their acceptance within the Syrian Democratic Forces (SDF).
Kurdpoor discussed the role of ethnic cleansing and the restrictions on indigenous languages. She argued that restricting a community’s language creates a disconnect between individuals and their cultural heritage, citing restrictions in Turkey and limits on Kurdish-language education in Iran. She also highlighted the continuing struggle to learn and preserve the language in Syria, describing it as central to the Kurdish community’s cultural survival.
Dean said that the Druze had historically spoken Aramaic before adopting Arabic, which she described as part of a broader effort to blend in with the surrounding occupying Arab population and protect Druze communities. She noted that the community’s historical efforts to assimilate had failed to ensure its safety, pointing to the July 2025 massacres in Sweida, continued attacks on Druze communities, and the ongoing siege of villages in southern Syria as evidence that conformity had not provided protection.
Dean also welcomed the growing use of Bashan, the biblical name for Sweida and the surrounding area, as it signaled that her community was moving away from what she described as failed attempts to secure peace with its occupiers through assimilation into their society. She condemned the labeling of Druze calling for freedom and self-determination as “separatists,” a term several speakers said had been used to discredit or suppress calls for freedom by Indigenous communities in the region.
Beyond their shared experiences of oppression and Islamist colonial occupation, the speakers also expressed concern about what they saw as a growing trend of Western women supporting regimes that would strip them of the rights and freedoms they currently enjoy.
Secular leftists paved way for Iran’s 1979 Islamic Revolution
Montazemi noted that secular leftists had helped pave the way for Iran’s 1979 Islamic Revolution, only to pay for it with their lives in the years that followed. She expressed concern at seeing women on social media proudly displaying the Islamic Republic’s symbols while wearing tank tops, clothing that would result in their arrest in Iran.
She pointed to Western women who had traveled to Syria to marry ISIS members, arguing that they had surrendered their rights in the process. Montazemi said more needed to be done to understand the appeal these groups held for women.
Explaining the importance of the event to The Jerusalem Post, Shmuel said, “Indigenous nations across Asia, the Middle East, and Africa face the same violent colonialism, yet our stories are routinely spun for Western audiences to portray Islamists as the victims and Indigenous communities as the cause of the conflict. We see this in Western reporting on attacks against Druze, Hindu, Kurdish, Persian, Jewish, Yezidi, Bahá’í, and other Indigenous communities.
Also, there is a sinister reason for this narrative: to manipulate the Western public into sympathizing with Islamist jihadi groups, paving the way for their expansion into the West,” she said.
Shmuel indicated her hope that the panels would provide a greater understanding to the global community of communities too often silenced and an understanding that “the safety and sovereignty of Indigenous communities across Asia, the Middle East, and Africa are deeply intertwined.”
The panel was the first in a series of events addressing the issue of Indigenous solidarity to be hosted by Indigenous Bridges. For more information, visit: https://indigenousbridges.com/

Barrett to build Northrop’s 25mm smart grenade launcher
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
11:57:26 UTC
20:57:26 KST

- Northrop Grumman and Barrett Firearms signed a teaming agreement under which Barrett will build the 25 mm Precision Grenadier System launcher in Nashville.
- Barrett will also integrate the inductive setter that programs Northrop Grumman’s 25 mm airburst and proximity rounds.
Northrop Grumman has teamed up with Barrett Firearms to build the launcher for its Precision Grenadier System, a shoulder-fired 25 mm grenade launcher meant to let infantry squads hit enemies hiding behind cover and shoot down small drones, the companies announced on Oct. 12 at the Association of the U.S. Army’s annual meeting in Washington.
Under the agreement, Barrett will manufacture the weapon at its plant in Nashville, Tennessee, and integrate the inductive setter, the device that programs each round with the distance at which it should detonate before it leaves the barrel. Northrop Grumman will continue to lead development of the overall system and of its family of 25 mm ammunition, and says it is offering the weapon to both U.S. and international customers. The companies say pairing Northrop Grumman’s ammunition and military programs experience with Barrett’s commercial and military firearms production will let them move quickly from prototype to delivery for U.S. and allied forces.
The Precision Grenadier System is designed to give an infantry squad a precise way to reach targets in defilade, meaning enemy soldiers sheltering behind walls, trenches or terrain that direct rifle fire cannot hit, as well as to fight at close quarters and engage small drones. Northrop Grumman’s 25 mm ammunition family includes a high-explosive airburst round that detonates above or beside a target at a programmed distance, a proximity round that senses a nearby drone and explodes without needing to be programmed, a close-quarters battle round, and a training round ballistically matched to the combat rounds. The weapon feeds from detachable box magazines.
The design builds on Northrop Grumman’s experience with the XM25, a 25 mm airburst weapon the company inherited through its 2018 purchase of Orbital ATK, which U.S. Army units tested in combat in Afghanistan before the program ended in 2018. The U.S. Army launched its Precision Grenadier System effort to replace the M203 and M320 40 mm grenade launchers carried by infantry squads today with a semi-automatic, magazine-fed weapon that combines the launcher, smart ammunition and a digital fire-control sight.
Several teams are working on solutions for the U.S. Army requirement in calibers from 25 mm to 40 mm. Barrett and MARS Inc. won the Army’s xTech Soldier Lethality competition in May 2025 with a 30 mm grenade rifle, and FN America has continued testing its MTL-30 launcher under a separate Army prototype award. Northrop Grumman earlier developed its 25 mm launcher with Colt before selecting Barrett to manufacture the weapon.
The U.S. Army plans to turn the Precision Grenadier System into a formal acquisition program and award a prototype agreement, and Northrop Grumman says it is continuing prototyping and ammunition development with Barrett to meet that requirement and interest from international buyers.

High Court challenges law excluding women from Israel's Chief Rabbinate elections
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
11:57:24 UTC
20:57:24 KST

The High Court of Justice last month made a small but consequential decision that has the potential to affect how chief rabbis and members of the Chief Rabbinate Council are chosen in the State of Israel.
The court issued a conditional order requiring the respondents to explain why legislation passed in December 2024 should not be interpreted as requiring the chief rabbis to appoint both men and women as representatives in the electoral assembly – or why the provision restricting eligibility for those appointments should not be struck down.
The petition was filed on December 19, 2024, ahead of elections to the Chief Rabbinate Council. Submitted by six women with advanced religious education, Bar-Ilan University’s Rackman Center, and Na’amat, it argues that the amendment passed earlier that month effectively prevented women from being appointed to the electoral assembly’s rabbinic contingent.
The case concerns the body that chooses the chief rabbis and the council’s elected members rather than membership in the council itself.
Why doesn't the Chief Rabbinate ordain women?
Under the Chief Rabbinate Law, the electoral assembly comprises 150 members: 80 rabbinic representatives and 70 public representatives. Most seats are linked to specified offices, such as rabbinic posts, local government leadership, and religious councils. Ten of the rabbinic representatives are appointed by the chief rabbis, in consultation with the religious services minister and with government approval.
Those 10 appointments are at the center of the dispute.
In an earlier Rackman Center case, the court ruled on January 14, 2024, that the chief rabbis must consider appointing women with suitable education in Torah and Halacha (Jewish law) to those seats. Justices Dafna Barak-Erez and Isaac Amit formed the majority, against Justice David Mintz’s dissent.
The ruling did not require the appointment of particular women or their ordination as rabbis. It rather held that, for this electoral role, the statutory term “rabbis” was not confined to people formally ordained by the Chief Rabbinate.
On May 19, 2024, however, the Chief Rabbinate Council adopted a decision saying that women could not be appointed as rabbis and that even considering such appointments was forbidden under its interpretation of Jewish law. The decision, cited in the petition and reproduced in the state’s response, argued that considering a woman would itself recognize the possibility of her holding a rabbinic role.
The Knesset subsequently passed Amendment No. 8 to the Chief Rabbinate Law on December 4, 2024. It defined a “rabbi” eligible for one of the 10 appointments as someone ordained by the Chief Rabbinate after passing its required written examinations or holding a certificate of eligibility for specified rabbinic posts.
Because the Chief Rabbinate does not ordain women, the petitioners argue, the new definition closed the route the court had recognized.
A separate ruling has since changed women’s access to the rabbinate’s examinations. On July 14, 2025, a unanimous panel, in a judgment written by Supreme Court Deputy President Noam Sohlberg, ruled that the Chief Rabbinate could not bar women from taking its exams.
The court explained that the examinations serve purposes beyond qualifying candidates for rabbinic office: Recognition of religious learning can also carry employment and salary benefits. Denying women access was therefore unlawful discrimination. That ruling did not, however, settle their eligibility for the electoral appointments challenged in this case.
At a High Court hearing last month, September 14, the petitioners’ lawyers emphasized that distinction: Passing examinations would not by itself satisfy a law requiring ordination. They argued that women’s expertise in Jewish law was being excluded from the assembly’s rabbinic representation because of their sex.
The state’s response argued that the amendment must be considered as a whole. Alongside the disputed qualification requirement, it introduced a minimum of 31 women among the assembly’s public representatives.
The state maintained that reserving the 10 appointments for rabbis recognized by the Chief Rabbinate served a legitimate purpose and that the broader increase in women’s representation supported the amendment’s constitutionality. The Knesset joined that position. The petitioners argued that additional public-representative seats did not remedy the exclusion of women as religious scholars.
Gov't argues petition would suspend statutory election arrangements
The government also argued that the petitioners’ request to halt the council elections pending a judgment would effectively suspend the statutory election arrangements.
Justice Gila Canfy-Steinitz rejected that interim request on December 31, 2024, citing the caution required before suspending legislation ahead of a ruling on its merits.
The September conditional order leaves the substantive challenge open. The respondents must submit their formal answers by December 15.

Does Saudi Arabia have any good options to deal with the Houthis? - analysis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
11:57:17 UTC
20:57:17 KST

The deadly Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia over the last week have put pressure on Riyadh to respond.
Saudi Arabia has carried out airstrikes on the Houthis in support of the Yemeni government forces over the past month. However, Riyadh has appeared reticent to respond in a massive way to the Houthi attacks. Rumors are swirling in the region about what might come next. Analysts tend to portray the Saudis as facing an uphill struggle with the Houthis.
Does Saudi Arabia really have no good options? Various recent reports have discussed different aspects of what Riyadh may be weighing in terms of what comes next.
For instance, there is the question of the US supporting Saudi Arabia. The US and many countries have condemned the attacks. However, US President Donald Trump has left media guessing as to whether the US will do more. The US appears to be supporting Saudi Arabia in terms of intelligence and targeting, according to the BBC.
The Houthis have threatened a "swift and painful" response if the US does intervene. "If the US becomes involved in the aggression against Yemen, we will not deliberate over the decision to respond; rather, there will be a swift and painful response targeting the US and all its interests in the region," Houthi political bureau member Mohammed Al Bukhaiti told the AFP.
All of this must weigh on US-Saudi coordination. There are questions about how a widening war in Yemen could also lead Iran to operationalize militias in Iraq.
Who should Saudi Arabia ally with to minimize spread of war in the Middle East?
Saudi Arabia has seen this before. It intervened in Yemen in 2015 to back the Yemeni government against the Houthis. The Houthis widened the war with ballistic missile and drone attacks on Saudi Arabia. In 2019, Iran directly attacked Saudi Arabia. Militias in Iraq also targeted Saudi Arabia. Therefore, Riyadh knows exactly what is at stake.
Meanwhile, there are questions about whether tensions in Yemen could lead to renewed fighting with Iran. Reports indicate that Israel could be involved in strikes on Iran again, or even on the Houthis.
There is intense interest in this among Saudi Arabia’s allies in Turkey and Pakistan. Those countries joined an alliance with Saudi Arabia over the last few months.
However, Turkey would likely not want to be on the same side as Israel fighting alongside Saudi Arabia. Anadolu media in Ankara noted that Riyadh had so far rejected Israel’s “bid to join fight.” It is not entirely clear if Israel wants to get deeply involved again in Yemen.
Israel already carried out strikes on Yemen in 2024-2025 in response to numerous attacks by the Houthis on Israel. The Houthis also attacked commercial ships they claimed were linked to Israel. They seized the Galaxy Leader, only releasing the crew in 2025. They tried to make the ship into a kind of tourist attraction. The Galaxy Leader finally partially sank in April 2026, the Maritime Executive noted.
How did Saudi Arabia get into tensions with the Houthis?
Further context might help explain how Riyadh got here.
Saudi Arabia intervened in Yemen in March 2015, leading a coalition against the Iranian-backed Houthis after the group seized Sanaa and advanced toward Aden. The intervention developed into a prolonged conflict involving airstrikes, ground fighting and Houthi missile and drone attacks on Saudi territory. A UN-brokered truce in April 2022 significantly reduced hostilities, and although it formally expired that October, a fragile period of relative calm followed.
That ceasefire has come under increasing pressure in 2026. Saudi strikes on Sanaa in July marked a renewed escalation, while the Houthis subsequently launched an offensive toward Bab el-Mandeb, the strategic strait connecting the Red Sea and Gulf of Aden. It’s worth recalling that Saudi Arabia and the Yemeni government did not want Sanaa airport used by Iran to fly in Iranian advisers to the Houthis.
Saudi-backed Yemeni forces launched a counteroffensive in October, supported by coalition airstrikes, to recover territory near Bab el-Mandeb and Mocha. The Houthis also escalated attacks on Saudi airports, including Riyadh’s King Khalid International Airport, where an October 10 strike killed 12 people and wounded 309. Riyadh vowed a firm response.
The conflict has also expanded beyond Yemen. On September 11, Saudi Arabia’s East-West oil pipeline was struck by drones that Saudi and Iraqi authorities said originated in Iraq. Riyadh temporarily shut the pipeline, a crucial alternative to shipping through the Strait of Hormuz. The attack highlighted growing concerns about coordination among Iran-backed terrorist groups across the region and the potential vulnerability of Saudi energy infrastructure.
On October 12, JINSA President and CEO Michael Makovsky spoke to Fox News about the latest Houthi attacks. “It’s very important that the [Saudi] Crown Prince be successful [in combating the Houthis], and it’s vital for US national security. But he’s alienated or distanced himself from a few key countries that could have been helpful here. I mean, he had a very well-known fight with the Emiratis, who were effective ... against the Houthis. ... He’s kept a distance from the Israelis, who have ... [been] very effective at hitting the Houthis, and, at times in this war, he’s been rather cool to the United States,” Makovsky said, according to a synopsis of the discussion released by JINSA.
He added, “I’d like to see the Saudis work with the Israelis, the Emiratis, and the US to deal with the Houthi threat. It is not only a threat to the Saudis, of course, but affects the whole world because of [the Houthi threat] to international commerce. ... There has to be an international coalition.”
Thomas Juneau, a Professor at the University of Ottawa, who focuses on Iran and Yemen and is a former Department of National Defense analyst in Canada, noted on October 11 on X that “Saudi Arabia faces no good options with the Houthis. Military escalation was inevitable and is likely to continue–but it will hurt Saudi Arabia more than the Houthis. Negotiations are inevitable too–though not in the short term. The Houthis hold stronger cards, and they know it; their goal will be to extract maximal concessions from Saudi Arabia, which remains reluctant to pay this very high price.”
Game theory can help Saudi Arabia face its Houthi dilemma
Might game theory help us understand the dilemma for Saudi Arabia in confronting the Houthis? The challenge is assessing how this spectacle connects with Iran, Israel, the United States, Iranian-backed militias in Iraq, Turkey and Pakistan.
The central problem is that Saudi Arabia may be militarily stronger than the Houthis, but military superiority does not necessarily translate into strategic leverage. The Houthis can impose high costs on Saudi Arabia without defeating its armed forces. Riyadh, meanwhile, must consider how its response affects not only Yemen but its economic security, regional alliances, and relations with Iran. This is what is called an “asymmetric” conflict.
This creates several overlapping strategic dilemmas. Saudi Arabia faces three calculations it has to make at the same time. It has to examine how it might deter more attacks, it has to manage its alliances, and it has to look at the regional context and potential escalation. Game theory does not provide a clear answer, because the outcomes depend on uncertain information, different objectives, and the decisions of several independent actors. Nevertheless, it might be helpful to model this problem more because Saudi Arabia is in a difficult position, but it has many options.
Saudi Arabia can weather the storm. It has done so in the past. It has a naturally cautious leadership, like most Gulf countries. The West tends to prefer quick solutions, and Western media appears to think that the lack of an immediate large response, like “shock and awe,” means nothing is happening. However, this illustrates the differences in calculations. The Iran war, for instance, has proven to be longer and more complex than many thought. This reflects differences in thinking between Washington, Jerusalem, Riyadh, Ankara, and other places in the region.

IAI and SIG SAUER conduct successful live‑fire test of FIRE STORM 250 armed UAS
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
11:57:01 UTC
20:57:01 KST

WASHINGTON - Israel Aerospace Industries (IAI) and SIG SAUER have completed a live‑fire demonstration of the FIRE STORM 250, the Apus 60 VTOL tactical unmanned aircraft equipped with SIG SAUER’s MICROLIGHT Remote Controlled Weapon Station (RCWS) and the new M250 machine gun.
Defense & Tech by The Jerusalem Post understands that the test, conducted ahead of the AUSA 2026 exhibition in Washington, took place in Israel and showed the platform’s ability to detect, identify, and engage targets while hovering over a simulated battlefield.
During the trial, the UAS loitered over the test area and used its onboard camera to identify targets before it fired in both single‑shot and semi‑automatic modes. Engagements were carried out from different altitudes and ranges to assess accuracy, stability, and safety under varied conditions.
While it is still a functional prototype, the companies said the live-fire test validated the system’s core concept of pairing airborne surveillance with stabilized, remotely controlled firepower to give small units organic close‑support capability.
The FIRE STORM 250 is built for long‑duration overwatch and armed reconnaissance. Powered by a multi-fuel internal-combustion engine, it can remain airborne for up to three hours and be refueled in the field, avoiding battery‑charging delays and specialized logistics. Its vertical take-off and landing (VTOL) configuration allows launch and recovery from forward positions without runways or aviation support.
200 rounds at 200 meters
SIG SAUER’s M250 airborne light machine gun can be configured to carry 200 rounds of either 7.62×51 millimeters or 6.8×51 mm. ammunition, depending on customer requirements. It has a targeting range of 400-600 meters at an altitude of 200 m. The MICROLIGHT RCWS brings the system’s total combat weight to 53 pounds, including the gun and ammunition.
Sensor feeds and fire‑control data are fused into a single targeting picture, giving operators real‑time imagery, tracking information, and engagement options. Operators control the platform by using advanced control algorithms that maintain shooting accuracy even while hovering and moving.
“One of the most dangerous positions is in a turret, and the main idea is to keep the soldier out of the line of fire,” Mike Joslin, defense product manager at SIG SAUER, told D&T at AUSA. “Rather than the soldier holding the gun, he holds the interface that controls it.”
Nevertheless, the platform’s architecture keeps a human in the loop, with operators receiving real-time sensor imagery, target-tracking data and engagement options, and authorizing each use of fire.
Sali Okanin, SIG SAUER’s Israel general manager, said the test highlights how lightweight weapons can expand what small unmanned aircraft can do.
"FIRE STORM 250 brings together the most advanced technologies in the world, including IAI’s drone platform and SIG SAUER’s MICROLIGHT RCWS mounted with the M250 machine gun to deliver a new level of operational flexibility,” he said, adding that the platform has “greater range than legacy systems and weight savings that not only provide squad-level benefits but also make drone capabilities possible."
It is intended to be deployed with small tactical units and support missions including persistent overwatch, intelligence gathering, force protection, border defense and special‑operations surveillance.
Joslin explained to D&T that multiple FIRE STORM 250 aircraft can operate together to maintain continuous day‑night coverage, provide advance observation along movement routes, and support maneuvering forces during operations and extraction.
“Our concept of operations is that with the platform’s flight time, you can have loitering support with more en route to provide constant support,” he said.
Moshe Levy, executive vice president and head of IAI’s Military Aircraft Group, said the demonstration reflects a shift in how tactical unmanned systems are being designed.
“The next generation of unmanned systems will be defined not only by autonomy, but by how effectively they integrate sensing, decision-making and action within the operational environment,” he said.
“FIRE STORM 250 brings these capabilities into a single operational loop, enabling tactical forces to extend their reach and maintain continuous awareness while retaining human control over engagement decisions,” he added. “The firing test demonstrates the potential of this approach in a realistic operational scenario."
The future
The collaboration between IAI and SIG SAUER, one of the world’s largest weapons manufacturers, comes as it expands its line of unmanned aerial platforms.
“Drones are the future,” said Ryan Scott, director of Advanced Concepts at SIG SAUER.
Scott, a 22-year US Army Veteran with over a decade in unmanned systems with the Army, explained that the 250-year-old company has been investing in drone design and development for the past several years.
The company’s new direction “shows our innovative capabilities to support our troops.”
Along with FIRESTORM, SIG SAUER displayed its fixed-wing SCYTHE platform, the SABER quadcopter with the M-HORNET 22 LR payload attachment. It also displayed the prototype XRAY-9 counter-UAS platform.
According to Scott, “If Israel wanted our drones, we would sell them.”
Joslin echoed Scott’s feeling towards Israel, telling D&T that “there is no same amount of passion as Israel defense tech companies. Serving is embedded in the culture.”

Houthis and Saudis show no intent to stop fighting
October 13, 2026
Iran-backed Houthi rebels on Tuesday said that Saudi Arabia had carried out overnight airstrikes targeting border regions in Yemen.
Rebel-run satellite television said two strikes had hit the Red Sea island of Kamaran and a third targeted Qanawis, north of Hodeida port.
Further strikes were reported in Jawf and rebels said their forces had downed a Saudi drone over Saada, a Houthi stronghold.
The strikes came just hours after air-raid sirens blared and loud explosions were heard in the Saudi capital Riyadh, which has come under intense fire for the past several days as fighting between the two belligerents intensifies.
The Houthis have clashed with Saudi Arabia since the kingdom stepped into Yemen's civil war to lead a military coalition against the Iran-backed fighters in 2015.
The rebels have pounded Saudi Arabia in recent days, repeatedly attacking the King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh. On Saturday, one of those attacks killed 13 people in what was the deadliest in the country in over a decade.
On Tuesday, Egypt's Foreign Minister Badr Abdelatty called for an immediate end to Houthi attacks on the kingdom, telling Iranian counterpart Abbas Araghchi that there is "no justification for these attacks and they cannot be accepted."
Houthi attacks' economic impact on Saudi Arabia
Beyond reigniting fighting tied to Yemen's civil war, increased Houthi activity has come as a result of the US-Israeli war on Iran, launched on February 28.
A regional proxy, the Houthis have helped Iran further destabilize the region by striking largely at the oil and transport infrastructure that brings oil and gas from US allies in the gulf to market.
Saudi Arabia is the world's top oil exporter and Houthi attacks have not only raised security issues, they have greatly hampered the kingdom's ability to get its product to market.
In its latest annual World Economic Outlook, the International Monetary Fund (IMF) estimates Saudi GDP will contract by 3.3% on the year as a result, with Iran's chokehold on the Strait of Hormuz compounded by Houthi maneuvering in the Red Sea and attacks on Saudi oil refineries and tankers.
Saudi Arabia quickly diverted oil exports away from Hormuz as Iran's blockade dragged on, making use instead, of its overland pipelines and Red Sea access. Houthi attacks, however, have also dramatically impacted these.
Saudi Arabia stops issuing air raids
The devastation of the Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia have prompted the kingdom to seek help from Washington and US President Donald Trump.
Although he previously ignored Saudi requests for assistance, on Saturday Trump mused about joining the fight against the rebels.
News of this consideration drew a quick response from the Houthis, with a representative saying US interests in the region would be targeted should DC enter the fray.
Despite at least 18 people being killed and more than 300 injured in recent days, Saudi Arabia has stopped issuing air raid alerts in the kingdom.
The government has not spoken of the policy change but observers suggest it may be an effort to avoid stirring public panic as the country's security vulnerabilities come into focus.
Still, analysts warn that the change could have the opposite effect by amplifying uncertainty over the current situation.
Last week, prior to a string of airport attacks, government officials said the alerts had been halted due to citizens' complaints about being woken by them.
Further, Saudi government officials on Monday reminded residents of regulations issued in March that forbid sharing any images related to Houthi air attacks, including missile interceptions or impact craters.
Former US Ambassador to Saudi Arabia Michael Ratney told Reuters news agency that Riyadh — which initiated public warnings in May before halting them on September 29 — was trying to balance public messaging with efforts to prevent disruption in the kingdom but that in his opinion leaders had ended up adding to a sense of unease about Houthi airstrikes.

SpaceX launches resupply mission to International Space Station
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

20:54:17 KST

Yasin Gungor
13 October 2026•Update: 13 October 2026
US aerospace company SpaceX launched its 35th commercial resupply mission to the International Space Station (ISS) on Tuesday morning, sending scientific research, critical hardware and operational cargo into orbit.
Loaded with more than 6,300 pounds (2,860 kilograms) of supplies, the SpaceX Dragon spacecraft launched aboard a Falcon 9 rocket from Space Launch Complex 40 at Cape Canaveral Space Force Station in Florida.
The rocket lifted off at 6.34 am local time (1034GMT), marking the fourth orbital trip for the Dragon cargo vehicle and the eighth flight for the first-stage booster.
 
Solar arrays, medical research
The cargo manifest includes the final pair of roll-out solar arrays designed to expand power capacity for station operations, upcoming research and eventual controlled deorbit procedures. Astronauts will install the units during spacewalks planned for late autumn.
The Dragon is carrying experiments to manufacture artificial retinas in microgravity to support vision restoration on Earth, alongside three-dimensional heart tissue models and brain organoids aimed at evaluating potential therapies for neurodegenerative conditions, including Alzheimer’s and Parkinson’s diseases.
The spacecraft is expected to complete an autonomous docking with the station’s Harmony module around 11 am local time (1500GMT) on Thursday.
The resupply mission comes as the International Space Station prepares for its final phase of operations, with the orbiting facility scheduled to conclude its orbital duties at the end of 2030.

A school revolution: how systemic problems in education have led to mass protests in France
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
14:54:00 EEST
20:54:00 KST

A school revolution: how systemic problems in education have led to mass protests in France
On Saturday 10 October, Gabriel Attal, a former education and prime minister, as well as a potential presidential candidate, unveiled what he called a "pact for youth".
The programme was presented as a response to the anger spreading through France’s upper-secondary schools. By the weekend, France’s lycée protests had acquired a new political life. The students are planning another national day of action on Tuesday.
On Friday, 141 lycées were closed, a sharp fall from the first days of the protests. But the fact that the protests have become less widespread does not mean that the political problem has gone away.
France has spent years accumulating the conditions for this outburst.
It has neglected the ordinary machinery of public education, allowed regional inequalities to harden, and then responded to a student movement as if the principal issue were public order.
The result is a crisis that cannot be reduced either to youthful disorder or to police repression. Both are present. Neither explains the whole story.
A protest born in the classroom
The movement began around 21 September in schools in the Créteil education district, which includes much of France’s poorer eastern suburbs. The first complaints were about the daily experience of attending a school that often seemed unable to provide the basics.
A student in Aubervilliers had no French teacher while preparing for an important examination. In Sevran, pupils showed photographs of damaged chairs, holes in ceilings, mould, leaking roofs and broken toilets.
Some classrooms were difficult to heat in winter and difficult to cool in summer. Timetables stretched from early morning into the evening, with long gaps that left pupils stranded in school buildings without adequate supervision or food.
France’s public secondary schools have fewer teachers than they did in 2008, despite having roughly 250,000 more pupils. More than 70 per cent of classes in public general and technical schools have more than 30 pupils, while one in five has more than 35. Long absences without replacement have increased sharply, particularly in the Créteil and Versailles regions.
Buildings tell the same story. The average French lycée is more than six decades old. Vocational schools are older still. Only a small proportion of secondary-school buildings were built or substantially renovated in the past academic year.
The problems are not evenly distributed. In Seine-Saint-Denis, where the movement first took hold, the poverty rate is close to 30 per cent, almost twice the national metropolitan average.
France’s republican school system promises that a child’s future should not be determined by family wealth, religion or geography.
Yet pupils in the poorest areas are often asked to accept the largest classes, the oldest buildings and the most unstable supply of teachers.
The students understand the contradiction. They are not necessarily demanding a new ideology, but that the Republic honour its existing one.
The struggle over order
The protests have also produced real violence, and some schools have been damaged or ransacked. Teachers and headteachers have been threatened or injured. Incidents have been reported in Bayonne, Toulouse, Saint-Chamond, Poitiers and Saint-Étienne. In one case, a fire spread to a teacher’s car. In another, a school cafeteria was damaged.
The Education Ministry has estimated the cost of repairs at about €30 million and warned that thousands of pupils could lose teaching time.
The state’s authority cannot survive if school staff are attacked and schools become targets.
Nor is the idea that French schools are becoming unsafe entirely invented. Official surveys show substantial levels of intimidation, defiance and verbal abuse.
Many teachers report that pupils challenge their authority or mock their work. A smaller but serious minority report threats, harassment or physical assault. At the same time, the latest official data does not support the claim that French schools are simply descending into generalised violence. Most staff say they feel respected by pupils and safe inside their schools. The number of recorded serious incidents per 1,000 pupils fell slightly in the latest year.
The memory of Samuel Paty hangs over this debate. Paty was murdered in 2020 after being targeted by an Islamist extremist for showing caricatures of the Prophet Muhammad during a lesson on freedom of expression.
Dominique Bernard, another teacher, was murdered in 2023 by a former pupil in a terrorist attack. France’s schools have since become the place where arguments about secularism, religion, free speech and state authority collide with particular force.
The figures recorded during the first national commemoration of Paty showed the scale of the challenge. Hundreds of pupils were reported for provocations, refusal to participate, threats or expressions of support for terrorism. That episode should not be used to label the current movement as Islamist, most of the present protests concern staffing, buildings, timetables and inequality.
But the Paty legacy does expose a larger question: how can teachers exercise authority in an open society when the state has not reliably protected them?
The deployment of riot police has opened another dispute over how the state exercises its authority.
Images of tear gas and riot police confronting teenagers have travelled quickly through France and abroad. In Saint-Denis, the mayor, Bally Bagayoko, was filmed facing police lines while trying to shield young people. In Lens, a 15-year-old lost a hand during an incident involving a police grenade. In the Paris region, a police officer has been placed under investigation after a teenager was seriously injured. By 9 October, more than 200 pupils and over 800 police officers or gendarmes had reportedly been injured,
while more than 6,800 people had been placed in police custody, 86 per cent of them minors.
The police have a duty to prevent arson, protect school staff and stop attacks on public buildings.
They also have a duty to use force lawfully and proportionately. Student violence does not excuse unlawful policing. Alleged police misconduct does not erase the violence committed by protesters.
The state has run out of easy answers
The government has now conceded that the grievances are legitimate. Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu has promised rapid action on teacher replacement, school buildings, timetables and Parcoursup. The Education Ministry has said it is contacting approximately 3,000 qualified teachers who could be sent to schools facing shortages.
That is a useful emergency measure, but it os not the same as solving the recruitment crisis. The government’s plan may demonstrate political responsiveness while leaving the structural weakness untouched. Ministers have recognised the problem, but recognition is cheaper than delivery.
The same tension is visible in the education budget. The government presents a 2027 allocation of roughly €64 billion, excluding pensions, compared with €48.8 billion in 2017.
Yet wider education spending barely increased in real terms last year. Inflation, salaries, energy costs, demographic change and the maintenance of old buildings consume money before it reaches the classroom.
France can still finance its debt, but the government has far less room to finance new promises.The European Central Bank has not judged that emergency intervention is necessary. But the country is in a politically dangerous financial position.
Public debt reached about 119 per cent of GDP at the end of the second quarter.
The government is working with a deficit of roughly 5.4 per cent of GDP this year, while annual interest costs are projected to rise from about €79 billion to more than €91 billion.
The ten-year borrowing rate has approached 5 per cent, its highest level in decades. Each rise makes the government’s promised concessions harder to fund. It means that markets are becoming less willing to treat French promises as costless.
The government therefore faces a narrow corridor. It must invest more in the services that citizens believe are collapsing while convincing creditors that public spending will eventually be brought under control. It must punish destruction without allowing the police response to define the entire crisis. It must restore authority in schools without turning schools into extensions of the security state.
There is no painless solution.
The government’s online consultation gives pupils a formal channel and produces a more precise map of their concerns. But consultation can become a substitute for decision. Students have already spent years being consulted about problems that remained visible afterwards.
France’s crisis is not simply a crisis of youth. It is a crisis of state capacity.
The young people on the streets are not all representative of the country’s lycéens. The movement is uneven, sometimes confused and occasionally violent.
It has not produced a coherent national programme. But it has revealed a common experience across very different schools: the sense that institutions ask for obedience while failing to provide the conditions in which obedience can appear reasonable.
France’s ability to sustain long-term European security commitments, including support for Ukraine, depends partly on whether it can rebuild domestic authority and fiscal credibility.
Charlotte Guillou-Clerc,
Journalist, France

Anthropic warns of self-replicating AI
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
11:46:18 UTC
20:46:18 KST

Anthropic warns of self-replicating AI
Small artificial intelligence models could be months away from copying themselves across internet-connected consumer devices without relying on data centers, Anthropic has warned, reports a Qazinform News Agency correspondent.
In its official research report, the company examined whether AI systems could move between machines, start operating on unfamiliar hardware and continue spreading without human intervention.
Researchers demonstrated that a model could run across 15 inexpensive Android TV boxes. Another small model successfully set up AI processing on eight of nine hardware types tested.
However, current small models still struggle to complete the entire replication process reliably. More capable models succeeded in simplified experiments, but required separate computing infrastructure.
Anthropic estimates that smaller models could reach the necessary capability by the end of 2026 if improvements continue at their historical pace. It stressed that this timeline is a rough projection.
“We don’t yet have a full rogue replicator,” researchers William Zhou and Daniel Freeman wrote.
The company warned that distributed AI could be difficult to shut down because it would lack a single central control point. Unlike conventional malware, it could adapt to unfamiliar hardware.
The experiments simplified the task of gaining access to devices, meaning their results do not establish reliable replication under real-world conditions.
Anthropic recommended stronger device security, monitoring unusual network traffic and isolating infected machines to limit potential spread.
