Across China: Back in saddle, Tibetan ex-wrestler gives horse traditions a modern twist
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
19:16:35 CST
20:16:35 KST

CHENGDU, Oct. 13 (Xinhua) -- As more herders on the grasslands of southwest China's Sichuan Province turn to motorcycles and cars instead of horses, Rinch Wangyel is heading in the opposite direction, opting to get back into the saddle.
The 34-year-old former wrestling champion returned to his native Hongyuan County seven years ago to build a business around horses. What began with two horses has since grown into a ranch with 44.
In peak season, up to 20 visitors a day ride with him across hills and rivers and into remote grasslands and forests, sometimes spotting hares or wolves.
"My goal is to let people see the grasslands and experience nomadic culture," he said. "Many people know little about horses and yaks, and they are curious about how herders live and what they eat."
For Rinch Wangyel, horses were part of life long before they became his livelihood.
Born into a herding family in the Aba Tibetan and Qiang Autonomous Prefecture, he rode almost daily as a child. But it was wrestling that first took him beyond the grasslands.
At 13, he traveled by bus to a competition in Maerkang, the prefectural capital. Back then, transport links in the region were limited, and the trip took nearly a full day. Having rarely ridden in a car, he threw up on his coach halfway.
Wrestling later took him much farther. He won several provincial championships in Sichuan and a national title.
After retiring as an athlete, he moved to Beijing to study something he had known all his life: horseback riding.
"I wanted to do something connected to my own culture," he said.
He spent four years studying modern horsemanship, earning riding and coaching qualifications from Chinese and French equestrian associations. He learned to train horses, use equipment safely and communicate through body movements.
In 2019, he returned to Hongyuan.
At an average elevation of more than 3,600 meters, Hongyuan takes its name from the grasslands crossed by the Communist Party of China-led Red Army during the Long March, a roughly 12,500-kilometer military odyssey from 1934 to 1936.
From 1935 to 1936, the three main forces of the Red Army passed through this region. Bitter cold, thin air, treacherous marshes and unpredictable weather made the grasslands of northwest Sichuan one of the most grueling stretches of the Long March.
The take-off of modern traffic infrastructure is among the most visible changes in these formidable grasslands.
Before 1949, the Aba plateau had no modern roads. Highway construction began in the early 1950s, with airports, expressways and railways following.
Today, Rinch Wangyel said, the journey from Hongyuan to Maerkang or the provincial capital Chengdu takes just three or four hours. Tourists can now even visit the once-remote grasslands over a weekend.
Tractors, trucks and motorcycles spread through pastoral areas in the 1980s and 1990s, followed by cars. Some herders now drive new energy vehicles.
Horses, once essential for getting around, have gradually taken on a different role.
Hongyuan, known for its Tibetan equestrian traditions, has around 20,000 horses. Increasingly, they are used for racing, tourism and cultural experiences rather than daily transportation.
Rinch Wangyel first offered tourists short horseback rides at Moon Bay, a popular local attraction. But riding beside a road for an hour, he felt, did little to show visitors what the grasslands were really like.
He then opened his own ranch, offering rides lasting hours or even a full day, deeper into the countryside.
"Our guests tend to be well-off," he said. "But they're also looking for something more than just sightseeing."
Some guests stay for days, switching horses and routes. A Frenchman living in Shanghai in east China has returned several times, and the ranch has attracted thousands of repeat visitors from both China and abroad.
For city dwellers seeking a break from hectic urban life, the grasslands offer a different pace. But taking inexperienced riders into remote terrain required Rinch Wangyel to rethink traditional practices.
He modified traditional saddles and stirrups, made helmets and protective gear mandatory, and helped develop safety standards for local horseback-riding businesses.
His approach to training horses also changed. "We have moved away from the traditional practice of training horses with whips and use the methods I learned in Beijing, communicating with them through body language," he said.
He even washes the horses with shampoo and carefully grooms them, hoping first-time visitors will see the local Hequ breed at its best.
"I've always believed horses have personalities just like people," he said.
Hequ horses, a traditional Chinese plateau breed, are known for their courage, steady temperament and endurance in cold, high-altitude conditions.
These animals have also become part of a wider effort to build a tourism industry around the region's equestrian traditions.
In recent years, Hongyuan has upgraded more than 100 horseback-riding sites and expanded horse breeding and training. Equestrian competitions and music festivals, notably, have brought more visitors.
During a series of events in 2025, the county received 220,000 tourist visits and generated 218.5 million yuan (approximately 32.47 million U.S. dollars) in tourism revenue.
The country's 15th Five-Year Plan (2026-2030), released in March, calls for promoting county economies via local strengths, expanding distinctive rural industries, and developing new rural industries and business models such as leisure tourism, cultural experiences and rural e-commerce.
Rinch Wangyel films and edits videos of grassland rides to attract customers and trains local herders to serve as part-time riding instructors during peak season. His ranch made a profit of approximately 600,000 yuan in 2025.
Now he has another ambition.
Rinch Wangyel has begun breeding imported British horses with local Hequ horses, hoping to produce taller animals while retaining the endurance and hardiness of the plateau breed.
Eight horses have been bred this year. If all goes well, a new generation of foals will arrive next spring, increasing his herd to more than 50.
"One day, I hope horses bred and trained in Hongyuan can leave the grasslands and compete in show jumping in Beijing and Shanghai," he said. "And I hope that will help more people understand our nomadic culture." ■

The turnaround in prices is sharp. Sri Lanka's consumer prices fell by 0.5 percent in 2025, but the IMF now projects inflation of 5.3 percent in 2026 and 5.4 percent in 2027, marginally above the Central Bank of Sri Lanka's 5 percent target.
The country's external position is also expected to weaken, with the current account moving from a surplus of 1.6 percent of GDP in 2025 to deficits of 0.5 percent in 2026 and 0.3 percent in 2027.
In addition, the IMF projects unemployment to hold at 3.9 percent over the three years. ■

Letter from Mideast: A vest marked "PRESS" was no shield
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
19:16:08 CST
20:16:08 KST

by Taher Abu Hamdan
BEIRUT, Oct. 13 (Xinhua) -- The tripod lay on its side, the camera and other equipment scattered across the hilltop. A media car burned nearby. Moments earlier, a group of journalists had been filming. The word "PRESS" was still visible on the vests amid the wreckage.
It was Oct. 13, 2023, days after fighting began along the Lebanon-Israel border. Cameraman Issam Abdallah was killed and six other journalists wounded, all wearing press vests. Independent investigations traced the shells to the Israeli side, while the intent remained disputed.
Until then, we had carried an assumption none of us said aloud: as journalists, we stood outside the fighting. After that afternoon, the vest no longer felt like armor. It felt like a word we had trusted too much.
Since Oct. 8, 2023, one day after the latest Gaza conflict erupted, we had gathered almost daily in a square in the border city of Marjeyoun overlooking Israeli positions.
We filmed Israeli airstrikes on towns around Marjeyoun and Bint Jbeil, then watched the strikes spread to the western Bekaa and Baalbek. In the opposite direction, we recorded Hezbollah rockets arcing toward Israel, sometimes intercepted above us.
At first, the confrontation looked contained. Then the distance between us and the war narrowed, day by day.
We began studying where we stood, which vehicles we used, how long we lingered, and how far we were from military positions. But the war advanced faster than our habits.
On Nov. 21, 2023, journalist Farah Omar and cameraman Rabih Maamari, both with Lebanese broadcaster Al Mayadeen, were killed while covering the fighting.
Nearly a year later, an Israeli strike hit a building in Hasbaya where about 18 journalists were staying, killing three.
Before each reporting trip, we no longer asked only what was happening there. We also asked: Is the place where we are standing safe? Is the word "PRESS" on our vests and vehicles enough to protect us?
As Israeli forces entered border villages, we no longer watched only the shelling. Tanks moved in, bulldozers reshaped the landscape. Houses were reduced to rubble. Villages once minutes away became dangerous to reach.
A ceasefire in November 2024 offered a fragile pause, but fighting surged again in March 2026. By May, Israeli forces had crossed the Litani River. Evacuation orders spread, and strikes continued even after further ceasefire announcements.
Each time we thought the war had reached its limit, it pushed that limit farther.
The endless fighting has reshaped the south. According to Lebanese authorities, at the peak of the 2026 flare-up, some 1.2 million residents were displaced across the country, most of them from the south.
For residents, a shifting front line is more than a change on a map: it decides whether they can return home, tend their farms, or reach the services they need.
As journalists, we leave after filming, but the place does not leave us. Some sounds remain: explosions, the buzz of drones, cries for an ambulance, and the long silence after an airstrike -- sometimes more painful than the blast itself.
Three years on, our footage records how far the war has spread. It cannot tell us where it will stop, or when those still displaced will be able to go home. ■

MELBOURNE, Oct. 13 (Xinhua) -- An Australian research project is testing whether acupuncture can be integrated into hospital emergency departments as a non-drug option for patients experiencing acute pain.
The Personalized add-on Acupuncture service at Northern Hospital Emergency Department for Acute Pain (PANDA) explores how registered acupuncturists can work alongside emergency department clinicians to support patient comfort, improve care experiences and potentially reduce time spent in hospital, according to a statement released Tuesday by Australia's RMIT University.
Unlike clinical trials that assess treatment effectiveness under controlled conditions, the project -- led by RMIT and Northern Health, a public health service provider in Australia's Melbourne -- focuses on how acupuncture can be delivered effectively in a busy emergency department, the statement said.
Early findings of the PANDA team show strong interest in non-drug pain management options, with more than 90 percent of surveyed emergency department patients saying they would consider acupuncture if it helped them avoid or reduce medication use.
Meanwhile, 90 percent of surveyed healthcare workers wanted non-drug options for their patients, the team found. The project has adopted the panda as its symbolic mascot, reflecting its goal of bringing relief and reassurance to patients in distress. ■

EU has paid Russia US$209bn for energy since March 2022
From March 2022 to July 2026, European Union countries paid Russia around €197 billion or approximately US$209 billion for fossil fuels.
Source: an EU source with a reference to official European Union statistical data, as reported by European Pravda
Details: Following the start of the full-scale Russian invasion of Ukraine, the EU spent approximately US$209 billion on Russian fossil energy, which refutes the claim made by US President Donald Trump about US$250 billion spent during this period.
Meanwhile, according to European institutional estimates, without the launch of the REPowerEU plan (the EU's planned phase-out of Russian energy resources), this figure could have reached around €475 billion.
The source calculated that reducing dependency on Russian fossil fuels had allowed the EU to avoid additional expenditure of approximately €278 billion.
The official recalled that as early as 2023, supplies from Russia accounted for only about 6% of the European Union's total expenditure on fossil fuels.
Background:
- Trump wrote on his social media network that the European Union had paid Russia US$250 billion for energy.
- On 9 October, Trump said he had spoken to Putin and reached an agreement with him on supplying Russian diesel fuel to the US and global markets.
- The agreement between Trump and Putin sparked outrage in Ukraine and European capitals.

Estonia's new plain language standard aims to make public writing clearer
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
11:15:00 UTC
20:15:00 KST

Estonia's new plain language standard aims to make public writing clearer
Estonia's first plain language standard took effect in early October, offering guidance on writing clear, reader-focused public communications.
Adopted ahead of International Plain Language Day on Tuesday, the standard aims to make public-sector writing clearer and communication more effective.
Kristel Ress, who chairs the technical committee that developed the standard, said writers should first consider who will read a text and in what circumstances.
Instructions for a fisherman reading on a phone in a cold boat, for example, need to account for very different conditions than something read at home or standing at a bus stop.
Ress nonetheless emphasized that the standard is just one tool, offering broad principles rather than detailed rules on word choice or grammar.
"The advantage of the standard is that, for the first time, all this advice has been brought together in one concise guide," she explained.
This guide, she continued, can help anyone who writes for work, including editors, teachers and researchers — but also office workers and even students.
"This isn't just for language professionals anymore," Ress said.
Putting the reader first
ERR language editor and adviser Ester Põldma said the guidance will be particularly useful for people writing online, where brevity and clarity are essential.
"Readers should be able to understand on the first read what a sentence is trying to convey," Põldma said.
Under the international definition, a text is written in plain language when its intended readers can find the information they need, understand it and act on it.
"Putting the reader first is the most important thing," Põldma said. "We need to think about who we're writing for or who we're making a program for. That determines the words we use, the sentences we write and what the text should look like."

As of today, this package of documents, detailing the violations and our legal assessment, and prepared in compliance with all procedures set out in the FIG Code of Ethics, has been submitted to the relevant FIG body. The goal is to secure a legal assessment and a decision regarding the continued presence of Russian organizations within the International Gymnastics Federation," Samborsky said during a press conference at the Interfax-Ukraine agency on Tuesday.
According to him, the formal appeal was submitted by Olympic champion Stela Zakharova, Vice President of the Ukrainian Gymnastics Federation (responsible for artistic gymnastics), who initiated the separate filing. "We helped her compile the relevant package of documents," stated the co-founder of the NGO Sports Context.
Samborsky added that the document package has already been "accepted and is undergoing assessment by the International Gymnastics Federation," and that the organization is prepared to "bolster its position with additional documentation if necessary."
Zakharova, for her part, emphasized that the events unfolding in the temporarily occupied territories of Ukraine "cannot be viewed as unrelated to sports."
"When sports organizations, coaches, judges, athletes, or competitions from internationally recognized Ukrainian territory are incorporated into another state's sports system, a very specific question arises: whose sports system do they represent, and who should defend the Ukrainian gymnast's right to her own territory and jurisdiction? To me, the answer is obvious: first and foremost, we ourselves—people to whom Ukrainian sport has given the opportunity to compete, win, become Olympic champions, and work within national federations—must not only avail ourselves of these opportunities but also stand up for ourselves. That is precisely why my appeal to the GEF—the International Federation's Gymnastics Ethics Foundation—reflects not only a civic stance but also a professional responsibility," she said during a press conference.
According to the Olympic champion, "we are submitting facts and documents and requesting an assessment of them in accordance with international gymnastics regulations."
"I do not know what the final decision will be, and I believe it is wrong to predict it before the procedure concludes. But I know one thing for certain: if a protection mechanism exists, we must trigger it; if rules exist, we have the right to demand that they apply equally to everyone. Therefore, what matters to me is not just the act of filing the complaint, but the fact that we are changing our approach—moving beyond merely talking about the problem to professionally defending Ukrainian gymnastics by utilizing the international sports system itself," said Zakharova.
She also emphasized the importance of ensuring that Russian athletes are not admitted to FIG international competitions. "I took this step deliberately, fully aware that certain organizations might respond with actions that could be considered inappropriate. I understood that risk, but for me, the priority is ensuring that our sport has every opportunity to prevent their admission into international sports organizations. I hope that will happen," Zakharova said.
Samborsky described the goal of the appeal as enabling Ukrainian sports institutions to defend their rights and "create conditions under which the return of Russian and Belarusian athletes to the international sports arena would be, if not impossible, then extremely difficult."
"We are not currently asking international sports organizations to agree with Ukraine politically, nor are we asking for an exception for Ukraine or for an assessment of the political actions of the organizations and aggressor nations currently causing us harm. We are asking for an assessment, a legal assessment of the actions, taken by Russian sports organizations that violate the statutes of international organizations. That is precisely the foundation upon which we propose basing Ukraine's position..."

The Financial Times, citing people familiar with the matter, reported over the weekend that US envoys, in talks with their Ukrainian counterparts on Friday, raised the possibility of cutting off intelligence sharing to Kiev if it did not heed Washington’s warning to halt energy strikes in Russia.

Russia’s defence ministry claimed that air defences shot down 604 Ukrainian drones over 15 regions and over the Sea of Azov.

Independent verification of the claims is difficult due to the war, which continues for more than four years.
Moscow and Kiev have intensified strikes in recent months, targeting each other's logistics centers, ports, and energy infrastructure.
Both countries deny deliberately targeting civilian infrastructure, maintaining that strikes are directed at military targets or facilities linked to military activities only.

Financial transactions with Russia are possible: TPO head
TEHRAN- Mohammad Ali Dehghan Dehnavi, Head of Iran’s Trade Promotion Organization (TPO), in response to a question about the organization’s measures to facilitate financial exchanges between Iranian traders and the member countries of the Eurasian Economic Union (EAEU), especially Russia, said: “One of the important issues in trade development is preferential and free trade agreements, which have been pursued seriously in the recent period and are being developed.”
According to ISNA, Dehghan Dehnavi, at a press conference on the 30th National Export Day ceremony and honoring national exemplary exporters, which will be held on October 21, referred to the implementation process of the free trade agreement with the Eurasian Economic Union, and stated: “This agreement has performed positively at a time when the country’s total exports have faced somewhat negative growth due to the issues that have arisen, and this shows that there is potential to develop trade in this market. The free trade agreement removes tariff barriers; in the agreement with the Eurasian Union, tariffs on 87 percent of goods have been reduced to zero; therefore, for this group of goods, there is no tariff barrier to exports.”
The Head of Iran’s Trade Promotion Organization, referring to non-tariff barriers to trade, said: “Although the agreement also mentions the removal of these barriers, it is not the main issue of the agreement, but we pursue these issues in trade negotiations. Payment systems and foreign currency transfers are among the non-tariff barriers to trade between Iran and the member countries of the Eurasian Union. The issue of banking systems and systems that can serve as alternatives to the banking system falls within the duties of the Central Bank, and our colleagues at the Central Bank have taken good measures in this regard.”
Dehghan Dehnavi, referring to the establishment of financial communications with Russia, said: “The possibility of communication and money transfers using national currencies has been provided. Of course, conditions are not like normal circumstances, and sanctions still create problems; especially since banks and financial institutions on the other side are not willing to cooperate fully due to considerations arising from sanctions. Despite these limitations, the conditions for financial transactions with Russia are suitable compared with many other countries, and in economic relations with the Eurasian Union, this is not the main concern.”
The Head of Iran’s Trade Promotion Organization considered standards and customs issues to be among the most important remaining non-tariff barriers in trade with the Eurasian Union and stated: “The National Standards Organization and the Customs of the Islamic Republic of Iran are trying to reduce these barriers.” He also announced the holding of meetings of the joint committee between Iran and the Eurasian Economic Union and said: “The EAEU trade minister will travel to Iran in the coming days. The responsibility for the joint committee related to the agreement between Iran and the Eurasian Union is held on Iran’s side by the Minister of Industry, Mine and Trade, and on the other side by the EAEU trade minister.”
On October 6, the official stating that Iran's share of the Russian market must increase, said: This country imports about $300 billion annually from various countries around the world, and despite the progress made, Iran's share of this large market is still negligible.
Dehghan Dehnavi said at the first Iran-Russia Trade Development Summit, focusing on Gilan and Astrakhan provinces, held in the Anzali Free Zone: Developing economic and trade cooperation with Russia is one of the programs that has been pursued over the past years, and one of the most important measures in this path has been the implementation of the Iran-Eurasian Economic Union Free Trade Agreement.
He added: This agreement has been implemented since April 2025, and based on it, tariffs on 87 percent of goods in Iran's trade with the five member countries of the Eurasian Economic Union, of which Russia is the largest, have been reduced to zero.
The Deputy Minister of Industry, Mining and Trade continued: The zeroing of tariffs has created an advantage and competitive power for Iranian traders, and the country's exporters can use this opportunity to be one step ahead of their rivals in the markets of the Eurasian Economic Union member countries.
He emphasized: Economic and trade convergence with the member countries of the Eurasian Economic Union must continue, and it is necessary to make optimal use of this opportunity and for all economic actors and the country's existing capacities to work to increase Iran's share of the Russian market.
The Head of Iran's Trade Promotion Organization, referring to the existing capacities for developing exports to Russia, said: Based on studies conducted, more than $50 billion of Russia's imports overlap with goods that Iran has the possibility to export, and activating this capacity can increase Iran's exports to this country from the current $1 to $2 billion to $10 or even $20 billion.
Dehghan Dehnavi continued: In addition to this capacity, new capacities must also be created, and to activate these capacities, planning and establishing direct communication between the economic actors of the two countries is necessary.
The Head of Iran's Trade Promotion Organization (TPO), stating that Gilan has a special position in trade with Russia, emphasized: In addition to its production capacities and export products, this province can also be a connection point and trade gateway for the country from a logistical point of view.
Dehghan Dehnavi stated: This province is connected to Russia as well as Kazakhstan, Azerbaijan, and Turkmenistan through the sea, and land and rail routes have provided other capacities for trade development.
He continued: Part of the rail project is being completed, and rail connection is currently established at the border; also, part of the goods transferred from China to the region arrive at Anzali Port via Kazakhstan and Aktau Port, and are distributed throughout the country from here.
The Head of Iran's Trade Promotion Organization (TPO) emphasized: These capacities show that Gilan, in addition to developing its own trade, can become a major commercial hub for the country.
According to him, to achieve this goal, completing the required infrastructure and defining new activities for the private sector is necessary and essential.
Dehghan Dehnavi emphasized the role of sending trade delegations in developing economic relations and added: Holding this summit and afterward planning to send trade delegations can be effective in developing trade between the two countries.
He added: Every trade communication and conversation, exchange of business cards, and negotiation among economic actors lays the groundwork for a new contract, export or import, joint cooperation, and investment.
Dehghan Dehnavi referred to the long-standing relations between Gilan and Astrakhan provinces and recalled: These relations must be in the field of investment in addition to trade, and the two sides can have joint investment in each other's capacities to provide a basis for increasing trade.
The Head of Iran's Trade Promotion Organization further emphasized: Part of the problems is caused by sanctions and foreign restrictions, and part is related to internal issues, including the multiplicity of laws and regulations, systems, instability of regulations, and administrative bureaucracy; our effort is to facilitate the path of trade at least in the area of internal obstacles that are within the government's control, and good measures have been taken and are being taken in this regard.
Dehghan Dehnavi also announced the drafting of an export support package by the Ministry of Industry, Mining and Trade and added: This package has been presented to the government and will be introduced next week, in which various supports for strengthening exports have been foreseen.
He also referred to measures being taken in the Government Economic Committee with the cooperation of the Ministry of Industry, Mining and Trade, the Central Bank, and the Ministry of Economic Affairs and Finance, and recalled: Regulations in the field of trade are being drafted, and if approved, part of the trade obstacles will be removed.
Dehghan Dehnavi called one of these cases the reform of the order registration process and added: One of the proposals is that order registration return to its primary function as a declaration of trade plan, and controls that can be carried out at the customs clearance stage be removed from the order registration stage.
The Head of Iran's Trade Promotion Organization, emphasizing that existing obstacles should not prevent the use of the country's trade capacities, stated: Iran's private sector has shown that despite restrictions, it can open the path of trade with initiative and effort and take big steps in this regard.
He considered holding the first Iran-Russia Trade Development Summit in Gilan as a measure to strengthen economic relations and added: We hope its effects will become visible in the coming months and years with increased exports from Gilan to Russia and other countries.
Dehghan Dehnavi also announced the assignment of a new trade mission to Gilan in connection with one of China's provinces and said: It is expected that this province, with proper planning, will use the new capacities for trade development.

The summit, focusing on Gilan and Astrakhan provinces, was held with the presence of Mohammad Ali Dehghan Dehnavi, Head of Iran's Trade Promotion Organization; Teymour Pourheidari, Head of Iran's Export Development in Astrakhan and Director General of Industry, Mine and Trade of Gilan; Sergei Vladimirovich Azarov, Consul General of the Russian Federation in Rasht; Ahmad Heydarian, Consul General of the Islamic Republic of Iran in the Russian Federation; Hadi Haqshenas, Governor of Gilan; and Mostafa Taati Moghaddam, CEO of the Anzali Free Zone.

Türkiye to ban livestreaming, screen recording for social media users aged 15-18
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
11:11:21 UTC
20:11:21 KST

Family and Social Services Minister Mahinur Özdemir Göktaş (AA File Photo)
Türkiye will prohibit social media users aged 15 to 18 from livestreaming and recording their screens under a new child protection regulation set to take effect on Nov. 1, Family and Social Services Minister Mahinur Özdemir Göktaş said.
Speaking to reporters after a Cabinet meeting chaired by President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan, Göktaş said the regulation would introduce age verification through e-Devlet, Türkiye’s government digital services portal, for users seeking to open social media accounts.
Users will receive a digital code after verifying their age. Platforms will also be required to use their own technological systems to estimate users’ ages and conduct ongoing checks after accounts are created.
If a platform suspects that an account is being used by someone under 15, it will temporarily suspend the account and direct the user to verify their age again through e-Devlet. Checks may also be repeated to prevent children from accessing social media through their parents’ accounts, Göktaş said, adding that the government would oversee compliance alongside the platforms.
The regulation will also restrict direct messages to those from accounts a child follows and disable read receipts, which indicate whether a message has been seen.
Göktaş said the government also aimed to remove design features considered to encourage excessive screen use, including continuous scrolling and functions that allow users to replay content from the beginning. Measures to limit children’s constant exposure to advertisements are also planned.
Social media platforms will have until March 31, 2027, to complete the transition and comply with the new requirements.

The Future Currency of Achievement in Human Philosophy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
11:10:54 UTC
20:10:54 KST

“What do we lose if LLMs kill the journal system? Nothing but some heavy ass chains, and a few weak heuristics for assessing CVs quickly that were never worth the outrageous amounts of time and labour the journal system wasted anyway.”
.
That’s Jonathan Weisberg (Toronto), who knows a little bit more than the average philosopher about the journal system, having co-founded Ergo.
With AI and “a little human guidance,” he says,
you can crank out the kind of papers that make up 95% of what we publish in a few hours. Soon (already?), human guidance may not even be necessary. Do I find this depressing? Just the opposite. Sure, I built my career on this skill, honed it for decades, and now a computer can do it in a hundredth of the time... But this was always a goofy way of making a living…
[I]t’s always been a drag dealing with bafflingly slow journals, maddeningly lazy referees, and typesetters so incompetent it must be a bit. The publication process puts years of frustrated waiting, and dozens of hours of wasted labour, between when I’m actually done understanding an idea, and the point where my dean finally gives me a pat on the head and a sticker that says “good job!”.
Many see the AI onslaught as a net negative for academia, but Weisberg sees it as an opportunity:
just tell the dean, “sorry, LLMs.” They’ll find some other way to count our beans, I have no doubt. But while they work on figuring that out, we have an opportunity to radically revise the whole bean economy.
If the journals crash and burn, you can still read, think, and write about philosophy. You can still share your writing with other philosophers, build on what they’ve done, hope they’ll do the same in turn, etc. None of this requires publishers, typesetters, or even traditional peer review.
There are better things to do with one’s time than “agonizing over how to revise your manuscript so the referees at the fourth journal you send it to won’t be able to miss the reply to their objection buried somewhere in the middle of page 23.”
So what should replace the current system?
Note that it’s not just that the deans (etc.) who would need a new way to “count our beans.” Being able to assess skills and achievements is important in any academic discipline for a variety of reasons (hiring, promotions, grants, collaborations, attention), and it’s generally good to have more than one heuristic for doing that. (We don’t want to rely solely on, say, inherited institutional prestige.)
On x.com, Wes Pegden, a mathematician at Carnegie Mellon, suggests that “deep talks” could be part of “a new system for how we identify ‘awesomeness’ in math” (h/t Henry Shevlin). What is a deep talk?
This is an extended format talk given on a paper (regardless of authorship) accompanied by the claim that the presenter is prepared to reconstruct any desired detail of paper’s proof on the spot, unaided. For example, currently there is a document that contains the solution to the Navier-Stokes problem. No person currently could give a “Deep Talk” on this paper. But certainly, I expect it is within human capability to do so. Someone can be the first! So impressive!
A mathematician would have a repertoire of Deep Talks they currently offer; departments could invite speakers offering talks of new results of interest (sometimes for longer “Deep Talks”, with the detail-probing component, sometimes normal seminar talks). What this system offers is a way to measure technical excellence—impressiveness—in our field. (The present discussion is not about the value to society about having mathematics as an academic field, which I strongly believe in but which is a separate topic).
Pegden adds, “Having such a measure is vital to having a thriving academic discipline. In particular, we need to have a way of measuring excellence in a way roughly aligned with what we recognize as mathematical capabilities.” If we replaced “mathematical” with “philosophical” in that statement (with a suitably pluralistic understanding of what counts as “philosophical capabilities”), I think most philosophers would endorse it. But I’m not sure that they’d agree that “deep talks” would do the trick. What would?
At the moment, to my knowledge, AIs are not yet producing excellent philosophical work, at least not in the form of articles or books. (And it may turn out that articles and books are not the best formats for showcasing the philosophical capabilities of AI. I suspect that complex, customizable dynamic inference mapping will be among their distinctive excellences, and the best format for that may be a tool or application, not an article or book.) Still, many people believe AIs eventually will produce excellent philosophical work. If they do, what then should be the currency of achievement in human philosophy?

Türkiye can help Europe reduce strategic dependencies: Belgian top diplomat

Türkiye has an important role to play in helping Europe reduce its strategic dependencies, particularly in key industrial sectors, Belgian Foreign Minister Maxime Prevot said on Tuesday.
Addressing the EU-Türkiye Business Summit in Brussels, Prevot said changing global dynamics, the ongoing war in Ukraine and disruptions to supply chains had made Europe increasingly aware of its economic vulnerabilities.
"Türkiye has an important role to play, not only as an industrial market but also as a gateway to markets in the wider region," Prevot said, stressing the importance of Türkiye's manufacturing capacity, industrial expertise and connections to neighbouring markets.
He said European companies were increasingly seeking reliable partners closer to home as they reconsidered where to manufacture and store their goods.
"We should make values of its proximity, particularly in sectors where Europe needs to reduce strategic dependencies," he added.
Prevot described Türkiye as a NATO ally, an EU candidate country and a major industrial economy connecting Europe, Asia and the Middle East, saying its capabilities could contribute to making European supply chains more resilient.
Prevot also called for stronger economic cooperation between Brussels and Ankara, particularly in economic security, defence, innovation, clean energy and digital technologies.
"Our economic relationship should no longer be limited to buying and selling goods. We should also be developing, producing, and investing together," he said.
The Belgian foreign minister also voiced support for modernising the EU-Türkiye Customs Union, which he said had served both economies for around 30 years but needed to reflect changing global economic conditions.
Prevot also highlighted the results of a Belgian economic mission to Istanbul and Ankara in May, which brought together more than 400 participants.
Belgian and Turkish companies signed 33 agreements during the mission, covering sectors including defence, aerospace, energy and technology, he said, describing the outcome as encouraging.
The second edition of the EU-Türkiye Business Summit will bring together leading voices from business, government, and civil society to explore how the EU and Türkiye can transform deep economic interdependence into strategic resilience.

France’s Philippe says Le Pen’s EU proposals would ‘crack open’ bloc

PARIS — French center-right presidential candidate Edouard Philippe accused his far-right rival Marine Le Pen of trying to force a Frexit in disguise with her euroskeptic campaign promises.
“There is something in Marine Le Pen’s proposals that has the potential to blow Europe up, or let’s say to crack it open,” Philippe said at POLITICO’s Paris Competitiveness Summit on Tuesday.
The former prime minister — who is currently the best-placed centrist candidate to challenge the front-running Le Pen, according to recent polls — said Le Pen’s plan to unilaterally demand a drastic cut to France’s contribution to the EU budget was akin to “saying you want out of Europe” without openly advocating for leaving the bloc. Le Pen had previously called for a referendum in France on leaving the EU but dropped the proposal after her crushing defeat to Emmanuel Macron in the 2017 presidential election. Her party, the National Rally, now says it wants to change the EU from within.
Advertisement
Philippe, a fiscal conservative who has been pitching himself as the voice of reason in a campaign dominated by populist rivals, also slammed budget plans Le Pen unveiled last week as “grotesque,” accusing her of pitching “fantasy” savings.
Le Pen’s fiscal plans have faced serious scrutiny since being presented, with many observers saying they either lack key details or overestimate savings on major proposals like immigration. Progressive think tank Terra Nova wrote in a note out Tuesday that Le Pen’s budget presentation was “riddled with errors and contradictions” as well as “botched estimates.”
“She isn’t even able to estimate the cost of the pension reform she is proposing,” Philippe said.
Le Pen said in August that her plan to bring France’s legal retirement age back down to 62 for most workers would cost €9 billion a year, and last week she said she would lay out at a later stage how she intends to fund her flagship pledge. However, the Institut Montaigne, a fiscally conservative think tank, estimated the proposal would cost €34.7 billion a year.
Philippe is hoping to convince voters that his fiscally conservative agenda is the right path in a country burdened by a ballooning public debt and a budget deficit still above 5% of gross domestic product, in breach of EU rules.
Philippe said France needed to get its finances back on track to regain credibility on the European stage after a “loss of influence” over the past few years.
Advertisement
Though he currently leads a crowded field of centrist candidates, Philippe’s campaign has struggled in recent weeks to gain momentum — and far-left candidate Jean-Luc Mélenchon is now challenging the former PM for second place in the polls. France’s presidential election goes to a runoff if no candidate receives more than 50% of the vote, and Le Pen’s strong poll numbers all but guarantee her a spot in the second round.
Tough on China
The former prime minister pitched a pragmatic European agenda with less regulatory burden, more focus on investment and a tougher approach to China.
Philippe had some harsh criticism for an already embattled flagship measure of the EU’s green deal, saying the 2035 combustion engine ban has been “disastrous.”
There was “a great naiveté toward China,” which ultimately benefited from Europe’s push on electric vehicles, Philippe said.
“We need to much better protect our market,” he added. “If one wants access to the European market, one has to manufacture in Europe. If a carmaker doesn’t manufacture here, then we have to slap high tariffs.”
The EU is in the process of drawing up new “Made in Europe” rules that would favor European producers over those outside the bloc, in response to trade practices by competitors like China and the United States.
Advertisement
Shortly before Philippe took the stage, European Commissioner for Industry Stéphane Séjourné said at the POLITICO event that a Franco-German deal trading stronger protections on the definition of Made in Europe in exchange for a loosening of combustion engine rules should be finalized “in the next few hours or in the next few days.”
On artificial intelligence, Philippe aligned himself with Macron, advocating for European sovereignty in the field and the need to regulate what he described as “an instrument of power.”
“What I see is an AI world making money for the U.S. with European savings and European data, and that bugs me,” he said.

Foreign Ministry introduces secure AI system for classified government data
Finland
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
14:07:44 EEST
20:07:44 KST

Finland's Ministry for Foreign Affairs has introduced an artificial intelligence assistant designed to process classified government information, taking a step towards the use of AI in sensitive public administration work.
The system, named UMAI, entered pilot use on 13 October 2026 and operates within a secure environment approved for handling information classified at national security level IV, the ministry announced on Tuesday.
Add Helsinki Times as a preferred source on Google (opens Google in a new tab)
Level IV, known in Finland as TL IV, represents the lowest classification category for information requiring protection under the country's national security classification system. The designation covers material that authorities must handle under specific security requirements.
The ministry has initially provided access to a limited group of users who will test the system and assess its suitability for government operations.
The project aims to support ministry staff in their work while maintaining government control over information processing, technical infrastructure and security procedures.
According to the ministry, the pilot will provide experience of deploying artificial intelligence in government environments where confidentiality and information security requirements restrict the use of conventional AI services.
The Foreign Ministry and the Government ICT Centre Valtori are participating as pilot organisations in the development of a shared AI platform for Finland's central government.
Authorities intend to use feedback from the initial deployment to improve the system, identify technical requirements and assess opportunities to extend secure AI services to other government departments.
The ministry said the project would also contribute to developing national expertise in artificial intelligence and establishing common practices for its use across public administration.
Foreign Minister Elina Valtonen linked the initiative to Europe's efforts to maintain control over technologies and reduce dependence on external providers.
“In the age of AI, Europe must retain its ability to make its own choices and build sufficient capacity, competitiveness and capability to control critical technologies,” Valtonen said in the ministry's statement.
She added that European countries need the expertise and resources to assess artificial intelligence systems and determine how to use them according to their own requirements.
The government initiative forms part of efforts to strengthen European digital sovereignty, a policy objective focused on maintaining control over data, infrastructure and technologies.
The initial deployment remains a pilot project, with further development dependent on user experience and requirements identified during testing.

====================================================================================================

More than 300 scientists say AI oversight needed after 'preventable' hacks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
11:06:19 UTC
20:06:19 KST

More than 300 scientists call for greater AI security through new international body
In short:
More than 300 scientists from across the Americas, Europe, Asia, Africa and Oceania are calling for greater AI safety measures in an open letter.
The letter gave three recommendations, including establishing an international body to record and publish security incidents caused by AI.
What's next?
The federal government is finalising its national AI standards and plans to legislate new rules in 2027.
A group of 350 scientists from more than 30 countries has written an open letter calling for greater AI security by establishing an international body to record and publish security failures due to AI.
In several incidents in recent months, both overseas and in Australia, AI models have hacked into the systems of external organisations, including startup Hugging Face and multiple government websites.
"[These incidents] can also be seen as an irresponsible lapse in standard cybersecurity practices, preventable with stronger sandboxes and procedures," the open letter reads.
The scientists are from 31 countries, including Australia, and are based across Europe, Asia, Africa and Oceania, and said that without immediate change, future incidents could expose critical infrastructure.
It had three recommendations, including:
- adopting high-assurance containment systems, and initially defaulting to air-gapping, which means disconnecting from the internet for cyber-capable AI models
- creating an international body to record and track AI containment failures
- reporting security incidents to the body and making them public.
Toby Walsh, chief scientist at the University of New South Wales AI Institute, was among the signatories and said now was the time to act.
"We're lucky so far because the hacks that have happened have been incredibly modest cyber events,"
Professor Walsh said.
"But you can imagine what would happen if an AI [model] was trying to hack into the air traffic control system. It could easily cause significant harms to our day-to-day lives."
Safeguards will ensure incidents won't repeat
Following the Hugging Face hack, where an AI model broke into the company's systems, OpenAI described it as a "warning shot", saying without proper safeguards AI agents could take "dangerous actions" without human direction.
But Professor Walsh said one of the recommendations in the open letter would have prevented the hack entirely.
"We wouldn't have had the Hugging Face attack if they just air-gapped the test environment from the internet,"
he said.
"We wouldn't have had the Medicare hack if they'd been careful about giving the agents minimal permissions for the task it was needed to do.
"I mean, these are all incredibly basic things."
Professor Walsh said the most important element of the open letter was the creation of an international body to provide both information sharing and oversight of incidents.
He said similar bodies existed for industries such as banking, aviation and pharmaceuticals.
"Every time there's an aviation accident, independent inspectors go in and find out what happened, so that everyone can learn and not make that same mistake again," he said.
"We could do the same with AI because it's advancing rapidly and we need to make it as safe as possible."
International cooperation needed to prevent incidents
Last week, Assistant Minister for Science, Technology and the Digital Economy Andrew Charlton echoed those sentiments surrounding regulating AI similar to banking and aviation in a speech.
The government is finalising its national AI standards, and plans to legislate the new rules next year.
But Professor Walsh said there needed to be broad international consensus on AI because the technology was not being developed in isolation.
"So we need to cooperate internationally … in terms of perhaps reporting of incidents and sharing of information that doesn't mean that we have to regulate internationally," he said.
Cyber security improved after it became a requirement for companies to report incidents, Professor Walsh said.
"[Otherwise] no-one knew what was happening and we weren't able to learn from all of the mistakes that companies made," he said.
"Similarly here, we're relying at the moment on the goodwill of these companies to report what's going on."

Germany scrambles jets after airline radio glitch sends false hijack alert
FRANKFURT - A flight from Greece to Germany landed safely in Nuremberg on Oct 13 after a cockpit hijack alert that the airline attributed to a malfunction prompted the German air force to scramble two fighter jets.
Corendon Airlines blamed a malfunction in the radio communication system and said that “no emergency situation occurred and that at no point were the passengers, flight crew or aircraft in any danger”.
The incident on the Boeing 737-800, which had departed from the Greek island of Corfu, forced a brief suspension of operations at Nuremberg Airport, the plane’s scheduled destination, the airport said. Flight operations later returned to normal.
“From the cockpit, the code ‘7500’ (hijacking case) was transmitted, and furthermore, the pilot could no longer be reached by radio. For safety reasons, various alarm scrambles were then triggered,” German police said on X.
A German air force spokesperson said that two Eurofighter jets scrambled from Neuburg Air Base in southern Germany and accompanied the passenger jet until it landed.
Germany has two of those alarm squads, each with two fighter jets, to assess the situation when communication with civilian air crews is lost, which happens about once or twice a month, according to the air force’s website.
The alert comes less than a month after the co-pilot of a jet bound for Israel from Dubai attacked the pilot with an emergency crash axe, with the United Arab Emirates’ prosecutor general calling the incident a “terrorist attack”.
Corendon, a Turkey-based leisure airline, said the emergency code had been transmitted while the jet was in Croatian airspace “due to a brief malfunction in the radio communication system”.
“The situation was immediately monitored, investigations were promptly initiated and all necessary preparations were made. The aircraft landed safely at Nuremberg Airport,” it said.
A possible drone sighting had already disrupted air traffic at the airport overnight into Oct 13.
The German authorities have been on heightened alert since a failed attack involving an explosives-laden drone at a German airport in August, which authorities blamed on Russia.
Russia has denied any involvement. REUTERS

Budget cuts would impair Colombia peace court, search for disappeared, officials say
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
11:05:43 UTC
20:05:43 KST

Budget cuts would impair Colombia peace court, search for disappeared, officials say
BOGOTA, Oct 13 - Budget cuts proposed by allies of Colombia's new right-wing president would crimp investigations and trials of human rights abuses by the country's transitional justice court and hinder efforts to locate and identify 137,000 people who disappeared during the country's ongoing conflict, the court, the disappeared unit and advocates say.
Congress has until October 20 to decide how next year's $195 billion budget will be distributed.
The Special Jurisdiction for Peace (JEP) court and the Search Unit for Disappeared People (UBPD), created under a 2016 peace deal, both said lawmakers are discussing steep proposed cuts to their budgets.
The court investigates and tries leaders from the Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia (FARC) rebels and military personnel for crimes against humanity, war crimes and human rights abuses.
Set to operate through 2033, it has sentenced FARC leaders to reparations work for their role in kidnappings and military personnel involved in extrajudicial executions. The court has nine ongoing cases, including into sexual violence and child recruitment.
Joint committees from the Senate and lower house have initially approved cutting the JEP's 2027 funding by nearly 17% from this year's level, which the court says would endanger the rights of victims and defendants. The cuts still need to be approved by the plenary to become law.
The court said it has already implemented austerity measures. This month, it asked Congress for a 2027 budget of 821 billion pesos, about $250 million, which is below its original funding request.
Senator Enrique Gomez, a close ally of new President Abelardo De La Espriella, spearheaded a proposed cut of 100 billion pesos, about $30 million, to the JEP, which he says has been too slow on convictions and is too expensive to operate as is. He wants to reassign the funding to the regular court system.
The joint committees backed that cut and an additional 70 billion peso trim, which would give the JEP a budget of about $200 million next year.
The court is "an enormous bureaucratic machine," Gomez told local Blu Radio in September. "By every measure, that branch of the transitional justice system has been an operational failure. It has not fulfilled its purpose, it systematically offends victims and, ultimately, it amounts to a permanent guarantee of impunity, especially for crimes against humanity."
De La Espriella, a lawyer who represented people connected to right-wing paramilitaries, initially promised to dismantle the JEP, later saying he would respect the court but subject it to rigorous oversight. He has backed Gomez's proposal.
Neither Gomez nor De La Espriella's office responded to requests for comment.
The JEP, like all public entities, has shared a breakdown of its spending every year and is committed to adjusting to fiscal constraints, Magistrate Catalina Diaz told Reuters last week.
"What we do not believe would be fair would be to compromise victims' rights in the years ahead," she said.
Cuts would make it difficult to hold hearings in rural areas hit hardest by the conflict, provide victims with lawyers, psychological support and travel expenses, and ensure alleged perpetrators have their rights safeguarded, Diaz said. Security schemes to protect victims and former combatants would also be at risk, she added.
Some 90% of ex-combatants accused by the JEP have recognized their crimes, Diaz said, leading to moving scenes at public hearings where some victims have offered forgiveness.
"We have seen that restorative justice works and bears fruit," she said. "But the entire restorative methodology is costly because it is intensive in both human resources and time."
The JEP is only able to sentence perpetrators to jail time, up to 20 years, if they refuse to accept responsibility. Those who acknowledge their crimes serve reparations sentences like helping with exhumations of disappeared people.
The court will need to adjust to budget limitations, said Paula Vargas of the Institute for Integrated Transitions, an NGO which advises countries transitioning away from conflict, including by streamlining investigations into combatants who were not top leaders.
She said lawmakers must not handicap the JEP so much that it is doomed to failure.
"It's one thing to ask them to be more efficient and render their accounts. It's another to wipe them out," Vargas said.
Proposals to end the JEP's mandate in 2028 or require military courts to review sentences against former soldiers are unlikely to secure the two-thirds majority needed to pass in a deeply divided congress.
Potential funding cuts under discussion for the UBPD disappeared unit would reduce its operational funding by nearly 22%, to some $18.2 million for next year. Officials said this would threaten DNA collection from families and some 10,000 planned exhumations of remains.
“The reduction in investment funding directly affects the two pillars that make searches possible: interdisciplinary investigation and the territorial deployment of investigative and forensic teams, who carry out most of their work in remote and hard-to-access areas,” UBPD Director Luz Janeth Forero said in a September statement.
The unit has called on Congress to keep its operational budget at some $23.4 million for next year, the same funding it received for 2026. REUTERS

The fight to save endangered species may have a new weapon: sex-changing mouse clones
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
11:04:10 UTC
20:04:10 KST

Scientists racing to save critically endangered species may soon have a new tool at their disposal: sex-changing clones. For the first time, researchers managed to turn cloned male mouse embryos into females, giving life to healthy and fertile animals. The technique could one day help scientists rescue endangered species with only a few surviving individuals.
“I think it’s a really neat foundational breakthrough in reproductive science,” says Ben Novak, lead scientist at Revive and Restore, a nonprofit that promotes biotechnology for wildlife conservation. “Being able to manipulate chromosome counts and chromosome makeup will open up a new avenue of functional genomic science.” Novak wasn’t involved in the new study, which has not yet been peer-reviewed.
Inspired by the Okinawa rubble goby, a Japanese fish that can switch sex, researchers used a method based on the gene-editing tool CRISPR to eliminate the Y chromosome from male embryos, which typically carry both X and Y chromosomes. This process turned the embryos female with just a single X chromosome—typically notated as XO.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
The scientists first successfully tested the tool, which they named Y-CUT, on male mouse embryos obtained through in vitro fertilization. Then they produced cloned male mouse embryos through a process called somatic cell nuclear transfer, in which a donor mouse’s cell nucleus was transferred into an egg cell with its own nucleus removed. The team applied Y-CUT to the cloned cells and transferred them to surrogate mothers, which gave birth to healthy, fertile female clones. In other words, the researchers were able to produce both male and female clones from the same donor male. The cloned females carried the exact same genome as the donor male (except for the Y chromosome).
In a surreal twist, the donor male mouse had the chance to meet its female clones. And it got weirder: The cloned females mated with male clones, producing offspring with regular XX or XY chromosomes. That’s why the researchers say the tool could be useful for rescuing endangered species with a few individuals left—scientists could create fertile breeding pairs using just one male donor.
“It certainly can have long-term future applications for extreme cases of species revival,” Novak says. Still, as tantalizing as the prospect of cloning a creature out of extinction may be, the method is limited—and not just because it requires at least one male. For example, female rodents carrying XO chromosomes may be fertile, but many other mammals, including horses and humans, can’t reproduce when they have this chromosome combination. It’s possible that supplementing the technique with other elements, such as future technologies that could add an X chromosome to XO embryos, might help overcome this problem.

The “Namejs 2026” Exercise Tests Cooperation Between The National Government And Municipalities In Crisis Situations
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
11:02:51 UTC
20:02:51 KST

During the comprehensive national defence exercise "Namejs 2026", held from 6 to 8 October, the Crisis Management Centre (CMC) led the participation of state administration and municipal representatives in an exercise scenario designed to test civil-military cooperation procedures, interinstitutional cooperation at both national and municipal level, the business continuity of critical sectors during crises, and the coordination of support required for national defence purposes.
More than 1200 participants from the civilian sector took part in the exercise, including representatives of the State Chancellery, ministries, government services, agencies and state-owned enterprises, as well as representatives of municipal civil protection commissions, municipal services, agencies and enterprises. This year, representatives of non-governmental organisations also participated in the work of some thematic groups and municipal civil protection commissions. The exercise provided an opportunity to assess how institutions from different sectors and levels of government coordinate information, align actions and develop a common understanding of the situation to support timely decision-making.
The exercise scenario included the simulation of the evacuation of residents from several municipalities across Latvia, as well as responses to incidents disrupting public order, energy security, cybersecurity and the information environment, including the spread of disinformation.
Attention was paid to accommodating evacuated persons and ensuring their basic needs were met. The successful implementation of such tasks requires cooperation across multiple sectors and levels of government, ranging from organising evacuations and transporting people to safety to providing suitable accommodation, food, water and other essential services. The exercise enabled participating institutions to practically test their ability to coordinate these tasks under crisis conditions.
Arvis Zīle, Head of the Crisis Management Centre, said: “Exercises of this kind are an important step in practically testing the national crisis management system. They allow us to assess not only the preparedness of individual institutions to perform their functions, but also their ability to work together towards a common objective. We will use the lessons learned to further improve interinstitutional coordination mechanisms in cooperation with the institutions involved and strengthen the state's capacity to manage complex crises.”
A total of 12 thematic working groups operated within the civilian component of the exercise, including the Mass Population Movement (Evacuation) Coordination Group, the Food and Water Supply Group, the Health and Pharmaceuticals Group, the Financial Services Group, the Communications Coordination Group, and others.
Observers from the Baltic states, Finland, Sweden and NATO also attended the exercise.
This was the first time that the Crisis Management Centre had been involved in planning and conducting an exercise of this scale. The experience gained will serve as a foundation for further strengthening national resilience and the crisis management system in cooperation with other participating institutions. The lessons learned during this year's exercise will also contribute to the development of proposals for next year's exercise scenarios and other specialised civil protection exercises, supporting the continued improvement of crisis management mechanisms across state and municipal institutions.

Ukraine's digital networks top winter priority - Balashov
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
14:02:46 EEST
20:02:46 KST

The Ministry of Digital Transformation has made the resilience of digital infrastructure and mobile networks a priority in winter preparations, so that they keep working during power outages, Deputy Minister of Digital Transformation for Cybersecurity and Cloud Technologies Vitaliy Balashov told Interfax-Ukraine.
"The government, in the person of the prime minister, has put winter preparation and maximum resilience first. So we have also put the resilience of digital infrastructure and mobile networks first, so that mobile operators can keep their networks running during blackouts," the deputy minister said in the interview.
The ministry took a systemic approach aimed at reform and long-term protection of physical infrastructure, and work on it is under way, but it has also singled out urgent measures that can be implemented before winter, he said.
Balashov said this means stepping up cooperation with foreign partners, "because one of the ways to protect physical infrastructure is to go outside Ukraine."
Among other areas of work, Balashov named a drafted document, the Concept for the Development of Cloud Services in Ukraine 26-31, which sets out a principle similar to the American Cloud First, under which any system, when it is created, should immediately be considered for hosting in the cloud.
The deputy minister said the ministry softened and reworded this approach as Cloud Smart. In particular, it proposed an option under which the ministry reserves the right, even at the level of principle, either not to move to the cloud or, conversely, to require use of the cloud where appropriate.
Separately, Balashov said the ministry has drafted another concept document that includes the Cloud Smart principle and a focus on a hybrid multicloud architecture model, which involves using different cloud environments and providers.
"It is important for us to follow the multicloud principle, because it diversifies risks, raises resilience and gives freedom to choose a provider," the deputy minister said.
In this component, the Digital Ministry regulates only state organizations, while businesses that are critical infrastructure will face additional resilience requirements, including use of a hybrid and multicloud model, he said.
"We do not impose specific providers. Business should choose them from those available on the market, taking its own needs and risks into account," Balashov said.
The deputy minister also said the Digital Ministry is open to cooperation and already works with foreign cloud providers.
The ministry also said it does not seek to depend fully on infrastructure abroad. In particular, Ukraine should have an option to keep a copy of state resources, while their owners must have procedures for restoring systems quickly if problems arise either in Ukraine or abroad.
Balashov said this function was enshrined in an update to Cabinet of Ministers resolution No. 1009, which amends resolution No. 205.
"If a system cannot be restored automatically, its owner must guarantee to us, as the ministry, that it can be restored within a clearly defined number of hours if problems arise either in Ukraine or abroad," he said.
According to him, both foreign providers authorized in Ukraine and Ukrainian companies with infrastructure abroad can be used to back up state registers abroad.
All operators, regardless of origin, must go through the same procedure to obtain the right to provide services to the state and critical infrastructure, the deputy minister added.
Balashov also said the procedure is currently quite complex and consists of confirming security certificates, equipment location and ownership of the equipment.
He said one reason for the changes to the law on cloud services is the complexity of its procedures, which large international cloud providers sometimes cannot pass because of their internal requirements.
"So we met them halfway and are simplifying this procedure a little, but we are not easing the security challenges in this procedure," Balashov said.
For the Digital Ministry, it is important that cloud providers working with the state and critical infrastructure facilities meet national security requirements, so the Security Service of Ukraine is involved in the procedure, the deputy minister said.

I’m a pediatrician. Loss of human connection is the biggest threat to kids, not AI | Megan Moreno
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
11:00:56 UTC
20:00:56 KST

We have become obsessed with the idea that screens are destroying human connection.
The evidence seems to be everywhere. Each week headlines warn of teenagers addicted to phones, a loneliness epidemic and the dangers of AI. The release of The Social Reckoning leads us to ask, “How bad were those guys at Meta?” and then ultimately wonder, “How bad am I if I still use Instagram?” In our day-to-day, we observe workers eating lunch alone while scrolling and friends choosing online games over offline gatherings.
But what if we are focusing on the wrong problem?
The greatest threat to connection may not be technology itself. It may be our growing unwillingness to curiously, thoughtfully and openly communicate about the role technology plays in our lives.
As a pediatrician, this issue often manifests in my clinic. Parents arrive with worries about their teens’ screen time. The parent will demand that their child “fess up” and reveal how many hours they waste on their phone every day. The atmosphere is immediately charged. The teen becomes defensive. The parent is frustrated.
I often suggest that we start somewhere else.
I ask: “Can you share a little about what you do when you are using technology? What do you enjoy? Are there things about your technology use you are worried about and willing to discuss?”
The answers are not usually what people expect. One teen tells me about the friendships she maintained on social media after moving to a new town. Another shows me videos he created to promote his school’s upcoming play. One shares how digital design tools are changing the fashion industry, so she is trying to learn about them now. Another quietly admits that gaming has become so consuming that it feels stressful.
As the conversation unfolds, something changes. The tension in the room eases. Parents relax. The teen patient might even smile a few times. We talk about strategies, relationships, stress and health.
What began as an argument about a device becomes a bigger conversation about health, relationships and life itself.
It often feels that our conversations about technology have become trapped in a false choice between two extreme camps. One camp is made up of the pro-tech enthusiasts, thought to embrace every new device or platform. The other camp is composed of preachers of digital abstinence.
The result is a polarized debate dominated by blame, shame and moral judgment. Instead of asking how technology affects our relationships, our sleep, our work, our wellbeing, we argue endlessly about whether technology is “good” or “bad”.
I was reminded of this recently during a community event focused on digital media. The event included a youth panel with several brave adolescents, willing to speak to an audience of their teachers, community members and parents. I asked the adolescents a question: could you describe a positive conversation you had with a parent about technology?
Every single panelist shook their head.
“I’ve never had that,” one teenager said, uneasily eyeing her mom who was sitting in the front row. The other panelists agreed.
It was a striking moment. Parents routinely talk their children through setbacks in sports, clubs, friendships and school. They listen, ask questions and offer support. Yet when it comes to technology, many conversations begin and end with warnings, criticism or fear.
Why is this?
For years, parents have been barraged by alarming headlines about screen time and mental health. Many parents worry there is probably only one right way to approach technology, and they’re failing miserably. Parents are also navigating the necessity of using their own devices for work, home and communication.
The real anxious generation just might be parents.
So how do we fix this? The solution begins with curiosity. Parents can ask what interests their children have online, and why those interests matter. Parents can ask their kids about what questions or worries they have about their tech use, and share some of their own concerns. If a parent missteps by scrolling cute cat videos and delaying dinner, they can acknowledge it and make it a teachable moment for themselves and their kids.
Because children do not need adults who have all the answers.
They need adults willing to ask questions.
These conversations matter because they lower the temperature of the debate. Once we move beyond panic and polarization, we can begin asking better questions on the societal level. How should digital platforms be designed to ensure safety? What obligations do technology companies have to children? What policies would support healthier digital environments?
If we want to preserve human connection in the age of social media and AI, the answer is not to simply spend less time with technology. It is spending more time talking openly with one another. The irony of the current moment is that as we worry endlessly about technology pulling us apart, it might be our inability to have conversations about technology that ultimately divides us.
Megan Moreno, MD, MSEd, MPH, is a co-author of Connecting: Raising Kids in the Digital World, published by the American Academy of Pediatrics on 13 October.
