Land, water, clay shape Çanakkale Biennial
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
10:33:34 UTC
19:33:34 KST

Spanning 15 venues, the biennial turns Çanakkale’s urban and rural landscape into an exhibition space.
Like tides that reshape coastlines, the 10th Çanakkale Biennial examines how nature, memory and human experience are transformed through the constant interaction between water and land, bringing together more than 60 artists from nine countries in northwestern Türkiye.
Titled “Metcezir // Ebb & Flow,” the biennial opened on Oct. 10 at the Troy Museum, drawing on Çanakkale’s coastal geography, ceramic traditions and archaeological heritage to explore the traces left by these encounters. Spread across 15 venues in the city center and surrounding rural settlements, the exhibition makes the region itself part of the experience.
The movement of the tides offers a framework for thinking about change: Shorelines erode and accumulate sediment, while landscapes preserve evidence of what has passed through them. The biennial extends this natural cycle to questions of cultural memory, material production and humanity’s relationship with the environment.
The setting lends the theme particular resonance. Situated along the Dardanelles, which connect the Aegean and Marmara seas, Çanakkale has long been shaped by the movement of water, its coastal livelihoods and its cultural history. The artworks explore how the natural world shapes human experience and how people, in turn, leave their mark on the environments they inhabit.
Ceramics take center stage
The Troy Museum anchors the biennial’s first “Special Focus: Ceramics,” bringing contemporary works by artists including Füreya Koral, Elif Uras and SEDNA into dialogue with the region’s archaeological heritage.
Among the participating artists is Lara Ögel, exhibiting ‘Gravity,’ who sees clay as more than a material, describing it as a body that reflects and carries lived experience. “The cracking, shedding, expanding and contracting of the clay are all deeply significant,” Ögel said. She views these physical changes as a visual map of inner experiences, with the material’s layers mirroring the emotional and existential changes people undergo. Working with ceramics, she added, requires patience, understanding and time, becoming a form of confrontation with one’s own soul.
SEDNA presents two new works inspired by memory and transformation. “İz” (Trace) draws on marks left by the sea on sand and the impressions experiences leave on the body and spirit. Its twisted form evokes sisterhood, interconnectedness and resilience. “TAÇ” (Crown), meanwhile, combines handmade glass scenes, plants collected from the museum garden and references to the sun and life cycles, presenting accumulated experience as a record of memory.
In the city center, Mavi Ev (Blue House) brings together ceramic and glass works, painting and digital art. Gülden Ataman’s ‘For Eyes That Listen, For Hands That Watch’ challenges conventional ideas about the material’s fragility and function. Rather than considering them musical instruments, she describes each piece as a “sound-seeking device” for acoustic exploration. “Their output depends entirely on the performer’s manual dexterity and acute listening skills,” Ataman said. The sounds that emerge depend on touch and the combinations chosen by each performer, potentially producing entirely new acoustic experiences. Local musicians explore these possibilities in a video installation at the venue.
German artist Gerrit Frohne-Brinkmann, meanwhile, juxtaposes a handcrafted ceramic snake with a mass-produced singing fish toy in ‘Pack.’ Drawing on Çanakkale’s historic ceramics, known for their animal motifs, he brings traditional craftsmanship into conversation with a familiar object of popular culture. “I really enjoy the confrontation between these two different styles of sculpture,” he said, highlighting the contrast between handmade and mass-produced objects that depict animals but carry different values and meanings.
The biennial extends into buildings whose previous uses reflect the city’s history. The Korfmann Library, housed in a former school and tobacco warehouse, presents works engaging with archaeological heritage and traditional building techniques, including Funda Susamoğlu’s response to a terracotta figure at the Troya Museum and Eymen Aktel’s work with adobe.
Along the Sarıçay riverbank, former acorn warehouses now house several exhibition spaces. MAHAL features Johannes Vogl’s Summer Rain – The Smell of Memories, which explores the scent of rain on Aegean soil and vegetation. The neighboring DemirHAN presents works by artists including Ozan Atalan and Mesut Öztürk, whose pieces draw on video, ceramic fragments and firebricks.
The Balıkhane, a working fish market, hosts works addressing marine ecosystems and coastal landscapes. These include Carmen Bouyer’s project connecting the Gediz and Rhône deltas and Annika Boll’s digitally constructed underwater environment. At the ASTİM industrial estate, visitors can see works by A. Serkan Aka and Gözde Mimiko Türkkan at Helin Boztepe Studio and by Manfred Heinze at Süleyman Yılmaz Studio. British artist Kay Aplin’s site-specific public artwork at Çanakkale Biennial Park draws on Troy’s nine archaeological settlement layers. Nine ceramic tile designs combine local botanical motifs with forms drawn from archaeological finds. Produced with the support of Kale Group, the installation is intended to remain in the city after the biennial closes.
Further afield, ORMOS in Yukarı Tartışık village hosts works by Can Altay, Renée Levi and Stijn Ank. The Adatepe Olive Oil Museum presents works by Andreas Treske and Fulya Çetin, while restored stone houses at İda Blue in Adatepe display works by Dilara Akay, Hakan Yılmaz and Meliha Coşkun.
The biennial also marks the 20th anniversary of the Çanakkale Biennial Initiative (CABININ), which has worked to sustain contemporary art in a city outside Türkiye’s main cultural centers. Together, the exhibitions, running until Nov. 20, invite visitors to consider change not as a clean break with the past, but as an ongoing process in which landscapes, materials and human experiences continually shape one another.

19:33:15 KST

Breadcrumb
'Haunting' accounts of Israeli sexual abuse of Palestinian children prompt calls for justice
Accounts of Palestinian schoolgirls afraid to cross Israeli military checkpoints after soldiers exposed themselves to women and girls stayed with Dr Rubin Minhas long after he reviewed the evidence.
For Minhas, a co-author of a new opinion piece in The BMJ, a leading medical journal, the descriptions were "haunting" – not only because of the sexual abuse, but because Palestinian children were forced to navigate military checkpoints simply to reach their classrooms.
"I think it just brought home to me how absolutely bizarre it is that having to go to school and pass through military checkpoints is the norm before we even get to the sexual violence," he told The New Arab.
The accounts include Palestinian schoolgirls in Hebron who feared passing through a checkpoint where Israeli soldiers had exposed their genitals to women and girls, according to a UN investigation cited by the authors.
Published on Tuesday, the article brings together evidence of conflict-related sexual violence against Palestinian women, men and children, exposing patterns of abuse across Israeli detention facilities, military checkpoints, raids and displacement sites, and demanding independent investigations and accountability.
Drawing on survivor testimonies, UN investigations and medical, humanitarian and human rights reports, the five authors examine how sexual violence has been used against Palestinians under Israeli occupation, and the devastating physical and psychological consequences for victims.
The purpose, Minhas said, was to draw together evidence "dispersed across accounts of detention, gendered abuse, humiliation, and displacement, and harm to children, to actually paint a picture of what was going on".
Conflict-related sexual violence, or CRSV, refers to sexual violence directly or indirectly linked to conflict. It encompasses rape, sexual torture, sexualised humiliation and reproductive harm, among other abuses.
'Occupation is violence'
For Palestinian children, the consequences of Israeli sexual violence extend far beyond the immediate abuse, affecting their education, relationships, psychological wellbeing and sense of safety.
The article cites a 2025 Save the Children report in which more than half of 165 Palestinian children, aged 12 to 17 at the time of detention, reported witnessing or experiencing sexual violence in Israeli detention, including rape threats, forced stripping and genital assault.
A separate 2026 UN investigation documented sexual and gender-based violence against Palestinian children during arrest and detention, including forced public nudity, sexual humiliation, rape threats, genital violence and allegations of rape.
In one particularly degrading incident documented in humanitarian and UN reports, a Palestinian boy was stripped and urinated on.
The Save the Children report also revealed the lasting psychological toll of Israeli detention, with former child detainees experiencing anxiety, panic attacks, nightmares, depression and social withdrawal.
Twenty percent reported intentional self-harm, while 45% did not return to school after their release. The figures reflect the wider consequences of detention, rather than harm attributed exclusively to sexual violence.
"We’re now moving away from the immediate act and are thinking about the long-term effects, the effects on their education, psychology, their development – it becomes intergenerational," Minhas said.
The evidence also documents sexual violence and humiliation against Palestinian women and girls at checkpoints, during military raids, in detention and in communities facing displacement.
Women described being forcibly undressed, sometimes in public or in front of their children, sexually touched during searches and threatened with rape.
Some were beaten after refusing to undress, while others faced rape threats in front of their children, threats to publish degrading footage online and the denial of sanitary pads while menstruating in detention.
The authors also cite Israeli soldiers posting photographs and videos of Palestinian women's underwear taken from homes in Gaza. Many of the images were subsequently removed, while the soldiers' social media accounts were closed or made private.
In the occupied West Bank, Israeli settlers have used sexual violence and humiliation to intimidate Palestinian communities, including exposing their genitals, threatening rape, attempting to touch women's bodies and stalking women on their way to latrines.
Fear of such violence has prevented women from going to work and girls from attending school, while some families have resorted to early marriage for their daughters.
Among 39 displaced households interviewed in Area C of the occupied West Bank, more than 70% identified threats to women and children, particularly sexualised violence, as a decisive reason for leaving, the authors write.
The article also details severe sexual torture inside Israeli detention facilities, including forced nudity, rape threats, genital violence, rape and assault with objects.
Palestinian detainees have suffered serious genital and rectal injuries following sexual torture involving batons and electric shocks.
One documented case involved a detainee whose rectum was ruptured, requiring surgery and the creation of a stoma. Other accounts describe detainees losing one or both testicles after being beaten on their genitals.
The authors also cite a February investigation by the Committee to Protect Journalists, which interviewed 59 Palestinian journalists released from Israeli detention. Seventeen, or 29%, described experiencing sexual violence, including two who recounted rape.
Minhas told The New Arab that these accounts exposed a reality of Palestinian life that remains poorly understood.
"People have very little understanding and awareness of what actually is going on and what the daily life of Palestinians entails, the kind of indignities that people have to suffer," he said.
"There is a fundamental aspect of living under military occupation that involves violence. And you know, at its very core, occupation is violence. You know, that’s the fundamental transaction that takes place, and it will manifest itself in various ways."
Sexual violence as a systematic yet underreported issue
The authors argue that the extensive evidence demonstrates recurring patterns of sexual violence against Palestinians rather than isolated incidents.
They cite a 2025 UN Commission of Inquiry finding that specific forms of sexual and gender-based violence "de facto form part of" Israeli security forces' "standard operating procedures" towards Palestinians.
The commission also concluded that sexualised torture, including rape and genital violence, was carried out with either explicit orders or implicit encouragement from senior Israeli civilian and military leaders.
It found that Israeli military and civilian justice systems were failing to ensure accountability for sexual crimes against Palestinians.
Despite the extensive evidence documented by human rights organisations and UN investigators, Minhas said medical research into sexual violence against Palestinians remained strikingly limited.
"The interesting thing here, from a medical perspective, was the remarkable lack of documentation and publication of conflict-related sexual violence in this setting," he said, contrasting it with the much larger body of research into sexual violence in other conflicts, including Ukraine.
He suggested that political pressures could discourage academics and researchers from investigating abuses against Palestinians.
"I think there’s a degree of personal and professional exposure for academics and for researchers seeking to try and study and understand this subject," he said.
The BMJ article brings together existing investigations and testimonies rather than presenting new primary research. Its authors warn that sexual violence remains significantly underreported, particularly among men and children, while restrictions on independent investigations have helped sustain impunity.
They also cite figures from Israeli rights group Yesh Din showing that, of 1,260 cases involving alleged offences by Israeli soldiers against Palestinians known to the military law enforcement system between 2017 and 2021, just 11, or 0.87%, resulted in indictments. The figures concern alleged offences more broadly, not sexual violence alone.
The authors identify the denial of independent access as a major obstacle to documenting abuse and holding perpetrators accountable.
The UN Commission of Inquiry has lacked access to Israel and the occupied Palestinian territories since October 2023, while the International Committee of the Red Cross has been unable to visit Palestinians held in Israeli custody.
Although Israel's Supreme Court ruled in June 2026 that the prohibition on Red Cross visits must be lifted, access had not resumed by the time the article was published.
The authors demand full, unrestricted access for independent investigators and medical and humanitarian organisations, arguing that accountability is impossible without scrutiny of the places where abuse occurs.
"The first instance is we need to get independent investigators into those settings," Minhas said. "And it’s only once you’ve got independent investigators in those settings that there’s actually a prospect that people may find that the impunity that they’ve enjoyed disappears."

Europe must switch to ‘war-mode’ defence production, Polish defence minister says

19:32:01 KST

Polish Defence Minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz said that Europe must accelerate the production of ammunition and weapons to match Russia’s pace, warning that failure to do so would negatively impact Europe.
Poland’s Minister of National Defence and Deputy Prime Minister, Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz, said Europe must adopt a “war-mode” mentality in its defence sector or risk harming Europeans in the future.
“I am actually an advocate for the war-mode when it comes to the production in defence sector,” he said at a press conference on the sidelines of the Warsaw Security Forum on Tuesday.
“This is what the Russian Federation does at the moment. We cannot overlook this fact.”
Russia shifted towards wartime defence production before its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, and is projected to spend 7.5% of its gross domestic product on its armed forces in 2026.
In 2025, Russia produced roughly seven million artillery, mortar, tank and rocket rounds, according to a recent Estonian intelligence report. Russian forces currently use roughly 10,000 to 15,000 rounds per day in their continued aggression against Ukraine.
In contrast, Europe’s defence industry has been shaped by decades of underinvestment and fragmentation.
Russia is outpacing the EU in ammunition production, with the 27 member states and Norway expected to produce just two million 150mm ammunition shells this year, according to a leaked report on Europe’s defence readiness.
Rearmament efforts by European countries and NATO members have driven the strongest annual increase in defence spending since the Cold War. Despite this, EU member states’ total defence spending in 2025 was estimated at €418 billion, or 2.2% of EU's total GDP, the report states.
Kosiniak-Kamysz said the “time has come” for Europe to prepare to defend itself by multiplying its defence production.
Failure to do so would be a “costly” mistake for Europeans, he warned, adding: “It's one of the disadvantages, but also it will impact (and) affect us negatively in future generations.”
Poland is among the biggest spenders of its GDP on defence capabilities, spending 4.7% on core defence capabilities, according to the US envoy to NATO, Matthew Whitaker.

Basic social assistance instead of several payments — Parliament adopted the law
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
13:31:53 EEST
19:31:53 KST

Basic social assistance instead of several payments — Parliament adopted the law
Kyiv • UNN
Parliament supported basic social assistance for low-income families instead of several payments. The law will take effect on January 1, 2028.
On October 13, the Verkhovna Rada adopted as a whole a bill providing for the introduction of a new type of state social assistance—a basic social assistance payment to replace several other payments, an UNN correspondent reports.
Details
Bill No. 15094, "On Basic Social Assistance," was supported in the second reading and as a whole by 247 members of parliament.
The document stipulates that "basic social assistance" is a monthly payment provided to a low-income family in cash, the amount of which depends on the average monthly aggregate income of the family and the property status of its members.
The concept of a "base amount" is also introduced—a statutory monetary indicator used to determine the amount of basic social assistance and established by the Law on the State Budget of Ukraine for the relevant year.
It should be noted that on September 15, the Cabinet of Ministers submitted to the Verkhovna Rada a draft State Budget for 2027. According to the document, among other things, it is proposed to establish that in 2027 the base amount used to calculate the amount of state social assistance for persons with disabilities since childhood and children with disabilities, as well as state social assistance and the care allowance, will be 4,000 hryvnias.
Who will be able to receive basic social assistance
"The right to basic social assistance is granted to Ukrainian citizens who belong to a low-income family or a family in a crisis situation and who permanently reside in Ukraine," the bill states.
Foreigners and stateless persons who legally permanently reside in Ukraine, as well as persons recognized in Ukraine as refugees or persons in need of additional protection, will also have the right to basic social assistance. In addition, Polish citizens who are legally present in Ukraine will have the right to basic social assistance on an equal basis with Ukrainian citizens.
How to apply for basic social assistance
A family representative will be able to submit an application for the appointment of basic social assistance:
-  through a CNAP; 
-  through an authorized structural unit (authorized official) of the executive body of a council (in the absence of a center for the provision of administrative services); 
-  through “Diia”; 
-  through the service center of the body that assigns basic social assistance; 
-  by mail.  
The transition to this assistance will be carried out exclusively upon the recipient’s application. Basic social assistance will not be assigned if its calculated amount is lower than the amount of state support that the family or individual was receiving on the date of application.
The application for the appointment of basic social assistance must be accompanied by the written consent of each adult family member to the processing of personal data, the initial assessment of the family’s needs for social services, and their obligations to fulfill the conditions of the social contract for the appointment of basic social assistance.
MP Olena Shuliak said that since July 1, 2025, Ukraine has already been implementing a pilot project providing basic social assistance that has combined several types of payments. These include assistance to low-income families, assistance to single mothers, assistance to large families, payments for children whose parents do not pay child support, as well as assistance to persons who are not entitled to a pension and to persons with disabilities. The new bill establishes this model on a permanent basis, taking into account the results of the pilot project.
Shuliak explained that the new model provides for a case-management method: each low-income family will be given an individual support plan based on an assessment of its actual needs. At the same time, the application-based principle, under which a family applies for assistance on its own, will be supplemented by the community’s active identification of such families.
The transitional provisions of the bill state that it will enter into force on the day following the day of its publication and will come into effect on January 1, 2028.
At the same time, from January 1, 2028, to December 31, 2028, families eligible to receive state social assistance for low-income families, assistance for children of single mothers, assistance for children raised in large families, temporary state assistance for children whose parents evade paying alimony, are unable to support the child, or whose place of residence is unknown, and state social assistance for persons who are not entitled to a pension and persons with disabilities, shall be entitled to apply for basic social assistance, provided that the payment of the specified types of assistance is terminated in accordance with the procedure established by the Cabinet of Ministers of Ukraine.
We remind you
A new service for applying for basic social assistance has been launched in "Diia"; it will replace five different payments. This pilot project is designed to run for two years, while the government is working to make it permanent.

fiat multiplay concept transforms family car into pickup with sliding rear module

fiat multiplay concept transforms family car into pickup with sliding rear module
fiat unveils the multiplay concept car at the 2026 paris motor show, with a sliding rear module that transforms a family vehicle into a pickup.
[FEATURED]
FIAT MULTIPLAY CONCEPT DEBUTS AT 2026 PARIS MOTOR SHOW
Fiat has unveiled Multiplay at the 2026 Paris Motor Show, a concept car that combines the space of an MPV, the character of an SUV and the versatility of a pickup truck. Measuring 4.45 meters in length, the vehicle explores how a single design could accommodate the changing needs of family life, from school runs to weekend adventures. At its heart is an adaptable architecture that allows the car to physically transform between two configurations. For now, Multiplay remains a design experiment rather than a preview of a specific production model.
The transformation revolves around a sliding rear module called Metamorfosi, developed around the vehicle’s C-pillar. Moving along dedicated guides, the structure converts the enclosed six-seat family configuration, which includes an additional multifunctional element, into a four-seat pickup with an open cargo bed. Bicycles, sports equipment and bulkier objects can occupy the newly exposed space. Even the rear spoiler has a second job, rotating into an integrated rack capable of carrying two bicycles.
FIAT MULTIPLA LEGACY RETURNS WITH FLEXIBLE SEATING
The concept revisits the unconventional spirit of the original Fiat Multipla, whose designs challenged expectations of how much could fit inside a relatively small car. The 1956 Fiat 600 Multipla accommodated six passengers within approximately 3.5 meters, while its 1998 successor arranged six seats across two rows in a body less than four meters long. Multiplay continues this fascination with spatial efficiency, although its approach goes beyond rearranging passengers to reconsider the vehicle’s entire configuration.
Inside, flexibility extends to smaller details. The so-called Petsenger seat can accommodate a child car seat, provide space for a pet, or function as a table or storage compartment. Part of its cushion can even be detached and used as a leash, while a folding bowl is tucked into the door. Another feature, the Sunseat, transforms the front passenger seat into a lounge chair when parked, using the dashboard as a backrest beneath the panoramic roof. Apparently, even the passenger seat deserves a little downtime.
WATERMELON COLORS AND MONOMATERIAL TEXTILES SHAPE THE INTERIOR
The color palette takes inspiration from an Italian summer, specifically a watermelon. Bright green bodywork recalls the rind, while red, pink and turquoise tones spread throughout the cabin. A soft pink floor and pixelated gradients introduce further contrast, turning the interior into a distinctly playful environment. Material choices follow a more practical logic, with monomaterial textiles produced through a stitch-free 3D knitting process intended to reduce waste. Waterproof finishes are incorporated into the areas designed for children and pets.
Large windows and a panoramic roof bring natural light into the cabin, while a horizontal dashboard references the Mediterranean horizon. Technology takes a comparatively discreet approach: the integrated display disappears from view when the vehicle is switched off, leaving a cleaner interior surface. Rather than introducing a new screen for every imaginable activity, Fiat uses Multiplay to investigate how adaptable architecture and multifunctional components might shape future mobility. Whether any of these ideas reaches production remains to be seen, but the concept makes a convincing case for giving family cars more than one personality.

Muslim American candidates make inroads in local races across US
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13

Breadcrumb
Muslim American candidates are making inroads within local races across US
At a recent fundraiser for local Muslim American candidates in the Fremont area of northern California, a young boy said he wanted to run for political office in the future.
For the three candidates, Aziz Akbari, Qasim Lodhi and Kashif Wasim, whose families hail from South Asia, this is part of what brings them joy on the campaign trail leading up to the 2026 midterms on 3 November–after decades of not seeing their own Muslim communities represented in politics.
"I went to my first city council meeting when I was seven. It was the very first council meeting after 9/11. My family had just moved to Fremont a year prior," Akbari said to The New Arab. He recalls how at the time the city was considered safe and affordable, in contrast with today’s exorbitant housing prices.
25 years later, as a city council candidate himself, he said, "That council meeting was specifically put together to welcome the Muslim community to Fremont to make sure we knew we were a part of this community."
"I juxtaposed that experience with what we saw in the media, where Muslims, immigrants were demonised just for their background, their religion. I would look at home, and though Fremont wasn’t perfect, it was a welcoming community, a safe community. It was a community that wanted us here. That was so empowering for me, and that stuck with me," he continued.
At 18, eager to give back to his community, he ran for mayor of Fremont (losing his first election, though undeterred from politics). He eventually worked his way up through politics at the city’s consumer affairs division, and now works in the water department.
According to the Council on American-Islamic Relations, there are currently around 225 Muslim American elected officials, the majority of whom serve at the local level.
"Local politics is incredibly important because 90 percent of your interactions with government happen at the local level. The roads you drive on, the schools your kids go to, the water your drink, the safety you rely on," he said.
Qasim Lodhi, who is running for city council of nearby Union City as a first-time candidate, said he was inspired to get into the race to bring people together and address common issues, such as the rising cost of living.
"The gap between people and their representatives has been growing exponentially over the last decade or so," he told TNA. "The more public pressure they have, the harder their job gets. It is up to the people who need to participate more. People are spending more time having to earn a living and less time at city council meetings. They can't take the extra stress."
Lodhi, whose professional background is in high-tech, believes he can help connect people through technology for day-to-day concerns, such as road safety.
Kashif Wasim, who is running for the local New Haven school board, also wants to see technology put to better use, particularly after the pandemic, which saw a general decline in test scores.
"I want to prepare our kids to be ready for the future," he tells TNA. He notes that many students are not getting jobs in their fields after graduation, and he worries this could get worse if they’re not prepared for the AI revolution. "We're looking for more creativity from students. If you want to change the world, change the education. I want to do impact that lasts longer."
In addition to a growing number of Muslims running for office, there are also more candidates who would identify as allies on issues such as Israel's genocide of Gaza, domestic surveillance, and academic freedom.
There are currently five Muslim-American members of Congress–Representatives Rashida Tlaib, Ilhan Omar, Aisha Wahab, Andre Carson and Lateefah Simon. If Abdul El-Sayed and Adam Hamawy win their races in Michigan and New Jersey for the Senate and the House, they will add to the Muslim leadership in Congress. Though the numbers are growing, Muslim Americans still have not reached proportional levels of the current populations in terms of political representation.
“We are around eight to 10 million Muslims in the US. Based on that number, we should have 12 to 14 in Congress. Now, we have five in Congress, ma sha’allah,” says IsTafa Zaidi, founder and president of the US American Muslim Public Affairs Council, noting that a decade ago there was essentially no Muslim representation in Congress.
"Our goal is to encourage our youth, our capable individuals to run for office and to serve the community," he told TNA. "We're encouraging people to go to the school board, to the city council, to engage where they live. They’re a part of the system and society."
"Our slogan is: A seat at the table. You need to have a seat at the table to make sure that you are at the decision-making table," he added.

How Elon Musk Learned to Love Political Spending Again
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
10:30:04 UTC
19:30:04 KST

Elon Musk, the world’s richest man who also spent more than $250 million for President Donald Trump’s re-election campaign, said in May last year that he planned “a lot less” in political spending for future elections—including the upcoming midterms. But newly disclosed donations to Republican groups have since made him the biggest known donor ahead of the November elections.
For the 2026 election cycle, which began in January 2025, the Tesla and SpaceX CEO has already spent $366 million—of which more than $276 million went to Republican groups and his super PAC since July—according to new reporting by the New York Times and Reuters. Representatives for Musk gave the media outlets data on his political largess ahead of the Thursday deadline when many super PACs must disclose their third-quarter spending.
Of the $276 million, $158 million reportedly went to the Senate Leadership Fund, a super PAC tasked with helping Republicans maintain their majority in the chamber; it is one of the largest known political donations in history. Another $20 million went to the Congressional Leadership Fund, which was set up to re-elect House Republicans aligned with House Speaker Mike Johnson of Louisiana.
Musk’s America PAC, which was created for the 2024 elections, received over $76 million to try to reach Republican voters and boost turnout. America PAC is boosting Republican candidates in seven battleground states and nearly three dozen House races.
Other conservative groups also received funds from the U.S.’s most high-profile billionaire. The Lone Star Liberty PAC, which backs Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton’s campaign for the U.S. Senate, received $10 million. Paxton, a Trump-backed Republican, is in a tight race with Democratic state lawmaker James Talarico.
Another $10 million went to the Republican Governors Association, and $2 million to the Republican Attorneys General Association. The Times also reported that Musk has donated more money through groups that have not disclosed their donors.
Andrew Romeo, spokesman for America PAC, told the Times that the “robust investments have allowed the G.O.P. apparatus to get its message out so Republicans can have a fighting chance to defy history.”
Musk’s donations signal his commitment to the political right and improving his relationship with Trump and the GOP after a public falling out with the President last year and threat to create a third political party. Republicans are looking to defend their majorities in Congress this November, but the task has appeared much harder as Democrats have made major gains among voters disgruntled by Trump’s policies.
Musk’s evolving attitude toward political spending
Musk’s massive donations for the 2026 midterms are a far cry from his previously conservative approach to political spending, though his positions have changed over the years.
At a 2015 Vanity Fair event, Musk said he would “get involved in politics as little as possible,” adding that he spends only a nominal amount for his business interests. Federal Election Commission records show that in 2015, Musk donated $5,000 to Hillary Clinton’s campaign, and another $5,000 to the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee.
But Musk shifted in 2017: his donations began to lean Republican, and he spent nearly seven times more on GOP campaigns than Democratic ones. In 2018, amid reports that he donated a large sum to a Republican House PAC, Musk posted on then-Twitter that he was “not a top donor to any political party.” Musk took over Twitter in 2022, reinstated Trump’s account, and, months later, rebranded it as X.
Since then, he’s continued to court the GOP through financing election efforts. During the 2024 election cycle, he created America PAC, though Musk denied reports at the time that he was donating as much as $45 million a month to boost Trump’s election campaign. He’s also targeted swing-state voters, even saying that he would give out a legally questionable $1 million prize to registered voters in a bid to boost turnout.
On an X livestream during the 2024 election, Musk said that America PAC “is going to keep going after this election, and prepare for the midterms and any intermediate elections.”
Musk then took a brief role in the Trump Administration as a special adviser to the President and led the so-called Department of Government Efficiency to reduce federal spending. He oversaw a government restructuring effort that disrupted services, eliminated hundreds of thousands of federal jobs, and led to numerous legal battles. As Musk officially stepped down in May 2025 amid a spat with Trump, he said that he thought he had “done enough” of political spending. But he included a caveat: “If I see a reason to do political spending in the future, I will do it. I do not currently see a reason.”
In 2025, Musk apparently saw a reason to channel more funds into political causes, namely midterm primary elections. He first threatened to help defeat lawmakers who voted for the Trump Administration’s gargantuan spending bill, vowing that he would help make them lose their primaries “if it is the last thing I do on this Earth.” Musk even suggested he would support Rep. Thomas Massie (R, Ky.), a vocal Trump critic, in his reelection campaign. (Massie would later lose the primary.)
The latest data on Musk’s spending isn’t surprising, given what’s at stake for him if Republicans lose.
House Democrats have called for probes into his companies’ government contracts that are worth tens of billions of dollars, as well as into his work running DOGE. He rejects accusations that his companies depend on those contracts: in an Oct. 2 post on X, Musk wrote that “roughly 90% of SpaceX’s revenue this year will be commercial” and that its government revenue for the last quarter of the year will be less than 5%. “SpaceX is FAR MORE commercial relative to the average company in America,” he said.
In a Bloomberg podcast published last month, New York Times reporter Maggie Haberman said that Democrats had privately told her they planned to subpoena Musk over DOGE if they gained the power to do so. House Democrats have had multiple unsuccessful attempts to subpoena him since Republicans repeatedly blocked them.

Alex Gibney’s ‘Musk’ Has a Unique Perspective on Daddy Issues
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
10:30:00 UTC
19:30:00 KST

Only one person agreed to be Alex Gibney’s new Elon Musk documentary immediately: Musk’s father. “We had Errol Musk at ‘hello,’” Gibney says.
Eventually, the director would speak with scores of Musk’s associates for his film. His first wife, Justine Musk, appears, as does his ex-girlfriend Ashley St. Claire. Journalist Kara Swisher, LinkedIn cofounder Reid Hoffman, myself, and WIRED global editorial director Katie Drummond also spoke to Gibney for Musk, which hits theaters nationwide on Friday. But landing Errol Musk, with whom the Tesla and SpaceX CEO has a complicated relationship, was a watershed.
“Everybody else took a lot of persuasion,” Gibney says. “It was very difficult to get people to appear because the risk profile for talking about Musk in a way that was honest was high.”
Once Gibney interviewed all of his subjects, he had enough material to make a documentary that runs nearly four hours, including a 10-minute intermission. It’s a damning portrait of the trillionaire CEO, detailing how much of his genius is based on his formidable ability to promote his own mythology—and the stock price of his public companies.
Musk never agreed to an interview with Gibney. Instead, the director’s team researched every public comment Musk ever made and created a simulated Elon Musk who appears throughout the film.
I spoke with Gibney earlier this month about his experience making the film, why he decided to make his simulated Elon attractive, and what material he had to leave on the cutting room floor.
This interview has been edited for length and clarity.
ZOË SCHIFFER: Alex Gibney, thank you so much for being with us today.
ALEX GIBNEY: Good to see you, Zoë.
This shouldn’t spoil anything, but in the four years that you spent making Musk, Elon Musk never agreed to sit down with you for an interview. Instead, your team looked back through the archives of everything he has said publicly, and you put together a sort of simulated interview, which appears throughout the film as a through line. Basically, it plays into Musk’s idea that we are all, in fact, living in a simulation. How did you decide on this approach for the film?
Well, what were we gonna do? He’s the main character.
I actually thought because he’d been so outspoken about this idea of a simulation, that cinematically we should lean into that. We should play in Elon’s sandbox and have a simulated interview. As we began to develop that idea, by using his real words, his actual audio recordings, but placing them in a kind of avatar which we would design, I think there became all sorts of thematic reasons to do it.
One was because he himself had said we’re living in a simulation. But two was the importance of this notion in the Elon Musk story of the shifting sands between what is real and what is unreal. Then also, because a lot of the film deals with his issues of AI, that discomfiting relationship that we’re beginning to explore, all of us on planet Earth, with these AI LLMs and how we begin to project things on these computer interfaces, it felt like this might be something interesting to do.
By the way, you’ll notice that when Elon is talking to people in a normal interview situation, he rarely looks at the interviewer or at the camera. He’s always looking this way or that way. So we designed this in a very different way, where he’s looking right down the barrel of the lens directly at the viewer, and we thought that that would be OK. We’re gonna give Elon a break, and actually, I thought our avatar made him look pretty good compared to some of the recent images of him.
I have a question about that because your simulated Elon Musk—I think it’s fair to say—looks a lot hunkier than present day Elon Musk. He’s kind of chiseled and tan, and …
It is kind of a two-day growth of beard.
Exactly. Was that an intentional choice? And if so, can you just talk about why that was?
It was. I joke about this, but he’s the star of my movie, I want my star to look good. But I think also it would’ve been a mistake to go into slop AI territory, like some of the images that Elon’s fans are posting about me right now, to sort of denigrate him visually.
Also, to some extent, the story is also about image building, too. So I thought, “OK, let’s have some fun with that as well.” Because we had a lot of choices. I mean, we started out with the design firm, like how should he look? What should he be dressed in? You know, we put him in a gamer chair, a leather jacket. There were conscious choices.
That extends to some of the comments he makes, where I don’t find like the most bumbling comments that Elon ever made.
When we have somebody speaking about something, I want a rejoinder from Elon. We looked for the best rejoinders, like how can he come back at us? Now, later on in the film, his statements become more and more fantastical, but that also is part of what happens.
I think it really worked for the film. I’ve seen it a couple times and I think there are these famous images of Elon Musk. I’m thinking of the one where he’s on the yacht and he’s shirtless. There, it seems like if you had leaned into a less flattering image, you would’ve been playing on his turf, but in a way that would undermine the message of the movie. Whereas elevating his look allowed you to hold him quite accountable in a way that comes across pretty fair.
Yeah, we were respectful. We gave him a good look. And much better by the time we go to the archive, particularly the archive of the SpaceX IPO, when he’s begun to start looking like Kim Jong Il.
I’m curious about your thoughts on ethics. It’s not putting words in someone’s mouth, because these are all statements that Elon Musk has really made, and it’s not even like you’re particularly mashing stuff together.
But your decision, for example, to have him look right at the camera, you are making decisions for him in a way that you couldn’t with a live interview subject. So I’m just curious if you could speak to the ethical implications of that.
I think that goes to the heart of what’s different about a documentary like this and maybe a podcast interview in the sense that we’re rendering that image in a kind of broader cinematic context. The imagery itself is intended to either convey meaning or to raise questions for the viewer that they should start to think about.
As you know from being interviewed for the film, we interviewed you in front of a green screen and then placed you in a background, which we sort of reveal at different times in the movie. All of this had to do with this kind of strange unreality, real unreal world we’re living in right now.
Mm-hmm.
But also by shooting him looking into the lens I sometimes do that and I sometimes don’t. There is this interesting psychological relationship that you begin to have with a subject that I think is both real and unreal at the same time, which was part of this larger conceit in terms of trying to find a way to make the movie and the formal devices in the film itself reflect some of the thematic concerns.
Right. It also makes him feel like there is a fair amount of conviction behind what he’s saying, and there’s this relationship between him and the audience.
I feel like over the course of his public life, he doesn’t appear to have had an allegiance or ideology to one coherent political identity or to even his colleagues or close friends. These things are shifting and changing. So I am curious how that kind of came up for you in the making of the film of wanting to convey an Elon Musk in the simulated interview that represented, to the best of your ability, the quote-unquote, “true Elon.”
I mean, it’s a shape-shifting image and one which is, after all, confected, which is useful, particularly when you’re using it as a vehicle to put these statements in. I agree with your point that you just made about Elon’s ideology. I think there are a lot of wise and very perceptive books that have been written that in my view sometimes make one kind of critical flaw. They try to render a coherence about Elon’s thinking that I’m not sure is there. I think he’s far more of an improviser and shape-shifter. He has an image of himself that he wants to convey, but he’ll sculpt and change that image according to conditions and evidence, like the way he acted with Obama versus the way he acted with Trump.
I mean, there was a history there, but still they’re both serving the same purpose for him, which is, “How do I cadge the most amount of resources out of the federal government?”
I’ve thought about this a fair amount as well. I think his acquisition of Twitter now acts as a very clear example where in the moment it was clearly this impulsive decision, but now that it’s become this big source of political power for him, there’s this tendency to be like, “Oh, he was playing a complicated game all along.”
My view has always been that if Elon has a superpower it’s that he has a pretty high risk tolerance, and so he’s able to make impulsive, rash decisions and then deal with the fallout in a way that a slightly more cautious person might not be able to, for better or often worse.
He’s so comfortable with risk. It’s as though he goes through life on a canoe moving down the rapids. When he sees a rock there, he goes this way. He sees another rock or a shifting current, he goes that way. In the case of Twitter, as you pointed out in your book, he kind of bought the company on a dare, and he grossly overpaid for it and also abandoned all due diligence.
From the standpoint of a businessman, it was just dumb. But he didn’t care, and he had so many resources, what did it matter? Twitter, now X, was always a vehicle for his ambitions and his ability to court retail investors.
I don’t think it occurred to him until later when he had virtually destroyed the value of the company for the rest of us, that actually this would be a good propaganda platform for me. That’s what it becomes. Then suddenly it actually has enormous political and economic utility in a way that I don’t think he thought through at the beginning.
So Musk aside, plenty of people did speak to you for this film: Musk’s first wife, Justine; his former girlfriend, the influencer Ashley St. Clair, who he has a kid with; his father; former business partners; former colleagues; people he’s fired; the former ambassador to the United Nations, Samantha Power; Kara Swisher.
Walk me through the process of getting these people to say yes, to trust you. Specifically, was there anyone who really surprised you in their immediate willingness to say yes, and anyone who really needed extra time and conversation with you in order to be able to say yes?
Almost everybody who appeared in this film needed time to be able to process and accept appearing, in part because there was a sense of risk associated with it. Only one person agreed immediately, and that was Errol Musk.
Oh my gosh.
It was almost like, what’s that line from that great film “You had me at …”
“You had me at ‘hello.’”
We had Errol Musk at hello. “Hello, Errol, would you like to appear in this documentary?” “Yes.” We quickly rushed a crew over to his house. I did a remote interview in South Africa. It was the one interview we did that was not green screen, and he was remarkably revealing, sometimes in intended and sometimes in unintended ways.
Everybody else took a lot of persuasion. I was having conversations with Justine for over a year, I think, before she agreed to sit down. Even somebody as powerful as Reid Hoffman, same thing. So it was very difficult to get people to appear because Musk’s—the risk profile for talking about Musk in a way that was honest was high.
In some cases I did talk to a lot of people, sort of powerful people in Silicon Valley, on background—some of whom had fond feelings toward Elon and some who didn’t. I found it interesting that there’s sort of like talking to people in a gentleman’s club, and one doesn’t talk about other people publicly.
While I did learn things when they were talking to me on background or off the record, I found that kind of revolting in a way. It’s like we’re dealing with a figure now who has enormous sway over all of us, and isn’t it important to weigh in on that kind of public debate?
But that wasn’t the view that they had. In fact, there’s a guy I know who is friends with Elon and treasures his friendship with Elon, and I said, “Let’s have a conversation off the record. You know, tell me what’s great about Elon and why you like him so much.” He said “I would never betray a friend like that.”
I got that for my book as well. I don’t feel as surprised. I think if we were talking about six, seven, eight, nine, 10 years ago, like, yes. But these are similar people to those who are flying to Washington, DC to pay fealty to Trump, and going directly against values that they were talking about not that long ago.
That’s right.
I do wanna talk about Errol Musk because you brought him up. There’s this very powerful interview in the film where he talks about his son. He seems to have had a very big impact on Elon Musk’s life, and not necessarily a positive one. This was kind of the central thesis of Walter Isaacson’s biography of Elon Musk.
It kind of came down to daddy issues. So I’m curious to get your perspective on Errol’s influence on Elon and how you balanced showing the hardship of his childhood without using that as an overly simplistic explanation for his behavior today.
I think that’s an important point. I do think that Errol Musk had a powerful impact on Elon, because of how Elon felt he was treated by his dad, sometimes cruelly, psychologically. We don’t know of any kind of physical abuse. But also I think, you know, by watching Errol, you grok—to use a term from the Heinlein book—the notion that the apple doesn’t fall far from the tree.
There’s an element you can see the character of Elon. We kept it in a kind of short contained section and as an element of how we can think about Elon Musk. But I think the Walter Isaacson conclusion, in a way, is a little bit too easy. There are a lot of people who’ve been bullied or abused by their parents who don’t end up becoming bullies or abusers.
And to say it’s a kind of a mechanical thing that happens is kind of letting Elon Musk off the moral hook. That was an issue I had with Walter’s book. To some extent, we’re all grateful for the fact that he was able to spend so much time with Elon. There’s an accretion of detail in the book that’s valuable.
But I think the conclusions were sort of a get out of jail free card for the performative cruelty that ultimately he engaged in. Yet you need to know about the origin story without—it can be an explanation without being an excuse, I guess is what I would say.
I would imagine that in the making of a film like this, there is an open question at the beginning in particular about whether you’re actually going to get enough access for this to work. It’s certainly a question with features that we write. I’m curious if there was a particular interview, maybe with someone close to him, where you knew like, “OK, we’re, we’re gonna be able to do this. I think we’re gonna have enough.”
Well, weirdly, it didn’t happen until very late, and I would say it was the Justine Musk interview. The Justine Musk interview gave me insights into his personality that were very powerful in both understanding him as a person, but also understanding some of what he did thematically.
Because I asked her—and this answer is not in the film, but it helped to guide me—“What was it that attracted you about him back in college?” They met in college in Canada. And she said it was his enormous confidence. And then the other thing she said that’s powerful that is in the film is that she learned about gaslighting from Elon Musk.
That gaslighting thing, the idea of trying to convince somebody that the truth is other than what it is, and to suggest that you’re crazy and if you don’t go along, is a super important insight into who Elon is. And confidence, of course, is what allows that to happen.
Justine’s was such a powerful interview in the film. There are multiple moments where she cries or is near tears. She comes across as just so genuine, and I think she also seems like someone who doesn’t appear to be in it for attention or power or money. Like, there’s a point in the film where I think she says, “I really wanted to have a say in how this story was told.”
I’m thinking specifically of when their first child died in a SIDS-related incident, and Elon Musk tweets that he was holding the child. The child died in his arms. And Justine says, “No, this was one of the most defining moments of my life. He died in my arms.” You really just see how Elon has hurt her over the years.
That’s right. That gets me kind of emotionally worked up even as I think about it, because of course that moment was deeply painful for Elon, which is what Walter Isaacson spent some time on in the book. But to credit-grab in the midst of a tragedy like that seems so petulant and small and, you know, talk about main character syndrome.
One of the defining things about Elon Musk is that over time, as he increased more and more power, there was only one character in all his companies, and that’s Elon Musk, and only one character in all of his marriages. That’s Elon Musk. Everyone else recedes into the background. It’s interesting.
Justine is a storyteller. She’s a talented novelist. I went deep into reading her blogs and also the article that she wrote for Marie Claire. You know, her ability to be a storyteller is actually quite profound precisely because she’s reaching for a deeper truth.
I think when Elon is a storyteller, he’s actually reaching for fiction. He’s reaching to mythologize in a way that undoes the truth, that steers us away from that kind of hard work of getting to the stuff that is really deep and painful because it’s true.
I am curious about your take on this because it’s a question that I have had about Elon Musk: Does he actually believe what he’s saying or is he knowingly lying?
I think it’s closer to the former, and I’ve dealt with a number of characters who are like this. Sam Harris in the film makes a distinction between liars and bullshitters, and liars, of course, have to assiduously keep track of the truth in order to know when and how they’re lying.
Bullshitters just say what comes to their mind. It’s a kind of—it’s on the right track, but sort of insufficient. I think for somebody like Elon Musk—or people in the past like that I’ve dealt with, like Elizabeth Holmes or the guys at Enron or even somebody like Lance Armstrong—in the moment, because you feel a kind of righteousness about your cause, you feel you’re kind of entitled to make things up, You feel over time so entitled and so corrupted by this notion that the end justifies the means, that some kind of psychological trick is played inside your own mind where in order to be forceful and confident about what it is you’re saying in the moment, you have to believe it.
I reckoned with that with Lance Armstrong, where he could look people in the eye at a press conference and say with great force, “How dare you say that I, as a cancer survivor, would ever use performance-enhancing drugs?” And then he’d get down off the podium and do a bag of blood.
But I think in the moment he did believe what he said, because that’s how you come off as being effective. You see it particularly for people who become kind of addicted to a growing power that they have, and they see that also they have an ability to convince, like Elizabeth Holmes did.
It’s a psychological quirk that kind of takes over, and it’s peculiar, but I think it’s real.
It’s so hard to remember when talking about Elon Musk that this goober in an Occupy Mars T-shirt who’s thrashing around with a chainsaw waxing poetic has had this undeniable impact on so many people’s lives and livelihoods, and a lot of that impact has been negative.
The part of your film about DOGE, Elon Musk’s Department of Government Efficiency, which is a short-lived stint in Washington, DC where he fired, I think, 300,000 federal workers to, quote-unquote, “solve the federal deficit.” Spoiler alert, he didn’t even come close. That was probably one of the hardest moments to watch.
Samantha Power, former ambassador to the UN, spoke specifically about the lives lost, thousands and thousands, and millions more projected, after he shuttered USAID. I’m curious, given all you know about Elon Musk at this point, and the reporting you did on DOGE, what do you think that period and that experiment was really about for him?
It wasn’t about waste, fraud, and abuse. There was an aspect of glee and performative cruelty that we tried to represent in the film by showing the DOGE cuts as a kind of first-person shooter game, juxtaposed of course, with the sober testimony of Samantha Power, who talks about how many children died as a result.
But I think in many ways the waste, fraud, and abuse was kind of the magician’s sleight of hand to say, “This is what we’re doing.” But what he was really doing was something very self-serving, which as a big tech baron, was literally destroying the regulatory state.
If there was a lot of collateral damage, people died, disease went up, who cared? It was the destruction of the inspectors general, the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau. He called everything corrupt without any evidence and so forth and so on.
The other thing, and the more controversial thing, which we’re all still chasing in a way, is the fact that the DOGE boys, who were clueless about the agencies they went into, nevertheless seemed to know an awful lot about data extraction and data access.
And they were granted, according to one head of IT at a federal agency I talked to, super admin status, which you know better than I, allows them to break through all sorts of silos that are intended to be erected to either protect classified information or protect our private data.
So the DOGE boys had access to vast amounts of data that no one has ever had access to in history. All of that didn’t go unnoticed, but it was the flash over the chainsaw all of the press conferences kind of hid a lot of what was really going on, I think.
Yeah, if you’re really worried about waste, fraud, and abuse, then there’s a certain level of care that you would take in your auditing. The DOGE boys were posting on X this kind of, quote-unquote, “wall of receipts” where they would talk about contracts that they’ve slashed, not understanding that in procurement paperwork, oftentimes you’ll put the total lifetime amount that could ever be spent on a contract, which is sometimes quite different, millions of dollars different, from the actual amount that was spent.
So they were claiming savings that were nowhere close to what had actually been saved. There was another, and this is in the film as well, moment where Elon Musk was talking about how they were finding tons of people who were getting Social Security benefits who were 150 years old, not understanding that when you don’t have a birthday for someone in the Social Security system, which is built on very arcane technology, really old code, it defaults to a birthday that shows someone as 150.
Anyone who had worked in SSA would’ve been able to tell them that, but they didn’t seem, to me, to be particularly interested in the details, which again, if you’re really worried about waste, fraud, and abuse, that’s all about details.
Correct. And indeed the detail that you mentioned about Social Security was actually posted on the Social Security website. So they could’ve read the website. But it goes to this kind of performative cruelty where it almost didn’t matter to them, you know?
One of the more chilling interviews, which I got from a deposition, was with one of the DOGE boys, a kid named Nate Cavanaugh.
Mm-hmm.
The questioner asked him, “Did you not care about the lives that were being affected by all of these mass firings and, and the kind of pain and suffering that would cause?” And he said, “Well, no, because we thought it was more important to reduce the federal deficit.” Next question: “Did you reduce the federal deficit?” “No.” But, you know, for a guy who’s supposed to be such a genius, you would think there would be some analysis done.
But that parallels what happened at Twitter, as you know better than anybody. In other words, they would fire people at Twitter who had actually critical jobs, without even knowing what they did.
Ezra Klein has talked about this. I think it’s really true. Like at Twitter, when you make a rash decision or you fire people, the feedback loop with the company or social media is pretty small. You can see the effects of that pretty quickly. The site starts to get glitchy.
In government, the feedback loop is really long. You don’t get to see immediately the impact of those decisions, and to me that appears to be a large reason why the effects were just so much more devastating, and honestly, while he has admitted publicly DOGE was a failure, it seems like there was no move made to kind of correct any errors.

Current account deficit to stay manageable, says Şimşek
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
10:29:57 UTC
19:29:57 KST

Treasury and Finance Minister Mehmet Şimşek said on Oct. 13 that Türkiye’s current account deficit was expected to remain manageable, supported by growth in goods exports and resilient services revenues.
His comments followed Central Bank data showing a current account surplus of $4.05 billion in August. The rolling 12-month deficit nevertheless widened to $42.1 billion from $41.5 billion in July.
Writing on X, Şimşek said Türkiye’s diversified energy suppliers and strong infrastructure continued to support energy security as risks to global supply increased.
Türkiye had spent $1.1 trillion on energy imports over the past 26 years, equivalent to 1.6 times its cumulative current account deficit over that period and twice its current gross external debt stock, he said. The figures demonstrated the strategic importance of the green transition, he added.
“We expect measures aimed at reducing dependence on imported energy to strengthen our resilience against global price shocks over the medium and long term, while also contributing to an improvement in the current account balance,” Şimşek said.
The government would continue policies to expand market access through free trade agreements, increase the value added of exports and improve competitiveness in services such as health tourism, contracting, software, education, engineering and design, he said.
The Central Bank figures showed a goods deficit of $3.75 billion in August, while services generated net inflows of $9.7 billion. Net travel receipts stood at $7.3 billion and net transportation receipts at $3.3 billion.
Excluding gold and energy, the current account recorded an $8.2 billion surplus.
Direct investment generated net inflows of $141 million, while portfolio investment recorded net outflows of about $1 billion. Official reserves increased by $7.14 billion during the month.
For January-August, the current account deficit totaled $31.5 billion, compared with $19.7 billion in the same period of 2025.
The government’s Medium-Term Program projects a deficit of $47.5 billion, or 2.6 percent of gross domestic product, in 2026. It forecasts a decline to $38.5 billion, or 1.9 percent of GDP, in 2027.

NEW DELHI: Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) founder Abhijeet Dipke on Monday backed the INDIA bloc’s protest march to the Supreme Court, saying demonstrations against Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar would continue across the country until he resigned.Dipke welcomed Monday’s INDIA bloc protest in Delhi, describing it as a “very large and important protest” and calling for more such demonstrations across the country.
“It is necessary for the entire country to unite and hold such protests, especially the INDIA bloc, as it is in the opposition,” he said.“Such protests will continue across the country until Gyanesh Kumar resigns. We hope that this happens,” Dipke added.
Reacting to the Congress Kerala unit’s now-deleted social media post demanding Chief Justice of India Surya Kant’s resignation over his remarks that law and order was not the Supreme Court’s responsibility, Dipke said he did not want to comment on the controversy at this stage.Dipke, however, questioned the Supreme Court’s response to alleged irregularities involving the Election Commission, asking what action the court had taken against the poll body.
“What action have they taken against the Election Commission? They have taken no action at all,” he said, referring to the court’s recent remarks on the issue.Citing the deletion of voters’ names in West Bengal, Dipke questioned the reasoning that those unable to vote could do so in a subsequent election.“Will the Supreme Court tell Narendra Modi the same thing, that he should not contest the election this time and can contest the next time? If they cannot say that, then on what basis are they telling voters this?” he asked.The remarks came amid a political row over the Congress Kerala unit’s post targeting the CJI. The post, which was later deleted, said: “Dear Surya Kant, if law and order is not your domain, resign now. We will find your replacement who can handle it.”
The BJP criticised the Congress over the post, accusing it of attacking constitutional institutions. Union minister Kiren Rijiju said that while protest was every citizen’s right, “brazenly abusing” constitutional authorities was deplorable.BJP spokesperson Sudhanshu Trivedi accused the Congress of seeking to create anarchy by undermining constitutional institutions. He also criticised the INDIA bloc’s march to the Supreme Court, alleging that the opposition was attempting to influence or intimidate the judiciary.
Earlier, CJI Surya Kant had said that law and order was not his domain when asked about the restrictions imposed amid anti-CEC protests in Delhi. He also said the Supreme Court’s doors remained open to everyone, including ordinary citizens and lawmakers.

Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“The United States continues to sell our equipment and munitions to our European and Canadian allies that then provide it to Ukraine,” Whitaker said.
“I know of no change to that program.”
Whitaker referred to NATO’s Prioritized Ukraine Requirements List (PURL) mechanism, where alliance members bankroll US weaponry for Kyiv.
The comments followed a Financial Times (FT) report on Sunday, citing unnamed European officials, that Washington is considering cutting arms flows via PURL over US President Donald Trump’s Friday diesel deal with Moscow.
The rumors stem from Kyiv’s hinted refusal to halt attacks on Russian refineries unless Washington secures a bilateral ceasefire that protects Ukraine’s energy grid, with the current terms, after Trump announced an energy truce, rumored to overwhelmingly favor Moscow by including only refineries.
Whitaker’s comments also echoed those of US Supreme Allied Commander Europe General Alexus Grynkewich at the same event, who called for Europe to bolster arms supplies to Kyiv via PURL in response to Russia’s hybrid threats.
However, Whitaker also told AFP he did not wish to comment on “unconfirmed reports” without referencing the FT report.
Zelensky Says Ukraine Received No Warning From Partners Before Russian Ballistic Missile Strike on Kyiv
Kyiv’s air defense challenges in winter
Whitaker also acknowledged the challenges Ukraine faces this winter, as Russia targets the country’s energy grid while Kyiv’s air defenses remain in short supply.
“Ukraine is facing a winter where, if there is not an energy ceasefire,... their electricity and heating infrastructure could be under a lot of pressure,” he said.
“Air defense largely is in high demand, and the availability is probably not as good as we would like,” he added.
Blackouts have already begun in Kyiv and other cities as the energy grid comes under attack. Strikes on Monday, one day after Trump boasted of an energy truce, also affected water supplies in Kyiv, less than two months before the arrival of subzero winter temperatures.
But Whitaker called it a “short-term challenge” as he said companies are coming up with alternatives to traditional air defense.
“You’re seeing a lot of companies try to come up with new and innovative ways to knock projectiles out of the air,” he said.
“Ultimately, we’re going to solve this problem… I think it’s a short-term challenge,” he added.
As Russia uses more jet-powered drones against Ukraine – with numbers spiking 10-fold from 350 in June to nearly 3,500 in September – Kyiv has also ostensibly explored more cost-effective ways to shoot down the drones.
Apart from using onboard 20mm autocannons from F-16 fighter jets, Ukraine also announced new models of faster interceptors to counter the jet-powered drones.
In Kyiv, automatic machine gun turrets are also being erected around the city after Russia began hitting the city’s bridges in October, with the Ukrainian Air Force hailing their successes in downing jet-powered drones.
But the quantity remains limited for now, and it’s unclear whether Kyiv can scale production enough to cope with the upcoming Russian onslaught this winter.

Zelenskyy: No warning from partners about Russian ballistic strike on Kyiv
Commenting on Russia's recent attacks on Ukrainian cities, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has said that Ukraine received no warning from its partners about the ballistic missile strike on Kyiv on the evening of 12 October.
Source: Zelenskyy on X (Twitter), as reported by European Pravda
Details: Zelenskyy noted that starting that evening and continuing into 13 October, Russia attacked Ukraine with more than 100 different weapons, including jet-powered drones, loitering munitions and ballistic missiles. A significant proportion were shot down, but not all of them.
"There was also a particularly vile ballistic missile strike on Kyiv – five missiles that hit civilian infrastructure. Unfortunately, we received no early warning from our partners about this strike," Zelenskyy said.
He stressed that intelligence about Russian ballistic missile launches helps save lives and is one of the most critical issues.
"This is precisely what helps prevent people from being killed – when there is an early warning about ballistic missiles," the president added.
Zelenskyy also said that Ukraine has not struck Russian oil refineries or the energy sector in general for two days since US President Donald Trump announced an energy ceasefire.
"During this time, the Russians have attacked both our energy facilities and our critical infrastructure, sending absolutely clear signals that they have no intention of refraining from strikes on Ukraine. [...] Our position remains unchanged: Ukraine is ready for reciprocal steps toward de-escalation, and effective pressure on Russia is needed to make de-escalation happen. Wars end when the aggressor realises that it cannot prolong the war," Zelenskyy stressed.
He added that international pressure on Russia contributes to bringing peace closer.
"But direct or indirect support for Russia, slowing down assistance to Ukraine, and making it harder to protect lives against ballistic missiles will certainly not help bring peace. Everyone needs peace. A strong America, a strong Europe, and strong partners are needed," Zelenskyy concluded.
Background:
- Earlier, it was reported that during talks with the Ukrainian team in Florida on Friday 9 October, Trump's envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner threatened to stop sharing intelligence with Ukraine because of Ukraine's strikes on Russian oil refineries.
- Reuters sources denied that any such threats had been made.
- Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha, meanwhile, has said that Ukraine continues to receive intelligence from the United States.

Drone attack targets two merchant ships off Bulgaria's coast, with Ukrainians among casualties
This was stated by Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev, according to Novinite, as reported by Ukrinform.
Radev also announced plans to hold talks with Russian Ambassador to Bulgaria Eleonora Mitrofanova and NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte.
During an emergency meeting of the Security Council under the Council of Ministers, Radev reported that the Maltese-flagged cargo ship CHELSEA 3 was struck by three drones approximately 18 nautical miles east of the city of Byala. A second vessel, identified as the Azov Concord, sank approximately 17 nautical miles east of the village of Krapets after being struck by a drone.
A distress signal from the CHELSEA 3 was received at 1:30 a.m. According to the crew, the drones struck the deck and side of the vessel. The Maritime Rescue Center in Varna immediately launched a rescue operation, and a border police unit evacuated all 15 people on board: seven Ukrainian citizens and eight Azerbaijani citizens.
The vessel, owned by a Ukrainian company and registered in Odesa, sails under the Maltese flag. The crew was taken to the port of Varna, where, according to preliminary reports, five sailors received medical treatment for minor injuries.
The second vessel sank approximately 17 nautical miles east of Krapets. One crew member was rescued, but the available information does not allow for determining the full composition of the vessel’s crew or the fate of other people who may have been on board.
“Another attack on merchant ships in the immediate vicinity of Bulgaria’s territorial waters is absolutely unacceptable,” Radev said.
He added that Bulgaria will seek international assistance to investigate these attacks and determine the origin of the drones. He emphasized that the available evidence is insufficient to pin the blame on a specific country, although, in his words, the outcome of these attacks appears to benefit Russia.
“The logic of what is happening suggests that the outcome of these attacks benefits the Russian Federation,” Radev said, explaining his intention to hold talks with Mytrofanova.
Bulgaria’s permanent representatives to NATO and the European Union have been informed of these incidents.
As Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha stated on social media platform X, Ukrainian citizens were injured during Russia’s latest attack on commercial vessels near Bulgaria’s territorial waters.
“Russia's latest attack on commercial vessels near Bulgaria's territorial waters, which injured Ukrainian and Azerbaijani citizens, once again demonstrates Moscow's deliberate disregard for civilian lives and maritime security in the Black Sea,” the foreign minister noted.
Sybiha called on partners to intensify pressure and sanctions against Russia and to take decisive measures to hold it accountable and protect freedom of navigation.
“The Black Sea is a lifeline for global food security. Russia is attacking it to weaponize hunger and hold the world hostage. This must be met with strength,” emphasized the head of Ukraine’s Foreign Ministry.
As reported by Ukrinform, Bulgaria is calling for the creation of a new EU mechanism to ensure free and safe navigation in the Black Sea amid recent attacks on civilian vessels.

ISLAMABAD, Oct. 13 (Xinhua) -- Pakistani President Asif Ali Zardari on Tuesday called for stronger disaster preparedness and greater international cooperation, stressing the need to prevent natural disasters rather than merely responding to their aftermath.
In a message marking the International Day for Disaster Risk Reduction, Zardari said Pakistan has experienced floods, earthquakes, heatwaves and droughts, which have caused heavy losses in lives, homes and livelihoods.
He said Pakistan is transforming its national disaster management system by using artificial intelligence, satellite technology and real-time data to identify risks and issue early warnings, helping communities move to safety before disasters strike.
Highlighting the role of local governments and communities, the president said they are often the first line of defense during disasters because they understand local conditions and can respond quickly.
He called for disaster preparedness to become a core priority for national and international organizations and urged countries to strengthen regional cooperation based on shared risks.
The president also proposed greater international cooperation on water resilience, protection of the cryosphere, food security, climate adaptation, environmental protection, and shared rivers. ■
