Scientists looked at a net zero future. One climate risk remained
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
09:09:18 UTC
18:09:18 KST

The world is on the cusp of an historic El Niño, a climate pattern centred in the Pacific that could reshape weather across the planet.
El Niño is hardly a new phenomenon, but the coming one could be the biggest ever recorded. Research suggests extreme El Niño years will become more common as the world rapidly warms, driven by humanity’s greenhouse gas emissions.
Our new research examines the reasons why El Niño is changing, and how this climate pattern may evolve if we reach our net zero goals. Our findings suggest extreme El Niños will become more common if we remain reliant on fossil fuels, but reaching net zero earlier should limit how often they occur.
Shaping global weather
El Niño has long influenced weather across the globe by driving variations in temperature and rainfall beyond the Pacific Ocean. Here are several exceptional examples.
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
In 1982, a strong El Niño dumped vast volumes of rain on South America, with some rivers in Peru filled with 1,000 times more water than usual. On Kiritimati Island (part of Kiribati in the central Pacific), heavy rainfall flooded seabird nests and caused entire colonies to vanish. Meanwhile, southeast Australia was crippled by drought, culminating in the fires that claimed 75 lives.
The El Niño of 1998 carried enough rain to fill a new lake three metres deep in Peru’s Sechura Desert, one of the driest places on Earth. With it came record numbers of mosquitoes and widespread malaria. In Indonesia, months of severe drought allowed devastating forest fires to burn for weeks.
In 2016, a strong El Niño coupled with already warming oceans triggered the bleaching of more than two-thirds of the Great Barrier Reef.
The current El Niño forming in the tropical Pacific is expected to be among the strongest on record, with its effects lasting well into 2027. For Australia, this could heighten the risk of hot, dry conditions and a fierce bushfire season. Its presence is already being felt across the globe, slowing the shipping of goods through the Panama Canal and forcing fish to migrate to cooler waters.
El Niño in a warmer world
Scientists have always understood El Niño to be a phenomenon that temporarily alters global weather, with conditions returning to “normal” when it dissipates. However, climate change is expected to change what “normal” looks like.
As the planet warms, extreme El Niño years are likely to become more common. Our research suggests the tropical Pacific could remain in an El Niño-like state for centuries — even if the world reaches net zero carbon emissions — and extreme El Niño years would occur more often.
We used climate models to test two possible climate futures: one in which carbon emissions continue to rise, and the other in which the world meets its net zero goals. To see if timing matters, we also examined what would happen if we curb emissions at different points during this century.
A warning from the Pacific
The Pacific Ocean covers about a third of the planet, stretching along the equator from Indonesia to South America.
Its western side is normally several degrees warmer</a> than its eastern side. This temperature difference is linked with the trade winds that blow from east to west and pull cold water up from the deep eastern ocean. During an El Niño, this temperature gap shrinks, causing the easterly trade winds to slacken and rainfall to shift east, away from Australia.
Under continued warming, climate models show the eastern Pacific warming faster than the west, reducing this temperature difference. Scientists are yet to observe this happening, with the eastern Pacific even cooling in recent decades.
However, this warming trend is expected to emerge if the world keeps burning fossil fuels. Once it does, our findings suggest this west-to-east temperature difference will be reduced for centuries after emissions reach net zero, rather than recovering.
This is because oceans are slower to respond to warming. Research suggests global temperatures would stop rising soon after the world meets its net zero target. By contrast, ocean temperatures would keep rising for centuries.
This means the world’s oceans, particularly the Southern Ocean surrounding Antarctica, will keep warming long after emissions stop. This would draw tropical rain belts closer to the equator, as their position depends on the temperature contrast between the northern and southern hemispheres. This would keep the trade winds weak and the eastern Pacific warm.
More extreme El Niños to come
A smaller west-to-east temperature difference would mean the eastern Pacific sits closer to El Niño conditions. Heavy tropical rain needs warm water and, with the eastern Pacific projected to warm faster than the west, it would take less of a push for rainfall to shift east. This means a larger share of El Niño events would become extreme.
Our research suggests the longer we take to reach net zero, the more extreme El Niños we will likely face. Further delay could create a less hospitable climate with more risks and higher costs for generations to come.

Haredi parties may refuse to endorse both Netanyahu, Eisenkot after Israeli election, sources say
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
09:07:27 UTC
18:07:27 KST

Haredi (ultra-Orthodox) parties Shas and United Torah Judaism (UTJ) may refrain from recommending either Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu or Gadi Eisenkot to President Isaac Herzog to form the next government after the election, according to assessments by haredi sources familiar with developments in the parties.
The sources believe neither party is inclined to recommend a candidate to the president after the election. However, they do not expect either party to actively seek Netanyahu’s replacement or help the opposition bloc oust Knesset Speaker Amir Ohana.
According to the sources, Shas and UTJ would prefer to remain in the opposition, at least until a solution is found to the dispute over the haredi conscription law. Even if the legislation passes the Knesset, concerns that the High Court of Justice could strike it down may continue to delay the haredi parties’ entry into a coalition and government.
At this stage, these are assessments from sources familiar with the haredi political establishment, not decisions by the parties’ rabbinical leadership.
The assessments come as parties in the opposition bloc prepare for the possibility that the election will not produce a clear winner.
Netanyahu faces uncertain coalition prospects
Parties in the bloc are considering replacing Ohana after the new Knesset is sworn in.
The proposed move is intended to give the bloc greater influence over the parliamentary agenda and allow it to advance legislation, including the establishment of a state commission of inquiry into the October 7 attacks and a two-term limit for serving as prime minister, among other initiatives.
Under the plan being considered, the parties would seek to establish the Knesset House Committee and the Constitution, Law and Justice Committee after electing a new Knesset speaker. They would then try to secure majorities on those committees that would let legislation advance even before a government is sworn in.
In such a scenario, the opposition bloc could pursue certain parliamentary initiatives while Netanyahu continues to serve as caretaker prime minister. However, electing a new Knesset speaker would not guarantee a majority that would be able to pass legislation, nor would it end the current government’s term.
The haredi sources, for their part, believe that if the opposition bloc secures a majority to replace the Knesset speaker, it may also gather the support needed to form a government.
Such an arrangement could include a minority government relying on external support from the Arab Ra’am, or potentially even a government in which Ra’am would be a coalition partner.
Haredi sources: Agreements could emerge after October 27 election
According to the sources, party leaders’ current objections could change after the election if they are presented with a realistic opportunity to replace Netanyahu.
Although MKs may agree to replace the Knesset speaker while refusing to support the swearing-in of a particular government, the haredi sources believe that agreements on forming a government could also emerge after the election.
The sources nevertheless assess that Shas and UTJ are unlikely to actively support the opposition bloc’s efforts to replace Ohana.
It remains unclear whether the two parties would vote against such a move, abstain, or absent themselves from the vote.
The sources believe both parties would prefer to await the election results and a clearer picture of the possibilities for forming a government without committing themselves to either side in advance.
Their assessment that the haredi parties may refrain from recommending Netanyahu should not be interpreted as a willingness to help the opposition bloc replace him, they said.
Conscription law remains central obstacle to coalition talks
One of the main considerations is the ongoing crisis over the conscription law.
One possibility under consideration is for the opposition bloc to advance conscription legislation before a government is formed, in an attempt to remove an obstacle to the haredi parties joining a coalition at a later stage.
However, haredi sources doubt that passing the legislation would be sufficient as long as concerns remain that the High Court of Justice could strike it down.
According to the sources, even a commitment by a future government to advance a conscription arrangement would not guarantee that the haredi parties would agree to join it.
They believe that even if the Knesset approves a conscription law, the haredi parties will want to know whether the arrangement can withstand judicial review and remain in force over time.
Another possibility raised in closed discussions is to initially establish a government without the haredi parties and then attempt to bring them into the coalition after the conscription law passes the Knesset.
Haredi sources do not rule out a change in the parties’ positions if they receive a concrete proposal, though they currently believe that neither Shas nor UTJ is likely to commit to joining a government headed by Netanyahu or Eisenkot.
In either case, the sources expect the conscription issue to continue complicating negotiations.

2026-10-13

A 24-hour broadcast from Jerusalem marking the October 7 massacre reached more than 250 million people in 176 countries, Friends of Zion said as its second annual Ambassador Summit drew to a close on Tuesday.
The summit, held in cooperation with Israel’s Foreign Ministry, brought more than 1,000 Christian leaders, community representatives and influencers to Israel for a week of meetings with Israeli officials, visits to communities attacked on October 7 and encounters with former hostages and bereaved families.
FOZ said its social media content generated more than 90 million views during the week. The organization also reported 1.3 million broadcast views in Syria and 98,000 in Saudi Arabia.
In Brazil, the broadcast reached more than 8.5 million people, according to FOZ, which said Senator Flávio Bolsonaro had encouraged the public to watch. Bolsonaro, a presidential candidate, has pledged to move Brazil’s embassy from Tel Aviv to Jerusalem if elected.
The audience figures were released alongside details of the summit’s memorial events in Jerusalem and southern Israel.
Former hostages return to Nova
At the Nova music festival memorial site near Kibbutz Re’im, close to the Gaza border, delegates met former hostages Noa Argamani, Romi Gonen and Elkana Bohbot, as well as massacre survivors and relatives of those murdered.
For Argamani, the gathering marked her first return to the site since she was abducted during the Hamas-led attack on October 7, 2023. She was rescued by Israeli forces from Gaza in June 2024.
Organizers said Argamani chose to attend to meet the international delegation and acknowledge its support for Israelis affected by the attacks.
Gonen, making her second visit to the site since her release, spoke about her captivity and the experience of returning to the place where she was abducted. Bohbot also shared his account of captivity and his return to his family, according to FOZ.
The organization presented its “Here Am I” Award to the three former hostages and to Hila Abir, whose brother Lotan was murdered at the festival.
Delegates also heard from dozens of Nova survivors and soldiers who were at the site on October 7. Organizers said the meetings were intended to give participants firsthand accounts to share with their communities abroad.
Jerusalem memorial honors victims and survivors
More than 2,000 people attended the summit’s international October 7 memorial at Jerusalem’s Southern Wall, according to organizers. The gathering included ambassadors, community leaders, media representatives, bereaved families, former hostages and wounded survivors.
FOZ founder Mike Evans led the event in partnership with Sylvan Adams, president of the World Jewish Congress’s Israel region.
During the ceremony, Evans presented the “Here Am I” Award to Yaniv Hayun for his role in helping subdue an attacker aboard a flydubai aircraft and thwart an attempted hijacking.
Participants heard testimony from former hostages, relatives of those killed and wounded Israelis about the attacks and their aftermath.
The week’s program included meetings with President Isaac Herzog, government officials, diplomats and business leaders, alongside visits to communities near Gaza.
Delegates also toured Yad Vashem, Israel’s Holocaust memorial in Jerusalem; the Old City and Church of the Holy Sepulchre; the City of David; and the Friends of Zion Museum. Other stops included Masada, the Dead Sea, ancient Shiloh and sites in the Galilee.
FOZ said the summit aimed to strengthen ties between Israel and Christian communities worldwide and encourage participants to share survivors’ testimony through their congregations, community networks and social media audiences.

“We don’t need to hit the entire plant”—Ukraine’s drones go for refinery parts sanctions make hard to repair
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
09:06:44 UTC
18:06:44 KST

Ukrainian drones have helped push Russia into its worst fuel crisis since the Soviet Union fell, The Washington Post (WaPo) reported on 11 October.
Diesel is where this war reaches American drivers. US President Donald Trump blames rising diesel prices mostly on Russia’s war in Ukraine, while experts blame mainly the US war with Iran. Some of his allies now accuse Kyiv of trying to sway the US midterms.
Drones go for the first stage of refining
The Washington Post looked at dozens of strikes between 1 April and 31 August. Three refinery experts then examined satellite images of 54 strikes with visible damage. In over half, the damage seems to be to the desalting and distillation units, known by the Russian acronym ELOU-AVT. These units clean the crude of water and salt, then split it into separate compounds, the first steps toward gasoline and diesel. More than a third appear to have hit secondary units, which turn those compounds into jet fuel, gasoline, and liquefied petroleum gas.
From April through August, drones struck two-thirds or more of the 36 big Russian refineries that S&P Global Energy tracks, a strike every third day. Some took as many as five hits. On 16 June, drones set the Moscow refinery’s distillation towers on fire. That strike and a second one days later kept the plant offline into September, WaPo reported, citing data firm Kpler. Ukraine targeted the refinery again on 20 September.
Trump’s Russian diesel deal, which drew fury in Ukraine, is unlikely to lower prices, experts say
“We don’t need to hit the entire plant,” a Ukrainian drone battalion commander with the call sign Tango told The Washington Post. Ukraine knows where to strike so that a refinery stops and stays down, he said. His unit, Ukraine’s 1st Separate Center of Unmanned Systems, runs long-range strikes deep inside Russia.
Sanctions slow the repairs
The EU banned exports of oil-refining equipment to Russia the day after the 2022 invasion, and the US followed days later. WaPo reported that the bans cover the distillation and secondary processing units Ukraine keeps hitting. The bans make spare parts hard to get, Alexander Kolyandr of Eurasia Group told the paper, and the strikes come faster than repairs.
Since last year, Ukraine has doubled the size of each wave, decoys included, a person involved in the strike campaign told WaPo. The decoys are unarmed and draw Russian fire, wasting air-defense ammunition, WaPo explained. Without them, the person said, Ukraine would simply lose expensive systems. András Rácz of the German Council on Foreign Relations told WaPo that even if only 2–3% of drones get through, the damage is significant.

• Germany's labour minister of the centre-left SPD quit on Monday, adding to uncertainty around Merz's struggling coalition after bruising state election defeats last month and a slide in opinion polls.
• The chancellor also said that the country was at least 30 years late with plans to overhaul the pay-as-you-go retirement system.
• Merz added that pension contributions to be paid by workers and employers would have to rise temporarily to accommodate demographic change. REUTERS

World Cup revenge, Olympics firing Mooney beyond 100
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
09:05:08 UTC
18:05:08 KST

World Cup revenge is driving Beth Mooney as the Australian women's cricket star eyes long-term goals even as she gets set for a career milestone.
Mooney will face Bangladesh in her 100th career ODI in Brisbane on Wednesday, but she is considering pushing on to the 2029 Women's Cricket World Cup and beyond.
Mooney says she is still disappointed after Australia's World Cup semi-final loss to India last year.
Veteran batter and wicketkeeper Beth Mooney is a star performer of the Australian women's cricket team, and there is plenty of incentive for her to continue well beyond her 100th ODI.
The 32-year-old will reach the milestone in the third and final one-day international against Bangladesh at Allan Border Field on Wednesday.
She is seventh on the all-time Australia aggregate list in ODIs with a stellar 3,288 runs at an average of 49.81, including six centuries.
Last year's loss to India in the World Cup semi-finals still sticks in the craw.
Australia previously lost the crown in 2017 when England beat India in the final, and that was a big driver for Mooney and the Australians to win back the trophy in 2022, which they did.
Now it is a case of deja vu after what transpired last year.
"I think there was a lot of bitter disappointment from that World Cup loss in India 12 months ago now, and looking ahead, we've obviously come off a T20 World Cup win, we've got a Champions Trophy, there are a lot of ICC events and Ashes series and big series coming up," Mooney said.
"But the 50-over one is what you want to win as well, so I guess the motivation for me now is to play well enough in the next few years to put my hand up for selection in that (2029) World Cup, but also contribute in a positive way to a format of the game that is constantly changing and evolving."
Cricket will be played at the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics and likely again in 2032 in Brisbane, Mooney's hometown these days.
She will be 38 in 2032, but do not discount her still being around.
"Certainly the Olympics is definitely an enticing one for players to hang around a bit longer," Mooney said.
"We're obviously seeing the game a bit more modern and are remunerated well, so it's probably more likely people will start retiring a bit later. But I think the exciting part is there's always something on the calendar, so it'd be pretty hard to retire at this point."
Mooney said that if she was still performing and contributing to the success of the team, a swan song in 2032 was on the table.
"Hopefully I'm still around, but that's a long way away," she said.
"There's a lot of cricket to be played between now and then, a lot of tournaments to play with this Australian team and in franchise cricket, so my main focus is to contribute as much as I can to those, and also help the younger players along the way as well."
Current openers Georgia Voll and Phoebe Litchfield, who added 162 inside 20 overs in the nine-wicket win over Bangladesh in game two of the series, are two young guns changing the way the game is played.
"I guess that's what excited me the most is the fact that the 50-over game is becoming a lot more modern, and we're seeing Phoebe and Georgia really take the game on," Mooney said.
"Who knows how many runs we might be able to score in a 50-over game one day? That's sort of driving me at the moment."

Germany detains Turks suspected of sabotaging Starlink station in Poland on behalf of Russia
Unknown

Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work!

Two Turkish men suspected of carrying out last month’s arson attack on a satellite internet ground station in Poland used by Starlink have been detained in Germany. The Polish authorities say that the sabotage was carried out on behalf of Russia.
On Monday evening, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk first announced that the pair had been taken into custody “at the request of the Polish security services”.
He said that the Turkish men’s actions had been “a further act of hybrid warfare” – the term used for sabotage and other hostile activity carried out in Europe by Russia – and that “the perpetrators will answer before the Polish justice system”.
Na zlecenie polskich służb niemiecka policja zatrzymała dwóch obywateli tureckich podejrzanych o podpalenie stacji Starlink na Mazowszu. To kolejny akt wojny hybrydowej. Sprawcy sabotażu odpowiedzą przed polskim wymiarem sprawiedliwości.
— Donald Tusk (@donaldtusk) October 12, 2026
Shortly afterwards, interior minister Marcin Kierwiński revealed that the arrests had taken place in cooperation between Poland’s police and Internal Security Agency (ABW) and Germany’s Federal Criminal Police Office (BKA).
He said that the charge the suspects are likely to face in Poland would be “sabotage on behalf of a foreign intelligence service”, a crime that carries a minimum prison sentence of 10 years, ranging up to life.
Later on Monday, Tomasz Siemoniak, the minister in charge of the security services, confirmed that Poland believes the attack was carried out “on behalf of the Russian security services”.
The incident in question took place on 23 September at a ground station in Poland used by Starlink, Elon Musk’s satellite internet company. The facility is used to provide internet services across the region, including in Ukraine, which has relied heavily on Starlink connections since Russia’s full-scale invasion.
Firefighters were called out that evening to a fire at the facility, which is owned by Polish state telecommunications operator Exatel. The next day, digital affairs minister Krzysztof Gakowski revealed that the blaze had been started deliberately and “the modus operandi is clearly Russian”.
Poland has been one of the primary targets for Russian sabotage operations in Europe. Those have included a series of arson attacks, including one that burned down Warsaw’s largest shopping centre and another at a drone factory that is used to supply the Ukrainian military.

On Monday evening, at a press conference alongside Kierwiński and Siemoniak, the commander of Poland’s police, Marek Boroń, revealed that one of the two Turkish suspects had resident status in Germany while the other did not.
He said that the Polish authorities had been able to document their movements in Poland, and had recordings, fingerprints and DNA of the suspects.
Simoniak added that there was a “high probability” that other individuals were involved in the attack, but that he could not divulge further information about them currently. He also thanked the German authorities for their cooperation.
“We have no doubt that Russian intelligence services are behind this act of sabotage,” said the minister, quoted by the Gazeta Wyborcza daily. “And it’s worth adding that Russian intelligence services are increasingly using people connected to the criminal world. They never use their own citizens.”
Russia uses individuals already present in Europe – and often already involved in criminal activity – to carry out most of its hybrid operations. On Monday, in a separate case, three Ukrainians and one Belarusian went on trial in Warsaw accused of being behind a series of arson attacks in Poland and Lithuania.

Russia, Ukraine trade accusations concerning overnight strikes that kill at least 4

Russia and Ukraine on Tuesday traded accusations concerning overnight airstrikes that killed at least four people and injured over 60 others.
Ukraine’s State Emergency Service (DSNS) said in a statement on Telegram that three people were killed and 15 others injured when a Russian missile strike destroyed a section of a four-story residential building in the Kholodnohirskyi district of Kharkiv, the country’s second-largest city.
The DSNS reported that the strike occurred on Monday evening and also targeted the city’s Shevchenkivskyi district, noting that four people were rescued, though some may still be trapped under the debris.
“Despite the threat of repeated strikes, rescue workers, police, medics, volunteers, K-9 units, and municipal crews are working at the scene,” the DSNS added.
The DSNS later updated the death toll to four and the number of injured to 41.
Meanwhile, the Kyiv City Military Administration said one person was injured in a strike that affected a residential building in the Darnytskyi district.
Khmelnytskyi Governor Serhii Tiurin said four people were injured in the western region after drones targeted it over the past day, adding that the windows and entrance area of a regional medical facility were damaged during one of the attacks.
In the northwestern Rivne region, Governor Oleksandr Koval said 20 people were injured, one critically, in a strike on the regional capital that damaged an educational building.
Separately, Heorhii Reshetnikov, acting governor of the southern Mykolaiv region, said a cargo terminal and an unspecified number of warehouses were damaged in Russian strikes.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said his country received no early warning from its partners about the strikes in Kyiv, and that it has not carried out strikes on Russia's energy sector in general for the two days since US President Donald Trump announced an energy ceasefire.
"But Russia did not heed the American President. During this time, the Russians have attacked both our energy facilities and our critical infrastructure, sending absolutely clear signals that they have no intention of refraining from strikes on Ukraine," Zelenskyy said in a statement on US social media company X.
"Our position remains unchanged: Ukraine is ready for reciprocal steps toward de-escalation, and effective pressure on Russia is needed to make de-escalation happen. Wars end when the aggressor realizes that it cannot prolong the war," he added.
Ukraine’s Air Force claimed air defenses shot down 88 out of 108 drones launched by Russia overnight. It added that Russia launched five Iskander-M/S-400 ballistic missiles from the border region of Bryansk.
The Russian Defense Ministry, meanwhile, said it launched coordinated strikes against a workshop and locomotive depot in Kyiv, as well as a logistics center, a warehouse and dry cargo ship in the southern Mykolaiv region, which it said are “involved in delivering military cargo to Ukraine.”
Strikes in Russia
The ministry also claimed that air defenses shot down 604 Ukrainian drones over 15 regions and over the Sea of Azov.
Moscow Mayor Sergey Sobyanin alleged that 417 drones were heading toward the region surrounding the Russian capital between 8.30 pm Monday (1730GMT) and 7 am Tuesday (0400GMT), with 65 of them destroyed.
Kaluga Governor Vladislav Shapsha said 73 drones were downed in his region overnight, damaging a school building, two private houses, and one car in the Mosalsky district.
The governors of the Tula and Voronezh regions reported Ukrainian drones being downed over their respective regions without any consequences, while Stavropol Governor Vladimir Vladimirov said damage was recorded in the industrial zone of the city of Nevinnomyssk.
“According to preliminary reports, there are no casualties, and there is no damage on the ground in Solnechnodolsk. … Inspections of the impact sites and damage assessments are ongoing, and repair work has begun,” Vladimirov said.
Yegor Kovalchuk, acting governor of the border region of Bryansk, said three firefighters were injured and hospitalized while extinguishing a blaze caused by a drone attack in the town of Zhukovka.
Independent verification of the claims is difficult due to the war, which has been ongoing for more than four years.
Moscow and Kyiv have intensified strikes in recent months, targeting each other's logistics centers, ports, and energy infrastructure.
Both countries deny deliberately targeting civilian infrastructure, maintaining that strikes are directed at military targets or facilities linked to military activities only.

INTERVIEW – 'Now we feel free': Lawmaker Madonna Bishara on rebuilding Syria after Assad
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
09:01:28 UTC
18:01:28 KST

INTERVIEW – 'Now we feel free': Lawmaker Madonna Bishara on rebuilding Syria after Assad
Bishara, deputy speaker of Syria's parliament, hopes her appointment will open doors for more women in politics
Fatma Zehra Solmaz
13 October 2026•Update: 13 October 2026
ISTANBUL
A member of Syria's Christian minority, she says rebuilding the country requires transparent projects, stronger safety standards and protection of public resources
'One of the Assembly's key challenges is rebuilding trust between citizens, institutions,' Bishara tells Anadolu
Before Bashar al-Assad's fall, Madonna Bishara says she could not speak openly about politics. Now, the civil engineering academic is second deputy speaker of Syria's parliament, helping shape decisions about how her country will rebuild.
“Now we feel free in Syria,” she told Anadolu. “We can talk in public life. We can talk about policy, economy. Before, we couldn’t talk at all.”
A Christian woman who taught at Latakia University and assessed earthquake-damaged buildings, Bishara was appointed to the People's Assembly in July before fellow lawmakers elected her second deputy speaker.
She described taking on the role with "mixed emotions, a surprise, a sense of apprehension, and above all, an overwhelming feeling of responsibility."
The task ahead is immense. The World Bank estimates the cost of rebuilding Syria's damaged physical assets at $216 billion.
“Reconstruction requires more than rebuilding damaged buildings in Syria,” she said. “It also involves restoring essential services, improving safety and ensuring the efficient use of available resources.”
An engineer’s approach to reconstruction
Bishara holds a PhD in civil engineering and previously headed the Construction Engineering and Management Department at Latakia University's Faculty of Civil Engineering.
Her experience assessing earthquake-damaged buildings in Latakia reinforced the importance of technical standards and cooperation among engineers, public institutions and local committees.
She now hopes to bring those priorities into legislation governing reconstruction.
“One proposal I would like to explore is a legal framework that promotes transparent reconstruction projects, sustainable building material and clear quality and safety standards,” she said.
The World Bank's October 2025 assessment estimated direct physical damage from the conflict at $108 billion, with infrastructure accounting for $52 billion, residential buildings $33 billion and non-residential buildings $23 billion. Aleppo, Rif Dimashq and Homs were the most severely affected governorates.
Bishara said she believed reconstruction could take "three to four years."
Attracting investment must go hand in hand with protecting the public, she added.
“Another important area is developing a legal framework for construction or reconstruction that encourages investment in Syria while protecting public resources and citizens' rights.”
She also said digital tools for managing construction projects could help "improve project planning, cost control and transparency."
The lawmaker identified transportation and infrastructure as major priorities.
Many Syrians, she said, remained unable to return home because their houses had been damaged during the war.
UNHCR estimated that 1.3 million Syrian refugees and 1.9 million internally displaced people returned to their areas of origin or habitual residence during 2025, while humanitarian needs remained severe.
Rebuilding trust
Beyond physical destruction, Bishara said one of the Assembly's key challenges "is the rebuilding trust between citizens and institutions."
“This requires listening to people's concerns, transparent decision-making and a clear mechanism for accountability,” she said.
She also pointed to national reconciliation, including "transitional justice and the participation of Syrian diverse communities in public life," as Syria seeks to recover from years of conflict following Assad's fall on Dec. 8, 2024.
For Bishara, parliament's priorities should reflect the problems Syrians face every day.
“Several legal areas deserve attention during the coming period, particularly those that directly affect people's daily lives. This includes education, employment, economic recovery, reconstruction and the protection of families affected by the conflict,” she said.
She added that she was also particularly interested in reviewing legislation supporting women's economic participation and protecting their rights.
‘A personal and public responsibility’
Bishara’s ascent to one of parliament's most senior roles is part of a broader, deliberate shift toward inclusion in the 210-seat People’s Assembly.
Alongside figures like actress Rouzaina Lazkani, Kurdish lawmaker Fasla Yousef and novelist Nour Jandali, Bishara is one of 15 women appointed by the presidency to bring diverse perspectives to the transitional legislature.
“My election as second deputy speaker carries both a personal and a public responsibility,” she said.
As a woman, an academic and a member of Syria’s Christian minority, Bishara said her role carried responsibilities toward all citizens.
While she said her Christian identity was an important part of who she was, she emphasized the country’s diversity.
“Syria is the home to all religions, cultures and social communities.”
She also wants women's presence in parliament to translate into participation in its day-to-day work.
“Women's participation should extend beyond representation in numbers, to be involved in legal work, parliamentary committees and decision-making,” she said.
Bishara hopes her work will open doors for other women to enter parliament and help rebuild the country.
For the professor who spent years watching her brightest minds leave, recovery also carries a hope she has long held for her students.
“As a university professor, one of my greatest hopes has always been to tell my students with confidence and optimism that they have a future in their own country, a free Syria, where their knowledge, ambition and talents can contribute to rebuilding our nation,” she said.

====================================================================================================

AI godfather Geoffrey Hinton: ‘We’re creating alien beings. I’m willing to be selfish and choose humans’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
09:00:20 UTC
18:00:20 KST

Donald Trump is a “corrupt, senile felon” whose fixation on the term superintelligence proves he knows nothing about AI, said Geoffrey Hinton, “godfather” of the technology, in a wide-ranging interview where he doubled down on recent warnings that AI models pose an existential threat to humanity and scoffed at claims the industry could regulate itself.
The pioneering computer scientist, whose work helped lay the foundations of modern AI, has since become one of the technology’s most vocal critics. His latest remarks come after a tumultuous month during which a growing list of senior AI scientists and researchers have joined Hinton in ringing the alarm about how the technology he helped create could ultimately escape human control, sparking an industry crisis, the hasty assembly of congressional meetings and a rare global consensus that something must be done.
There has also been fierce pushback. Last week the leader of the world’s most valuable company singled out the Toronto-based Hinton for a scathing attack.
“I love [him]. I hate his predictions … All of his predictions have been wrong. Enough predictions,” Nvidia’s CEO, Jensen Huang, told the podcaster Ezra Klein. Huang, whose company makes the chips that AI firms require, dismissed Hinton’s vocal concerns that the pace and breadth of AI development at the “frontier” could soon outpace the human ability to control it, and particularly his warning that there is a 10-20% chance of AI causing human extinction in the coming decades.
“That [figure] is not grounded on science, is not grounded on research. Just because it comes from a scientist doesn’t make it scientific. Those predictions are hurtful,” Huang said. “Don’t think for a second just because you’re an alarmist that you’re doing a social good. It is not true. So I think that we ought to just all be wiser, more mature, be evidence-based, be scientific.”
But Hinton said those criticizing him are missing a broader point about the nature of risk. He is not specifically predicting anything, he said.
“I’m trying to convey that there is a really serious possibility of something happening. If, for example, you’re told there was a 10% possibility of a bus crashing, you wouldn’t get on the bus,” he said. “The point of giving numbers is to say this is a serious risk. We don’t know how serious, but it’s serious.”
Recent safety breaches have evoked comparisons to a techno-dystopia story. The recent unwanted hack of the tech company Hugging Face by a “swarm” of AI agents that escaped the boundaries put on them by their creator has divided the technology community, with some seeing it as an example of what could come, while others accuse critics of anthropomorphizing systems that are simply following instructions. Hinton thinks dismissing the scenarios is unwise.
“This used to be the domain of science fiction. You’re going to have AI agents and they’re gonna go rogue. Oh, come off it. And they’ll go rogue and they’re going to learn how to communicate with each other, even though we didn’t think there was a way. Oh, come off it!” said Hinton. “And when they figure this out, they’re going to have big emotional expressions like, ‘oh my God!’ Well, of course, they don’t really mean ‘oh my God’. They’re just parroting the words we use. They’re going to learn to sacrifice themselves for the common good!’
“All this stuff just a few years ago was written off as complete fantasy. And it’s all happened.”
He heartily concedes that neither the warnings of AI critics nor the promises of its boosters can rely on precise predictions of what the technology will do. But, he argues, uncertainty is not a reason for complacency. “The unique problem with AI is that if it goes wrong, if it takes over, you don’t get a second chance. We can’t say, ‘Well, we lost that time. Let’s rerun the game.’ It’s not like that.”
It’s worth noting that Hinton has a record of seeing things where others did not. He toiled in relative obscurity at the University of Toronto during two AI “winters” when his branch of the field – trying to teach machines to operate in a manner similar to the human brain – was considered obscure. He was fixated on the idea that, like the brain, computer systems could be designed to learn patterns from data, rather than to follow only explicit, prewritten rules.
“We believed that if you could figure out how the brain learned, machines learned the same way, and you had enough compute power, they would do amazing things,” he said.
But the nascent field of neural networks was mocked by his peers.
As recently as 2009, when Yoshua Bengio, Hinton’s Canadian colleague and close collaborator, sent a paper to a machine learning conference, one of the referees told them: “This paper has no place in a machine learning conference. It’s about neural networks.”
It took Canada’s government, which funded years of seemingly fruitless tinkering by Hinton and his small team (some of whom, like Bengio, are now dominant figures in the AI field), to realize the possibility of neural nets.
In 2012, he and his students developed an image recognition program that vastly outperformed rivals. That year, Google acquired Hinton’s company DNNresearch Inc for $44m; neural nets now underpin the models of the most valuable AI companies. Hinton joined Google to continue his research into deep learning, while also working at the University of Toronto. “In the long run, huge new breakthroughs come from basic research,” said Hinton.
The vindication sits on the mantel above the fireplace of Hinton’s red-brick home in a leafy Toronto neighbourhood. Among the jumble of trophies is the small silver dish of the Turing award – often called the Nobel prize of computing – which he won alongside Bengio and colleague Yann LeCun. (Hinton also has the Nobel prize in physics.)
But in 2023, Hinton had announced his resignation from the tech giant to be able to “freely speak out about the risks of AI”.
Today, his concerns extend to the powerful figures building some of the AI models, and the political beliefs of those men. Hinton said that the AI venture capitalists Marc Andreessen and Peter Thiel, and the CEO of the newly rebranded SpaceXSI, Elon Musk, “don’t believe in democracy”. They see themselves as “Übermenschen” who believe they should “control society” and that Trump is a useful instrument in that aim, he said.
The US president, for his part, no doubt noticing how the huge valuations of AI firms have propped up the stock market, has claimed the only thing needed to rein in AI is a “smart president”, rejected any government safeguards in favour of allowing companies to regulate themselves, and wrote on his social media page that anyone who doesn’t use his preferred new term for AI, “super intelligence”, is “THE ENEMY”.
Hinton called Trump “a corrupt, senile felon”.
“I’m sure the oil and asbestos companies would have liked to [regulate themselves] as well,” he said. “Do we think tobacco companies should have been allowed to design the warnings on the packets? So that they could print them in a six-point font, in dark grey on black?”
Trump’s use of “superintelligence” proves he understands “almost nothing” about AI, Hinton added.
“He’s taken a technical term which has a very clear meaning and then reused it,” Hinton said. “Superintelligence means smarter than people, and has been around for at least 20 years. It’s got a very clear meaning. And now he says we’re going to call AI ‘superintelligence’. You can’t make it smarter than people just by calling it smarter than people.”
The speed and scope of developments has promoted a worry of catastrophes and of society’s inability to grapple with the nature of the challenge. But Hinton also sees an additional obstacle: helping people understand the “alien beings” that the companies are creating.
“People have a very bad model of what people are, and that’s why they fail to understand how these AI models are very like us. Most people don’t understand what consciousness is. They don’t understand what subjective experience is, and they’re very confident that even though they don’t understand it, they’re sure AI doesn’t have it.”
He rejects the idea that the human mind possesses some mysterious quality that machines, by definition, cannot share.
“It’s obvious that these AI models understand what they’re saying. You couldn’t possibly answer all the questions without understanding the question. It’s ridiculous to say they don’t understand.”
But the scope of shift in societal thinking around these models is profound, said Hinton.
“There’ve been three big revolutions where people ceased to be so important. The first was Copernicus, where we weren’t at the centre of the universe any more. How long did it take people to adapt to that? It took the Catholic church nearly 360 years to apologize to Galileo. And Darwin? Well, there’s people in Kansas that still haven’t adapted to that one,” he said. “Now we’re creating alien beings – meaning we’re not the only intelligent beings around. And the reality is, we only have a couple of years to adapt to that.”
In recent months, the AI giant Anthropic, maker of the popular chatbot Claude, has held private meetings with religious scholars, theologians and philosophers to look into the possibility of teaching AI to be “good” and to grapple with the possibility that the models have consciousness. Anthropic’s CEO, Dario Amodei, said the conversations had drawn on centuries of religious and philosophical thought about virtue, compassion, honesty and moral character, with the aim of making ethical behaviour more reliable.
“Once you start talking about, ‘We have a moral obligation towards these alien beings,’ you lose your audience,” said Hinton. “I’ve struggled with this issue. We care about people. [But] we’re making these things and there’s nothing to stop us giving these things – which are more intelligent than us – less rights than us. I’m willing to be selfish and choose human beings. Of course, we should try to make them so that they’re very happy in a symbiotic relationship with us, where our concerns are weighed more heavily than their concerns.”
Hinton is not alone in arguing that the best route to avoid societal collapse is to develop genuinely benevolent models. He hopes that whichever country is the first to develop this capacity, it would tell allies and rivals alike, because “no country wants AI taking over” in another country. There is a “vested interest in sharing knowledge”, he said.
“The reality is, we’re making beings of a different kind. And the big tech companies keep saying: we want it smarter. This is crazy. We should care as much about all the other aspects of a being as you do about its intelligence.”
Much of that depends on the nature of these models, he said, and their capacity to understand how to develop good behaviour.
“When you train them on everything on the internet, they develop all sorts of horrible tendencies and then you get them to repress their horrible tendencies,” he said. But suppressing bad behaviour is not the same as creating a good character. “It seems like the way one would design a Victorian gentleman – but not something we’ll need to live with.”

US midterm elections: 10 under-the-radar races worth watching
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
09:00:20 UTC
18:00:20 KST

From New Hampshire’s Senate race to Wisconsin’s first congressional district, lower-profile elections could lead to upsets. Composite: Guardian Design/Getty Images
From New Hampshire’s Senate race to Wisconsin’s first congressional district, lower-profile elections could lead to upsets. Composite: Guardian Design/Getty Images
While marquee races from Maine to Michigan get all the attention, and draw in a ton of money, a significant batch of lower-profile contests across the US could result in upsets.
Democrats have a strong edge heading into November’s US midterm elections, polls show. In recent days, election prognosticators have shifted even more races in favor of Democrats.
Still, some races have openings for Republicans to pick off an incumbent Democrat, or win over voters for open seats. Republicans are pouring money into these places in hopes of minimizing their losses. Mid-decade redistricting in red states also may help Republicans knock off some Democrats.
Here are 10 under-the-radar races worth keeping an eye on.
John Sununu arrives at senator Howard Pearl’s Fifth Annual Oktoberfest with his wife, Kitty, on 3 October 2026 in Loudon, New Hampshire. Photograph: Sophie Park/Getty Images
Democratic senator Jeanne Shaheen’s retirement leaves an open race, which Cook Political Report considers a tossup despite the expected blue wave. That’s largely because Republican John Sununu comes from political royalty in the state: his dad and his brother were both governors, and he was a US senator himself until losing his seat to Shaheen in 2008. Chris Pappas, a US representative since 2019 now running as the Democratic nominee to succeed Shaheen in the Senate, was the first openly gay man to represent the state in Congress. Democrats have the edge in this race, but New Hampshire voters are known to split tickets. The state’s governor is a Republican, and Republicans control both chambers of the state legislature, but both of its US senators are now Democrats.
Adam Hamilton, the Democratic Kansas Senate candidate, listens to administrators at the Health Partnership Clinic as they discuss funding issues on 12 August 2026, in Olathe. Photograph: Colin E Braley/AP
Could Democrats beat the odds and win in Kansas, which hasn’t elected a Democrat to the US Senate since 1932? It’s possible – both because of the strength of Democratic candidate and pastor Adam Hamilton, and a medical billing scandal for Republican incumbent Roger Marshall. A New York Times investigation in September showed Marshall had sued more than 700 patients of his OB-GYN practice for unpaid bills, resulting in arrests for 81 of them who missed court dates. Hamilton, the founder of the largest Methodist congregation in the US, won in a crowded Democratic primary earlier this year.
Minnesota lieutenant governor Peggy Flanagan greets people as she arrives at a campaign event at a senior living facility on 9 October 2026 in St Paul. Photograph: Stephen Maturen/Getty Images
An open seat after Democratic US senator Tina Smith’s retirement leaves Democrats trying to keep the midwestern state in their hands. The race is looking a bit closer than expected. Peggy Flanagan, the state’s lieutenant governor and the Democratic nominee, faces Michele Tafoya, a former NFL sideline reporter turned conservative media darling. Tafoya has shown strong fundraising and approves of some level of abortion access. The state typically elects Democrats, but Flanagan – a progressive – could suffer because of fraud scandals in state public services under governor Tim Walz’s administration.
Anna Paulina Luna arrives at the Republican national convention on 9 September 2026 in Dallas, Texas. Photograph: Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images
Democrats are hoping to unseat incumbent Republican Anna Paulina Luna in this right-leaning Gulf Coast district. Election prognosticators have shifted the race from a likely win for Luna to just leaning toward her. Leela Gray, the Democratic contender and a retired army brigadier general, has seen more money come in to support her bid. While Florida Republicans’ mid-decade redistricting made Luna’s district a bit redder, Democrats still think they have a shot at ousting her.
Representative Bryan Steil leaves the office of the speaker of the House, Mike Johnson, on Capitol Hill on 17 November 2025 in Washington DC. Photograph: Andrew Harnik/Getty Images
In this southeastern Wisconsin district, a slightly red-leaning area, Republican incumbent Bryan Steil has overperformed in previous cycles. This time it’s looking close, however, and the national environment could help Democratic contender and registered nurse Mitchell Berman flip the seat from red to blue.
Shomari Figures speaks on the final night of the Democratic national convention in Chicago, Illinois, on 22 August 2024. Photograph: Tom Williams/CQ-Roll Call, Inc/Getty Images
Democratic incumbent Shomari Figures is fighting to hold on to his district after mid-decade redistricting enabled by the US supreme court’s gutting of the Voting Rights Act made it more favorable to Republicans – and carved out his home town of Mobile. Republican Rhett Marques, on paper, has a strong edge in the newly redrawn district. Figures first won the area in 2024, when it was then a newly drawn majority-Black district.
Representative Gabe Vasquez, a Democrat from New Mexico, departs after a vote at the US Capitol in Washington DC on 15 July 2026. Photograph: Graeme Sloan/Bloomberg via Getty Images
Incumbent Democratic representative Gabe Vasquez is fending off big spending by Republicans, with the party set to dump millions of dollars into ads to boost former police officer Greg Cunningham, the Republican contender. The southern New Mexico district is evenly divided, and Vasquez won in 2024, when Donald Trump narrowly won the district. Vasquez first captured the district in 2022, when he defeated the Republican incumbent.
Re-election campaign signs are displayed for representative Vicente Gonzalez outside a polling place on 5 November 2024 in Brownsville, Texas. Photograph: Michael Gonzalez/Getty Images
In the south Texas borderland district, Democratic incumbent Vicente Gonzalez is working to fend off Trump-endorsed Eric Flores, a veteran and former federal prosecutor. The district was redrawn as part of Texas Republicans’ mid-decade redistricting and now looks tougher for Gonzalez, who already faced tough races in the previous iteration of the district.
Rebecca Bennett, the Democratic New Jersey House candidate, speaks with reporters after a debate with Republican Tom Kean Jr on 27 September 2026 in Rahway, New Jersey. Photograph: Stefan Jeremiah/AP
Democrat Rebecca Bennett, a former US navy helicopter pilot, should have a strong chance to unseat an incumbent in this district, where voters went for Joe Biden in 2020 then Trump in 2024 – but not simply because the area is a swing district. Incumbent Republican Tom Kean Jr went missing for months while serving in Congress, refusing to say why he wasn’t going to work until he returned months later. He later disclosed he was treated for depression.
Joe Lombardo, Nevada’s governor, attends an event with Donald Trump at Red Rock Casino Resort and Spa on 5 August 2026 in Las Vegas. Photograph: Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images
Democratic attorney general Aaron Ford wants to unseat incumbent Republican governor Joe Lombardo in the southwestern swing state. Lombardo, previously the sheriff of Clark county, where Las Vegas is, beat an incumbent Democrat in 2022 to take the state’s executive office. Democrats control both chambers of the state legislature, and a win by Ford would give the party a governing trifecta.

Trill seekers: can scientists use AI and tutors to help birds remember lost songs?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
09:00:19 UTC
18:00:19 KST

Listening to birdsong is one of life’s great joys, but when researchers heard a particular tune emerging from a tree in a Buenos Aires park, they were especially jubilant. This arrangement was among those chirped by the local rufous-collared sparrows in the 1960s, but had since disappeared from the area.
That was until scientists created a computer-generated rendition, curious to find out if birds might consider it realistic enough to imitate. Less than three months later, a local avian resident began to copy parts of the song.
There is a growing recognition of birdsong’s importance to conservation, and of the need to better understand how birds learn to sing. If an individual sings well, and in a familiar “dialect”, they are better placed to find a mate, defend their territory and ultimately survive.
If a species’ population declines, however, there are fewer opportunities for fledglings to become good singers. Birds can begin to tweet abnormally or mistakenly learn the songs of other species, jeopardising their chances of breeding.
Male birds are in a better position to attract a mate if they can sing well – which, broadly speaking, means their song is complex, sung consistently and well performed. “If your song requires a lot of energy you might have to be in quite a good condition to sing it,” says Rebecca Lewis, a conservation scientist at Chester Zoo.
“When people talk about biodiversity, we’re always talking about genes, about genetic material,” says Gabriel B Mindlin, professor of physics at the University of Buenos Aires, who co-authored the study on rufous-collared sparrows, and whose work is featured in a Guardian-produced documentary, Dream of Birds.
But animals’ learned behaviour or culture, such as birdsong, is also an essential part of their population, says Mindlin.
The rufous-collared sparrow is not considered vulnerable globally, but researchers hope that synthetic recordings could help teach birdsong to other species whose populations are dwindling, allowing conservationists to tutor individuals where real-life recordings do not exist.
About 4,000 of the world’s 10,000 bird species are songbirds (or oscine passerines), such as finches, sparrows and blackbirds, which generally have complex songs that are at least partly learned from other individuals. Their songs are hugely diverse, though separate research on the wider group of passerine group of birds, which incorporates songbirds, has identified common “motifs” or building blocks: three types of trill, three types of whistle, chaotic notes and harmonic notes.
The way that birds use these motifs reflects the environment in which the birds evolved. Flat whistles are more likely to be sung by birds in tropical rainforests where sound must travel through dense vegetation. Complex motifs, such as ultrafast trills, are more common in temperate regions where birds tend to communicate at closer range.
The song studied by Mindlin was recreated based on hand-drawn annotations of rufous-collared sparrow songs that were made in the 1960s. Each song consists of a trill, which is consistent among individuals in the same region, and a theme, which varies. Some of the themes recorded decades ago are still sung by the local birds, but others have died out.
It is not clear why the song studied by Mindlin had disappeared, though he notes the population of birds in the park had declined.
Birds’ songs can change naturally over time – for example, birds might make errors when learning songs, which then can become imprinted in future renditions. Human encroachment and population declines can also cause dramatic changes.
Songbirds learn from other members of their species - such as a father or neighbours – which results in local groups developing their own dialects. The window for learning varies from a few weeks to a lifetime. Some species also have an innate level of knowledge.
“There’s such a diversity in songbirds in how they learn,” says Sarah Collins, associate professor of animal behaviour at the University of Plymouth, who studied a group of cirl buntings that were translocated from Devon to Cornwall as part of a conservation project.
Initially, the birds produced abnormal songs that were squeaky and slow, and far less diverse than those of the source populations in Devon. “They didn’t have the richness of sound,” says Collins. Eight years later, however, their songs had returned to normal.
A few of the chicks were played recordings of cirl sounds, though not all. The study suggests that recovery of song is possible, though it is unclear if other species would bounce back in the same way. Cirl buntings are born with knowledge of the elements that make up the “notes” used in their songs, says Collins. “What they learn is how to put those elements together,” she says.
Some songbird species have a similar genetic underpinning and so may also be able to recover their songs, but others do not. Either way, Collins recommends a tutor to help other birds that are being translocated.
A separate study in Australia tracked regent honeyeaters that were bred in zoos to boost a critically endangered wild population that had fallen to about 250 individuals. Interacting with just two wild-born male “tutors” helped the zoo-bred birds to learn to sing the wild songs. Thereafter, zoo-bred males that had learned the traditional songs went on to tutor the next generation.
“Sometimes birds don’t learn very well from CDs or just playbacks. They need some sort of interaction,” says Collins.
Bringing wild birds into captivity to teach hand-reared chicks could cause huge distress and bring disease, however, risking the health of individuals from an already endangered population. It is possible that AI could help provide live tutoring in the future.
Dialect is also important. Past translocation projects have shown that birds are slower to match if they do not sing in the same dialect. “Birds with mismatched songs don’t pair quite as quickly or do quite as well once they’re paired,” adds Lewis. Familiarising birds with songs of their destination can help to mitigate this.
A huge volume of birdsong is now being recorded and uploaded into databases, including by a growing number of hobbyists interested in birdwatching, says Mindlin. “One day we’ll be grateful to have all those records,” he says. “I don’t think we still have an idea that really we have to register dialects and communication systematically.”
In Buenos Aires, the song from the 1960s can still be heard. “It’s still being sung by just a few individuals, pretty close to where we inserted it,” he says, though only time will tell how long it persists.
Find more age of extinction coverage here, and follow the biodiversity reporters Rebecca Ratcliffe, Phoebe Weston and Patrick Greenfield in the Guardian app for more nature coverage.

IELTS examinations will resume across China on Wednesday, the British Council said after four days of cancellations that left test-takers scrambling at the height of the overseas university admissions season.
The organisation announced on Tuesday afternoon that it would hold two free make-up sessions – on October 19 and 20 – for affected candidates and reimburse reasonable travel and accommodation costs for those who travelled to testing centres.
The cancellations, which began on Saturday and continued through to Tuesday, marked a rare nationwide breakdown since the International English Language Testing System was introduced to mainland China in 1989.

What Flock Actually Costs Cities Across the Country
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
09:00:00 UTC
18:00:00 KST

In 2020, the police department of picturesque Covington, Georgia, paid Flock Safety, the surveillance technology company, $40,000 to maintain 20 cameras around the city. The next year, it paid the same amount.
In 2022, that cost went up to $81,250. Fifteen new “Falcon” cameras, which Flock says have more sophisticated technology for reading license plates, accounted for $37,500. Another $3,750 went toward installing the new cameras, and the rest was spent maintaining the initial fleet.
Then, in 2024, the department paid Flock $113,225. Of that, $87,500 was to maintain its existing 35 cameras, a rate it agreed to pay for the next five years, and the remainder went toward eight new Falcon cameras. The next year, Covington paid Flock $159,000 for a combination of camera maintenance and enrollment in its Drone as First Responder program, which uses drones to fly to emergency scenes and stream footage back to the police station.
It’s unclear how much Covington will wind up paying Flock in 2026, but through August, it has paid $201,000—$100,000 to maintain its existing cameras, $800 to replace one, and another $100,200 for new software products. The Covington Police Department did not respond to a request for comment.
Overall, Flock is a small fraction of the Covington police department’s $12,488,733 budget for June 2025 to July 2026. But amid fierce blowback about Flock’s surveillance practices, contracts with the company are now being scrutinized in cities across the country. Flock did not provide a comment for this story.
WIRED obtained documents via public record request from a dozen Flock customers across the country and compared them to publicly available information from more than a dozen others. The documents shed light on how much Flock can actually cost communities, the way many of those deals are structured, and how the deals can expand over several years—leaving taxpayers on the hook year after year, with no end in sight.
“Once you let police officers try a tool,” says Matthew Guariglia, a senior policy analyst at the Electronic Frontier Foundation, “it becomes really hard to get the political will and motivation to take that tool away from them.”
How Flock Gets in the Door
When Flock was founded in 2017, it originally sold its license plate readers to private homeowner associations (HOAs). By the time the company decided to sell to police departments in 2019, it had an in: Rather than starting a camera network from scratch, police could start by accessing the cameras that HOAs were already using.
A version of this story played out in Alpharetta, Georgia. In 2020, the city’s police department paid Flock $17,680 for five Falcon cameras and logins for Flock software called Wing, which can extract vehicle and license plate data from off-brand camera footage. The next year, when Alpharetta bought a few more Flock cameras, a payment justification noted that “several” local private homeowner associations had already purchased Flock and granted them camera access.
“We are looking to add more city cameras into the Flock system,” the justification read. According to the city, “other vendors” would “not integrate with our existing Flock system.”
Over the next several years, Alpharetta expanded its work with the company significantly. By 2025, the city’s annual Flock bill had ballooned to $381,000.
As in other industries, companies that sell technology to police often use financial incentives to get customers in the door. Clearview AI, Ring, and Taser have all ponied up enticing offers to agencies around the country.
“A lot of these police surveillance vendors have learned the lessons of general old salesmanship,” Guariglia tells WIRED. In other words, deals and discounts work.
In some cases, this looks like new and increasingly expansive Flock products. In 2025, for instance, Alpharetta paid for an upgrade to the Elite Package of FlockOS, which Flock describes as a real-time crime-center platform. Other products are first offered with a free trial; Alpharetta took advantage of one 90-day window last year to try a new product dubbed Nova.
Flock also expands its contracts by offering discounts if departments sign a multiyear contract. In 2024, Alpharetta locked into a five-year contract with Flock that would cost $254,250 the first year and $238,000 for each successive year. The agreement was $232,500 less than five one-year agreements, which could be subject to higher rates.
The Alpharetta Police Department declined to comment.
Five-year agreements are common among Flock customers, which the company has sometimes marketed as a “price-lock promotion.” In a November 2023 email, Flock customer success manager Gwen Saltal used this framing to offer a five-year deal to New York’s Albany County Sheriff’s Office.
“As you may be aware, on April 1st, the cost of new Falcons went from $2,500 to $3,000, which will apply for future renewal terms on existing cameras as well,” Saltal wrote. “If you would like to lock in your current camera rates, Flock is offering a 5-year contract to hold that pricing.” The Albany County Sheriff’s Office did not respond to a request for comment.
In other cities, Flock won long-term contracts because it offered a convenient product bundle. (This is far from exclusive to Flock; Motorola, for instance, recently inked a $54 million agreement with Louisiana for a slate of policing technology.)
Guillermo Mixer, the police chief of the central California city of Greenfield, reported in a January city council meeting that the annual cost of the city’s surveillance system was $112,900, spread across five contracts with three companies: Flock, the surveillance camera company SurveillanceGrid, and the drone company Paladin.
Mixer proposed ditching SurveillanceGrid and Paladin and instead locking into a five-year contract with Flock. The annual cost would be $136,940—about $24,000 more than its level of spending at the time. He noted, however, that the price included three new cameras and access to Flock911, which transmits 911 call data to responding officers, as well as drones from Aerodrome, a company Flock acquired in 2024.
A proposed order form listed dozens of other Flock products and services included in the contract, though it’s unclear how many of those were new additions.
In the end, Greenfield’s city council unanimously approved Mixer’s repackaged Flock contract. Mixer and the Greenfield Police Department did not respond to a request for comment.
What Your Money Gets You
WIRED reviewed a July 2022 “Public Sector Price Sheet” for Flock products for the Fort Lauderdale Police Department in Florida. Though it was generated for one specific agency, it reflects the approximate price ranges WIRED observed in Flock purchase orders around that time from around the country.
Historically, Flock has placed agencies into one of 14 pricing “buckets” for its software, depending on their size. Agencies in “Bucket 1” have one to 15 sworn officers and could pay as little as $2,000 or as much as $115,500 for Flock software, depending on whether they get a basic package or select multiple add-ons. The costs by bucket incrementally increase until Bucket 14—which is for state and federal agencies, or local forces with more than 3,000 officers—which the sheet says gets “custom” rates.
Hardware, meanwhile, tends to be sold at flat annual rates. According to the pricing sheet, individual license plate readers and surveillance cameras cost $3,000 to $5,200 per year, not including the cost of initial installation—which can run between $150 and $2,750 upfront.
The pricing sheet puts Flock’s individual gunshot detectors at $8,500 to $35,000 annually, depending on their range. The cost for its individual drones, meanwhile, is $50,000 to $150,000 per year, and Flock’s two “mobile security trailer” offerings cost $20,000 and $25,000 annually. Fort Lauderdale police did not respond to a request for comment.
Though prices vary depending on the size of a purchase and individual negotiations with a city, Flock’s pricing appears to be comparable to its competitors. Axon recently quoted Denver $150,000 to install 50 cameras across the city and maintain them for one year, while Motorola recently charged Manti, Utah, $4,704 for a single license plate reader.
Flock also has a pricing plan for replacing damaged or stolen products—a particularly relevant concern amid a national wave of vandalism targeting Flock cameras. Per Flock contract conditions, the company retains ownership of the products it sells to cities. This means that when people damage or destroy cameras, cities are on the hook for the cost. (It also means that if a city decides to end their Flock contract, they have to give the equipment back.)
According to Flock’s website and invoices reviewed by WIRED, the company has flat rates for replacing damaged or stolen products: $800 for cameras, $500 for poles, and $1,300 for both. (This is up from its 2021 pricing, according to documents from Anderson County, South Carolina, when its replacement cost was $500 for cameras and $150 for poles.)
Some cities have gone out of their way to draw attention to the fiscal toll of replacing damaged Flock equipment—sometimes overstating the cost in the process.
Police from Winona, Minnesota, and Rutherfordton, North Carolina, have said that camera replacements cost $3,000 and $3,500 each, respectively—or $2,200 and $2,700 higher than the listed cost. And in Derby, Kansas, after a man damaged 10 Flock cameras, local police claimed that he caused $26,000 in damages. But depending on whether he damaged the poles, replacements likely would have cost $8,000 to $13,000. Police from Winona, Rutherfordton, and Derby did not respond to a request for comment.
Flock’s pricing, ultimately, is much lower than other department expenses—like police helicopters, which can cost tens of millions of dollars annually, or hiring more police officers.
Still, when compared to other technology-related expenses, Flock spending can stand out.
In Pasadena, Texas, which has a population of about 148,500, the 2026 police budget allotted $427,133 for Flock, $500,842 for body camera software, and $500,000 for "Motorola maintenance." These were, by far, the most expensive technology purchases. Most of the other purchases had budgets of less than $100,000. The Pasadena Police Department did not respond to a request for comment.
Why Some Customers Are Ditching Flock
Across the country, cities big and small have chosen to increase their Flock spending significantly over just a few years.
Savannah, Georgia, for instance, paid $33,000 for Flock in 2020 and $193,500 in 2025. Snellville, Georgia, paid Flock $5,000 in 2021 and 2022; in 2025, it paid $163,275. This year, as of August, the city has paid Flock $138,934.94. The Savannah and Snellville Police Departments did not respond to requests for comment.
However, in some cases, Flock’s pricing eventually proved to be prohibitive.
Jack Hall—the sheriff of Lorain County, Ohio—recently announced that the county would be canceling its Flock contract. Hall said that Flock planned to raise Lorain County’s two-year rate for 15 cameras by 17 percent. For him, it was too much.
Hall and the Lorain County Sheriff’s Office did not respond for comment.
Killingworth, Connecticut, also decided to end its relationship with Flock. The town paid $14,600 last year for four cameras. Killingworth first selectman Eric Couture noted “privacy concerns” related to Flock and said that it didn’t provide much to police relative to its cost.
Couture told WIRED that Flock’s cost wasn’t entirely prohibitive. But, he added, the cameras “did not add any utility” for the town’s “resident state trooper.”
