fifty oak trees and stone-paved clearing shape contemporary italian piazza by ghisellini architetti
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
08:45:07 UTC
17:45:07 KST

fifty oak trees and stone-paved clearing shape contemporary italian piazza by ghisellini architetti
ghisellini architetti reorganizes public square madre francesca cabrini around shaded gathering areas, layered planting, and integrated rainwater systems that reconnect the town center with the surrounding lowland landscape.
[FEATURED]
a grid of oak trees frames porphyry-paved piazza in northern Italy
Ghisellini Architetti has redesigned Public Square Madre Francesca Cabrini as a contemporary Italian piazza framed by architecture and trees. Located in a small town in the lower Lodi area of Italy, the project reinterprets the open clearings of the region’s former lowland forests, creating a defined public space enclosed by three planted edges and the existing town hall.
Ghisellini Architetti reimagines the square as a tree-lined clearing
A continuous paving surface of Italian porphyry extends from north to south, aligning with the town hall’s facade and volume. Fifty oak trees representing three species are arranged in a 7-by-7 grid, providing shade and forming sheltered green spaces around the square. Paths weave through flowers, lawns, shrubs, and shade-tolerant undergrowth, while wooden benches, drinking fountains, trash bins, and bike racks support public use. The design team at Ghisellini Architetti uses concrete monoliths to separate pedestrian areas from vehicles.
A dual-level lighting system illuminates the square after dark
A two-level lighting system combines multi-projector poles with ground-level fixtures to illuminate the square after dark. The landscape and paving also integrate rainwater management and climate-responsive measures. Permeable surfaces and lawns help replenish groundwater and reduce summer heat, while the porphyry paving directs rainfall to an underground storage system. Collected water is reused to irrigate trees, lawns, and undergrowth, with excess water gradually released into the drainage network during heavy rainfall.

name: FOREST JUMP | Public Square ‘Madre Francesca Cabrini’

location: Public Square Madre Francesca Cabrini, Lodi, Italy

====================================================================================================

Cyberattack on Supermarket Fridges in France Highlights Food Systems’ Vulnerability
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
08:45:00 UTC
17:45:00 KST

Cyberattacks aren’t just stealing your passwords; they’re spoiling your food.
The Paris prosecutor’s office opened an investigation on Monday into an overnight cyberattack on refrigeration systems at hundreds of French supermarkets. Hackers raised the temperature of refrigerators and freezers, sparking fires and causing food to spoil.
In a statement to TIME, French retailer Les Mousquetaires, which runs supermarket chains Intermarche and Netto, said damage from the attack could amount to several million euros in losses.
“Targeting equipment essential to the preservation of fresh products and to the food supply of the French people is of extreme gravity and is unprecedented,” Dominique Schelcher, CEO of French supermarket chain Cooperative U, posted on X.
France’s National Cybersecurity Agency (ANSSI) confirmed to TIME that it is investigating the attack “both at the national level, to accompany potential victims, and at the European level to coordinate with its counterparts.”
The incident has raised concerns about the threat of cyberattacks on food security as food supply chains increasingly rely on network-connected systems.
Christophe Hansen, the European Union’s food and agriculture commissioner, condemned the attack, noting in a post on X: “Food security requires more attention at all levels, because the exploitation of food has become a reality.”
Hackers target connected refrigerators, spoiling food across hundreds of stores
BFM-TV, which first reported the attack, said hackers “managed to remotely trigger the forced defrosting of the refrigeration systems in numerous stores.” The French broadcaster said the cyberattack involved forcing a continuous defrost cycle, setting temperatures to 50°C (122°F). French newspaper Le Monde reported that hackers also extended the defrost cycle in some freezers and cold-storage rooms from one hour to eight hours to delay alarms.
Supermarkets typically use central control panels to manage multiple refrigeration units. Many of these control panels are connected to the internet to allow maintenance companies to remotely access them. But the French government said Monday that exposing a management interface to the internet is “contrary to best practices,” and that remote administration should be restricted to trusted IP addresses if it is necessary.
Monday’s attack affected two refrigeration management product series by Danish company Danfoss, AK-SC and AK-SM, according to an ANSSI alert.
Danfoss told news outlets that it was “aware of incidents in France affecting a limited number of refrigeration management systems.” The company said the affected units “were running outdated firmware” and that it “long advised customers to keep supported systems updated with the latest firmware and to migrate legacy systems to current-generation solutions.”
Investigators have yet to publicly identify how attackers gained access to the Danfoss systems.
Around 180 Intermarche or its Netto brand supermarkets were targeted, parent company Les Mousquetaires told TIME, although BFM-TV reported a higher count of 300. At least 100 Cooperative U stores, 80 Carrefour outlets, 30 Monoprix stores and several E.Leclerc outlets were also affected, the retailers said. Independent grocery stores and butchers that use the same refrigeration system may also have been affected.
Intermarche CEO Thierry Cotillard told BFM-TV that the “unprecedented” attack resulted in losses amounting to “tens of millions of euros nationwide in a single day.”
Two supermarkets in Alsace, Intermarche and Super U, reported losses of 270,000 euros, according to BFM-TV. An Intermarche in La Haye, Normandy, posted on Facebook that temperatures reached 80°C (176°F), causing some equipment to melt. Supermarket owners described throwing out nearly a dumpster’s worth of frozen food.
TIME has reached out to Danfoss and major French retailers for comment.
Growing cyber threat to food and agriculture
France’s ANSSI told TIME that it is coordinating with European counterparts given that stores in other countries may also use the same software and be at risk. Reuters reported, citing a cyber threat intelligence analyst, that Spain, Portugal, Poland, Germany, and Belgium were affected. Internet scans found Danfoss refrigeration controllers exposed in South Africa, the U.S., the U.K., and other countries. France had the largest observed concentration, holding nearly 60% of the world’s exposed Danfoss controllers detected by scans, according to cyber intelligence firm U.K. Cyber Defence.
No other countries have confirmed related breaches so far.
The attack is also not the first time cyber incidents have disrupted food systems.
In late August, at least six U.S. military commissaries reported refrigeration outages, resulting in spoiled chilled and frozen products. Military investigators are investigating the outages, but have not commented on the nature of the investigation.
In June 2025, U.S. food distributor United Natural Foods also temporarily took certain systems offline during a suspected breach, which impacted order fulfillment and distribution.
Also on Monday, Dutch retailer Ahold Delhaize took several systems offline as a precautionary measure amid “a security issue within its network.” The retailer operates the Netherlands’ biggest supermarket chain Albert Heijn, as well as several U.S. grocery brands, including Stop & Shop, Hannaford, and Food Lion. In a Monday statement, Dutch retail brands Albert Heijn, Etos, and Gall & Gall said they were dealing with a cybersecurity incident. There is no established link between these incidents and the French cyberattack.
Food systems are becoming increasingly exposed to cyberattacks as farms, processors, distributors, and supermarkets rely on network-connected equipment throughout their supply chains, analysts have warned. The Food and Ag-ISAC, a nonprofit industry group based in Washington, D.C., tracked 227 ransomware incidents in the food and agriculture sector from January through July, up 62% from the same period last year.
The European Union’s cybersecurity agency ENISA also noted that food production, processing and distribution were among the sectors most affected by ransomware claims in its latest E.U. threat assessment.
Prior to Monday’s attack in France, cybersecurity firm Claroty published an August report that showed how flaws in Danfoss’s AK-SM 800A controller could allow an intruder to bypass a login and gain control of software used to control supermarket refrigeration. Danfoss’s firmware updates included fixes for those flaws.

Warsaw Security Forum on the "theory of victory”, security, the future of NATO and the war in Ukraine
12.10.2026
- The choice of place was not arbitrary - we picked Warsaw to show the theory of victory, as Poland has been demonstrating for the last few years how to place large investments for freedom to have strength with which to defend itself - said the Deputy Prime Minister W. Kosiniak-Kamysz during the Warsaw Security Forum.
On Monday, 12 October in Warsaw, the Deputy Prime Minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz and Deputy Minister Magdalena Sobkowiak-Czarnecka took part in the Warsaw Security Forum.
During the event, the Deputy Prime Minister met with the Supreme Allied Commander Europe (SACEUR), gen. Alexus Grynkewich. The Minister of National Defence has also attended a number of bilateral meetings and gave opening remarks for the panel “How Can Europe Build the Military Power It Needs?”.
- What to do for Europe to be stronger – that’s the topic of today’s debate. How to forge the difficult achievements and experiences of these last few months into being able to build strength and the resilience and defence potential for the whole of Europe? I will begin by saying that Europe has to take greater responsibility on itself. This is not just a buzzword anymore, but something European countries are fully aware of since the decision from the Hague in 2025 on spending 5% of GDP for defence by 2035. (…) We are the leader of using European funds from the SAFE programme – 44 billion euros, or almost a third of the entire amount went to Poland, and of that sum, two thirds has already been given to the Polish defence industry. Europe has to make its defence industry supply chain independent, that is the task that needs to be fulfilled first. (…) Military mobility is another matter with which the European Union has been struggling with for years now, and there is still no decision allowing for the free movement of troops without prior approval of all the regions or lands. This needs to end as soon as possible. (…) Poland wants to take greater responsibility for its partners, especially on the eastern flank of NATO. The more American soldiers are stationed in Poland, if we were to have a permanent base and presence of US troops, the more responsibility for the eastern flank of NATO we can take. (…) Europe has to do more not to replace America. We want an alliance with the United States. A lasting, predictable alliance, not just in the areas of intelligence exchange or military capabilities, but also for our defence industries. I believe that the defence industry strategy should be highlighted as part of plans for NATO 3.0, show it prominently. Things like moving production lines and service centres to Europe, for example those for the Patriot missiles
- said the Minister of National Defence during the Warsaw Security Forum.
Earlier, the Deputy Prime Minister was present for the discussion of gen. Grynkewich with prof. Katarzyna Pisarska, the head of Warsaw Security Forum, entitled: “The Theory of Victory: How To Achieve Military Success in Deterrence and Defence Against Russia?”.
- NATO is a defensive alliance. However, no one should mistake our defensive nature for weakness or lack of determination. If anyone was so reckless as to attack us, we will fight. (…) If we are attacked, we are ready to fight tonight, but we will not fall into complacency. We will still prepare and train every day, so tomorrow we will be even more ready, and even more the day after that. (…) If an adversary will threaten escalation, rattling their sabre, or actually decides on escalation during a conflict, this will not fracture our Alliance. On the contrary – it will make us even more united
- noted the Supreme Allied Commander Europe gen. Alexus Grynkewich, presenting his „theory of victory” during the Warsaw Security Forum.
Warsaw Secuirty Forum is an annual conference, organised by the Casimir Pulaski Foundation. WSF is a place for exchanging experiences and views on the security policy of the member states of the North Atlantic Treaty Organisation and the European Union, as well as partner countries. The guests are high-level country representatives, ambassadors, politicians and experts in international affairs and security.
- We do not want to waste time. Poland remembers, especially from the time of the Second World War, when not everything was yet ready, that the only boundless thing was the bravery of the Polish soldier and everything else had limits – the alliances had limits, deliveries had limits, supplies had limits. We do not want to have this history lesson, which our ancestors have learned once before, in their experience and the experience of all the Polish families, we do not want to repeat it
- noted the Deputy Prime Minister.
On the sidelines of the Forum, the Deputy Prime Minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz met with the US Permanent Representative to NATO Matthew Whitaker, the Chair of the NATO Military Committee, adm. Giuseppe Cavo Dragone and the Ministers of Defence of the Netherlands, Hungary, Norway, Kosovo and Belgium.
- I believe that this is the moment when the US government and companies will agree to co-production with Europe. The cooperation between the European Union and America is necessary. We have the SAFE instrument. We have decided to invest almost all the funds into our defence industry to make ourselves independent from other supply chains. (…) The lesson from Ukraine is that on the first day it is important how much equipment we have in place, but on the second and further days it is important to maintain what we have. This is something we are preparing for. Is Poland open to companies from other countries? Yes, this is one of the ideas present in the Ministry of National Defence. If a company wants to sell something to the Polish government, then we don’t look only at the price and quality. We are looking at four additional conditions. The first is a maintenance centre, co-production, local suppliers or at least investing in local training. So there is no chance for anyone to sell us something without investing in the region. This is also a matter of maintenance
- stressed the Secretary of State in the Ministry of National Defence Magdalena Sobkowiak-Czarnecka, who took part in the panel entitled: “How Can Europe Build the Military Potential It Needs?”.

Ukraine’s swimming robot can tow 10 tons, its maker says. Hook up a gun, and the shells ride aboard
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
08:43:52 UTC
17:43:52 KST

Ukraine’s amphibious ground robot UNEX UGV can tow artillery guns, its project lead said in a video interview, Militarnyi reported on 13 October. The electric platform from ABRIS Design Group (ABRIS DG) also swims, climbs, and hauls cargo on its own deck.
The Defense Ministry’s robot tally, kept in its DELTA system, counts supply and evacuation runs. It logged 25,143 of them in August, a monthly figure that has climbed all year. In April, then-Defense Minister Mykhailo Fedorov said the goal was for robots to handle all frontline logistics. A robot that brings a gun and its shells to a position adds artillery moves to that workload.
A gun behind, shells aboard
The robot can pull a gun or another wheeled vehicle of up to 10 metric tons (about 22,000 lb), the project lead said. Ammunition can ride aboard, so the gun and its rounds reach the position together. No crew has to go with them, he said, and the team has already demonstrated the setup. On its own deck, ABRIS DG says, the robot carries up to 1.7 tons (3,750 lb) on land and 1.25 tons (2,760 lb) on water.
ABRIS DG said US Army testers ran UNEX through scenarios that included towing Joint Light Tactical Vehicles (JLTVs), which are armored US military trucks. The trials took place at the Army’s XTech competition in Vilseck, Germany, in March 2026. UNEX was picked as one of five winners, the company said.
Swims, climbs, backtracks
The robot can float for more than an hour. The team has already crossed the Desna River and narrow stretches of the Dnipro with it, the project lead said. Ultra-low-pressure tires spread its weight over soft ground and swamps. ABRIS DG says it climbs obstacles up to one meter (3.3 ft) high and drives out of water onto ice.
Ukraine turned ground robots into a frontline workhorse. Its first competitive tender may reward cheap copies over proven machines, an officer warns
Operators steer it via Starlink or radio. An escort drone can add an overhead view to the robot’s own cameras. If the link drops, the robot retraces its route to where the signal last held.
It runs on a Ukrainian-made 78 kWh battery. The project lead puts its work time at up to six hours and its range at up to 120 km (75 miles), with a top speed of 20 km/h (12 mph). Load and terrain cut into those figures, he added. With a generator now in development, a mission should stretch to about 12–14 hours, he said.
The robot is not built for the zero line, the project lead said. It works 20–30 km behind the front, at night, where armor would add little. Developers also plan demining and air defense versions. Ukraine’s Defense Ministry codified the robot and cleared it for use in its forces in April 2025.

The escalation in Yemen is a turning point
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
08:42:55 UTC
17:42:55 KST

The escalation in Yemen is a turning point
The risk of a region-wide war is increasing, but if cooler heads prevail, a peaceful arrangement can still be reached.
Yemen is witnessing a major military escalation that has once again brought the western coast and the area around the Bab al-Mandeb strait to the forefront of regional developments. Operation Yemen’s Dawn, launched by the forces loyal to the internationally recognised Yemeni government, has produced some results.
Government forces have advanced towards the strait of Bab al-Mandeb and are now fighting against reinforced Houthi positions. Clashes continue in parts of Dhubab District and around Dhubab Airport.
The central question now is whether these military moves can bring about a lasting change in the balance of power and whether they will widen the confrontation or open the way for a new negotiating process.
Control of Bab al-Mandeb
Fighting has concentrated around Bab al-Mandeb because of its strategic position in global trade and energy flows. It is especially significant to the parties to the Yemeni conflict because control of the coastline, islands and surrounding highlands offers varying capabilities for surveillance, military deployment and threats to maritime traffic.
An advance along the coast may enable government forces to retake key positions and restrict the Houthis’ space for manoeuvre. However, it does not, by itself, guarantee the security of the strait or eliminate threats to navigation.
Even if the Houthis lose coastal positions, they could still retain their ability to launch attacks in the Red Sea. Threats to maritime traffic do not necessarily depend on direct control of the strait; they also depend on the availability of missiles, drones, launch platforms, supply networks and the ability to operate from other locations.
As operations move from the coastal strip into the highlands, particularly the Kahbub Mountains in Lahj governorate and the highlands to the west and south-west of Taiz governorate, the challenges posed by the terrain, defence, movement and supply become more severe.
In this context, three distinct levels must be differentiated: retaking coastal positions, consolidating military control over them and establishing a sustainable capacity to secure the strait and its surrounding area. Confusing these levels may lead either to an exaggerated assessment of the operation’s results or to an underestimation of the adversary’s ability to continue fighting.
Unity and cohesion
Recent statements by Dr Rashad Al-Alimi, president of Yemen’s Presidential Leadership Council, signal a shift in objectives: from containing the Houthi threat to restoring state institutions and liberating Sanaa.
This shift gives the ongoing fighting a national dimension that goes beyond limited gains on the ground. Its success, however, remains contingent on the government forces’ ability to unify command, secure supplies and coordinate the various military formations.
Containing divisions within the components of the government—particularly over the southern issue—is essential to preserving gains and preventing the confrontation from turning into an internal conflict.
Success requires coordination among participating formations, avoidance of competition over spheres of influence and the linking of military gains to security and political governance capable of preventing fighting between factions.
This is especially important because the formations playing the most effective role in the coastal battles, the Southern Giants Brigades, originate from the southern governorates.
The regional dimension
The Houthi escalation is difficult to understand in isolation from the Iran war. Iran’s support for the group is well-known, but recent media reports have also revealed the extent of it. The Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps reportedly has directed Houthi movements along the coast and encouraged escalation against Saudi Arabia, with commitments to provide further support.
Control of Bab al-Mandeb is strategically important to Iran and its allies, as increased pressure there can provide more leverage in the Iran conflict.
For Saudi Arabia, involvement in the Yemen conflict is driven by direct security concerns and a desire to reduce threats to its territory and nearby maritime routes.
Against this backdrop, a Saudi response to the deadly airport attacks appears highly likely. Riyadh may be less inclined to limit itself to familiar exchanges along existing front lines and could instead target sites or capabilities of greater importance within the Houthis’ military structure. What form the response takes may reflect efforts to impose significant costs without immediately widening the confrontation into a broader regional war.
At the Gulf level, collective military participation appears less certain. The attacks could prompt an emergency GCC meeting, stronger political statements, or greater defensive coordination, but reviving a joint military campaign against the Houthis would be more difficult. Gulf states no longer share the same degree of strategic alignment over Yemen, while differences, particularly between Saudi and Emirati priorities, continue to constrain collective action.
Pakistan and Turkiye, for their part, have announced support for Saudi Arabia under the Mecca Pact, although the exact parameters of their participation are yet to be defined. The current escalation may therefore test whether these partnerships remain political and defensive frameworks or translate into practical military support, including stronger air defence deployments.
US involvement also remains possible, but any direct role would likely be limited. Previous US intervention in Yemen has focused more on deterrence, maritime security and containing threats rather than on decisively shifting the battlefield balance in favour of the government forces.
An expanding confrontation does not automatically mean that all parties seek an open war. Some may use escalation to improve their deterrence or negotiating position, although the risk of miscalculation remains.
What happens next
Developments in the Yemen war in the near future depend on the government forces’ ability to hold the positions they have retaken, secure the area around the strait and the connecting roads and remove the Houthi threat from the highlands. If these conditions are met, the balance of military and political pressure could shift, though this would not necessarily end the Houthis’ maritime threat.
However, if the advance stalls at positions that are difficult to overcome and the Houthis are able to continue using missiles and drones to conduct counterattacks, this could create a protracted confrontation. A war of attrition could have a devastating humanitarian and economic impact not just on Yemen, but across the region.
The risk of escalation and region-wide war may still push the parties to seek an understanding or an arrangement to halt the fighting. Turning military advances into a settlement, however, would require addressing broader political and security issues, including power-sharing arrangements, mutual guarantees and the security of maritime routes.
In other words, the ongoing coastal battle could become a gateway to a broader change in the course of Yemen’s crisis rather than another round in a protracted war.
The views expressed in this article are the author’s own and do not necessarily reflect Al Jazeera’s editorial stance.

MI5 chief Ken McCallum confirms Russia did interfere in Brexit referendum - but says it had little impact
Dan Sabbagh
Dan Sabbagh is the Guardian’s defence and security editor.
MI5 chief Ken McCallum said today that Moscow did attempt to interfere in the 2016 Brexit referendum with anti-EU coverage on RT and Sputnik media and via troll social media accounts. But there was a big difference between “what may have been attempted and what actually resulted”, he added.
The head of the Security Service said that he agreed strongly with what the prime minister had said on Sunday and Monday, when he raised the issue of attempted Russian interference a decade ago – though Burnham then backed off when he was challenged by the Conservatives as to whether this meant he regarded the Brexit vote as illegitimate.
McCallum did not put any new evidence into the public domain but cited already known concerns about Russian broadcasters who “came in pretty strongly around the time of the referendum” in favour of Brexit. He also said that “there was a second line of interference attempted through [internet] trolls”.
However, he argued there was no evidence to suggest the result of the Brexit vote had been swayed as a result of the effort, which is generally believed to have been marginal, and said that it would be to Russia’s benefit if the issue was talked about further.
He explained:
It is up to us how far we allow our adversaries to divide us.
I’m a little bit worried that if we all stay in this debate for another few days, the Russian trolls who didn’t appear to do all that much at various points over the years, they’ll be delighted they are front page news once again despite the comparative unimpressedness of what they do at all points along the journey.
I am a little bit anxious that we don’t play into our adversaries’ hands by making these trolls look 10ft tall.
UPDATE:McCallum said:
There is a really important difference between interference attempted and outcome swayed … It’s quite important to focus on the difference between what may have been attempted and what actually resulted.
It is a matter of public record including in select committee reports published in 2019 – the DCMS [digital, culture, media and sport] committee did a bit and the intelligence and security committee did a bit also – that in 2016, before you even get to any secret intelligence … it is openly on the record that Russia Today and Sputnik and other Russian media organisations came in pretty strongly around the referendum.
And it is also a matter of open source record that there was a certain amount of interference attempted through trolls and bots and so forth.
I agree strongly with what the prime minister said yesterday, we did see a hack and leak thing inside the 2019 general election campaign.

Streeting tells MPs committing to spending 3% of GDP on defence without plan to fund it would risk Truss-type backlash
The government could trigger a Liz Truss mini-budget-type economic incident if it committed to spend 3% of GDP on defence by 2030 without saying where the money will come from, Wes Streeting has suggested.
Streeting used the argument as he gave evidence to the Commons defence committee, where he as pressed to confirm that the government will raise defence spending to 3% of GDP by 2030.
The defence investment plan (Dip) currently sets out a path to spending 2.7% of GDP on defence by the 2027-28 financial year. We have had very bitter recent experience of a former prime minister making unfunded commitments to spend more, tax less, and borrow more all simultaneously, and it led to enormous loss of confidence, people’s mortgages going up, and a level of fundamental loss of confidence in Britain among investors, and this country is still recovering from that.

Veterans to get more protection under significant amendments to Northern Ireland Troubles bill, ministers claim
Later in the Commons, MPs are expected to pass a motion allowing them more time to consider the Northern Ireland Troubles bill before it has to be passed. The bill was introduced in the last session of parliament, which means it is subject to the carry-over procedure.
The bill replaces legislation passed by the last Tory government which in effect gave immunity to terrorists and members of the armed forces accused of crimes during the Troubles, provided they gave evidence to a Legacy Commission trying to establish the truth about unsolved Troubles-era murders. The Conservative law was hugely unpopular in Northern Ireland, and the Labour alternative – which is similar – has also been widely criticised.
In an article in the Times today, Chris Byrant, the Northern Ireland secretary, and Wes Streeting, the defence secretary, highlight amendments being made to the bill which they argue will reduce the risk of retired soldiers being subject to vexatious investigations. Under one change, in future the attorney general would have to approve any serious, Troubles-related prosecution.
They say:
By setting up a fair, workable system to deliver as many answers as possible, we will help communities to heal so that we can finally turn the page on one of the darkest periods in our recent history.
More than a quarter of the families seeking answers from the Legacy Commission are veterans’ families. Nearly one in five are the families of police officers. No one should be in any doubt how important this is.
And describing the way the legislation has been changed, they say:
Over the last few months, we have listened to veterans, victims’ groups, including those representing service families, and the wider defence community to hear their concerns. We are responding by making sure the Troubles bill properly protects all those troops who served with honour.
Under the previous government’s scheme, terrorists would have enjoyed the same immunity as veterans – something so abhorrent it should never have been considered in the first place. And so we will not only repeal it, we will make clear – in black and white – that there is no equivalence between paramilitaries, who waged campaigns of violence, murder and destruction, and the lawful actions of our armed forces sent to stop them.
For too long, our servicemen and women have had to fear the knock at the door, the call from an unknown number or the ping of an email notification, as they bear the brunt of incidents being reinvestigated years or decades after the events in question. The bill spells out that there can be no duplication of previous investigative processes unless it is essential, and that witnesses cannot be contacted unless it has been clearly demonstrated that there is compelling new evidence. Nor will veterans be forced to traipse to Northern Ireland to attend hearings. And any decision to prosecute a serious Troubles-related crime will now require the consent of the attorney general.

MI5 chief Ken McCallum confirms Russia did interfere in Brexit referendum - but says it had little impact
Dan Sabbagh
Dan Sabbagh is the Guardian’s defence and security editor.
MI5 chief Ken McCallum said today that Moscow did attempt to interfere in the 2016 Brexit referendum with anti-EU coverage on RT and Sputnik media and via troll social media accounts. But there was a big difference between “what may have been attempted and what actually resulted”, he added.
The head of the Security Service said that he agreed strongly with what the prime minister had said on Sunday and Monday, when he raised the issue of attempted Russian interference a decade ago – though Burnham then backed off when he was challenged by the Conservatives as to whether this meant he regarded the Brexit vote as illegitimate.
McCallum did not put any new evidence into the public domain but cited already known concerns about Russian broadcasters who “came in pretty strongly around the time of the referendum” in favour of Brexit. He also said that “there was a second line of interference attempted through [internet] trolls”.
However, he argued there was no evidence to suggest the result of the Brexit vote had been swayed as a result of the effort, which is generally believed to have been marginal, and said that it would be to Russia’s benefit if the issue was talked about further.
He explained:
It is up to us how far we allow our adversaries to divide us.
I’m a little bit worried that if we all stay in this debate for another few days, the Russian trolls who didn’t appear to do all that much at various points over the years, they’ll be delighted they are front page news once again despite the comparative unimpressedness of what they do at all points along the journey.
I am a little bit anxious that we don’t play into our adversaries’ hands by making these trolls look 10ft tall.
UPDATE:McCallum said:
There is a really important difference between interference attempted and outcome swayed … It’s quite important to focus on the difference between what may have been attempted and what actually resulted.
It is a matter of public record including in select committee reports published in 2019 – the DCMS [digital, culture, media and sport] committee did a bit and the intelligence and security committee did a bit also – that in 2016, before you even get to any secret intelligence … it is openly on the record that Russia Today and Sputnik and other Russian media organisations came in pretty strongly around the referendum.
And it is also a matter of open source record that there was a certain amount of interference attempted through trolls and bots and so forth.
I agree strongly with what the prime minister said yesterday, we did see a hack and leak thing inside the 2019 general election campaign.

====================================================================================================

Pakistan Imposes Emergency and Governor’s Rule in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
08:42:00 UTC
17:42:00 KST

On October 11, Pakistan’s federal government imposed an emergency and governor’s rule in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa (KP) province, which was being governed by former Prime Minister Imran Khan’s Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI).
The move, which was approved by President Asif Ali Zardari on the advice of Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif following a federal cabinet meeting, marks a decisive takeover by the federal government of a province that has long been a PTI stronghold. The federal government justified the decision by pointing to a sharp surge in terror attacks across KP, alleging that the provincial administration was obstructing counterterrorism efforts, failing to maintain public order and allowing militant groups space to operate.
The federal government invoked Articles 232 and 234 of the constitution, which grant extraordinary powers to the federal government over provincial affairs.
However, the two articles address different circumstances and operate within distinct mechanisms. For instance, Article 232 empowers the federal government to declare a state of emergency when security is threatened by war or internal disturbance beyond the provincial government’s control. Under this provision, the provincial assembly continues to function, but federal laws take precedence in cases of conflict.
On the other hand, Article 234 allows the president to impose governor’s rule when a provincial government is judged unable to function in accordance with the constitution. Once implemented, the article suspends the provincial cabinet, transfers executive authority to the federal government or the governor, and permits parliament to exercise the assembly’s powers.
By deploying the two articles together, the federal government has essentially neutralized PTI’s institutional presence in the province. Article 234 has removed the PTI provincial cabinet and chief minister, which has effectively cut the party off from the province’s administrative system, official resources, and day-to-day levers of governance.
Moreover, Article 232 has shifted key legislative and public order authority to the center and provided federal authorities with stronger legal tools to enforce order, restrict street mobilization and limit any form of organized political activity.
By invoking Articles 232 and 234, the federal government has made a comprehensive effort to deny PTI any realistic prospect of regaining political or institutional influence in KP province in the near term.
This institutional confrontation is the culmination of months of friction between the federal government and PTI. The current setup in Islamabad is governed by a multi-party coalition, which is led by Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif of the Pakistan Muslim League-Nawaz (PML-N) and supported prominently by the Pakistan People’s Party (PPP) under President Asif Ali Zardari. It is pertinent to mention that after having assumed power following a highly contested election in 2024, the ruling coalition in Islamabad has remained engaged in an intense political feud with Imran Khan’s party.
The latest decision indicates that the relationship between the PTI-led provincial government and the federal government had become virtually unbridgeable.
From Islamabad’s perspective, the core dispute between the two sides centered on counterterrorism policy and the provincial government’s perceived defiance of federal priorities. It is important to note that security conditions in the province have deteriorated sharply in recent months with a marked rise in militant attacks.
Information Minister Attaullah Tarar on Sunday went as far as saying that the PTI-led government had developed a nexus with terrorist groups and that a “power-sharing formula was gradually taking shape between terrorists and the PTI’s KP government, which was starting from southern districts and was ingressing further into the entire KP.”
The PTI leadership has questioned these assertions, arguing that security concerns are being leveraged to justify political measures aimed at diminishing the party’s footprint in the province. Furthermore, PTI leaders maintain that the central government refused to adopt a consultative approach to address the militancy challenge and also consistently denied party leaders access to consult with Imran Khan, who is languishing in prison.
The timing of this development is significant for many reasons. The emergency measures were imposed as the PTI prepared a long march from KP to Islamabad, the national capital, to demand Khan’s release from prison. Moreover, the provincial leadership, particularly Chief Minister Sohail Afridi, have refused to come on board the federal government’s counterterrorism policy. This stance hardened in recent months.
For decision makers in Islamabad, the provincial government had become both a political irritant and a security liability that was obstructing coordinated action against the militancy emanating from KP, which has become a threat to national security.
Following the declaration of emergency, one of the central government’s first administrative steps has been to establish a direct administrative framework for KP’s border and former tribal districts. The federal government has approved the immediate establishment of an Area Development Secretariat, which will be supervised by an Area Representative and Development Council and covers Dera Ismail Khan, Tank, Lakki Marwat, Bannu, Bajaur, Mohmand, Khyber, Kurram, Orakzai, North Waziristan, and both Upper and South Waziristan. The ADS will be responsible for restoring law and order, protecting citizens, and ensuring governance and development.
Under this arrangement, civil administration, police and military coordination have been placed under a streamlined federal framework. It has created a more direct channel for Islamabad to manage high-risk districts. Moreover, this has also arguably reduced the scope for any future provincial government to impede security operations in these areas.
The move also carries clear external implications.
On Monday, KP Governor Faisal Karim Kundi stated that the days of lack of coordination between the center and the province on terrorism related issues are over, adding that “our policies will come from Islamabad … not Kabul, Jalalabad or Kandahar.” Arguably, Kundi’s statement was meant to emphasize that the state will not entertain dialogue or local deals with militant elements. By emphasizing that policy will originate from Islamabad rather than Afghanistan, he signaled that the federal government will no longer tolerate cross-border sanctuaries and will implement security policy unilaterally.
Kundi’s statement is important as it carries clear policy-level implications. If the new administrative framework is any indication, Pakistan is set to confront Tehreek-e-Taliban Pakistan (TTP) threats and presence in its border regions more forcefully than before, and will likely pursue an uncompromising approach toward the Afghan Taliban on issues of militancy, border management, and cross-border sanctuaries.
One can argue that while the PTI government in Peshawar had become a political problem for the center, it had also evolved, in Islamabad’s assessment, into a security challenge. The party’s resistance to the measures now being imposed in the former tribal districts was viewed as untenable by both the federal government and the military leadership.
For now, the federal government has imposed its will in the province. Whether the new direct-rule arrangement can deliver improved security and reduced terrorist threats will determine whether it ultimately gains public acceptance. The immediate challenge for Islamabad is to ensure that the policy it is seeking to implement actually produces results on the ground.

LVMH sales miss growth forecasts as China luxury demand slows
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
08:41:04 UTC
17:41:04 KST

LVMH, the world's leading luxury group, said its sales edged higher in the third quarter despite a slowdown in demand in China hitting its fashion and leather goods segment.
The fashion giant, once Europe’s most valuable listed company, reported revenue of €18.5 billion in the three months to the end of September.
The firm, whose brands include Louis Vuitton, Dior, Celine and drinks maker Hennessy, saw a revenue increase of 1.2% year on year in the third quarter, after a 0.1% rise in the second quarter and a 5.9% fall in the first.
However, organic sales growth, which excludes currency movements and changes to the group's business portfolio, fell short of expectations. Growth slowed to 1% in the third quarter from 3% in the second.
Overall, in the first nine months, sales were €57.1 billion, with organic sales up 2%.
The company praised its diverse business portfolio in a statement, saying it provided resilience in an uncertain geopolitical and economic environment.
LVMH said sales growth was good in the United States, Europe and Japan, but it faced a less favourable environment in China.
As a result, the fashion and leather goods segment saw sales drop 5% on an organic basis as weaker demand in the world's second-largest economy weighed on the business. The decline was steeper than the roughly 2% fall expected by analysts, according to Deutsche Bank.
Louis Vuitton also saw its public image take a hit in China after suing local tea company Molly Tea for copying its logo. While it won the case, the dispute provoked a wave of indignation on social media and calls to boycott the brand.
Overall, the quarter proved to be a setback for the fashion and leather goods segment, as the drop in sales followed the division posting its first organic sales gain in two years in the previous quarter.
But LVMH's selective retailing division, which includes the Sephora perfume and cosmetics retail chain, posted an 8% organic sales increase, while the watches and jewellery and wines and spirits segments both managed 6% organic gains.
Deutsche Bank analysts said the results could prompt further cuts to earnings forecasts for the second half of 2026 and 2027.
“It is hard to see what could change investor sentiment in the short term,” they wrote, although they viewed the weakness as cyclical rather than structural.
"Overall, recovery is taking longer due to the weaker Chinese demand, but the company do not see it as a structural issue. Brand initiatives are producing results and they expect these bottom-up measures to be more gradual," they wrote.
LVMH's share price has dropped nearly 40% since the start of the year. In September, L'Oréal overtook the group as France's most valuable listed company. LVMH’s share price was down more than 1.6% at around 10am CEST in Paris.

Lithuanian fintech is growing abroad and strengthening the export of financial services
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
08:39:55 UTC
17:39:55 KST

In Lithuania, licensed electronic money and payment institutions had 2.5 million active customers in 2025 – 14 percent more than a year ago. As many as 87 percent of them were foreign customers, according to data from the Bank of Lithuania. According to the Lithuanian Fintech Association, these results reveal the improving opportunities for the country’s fintech companies to grow in international markets and strengthen the export potential of Lithuania’s financial services.
The international orientation of the sector is also visible in the business client segment. Of the 146 thousand legal entities served by electronic money and payment institutions, only slightly more than a fifth were established in Lithuania. This shows that foreign companies also widely use the payment services of institutions licensed here.
As Greta Ranonytė, CEO of the Lithuanian Fintech Association, notes, the large share of foreign clients shows that the services of payment companies licensed in Lithuania are in demand on the international market. According to her, this provides opportunities for companies to grow and strengthen Lithuania’s role as a financial services center.
“Lithuania’s small domestic market does not limit the opportunities of payment companies operating here. The expertise of specialists, technological solutions, payment infrastructure and opportunities provided by the regulatory environment accumulated in our country help them to serve foreign residents and businesses. For Lithuania, this is an opportunity to expand the fintech sector, export of financial services and create high-value-added jobs here, even though the users of the services are in other EU countries,” she says.
Both income and payment volumes grew
The expansion of the customer base was accompanied by growing revenues of electronic money and payment institutions, which constitute an important part of the Lithuanian fintech sector. According to the Bank of Lithuania, the revenues of these institutions from licensed activities in 2025 increased by 13 percent and reached EUR 643.1 million. The total amount of payment transactions increased by 5 percent over the year to EUR 161.6 billion.
At the end of 2025, there were 117 electronic money and payment institutions operating in Lithuania.
As G. Ranonytė notes, when assessing Lithuania’s positions in the international financial technology market, it is important to take into account the ability of companies operating here to expand their activities and earn income.
“It would be too narrow to judge the development of the sector solely by the number of licenses issued. What is also important is the scale of activities carried out by companies, how many clients they serve and whether they are able to retain them. Growing income and payment volumes show that licensed institutions in Lithuania are expanding their activities. For the further growth of the fintech sector, it is important to invest in the quality of services, technologies and people who help compete in different markets,” she says.
Currently, there are a total of almost 250 financial technology companies operating in Lithuania, employing about 7.8 thousand specialists.

AI models improve long-term flood forecasting: study
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
16:38:25 CST
17:38:25 KST

SYDNEY, Oct. 13 (Xinhua) -- An international research team has developed artificial intelligence (AI) models that could improve long-term flood forecasting, helping communities get warnings weeks ahead of floods.
Researchers used two decades of historical precipitation and streamflow data from the DuPage River basin in Illinois, the United States, to develop deep learning models incorporating attention mechanisms to identify patterns in rainfall and river flow, according to a statement released Tuesday by Australia's University of Technology Sydney (UTS).
By combining the models' predictions, the team improved forecasting accuracy, with the ensemble deep learning models reducing prediction errors by about 38 percent and the proposed fusion framework improving predictive performance by about 47 percent, according to the study published in the Journal of Hydrologic Engineering.
The approach remained highly accurate for forecasts up to 12 weeks ahead, said UTS Professor Amir H. Gandomi, the study's co-author, stressing that additional warning time could help communities prepare for floods.
The findings could have implications for flood risk management, including disaster preparedness, infrastructure resilience and water resource management, according to the team.
"Ultimately, the goal is not simply to predict floods more accurately, but to turn better predictions into better decisions," Gandomi said. ■

"Israel’s continued violations of Syrian sovereignty and territorial integrity undermine these prospects and show disregard for international law,” he said.
"The situation is particularly alarming in southern Syria, where continued military incursions and expansionist actions and words are getting out of control,” he added.
Yıldız said Israel’s recent resumption of activities along the so-called "Sufa 53 line” in Quneitra was a further attempt to undermine the 1974 agreement and impose a fait accompli on the ground. "These reckless acts must stop,” he said.
He urged Israel to comply with the 1974 agreement and relevant Security Council resolutions, particularly Resolution 497, and to withdraw from the occupied Syrian Golan Heights. "A stable, sovereign and unified Syria capable of securing its borders, defeating terrorist organizations and contributing to regional peace and economic cooperation serves the interests of all, including Israel,” he added.
"The dissolution of the so-called SDF has opened a new chapter in the integration process,” Yıldız said. "Remaining arrangements should be finalized and fully implemented without delay, in a manner that reinforces Syria’s sovereignty, unity and social cohesion,” he added.
Yıldız described the fight against terrorism as "a critical priority” and welcomed Damascus’ cooperation with the global coalition for the enduring defeat of Daesh. "Security and economic recovery must advance hand in hand,” he said.
On refugees, Yıldız said the number of Syrians under temporary protection in Türkiye once exceeded 4 million and now stands at around 2.2 million.
He said returns have been gradual because of economic conditions, security concerns and Israeli incursions. Since Bashar Assad’s fall on Dec. 8, 2024, Israel has expanded its military operations in Syria, moving troops into the Golan buffer zone and nearby positions. Syria demands the withdrawal of Israeli forces from the areas they occupied and maintains its commitment to the 1974 Disengagement Agreement. Israel claims its movements are driven by security considerations.
Addressing the same session, Syria’s U.N. representative Ibrahim Olabi said those claiming to seek security "should not be killing Syrian citizens within Syrian territory.”

BEIJING, Oct. 13 (Xinhua) -- Chinese President Xi Jinping has called for efforts to firmly follow a path with Chinese characteristics in developing the country's health programs, to secure decisive progress in the Healthy China Initiative over the 15th Five-Year Plan period (2026-2030).
Xi, also general secretary of the Communist Party of China (CPC) Central Committee and chairman of the Central Military Commission, made the remarks at a national meeting on health held in Beijing on Monday and Tuesday.
Xi stressed that people's health is a key benchmark of a nation's prosperity and strength.
Since the 18th CPC National Congress in 2012, the Party has made a major decision to launch the Healthy China Initiative, promoting the establishment of the world's largest systems of medical services, traditional medicine, disease prevention and control, and healthcare security, said Xi, noting that the country has achieved historic accomplishments and made all-round progress in healthcare.
He said the goal is to build a Healthy China, where health services are ensured in a balanced, inclusive, high-quality and efficient manner.
Xi stressed that people's health should be factored into all policies and reflected in every aspect of work.
Prevention, he said, is the most cost-effective and efficient approach to protecting public health. He called for greater emphasis on foundational health work, addressing risks at their source, and encouraging the public to adopt a sound understanding of health and take an active role in managing their own well-being.
He also called for a stronger disease prevention and control system to guard against large-scale outbreaks.
Xi underscored the need to optimize the functions and structural layout of medical institutions so that people can access medical care close to home and receive effective treatment.
He also urged efforts to improve mechanisms for the preservation and innovative development of traditional Chinese medicine, strengthen basic research and original innovation in the health sector, and enhance the patient experience.
Xi stressed that coordinating the development and regulation of medical services, medical insurance, and pharmaceuticals should be a key priority in reforming China's medical and healthcare systems.
He also called for efforts to train and develop a sufficient number of highly qualified medical professionals.
Efforts will also be made to actively promote the building of a global community of health for all, work with other countries to address major challenges in the health sector, and continuously improve the health and well-being of people around the world, he said. ■

Economy Minister Giancarlo Giorgetti
said the government will continue to take a prudent approach to
managing the public finances as there are storm clouds ahead as
he presented its Public Finance Planning Document (DPFP) in the
Lower House on Tuesday.
                                    
The DPFP features the government's plan to use the escape clause
granted by the EU for 0.3% budget deviations for both energy and
defence investments in the 2027 budget law.
                                    
"Planning three years ahead (in the DPFP) is highly complex
especially amid great turbulence, and updates come weekly, as
IMF data show," Giorgetti said.
                                    
"The fundamental premise underlying our reasoning is that when
the weather forecast predicts a storm, it is wise to check the
vessel's condition before heading out to the open sea, and that
is precisely what we have sought to do in recent years.
                                    
"We believe it is essential to stay on this course at a time
when storm clouds are gathering on the horizon.
                                    
"This document is a reflection of that approach, aiming to
adhere to the path of fiscal consolidation and meet the targets
set by the new European governance framework, with a view to
exiting the (excessive-deficit) procedure in the spring,
conditions permitting".
                                    
Italy's budget deficit needs to come within the 3% of GDP
threshold for it to be able to emerge from the procedure.
                                    
Giorgetti has said he is expects this to be the case for 2026,
after the deficit came in at 3.1% for 2025, before going up to
3.4% in 2027 with the use of the escape clause.
                                    
"The request to adjust the budget in order to activate the
national escape clause for defence and energy is a deliberate
departure from the prudent stance I have previously advocated,"
Giorgetti said.
                                    
"These are measures that the Commission acknowledges, and that
the markets have deemed sustainable within the framework of
ensuring the long-term sustainability of Italian public debt".

Chiang rejected claims that his campaign had proposed Oct. 31, saying the date came from the two broadcasters. He said organizers needed at least two weeks to prepare, making Oct. 31 the earliest possible date, per Newtalk.
Chiang said his team had agreed to the date despite existing commitments. He criticized Shen's representatives for leaving the talks without approving it, questioning whether they had the authority to make decisions.
Chiang also accused Shen of using calls for a debate as a campaign issue rather than making a serious effort to arrange one. Shen rejected the criticism, saying his campaign had sent senior staff with decision-making authority to the meeting.
Shen's campaign manager, DPP Legislator Wu Szu-yao (吳思瑤), also criticized Chiang's team for failing to clarify how many debates it would accept. She accused the campaign of trying to limit the candidates to one debate by insisting that the first event be arranged before discussing others.
Chiang maintained that his position was consistent with Lo's and said both campaigns should focus on holding the first debate. He added that he remained open to discussing a second or third debate afterward.

Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) leaders Ashutosh Ranka, Saurav Das and Ajinkya Shinde were among about 20 volunteers who “sneaked” into Jantar Mantar to “reclaim” the popular protest site and were detained on Tuesday.
CJP supporters and opposition parties have held protests nearly every day this month to demand CEC Gyanesh Kumar’s resignation over the revisions, which critics say favour Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP).
Thousands joined a protest march on Monday, after a clampdown foiled CJP plans for a weekend demonstration. Earlier, police detained thousands of protesters, including CJP leaders, over the weekend.
Following the mass detentions, Human Rights Watch urged the government to stop “the ill-treatment” and “arbitrary” arrests of protesters and to allow people to protest peacefully.
“The Modi government should stop throwing young protesters in jail and instead engage with them to address concerns over the right to vote and fairness of elections,” Elaine Pearson, HRW’s Asia director, said in a statement on Tuesday.
“Peaceful protest and freedom of expression are fundamental rights protected under the international human rights law that India’s leaders claim to uphold,” she added.
The Delhi Police announced on Monday that the Jantar Mantar open-air astronomical observatory was no longer designated an official protest site and that three new venues had been identified for demonstrations.
However, CJP leaders and supporters went ahead with their protest plan at Jantar Mantar and were taken into custody.
“You cannot denotify the resistance,” CJP founder Abhijeet Dipke said on X after their detention.
A video posted to his account shows about a dozen volunteers jumping a gate and barricades to reach the site, where they waved the Indian flag and chanted slogans as police arrived and detained them.
The Delhi Police did not immediately respond to a request for comment from the Reuters news agency.
In an earlier post, Dipke said the government’s efforts to block the site would do nothing to deter their campaign.
“If Modi thinks taking away Jantar Mantar will put an end to protests, he is mistaken. Jantar Mantar is not just a location but a spirit of resistance that nobody can ever take away,” he said.
The youth-led movement, which has mobilised protests in recent months over a range of issues, is among the biggest political challenges to the BJP and Modi in his 12 years in power.
The Election Commission has denied favouring any party with its revisions to the voter list and said wrongly deleted voters can re-enrol.

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Shareholders of Taiwan Cement Corp. (TCC) approved a plan Monday to take subsidiary Cimpor International Holdings public in Europe.

In 2024, TCC fully acquired the Portuguese cement group Cimphor’s businesses in Europe and Africa through OYAK Group, a Turkish holding company.
In September 2026, TCC authorized its Dutch subsidiary to acquire Ivano-Frankivsk Cement, Ukraine’s second-largest cement maker, for up to 750 million euros (NT$27 billion). The deal remains subject to government approval.
Chair Chang said AI is creating new demands for the cement industry. TCC will continue developing low-carbon, durable materials, upgrading its plants, improving energy efficiency, and investing in renewable energy, energy storage, and recycling, he said.
The European listing plan requires approval from regulators in both Europe and Taiwan, Chang said. The offering price, number of shares to be issued, and final listing venue have yet to be determined.

Fertility Treatment in Iran
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
08:35:42 UTC
17:35:42 KST

This article explores why Iran has become an option for international patients seeking fertility treatment. It covers the global prevalence of infertility, Iran’s position in reproductive medicine, and factors such as specialized treatments, accessibility, and comparatively lower costs. The article also introduces VitaLife Fertility Center and its support for international patients seeking IVF, egg donation, surrogacy, and other fertility services in Iran.
Infertility is no longer a health challenge limited to a small group of couples. According to the World Health Organization (WHO), approximately one in six people of reproductive age experience infertility during their lifetime, making access to effective and affordable fertility care a growing global health priority.
As demand for assisted reproductive technologies continues to grow, patients are increasingly looking beyond their home countries for fertility treatment. Cost, access to advanced reproductive technologies, legal restrictions, waiting times, and the availability of specialized services can all influence where international patients seek care.
Among the destinations receiving increasing attention is Iran, where assisted reproductive medicine has developed substantially over the past several decades.
Infertility can result from male factors, female factors, a combination of both, or unexplained causes. Treatment may involve medication, surgery, intrauterine insemination (IUI), in vitro fertilization (IVF), egg donation, embryo-related genetic testing, or other assisted reproductive technologies.
The challenge, however, is not simply whether treatment exists. Access matters.
WHO notes that fertility treatments remain inaccessible or unaffordable for many people, with the high cost of assisted reproduction creating a significant barrier in numerous countries.
This has contributed to the growth of cross-border reproductive care, in which patients travel to another country to obtain fertility services that may be more accessible, affordable, or legally available there.
Research examining international reproductive care has found that cost and the legal availability of assisted reproductive technologies are among the most frequently reported reasons patients seek treatment abroad, alongside cultural and practical considerations.
Where Does Iran Stand in Fertility Treatment?
Iran has developed a substantial medical infrastructure for assisted reproduction. Assisted reproductive technologies have been used in the country since the 1980s, and a national report published on Iranian ART centers documented tens of thousands of IVF/ICSI cycles across dozens of centers. Researchers concluded that Iran has considerable potential to provide IVF services not only to Iranian patients but also to patients from other countries in the region.
Iran's position has also been highlighted by Iranian medical authorities. In a report published by Mehr News, Hamid Choubineh, head of the Iranian Scientific Association of Infertility and Reproductive Health, described Iran as being among the top 10 countries in the world for infertility treatment, while emphasizing the country's access to modern assisted reproductive techniques.
The country's reproductive medicine sector includes IVF, ICSI, genetic testing, donor programs, and gestational surrogacy. Iranian research has also documented the use of preimplantation genetic diagnosis for conditions such as beta-thalassemia, aneuploidy screening, and sex selection.
For international patients, this combination of medical expertise and comparatively lower treatment costs can make Iran an option worth investigating.
Why Do International Patients Consider Iran?
The reasons vary from patient to patient, but several factors frequently influence the decision.
Access to Specialized Fertility Services
Some reproductive treatments are heavily restricted in certain countries. Regulations concerning donor eggs, donor embryos, gestational surrogacy, and embryo testing vary significantly around the world.
Iran occupies a distinctive position within the Muslim world in this regard. Islamic bioethics literature notes that the late Ayatollah Ali Khamenei issued a fatwa permitting certain third-party reproductive arrangements, including egg donation and surrogacy, and that these practices subsequently became incorporated into Iran's reproductive medicine framework.
This religious and legal context differs from the position adopted by many Sunni authorities regarding third-party gamete donation. For international patients, therefore, Iran can provide an alternative where certain fertility treatments are available within a Shia Islamic legal and medical framework.
At the same time, eligibility is not unlimited. Iranian fertility programs operate within local medical and legal requirements, and international patients should confirm their eligibility before traveling. For example, VitaLife's current program information specifies eligibility requirements for international intended parents and states that its surrogacy pathway is designed for legally married heterosexual couples.
Surrogacy, Egg Donation and Gender Selection
For patients who cannot safely carry a pregnancy, surrogacy in Iran can provide another reproductive pathway. In gestational surrogacy, an embryo created through IVF is transferred to a gestational carrier.
Egg donation is another important option for patients whose own eggs may not be suitable for treatment. Iran has developed clinical experience with donor-assisted reproduction, making it an area of interest for some international patients.
Another service sought by some international couples is gender selection through IVF and preimplantation genetic testing. Iranian medical research has documented PGD-based sex selection in clinical settings, although the medical, ethical, and legal circumstances surrounding its use should always be discussed with a qualified fertility specialist.
The important point is that international fertility care should not be viewed simply as a search for the cheapest treatment. Patients need to consider medical suitability, legal requirements, laboratory standards, documentation, and the process for returning home with a child born through assisted reproduction.
How VitaLife Supports International Patients
For someone traveling abroad for fertility treatment, the medical procedure is only one part of the journey.
International patients may also need help with medical records, treatment planning, translation, travel arrangements, legal documentation, surrogate coordination, and communication with clinics.
This is where an international surrogacy agency and fertility coordinator can play an important role.
VitaLife Fertility Center in Iran works with international intended parents seeking coordinated fertility and reproductive services. Its programs include IVF, egg donation, gestational surrogacy, embryo-related genetic services, and support with the practical aspects of treatment in Iran.
The center's international support model is designed to coordinate different stages of treatment rather than leaving patients to manage each component independently. According to VitaLife's published program information, this includes medical coordination, surrogate matching, legal documentation support, international patient coordination, and assistance throughout the treatment process.
For intended parents considering treatment abroad, this type of coordinated approach can make an otherwise complicated process easier to navigate.
Choosing Fertility Treatment Abroad
Choosing fertility treatment abroad involves more than cost. International patients should consider the medical team, clinic facilities, legal requirements, treatment eligibility, timeline, total costs, and support throughout the journey.
Fertility treatment cannot guarantee pregnancy or live birth, as outcomes depend on individual medical factors such as age, reproductive history, and embryo quality.
Your Treatment Journey with VitaLife
At VitaLife Fertility Center, international patients are supported throughout their treatment journey in Iran, from the initial consultation to delivery. Mobina Hosseini, a midwifery specialist with a master’s degree in midwifery, serves as the dedicated patient coordinator, helping international intended parents navigate their treatment from A to Z.
Medical care is provided under the supervision of Dr. Farah Ghasemi, the treating physician, with IVF procedures carried out at Baharan Negar Infertility Treatment Center. For patients undergoing surrogacy, delivery takes place at Nikan Aghdasieh Hospital, providing a coordinated pathway from fertility treatment through pregnancy and birth.
This integrated approach allows international patients to have one coordinated team supporting their medical, communication, and practical needs throughout the process.
A Growing Role for Iran in International Fertility Care
Iran’s experience in assisted reproduction, specialized fertility services, and comparatively accessible treatment costs has made it an option for international patients. For intended parents, choosing the right pathway means finding medically appropriate, legally compliant, and well-coordinated care. VitaLife Fertility Center supports international patients throughout their fertility journey in Iran.

NATO's top commander outlined tough military response in the event of "foolish" Russian attack
Kyiv • UNN
General Alexus Grynkewich said that NATO would make an attack on any ally completely futile. He also vowed to dismantle the entire system of warfare.
NATO's Supreme Allied Commander warned Russia on Monday, October 12, that his forces would destroy "everything and everyone" that could be involved in any attack if Moscow were "foolish enough" to launch an assault on alliance territory. UNN reports this with reference to Reuters.
Details
Speaking at the Warsaw Security Forum, U.S. Air Force General Alexus Grynkewich emphasized that NATO is a defensive alliance. But he outlined a three-pronged approach of blocking, blunting and breaking enemy forces to make any attack "utterly futile."
His remarks came amid rising tensions between Europe and Russia and continued concern among European allies about U.S. President Donald Trump's commitments to NATO's mutual defense pact.
In recent days, Trump announced an agreement with Kremlin chief Vladimir Putin allowing Russia to supply diesel fuel to world markets, and renewed his criticism of Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, the publication writes.
European governments accuse Moscow of intensifying a campaign of sabotage, drone incursions, and cyberattacks against them, while Russia warned last month that it could use nuclear weapons if NATO attempted to cut off its exclave, the Kaliningrad region.
EU commented on Russia's nuclear threat against NATO over Kaliningrad01.10.26, 16:32 • 4714 views
Grynkewich did not mention Russia by name, but much of his message was clearly directed at Moscow, the publication writes. NATO's 2022 Strategic Concept describes Russia as the most significant threat to the alliance's security.
If anyone is foolish enough to attack us, we will fight. In short, we will ensure that any attack on any ally proves absolutely futile
Grynkewich said NATO's response would not be limited to the forces involved in the initial attack.
"If the adversary decides to continue the attack or commit its reserves, we will break the warfighting system that is being waged against us," he said.
"This includes not only the attacking forces themselves, but everything that supports, sustains, and controls those forces," Grynkewich noted.
Putin said this month that Russia does not plan to attack any European country and wants to coexist peacefully. Such statements have not reassured European leaders, given that Russia made similar statements before invading Ukraine in 2022, the publication points out.
Russia has also repeatedly denied involvement in sabotage and other hybrid operations.
Grynkewich said he decided to speak publicly about NATO's plans because recent acts of sabotage and arson had made people across the alliance nervous.
"I want to assure the one billion citizens of our alliance that we will deal with this. We know what we need to do. We know how we will do it," he said.
He said he also wanted to send a message to anyone considering the possibility of harming NATO members.
Grynkewich sought to downplay concerns about Washington's commitment to the alliance, recalling that Trump spoke of "love" at the NATO summit in Ankara in July.
"I was in the room and I felt the love," he said.
