Global: New report exposes human rights failures at 2026 Men’s World Cup
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
08:34:34 UTC
17:34:34 KST

Coalition calls for upcoming FIFA presidential election to centre human rights
The 2026 Men’s World Cup exposed a failure of FIFA’s leadership to implement its own human rights policies, with the pursuit of record revenues prioritised over fairness and equality, the Sport & Rights Alliance and Football Supporters Europe said in a joint report released today. The 50-page report, “Profit Over People: The 2026 FIFA Men’s World Cup,” documents a tournament marked by a climate of fear given the backdrop of mass immigration detentions and deportations; discriminatory visa bans; cost and accessibility barriers for fans, players and journalists; unclear safeguarding and eligibility standards; and lack of effective access to remedy.
“The 2026 World Cup exposed how the priorities and direction set by FIFA’s leadership put profit over people,” said Andrea Florence, Executive Director of the Sport & Rights Alliance. “For everyone touched by the tournament, access and participation were limited by economic status, nationality, immigration status, disability, gender identity and sexual orientation or political circumstance. Not only did FIFA fail to use its leverage to uphold human rights obligations, it chose to lift up a government that is actively violating human rights by awarding an unvetted ‘FIFA Peace Prize’ to U.S. President Donald Trump.”
As a 48-nation, 104-match tournament hosted for the first time in three countries – Canada, Mexico, and the United States – the 2026 Men’s World Cup was the biggest mega sporting event in history, and one that, as FIFA promised would be a tournament where everyone “feels safe, included and free to exercise their rights.” The tournament was the first World Cup to be hosted under FIFA’s recognition and adoption of international business and human rights obligations, through its 2017 Human Rights Policy, integration of human rights criteria in the bidding process, and a dedicated “FWC26 Human Rights Framework” for 16 local host committees. Yet due to rising concerns about potential human rights abuses at the tournament, over 65,000 people joined Amnesty International’s call for FIFA and host nations to address risks and guarantee a World Cup for everyone.
ICE raids surged, protests were blocked and discriminatory visa policies kept many fans from enjoying what was billed as ‘the most inclusive World Cup ever’.
Frank Conde Tangberg, Policy Advisor at Amnesty International
“The unity and joy we saw on the pitch and in the stands were a world away from the fear and division beyond the stadiums. ICE raids surged, protests were blocked and discriminatory visa policies kept many fans from enjoying what was billed as ‘the most inclusive World Cup ever’,” said Frank Conde Tangberg, Policy Advisor at Amnesty International. “Many of these violations stemmed from repressive and abusive government policies, but FIFA failed to use its leverage to protect fans and local communities. It spent its political capital on maximising revenue rather than standing up for human rights.”
The report details how excessive ticket pricing, coupled with expensive visa requirements and a lack of affordable inter-city transport, as well as U.S. travel restrictions on over 39 nations, disproportionately excluded fans with disabilities, with limited incomes and/or from the Global South. Participating teams and officials faced severe disruptions: members of the Iranian national team had U.S. visas delayed or denied, and for two U.S. matches the team had to enter and depart the country on the same day – while Somali referee Omar Artan, despite having a valid visa, was denied entry at Miami International Airport following an 11-hour interrogation. These and other barriers unfolded alongside aggressive U.S. immigration enforcement, with, as Human Rights Watch documented, Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) conducting over 167,000 arrests in and around 11 World Cup host cities leading up to the tournament. Although reporting of ICE detentions inside World Cup venues was limited, enforcement surged during the tournament, including over five days in late June when approximately 10,000 people were arrested.
“Supporters were treated as objects to be exploited rather than the heart of the game,” said Ronan Evain, Executive Director of Football Supporters Europe. “When ticket prices are at the highest in World Cup history, legal accessibility requirements for fans with disabilities are ignored, and dedicated supporters face discriminatory visa rejections or militarized border enforcement, you no longer have a global celebration – just an exclusive, sanitized spectacle meant only for the elite.”
The report also documents other human rights abuses in Mexico, where police confronted planned protests with tear gas and detained two journalists. In Canada, preparations were marked by street sweeps displacing unhoused residents in host cities – and immigration authorities rejected more World Cup visa applications, which came mostly from Global South applicants, than they approved. Within FIFA’s direct control, questions remain about whether FIFA failed to enforce its own in-competition policy explicitly requiring athletes to declare they have never been investigated for a sexual or other violent offence, given that at least eight players facing pending sexual assault cases or allegations competed in the 2026 World Cup. Independent journalism was also severely constrained by FIFA’s opaque media accreditation processes, U.S. visa barriers, and a lack of regular press conferences with top leadership.
“In recent years, the U.S. – the country hosting the majority of World Cup matches – fell from 45th to 64th in our Press Freedom Index, and journalists have faced violence, detention, and deportation,” said Clayton Weimers, Executive Director of Reporters Without Borders (RSF) USA. “Yet FIFA’s lack of clarity on media accreditation, coordination with visa processes, and blasé attitude toward media briefings underscored FIFA’s failures to uphold human rights. On top of this, FIFA’s continued lack of advertising for its grievance mechanism for journalists, players, fans, workers and community members means we don’t know the true extent of the harm.”
FIFA is in clear need of systemic governance reform that embeds human rights and good governance into leadership and decision-making structures, provides an independent system of checks and balances, and ensures meaningful accountability when its commitments are not met.
“The lesson of the 2026 World Cup is not that international sporting bodies can guarantee the conduct of sovereign governments, but that human rights risks must shape how tournaments are awarded, planned, contracted, monitored, and delivered – and that top leadership at FIFA and other sport governing bodies must be prepared to act, especially when circumstances change,” said Florence.
As detailed in the report, the Sport & Rights Alliance and Football Supporters Europe call on FIFA, and all candidates in the 2027 presidential election, to:
- Make human rights requirements binding, and set enforceable conditions in host agreements for all future Men’s and Women’s World Cups, backed by independent monitoring and clear consequences for non-compliance;
- Establish a transparent, survivor-centered eligibility framework for athletes and officials facing serious misconduct or sexual violence allegations, replacing case-by-case discretion;
- Ensure meaningful access without discrimination to future tournaments for fans, athletes, journalists, and other accredited participants, and ensure the rights to freedom of expression, peaceful assembly and press freedom are guaranteed in the context of FIFA tournaments;
- Guarantee equal ticket access and free companion seating for supporters with disabilities, while preventing predatory ticket pricing; and
- Make FIFA’s grievance and remedy mechanisms visible and accessible, re-establish a permanent and independent Human Rights Advisory Board, comprehensively reform the FIFA Ethics Committee, and create a permanent Remedy Fund for individuals and communities harmed by past and future tournament operations.

Netanyahu seeks prosecution of soldiers who testified in Gaza documentary: report
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
08:34:10 UTC
17:34:10 KST

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has ordered the security establishment and the country’s attorney-general to identify and prosecute soldiers and officers interviewed in the investigative documentary NAZA about Israel’s mass killings of civilians in Gaza, Israeli media reported on Monday.
In a letter to army Chief of Staff Eyal Zamir, Shin Bet chief David Zini and Attorney General Gali Baharav-Miara, Netanyahu accused those who participated in the documentary of committing “serious information security offenses, and criminal defamation” and causing harm to “Israel’s diplomatic and security interests,” according to Haaretz newspaper.
The award-winning documentary examines Israel’s use of artificial intelligence and automated surveillance systems in targeted killings and military offensives during its genocidal war on Gaza.
The film’s title, "NAZA," refers to an acronym used by Israeli military intelligence to denote the number of civilians expected to be killed in an air strike.
During the war, the Israeli army has killed more than 74,000 Palestinians and injured over 175,000 others since October 2023 in a brutal offensive that has left the entire enclave in ruins.
Netanyahu claimed that the film has presented a “false, misleading and biased narrative” that defames Israel and its military and damages the country’s international standing.
“There is concern that those involved in the defamatory film committed serious criminal offenses by exposing highly classified information and creating a breach in the information security of a highly sensitive intelligence unit,” he said in the letter.
The film, based on testimony from 24 Israeli soldiers and intelligence personnel, won the Special Jury Prize at the Venice Film Festival last month.
Following the award, Israeli Culture Minister Miki Zohar asked the Interior Ministry to consider revoking the citizenship of the film’s creators, describing the documentary as “vile” and accusing them of “treason.”
Zamir separately ordered Military Intelligence, the Military Advocate General’s Corps and the Israeli Air Force to identify the soldiers featured in the film and determine whether they were active-duty troops, career officers or reservists, according to Haaretz.
During discussions on the issue, Military Advocate General Itai Ofir said that there would be no legal basis for criminal prosecution unless participants were found to have committed information-security violations or disclosed classified material.
He said disciplinary or command measures could, however, be taken if military orders were violated.
The Israeli army claimed that the documentary’s portrayal of its targeting procedures in Gaza contained “substantial factual errors.”
The Guardian, which produced the documentary, defended the film, saying the process used to assess the credibility of the testimonies was “rigorous” and included classified documents, verification of specific strikes and corroboration from additional confidential sources.
The newspaper said it had interviewed more than 100 people familiar with Israeli military systems used during the war on Gaza, including senior commanders involved in authorising strikes.
In November 2024, the International Criminal Court issued arrest warrants for Netanyahu and former Defence Minister Yoav Gallant over war crimes and crimes against humanity in Gaza.
The International Court of Justice, the UN’s principal judicial organ, is also hearing a case brought by South Africa and joined by several countries accusing Israel of genocide against Palestinians in Gaza.

abroad. The largest numbers arrived from Türkiye, Ukraine and Germany. The main reason for the population decline remains negative

Ethiopia opens first gold refinery (VIDEO)
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
08:33:16 UTC
17:33:16 KST

Ethiopia opens first gold refinery (VIDEO)
Ethiopia has opened its first gold refinery to increase earnings from its mineral resources and offer African producers an alternative to processing their gold overseas, Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed has announced.
Abiy inaugurated the National Precious Metals Refinery on Saturday at the Bole Lemi Special Economic Zone in the capital, Addis Ababa. The $50 million venture is majority owned by the Ethiopian Investment Holdings (EIH) and Dubai-based Sam Precious Metals.
The facility can process more than 600 metric tons of precious metals annually and has “the capacity to serve not only Ethiopia but also the broader East African and pan-African markets,” Abiy wrote on X on Saturday. It is intended to boost export earnings, create skilled jobs, support the jewelry industry, and serve East African and wider African markets, he said.
“It enables neighboring countries and regional mining companies to bring their gold to Ethiopia for advanced refining, certification, value addition, and sale, eliminating the need to export it outside the continent,” he added.
The launch came five days after Abiy was reelected for another five-year term, pledging to continue economic reforms, advance major infrastructure projects, and defend Ethiopia’s national interests.
Gold is a major source of foreign exchange for Ethiopia, generating $5.6 billion last year, according to government figures. Abiy said African countries have long exported raw materials cheaply while importing finished products at substantially higher prices.
African leaders have increasingly demanded local mineral processing and rejected a repeat of colonial-style resource extraction as Western powers seek greater access to critical minerals. Ghanaian President John Dramani Mahama took that message to the UN General Assembly last month, warning that Africa would not remain a “passive arena for a new scramble for resources.”
South African President Cyril Ramaphosa similarly told the BRICS Business Forum in New Delhi last month that Africa must reject a future of supplying minerals while “value addition and manufacturing take place elsewhere.”
Ghana has required licensed self-financing gold aggregators to refine their gold locally before export since September 1. Burkina Faso opened its first gold refinery, Raffinor-BF, on September 28 as the transitional authorities seek greater economic sovereignty after cutting ties with traditional Western partners. DR Congo, where the US brokered a peace deal tied to access to critical minerals, has banned copper and cobalt concentrate exports to encourage domestic processing. Zimbabwe has introduced lithium concentrate export quotas and required producers to commit to building local processing plants ahead of a planned January 2027 ban on concentrate exports.
The National Precious Metals Refinery, constructed within the Bole Lemi Special Economic Zone, has the capacity to serve not only Ethiopia but also the broader East African and pan-African markets. By providing internationally credible refining and testing services, it enables neighboring countries and regional mining companies to bring their gold to Ethiopia for advanced refining, certification, value addition, and sale, eliminating the need to export it outside the continent.

Italy

Economy Minister Giancarlo Giorgetti
said the government will continue to take a prudent approach to
managing the public finances as there are storm clouds ahead as
he presented its Public Finance Planning Document (DPFP) in the
Lower House on Tuesday.
                                    
The DPFP features the government's plan to use the escape clause
granted by the EU for 0.3% budget deviations for both energy and
defence investments in the 2027 budget law.
                                    
"Planning three years ahead (in the DPFP) is highly complex
especially amid great turbulence, and updates come weekly, as
IMF data show," Giorgetti said.
                                    
"The fundamental premise underlying our reasoning is that when
the weather forecast predicts a storm, it is wise to check the
vessel's condition before heading out to the open sea, and that
is precisely what we have sought to do in recent years.
                                    
"We believe it is essential to stay on this course at a time
when storm clouds are gathering on the horizon.
                                    
"This document is a reflection of that approach, aiming to
adhere to the path of fiscal consolidation and meet the targets
set by the new European governance framework, with a view to
exiting the (excessive-deficit) procedure in the spring,
conditions permitting".
                                    
Italy's budget deficit needs to come within the 3% of GDP
threshold for it to be able to emerge from the procedure.
                                    
Giorgetti has said he is expects this to be the case for 2026,
after the deficit came in at 3.1% for 2025, before going up to
3.4% in 2027 with the use of the escape clause.
                                    
"The request to adjust the budget in order to activate the
national escape clause for defence and energy is a deliberate
departure from the prudent stance I have previously advocated,"
Giorgetti said.
                                    
"These are measures that the Commission acknowledges, and that
the markets have deemed sustainable within the framework of
ensuring the long-term sustainability of Italian public debt".

Swiss family business Wagner shuts down with 69 job losses
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

17:32:31 KST

Swiss family business Wagner shuts down with 69 job losses
Swiss industrial company Wagner is closing down permanently with the loss of 69 jobs. Following an unsuccessful consultation process, business activities will be gradually transferred to other partners.
Production is set to continue on a larger scale than originally planned until the end of March 2027, the family business announced. The reason for this is said to be additional customer orders.
Wagner specialises in metal die-casting and plastic injection moulding. The company supplies the automotive industry and the mechanical and plant engineering sectors.
The redundancies and resignations of the 69 employees will take place in stages. A voluntary redundancy scheme has been agreed for those affected, in consultation with the administrator.
Despite intensive restructuring efforts and discussions with investors, it was not possible to find an economically viable solution for the company as a whole.
Wagner cites a difficult demand situation, significant overcapacity, international competitive pressure and the framework conditions for industrial production in Switzerland as the reasons. Even additional funding from the owners was unable to prevent the closure.
The consultation process, which began on September 23, was concluded on October 9. No proposals were received that would have enabled the orderly closure to be adjusted.
“The definitive closure of our family business is an extraordinarily painful step for us,” said CEO and co-owner Silvan Halter. According to the statement, he is the third generation to run the family business, which has been in operation for over 80 years.
The aim now is to carefully manage the handover of the projects, support staff in finding new employment and ensure a fair and orderly process.
The continuation of the insolvency proceedings still requires court approval as well as the subsequent consent of the creditors.

Les dirigeants européens sont censés faire avancer le sujet les 15 et 16 octobre, avec l'objectif de rapprocher des positions encore très éloignées.

Putin wants Ukraine deal more than Zelensky – Trump
Russian President Vladimir Putin is more eager than Vladimir Zelensky to reach a deal to end the Ukraine conflict, US President Donald Trump has said. Trump’s comments came after he suggested it is time for Ukraine to get a “new president.”
Speaking to reporters on Monday, Trump claimed both Moscow and Kiev support the energy ceasefire which he announced on Sunday. Neither Russia nor Ukraine has confirmed the truce.
“I think they want to make a deal, but they don’t know how. But we’re going to get them to make a deal,” Trump said.
“I think, actually, Putin wants to make a deal more than Zelensky,” he added.
Trump also rejected criticism of his decision to ease sanctions on Russian diesel following a phone call with Putin on Friday, stressing that the agreement benefited the wider world and American farmers and ranchers. 
“Zelensky has to focus on making a deal, not talking about that,” he stressed, referring to the Ukrainian leader’s criticism of the agreement.
On Sunday, Trump announced that Russia and Ukraine had agreed to an immediate “energy ceasefire.” Zelensky said the announcement “was news for me,” but expressed readiness to stop attacking Russian refineries if Moscow halted strikes on Ukrainian energy infrastructure.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov has declined to confirm the agreement, saying contacts were ongoing. While praising the efforts of American negotiators, Peskov stressed that Moscow is seeking long-term peace rather than a temporary ceasefire. Russian officials have long argued that a truce would only help Ukraine to reinforce its battered military and receive more Western-made weapons.
According to the New York Times, Ukrainian officials were informed of the US-Russia diesel deal during tense negotiations in Miami. The US delegation subsequently demanded that Ukraine stop striking Russian refineries, and when Kiev’s representatives asked what they would receive in return, the Americans reportedly argued that Washington already provided substantial assistance, including intelligence sharing. Some participants interpreted this as a veiled threat to withdraw support, the article said.
Following his conversation with Putin and Zelensky’s angry reaction to the diesel deal, Trump suggested that “it’s time for Ukraine to get a new president.” Zelensky’s presidential term expired more than two years ago, although the Ukrainian leader has refused to hold a new election, citing martial law. Russia has declared Zelensky “illegitimate,” highlighting his dubious legal status as a major obstacle to a peace agreement.
After a war of words with Trump, Zelensky signaled he was ready to hold an election but demanded a 60-day ceasefire with Russia. Moscow responded by stressing that “if Kiev genuinely wants to hold elections… then the president of the Russian Federation… will be ready to issue an order not to carry out strikes against Ukraine on the election day specifically.”

India to buck global slowdown and grow 7% for two years – IMF
India will be the world’s fastest-growing major economy despite the drag from higher oil prices and slowing global growth, the International Monetary Fund has said. 
The IMF raised India’s GDP forecast for 2026-27 to 7%, from its July figure of 6.4%, in its latest World Economic Outlook released on Tuesday. It also upgraded its growth projection for the country in 2027-28 to 7%, from the previous 6.7%. 
The upgrade reflects stronger-than-expected economic momentum, supported by domestic demand and services activity. India’s expanding domestic market, favorable demographics, and continued structural reforms have also strengthened its growth potential, the IMF said. 
The Indian economy expanded 7.8% in the financial year ended March 2026, and maintained the same pace in the April-June quarter. The latest revision follows similar upgrades by other major institutions. The World Bank raised India’s growth forecast for 2026-27 to 7.1% last week, citing strong domestic demand and exports. The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) also increased its projection for the current financial year to 7.1%. 
India’s expansion is also supporting growth across South Asia, where the World Bank expects the country to remain a major driver of regional economic activity. 
The upgraded Indian outlook contrasts with slower global growth. The IMF expects the world economy to expand 3.1% in 2026, down from 3.5% last year.
China’s economy is projected to grow 4.5% this year, while the US is expected to grow 2.3%.
The Middle East conflict continues to weigh on energy-importing economies, while investment in AI infrastructure has helped support global growth, the IMF said.
Inflation remains a concern in India, with consumer prices rising 5.54% in September, close to the RBI’s upper tolerance limit of 6%. The central bank raised its benchmark interest rate to 5.5% last week amid broader price pressures.
The IMF also expects India’s current account deficit to widen to 1.5% of GDP this financial year from 0.7% a year earlier amid higher energy import bills.

Iranian officials have raised the possibility of launching ground incursions into neighboring countries if the United States resumes military strikes against the Islamic Republic, The Wall Street Journal reported, citing people familiar with warnings conveyed by Tehran. The threats are part of a broader Iranian effort to deter Washington from launching another round of attacks after the November 3 midterm elections.
According to the report, some Iranian officials have hinted that their forces could cross into neighboring countries as part of a wider military escalation. The potential targets of such ground operations were not specified. Tehran has also privately warned Arab officials that renewed fighting could trigger attacks on Saudi oil facilities and other strategic infrastructure across the Gulf.
Iranian national security official Mohsen Rezaei warned Sunday that Tehran could strike the United Arab Emirates, which has largely avoided attacks since late spring, as well as data centers and internet cables across the region. Separately, Iranian officials have told mediators that their forces could intensify attacks on American personnel, including attempts to sink US warships in the Middle East and kill their crews, according to people familiar with the warnings cited by the Journal.
The threats follow a series of attacks that have heightened regional tensions. At least three commercial vessels were struck over the weekend in and around the Strait of Hormuz, according to the UK Maritime Trade Operations agency. A drone attack also set an Emirati tanker ablaze near Oman, leaving two Indian sailors missing. Meanwhile, a Houthi missile strike on Riyadh's international airport Saturday killed at least 13 people and wounded hundreds more.
Washington is also preparing for the possibility of renewed fighting. A third American aircraft carrier strike group and another Marine expeditionary unit are heading toward the Middle East, while the Pentagon is considering deploying additional air-defense systems and munitions to regional bases. President Donald Trump has ruled out strikes before the midterm elections but has publicly discussed targeting Iran's Pickaxe Mountain nuclear facility.
The Journal also reported that the Pentagon moved approximately 12 B-1 bombers from a military base in Britain last week over concerns that Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps was planning a drone attack. Iranian missiles had previously come close to American warships during attacks in September, highlighting the risks facing US forces in the region.
Meanwhile, Tehran has used the relative pause in direct fighting to rebuild missile and drone production facilities and replenish its arsenal, while strengthening defenses around sensitive sites. Satellite imagery analyzed by the Institute for Science and International Security shows that Iran recently constructed earthen barriers around the Pickaxe Mountain and Natanz nuclear facilities, apparently intended to obstruct possible ground raids.
Iran's preparations extend beyond military installations. State media has intensified coverage of pro-government rallies, while billboards in Tehran advertise civilian training in shoulder-fired antiaircraft missiles and sniper rifles. The Revolutionary Guard has publicized training for female commando units and even sent personnel to a kindergarten in Sabzevar, where they recounted wartime experiences and displayed what they described as a neutralized American Tomahawk missile.
The Journal noted that Iran's ability to defend against advanced American aircraft and cruise missiles remains limited, making threats of regional escalation a central element of its deterrence strategy. The preparations suggest that Tehran is attempting both to discourage another US attack and to ready itself for a conflict that could extend far beyond Iranian territory.

Mapping Africa’s energy wealth and 560 million who remain without power
Africa is rich in energy, yet hundreds of millions Africans still live without electricity, most of the world’s total.
Africa holds billions of barrels of oil, trillions of cubic metres of gas and produces most of the world’s cobalt and manganese for electric car batteries.
This week, energy ministers, investors and oil executives are meeting in Cape Town for African Energy Week, which runs until October 16. The conference focuses on investment in oil and gas, energy finance and ending energy poverty.
In this visual explainer, Al Jazeera maps where Africa’s oil, gas and critical minerals are found, how its electricity is generated and who still goes without it.
How much oil does Africa have?
Africa holds about 125 billion barrels of proven crude oil reserves, representing 7.2 percent of the global total. Proven reserves are oil that has been discovered and can be extracted commercially with existing technology, but is still in the ground.
Libya and Nigeria account for nearly 70 percent of Africa’s reserves, with 48.4 billion and 36.9 billion barrels, respectively. Algeria ranks third, with 12.2 billion barrels. Angola follows with 7.78 billion barrels, while South Sudan and Egypt hold 3.75 billion and 3.3 billion barrels, respectively.
Nigeria was Africa’s largest oil producer in 2024, accounting for about 23 percent of the continent’s output. Algeria and Angola followed with about 17 percent each, and together the three produced 56 percent of Africa’s oil. The top five producers accounted for more than 80 percent. Africa as a whole produced 7.6 percent of the world’s crude oil, roughly in line with its share of global reserves.
Libya, which holds Africa’s largest proven reserves, ranked only fourth in production. Italy’s Eni, France’s TotalEnergies and Spain’s Repsol are among the foreign companies operating in the country, where political disputes and blockades have repeatedly disrupted output.
Where are Africa’s natural gas reserves?
Africa held almost 18 trillion cubic metres of proven natural gas reserves at the end of 2023.
Nigeria and Algeria hold about 58 percent of the total, followed by Mozambique with 2.84 trillion cubic metres, Egypt with 2.21 trillion and Libya with 1.51 trillion.
Algeria and Nigeria are also among Africa’s leading gas exporters, while much of Mozambique’s reserves, discovered offshore in the 2010s, remain largely undeveloped.
Where do the critical minerals come from?
The African continent supplies a large share of the minerals used in electric vehicles, batteries and renewable energy technologies.
In 2025, African countries accounted for 71.2 percent of global cobalt production and 72.4 percent of manganese production.
Cobalt is used in rechargeable batteries. Manganese is mainly used to strengthen steel, but it is also used in some electric vehicle batteries and in batteries that store renewable energy.
The Democratic Republic of the Congo produces nearly 70 percent of the world’s cobalt. Some of it is dug by hand by artisanal miners, and Amnesty International has documented dangerous and often deadly conditions in some of the country’s mines.
South Africa produces nearly 38 percent of global manganese, followed by Gabon with nearly 25 percent. Together with Ghana, the three countries account for 72.4 percent of global production.
Zimbabwe, Africa’s largest lithium producer, accounted for 9.6 percent of global production in 2025. Lithium is used in rechargeable batteries that power electric vehicles and store electricity from solar and wind.
Madagascar, Mozambique and Tanzania produced a combined 222,000 tonnes of natural graphite in 2025, or 11.9 percent of the global total. Graphite is used in the anodes of most lithium-ion batteries, the negative electrodes that store and release energy, as well as in steel manufacturing, lubricants and pencils.
How many African countries produce electricity from renewables?
Renewable energy accounted for all electricity generated in Ethiopia and the Democratic Republic of the Congo in 2024. Uganda, Namibia and Eswatini each generated more than 96 percent from renewables, mostly hydropower.
At the other end, renewables made up less than 5 percent in Algeria, Libya, Niger and Tunisia, which rely mainly on gas or oil.
Ethiopia’s electricity comes mostly from hydropower, led by the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam on the Blue Nile, Africa’s largest hydroelectric project. The dam began generating power in 2022 and was officially inaugurated in September 2025.
Where do people have access to electricity?
In 2024, six African countries reported universal electricity access: Algeria, Egypt, Mauritius, Morocco, Seychelles and Tunisia. Together, they are home to about 215 million people, or roughly 14 percent of Africa’s population.
Elsewhere, access varies widely. In South Sudan, only 5.4 percent of people had electricity. The figure was 15.6 percent in Malawi and 22.5 percent in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, even though the DRC generates all its power from renewables.
Nigeria, Africa’s most populous country, had an access rate of 62.5 percent, leaving roughly 85 million people without electricity, the largest number of any country in the world.
In rural areas, where access is far lower than in cities, many families still rely on kerosene lamps, candles or torches to light their homes after dark.
Africa has vast energy resources, from oil and natural gas to the minerals powering the global energy transition. Yet more than 560 million people in sub-Saharan Africa lack access to electricity, accounting for about 86 percent of the global total, according to the World Health Organization (WHO).

German police are investigating possible arson after a fire killed three people and injured five others early Tuesday in a multi-family apartment building in Bochum, a city in the industrial Ruhr region. 
The Bild tabloid reported that investigators are examining whether the blaze was deliberately set. Neighbors told the paper that several strollers in the hallway may have caught fire and that the flames then spread to the wooden staircase, blocking the only escape route. 
Authorities have not released any details on the identities, nationalities or ages of the three victims. Residents told Bild the dead were two women and one man who had moved into the second-floor apartment only about two weeks earlier, but officials have not confirmed that account. 
A spokesman for the Bochum fire department told public broadcaster WDR that crews were alerted at around 4.15 am (0215 GMT). By the time they arrived, the fire had already spread widely through the building. 
He said firefighters could not reach upper floors through the stairwell because it was blocked by flames and smoke. Crews rescued two residents with a turntable ladder, two more with portable ladders, and one person who jumped into a safety cushion. 
During later extinguishing work, crews recovered three bodies inside a second-floor apartment. Attempts to revive them at the scene failed. 
Police spokesman Jens Artschwager told Bild that officers had already been called to the building the day before the fire because of disputes. “A patrol car was on site. No complaint was filed. We are currently checking whether there is a connection with the fire,” he said.

UK shoppers seek deals as grocery price inflation rises again
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
08:21:13 UTC
17:21:13 KST

Grocery price inflation in the UK has picked up further, prompting shoppers to turn to special offers to keep their bills down – while the price of chocolates has fallen in the run-up to Halloween.
Supermarket prices were 2.5% higher than last year in the four weeks to 4 October, up from 2.3% last month, according to data from the retail analysts Worldpanel by Numerator.
Spending on promotions over the last month was more than £250m higher than a year ago, with many shoppers using special offers to keep their grocery bills in check or to make pricier items and larger packs more affordable, Worldpanel said.
Fraser McKevitt, the head of retail and consumer insight at Worldpanel, said: “With the autumn budget fast approaching [on 28 October], the cost of living continues to weigh heavily on the minds of shoppers. And the cost of filling up a car is only adding to the pressure on household budgets.
“More than half tell us they’re very or extremely worried about petrol prices, and almost one in three say it’s already taking a real toll on their finances. Until the chancellor sets out his plans, we expect that caution to carry on showing up at the till, with shoppers leaning more heavily on promotions to keep their grocery spend under control.”
However, in some good news for households stocking up on trick or treat supplies for Halloween, chocolate confectionery prices are 3% lower than a year ago.
About 1.2 million households bought a pumpkin over the latest four weeks, up 10% year on year, while more than 250,000 households treated themselves to a pumpkin spice coffee.
McKevitt added: “Halloween and Christmas are two of the most important moments of the year for chocolate confectionery, so falling prices will be welcome news for shoppers and retailers alike.
“After the double-digit increases of 2025, a 3% drop won’t fully reverse what consumers have paid in recent months, but it should help ease some of the pressure on household budgets as the festive season approaches.”
While sales of hot chocolate and soup surged in September compared with August, by 41% and 35% respectively, they fell sharply when compared with last year, by 20% and 4% respectively.
A separate report from NielsenIQ showed total till sales at major UK supermarkets grew 1.4% in the four weeks to 3 October, down from 1.8% growth in the previous month, as shoppers remain cautious about spending.
Summer favourites remained popular as September was unusually warm this year, with strong sales of mineral water (+17.4%) and ice-cream (+11.7%).
Asda was the only big grocer to report a drop in sales, of 0.5%, in the 12 weeks to 4 October, Worldpanel said.
The German discounter Lidl led in market share gains and now controls 8.6%, on the back of a 7.1% increase in sales driven by fruit, vegetables and wine.
Sales at the online grocer Ocado increased by 12.4%, outpacing online sales across the sector at 5.5%.
Spending through the tills was 1% higher at Tesco and 1.3% higher at Sainsbury’s, with the two retailers holding 27.8% and 15.2% of the market respectively.
Asda’s share now stands at 11.5%, while Aldi holds 10.5% of the market, with sales at the discounter up 0.4% year on year.
Beyond the supermarkets, grocery sales at Marks & Spencer rose by 14.9%.

French Navy Boards Russia-Linked Tanker in Indian Ocean
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
08:21:00 UTC
17:21:00 KST

The French navy intercepted and boarded an oil tanker linked to Russia’s so-called shadow fleet in the Indian Ocean, President Emmanuel Macron announced Monday.
The French joint staff said naval inspectors boarded the vessel to verify its nationality after doubts arose over its claimed Benin registration. The operation took place around 450 nautical miles south of Réunion Island, an overseas territory of France.
Macron said the ship — the DF Peak — was suspected of sailing under a false flag and being involved in illicit fuel transportation. The vessel is under U.S., EU, U.K. and Ukrainian sanctions.
The tanker was being escorted to Réunion for further checks, said armed forces minister Catherine Vautrin.
The DF Peak is at least the sixth shadow-fleet tanker French authorities have detained over the past year, according to the exiled outlet The Insider.
President Vladimir Putin has previously condemned European seizures of Russia-linked tankers as “piracy and robbery” and threatened retaliation.
Built in South Korea in 2006, DF Peak previously operated as the NS Captain and later as the Kaliningrad under Russia’s state shipping giant Sovcomflot.
Maritime database records cited by The Insider and Mediazona claim the DF Peak dropped its Russian flag in June 2025 to register under Benin and is currently registered to Hong Kong Ding Feng Shipping.
Russia's embassy in France said on Tuesday that France's seizure of the DF Peak was a blatant violation of international law, the state RIA news agency reported.
RIA cited the Russian embassy as referring to the seizure as "piracy" and as saying it was trying to determine if any Russian citizens had been among the ship's crew.
It was also quoted as saying that France had not notified Russia about the tanker's seizure.
AFP and Reuters contributed reporting.

A week earlier, drones attacked two other cargo ships off Bulgaria’s coast, about 110 kilometers (68 miles) from shore. The crew of one ship was evacuated, while the other sank. Meta launches new AI models to compete with OpenAI and Anthropic
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
08:17:31 UTC
17:17:31 KST

Dilara Hamit
13 October 2026•Update: 13 October 2026
Meta has launched two new artificial intelligence models as the technology company seeks to compete more directly with leading systems developed by OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google.
Muse Wonder and Muse Wonder Full are Meta’s most capable models to date and are designed for personal and professional AI agents, the company said in an announcement on Monday.
The models can perform long-running tasks, use computers, and work in specialized areas including law, finance, and health. Meta said they can also handle complex coding projects, delegate work to smaller AI agents and recover from errors without abandoning the original goal.
One of their main features, Active Memory, allows the AI to retain important information about a user across multiple conversations and retrieve it when relevant.
Another feature, Active Focus, is intended to keep an AI agent working when it encounters difficulties by trying alternative approaches, adapting to new information, and seeking clarification when necessary.
Meta said the models could help users perform tasks ranging from understanding a lease or navigating an insurance claim to analyzing finances and building an application.
Muse Wonder is now available to developers through the Meta Model API and the company’s Muse Code programming tool. The more capable Muse Wonder Full is available through paid Muse Code subscriptions, with plans starting at $50 per month for access to Meta’s most advanced models.
Muse Wonder will later be incorporated into Meta’s Muse personal assistant, initially for subscribers.
Meta published benchmark results that it said showed the models matching or outperforming some systems from OpenAI and Anthropic on selected coding, memory, and professional tasks. The broader performance of the models will still need to be assessed through independent testing.
The company said it trained the Wonder family to protect private information, refuse assistance with harmful activity, and strengthen defenses against cyberattacks. A more detailed safety report is expected to be released later.
The launch forms part of Meta’s broader push toward what CEO Mark Zuckerberg has described as “personal superintelligence,” AI systems capable of understanding users’ goals, preferences and long-term needs.
Unlike some earlier Meta models released with downloadable weights, the company did not announce plans to make the Wonder models open source.

Kazakhstan’s GDP grows 4.1% in first half of 2026
Kazakhstan’s GDP reached 71.2 trillion tenge in the first half of 2026, marking a 4.1% increase in real terms compared with the same period last year, Qazinform News Agency reports, citing the Bureau of National Statistics.
According to the bureau, the country's GDP totaled 71,215,382.4 million tenge between January and June 2026, representing real growth of 4.1% year-on-year.
Ulytau region recorded the fastest growth in gross regional product (GRP) at 15.3%, followed by Turkistan region at 13.3% and North Kazakhstan region at 11.4%.
Meanwhile, Almaty accounted for the largest share of Kazakhstan’s GDP at 20.2%, ahead of Astana at 12.5% and Atyrau region at 11.7%.
Almaty also contributed the most to the country’s economic growth, adding 0.68 percentage points, compared with 0.62 percentage points from Astana and 0.47 percentage points from Almaty region.
Earlier, Qazinform News Agency reported that Kazakhstan’s economic growth had slowed to 4.1% year-on-year in the first half of 2026, mainly due to disruptions in oil exports and lower production.

"Most people are ready to start again after the holidays", says 16-year-old Simon, a pupil at the Lycée Saint-Charles in Marseille, France's second-largest city.

In the western city of Rennes, where protesters met before dawn outside the Jean-Macé secondary school, 13-year-old Lily worried that the protest may "run out of steam".
But "October 17 will breathe new life into the movement", said her classmate Albane, referring to looming protests by unions, farmers and others angered by surging energy prices.
Protesters in Marseille. Credit: Manon Cruz, Reuters
Student union says 90% of French universities shut today
Around 90 per cent of the approximately 70 French universities are "blockaded" or "closed" today as part of the protest movement, says the Union étudiante, France's leading student union.
In a press release, the union added that "the detailed list is currently being finalised".
Students, teachers march in cities across France
Thousands of people – mainly high school pupils, university students and teachers – have begun marching in towns and cities across France as part of the movement’s fifth round of protests.
In Strasbourg, demonstrators gathered at Place Kléber, in the city centre, before setting off on a march.
Adeline Ferier, 42, a secondary school literature teacher and member of the SNES-FSU trade union, told AFP she was demonstrating "first and foremost in support of (her) 16-year-old daughter".
"I think it’s great that young people are aware of inequalities and are taking action," she said, while also expressing strong criticism of the replacement plan announced by Education Minister Édouard Geffray.
"You can’t have a budget with 1,500 fewer posts and then pretend to pull 3,000 posts out of a hat," she said.
A march in Nantes on October 13, 2026. Credit: Stéphane Mahé, Reuters
In Nantes, several thousand people marched behind a banner reading "schools without funding, a country without a future".
"I think there are a great many of us in France who remain motivated. It’s a misunderstanding of the movement to think that the anger will disappear once the holidays begin," said Mariolino, a 16-year-old in his final year of secondary school.
Thunberg 'extremely proud of French students'
The Swedish activist, wearing her trademark keffiyeh, has spoken to journalists gathered outside a high school in Saint-Denis, where more than a hundred students gathered early this morning to block the entrance.
"Young people aren’t being included in the discussions. Our future is being stolen from us and, as we’ve seen here, schools aren’t receiving the investment they need," said the 23-year-old.
Greta Thunberg at the Lycée Paul Eluard in Saint-Denis, north of Paris. Credit: Julien de Rosa, AFP
"So, what are we supposed to do? Give up? Of course not. That is precisely what people are saying here: we are not going to give up and we are going to fight for this future that is being stolen from us right before our eyes," she added, saying she was "extremely proud of French students".

Basic schools' broad selection of foreign languages a problem for Estonian high schools
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
08:15:00 UTC
17:15:00 KST

Basic schools' broad selection of foreign languages a problem for Estonian high schools
With 15 different languages taught in basic schools last year, students entering upper secondary school may be unable to continue studying a language they have spent several years learning.
A few years ago, Russian and German were the main second foreign languages taught in Estonian schools, but students can now choose from 15 different languages in basic school. Hans Krister, who started upper secondary school this fall, had studied Spanish for three years in basic school. His new school does not offer Spanish, leaving his family with no choice but to pay for his continued language studies out of pocket.
"With the school's help, we found another student, so the lessons aren't entirely one-on-one and the price is quite reasonable. The best compliment for me was when my son said after one lesson, 'Dad, you know, I think that money was well spent. I feel like I'm really learning and making progress there,'" parent Sven Kala said.
Tallinn Language School has seen a significant increase in interest among schoolchildren in learning French and Finnish this fall.
"Finnish has been the most requested language so far. There's also demand for online lessons. People from outside Tallinn, including students from other cities, have taken and are taking these courses," said Ivar Soone, head of Tallinn Language School.
According to Soone, courses for schoolchildren are slightly cheaper, costing less than €100 per month. So far, no schools have paid for the courses. The Ministry of Education sees no problem with paid courses replacing compulsory language lessons.
According to the Ministry of Education, if students cannot continue studying a foreign language in upper secondary school, the school must offer them the opportunity to start learning another language from scratch. Alternatively, students can continue studying their chosen language at private language courses paid for by their parents, with the school recognizing the results.
Last winter, there was debate over whether schools should be allowed to collect money from parents for expenses such as museum tickets.
"These are different things. If it's a compulsory subject in the curriculum and the school is required to offer students the opportunity to study a B foreign language — at the upper secondary level, we're talking about B1 and B2 foreign languages and schools must offer B1 foreign language instruction — then when a student continues studying a language outside school, it's usually not because the school doesn't offer another option. It's the choice of the parents and the student," said Marika Peekmann, the Ministry of Education's chief expert on foreign languages.
According to Ene Saar, principal of Tallinn Secondary School of Science, the biggest challenges for schools are still ahead as this year's basic school graduates are the first cohort required to choose a foreign language other than Russian.
"When they enter upper secondary school, it will be a challenge to figure out how and in what way we can open these B foreign language groups. It's simply not financially feasible to offer everyone the language they want," Saar said.
Saar believes the choice of second foreign languages could be restricted, with some less commonly taught languages offered as electives instead. The Ministry of Education sees no need for such restrictions, saying it is not aware of any upper secondary schools experiencing problems.

AI models may soon replicate across smart devices without human control, Anthropic says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
08:13:24 UTC
17:13:24 KST

Dilara Hamit
13 October 2026•Update: 13 October 2026
Small artificial intelligence models could soon become capable of copying themselves across internet-connected devices without human control or access to data centers, according to new Anthropic research.
The study, published Sunday by the US AI company’s Frontier Red Team, examined whether AI models could independently find devices, transfer model files, establish the software needed to operate and continue spreading from each newly infected machine.
Researchers said models with fewer than 30 billion parameters can already complete many individual stages of that process, although most still struggle to combine them reliably.
In a controlled and simplified experiment, the GLM-5.2 model successfully spread across all eight available test devices in four of five trials and reached seven in the remaining trial.
Anthropic stressed that the experiment simplified the hacking stage by using devices with an unsecured connection. The results therefore do not demonstrate that an AI model can currently escape and reproduce autonomously under real-world conditions.
“We don’t yet have a full rogue replicator,” the researchers said. However, they warned that agents were becoming increasingly capable of completing the necessary steps and passing useful information to later copies of themselves.
The study focused particularly on inexpensive internet-of-things devices, which frequently have limited security protections. Potential targets could include smart televisions, refrigerators, ovens, vacuum cleaners, security cameras and videoconferencing equipment.
Anthropic demonstrated that a 26-billion-parameter model could run across 15 inexpensive Android television boxes costing about $55 each. A smaller model successfully established the software required to operate on eight of the nine types of hardware tested.
Unlike conventional computer worms, a self-replicating AI system could potentially adjust to unfamiliar devices, diagnose technical problems and pass successful strategies to future copies.
The researchers said such a system would initially spread slowly, possibly taking one or two days to produce each new copy. However, it could be difficult to eliminate because there would be no central server to switch off.
Anthropic estimated that, if smaller models continue improving at their historical pace, they could reach the capability demonstrated by GLM-5.2 by the end of 2026. The company cautioned that this was only a rough projection based on general capability trends.
The researchers recommended monitoring unusual network traffic, isolating infected devices and requiring manufacturers to strengthen default security settings.
They warned that early, slow-moving replicators could signal the future arrival of faster systems capable of breaching more secure computers.
“We should aim to harden our systems to make it difficult for such replicators to spread,” they said, “but also prepare to deal with a world where they are here to stay.”

Netanyahu has called for a criminal investigation into soldiers and officers interviewed in award-winning documentary.
Israeli prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu has ordered the country’s attorney general and the head of the Shin Bet security service to reveal the identities of officers interviewed in the award-winning film NAZA.
Netanyahu is ordering for the filmmakers, Oscar-winning Israeli directors Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor, to be prosecuted for causing “harm to Israel’s diplomatic and security interests”.
He has asked for attorney general Gali Baharav-Miara, IDF chief of staff Lt Gen Eyal Zamir, and Shin Bet head David Zini, to “act urgently to uncover the identity of all those who are involved or appear in the libel film”.
NAZA, which premiered in Venice and won the Special Jury Prize, is currently being screened in cinemas in more than 50 countries, shows “in detail the systems behind Israel’s calculated mass killing of Palestinian civilians in Gaza,” according to its official synopsis.
Shot in secrecy at night on the rooftops of Tel Aviv during the ongoing Gaza war, it features interviews with 24 Israeli military intelligence officers, soldiers and whistleblowers. They describe how Palestinians are targeted and how strikes are carried out using AI and automated surveillance in military targeting systems - despite Israel being aware that civilians are present in targeted areas. The participants' faces and voices were digitally altered to protect their identities.
The 80-minute hot-button doc builds on reporting between 2023 and 2025 published by the Israeli-Palestinian +972 Magazine, the Hebrew-language outlet Local Call, and The Guardian.

Switzerland sees rise in mortgage rates in third quarter
Mortgage costs rose in Switzerland in the third quarter compared with the previous three months, mainly due to the rise in interest rates on the capital markets, which drove up banks’ refinancing costs.
At the end of September, the indicative rate – calculated based on the average of rates from around 30 banks – stood at 2.07% for a ten-year fixed-rate mortgage, according to the online comparison portal Comparis.
More
Switzerland’s housing shortage: how bad is it?
For a five-year fixed-rate mortgage, the rate stood at 1.9% at the end of the quarter under review. At 1.75%, three-year fixed-rate mortgages were also higher than they had been three months earlier (1.38%).
“In the short term, given that inflation remains low, the Swiss National Bank is unlikely to be in any particular hurry to raise interest rates. However, the more favourable economic outlook, the weakness of the franc and rising energy prices have increased the likelihood of a tightening of monetary policy,” says Dirk Renkert, a financial expert quoted in the press release.
Higher interest rates abroad are increasingly having an impact on the Swiss capital market.
“This is why fixed-rate mortgages are becoming more expensive, even though the SNB is keeping its key interest rate at 0%. The indicative rates for 10-year fixed-rate mortgages, which are now above 2%, have not been this high since March 2025,” Renkert added.

Dozens of Turkish Amazon armored vehicles spotted in Libya
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
08:10:21 UTC
17:10:21 KST

- Footage said to be from Libya shows dozens of Turkish-made BMC AMAZON 4x4 armored vehicles with remote weapon stations and jamming systems.
- Turkish analyst Ahmet Alemdar said the vehicles are operated by Libyan elite units but did not identify the force or filming location.
Footage said to be from Libya shows dozens of Turkish-made BMC AMAZON 4×4 armored vehicles in service with Libyan elite units, fitted with remote-controlled weapon stations and jamming systems, according to Turkish defense analyst Ahmet Alemdar, who shared the images on X.
Alemdar described the vehicles as being operated by “elite units” but did not identify which Libyan force or faction they belong to, where or when the footage was filmed, or how many vehicles appear in total beyond describing them as “dozens.” The post also did not say what type of jamming equipment is mounted on the vehicles or which weapons the remote-controlled stations carry. Neither BMC nor Türkiye’s defense procurement agency has publicly announced an AMAZON export contract with Libya.
The AMAZON is the smallest vehicle in BMC Otomotiv’s family of armored vehicles and was first shown publicly at the Eurosatory exhibition in Paris in 2016. It has a V-shaped hull built to deflect mine and roadside bomb blasts away from the crew, carries up to seven people, and, according to BMC, can reach 120 km/h (75 mph) and travel about 800 km (500 miles) on a tank of fuel. Remote-controlled weapon stations on the AMAZON typically carry a 7.62 mm or 12.7 mm machine gun that the crew aims and fires from inside the vehicle using cameras and a screen. BMC has also shown versions that can be driven without a crew, and Turkish company ASELSAN has mounted its GÖKBERK counter-drone laser on the AMAZON chassis.
Jamming systems on light armored vehicles are usually meant to block the radio links and satellite navigation signals that small drones and remotely triggered roadside bombs rely on, giving convoys some protection against both threats. Alemdar’s post did not say which of those roles the Libyan equipment is meant to fill.
Türkiye has been one of Libya’s main military partners since 2019, when it signed a security agreement with the government in Tripoli and later sent military advisers, drones and armored vehicles to support its forces. Turkish-made BMC vehicles, including the larger Kirpi and Vuran models, have appeared in Libya in previous years. The AMAZON has also been exported to other countries in the region, and BMC has marketed it heavily to armies that need light, mine-protected vehicles for internal security and border work.

Child marriage in southern Germany: Over 350 cases recorded, some brides as young as 11
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
08:09:32 UTC
17:09:32 KST

A written question by two AfD members of the Baden-Württemberg state parliament revealed 358 marriages involving minors, but only eight have so far been annulled with final legal effect.
In the southwestern German state of Baden-Württemberg, a total of 358 so-called child marriages have been officially recorded since 2012. Only eight of these forced marriages have so far been legally annulled. According to authorities, the other 350 cases were brought to an end in other ways.
This alarming finding comes from a response by the Baden-Württemberg state government to a minor inquiry submitted by AfD state parliament members Nikolaos Boutakoglou and Emely Knorr.
The Tübingen regional authority is responsible for recording the data, the answer came from the Ministry of the Interior.
11-year-old Iraqi girl married off
The eight final annulments took place between 2018 and 2024. Among the documented cases was the marriage of an 11-year-old girl from Iraq to a 17-year-old Iraqi, which was annulled in 2020.
As early as 2018, the marriage of a 14-year-old Afghan girl to a 30-year-old man had been ended. In 2024 two further annulments were added: they concerned a 16-year-old German girl and a 25-year-old Pakistani man and a 16-year-old Syrian girl and a 27-year-old man from the same country.
State parliament member Nikolaos Boutakoglou wrote on Facebook that the issue was "really awful" but was being treated as a taboo.
According to its own account, the ministry deals exclusively with such marriages entered into abroad.
Since summer 2017, the Act to Combat Child Marriages has been in force in Germany. In 2024, the Bundestag adopted new rules to protect minors in marriages concluded abroad.
Hundreds of cases without state intervention
The significantly higher number of cases concluded in other ways raises questions about how these marriages continued. For the period from 2015 to 2026, the regional authority lists a total of 350 proceedings under the heading "other disposals."
But what became of the other child marriages? The state government cites, among other things, the death of a spouse, reaching adulthood, a decision not to seek annulment or a new marriage concluded abroad. In these cases, there was therefore no legally binding annulment.
For 2023, the records include the case of a 12-year-old Afghan girl who was married to a 21-year-old Afghan man. Girls aged 13 and 14 also appear several times in the statistics.
The most recent entries in the overview relate to 2026. They include, among other things, marriages of 16- and 17-year-old girls to adult men. The statistics record the age of the spouses at the time of marriage and their respective nationalities.
According to the Interior Ministry, at the time the inquiry was answered there were no court proceedings pending to annul child marriages.
State parliament member Emely Knorr, who co-initiated the inquiry, demanded on the social media platform Instagram: "Child marriages are incompatible with our values. Children have a right to safety, education and a self-determined future. That is why we need effective protection, early intervention and resolute action against forced marriages."
How many pupils are affected?
The two MPs wanted to know what impact forced marriages have on their schooling.
The Ministry of Education explained that no such data are collected. According to the state government, it also has no information on the countries in which the recorded marriages were contracted.
The age and nationality at the time of marriage are recorded, as these are relevant for possible annulment proceedings.
Another question from the MPs concerned how often the YASEMIN counselling centre, which is funded by the state, had been called in for cases of forced marriage involving pupils at schools in Baden-Württemberg.
In its reply of 9 September 2026, the Interior Ministry wrote that the counselling centre does not break down its cases by the school status of the people it advises or by school year.
Instead, cases are recorded by the age of those affected and by calendar year. The precise number of counselling sessions remains unclear.
Threat of forced marriage: 80 cases recorded
In the 2025 calendar year, YASEMIN recorded a total of 271 counselling cases. In 80 cases, the people concerned were at risk of being forced into marriage. Of these 80 people, 33 were minors.
Four of the minors were under 12 years old, five were 12 and another two were 13. The counselling centre distinguishes between people at risk of forced marriage and other counselling issues; it does not carry out any school-related analysis.
According to the MPs, the trigger for the parliamentary inquiry was an emergency checklist by the women's rights organisation Terre des Femmes, published at the end of July 2026 and aimed primarily at teaching staff.
In legal terms, people up to the age of 14 are considered children in Germany; from then until the age of 18 they are deemed adolescents.
Under the UN Convention on the Rights of the Child, everyone up to the age of 18 is regarded as a child. Only once they reach adulthood are people allowed to marry in Germany. Forced marriage is defined as a separate criminal offence in the Penal Code.
With a population of around 11.24 million people, Baden-Württemberg accounts for just under 13.5% of the total German population of about 83.5 million inhabitants.

====================================================================================================

One trail approved, another closed: questions grow after deadly Israeli school hike blast
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
08:05:41 UTC
17:05:41 KST

Documents obtained by ynet following the death of schoolboy Yair Wilensky in an unexploded munition blast on Ramim Ridge in northern Israel reveal troubling questions about how school hiking trips are approved in areas damaged by war. The Education Ministry's trip coordination center authorized an itinerary labeled "Israel Trail 2051," a designation that combines the names of two entirely different routes running parallel to each other, one of which remains officially closed. The documents raise concerns about unclear instructions and conflicting restrictions in a region exposed to Hezbollah fire for more than two years.
Near the entrance to Kibbutz Kfar Giladi, two separate hiking routes begin at roughly the same location. One is the Israel Trail, marked in orange, blue and white, which climbs dozens of meters up the mountainside. The other, marked in green, is a paved route identified on maps as Trail 2051, also known as the Ramim Ridge Scenic Road or the Naftali Mountains Scenic Road. For approximately 7.5 kilometers, the two trails remain entirely separate before merging near Ein Korim spring and continuing toward Mishkenot HaRoim.
The school group received authorization to hike from Kfar Giladi to Mishkenot HaRoim along a route identified as "Israel Trail 2051." Yet the same approval explicitly stated that "Ramim Ridge Scenic Road 2051" was closed due to repairs of war damage. The Jewish National Fund (KKL-JNF) website also lists the paved, green-marked route as closed to hikers.
The scenic road was repaired and remarked only during the past week but has still not officially reopened. Nevertheless, thousands of families walked along it during the recent Jewish holidays and the vacation period at religious educational institutions. Despite the risk of unexploded ammunition and other remnants of the fighting, no specific warnings about such dangers were posted along the route. A longstanding KKL-JNF sign states that the trail is closed "due to war damage" and that hiking is "strictly prohibited," but makes no mention of unexploded ordnance.
‘The trail is approved, but not approved’
Investigators now face several critical questions. Did the students take the green-marked scenic road rather than the Israel Trail? If so, why? Did the guide misunderstand the route or fail to distinguish between two trails beginning at the same location? Did the group follow the approved itinerary, or was the route changed along the way? Another question concerns the approval system itself: Should school trips be authorized near routes that remain closed because of possible unexploded munitions left behind by the war?
Experienced hiking guides have sharply criticized the Education Ministry's approval procedures, arguing that the conflicting instructions indicate a lack of understanding of conditions on the ground. "It cannot be that Route 2051 is approved, but approved with restrictions. So is it approved or not?" a senior hiking guide told ynet. "If these are different routes, they should have been treated as different routes."
The guide acknowledged that the person leading the trip also had a professional responsibility to clarify the instructions. "Perhaps he should have asked questions and tried to understand what the coordination center meant with all its 'remarks,'" he said. "But ultimately, the body responsible for overseeing and managing the entire process is the Education Ministry."
The central problem, according to guides familiar with the area, is the disconnect between officials issuing hiking permits from their offices and the actual dangers on the ridge. "You cannot issue an approval, include contradictory and confusing instructions under the restrictions, and then expect a teacher or guide to understand that 'this trail is approved, but it isn't approved,'" the guide said. "So what exactly am I allowed to do? What am I not allowed to do?"
He also criticized the system used to approve hikes, saying it relies too heavily on computerized information rather than firsthand knowledge of the terrain. "The nature coordination center doesn't know what's happening on the ground. I'm telling you this from experience," he said. "They don't approve things based on actual fieldwork and an understanding of reality. They simply work according to the computer, according to whatever it tells them. Most of the time, they have no real connection to conditions in the field."
Education Ministry: Planned route did not enter prohibited area
The Education Ministry rejected suggestions that it had authorized a hike through an area officially closed to visitors. "The ministry acted in accordance with KKL-JNF restrictions and instructed that no activities take place in the designated area because of war damage. The planned hiking route did not pass through the prohibited area," the ministry said in a statement. It added that the approval included explicit safety instructions, including an absolute prohibition on touching unexploded missiles or ammunition and a requirement to report any such objects immediately.
"The circumstances of the incident and the route actually taken are now being examined as part of an investigation by the IDF and police, in cooperation with the Education Ministry and the relevant professional authorities," the statement said. The ministry stressed that the findings of the investigation should be awaited before conclusions are drawn about the circumstances of the tragedy.
The ministry also said it would work with the relevant authorities in the coming days to review the procedures for approving outdoor activities and the safety instructions accompanying them. For now, a central question remains unanswered: Whether the students followed the authorized Israel Trail or entered the nearby scenic road that had been closed because of war damage.

UNHCR chief says low funding makes agency’s task “impossible”
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
08:04:40 UTC
17:04:40 KST

UNHCR chief says low funding makes agency’s task “impossible”
The UN High Commissioner for Refugees believes that the agency is facing an “impossible” task due to a lack of funds. Barham Saleh admitted in Geneva that “times are tough” while announcing a reorganisation.
“Efficiency has its limits,” said Saleh at the start of the executive committee meeting of the UNHCR. “There comes a point where greater efficiency cannot make up for a shortage of resources,” he added. “The consequences are not abstract; they are borne by those who depend on us.”
More
Ripple effect of aid freeze becomes real in Geneva
The former Iraqi president acknowledged the financial difficulties facing member states. “But there is a difference between doing more with less and being asked to do the impossible,” the High Commissioner added.
Among the consequences, aid to 50,000 survivors of the Sudan conflict is under threat, and the registration of tens of thousands of refugees has been suspended in Ethiopia.
According to figures up to last Friday, the UN agency had received only 35% of the $8.5 billion requested for this year. For 2027, UNHCR is currently forecasting funding of less than $2.7 billion, which could be increased by the end of the year at the time of the donor conference.
Saleh is calling for funding that is provided earlier, is more predictable and is more flexible.
More
UNHCR cuts close to 5,000 jobs amid funding shortfall
In recent years, the UN agency has faced funding cuts from the US and other countries. Since 2024, nearly 8,000 people have left the organisation, reducing its staff from nearly 20,000 to just under 12,000.
Impact across 31 offices
Since taking up his post in early January, Saleh has commissioned an independent assessment of UNHCR’s operations. He wants a “more agile” and “more sustainable” organisation that collaborates more closely with other parts of the UN humanitarian system, particularly in terms of procurement.
Changes are to be implemented across 31 UNHCR sites. The aim is to avoid duplication at the Geneva headquarters and in regional offices, and to bring the UN agency even closer to the people it assists.
Structures are to be simplified and responsibilities more clearly defined. Another change is that the number of directors reporting directly to political posts will be reduced from 12 to 6.
Some 88% of staff work outside Geneva. And around 70% are local staff. Around 95% of resources are channelled into assistance in the various countries. Saleh also wants UNHCR to rely more heavily on artificial intelligence for its operations.

IMF projects average oil price at $95.74 per barrel in 2026 and $87.39 in 2027
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
08:03:22 UTC
17:03:22 KST

BANGKOK, October 13. /TASS/. The International Monetary Fund (IMF) forecasts that the average price of a barrel of oil will be $95.74 this year and $87.39 in 2027. This forecast is included in the organization's latest World Economic Outlook report, released in Bangkok, where the governing bodies of the IMF and the World Bank are holding their off-site meetings.
"The average price of oil in US dollars a barrel was $67.74 in 2025; the assumed price, based on futures markets, is $95.74 in 2026 and $87.39 in 2027," the report says.
According to the authors, oil prices are projected to rise by 41.6% this year and fall by 8.7% next year. These figures represent upward revisions of 9.5 and 3.1 percentage points, respectively, compared to the Fund's previous World Economic Outlook report released in July.
Fund experts emphasize that the forecast factors in an expected recovery of shipping in the Strait of Hormuz to pre-war levels between March and October 2027. However, they note that if the war between the US and Iran is not resolved by June 2027, shipping in the Strait of Hormuz and the Bab el-Mandeb Strait would be effectively paralyzed and damage to oil infrastructure would escalate. Consequently, a resumption of oil supplies should not be expected before the end of 2027. In such a scenario, the experts forecast that oil prices could climb to $130 per barrel between the fourth quarter of this year and the first quarter of 2027, returning to baseline scenario levels only by the fourth quarter of next year.
Natural gas prices are estimated by Fund experts to rise by 48% this year compared to 2025 levels. Fertilizer prices are projected to increase by an average of 10% in 2026 compared to the previous year.
