- A child and his mother were killed Thursday when Israeli warplanes struck a home in Gaza City’s al-Sabra neighbourhood after an evacuation warning.
- A drone strike on a charging point west of Khan Younis killed four people on Sunday, the Palestinian news agency Wafa reported.
- Two more men were killed in a strike near a mosque in al-Mawasi in the south on Monday.
In statements describing attacks, Israel’s military claimed several of those killed this week were Palestinian fighters.
The Israeli military said two men killed near the Jordanian Field Hospital were Islamic Jihad operatives; Wafa identified one as a recently released former prisoner.
It separately said a civil defence worker killed while responding to the wounded near Kamal Adwan Hospital in northern Gaza had been a Hamas sniper; Hamas rejected the claim, and it has not been independently verified.
Gaza’s health system continued its collapse:
- Gaza’s Ministry of Health said that 44 percent of essential medicines are completely out of stock.
- A Physicians for Human Rights Israel report found that a year into the ceasefire, not one of Gaza’s 36 hospitals is operating at full capacity.
- More than 18,500 patients need medical evacuation and more than 1,000 have died waiting, according to the joint NGO statement.
- The Health Ministry said this week that no patient had been permitted to leave through Rafah crossing in the last week.
Israeli forces have also continued pushing the so-called Yellow Line demarcating Israeli control further into residential Gaza City neighbourhoods this week, triggering fresh displacement.
One year into the ceasefire, the Board of Peace – Gaza’s transitional oversight body – has failed to meet most of its central commitments: no international stabilisation force has deployed, aid trucks are entering at roughly a third of the agreed rate, and Israel now controls nearly two thirds of the Strip — well above the roughly 50 percent it was supposed to retain before further withdrawal and a future handover of control to Palestinians.
Olive harvest under coordinated assault
The Palestinian olive harvest – traditionally a time of family and celebration – gathered pace as Israeli settlers and soldiers intensified efforts to disrupt it. Harvesters were killed, attacked and blocked, while isolated families faced dayslong settler sieges.
Pogrom attacks included:
- On October 7, Ali Hassan Yasser al-Bazzari, 44, was shot dead when settlers and soldiers opened fire on olive pickers on farmland between Burqa and Ramin, northwest of Nablus in the occupied West Bank. At least 16 others were wounded during the pogrom, according to the Palestinian news agency Wafa.
- The Palestine Red Crescent Society said Israeli forces assaulted ambulance crews trying to reach the wounded olive pickers and briefly detained three paramedics. Soldiers later raided the nearby village and made arrests, while the settlers who carried out the attack marched past unimpeded.
- The Palestinian Colonization and Wall Resistance Commission recorded 19 settler attacks on Friday alone, another 12 on Saturday and 18 more on Sunday, according to Wafa.
- The Israeli rights group Yesh Din had already documented 109 harvest-related settler incidents across 75 Palestinian communities in a 10-day period between September 27 and October 6.
- The commission says settlers and soldiers have destroyed roughly 50,000 trees so far this year.
The attacks followed a familiar shape village to village, according to Wafa and field reports from local residents and activists:
- Settlers in Qusra stole a farmer’s olives before bulldozing more than 50 of his trees.
- In Birin, settlers from the recently established Adorim outpost set a dog on a 79-year-old woman harvesting nearby, hospitalizing her.
- Settlers from the same outpost cut power to roughly 20 homes repeatedly over the week.
- In al-Mughayyir, northeast of Ramallah, soldiers followed settlers into the village’s residential streets on Sunday, kicked an elderly woman trying to reach her home, and fired live rounds and tear gas into houses “without apparent reason,” according to Israeli field monitor Jonathan Pollack. The daily incursions are part of a monthslong campaign by settlers against villagers there.
- At Deir Abu Mash’al, a solidarity harvest organised by the Wall and Settlement Resistance Commission drew an attack by settlers in Area B that left eight people wounded, including a photojournalist shot in the thigh, Wafa reported.
Israeli forces frequently blocked the harvest, too. Soldiers used drone-mounted loudspeakers to drive farmers out of Wadi Abwein and turned pickers away in several locations elsewhere.
Israeli settlers’ own chat groups reveal how they frame such attacks in reverse — through a messianic lens, casting Palestinian harvesters reaching their own land in Deir Abu Mash’al as attempting to “seize” the land, and the olive harvest itself as cover for Palestinians gathering “intelligence” rather than picking olives that families have harvested there for generations. Settlers have been documented repeatedly stealing olives from Palestinians’ lands since harvesting unofficially started late last month.
Political jockeying ahead of elections
Once again, Palestinian Authority President Mahmoud Abbas postponed Palestinian legislative elections – this time to September, citing Israeli restrictions on election materials and observers entering Gaza and East Jerusalem, and ongoing settler violence. Mustafa Barghouti, of the Palestinian National Initiative, said the decision reflects that “everything is concentrated in the hands of the executive authority”, with no parliament or independent judiciary to check it.
In Israel, with high-stakes parliamentary elections scheduled for October 27, Joint List leader Yousef Jabareen said his alliance – made up predominantly of Palestinian citizens of Israel – was prepared to support a coalition against current Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu from outside government.
The support would be given in exchange for policy commitments, including a pathway to Palestinian statehood, The Times of Israel reported – a potential route to a majority that polls suggest neither bloc can reach without Arab party support.
Israeli authorities also began demolishing homes this week in al-Dahiya, an unrecognised Bedouin village in the Naqab, after a district court rejected a request to freeze the orders; roughly 60 homes face demolition.
In diplomatic news, the UK’s consulate in occupied East Jerusalem formally became a reduced “mission” after Israel’s deadline for its closure passed; it has long handled the UK’s relations with Palestinians.

Microsoft president says milk faces more regulation than AI
Unknown

2026-10-13

16:45:00 KST

Microsoft president says milk faces more regulation than AI
- Microsoft president Brad Smith said AI needs urgent global rules, with independent checks, incident reports and an “emergency brake” for rogue systems.
- Smith said AI has fewer safety rules than milk or washing machines, and warned that companies should disclose breaches and harmful behaviour.
- He said Britain could lead regulation through its AI Security Institute, while the UK may tighten rules if the current voluntary system fails.
AI generated
LONDON – Artificial Intelligence needs urgent global regulation with independent evaluators able to vet new developments, the president of Microsoft said, warning that AI currently faces fewer safety requirements than milk.
In an interview with the BBC published on Oct 12, Brad Smith said a set of global safety rules needed to be in place, requiring a “victim” to be informed if their system is breached by a rogue AI agent and an “emergency brake” available.
He said there should also be a legal requirement for companies to write “incident reports”.
“We know how to do this for other products,” Smith said. “We should build on that knowledge and think about how to apply it to AI.”
“Right now, your washing machine is subject to more safety rules than AI. Every carton of milk that you see in the grocery store is subject to safety rules and inspection.”
Tech companies such as Anthropic and OpenAI have started disclosing rogue or undesired behaviour by AI agents as part of a global debate about the fast-advancing technology that has included researchers’ warnings of an eventual existential threat to humanity.
Some companies have called for AI development to slow down, but that has sparked a debate as to whether executives have ulterior motives such as setting rules that preserve the lead of their firms, pre-empting a broader government backlash, or simply slowing breakneck spending.
Microsoft’s Smith said the one country that was well-placed to lead the way on regulation of AI was Britain, due to the AI Security Institute which was launched under former prime minister, Rishi Sunak.
Smith said officials in Washington viewed London very differently to how they viewed Brussels, which regulates AI based on the level of risk via its AI Act.
Britain’s institute receives pre-deployment access under voluntary agreements with the major AI models, allowing it to assess their capabilities and risks.
AI Minister Kanishka Narayan has told Reuters that Britain would consider regulating advanced models if the current system proved insufficient. REUTERS

Such exercises can also expose potential weaknesses in fire support coordination and logistics, he said.
The military should also strengthen training with various types of drones and assess its ability to counter enemy reconnaissance and strike capabilities to identify existing gaps in combat readiness, Shu added.

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — The International Monetary Fund (IMF) has raised Taiwan's 2026 economic growth forecast to 10.7%, up from 5.2% in April. That would make Taiwan the fastest-growing economy in Asia-Pacific and one of only three economies worldwide forecast to post double-digit growth.
The fund released its latest World Economic Outlook report on Tuesday, forecasting global economic growth of 3.1% this year. Taiwan's projected growth is more than double Singapore's 5%, while Hong Kong is forecast to grow 3.8%, South Korea 3.3%, and Japan 0.7%.
Guyana's economy is forecast to grow 22.3% this year, while South Sudan's is projected to expand 10.5%, making them the only other economies expected to record double-digit growth. Taiwan's current account surplus is projected to reach 22% of GDP this year, among the highest of any major economy, reflecting strong export performance.
The fund forecasts Taiwan's consumer price index to rise 2% this year, up from its April estimate of 1.5%, while the unemployment rate is projected to remain at 3.4%. Taiwan's nominal GDP is projected to reach NT$32.59 trillion (US$1.02 trillion) this year, with GDP per capita at NT$1.40 million.
Among emerging Asian economies, Vietnam is forecast to grow 8.4%, India 7%, and Indonesia 5.1%. The IMF projects US economic growth of 2.3% in both 2026 and 2027, while the euro area is expected to expand 1.1% in 2026 and 1.2% in 2027.
China's economy is forecast to grow 4.5% this year and 4% next year. China's second-quarter growth fell short of expectations at 4.3% year over year, as weak consumption and investment partly offset robust exports, the report said.
The fund sharply downgraded its 2026 growth outlook for the Middle East and Central Asia, citing severe economic disruption from the ongoing Iran war. Saudi Arabia's economy is projected to contract 3.3% this year, although the fund expects a recovery next year if shipping through the Strait of Hormuz returns to normal.
The report also highlighted how AI-related technology exports and investment are helping offset geopolitical headwinds. Taiwan and South Korea are among the few economies producing advanced semiconductors at scale, and together account for 62% of net trade in AI-related computing hardware.

Taiwan to impose anti-dumping duties on Chinese polyamide film
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
07:44:23 UTC
16:44:23 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Taiwan will impose provisional anti-dumping duties on certain Chinese-made polyamide film for four months starting Oct. 19, the Customs Administration said Tuesday.
Polyamide film, also known as nylon film, is used in food packaging, industrial materials, and electronics because of its strength and resistance to heat and chemicals. The provisional rate will be 0% for three Yuncheng Group affiliates and 40.21% for all other manufacturers or exporters, per Tai Sounds.
The three companies assigned the 0% rate are Kunshan Yuncheng Plastic Industry Co., Ltd., Yuncheng Qilong New Material Co., Ltd., and Yuncheng Heshan New Materials Co., Ltd.
Yuncheng Group provided documents to show that it sets prices based on production costs and operates independently of the Chinese government, per CNA. Based on its calculations, investigators found no positive dumping margin for the group.
Exporters that did not cooperate with the investigation were assigned a 40.21% dumping margin, matching their provisional duty rate. The Customs Administration said the provisional duties are intended to prevent further harm to local producers while the investigation continues.
The Ministry of Finance must make a final determination on dumping within 60 days of the preliminary announcement. If dumping is confirmed, the Ministry of Economic Affairs will have 40 days to determine whether it injured the domestic industry.

ArcelorMittal Kryvyi Rih has begun the process of placing its plant in cold shutdown following four Russian missile attacks, the company said on 10 October. The attacks killed six workers, injured more than 18 others, and forced the suspension of primary steel production.
ArcelorMittal Kryvyi Rih is Ukraine’s largest steelworks, so its shutdown adds to the pressure on an industry already hit by Russian attacks and disrupted exports.
ArcelorMittal Kryvyi Rih CEO Mauro Longobardo said the company’s priority was to protect workers and industrial assets. He said the ArcelorMittal Group would remain in Ukraine, but that its assessment was that safe operation was impossible while the war continued.
Workers and the city

On 29 September, the outlet reported that the company had not said how many workers could lose their jobs and was assessing its staffing needs after production stopped. It also said municipal water and heating utilities had about 1,000 vacancies and had been instructed to help ArcelorMittal workers find jobs. The outlet noted that it was unclear whether the vacancies were new and that the announcement did not specify the roles or salaries.
In late September, Kryvyi Rih defense council head Oleksandr Vilkul wrote on Telegram that the city would cut spending and stop a number of projects as tax revenues fell. He attributed the pressure to Russian attacks and the inability to export through seaports, and said several major industrial facilities were idle, including ArcelorMittal Kryvyi Rih and three mining and ore-processing plants.
September steel output down 4.7-fold
Ukraine’s steel production fell 4.7-fold year on year in September, to 131,000 tons, the steelmakers’ association Ukrmetalurhprom said, NV reported. Metinvest chief operating officer Oleksandr Myronenko told Forbes Ukraine on 15 September that the group would declare force majeure on some contracts after Zaporizhstal and Kametstal halted operations.
An expected $1 billion impairment
The ArcelorMittal Group said on 25 September that it expected to record a non-cash impairment of about $1 billion, mostly related to property, plant, and equipment. It also said it had provided more than $700 million in financial support to its Ukrainian business.

Christian tourists buy West Bank settlement goods in protest of European trade restrictions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
07:41:11 UTC
16:41:11 KST

“This piece of legislation written by the Irish parliament shall not stand,” said Paul Coulter, national director of the International Christian Embassy Jerusalem (ICEJ) in Ireland, as he held up a copy of Ireland’s new law restricting imports from Israeli settlements. Then he tore the document apart in front of the camera.
For more stories from The Media Line go to themedialine.org
The gesture came during an ICEJ visit to Israeli communities in the West Bank, also known as Judea and Samaria, where Christian visitors traveled through Samaria, Gush Etzion and Efrat and were encouraged to shop at local businesses. The tour, organized during ICEJ’s annual Feast of Tabernacles gathering in Jerusalem, was intended as a direct response to a growing set of European measures restricting trade in products from Israeli settlements. Some of those measures are already in force; others remain proposed legislation.
Ireland’s ban took effect on Sept. 15. The Netherlands followed with a broader restriction on Sept. 22 that reaches even goods carried in personal luggage. Norway, meanwhile, is considering legislation that would prohibit imports from and exports to Israeli settlements, along with certain property transactions and services. The Norwegian proposal remains under consideration after a public consultation that closed Sept. 19.
David Parsons, ICEJ senior vice president and spokesman, said the organization brought Christians attending the Feast of Tabernacles into the area specifically to support businesses affected by the measures.
“In recent weeks, several European countries and even Canada and others have announced that they’re going to pass sanctions against the Jewish communities in Judea and Samaria,” Parsons told The Media Line. “We brought them here to the Shomron, to Samaria, also down to Gush Etzion, Efrat, to go and show support by buying goods here.”
Christians protest European settlement boycotts
The governments imposing or considering the restrictions present them as measures directed at settlements they consider illegal under international law, rather than at Israel as a whole. Ireland says its law is part of an effort to comply with international legal obligations identified in the International Court of Justice’s 2024 advisory opinion. The Irish government argues that Israeli settlements in what it refers to as occupied Palestinian territory are unlawful and undermine prospects for a two-state solution. Its law prohibits imports originating in designated settlement postal codes and makes violations subject to existing customs law, including search, seizure and forfeiture powers.
Parsons rejected that reasoning and argued that the economic effect was precisely the point. “The real intent of these European countries is to dry up the settlements and their livelihoods, the way of life, so they’d have to leave here,” he said. That characterization is disputed by the governments behind the measures, which describe them as a legal and political distinction between Israel and territory captured in 1967.
The Irish measure, however, stops short of restricting what tourists bring home for themselves. Noncommercial goods in personal baggage are exempt when intended for the traveler’s own consumption or use. That distinction became part of Coulter’s message during the trip.
“Come and buy Israeli wine. It’s some of the best wine in the world,” he said. Later, addressing Irish visitors specifically, he added: “Break the boycott. If you can buy Israeli wine, buy it.” Coulter noted that Irish law does not prevent tourists from returning with those products for private consumption.
Coulter said opposition to ICEJ’s position has also followed the organization at home. He described venues receiving calls demanding that ICEJ events be canceled and demonstrations outside meetings that went ahead.
“We have our own hashtag, #BoycottApartheidICEJ,” he said. “Our venues are lobbied and phoned to cancel our meetings, and when the venues won’t cancel, we actually have protest mobs screaming and shouting at the gates of our meetings.”
Norway has not yet enacted its proposed trade ban. Its Foreign Ministry opened the proposal for public consultation in June, saying Norwegian citizens and companies should not contribute economically to maintaining settlements that the government considers unlawful. The proposal would prohibit importing goods from Israeli settlements and exporting goods to them. It would also restrict certain real estate purchases, construction and property-related services, and acquisitions of businesses based in the settlements. Violations would carry criminal liability.
Dag Øyvind Juliussen, national director of ICEJ Norway, said the prospect of criminal penalties has sharpened opposition among supporters of Israel in his country. “They want to pass a bill that would make it a crime to trade with the Jewish inhabitants in Judea and Samaria, the so-called settlements,” he told The Media Line, adding that the legislation must still go through the Norwegian parliament.
For Juliussen, joining the shopping tour was a way to turn that opposition into a physical act. “This is what we need to do,” he said. “This area has been the heartland of the Jewish people for 3,000 years.” He said Christians who share that view should make their position visible by supporting the people and businesses living there.
Christian groups challenge European trade bans on Israeli settlements
The Netherlands has taken a different approach. Since Sept. 22, travelers entering the country have also been barred from bringing in products that Dutch authorities identify as coming from Israeli settlements covered by the measure. That includes items bought for personal use, such as gifts or souvenirs.
Dutch customs officers can check luggage and ask where an item was made or purchased. Products found to fall under the ban may need to be surrendered or seized. The measure does not apply to Israeli goods generally, but specifically to products linked to the settlements covered by the Dutch restrictions. Customs authorities say inspections are selected on the basis of risk assessments and objective information rather than a traveler’s nationality, religion, ethnicity or appearance.
Parsons said the possible long-term consequences went beyond lost sales. He accused European governments of pursuing policies that could eventually pressure Jews to leave the communities. “Are you really willing to support ethnic cleansing of that nature through these sanctions and criminal laws against buying goods from this area?” he asked. His language went far beyond the stated position of the governments involved, which say their measures are aimed at settlements and at preserving the possibility of a negotiated two-state outcome.
ICEJ’s response during the tour was deliberately practical. “We’ve done that now by bringing dozens of Christians on several buses to these areas to shop,” Parsons said. His instruction to participants was straightforward: “Take out your plastic, take out your dollars, your shekels and buy goods from Judea and Samaria.”
That leaves people traveling together on the same ICEJ tour subject to different rules once they return home. An Irish visitor can bring a bottle of locally produced wine back for personal consumption under Ireland’s exemption. A Dutch traveler carrying the same bottle from a location covered by the Netherlands’ restrictions may have to surrender it at customs. The United States Has an Industrial Problem in the Indo-Pacific
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
07:41:00 UTC
16:41:00 KST

The United States has spent years warning about China’s growing military power. Much of that discussion focuses on ships, missiles, aircraft, artificial intelligence, and other weapons, but considerably less attention is paid to the industrial capacity behind them. China has built an enormous manufacturing base capable of producing ships, electronics, machinery, batteries, components, and other goods at a scale the United States cannot easily match. In a prolonged conflict, that difference could become as important as the capabilities of the weapons themselves. The United States would need to replace damaged equipment, replenish munitions, repair ships and aircraft, and keep production running under wartime conditions. Its allies in the Indo-Pacific would face similar demands.
Washington is increasingly aware of the problem and is trying to bring new companies, private investment, and manufacturing methods into the defense sector. The Navy’s recently announced Arsenal-2 project with Anduril Industries is one example. Announced October 6, Arsenal-2 is a planned $6.6 billion manufacturing facility at Tradepoint Atlantic in Maryland. Anduril plans to invest $3.7 billion of private capital, while the Navy could provide up to $2.9 billion. The facility is intended to manufacture components and large assemblies for Virginia-class submarines, initially including torpedo tubes and potentially expanding to larger sections of the boats. The project addresses a genuine weakness in the American defense-industrial base: the Navy needs more production capacity, particularly as it tries to expand the submarine fleet.
The difficulty is that Arsenal-2 will not be operational tomorrow. Initial operations are not expected until 2030, and the manufacturing methods that will underpin the facility still have to be developed and validated. Anduril will have to establish the workforce, suppliers, quality systems, and production processes needed to meet the demanding requirements of the submarine industry. That raises a broader question for Washington as it tries to rebuild the defense-industrial base: how quickly can the United States create industrial capacity that can actually be relied upon in times of crisis?
The question is particularly important in the Indo-Pacific. A conflict with China would place enormous demands on American production while US forces were operating thousands of miles from the continental United States. Ships would require repairs, missiles and drones would need to be replaced, and munitions stocks would have to be replenished. The United States would also be relying on its allies. Japan, Australia, South Korea, the Philippines, and other partners are increasing their defense capabilities, but American credibility in the region depends partly on whether Washington can continue supplying and supporting those forces during a prolonged crisis. A military that can deploy advanced systems but cannot replace them at the required rate has a very different deterrent value from one that can sustain production.
China’s advantage is not limited to the size of its military. Its civilian manufacturing base supports military production in ways that are difficult for the United States to replicate quickly. China is already a major producer of ships, electronics, machinery, industrial components, and many of the materials and products that underpin modern manufacturing. The United States, by contrast, is trying to rebuild capacity that has contracted over decades. This is why the defense-industrial debate should be viewed as part of the broader strategic competition with Beijing rather than simply as a question of Pentagon procurement.
That effort will require private capital and new companies capable of challenging established defense contractors. It will also require the government to create sufficient and predictable demand for companies to invest in factories, equipment, workers, and supply chains. The traditional defense industry cannot simply be expected to expand on its own after years of consolidation. At the same time, Washington cannot assume that every new company or manufacturing concept will succeed merely because it offers a different approach.
The Pentagon has considerable experience with the consequences of moving production ahead of development and testing. The F-35 is the most prominent example, while the Littoral Combat Ship provides another. The issue is not that these programs were necessarily wrong to pursue, but that the government has repeatedly faced substantial costs when production proceeds before key technologies and capabilities have been sufficiently demonstrated. A 2013 GAO review found that the F-35’s concurrent acquisition strategy had led to substantial rework costs as deficiencies were discovered in testing. A later GAO review found continuing delivery delays and recommended that the program better align incentives with production outcomes. The LCS program likewise faced significant operational and testing problems, including delays in developing mission modules.
Arsenal-2 presents a related question at the industrial level. The United States is investing in a new production facility while the manufacturing processes behind it are still being developed and validated. That does not mean Arsenal-2 should be delayed or that Anduril should not receive the opportunity to build it. The more useful question is how Washington structures the relationship. What production targets will the Navy require? How quickly must the facility reach them? Who will independently verify performance? What happens if production falls short? And can procurement shift toward other suppliers if a new approach does not deliver? Those are basic questions for any major defense investment, particularly when the United States is trying to rebuild capacity under pressure from a much larger industrial competitor.
There is a strong argument for taking risks on new defense companies. The existing defense-industrial base has its own shortcomings, and established contractors have not always been able to deliver new capabilities quickly or at the required scale. Private investors should be able to back companies they believe can change that, and Washington should encourage competition rather than protecting incumbents. But government support should not become a substitute for performance. Companies should have the opportunity to demonstrate that they can deliver, and successful performance should lead to greater opportunities. If a project fails to meet its targets, the government needs to retain the ability to limit further exposure and turn to alternatives.
There are precedents for Washington taking early risks on companies that had not yet demonstrated their full capabilities. NASA supported SpaceX before Falcon 9 had flown, while the Department of Energy provided Tesla with a $465 million loan in 2010 that the company later repaid. Some early bets work and some do not. The lesson is not that the government should avoid risk. It is that government needs mechanisms that allow successful companies to grow while preventing unsuccessful projects from consuming resources indefinitely.
That approach is particularly important when the objective is to compete with China’s industrial capacity. The United States cannot deter China simply by developing more sophisticated technology or fielding a small number of advanced systems. It needs the ability to produce, repair, replace, and sustain military equipment over time. For the Indo-Pacific, that is a central part of the deterrence equation.

Israeli authorities have notified foreign airlines operating flights to Ben Gurion Airport of new restrictions on crew members holding dual nationality if one of their nationalities is among 29 countries on a list drawn up by Israel, according to aviation news website Paddle Your Own Kanoo (PYOK).
The Hebrew-language Walla website reported that the measures follow the thwarting of an alleged attack aboard a Flydubai flight on 30 September. Co-pilot Hamam al-Hamahi is accused of attempting to incapacitate the captain and take control of the passenger aircraft, which was heading to Ben Gurion Airport, with the alleged aim of crashing it into the terminal building.
PYOK reported that several passengers and two pilots who were not assigned to the flight helped prevent the suspected attack.
The new restrictions expand existing Israeli measures targeting crew members from countries that do not have diplomatic relations with Israel to include dual nationals. Under the rules, a crew member could be barred from working on a flight to Israel if they hold a US passport alongside the nationality of one of the countries on the list.
According to Walla, the published list contains 29 countries, although the PYOK report says the restrictions cover 31 countries without identifying the remaining two.

Attack scale
- On-duty air defense systems intercepted and destroyed 604 Ukrainian fixed-wing unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) over Russian regions between 8:00 p.m. Moscow time (5:00 p.m. GMT) on October 12 and 8:00 a.m. Moscow time (5:00 a.m. GMT) on October 13, the Defense Ministry reported.

- Air defense forces shot down 13 Ukrainian UAVs over the Voronezh Region overnight, Governor Alexander Gusev wrote on his Max channel.
Aftermath
- Air defenses repelled a large-scale aerial attack on the Stavropol Region, Governor Vladimir Vladimirov reported on Max.
- There have been no casualties reported so far.
- Damage from falling UAV debris was recorded in the industrial zone of the city of Nevinnomyssk.
- Inspection of the crash sites and assessment of the damage are underway.
- Emergency services began cleanup operations.

Ukrainian companies The Fourth Law and Odd Systems have announced signing a memorandum of understanding with U.S. defense technology company Performance Drone Works (PDW), under which the integration of Kurbas cameras into PDW drones will be assessed, with the possibility of localizing production in the U.S. later, the companies said.
"Ukraine is showing how fast technology can evolve when engineers and operators work closely together. We aim to combine proven technology with the U.S. engineering and production capacity needed to deploy it at scale," PDW CEO James Slider said, according to the release.
The Fourth Law and Odd Systems said in a joint release that the document was signed at the annual AUSA exhibition in Washington.
Under the agreement, the companies plan to assess the integration of cameras developed by Odd Systems, as well as technical specifications and requirements for further production in the U.S. In particular, PDW will become a manufacturing and industrialization partner for The Fourth Law and Odd Systems in the U.S.
Among other things, the companies also intend to set up production of thermal sensors in the U.S. under the newly created Project Foundation initiative, headed by Ihor Nakonechny.
"Kurbas cameras were created and tested at the front. Together with PDW we can bring this technology to American platforms and, through Project Foundation, build a thermal sensor supply chain directly in the United States," The Fourth Law CEO and Odd Systems co-founder Yaroslav Azhniuk said in the release.
The release also said PDW is building capacity to integrate selected partner technologies and produce components for its platforms, and over time for the entire industry of unmanned systems in the U.S. and allied countries.
Performance Drone Works is a U.S. defense technology company specializing in the development of multipurpose aerial robotic systems, as well as software, communications, training systems and production capacity. It is headquartered in Huntsville, Alabama.
The Fourth Law and Odd Systems were founded in Kyiv in 2023 by entrepreneur Yaroslav Azhniuk. They operate in Ukraine, elsewhere in Europe and in the U.S.
The Fourth Law specializes in developing scalable autonomy for robotic systems, with a primary focus on defense.
Odd Systems develops and makes thermal and daytime cameras for drones and other robotic systems.
Last week The Fourth Law and Odd Systems announced the launch of a joint project, Project Foundation, to produce uncooled thermal sensors in Europe and the U.S.

U.S. Army names its new Korean-designed cannon XM1776
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
07:38:14 UTC
16:38:14 KST

- The U.S. Army and Hanwha Defense USA named the wheeled K9-based howitzer the XM1776 Mobile Tactical Cannon at AUSA 2026.
- The U.S. Army has ordered nine XM1776 prototypes with an option for nine more; the value of the change was not disclosed.
The U.S. Army has given its new wheeled howitzer an official name, the XM1776 Mobile Tactical Cannon, and has raised its prototype order from Hanwha Defense USA to nine systems, with an option for nine more.
The Army and Hanwha unveiled the designation at a naming ceremony at the company’s booth at the Association of the U.S. Army’s annual meeting in Washington on Oct. 12. The XM1776 is the American version of Hanwha’s K9 Mobile Howitzer, an eight-wheeled 155 mm self-propelled gun the U.S. Army is testing as a replacement for the towed M777 in some units. The number in the name points to 1776, the year of American independence, and Hanwha tied the unveiling to the country’s 250th anniversary this year.
When the U.S. Army picked Hanwha in August, the agreement called for six prototypes delivered on an accelerated schedule, with options for 12 more, worth up to about $263 million in total. Hanwha now says the U.S. Army has ordered nine prototypes with an option for nine more, keeping the possible total at 18. Neither the company nor the U.S. Army disclosed the value of the added systems, when they will be delivered, or how many have already been handed over. The first prototype arrived earlier this fall and was shown at a U.S. Army event on Capitol Hill this month.
“The XM-1776 Mobile Tactical Cannon represents the launch of the U.S. Army’s new long-range precision fires modernization effort and its powerful partnership with HDUSA to produce this system at speed and scale,” said Mike Smith, Hanwha Defense USA chief operating officer and president of land systems.
The XM1776 is built around the same 52-caliber gun used on Hanwha’s tracked K9, which serves with South Korea and about 10 other countries. Hanwha says more than 2,500 K9 howitzers have been fielded worldwide. A self-propelled gun can fire and drive off before enemy counter-battery fire arrives, something a towed M777 crew cannot do as quickly, and the K9’s longer barrel gives it more range than the M777.
Hanwha is setting up an integration and test site in Opelika, Alabama, as the first phase of U.S. production for the XM1776 and other K9 wheeled variants. Company leaders are meeting with more than 70 current and potential American suppliers this week as part of an effort to build what Hanwha calls an Artillery Industrial Base Coalition, aimed at moving more of the supply chain to the United States.
The U.S. Army plans to field the new cannon first to Stryker brigade combat teams, followed by mobile and infantry brigades, and wants a ready version in units by 2031. It has also opened a separate competition for a tracked Mobile Tactical Cannon.

Minister: Iran's role in RAF Fairford incident affects Estonia's security
Foreign Minister Margus Tsahkna says Iran's involvement in the RAF Fairford incident has implications for Estonia's security.
Fairford is used by US forces. Tsahkna said that matters to Estonia because NATO collective defense depends on allied infrastructure working and troops moving quickly across Europe in a crisis.
The UK has attributed the 27 September incident to Iran. Estonia is joining a joint statement by the foreign ministers of 28 nations condemning it.
"Estonia joins the joint statement by other foreign ministers, in which we acknowledge the United Kingdom's attribution and condemn Iran's violent attacks and other hybrid activity," Tsahkna said.
"European security threats are not limited to Russia's activities. According to the UK's assessment, what happened at Fairford shows the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps's continued readiness to operate through covert networks beyond Iran's borders. This means Iran's hostile activity must be treated as a European security question, not only a Middle East problem," he went on via a ministry press release.
I join my fellow foreign ministers in recognising the UK's attribution of Iranian involvement in the 27 September incident at RAF Fairford and condemning Iran's violent attacks and other hybrid activities. Threats to military facilities used by our Allies affect us all. We need closer coordination between Allies to expose hostile networks and prevent further attacks. We will not be intimidated. https://t.co/VaRvmwTZ7M

Five men, all UK nationals in their twenties, were arrested near the base in Gloucestershire in the early hours of 27 September after police were alerted to three suspicious vehicles. They were released on bail. Dozens of nearby homes were evacuated. US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the incident "clearly involves the hands of a foreign actor."

16:36:38 KST

Drone attack sinks ship off Bulgaria’s Black Sea coast, PM says
Two ships were hit in the attack, including the Ukrainian-owned Chelsea 3, which sustained damage.
Two ships have been hit in drone attacks off Bulgaria’s Black Sea coast, with one of them sinking, Prime Minister Rumen Radev said.
The Ukrainian-owned Chelsea 3, which was sailing under a Maltese flag, was hit by three drones and damaged about 18 nautical miles (33km) off Bulgaria at about 1:30am on Tuesday, Radev said.
Radev said its 15-man crew, seven of them Ukrainians and eight Azerbaijanis, was rescued. Five crew members received medical assistance, and no one was seriously injured.
Bulgarian officials said five crew members had been rescued from the ship that sank but 11 remain missing at sea. The vessel went down off the coast of the village of Krapets, near the Romanian border and was identified as the Guinea-Bissau-flagged cargo ship HS Dignity by President Iliana Iotova. A search and rescue operation is ongoing, she said.
Radev called the incident “absolutely unacceptable”.
“Another attack in the immediate vicinity of Bulgarian territorial waters,” he said in a televised address.
Radev also said there was no clear evidence of who carried out the attack, but “the outcome benefits” Russia and that the Russian ambassador would be summoned over the incident.
As a member of the NATO military alliance, Bulgaria holds a strategic position on the Black Sea, where Russia and Ukraine have vital ports.
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen condemned the attack on the ships.
“The Black Sea has become another front of escalation of the Russian war in Ukraine,” she said.
“This is unacceptable. I strongly condemn the drone attacks on merchant ships near Bulgaria’s coast. Putting the lives of the crew in grave danger and threatening security in the Black Sea,” she wrote on X.
“We stand with Bulgaria and thank its rescuers for their swift response. Those responsible should be held accountable,” von der Leyen added.
NATO chief Mark Rutte said the alliance would adjust its defences “as needed” following the incident.
“NATO will continue to work closely with our allies in the Black Sea. We have already strengthened our posture along the eastern flank and will continue to monitor the security environment, adjusting our deterrence and defence posture as needed,” Rutte said on X after talking to Radev.
The incident comes as concerns grow over hybrid attacks involving Russia.
Last week, drones hit two ships off Bulgaria’s Black Sea coast, causing one to sink. All 10 crew members from the ship that sank remain unaccounted for.

Hong Kong police arrest 20 over prostitution syndicate that trapped women in debt
Police say women from Southeast Asia had to provide unpaid sexual services to repay travel and accommodation costs before sharing earnings with the syndicate
Hong Kong police have arrested 20 people in connection with a cross-border prostitution syndicate that allegedly recruited women from Southeast Asia and required them to provide unpaid sexual services to repay travel debts.
Police said on Tuesday that the syndicate paid for the women’s travel and accommodation but required them to provide sexual services 30 to 45 times without payment before they could earn money from prostitution. The women then had to hand over half their earnings.
“This method left the women completely under the group’s control when they first arrived in Hong Kong, while allowing the syndicate to make huge profits,” Senior Inspector Lam Wa-yan of the special duties squad said.

Syria holds 19 hearings for war crimes suspects in Damascus
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
07:35:03 UTC
16:35:03 KST

Breadcrumb
Syria holds 19 hearings for war crimes suspects in Damascus
A Damascus court held 19 hearings involving suspects accused of war crimes and crimes against humanity under the ousted Assad regime.
A Syrian court specialising in transitional justice held 19 hearings on Monday involving defendants accused of war crimes and crimes against humanity committed against civilians during the rule of ousted president Bashar al-Assad.
The hearings, held at Damascus's Fourth Criminal Court, form part of ongoing efforts to prosecute those responsible for abuses committed under the former regime.
Radif Mustafa, director of the Accountability Department at the National Commission for Transitional Justice, said late on Monday that the court had held 19 sessions, during which public trial proceedings continued, case files were read out, and evidence submissions and legal claims were presented.
The court also adjourned several cases to allow for the completion of legal procedures, including prosecution and defence submissions, the summoning of witnesses and the renewal of legal notifications.
Mustafa said the trials were continuing, adding that the number of cases and defendants reflected the scale of the judicial work required to address the legacy of serious violations committed under Assad's rule.
He stressed that accountability proceedings were moving forward in accordance with legal procedures, with defendants guaranteed the right to defend themselves, while responsibility for determining guilt and assigning criminal liability remained with the judiciary.
Mustafa also urged victims and their families, as well as anyone with complaints against the defendants or credible testimony, documents or information relating to abuses, to submit them to transitional justice courts through official channels.
He said documented complaints should not be overlooked and that relevant information must be brought into the legal verification process to help establish the truth and hold those responsible accountable based on evidence and the law.
The hearings follow a series of trials in Damascus in recent months targeting former security and military officials and other figures associated with Assad's government.
On 11 August, the Fourth Criminal Court sentenced Atef Najib, the former head of political security in Daraa, to death. It also handed down death sentences in absentia against Bashar al-Assad, his brother Maher al-Assad and several senior former officials.
Those sentenced included former defence minister Fahd Jassem al-Freij and former air force intelligence chief Jamil Hassan, following convictions for murder, torture and other violations classified as war crimes and crimes against humanity.
On 18 August, the court sentenced Wassim al-Assad, a relative of the ousted president, to death after convicting him of war crimes and crimes against humanity.
Six days later, on 24 August, it sentenced former Syrian grand mufti Ahmad Badr al-Din Hassoun to life imprisonment over crimes linked to the former regime.
The rulings form part of Syria's transitional justice process, which aims to hold those responsible for abuses against Syrians accountable following the collapse of Assad's regime in December 2024.

Former commander-in-chief Syrskyi explains why he sent troops to Kursk operation instead of defending Pokrovsk
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
10:31:00 EEST
16:31:00 KST

Former commander-in-chief Syrskyi explains why he sent troops to Kursk operation instead of defending Pokrovsk
Oleksandr Syrskyi, former commander-in-chief of the Armed Forces of Ukraine, considers the Kursk operation a successful manoeuvre and says that Russia had concentrated a force of nearly 100,000 troops near Pokrovsk at the time, meaning that redeploying Ukrainian units there would not have changed the situation.
Source: Syrskyi in an interview with BBC News Ukrainian
Quote from Syrskyi: "You have to understand that this operation was a necessity. If we recall 2024, after substantially increasing the pay of its military personnel and expanding the size of its forces, the enemy launched offensive operations in early summer 2024. This was effectively happening across all 13 operational sectors, with the enemy enjoying a 4½-fold advantage in some areas and, at times, even a sixfold advantage.
Under those conditions, with Russian aircraft dominating the skies, we were engaged in heavy defensive fighting, and we simply had to disrupt the enemy's plans, given the significant advantage it had."
Details: Syrskyi said the military leadership had studied the entire front line in detail and selected the Sumy front, where the Russians initially had 26,000 troops. During Russia's unsuccessful offensive on the Kharkiv front, however, it gradually redeployed all of its forces and assets from the Sumy front to Kharkiv. This failed to give the Russians any significant advantage, and they became bogged down in fighting along the border.
Syrskyi's decision to conduct an offensive operation on the Kursk front was approved by the Ukrainian president.
As a result, within a month, Ukraine's defence forces took control of 1,273 sq km of Russian territory, while the Russians were forced to halt their offensive on all operational-strategic fronts except the Pokrovsk front. Russia redeployed around 70,000 troops to the Kursk front, including airborne forces, marines and its best-trained motorised rifle units.
"This effectively gave us an opportunity to prepare reserves, give our troops some respite and restore the combat capability of units that had suffered losses in such heavy fighting. So the Kursk operation provided a major boost to the morale of our troops," Syrskyi said.
The interviewer pointed out that Russian forces had meanwhile been able to advance rapidly towards Pokrovsk and asked the general whether it would have been better to use the resources committed to the Kursk operation to defend the eastern front.
Quote from Syrskyi: "No, it would not. The point is that only three understrength air assault brigades and two assault battalions were used as part of the offensive force on the Kursk front.
Other units were involved in the second echelon as consolidation forces, but they too were only at 60-70% strength. They were effectively holding the front in this sector and only advancing behind the brigades. Their primary task was to consolidate their positions and hold the territory.
Two brigades spent a month preparing for the operation. The third, the 95th Brigade, was coming out of combat after heavy fighting on the Toretsk front and had very little time to restore its combat capability. So in practice, only one brigade attacked at full strength, while two brigades initially attacked with two battalions each, with their third battalions joining later once they had recovered.
So if they had been deployed on the Pokrovsk front – and we regard the Pokrovsk front as two separate sectors, Dobropillia and Pokrovsk – the Russians had concentrated a force of almost 100,000 troops there. Those two brigades, and later the third, would not have made any difference, given their technical condition.
On the Kursk front, however, the enemy had very weak defences and units covering the state border, consisting mainly of conscripts and stretched out thinly along the front. Some battalions covered 10 km, while others 12. So the defences there really were weak, and that was precisely why our forces achieved such enormous success.
When the enemy began redeploying its units, it was chaotic because there genuinely was a state of panic. I remember how much the Russian media were panicking at the time about the advance of our best brigades. The units being redeployed were thrown straight into battle and also suffered enormous losses.
According to the Russians' own figures, on some days during the fighting on the Kursk front, the casualty ratio for the enemy – which was hastily switching over to defence – was one to five. In other words, the enemy suffered five times as many casualties while defending as our troops did while attacking. I hope that answers your question."

Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“A loud morning. The enemy attacked Dnipro with guided aerial bombs. A man was injured. Apartment buildings, transport infrastructure, and vehicles were damaged,” Lukashuk wrote.
Oleksandr Hanzha, head of the Dnipropetrovsk Regional Military Administration (OVA), said the injured man was 64. Medics provided him with the necessary care, but he declined hospitalization.
The type of weapon used in the attack has not been independently confirmed. If the use of guided aerial bombs is verified, the strike could mark a new escalation in Russian attacks on Dnipro.
Previous reports of guided bomb strikes on Dnipro
Reports of a Russian guided aerial bomb attack on Dnipro also emerged in early October last year. However, the weapon was later identified as a Hrom-1 missile, which had reached the city for the first time.
The Hrom-1 is a missile-bomb system that can be used as either a missile or a glide bomb. The two versions differ in their warheads and range: the missile carries a 315-kilogram warhead and has a range of up to 120 kilometers, while the bomb variant carries a 480-kilogram warhead and can travel up to 65 kilometers.

“The difference is due to the fact that the missile has a jet engine, while the bomb does not,” Ukrainian outlet NV reported.
Recent Russian attacks on Dnipro

In the early hours of Oct. 11, 2026, Russians attacked Dnipro with drones, damaging a high-rise building and setting warehouses ablaze. Several people were also injured.
On Oct. 10, Russia attacked the city three times throughout the day. The third strike sparked fires at food warehouses.

Albert Heijn and sister chains abroad hit by likely cyberattack
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13

Albert Heijn and sister chains abroad hit by likely cyberattack
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
Cybersecurity experts say it is very likely someone broke into Albert Heijn’s IT systems, as the outage at the Netherlands’ biggest supermarket chain leaves empty shelves in its stores.
Albert Heijn and its parent company Ahold Delhaize have kept systems switched off since Sunday afternoon and still describe the problem only as a “cybersecurity incident”. “An organisation that big doesn’t take measures like this lightly,” cybersecurity expert Joey Fennis told broadcaster NOS.
Fennis said that if attackers had got in, they may also have viewed or stolen data. Pim Takkenberg told current affairs programme Nieuwsuur it seemed “fairly clear” that someone malicious had been in the system. “An outage doesn’t usually last this long,” he said.
A third expert, Eward Driehuis, said the chain may instead have found a weakness it could not fix quickly, and shut its systems down as a precaution. Albert Heijn says its investigation is ongoing and has not said when services will be restored.
Supply chain
Albert Heijn has six distribution centres in the Netherlands. CEO Margaret Versteden-van Duijn told NOS on Monday that work at some of them had stopped completely, but she would not say which ones.
According to an email to suppliers seen by RTL Z, only the Zaandam centre is still operating, and suppliers have been asked to deliver there alone, in agreed time slots. Albert Heijn has not confirmed this.
The chain says fruit, vegetables and other fresh produce will be hardest to find, while frozen goods, bread and long-life products should remain more widely available. “Of course shelves will empty if this goes on longer,” Versteden-van Duijn told NOS. “That will vary from store to store.”
Beyond the Netherlands
Belgian supermarket chain Delhaize, also owned by Ahold Delhaize, has reported IT problems. Albert Heijn’s stores in Belgium, which are supplied from the Tilburg distribution centre, may run short of some products, broadcaster VRT reported, although the chain says the impact there is limited so far.
In the US, the websites of all five Ahold Delhaize supermarket chains, including Stop & Shop and Food Lion, were offline on Monday, according to trade publication Grocery Dive. Online ordering and deliveries were also suspended, Supermarket News reported.
The incident came on the same weekend as a separate cyberattack on hundreds of supermarkets in France. There, hackers remotely forced refrigeration systems to defrost, and chains including Intermarché and Coopérative U had to throw away fresh and frozen food. The Paris prosecutor’s office has opened an investigation.
The French attack targeted refrigeration equipment supplied by Danish firm Danfoss. Albert Heijn’s CEO told NOS she could not say whether the two incidents were linked, but an Ahold Delhaize spokesperson later told the news agency Reuters there was no reason to see a connection.

Fuel shortage in Bali: hours-long queues have formed at gas stations
Kyiv • UNN
At gas stations in Denpasar and southern Badung, drivers spend hours searching for Pertalite and Pertamax. Authorities say supplies are gradually being restored.
Drivers in various parts of the Indonesian island of Bali are facing long queues at gas stations, with some drivers spending hours trying to fill their tanks due to fuel shortages. UNN reports this, citing 7NEWS.
Details
Long queues have formed at gas stations across Denpasar and southern Badung, including Kuta, as Pertalite fuel—and, in some places, Pertamax—becomes increasingly difficult to find.
Some queues stretched beyond gas station entrances and onto surrounding roads, while drivers reported visiting several stations only to find that fuel supplies had run out. Traffic congestion has been reported, according to detikNews, affecting the flow of traffic.
One resident said the shortage had forced his wife to queue until dawn. "This morning, my wife joined the queue at 4:30 a.m. and waited for two and a half hours before she was finally able to refuel. This is crazy," he said.
The head of Bali's Manpower, Energy and Mineral Resources Agency, Ida Bagus Setiawan, said last week that the authorities were working with fuel supplier Pertamina and distributors to restore normal supplies.
"Technically, we were informed that the fuel flow was being redirected from the Pesanggaran depot to the Manggis transit terminal. The situation is gradually recovering," he said.
Setiawan said officials were still awaiting more detailed information about the cause of the distribution disruptions and their broader impact on fuel availability.
Badung Police Chief AKBP Joseph Edward Purba, as reported by detikNews, said that congestion at several gas stations in Badung had been caused by technical problems with fuel supplies from providers.
The shortage occurred after similar disruptions in late August, when fuel supply problems also led to long queues at gas stations in various parts of Bali.
Authorities say fuel distribution is gradually recovering, but its availability continues to vary depending on the location.

New safeguards sharply reduce AI distillation attacks: Anthropic
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
07:25:00 UTC
16:25:00 KST

New safeguards sharply reduce AI distillation attacks: Anthropic
- Anthropic said new safeguards cut Claude distillation attacks by 90% to 99%, or “10 to 100 times lower” reasoning tokens extracted.
- The company said it blocked proxy networks and repeated probing, making large-scale copying of Claude’s protected reasoning much harder.
- Anthropic banned tens of thousands of accounts and warned that distillation, including by Z.ai, poses safety and national security risks.
AI generated
SAN FRANCISCO – Anthropic said on Oct 12 that new measures designed to prevent rivals from copying the capabilities of its Claude AI models have reduced data harvested in so-called distillation attacks by about 90% to 99%.
Model distillation has emerged as a key concern for leading artificial intelligence companies due to intensifying US-China competition, with firms including Anthropic, OpenAI and Google arguing the practice enables rivals to reproduce advanced capabilities more quickly and at lower cost.
Anthropic said safeguards restricting access to Claude’s reasoning have sharply reduced extraction attempts, with “the number of reasoning tokens extracted by distillers” now “10 to 100 times lower than it was before”.
The California-headquartered company said it had made it harder to use proxy networks to repeatedly probe Claude’s protected reasoning, blocking extraction attempts and hindering large-scale distillation efforts.
Anthropic said its safety system is “roughly as robust as those that prevent Claude from helping build bioweapons” and has “a false positive rate of less than 0.1%”.
Anthropic banned tens of thousands of accounts linked to distillation campaigns and cited Chinese AI startup Z.ai, also known as Zhipu, as an example of a company that attempted to distil capabilities from Claude while developing its GLM-5.3 model, warning such practises pose safety and national security risks
Z.ai did not immediately respond to a request for comment. REUTERS

Fewer properties sold due to higher interest rates
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
07:22:35 UTC
16:22:35 KST

Over the past three months, 2.2 per cent fewer homes have been sold in Belgium in comparison with the same period last year. This is clear from the latest information from the estate agents’ property barometer. The cause is the sharp rise in interest rates on mortgages. “You’re now paying 8.9 per cent more per month than a year ago,” calculates John Romain of independent mortgage advisers Immotheker Finotheker. House prices, too, continue to rise.
Sales of houses in Belgium have fallen particularly sharply, according to figures from the quarterly property barometer published by Fednot, the Federation of Notaries. Over the past three months, 2.8 per cent fewer houses were sold, whilst the decline in flat sales remained relatively limited at 0.4 per cent. Taken together, this means the overall Belgian housing market has contracted by 2.2 per cent.
In Flanders, the decline is smaller. Over the past quarter, 1.2 per cent fewer houses were sold and 0.7 per cent fewer flats. The number of property purchases has fallen in all Flemish provinces, with the exception of Flemish Brabant, where a slight increase of 1 per cent has been recorded.
Limburg, on the other hand, is the worst performer, with a fall of 5.1 per cent for flats and 2.4 per cent for houses.
Interest rates are to blame
The reason for this decline is the sharp rise in interest rates on mortgages, says notary Bart Van Opstal. “Interest rates have risen, which means that mortgages have also become more expensive.”
In August, interest rates reached their highest level in 12 years and have since risen even further. And that has a twofold effect, explains Van Opstal. “It is more expensive to take out a loan. If you take out a loan for an average house price and the interest rate rises by 1 per cent, you can easily end up paying hundreds of euros more per month.”
As a result, investors are also looking for alternatives to the property market: “They are now opting more for alternatives that offer higher returns, such as bonds. That is why they, too, are less active in the property market.”
Logically, a cooling of the market should be followed by price falls, but these have yet to materialise, Van Opstal observes. “We are in a prolonged period of price rises. House prices have risen by around 3 per cent since last year, whilst flat prices have risen by 2 per cent.”
A house in Flanders cost an average of 398,182 euros during the past three months. Last year, the figure was 384,781 euros, according to the notary barometer. Prices have risen by 3.5 per cent in the space of a year. Over the past five years, there has even been a price increase of 21.5 per cent. In 2021, a house in Flanders cost an average of 327,785 euros.

Ukraine Secures EU-Wide Agreement on Two More Accession Clusters Following Minority Rights Reform
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
07:22:29 UTC
16:22:29 KST

- Category
- World
Ukraine Secures EU-Wide Agreement on Two More Accession Clusters Following Minority Rights Reform
All 27 European Union member states have agreed to open two additional accession negotiation clusters with Ukraine and Moldova, Irish Minister of State for European Affairs and Defense Thomas Byrne confirmed on October 12.
Byrne announced the agreement on X, outlining a series of EU enlargement decisions involving Ukraine, Moldova, Montenegro, and Albania.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
“I can confirm that all EU member states have agreed to open clusters 2 and 3 for Ukraine and Moldova,” Byrne wrote.
The agreement covers two major areas of EU accession negotiations: Cluster 2, which addresses the internal market, and Cluster 3, which focuses on competitiveness and inclusive growth.
Cluster 2 covers the rules governing the EU's single market, including the free movement of goods, workers, services, and capital. It also addresses company law, intellectual property, competition policy, financial services, and consumer protection.
Cluster 3 focuses on economic and social development. Its eight negotiating chapters cover digital transformation and media, taxation, economic and monetary policy, employment, industrial policy, science and research, education and culture, and customs policy.
The EU accession framework divides negotiations into six thematic clusters, each covering specific areas of legislation that candidate countries must align with European standards.
Opening a cluster allows negotiations to proceed across its policy areas, but it does not mean the country has completed the required reforms. Individual chapters can be provisionally closed once the EU determines that the relevant conditions have been met.
Byrne also confirmed that EU member states had agreed to close three negotiating chapters with Montenegro: economic and monetary policy, statistics, and social policy and employment.
Albania will close Chapter 20, covering enterprise and industrial policy.
The Irish minister described the forthcoming developments as another "Super Tuesday" for EU enlargement, following what he called "Montenegro Monday."
The agreement follows Ukraine's adoption of legislation expanding educational rights for national minorities and indigenous peoples on October 12.
The amendments address an issue that had contributed to Hungary's objections to the advancement of Ukraine's EU accession negotiations.
The law allows greater use of eligible minority languages in schools while preserving Ukrainian's status as the state language. Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha had earlier indicated that Kyiv expected the EU to formally open the two clusters on October 13.
Ukraine's accession negotiations began in June 2024, and the EU subsequently opened Cluster 1, covering fundamental reforms, in June 2026. Cluster 6, covering external relations and foreign, security, and defense policy, opened on July 14, 2026. Under the EU's accession methodology, the Fundamentals cluster opens first and closes last, with progress in that area determining the overall pace of negotiations.

France’s navy detained an oil tanker called the DF Peak that belongs to the “shadow fleet” on October 12, French President Emmanuel Macron said.
The tanker was detained more than 450 nautical miles south of Réunion Island in the Indian Ocean. Authorities suspect it was flying a false flag and illegally transporting fuel.
According to data from Marinetraffic, the tanker was sailing under Benin’s flag and was headed to the port of Cruz Grande in Chile. It wasn’t clear where the vessel had sailed from.
The magazine Maritime Executive writes that the tanker was built in 2006 and originally belonged to the company Sovcomflot, sailing under the name NS Captain. It was renamed Kaliningrad in 2024 and took its current name in 2025. Its operator is now a company based in Hong Kong.
Maritime Executive also says that Benin’s national registry, whose flag the tanker flies, was once “considered a haven for Russia-linked shadow fleet vessels.” The U.S. sanctioned the tanker in February 2024. The European Union, Switzerland, Canada, the U.K., and Ukraine followed with sanctions of their own.
France has detained tankers belonging to the “shadow fleet,” including some reportedly linked to Russia, several times since the start of 2026. In January, French authorities detained the tanker Grinch. In March, they detained the tanker Deyna, which was allowed to leave the port of Marseille a month later. In June, French authorities detained the tankers Tagor and Deliver. Also in mid-June, the U.K. detained a Russian “shadow fleet” tanker for the first time after it tried to pass through the English Channel.

The politics of gratitude: The corruption no one sees
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
07:21:59 UTC
16:21:59 KST

Not all political corruption begins with money. Sometimes, it begins with success. Public imagination has long been trained to look for corruption in suitcases of cash, shady contracts, and secret deals. Yet some of the most consequential distortions of political judgment emerge from a far subtler source: a politician’s emotional attachment to a project they helped create.
This hidden dynamic lay beneath the recent controversy surrounding Andy Burnham’s comments on Manchester City. After initially suggesting that the club deserved fair treatment before later reaffirming that no institution stands above the rules, Burnham found himself at the center of a debate that extended far beyond football.
At first glance, the story appeared to involve a politician defending a football club or perhaps its wealthy owners. In reality, something more interesting was taking place. Burnham was defending, consciously or otherwise, part of his own political story.
The transformation of Manchester over the past two decades has become one of Britain’s most celebrated urban success stories. Manchester City’s ownership was not solely responsible for that transformation, but it undeniably became part of it.
Investments around the Etihad complex and across large sections of East Manchester helped reinforce a narrative of renewal that politicians, civic leaders, and business interests collectively embraced. For Burnham, separating the success of modern Manchester from his own political identity has become increasingly difficult.
This is not primarily an ethical problem. It is a human one.
People instinctively defend the institutions, ideas, and projects that have given meaning to their lives. Politicians are especially vulnerable to this tendency because politics is ultimately a profession obsessed with legacy. Few enter public life merely to exercise power. Most hope to leave behind a lasting achievement. The moment that achievement comes under scrutiny, criticism of the project begins to feel like criticism of the self.
Britain has witnessed this phenomenon before.
Tony Blair spent years trapped within the narrative of “New Labour” and the promise of a modernised Britain. The project was initially so successful that its architect struggled to recognise its deeper flaws. This became most visible in the Iraq War.
Blair’s persistence was not simply a matter of defending a policy. Over time, the war became intertwined with his broader conception of leadership and international responsibility. Retreat no longer meant revising a political decision. It meant acknowledging that one of the defining chapters of his public life may have been built upon a profound misjudgement.
A similar pattern can be observed in Boris Johnson’s relationship with Brexit. Long after leaving office, Johnson has remained attached to the project not merely because he believes in its outcomes but because Brexit became inseparable from his political identity. It delivered power, fame, and a place in history. To distance himself from it would require a form of self-criticism that few politicians are willing to undertake.
Yet this phenomenon extends beyond individuals.
Governments fall in love with their achievements. Cities fall in love with their redevelopment schemes. Nations fall in love with the narratives they construct about themselves.
READ: UAE warns UK over potential fallout from Manchester City sanctions: Report
At a certain point, success ceases to be a project and becomes a creed.
And that is when the trouble begins.
The paradox is that failure often encourages self-examination, while success produces the illusion of infallibility. A failed policy invites scrutiny. A successful one tends to acquire defenders. The more celebrated an achievement becomes, the more difficult it is to assess honestly.
The true responsibility of a statesman is not to adore achievements but to question them. It is not to protect them from criticism but to subject them to it. A good engineer is not the person who loves a building most. It is the person who knows where it might collapse.
Modern politics, however, rewards precisely the opposite behaviour. It rewards the conversion of political accomplishments into heroic narratives. Eventually, the narrative becomes more valuable than reality itself. Protecting the legacy becomes more important than examining its weaknesses.
This is why one of the most dangerous forms of political corruption is not financial corruption but what might be called the corruption of gratitude.
A politician becomes indebted to a project, a business leader, an idea, a movement, or even an electorate that helped create their success. Once that bond is formed, impartial judgment begins to erode. Not because of bribery or coercion, but because emotional loyalty quietly replaces critical distance.
The politician who takes a bribe can be exposed.
The politician imprisoned by personal success is far more difficult to detect.
In many cases, such individuals sincerely believe they are acting in the public interest. They do not recognize their own bias because they are not protecting a benefactor. They are protecting a cherished part of themselves.
Nor is this tendency confined to politics. Revolutionaries often become prisoners of the narratives they once created. Writers become captives of their most celebrated books. Leaders cling to decisions that history has already judged harshly because they can no longer separate the truth from their own reflection in it.
This is what makes the Burnham episode more interesting than Manchester City itself.
The fundamental question is not whether the club’s owners are good or bad, nor whether the club is guilty or innocent. The deeper question is what happens when a politician can no longer distinguish between the interests of a city and the story they tell themselves about their role in its success.
That is where the quiet tragedy of politics begins.
And it is also where the most elusive form of corruption emerges.
Not from the pocket, but from the heart.
OPINION: Political failure, not economic shock, unmasks Iraq

Kaunas is phasing out paper tickets and cash payments in public transport
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
07:21:00 UTC
16:21:00 KST

Kaunas will eliminate paper tickets and cash payments on public transportation starting in December, following a vote by the city council on Tuesday.
Twenty-seven council members voted in favour of the proposal, one opposed it and 10 abstained.
The city says eliminating cash payments will allow drivers to focus on operating vehicles instead of handling money and issuing tickets, helping public transportation run on schedule.
The proposal drew concerns from opposition politicians about access for senior citizens, tourists and passengers affected by banking or payment system disruptions.
Conservative council member Rasa Duobaitė-Bumbulienė asked whether the change would make it harder for older people traveling to Kaunas for medical appointments to use public transportation.
Martynas Matusevičius, head of the city’s Transport and Traffic Organisation Division, said older passengers receiving discounted fares accounted for a small share of those who currently pay drivers in cash.
Passengers can switch their discounted fares to bank cards, and Kaunas Public Transport’s information centre will provide assistance by phone and in person, he said.
The city is also considering installing ticket vending machines at planned public transportation transfer terminals, although their cost and maintenance requirements remain concerns, Matusevičius said.
He added that the contactless payment system had been tested and could continue operating even during internet disruptions, with payments processed later.
Under the new rules, passengers will still be able to use cash to buy or top up public transportation cards at designated sales points, including customer service offices, shopping centres and kiosks.
According to Kaunas Public Transport, tickets bought from drivers with cash accounted for just 4.5% of all fare payments during the first eight months of this year, about one-third fewer than in the same period last year.
About 60% of passengers use public transportation cards, while nearly 35% use the special mobile app, Žiogas. Bank cards and smart devices account for less than 1% of payments.
Contactless payments were introduced on Kaunas public transportation in August last year. Since September, passengers have also been able to buy discounted tickets using contactless validators.
