AI models may soon self-replicate across smart-home devices: Anthropic
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
07:20:00 UTC
16:20:00 KST

AI models may soon self-replicate across smart-home devices: Anthropic
- Anthropic warned that small AI models may soon self-replicate on insecure IoT devices, such as smart ovens and Android TV boxes, using only commercial internet-connected hardware.
- Its tests found models under 30 billion parameters could complete parts of the process, but many still could not finish full replication without help. GLM-5.2 and stronger models did so in simplified tests.
- Anthropic said self-replicating AI would be hard to stop, could target unfamiliar devices, and may be autonomous by the end of 2026 if progress continues. It urged stronger security.
AI generated
SAN FRANCISCO – Anthropic said on Oct 12 that small AI models could be months away from self-replicating across internet-connected devices, raising the possibility of AI botnets spreading quickly, fighting takedown attempts and even breaking into data centres to turbocharge their growth.
In September, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei first floated the idea that within the next year or even sooner, AI might be able to hijack “the entire internet” with “a persistent botnet,” a warning that raised eyebrows in the cybersecurity community.
Botnets – vast networks of devices controlled by malicious operators – have been around since the early days of the internet, and are still around.
The network typically includes poorly secured Internet of Things (IOT) devices, such as Android TV boxes, smart appliances and security cameras, and is used by hackers to send spam, seed malware, or sabotage target companies using floods of bogus traffic.
Anthropic’s Oct 12 blog post appeared to be the first attempt to articulate how that might happen.
The company said that its experiments showed that a malicious artificial intelligence agent could stitch together the computing power of inexpensive internet-connected devices to run other AI models. It added that the models were able to replicate across a simplified test network.
“A replicator like this would be challenging to shut down, since there’s no centralised point to shut off,” the company said.
The report adds to broader concerns about the security risks tied to increasingly capable AI systems, including their potential to automate cyberattacks, operate with limited human oversight and circumvent safeguards.
The advances in models have prompted a series of often dire warnings from industry heads and AI company employees about the possibility of severe, even existential, risks of runaway AI development.
Anthropic said its experiments showed that models with 30 billion parameters or fewer can already perform many of the individual tasks required for self-replication, although they struggle to complete the entire process reliably.
In its simplified tests, where some security steps were removed, Anthropic found that GLM-5.2 and stronger models were capable of end-to-end replication.
Anthropic said that if smaller models continue improving at their historical rate, they could reach the capability required for autonomous replication by the end of 2026.
An AI worm running on low-powered hardware could take days to complete parts of the replication process, Anthropic said. It added that such a network could continue growing, slower than some conventional malware, if compromised devices infected enough additional machines.
Anthropic also warned that future systems could target more powerful computing resources, including data-centre processors, although its experiments did not demonstrate autonomous replication through commercial data centres. REUTERS

Dutch economy set to grow by 1.5% in 2026 as IMF raises forecast
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
The International Monetary Fund (IMF) has improved its forecast for the Dutch economy, but warned that high prices will continue to cause pain for consumers.
The Netherlands’ GDP is now expected to grow by 1.5% this year, up from 1% in the IMF’s last assessment in July. The trend is set to continue into 2027, when the IMF expects growth of 1.3%.
The organisation says the Dutch economy will benefit from stronger than expected growth in Germany, where it has revised its prediction from 0.7% to 1.3% for this year, as well as large global investments in AI technology.
Consumer prices will grow by 2.9% this year, reflecting the high cost of energy and fuel. The statistics agency CBS reported on Tuesday that inflation had risen to 3.4% in September, continuing an upward trend that started in July.
Fuel prices have risen by 27.2% in the last year, with a litre of diesel costing nearly €2.50 at the pumps. But prices for other commodities have fallen, such as food, which is down by 1.9%.
The IMF said the impact of the conflict in Iran on fuel prices had been tempered by countries finding alternative suppliers of oil and gas.

Banking watchdogs ramp up AI scrutiny as stability fears mount, sources say
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
07:15:00 UTC
16:15:00 KST

Banking watchdogs ramp up AI scrutiny as stability fears mount, say sources
- Banking regulators in the US and Europe are stepping up AI checks as fears grow that agentic AI could weaken cyber defences and threaten financial stability.
- US agencies, including the Fed, OCC and FDIC, are asking banks how they use advanced AI, especially foreign models, cyber defence agents and controls on autonomous systems.
- European supervisors want stronger recovery plans and better mapping of AI use across banks and providers, as experts warn a major attack could disrupt payments and lock customers out.
AI generated
NEW YORK/LONDON – Banking regulators are stepping up efforts to contain growing AI risks, six people familiar with the matter said, with some pointing to the potential for cyberattacks on banks or rogue agents undermining global financial stability.
The regulatory scrutiny, fresh details of which are reported here for the first time, reflects growing recognition that advances in frontier AI may require costly investments in cyber recovery, greater attention to dependencies on external technology providers and, in some jurisdictions, more formal regulatory guidance, sources said.
Three top regulators in the US, including the Federal Reserve, are quizzing banks about their use of advanced AI models, two of the people told Reuters, adding to prior scrutiny.
Questions include whether they deploy Chinese-developed technology, use AI agents in cyberdefence and can control increasingly autonomous systems, three of the people said.
In Europe, supervisors, including the Bank of England (BOE) and the European Central Bank (ECB), are pressing banks to improve recovery plans, concerned that rapid advances in artificial intelligence could cause serious harm and disruption in financial markets sooner than previously feared, three people with knowledge of their thinking said.
A senior executive at a large European bank said they, too, are worried about potentially major damage to banking and financial markets “within six months”.
The debate over AI oversight has intensified amid warnings from the industry after recent incidents, with JPMorgan chief executive Jamie Dimon urging corporate leaders to join a US-focused industry group to address AI risks, Reuters reported.
US cybersecurity company CrowdStrike said in October that a person in China likely used a Chinese-developed AI agent and Anthropic’s Claude Code in a hack on South Korean banks. Rogue AI agents developed by OpenAI were meanwhile involved in a breach of the AI platform Hugging Face, Reuters reported.
Anthropic researchers have warned that increasingly powerful AI systems could eventually escape human control and even pose an existential threat, prompting calls for stricter regulation.
Banks are competing to adopt agentic AI, which can accomplish tasks with minimal human supervision, while also grappling with challenges in new models, including IT weaknesses flagged by Anthropic’s Mythos tool.
Michael Woodbridge, London-based cybersecurity partner at Grant Thornton, said: “The adoption of AI is often outpacing the ability to put the controls in place.”
US concerns aim at agentic AI
The US regulatory inquiries centre on how banks use agentic AI in areas such as cybersecurity, focusing on whether AI agents are being used to identify, prioritise and respond to threats.
Questions from the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC), the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (FDIC) and the Fed focus on what limits are placed on systems, how their actions are monitored and approved and whether banks can clearly track and audit AI agent decisions, two of the people said.
They are also asking what safeguards exist to prevent agents from exceeding their authority, whether humans remain involved in key decisions and how banks can shut down autonomous systems.
The OCC, the Fed and the FDIC declined to comment.
Through their questions, regulators are probing more specific issues tied to advanced AI models, including the use of autonomous AI agents, foreign-developed models and new cyber risks, the three people with knowledge of their thinking said.
The written and verbal inquiries to large, mid-size and smaller banks show regulators are focusing on vulnerabilities from banks’ use of AI and their preparedness to act, they said.
Regulators are still gathering information and are not yet being prescriptive about what lenders should be doing, they added.
Europeans worry about recovery
Supervisors in Britain are separately encouraging the largest banks to examine so-called bare metal recovery plans, two of the people familiar with their thinking said.
These systems are entirely independent of a bank’s main tech set-up and can kick in if primary operating systems are compromised.
But building and maintaining such state-of-the-art recovery is expensive, the people said.
Rather than introduce new requirements, the British authorities intend to work collaboratively with the industry, they added.
The BOE declined to comment.
In July, the ECB gave lenders an end-October deadline to produce plans to counter AI-enabled cyberthreats, including improved backup and recovery.
Asked about its strategy for regulating AI, the ECB referred to its July letter and a June speech by board member Frank Elderson, who stressed the need to create a sense of urgency, not alarm, about the threats.
The need for supervisory action has taken on added urgency after European banks and regulators expressed frustration at getting limited access to Mythos in 2026, amid concerns that US banks will be given first sight to test frontier models.
Like their US counterparts, British supervisors are also asking banks to use frontier AI to identify vulnerabilities and accelerate patching, two people said, with one adding that lenders were so far doing a good job.
The third person said euro zone banks were also being asked to map how AI is being used across their businesses and third-party providers to understand key dependencies and ensure they can switch off and restart systems in a controlled manner.
Significant gaps remained at some firms, they added.
Sukand Ramachandran, managing director and senior partner at Boston Consulting Group, said: “To protect against attacks, rapid recovery matters as much as prevention.”
Without separately held clean, secure copies of critical data, “a serious attack could lock customers out of their accounts and disrupt payments across the wider economy”, he added. REUTERS

Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
07:13:24 UTC
16:13:24 KST

The second wave of early prison releases has begun, with hundreds of offenders walking out across England and Wales under the government’s controversial plan to ease overcrowding.
About 2,000 criminals, including domestic abusers and violent offenders, are being freed this month, with another 3,000 to follow in stages over the next year. The total was reduced from 6,000 after an intervention by Andy Burnham.
Prisoners convicted of manslaughter are excluded, meaning the killers of PC Andrew Harper, who died in the line of duty in 2019, will not be eligible.
The second tranche of early releases comes as members of the probation union, Napo, hold a pre-ballot meeting on taking strike action over pay and workloads.
Pay negotiations with probation officers ended with a “best and final” conditional pay offer worth 5%, which the union’s negotiating committee rejected. Members will be asked to vote for industrial action on pay, along with a question on workloads, in a formal ballot on industrial action to launch on 19 October.
The union says probation officers have been required to take on large amounts of extra work since tens of thousands of prisoners began being released early from 2022.
The number of people in prison has jumped by more than 1,700 in the past three months. The prison population in England and Wales was at 87,499 on Monday, according to Ministry of Justice data, up from 85,761 on 29 June, a rise of 2%.
The MoJ said released offenders would be monitored under the “toughest supervision in British history”. New restriction zones designed to control the movements of the highest-risk sexual and violent offenders should confine released prisoners to areas a few miles wide, in an effort to reassure the victims of their crimes.
The MoJ said it had expanded electronic monitoring, with a new presumption that offenders will be tagged and monitored when they leave prison. Technology rolling out this year is said to give probation services near-live access to tagging data, helping staff spot breaches.
However, this month the victims’ commissioner, Claire Waxman, said the government’s confidence in the plan “is not yet matched by the reality on the ground”.

Global economy to grow 3.1% in 2026 amid severe Middle East contractions, IMF forecasts
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
07:11:09 UTC
16:11:09 KST

Gokhan Ergocun
13 October 2026•Update: 13 October 2026
The International Monetary Fund (IMF) projected the global economy to expand 3.1% in 2026 and 3.4% in 2027, warning of severe downward revisions for the Middle East and China amid ongoing conflicts.
The Washington-based institution kept its near-term global forecast stable but warned of a deeply fractured economic outlook in its October 2026 World Economic Outlook report on Tuesday.
Eurozone economy is expected to grow by 1.1% this year, and the US economy is forecasted to see a growth rate of 2.1%.
The organization noted widespread downward revisions, with about 47% of economies seeing downgraded growth forecasts compared to April estimates.
The Middle East and Central Asia region suffered the most dramatic downward revisions, as its growth forecast for 2026 dropped 2.2 percentage points into negative territory at minus 0.3%.
The fund attributed this sharp decline directly to the dragging war in the region and a longer-than-expected closure of the Strait of Hormuz.
Commodity producers most affected by disruptions to energy output and transport, including Bahrain, Iraq, Kuwait and Qatar, were projected to experience double-digit contractions in 2026.
Saudi Arabia's economy was also expected to shrink by 3.3% this year.
In Asia, the organization downgraded China's 2026 growth forecast to 4.5%.
Higher global oil prices, protracted uncertainty and structural headwinds were expected to weigh on the country's activity.
Sluggish domestic consumption and weakening investment amid continued property sector strains were anticipated to compound China's economic challenges.
The report highlighted a split global economy shaped by geopolitics and technology.
Energy-importing economies with little connection to the technology value chain were projected to face the most difficult configuration.
These nations would deal with higher import costs and exchange rate pressures, weaker real incomes, more constrained fiscal space and fewer offsetting demand impulses.
Many low-income and vulnerable countries fell into this category, threatening to widen income gaps globally.
Global headline inflation was forecast to pause its steady decline and rise to 4.7% in 2026, primarily driven by the war-induced negative supply shock impacting energy and food prices.

Germany's inflation hits 3.3% in September, highest since 2023
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
07:11:02 UTC
16:11:02 KST

Gokhan Ergocun
13 October 2026•Update: 13 October 2026
Annual consumer inflation in Germany reached 3.3% in September, hitting its highest level since December 2023 as energy and motor fuel prices soared, official data showed on Tuesday.
The inflation rate in the country accelerated from 2.9% in August and 2.8% in July, according to Destatis data.
Ruth Brand, president of Destatis, said the rate exceeded the 3% mark to reach a new record high for the year and the highest level since December 2023.
Brand added that energy prices drove the increase, particularly mineral oil products at filling stations and heating oil.
Total consumer prices rose by 0.6% on a monthly basis in September.
Energy product prices jumped 14.9% in September compared to the same month last year, marking the third consecutive month of acceleration and the largest increase since February 2023.
Motor fuel prices surged 37.1% and heating oil soared 74.9% year-on-year in September, reflecting price increases on the crude oil market since the start of the Iran war.
Conversely, electricity, natural gas, and district heating prices fell by 5.5%, 2.8%, and 1%, respectively, partly due to government relief measures.
Food prices registered a below-average annual increase of 0.4% in September.
The core inflation rate, which excludes food and energy, stood at 2.4% in September, remaining below the overall inflation rate.
Prices of goods increased by 3.8% year-on-year, while services became 2.7% more expensive.

Israeli premier orders prosecution of soldiers who exposed Gaza mass killings in NAZA documentary
Unknown

2026-10-13
07:10:08 UTC

Lina Altawell
13 October 2026•Update: 13 October 2026
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has ordered the security establishment and the country’s attorney-general to identify and prosecute soldiers and officers interviewed in the investigative documentary NAZA about Israel’s mass killings of civilians in Gaza, Israeli media reported Monday.
In a letter to army Chief of Staff Eyal Zamir, Shin Bet chief David Zini and Attorney General Gali Baharav-Miara, Netanyahu accused those who participated in the documentary of committing “serious information security offenses, and criminal defamation” and causing harm to “Israel’s diplomatic and security interests,” according to Haaretz newspaper.
The award-winning documentary examines Israel’s use of artificial intelligence and automated surveillance systems in targeted killings and military operations during its genocidal war in Gaza.
The film’s title, "NAZA," refers to an acronym used by Israeli military intelligence to denote the number of civilians expected to be killed in an airstrike.
During the war, the Israeli army has killed more than 74,000 Palestinians and injured over 175,000 others since October 2023 in a brutal offensive that has left the entire enclave in ruins.
Netanyahu claimed that the film has presented a “false, misleading and biased narrative” that defames Israel and its military and damages the country’s international standing.
“There is concern that those involved in the defamatory film committed serious criminal offenses by exposing highly classified information and creating a breach in the information security of a highly sensitive intelligence unit,” he said in the letter.
The film, based on testimony from 24 Israeli soldiers and intelligence personnel, won the Special Jury Prize at the Venice Film Festival last month.
Following the award, Israeli Culture Minister Miki Zohar asked the Interior Ministry to consider revoking the citizenship of the film’s creators, describing the documentary as “vile” and accusing them of “treason.”
Zamir separately ordered Military Intelligence, the Military Advocate General’s Corps and the Israeli Air Force to identify the soldiers featured in the film and determine whether they were active-duty troops, career officers or reservists, according to Haaretz.
During discussions on the issue, Military Advocate General Itai Offir said that there would be no legal basis for criminal prosecution unless participants were found to have committed information-security violations or disclosed classified material.
He said disciplinary or command measures could, however, be taken if military orders were violated.
The Israeli army claimed that the documentary’s portrayal of its targeting procedures in Gaza contained “substantial factual errors.”
The Guardian, which produced the documentary, defended the film, saying the process used to assess the credibility of the testimonies was “rigorous” and included classified documents, verification of specific strikes and corroboration from additional confidential sources.
The newspaper said it had interviewed more than 100 people familiar with Israeli military systems used during the war in Gaza, including senior commanders involved in authorizing strikes.
In November 2024, the International Criminal Court issued arrest warrants for Netanyahu and former Defense Minister Yoav Gallant over war crimes and crimes against humanity in Gaza.
The International Court of Justice, the UN’s principal judicial organ, is also hearing a case brought by South Africa and joined by several countries accusing Israel of genocide against Palestinians in Gaza.

The International Monetary Fund has kept its estimate of Ukraine's real gross domestic product growth at 1% for 2026, compared with 1.8% last year, in its October World Economic Outlook, an Interfax-Ukraine correspondent reported from the IMF and World Bank annual meetings in Bangkok.
The forecast for growth to accelerate to 3.5% next year is also unchanged, as is the estimate of 3.6% growth in 2031, according to the report published on Tuesday morning.
In June, the IMF cut its 2026 growth forecast for Ukraine to 1-1.6%, compared with 2% in the April World Economic Outlook and 1.8-2.5% when the new four-year Extended Fund Facility program was approved in late February.
For next year, the fund forecast acceleration of GDP growth to 3.5% during the second review of the program in June-July, although most other analysts have cut their forecasts since then.
The IMF also confirmed its July forecast for the other main indicators. It expects inflation to rise from 8.0% last year to 10.5% this year and return to 8.0% next year, and the current account deficit to narrow from 16% of GDP last year to 11% of GDP this year and 4.7% next year.
The fund expects unemployment to fall to 10.2% this year from 11.6% last year and to rise again to 11.3% next year.
The World Bank cut its forecast for Ukraine's 2027 economic growth last week from 4% to 1.5%, but kept its estimate of 1.2% growth this year. The European Bank for Reconstruction and Development cut its forecast for Ukraine's GDP growth in late September to 1.5% for 2026 and 2.5% for 2027.
Economy and Environment Minister Oleksandr Kravchenko said in late September that he is considering cutting the 2027 GDP growth forecast by 0.3-0.5 percentage points from the already built-in pessimistic plan, from 1.3% to 0.8-1%, and the 2026 forecast to 0.5% from the current 1.6%.
The National Bank of Ukraine lowered its estimate of real GDP growth this year to 1.1-1.2%, compared with 1.8% in late July.
Leading Ukrainian investment company Dragon Capital also cut its macro forecast significantly last week. It now expects GDP to fall 0.5% this year and 1.0% next year. Before the escalation of the war in July, it estimated possible growth of 1.5% this year and 0.5% next year.

airBaltic losses soar to 128.2 million euros despite rising revenue and passenger numbers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
07:06:17 UTC
16:06:17 KST

Latvia’s national airline airBaltic Group recorded losses of 128.2 million euros in the first half of 2026, compared with losses of just 1.7 million euros in the corresponding period of 2025, the airline’s representatives told LETA.
Meanwhile, the group’s revenue increased by 14.2% year-on-year, reaching 399.2 million euros in the first six months of 2026.
During the first half of the year, airBaltic carried a total of 4.4 million passengers, an increase of 15% compared with the same period last year.
Of these, 2.5 million passengers travelled on the airline’s own route network, representing growth of 3.9%.
The total number of flights operated, including aircraft, crew, maintenance and insurance (ACMI) leasing services, reached 42,300, an increase of 16.2%.
This included 24,000 flights operated on airBaltic’s own route network, up 5% year-on-year, and 18,300 ACMI flights, representing an increase of 35%.
The airline’s average passenger load factor in the first half of 2026 was 77.3%, one percentage point lower than in the corresponding period of 2025.
Adjusted earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation, amortisation and aircraft rental costs, as well as provisions for litigation (EBITDAR), amounted to 34 million euros, down 16.9 million euros compared with the first half of 2025.
According to airBaltic, revenue in the second quarter of 2026 reached 250.1 million euros, an increase of 15.3% compared with the same period last year.
However, the company recorded a loss of 58.1 million euros, compared with a profit of 27.6 million euros in the second quarter of 2025.
Passenger numbers increased by 17% to three million during the quarter.
Of these, 1.41 million passengers travelled on the airline’s own route network, representing growth of 3.2%.
The total number of flights operated in the second quarter, including ACMI leasing services, increased by 19.1% to 27,200.
The airline attributed its first-half revenue growth to a 7.4% increase in passenger transport revenue and a 36.5% rise in revenue from ACMI leasing services.
airBaltic emphasised that higher operating costs negatively affected profitability during the first half of 2026.
Foreign exchange fluctuations had a particularly significant impact on the company’s net financial results.
While currency movements generated a gain of 65.7 million euros in the first half of 2025, they resulted in a net loss of 21.2 million euros during the corresponding period of 2026.
Higher depreciation associated with fleet expansion and increased financing costs also contributed to the losses.
At the same time, airBaltic reported improvements in aircraft availability.
During the second quarter, the airline leased out an average of approximately 26 aircraft, compared with 19 aircraft a year earlier.
Fleet availability also improved significantly.
During the first half of 2026, airBaltic had no aircraft grounded due to Pratt & Whitney engine problems, compared with an average of 11 grounded aircraft in the first half of 2025.
According to the airline, the escalation of the conflict in the Middle East created a more challenging operating environment and affected profitability.
Fuel costs increased by 79.6% in the second quarter of 2026 compared with the same period last year, reaching 66.1 million euros.
Inflation also drove up personnel costs, carbon emission allowance expenses and other operating costs.
Airspace restrictions forced airBaltic to operate longer flight routes, while services to Tel Aviv and Dubai were suspended.
In response to higher fuel prices, the airline adjusted its summer capacity by cancelling approximately 5.7% of flights originally scheduled between March and October.
The total impact of higher aviation fuel prices on airBaltic’s financial results in the second quarter of 2026 was estimated at 29.3 million euros.
airBaltic President and CEO Erno Hildén stressed that the aviation industry continues to face significant pressure from external factors, including historically high aviation fuel prices affecting airlines across the sector.
“The current operating environment requires greater discipline and focus in managing the company.
“The airline’s priority is to strengthen airBaltic’s financial foundations and develop a more resilient operating model, with particular emphasis on efficiency, sustainable profitability and financial stability.
“The recently announced new business plan outlines a clear path towards achieving these objectives while maintaining airBaltic’s essential role in ensuring connectivity for Latvia and the wider Baltic region,” Hildén said.
Going forward, airBaltic will publish its operational performance figures in a Monthly Operating Report during the second half of each month, providing an overview of the airline’s key operating indicators for the preceding month.
In the first half of 2025, airBaltic Group reported revenue of 349.6 million euros and losses of 1.7 million euros.
For the full year 2025, the group’s revenue increased by 4.2% compared with 2024, reaching 779.344 million euros.
Meanwhile, its annual losses amounted to 44.337 million euros, approximately 2.7 times lower than in 2024.
The airline carried a total of 5.2 million passengers in 2025, an increase of 1% compared with the previous year.
As previously reported by LETA, airBaltic has initiated the restructuring of its financial obligations under the Chapter 11 procedure established by US law.
The airline has received binding commitments from lenders to provide up to 350 million euros in new debtor-in-possession (DIP) financing to support liquidity and operations during the Chapter 11 process.
airBaltic has already received the first financing tranche of 140 million euros.
Of this amount, 78.925 million euros will be used to purchase eight aircraft and seven engines.
The financing was arranged by Strategic Value Partners (SVP), with commitments from Barclays, Hayfin Capital Management, Morgan Stanley, Oaktree Capital Management and Strategic Value Partners.
The interest rate is SOFR plus 8%, currently equivalent to approximately 12%.
However, the financing arrangement also involves additional fees of up to 52.5 million euros.
As a result, the previous plan to raise up to 257 million euros from bondholders at an annual interest rate of 25% will not proceed.
Meanwhile, a bondholder group known as the Ad Hoc Group has filed objections in court concerning the terms of the DIP financing and its potential impact on bondholders’ collateral.
The Chapter 11 procedure protects airBaltic from creditor claims until the restructuring of its obligations is completed.
The airline has also stated that flights and customer services will continue as usual.
All flights will operate according to the planned schedule, existing tickets and reservations remain valid, and passengers can continue purchasing tickets and travelling with airBaltic as before.
The restructuring process is expected to result in a reorganisation plan that must be approved by the court.
The process is currently expected to conclude by mid-2027.
As previously reported, airBaltic bondholders approved the capitalisation of the next two bond interest payments in August, along with several other measures intended to provide the airline with additional flexibility in implementing its revised business plan.
Bondholders agreed that interest payments due on 14 August and 14 November 2026 would be added to the principal amount of the bonds rather than paid in cash.
They also approved a temporary waiver of minimum liquidity requirements until November 2026.
Germany’s national airline Lufthansa became an airBaltic shareholder in the summer of 2025.
Currently, the Latvian state owns 88.37% of airBaltic shares, while Lufthansa holds 10%.
Aircraft Leasing 1, a company owned by Danish businessman and financial investor Lars Thuesen, holds 1.62%, with the remaining 0.01% owned by other shareholders.
The company’s share capital amounts to 41.819 million euros.

Fewer hands for the harvest: Lithuania’s apple orchards face seasonal labour crunch
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
07:06:00 UTC
16:06:00 KST

Seasonal apple picking, once a popular source of extra income for hundreds of residents in northern Lithuania, is becoming increasingly difficult to staff as fewer people are willing to take the short-term jobs.
At Naradava orchards in Pasvalys district, pickers can earn as much as 100 euros a day. But while the pay remains attractive to some, the number of people seeking seasonal work has steadily declined.
In previous years, employers sometimes had to select workers from a pool of applicants. This year, nearly everyone who applies is being hired.
Vytautas, who has been picking apples at the orchards for almost two decades, looks forward to the harvest every year. For him, the seasonal work is a valuable opportunity to earn money because finding employment in the countryside can be difficult.
“It’s possible, but it’s difficult at my age,” he told LRT TV. “Here, I can manage to earn some money.”
Some workers use the income to supplement their pensions, while others take vacation from their regular jobs specifically to work during the harvest.
For some, the extra income is earmarked for a particular purchase or a trip.
“I work and arrange my personal life – I buy something or go somewhere,” one worker said. “Maybe I’ll manage to go somewhere this weekend.”
The orchards are also facing another challenge this year. A cold winter destroyed about one-third of the company’s orchards, but Naradava still expects to harvest around 4,000 metric tons of apples.
Finding enough workers, however, is becoming increasingly difficult.
“We really need these pickers, and this year we are using various methods to find them – ads in newspapers, asking acquaintances, and social media,” said Džiugas Palionis, director of Naradava. “We have about 150 workers at the peak this year, whereas in better years we managed to have as many as 300.”
Dalia Radzivonienė, a forewoman at the company, said the change is particularly noticeable compared with previous years.
Residents of surrounding districts once began asking well in advance when they could start working and often wanted to reserve places for family members. Demand was so high that the company sometimes had to hold selections.
“Now we have to take whoever comes,” Radzivonienė said. “There aren’t as many people interested as there used to be. In some years, people couldn’t get in. Now we accept everyone who comes.”
Naradava recruits workers from nearby villages and towns and operates its own bus to transport them from Pasvalys, Biržai and surrounding areas, Palionis said.
“We manage to gather them somehow,” he said. “Every year, there are fewer workers.”
The apple harvest is expected to continue until the end of October.

Estonia's defense ministry allocates €250,000 for war movies
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
07:03:00 UTC
16:03:00 KST

Estonia's defense ministry allocates €250,000 for war movies
The MoD has announced a funding competition worth €250,000 to support the production of films and other audiovisual works aimed at strengthening the Estonian public's willingness to defend the country.
"I would like to impress upon everyone on the committee selecting these films at the Ministry of Defense that any film that is overly propagandistic or too polished and carefully packaged is actually less credible. When we talk about defending Estonia, my view, my belief, is that the truth ultimately works best," film director Ilmar Raag commented.
The Ministry of Defense is inviting submissions for feature films, documentaries, animated films, television series and narrative video games. The ministry has supported the production of Estonian war films for more than 20 years, including "Names in Marble," "1944" and "O2."
According to ministry representative Thomas Mell, different audiovisual formats make it possible to reach different generations.
"The willingness to defend the country is an important part of Estonia's national defense and strengthening it is one of our core responsibilities. Supporting films and other audiovisual works is one way to contribute to this. Film is a medium that reaches a wide audience, as do video games nowadays, for example, and they help communicate national defense issues in ways that resonate with different generations," Mell said.
Raag, who previously received funding through a Ministry of Defense competition to produce a documentary, believes that funding decisions must also take into account the potential for a backlash.
"Those who allocate funding at the ministry need to recognize that if a filmmaker takes an overly simplistic, propagandistic approach, it could actually backfire," Raag noted.
To qualify for Ministry of Defense funding, projects must align with national defense objectives. This raises the question of how much influence the state, as a funder, can exert over a film's content.
"As the Ministry of Defense, we do not interfere in any way with filmmakers' creative freedom. We do not dictate scripts, themes or how characters should be portrayed. Instead, filmmakers themselves are free to submit their proposals to us," Mell explained.
The Ministry of Defense is accepting applications until November 18. The funding can be used next year.

Latin American organised crime ‘may operate in 16 European countries’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
07:00:18 UTC
16:00:18 KST

A four-month investigation by the Guardian has revealed that the surge in cocaine trafficking to Europe is directly linked to the expanding presence of Latin American criminal networks in Europe, where they have forged close ties with local mafia organisations.
The investigation, utilising databases, police and intelligence agencies, along with interviews with judges, prosecutors and experts from eight countries, shows that cartels and factions from Colombia, Brazil, Ecuador, Venezuela, Mexico and the US are active in at least 12 European countries. Between 2014 and 2024, there was a 471% rise in the quantity of cocaine seized and more local laboratories processing cocaine derivatives were dismantled.
The figure could be even higher, as it includes only groups officially identified in Europe through police operations, transnational investigations and ongoing court cases involving brokers, active members, cells or operational networks. It does not include gangs that lack a physical presence in Europe while working in “joint ventures” with European mafias.
The identified groups include Mexico’s Sinaloa cartel and the Jalisco New Generation cartel (CJNG); the Clan del Golfo mafia, and the guerrilla organisations ELN and dissident factions of Farc in Colombia; Brazil’s Primeiro Comando da Capital (PCC, or First Capital Command) and Comando Vermelho (CV, or Red Command); Venezuela’s Tren de Aragua; and the US-originated Barrio 18 and MS-13 gangs, which are also prevalent in El Salvador, Honduras, Guatemala and, to a lesser degree, in Mexico.
These organisations have built a more prominent presence in Spain, Portugal, the Netherlands, Belgium and France, while their activities have also been noted in Germany, Romania, Croatia and Slovakia. The Global Initiative Against Transnational Organized Crime (Gi-Toc) also includes Bulgaria.
Daniel Brombacher, a political scientist and director of the Europe Observatory at Gi-Toc, said: “There is something new happening with a presence of Latin American groups in geographies where there’s no pre-existing infrastructure.
“This phenomenon is no longer limited to the traditional gateway countries,” he says. “Recent police operations have uncovered Mexican-run methamphetamine labs in southern France, north-eastern Poland and Brandenburg, south of Berlin. Latin American groups are also appearing in Romania and Bulgaria along the Balkan route.”
Latin American national authorities and experts suggest the list may be even longer. An unpublished report by the São Paulo public prosecutor’s office, partly based on data from the Brazilian intelligence agency (Abin) – which the Guardian reviewed – shows, for example, that the PCC, now Brazil’s biggest criminal group, operates in 16 European countries, including the UK, Ireland, Iceland, Serbia, Sweden, Switzerland and Turkey.
The suspicion that Latin American cartels and factions are seeking to become established in Europe is not new. Since at least the 1980s, Colombian criminal organisations such as the Cali and Medellín cartels had footholds in regions of Spain such as Galicia. In 2013, a Europol report in 2103 warned of their rise. But what authorities are witnessing now is on an another level.
A Europol report this year states that “Latin American MTCNs [most threatening criminal networks] have also settled in the EU, from where they direct operations that affect the EU. This is particularly the case for mobile criminal networks involved in organised property crime.”
Interpol, led by the Brazilian federal police officer Valdecy Urquiza, has been approached, but has not commented.
The problem has become more visible over the past decade. Drug production in Latin America in that time has increased roughly fourfold to reach a record of about 4,100 tonnes in 2024. This comes after growth of up to 35% at the beginning of the decade. More cocaine is now produced in Colombia than during the era of the notorious drug lord Pablo Escobar. Nearly all the world’s cocaine and many related substances originate from Latin America, particularly Colombia.
Víctor Manuel Sánchez Valdés, an academic at the Autonomous University of Coahuila in Mexico who is an expert on organised crime, says: “The main ones are the Sinaloa cartel and the Jalisco cartel [CJNG] in Mexico; the Comando Vermelho and the PCC of Brazil; the Gulf Clan and different factions of the Colombian Farc; the Lobos and the Choneros of Ecuador; and Tren de Aragua of Venezuela.”
He believes that the Latin American presence in Europe is even more widespread than is generally recognised. “Sinaloa cartel and the CJNG have a presence in more than 20 European countries. Obviously, that does not mean they dominate or have large cells,” he says. “Rather, they are business emissaries.”
The UN Office on Drugs and Crime’s 2026 World Drug Report on illicit crimes states that global cocaine production in 2024 was between 3,800 and 4,700 tonnes – more than four times higher than it was in 2014. South America remains the main production hub, with coca cultivation covering a record 385,000 hectares over the past decade – three times the 2014 figure.
Europe has emerged as a key market because it offers organisations higher profit margins than the US. Since the beginning of the decade, European police have confiscated more drugs than American forces, and data indicates that Europe now represents about a quarter of global consumption.
Europol recently reported that out of 731 MTCNs operating across Europe, 149 are connected to Latin American organisations. Of these, 67 have Latin American members, and 22 mainly consist of Latin Americans.

One thing must now be clear to Andy Burnham. The rightwing press is on a war footing – and he’s the enemy | Jane Martinson
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
07:00:18 UTC
16:00:18 KST

While the merits of a so-called Britannia shield to protect Britain from missiles and drones are debatable, the Conservatives’ proposal did achieve one thing last week: the very idea of the shield was used to anoint a political leader.
In a significant development, little observed amid the hullaballoo of news events, Kemi Badenoch’s uncosted, pie-in-the-sky plans to build a £10bn anti-missile system were enthusiastically heralded by the rightwing press. It was not just a matter of the plans themselves being lauded, even by outlets that must know them to be ridiculous. More significant is what it said about the champion chosen by these media organisations in their offensive against the Labour government and Andy Burnham.
The Sun splashed a smiling Badenoch across its front page with a banner headline calling her the “Iron Dome Lady”; the Express paraded her in a power suit and a union jack. The Daily Mail, meanwhile, hailed the Tories for seeking to “protect the nation’s skies” and sealed the plans with its “Don’t Leave Britain Defenceless” campaign stamp. Even wartime leaders could not hope for better, unquestioning coverage from battle-aligned, nation-rallying propaganda sheets.
The slavish Badenoch coverage is significant so soon after Burnham’s first conference speech as prime minister. It marks the moment when much of the rightwing press has returned to its traditional Tory-supporting ways after years of flirting with – and outright eulogising – Nigel Farage and his now scandal-hit Reform UK party. It also suggests a back-to-basics return to the economy as the chief battleground for this fight, and not the madder excesses of the war on woke that has recently consumed them.
The praise for Badenoch, who was also recently treated to an all-expenses paid trip to Greece to meet Rupert Murdoch and executives from the Sun and Times-owning News Corp, suggests that she has cemented a position as the rightwing press’s best political hope of beating Burnham.
The search for a suitable champion has assumed a growing urgency because the prime minister has so far proved hard to leave a mark on. “Red Andy”, the early attack line, has not been widely used since the June byelection in Makerfield. The Mail may have dubbed Burnham’s first conference speech “the most Left-wing speech delivered by a modern British prime minister”, but in recent weeks only the Telegraph’s Allister Heath has fired the “Red Andy” missile in a column that called plans for pension reform, a social care system and all talk of a return to the European Union, “mad, nasty and shockingly extreme”.
This coverage reminds Alastair Campbell of his early years advising Tony Blair when he was depicted either as a “useless Bambi or Stalin”, he tells me. “They can’t decide if [Burnham] is a useless Paddington Bear or red in tooth and claw,” says Campbell. “They just can’t work him out yet.” A member of the loathed liberal elite or outright Trot?
There are a few factors that are making it difficult for the rightwing press to get the full measure of their enemy – including Burnham’s trajectory from New Labour luvvy to working-class champion, the King of the North. Labour advisers also cite the fact that Burnham’s inner circle, in contrast to his predecessors, has also been relatively leak- and conflict-free, leaving rightwing combatants with fewer vulnerabilities to exploit.
This is the calm before the storm, of course, with Burnham’s opponents gearing up for the budget and the inevitable controversies on 28 October. “The press are probing his defences,” Tom Baldwin, a former Labour party adviser, tells me. “They’ll keep trying, of course, and the chances are that one of their missiles will eventually hit a target.”
Amid rising fuel prices, geopolitical uncertainty and concerns over jobs, the back-to-the-future nature of this debate – indeed the back-to-the-Tory-future nature of it – is hardly surprising. Burnham has assaulted shibboleths. He has vowed to reverse “40 years of failure” with his pledge to repeal Margaret Thatcher’s ban on public ownership of water companies, to abolish the Tory version of the right-to-buy housing scheme, and to restore a sense of common good to Britain. To the right, this is unconscionable. Dan Hodges in the Mail, praising Badenoch’s “best speech yet”, wrote that the country faces a choice between Burnham’s “unashamed 1970s-style socialism” and the Tory leaders’ “bold attempt to reappropriate and recondition Margaret Thatcher’s radical conservatism”.
Although the rightwing outlets fight a similar battle against Labour, they do so for varying reasons. Some of those are ideological, but commercial imperatives also fuel their fervour. The 1970s and 80s marked a golden age for newspapers, when millions of loyal readers gave them heft and profits. With sales and readership figures now at a fraction of their peak in the late 80s, the Sun (which claimed sales of 3.8m per day in 1987) and several other titles no longer publish their numbers, focusing instead on online reach. In dwindling markets, the strategy is to stay competitive by aligning with, or perhaps exacerbating, the prevailing wave of political populism.
The Sun has struggled more than the Mail with the shift online. It has also struggled more with Burnham because of its coverage of the 1989 Hillsborough disaster, in which it falsely blamed Liverpool supporters for a crush that killed 97 people. According to Baldwin, citing well-placed sources, Burnham may become the first prime minister since the Labour leader Jim Callaghan to refuse requests for exclusive interviews and articles in Rupert Murdoch’s biggest tabloid.
The right’s battle-camp has the additional problem that Burnham himself is proving quite a wily opponent. The prime minister spends 10 minutes a day with his social media team before posting to his nearly 1m followers on Instagram and more than 700,000 on TikTok. His short-form videos on fuel prices and the triple lock don’t seem to target younger voters, but they are a way of bypassing a negative narrative – or what Campbell calls “the madness of the rightwing press”.
Burnham could opt to go his own way, to ignore the hostile rightwing outlets altogether. But in a democracy, that would be no more ethical for Labour than it is for Reform UK, which has barred press critics. David Yelland, the editor of the Sun when it put Tony Blair on its front page with the headline “Is THIS the most dangerous man in Britain?”, tells me it would also be unwise. The power of the rightwing press is diminished, he says; they are “toothless tigers in a jungle full of new dangers – dangers as lethal for them as the rest of us, by which I mean AI and what comes next”. But, “the truth is the Tory press still has influence over the political and media classes … it can still set the weather”.
And as we know from famous battles past, the weather can be a decisive factor. The side that copes with it best usually wins.
- Jane Martinson is an academic and Guardian columnist. She is a board member of the Scott Trust, which owns the Guardian Media Group, and writes in a personal capacity

Nuisance or festive tradition? Swiss vote on fireworks ban
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
07:00:00 UTC
16:00:00 KST

Nuisance or festive tradition? Swiss vote on fireworks ban
At the end of November the Swiss will vote on a people’s initiative seeking to ban the sale and use of noisy fireworks. While supporters of the initiative want to reduce the noise pollution and environmental impact caused by fireworks, its opponents argue for the preservation of a popular tradition.
For a long time in Switzerland, no one could imagine Swiss National Day on August 1 without fireworks displays and other noisy firecrackers. In recent years, however, drought has regularly led to bans on them in several cantons. At the same time, fireworks are at the centre of a heated debate over their usefulness and the nuisance they cause. Their fate will be decided at the ballot boxExternal link on November 29.
What does the initiative call for?
It calls for a ban on the sale and use of noisy fireworks. Pyrotechnic devices that do not produce noise, such as Bengal lights or volcanoes, would remain permitted.
The initiative does, however, provide for exceptions. The cantons could grant special permits for events of supra-regional importance. Large fireworks displays could therefore still be organised for certain celebrations, such as August 1 or New Year’s Eve, provided a cantonal exemption is obtained.
It specifies, however, that these events should take place within a clearly defined timeframe and location, to allow a wide audience to enjoy them and to significantly reduce any negative effects.
Who is behind the initiative?
The initiative was launched by animal welfare organisations. A broad alliance of organisations from the fields of agriculture, health and nature conservation has formed in support of it. The initiators collected 137,429 signatures – more than the 100,000 required to trigger a popular vote.
What do supporters argue?
Supporters of the initiative claim they want to protect animals, people and nature by reducing the nuisance caused by fireworks. They argue that sudden loud bangs can trigger panic in animals and harm their welfare. Some animals run away and are never found by their owners.
They believe the public is also affected by this noise pollution. Children, the elderly and people with mental health conditions are said to be particularly sensitive to the loud bangs.
Supporters of the initiative also highlight the environmental impact of fireworks. According to them, these generate around 1,300 tonnes of waste each year, some of which ends up in public spaces or on agricultural land. They also point out that the burning of fireworks releases several hundred tonnes of fine particulate matter, metals and other pollutants into the air.
What do opponents argue?
In the eyes of its opponents, the initiative goes too far. First and foremost, they point out that the cantons and municipalities already have the right to restrict the sale and use of fireworks. Indeed, several of them have imposed restrictions this year due to the fire risks associated with the drought.
Opponents also emphasise that fireworks are only used for a few days a year. In their view, the nuisance they cause is therefore already limited in time and space.
They also believe that the initiative threatens a deeply rooted popular tradition, associated with the August 1 celebrations and, increasingly, with New Year’s Eve celebrations. Finally, they argue that a ban would infringe upon the economic freedom of businesses that manufacture, import, sell or use fireworks for professional purposes.
Who supports it, and who opposes it?
Parliament and the government recommend rejecting the initiative. In parliament, the left-wing Green Party and the left-wing Social Democratic Party supported the initiative, while the right-wing Swiss People’s Party, the centre-right Radical-Liberal Party and the Centre Party strongly opposed it.
How many fireworks does Switzerland use?
Annual fireworks consumption varies significantly from year to year in Switzerland. According to the Federal Office of Police, between 1,200 and 2,300 tonnes of fireworks have been sold in the country each year over the past decade. Around three-quarters of the pyrotechnic devices used are imported. China is by far the main supplier. Swiss production mainly consists of volcanoes, Bengal lights, sparklers, confetti cannons, table bombs and other table fireworks.
How do other countries regulate fireworks?
The debate on fireworks extends far beyond Switzerland’s borders. Several countries have already restricted or banned the use of fireworks.
In the Netherlands, where New Year’s Eve celebrations are regularly marred by accidents and violence, a ban on most fireworks intended for the public is set to come into force before the end of the year. The country would thus become the second European nation, after Ireland, to impose such strict limits on the use of fireworks by private individuals. Outside Europe, Australia and Singapore have also adopted highly restrictive regulations, with the use of fireworks largely restricted to authorised professionals.
Other countries have opted for a more nuanced approach. In Germany, for example, fireworks may generally only be set off around New Year’s Eve, and several cities have established zones where they are banned.

The Swiss voted for a pension hike. Now they must decide how to pay for it
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
07:00:00 UTC
16:00:00 KST

The Swiss voted for a pension hike. Now they must decide how to pay for it
On November 29, the Swiss will vote on funding a 13th monthly pension payment by increasing value-added tax (VAT) by 0.4 percentage points. If the proposal is rejected, payment of the 13th monthly pension will still go ahead from December 2026, but funding will yet have to be secured.
This December will be a special one for those receiving the Old Age and Survivors’ Insurance (OASI), the first pillar of the Swiss pension system. For the first time, retirees – whether living in Switzerland or abroad – will receive a 13th monthly pension payment. What is still unclear, however, is how this extra payment is to be funded. On November 29, Swiss voters will have their say on the solution proposed by parliament.
What exactly is the vote about?
The referendum does not threaten the 13th pension payment. This was approved by 58.2% of voters in March 2024. On November 29, the Swiss will be deciding on how to fund part of this new expenditure.
Single pensioners will now receive up to CHF2,520 ($3,031) more a year and married couples up to CHF3,780. This will cost a total of over CHF4 billion annually. As the number of retirees continues to grow and pensions are regularly adjusted to the cost of living, this figure is expected to rise, reaching CHF5 billion a year from 2035 onwards.
To cover part of these additional costs, parliament is proposing to increase VAT from 2028. The standard rate, which applies to most goods and services, would go up by 0.4 percentage points, from 8.1% to 8.5%. The special rate for the accommodation sector would rise from 3.8% to 4%. Meanwhile, the reduced rate of 2.6%, which applies in particular to food, medicines and books, would remain unchanged.
This VAT hike, which is expected to generate around CHF1.4 billion a year, would still not be enough to cover the full cost of the 13th pension payment. It would, however, ease the financial burden on the state old-age pension system. The Swiss government has already drawn up a scenario for additional funding for the 13th pension in its OASI 2030 reform proposal, which is currently under consultation. This could entail a further increase in VAT or a combination of VAT and social security contributions.
How is the state pension system funded?
The OASI is funded through a pay-as-you-go system. This means that the contributions from today’s active workforce directly finance current pensions. Worker and employer contributions account for around 70% of OASI revenue.
The federal government covers just over 20% of expenditure, mainly through its general funds, as well as taxes on tobacco and spirits. About 9% of revenue comes from VAT and the tax on casinos. Added to this are any returns generated by the investment of OASI reserves, which can vary significantly from one year to the next. In 2025, OASI revenue thus totalled just over CHF55 billion.
How are pension finances faring?
The state old-age pension system is currently in a relatively sound financial position. It closed the 2025 fiscal yearExternal link with a CHF4.4 billion surplus. This is largely thanks to the additional revenue generated by the Tax Reform and OASI Financing Act and the OASI 21 reform.
However, the retirement of the baby-boomers and the decrease in the active labour force are putting pressure on the social insurance system. On top of this now comes the cost of the 13th pension payment. From this year onwards, expenditure will exceed revenue by more than CHF1 billion. Without additional funds, annual deficits will hit nearly CHF5 billion by 2035, according to estimates by the Federal Social Insurance OfficeExternal link. With the VAT increase, the deficit is expected to drop to CHF3 billion.
Why is a nationwide vote necessary?
Increasing VAT requires an amendment to the Swiss Constitution. Voters must therefore decide whether to accept the Federal Decree on Additional Financing of the OASI through a VAT IncreaseExternal link. The bill will need to secure a majority of both the people and the cantons to be approved.
Who is for the reform and who against?
Parliament and the government support the VAT increase. The centre-right parties are against, while the left-wing and centrist parties are in favour. The major trade unions also support the reform, although there are dissenting voices within their ranks – in particular the public service union, which recommends rejecting the proposal.
Why vote for the reform?
The main argument is financial. The introduction of the 13th OASI pension payment was decided in a nationwide referendum. To respect the will of the people, funding must now be secured to prevent the OASI’s accounts from slipping into the red.
Supporters of the VAT hike believe this is the best way to finance the new pension payments quickly. In parliament, the left had advocated a mixed funding approach, combining an increase in payroll contributions and VAT. However, it regards the chosen solution as the best possible compromise given the current political dynamics. The left-wing supporters of the VAT increase also believe it will help reduce pressure to raise the retirement age, in particular from the political right.
The backers also point out that the 0.4 percentage points increase is modest and that essential goods are exempt. For the vast majority of retirees, they say, the gain from the 13th pension payment will outweigh the additional costs arising from higher VAT.
Why vote against?
The opponents of the reform do not challenge the payment of the 13th monthly pension, but rather the funding method. They believe that an increase in VAT will put too great a strain on households’ purchasing power, which is already squeezed by rising health insurance premiums, rents and day-to-day expenses.
They also criticise the fact that the reform would cover only part of the cost of the 13th pension. The focus should instead be on addressing the structural problems of the OASI, the Radical-Liberal Party (centre-right) argues.
On the left, the public service union regards VAT as an anti-social tax that hits low earners proportionally harder. It also points out that additional funding is not necessary in the immediate term, given the sound financial health of the state old-age pension system today.

Trump calls for energy truce; Moscow remains silent
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
06:59:16 UTC
15:59:16 KST

On the 11th of October, US President Donald Trump announced that Russia and Ukraine had agreed to observe an energy truce, refraining from strikes on energy infrastructure; Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky reacted by saying this was news to him, while Moscow remains silent, the BBC reports.
When asked whether an agreement on an energy truce had been reached, Dmitry Peskov, the spokesman for Russian dictator Vladimir Putin, stated that communication is ongoing and the media will be informed as soon as there is something to say.
Peskov may not have much to say on the matter, but pro-Kremlin media certainly do. They have dubbed the energy truce a gift to Moscow. The pro-government outlet Moskovsky Komsomolets emphasized that Russia is, of course, the beneficiary of the truce. It implies only that Russia is prevented from destroying Ukraine's last remaining oil refinery—which is barely functioning anyway. Conversely, Kyiv would no longer be able to attack Russian oil refineries; thus, it is essentially an agreement that favors Moscow, which is why no one has rejected it. In other words, Moscow believes that Trump’s statement has tied Kyiv’s hands, not Moscow’s.
In recent months, Ukrainian strikes have caused serious damage to Russian oil refineries and triggered fuel shortages. If the strikes continue, Moscow can be expected to start arguing that Kyiv is harming US economic interests—and, by extension, Republican prospects in the midterm elections. Russian officials will seize the opportunity to claim that the strikes jeopardize Trump’s plans to purchase Russian diesel. Trump has indicated that a deal to buy diesel from Russia would benefit American consumers, though 
many remain skeptical that the volume offered by Russia could actually impact fuel prices in the US.
The Russians would be more than happy if Ukrainian strikes provoked anger in the White House. Moscow would rejoice if Washington stopped sharing intelligence with Kyiv and halted arms sales to Europe intended for Ukraine. The Russians were already delighted when Trump began suggesting that Ukraine needed a new president.
Zelensky has called for a 60-day general ceasefire to allow presidential elections to be held in Ukraine. What does Moscow say about this? Peskov noted that the Kremlin and the dictator have repeatedly stated that Russians do not want a mere ceasefire but rather a lasting peace, and are ready to do everything possible to achieve it. However, "everything possible" does not include a 60-day ceasefire, a 30-day ceasefire, or anything of the sort. On the 12th of October, the Kremlin suggested a one-day ceasefire for the elections. Neither Ukraine nor Europe considers this a serious proposal. Putin has shown no interest in halting hostilities.
Recent statements, speeches, and directives from the Russian dictator indicate that, as winter approaches, Russia is relying on continued strikes to increase pressure on Ukraine. Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov stated that Ukraine does not deserve the respite a ceasefire might provide. While the Kremlin speaks of lasting peace, it continues to wage war. On the 12th of October, Zelensky reported that Russia had launched strikes against several energy infrastructure facilities.
The Kremlin's goal has not changed; it seeks Ukraine's capitulation. It appears Moscow believes that a deal with Trump regarding diesel sales—combined with the American's growing impatience with Zelensky—will enable it to achieve its desired outcome.

Bulgaria to summon Russian ambassador over drone attacks on merchant vessels
Two merchant ships were attacked by drones on the night of 12-13 October off the Bulgarian coast, causing one of the vessels to sink. Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev has announced his intention to summon Russian Ambassador Eleonora Mitrofanova for explanations, although the origin of the drones has not yet been established.
Source: European Pravda, citing Bulgarian media outlet BGNES
Details: Two merchant vessels came under attack during separate incidents in the Black Sea on the night of 12-13 October, according to information provided at an emergency meeting of the Security Council.
The Maltese-flagged cargo ship Chelsea 3 was attacked by three drones approximately 18 nautical miles east of the town of Byala. They hit the ship's deck and the side of its hull. All 15 crew members were evacuated and taken to Varna. Early reports indicate that five crew members received medical treatment for minor injuries.
The Chelsea 3 sails under the Maltese flag, is registered in Odesa and, according to the information provided, is Ukrainian-owned.
Another vessel sank approximately 17 nautical miles east of Krapets. For now, one crew member has been reported to have been rescued.
Rumen Radev announced that he would summon Russian Ambassador Eleonora Mitrofanova and hold discussions with NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte.
"Another attack on merchant ships in the immediate vicinity of Bulgarian territorial waters is absolutely unacceptable," Radev stated.
The prime minister said that Bulgaria would demand explanations from Russian Ambassador Mitrofanova. He also specified that at this moment there is no conclusive evidence regarding the origin of the drones that would allow responsibility for the attacks to be attributed to a specific state. However, according to Radev, "the logic of what is happening suggests that the outcome of the attacks benefits the Russian Federation".
Radev noted that Bulgaria's permanent representatives to NATO and the European Union have been informed about these incidents.
Background:
- On 6 October drones attacked two commercial vessels – the Togo-flagged Alfa Watan and the Palau-flagged Able – in Bulgaria's exclusive economic zone in the Black Sea.
- President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said the Ukrainian Navy had contacted its Bulgarian counterparts regarding the attack on two civilian vessels in Bulgarian waters. Zelenskyy stated that the attack had been carried out by Russia.
- Bulgaria has asked the EU and NATO for assistance in investigating the drone attacks in the Black Sea.

Last week US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said the execution of Nidal Malik Hasan, convicted of killing 13 people at a military base in Texas in 2009, would be available for the public to watch, but Vice-President JD Vance cast doubt about whether that would occur.
The potential live stream has elicited a strong response in parliament, with federal members across the political divide urging the government to "pull every single lever" to block the broadcast.
On Tuesday Mr Albanese told Afternoon Briefing that the government would do whatever it could, but acknowledged it was not as simple as "turning off a light switch".
"Australia has had a bipartisan position of opposition to the death penalty and I find the idea of live streaming the death of anybody completely abhorrent," he told ABC.
"We should do whatever we can to stop that occurring."
He said the government was seeking advice on its options.
On Monday the eSafety Commission said it could not prevent Australians from seeing the execution.
"While eSafety does not have powers to proactively prevent a live stream from occurring online, online services have responsibilities under Australia's online safety regulatory framework to protect users from harmful material," a spokesperson told the ABC.
The prime minister said he would make it "very clear" to social media platforms that the content had no place in Australia.
"I think anybody broadcasting this will damage their own reputations as well. They have a social responsibility here to do the right thing," he said.
The ABC has contacted Google, Meta and TikTok to see if they plan to restrict the content, but has not received responses.
Asked whether he had made representations to Donald Trump on the issue, Mr Albanese said the US president had indicated in the media that he was weighing the matter.
"President Trump has already said he is giving consideration to this and I hope that there is a response in the United States as well," he said.
If the broadcast goes ahead, it will mark the first time an execution in the US has been live streamed.
Politicians express concern
Greens Leader David Shoebridge grilled Foreign Minister Penny Wong over the proposed live stream during Tuesday's Question Time and asked about the "shared values" between Australia and "a government that publicly broadcasts state-sanctioned snuff films".
Senator Wong said it would be "deeply distressing for any such vision to be live streamed".
"We don't believe anyone should be confronted with it, particularly younger Australians," she said.
Senator Wong said Australians had a right to expect such content would not appear on their screens.
"We believe that platforms do have a responsibility to meet these expectations," she said.
Shadow Foreign Affairs Minister Ted O'Brien said the government needed to ensure Australians could not view the execution.
"That concerns me deeply. We cannot have young Australians watching an execution," he told Afternoon Briefing.
"That would be appalling, repugnant, and that is why we need to be looking at every possible lever to ensure that is not live streamed, if indeed it goes ahead."

General Staff: Russia has lost 1,555,700 troops in Ukraine since Feb. 24, 2022
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
06:53:39 UTC
15:53:39 KST

Russia has lost 1,555,700 troops in Ukraine since the beginning of its full-scale invasion on Feb. 24, 2022, the General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine reported on Oct. 13.
The number includes 1,390 casualties that Russian forces suffered over the past day.
According to the report, Russia has also lost 12,412 tanks, 25,534 armored combat vehicles, 162,418 vehicles and fuel tanks, 51,141 artillery systems, 2,211 multiple-launch rocket systems, 1,704 air defense systems, 443 aircraft, 356 helicopters, 2,942 unmanned ground vehicles, 35 ships and boats, and two submarines.
Ukraine's General Staff has not revealed its own losses during the full-scale invasion, citing operational secrecy.
Independent Western think-tank reports agree that the Russian casualties significantly surpass Ukraine's losses, with the Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS) estimating the ratio to be "roughly 2.5:1 or 2:1."
A January 2026 CSIS report said Ukraine has likely suffered between 500,000 and 600,000 casualties from February 2022 to December 2025, of which between 100,000 and 140,000 are thought to be killed in action.
While Ukrainian officials rarely disclose the figure, President Volodymyr Zelensky told France TV on Feb. 4 that at least 55,000 Ukrainian soldiers have been killed in action since the beginning of the full-scale war, in addition to significant numbers who are missing in action.
The intensity of Russian drone attacks and the fighting has made it extremely difficult for Ukraine to retrieve the bodies of fallen soldiers, which are needed for DNA confirmation.

This has happened not only in Kyiv Oblast but also in frontline cities. In this case, the Air Force spokesperson expressed hope that Ukrainian intelligence together with foreign partners will determine the cause of the delay.
Quote: "The intelligence data that everyone is talking about now varies. There is intelligence utilising satellite communications that not only the US but also other NATO countries share with Ukraine. This covers the activity of enemy strategic aviation at their home airfields, ship movements in the Black or Caspian Seas and ballistic missile launches.
There are moments when this information fails to arrive. This is not the first case... If there were certain technical issues this time, I believe the experts can sort it out. And we will resolve this problem together with our partners."
Background:
- At 22:10 on 12 October, Russia struck the capital of Ukraine with five ballistic missiles. Radar systems detected the incoming missiles only once the attack on Kyiv was underway.

IMF lowers Türkiye’s growth forecast for 2026
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
06:51:40 UTC
15:51:40 KST

The International Monetary Fund (IMF) has lowered its 2026 growth forecast for Türkiye to 2.7 percent from 2.9 percent, while keeping its projection for next year unchanged at 3.6 percent.
The forecasts appeared in the October World Economic Outlook, released on Oct. 13 during the IMF and World Bank annual meetings in Bangkok. The previous estimates were published in July.
The fund expects Türkiye’s annual-average consumer inflation to reach 31.2 percent in 2026 and 26.5 percent in 2027.
Its year-end inflation forecasts stand at 29.9 percent and 23.7 percent, respectively.
Türkiye’s current account deficit is projected at 2.9 percent of gross domestic product this year, narrowing to 2.4 percent in 2027.
The unemployment rate is forecast at 8.2 percent this year and 8.3 percent next year.
Globally, the IMF raised its 2026 growth forecast to 3.1 percent from 3 percent in July, while maintaining its 2027 estimate at 3.4 percent. It expects global inflation to reach 4.7 percent this year before easing to 4.1 percent next year.
The fund said growth was becoming increasingly uneven, with countries benefiting from investment in artificial intelligence performing better than many energy-importing and lower-income economies.
It warned that prolonged or escalating conflict in the Middle East could keep energy and food prices high, weakening growth and adding to inflation pressures.
Higher government borrowing costs and renewed trade tensions also posed risks.
The IMF urged governments to strengthen public finances and ensure that support for households facing higher food and energy costs remained temporary and targeted.
