China Focus: China's key wine-producing base pioneers ecological transition models
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
14:51:38 CST
15:51:38 KST

YINCHUAN, Oct. 13 (Xinhua) -- Since opening in August this year, a 22.77-kilometer avenue in northwest China's Ningxia Hui Autonomous Region has been drawing a steady stream of visitors from both home and abroad.
"To the west is the majestic Helan Mountain, and to the east are endless vineyards. It is full of surprises and so much fun," Wang Xiaotong, a tourist from north China's Shanxi Province, said in describing the avenue flanked by vast vineyards.
She was unaware that, just decades ago, this place had been a barren stretch of desert. Through years of sustained effort, Ningxia has turned over 400,000 mu (about 26,667 hectares) of barren land at the eastern foot of Helan Mountain into a world-renowned ecological wine-producing base.
At a local winery, the owner Ding Jian boasts an underground wine cellar that she describes as able to "breathe." The cellar is designed with a naturally constant-temperature, constant-humidity structure, and a natural circulation system formed by ventilation holes in the walls.
Without any refrigeration or heating equipment, it maintains a stable environment suitable for wine aging and storage while consuming minimal energy, no matter how extreme the outdoor temperature is.
Another local winery has adopted an environmentally friendly layout at its production area, using dense windows to create a "chimney effect" that allows free air circulation and significantly reduces reliance on temperature control equipment.
The winery's manager, Zhang Xueyan, outlined a comprehensive ecological scheme. "Grape skins from the winery are supplied to cosmetics companies as raw materials, while discarded vines are provided to farmers free of charge to feed their cattle and sheep. The manure is then returned to the fields to nourish the organic vineyards," she said.
"Every step, from planting to brewing, is aimed at saving energy and cutting emissions, which is also the key to the sustainable and sound development of the industry," the manager concluded.
Ningxia has also explored "carbon asset" models since 2023, seeking to transform a vineyard's ability to absorb carbon dioxide into a tradable asset. In December 2025, the country's first wine vineyard carbon transaction was completed in Ningxia.
This transaction was of great significance as it verified that the "carbon asset" has a market-oriented foundation, while also providing a replicable and scalable practical model for the green transformation of the global wine industry, according to the management committee of the wine industrial park at the eastern foot of Helan Mountain.
In December 2025, the wine region at Ningxia's eastern foot of Helan Mountain was awarded the International Sustainable Development Award at the 20th Bettane & Desseauve Ministry of Foreign Affairs Celebration held in France, becoming the first Chinese wine region to receive this honor.
Sergio Cabrera, ambassador of Colombia to China, said Ningxia's wines not only excel in quality but also embody an outstanding environmental protection philosophy that puts ecology first in industrial development, an approach worthy of global reference.
The 47th World Congress of Vine and Wine, meanwhile, opened on Monday in Yinchuan, capital of Ningxia. This is the first time the congress, held alongside the 24th General Assembly of the International Organization of Vine and Wine (OIV), has been hosted in Asia since its launch in 1924.
Yvette van der Merwe, OIV's president, hailed China's important role and its growing contribution to the international vine and wine industry, highlighting Ningxia's significant development as a wine-producing region.
The eastern foot of Helan Mountain in Ningxia has become China's largest contiguous wine grape production area. This region has roughly 40,467 hectares dedicated to wine grape cultivation and development, accounting for nearly 42 percent of China's total planting area. ■

Across China: 5 years on, preservation efforts bear fruit in tropical rainforest park in south China's Hainan
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
14:50:59 CST
15:50:59 KST

HAIKOU, Oct. 13 (Xinhua) -- Streams babble through the forest. Birds chirp in clear and crisp notes. Dense vegetation thrives everywhere.
Hainan in south China is typically known for its coconut palms, beaches and sea breezes, but tucked away in the central part of this tropical island province is a different world.
The tropical rainforest in central Hainan is the most concentrated, best-preserved and largest contiguous continental-island-type tropical rainforest in China, and forms an important part of the world's tropical rainforest system.
In 2021, China formally established its first batch of five national parks, including the National Park of Hainan Tropical Rainforest. With a total area of 4,269 square kilometers, the park spans nine cities and counties and accounts for about one-eighth of Hainan Island's land area. Monday marked the fifth anniversary of its establishment.
Over the past five years, construction of the park has made solid progress. According to the latest figures from the Administration of Hainan Tropical Rainforest National Park, 91 new wildlife and plant species have been discovered, and more than 95 percent of Hainan's primary forest and over 55 percent of its natural forest have been effectively protected.
Data from the National Forestry and Grassland Administration showed the population of Hainan's resident gibbons has increased to 44 in seven groups, making it the only gibbon species in the world with a continuously growing population.
During this year's Mid-Autumn Festival and National Day holidays, the park's Yinggezui nature experience area opened to the public by reservation for the first time, with visitors from across the country coming in awe of the quietness and grandeur of this hidden rainforest realm. The experience area followed the principle of "ecological protection first, limited and orderly opening," offering free reservations with a daily cap of 800 visitors.
Fu Mingkai, a local staff member, said the area had been fully booked every day from Oct. 1 to 6.
"The area has not undergone excessive commercial transformation," Fu said, adding that visitors can get a close-up view of highly representative original rainforest landscapes, such as buttress roots and cauliflory, by slowly walking along a dedicated ecological route.
"This is a globally important gene pool of germplasm resources, and it is home to many plants and animals unique to Hainan," Fu said. "For example, the Hainan gibbon and the Hainan peacock-pheasant, which have very high requirements for their habitat, have both been found here."
The fact that the species appear here and that their populations have recovered shows the rainforest is healthy and full of vitality, he added.
"Thanks to strict protection in recent years, the vegetation has recovered and wildlife in the rainforest is improving," Fu said.
After the holidays, the Yinggezui experience area will continue to open by reservation on holidays, weekends and other periods to better meet public demand for ecological sightseeing and science education, he said.
Hainan has been sparing no effort in ecological protection.
Fu Cairui, another local staff member, has worked in rainforest protection for more than 20 years.
"More than 20 years ago, the surrounding mountains were full of life, but some local residents practiced slash-and-burn farming, and some primary forests were slowly eroded," he said. "Forests that once extended to low elevations could later only be seen at middle and high elevations."
Species such as the clouded leopard, Hainan peacock-pheasant and pangolin were common in his grandparents' time, but later became critically endangered, he said.
In his view, protecting the tropical rainforest is vitally important.
"Tropical rainforests have extremely high ecological value. They absorb carbon dioxide, release oxygen and slow climate change. They conserve water, purify water quality and maintain the regional water cycle. They also contain rich species resources and are a natural gene bank. To protect the tropical rainforest is to protect the habitats of rare plants and animals," he added.
Everyone is responsible for protecting the rainforest, Fu said.
"People can actively take part in environmental public welfare activities," he said. "We also go to schools and villages around communities to give lectures, and we hope the public will pay more attention to and support our work." ■

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — The Air Force has proposed allowing eligible pilots to serve until age 58, Defense Minister Wellington Koo (顧立雄) said Tuesday.
Under the existing system, lieutenant colonels face a service limit of 26 years, or approximately age 48, while colonels face a limit of 30 years, or approximately age 52. Pilots who leave the military lose their flight allowances, Koo said. The proposed extension would help the Air Force retain experienced officers, per Liberty Times.
Eligible lieutenant colonels and colonels could serve until age 58 regardless of those limits, per CNA. The plan would still require annual health checks and other regular reviews, the minister said. Officers who failed the tests could no longer continue flying.
Koo said he believed pilots loved flying and would be proud to continue serving. Maintaining their flight allowances until age 58 would also reduce the pressure to change careers in middle age and seek work in the private sector, he said.

Spain's royal couple are expected in Ceuta on Tuesday, 13 October, as the North African enclave continues to recover from an unprecedented migration crisis. On 30 and 31 July, more than 70,000 people crossed the border from Morocco, a figure approaching the city's entire population of 80,000.

Morocco's territorial claims add a further diplomatic dimension to the trip.

Healey should ‘stay the course’ and repair UK finances, says top IMF economist
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
06:49:39 UTC
15:49:39 KST

John Healey should “stay the course” and continue repairing the UK’s public finances, the International Monetary Fund’s top economist has said, after the fund lifted its growth forecast for Britain.
Little more than a fortnight before Healey’s first budget, Silvana Tenreyro, the IMF’s economic counsellor, said the UK “stands out” among G7 countries in having a plan to narrow its deficit.
“The UK has already started a consolidation process,” she said. “The message for the UK is simply, stay the course.”
Tenreyro, a former member of the Bank of England’s monetary policy committee, was speaking at the launch of the IMF’s twice-yearly World Economic Outlook (WEO) at the fund’s annual meetings in Bangkok.
Healey is under pressure to announce a generous energy support package in the budget, before the sharp rise in energy bills expected in January.
But in its WEO report, the IMF advises member governments against across-the-board subsidies, saying any support should be “temporary, targeted and non-distortionary”.
In a fillip for the chancellor, who is due to arrive in Bangkok later this week, the IMF has upgraded its growth forecast for the UK this year, but it expects a modest slowdown in 2027 as higher energy prices take their toll.
Responding, Healey said: “Conflict in the Middle East and Europe is hitting people in the UK and around the world. But Britain’s economy is showing strong international resilience in the face of these challenges.”
The IMF predicted GDP growth of 1.3% for the UK this year, up 0.3 percentage points from its most recent update in July.
UK GDP growth has been stronger than expected in early 2026, at 0.6% in the first quarter and 0.5% in the second quarter. The Office for National Statistics has pointed to the strong expansion of AI-related businesses as one factor behind the upside surprise.
However, the IMF warned that prolonged high oil prices and rising interest rates meant growth was likely to “edge down” in 2027 “as higher energy prices and long-term interest rates weigh on consumption and investment”.
It cut its UK growth forecast for next year modestly to 1.2%, from 1.3%.
Markets have been revising up their expectations of future inflation and interest rates across big economies since the Middle East conflict re-escalated in the summer.
The Bank of England’s nine-member monetary policy committee is now widely expected to raise the policy rate at its November meeting, echoing similar moves by the Federal Reserve, European Central Bank and Bank of Japan.
Mortgage rates in the UK have already been rising in response to higher funding costs for banks in financial markets.
The BoE policymaker Megan Greene argued on Tuesday morning that the IMF’s growth upgrade was proof that UK interest rates should be higher.
Speaking to the Atlantic Council at the IMF meetings in Bangkok, Greene argued that interest rates were currently not very restrictive.
“There’s more recently been some labour market data that has also suggested that maybe slack in the labour market has peaked, so the labour market is loose,” Greene said.
The IMF singled out the UK as among the countries – also including Japan – where core inflation, which excludes volatile commodities such as energy, was not expected to return to the 2% target until late next year.
It expects average inflation in the UK to be 3.3% this year and to remain at 2.8% in 2027 – a challenge for Healey and the prime minister, Andy Burnham, who are promising to offer voters a “breathing space” from rising costs.
Healey will spend little more than 24 hours in the Thai capital before flying home to put the finishing touches to his 28 October budget.
He is expected to focus on plans to devolve more tax revenues to mayoralties, alongside measures to help households cope with higher energy bills before the winter.
A string of other challenging decisions, including when the UK should be aiming to spend 3% of GDP on defence, is expected to be delayed until a big spending review at some point next year.
The Institute for Fiscal Studies (IFS) warned this week that the budget would be a “work of fiction” unless Healey explained how he would deal with what it said were £35bn of future spending pressures.

Fuel prices: Sébastien Lecornu promises €10 cut per fill-up
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
06:45:00 UTC
15:45:00 KST

In France, pump prices are among the highest in the European Union. The government has moved to cut the price per litre by 12 to 18 centimes, the prime minister said on Monday.
Diesel prices in France will fall by up to 18 cents per litre from Sunday 1 November as the government releases fuel from its strategic reserves. The prime minister promises savings "of around €10 for a full tank".
Sébastien Lecornu announced the measure on X on Monday 12 October after meeting fuel distributors.
"Facing a crisis we did not choose, [...] the state is shouldering its responsibilities," he said.
The reduction will also apply to domestic heating oil, diesel sold to transport professionals and off-road diesel used by farmers, fishers and construction workers.
The measure will run until the end of January. The government will sell 10 million barrels of diesel at cost price from its strategic reserves, bought before the start of the war in Iran at €0.28 per litre.
53 litres of diesel for one day’s wages
Government support seemed inevitable. France is currently one of the EU countries where pump prices are highest, with an average of €2.355 per litre of diesel as of 5 October, according to the comparison site fuel-prices.eu. That is well above the EU-27 average of €2.149 per litre. Only Finland (€2.553), the Netherlands (€2.506) and Denmark (€2.488) are more expensive.
However, the surge in prices at the pump is not limited to France. Prices are also reaching record levels in neighbouring countries. In Belgium, a litre sells for an average of €2.349, compared with €2.254 in Germany and €2.273 in Italy.
Spain, meanwhile, is one of the countries with the lowest average price, with a litre selling for €1.918.
But the price displayed at the pump is not enough to gauge how hard the bill hits motorists. Wage levels also play a decisive role. While Spain appears to be doing better, a worker on the country’s average wage can buy 54.2 litres of diesel with one day’s pay. In France, one day’s pay buys 52.8 litres, compared with 47 litres in Italy and 62.3 litres in Germany.
And when it comes to filling up the tank, France sits around the EU average, with a full tank equivalent to 4.4% of the average net monthly wage.
The situation is broadly similar for petrol. France is among the countries where a litre is most expensive, at an average of €2.212 on 5 October. Here too, the country’s average prices are much higher than those in the EU (€2.006), but below the average price per litre in Denmark (€2.605, a figure that takes into account potential discounts), the Netherlands (€2.432) and Finland (€2.370).
However, France is also close to the European average when petrol prices are compared with average wages. One day’s pay buys 56.2 litres, compared with an EU average of 57.4 litres.
Heating oil far pricier than the European average
Motorists are not the only ones bearing the brunt of soaring energy prices. As winter approaches, heating costs are also a source of concern for households that use heating oil. On 5 October, 1,000 litres of domestic heating oil were selling for €1,907.08 in France, €165.14 more than the EU average and €179.09 more than in the euro area, according to the European Commission’s figures.
In recent months, prices in France have followed the same trend as in Portugal and Italy, where 1,000 litres of domestic heating oil now sell for €2,204 and €2,063.10 respectively.
Other countries have nonetheless managed to keep prices more affordable. In Germany, heating oil sells for €1,726.40 per 1,000 litres. In Belgium and Spain, heating oil is cheaper still, at €1,533.40 and €1,495.34 respectively, 19.6% and 21.6% less than in France.

Built-in Agility and the Architecture of the Infinite Lifecycle
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
06:45:00 UTC
15:45:00 KST

While architecture often responds to a specific program of uses, taking into account areas, contexts, and various economic and technical conditions, buildings rarely remain the same throughout their lifespan. Programs, spatial dynamics, and users' needs change, as do environmental, economic, and technological conditions, requiring interventions that were likely not anticipated at the beginning of a project. Steel structures make it possible to envision architecture capable of growing, transforming, being disassembled, and reassembled. Their dimensional precision, industrialized components, and potential for mechanical connections enable the design of open systems prepared for future interventions.
Just as Mies van der Rohe designed the Neue Nationalgalerie in Berlin and Richard Rogers and Renzo Piano designed the Centre Pompidou in Paris, steel was embraced by numerous architects throughout the 20th century, enabling them to create everything from large-span and high-rise structures to more flexible spaces with greater degrees of freedom. As its applications have evolved over time, steel has continued to support the development of adaptable architecture, even allowing future expansions to be planned from the earliest stages of a project.
Rather than understanding buildings as closed and definitive volumes, structural systems can establish growth strategies that anticipate future connections, reserve areas for extensions, or dimension certain elements to accommodate additions at a later stage. Planning for expansion thus becomes part of an architectural approach conceived as an ongoing process, in which a building can begin with a given floor area and later incorporate new modules, levels, or spaces without altering its existing structure. By working with standardized components and repetitive systems, steel supports this logic of incremental growth, allowing new elements to be integrated into preexisting structures.
When Steel Adapts to New Uses
However, adaptability also means responding to transformations that do not necessarily require more floor area, but instead accommodate new uses. An office can be converted into housing; an industrial building can host cultural activities; and a commercial structure can house educational or community programs. The capacity for adaptation depends on how much of the existing architecture can be retained while its interior components and building systems are modified. Steel supports this approach by allowing different components to be joined through mechanical connections, reducing reliance on permanent construction methods. Bolted connections, for example, make it possible to disassemble and reassemble certain elements, avoiding the need for extensive demolition.
At the heart of a historic village, "Laab Is More" reflects a model of community life rooted in mutual support and shared assistance. Blending modern and traditional elements, the house's aesthetic responds to the owner's appreciation for traditional ways of living, while the strategic use of steel reflects the spirit of northern craftsmanship and integrates with the community's simple, rural character. The layout draws on the region's traditional vernacular architecture and makes use of locally available materials, adapting them to new applications and a contemporary design.
The commission called for a shelter that would provide privacy and an inviting space for gathering while moving away from the traditional wooden structures of neighboring houses and minimizing the use of wood. The architecture tells a story about an emotional connection to the region's vernacular culture, where people traditionally sit on the floor and enjoy a staple dish called "Laab," as their ancestors did.
To ensure strength and durability, the foundations and structural system were built in concrete, supporting the steel columns, beams, and roof truss. Studio Sifah selected corrugated steel roofing sheets—made from BlueScope Zacs Cool steel in Asian White color with corrugated profile—to complement the zinc and fiber-cement roofs found throughout the surrounding area. The wall cladding echoes the dimensions and texture of the wooden panels traditionally used in rice barns, a familiar element of the northern region. The roof is separated from the walls, creating an intermediate space that visually lightens the structure. BlueScope Zacs Cool sheets in Asian White color were folded and finished with rubber strips, while concrete and steel were used to evoke the lightness of traditional vernacular wooden houses.
Steel as a Resilient and Functional Technology
Beyond the durability of steel and its ability to establish relationships with its surroundings, the material can also serve practical functions that extend beyond aesthetics. For example, designing for disassembly introduces a new perspective. A beam, column, or industrialized component can become a potential resource for recovery, allowing building components to be replaced, relocated, or reused once a program changes or an existing structure requires intervention. Partial disassembly can be useful for renovating specific parts of a building without affecting the entire structure, while a more comprehensive approach can allow recovered components to find new applications elsewhere.
Trinity House, clad in COLORBOND® steel in Gull Grey color, demonstrates how material selection can serve a practical function beyond aesthetics. From the roof to the walls, the building features a consistent palette and pattern defined by gray tones. But the material does more than establish a visual identity: COLORBOND® steel with THERMATECH® solar reflectance technology reduces heat absorption at the surface, helping maintain comfortable interior temperatures. In addition, CLEAN TECHNOLOGY, which uses a Super Polyester paint system, helps preserve the home's color over time. By combining aesthetics and performance, the use of COLORBOND® steel and advanced technologies demonstrates how material choices can contribute to attractive, comfortable, and adaptable environments.
Another example is FNI Office & Workshop, designed by architect Heru Mudito Prasetyo. The factory and office complex combines aesthetics and resilience through elevated structures, effective ventilation, optimized natural lighting, and minimal maintenance requirements. The project responds to a series of environmental and operational challenges. The client operates in the steel fabrication industry, where the production process relies on conveyor belts and rollers. The workshop was commissioned to accommodate and optimize these processes, which had become increasingly inefficient after years of use, limiting the production line. The building's volume responds to the project's requirements and challenges, seeking to accommodate the steel fabrication process, address the constraints of the site, and improve the quality of life of its users.
Designing adaptable architecture does not necessarily mean attempting to anticipate every transformation that may occur throughout a building's lifespan. It means creating structures flexible enough to accommodate different future scenarios. While the structural system establishes certain conditions—such as module dimensions, spans, load-bearing capacity, and connections—its components can be modified with greater freedom. From this perspective, a building's efficiency would depend not only on how much material or energy is required to construct it, but also on how many transformations it can accommodate without losing architectural or material value.
The potential of steel lies not only in its ability to achieve long spans, reduce construction time, or facilitate industrialized building processes. It also involves conceiving buildings as modifiable systems: structures capable of growing, adapting, being disassembled, and reconfigured. Rather than designing buildings that are intended to remain unchanged, this approach proposes creating buildings prepared to evolve, incorporating new needs without resorting to demolition and reconstruction. In a context where extending the lifespan of buildings and reducing material waste are becoming increasingly important, considering how buildings can transform becomes just as relevant as considering how they will be constructed in the first place.

IDF: mystery object that entered Israel from Lebanon was likely a balloon, not a drone
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
06:43:39 UTC
15:43:39 KST

An unidentified object that entered Israeli airspace Saturday night was most likely a balloon or another device kept airborne by hot air, rather than a drone, the IDF said Tuesday, following an extensive investigation into the incident.
According to the military, the object's origin and purpose remain unknown, and investigators cannot rule out the possibility that it was harmless and had simply drifted into Israeli territory.
"At this stage, it is not possible to determine with certainty its origin or purpose," the IDF said. "It can be established that it was not a drone or unmanned aerial vehicle, and it may have been an innocent object that drifted into Israeli territory."
The object was detected by Air Force observation personnel and detection systems, which tracked its movement and directed forces on the ground as they responded to the incident.
At the same time, security measures were reinforced in nearby communities, including the activation of local defense units, pending completion of the relevant checks.
The military said the object has still not been located despite continued searches. No changes have been made to Home Front Command instructions for civilians.
Addressing a recent increase in reports of false detections and interceptions, the IDF explained that distinguishing between a small drone and a bird can be extremely difficult for aerial detection systems.
Throughout the war, the Air Force has been responsible for detecting and intercepting threats across multiple fronts, with protecting civilians and deployed troops its primary priority.
"The difference between a drone and a bird is very small," the military said, explaining that it cannot afford to take risks when a potential threat is detected. Once a suspected threat is identified, forces must make rapid decisions that can lead to interception.
The IDF said it continues to search the area from the air and on the ground while reviewing its detection systems, with the aim of improving identification capabilities and applying lessons from recent operational incidents.

Sumykhimprom sale fails again for lack of bidders
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
09:42:59 EEST
15:42:59 KST

An auction to sell the state’s 99.9952% stake in Sumykhimprom, one of Ukraine’s largest chemical companies, did not take place because there were no buyers. It had been scheduled for October 13 in the Prozorro.Sale trading system with a starting price of UAH 1.005 billion.
“The asset is complex, with a heavy background, but for an investor in agrochemicals or building materials it is a ready site for building a national champion,” State Property Fund head Dmytro Natalukha said on Facebook on the eve of the auction.
A repeat online auction scheduled for January 13, 2026, with the price cut 9.3% to UAH 1.088 billion (excluding VAT), also failed for lack of participants, as did the previous auction on June 11, 2025.
On July 8 this year the government approved the terms and a starting price of UAH 1.005 billion for the stake.
Under the terms, the new owner had to keep the company’s main activities and invest at least UAH 150 million in technical re-equipment and modernization of production. The buyer also had to repay wage arrears, debts to the budget and overdue payables within six months, observe employees’ social guarantees under labor law and not lay anyone off for six months after the purchase.
The fund will offer several more big and interesting assets at auction next week, Natalukha said. First, the Odesa Portside Plant will go on sale on October 19.
“It is a pearl of Ukrainian industry, but also a monument to corruption that has survived five failed auctions and endless backroom games. It is the biggest and practically unique ammonia and urea transshipment hub on the Black Sea, with its own sea berths, terminals and direct access to deep water. It is a ready, world-class logistics and production hub,” he said, promoting it.
Two other assets, transferred to the state under the law on sanctions against Russians, are the Demurynsky Mining and Processing Plant and Motordetal-Konotop. Their auctions are scheduled for October 20.
Sumykhimprom is one of Ukraine’s largest producers of complex mineral fertilizers, titanium dioxide, sulfuric acid and other inorganic chemicals. It is one of the three biggest budget contributors in Sumy and the region, and it makes more than 30 grades of NPK fertilizers with different nutrient ratios for different soil and climate zones.
For more than 10 years the plant was managed by a group of companies linked to Group DF of entrepreneur Dmytro Firtash. In November 2023 the Sumy Region Commercial Court granted a motion by the State Property Fund and the Justice Ministry and closed the bankruptcy and rehabilitation proceedings against Sumykhimprom.
The fund planned to sell the company to a private investor even before the full-scale war, but privatization dragged on because of the position of Firtash, a minority shareholder who received 0.005% of the shares in 2010 and control of management. Sumykhimprom piled up debts, which made it possible to form a creditors’ committee and start rehabilitation proceedings.
The fund tried through the courts to end the bankruptcy proceedings from 2015 but succeeded only in 2023, which unblocked privatization.
Russian forces shelled the plant in March 2022, causing an ammonia leak. The plant stood idle for a year and resumed operations in spring 2023. As of June 2025 the front line was less than 30 km from Sumykhimprom.
According to its 2025 report, the company’s payables at the end of the year were UAH 4.135 billion, of which UAH 1.292 billion was debt in the bankruptcy case opened by the Sumy Region Commercial Court in October 2011, formed under the court-approved register of creditors.
“The lack of working capital, loss-making operations and plant downtime cause growth of payables,” the report said.
Sumykhimprom’s 2025 revenue was UAH 129.2 million (UAH 395.9 million a year earlier), gross profit UAH 53.3 million (UAH 9.9 million) and net loss UAH 405.7 million (UAH 600.2 million).
“The main reason for Sumykhimprom’s losses in 2025 is the forced downtime of production capacity from November 2024 to July 22, 2025 and the downtime of all structural units in the fourth quarter of 2025. In 2025, sulfuric acid shop No. 5 worked for only two months,” the report said.
Because of the worsening dangerous situation in the region, the regional military administration did not give permission to buy ammonia, which kept the company from launching its complex mineral fertilizer program as set out in the approved financial plan for 2025, the report said.

Malaysia’s Firefly cancels flights to Singapore over haze from Indonesia
Move comes as haze from Indonesian fires makes Singapore and Kuala Lumpur the world’s most polluted cities.
Firefly, a Malaysian low-cost airline, has extended the suspension of its flights between Kuala Lumpur and Singapore through Wednesday as smoke from fires in Indonesia continued to blanket the region.
The announcement came as IQAir, an air quality monitor, ranked Singapore and the Malaysian capital Kuala Lumpur as the world’s two most polluted cities on Tuesday.
Firefly said in a statement that flights between the Sultan Abdul Aziz Shah Airport (SZB) near Kuala Lumpur and the Seletar Airport in Singapore (XSP) have been cancelled up to Wednesday due to “weather and haze conditions”.
It called the action a “proactive safety measure”.
The fires, mostly on the Indonesian islands of Sumatra and Borneo, are the country’s most intense in 11 years. They have been spurred by El Nino, a weather pattern expected to be among the strongest in four decades.
IQAir, a Swiss air quality monitoring company, said Air Quality Index in Singapore stood at 199 on Tuesday and 183 in Kuala Lumpur. Readings above 150 are generally considered unhealthy, and those above 300 are classified as hazardous.
Firefly, a subsidiary of Malaysia Aviation Group, which includes Malaysia Airlines, first announced the flight cancellations on October 10, citing “low visibility” due to the haze conditions.
Firefly said that affected passengers were being rebooked on Malaysia Airlines flights between Kuala Lumpur International Airport and Singapore’s Changi Airport, subject to seat availability.
The Singapore government has reintroduced subsidised care for haze-related illnesses, as it last did in 2015, when smoke from Indonesian fires hung over the region for weeks.
In Malaysia, schools reopened in most states on Tuesday as air quality improved slightly, but they remain closed in three states, one federal territory and several districts.
Malaysia’s foreign minister, Mohamad Hasan, said on Monday that he would press for stronger regional mechanisms when foreign ministers of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) meet next month.
“We already have an ASEAN mechanism for natural disasters, but haze is not included or classified as a natural disaster,” he told reporters in Sepang, according to Bernama, Malaysia’s state news agency.
The Philippines, which chairs the bloc this year, confirmed that the issue would be on the agenda.
“It’s in the agenda,” Dominic Xavier Imperial, a spokesman for the Philippine Department of Foreign Affairs, said of the November meeting, which will precede the 49th ASEAN summit in Manila.
Mohamad, the Malaysian minister, said Indonesia had deployed about 60,000 personnel to fight the fires, but thick smoke had grounded 34 aircraft, including planes and helicopters.
Remote terrain and limited water supplies have also hindered the effort, he said, and cloud seeding is not possible without suitable rain clouds. He acknowledged Indonesia’s efforts but urged more effective action, citing the toll on Malaysian communities.

Video: Why does Finland celebrate failure?
Finland
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
09:41:36 EEST
15:41:36 KST

Back in 2010, a student group at Aalto University in Helsinki came up with an idea: what if failure was something to be celebrated, instead of lamented?
Their initiative became 'Epäonnistumisen päivä', or 'Failure Day', and it was marked for the first time on 13 October that year.
Since then, the concept has been picked up by organisations and businesses in dozens of countries around the world — from 'failure panels' in the US to 'failure meetups' in Japan.
October 13 has now become the 'International Day for Failure', and it seeks to remove the social stigma around making mistakes as a means of encouraging open discussions about setbacks, reframing failure as a normal aspect of every day, and to encourage people to create and innovate.

How Ukrainians Can Process an Inheritance While Abroad – Explanation by the Ministry of Justice

How Ukrainians Can Process an Inheritance While Abroad – Explanation by the Ministry of Justice
Kyiv • UNN
An inheritance can be accepted from abroad without traveling to Ukraine within six months. The application is submitted in person through a consulate or a notary.
Ukrainians residing abroad can accept an inheritance without personally traveling to Ukraine. This was reported by the Ministry of Justice of Ukraine, according to UNN.
It is not necessary to travel to Ukraine to accept an inheritance. If, at the time the inheritance was opened, you did not permanently reside with the deceased, you must submit an application to accept it. The general time limit is six months from the date the inheritance was opened. For those who permanently resided with the deceased at that time, a different rule applies: they are considered to have accepted the inheritance unless they rejected it within the established time limit
How to submit an application from abroad
According to the available information, to submit an application, the heir must have their signature certified at a Ukrainian consular office or by a foreign notary. If the document is оформed by a foreign notary, the requirements regarding an apostille or legalization and translation depend on the country and Ukraine’s international treaties.
Send the application by mail to a notary in Ukraine. It is advisable to first coordinate with the notary whether they can open or continue your inheritance case. Keep proof of dispatch: an application sent before the deadline for accepting the inheritance is considered timely, even if it reaches the notary later
The ministry emphasizes that the application to accept an inheritance must be submitted by the heir personally—a representative acting under a power of attorney cannot do this on their behalf. At the same time, the heir may authorize a representative in Ukraine to submit the documents required for the further processing of the inheritance and to obtain a certificate of the right to inherit.
Recall
All heirs under the law have equal shares in the inherited property unless otherwise provided by a will. However, the division of the inheritance may be changed by agreement among the heirs. What rules apply to inheritance and what should be taken into account.

‘People have a right to seek answers’: Inside India’s unrest over the electoral process
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
06:41:21 UTC
15:41:21 KST

‘People have a right to seek answers’: Inside India’s unrest over the electoral process
The administration in the Indian capital, New Delhi, has been on its toes since last week as Indian opposition parties and an informal movement known as Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) are staging protests over the removal of millions of names from voter lists.
New Delhi became a fortress over the weekend, with barricades made of iron and armed personnel stationed at nearly all major intersections ahead of the protests. Still, people showed up, thousands were detained, and the formal opposition parties took the baton with a massive march towards the Supreme Court on Monday.
The key demand of the protesters is the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar over allegations that a country-wide revision of the electoral database is helping the ruling Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) party, led by Prime Minister Narendra Modi, to stay in power and win elections across states. Both the BJP and the Election Commission have rejected the accusations.
CJP back in action
The CJP, a youth movement born out of an online meme, became prominent earlier this year for staging massive protests against irregularities in the examination system that eventually led to the resignation of the country’s education minister.
This time, the protests are challenging the nationwide Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of the electoral rolls done by the Election Commission of India earlier this year. The CJP and formal opposition parties allege that the SIR exercise caused the widespread and irresponsible deletion of people from electoral rolls. Reports say there have been 130 million names deleted from the provisional electoral rolls through the ongoing revision process. The Election Commission says this is necessary to eliminate duplicate names, names of deceased people, and those who have migrated. It also maintained that it operated strictly under constitutional and legal frameworks.
On Saturday, thousands of young activists, students, and opposition leaders gathered around Jantar Mantar and several other prominent locations in the center of the Indian capital. This is despite warnings from the police and the lack of official permission to protest.
The Delhi Police formally denied permission for the Jantar Mantar protest on Saturday, citing public order and traffic concerns. A 24-hour temporary mobile internet shutdown was enforced across central Delhi and key border points. Entry and exit were restricted or closed across 57 Delhi Metro stations around the central corridor, and over 60 incoming regional trains were canceled or short-terminated.
Over 23,000 police and paramilitary personnel were deployed across central intersections, converting locations like Connaught Place and Janpath into restricted zones.
“We have a right to protest against the Election Commissioner,” Ariba Fahim, 19, a student activist who was detained briefly near INA on Saturday during the demonstration, said.
Shiv Tanakiya, 21, a college student who traveled from Meerut in the neighboring state of Uttar Pradesh a day before the protest, said young people have a right to seek accountability from the government.
“We are the youth of this country wanting to be heard. We live in a democracy. We are not doing this at the behest of any opposition party, but this is a concern for the whole country,” he said.
Early Saturday morning, key CJP organizers Abhijeet Dipke, Saurav Das, and Ashutosh Ranka were taken into preventive custody directly from an incoming flight at Delhi Airport. After over 24 hours of preventive detention, all three were freed after a peace bond.
At a press conference shortly after their release on Sunday afternoon, the leaders condemned the government’s response, saying the use of thousands of security personnel and internet shutdowns against peaceful demonstrators exposed the administration’s fear of youth-led accountability.
“Picking up citizens off airplanes and shutting down an entire city just to block a peaceful protest is not governance; it is intimidation,” Das told reporters, reaffirming that the CJP would continue its pan-India campaign for electoral transparency despite the state restrictions.
Prominent YouTuber and influencer Dhruv Rathee, who traveled to Delhi from Germany where he resides, to take part in the protests was detained from his parents’ residence before he could do so. “I was not arrested or detained, I was KIDNAPPED,” Rathee said in a post on X after he returned home.
Official police reports indicate that over 7,000 individuals were taken into preventive detention across Delhi and surrounding border checkpoints throughout the day; most of them were freed on Sunday.
“We are educated peaceful protesters exercising our constitutional rights,” Kirti Sahu, 22, a university student who was detained near CP before being loaded onto a police bus, said. “The government caused inconvenience to people by shutting down metro stations, cutting the internet; you are proving our point about highhandedness.”
Another student protester, Rinku Singh, said the key demand is transparency in public institutions.
The CJP seemed to be prepared for the police crackdown. Just as the detentions started, founder Abhijeet Dipke dropped a pre-recorded video telling protesters to spread out. Prominent student leader Neha Bora, the president of All India Students’ Association, quickly shifted the crowds away from a blocked Jantar Mantar toward Connaught Place, outsmarting police barricades and keeping the protest moving across the city.
“Narendra Modi’s government cannot simply ignore young people. India has a massive youth population with high ambitions, but millions of educated graduates are struggling to find decent jobs, creating deep frustration,” Asim Ahmad, a researcher from Jamia Nagar, Delhi, who was also part of the protest, said.
Nitin Nabin, the president of the ruling BJP, lambasted the CJP protests and said the leaders working at the behest of the opposition cannot see India moving forward.
“PM Modi has the trust of [the 1.4 billion] people of India. We will ensure the Viksit Bharat dream will be taken forward, and any forces, whether they live in this country or outside trying to destabilize India will be strictly dealt with,” Nabin said in a post on X, adding that the opposition is attempting to destabilize the country in collusion with foreign powers.
Special attention
The Delhi protests were widely covered by international media, drawing immediate attention from the UN High Commissioner for Human Rights (OHCHR). It released a statement on Saturday, expressing concern over “mass detentions” and urging the Indian authorities to “ensure that the right to peaceful assembly is fully respected and fulfilled, and that those detained arbitrarily are released immediately.”
The Ministry of External Affairs issued a firm response, calling the OHCHR’s remarks “an unwarranted interference in the internal affairs of India”
“As in every democracy, Indian citizens exercise this right subject to the maintenance of public order and safety. Our law enforcement authorities act strictly in accordance with the law, and our courts remain available to all for the redressal of any grievances,” New Delhi said. It also noted that OHCHR’s “double standards” in commenting on protests – and the way local authorities respond to it – in various parts of the world.
“Violent responses to protests in our neighborhood have gone uncommented, as indeed have law enforcement actions in its own vicinity. Such double standards only erode the credibility of its standing and contribute to the loss of faith in multilateralism,” New Delhi said.
While images of detentions in India are dramatic, they are hardly comparable to those coming out of France, where student protesters have clashed with fully equipped riot police using tear gas and water cannons.
No official statement came from the OHCHR office regarding the French protests, though the spokesperson for the UN human rights office on Friday said the body is “following with concern incidents related to the student protests and high school blockades in France.”
“We call on everyone to ensure that they remain peaceful and that there is no disproportionate use of force by law enforcement,” the spokesperson said, according to Le Monde.
Opposition springs into action
The official opposition has called for new protest, with Rahul Gandhi, the head of the main opposition Congress party, leading a march to the Supreme Court on Monday. He was joined by other opposition leaders who form the INDIA (Indian National Developmental Inclusive Alliance) bloc.
At a press conference ahead of the march, Gandhi said the opposition’s fight will continue until the Election Commission’s leadership changes, the Constitution is upheld, and the electoral system is overhauled.
INDIA leaders filed a petition in the Supreme Court against the Election Commission, alleging large-scale voter deletions and irregularities in the electoral roll revisions. The plea also raises concerns over restrictions on peaceful demonstrations.
In anticipation of the opposition march, Delhi Police not only barricaded all major access roads with multiple layers of barriers and closed nearby metro stations, but also de-notified Jantar Mantar as a designated protest site – a role it had served for more than three decades.
Under the new arrangement, protests will be permitted only at Ramlila Maidan in central Delhi, Burari Ground in north Delhi, and CBD Ground in east Delhi.
However, in a special hearing on Sunday following the October 10 security lockdown, a Supreme Court bench comprising Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V. Mohana reasserted the constitutional right to peaceful assembly, ordered an immediate halt to all unauthorized preventive detentions, and demanded the full restoration of normal transit and mobile internet services across the capital. The court stressed that while law enforcement can enforce prohibitory orders in specific restricted zones, citizens holding peaceful, unarmed demonstrations cannot be subjected to city-wide blackouts or arbitrary detentions.
Thousands took part in the march on Monday, with drone footage showing massive crowds in the streets of central Delhi leading to the Supreme Court building, which Gandhi and other opposition leaders reached by the evening. Chief Justice of India Surya Kant earlier declined the request of the opposition for a meeting, arguing, according to the media reports, that the meeting would be inappropriate as the issues to be raised are already sub judice before the Supreme Court.
While local protests over the electoral rolls have been seen in other large cities, including Mumbai and Bengaluru, agitation is yet to become nationwide. What is clear, however, is that it is unlikely to die out easily.
“It is the people who choose the government. People have a right to seek answers, but this government is not listening and is using police to stop peaceful demonstrations,” Shiv Tanakiya said. “We are the future of this country, and we must be heard.”

IMF upgrades 2026 growth forecast but warns of ‘split’ outlook
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
06:40:36 UTC
15:40:36 KST

In its latest edition of the World Economic Outlook, the IMF has warned that low-income countries remain vulnerable to the supply shocks. (AA Photo)
The International Monetary Fund on Oct. 13 forecast global growth in 2026 would slow less than previously expected because of advanced economies’ “resilience” in the face of war-fuelled energy prices, but warned low-income countries remained vulnerable to the supply shock.
In its World Economic Outlook (WEO) released at the organization’s Annual Meetings in Bangkok, the IMF raised its 2026 global growth forecast by 0.1 percentage points to 3.1 percent, compared with 3.5 percent growth in 2025.
It warned that while many advanced economies have been buoyed by rising investment in artificial intelligence (AI) technology, poorer countries that are not benefiting from that boom face stark choices as they deal with high energy prices caused by the Iran war.
“The global economy has been resilient, but that resilience is under strain, with risks tilted to the downside,” Silvana Tenreyro, the IMF’s chief economist, told journalists in Bangkok.
With global debt-to-GDP ratios at sky-high levels, including in advanced economies, the IMF has called on governments to cut spending and manage borrowing -- a difficult task for those in the developing world struggling with the Iran war shock.
“What we are advocating for is for policymakers to balance the near-term needs of inflation, and that involves food security, that involves energy security... while also keeping in mind the medium-term stability,” said Deniz Igan, chief of the IMF’s World Economic Studies division.
The United States’ war on Iran, launched in February, has plunged the Middle East into violence and seen global energy prices skyrocket as a result of Tehran’s retaliation.
Prices of refined petroleum products remain between 70 and 95 percent above pre-war levels, putting pressure on countries dependent on energy imports for economic activity.
“A more prolonged disruption of production and transport in the Middle East could lead to” higher inflation and a drag on growth, said Tenreyro.
Energy-importing countries not exposed to the AI boom remain the most vulnerable, creating what the IMF termed a “bifurcated outlook” in its WEO report.
The report detailed that the twin economic forces of the war in Iran and the AI technology boom had created a “fragmented” world economy.
“Headwinds from a prolonged war and persistent geopolitical tensions could revive inflationary pressures, strain fiscal and external positions, and hit energy-importing and low-income countries hardest,” it said.
“At the same time, the current technology tailwind could stop abruptly if expectations about AI-related profits and productivity gains are reassessed, weakening investment and tightening financial conditions.”
Responding to AFP, Tenreyro said AI had been a major factor driving the world economy, accounting for almost half of the increase in global trade from 2023 to 2025.
The IMF’s split view of the world economy was evident in its specific projections.
The Middle East and Central Asia region is expected to suffer a 0.3 percent contraction in 2026. Saudi Arabia’s is one of the worst affected, with its economy projected to shrink 3.3 percent — representing a 5 percentage points cut in the Fund’s forecast.
The IMF said the region is expected to bounce back quickly once the war is over, but there remains high uncertainty as to when that will be.
In advanced economies, growth fueled by the AI boom and other factors remained strong.
The world’s advanced economies were forecast to grow 2.1 percent in 2026, with those in the AI supply chain such as Taiwan and South Korea posting significantly higher figures.
Growth in China, the world’s second-largest economy, was expected to slow, the IMF said, mainly because of weak domestic demand.
Global inflation remained set to accelerate to 4.7 percent in 2026, with effects spread across advanced and developing economies.
Tenreyro warned that urgent action was required by all countries in the face of downside risks, and called on governments to only use temporary, targeted measures to help ease the burden on the public of high energy and other costs.
In lockstep, “monetary policy should remain firmly focused on price stability”, she added, indicating that interest rate hikes to curb high inflation were appropriate.
“The economy has been resilient, but that resilience is reaching its limits,” she said. “The task ahead is to move from coping to rebuilding, restoring fiscal space and supply-side resilience.”

Heavy rain and strong winds have caused serious damage in Baja California and Guerrero, where authorities seek six missing and deploy thousands of rescue workers amid further flood risk.
Hurricane Simon battered Mexico's west coast on Monday with powerful winds and torrential rain, after several weather systems left at least five people dead and caused widespread damage to property in Pacific coastal communities.
The eye of the Category 2 hurricane has remained offshore, although its outer bands have lashed communities located between the Sierra Madre and the Pacific Ocean, near Puerto Vallarta.
In the state of Baja California, rescue teams have continued searching for missing people in the coastal city of Ensenada, where floods have swept away vehicles and damaged homes. Another six people remain missing, four in Ensenada and two in San Felipe. Landslides and overflowing rivers have cut off a number of communities.
The Mexican army has rescued 32 people by helicopter, including 22 foreign nationals, who had been trapped on a ranch in Ensenada. According to the authorities, the group included German and US citizens, as well as several missionaries.
The governor of Baja California, Marina del Pilar Ávila, said that around 14,000 federal and state personnel have been deployed to assist those affected and respond to the emergency.
Simon threatens further flooding and landslides
Further south, Simon has brought down trees and power lines, blocked roads and flooded homes in several coastal communities in the state of Guerrero, including the port of Acapulco. The governor, Evelyn Salgado, has confirmed the death of a 71-year-old man after a wall collapsed in Chilpancingo, the state capital.
By late Monday, the hurricane was producing sustained winds of up to 155 kilometres per hour and is expected to maintain its strength for much of the week, according to the US National Hurricane Center, which has warned of potentially life-threatening flooding and landslides before a possible landfall on Friday.
In Puerto Vallarta, easing rainfall has allowed the reopening of some shops, although the international airport has suspended operations until Tuesday morning. The authorities remain on alert amid uncertainty over the storm's trajectory.
Meanwhile, in the south-western United States, most flood warnings have been lifted after surges caused over the weekend by the remnants of tropical storm Rachel in Las Vegas.

Germany news: Left-leaning Berlin coalition talks break down
Published October 13, 2026last updated October 13, 2026
What you need to know
- Berlin's SPD and Greens stop regional parliament coalition talks with the Left Party, disappointed with its pledges on Israel and organized crime
- They did leave the door open to potentially restart the exploratory talks, however
- International Monetary Fund raises Germany's 2026 growth forecast to 1.3%, up from just 0.7% in July
- Investment in infrastructure and defense, stronger exports and demand linked to artificial intelligence are helping the recovery
- Germany's 2026 wine harvest is expected to be around 20% below the ten-year average
Here is a roundup of top stories from and about Germany on Tuesday, October 13, 2026:
Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add DW as a Preferred Source on Google.
Why have the Berlin exploratory talks broken down within a week?
The breakdown in the exploratory talks can be traced back to concerns about the often highly critical stance on Israel adopted by some members of the Left Party, coupled with criticism of the appearance of a figure linked to organized crime at an election night party.
The Left scored well with parts of Berlin's population, not least the young and communities with more people of migrant backgrounds, with an unusually stern line on Israeli wars in Gaza and elsewhere in the Middle East by the often muted standards of German politics.
But comments from its more outspoken members and controversies like an organized crime boss attending an election-night after-party led to questions — particularly in some newspapers and from the conservative Christian Democrats — about whether center-left parties could work under the Left's leadership.
In a bid to settle this, the Greens, SPD and Left drafted a joint statement on antisemitism, Israel's right to exist and maintaining a distance from organized crime before starting their talks.
But the text subsequently faced criticism from within the Left's own ranks.
On Tuesday, as 44 Left Party members of the new Berlin parliament met, they instead signed off on a different text more closely aligned to the party's past internal position papers.
"We stand by Israel's right to exist and for equal rights for all people in Israel. Equally we stand by Palestine's right to exist and for equal rights for all people in Palestine," the Left Party's text read.
Among other things, this omits a reference in the joint text to Israel's right to exist being "non-negotiable," and to listing potential sanctions for transgressions potentially extending as far as being ejected from the party.
The CDU — which emerged as the second-largest party in the vote, well adrift of the Left on 18.8% — argue that the SPD and Greens should negotiate a coalition government with them instead.
Chancellor Merz had also weighed into the discussion, saying that the allegations of impropriety facing the Left Party cannot be "dismissed with a piece of paper." In the meantime, the party's state lawmakers appear to have disavowed that piece of paper anyway.
Berlin: SPD and Greens halt exploratory coalition talks with Left Party
Berlin's center-left Social Democrats (SPD) and environmentalist Greens have halted exploratory coalition talks with the socialist Left Party , which followed last month's regional elections.
The two parties' lead candidates from the state elections, Werner Graf of the Greens and Steffen Krach of the SPD, announced the move in a joint statement on Tuesday evening.
They referred to Left Party meetings earlier in the day in which party members signed a statement on handling antisemitism and on Israel's right to exist, but using a text that differed from a statement the three parties had jointly agreed to when opening the negotiations.
"We have taken note that the Left Party have reached a different arrangement within their own party," Graf and Krach's statement said.
However, the SPD and Greens also made clear that they were not closing the door on the Left Party entirely.
"This means that at this point we have to interrupt the coalition negotiations, so as to evaluate whether or not our agreement from last week still stands," they wrote. "We expect the Left Party to make clear to us to what extent they take the agreements they made seriously and intend to implement them."
The Left Party emerged as the largest party Berlin's close-fought election last month, claiming just under 26% of the vote, faring particularly well with young voters.
The Greens won just over 14% and the SPD just over 12% — meaning that the three left-leaning parties would command a slim majority if combined.
In theory, the SPD and Greens could also ally with the conservative CDU, but this would yield an even more fragile majority in the city-state's parliament, with stiff populist opposition from the AfD on the far-right and the Left on the other flank.
Astronaut Adenot: Mars voyage with current tech would be 'disaster'
French astronaut Sophie Adenot spoke to reporters at the European Space Agency (ESA) headquarters in Cologne on Tuesday, shortly after her return from the International Space Station.
She said that based on her experiences, it was too early to consider a mission to Mars the likes of which Elon Musk has been touting for years.
"We are not ready, we need technological breakthroughs," Adenot said, recalling her thoughts on landing in the Pacific Ocean five days ago after months in orbit.
"The moment the capsule opened, the first thing I said was, 'send me back to space,' because I was getting seasick on the waves," Adenot said. "But the second thing I said was that we are not ready to fly to Mars."
Adenot explained how around half of astronauts experienced symptoms like she did on returning from a long stretch in space, like pronounced frailty and nausea.
"With the technology that we currently have, a very long mission, a journey to Mars lasting months — just imagine the disaster," Adenot said.
Adenot said that technological breakthroughs were needed, either to drastically shorten the travel time, "or for example to artificially generate gravity," perhaps by having the spacecraft in a permanent state of rotation.
Adenot spent eight months on the International Space Station — a comparable amount of time that it would theoretically take to fly to Mars with current propulsion methods.
But she said that on the ISS there was much more space and much better facilities for exercise and movement than any transport vessel could offer. 
Boateng 'proud and happy' in Trabzonspor coaching role after Bayern job fell through
Former Germany defender Jerome Boateng has confirmed reports of him taking up a coaching role with Turkish top-flight club Trabzonspor.
"I am very proud and happy to be a part of the coaching staff," Boateng wrote on Instagram, saying it meant "a great deal to me" to learn from Trabzonspor's German head coach and his team every day.
The 2014 World Cup winner Boateng also said the role allowed him to share his experience and work with players "on and off the pitch, which is very valuable to me."
One of those Trabzonspor players is Egyptian superstar Mohamed Salah, who joined from Liverpool in the offseason and has hit the ground running scoring a goal a game.
Boateng's appointment follows around a year after a planned start to his coaching career at his former club Bayern Munich fell through.
Boateng retired as a player in September 2025. He was then invited by head coach Vincent Kompany to gain experience with the Bundesliga champions. But after vocal fan protests, Boateng said he had decided to focus on other matters given the "recent discussions about me."
The protests appeared to be linked to a 2024 Munich court ruling, which found Boateng guilty of intentionally causing bodily harm to a former girlfriend and issued him a formal warning. Boateng denies ever having hit a woman.
Ukraine allies in Poland after 'very difficult few days' with Trump
The foreign ministers of Germany, Norway, Poland and the UK spoke at the Warsaw Security Forum on Tuesday.
They expressed criticism and skepticism about US President Donald Trump's approach to the conflict in Ukraine in the past week.
German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul bemoaned the US decision to lift sanctions on Russian diesel as part of a deal to supply the US — seemingly struck as Trump panics about fuel prices with the Iran war still unresolved and a month to go until mid-term elections.
"I would say this is not the time to lower the sanctions regime but to strengthen this," Wadephul said.
"We are keeping our course," he said, adding that Europe was asking the authorities in Washington to do the same.
UK Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband arguably found even clearer words.
"Within the bounds of diplomacy we should acknowledge that it's been a very difficult few days," Miliband said in the Polish capital that's just a few hours' drive from Ukraine's western border.
He lauded Zelenskyy for showing "extraordinary leadership ... in the most difficult of circumstances" since Putin's 2022 full-scale invasion, shortly after Trump's call — mirroring Russian messaging — for presidential elections in war-torn Ukraine.
However, Miliband also said the notion of an "energy ceasefire" raised by Trump — seemingly unilaterally — was nevertheless worthy of consideration given the attacks on Ukrainian energy infrastructure and the onset of winter.
"So let us take up this idea of the full energy ceasefire and let us seek with President Trump to hold Putin to this full energy ceasefire, because that is what we need."
Miliband noted how Zelenskyy had expressed a willingness in theory, even if Russia was yet to do so.
IMF nearly doubles German growth forecast to 1.3%
The International Monetary Fund (IMF) has raised its forecast for German economic growth this year to 1.3%, almost double the 0.7% it predicted in July.
It now expects Europe's largest economy to expand by 1.1% in 2027, an upward revision of 0.1 percentage points.
The figures match the German government's forecasts released last week. The Economy Ministry said the economy had proved more resilient than expected despite higher energy prices and uncertainty over US tariffs.
Government investment in infrastructure and defense, alongside stronger exports, has helped support the recovery. German suppliers are also benefiting from investment in artificial intelligence.
The IMF slightly raised its global growth forecast for 2026 to 3.1%, from 3.0%, while keeping its projection for next year unchanged at 3.4%.
Strong investment in AI has helped offset the energy shock caused by the war in the Middle East. Higher oil production outside the Gulf, releases from strategic reserves and weaker demand in China have also cushioned the impact.
The IMF raised its eurozone growth forecast for this year by 0.2 percentage points to 1.1%. It still expects growth of 1.2% in 2027.
However, higher energy prices and weak consumer confidence continue to weigh on the currency bloc's economy.
Berlin airport cuts outlook as Ryanair scales back
Berlin Brandenburg Airport (BER) expects passenger numbers to fall this year and next as Ryanair cuts its services, airport chief Aletta von Massenbach said.
The airport now forecasts 25.7 million passengers in 2026, down from 26.1 million last year, a decline von Massenbach described as the "Ryanair effect."
Other airlines would partly offset Ryanair's cuts, but would not fill the gap entirely, she said.
The airport is reviewing all costs and postponing investments in response.
"This is a heavy blow," von Massenbach said of Ryanair's decision to close its BER base, comprising seven aircraft and their crews, on October 24.
Europe's largest budget airline will continue flying to Berlin but will cut roughly half its services, removing around 2.5 million seats a year, she said.
Ryanair has called BER "Europe's most unsuccessful airport." Von Massenbach said she understood the airline's frustration over high costs in Germany, interpreting its criticism as primarily directed at the federal government.
"Everything they say against BER, they are saying against Germany," she said.
The aviation industry has long criticized Germany's comparatively high taxes and fees, arguing that they are a main reason air traffic has recovered more slowly from the pandemic than elsewhere in Europe.
Fighter jets escort plane to Nuremberg airport
German fighter jets escorted a passenger plane from Greece to Nuremberg, prompting a temporary airport closure. Police later gave the all-clear, saying everyone on board was safe.

Pistorius says Trump has his 'back against the wall'
German Defense Minister Boris Pistorius says US President Donald Trump is under severe domestic political pressure and that his threats should be viewed in the context of the upcoming US midterm elections.
Trump has his political "back against the wall," Pistorius, of the center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD), told an employers' conference in Berlin.
History shows that leaders under pressure at home seek opportunities abroad to score political points, he said, adding that he believed the strategy would backfire.

Merz made the remarks after being asked whether he was prepared to confront opposition to potentially unpopular reforms aimed at making Germany more competitive.
"I am right in the middle of this conflict," he said. "If I weren't, my personal poll ratings would be better."

Germany news: Left-leaning Berlin coalition talks break down
