Germany news: Left-leaning Berlin coalition talks break down
Published October 13, 2026last updated October 13, 2026
What you need to know
- Berlin's SPD and Greens stop regional parliament coalition talks with the Left Party, disappointed with its pledges on Israel and organized crime
- They did leave the door open to potentially restart the exploratory talks, however
- International Monetary Fund raises Germany's 2026 growth forecast to 1.3%, up from just 0.7% in July
- Investment in infrastructure and defense, stronger exports and demand linked to artificial intelligence are helping the recovery
- Germany's 2026 wine harvest is expected to be around 20% below the ten-year average
Here is a roundup of top stories from and about Germany on Tuesday, October 13, 2026:
Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add DW as a Preferred Source on Google.
Why have the Berlin exploratory talks broken down within a week?
The breakdown in the exploratory talks can be traced back to concerns about the often highly critical stance on Israel adopted by some members of the Left Party, coupled with criticism of the appearance of a figure linked to organized crime at an election night party.
The Left scored well with parts of Berlin's population, not least the young and communities with more people of migrant backgrounds, with an unusually stern line on Israeli wars in Gaza and elsewhere in the Middle East by the often muted standards of German politics.
But comments from its more outspoken members and controversies like an organized crime boss attending an election-night after-party led to questions — particularly in some newspapers and from the conservative Christian Democrats — about whether center-left parties could work under the Left's leadership.
In a bid to settle this, the Greens, SPD and Left drafted a joint statement on antisemitism, Israel's right to exist and maintaining a distance from organized crime before starting their talks.
But the text subsequently faced criticism from within the Left's own ranks.
On Tuesday, as 44 Left Party members of the new Berlin parliament met, they instead signed off on a different text more closely aligned to the party's past internal position papers.
"We stand by Israel's right to exist and for equal rights for all people in Israel. Equally we stand by Palestine's right to exist and for equal rights for all people in Palestine," the Left Party's text read.
Among other things, this omits a reference in the joint text to Israel's right to exist being "non-negotiable," and to listing potential sanctions for transgressions potentially extending as far as being ejected from the party.
The CDU — which emerged as the second-largest party in the vote, well adrift of the Left on 18.8% — argue that the SPD and Greens should negotiate a coalition government with them instead.
Chancellor Merz had also weighed into the discussion, saying that the allegations of impropriety facing the Left Party cannot be "dismissed with a piece of paper." In the meantime, the party's state lawmakers appear to have disavowed that piece of paper anyway.
Berlin: SPD and Greens halt exploratory coalition talks with Left Party
Berlin's center-left Social Democrats (SPD) and environmentalist Greens have halted exploratory coalition talks with the socialist Left Party , which followed last month's regional elections.
The two parties' lead candidates from the state elections, Werner Graf of the Greens and Steffen Krach of the SPD, announced the move in a joint statement on Tuesday evening.
They referred to Left Party meetings earlier in the day in which party members signed a statement on handling antisemitism and on Israel's right to exist, but using a text that differed from a statement the three parties had jointly agreed to when opening the negotiations.
"We have taken note that the Left Party have reached a different arrangement within their own party," Graf and Krach's statement said.
However, the SPD and Greens also made clear that they were not closing the door on the Left Party entirely.
"This means that at this point we have to interrupt the coalition negotiations, so as to evaluate whether or not our agreement from last week still stands," they wrote. "We expect the Left Party to make clear to us to what extent they take the agreements they made seriously and intend to implement them."
The Left Party emerged as the largest party Berlin's close-fought election last month, claiming just under 26% of the vote, faring particularly well with young voters.
The Greens won just over 14% and the SPD just over 12% — meaning that the three left-leaning parties would command a slim majority if combined.
In theory, the SPD and Greens could also ally with the conservative CDU, but this would yield an even more fragile majority in the city-state's parliament, with stiff populist opposition from the AfD on the far-right and the Left on the other flank.
Astronaut Adenot: Mars voyage with current tech would be 'disaster'
French astronaut Sophie Adenot spoke to reporters at the European Space Agency (ESA) headquarters in Cologne on Tuesday, shortly after her return from the International Space Station.
She said that based on her experiences, it was too early to consider a mission to Mars the likes of which Elon Musk has been touting for years.
"We are not ready, we need technological breakthroughs," Adenot said, recalling her thoughts on landing in the Pacific Ocean five days ago after months in orbit.
"The moment the capsule opened, the first thing I said was, 'send me back to space,' because I was getting seasick on the waves," Adenot said. "But the second thing I said was that we are not ready to fly to Mars."
Adenot explained how around half of astronauts experienced symptoms like she did on returning from a long stretch in space, like pronounced frailty and nausea.
"With the technology that we currently have, a very long mission, a journey to Mars lasting months — just imagine the disaster," Adenot said.
Adenot said that technological breakthroughs were needed, either to drastically shorten the travel time, "or for example to artificially generate gravity," perhaps by having the spacecraft in a permanent state of rotation.
Adenot spent eight months on the International Space Station — a comparable amount of time that it would theoretically take to fly to Mars with current propulsion methods.
But she said that on the ISS there was much more space and much better facilities for exercise and movement than any transport vessel could offer. 
Boateng 'proud and happy' in Trabzonspor coaching role after Bayern job fell through
Former Germany defender Jerome Boateng has confirmed reports of him taking up a coaching role with Turkish top-flight club Trabzonspor.
"I am very proud and happy to be a part of the coaching staff," Boateng wrote on Instagram, saying it meant "a great deal to me" to learn from Trabzonspor's German head coach and his team every day.
The 2014 World Cup winner Boateng also said the role allowed him to share his experience and work with players "on and off the pitch, which is very valuable to me."
One of those Trabzonspor players is Egyptian superstar Mohamed Salah, who joined from Liverpool in the offseason and has hit the ground running scoring a goal a game.
Boateng's appointment follows around a year after a planned start to his coaching career at his former club Bayern Munich fell through.
Boateng retired as a player in September 2025. He was then invited by head coach Vincent Kompany to gain experience with the Bundesliga champions. But after vocal fan protests, Boateng said he had decided to focus on other matters given the "recent discussions about me."
The protests appeared to be linked to a 2024 Munich court ruling, which found Boateng guilty of intentionally causing bodily harm to a former girlfriend and issued him a formal warning. Boateng denies ever having hit a woman.
Ukraine allies in Poland after 'very difficult few days' with Trump
The foreign ministers of Germany, Norway, Poland and the UK spoke at the Warsaw Security Forum on Tuesday.
They expressed criticism and skepticism about US President Donald Trump's approach to the conflict in Ukraine in the past week.
German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul bemoaned the US decision to lift sanctions on Russian diesel as part of a deal to supply the US — seemingly struck as Trump panics about fuel prices with the Iran war still unresolved and a month to go until mid-term elections.
"I would say this is not the time to lower the sanctions regime but to strengthen this," Wadephul said.
"We are keeping our course," he said, adding that Europe was asking the authorities in Washington to do the same.
UK Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband arguably found even clearer words.
"Within the bounds of diplomacy we should acknowledge that it's been a very difficult few days," Miliband said in the Polish capital that's just a few hours' drive from Ukraine's western border.
He lauded Zelenskyy for showing "extraordinary leadership ... in the most difficult of circumstances" since Putin's 2022 full-scale invasion, shortly after Trump's call — mirroring Russian messaging — for presidential elections in war-torn Ukraine.
However, Miliband also said the notion of an "energy ceasefire" raised by Trump — seemingly unilaterally — was nevertheless worthy of consideration given the attacks on Ukrainian energy infrastructure and the onset of winter.
"So let us take up this idea of the full energy ceasefire and let us seek with President Trump to hold Putin to this full energy ceasefire, because that is what we need."
Miliband noted how Zelenskyy had expressed a willingness in theory, even if Russia was yet to do so.
IMF nearly doubles German growth forecast to 1.3%
The International Monetary Fund (IMF) has raised its forecast for German economic growth this year to 1.3%, almost double the 0.7% it predicted in July.
It now expects Europe's largest economy to expand by 1.1% in 2027, an upward revision of 0.1 percentage points.
The figures match the German government's forecasts released last week. The Economy Ministry said the economy had proved more resilient than expected despite higher energy prices and uncertainty over US tariffs.
Government investment in infrastructure and defense, alongside stronger exports, has helped support the recovery. German suppliers are also benefiting from investment in artificial intelligence.
The IMF slightly raised its global growth forecast for 2026 to 3.1%, from 3.0%, while keeping its projection for next year unchanged at 3.4%.
Strong investment in AI has helped offset the energy shock caused by the war in the Middle East. Higher oil production outside the Gulf, releases from strategic reserves and weaker demand in China have also cushioned the impact.
The IMF raised its eurozone growth forecast for this year by 0.2 percentage points to 1.1%. It still expects growth of 1.2% in 2027.
However, higher energy prices and weak consumer confidence continue to weigh on the currency bloc's economy.
Berlin airport cuts outlook as Ryanair scales back
Berlin Brandenburg Airport (BER) expects passenger numbers to fall this year and next as Ryanair cuts its services, airport chief Aletta von Massenbach said.
The airport now forecasts 25.7 million passengers in 2026, down from 26.1 million last year, a decline von Massenbach described as the "Ryanair effect."
Other airlines would partly offset Ryanair's cuts, but would not fill the gap entirely, she said.
The airport is reviewing all costs and postponing investments in response.
"This is a heavy blow," von Massenbach said of Ryanair's decision to close its BER base, comprising seven aircraft and their crews, on October 24.
Europe's largest budget airline will continue flying to Berlin but will cut roughly half its services, removing around 2.5 million seats a year, she said.
Ryanair has called BER "Europe's most unsuccessful airport." Von Massenbach said she understood the airline's frustration over high costs in Germany, interpreting its criticism as primarily directed at the federal government.
"Everything they say against BER, they are saying against Germany," she said.
The aviation industry has long criticized Germany's comparatively high taxes and fees, arguing that they are a main reason air traffic has recovered more slowly from the pandemic than elsewhere in Europe.
Fighter jets escort plane to Nuremberg airport
German fighter jets escorted a passenger plane from Greece to Nuremberg, prompting a temporary airport closure. Police later gave the all-clear, saying everyone on board was safe.

How third-party systems leave supermarkets vulnerable to cyber attacks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
06:36:30 UTC
15:36:30 KST

French supermarket hack could happen in Australia, experts say
French authorities are investigating after a "large-scale" cyber attack targeted supermarkets and resulted in millions of euros of food wastage.
It raises questions about whether Australian supermarkets could be vulnerable to similar attacks.
What happened to the French supermarkets?
Hackers turned up the temperatures on fridges and freezers in hundreds of stores, spoiling food that had to be discarded.
Les Mousquetaires, owner of retailer Intermarche, said fridges at about 150 of its stores were heated up to 50 degrees Celsius for six hours overnight.
Many major supermarkets manage their fridges and freezers by control panels that can be accessed over the internet, allowing maintenance companies to change settings without having to physically enter a store.
"Attackers do not necessarily need to hack individual fridges," University of Queensland's Cyber Research Centre director Ryan Ko says.
"More commonly, they gain access through compromised credentials, vulnerable remote access services, third-party suppliers, or inadequately secured operational technology management platforms.
"Once inside, they can potentially change temperature set points across many locations at once."
'Outdated firmware'
France's National Cybersecurity Agency (ANSSI) identified a vulnerability in software supplied by Danish company Danfoss, a source close to French Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu told Reuters.
Danfoss said it was "aware of incidents in France affecting a limited number of refrigeration management systems".
The company said the affected units "were running outdated firmware".
Danfoss also said it had "long advised customers to keep supported systems updated with the latest firmware and to migrate legacy systems to current-generation solutions".
In August, cybersecurity firm Claroty's Team82 published research detailing vulnerabilities in the Danfoss AK-SM 800A controller.
That report detailed software updates released by Danfoss that addressed the vulnerabilities that may have allowed attackers to bypass authentication controls and execute code on compromised devices.
How did it happen?
We don't have the confirmed details of that yet, so we can only speculate.
Macquarie University cyber security lecturer Jennifer Williams says hackers could have taken advantage of an outdated software system.
"It could be that there was a vulnerability that was already known with the software, but it wasn't patched because they didn't update it," Dr Williams says.
"The other possibility is there's something called a zero-day vulnerability, which is there's been zero days that that vulnerability has been made public.
"That means that no-one knows about it.
"Even the software providers might not be aware and able to control some of those security vulnerabilities."
We'll find out more about exactly how this happened once the ANSSI investigation wraps up.
How widespread was the attack?
Hundreds of stores were affected.
At least 300 shops of Intermarche or its Netto brand were targeted, along with over 100 Cooperative U outlets as well as several E Leclerc stores, according to Agence France-Presse.
Reuters reported that 80 Carrefour Market stores and 5 per cent of Monoprix stores were also affected.
There was no immediate estimate of industry-wide losses.
However, Intermarché chief executive Thierry Cotillard told local media the attack would result in "tens of millions of euros nationwide".
Could the same thing happen here?
It's possible, especially if our supermarkets are using similar systems, Professor Ko says.
"A likely scenario would involve attackers compromising a retailer's corporate network or a centralised refrigeration management platform, then moving into the operational systems that control refrigeration equipment," he says.
"The incident might initially appear as an equipment fault, but could quickly escalate into food spoilage, store closures, lost inventory, supply chain disruption, and reputational damage.
But Dr Williams says it's likely Australian supermarkets are on alert in case of "copycat" attacks.
"They're aware that this is now an exploit [and] they need to do something about it," she says.
"It's a little bit of cat and mouse in the sense that the criminals might be out there trying to exploit it but, at the same time, the industry is trying to prevent that from happening."
Which supermarkets could be targeted?
"Places like Woolworths and Coles and Aldi … they're very centralised," Dr Williams says.
"They might be slightly more vulnerable to that because they're more likely to have those centralised systems."
However, independent stores like IGA could be less vulnerable to the attacks if they're not using a wide-ranging centralised system like the supermarkets.
Professor Ko says Coles or Woolworths would be more attractive targets for cyber criminals because of the wider scope of an attack.
"However, being a target is not the same as being vulnerable," he says.
"Larger organisations typically invest significantly in cyber security, monitoring, and incident response capabilities.
"Smaller retailers and independent operators may have fewer resources dedicated to cyber security and could therefore be more vulnerable to compromise.
"In practice, every organisation connected to digital systems is potentially exposed, regardless of size."
The ABC has contacted Woolworths, Coles, Aldi and IGA for comment.
The future of cyber attacks?
Rahat Masood, a senior lecturer in computer science at the University of New South Wales, says the French incident demonstrates a shift in the cybersecurity threat landscape.
"Traditionally, when we think about cyber attacks, we think about stolen personal information, ransomware or disrupted websites," Dr Masood says.
"However, our physical infrastructure is becoming increasingly dependent on interconnected digital technologies.
"Supermarkets, hospitals, manufacturing facilities, transport systems and even commercial buildings now rely on software and internet-connected devices to manage essential operations."
While this technology can make things more efficient, Dr Masood says they offer new opportunities for cybercriminals, especially when dealing with aging systems.
"Operational technology systems are often designed to operate for many years," she says.
"Some were developed when cybersecurity was not a major design consideration.
"As a result, organisations may continue using equipment with outdated software, limited security protections or vulnerabilities that are difficult to patch."
It comes at a time when artificial intelligence (AI) is advancing, giving cyber criminals more tools.
"AI models are very aggressive," Dr Masood says.
"If you instruct them to find the vulnerability in that system, they can go by any means to find that vulnerability.
"It's not just a human mind who actually gets tired … they don't get tired."
ABC with Wires

European Aquatics president visits Russia and discusses possibility of holding competitions there

European Aquatics president visits Russia and discusses possibility of holding competitions there
António Silva, the president of European Aquatics, the governing body for aquatic sports in Europe, has visited Russia at the invitation of Dmitry Mazepin, head of the Russian Aquatics Federation, and assessed the possibility of holding international competitions there.
Source: Russian propaganda media outlet Match TV
Details: After arriving in the country, the sports official spoke to local journalists. Responding to their questions, Silva said he was pleased that Russian athletes had returned to the international stage.
When asked about when international competitions might once again be held in Russia itself, he said the matter was still under consideration.
"We are in constant contact with the Russian side. And now I have seen how well developed aquatic sports are in your country. We are pleased that Russian athletes have returned to competitions.
Unfortunately, there is currently no exact date set for when international competitions will once again be held in Russia. We are discussing this issue," Silva said.
He said that hosting competitions in Russia involving other countries would require appropriate infrastructure and guarantees for the safety of all participants.
"Organising a high-quality international competition requires a whole range of factors to be taken into account. First and foremost, there must be appropriate infrastructure, a willingness to host the competition, and guarantees for the safety and well-being of all participants.
In addition, it is important that other countries are prepared to travel to wherever the competition is being held.
Following our productive talks with the Russian Aquatics Federation, I can say that when considering future bids to host competitions, we, together with Russia and the regional authorities interested in organising such events, will have to take all these criteria into account," he said.
Meanwhile, Silva stressed that there are currently no countries opposed to Russian athletes participating in international competitions. He reiterated that there were concerns about ensuring safety at such events, mentioning Ukraine in this context.
"As for the second part of the question, there are no countries that oppose the participation of Russian athletes in international competitions.
There are certain concerns related to security arrangements when organising competitions. This is natural, as the actual conditions under which competitions are held need to be taken into account.
And this concerns not only Russia but other countries as well, such as Ukraine. Security issues should be considered in light of the specific circumstances," Silva stressed.
Background:
- In April 2026, World Aquatics, the global governing body for aquatic sports, decided to lift all restrictions on the participation of Russian and Belarusian athletes in international competitions.
- However, it later emerged that European Aquatics had asked World Aquatics to postpone lifting the sanctions on athletes from the aggressor countries.
- World Aquatics subsequently issued a ruling stating that organisers of international competitions may not refuse to allow Russian athletes to participate.
- António Silva also visited Kyiv in mid-May this year, where he spoke about plans to hold the European Diving Championships in Ukraine.

Gallery: See what the Pirita River estuary will look like in the future
The winning design for developing the area near the mouth of the Pirita River envisions residential buildings, commercial spaces, a hotel and a promenade.
The aim of the competition announced this summer was to find a cohesive architectural design for the area that would be practical, technically feasible and economically viable. A total of 15 entries were submitted.
"While the quality of the entries varied and not all the proposals met the client's expectations, the competition nevertheless achieved its goal: We found a very strong design that clearly stood out from the rest and the jury's decision was unanimous," said jury chairman Aivar Tuulberg, chairman of the supervisory board of the Tallinn Olympic Sailing Center (TOP).
The winning entry was designed by Maarja Kask, Ralf Lõoke and Martin McLean of architecture firm Salto. Their design draws on the site's location between the sea and the river. The proposal's defining architectural feature is its stepped buildings.
In addition to apartments, the development will include a hotel, spa, swimming pool, curling facility, sports and fitness facilities and a health center. Plans also call for a restaurant and cafe, retail, service and office space, a childcare facility and an event and conference hall.
The development's largest public square is planned for the waterfront, overlooking the Tallinn skyline and will connect to the seaside promenade. A separate plaza will be created in front of the hotel entrance.
An underground parking garage will be built, with its entrance located on Topi tänav.
The developer's next step is to proceed with the detailed spatial plan and work with the winning architects to further develop the design.
"It is still too early to give specific dates, but our goal is to move forward as smoothly and quickly as possible in cooperation with the City of Tallinn," Tuulberg added.
The architectural competition jury comprised chairman Aivar Tuulberg, TOP representative Margus Hütt, Tallinn Urban Planning Department architect Kalle Rannula and architects Mari Hunt and Emil Urbel, representing the Estonian Association of Architects.

Hydrocarbon sales to Europe since 2022 hit $320 bln: Russia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
06:34:48 UTC
15:34:48 KST

A motorist fills his car at petrol station near Lille, northern France. (AFP Photo)
Russia said that it had sold European countries more than $320 billion worth of hydrocarbons since 2022, despite sanctions imposed over the war in Ukraine.
“For the period from 2022 to today, this figure amounts to $320.7 billion. This is the volume of energy resource deliveries to European Union countries,” Russian Deputy Prime Minister in charge of energy Alexander Novak said on television on Oct. 12.
He said European countries purchased $21.3 billion worth of Russian hydrocarbons in the first nine months of 2026 alone.
“In other words, despite sanctions-related restrictions, we continue to supply energy resources in certain areas for which exemptions have been granted,” he added.
Novak said Russian oil exports may reach their pre-war levels by the end of the year.
The European Union has adopted numerous sanctions against Russia since the start of the war in Ukraine in 2022, yet many countries — including France — continue to source hydrocarbons, particularly liquefied natural gas (LNG), from Moscow.
Several landlocked countries, including Slovakia and Hungary, also benefit from exemptions allowing them to purchase Russian oil transported via pipeline.
This total does not include Russian output reaching Europe indirectly after being processed in third countries such as India or Türkiye, which, like China, have massively increased their purchases of Russian crude oil since 2022.

Imran Khan’s PTI braces to fight federal takeover of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
06:32:43 UTC
15:32:43 KST

Imran Khan’s PTI braces to fight federal takeover of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa
Islamabad says the PTI failed to lead the fight against armed groups, but analysts question the takeover.
Islamabad, Pakistan – The Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI) party of jailed ex-Prime Minister Imran Khan is planning to legally challenge the federal government’s Sunday takeover of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, a province that the party governed.
Sheikh Waqas Akram, the PTI’s central information secretary, told Al Jazeera that the party would challenge the imposition of emergency laws – suspending civil liberties – and governor’s rule in the province in court on Tuesday. A petition had been drafted by a legal committee headed by PTI Secretary-General Salman Akram Raja, but Akram did not say whether it would be filed in the Supreme Court or the Federal Constitutional Court.
The federal government’s moves have emerged as Pakistan’s latest political flashpoint, with competing narratives from the government and the PTI, at a time when the party was in the middle of a delayed march towards Islamabad, aimed at pressuring authorities to release former PM Khan, who has been jailed for more than three years.
Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi on Monday justified the government’s moves by arguing that federal rule in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa was needed for Pakistan to effectively combat “terrorism” in the province that shares a porous border with Afghanistan.
“No war can be won, however many resources you bring, whatever you do, until the government there leads it,” Naqvi said in Peshawar on Monday.
On Sunday, President Asif Ali Zardari imposed emergency rule and governor’s rule, suspending the PTI government in the northwestern province. The party has governed Khyber Pakhtunkhwa since 2013.
Sohail Afridi, the suspended chief minister, and some members of his cabinet have been taken into preventive custody, Minister of State for Interior Talal Chaudhry confirmed on Monday. Afridi had been leading the march towards Islamabad seeking to free Khan, and despite the setbacks to the party, PTI leaders said the protest was still on.
“The long march has not ended. But a historic crackdown against the party has begun,” Akram said.
The case for intervention
According to the proclamation signed on Sunday, the provincial government had “failed to demonstrate the ownership, will and intent to adequately deal with the menace of terrorism”.
“The federal government’s position is clearly described. ‘A deliberate disengagement from the fight against terrorism’ as communicated after cabinet meeting. That’s the constitutional premise needed for imposition of emergency,” Aasiya Riaz, joint director of the independent political think tank the Pakistan Institute of Legislative Development and Transparency (PILDAT), told Al Jazeera.
However, Hassan Abdullah Niazi, an adjunct faculty member at the Lahore University of Management Sciences (LUMS) and a lawyer based in Lahore, disputed that premise.
“If all of this was true, then KP would be in a state of anarchy, but we know that is not the case. It had a functioning legislature and executive that commanded the confidence of the people, hence this entire exercise is an unconstitutional move against provincial autonomy,” he told Al Jazeera.
A more detailed case was set out last month in a 14-page white paper presented in Islamabad by Ikhtiar Wali Khan, a political adviser to Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif from the ruling Pakistan Muslim League-Nawaz (PMLN).
The paper pointed to rising police deaths, staff and equipment shortages in the provincial counterterrorism department, and spending priorities.
However, Akram rejected the charge that the PTI had failed to lead the fight.
He said the provincial government had paid 1.83 billion rupees ($6.6m) from its own funds to the families of more than 900 soldiers, police and paramilitary personnel killed fighting armed groups, a contribution he said no other province had made.
What Islamabad wanted
Naqvi said at a news conference in Islamabad on Sunday that the federal government had been involved in negotiations with the PTI on a proposed “sit-in” by the party in support of Khan.
“We have no problem with the sit-in. Do the sit-in as eagerly as you like; we have no issue with the sit-in. Our issue is entirely terrorism-related, and we want to get you on board on that,” he said.
Taimur Jhagra, a PTI leader and former provincial finance and health minister, said the talks with the government that the party had agreed to were meant to focus on Khan.
“It’s absurd that a negotiation about a protest movement to give Imran Khan Supreme Court-ordered medical and visitation rights becomes a negotiation about terrorism strategy,” he told Al Jazeera.
Naqvi also said the PTI had agreed during the talks that emergency rule should be imposed in 12 districts of the province.
Akram rejected that claim and said the party had refused. The party feared residents would bear the cost of military operations, he said.
“We said ‘No, this cannot be. You cannot do whatever you like with them. We took the votes from them. Tomorrow they will blame us: ‘You got us killed,’” he said.
Akram said the PTI negotiators referred the federal government’s proposal to Afridi, who rejected it.
Federal Information Minister Attaullah Tarar went further at Sunday’s news conference.
“This government, which has been suspended through a constitutional option, is responsible for the deaths of thousands of citizens of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa,” he said, accusing Afridi’s PTI government of being hand in glove with the Tehreek-e-Taliban Pakistan – an armed group known as the Pakistan Taliban – and the Afghan Taliban.
There is no known or public evidence of any such links.
Security or politics?
According to a government white paper, 122 police personnel were killed in the province in the first half of this year, up from 63 during the same period in 2025.
Independent trackers also point to rising violence. The Centre for Research and Security Studies (CRSS), an Islamabad-based think tank, recorded 556 violence-linked deaths in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa between July and September, up from 475 in the previous quarter and 311 in the one before.
Balochistan was hit harder. Deaths there rose by 213 percent to 829, making it the worst-affected province, according to CRSS.
The government says it acted because the provincial administration would not lead the fight against armed groups, but analysts disagree over the takeover’s purpose.
“I would say this decision is political, administrative and security. All three elements are present in it,” Zaigham Khan, an Islamabad-based political analyst, told Al Jazeera.
Ali Arqam, a longtime observer of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, disagreed.
“This is not really about security at all. It is basically a political move that they are just dressing up as some kind of administrative necessity,” he told Al Jazeera.
Jhagra said the government believed the takeover would break the PTI, but argued that people across the country still saw Khan as their leader.
“It is trying to solve for legitimacy,” he told Al Jazeera, referring to the government.
For his part, Federal Law Minister Azam Nazeer Tarar said at a news conference in Islamabad on Sunday that the decision was a purely constitutional step.
A party under pressure
For the PTI, the immediate concerns are its leaders and the courts.
“There has been no contact. No one in the party has had any contact with the chief minister,” Akram said.
But the party remains widely popular, in the province and nationally.
At Monday’s meeting, Naqvi said results against “terrorism” would not come in a day. There would be ups and downs, he said, and harder times lay ahead.
But Arqam, the Khyber Pakhtunkhwa observer, said Islamabad should be judged by the same measures as the PTI government.
“You test this government by looking at the exact same hard metrics: Does security actually improve, do the basic services get better, and do the promised fiscal resources finally show up?” he said.

“Our concert occupancy rates were between 40 and 50 percent in 2024. We have been gaining momentum. We ended last season with occupancy rates of 80 to 90 percent. Many of our concerts sold out days in advance. We expect the same level of interest this season,” he said.

Ongoing digs at Klaros Sanctuary reveal Roman Imperial complex
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
06:31:32 UTC
15:31:32 KST

Works have uncovered buildingsfrom the first and second centuries. (AA Photo)
Excavations are continuing in two areas of Klaros Sanctuary in the western province of İzmir’s Menderes district, including structures where visitors stayed and a building complex containing seven rooms dating to the Roman Imperial period.
According to a statement from İzmir Municipality, the excavations are being carried out in cooperation with the Culture and Tourism Ministry and Ege University’s Department of Archaeology, with support from the municipality.
An interdisciplinary team of archaeologists, architects, restorers, conservators, epigraphers and numismatists has been working at various parts of the site throughout the excavation season.
Excavation head Associate Professor Onur Zunal said work was continuing in two separate areas of the sanctuary.
Excavations east of the sanctuary’s entrance structure have uncovered buildings where visitors stayed during the first and second centuries A.D. Zunal said these structures were known as “katagogeion” and could be compared to modern motels or guesthouses.
Zunal said excavations have also been underway since 2016 at a building complex covering approximately 2,500 square meters toward Notion, the main city associated with the sanctuary. The complex was used during the Roman Imperial period, between the first and third centuries A.D., he said.
The northern section of the structure contains seven rooms, while archaeologists believe another seven rooms may have stood parallel to them in the southern section. An open courtyard lies in the middle of the complex, Zunal said.
The building’s function has not yet been definitively established. Everyday vessels and coins found at the site are helping researchers determine its date, he added.
Klaros Sanctuary was one of the important centers where oracles were delivered in the name of Apollo in antiquity. Believed to have been established in the 13th century B.C., it is considered one of the ancient world’s three major oracle centers, alongside the temples of Apollo at Didyma and Delphi.

The FIR names Akoijam, and an investigation is underway.Meanwhile, the BJP Mahila Morcha staged protests outside the Congress headquarters in Delhi and at several locations in Himachal Pradesh on Monday, demanding Akoijam’s expulsion from the party.
Union Women and Child Development Minister Annpurna Devi, who took part in the Delhi protest titled 'Nari Shakti Hunkar Andolan', accused Congress leader Priyanka Gandhi Vadra of giving "hollow slogans" in support of girls.BJP Mahila Morcha in-charge D Purandeswari said the JNU Internal Committee’s report had brought to light allegations of molestation involving 11 female students. She criticised Rahul Gandhi and Priyanka Gandhi for their silence and demanded that Rahul Gandhi apologise to women across the country and that the Congress immediately expel Akoijam.

Lufthansa Group boosts Japan network with up to 50 flights per week from summer 2027
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
06:31:07 UTC
15:31:07 KST

Due to a ‘strong increase in demand’, the group’s airlines will offer up to 50 weekly flights to four Japanese airports next summer.
Lufthansa Group is boosting its Japan network for 2027, bringing back its Frankfurt-Nagoya route and adding a daily service between Frankfurt and Tokyo-Narita in response to a “strong increase in demand”.
The group’s airlines – including Lufthansa, Austrian Airlines, SWISS and ITA Airways – will offer up to 50 flights per week next summer to four Japanese airports: Tokyo-Haneda, Tokyo-Narita, Osaka and Nagoya.
The expansion follows a record year in 2025 for international arrivals in Japan, with the country welcoming 42.7 million overseas visitors, up 15.8% on 2024, according to the Japan National Tourism Organization (JNTO).
Visitor arrivals from several European markets have continued to grow in 2026. Japan recorded 27.6 million international visitor arrivals between January and August, down 2.7% compared with the same period in 2025.
However, arrivals from Germany rose 5.6% to 281,500, while arrivals from the UK increased 5.8% to 364,800. France, Italy and Spain also recorded growth.
Frankfurt-Nagoya flights return in March
Lufthansa’s seasonal Frankfurt-Nagoya service will resume on 29 March 2027, operating three times a week on Mondays, Wednesdays and Saturdays.
Outbound flights will leave Frankfurt at 2:10 pm and arrive in Nagoya at 9:35 am the following morning. Return services will depart Nagoya at 11:30 am and land in Frankfurt at 6:30 pm. All times are local.
Nagoya, in Aichi Prefecture, is one of Japan’s major industrial centres, with strong links to the automotive sector. For holidaymakers, the city also offers samurai history and a gateway to destinations including Kyoto.
Passengers travelling from Nagoya will be able to connect through Frankfurt to destinations across Europe and South America.
Daily service to Tokyo-Narita
A daily seasonal service between Frankfurt and Tokyo-Narita will begin on 28 March 2027, complementing Lufthansa’s existing daily flights to Tokyo-Haneda from Frankfurt and Munich.
The new Narita service will depart Frankfurt at 1:45 pm, arriving at 9:30 am the next day. Return flights will leave Narita at 11:20 am and reach Frankfurt at 6:40 pm.
Both the Nagoya and Narita routes will use Boeing 787-9 aircraft equipped with Lufthansa’s Allegris cabins, offering 28 business class seats, 28 premium economy seats and 231 economy seats.
“Japan is a key market for the Lufthansa Group, and we are pleased to further strengthen our presence with additional capacity and the resumption of flights to Nagoya,” says Dieter Vranckx, the group’s chief commercial officer.
“Together with our expanded Tokyo services, these investments provide our customers with more travel options and support the continued diversification of our intercontinental network.”
SWISS will also increase its Japan services, offering up to seven weekly flights between Zurich and Tokyo-Narita during summer 2027.

Çukurova’s traditional cuisine kept alive in 531-year-old building
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
06:30:47 UTC
15:30:47 KST

The two-story building now serves as the ‘Selamlık Table Heritage House.’ (AA Photo)
A 531-year-old building in Adana, once used as the selamlık, or reception quarters for male guests, of the Ramazanoğulları Beylik palace, has been restored and transformed into a venue showcasing the region’s traditional cuisine and dining culture.
Located in the Ulucamii neighborhood, the two-story building was commissioned by Ramazanoğlu Halil Bey during the rule of the Ramazanoğulları principality. It served as a reception area for male guests and a place where official affairs were conducted.
The historic structure was later used for various purposes and became known as “Tuz Hanı” and “Tuz Pazarı Hanı” due to the salt trade once conducted there.
After remaining unused for a period, the 531-year-old building was restored by the governor’s office last year. It was then allocated to the Adana Maturation Institute to help pass on Çukurova’s rich culinary and dining heritage to future generations.
Under a project prepared by the institute in coordination with the governor’s office, the building was transformed into the “Selamlık Sofra Mirası Evi” (Selamlık Table Heritage House).
Visitors can sample traditional dishes prepared by local culinary experts while learning about their recipes and the region’s food culture.
HH Visitors can learn how traditional dishes are made
Adana Maturation Institute Director Seher Coşkun told state-run Anadolu Agency that the institute was proud to operate in a historic building.
Describing dining culture as an important heritage passed down through generations, Coşkun said the aim was to preserve the region’s cultural richness in its authentic form.
“Our goal is to keep our cultural heritage alive in its original form. Our culinary tradition is also a source of richness, and we have a strength rooted in history. We will continue our work here by sharing recipes and demonstrating the preparation stages of these dishes,” she said.
Coşkun said the venue initially offered 15 regional specialties, including “içli köfte” (stuffed meatballs), “börek soup,” “analı kızlı” (a traditional meatball and chickpea dish) and stuffed okra.
Visitors can learn how the dishes are prepared in addition to tasting them, she said, inviting guests to experience the traditional cuisine in the historic setting.

Water safety concerns close schools in northern Türkiye
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
06:30:25 UTC
15:30:25 KST

People gather outside a hospital’s emergency unit in Tokat.
Schools in the city center of Türkiye’s northern province of Tokat were closed on Oct. 12 for disinfection amid a water safety scare that led nearly 3,000 people to seek medical treatment.
The Tokat Governor’s Office said the one-day closure covered all public and private formal and nonformal education institutions and rehabilitation centers to allow thorough disinfection.
Nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain and diarrhea began on the evening of Oct. 9, first among children, before adults also sought treatment. As of 8 a.m. on Oct. 11, 2,914 people had sought medical care. Six of the 18 hospitalized children were discharged, while those still receiving treatment were in good condition.
Authorities investigating the cause sent drinking water samples from across the city to the Ankara Public Health Reference Laboratory. Results were expected within three days.
The Governor’s Office advised residents to use reliable bottled water for drinking and cooking until the results were available. Tap water could be used for other daily needs but should not be swallowed, it said. Findings and updates would be shared with the public.
Tokat Municipality said on Oct. 11 that sewage had not entered the drinking water network, citing its Water and Sewerage Directorate’s technical assessment. It said no technical evidence linked the illnesses to municipal infrastructure and urged residents to follow official statements rather than unverified claims.

Shock, anger and a crackdown: why a contentious electoral revision has sparked outrage
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
06:30:16 UTC
15:30:16 KST

Months of simmering public anger have given rise to a season of discontent in India. In its latest iteration, the demand is for the removal of chief election commissioner Gyanesh Kumar and the scrapping of a controversial electoral rolls revision that has struck 130 million people off the register. Protests have erupted every day over the past week, prompting a violent crackdown on dissenters in the capital.
Over the weekend, Delhi was effectively under lockdown, transformed into a militarised landscape of barricades, road closures and paramilitary forces marching through the streets. Ahead of a protest led by the Cockroach Janta party on Saturday, authorities deployed a massive dragnet: 245 trains to Delhi were cancelled, 45 metro stations were shut, liquor shops were closed, internet services were cut off in the heart of the city and activists were put under house arrest.
The founders of the Cockroach party were removed from an Air India flight shortly after it landed at Delhi airport on Saturday. Opposition leaders were held for more than eight hours in various police stations. Video footage showed students and activists being manhandled, beaten and dragged off the streets while some journalists were also swept up in the detentions. A supreme court lawyer assisting those detained was carried away by police, his shirt torn in the process. The crackdown extended to Mumbai, where Tushar Gandhi, the great-grandson of Mahatma Gandhi, was whisked away by the police to prevent him from participating in a local demonstration. On Monday, the Delhi police denotified Jantar Mantar as a designated protest site, instead recommending three alternative locations.
“I have been in public life and have watched politics for four decades now, and I have never witnessed this kind of preparation for a demonstration. It was extraordinary by any stretch of the imagination,” political activist Yogendra Yadav, who was also detained, said of Saturday’s crackdown. Despite what he described as “terror unleashed by the state”, he said, small groups staged flash protests in several areas of Delhi defying the heavy security presence.
The crackdown was preceded by similarly aggressive police action against Congress party’s protests, led by Rahul Gandhi. Dramatic images of police personnel detaining Gandhi and his sister, Priyanka, amid scenes of chaos flashed across screens nationwide.
The ruling Bharatiya Janata party has defended its position, with spokesperson Ravi Shankar Prasad accusing the opposition of weaponising protests after electoral defeats. “One, Indian democracy has thwarted attempts to incite anarchy. Two, the country will be governed by parliament, not by the streets,” he said at a news briefing.
While suppression of protests is not new, what stands out this time is the scale of the crackdown in the capital. Government clampdowns in Indian-administered Kashmir have been far more severe, particularly in 2019, when sweeping restrictions were imposed after the revocation of Article 370.
The ferocity of the state response reflects the high political stakes for Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s government, which faces mounting resistance over the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) and questions about the credibility of the electoral process.
The latest protests began with a demand for Kumar’s resignation after an Indian Express investigation reported that the ECI’s two other commissioners, Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi, had raised concerns about changes to electoral rolls, registration procedures, and digital systems. While Kumar has not responded to the investigation, the ECI said in a statement that “differing views” were part of the “decision-making process”. But the anger runs deeper. The SIR exercise has faced criticism for putting citizens through a trial by fire and leaving the most marginalised in a Kafkaesque limbo. Critics and opposition leaders have gone further, charging that the exercise was designed to benefit the ruling regime.
Former election commissioner Ashok Lavasa told me that the SIR process is unprecedented and unfair, marking a departure from the Commission’s traditional emphasis on inclusion. “For more than seven decades the ECI took it upon itself, as a duty, to enrol everyone who was eligible to vote. And that was one of the basic differences between how Indian democracy works and how other democracies function, where you need to apply to get enrolled,” he said. Voters accustomed to a “friendly procedure” now face a hostile system, which he said “is not good for democracy” in the long run.
Yadav argued that the SIR controversy has exposed what he describes as a deeper process of democratic capture by the ruling party. “Elections are the only mechanism now left for the regime to stamp its legitimacy and election capture is critical to their survival. And therefore, Gyanesh Kumar is critical,” he said. He pointed to a 2023 law giving election commissioners legal immunity for actions performed in their official capacity, which he said is broader than even the protection afforded to judges.
As to what comes next, he envisions potential for three strands to find common ground: the opposition parties, organised civil society groups, and ordinary citizens. For a government that has shown no sign of budging yet, he said, the calculus will get harder. “The longer they delay, the higher the stakes.”
On Monday, the Keralam assembly passed a resolution seeking Kumar’s removal, as opposition parties marched toward the supreme court demanding action against him. And the Cockroach movement and leftist student groups have vowed to continue protesting. “People have refused to be fearful any longer. They will come again and again,” said left-wing student leader, Danish Ali. “We are living in a democratic country, and protest is a fundamental right that no one can snatch away from us.”

Human rights | South African jurist and former international criminal court judge, Navi Pillay, who is of Indian Tamil heritage, has won the 2026 Nobel Peace Prize. In a first-person account published in 2023, she wrote about her grandparents, who came from India and worked on a sugarcane farm in South Africa for five years before being allowed to buy land.
Technology | The United States has suspended labour-certification processing for several major technology companies, including top Indian IT firms, as part of a crackdown on what it alleges is a misuse of its flagship green card program, fraud and the displacement of American workers. The impacted companies include Cognizant, Infosys, Tata, Wipro, HCL, Capgemini, Microsoft and Adobe. “We will not accept any new or process any pending permanent labour certification applications involving these companies,” the US labour secretary Keith Sonderling announced last week.

Guest shelf
A recommendation from someone with great taste
With Delhi in the news for all the wrong reasons, I turned to Mayank Austen Soofi, who writes a daily Delhi column for Hindustan Times, to share a spot he returns to for a moment of reprieve. “Whenever I can, I spend a solitary afternoon at the tiny Sufi shrine of Hazrat Sarmad Shaheed, beside the Jama Masjid mosque. The bazaar outside the shrine is the Walled City’s noisiest quarter, yet inside one can sit in silence beneath the neem tree growing beside Sarmad’s grave. An Armenian Jew from Iran, Sarmad fell in love with a Hindu boy in Sindh, eventually became a naked fakir and settled in Mughal Delhi. Executed by Emperor Aurangzeb, his grave lies beneath a red cloth that recalls his blood-soaked beheading. These days, I linger a little longer at the resting place of a man who would just not submit to power.”

A number worth knowing
32
At least 32 children from the Indigenous community in Balaghat, Madhya Pradesh, have died since June, the Indian Express reported. An inquiry found evidence of measles and malaria. The children, aged between one and 13, experienced symptoms including high fever, skin rashes and abdominal pain.
Vibe check
For Mumbai-based cinematographer, Arbab Kamal Khan, the fleeting, unguarded moments of everyday life offer the most honest form of documentation. His Instagram account is an extension of this cinematic vision, capturing the languor of slow days, the beauty of the mundane and the quiet air of romance.
“When someone passes away, we don’t remember the curated moments,” he told me. “We always go back to the little things, the moments that are small or intricate.”
For me, the images and videos featuring his parents – their feet across each other besides teacups resting atop an Urdu newspaper, or his dad resting under his wife’s dupatta as she brushes her hair – are particularly striking because older people are rarely afforded such tenderness in visual culture. In his frames, his parents are not only elderly figures but also lovers who continue to find intimacy in each other’s presence.

Touristic Eastern Express to make 70 trips in 2026-2027 winter season
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
06:30:15 UTC
15:30:15 KST

The Touristic Eastern Express is designed to combine long-distance rail travel with sightseeing stops at destinations along its route from Ankara to Kars. (DHA Photo)
Türkiye’s Touristic Eastern Express will make 70 trips between Ankara and Kars during the 2026-2027 winter season, offering passengers a chance to explore the country’s historical sites, cultural heritage and landscapes along the route, Transport and Infrastructure Minister Abdulkadir Uraloğlu has said.
The train will run 35 services in each direction, with Ankara-Kars journeys scheduled from Dec. 21 to March 10, 2027, and return services from Kars to Ankara operating between Dec. 23 and March 12, 2027, Uraloğlu said in a written statement.
Trains departing from the capital Ankara in central Türkiye will run on Mondays, Wednesdays and Fridays, while services from the eastern province of Kars will depart on Wednesdays, Fridays and Sundays. The final Ankara-Kars journey will take place on March 10, with the last return service scheduled for March 12.
The Touristic Eastern Express is designed to combine long-distance rail travel with sightseeing stops at destinations along its route. Trains traveling from Ankara to Kars will stop in Erzincan and Erzurum, while those heading back to Ankara will make sightseeing stops in İliç, Divriği and Sivas.
The stops will allow passengers to visit locations known for their historical and cultural significance while traveling across central and eastern Anatolia, Uraloğlu said.
The train will feature sleeper and dining cars. Each sleeper car will have 10 compartments, with two beds in each compartment, providing accommodation for 20 passengers per car. A dining car will also serve passengers during the journey.
Individual ticket sales for the new season will begin on Oct. 26 through the sales channels of TCDD Taşımacılık, Türkiye’s state railway passenger transport operator, according to the minister.
Rising to fame through social media and travel photography, the seasonal service has become a popular option for travelers seeking to experience Anatolia by rail, particularly during the winter months, when the route offers views of snow-covered landscapes and opportunities to explore destinations along the way.
Since its debut in 2019, the Touristic Eastern Express has brought together people of all ages and nationalities with the unique nature and culture of Anatolia. In its 2025-2026 season, the route welcomed more than 10,000 passengers with a total of 60 round-trip services.

Türkiye develops three drought-tolerant wheat varieties
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
06:30:04 UTC
15:30:04 KST

Signs identify newly developed wheat varieties in experimental plots in Kırşehir.
Researchers in Türkiye’s central province of Kırşehir have developed three drought-tolerant wheat varieties to raise yields and reduce disease losses for farmers working in dry conditions.
Kırşehir Ahi Evran University Rector Professor Mustafa Kasım Karahocagil told Anadolu Agency the Faculty of Agriculture’s Cereal Breeding Program had produced candidates yielding over 850-900 kilograms per decare.
The university specializes in agriculture and geothermal energy. Following more than a decade of research, it expects the varieties, bred for local soil and climate conditions, to be widely grown in Central Anatolia and other dry areas.
Faculty Dean Professor Selahattin Çınar said 20 candidates were compared with standard varieties in 2026 regional yield trials at the university’s research fields. Three stood out for their yields.
Applications will be submitted in stages over the coming years to the Agriculture and Forestry Ministry’s Seed Registration and Certification Center. Once registered, the varieties will be multiplied and supplied to farmers.
Field Crops Department Associate Professor Ramazan Ayrancı said the bread wheat crossing program began in 2013. Researchers selected 20 lines from 1,600 for their performance under local conditions and tolerance of winter cold, summer heat and uneven seasonal rainfall.
Ayrancı said the candidates resulted from 12 years of continuous work and were suited to rain-fed farming, including areas where fields are left fallow. Breeding for dry conditions is harder than for irrigated, more productive land, he said.
Research will continue to address low yields. Wheat has been grown in Anatolia for 10,000 years, Çınar said.

Could the European Security Council be the EU’s answer to hybrid attacks?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
06:30:03 UTC
15:30:03 KST

The European Commission proposed a new European Security Council (ESC) to respond to a recent surge in state-sponsored hybrid warfare, like cyberattacks and sabotage.
The European Security Council would fast-track traditional EU bureaucratic gridlock during security emergencies. Under the proposal, it would rely on what European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen called a "counter-hybrid playbook" to address grey-zone hostile actions.
In her 2026 State of the Union address, she explicitly said that these new mechanisms are meant to be "fully aligned" and "complementary" to NATO rather than replacing it. And speaking at Euronews' Defence & Space Summit, EU defence chief Andrius Kubilius said the ESC would "not [be] against NATO" but be "exactly the opposite”.
“It is how to make Europe stronger, which will make NATO stronger", he said.
The full initiative would feature three main elements. First, there’s the ESC itself, which is envisioned as an agile political forum that expands the EU leaders' summit to include key non-EU partners. Second, the Emergency Security Protocol would require member states to convene immediately if one faces a hybrid threat. The third part is a dedicated fund for Strategic Defence Enablers, which focuses on joint investments in air defence, cyber security, and space systems.
The EU’s goal
The EU wants the ESC to address a critical gap in Europe's fragmented and slow defence architecture.
State-sponsored hybrid warfare involves hostile "grey-zone" actions, like infrastructure sabotage, cyberattacks and drone incursions. Since these operations fall below the threshold of conventional military conflict, they do not automatically trigger NATO's collective defence mechanisms.
“The idea has got a new lease on life amid growing doubts about the US willingness to uphold NATO's Article 5 security guarantee and fears that Washington might block political decision-making [...] or frustrate operational command within NATO, and that therefore European fallback options should be strengthened,” said Steven Blockmans, deputy director at the International Centre for Defence and Security.
The ESC aims to address three problems. First, it seeks to bypass the EU's unanimity deadlock through qualified majority voting to prevent vetoes from paralysing foreign policy. Second, the Emergency Security Protocol would act as Europe's version of NATO's Article 4, bringing member states together to coordinate responses to non-military crises. Third, it includes non-EU partners like the UK, Ukraine, Norway and Canada, turning ad-hoc coalitions into a permanent security framework.
This fits into the EU's long-term goal of strategic autonomy and a self-reliant European Defence Union. Over the next decade, the bloc aims to reduce its dependence on US military logistics by unifying Europe's fragmented defence sector and streamlining joint procurement and manufacturing.
What’s on the proposal?
The ESC would provide a permanent year-round forum for crisis management. The idea is “having dedicated meetings of the EU Council, calling it the European Security Council [to] have more structured discussions about security and defence in a way that the EU Council wouldn't always have”, explained Luigi Scazzieri, senior policy analyst at the EU Institute for Security Studies.
The goal is to strengthen political coordination on defence and security, and provide strategic, long-term direction. It would bring together EU leaders and international partners, including Ukraine, Canada, Norway, and the UK.
The ESC would also allow members to plan and carry out rapid defence responses, including to growing hybrid and unconventional military attacks.
“The ESC would close the gap between detecting a threat and deciding what Europeans will do about it”, said Ionela Maria Ciolan, Research Officer on security and defence at the Wilfried Martens Centre for European Studies.
Under the proposed “Emergency Security Protocol”, modelled on NATO’s Article 4, members may call consultations if they believe their security, territorial integrity, or political independence is under threat, and coordinate a response.
According to Ciolan, the protocol would not replace Articles 42(7) or 222 of the treaties, which require member states to intervene when another member state is subjected to armed aggression or terrorist attacks. Rather, it would provide “an earlier political entry point,” trigger an emergency meeting, and assess whether the situation calls for national action, EU crisis tools, NATO consultations, or, in the worst cases, consideration of a treaty clause, she added.
The ESC and NATO
The proposed ESC is not supposed to override NATO. Crucially, it would act independently of Washington while keeping NATO as the central framework for defence. Scazzieri, said the division of labour is clear: “Essentially NATO does collective defence, this European Security Council would not”.
NATO handles collective military defence under Article 5, while the ESC focuses on grey-zone and hybrid threats. The Emergency Security Protocol would trigger immediate security consultations without relying on the US.
“It would be about sanctions, [...] how to prioritise spending limited EU money, [...] bringing together a slightly different group of countries that doesn't come together in a NATO context, including those EU members that are not NATO members,” said Scazzieri.
But despite official claims of synergy, the initiative has raised concerns among member states like Estonia, which fear it could duplicate NATO functions. Parallel alert systems and consultation bodies could create bureaucratic confusion, while excluding the US could increase tensions.
However, Scazzieri sees little risk of duplication because the two would use different tools and perform different functions.
“There's obviously always going to be a bit of turf-war bias in institutions where NATO, for example, might see the EU is now setting up a European Security Council. Are they going to discuss the same things? I see little risk of that because all of this would be seen from the EU's toolbox,” he said.
For Blockmans, a more ambitious ESC would eventually need to connect political decisions with military capabilities.
“It would need to be compatible with NATO and the European Union. And that would presuppose [...] an intergovernmental agreement that foresees [...] the participation also of, for example, the NATO secretary general, just as you might imagine the European Commission president and the European Council presidents to be included as well.”
Powers remain to be defined
The Commission’s proposal does not resolve the unanimity gridlock within NATO or the EU Council, Blockmans argued.
“A new body composed of like-minded and trusted states […] would be breaking through these decision-making blockages, of course, although one might assume that decision- making within that new body would also proceed on the basis of consensus”.
For Scazzieri, the ESC won't speed up decision-making either. “It cannot exist as a legal body in its own right” and therefore will not make binding decisions, unlike the EU Council. Yet real decision-making power is key to boosting the ESC’s legitimacy and “provide national parliaments of the participating states with a democratic backstop,” Blockmans explained, delivering the change the EU plans for its security and defence policy.
The structure and composition have yet to be decided too. Besides the UK, Norway, Canada and Ukraine, Blockmans says nothing excludes the possibility of Korea or Japan joining too.
The EU would also need to define how EU member states fit into the configuration alongside international partners, what role they will play in discussions, and whether they will carry more weight than non-EU states.
“Whether it should replicate a sort of United Nations Security Council system with a two-tier mechanism of permanent members and then rotating non-permanent members, there's no clarity on this whatsoever,” said Blockmans.
The ESC would need practical military capabilities, including NATO- and EU-compatible command structures, a dedicated defence budget, and a multinational European defence force. Without these resources, Blockmans argued, the ESC could make political decisions but would lack the means to turn them into military operations.
What do the member states think about it?
The Commission has not made a formal proposal, nor have the national governments been asked to endorse a detailed plan yet, so it remains to be seen who will support or oppose the ESC. Still, for Ciolan, it's possible to identify a group of potential supporters.
Italy is likely to join the initiative, as it backs stronger European defence cooperation and a single EU representative in the Ukraine peace talks, while Spain generally favours deeper common defence, Ciolan said.
Germany and France have suggested a coordinated defence approach through the ESC in the Meseberg Declaration, “Renewing Europe’s promises of security and prosperity”, in 2018. Generally, she added, national governments affiliated with the European People’s Party (EPP) are expected to be more supportive of the initiative.
Resistance, Ciolan argued, is more likely to come from those that fear losing their national veto over foreign and defence policy, being marginalised by other, more influential member states, or weakening the transatlantic framework.

On the International Day for Disaster Risk Reduction: "Resilience Starts at Home"
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
06:30:00 UTC
15:30:00 KST

Every year on October 13, the International Day for Disaster Risk Reduction (IDDRR) draws attention to the ways communities can reduce exposure and vulnerability to hazards. Established by the United Nations in 1989, the day provides an opportunity to consider how governments, communities, and professionals can strengthen preparedness and resilience before disasters occur. For its 2026 edition, the United Nations Office for Disaster Risk Reduction (UNDRR) has selected "Resilience Starts at Home" as its theme, placing housing at the center of this year's campaign.
The theme recognizes the home as both a primary site where disaster impacts are experienced and a starting point for building resilience. The location, design, construction, financing, and maintenance of housing can either reduce or create risk, while inadequate building standards and development in hazard-prone areas can increase the consequences of earthquakes, floods, extreme heat, and other events. The campaign calls for risk-informed land-use planning, resilient building codes, accessible early-warning systems, inclusive design, and greater investment in safe and affordable housing, while also emphasizing the roles of local communities, developers, construction companies, financiers, and households.
The focus comes amid another year of disasters affecting homes, infrastructure, and settlements around the world. In June, two major earthquakes struck northern Venezuela within seconds of one another, while four significant earthquakes occurred across Japan, Northern California, and Venezuela within a 36-hour period. In August, a magnitude 7.4 earthquake in Colombia damaged housing, healthcare and educational facilities, infrastructure, and historic architecture, while a glacier collapse in the Himalayas triggered flash floods that destroyed villages along the Nepal-Tibet border. These events highlight how the consequences of natural hazards are shaped not only by their intensity, but also by the resilience of the built environment and the preparedness of the communities living within it.
Related Article
On World Architecture Day 2026: A Call to Build Better, Build Differently, and Share Resources
Designing Homes for Climate and Disaster Resilience
At the scale of the home, resilience increasingly involves designing for environmental conditions that may be recurrent rather than exceptional. Elevated and amphibious structures can respond to seasonal flooding, while robust envelopes, passive cooling, fire-resistant materials, protected openings, and adaptable energy systems can help homes withstand extreme heat, storms, wildfires, power outages, and other disruptions. These approaches shift the focus from repairing or replacing damaged buildings toward anticipating hazards through decisions about site, structure, materials, and everyday domestic spaces.

Post-Disaster Reconstruction and Emergency Architecture
Emergency architecture encompasses a range of responses to displacement and destruction, from rapidly deployable shelters to reconstruction strategies intended to support longer-term recovery. Modular and prefabricated systems can accelerate construction where time, labor, and resources are limited, while vernacular techniques and locally available materials can make rebuilding more responsive to climate, culture, and existing construction knowledge. Lightweight and recyclable materials have also been explored as alternatives for temporary structures, raising broader questions around dignity, adaptability, cost, transportation, and the transition from emergency accommodation to permanent housing.

The Role of Biomimicry in Disaster-Resilient Architecture
The Impact of Wildfires on Building Codes: Reflections on the Recent Los Angeles Fires
Resilient Materials, Infrastructure, and Urban Adaptation
Beyond individual buildings, disaster resilience is shaped by the materials, landscapes, infrastructure, and public spaces that connect homes to their wider environments. Fire-resistant and self-repairing materials, permeable surfaces, green roofs, water-retention systems, passive cooling strategies, and other forms of green and blue infrastructure can help cities manage heat, flooding, fire, and other environmental pressures. At the same time, the uneven distribution of these measures raises questions of access and inequality, emphasizing the need to consider resilience not only as a technical challenge but also as a question of who is protected, where investment is directed, and how urban systems can adapt over time.

BYD unveiled the flagship Atto 8 with &quot;breakthrough&quot; fast charging, but there is a catch
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
09:29:16 EEST
15:29:16 KST

BYD unveiled the flagship Atto 8 with "breakthrough" fast charging, but there is a catch
Kyiv • UNN
The seven-seat BYD Atto 8 has debuted in Europe with a 115 kWh battery and a range of up to 640 km. Charging in 9 minutes is possible only at Flash stations.
The new BYD Atto 8 electric vehicle from Chinese automaker BYD debuted in Europe with a 115 kWh Blade battery, impressive WLTP-range figures, and nine-minute fast charging under certain conditions. UNN reports this, citing Motor1.com.
Details
At the Paris Motor Show, BYD presented a figure that most electric-vehicle manufacturers would not dare to claim: nine minutes. According to the automaker, that is how long the new Atto 8 needs to charge from an almost depleted battery to full, provided it is connected to the right charger.
Paris Motor Show Mondial de l'Auto: dates and main premieres09.10.26, 16:46 • 129088 views
The Atto 8 is BYD's first seven-seat electric flagship for Europe, built around a second-generation 115 kWh Blade battery. It will appear in European showrooms in the first quarter of 2027, and its specifications are just as impressive as its claimed charging figures, the publication notes.
BYD's largest and most expensive crossover in Europe
BYD unveiled the Atto 8—the brand's largest and most expensive crossover (SUV) in the region—on October 12. The crossover is approximately 5 meters long, about 2 meters wide, and approximately 1.8 meters high, placing it among the largest three-row crossovers sold in Europe.
Inside, BYD has installed a panoramic glass roof measuring approximately 2.4 square meters and a 15.6-inch central touchscreen—technologies that have become standard in flagship SUVs. BYD Executive Vice President Stella Li called the model confirmation of the brand's broader ambitions, describing the Atto 8 as an "ideal example" of bringing intelligent technologies into reality.
The seven-seat layout places the Atto 8 in Europe's crowded three-row electric-vehicle segment, including the Skoda Peaq. BYD is betting that battery size and charging speed, rather than seating-layout flexibility alone, will be what distinguishes its flagship model from competitors.
A common mistake among buyers of any three-row electric vehicle is assuming that seven seats mean seven adults can sit comfortably on a long journey. The third row in vehicles of this size is generally best suited to children or short trips, regardless of the brand, the publication writes.
What configurations are available
BYD offers the Atto 8 in two configurations. The rear-wheel-drive Design version develops 455 horsepower, accelerates to 100 km/h in approximately 5.8 seconds, and has a claimed WLTP range of 640 km.
The all-wheel-drive Excellence version sacrifices some range for speed. Its two electric motors produce a combined 764 hp and approximately 774 Nm of torque. BYD claims that acceleration to 100 km/h takes just 4.6 seconds, more than three seconds faster than the rear-wheel-drive model, although the claimed WLTP range falls to 500 km.
Fast charging, but there's a catch
The main feature is fast charging. BYD claims that the Atto 8 can charge from 10% to 70% in five minutes and from 10% to 97% in nine minutes. Li called this "the breakthrough in electric vehicles that everyone has been waiting for," comparing the charging speed to refueling a gasoline tank.
These figures come with conditions that BYD "does not put in the headline." Achieving the nine-minute result requires a second-generation Blade battery paired with special BYD Flash chargers capable of delivering up to 1,500 kilowatts.
When connected to a fast-charging station operated by a third-party provider, the Atto 8's charging power will be limited by that network's capabilities. This distinction matters because BYD plans to install only 3,000 Flash stations across Europe by the end of 2027.
Cold weather also changes the situation. At temperatures as low as minus 30 degrees Celsius, BYD says charging from 10% to 97% takes 12 minutes, which is three minutes longer than claimed by the manufacturer.

More than 193 million passengers traveled through Türkiye’s airports in the first nine months of 2026, Transport and Infrastructure Minister Abdulkadir Uraloğlu has said, citing data from the General Directorate of State Airports Authority (DHMİ).

Total passenger traffic grew 2.9 percent year-on-year.

Istanbul Airport handled 64.5 million passengers in the first nine months of the year, including 13.57 million domestic and 50.94 million international travelers. Aircraft traffic at the airport totaled 414,553 flights during the period.
Istanbul Sabiha Gökçen Airport served 37.95 million passengers in January-September, with 17.47 million traveling on domestic routes and 20.48 million on international routes.
Airports in the country’s tourism hubs welcomed 49.63 million passengers during the first nine months of the year, including 16.32 million domestic and 33.31 million international travelers.
