Kyiv won’t turn into dead city - energy expert
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
09:28:48 EEST
15:28:48 KST

Kyiv can fully avoid becoming a dead, frozen city because energy workers prepared for any scenario, as the speed of power restoration after Russian strikes shows, Center for Energy Research Director Oleksandr Kharchenko said.
“Right now this is a scenario Russia is carrying out. It is not a horror, the situation is under control. What is happening is clear. How to fix it is clear. And it will keep repeating as long as massive missile and drone strikes are carried out… Without the ability to restore quickly, we would face a long prospect of bad days… There will be no dead-city situation,” Kharchenko said on the Tse Baza podcast on YouTube.
After each Russian strike on the capital there will be difficult periods when, on frosty days, electricity is available only six to eight hours a day, he said.
Kharchenko said he is convinced that “Russia will not manage to knock Kyiv down to worse than six to eight hours with electricity.”
The capital, which lost its three main combined heat and power plants to ballistic strikes in January, will be supplied from external sources through power lines that the Russians cannot disable, for certain reasons, and from new generation, Kharchenko said.
“About 250 MW [of new capacity] will be working. That will not be enough for households, which will come after heat, water and sewage. But I do not believe in collapse, I see how much and what has been done,” he said.
“A sewage problem for three to four hours is not a problem,” he said.
If there is no shelling, restrictions in Kyiv could be lifted in about a week and a half, Kharchenko said.
A mild but realistic scenario for Kyiv under Russian shelling includes periodic emergency power outages every two to three weeks, plus scheduled restrictions of four to six hours a day in between, he said.
A harsh scenario means up to 18 hours without electricity in scheduled outages and at times no water, he said.
“I think we will not reach serious loss of heating, although that is possible too, but not for the whole city and not for long. There will be restoration, and mobile boiler houses and generators,” he said.
Among other cities that Russia constantly shells, Odesa is at risk this winter because it has no generation of its own but is home to many people, Kharchenko said. Kryvy Rih and Dnipro have generation, but it is under threat of being lost to shelling, he said.
Consumption in Chernihiv and Sumy is much lower, but they are even more vulnerable to shelling, he said. The situation in Zaporizhia is better, in his view, because it has a large hydropower plant and no large concentration of thermal sources. In Kharkiv, “a lot has been done,” he said.

What is holding back Cyprus's Schengen ambitions?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
06:26:00 UTC
15:26:00 KST

What is holding back Cyprus's Schengen ambitions?
October 13, 2026
Cyprus is closer than ever to joining the Schengen Area.
Together with Ireland, Cyprus is currently the only member of the European Union not to be part of Europe's border-free travel zone.
After years of preparations and the implementation of 120 technical recommendations, Nicosia received a positive assessment from the European Commission in July, confirming its technical readiness.
The recommendations, issued as part of EU evaluations dating back to 2021, covered areas including border controls, visa policy, access to European security databases and police cooperation. Their implementation required technological upgrades as well as legislative and administrative reforms.
On October 1, Cyprus's Deputy Minister for Migration and International Protection, Nicholas Ioannides, confirmed that "all recommendations made by the European Commission are now considered to have been implemented."
According to Ioannides, Cyprus is technically ready to join Schengen, with the next step being to secure the necessary political agreement.
Austria, the Netherlands express reservations
However, a positive technical assessment alone is not enough for Cyprus to join the Schengen Area.
Accession requires a unanimous decision by the EU Council following consultation with the European Parliament.
According to information obtained by DW, Austria and the Netherlands have already informally expressed reservations over security concerns linked to the Green Line, which divides the island of Cyprus, and the special status of the British Sovereign Base Areas.
Although neither country has officially threatened to veto Cyprus's accession, their reservations carry particular weight.
Both Austria and the Netherlands have previously raised objections to the expansion of the Schengen Area to Bulgaria and Romania.
What is the Green Line?
Perhaps the most significant obstacle is the Green Line, the approximately 180-kilometer-long (112 miles) ceasefire line that has divided Cyprus since Turkey's military intervention in 1974.
It separates the areas controlled by the internationally recognized Republic of Cyprus from the Turkish-controlled northern part of the island.
The buffer zone is monitored by the United Nations Peacekeeping Force in Cyprus (UNFICYP), while the Green Line itself is not an internationally recognized state border.
Crossings between the two sides take place at nine designated crossing points and are governed by a special EU regulation.
This unique arrangement poses a challenge to Schengen membership, as the Republic of Cyprus does not exercise effective control along the entire length of the line. At the same time, Nicosia rejects any arrangement that could turn the Green Line into an external border, either legally or even symbolically.
"The issue raised by some Schengen countries is that the Republic of Cyprus does not control the entire Green Line. It may control the crossing points, but there are also open stretches of land," Dr. Nasia Hadjigeorgiou, associate professor of Transitional Justice and Human Rights at the School of Law of UCLan Cyprus, told DW.
"For it to be considered to have full control, something would have to change. Either the Cyprus problem would have to be resolved, or a strictly controlled physical border would have to be established. There is no other way," said Hadjigeorgiou.
Why are the British Sovereign Base Areas an issue?
Another obstacle to Cyprus's Schengen ambitions is the presence of the British Sovereign Base Areas of Akrotiri and Dhekelia, which remained under UK sovereignty when Cyprus gained independence in 1960.
Together, the two areas cover 254 square kilometers (98 square miles), almost 3% of the island, and remain British sovereign territory.
The main complication concerns the Dhekelia base area, which borders both the territory controlled by the Republic of Cyprus and the self-declared Turkish Republic of Northern Cyprus, which is not internationally recognized.
Two crossing points, at Pergamos and Strovilia, are located in this area, where checks are carried out by British authorities. The UK is no longer a member of the European Union.
Dr. Nasia Hadjigeorgiou explains the difficulties arising from this unusual arrangement: "This is problematic because the area in question is controlled on one side by the authorities in the occupied north and on the other by the British Sovereign Base Areas."
"As a result, the United Kingdom would be controlling who enters and leaves the Schengen Area. This is an unusual situation, since it is normally the Schengen member states themselves that decide who can enter and leave the area," she said.
According to information obtained by DW, Nicosia and the British Sovereign Base Areas have already begun discussions on upgrading border control procedures at Pergamos and Strovilia to bring them into line with EU requirements.
Political negotiations with EU countries
In the meantime, Nicosia has stepped up its diplomatic efforts to secure the necessary consensus.
Deputy Minister for Migration Nicholas Ioannides held bilateral meetings with his counterparts from Austria, the Netherlands and Finland on October 1 on the sidelines of the EU Justice and Home Affairs Council meeting in Luxembourg. Cyprus's accession to Schengen was among the issues discussed.
Cyprus also secured significant political backing on October 7 during the summit of the nine Mediterranean EU member states (MED9) in Croatia.
In their joint declaration, the leaders welcomed the European Commission's positive assessment and called for the timely completion of Cyprus's accession process.
Nevertheless, diplomatic sources speaking to DW on condition of anonymity cautioned that despite the positive signals, Cyprus's entry into the Schengen Area should by no means be taken for granted.
The same sources consider it highly likely that the EU may choose to wait for the outcome of the ongoing efforts to resolve the Cyprus problem before making a decision that could create additional political and practical complications.

“If attacked, we are ready to fight tonight,” Grynkewich told the audience in the Polish capital, which broke into applause. “We will continue to prepare and rehearse each and every day, so we will be more ready tomorrow, and even more ready the day after that.”
According to NATO officials, the battle plan involves the use of capabilities from across the alliance, including traditional fighting methods such as frontline ground forces as well as military aircraft, our NATO correspondent Shona Murray reports.

IMF warns AI market correction, cyberattacks threaten global financial stability
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
06:22:57 UTC
15:22:57 KST

The International Monetary Fund has warned of elevated risks to the global financial system, citing the possibility of an AI-related market correction, severe cyberattacks and a surge in bond yields.
The warning came in the IMF’s latest Global Financial Stability Report, published on Tuesday during its annual meetings with the World Bank in Bangkok, Thailand.
“These risks are plausible near-term catalysts for a sharp tightening of financial conditions and market turmoil,” the report said.
The AI boom, fuelled by investment in semiconductors and data centres, has supported global growth despite geopolitical pressures, including the war in the Middle East.
However, the IMF warned that AI capabilities could be delivered with less investment than expected, while the potential economic gains might also fall short of forecasts.
“Weaker or less durable AI investments and profitability could be a shock that triggers a market correction,” the report said.
The fund also warned that increasingly sophisticated cyber threats could undermine confidence and disrupt critical financial infrastructure.
“Severe cyber incidents could undermine market confidence and disrupt critical financial market infrastructure and operations,” it said.
Athanasios Vamvakidis, deputy director of the IMF’s Monetary and Capital Markets Department, told reporters that cyber risks to the financial system were both “known and very much unknown”.
“The policy priority should be to strengthen resilience before new shocks hit the economy,” he said.
Cyber risks and bond yields
The IMF warned that the risk of successful cyberattacks on critical financial institutions and market infrastructure was worsening as AI capabilities advanced and financial systems became more digitised.
“The impact could be severe as rapid digitisation has increased the attack surface,” the report said.
Caio Ferreira, deputy division chief at the IMF’s Monetary and Capital Markets Department, said emerging markets were particularly vulnerable where resources for cyber defence were insufficient.
The report added that advanced AI models could be used to carry out cyberattacks but could also help strengthen defences.
Another major risk is a rise in bond yields, which could trigger significant shocks because sovereign bond markets underpin the global financial system.
The IMF warned that higher energy prices could reignite inflation and force central banks to tighten monetary policy, putting further pressure on bond markets.

He added that any assistance, if being provided, would be at a very low level.

He said Xi’s assurance also covered Chinese companies.

One official said Russia was supplying missiles to Iran. The White House rejected the assessment of Iran’s military capabilities, while Russia’s Defense Ministry did not respond to Bloomberg’s request for comment.

Washington had imposed sanctions in May on Chinese companies accused of supporting Iranian military procurement and supplying satellite imagery.
Meanwhile, Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baghaei said on Oct. 12 that Tehran was still assessing the U.S. response to its proposal on reopening Hormuz and would reply through intermediaries once the review was complete.
His comments followed a statement by Iranian security chief Mohsen Rezaei that Washington’s response did not sufficiently address Tehran’s seven conditions for reopening the waterway and returning to negotiations.
Washington wants Iran’s nuclear program addressed from the outset. Tehran says discussions should first focus on reopening the strait and restoring security there.
Qatar and Pakistan have been among the mediators seeking to end the war, which began with U.S. and Israeli strikes on Iran on Feb. 28.
An interim ceasefire reached in June broke down, and intermittent strikes resumed.
Before the war, the Strait of Hormuz carried about a fifth of global trade in oil and liquefied natural gas.
Disputes over navigation through the waterway remain central to efforts to reach a settlement.

Eleven sailors missing after drone sinks ship off Bulgaria
SOFIA, Oct 13 - Eleven sailors were missing at sea on Tuesday from a ship sunk by a drone attack off the coast of Bulgaria, possibly the second deadly sinking of a cargo vessel in the area in a week, prompting Bulgaria to summon Russia's ambassador.
Two cargo ships were hit by drones overnight and one was sunk, Bulgarian officials said. Bulgaria stopped short of explicitly accusing Russia of carrying out the attacks but Prime Minister Rumen Radev said their outcome "benefits the Russian Federation".
There was no immediate comment from Moscow on the incidents.
"This is absolutely unacceptable — another attack in the immediate vicinity of Bulgarian territorial waters," Radev said in a televised address.
The attacks were also condemned by Ukraine and the EU.
"The Black Sea has become another front of escalation of the Russian war in Ukraine," European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said on X. "Those responsible should be held accountable."
Ukraine's Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said on X on Tuesday that the strike "once again demonstrates Moscow's deliberate disregard for civilian lives".
"The Black Sea is a lifeline for global food security. Russia is attacking it to weaponise hunger and hold the world hostage," he said.
Speaking with von der Leyen and NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte by telephone on Tuesday, Radev urged their support to bolster his country's maritime and airspace surveillance, the Bulgarian government said in a statement.
NATO would continue to adjust its military presence on its eastern flank "as needed", Rutte said.
Defence Minister Dimitar Stoyanov spoke on the phone with his counterparts from Romania and Turkey and discussed security in the Black Sea region.
BLACK SEA SHIPPING DRAWN INTO WAR
Bulgarian officials said five crew members had been rescued but 11 were still listed as missing from the ship which sank off the coast of the village of Krapets, near the Romanian border. President Iliana Iotova identified the vessel as the Guinea-Bissau-flagged cargo ship HS Dignity and said a search and rescue operation was ongoing.
Another ship, the Chelsea-3 sailing under a Maltese flag, was also hit by three drones overnight, Bulgarian officials said. All crew from that ship — seven Ukrainians and eight Azerbaijanis — were rescued and none seriously injured.
The Chelsea-3 called at the Romanian port of Tulcea on October 3 before sailing towards the Bulgarian coast, according to ship tracking data on LSEG and MarineTraffic. The vessel was showing it was at 72% of its full load, indicating it had cargo onboard.
The sunken HS Dignity, which was also part-loaded, was sailing to the Romanian port of Braila and had previously called at the Algerian port of Mostaganem, ship tracking data showed.
A week ago nine Syrian sailors and one Egyptian were lost at sea from a ship that sank when hit by drones in Bulgaria's Black Sea exclusive economic zone. Another ship was also hit that night but the crew was rescued.
After meeting Radev in Sofia, Russian Ambassador Eleonora Mitrofanova said she had no information from the Russian Defence Ministry about attacks on commercial vessels in the Black Sea but did not rule out they could be a provocation by a third party, the Bulgarian government said.
More than four and a half years into the war that Moscow launched with its full-scale invasion in 2022, Black Sea shipping has increasingly been drawn into a prolonged battle of economic endurance.
Ukraine and Russia are both among the world's largest exporters of grain.
Russia has been bombing Ukraine's Black Sea ports, forcing Ukraine to rely increasingly on river ports on the Danube and shipping routes close to the coasts of NATO members Bulgaria and Romania.

JSC Grindeks invested €1.87 million to expand finished dosage form packaging capacity
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
06:18:47 UTC
15:18:47 KST

JSC Grindeks has invested €1.87 million in a new packaging line at JSC Tallinna Farmaatsiatehas. During its first eight months of operation, the line produced 719,700 packs of solid oral dosage forms, accounting for 9% of the total volume of finished dosage form packs handled by Grindeks.
The investment covered the development and equipping of a dedicated finished dosage form packaging area, installation of the packaging line, acquisition of technological equipment, and implementation of quality control and traceability solutions. The packaging processes comply with EU Good Manufacturing Practice (GMP) requirements governing pharmaceutical manufacturing, quality control and packaging operations.
Baiba Galviņa, Head of Production at JSC Grindeks, comments: “As demand for Grindeks products increased, we looked for ways to ease pressure on production capacity in Riga while retaining sufficient flexibility in future production planning. The additional equipment required to introduce a new packaging format can cost €50,000–60,000, while the packaging lines in Riga and Tallinn are technologically identical. Using compatible lines at both manufacturing sites allows us to reduce dependence on a single location, plan production more efficiently and introduce new products or packaging formats with greater flexibility. In practice, this kind of setup contributes both to cost efficiency and to long-term operational resilience.”
Kadri Randveer, Head of JSC Tallinna Pharmaceutical Plant, informs: “In the pharmaceutical industry, competitiveness is increasingly determined not only by manufacturing capacity, but also by the ability to adapt flexibly to changing market conditions. Our focus is on gradually expanding the plant’s manufacturing capabilities so that, over time, it can take on a broader range of projects and strengthen its role within the Grindeks Group. This direction also supports Europe’s broader objective of strengthening the resilience of pharmaceutical manufacturing and improving access to critical medicines.”
At present, JSC Tallinna Pharmaceutical Plant packages five medicinal products across several therapeutic areas. The plant also has additional capacity for the manufacture of finished dosage forms, as well as infrastructure for further expansion of packaging capacity. This enables a growing share of manufacturing and supply activities to be carried out within the Group, strengthening control across the manufacturing and supply chain.
About JSC Grindeks
JSC Grindeks is the parent company of the international pharmaceutical group Grindeks. The Group is engaged in the research, development, manufacturing and commercialization of original medicines, generic medicines and active pharmaceutical ingredients.
The Grindeks Group comprises JSC Grindeks and its subsidiaries, including JSC Kalceks in Latvia, JSC Tallinna Farmaatsiatehas in Estonia and HBM Pharma s.r.o. in Slovakia. In total, the Group includes 38 subsidiaries and 11 representative offices.
JSC Grindeks specializes in the development and manufacture of medicines in the therapeutic areas of cardiovascular diseases, central nervous system disorders, oncology, dermatology and diabetes. JSC Kalceks focuses on the development and manufacture of medicines for the hospital segment, while JSC “Tallinna Farmaatsiatehas” specializes in the manufacture of ointments.
The Group’s products are exported to more than 100 countries worldwide. Key export markets include the European Union, Australia, the United Arab Emirates, Israel and CIS countries.

Türkiye urged Israel on Oct. 12 to halt its military incursions in Syria and comply with the 1974 disengagement agreement, saying its actions were undermining the country’s stability and economic recovery.
“The situation is particularly alarming in southern Syria, where continued military incursions and expansionist actions and words are getting out of control,” Türkiye’s U.N. envoy Ahmet Yıldız told the Security Council.
He cited renewed Israeli activity along the “Sufa 53 line” in Quneitra, describing it as an attempt to undermine the agreement and impose new facts on the ground.
“These reckless acts must stop,” he said.
Yıldız called for Israel’s withdrawal from the occupied Syrian Golan and compliance with relevant Security Council resolutions, particularly Resolution 497.
He said Syria needed stability to rebuild its economy, attract investment and participate in regional energy and connectivity projects.
A sovereign and unified Syria capable of securing its borders would also serve Israel’s interests, he added.
Israel moved troops into the Golan buffer zone and nearby positions after Bashar al-Assad’s fall on Dec. 8, 2024.
It says its deployments are driven by security concerns, while Damascus demands their withdrawal.
Yıldız also said the dissolution of the Syrian Democratic Forces had opened a new phase in the integration process and urged the remaining arrangements to be fully implemented without delay.
He welcomed Damascus’ cooperation with the international coalition against ISIL.
Around 2.2 million Syrians remain under temporary protection in Türkiye, Yıldız said, adding that economic conditions, security concerns and Israeli incursions had slowed returns.
Addressing the same session, Syria’s U.N. envoy Ibrahim Olabi said those claiming to seek security “should not be killing Syrian citizens within Syrian territory.”
He said security depended on international legitimacy and Security Council resolutions, and urged support for Syria’s economic recovery and reconstruction.
Olabi called for help restoring schools, hospitals and water and electricity networks, as well as resources and expertise to clear mines and other remnants of war.

“They tasked me with getting him to admit he was LGBTQ too”: A Russian trans girl&#039;s first-hand account of how to escape the FSB
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
06:17:56 UTC
15:17:56 KST

In January 2025, FSB officers searched the home of an 18-year-old trans girl from Tyumen, found correspondence with the Combat Organization of Anarcho-Communists (BOAK) on her phone, and threatened her with criminal charges that could have led to years in prison. Under pressure, she agreed to cooperate with the authorities, and her handlers tasked her with approaching LGBTQ people, gaining their trust, and trying to obtain compromising information on them. In an interview with The Insider, she described how recruitment works, how she managed to outwit the FSB, and how she fled the country without contacts, money, or an international passport.
“They found my messages with BOAK and said, ‘Now you’re really f***ed’”
On January 15, 2025, I woke up to a masked man shouting at me and shaking my shoulder. I was living with my parents at the time, and they had let FSB officers into the house. The officers arrived with a prosecutor’s warrant and, for some reason, said they were looking for an IED.
They barely let me look at the paperwork. They waved the warrant in front of my face and immediately put it away. There were two investigators, plus attesting witnesses and another FSB officer in a balaclava and body armor. They seized my computer, phone, and portable camera.
When I refused to unlock my phone, the masked officer hit me on the back several times, asking, “Want to cough?” I said, “No.” He hit me again.
Then they pulled a hat down over my face, led me into the stairwell, put me in a car, and drove me to the FSB’s city headquarters at 40 Sovetskaya Street. It was around six in the morning. They took me up to the third or fourth floor and questioned me until almost evening.
At first, they asked if I wanted to tell them anything. Then they took my phone to another office and brought it back about 15 minutes later, with all the passwords already reset.
There were two officers, and they played good cop, bad cop in the most ham-fisted way imaginable. One shouted, threatened me, and searched my phone. The other asked questions based on what his colleague told him about its contents.
I decided that since they already had access to my phone, I might as well take responsibility for anything they had found about our initiative’s activities. I said I had put up the leaflets on my own and had done the graffiti by myself, too.
Then I remembered that I hadn’t deleted everything. But it was too late: they had found my email correspondence with BOAK, the Combat Organization of Anarcho-Communists. We had discussed instructions for making anonymous phone calls and how to establish contacts among comrades for the initiative. One email also mentioned a “fascists’ car.”
They later used this correspondence as the basis for a case on “training in terrorist activity.” As soon as they found it, they broke into smiles and said, “That’s it. Now you’re really f***ed.”
They kept searching, but apart from photos of the leaflets, my small left-wing channel with around 30 subscribers, and the emails, they found little else. They tried to get me to confess to something beyond the leaflets, graffiti, and correspondence with BOAK.
For some reason, they believed I had been planning some form of action targeting the car of the head of the Russian Community in Tyumen. I said that the most we had discussed was slashing its tires, but that I had since abandoned the idea altogether — which was why the car was still intact.
Where the security services might have obtained their information
They didn’t beat me at FSB headquarters. The pressure there was mainly psychological, and the conditions were uncomfortable. Instead of a chair, for example, I had to sit on my computer tower. They pointed to a safe in the corner of the office and said they stuffed people inside. They claimed that one person had been kept there for three days without being let out.
They pointed to a safe in the corner of the office and said they stuffed people inside
They also said that if they had caught me not in Tyumen but in Ukrainian territory occupied after the full-scale invasion, they would have killed me. The officer playing “bad cop” threatened to throw me into a cell where five people would rape me.
Toward evening, they drove me home and, you could say, handed me over to my father. Once again, they gave me no documents. I wasn’t formally under house arrest, but they told me I must not leave the apartment or they would take me to a pretrial detention center.
They kept my phone, computer, and camera.
After that, I began noticing signs of surveillance around the house. Cars with unfamiliar license plates appeared, and for the first three days, a strange man in camouflage sat outside the entrance with a bicycle from morning until evening. My mother noticed him too when she left for work. He made little effort to hide the fact that he was there for a reason.
I spent about a week and a half cooped up at home.
“You’re facing 15 to 25 years. Your only way out is to cooperate.”
About a week and a half later, my father and I were summoned to the FSB building. The investigator who had played “good cop,” a man named Daniil, told my father that everything was fine: I would supposedly receive an administrative penalty, and that would be the end of it.
They returned my computer and camera but kept my phone. They said I could go to university again, but nowhere else — moving only between home and the university.
Soon afterward, Daniil called my father and told him I had to report immediately to Room 300 in Tyumen State University’s building at 16 Lenina Street. I went. He locked the door and told me I was facing charges of “training in terrorist activity” and “justifying terrorism.” He showed me a printout listing the charges.
I still don’t understand what grounds they had for accusing me of “justifying terrorism.” I hadn’t posted anything about Russian partisans on my channel. Maybe they planned to use some tangentially related post.
He said I was facing 15 to 25 years in prison and that my only way out was to cooperate. I decided I would find out whom they wanted me to entrap, escape in time, and warn the person they were targeting.
The FSB officer said that because I was LGBTQ, I had to frame another LGBTQ person.
The FSB officer said that since I was LGBTQ, I had to frame another LGBTQ person
I formally agreed to cooperate and signed a piece of paper. He dictated the wording, and I wrote it out by hand on a sheet of A4 paper: “I, [surname, first name, patronymic], undertake to cooperate with the state security agencies.” That was it — just my signature at the bottom. There wasn’t even a stamp on it. He also warned that disclosing any of this could get me charged with treason.
After I signed, they returned my phone. The FSB officer said he would message me on Telegram, then they let me go.
I had no intention of carrying out their assignment. I just needed to find out whom they wanted me to frame, buy time, and get out of the country before they realized I wasn’t going to do anything for them.
“Gain his trust and get him to admit he’s LGBTQ”
Soon afterward, Daniil messaged me on Telegram. He sent me a dating chat and identified the person he wanted me to entrap.
The chat was called “The Gym.” It was disguised as a place where people simply chatted and worked out together, so creeps like Daniil wouldn’t raid it. Somehow, though, he had apparently figured out that it was more about dating than sports.
It was a nationwide chat with several hundred members. Daniil said there was a man from Tyumen in the group. He sent me his username and told me to message him. The man had mentioned that he enjoyed swimming, so the FSB officer told me to write, “I want to swim too. Let’s get to know each other.”
My task was to get him to admit that he was LGBTQ too, then send the entire exchange to the FSB. They didn’t tell me what they planned to do with him afterward. When I asked why they needed this, Daniil said I wouldn’t be told.
I messaged the man but deliberately dragged things out: I’d go several days without contacting him or talk about unrelated topics. I pretended to be carrying out the assignment, but I wasn’t doing what they’d asked — trying to get him to disclose his sexual orientation.
Meanwhile, I was preparing to flee.
I also suspected they might have installed some kind of software on my phone. After the FSB returned it, all the apps ran much more slowly, and calls were plagued by interference. Telegram also showed a device other than my own among the active sessions. I left it there to avoid arousing suspicion. I handled all communications unrelated to the FSB on devices they didn’t know about, including a spare phone the officers hadn’t found during the search.
This went on for about a week or a week and a half. I kept stalling, but I knew it couldn’t last: sooner or later, I’d either have to entrap the man or end up in pretrial detention myself.
So I began preparing to flee as soon as they returned my phone.
“Sometimes it’s do or die”
My plan was to cross the border into Kazakhstan. Tyumen is not far from the Kazakh border, and I decided that my priority was to get to safety and warn others. I’d figure out the rest once I got there.
The main problem was that I didn’t have a passport for international travel. However, Russian citizens could enter Kazakhstan using their domestic passports. I was worried they might detain me at the border, of course, but I decided that sometimes you have to take a risk. If there was a chance to escape, I had to try.
I rehearsed what I would tell the border guards: the university was on holiday, and I’d decided to take a trip to see the local sights. I agreed with my comrades that if I didn’t contact them within 24 hours, it meant I’d been caught.
I fled on February 24, leaving home late that evening. People I suspected were FSB agents still occasionally kept watch outside the building, so I first had to shake off surveillance. Then I made my way to the bus station.
I bought my ticket just two hours before departure, deliberately leaving it until the last minute so they wouldn’t catch wind of my plans. But when I arrived to board, I discovered that my ticket had been canceled for some reason about an hour earlier. The bus station staff couldn’t explain why.
I approached the driver and told him I desperately needed to get to Kazakhstan. I made up some story, and he believed me and agreed to take me.
At the Russian border, I encountered an ordinary, tired-looking official. He checked my passport, logged my border crossing in the system, and that was it. The Kazakh border guards asked why I was traveling. I gave them the story I’d prepared, and they let me through, too.
As it turned out, the FSB officers hadn’t learned in time that I’d left home late that evening and was heading abroad. They found out I’d crossed the border only about an hour to an hour and a half after I’d reached the other side.
The FSB didn’t find out I’d crossed the border until about an hour or an hour and a half after I’d reached the other side
When I got off the bus in Kazakhstan, I sat on my bag and lit a cigarette. Then I rushed to find a SIM card. I bought one and messaged my comrades to say I’d made it out. Next, I messaged the person the FSB wanted me to entrap and the admin of “The Gym,” warning them that the authorities were planning a provocation against members of the chat. They read my messages but didn’t reply.
“Crossing the border was easier than getting any farther”
The next morning, the FSB summoned my father and asked if he knew where I was. They told him that if he found out, he had to inform them immediately.
I spoke to my parents a few days later. My father told me the FSB had sent me a message through him, saying more or less that I could stay in Kazakhstan legally for only a limited time and offering me the chance to return to Russia voluntarily.
Of course, I had no intention of returning. I knew Kazakhstan extradited people for political reasons, so I began looking for a way to get farther away. Crossing into Kazakhstan was only the first stage of my escape. The biggest problem was that I didn’t have an international passport.
Without one, you’re in an extremely precarious position. While your legal stay remains valid, you can somehow get by, but after that, things become much harder. It’s almost impossible to find legal work, obtaining legal status is difficult, and there are few places you can go next.
A Russian domestic passport allows you to enter only a handful of countries: Belarus, Armenia, Kazakhstan, and Kyrgyzstan. Most of these options are unsafe for someone fleeing political persecution in Russia.
That’s why you need to apply for an international passport as soon as possible, but that proved to be a slow process for me. The first time I went to the consulate to apply, I discovered that I had to fill out a form on its website and bring a printed copy, even though the published instructions didn’t mention the latter requirement. I rushed off to print it, but when I returned, they told me I was too late and they wouldn’t accept my documents that day.
I made another appointment, and the process dragged on. More than two months passed between my attempts to submit the application, waiting for appointments, and dealing with other problems. For a while, I also lacked a suitable device that could reliably access the consulate’s website.
One option for getting farther away is a humanitarian visa. I applied for one from France. Someone persecuted for their political views, activism, or identity has ample grounds to seek a humanitarian visa.
The main problem is the wait. Getting a decision within five months is already lucky; often, the wait stretches to eight months or longer. All that time, you have to somehow survive in a country where you have no secure legal status, no job, and no easy way to simply buy a ticket and leave.
To anyone who has found themselves in this situation, anyone forced under threat to agree to cooperate, I want to say this: don’t let them break you. Even if you’ve already signed a paper agreeing to cooperate, as long as you haven’t betrayed anyone or helped entrap them, don’t get your hands dirty. Try to save both yourself and those whom the authorities want to throw into the machinery of repression using you. There is a way out — not always, perhaps, but in many cases. Don’t betray others, and don’t betray yourself.
I used to read a lot about revolutionaries: how Mikhail Bakunin escaped tsarist exile by making his way across Siberia, how people broke out of prisons, and how they outwitted the tsarist secret police. History offers examples that can inspire us to take the right course of action.
Lawyers’ advice: what to do if the security services try to recruit you
There is no one-size-fits-all guide to such situations. Much depends on whether the person has been detained, whether the authorities have evidence that could be used to bring criminal charges, how serious the threats are, and whether the person can physically leave Russia. The following recommendations draw on the guidance published by First Department, advice from EQUAL PostOst director Evi Chaika, and the author’s own experience.
If you can safely refuse, do so clearly and briefly. There is no need to argue at length with security officers or explain your beliefs. If the situation is relatively straightforward — for example, you have been detained over an administrative offense and have no reason to believe a criminal case is being prepared against you — firmly state that you will not cooperate. As First Department lawyer Yevgeny Smirnov points out, hesitation can signal to security officers that you may still be persuaded.
If you effectively have to choose between cooperating and being imprisoned immediately, there is no universal answer. Everyone must assess their own risks. But agreeing to cooperate does not mean you must carry out the security services’ subsequent demands. There have been cases in which people agreed under pressure, were released, then cut off contact and left the country.
Do nothing that could put another person at risk. Do not try to provoke people into making statements or taking actions that could lead to prosecution, do not gather compromising information, and do not pass on sensitive data. If the security services have already given you an assignment, bear in mind that it may itself be a test, and the person you have been instructed to target may be part of an operational scheme. It is therefore safer to warn the potential target only after leaving Russia.
If you have agreed to cooperate, time is usually limited. The security services may demand a concrete action fairly quickly. Ordinary excuses — illness, being busy, or needing to clarify something — may buy you a few days, but pretending to cooperate for an extended period is dangerous. If you have decided to try to get out of the situation, start preparing to leave immediately.
Contact human rights organizations as soon as possible, and be honest about what has already happened. Even if you have signed a document, handed over information, or complied with a request from the security services, it is not too late to seek help. Do not try to deal with the consequences alone. Human rights advocates can help you assess the risks to yourself and others and find the safest way to end the cooperation. EQUAL PostOst recommends this approach, and First Department likewise advises seeking help immediately if you were unable to refuse at first.
Treat any device that has been in the hands of the security services as potentially compromised. Use another device for sensitive communications, including contact with human rights advocates and preparations to leave the country. The device itself is not the only concern — the location and method of communication matter, too. Avoid talking near a compromised device, and always use secure communication channels.
Document what happens whenever possible. Phone numbers, operatives’ accounts, correspondence, assignments, and the dates and locations of meetings may all prove useful. Save screenshots somewhere other than on a device that may be under the control of the security services. This information can help you obtain assistance and later serve as evidence of persecution, including when applying for international protection.
If the pressure becomes systematic, consider leaving Russia. A chance encounter with an operative does not necessarily mean you are the target of a focused investigation. However repeated summonses, credible threats of criminal prosecution, persistent calls or meetings, surveillance, and pressure on family members are signs that the situation really is serious. EQUAL PostOst director Evi Chaika recommends temporarily leaving Russia, if possible, and assessing the situation from a safer location.
If you decide to leave, your priority is to get yourself out. Do not try to take your entire life with you. Focus on travel documents, money, and a route. Ideally, arrange support from at least one trusted person outside Russia who knows your route, expects messages at agreed times, and knows what to do if you lose contact. Prepare a communication plan, a backup device, and any necessary apps in advance. The fewer people who know about your departure before you have left, the lower the risk that the information will reach the security services.

“Rig the vote or be shipped off to war”: How United Russia &quot;won&quot; its electoral victory in Voronezh
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
06:17:06 UTC
15:17:06 KST

From the Kremlin's perspective, one of the top performers in the 2026 State Duma elections was leadership of the Voronezh Region, where the ruling United Russia party claimed a whopping 72% of the vote. Only four national republics – Chechnya, Dagestan, Ingushetia and Tuva – and the Russian-occupied territories of Ukraine posted higher figures. In previous years, Voronezh — the second-most populous city in the Central Federal District after Moscow — had delivered far less impressive results, and as a local official responsible for liaising with election commissions told The Insider, it was no accident that the region achieved such extraordinary figures this time around. Election commissions were ordered to ensure that at least a third of voters cast their ballots either at home or early, and opposition observers were barred from almost all of the region’s 500 polling stations. In their place, students from Colombia, Chile, and Pakistan were brought in. Unsurprisingly, official turnout nearly doubled, as did United Russia’s share of the vote.
“They dismantled election monitoring the day before the vote”
I’ve worked in this system for more than 25 years, over 20 of them organizing elections.
By the evening of September 20, when the polling stations closed and the count began, I found myself wondering why I was still in this job. What good could any of this do for the city? If I spoke out, they’d laugh at me, then find a reason to fire me – or even build a criminal case against me. But staying silent would mean proving my colleagues right. They’re now congratulating themselves on how neatly we pulled it off in terms of information management. So let my confession at least remain on the record for posterity.
How many votes did United Russia receive in Voronezh and Voronezh Region?
Turnout in Voronezh in State Duma elections had never topped 40%, while United Russia typically won 35–42% of the vote.
The region’s rural districts showed a very different level of loyalty. Turnout exceeded 65% almost everywhere, and in two districts – Anninsky and Bobrovsky – United Russia’s share of the vote approached 100%, with turnout similarly high.
Across the region, the ruling party won 58% of the vote in 2016 and 55% in 2021. In 2026, however, the region unexpectedly gave United Russia 72%.
In May of 2021, Ilya Ivanov, a former deputy head of the regional department for domestic policy, took over as head of the regional election commission. He was reportedly well regarded there because his guiding principle was that all the paperwork and figures had to be in order.
Ahead of the 2021 State Duma elections, he was still finding his feet. By this year’s vote, however, he already had a detailed plan: regional officials set targets for vote share and turnout (presenting them as recommendations), and the mayor then turns them into strict requirements.
This time, there was no direct order to deliver a specific percentage for United Russia. Instead, the requirement was that at least a third of voters cast their ballots either at home or early.
A deliberate purge of election commissions to remove “undesirable” members began last autumn. The regional commission replaced its Communist Party representative, swapping an election-law expert for a “vegetable.” Several heads of territorial election commissions (TECs) were also replaced.
In Voronezh’s Sovetsky District, a notorious stronghold of protests and controversy, the commission was taken over by a former TEC chair from some remote rural district where United Russia gets the “right” result in every election — more than 80% of the vote.
Next came the grassroots level: the chairs of precinct election commissions. Here, too, the pattern was clear. Relatively independent people — a kiosk owner, a construction foreman, or an ordinary pensioner — were replaced by school deputy principals. Many had never taken part in an election before and didn’t know even the basics. They came to us for instructions, looking bewildered and afraid of everything.
CEC, TECs and PECs – how Russia’s electoral system works
Those they couldn’t get rid of were simply intimidated. The night before voting began, one precinct election commission chair received a call from the “higher-ups,” who threatened him: refuse to rig the vote, and you’ll be shipped off to fight in Ukraine. He told the caller to go fuck himself and counted the votes honestly. Several polling stations were housed in the same school. At his station, United Russia received just over 30% of the vote, with the Communist Party and New People close behind. At the other stations, the deputy principals delivered the “right” results.
The day before the election, they crushed election monitoring. More than 400 Communist Party observers were barred from polling stations across the city over a paperwork error – the same error in all their documents. The Communists corrected it in 15 minutes and returned to the election commission with revised lists. But then it was lunchtime, or the door was locked. And then the deadline passed. They really did a number on our Bolshevik comrades – and on the city’s voters, too.
Foreign “observers,” meanwhile, were hauled in by the busload: students from Colombia, Chile and Pakistan. They had no official status as election observers, weren’t stationed at polling stations and had never even observed elections in their own countries. They were given a guided tour and told that ballot boxes were brought to anyone who had difficulty walking. The organizers had supposedly made voting convenient for people by giving them a whole 12 days to cast their ballots. The students were only too happy to repeat all this on camera.
“The key manipulation occurred in the first few days”
What followed was unprecedented in my 20 years of working on elections in Voronezh.
The main manipulation took place in the first few days. You have three days to vote, an order to visit voters at home, and no election observers. It couldn’t be simpler: stuff the mobile ballot box with the required number of ballots, and there’s your result. We’re talking dozens, if not hundreds, of ballots. With no observers around, you can also wait until voting ends and forge the signatures of voters who never turned up, making it look as though they collected their ballots and voted.
Commission chairs fell into two camps: those who fabricated the results and those who refused. They could even be working in the same gym.
One chairwoman said, “I’m not falsifying anything. I have no desire to spend the 20,000 rubles [$238] I’ll earn for working the election dealing with courts and investigators.”
Incidentally, this year almost all payments were official — no cash in envelopes. The only exception was that district administrations allocated a couple of million rubles to each territorial election commission, supposedly to feed commission members during the voting days.
But the chairwoman’s neighbor took a different view: “Well, the city administration called, didn’t they? We have to do it if the motherland asks.” Quite the patriot.
This time, commission chairs who worked in the public sector were actually calling us to ask, “My turnout is 45%. Is that enough, or does it need to be higher?” And this was Saturday afternoon, with another day and a half of voting still to go.
Commission chairs with public-sector jobs were actually calling us this time to ask, “My turnout is 45%. Is that enough, or does it need to be higher?”
Later, when those same school deputy principals submitted their results protocols to the territorial election commissions and were told to their faces that they had obviously falsified the results, they burst into tears and swore they would never, ever take part in elections again. But they were reassured: “You’ve done a great job. The motherland won’t forget you.”
One TEC told me about a commission chair who actually called during the vote count to ask how he should rig the results. When they replied, “Rig them however you like,” he protested: “But I was promised support at every level!” The answer was: “Then take it up with whoever made you that promise.” That polling station was one of the last in the city to submit its results, and United Russia scored a complete triumph there, taking nearly 80% of the vote. Help had arrived after all — they finally explained how to fill in the paperwork.
You could identify the vote-riggers even before their results protocols arrived by how long they spent counting. Actual turnout in Voronezh ranged from 20% to 30%, depending on the polling station, and it reached 40% at the highest. This was despite precinct election commissions spending nearly two weeks going door to door, persuading people to vote at home or vote early. They had been given a clear target: at least a third of voters had to cast their ballots at home.
Those who counted honestly submitted their results protocols to the territorial election commissions first. There wasn’t much to count – just 400–500 ballots. The vote-riggers had a harder job: after the polls closed, they had to forge the signatures of several hundred people who hadn’t shown up, making it appear that they had received ballots and voted.
They couldn’t put this off until later: under the rules, a territorial election commission cannot accept a precinct’s results protocol if the turnout figures don’t match the voter lists. As a result, the vote-riggers submitted their protocols at around dawn — or even later on Monday morning.
The “wrong” exit polls
That morning, Ivanov and our political analysts were officially declaring that the elections in Voronezh had gone smoothly, with no violations reported. It was quite something to hear.
Of course, we’d done everything to ensure that no violations were reported. But even a cursory look at the figures would tell anyone with a basic grasp of math that something was wrong. Results don’t vary that wildly between neighboring polling stations serving the same residential complex. At one, United Russia narrowly trailed the Communists and even New People, getting just 150 votes. Yet right next door, where residents of the building across the street voted, it received more than 1,000!
That morning, we learned that the regional department for domestic policy had commissioned exit polls from a reputable research agency. They showed that United Russia actually had no more than 35% support in Voronezh. The findings were never published. They probably had no intention of publishing them anyway: the point of the exit polls was to get a reasonably accurate picture of the actual vote and use it to manage the voting process.
Exit polls conducted by a reputable local research agency showed that United Russia had no more than 35% support in Voronezh
One of my fellow officials, a rather naive man, even complained at a meeting: "why pay the agency if its findings didn’t match the official results? They were amateurs," he said. How do you respond to that? You can either laugh or cry.
There were rumors that Moscow might call Ivanov and his subordinates to account for such blatant vote-rigging, but I find that hard to believe. The figures and paperwork all line up perfectly. Everything is formally in order. Nobody cares about the substance.

More parks, rivers and green corridors: How Guimarães is preparing for extreme heat
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
06:16:47 UTC
15:16:47 KST

Guimarães, the current European Green Capital, is reshaping the city to tackle extreme heat and climate change.
Guimarães, the current European Green Capital, is the second Portuguese city to receive this title, after Lisbon.
The Minho city in northern Portugal beat Heilbronn in Germany and Klagenfurt in Austria to become European Green Capital for 2026.
The European Commission assesses candidates in seven areas: air quality, noise, water, biodiversity and green spaces, waste and the circular economy, climate mitigation and climate adaptation.
Behind this recognition lies more than a decade of work on green corridors, the restoration of waterways and cutting waste.
Known as the cradle of the nation, the city’s historic centre has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2001. It is in this centuries‑old centre, built in stone and now facing summer temperatures of 40 degrees Celsius, that the municipality is trying to preserve liveable conditions, across an area of 241 square kilometres, home to around 166,000 people.
'We need to design cities with a better quality of life'
The initiatives for the Green Capital year are coordinated by the Guimarães 26 Mission Unit, based at the Landscape Laboratory, set up in 2014 by the municipal council together with the University of Minho and the University of Trás‑os‑Montes and Alto Douro.
For Carlos Ribeiro, head of the Landscape Laboratory, redesigning cities has now become a public health issue.
"We are seeing an increase in diseases linked to heatwaves. So we need to transform our cities. We need to design cities with a better quality of life. And these cities are cities with strong connectivity between green areas but, more importantly, they are cities where people actually use those green areas, the parks," he explains.
The city is developing a green infrastructure strategy based on a radial model, a network of corridors that stretch out from the centre to connect parks, waterways, farmland and forests.
The stated goals include increasing green cover, promoting biodiversity and reducing urban heat islands.
'We have managed to reduce temperatures by two degrees'
Water is central to this effort. The rivers Ave and Vizela are used for leisure as well as for cooling. Low‑impact paths for pedestrians have now been created along their banks.
This is because in summer temperatures in Guimarães can easily reach 40 degrees Celsius.
"We know we are facing climate change and we need to act on it," says Ribeiro. "That is why in recent years we have been preparing the city for climate change and trying to improve connectivity in order to enhance green areas and bring temperatures down. We have managed to reduce temperatures by two degrees. So we know we need to create more green parks, more green areas, and then we need to improve this kind of solution."
The two degrees are not a rough estimate.
Researchers from the Landscape Laboratory and the University of Minho, working with universities in Texas and Colombia, used a decade of satellite images to measure the impact of the city’s green interventions.
Published in September 2025, the study shows that land surface temperatures fell by up to 2.49 degrees Celsius in areas where green roofs and urban gardens were introduced.
However, the authors warn that stronger environmental policies will be needed to sustain the progress achieved so far.

New Delhi – The United States-led global order “is over” and the world has entered a period of heightened geopolitical uncertainty, former British prime minister Rishi Sunak said on Oct 13.
US President Donald Trump is “not a cause of that, he’s a symptom of that”, Sunak said on the first day of Bloomberg’s New Economy Forum in New Delhi.
“The world that we’re in now is one where we don’t quite know what we’ve settled down to, and that creates an enormous amount of geopolitical uncertainty and indeed danger.”
The world is adjusting to a new geopolitical reality, with China now a peer competitor to the US across economic, military and technological spheres, while countries including India and the Gulf states have greater freedom to chart their own course, Sunak said.
Sunak, who remains a British lawmaker, also warned of the risks stemming from dependence on China for critical minerals and key ingredients used in medicines.
Efforts to reduce those vulnerabilities could make India a “massive beneficiary”, as the US, Britain and others look to trusted partners to diversify their supply chains, he said.
“If you want a trusted partner like India that can provide that resilience for you. That to me seems the right type of avenue to pursue.”
Sunak also said that technology companies are on track to become larger net issuers of long-term debt than the US government in 2027. Bloomberg

Anthropic warns AI models may soon replicate themselves without data centres
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
06:13:35 UTC
15:13:35 KST

Anthropic said on Monday its experiments suggested small AI models may be months away from being capable enough to self-replicate on commercial internet-of-things (IoT) devices, such as smart ovens and off-brand Android TV boxes.
In its experiments, Anthropic looked at whether AI models could find vulnerable devices, copy themselves into those devices, and continue spreading without human help.
It found that small models under 30 billion parameters could complete the many steps needed for replication.
However, the firm found that such AI models also struggled to complete the entire sequence from start to finish.
In its simplified tests, where some security steps were removed, Anthropic found that GLM-5.2 and stronger models were capable of end-to-end replication.
Replicating models would be hard to shut down as there is no central switch-off point and, unlike non-AI malware, they could also figure out unfamiliar devices on their own, targeting data centre processors, Anthropic warned.
The firm focused on IoT devices like Android TVs, smart appliances, and other internet-connected gadgets in its research as these are typically poorly secured.
The AI major also warned that if small models improved at their historical rate, they would be able to autonomously replicate by the end of this year, with small weight-based replicators following suit soon after.
Anthropic also said such autonomous AI systems were likely to replicate slowly and rely on widely available, relatively insecure computing resources. It added that systems should be strengthened to make it harder for such AI agents to spread.

PKK withdraws from four bases in northern Iraq
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
06:12:48 UTC
15:12:48 KST

The PKK has withdrawn from four cave bases in northern Iraq near the Turkish border, Turkish security sources said on Oct. 12.
The group vacated the Hebat, Yajk, Sabri and Sason shelters in Metina’s Baze area on Oct. 8, the sources said.
The area had long served as a base and transit point for the group.
The withdrawal is part of the government’s “terror-free Türkiye” initiative, under which the PKK decided to dissolve last year.
Speaking in Gaziantep on Oct. 12, Parliament Speaker Numan Kurtulmuş said some caves and weapons in Metina had been handed over to state institutions, describing the handover as an important step.
He said applying legal measures covering PKK members required security agencies to confirm the group’s disarmament and dissolution, followed by an announcement by the National Security Council.
The Law on Strengthening National Solidarity and Social Integration was published in the Official Gazette on Aug. 18.
Kurtulmuş said a board chaired by the vice president would oversee the process, alongside a parliamentary monitoring committee.
He also called for complete disarmament and steps to strengthen the rule of law and democratic standards.
Nechirvan Barzani, president of Iraq’s Kurdistan Region, meanwhile voiced support for the process at the Middle East Research Institute forum in Erbil on Oct. 12.
Barzani said the initiative was serious and that concerns about its pace were understandable, adding that the issue could not be resolved overnight.
“It may not be moving as quickly as we would like, but it is moving in the right direction,” he said.
Barzani said Erbil was ready to contribute. He also said whoever resolved the issue would deserve the Nobel Peace Prize, singling out President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan.

Ukraine strikes on Yandex data centers cut traffic to Estonian sites nearly 100%
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
06:09:00 UTC
15:09:00 KST

Ukraine strikes on Yandex data centers cut traffic to Estonian sites nearly 100%
Traffic from Russia's Yandex network to Estonian websites has fallen nearly 100 percent following Ukrainian strikes on the internet company's data centers.
The Information System Authority (RIA) says average requests from Yandex fell roughly 420 times by October 13 compared with September's average, following strikes last week. RIA puts the overall drop in Yandex traffic to Estonian sites at 99.8 percent.
Ukraine struck three Yandex data centers last week — one near Moscow on Sunday, one in Sasovo on Thursday and one in Kaluga on Friday.
"The average number of queries coming from the Yandex network has decreased by 99.8 percent, or roughly 420 times, compared with the September average, as of October 13," said Simon Berner, an analyst at RIA's analysis and prevention department.
Yandex was forced to suspend operations at the data center near Moscow on Sunday after the facility was damaged in a Ukrainian drone strike.
Foreign media has reported that the strikes on Yandex also dealt a blow to the Kremlin's online influence operations, including via bot activity in English, which often takes a far-right perspective.
RIA says, however, that it is too early to assess possible changes in the activity of cyberattacks carried out by Russia.
"At the same time, there is no reason to assume that disruptions to Yandex data centers would have a significant effect on the frequency of cyberattacks directed against Estonia. Various infrastructures are used to carry out attacks, and these do not depend on the functioning of Yandex services," Berner said.
Monitoring Russia's influence activities, including the activity of social media bots and troll accounts, does not fall within RIA's competence, so the authority cannot confirm or refute claims that their activity has decreased.
Yandex also operates food delivery and taxi apps used by tens of millions of people; it has previously said its data centers are essential to the normal functioning of its services.
Yandex taxi services in Estonia were banned shortly after the start of the full-scale Russian invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.

China has caused luxury giant LVMH’s sales to plunge
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
09:08:47 EEST
15:08:47 KST

China has caused luxury giant LVMH’s sales to plunge
Kyiv • UNN
LVMH’s sales on the mainland fell by a double-digit percentage, while Chinese consumers’ purchases abroad declined. In the United States, spending increased.
LVMH Moët Hennessy Louis Vuitton SE this week provided a more detailed analysis of the deepening downturn in China’s luxury goods market, reporting that sales in mainland China fell by a double-digit percentage in the third quarter, while the group, which traditionally relies on big-spending consumers, also saw overseas sales decline. UNN reports this, citing Bloomberg.
Details
Weak spending contributed to a 5% decline in organic revenue in Asia, excluding Japan, the only region where the luxury giant recorded a year-on-year decrease. Purchases by Chinese shoppers abroad fell by several percentage points, while overall demand improved toward the end of the quarter ended September 30, Chief Financial Officer Cécile Cabanis told analysts during a conference call.
China’s slowing economic growth, long regarded as an indicator of the industry’s health, is raising doubts about the sustainability of the broader luxury market recovery and could be a warning sign for competitors, including Yves Saint Laurent owner Kering SA and Hermès International SCA, which are due to report their financial results, the publication writes. Less than a year ago, China was contributing to the industry’s recovery, but deteriorating economic sentiment is once again putting pressure on spending in the luxury goods segment.
"The news flow from China over the summer was not particularly good," Cabanis said. "So it really affected positive sentiment and created a short-term subdued environment in China."
Demand for luxury goods in China is declining across many categories. Consumer caution amid the broader economic downturn is restraining domestic spending and prompting some shoppers to turn to cheaper local brands. At the same time, the recent weakening of the stock market and tighter taxation of overseas assets are putting pressure on some of the country’s wealthiest consumers.
"It’s difficult for everyone right now," said Jacques Roizen, co-founder of Shanghai-based consulting firm Foresight Performance Partners. "LVMH’s portfolio, as a major company, is an industry index, and other publicly traded companies in the luxury goods segment will not be able to significantly outperform it."
The slowdown in demand in China contrasted with spending by American shoppers, which rose by several percentage points.
Louis Vuitton also faced a public backlash following a trademark dispute with local tea shop chain Molly Tea, which drew criticism in China during the quarter and added pressure on LVMH’s largest brand. Cabanis said that, although it was difficult to quantify the impact, consumer resistance hurt Louis Vuitton, at least at the beginning of the period.
Chinese tea chain ordered to pay Louis Vuitton $1.5 million over logo03.07.26, 15:00 • 64471 view
The downturn in China is occurring against the backdrop of an overall slowdown in the recovery of the luxury goods market, which is facing pressure from the conflict in the Middle East and cost-of-living concerns that are curbing spending on goods and services worldwide.
This pressure is already being felt in the luxury goods sector. Sales of the 25 largest luxury brands in China fell by more than 10% in July, Bloomberg previously reported. This threatens to derail the recovery that began less than a year ago, when an artificial intelligence-fueled stock market boom helped revive luxury spending.
LVMH’s renewed growth in revenue and earnings per share this year "has become unstable" as China’s slowdown deepened in the third quarter, Bloomberg Intelligence analysts Deborah Aitken and Karin Pitton wrote.
"There have been changes in China’s consumer environment, and this is prompting us to intensify our self-help efforts," CFO Cabanis said. "We need to do more, but we have not stopped investing in China."

NATO fund targets drone defence technologies as Ukraine reshapes priorities
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

NATO fund targets drone defence technologies as Ukraine reshapes priorities
Oct 13 - Russia's invasion of Ukraine is reshaping NATO's defence technology priorities, with counter-drone systems and space-based surveillance emerging as some of the alliance's most urgent capability gaps, the head of the NATO Innovation Fund told Reuters.
The 1 billion euro ($1.12 billion) fund, backed by 24 NATO nations, is expanding into Poland and looking for direct investments as it seeks to accelerate the development of dual-use technologies on NATO's eastern flank.
"We have seen drone incursions into countries here to an extent that is not being seen elsewhere," NIF President Ari Jonsson said.
"That really creates a different mindset when it comes to threats that you can actually see."
The most pressing needs on NATO's eastern flank are technologies that can detect, track and neutralise drones as well as space-based intelligence and reconnaissance capabilities, he said.
Lessons from the war in Ukraine had significantly influenced the fund's investment strategy, Jonsson said.
Poland's high defence spending, openness to new technologies and strong engineering base have made it an attractive destination for investment, he said.
Jonsson said the fund was deliberately looking beyond traditional defence contractors for the next generation of defence technologies.
To support that effort, the fund is opening a presence in Warsaw to speed up the identification and adoption of promising innovations.
"The NATO Innovation Fund is the first major fund, not originating from Poland, to establish a substantial presence in our country," Polish Finance Minister Andrzej Domanski said in a statement. REUTERS

Meta challenges UK media regulator over fees, fines
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
06:04:44 UTC
15:04:44 KST

Burak Bir
13 October 2026•Update: 13 October 2026
A UK High Court will hold a hearing Tuesday on a challenge brought by Meta, the tech giant that owns Facebook and Instagram, over fees and potential fines introduced under the country's Online Safety Act.
Meta is challenging Ofcom in the High Court, claiming that the UK media regulator acted unlawfully, specifically regarding their definition of "qualifying worldwide revenue," which is introduced under the act.
The law, which came into force last year, introduced protections against harmful online content, with Ofcom's operating costs for carrying out its online safety work funded by tech firms.
Under regulations introduced in September 2025, the fees are based on a company's qualifying worldwide revenue and apply to firms earning more than £250 million a year.
Meta explicitly argues that Ofcom's calculation methods are disproportionate and unlawful, while Ofcom said it would "robustly defend" its position.
The BBC reported in May that lawyers acting for Meta argued that the regulations should be reconsidered by the regulator.
Monica Carss-Frisk KC, for the tech giant, has said in court documents that Ofcom's approach is "troubling" and leads to "a handful of companies such as Meta bearing the vast majority of Ofcom's costs, despite the act making clear that it is concerned with a wide range of internet services offered in the UK.”
Under the Online Safety Act, firms found to have breached safety rules can face fines of up to 10% of qualifying worldwide revenue or £18 million ($23.7 million), whichever is greater.
Meanwhile, a senior director at the regulator told a committee in the House of Lords earlier this year that Ofcom was "operating in a highly litigious environment," including facing two actions by Meta and others from "a raft of services" bringing judicial reviews against the body for trying to collect data.
"We absolutely are looking to drive change in the best way we can," Oliver Griffiths, the Ofcom group director for online safety, told peers hearing evidence about the Online Safety Act.

Taiwan allies Paraguay, Belize reject China sanctions on ministers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
06:00:32 UTC
15:00:32 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Taiwan’s diplomatic allies Paraguay and Belize vowed Monday to maintain ties with Taipei after Beijing sanctioned two of their ministers for supporting Taiwan.
China’s foreign ministry on Monday announced sanctions against Paraguay’s Minister of Information and Communication Technologies Gustavo Emigdio Villate Samaniego and Belizean Minister of Foreign Affairs and Foreign Trade Francis Fonseca. The measures freeze their assets in China, prohibit Chinese organizations and individuals from conducting transactions or cooperating with them, and ban them from entering China, Hong Kong, and Macau.
Villate told ABC Color that the sanctions “were to be expected” given the major technology cooperation projects Paraguay is pursuing with Taiwan, including data centers and AI infrastructure. “We will continue working on all the projects we have, and we will push this even more strongly,” Villate said.
Villate said the initiatives that may have angered Beijing include the planned Binational Data Center in Chaco’i and an invitation to Taiwan-based Foxconn to join the Yguazu Digital AI hub. He described the sanctions as a “medal of honor” and said Paraguay would accelerate its joint technology development agenda with Taiwan at President Santiago Peña’s direction.
Paraguay’s foreign ministry also rejected the sanctions in a statement posted on X, saying they created “unnecessary friction” with the country. The ministry reaffirmed Paraguay’s firm support for Taiwan and its commitment to democratic values and principles.
Belize’s foreign ministry condemned China’s sanctions, saying the measures were unwarranted and would not change the country’s foreign policy. “Belize is a sovereign and independent state,” the ministry said, adding that every country has the right to conduct its foreign policy free from external pressure under the UN Charter.
The ministry said Belize established diplomatic relations with Taiwan through a sovereign decision and described the relationship as a partnership that has benefited Belizeans through cooperation in development, health, education, infrastructure, environmental protection, and agriculture. It added that Fonseca had acted in his official capacity and in Belize’s national interest, rejecting measures targeting him for carrying out his duties.
“These measures will not alter Belize’s foreign policy, nor will they deter the Government from carrying out its responsibilities,” the ministry said. It added that the government continued to “stand fully behind Minister Fonseca.”
“The Trump Administration opposes coercion and aggression by China against countries in our hemisphere for exercising their sovereign rights,” State Department spokesperson Tommy Pigott told Reuters.

Taiwan’s Thunder Tiger showcases drones at US defense expo
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
06:00:30 UTC
15:00:30 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Taichung-based Thunder Tiger said Monday it would showcase drone technology at the 2026 Association of the United States Army exhibition in Washington, DC, CNA reported.
The three-day event runs from Oct. 12 to 14 and hosts defense contractors including Boeing, Lockheed Martin, and BAE Systems. Thunder Tiger said its exhibits include the Papadelta x Ultrabuggy unmanned ground vehicle, SeaShark 600 unmanned surface vessel, and Blue UAS-certified Overkill first-person-view drone, built using non-Chinese parts.
Thunder Tiger said its unmanned ground vehicle uses a pneumatic catapult to launch the drone while moving, without a runway or launch pad. The drone can be equipped with 175cc or 250cc piston engines, or the National Chung-Shan Institute of Science and Technology’s CS-80 microturbine jet engine, depending on mission requirements.
Thunder Tiger said its SeaShark 600 drone boat has a 6-meter aluminum alloy hull fitted with US-based Allen Control Systems’ Bullfrog precision aiming system and AeroVironment’s four-launcher Switchblade system. It can reach a top speed of 50 knots (92.6 kilometers per hour), travel more than 190 nautical miles (350 kilometers), and carry 300 to 600 kilograms for coastal patrols or assault missions.
Thunder Tiger said its Overkill drone has obtained US Department of Defense Blue UAS status. The series includes the complete drone as well as fiber-optic communications, motors, and other components. The drone can fly for up to 30 minutes at a top speed of 120 kph and carry a maximum payload of 3 kilograms.
Blue UAS certification supports the sale of unmanned systems for US defense use, though the US Department of Defense can also purchase systems without it. Green UAS certification applies to vendors seeking to sell to non-Defense Department agencies, such as the US Coast Guard and US Border Patrol.
Thunder Tiger also presented systems developed with US-based Auterion and Israeli and Taiwanese partners to reduce dependence on Chinese parts. It is pursuing rapid, modular, and standardized mass production to secure US defense contracts.
