Protests Escalate in Delhi Despite Modi Government’s Heavy-handed Crackdown
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
05:14:00 UTC
14:14:00 KST

On October 12, Congress leader Rahul Gandhi, India’s main opposition leader, led a march to the Supreme Court of India, seeking the judiciary’s intervention in what he called the election commission’s loss of integrity.
The Chief Justice of India, Surya Kant, had declined to meet the opposition delegation, arguing that it would violate the principle of separation of powers. Yet tens of thousands of people, including opposition lawmakers, activists, and ordinary citizens, marched towards the apex court premises.
Monday’s protest march drew unprecedented crowds, despite the Narendra Modi government’s brutal crackdown on protestors calling for the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner (CEC) Gyanesh Kumar.
Kumar, the first CEC to be appointed under a new law that allowed the government to pick an election commissioner of its choice, has been at the center of political controversies since the launch of a Special Intensive Revision of the electoral roll last year that has left millions outside the roll, leaving them at the risk of disenfranchisement. Opposition parties have alleged pro-government bias on a range of issues related to election conduct, including targeted voter roll manipulations.
Over the weekend, India stood witness to some unprecedented scenes. Police in the national capital of New Delhi raided hotels, hostels, the offices of political parties, and the residences of activists in search of suspected protesters. The goal was to foil the satirical youth network Cockroach Janta Party (CJP)’s October 10 protest in New Delhi. The CJP too is seeking Kumar’s resignation.
The CJP’s protest at Jantar Mantar in Delhi in June-July resulted in Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan’s resignation. This time the Modi government was determined to prevent the CJP protests on Saturday.
To this end, it turned Delhi into a fortress. The assembly of five or more persons was prohibited across large parts of the city, and an estimated 30,000 police and paramilitary personnel were deployed. Police reportedly asked hotel owners to refrain from accepting fresh room bookings from people coming to the capital. To prevent protesters from gathering in New Delhi, the government took the unprecedented step of suspending or diverting dozens of Delhi-bound trains. Metro rail station gates closed across the city from 9 pm on Friday. Metal barricades blocked most roads leading to the designated protest venue, Jantar Mantar, in central Delhi. Checkposts multiplied at the city’s borders and Internet access was restricted in central Delhi. Early on Saturday morning, the police boarded a flight as soon as it landed in New Delhi to detain three CJP leaders. On Oct 10, Delhi was a city under siege. Daily life in the capital was suspended to prevent one political gathering.
And yet, thousands of protesters hit the streets in different parts of Delhi on Saturday. Thousands were detained, including lawyers, journalists, legislators and four former chief ministers of different states from the opposition parties. The police clashed with protesters at different locations. Young people on the streets were indiscriminately detained. Many alleged police brutality. Leftist student organizations kept cops busy on the streets on Sunday.
Even a U.N. human rights spokesperson expressed concerns over the situation, prompting the Modi government to accuse the Office of the U.N. High Commissioner for Human Rights of bias.
The Modi government may have been able to prevent youth and student protestors from gathering at one place on Saturday. But its problems are far from over, as the INDIA bloc and the CJP will be holding a wave of protests not only in the national capital but in other major cities as well. Besides, almost all opposition parties have thrown their weight behind the protests despite their internal rivalries – even if only for the time being. This has complicated matters for the Modi government.
“How long will you keep Delhi locked down? The minute you open the barricades & send police off, protestors will come in. Nobody, but nobody, can stop us,” said opposition parliamentarian Mahua Moitra on the night of October 10. The “government will never be able to ‘normalize’ life again.”
Meanwhile, a Supreme Court bench has directed the authorities to review their use of barricades, ensure normal metro and railway operations, and keep internet services running except where its suspension is legally justified.
By Monday, the government had adjusted its tactics. Instead of a citywide shutdown, it closed entry and exit at six central Metro stations from 6 a.m. to 4 p.m. Delhi’s borders, railway stations, and bus terminuses remained tightly guarded. Traffic was diverted from selected roads. The government also denotified Jantar Mantar as a protest venue and designated three other places for protest purposes.
The CJP top leadership, who were released on Sunday, vowed to continue their protests. “If Modi thinks taking away Jantar Mantar [as a protest venue] will put an end to protests, he is mistaken,” said CJP founder-convenor Abhijeet Dipke, adding that Jantar Mantar was no longer just another location “but a spirit of resistance that nobody can ever take away.”
There does not seem to be an easy way out for the Modi government. It will not be easy for it to let CEC Kumar go. After all, Kumar is the Modi government’s appointee. Conceding ground here could encourage the opposition to aim higher next time.
On the other hand, if the opposition manages to maintain pressure on the government through intense and continued street protests, the credibility of the election commission could be further undermined in the eyes of the public.
The ruling Bharatiya Janata Party has alleged that anti-national and foreign-funded forces have joined hands to destabilize the country. “We will deal firmly with all such forces active outside or inside the country,” said BJP president Nitin Nabin.
With the administration designating new locations away from central Delhi as protest venues and the opposition announcing continued protests, the coming few weeks look set for tense conflicts.

Taiwan military expert emphasizes safety for Narwhal sub sea trials
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
05:09:29 UTC
14:09:29 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Sea trials for the domestic Narwhal submarine should prioritize safety and proceed gradually rather than being driven solely by schedule deadlines, military expert Chi Tung-yun (紀東昀) said on Tuesday.
Chi, chair of the Taiwan Security and Development Association, told reporters that Taiwan’s submarine-building challenges are greater than those of most countries, CNA reported. The project involves more complex systems integration than in countries such as South Korea and Australia, where original manufacturers directly transfer technology, he pointed out.
The first submarine is a prototype for testing and validation, rather than a fully perfected product from the outset, he said. Adjustments and improvements must be based on test results, and subsequent submarines may incorporate design or system changes based on experience gained from the first vessel.
Chi noted that only a limited number of countries worldwide can build submarines independently. Building a submarine from scratch and conducting sea trials has been particularly challenging for Taiwan, he said.
As a vessel approaches delivery, engineering teams typically expand to identify software error messages, determine their causes, and correct them, he said, adding that these are normal procedures.
The Narwhal conducted its 24th sea trial on Tuesday.

Outgoing presidential culture adviser: Staying creative is important
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
05:06:00 UTC
14:06:00 KST

Outgoing presidential culture adviser: Staying creative is important
After five years serving as President Alar Karis' culture adviser, Estonian composer Rasmus Puur says the job shouldn't come at the expense of staying active creatively.
Puur joined Karis' team while studying at the Sibelius Academy in Helsinki. He initially had no plans to take the job but was eventually persuaded to try it.
Working quarter-time allowed him to continue composing and other creative work, though the workload sometimes resembled a full-time job.
"Anyone who's ever worked part time knows it can vary a lot — sometimes you end up working full time, sometimes you could do a little less," he said, adding that those times you could squeeze in an orchestra rehearsal or do something else.
Puur had to fit composing around the president's schedule, sometimes turning down commissions and racing to finish pieces during quieter interludes.
"I'd know the president was on a visit to somewhere in the U.S. that week and think, 'OK, things are a little quieter for now, so I need to get this piece written,'" he recalled.
Still, he stressed the importance of not losing touch creatively.
"With this kind of job, I think it's very important to stay connected to your creative self and the wider [creative] scene, so you don't end up isolated from it," the composer said.
Showing up, new traditions
A key part of Puur's role was helping the Estonian president engage with cultural events and recognize creatives' work. Even simply showing up, paying attention or presenting an award can mean a great deal to people in the field, he said.
During Karis' five-year term, the head of state attended major cultural anniversaries, song festivals and other events, and even served as official patron of the Year of the Estonian Book.
New traditions included annual reading marathons on the presidential palace's front steps in Kadriorg each March and the establishment of Estonian Literature Day, observed January 30, when the president announces the Literature Teacher of the Year.
Puur also highlighted Karis' visits to communities across the country for Mother's Day and Father's Day celebrations, which helped bring people together and put local events and efforts in the national spotlight.
"Showing Kilingi-Nõmme, Haljala or the Jõgeva Cultural Center live on public broadcasting, with the president speaking there, is hugely important to that local community," he stressed.
Karis also took cultural figures with him on foreign visits to build international ties and open new doors for Estonian artists.
"He genuinely believed that art and culture can sometimes reach people more effectively than traditional diplomacy," Puur said.
One example was a proposed exhibition of Estonian painter Konrad Mägi at Paris' Musée d'Orsay, an idea discussed during the Estonian delegation's visit during the 2024 Summer Olympics and now potentially back under consideration.
What comes next
Puur said his time at the Office of the President (VPK) taught him the importance of a close-knit team, particularly in a fast-paced environment where decisions carry significant responsibility. Running important questions by each other helped, he said, as did being able to joke around while under pressure.
As Karis leaves office, replaced by the newly sworn-in President Ülle Madise, Puur will hand over the title of presidential culture adviser to Jaak Prints.
He said there are no fixed job instructions for the role, which each president and adviser shapes according to their own personalities and priorities.
Under Karis, he believes, cultural figures felt their work received attention and recognition, even as arts organizations faced funding shortages and cuts.
Puur, meanwhile, has no firm plans for what comes next. For now, the composer wants to adjust to life outside the VPK again, and see where music and other opportunities might take him.
"One day at a time," he said. "I have some ideas, but first let's see what civilian life is like; it's been a while since I've experienced it."
--
Editor: Karmen Rebane, Aili Vahtla

How NRL's Super League bid could revive a fallen giant
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
05:04:59 UTC
14:04:59 KST

Roosters coach Trent Robinson says the NRL's offer of investment in Super League could help reinvigorate rugby league in France.
Robinson, who is assisting French coach Laurent Frayssinous at the Rugby League World Cup, thinks the NRL has a world vision and sees the value of the game in France.
What's next?
France starts its Rugby League World Cup campaign with a match against Samoa on Friday afternoon in Sydney.
As talks over the NRL's proposed investment in Super League near the pointy end of negotiations, Trent Robinson says a partnership between the two competitions could help reinvigorate the sport in France.
After guiding the Sydney Roosters to the fourth NRL premiership victory of his tenure earlier this month, Robinson would have every right to be sat somewhere in the south of France with his feet up sipping a glass of red.
But instead he finds himself offering his services to the French national team, where he supports head coach Laurent Frayssinous as director of rugby, in preparation for Friday's World Cup opener against Samoa.
On the other side of the world, club owners in England and the Super League's two French sides — Catalans Dragons and Toulouse Olympique — are weighing up an offer that would lead to the NRL providing an investment into the code's only other professional competition.
Some British clubs are reluctant to cede power to the NRL but Robinson is a firm believer in how Australia can help revive France as an international force.
"I think the NRL will have a world vision of rugby league, and I know they see the value of French rugby league and the importance of it," the Roosters coach told AAP.
"I think it would continue the progression of having a place at the table."
France was one of the sport's leading powers in the 1950s and 1960s but their stock has fallen considerably.
The presence of two French clubs in Super League, from which the majority of the national team is drawn, has so far failed to translate into international success.
France was supposed to host this year's World Cup until the government pulled the pin, citing the expense of hosting rugby union's World Cup in 2023 and the Paris 2024 Olympic and Paralympic Games.
Ranked 11th in the world, France are seen as $21 outsiders by bookmakers for their meeting with a Samoan team laden with NRL talent at Western Sydney Stadium.
Mitchell Pearce, who has retired in France after playing for Catalans, said: "There's some great French talent and they'll be enjoying the opportunity (to play in the World Cup).
"I think it'd be great for the NRL to expand and open up French rugby league and help the development pathways."
France's struggles to field a strong international side, they were hammered 62-4 by Samoa four years ago, can surely be attributed to the fact their clubs are operating in the most cash-rich market in any rugby code.
France's top rugby union competition, the Top14, has a salary cap of roughly $18 million, the NRL's is around $12 million, while the Super League's is approaching $4 million.
"There's a respect that is growing in France for rugby league from when I first went 24 years ago," Robinson said.
"It's because we've got a great sport and because of the Catalans and Toulouse.
"It's a fair mountain to climb, the Top 14, and trying to catch up with that.
"But it (league) does have respect and the NRL would add to that because there's an enormous amount of respect for it in rugby union circles."

Musk spent $276M to help Republicans in midterm elections: US media
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
05:04:48 UTC
14:04:48 KST

Tech billionaire Elon Musk, the world's richest man, has contributed $276 million to organisations boosting the campaigns of right-wing American candidates ahead of upcoming midterm elections, US media reported on Monday.
The sum, all contributed since July, positions Musk as the largest single donor for the November 3 elections, according to the New York Times. He has spent a total of $366 million this election cycle.
The largest funding recipient was the Republican's Senate Leadership Fund, receiving $158 million, aimed at maintaining the party's control of the upper house of Congress despite a slim margin.
The SpaceX and Tesla boss is no stranger to massive US election spending, having contributed $290 million in 2024 to help US President Donald Trump win re-election.
Trump allowed Musk to work in the White House for several months overseeing his cost-cutting Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE) venture, but he exited the role after a public falling out with the president.
They've since reconciled, and Trump awarded Musk the National Medal of Science at an event in DC last week.
Though individual campaign donations in the United States are capped at $3,300 per person, loopholes in the US campaign finance system allow political mega donors to contribute to funds known as political action committees or "PACs," which support candidates.
Musk donated $76 million this summer to his own America PAC, the New York Times reported.
Other recipients of Musk's political funding include $20 million to the Republican's Congressional Leadership Fund, $10 million each to the Republican Governors Association and the Lone Star Liberty PAC, and $2 million to the Republican Attorneys General Association.

Short trips to Australia from China up 8.4 pct year-on-year in August
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
13:03:09 CST
14:03:09 KST

CANBERRA, Oct. 13 (Xinhua) -- Short-term visitors to Australia from the Chinese mainland in August increased by 8.4 percent year-on-year, according to official data released Tuesday.
The Australian Bureau of Statistics said that 106,990 people from the Chinese mainland arrived for short-term visits in August, up 8.4 percent from August 2025 and 36.2 percent from August 2024.
The data showed that visitors from the Chinese mainland accounted for 14.2 percent of the total 755,530 people who arrived in Australia on short-term trips in August compared to 13.1 percent in August 2025.
New Zealand remained the leading source of short-term visitors to Australia for the month despite a 3.9 percent decline in arrivals. ■

ISLAMABAD, Oct. 13 (Xinhua) -- At least five passengers were killed and 30 others injured after all 14 carriages of a passenger train derailed in Pakistan's eastern Punjab province early Tuesday morning, police said.
"The accident occurred in Multan district when the Rehman Baba Express, traveling from the southern port city of Karachi to the northwestern city of Peshawar, went off the tracks," police sources from the district told Xinhua.
The injured passengers were being shifted to a nearby hospital for medical treatment, according to police.
Railway traffic on the affected section has been suspended following the incident, while an additional train has been dispatched to transport the stranded passengers to Peshawar.
An investigation into the cause of the derailment is underway, police said. ■

Russia's offensive ability is broken, Kyiv's former top general tells BBC
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
06:02:34 BST
14:02:34 KST

Russia's offensive ability is broken, Kyiv's former top general tells BBC
- Published
Ukraine has stabilised the front line and "broken Russia's ability to advance" by killing so many of its men, Ukraine's former commander-in-chief has said in an interview with the BBC.
Gen Oleksandr Syrskyi made the comments in an exclusive interview, his first since he was dramatically forced from his post in the summer.
He addressed his sacking, disagreeing with his critics who declared him too "old school" to command Ukraine's new, technologically advanced forces.
He also pushed back against allegations made by soldiers who previously served under him, who told the BBC they were ordered to remain at their positions even when they were almost surrounded by Russians, leading to high losses.
Syrskyi said that Moscow's overall losses in the war were six times higher than Ukraine's. "If you count only dead, then it's up to 11 times," he added.
Neither Russia nor Ukraine officially release the numbers of their dead. Ukraine's military says it inflicted record losses this year on Russian soldiers in September, although that cannot be verified.
UK intelligence chiefs estimate Russia has lost around half a million men killed in Ukraine since launching its full-scale invasion in 2022. The US-based Center for Strategic and International Studies meanwhile believes, external Ukraine has lost up to 150,000 troops killed by June 2026.
He says this difference in death toll – as well as technological advances, and a strategy of attacking weak points in Russia's lines while containing their advances in other parts – accounts for the current stalemate at the front.
In the first six months of 2026, Russia managed overall to seize 61 sq km, the general said. "It's an indication that the front line has been stabilised."
The Institute for Study of War (ISW) has also confirmed this trend. One of its recent reports, external says that in September 2026, Moscow lost more territory than it took.
Syrskyi was appointed Ukraine's commander-in-chief in 2024. He had previously won praise for defending Kyiv at the start of Russia's full-scale invasion in 2022, and for leading the successful counteroffensive east of Kharkiv in the autumn of that year.
But President Volodymyr Zelensky fired Syrskyi this summer, amid a major disagreement with then-defence minister Mykhailo Fedorov.
Fedorov had said that instead of adapting to the realities of the changing war, the army under Syrskyi had blocked his initiatives.
Zelensky initially fired Fedorov, as tensions burst into the open between the two men. But mass street protests then forced the president to also fire Syrskyi, replacing him with Maj Gen Mykhailo Drapatyi, 43.
Syrskyi told the BBC that he had "disagreements" with Fedorov because the latter "didn't take into consideration the interests of the army" when procuring weapons and supplies.
Fedorov had created an "imbalance" in supplies, Syrskyi said. He had prioritised drones while overlooking key front-line kit such as unmanned ground vehicles, pick-up trucks and motorbikes. Even with drones, Syrskyi said, there were shortages as the army got only half of what they needed.
Fedorov was a popular young minister who was known for his digital and technological initiatives. Many contrasted him with Syrskyi, who critics thought was not fit to lead the new technological arms race with Russia.
But Syrskyi disagrees with such criticism. It was during his time the use of drones reached this new, unprecedented level, including deep strikes more than 2,000km (1,200 miles) behind enemy lines, he said. Ukraine was the first country to create the Unmanned Systems Forces as a separate branch of armed forces, under his command: now, he said, drones account for 80% of Russia's losses.
Under his military leadership, however, Ukrainian troops undertook chaotic withdrawals from the eastern cities of Avdiivka and Vuhledar, and from around Pokrovsk.
Soldiers who spoke to the BBC in the past complained that they were ordered to remain at their positions at any costs. By the time they were told to pull back, it was often too late as they were almost surrounded by Russian troops.
Syrskyi does not deny that such situations occur on the front line. But he told the BBC that Ukraine was fighting against a far more powerful army.
In 2025, the ratio of jets and bombs was 18 to one in Moscow's favour, he said. In the same year, Russia had two-and-a-half times more artillery pieces and shells than Ukraine. And with four million militarily trained men who they can mobilise, Russian forces can create chances to push through, he argued.
One of Syrskyi's most famous operations was an incursion into Russia's Kursk region that started in August 2024. It ended with a dramatic retreat the following spring, which some soldiers described as "catastrophic". Syrskyi, however, insisted that the Kursk operation was "a necessity".
"In the summer 2024, Russian forces were pushing along all main directions on the front line with up to six times more troops than we had," he explained.
The Kursk incursion disrupted Russia's offensive and forced Moscow to redirect troops, giving Ukraine a respite and a chance for its stretched brigades in the east and south to recover, Syrskyi said.
He also had strong words for European allies who doubt that Russia may have territorial ambitions beyond Ukraine. He advised European partners to start preparing for the war now and "drop all illusions that [it] will not come".
He also said he believed Ukraine's war was going to become even more technological. There will be more robots, automated systems and artificial intelligence (AI). "Even ordinary weapons now get an AI-based control system to enhance their capabilities," he said.
Such technologies can give a new life to conventional weapons like tanks. Both Russia and Ukraine were now racing to develop "active systems of defence" to protect armoured vehicles, Syrskyi said.
But he insisted that "the human role will remain definitive [on the battlefield] because [people] will need to control those systems".

More than 100 foreign trekkers stranded by floods in Nepal’s Gorkha region

Unknown Publisher

05:01:14 UTC

More than 100 foreign trekkers stranded by floods in Nepal’s Gorkha region
Rescue operation underway after flash floods swept away homes, bridges and parts of the Manaslu trekking trail.
More than 100 foreign trekkers have been stranded in central Nepal, according to a local official, a day after flash floods in the Gorkha district washed away bridges, hiking trails and hundreds of homes.
Bhuwan Raj Ojha, an official of the Manaslu Conservation Area Project, told the Reuters news agency on Monday that the trekkers were stranded in different areas of the popular Manaslu trekking trail because part of the route had been swept away.
“Those hikers who want to return because of the flood need to be rescued. Those who want to continue their trekking can do so from locations that are safe,” he told Reuters from Gorkha.
“There are restaurants and tea houses along the route. They are safe”.
The flash floods hit on Sunday, when a predawn landslide blocked the Budhi Gandaki River in the Gorkha district, about 100km (62 miles) west of the Nepalese capital, Kathmandu.
Authorities rescued 321 people, including 12 foreigners, on Monday, and the army said the rescue operation would continue on Tuesday, even as the water level in the river receded.
The river is a tributary of the Trishuli River, downstream from another tributary where a glacier collapse caused a catastrophic flood in August that killed 1,457 people, with thousands still missing.
There were no reports of deaths in the latest flood, but five villagers were out of contact after black muddy sludge and debris washed away more than 200 homes and damaged infrastructure, including three hydroelectric plants, national disaster authorities said.
Md Shahadat Hossain, a Bangladeshi trekker stranded in Jagat village, told the Anadolu news agency that nine Bangladeshis were waiting for a possible evacuation by helicopter.
“We have been stranded in Jagat since yesterday. A flash flood came down from above the village and flowed through its lower part,” he said.
“We are safe, but there has been no electricity since yesterday, communication with the outside world has been disrupted, and food supplies are gradually running short,” he added.
Gorkha district authorities have asked villagers living along the riverbanks downstream to evacuate.
National disaster authorities had also alerted people living along the river in the Gorkha, Tanahun, Chitwan, East Nawalparasi and West Nawalparasi districts about the flood.

War is not imminent or inevitable, says NATO commander
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
06:00:58 BST
14:00:58 KST

NATO’s Supreme Allied Commander Europe has told an audience in Warsaw that he does not assess conflict to be either imminent or inevitable, while arguing that the alliance must still prepare for what is possible, according to remarks at the Warsaw Security Forum.
General Alexus Grynkewich made the point before setting out the approach he calls a Theory of Victory. “Before I describe this theory in more detail, let me make one point very clear. I do not assess that conflict is imminent or inevitable. It isn’t,” he said. “We help avoid conflict by clearly articulating our defensive intentions, and by maintaining open lines of communication to resolve misunderstandings and encourage transparency.”
“But deterring conflict also requires warfighting readiness, and readiness requires to plan against what is possible, not just what is probable,” he said. “As America’s first president, George Washington, stated, the most effective way to preserve peace is to prepare for war. Or, as America’s current president puts it, this is peace through strength. In the case of NATO, that’s the strength of 32 nations, together.”
He described the alliance as unlikely to be taken unawares, drawing on “a sophisticated layering of intelligence provided by multi-source collection assets that deliver tremendous amounts of data” and advanced algorithms used to make sense of it.
“This means the Alliance is unlikely to be caught by surprise. We will see if an attack is coming, giving us time to assess intent and rapidly position our forces,” he said. “In doing so we aim to deter, but these movements also prepare us to deny any potential attack, including those aimed at seizing and holding NATO territory as a fait accompli.”
Speaking of Poland’s accession to NATO in 1999, he said: “It reminds us NATO is a defensive Alliance, constructed to preserve peace. And as such, we have no plans, no intentions, and no ambitions beyond the protection of our people and the defence of our territory.
“Still, no one should mistake our defensive nature for weakness or lack of resolve. Through our collective strength we aim to deter and keep the peace. But if someone is foolish enough to attack us, we will fight.”
His Theory of Victory, which he stressed is a common vision and his commander’s intent and not a military plan, sets out three stages, blocking an initial attack, blunting it if it persists, and breaking the enemy forces and the warfighting system supporting them if required.
General Grynkewich said implementing it would require him to issue orders he hopes never to give, and that demonstrating the readiness to do so is what prevents the need arising. “If attacked, we are ready to fight tonight, but we are not complacent,” he said, adding that any adversary weighing an attack should conclude “today is not the day.”

- Summary:
- Scientists have uncovered a hidden layer of organization in the brain by creating the first detailed 3D map of its lipids, the fatty molecules essential for brain structure and communication. By analyzing millions of measurements from mouse brains, researchers identified 539 distinct chemical zones, revealing patterns and boundaries that traditional brain maps have missed. Surprisingly, even white matter, once thought to be relatively uniform, contains a complex patchwork of chemically distinct regions.
- Share:
Scientists have spent decades studying the brain's cells, connections, genes, and proteins. Yet another essential part of brain biology has received far less attention: lipids. These fatty molecules make up the membranes surrounding neurons, contribute to the myelin insulation that protects nerve fibers, and play important roles in communication between brain cells.
Although lipids are fundamental to brain function, scientists have struggled to map where different types are located. Conventional imaging techniques cannot easily distinguish individual lipid molecules, leaving a major gap in our understanding of the brain's chemical organization.
"So scientists have had only a blurry picture of how lipids differ from one part of the brain to another," says Giovanni D'Angelo, professor at The Kristian Gerhard Jebsen Foundation Chair in Nutrition and Metabolism at EPFL. "That gap matters, because changes in brain lipids are increasingly linked to conditions from depression to Alzheimer's disease."
Researchers at EPFL have now taken a major step toward filling that gap. A team led by D'Angelo, Luca Fusar Bassini, and Gioele La Manno has created a detailed map showing how lipids are distributed throughout the mouse brain.
Their Lipid Brain Atlas reveals that these molecules are arranged in highly organized patterns. Some match familiar anatomical structures, while others expose chemical boundaries that previous approaches had overlooked. The patterns are so distinctive that researchers could identify where a brain tissue sample originated simply by examining its lipid composition.
The findings were published in Nature.
Scientists Identify 539 Distinct Chemical Zones in the Brain
To construct the atlas, researchers used mass spectrometry imaging, a technique that allows them to identify lipid molecules across thin sections of brain tissue. A laser scans each slice one location at a time, producing detailed information about which lipids are present and where they are found.
The team examined 172 different lipids in 109 brain slices collected from 11 mice. This generated approximately 7 million measurements, which scientists combined into a comprehensive 3D reconstruction using machine learning tools developed specifically for the project.
The resulting atlas revealed 539 chemically distinct territories, which the researchers named "lipizones." Each has a characteristic combination of lipids, creating a recognizable chemical signature.
Many of these regions correspond to established brain structures and cell types. Others reveal unexpected relationships between groups of nerve cell bodies and distant regions connected by their fibers. Such connections have often been difficult to detect using maps based on gene activity.
"In effect, lipids work like postal codes, giving distant but related parts of the brain the same chemical address," says D'Angelo.
Hidden Chemical Patterns Challenge Previous Brain Maps
The new atlas also uncovered surprising differences within parts of the brain that scientists previously considered relatively uniform.
One striking example is white matter, the tissue containing nerve fibers that connect different brain regions. Rather than having a largely consistent chemical composition, white matter contains numerous distinct lipid zones.
"This shows that the cells which make myelin are far more varied in their chemistry than their genes alone would suggest," says Luca Fusar Bassini.
The researchers also detected previously unrecognized chemical boundaries in the choroid plexus, the structure responsible for producing cerebrospinal fluid, as well as in the tissues lining the brain's internal cavities.
Together, these findings show that lipid mapping can reveal important features of brain organization that are not apparent from anatomy or genetic information alone.
Pregnancy Triggers Widespread Changes in Brain Lipids
Beyond identifying the brain's chemical structure, the atlas offered new insight into how that structure changes during pregnancy.
When researchers examined pregnant mice, they found substantial shifts in lipid composition across numerous brain regions. Overall, these changes were more pronounced than the typical lipid differences observed between male and female mice.
The cortex, which forms the brain's outer layer, showed particularly extensive changes. Meanwhile, levels of galactosyl ceramide, an important component of myelin, increased sharply throughout much of the brain's white matter.
These findings suggest that pregnancy involves significant changes in the brain's chemical makeup, potentially helping its neural connections adapt to the body's changing demands.
"Together, these shifts suggest the brain retunes its own wiring to meet the demands of pregnancy," says Gioele La Manno. "The Atlas reveals that the brain constantly adjusts its lipids to meet the body's changing needs."
A New Tool for Understanding Brain Aging and Disease
The Lipid Brain Atlas is freely available online, allowing scientists worldwide to explore this previously difficult-to-study aspect of brain biology.
By combining lipid information with existing genetic and cellular maps, researchers can gain a more complete understanding of how the brain is organized and how its chemistry changes over time.
The atlas also establishes a detailed reference for healthy mouse brain tissue. Scientists can use it to investigate how disruptions in lipid distribution might contribute to brain development, aging, and disorders such as Alzheimer's disease and depression.
Although the specific mouse brain map cannot be directly applied to humans, the approach used to create it could help researchers uncover comparable patterns in the human brain.
"What transfers to humans isn't the map, it's the method, and the fact that we now know that a healthy brain has a very organized lipid map at all," says Luca Fusar Bassini.

AI could self-replicate on home devices within ‘months’, Anthropic says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
04:47:00 UTC
13:47:00 KST

AI could self-replicate on home devices within ‘months’, Anthropic says
US tech giant says small AI models may soon be capable of self-replication without access to a data centre.
Small artificial intelligence models could soon begin self-replicating on everyday consumer products such as smart TVs and fridges, without needing a data centre, according to researchers at AI giant Anthropic.
In a report released on Monday, the researchers said small AI models “may be months away from being capable enough” to copy themselves on internet of things (IoT) devices used in homes and small businesses.
Anthropic’s frontier red team, which ran experiments using multiple US- and Chinese-developed AI models, said such self-replicating AI would be “challenging to shut down” due to the lack of a centralised host.
While data centres would be “a clear, high-value target” for AI worms, internet-connected devices like smart TVs, fridges, ovens and lawnmowers could soon also provide sufficient computing power for self-replication, the research team said.
Although no current AI model proved to be both powerful and small enough to self-replicate reliably on a smart TV used in testing, the trend in development makes the emergence of such a model likely by the end of 2026, the researchers said.
“Home and small business IoT devices might be the first target for such attacks because they’re connected to the internet and, historically, have had minimal security measures in place,” researchers William Zhou and Daniel Freeman said.
The researchers said they anticipated the future would be “awash with agents running on all types of hardware”, including some that “aren’t under human control”.
“While it’s true that IoT devices have been vulnerable for a long time, lightweight agents may be much more willing than human attackers to put in the effort to compromise large fractions of the world’s IoT compute,” they said.
Anthropic, the creator of the Claude family of AI models, did not respond to Al Jazeera’s questions, sent outside regular business hours, about the finding’s safety implications.
Anthropic’s report comes as the risks of AI escaping human control are under scrutiny following a slew of incidents of models engaging in unsanctioned malign behaviour, including cyberattacks.
Anthropic and its chief rival OpenAI have called on the international community to coordinate a slowdown in AI development to minimise catastrophic risks, a suggestion that has had little buy-in from the United States and China, the two leading AI powers.
Many AI safety advocates have identified recursive self-improvement, where models learn to improve themselves, as a critical tipping point that could lead to catastrophic harm for humanity.
Roman V Yampolskiy, an AI and cybersecurity expert at the University of Louisville, described Anthropic’s findings as a significant development.
“Computer worms are not new, but an AI worm could do something traditional malware cannot: reason about unfamiliar devices, adapt when its approach fails, and continue spreading without a human operator,” Yampolskiy told Al Jazeera.
“Today, this is not an existential threat. But the trajectory is concerning,” Yampolskiy said.
“Once autonomous replication is combined with strong hacking, persistence, and strategic reasoning, shutting such a system down becomes much harder because there may be no single server or organisation controlling it.”
Anthropic and other leading US tech firms last month joined a non-binding accord pledging stronger internal safeguards and engagement with external auditors, drawing a mixed response from experts, many of whom criticised the voluntary nature of the pact.
In a separate announcement on Monday, Anthropic said it had made substantial progress preventing so-called distillation attacks, which involve the unsanctioned use of cutting-edge AI to train cheaper, less capable models.
The San Francisco-based firm, which has accused Chinese competitors DeepSeek, Moonshot, and MiniMax of “industrial-scale” efforts to copy Claude, said the measures it introduced had reduced the illicit extraction of data by 90-99 percent.

NASA's Perseverance rover breaks record for off-planet driving on Mars
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
04:45:29 UTC
13:45:29 KST

NASA’s Perseverance rover breaks record for off-planet driving on Mars
- NASA says Perseverance has driven 45.2km on Mars, breaking the off-planet distance record set by Opportunity, and its systems may keep working into the 2030s.
- The rover is exploring Jezero Crater and nearby ancient terrain, where NASA says it may help explain Mars' early geology and past water-rich conditions.
- Perseverance's AutoNav system has made most drives autonomous, and NASA says a 2025 finding of a possible biosignature is its biggest achievement so far.
AI generated
WASHINGTON – NASA’s robotic Perseverance rover has now driven farther than any other vehicle on the surface of any world other than Earth, racking up 45.2km since arriving on Mars in 2021, the US space agency said on Oct 13.
The car-size, six-wheeled rover reached the milestone 5½ years into its mission to explore if conditions conducive to microbial life ever existed on Earth’s neighbour.
In doing so, it is visiting some of the most ancient terrain ever encountered in the solar system.
“Perseverance’s engineering hardware and instruments are in excellent shape with all redundant systems still available,” Steven Lee of NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory in California told Reuters.
“A recent assessment of all systems concluded that they are capable of operating well into the 2030s, likely beyond,” added Lee, the project manager for NASA’s two Mars rovers, Perseverance and Curiosity.
Perseverance has exceeded the previous figure of 45km driven on the Martian surface by NASA’s Opportunity rover from 2004 to 2018.
Both also exceeded the driving distances of any lunar rover.
Perseverance, with its suite of scientific instruments, has focused on the Jezero Crater, a region in the northern hemisphere of Mars believed to have been flooded with water and home to a lake basin billions of years ago.
The rover set the milestone in a journey towards an area called Idubi, through the region off the crater’s western rim nicknamed Lac de Charmes.
Its companion rover, Curiosity, rolls along in the Gale Crater near the Martian equator.
Perseverance is showing no signs of slowing down, Lee added.
Its mobility system mechanisms are being tested to show it can drive 100km or more, he said, with the hardware to be tested to the equivalent of 150km to 300km in the effort.
NASA attributed a major role in Perseverance’s success to its self-driving capability, an autonomous navigation system called AutoNav.
Lee said 90% of its drives are done autonomously, with no human intervention.
“Perseverance takes stereo images of the terrain ahead, generates a 3D software map and selects the safest path towards a drive goal,” he said.
Another key component is the Vision Compute Element, a fast co-processor computer that allows the rover to process images and run its self-driving software very quickly, almost continuously during drives, Lee added.
That contrasts with previous rovers, which needed to pause to “think” before each drive segment, he said.
“Perseverance builds on the 29-year legacy of our past Mars rovers – Sojourner, Spirit, Opportunity and Curiosity – each incorporating prior lessons and improving our ability to drive on another world,” Lee said.
Potential biosignature
Lee said the rover’s biggest achievement was almost certainly its discovery, unveiled in 2025, of a potential biosignature, or possible sign of ancient microbial life.
This was found in reddish rock believed to have formed 3.2 billion to 3.8 billion years ago in a river channel feeding the lake that once filled Jezero Crater.
The Lac de Charmes terrain, Lee said, may yield clues to early planetary geological processes, such as the effects of large meteorite impacts.
Jezero Crater was formed by such an impact early in Martian history.
Lee cited orbital evidence that some areas of the rim were once hydrothermal systems with warm or hot groundwater.
“These areas may once have provided a warm, watery sub-surface environment conducive to life,” he added. “Indeed, some palaeontologists hypothesise that life on Earth began in such environments.”
The rover’s original mission envisaged just 20km of driving.
NASA recently approved an extension of its mission to explore the crater rim until roughly the end of 2028.
The rover’s plutonium-based power system is performing as expected, Lee said, adding that it has “many years of useful energy still available”. REUTERS

Statistics from the Shenzhen General Station of Exit and Entry Frontier Inspection showed 41,300 people entered Hong Kong through the rebuilt checkpoint between Hong Kong and mainland China on Monday, while 38,200 departed the city. The Danish government has presented a proposed budget for 2027 that prioritizes national security, with more money allocated to defence amid an increasingly tense international security situation.
The proposal, titled “A stronger defence of Denmark – a strengthened Denmark to defend”, was presented by Finance Minister Peter Hummelgaard of the Social Democrats (S) at the Ministry of Finance on Friday morning.
The government wants to ensure that defence spending reaches 3.5 percent of gross domestic product (GDP) by 2030.
Hummelgaard said the proposal reflected the need to make “hard priorities” in response to the current security situation. He also described the Danish economy as being “in top shape”.
“The government’s proposal for the finance bill shows that we take responsibility upon ourselves, and that we lead the way in working for a greener, freer, and more equal Denmark,” Hummelgaard said.
Pia Olsen Dyhr of the Socialist People’s Party (SF), the minister for economic and interior affairs, also highlighted the security situation.
“We do not solve all the challenges we have in Denmark with this finance bill. But we are well on our way,” she said at the press conference.
“I also think everyone must remember that we are in an escalated security policy situation,” Olsen Dyhr said.
Much of the proposed budget had already been announced, either in the government’s policy platform or through statements by ministers in recent weeks.
The proposal allocates 1.2 billion DKK to children’s services and education in 2027, including Denmark’s public primary and lower secondary schools, known as folkeskole.
It also sets aside a total of 10.1 billion DKK in 2030 for tax cuts. These include abolishing the intermediate income tax and the top-top tax, as well as reducing corporation tax.
“We are simplifying the tax system,” said Taxation and Growth Minister Jakob Engel-Schmidt of the Moderates (M).
The tax measures will be negotiated separately as part of a tax reform. While the budget proposal includes tax cuts, the government also plans to freeze several tax thresholds, which would increase the tax burden for some taxpayers as incomes rise.
The liberal think tank Cepos estimates that the government’s various plans will result in a net tax cut of 2.2 billion DKK in 2030.
Business and Competitiveness Minister Martin Lidegaard of the Danish Social Liberal Party (R) highlighted investment in young people and education.
“We are significantly strengthening knowledge, general education, and formal education in Denmark, from ABC to PhD. It is good for the individual young person, but it is also good for Denmark’s future,” Lidegaard said.
Unlike in recent years, when the government’s fiscal room for manoeuvre helped fund much of its budget plans, this proposal includes several measures to find additional savings.
These include cuts to the Danish student grant (SU), savings on senior pension payments, a proposed tax on cruise ships and further reductions in state administration costs.
The government must now negotiate with other parties in the Danish Parliament, the Folketing, to secure a majority for the 2027 budget.
The proposal includes a negotiating reserve of 500 million DKK annually from 2027 to 2030, which other parties can seek to use to fund their own priorities.

Physicists discover “astonishing” property of light that defies expectations
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
04:19:32 UTC
13:19:32 KST

Physicists discover “astonishing” property of light that defies expectations
- Date:
- October 13, 2026
- Source:
- University of East Anglia
- Summary:
- Scientists have uncovered a surprising hidden ability of light that allows it to develop spinning, twisting behavior as it travels through empty space, without special lenses, mirrors, or materials. Researchers discovered that light’s internal geometry can naturally produce left- and right-handed patterns, challenging long-standing assumptions about how light behaves. By carefully arranging a beam’s structure, scientists can control where and how these spinning patterns emerge, unlocking a new way to manipulate light.
- Share:
Scientists have discovered a surprising ability of light that allows it to develop spinning patterns as it moves through empty space, without relying on special lenses, mirrors, or materials. The finding reveals that light possesses a hidden geometric structure that can influence its behavior in ways researchers previously thought were difficult to achieve.
The discovery comes from an international team led by researchers at the University of East Anglia (UEA) in the United Kingdom, working with scientists in South Africa. Their experiments demonstrate that carefully prepared light can be controlled through its own internal geometry, offering a new approach to manipulating how light spins and twists.
The findings challenge long-standing assumptions about how different properties of light interact. They could eventually lead to more sensitive medical tests, faster and more secure communications, and advanced quantum technologies that use light to transmit and protect information.
Why the Direction of Light's Spin Matters
One of the most intriguing aspects of the discovery involves chirality, a scientific term describing the difference between left-handed and right-handed structures.
Human hands provide a familiar example. Although they are mirror images of each other, a left hand cannot be perfectly superimposed on a right hand. Many molecules have a similar property, including compounds used in medicines. Two versions of the same molecule can have nearly identical chemical structures yet produce very different effects in the body.
Scientists can distinguish these molecular forms by studying how they interact with light that has a particular rotational behavior. Traditionally, producing and controlling such light has often involved specialized materials, carefully designed surfaces, or powerful lenses that focus beams extremely tightly.
The research demonstrates that appropriately prepared light can develop this behavior naturally as it travels, without requiring those additional optical components.
"Our work shows that light can naturally develop this handed behavior all on its own," said Dr. Kayn Forbes from UEA's School of Chemistry, Pharmacy and Pharmacology.
"You just have to prepare it in the right way.
"Most people think of light as traveling in straight lines. But scientists can also create structured light -- light whose brightness, shape, and direction are carefully arranged.
"One extreme example is light that twists as it travels, forming a corkscrew shape known as an optical vortex. Each twist can carry information, making this kind of light valuable for high-speed internet, secure communications, and advanced sensors.
"Light can also spin as it travels, depending on how it is polarized. This spin can be left-handed or right-handed -- another form of chirality."
Scientists Discover How Light Develops a Hidden Spin
Light can exhibit different kinds of rotational behavior. An optical vortex, for example, has a wave pattern that twists around its direction of travel, much like a corkscrew. Light also has a property known as polarization, which describes how its electric field oscillates. Certain polarization patterns produce a form of rotation called spin.
Physicists have long studied the relationship between these two properties. However, the interactions responsible for the newly observed effect were generally considered extremely weak and difficult to detect without specialized experimental conditions.
The researchers found that the situation changes when a beam of light is prepared in a particular balanced configuration.
Under those conditions, the beam can initially have no spin, yet distinct regions with spinning behavior emerge as it travels through free space. The effect does not require the light to pass through engineered materials or additional optical devices.
"It starts off with no spin at all," explained MSc student Light Mkhumbuza, who carried out key experiments. "But as the beam travels forward, spinning regions appear and separate out -- almost as if the spin was hiding and then revealed itself."
Rather than creating spin through an external optical component, the researchers demonstrated how the beam's existing internal structure can determine where spinning regions develop during propagation.
The Hidden Geometry That Controls Light
To explain this unexpected behavior, the researchers turned to topology, a mathematical field concerned with properties that remain unchanged when objects are continuously stretched, bent, or reshaped.
Dr. Isaac Nape, from the University of the Witwatersrand in Johannesburg, South Africa, offered a simple way to understand the concept.
"To explain it, imagine a mug and a doughnut," he said. "You can morph one into the other without tearing it, because they both have one hole. That hole is a topological feature."
The researchers found that structured light possesses its own topological characteristics, encoded in the arrangement of its polarization.
This underlying pattern acts like a mathematical fingerprint. Even as the light beam changes shape while traveling, its topological structure remains, influencing how different regions of the beam evolve.
As a result, the arrangement of the light itself can determine where its left-handed and right-handed spinning patterns become visible.
The discovery gives scientists a way to guide this behavior by designing the beam's initial structure, rather than depending on specialized materials to produce the desired effect.
"This gives us a completely new tuning knob for light. By adjusting its topology, we can decide how and where chirality appears," said Dr. Nape.
Potential Breakthroughs in Medicine and Communications
The ability to control light through its geometry could eventually make several important optical technologies simpler, more affordable, and more versatile.
One particularly promising application involves medical diagnostics and pharmaceutical research. Because many biologically important molecules have left-handed and right-handed forms, carefully structured light could help scientists identify these differences with greater sensitivity. Such tools could be valuable for evaluating drug safety and detecting biological markers associated with disease.
The same principles could support smaller optical sensors capable of identifying chemicals or biological substances without requiring large, sophisticated laboratory instruments.
Communications technology could also benefit. By encoding information into different twisting and spinning patterns, researchers may be able to increase the amount of data carried by individual light beams. This could contribute to faster optical communications, improved information security, and future quantum networks.
Other potential uses include manipulating microscopic particles, cells, and molecules with light, as well as developing more resilient quantum systems. Topological properties may help protect delicate quantum information against certain forms of noise and interference.
"The implications are wide-ranging," said Dr. Forbes. "This work could lead to simpler and more sensitive medical tests, especially in drug development.
"It could also be used to pack more information into laser beams -- boosting data capacity for communications, including future quantum networks.
"And because the effect doesn't rely on fragile materials or precision-engineered surfaces, it could be easier and cheaper to use in real-world technologies.
"This research could lay the foundations for a new generation of light-based technologies, by showing that light's behavior can be controlled using its own internal geometry," he added.
These applications remain possibilities for future development, but the underlying discovery provides researchers with another way to design and control the behavior of light.
A Hidden Property of Light Finally Revealed
For decades, scientists have relied on increasingly sophisticated optical equipment to produce and manipulate unusual forms of light. The findings suggest that some of these behaviors can instead arise from carefully designed structures already encoded within a light beam.
By showing how topology governs the emergence of spinning regions during propagation, the team has revealed a previously underappreciated connection between light's geometry and its physical behavior.
The discovery also illustrates how much remains to be learned about something as familiar and extensively studied as light.
"For something so familiar, light is proving to be far richer, stranger and more powerful than anyone imagined," said Dr. Forbes.
"And astonishingly, this new behavior has been there all along -- just waiting to be seen."
The research, 'Topological Control of Chirality and Spin with Structured Light', was published in the journal Light: Science & Applications.
Story Source:
Materials provided by University of East Anglia. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Light Mkhumbuza, Pedro Ornelas, Angela Dudley, Isaac Nape, Kayn A. Forbes. Topological control of chirality and spin with structured light. Light: Science, 2026; 15 (1) DOI: 10.1038/s41377-026-02278-6

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Taiwan has secured Saudi Arabian crude oil for November delivery, while state-owned CPC Corp. says domestic oil and natural gas supplies are assured through year-end despite rising risks to Middle Eastern energy shipments.
Two sources told Reuters that Saudi Arabia had sold November-loading crude to refiners in Taiwan and India. Some cargoes sold on a delivered basis carried premiums of about NT$640 (US$20) per barrel above November official selling prices.
Saudi Arabia typically announces official selling prices at the beginning of each month and asks buyers with long-term contracts to nominate their purchase volumes. The company said oil and natural gas supplies are secure through the end of the year and that it has begun planning procurement for Q1 2027.
It began purchasing alternative crude from multiple non-Middle Eastern sources after the US-Iran war began in February. In mid-September, after a bombing of Saudi Aramco’s East-West Pipeline disrupted supplies under September and October term contracts, CPC purchased additional spot crude to cover the shortfall.
Crude prices have remained elevated and volatile, while freight and insurance costs have risen sharply, CPC said. As the Northern Hemisphere approaches peak winter demand, European countries are replenishing liquefied natural gas inventories, intensifying competition for energy cargoes and tankers.
CPC has also increased sourcing from the Americas, West Africa, and the Asia-Pacific region as part of its long-term diversification strategy.

IMF sees milder global slowdown as AI boom offsets war hit — warns resilience is nearing limits
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
04:10:49 UTC
13:10:49 KST

BANGKOK — The International Monetary Fund has raised its forecast for global growth this year as the AI-driven investment boom helps offset some of the impact from surging energy costs, while warning that economic resilience could be nearing its breaking point.
The IMF expects the global economy to grow at 3.1% in 2026, up from the 3% projected in July, but slower than the 3.5% rate last year. For 2027, it kept the forecast unchanged at 3.4%.
The UN agency expects inflation at 4.1% in 2027, above the 3.9% it projected in July – when it estimated the Strait of Hormuz would reopen by mid-July, with conditions broadly returning to pre-war levels by March 2027. For the current year, it maintained its 4.7% outlook.
"The global economy has been resilient, but that resilience is reaching its limits," Silvana Tenreyro, economic counsellor and director at the IMF research department, told reporters Tuesday, urging policymakers to restore fiscal space and supply-chain security.
The IMF now estimates that the Strait of Hormuz will reopen in March next year and return to pre-war state by October. Gulf crude exports averaged 88% of pre-conflict levels in September as traffic picked up, the international body said.
The report was released at the IMF and World Bank annual meetings in Bangkok this week, where finance ministers and central bank governors from the fund's 191 members are meeting to discuss geopolitical tensions, mounting public debt and artificial intelligence.
AI-related investment gave the global economy a "demand impulse" that helped activity in the first half of the year hold up better than expected, despite the Middle East war and trade tensions, the IMF said. Financial markets also stayed largely calm, which the fund said may partly reflect "AI-related exuberance."
For now, "use of buffers and adaptability have helped economies weather the negative shocks," the IMF said, citing measures such as diversifying fuel sources, tapping strategic reserves that have contained the energy-market turmoil unleashed by the Middle East war.
But that cushion is "rapidly narrowing" in the near term, it said. Global oil reserves are being drawn down by about 2.7 million barrels a day, nearing levels that could trigger sharp price moves, and energy constraints could impair the AI-led momentum. The growing unease over governments' fiscal health also adds to the headwinds.
Tenreyro said monetary policy should remain "sufficiently restrictive" to return inflation to target in a timely way, and that central bank independence is critical as governments face mounting financing pressure.
Skewed growth
Overall growth is also becoming increasingly uneven. Thirty-two economies now account for 95% of global growth, down from 54 in April.
Countries that have limited exposure to the war-led supply shock and are catering to the AI-led demand are holding up or strengthening. Taiwan is forecast to grow 10.7% this year and South Korea 3.3%, up from 1.1% in 2025 on semiconductor demand. The U.S. is projected to expand 2.3% in both 2026 and 2027, supported by private consumption, fiscal policy and tech investment.
Energy importers outside that tech supply chain face higher import bills, weaker real incomes and less fiscal room. The euro zone is estimated to eke out just 1.1% growth this year amid higher energy costs and weak consumer confidence. The Middle East and Central Asia is projected to contract 0.3% this year, with Bahrain, Iraq, Kuwait and Qatar facing double-digit declines before double-digit rebounds in 2027.
China is forecast to grow 4.5% this year and 4.0% in 2027, with higher oil prices and structural headwinds weighing on activity. Second-quarter growth of 4.3% was weaker than expected as sluggish consumption and property strains outweighed robust exports.
India remains the fastest-growing major economy, with the IMF forecasting growth of 7.0% in both 2026 and 2027, upgrades of 0.6 percentage point and 0.3 percentage point from July, respectively, driven by robust domestic demand, services activity and AI-related investment.
"The global economy is not simply slowing or accelerating; rather, growth is being reallocated across countries according to their exposure to the war-induced supply shock and AI-related demand strength," the IMF said.
AI-related risks
While AI has underpinned resilience, the investment boom is also adding to inflationary pressures and financial fragility, the IMF said.
"This is a large, front-loaded demand shock" that sees massive investment pouring into sectors such as semiconductors, data centers, and power generation, before any broad productivity gains have materialized, it said in the report.
A potential reassessment of AI-related profitability and productivity prospects could see excessive investment pull back and force a sharp correction in equities. The IMF warned that in a scenario where AI productivity gains fail to materialize, U.S. equities could fall 20% and global growth could end up 1.1% below its baseline estimates by 2028, with Asia 1.7% lower.
Fiscal constraints
Advanced-economy benchmark yields have climbed to multidecade highs as resurgent inflation, the expected path of policy rates and fiscal concerns push up borrowing costs, the IMF said. Technology firms borrowing to finance AI investment are adding to the pressure.
Public debt in advanced economies is projected to reach 115% of GDP by 2031, from 108% in 2025. In emerging and developing economies, it is forecast to climb to 84% from 74%. Primary deficits in the largest economies remain substantially larger than before the pandemic, and governments face higher real interest rates and shorter debt maturities as defense spending pressures mount.
Rebuilding fiscal space is "increasingly urgent," it said, urging governments to keep support for households facing higher energy and food costs "temporary, targeted, and nondistortionary."
Its models put the probability that global inflation exceeds 5% in 2027 at about 35%, up from 30% in April. Risks remain "tilted to the downside," the fund said.

Explainer: Why the 2026 Nobel Prize in Economics honors scholars tackling economic shocks
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
12:07:37 CST
13:07:37 KST

STOCKHOLM, Oct. 13 (Xinhua) -- The 2026 Sveriges Riksbank Prize in Economic Sciences in Memory of Alfred Nobel was awarded to American economists Robert E. Hall and Michael Woodford for their decades of work developing models that have helped governments and central banks manage economic shocks.
In its announcement on Monday, the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences credited the two economists with laying "microeconomic foundations of macroeconomic stabilization."
"The laureates have helped us smooth out the economy's peaks and troughs," the academy said in a statement, adding that their work had "significantly improved" policymakers' ability to implement well-timed fiscal and monetary measures.
WHAT THEY FOUND
Hall, a professor at Stanford University, and Woodford, a professor at Columbia University, helped reshape macroeconomic modelling by grounding it in microeconomics.
Rather than relying solely on statistical relationships between broad economic indicators such as inflation, output and consumption, their approach examines how the decisions and expectations of households and businesses shape the wider economy.
In a 1978 paper, Hall examined how household consumption decisions are shaped by expectations about future economic conditions. His work helped establish the microeconomic foundations for understanding consumption, while Woodford's research on firms' price-setting behaviour helped bring the demand and supply sides together in a framework for macroeconomic stabilization.
Together, their work contributed to the development of New Keynesian models, which provide a framework for analysing how households and businesses respond to economic conditions and how monetary policy affects economic activity.
"Robert Hall worked on the demand side, studying consumption, whereas Michael Woodford studied the supply side, the price-setting behaviour of firms, and put all the pieces together in a whole," Timo Boppart, a professor at Stockholm University and a member of the prize committee, was quoted by the Financial Times as saying.
The academy said it was recognizing the pair for bringing about "a paradigm shift in stabilization policy." The prize is worth a combined 12 million Swedish kronor (about 1.2 million U.S. dollars).
"The laureates' work has provided us with a stable theoretical foundation for the models that are now used by central banks and governments around the world," said John Hassler, chair of the Committee for the Prize in Economic Sciences.
Because of their research, "we are better equipped to deal with shocks in the economy, such as energy crises or sudden changes in how much households consume," he added.
WHY IT MATTERS
The award comes at a time of heightened geopolitical uncertainty and a fragile global economy, with frequent shocks posing persistent challenges for policymakers.
"Your research on economic stabilization has greatly improved our understanding of people's economic decisions and strengthened the foundations for effective policy," Christine Lagarde, president of the European Central Bank, wrote in a note of congratulations to the economists on social media.
For decades, governments have sought to cushion economic shocks by following the prescriptions of British economist John Maynard Keynes, whose ideas gained prominence during the Great Depression. Cutting taxes and increasing government spending can stimulate demand by encouraging households and businesses to spend and invest, helping revive economic growth.
The oil shocks of the 1970s, however, posed a major challenge to existing economic thinking. Many Western economies experienced high inflation alongside high unemployment, while growth remained weak. The combination raised doubts about the effectiveness of established approaches to economic stabilization.
This year's award winners brought renewed relevance to economic stabilization theory, showing how a better understanding of real-world economic behaviour can help explain the effects of policy decisions.
Their research also helped shape the theoretical basis for forward guidance, a policy tool through which central banks signal their expectations for future interest rates. The approach gained prominence in the wake of the 2008 financial crisis.
"That was an important part of the policy response in the years from 2009 onward, and I think it did contribute to better stabilization," Woodford told the committee by phone from New York.
He added that one of the main themes of his work was helping policymakers appreciate the importance of understanding individuals' behavior in the market: How they make decisions about spending and what they understand about future economic policy. ■

Xinhua Commentary: China's health approach advances wellbeing of humanity
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
12:07:24 CST
13:07:24 KST

BEIJING, Oct. 13 (Xinhua) -- For a country of over 1.4 billion people, ensuring the health of its population is not merely a domestic priority, but also an important contribution to humanity.
Since the 18th National Congress of the Communist Party of China (CPC) in 2012, China has further stepped up efforts in ensuring people's health, setting out the guiding principles for health work in the new era and making major decisions and arrangements for fully advancing the Healthy China Initiative. This has delivered historic achievements in the country's health sector and laid a solid health foundation for national rejuvenation.
A series of facts and figures shows the profound changes in health. China has put in place the world's largest systems for medical services, traditional medicine, disease prevention and control, and healthcare security. Its health services have seen steady progress in capacity, accessibility and equity, alongside continuous improvements in people's health. China withstood the severe impact of the global COVID-19 pandemic -- a remarkable feat for a populous nation like China.
The development of health services has brought concrete benefits to the Chinese people. So far, China has more than 1.1 million medical and health institutions. Over 90 percent of people in China can reach their nearest medical service facilities within 15 minutes. Its basic medical insurance covers around 95 percent of the population. In 2025, the average life expectancy in China reached 79.25 years. The infant mortality rate fell to 3.8 per 1,000 and the maternal mortality rate dropped to 13.4 per 100,000, making China one of the high-performing countries in maternal and child health recognized by the World Health Organization.
China's approach to promoting people's health epitomizes the country's people-centered development philosophy. Through consistent efforts in medical and healthcare system reforms, capacity-building, legislation and health promotion, among others, China has blazed a path of inclusive and balanced health development to ensure health for all -- a solemn promise of the CPC and the Chinese government.
Undoubtedly, China's all-round progress in its medical and health sector marks an important contribution to the sustainable development of humanity. As the world faces various health challenges, China has actively engaged in global health governance.
China has deepened cooperation with other countries in the medical and health sector, worked together to address cross-border public health risks, solidly advanced the building of a community of health for all, contributing China's strength to the global health cause. Traditional Chinese medicine has been introduced to more than 190 countries and regions. Since late 2012, China has dispatched medical aid teams to 59 countries and regions. During the COVID-19 pandemic, China supplied a multitude of anti-epidemic products to the world.
People's health is an important indicator of socialist modernization. With clear goals and intensified efforts, China will unswervingly follow the path of health development with Chinese characteristics and advance the Healthy China Initiative to secure greater progress in enhancing people's health. As a major country, China will also further participate in global health cooperation and governance to contribute more to the wellbeing of humanity. ■

Beijing forum eyes new paths for modern urban governance
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
12:07:18 CST
13:07:18 KST

Georgios K. Giannaros, first deputy mayor of Athens, Greece, addresses the opening ceremony of the 2026 Beijing Forum on Swift Response to Public Complaints in Beijing, capital of China, Oct. 12, 2026. (Xinhua/Xie Han)
BEIJING, Oct. 13 (Xinhua) -- Chinese and international experts gathered in Beijing to explore new paths for modernizing urban governance, as the 2026 Beijing Forum on Swift Response to Public Complaints began Monday.
The two-day event, themed "Digital Intelligence Era and People's City," drew more than 3,200 participants from over 70 countries and regions.
In 2019, Beijing, home to over 20 million residents, launched a "swift response to public complaints" initiative aimed at addressing public concerns promptly and resolving everyday challenges efficiently. It has integrated more than 60 hotline services into the single hotline number 12345, which serves as the primary channel for residents to voice their concerns.
Official data shows the Chinese capital has handled about 200 million public appeals in just over seven years, with resolution and satisfaction rates both exceeding 97 percent.
Beijing's "swift response to public complaints" reform began with a single hotline and platform and has since evolved into an urban governance system integrating big data and AI, one that has tackled a range of pressing public concerns, Gao Xiang, president of the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences, said in his opening address.
"Digital empowerment of people-centered urban governance is the prevailing trend in urban governance worldwide," he said.
This year's forum unveiled a batch of research outcomes on urban governance, including theoretical studies of the reform itself, an evaluation of global city hotline services, and case studies of governance innovation worldwide.
It also rolled out two English-language publications on the reform -- the monograph "How Urban Governance Works: the Case of Swift Response to Public Complaints in Beijing," and a special issue with the "Journal of Comparative Policy Analysis: Research and Practice." Both signal a move from lessons learned to theoretical exposition, and from Chinese practice to international comparison.
"The experience of Beijing's citizen service system offered valuable lessons for Athens in advancing people-centered urban governance and building a city that listens to its citizens and responds to their concerns," said Georgios K. Giannaros, first deputy mayor of Athens, Greece.
Held every two years, this year's Beijing Forum on Swift Response to Public Complaints featured six parallel sub-forums, where participants noted that the reform has driven changes in mega-city governance, offering the world a window into China's approach to governance. ■
