Helping a boy with anxiety find his way
How do we help a teenage boy who has social anxiety, is refusing to go to school, and is captured by the internet. The school he used to go to is overwhelmed by the numbers needing support.
- Sally
Billy says:
Sadly I hear this story every week in our developmental clinics, but there is a path through it that isn't giving up or forcing them to attend.
First we see that this is anxiety, not defiance. These boys don't feel safe and this is how they protect themselves. Telling them to push through will only make it worse. We have to validate that feeling, help them understand it and then develop strategies that help him to process it in a healthy way that means he can still walk towards things that are scary.
We do this gently and alongside him. Instead of "you return to school on day one of term three", we ask "I wonder if we could connect with your class mates on the weekend to play basketball" or "I wonder if Ms McKenzie would like us to send a letter about the comics you've been reading". These approaches are small steps towards succeeding at the school community that help children get back their long term and successfully too.
On the internet, we should see it as meeting a need. Maybe connection, a sense of belonging, distraction from anxiety or just boredom. Sometimes, the first step here is learning what they use it for and seeing if we can enter that world too, such as their favourite video game or youtuber.
Finally GPs, our most important medical specialists, can be an amazing point of contact when things are too much for us alone.
How big is this shift?
Earlier, Stuart asked whether the current mood around the manosphere could be considered a "passing wave" or more of a societal shift.
Zac says there are a few ways to tell:
A few things to consider when trying to discern if this is a wave or a tectonic shift as you suggest:
Does it follow them as they age? If attitudes soften as young men get jobs, relationships and stability, it's a phase of life. If they hold into their 30s, it's a lasting generational change.
Does it leave the screen? We are already seeing how online vitriol and narratives are trickling into everyday life. We need to get better at measuring this and being able to tell what caused what.
Does it outlast the algorithm? If changing platform design (e.g. Fix Our Feeds) or a few influencers falling from grace makes it fade, it is probably amplification rather than root values.
Are institutions shifting? When policy, political platforms or workplaces start echoing it than we know there are lasting social shifts.
What changes the outcome is whether we give boys something better to belong to. Shaming them hasn't worked so far and sadly women and girls are bearing the brunt of this.
Key Event
'It feels like he is part of a cult'
Wondering how to keep in touch with my 19-year-old son, whom I evicted in February partly over his misogynist behaviour towards me and his younger sister. He is now living with friends who share these views and rarely responds to my attempts to communicate. He has body image problems, fasting, working out at the gym (looksmaxxing) and looks up to Andrew Tate and Elon Musk. It feels like he is part of a cult. He is focussed on popularity (social media following) and has unrealistic ideas about becoming a multimillionaire within a year or so. As he is legally an adult, but emotionally and socially very immature, it's hard to watch. Any tips?
- Lila
Zac says:
Lila, that sounds painful, and I want to say first that protecting yourself and your daughter sounds like the best decision you could make in such a circumstance. Boundaries around how he treats the women in his family are fair, and you can hold them while still loving him.
Some quick thoughts that I'm sure you may have already tried, but good to keep in mind:
- Keep the door open, keep the pressure low. Send short, warm messages that don't need a reply: a photo of the dog, "thinking of you", "saw this and thought of you". The message underneath is "I'm still here." Don't judge him for not responding. He's likely reading them even when he doesn't reply.
- Don't debate Tate or Musk. Arguing about them puts him in the position of defending them, and that pushes him closer.
- Get curious about what he's chasing instead: money, respect, status, feeling like he matters. Those goals aren't the problem. Stay away from misogyny and try to talk about things that don't get you riled up
- Find neutral ground. Shared meals, sport, practical help. One-on-one time doing something side by side is often easier than a big conversation.
- Hold your boundary and the relationship together. You can say, "I love you, and I want you in my life, and I won't be spoken to that way". Both can be true.
- Watch the body image stuff closely. Fasting, compulsive training and a fixation on appearance in young men can be signs of disordered eating or muscle dysmorphia. These are serious and often missed in boys. If you get an opening, raise it gently, out of care rather than criticism. The Butterfly Foundation supports families too, including with sons.
- Look for the cracks. Get-rich-quick plans and chasing followers often run into reality. When that happens, he may feel humiliated, and that's when he'll need somewhere soft to land. Make sure he knows that's you.
- Look after yourself. This is a long game. Talking to a psychologist or a parent support service for your own sake isn't a luxury.
At 19, his brain and identity are still very much under construction. This chapter isn't the whole story and just know I've seen many guys come through this and are better men on the other side.

Genetic scores linked to depression and neuroticism are associated with lower voter turnout
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
00:00:39 UTC
09:00:39 KST

A study published in Political Behavior shows how genetic scores related to health and psychological traits can predict a person’s likelihood of voting or engaging in politics. Analyzing genetic data from more than 50,000 people in the United States and Sweden, researchers found that genetic predispositions for traits like cognitive performance and subjective well-being were linked to higher voter turnout, and comparisons between siblings suggested that some of these links reflect causal genetic effects.
Political scientists typically focus on environmental factors, such as education, income, or family upbringing, to explain why some people vote and others stay home. Over the past 15 years, however, twin, adoption, and molecular genetic studies have indicated that political orientation and civic participation are also partly heritable. Integrating these findings into mainstream political science has been difficult, in part because early attempts to link political behavior to a handful of specific genes largely stalled as it became evident that complex traits are shaped by thousands of genetic variants with tiny effects.
To overcome these limitations, a research team set out to introduce a new tool to the study of political behavior. The team included Rafael Ahlskog and Sven Oskarsson of Uppsala University, Christopher Dawes of New York University, and Aaron Weinschenk of the University of Wisconsin-Green Bay. They proposed using polygenic indices, which are individual-level scores that summarize a person’s genetic propensity for a specific trait.
A polygenic index is created by looking at hundreds of thousands of tiny variations in a person’s DNA. Researchers assign a weight to each variation based on how strongly it correlates with a given trait in massive genome-wide association studies. These underlying studies analyze the DNA of very large samples, sometimes more than a million people, to find tiny statistical links between specific genetic markers and specific outcomes. By adding all these weighted variations together, researchers can generate a single score that estimates an individual’s genetic likelihood of exhibiting traits like extraversion, depression, or high cognitive performance.
To demonstrate the method, the researchers analyzed data from four large samples: the National Longitudinal Study of Adolescent to Adult Health, the Wisconsin Longitudinal Study, and the Minnesota Twin Family Study in the United States, and the Swedish Twin Registry. The combined datasets included more than 50,000 individuals, and the analyses were limited to people of European ancestry. The researchers gathered information on self-reported voter turnout, turnout validated from official records in both high-profile elections (such as presidential or national parliamentary elections) and lower-profile ones (such as U.S. midterms and European Parliament elections), and engagement in non-voting political activities, such as attending a political rally or contacting a politician.
Alongside the political data, the researchers calculated polygenic indices for ten health and psychological traits. These traits included cognitive performance, adventurousness, extraversion, being a morning person, neuroticism, risk tolerance, self-rated health, depression, subjective well-being, and physical activity. They also included a genetic score for educational attainment as a benchmark for comparison, and the main analyses followed plans the researchers had registered in advance.
The researchers first compared people across different families. To account for broad genetic differences that arise from human demographic history rather than specific traits, they controlled for participants’ genetic ancestry, along with birth year and sex.
Several genetic scores were associated with voter turnout. Higher genetic propensities for cognitive performance, self-rated health, subjective well-being, and physical activity predicted a higher likelihood of voting, while scores for neuroticism and depression predicted lower turnout. A genetic tendency toward being a morning person was associated with higher turnout in high-profile elections, and the score for adventurousness with higher turnout in lower-profile ones. Results for risk tolerance were mixed, with higher scores linked to lower turnout in high-profile elections but higher turnout in lower-profile ones.
The associations were modest but not trivial. A one standard deviation increase in the genetic score for cognitive performance or self-rated health was associated with a roughly 4 percentage point higher likelihood of voting in lower-profile elections, and each of these scores accounted for almost 1% of the variation in turnout in those elections.
When looking at non-voting political participation, the researchers found a different pattern. Genetic scores for extraversion, risk tolerance, and adventurousness were positively associated with activities like contacting a politician or attending rallies. This aligns with previous research suggesting that outgoing and novelty-seeking people are drawn to the more social aspects of political activism.
Additional analyses suggested that, on average, about 30% of the scores’ links with participation ran through the traits they were designed to predict. This varied widely: measured cognitive performance accounted for almost all of the link between its genetic score and participation, while measured physical activity explained very little of its score’s link.
While comparing people across families reveals an association, it does not prove a direct causal link. The study authors point to two main sources of bias in such comparisons: population structure and genetic nurture. Population structure refers to genetic differences that align with social or cultural groups due to historical mating patterns, which can create false correlations. Genetic nurture occurs when parents’ genes influence the environment they create for their children, meaning a child’s behavior might be shaped by their upbringing rather than their own DNA.
To establish a firmer causal connection, the researchers conducted a second set of analyses that restricted the data to pairs of full siblings. Because biological siblings receive a random mix of their parents’ genes, any genetic differences between them are the result of chance. Comparing siblings to each other effectively removes the influence of their shared family environment and broad population-level genetic differences.
In the sibling analyses, many of the links between the genetic scores and voter turnout held up, particularly for high-profile elections. For lower-profile elections, the estimates comparing siblings tended to be smaller than those comparing different families, suggesting that the earlier results were partly inflated by genetic nurture or population structure. Results for self-reported voting and non-voting participation were less precise.
Because genetic differences between siblings arise by chance, the authors argue that the within-family results can be given a causal interpretation: the genetic variants captured by these scores affect the likelihood of voting. That does not necessarily mean they work through the traits the scores were designed to measure.
The authors note several limitations to how these findings should be interpreted. A genetic effect does not mean that a person’s political behavior is biologically predetermined. Genetic influences often work through environmental pathways; for example, a genetic propensity for height might affect political participation because of wage discrimination against shorter people, rather than through any direct biological drive to vote.
Genes frequently affect multiple traits at the same time, a concept known as pleiotropy. A genetic score designed to predict depression might also capture genes related to entirely different characteristics that ultimately influence political behavior. The scores also capture only a fraction of the total genetic influence on a trait, as they are based on estimates containing some statistical noise, so the authors describe their results as a lower bound.
A major limitation of current polygenic indices is that they rely on genetic databases that predominantly feature individuals of European ancestry. Because genetic markers differ across populations, these scores are currently less accurate when applied to people of other ancestral backgrounds, which is why the analyses were limited to people of European descent.
Future research could use genetic scores to better understand how parents socialize their children politically. By comparing the genetic scores of parents and children, researchers can tease apart which political behaviors are passed down through a shared environment and which are inherited biologically.
The method also offers a way to study how different environments might amplify or suppress a person’s genetic predispositions. In one exploratory analysis that was not part of the preregistered plan, education appeared to buffer the negative link between depression-linked genes and voter turnout. The lower turnout associated with the depression genetic score appeared to be driven entirely by people at the lower end of the education distribution.
The study, “The Genetics of Political Participation: Leveraging Polygenic Indices to Advance Political Behavior Research,” was authored by Rafael Ahlskog, Christopher Dawes, Sven Oskarsson, and Aaron Weinschenk.

1930s cider press screw becomes sculptural stool in reclaimed wood and brushed aluminum

1930s cider press screw becomes sculptural stool in reclaimed wood and brushed aluminum
le pressoir gives new life to a 1930s french cider press, reworking the agricultural object into a contemporary sculptural stool that brings its raw history into dialogue with refined aluminum craftsmanship.
[FEATURED]
Reclaimed wooden cider press screw forms sculptural stool
LE PRESSOIR is a sculptural stool by Studio Jumel in collaboration with Ariane Ronot, made from a French cider press dating to the 1930s. Rooted in Normandy’s apple-growing and cider-making traditions, the design reuses the original wooden screw mechanism as the stool’s four legs, retaining the aged texture and irregularities accumulated through decades of use.
A cross-shaped structure made from 3 mm-thick aluminum connects the wooden elements, contrasting the material’s precise finish with the timber’s weathered surface. Its openwork form references apple blossoms, while the seat’s helical profile echoes the original screw mechanism.
Brushed aluminum meets weathered timber in LE PRESSOIR stool
The design by Studio Jumel and creative Ariane Ronot combines preserved wooden elements with newly fabricated aluminum components, whose brushed, vibrated finish complements the texture of the reclaimed timber. Measuring 45 cm high and 42 cm wide and deep, LE PRESSOIR balances everyday function with a sculptural silhouette, retaining the physical traces of its agricultural past while giving the historic object a new role in contemporary furniture design.
project info:
name: LE PRESSOIR
designer: Studio Jumel | @studio.jumel, Ariane Ronot | @ariane.ronot
photographer: Wallys.M | @wallygatooor

Magnitude 6 earthquake strikes Panama, EMSC says
PANAMA CITY, Oct 12 - An earthquake of magnitude 6 struck Panama on Monday, the European-Mediterranean Seismological Centre (EMSC) said.
The quake was at a depth of 35 km (22 miles), the EMSC said.
Panama recorded more than 300 aftershocks following Friday's magnitude 7.7 earthquake that damaged hundreds of homes and infrastructure across the country's central provinces, prompting the government to declare a national state of emergency over the weekend.
No deaths were reported, but at least 27 people were injured and nearly 900 homes were damaged, according to emergency authorities, who warned the toll could rise as assessments continue in remote communities.
Among the most affected provinces are Los Santos, Cocle, Veraguas, and Herrera, authorities added. REUTERS

In recent days, The Wall Street Journal has published a series of highly embarrassing articles about the former Fox News host, who became a prominent figure in Trump’s Make America Great Again movement.
According to the newspaper, which posted supporting screenshots, Guilfoyle asked Eric Deters, an influential supporter of the President, to write off US$100,000 (S$128,000) in personal credit card debt.
“Honey please I need you to get this done for me today,” she texted Deters in July 2025, the Journal reported, along with a PDF of bill payment instructions from her credit card company.
Deters did not make the payment, “telling Guilfoyle it would cost him his marriage,” the Journal reported.
The allegation became public as US Secretary of State Marco Rubio was touring Europe last week, with Athens among his stops.
The texts were part of a tranche of hundreds of messages, e-mails and letters reviewed by the Journal, including recorded conversations in which the ambassador boasts of luxury trips and stays paid for by wealthy Greek businessmen.
She flew to Davos on a private jet with Alexandros Exarchou, chief executive of Greek construction company Aktor Group.
She also spent Christmas in the exclusive Swiss luxury resort of Gstaad with Greek shipping tycoon Nikolas Tsakos.
“Honey, I spent Christmas with him. New Years. OK? Gstaad. Like, everywhere,” she said, per the Journal.
When she travelled with Tsakos to Paris to attend his wife’s fashion show, they stayed at the Four Seasons Hotel George V for a week, and he footed the bill, the Journal reported.
In another exchange quoted by the newspaper, Guilfoyle launched into an expletive-laden tirade over being left off the guest list for a dinner on the sidelines of the Davos economic forum in January 2025.
American media have also reported in recent days on other possible conflicts of interest involving Guilfoyle, who was previously married to California’s Democratic Governor Gavin Newsom. AFP

Europe's new Sentinel-3C satellite just sent back spectacular images of Earth
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
23:48:22 UTC
08:48:22 KST

Europe's new Sentinel-3C satellite just sent back spectacular images of Earth
Just two weeks after launch, Europe's Sentinel-3C satellite is revealing stunning views of Earth while preparing to track the dramatic changes transforming our planet.
- Date:
- October 12, 2026
- Source:
- European Space Agency (ESA)
- Summary:
- Europe's Sentinel-3C satellite has returned breathtaking images of Earth just two weeks after launch, revealing the snowy Alps, frozen Arctic islands, and brilliant turquoise Caribbean waters. Its first measurements also show promising results for tracking rising seas, melting ice sheets, and other changes reshaping our planet.
- Share:
Just two weeks after reaching orbit, Europe's new Copernicus Sentinel-3C satellite has delivered its first spectacular images of Earth, revealing everything from the snow-covered Alps to the frozen Arctic and the brilliant turquoise waters of the Caribbean.
But the satellite is doing much more than taking beautiful pictures. Its instruments have also begun measuring ocean heights and the elevation of Greenland's massive ice sheet, providing an early demonstration of technology designed to monitor Earth's changing climate.
The first images and measurements come from two of Sentinel-3C's key instruments. Both are performing well in initial tests, bringing the satellite closer to its mission of tracking environmental changes across the planet.
A Powerful New Satellite to Monitor Earth's Changing Climate
Sentinel-3C is the third spacecraft in Europe's Sentinel-3 satellite series, a central part of the Copernicus Earth observation program. The satellites are equipped with matching sets of instruments that continuously gather information about the oceans, land, atmosphere, and cryosphere, which includes Earth's frozen regions.
Over the oceans, Sentinel-3 measures sea surface temperature, color, and height, along with sea ice thickness. These observations help scientists investigate marine pollution, track marine heatwaves, and understand changes in ocean conditions.
On land, the mission provides valuable information about droughts, wildfires, vegetation health, and how different areas are being used. It also measures water levels in rivers and lakes, as well as changes in the elevation of polar ice sheets.
The data support weather forecasting by providing timely observations of environmental conditions. They also help researchers identify long-term trends linked to climate change.
The European Space Agency (ESA) is still preparing Sentinel-3C for full operation through a detailed testing and commissioning process expected to take another five months. Nevertheless, the satellite's first two weeks in orbit have already produced encouraging results.
Stunning Satellite Images Reveal Italy's Diverse Landscape
One of Sentinel-3C's first images, captured on September 30 by its ocean and land color instrument, offers a remarkable natural-color view of Italy and its surrounding seas.
The image extends from southern Germany across the Italian peninsula to Sicily and the southern Mediterranean. It reveals an extraordinary variety of landscapes, from towering mountains and fertile farmland to deep blue waters.
Near the upper center of the scene, the Po Valley stands out as a broad expanse of green and brown. This fertile region is the heart of Italy's agricultural production. Immediately to the north, the snow-covered Alps rise dramatically above the lowlands, their bright white peaks creating a striking contrast with the surrounding terrain.
Elsewhere across Italy, different shades of green and brown reveal variations in vegetation, farming activity, and land cover.
To the east, the Adriatic Sea separates Italy from the partially visible Balkan Peninsula. Along Italy's eastern coast, bands of lighter blue water stand out against the deeper blue offshore. Scientists believe these color differences are likely caused by sediment carried into the sea by rivers and redistributed by coastal currents.
On the opposite side of the peninsula, the dark waters of the Tyrrhenian Sea surround Sardinia and Sicily. Corsica is also within the image, although clouds obscure much of the island.
Together, the contrasting colors of mountains, farmland, islands, and surrounding seas create a vivid portrait of Italy as seen from space.
A Dramatic View of the Arctic's Vulnerable Ice
Another image captured on September 30 shifts the focus far north to the Canadian Arctic Archipelago, located west of Greenland.
Here, the landscape looks dramatically different. Snow and ice blanket many of the islands, while exposed rock, rugged coastlines, and deep fjords form intricate patterns across the frozen region.
The image was taken near the time of year when Arctic sea ice typically reaches its annual minimum. Much of the surrounding water appears dark and open, although scattered fragments of floating sea ice remain visible.
These observations are particularly important because the Arctic is warming much faster than the global average.
As temperatures rise, glaciers and ice sheets lose mass, while sea ice continues to melt. The disappearance of reflective ice also exposes darker ocean water, which absorbs more solar energy and can accelerate regional warming.
Sentinel-3's different instruments observe ice in complementary ways, helping scientists better understand changes across these vulnerable polar environments.
Brilliant Caribbean Waters Seen From Space
Sentinel-3C's third featured image, captured on September 29, reveals an entirely different side of Earth.
The scene shows part of the Caribbean, with Cuba near the bottom and the Bahamas toward the top. Around the islands, shallow waters glow in brilliant shades of turquoise, contrasting sharply with the dark blue of the deeper surrounding ocean.
These dramatic differences in color help reveal variations in water depth and the characteristics of the marine environment.
The Caribbean image is also a reminder of the challenges facing low-lying islands and coastal communities as global sea levels continue to rise.
One of Sentinel-3C's most important instruments, its synthetic aperture radar altimeter, is designed to measure the height of the ocean surface with high precision. By tracking how that height changes over time, scientists can better understand sea-level rise and support efforts to prepare for its consequences.
New Measurements Show the Satellite Is Performing Well
Beyond its striking photographs, Sentinel-3C has already begun demonstrating its ability to gather precise scientific measurements.
Its radar altimeter has collected sea surface height data across the Atlantic Ocean and Mediterranean Sea. Researchers compared these observations with the Copernicus Marine Service's multimission sea-level anomaly data, which combine measurements from multiple satellites.
The early results show good agreement with existing measurements, indicating that the new altimeter is operating as expected.
Once Sentinel-3C completes commissioning, it will contribute to global sea-level monitoring alongside established satellite missions such as Copernicus Sentinel-6 and Jason.
These long-running observations are essential for understanding how quickly the world's oceans are rising.
Thanks to precise satellite measurements, scientists have determined that global sea levels have increased by an average of 3.64 mm per year since 1999. The rate of sea-level rise has also been accelerating, making continued monitoring increasingly important.
Sentinel-3C's altimeter will contribute more than ocean measurements. It will also observe changes in the height of rivers, lakes, sea ice, and land ice, complementing future observations from the upcoming Copernicus CRISTAL mission.
Tracking Greenland's Massive Ice Sheet From Orbit
Some of Sentinel-3C's most encouraging early results come from Greenland.
Between September 30 and October 4, the satellite collected measurements of the Greenland Ice Sheet's surface elevation. An accompanying animation shows the tracks of these observations across the enormous ice-covered landscape.
When scientists compared the measurements with a reference digital elevation model, a detailed representation of the ice sheet's surface, the satellite's observations closely matched the existing data.
This agreement offers further evidence that the radar altimeter is functioning properly.
Accurately tracking ice sheet elevation is particularly important as the planet warms. Greenland and Antarctica contain vast amounts of frozen water, and changes in their ice sheets can have major consequences for global sea levels.
Ice loss from these regions is already a major contributor to sea-level rise. By repeatedly measuring the height of their surfaces, satellites can help scientists monitor changes over time and improve predictions of future sea-level rise.
What's Next for Europe's New Earth-Watching Satellite?
Although Sentinel-3C is still in its early testing phase, its first observations represent an important step toward full scientific operations.
The satellite's ocean and land color instrument has already delivered detailed images of landscapes and coastlines, while its radar altimeter has produced encouraging measurements of ocean and ice sheet elevations.
Another milestone is approaching. The mission is preparing to release the first observations from its sea and land surface temperature radiometer, an instrument designed to measure the temperature of Earth's land and ocean surfaces.
Sentinel-3C is part of Copernicus, the Earth observation component of the European Union's Space Program. ESA is responsible for developing and implementing the Sentinel-3 satellites and operating them through the commissioning period.
After commissioning, ESA and the European Organisation for the Exploitation of Meteorological Satellites (Eumetsat) jointly manage the Sentinel-3 mission.
Eumetsat handles routine satellite operations and supplies marine and atmospheric observations, while ESA provides data covering land, the cryosphere, inland waters, and atmospheric products processed after acquisition.
Together, the two organizations make Sentinel-3 observations available to Copernicus services and users around the world.
With its first images and measurements already demonstrating promising performance, Sentinel-3C is on its way to becoming another important tool for observing Earth's oceans, landscapes, ice sheets, and atmosphere as the planet continues to change.

Saudi warning system stayed silent before deadly airport attacks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
23:40:27 UTC
08:40:27 KST

Saudi warning system stayed silent before deadly airport attacks
- Saudi Arabia’s public warning system went silent before deadly Houthi attacks on Riyadh airport, which killed at least 18 people and wounded more than 300.
- Officials gave no clear reason for the missing alerts, but analysts said Riyadh was trying to avoid panic while still showing calm.
- The attacks exposed Saudi Arabia’s security gaps, while embassies issued their own internal warnings and the kingdom later resumed alerts on Oct 12.
AI generated
RIYADH – Saudi Arabia stopped issuing public warnings of imminent military attacks days before a series of deadly strikes on Riyadh airport that killed at least 18 people and wounded more than 300.
The government has not said why there were no alerts to the public before the four Riyadh attacks in the past week.
The warnings had served to highlight the violence undermining the kingdom’s efforts to project an image of calm to its people and the world during its war with Yemen’s Iran-aligned Houthis.
Their absence during the airport strikes raised questions about Saudi Arabia’s vulnerability to attack and about its ability to protect residents and visitors, four Western and Arab officials in the region and political analysts told Reuters.
It also reflected efforts to maintain a sense of normalcy, they said.
“They (the Saudi government) want to have it both ways: to launch a military operation and at the same time try to give confidence to the population and external stakeholders,” said Sultan Alamer, a US-based Saudi academic and Senior Resident Fellow at the Middle East Policy Council think tank.
The Saudi civil defence – a national emergency management, rescue and firefighting agency which operates under the interior ministry and issues early warning alerts – and the Saudi government media office did not respond to emailed questions on why no alerts were issued.
Saudi Arabia’s approach is also one that some regional analysts said risked backfiring because the absence of warnings has heightened uncertainty in the kingdom.
On Oct 12, Saudi Arabia’s civil defence authority issued its first alerts since Sept 29, warning of potential threats in Riyadh and southern cities.
Reuters was unable to ascertain whether the decision to issue alerts again was a response to the airport attacks, and the Saudi government did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the matter.
System goes silent
All Gulf countries have been hit by Iranian drones and missiles since the US-Iran war began in February, but their governments have handled public warnings differently.
Qatar’s interior ministry has issued mobile phone alerts before nearly every attack, including most recent attacks in July, when residents were warned to stay inside and away from windows.
Bahrain and Kuwait have repeatedly sounded sirens urging people to take shelter.
Saudi Arabia began issuing threat alerts to mobile phones and social media accounts via a national early warning system in May. But despite increasing Houthi attacks leading up to last week, the system went silent.
The last alert before last week’s attacks was issued on Sept 29, for the southern province of Najran, according to posts on the civil defence X account.
The civil defences authority has continued to issue warnings about staying out of harm’s way during adverse weather, including rain and flooding, and did so as recently as Oct 12.
It also warned residents not to share images, rumours or information about interceptions and impact sites, including in a post on Oct 12, under government regulations issued in March.
Reuters could not determine whether anyone had faced prosecution for sharing such information, and the Saudi government media office did not respond to a request for comment on the matter.
Before last week’s airport attacks, officials from an allied Western government asked Saudi authorities why the alerts had stopped, two officials with direct knowledge of the matter said.
The response was that the alerts were too disruptive and many citizens had complained they were being woken by them at night, the officials said.
The Saudi government media office and Saudi officials did not respond to requests for comment on the assertion.
Former US ambassador to Saudi Arabia Michael Ratney said Riyadh was trying to balance public messaging on attacks with efforts to prevent disruption in the kingdom but had ended up adding to a sense of unease about the strikes.
“Their approach to public messaging seems like a corollary to the quandary they are in: They need to respond to the Houthis but don’t want that to result in societal disruption and their public messaging is a reflection of that,” he said.
“But the lack of alerts of incoming Houthi attacks creates the very nervousness they are trying to avoid.”
New threat alert
Ali Shihabi, a Saudi analyst close to the government, said that with or without early warnings, the kingdom would struggle to defend all of its assets because of its size.
“In Saudi Arabia you have too much to protect. It’s a huge country with airports, pipelines and oil facilities. There is just not enough coverage to defend everything at once, not enough Patriots (missile defence systems), interceptors and missile batteries to do it all,” he said.
“Saudi Arabia has an unlimited need for air defences,” he added.”
Despite the attacks, Saudi Arabia hosted an international conference on Monday, though major oil bosses dropped out.
At the World Petroleum Council Energy Congress in Riyadh, Saudi Prince Abdulaziz bin Salaman, a brother of the Saudi crown prince and the kingdom’s energy minister, struck a defiant tone while acknowledging risks and Saudi Arabia’s intent to keep its economic plans on track.
He thanked all who had travelled to Riyadh “because you know this country is safe” but added: “Our gathering here does not mean the risk is gone.”
“We will never forfeit any chance to maintain our commitment and our vision,” he said.
Embassies issue their own internal alerts
Despite no public alerts being issued in October until Oct 12, Riyadh has been attacked about a dozen times, two of the Western officials said.
During that time, Western embassies in the kingdom have been issuing their own internal missile and drone alerts to staff, according to three people familiar with the matter and alerts seen by Reuters.
These internal alerts are compiled from a mixture of US and other Western government intelligence and input from Saudi authorities, one of those people said.
They include alerts sent to staff around the time of two first airport strikes last week according to the people familiar with the matter.
They said that even the embassies had received no internal warning before the Oct 10 airport strike, without offering an explanation.
Reuters could not determine why no warning came before the attack on Oct 10, the deadliest of last week’s attacks.
On Oct 11, Saudi state TV released footage of the Oct 10 strike.
It showed several shots of travellers in the airport terminal. Dozens lined up to board a flight. Men and women sat in chairs waiting, their eyes trained on the screens of their mobile phones as they scrolled.
Then, the bright orange flash of a missile explosion. REUTERS

Hackers hit French supermarkets in attack disabling fridges, forcing stores to discard food
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12

Hackers hit French supermarkets in attack disabling fridges, forcing stores to discard food
- Hackers attacked hundreds of French supermarkets on Oct 11 and disabled fridges, forcing stores to throw away meat, frozen food and vegetables.
- About 150 Intermarche stores, fewer than 100 Cooperative U stores and 80 Carrefour sites were hit. Danfoss said it was “aware of incidents in France” and is helping customers.
- The attacks raised fears of physical sabotage through “operational technology” systems. Experts said older Danfoss equipment lacked updates, and France is preparing to protect critical infrastructure.
AI generated
PARIS – Hundreds of supermarkets in France were hit by cyberattacks on the night of Oct 11 that disabled refrigeration systems and forced stores to throw out damaged food, following warnings that hackers are seeking to cause physical damage.
Around 150 Intermarche stores were hit, a spokesman for owner Groupement Mousquetaires told Bloomberg.
Hackers accessed cooling systems and set them to defrost, with refrigerators and freezers heating to 50 deg C for around six hours.
Meat, frozen items and vegetables had to be tossed out.
Mousquetaires said the systems were managed by Danish refrigeration firm Danfoss and that it would be up to the supplier to file a complaint with the authorities.
Cooperative U was also hit by the cyberattacks, chief executive Dominique Schelcher said on X. Fewer than a hundred of its stores were affected, AFP reported.
A spokesperson for Carrefour said 80 supermarkets were impacted out of a total of 6,000 sites.
Some Leclerc stores were also targeted, BFM said. Leclerc did not immediately respond to a Bloomberg request for comment.
Danfoss said it was “aware of incidents in France” and working with customers to implement mitigation measures.
It was not immediately clear who was behind the refrigeration cyberattacks, but the intrusions occurred against a backdrop of disruptive cyberattacks internationally.
Hackers can target physical processes and equipment too
In August, Britain’s National Cyber Security Centre warned that hackers were increasingly seeking to cause physical disruption with their attacks, which it linked in part to increased geopolitical instability.
The centre said that such attacks were targeting multiple sectors globally and had been carried out by a range of threat actors.
Hackers are more frequently associated with stealing data and extorting companies. But they can also target what are known as operational technology systems, which control physical processes and equipment, such as machinery or temperature controls in refrigeration systems.
In the US in July, suspected Iranian hackers targeted water facilities in at least seven states and in some cases degraded water operations.
Unidentified hackers separately targeted oil and gas tankers this summer, temporarily accessing the propulsion system of a tanker approaching the Texas coast.
In September, French President Emmanuel Macron said that he had instructed his government to prepare a plan to protect France’s critical infrastructure and defence industrial and technological base against drone and cyberattacks.
He said the country was facing intensifying hostile actions from Russia.
Muhammad Yahya Patel, virtual chief information security officer and cybersecurity adviser for EMEA at the cybersecurity firm Huntress, said the refrigeration attacks are the type that the security industry has been warning about as the “next frontier for sabotage attacks”.
“They’ve now been weaponised against food retail infrastructure in one of Europe’s largest economies. The immediate financial consequences are significant and visible.”
Danfoss spokesman Lars Grubak Lohff told Bloomberg that the majority of the affected products are old technologies, including the company’s AK-SM 800 and AK-SC 355 refrigeration systems, which no longer receive software or security updates.
“Danfoss has long advised customers to keep supported systems updated with the latest firmware and to migrate legacy systems to current-generation solutions,” Lohff wrote.
In August, cybersecurity researchers at Team82, part of Claroty, wrote a report flagging vulnerabilities in Danfoss controllers used to manage refrigeration in supermarkets and other cold storage facilities.
The group said it had found a hidden authentication mechanism that could be used to tamper with the operations of refrigeration systems.
Danfoss sold a €500 million (S$715 million) 5.5-year bond on Oct 12 that drew more than €3 billion of investor bids, according to a person familiar with the matter who asked not to be identified.
The lead managers moved the pricing level by as much as 37 basis points tighter during the process. BLOOMBERG

Philippine Lower House Passes Bill Restricting Social Media Access of Minors
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
23:22:00 UTC
08:22:00 KST

The Philippine House of Representatives yesterday approved a measure barring children under the age of 13 from social media. It has become the latest nation in Southeast Asia to tighten online safety provisions for minors.
The Safe and Friendly Environment for Kids in Digital Spaces Act was passed nearly unanimously, with 287 lawmakers voting in favor and three against, Inquirer.net reported.
The measures align the Philippines with a growing global effort to restrict minors’ access to social media platforms, in the interests of protecting them from cyberbullying, online fraud, and exposure to pornography, among other perceived threats.
In the Philippines, the legislative push has come after a string of incidents of school violence that the government believes were driven by online content. Last month, a 16-year-old shot dead two fellow students and injured eight others at a school in the southern Philippines, before taking his own life.
This followed a similar incident in the same region in August, in which a student at a Catholic school live-streamed himself shooting and killing a classmate before taking his own life. Also in June, two students shot and killed three and injured seven of their peers at a school in Tacloban, allegedly in response to bullying.
Under the proposed bill, children aged 13 and below would be prohibited from creating social media accounts. Meanwhile, a variety of restrictions would be put in place for those under 18 years of age. They will be barred from making online purchases and engaging with “gambling-like mechanisms” and other features that may pose “reasonably foreseeable and material risks” to their well-being. They would also be shielded from harmful ads and algorithmic short-video feeds that encourage limitless scrolling, according to Inquirer.net.
Filipinos are heavy users of social media. The country has the sixth-largest pool of Facebook users in the world, with more than 102 million accounts registered, and an estimated 78.1 million TikTok accounts, the seventh-largest of any country. According to research, Filipinos spend an average of nearly 34 hours per week on social media.
Yesterday’s vote came after the Senate’s recent endorsement of a similar but slightly stricter bill, which would ban a minor under 18 years of age from registering, accessing, using, or maintaining an account on any age-restricted social media platform. According to Inquirer.net, the two dueling bills are now set for a “legislative showdown,” and it remains to be seen exactly what the final version of the legislation will look like.
These moves follow Australia’s introduction of the world’s first social media ban for under 16s. The policy, which took effect in December of last year, forces social media firms to block users under 16 from having accounts on their platforms, rather than penalizing young people or their parents. Despite the lingering questions about the effectiveness of such restrictions, a long list of countries, including India, China, Türkiye, the United Kingdom, the European Union, and several in Europe, have since followed suit and announced the introduction of curbs of some kind.
Within Southeast Asia, Indonesia in March became the first nation to ban under-16s from having accounts on what it termed “high-risk” digital platforms, including YouTube, TikTok, Facebook, Instagram, Threads, X, Bigo Live, and Roblox. Malaysia started enforcing a similar ban on June 1, and ordered major social media platforms to conduct age verification against government-issued records. It has given them until January to implement the measure.
Vietnam also announced in July that it planned to introduce social media restrictions for minors. While Hanoi will not ban minors’ access to social media platforms, the new rules would bar under 16s from posting, commenting, sharing, or reacting to posts on social media.

SC to government: Cap prices of non-patented medicines
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
23:18:55 UTC
08:18:55 KST

A bench of Justices Vikram Nath and Sandeep Mehta said there was no rationale for controlling the price of a few scheduled medicines and allowing the rest to be sold at inflated prices as all medicines are essential. It suggested a uniform rule limiting the MRP to not more than 16% above the price to the retailer (PTR).
NEW DELHI: With the Centre failing to give even "one justification" to the satisfaction of the court in favour of patients for keeping the maximum retail price of medicines at exorbitant levels but also accepting that profit margins for drugs and medical consumables reach up to 1,000%, Supreme Court on Monday said that the price of all non-patented drugs and consumables should also be controlled and it should not be confined only to anti-cancer medicines as done by govt recently.As solicitor general Tushar Mehta and ASG Aishwarya Bhati informed SC about the decision to cap the trade margins on anti-cancer drugs at 30% of the maximum retail price, the court appreciated govt's decision but raised questions on why pricing of other medicines should not be capped. The bench pointed out various examples to drive home the point that patients are fleeced because of sky-high pricing.SC to government: There is a great divide... why can’t you control the entire range of drugsThis relates to only cancer drugs. What about the overall? For an ordinary cardiac stent, Indian made stent, price to retailer (PTR) is Rs 5,000 but MRP is Rs 25,000... This is not even a tip of the iceberg. It (decision) has come only because of harsh observation from the court,” the bench of Justices Vikram Nath and Sandeep Mehta asked SG Tushar Mehta and also applauded his intervention resulting in a quick decision.It said the price of a drip line for saline for the retailer is Rs 11 but the MRP is around Rs 270. It said MRP for Azithromycin is Rs 78.29 but the PTS (price to stockist) is Rs 28.5.
“There is a great divide... There are thousands of examples,” court said, asking govt to explain why all non-patented medicines shouldn’t be brought under price control.“Give me just one justification in favour of patients (for not controlling the prices). Why can’t you control the entire range of drugs?” the bench asked the ASG.Bhati submitted that areas with lower sales, such as rural areas, may require higher margins for the retailer so as to provide sufficient income and livelihood to the retailer, failing which the access to and availability of drugs in such areas may be adversely affected. She told the bench the Indian drug market is fairly competitive, with a large number of pharmaceutical companies in every drug segment, resulting in one of the lowest prices in the world. “If there is too much intervention by govt, it will lead to the market suffering. It will affect availability.”But court said all the justifications given by govt were not in favour of patients who had to pay the higher price. Intervening in the proceedings, the SG submitted govt was not averse to the plea and the bench also made it clear that its proceeding was only intended to “strengthen the hands of the govt and nothing else”.Govt, in its affidavit, said, “Another area of concern in the sector is supply of consumables in hospitals, where margins of 100-1000% or more are prevalent, along with a tendency of hospitals to purchase consumables that have a high MRP, with a low price to the distributor/hospital.”
It admitted that patients have a very low bargaining position vis-a-vis the hospital, and a patient’s knowledge of drugs, their substitutes and their prices is also limited.“These bargaining and information asymmetries result in malpractices despite strong competition among manufacturers, leading to the need for regulation. That hospitals purchase medicines from manufacturers who provide the highest trade margin and then sell those to patients at the MRP, with margins ranging from 170% to 700% or more in the case of anti-cancer (oncology) drugs,” the affidavit said.The apex court thereafter adjourned the case for Oct 27.

Jantar Mantar out as protest hub; 3 new venues named
Unknown

2026-10-12

08:11:41 KST

NEW DELHI: For decades, Jantar Mantar offered protesters a place within earshot of Parliament and the seat of govt they sought to hold accountable. Now they will have to make themselves heard from further away.Ramlila Maidan in central Delhi, Burari ground in the north and CBD ground in Shahdara have been designated as the city's new protest sites, replacing Jantar Mantar Road. An order issued by police commissioner Anurag Kumar on Oct 11 said the decision followed recommendations by a ministry of home affairs committee set up to identify suitable venues where citizens could exercise their right to protest.
The order said: "On the committee recommendations, Jantar Mantar as a protest venue has been de-notified".While the protest site is called Jantar Mantar, the protests never took place inside the 18th-century, ASI-protected astronomical observatory. They were held on the adjoining Jantar Mantar Road, the starting point of many historic movements.On the face of it, the road is hardly an ideal protest venue. Hemmed in by bungalows and shops, it offers limited space. But crowds find room, spilling into lanes and roads, as was seen during June-July CJP protests and the 2011 India Against Corruption movement.
Shifting protests to Burari will reduce chances of traffic congestion: PoliceBut its location more than makes up for the lack of space. Around 3km from Parliament and barely a kilometre from Connaught Place, it sits amid key govt buildings. It also offers the practical comforts a protest site needs: water, inexpensive food, toilets and tree shade. But its biggest advantage, however, may be that it comes free.The alternatives come with a price. Booking Ramlila Maidan for functions costs Rs 66,080, while Burari and CBD grounds cost approximately Rs 90,000 each (without security deposit). No separate booking category for protests has been introduced yet.Jantar Mantar’s denotification as a protest site came after Supreme Court, on Oct 9, asked authorities to designate a suitable alternative venue for protests. During the hearing, the CJI-led bench said, “The govt and parties are agreeable to the suggestion that it is high time to identify and designate a proper protest site, instead of Jantar Mantar, with basic amenities like water, toilets and healthcare facilities. The competent authorities would consider the suggestion and take an appropriate decision in this regard.”An officer said at Jantar Mantar, a crowd beyond 1,000 leads to crowding and traffic congestion on approach roads. Another officer said the presence of sensitive installations in the vicinity was also a security concern.“If someone disguises themselves as a protester and then moves towards a sensitive installation, it could pose a security threat,” the officer said.Ramlila Maidan can accommodate a crowd of up to 50,000, while Burari ground, which is the largest of the three sites, can hold more than 50,000 people. CBD Ground in Shahdara is across 12 acres.A senior police officer said Ramlila Maidan can host protests and large gatherings. Organisers must apply 10-12 days in advance, after which police coordinate with them on turnout, venue requirements, timings, VIP attendance and the agenda. In 2011, the Anna Hazare-led India Against Corruption movement, which later gave rise to AAP, shifted from Jantar Mantar to Ramlila Maidan as crowds swelled.The proposed shift from Jantar Mantar also raises questions about managing exceptionally large gatherings. One of the organisers of Ramlila events claimed that the turnout at some programmes could exceed 50,000, potentially putting pressure on the arrangements at the designated venues.
Police sources said the area of the site at Shahdara will be finalised before infrastructure is set up. With malls, banquet halls and other commercial facilities nearby, clearly demarcating the venue and managing traffic will be key, they said. Once the site is finalised, police infrastructure, including a police post, would be made, the sources added.Burari Ground is an open space. Police sources said the likelihood of such gatherings significantly affecting traffic was relatively low here.

Zelenskyy says Russia isn't honoring Trump's energy ceasefire
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

Ukraine's Zelenskyy says it's "increasingly evident that Russia is unwilling to accept an energy ceasefire"
Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Monday that so far, "there is no indication that Russia is complying" with an energy ceasefire announced by President Trump the day before.
Just hours after Mr. Trump's announcement, Zelenskyy said Russia struck a power plant in eastern Ukraine. By Monday afternoon, Russia had attacked six additional energy facilities across Ukraine.
"Ukraine is ready to guarantee the energy ceasefire, as announced by the American President, and Russia must take corresponding steps," Zelenskyy wrote on X. "As of now, there is no indication that Russia is complying with the conditions outlined by the American President."
Asked Monday about reports that Russia had violated the energy ceasefire, Mr. Trump said: "I'm not sure about that, and we'll take a look. But all I know is that Zelenskyy and Putin have to get together and end that ridiculous war." He also said "there's been violations on both sides."
The U.S. president later told reporters that he believes Russian President Vladimir Putin "wants to make a deal more than Zelenskyy."
Over the last year, Mr. Trump has made several attempts at brokering deals to halt strikes on energy infrastructure between Russia and Ukraine that failed to materialize or were quickly violated.
In January, Mr. Trump claimed that Putin agreed not to strike Ukrainian energy infrastructure for a week, but Russia attacked Kyiv's power and heating plants four days later. In September, Mr. Trump said both Putin and Zelenskyy had agreed to refrain from striking one another's energy infrastructure, but neither side halted attacks.
Zelenskyy told CBS News in an interview after the September proposal that Ukraine would be willing to agree to such a moratorium but doubted Russia would ever reciprocate.
One reason for the Kremlin's intransigence is that Russia's attacks on Ukrainian energy infrastructure have a relatively greater impact than Ukraine's. Ukrainian strikes primarily target Russian oil and gas infrastructure, attempting to cut into the energy revenues Russia uses to fund its war effort.
The attacks have brought Russian oil refining to a 20-year low and reduced diesel production by 30% in 2026, according to the International Energy Agency, but Russia's economy has shown little sign of collapse.
"For Russia, Ukraine's attacks are an inconvenience and an inflationary pressure," Alexander Kolyandr, director for Europe at Eurasia Group, told CBS News. "It is definitely damaging Russia's economy, but it isn't putting it on the verge of collapse."
Russia — with more drones and missiles and an economy 10 times the size of Ukraine's — is able to inflict more relative pain on both the country's economy and its civilians. Ukraine has already begun to experience power outages this fall as Russia hammers its power grid heading into winter.
"Because the Ukrainian economy is so much smaller than the Russian one, the relative effect is much higher," Kolyandr said. "And the Russians by and large do not distinguish between civilian and military infrastructure. Their theory is that any kind of infrastructure is used or can be used for military purposes."
Last winter, as Ukrainians faced frequent power and heating outages through one of the coldest winters in recent memory, Mr. Trump requested Putin stop striking Ukraine's energy infrastructure. This week, though, he has directed pressure toward Ukraine.
The pressure comes as Mr. Trump grapples with high global energy prices — a situation he has argued has more to do with the Russia-Ukraine war than the Iran war. Last week, Mr. Trump announced a deal to allow Russia to sell some diesel to the U.S. and global markets, a change of course after years of U.S. efforts to block Russia from financing its war effort by selling petroleum products abroad.
A European official and a Ukrainian official told CBS News that the Trump administration has threatened to stop sharing intelligence and to halt the purchase of U.S.-made weapons by European allies for Ukraine via the PURL procurement system if Ukraine does not stop deep strikes against Russian energy infrastructure.
The Ukrainian official said that Ukraine's government is taking the threats very seriously as intelligence sharing allows Ukraine to know where and when Russia launches its ballistic missiles from, and the PURL program is the only way Ukraine can purchase its Patriot air defense missiles, already in short supply.
The Financial Times was first to report the American threats to pause intelligence and weapons shipments to Ukraine.
CBS News has reached out to the White House for comment.
Zelenskyy said progress toward an energy ceasefire hinges on the White House's willingness to impose more pressure on Russia.
"A lot depends on America's position for de-escalation to actually succeed," he wrote on X. "Pressure on Russia is needed."

The Dow Jones Industrial Average rose 195.6 points, or 0.38 percent, to 51,850.55. The S&P 500 shed 4.3 points, or 0.06 percent, to 7,807.24. The Nasdaq Composite Index dropped 120.27 points, or 0.44 percent, to 27,245.9.
Eight of the 11 primary S&P 500 sectors ended in the green. Energy was the day's best-performing S&P 500 sector, while technology led the laggards as memory-chip and AI-hardware stocks slumped.
The cash U.S. Treasury market was closed for Columbus Day, leaving investors without a fresh read on bond yields. The benchmark 10-year Treasury yield ended Friday at about 5.24 percent, just off the more-than-two-decade high it touched earlier in the week, while the 30-year yield hovered near 5.6 percent.
Oil prices rose as supply worries persisted, despite U.S. President Donald Trump's weekend announcement of an "energy ceasefire" between Russia and Ukraine. West Texas Intermediate for November delivery went up 1.89 U.S. dollars, or 2.06 percent, to settle at 93.74 dollars a barrel. Brent crude for December delivery increased by 1.93 dollars, or 1.84 percent, to settle at 106.65 dollars a barrel on the London ICE Futures Exchange.
"While this week's inflation data could be a near-term volatility trigger, the new earnings season may play a bigger role in shaping the market's momentum into year end, since it may signal how strong those tailwinds really are," said Chris Larkin, managing director of trading and investing at E*TRADE from Morgan Stanley.
On the corporate front, chip stocks sold off after Broadcom CEO Hock Tan warned at a Singapore conference that capital constraints could become a bigger obstacle to the AI buildout than shortages of chips, memory or electricity. He likened many AI investors to casino gamblers. Intel CEO Lip-Bu Tan echoed the financing concerns.
The Philadelphia Semiconductor Index dropped about 2.6 percent, marking its fourth straight session of losses following the concerns. Broadcom slipped nearly 2 percent and Intel fell more than 3 percent. Micron Technology was down nearly 4 percent and SK Hynix was down more than 4 percent.
Meanwhile, Lumentum Holdings tumbled 9.78 percent, marking the worst performance on the Nasdaq, while Salesforce rose more than 2 percent after Bank of America upgraded the stock to "Buy" from "Underperform." Meta Platforms bounced up more than 3 percent. Exxon Mobil and Chevron rose 1.9 percent and 1.42 percent, respectively.
Investors now turn to a heavy week of catalysts. Third-quarter earnings season kicks off Tuesday with results from JPMorgan Chase, Goldman Sachs, Wells Fargo and Citigroup, followed by ASML later in the week. Johnson & Johnson and UnitedHealth Group are also slated to issue results before the bell on Tuesday. ■

Egypt posts 2.8 bln USD balance-of-payments surplus in FY 2025/2026
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
07:00:50 CST
08:00:50 KST

CAIRO, Oct. 12 (Xinhua) -- Egypt recorded a balance-of-payments surplus of 2.8 billion U.S. dollars in the 2025/2026 fiscal year, reversing a deficit of 2.1 billion dollars a year earlier, the Central Bank of Egypt said Monday.
The capital and financial account posted a net inflow of 23.2 billion dollars during the fiscal year, which runs from July 1 to June 30, up from 10.2 billion dollars a year earlier, according to a statement by the central bank.
It included 18 billion dollars in net foreign direct investment (FDI) and 4.2 billion dollars in net portfolio investment, the statement said.
Remittances from Egyptians working abroad surged 29.6 percent to 47.3 billion dollars, while tourism revenues rose 10.3 percent to 18.4 billion dollars, it said.
Suez Canal transit receipts increased 21.6 percent to 4.4 billion dollars, it added.
However, the current account deficit widened to 22.5 billion dollars from 15.4 billion dollars a year earlier, driven by a larger merchandise trade deficit and the investment income deficit, according to the bank.
The non-oil trade deficit expanded 25.4 percent to 46.6 billion dollars, mainly as non-oil imports grew faster than non-oil exports.
Abu Bakr al-Deeb, an economic researcher at the Cairo-Abed Arab Center for Research and Studies, said strong financial inflows helped Egypt improve its overall external position despite continued pressure from the trade balance.
Al-Deeb noted, however, that the surplus, while a positive development, should not be taken alone as evidence that external imbalances had been resolved.
"Egypt needs to strengthen its export capacity and competitiveness and direct investment toward productive sectors that can expand domestic production and generate foreign currency earnings," he explained. "Continued tourism growth and remittances will remain important, but reducing the structural trade gap is essential to strengthening the country's external position." ■

In a statement Monday, El Mansouri said the agreement followed two rounds of consultations aimed at building a politically coherent majority.
The four parties will propose candidates for ministerial posts, while negotiations continue on the cabinet's composition and the government program. ■

The Role of Beneficial Ownership Transparency in the Hard Power Era
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
23:00:00 UTC
08:00:00 KST

The Role of Beneficial Ownership Transparency in the Hard Power Era
In the age of hard power, beneficial ownership transparency must shift from an anti-corruption ideal to a national security capability for Britain and its allies.
In the halcyon days of geopolitical stability in 2013, the UK government launched its campaign for raising global standards on beneficial ownership transparency (BOT) during its G8 presidency. One thing that has survived the turmoil in the intervening period is the UK government’s continued, cross-party support for this mission. This campaign has certainly achieved a measure of success, especially domestically, with a much-enhanced Companies House register and the novel introduction of the Register of Overseas Entities for improved property transparency, as the two stand-out achievements.
In a political culture of hyperbole, the UK can genuinely see itself as a global leader in championing – and delivering – BOT but as the UK prepares for its presidency of the G20 next year and the now-G7 in 2028, it cannot look at the state of global progress with great satisfaction.
In August this year, the US government defanged its Corporate Transparency Act by announcing the permanent removal of the requirement for US individuals and businesses to register, in a move which made permanent a 2025 suspension celebrated by President Trump as ending the ‘economic menace’ of BOT. In the EU, the 2022 Court of Justice of the European Union ruling has effectively put an end to public registers, the UK’s policy preference, with focus shifting to a Legitimate Interest Access model. Finally, closer to home for the UK, genuine access to beneficial ownership information in the highest-risk Overseas Territories can be mildly described as suboptimal.
With the tide turning against it, how can the UK find a new argument to support its campaign for BOT to regain its relevance in an era of slipping standards and hard power politics?
A New Register
The anti-corruption framing which has long accompanied BOT advocacy is technically correct and morally justified. It has proven effective in driving significant progress in the UK, especially when viewed through the prism of Russian kleptocrats. The challenge is not the veracity of these arguments but that the BOT argument is now being made in a world focused on hard security choices over development priorities, while integrity-based politics is suffering at the ballot box. With global norms slipping and the Financial Action Task Force not moving its baseline towards a requirement for public registers, the UK risks continuing to play the old classics to an audience which is not listening anymore.
As Russian sabotage attacks spread across Europe, opaque ownership over who owns what should be considered as a national security risk rather than simply a concern of anti-corruption campaigners
Much as the security crisis of Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine proved to be the catalyst for long-overdue illicit finance reforms in the UK, the next salient framing – both rhetorically and substantially – is identifying and articulating the importance of BOT in supporting the UK and its allies in the ‘space between peace and war’ in which they currently operate, rather than proposing transparency as an intrinsic good.
Hard Power Necessity, Not Only Integrity
Open economies and societies such as the UK face an asymmetric disadvantage in comparison to more closed adversaries as they present a wider attack surface for these adversaries to exploit. This openness is a key feature and benefit of European countries but also requires greater efforts to protect against those who seek to do harm.
As Russian sabotage attacks spread across Europe, opaque ownership over who owns what should be considered as a national security risk rather than simply a concern of anti-corruption campaigners.
Shoots of this argument already exist across Europe with Nordic and Baltic countries taking measures to restrict the rights of Russian citizens to purchase property near Critical National Infrastructure (CNI) sites, or even across the entire country in some circumstances. This is based on fears that the Russian state will use these properties as ‘Trojan horses’ in hybrid or full-scale attacks against Europe. Critically, none of these measures could be successful without understanding who owns what in the first place.
High-quality beneficial ownership information does not just reveal property ownership; it is also crucial for unveiling shell ownership structures of shadow fleet operations, companies linked to the evasion of dual-use controls and even where ownership of CNI itself is at risk.
This is not confined to Russia; clear examples emerge from China too. As detailed by the OCCRP (Organized Crime and Corruption Reporting Project) and others, China’s authority for foreign exchange reserves (SAFE) was able to acquire equity in a range of European assets from fibre-optic companies, natural gas distributors or renewable infrastructure in the UK through a network of seven shell companies registered in the British Virgin Islands, which in turn controlled 28 registered holding companies in Luxembourg. A lack of transparent corporate ownership represents a clear national security risk.
Beyond Russia and China, the irony should not be lost on the US government that it weakened both its own domestic standards and consequently the international norms on BOT in the same month that it declared an economic D-Day on Iran, itself a frequent abuser of corporate secrecy to evade sanctions and the very pressure the US has unleashed.
Deeds over Discourse
So how can BOT improve our national security capabilities? The focus should not merely be on the availability of more data but critically its quality, and the systems built to exploit it. A public register with poor-quality data achieves as little as excellently verified data that is not accessed, analysed and exploited.
Starting at home, the UK government can use the proposed Defence Readiness Bill as the legislative vehicle to plug the remaining gaps in the UK’s beneficial ownership framework such as the role of discretionary trusts. Gaps that are relevant to CNI are especially relevant given its existing prevalence in the Bill. An exercise that separates what legislative gaps exist from the capability gaps in accessing, analysing and exploiting beneficial ownership information from a national security perspective would identify what requires investment rather than statute.
One step removed is the UK’s relationship with its Crown Dependencies (CDs) and Overseas Territories (OTs) that are viewed by many as the soft underbelly of the UK’s BOT campaign. Glacial progress in public registers has resulted in the stop-gap solution, and wonderful acronym, of LIARBOs (Legitimate Interest Access Registers of Beneficial Ownership). LIARBOs are in their infancy but the flaws have already been documented, and after eight years of protracted negotiations since the UK government first pledged public registers in the Overseas Territories, the status quo is likely to be as far as this process will go. This does not mean the UK should reduce its efforts, but with public registers still a mirage, an alternative option – the expansion and more active use of the Exchange of Notes (EoN) concept – that allows for better government-to-government information sharing should be more closely considered.
Ten years on from the original EoN agreement, which allowed for law enforcement agencies in the UK to receive accurate beneficial ownership information on request from their counterparts in the CDs and OTs in a timely and private manner, the 2019 review remains the sole public record of its success. An updated and transparent Exchange of Notes review would provide either the grounds for practical improvements in the arrangements such as direct UK government access to the registers or, in the best-case scenario, a strong footing for the CDs and OTs in the narrative and policy debates they face on BOT. Furthermore, such an intimate government-to-government approach embracing other international financial centre registers that remain closed to public access could be expanded to boost security access to beneficial ownership data and could be integrated into the final leg of the UK’s influence on the international stage via initiatives such as the planned Illicit Finance Summit as well as the upcoming G7 and G20 presidencies.
Given that the UK’s preferred model of public registers is unattainable at present, an EoN model of government-to-government access built on collective security interests may provide a different pathway for continued progress. Expanding the UK’s EoN model with like-minded countries offers the most practical step forward, which might also include creating system-to-system access with the Beneficial Ownership Registers Interconnection System (BORIS), the EU’s interconnected and internal database linking national central beneficial ownership registers.
Whatever the policy direction, recognising that corporate secrecy has become more than a mere criminal threat and is being weaponised would help secure another decade of political support for advancing BOT standards and ensure that access to and analysis and exploitation of accurate beneficial ownership information plays its part in the national security apparatus of the UK and its allies.

CJI rejects INDIA bloc leaders’ request for meeting over ‘vote chori’
NEW DELHI: A day after CJI Surya Kant turned down Congress leadership's request to meet them privately on their "vote chori" charge, saying doing so will violate the principle of separation of powers, SC Monday reiterated that it should not be dragged into political battlefields nor politics be brought into the court."We are not concerned with political parties or their activities. But courts should not be dragged into such kinds of things," said a bench of CJI Kant and Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana.
In an email response, through which he turned down the request from leaders of opposition in the two Houses of Parliament, Rahul Gandhi and Mallikarjun Kharge, for a face-to-face meeting, CJI had pointed out to them that it was duty-bound to hear petitions against CEC Gyanesh Kumar and those challenging SIR, and indicated that the court will hear those on priority.Wherever identified locations are there, protests can be held: SCThe CJI-led bench Monday emphasised the need for it to exercise restraint and not enter the political thicket while hearing the complaint that protests and barricades were obstructing lawyers from working.At the commencement of proceedings, senior advocate Atmaram Nadkarni sought urgent hearing on a writ petition filed by a lawyer, saying he could not represent his client at an international arbitration because of protests and preventive measures.
Nadkarni was joined by SCBA president Pradeep Rai who said the right to protest must co-exist with the right of other citizens to move and function without hindrance. SC agreed to list both the petitions for hearing on Tuesday along with pleas by Shailendra Mani Tripathi, opposition MPs M A Baby, Manoj Jha and Menaka Guruswamy, who have accused police of using excessive force to quell protests.Rai said, “Institution is performing its institutional duty and we are doing our professional duties. Political parties must not interfere with our domain.”CJI Surya Kant, while saying that court would not wade into others’ turf, said, “Democratic institutions should be allowed to function peacefully and there should not be any impediment in the functioning or movement of lawyers, court staff and litigants.”Following Nadkarni and Rai, advocate G Sankaranarayanan mentioned another petition repeating what was argued — detention of senior advocate Shadan Farasat in an “unseemly” manner — before SC on Sunday and suggested that asking protesters to exercise restraint, be peaceful and cooperate when police was using excessive force, was not fair.“I know SC has repeatedly said we must try to cooperate and exercise restraint. For once I would hope that court would say the same thing to police. That has not come from this bench so far. I am hoping that happens because of excesses they are allowing... the hooligans were roaming around with sticks,” he said.
“They have hit children on the head and put out videos and proudly posted the videos saying they have done this and police have done nothing. And we are being told to exercise restraint. I do not know what we have done to be told to exercise restraint. At some point the bench will come to the rescue of the bar and the citizens of this country and send a strong message to the police,” he added.CJI agreed to list the petition on Tuesday but stressed yet again: “I will not allow SC or SC campus to become a political battlefield. We do not want advocates and lawyers to be part of the political battles inside the court premises. Wherever identified locations (for protest) are there, the protests can be held there.”

NEW DELHI: Opposition INDIA bloc members, led by leader of opposition in Lok Sabha Rahul Gandhi and joined by thousands of supporters, undertook their march to Supreme Court on Monday to file a joint petition seeking intense scrutiny into a host of issues - functioning of EC, preventing CEC Gyanesh Kumar from taking decisions "unilaterally", "arbitrary" deletion of voters during SIR, and the architecture governing use and deployment of EVMs.Rahul and other petitioners - Congress chief Mallikarjun Kharge, TMC's Saugata Roy, Samajwadi Party's Akhilesh Yadav, RJD's Tejashwi Yadav, Sena (UBT)'s Sanjay Raut, CPM's M A Baby, CPI's D Raja, JMM's Mahua Majhi, NCP(SP)'s Supriya Sule and IUML's E T Mohammed Basheer - sought suspension of SIR without questioning its legality, and, inclusion of eligible voters in rolls of Punjab and other poll-bound states.
