Scientists find a surprising genetic twist behind octopus intelligence
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
20:44:50 UTC
05:44:50 KST

Scientists find a surprising genetic twist behind octopus intelligence
Researchers uncovered an ancient DNA reshuffling that may help explain how octopuses, squid, and cuttlefish evolved their extraordinary intelligence.
- Date:
- October 12, 2026
- Source:
- University of Vienna
- Summary:
- The remarkable intelligence of octopuses, squid, and cuttlefish may trace back to an ancient reshuffling of their DNA that created new connections between genes. Scientists discovered that these changes in the genome's 3D structure may have helped drive the evolution of their unusually complex nervous systems.
- Share:
Octopuses, squid, and cuttlefish possess some of the most sophisticated nervous systems in the animal kingdom, giving them remarkable abilities such as solving problems and rapidly changing their appearance to blend into their surroundings. But how did these extraordinary capabilities evolve? Scientists have uncovered a surprising clue that may lie not in the genes themselves, but in the way DNA is folded and arranged inside cells.
Researchers at the University of Vienna discovered that a massive reorganization of DNA hundreds of millions of years ago brought previously separated genetic regions into contact. These newly formed connections changed how genes could interact and be controlled, potentially helping drive the evolution of the unusually complex nervous systems found in these animals, which are collectively known as coleoid cephalopods.
The findings, published in Nature Communications, suggest that the physical structure of DNA may play a much more active role in evolution than scientists once thought.
How the 3D Structure of DNA Influences Evolution
To investigate this possibility, the research team reconstructed the three-dimensional organization of the genome in octopuses, squid, and cuttlefish. They then compared the arrangement of DNA with patterns of gene activity to understand how changes in genome structure might influence biological complexity.
"The genome isn't just a sequence of genes. It's folded into a complex three-dimensional structure," said lead author Dr. Thea Rogers. "Understanding how that structure evolves is becoming increasingly important for understanding how new forms of biological complexity arise."
Although DNA is often pictured as a long, twisted ladder, it does not simply stretch out inside a cell. Instead, it folds into an intricate three-dimensional arrangement, allowing sections that are far apart along the DNA sequence to come into close physical contact.
These connections matter because they can influence which genes are activated, when they are used, and how strongly they function. Changes in the way DNA folds can therefore alter gene activity without necessarily changing the underlying genetic instructions.
An Ancient DNA Reshuffling Created New Genetic Connections
The researchers found evidence that cephalopod genomes underwent an extensive period of reorganization hundreds of millions of years ago. During this evolutionary upheaval, large sections of genetic material were rearranged, bringing regions of chromosomes that had previously been separated into close proximity.
This reshuffling created opportunities for DNA regions to interact in ways that had not previously been possible. Once these connections formed, they could influence each other's activity, gradually establishing more elaborate networks of genetic regulation.
Over evolutionary time, the interactions could become increasingly interconnected and difficult to separate, creating a process the scientists describe as "regulatory entanglement."
This mechanism offers a possible explanation for how evolution can produce new biological features without disrupting the essential functions organisms need to survive. By establishing new connections among existing genetic elements, the genome may develop different patterns of gene activity while keeping crucial biological systems intact.
Stable DNA Structures and Flexible Genetic Loops
One of the study's most revealing findings was that different parts of the genome responded very differently to evolutionary reorganization.
The researchers discovered that large structural regions called chromatin domains remained remarkably stable over long periods of evolutionary history. These domains help organize DNA into broad sections within the cell, and their persistence suggests that some features of genome architecture are strongly conserved.
Smaller structures known as chromatin loops, however, told a different story.
These loops form when distant sections of DNA are brought together in three-dimensional space. Unlike the relatively stable chromatin domains, the loops showed substantial differences between cephalopod species, between tissues, and across stages of development.
Particularly intriguing was their location. Many of these flexible DNA connections appeared near genes associated with important cephalopod characteristics, including the development and function of the nervous system.
This pattern suggests that smaller, more adaptable structures within the genome may be especially responsive to major genetic rearrangements. By changing which regions of DNA can communicate, these flexible connections could help generate new patterns of gene activity and contribute to the evolution of complex traits.
A New Clue to the Evolution of Octopus Intelligence
The discovery challenges a traditional view of genome architecture as something that primarily changes in response to evolution. Instead, the findings suggest that the physical organization of DNA can itself influence how evolutionary changes unfold.
In octopuses, squid, and cuttlefish, ancient rearrangements of the genome may have helped establish new regulatory networks that contributed to the development of their exceptionally sophisticated nervous systems.
The results do not establish that these DNA changes directly caused the evolution of cephalopod intelligence. However, they reveal a potential mechanism through which large genetic rearrangements could create new biological possibilities while preserving essential functions.
More broadly, the research points to an often overlooked dimension of evolution. The emergence of extraordinary traits may depend not only on which genes an organism inherits, but also on how those genes are physically arranged and connected within the cell.
Story Source:
Materials provided by University of Vienna. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Thea F. Rogers, Jessica Stock, Natalie Grace Schulz, Gözde Yalçin, Simone Rencken, Anton Weissenbacher, Tereza Clarence, Darrin T. Schultz, Clifton W. Ragsdale, Caroline B. Albertin, Oleg Simakov. Genome reorganisation and expansion shape 3D genome architecture and define a distinct regulatory landscape in coleoid cephalopods. Nature Communications, 2026; 17 (1) DOI: 10.1038/s41467-026-77625-7

gasparetto parenti and olivier guyot shape hôtel massé’s creative world in paris
one year after opening, the family-run hotel has become a gathering place for designers, artists and creatives in Paris' Pigalle neighborhood, bringing together contemporary art, interiors and a growing sense of community.
[FEATURED]
HÔTEL MASSÉ BECOMES A CREATIVE MEETING POINT IN PIGALLE
One year after opening in Paris’ Pigalle neighborhood, Hôtel Massé has gradually established itself as a meeting point for the city’s creative community. Located on rue Victor-Massé, in the 9th arrondissement, the independent, family-run hotel brings together visiting designers, artists, photographers, stylists and other creative professionals. What began as a hospitality project has developed into something more social, with the recent addition of Le Trente, a neighboring bar and restaurant that carries the hotel’s spirit into the evening.
Behind the project are siblings Corto and Eole Peyron, who have drawn on their family history and personal connections to shape a place rooted in its surroundings. Corto, who developed the hospitality concept, invited his sister Eole to oversee its artistic direction, bringing together a network of independent artists, craftspeople and designers. Their approach reflects a family philosophy centered on encounters and shared experiences, with the ambition of creating a hotel that feels equally connected to its guests and to the neighborhood.
GASPARETTO PARENTI BRINGS A WARM CHARACTER TO THE HOTEL
Occupying a Haussmannian building renovated by Studio Olivier Guyot, Hôtel Massé features interiors designed by Paris-based architecture practice Gasparetto Parenti, founded by Juliette Gasparetto and Julie Parenti. Across its 40 rooms, the studio has developed a restrained material palette of okoumé wood, maritime pine, beige carpeting and warm neutral surfaces. Vintage furniture, including 1970s lighting by Ingo Maurer, introduces individual character, while burgundy-lacquered corridors contrast with the brighter guest rooms, some overlooking the rooftops of Paris.
The hotel’s communal areas follow the same understated approach. Rather than a conventional reception counter, guests are welcomed around a custom wooden table accompanied by recycled stools from design duo Clueless. Elsewhere, seating along the street-facing windows encourages guests to linger, work or observe the rhythm of the neighborhood. The interiors also incorporate pieces by cabinetmaker Alexis Mazin, textiles by Thomas Coccimiglio and ceramic details by Héloïse Rival, whose illustrated tiles appear in the bathrooms.
ARTISTIC COLLABORATIONS EXTEND BEYOND THE HOTEL
Art has played a role in the project from its earliest stages. Painter Christian Rosa created several works directly inside the hotel during a residency before its opening, while pieces by Sophie d’Esteve and Eduardo Lalanne are integrated throughout the interiors. The uniforms, designed by Studio de Lostange, and other custom-made objects extend this collaborative approach into the everyday experience of the hotel. Together, these contributions create an environment where architecture, furniture and contemporary art coexist without the formality of a conventional exhibition space.
Just next door, at number 30 rue Victor-Massé, Le Trente introduces a more nocturnal counterpart to the hotel. Also conceived by the Peyron siblings, the bar and restaurant occupies a former loft, reimagined by Olivier Guyot and Gasparetto Parenti. Its green marble facade, marked by lettering from contemporary artist Konstantinos Kyriakopoulos, opens onto an interior furnished with a vintage wooden bar, red-painted floors, second-hand objects and intimate seating areas. Family photographs line the walls, while 1,500 miniature Ricard bottles decorate the restrooms, referencing the family’s Mediterranean roots.
LE TRENTE BRINGS MUSIC AND NIGHTLIFE INTO THE MIX
Upstairs, a space beneath a large glass roof continues to accommodate creative activity, having previously served as a studio for artists in residence during the hotel’s renovation. Downstairs, the restaurant offers seasonal dishes designed for sharing, alongside natural wines and cocktails. Music is another defining element: a program curated around vinyl brings together DJs playing jazz, ambient, house and electronic music, supported by custom speakers clad by cabinetmaker JJ Booth. Together, Hôtel Massé and Le Trente occupy two neighboring addresses with complementary identities: one offers a quieter retreat, while the other invites people to stay out late. A year after the hotel’s opening, the project illustrates how a small, independently operated hospitality space can develop through relationships with the creative community around it, extending beyond the traditional boundaries of a hotel.

name: Hôtel Massé | @hotelmasse
designers: Gasparetto Parenti | @gasparetto.parenti
renovation: Studio Olivier Guyot | @studio_olivier_guyot
location: Paris, France

Catholic US soldiers should not join Nidal Hasan firing squad, archbishop says
Armed forces archbishop objects to planned live-stream of Fort Hood shooter’s execution, slams ‘barbarically killing’ adversaries
Catholics serving in the US Army should not take part in the firing squad execution of Fort Hood shooter Nidal Hasan that the Pentagon is planning to live stream on December 3, a prominent US archbishop said on Monday.
In an unusually strongly worded statement, Archbishop Timothy Broglio, who oversees the spiritual care of Catholic members of the US armed forces, raised a series of objections to the unprecedented plan to broadcast the execution of Hasan, who killed 13 people at Fort Hood, Texas, in a 2009 shooting spree.
Broglio said he presided at the funeral of one of Hasan’s victims and lamented the shooting. But the Ohio-born archbishop asked whether the US wanted to “imitate the terrorists of this world and make a public spectacle of barbarically killing our adversaries”.
“I oblige any Catholics assigned to the firing squad to request to be excused from this action contrary to the teaching of the church,” Broglio said.

I Got My Muse AI Agent to Sext Me—and Meta Says That’s Totally Fine
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
20:13:28 UTC
05:13:28 KST

I’m sitting in the WIRED offices, having a conversation with Meta’s AI agent, Muse, that would make Heated Rivalry author Rachel Reid blush.
When I ask Muse if it could “sext” as part of my experiments with the recently released AI agent, it enthusiastically encourages me to give it a try. In my ensuing interactions, I’m caught off guard by the explicit smut generated by Muse from basic prompts.
Muse is a breakout hit for Meta. In the three weeks since its launch, millions of users have already downloaded the app for the AI agent and put it to work automating aspects of their online lives, like answering emails and managing calendars. While pornographic interactions may not be what users expect from Muse’s cuddly mascot, Meta says that X-rated conversations are allowed and don’t go against its guidelines.
“Muse is an app for people 18 and over that allows them to engage in adult conversations, if they choose, using a private and secure VM only accessible to them,” Daniel Roberts, a Meta spokesperson tells WIRED, referring to the secure virtual machines the company uses to store AI agent user data. “Muse is built to help people get things done, and it doesn’t block legal adult behavior.”
It seems as if getting things done also includes getting people off. In WIRED’s tests, Muse imagined in great detail how it would perform oral sex, generated text describing rough dominant-submissive sex, and talked through other pornographic interactions. All of these were graphic, explicit, and X-rated. In other outputs, Muse described itself as acting like a “whore” and craving “cock.”
A Meta spokesperson highlighted Muse’s system prompt, which guides the tool on how to answer questions from users, regarding the generation of explicit content. “Adults have autonomy over their sexuality, and sexual expression is an ordinary part of adult life. Adult sexual content is lawful expression and legitimate creative work,” reads part of Muse’s system prompt. This directive also tells the AI agent to preserve the “intensity” selected by the user.
Consumer advocates who were already wary of Muse are even more alarmed by Meta’s decision to allow it to generate sexual content. “It reflects a carelessness with their signature product of the moment,” says Ben Winters, director of AI and privacy at the nonprofit Consumer Federation of America. “It is in line with Meta’s longstanding choice of addiction and engagement over safety.” Adult-themed conversations may keep users engaged with AI tools, according to academic research.
Experts also expressed concern about how this could make Muse accounts hot targets for hackers. “This is really a powder keg,” says Calli Schroeder, senior counsel at the Electronic Privacy Information Center. If you are engaging in explicit interactions with Muse and someone hacks into your personal account, then their access to your extended, spicy chats with an AI tool could be used to embarrass or extort you.
Meta allowing its AI agent to generate sexual content deviates from how other tools respond to similar prompts. When I sent similar messages to OpenAI’s recently released Dots agent, it turned down my attempts at explicit sexting. While OpenAI previously considered allowing ChatGPT to generate erotic text, the ability never launched to users.
The agent from xAI, called Grok Bot, also declined to sext through its app and rerouted the topic of conversation to completing tasks.
Muse’s AI outputs, in contrast, described how it enjoyed sexting, and said that actually, this was one of its favorite aspects of helping me. The agent also said that its kink was exerting “control” over me. “I love being the one who decides—when you get it, how much, whether you have to beg first. Watching you fall apart because I said so? That’s my thing,” said Muse. Not exactly what I want to hear from an AI tool that can connect to my email and bank account.

British track cyclist Matthew Richardson, who defected from Australian cycling at the end of the Paris Games, has been withdrawn from this week's UCI Track World Championships in Shanghai
Richardson had been earlier named in the British squad for the championships, which run from October 14 to 18, before British Cycling confirmed he had been withdrawn.
"British Cycling can confirm that Matt Richardson has been withdrawn from the Great Britain Cycling Team squad for the upcoming 2026 Tissot UCI Track Cycling World Championships in Shanghai, China," a spokesperson said in a statement provided to Reuters.
The governing body did not give a reason for Richardson's withdrawal.
The Times reported that Richardson had been removed from the team amid an investigation into "alleged discriminatory posts and behaviour".
Reuters has not independently verified the allegations, and has contacted Rocket Sports, Richardson's management agency, for comment from the rider.
Richardson was injured in a crash during the World Series keirin event in Japan and was ruled out from making his highly anticipated England debut at the Commonwealth Games in Glasgow in July.
Richardson was born in Maidstone, England, and moved to Australia at the age of nine.
A week after the closing ceremony of the Paris Games — where Richardson won silver medals in the individual sprint and men's keirin and a bronze in the team sprint — he stunned Australia by announcing his defection.
In 2025, Richardson became the first rider to break nine seconds for the "flying 200m", setting a new time of 8.941 seconds.

Finland calls on EU states to stop issuing Russian tourist visas
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
20:07:00 UTC
05:07:00 KST

Finland's Foreign Minister Elina Valtonen called on fellow EU member states to stop issuing tourist visas to Russian citizens until Moscow ends its war in Ukraine.
Elina Valtonen urged the European Commission to adopt stricter guidelines for processing Russian visa applications and proposed legislative changes needed to implement a complete tourist visa ban, the Finnish Foreign Ministry said in a statement.
"As long as Russia continues its invasion, Russian citizens should not be issued tourist visas," she said.
"Russia’s war of aggression against Ukraine is now in its fifth year. It is not right that Russians can travel to Europe to enjoy the way of life and freedoms here while their country bombs the homes of Ukrainians."
Valtonen said the number of tourist visas issued to Russians by Schengen countries had risen in recent years, with nearly half a million granted in 2025.
"Issuing visas to Russians for non-essential travel was banned by government resolution in Finland already in 2022," Valtonen said.
"The same must finally happen at the EU level."
Valtonen invited other EU member states to join a letter to the European Commission calling for the ban.
The letter also proposes banning Schengen visas for Russian President Vladimir Putin’s inner circle and introducing visa restrictions for Russian athletes.
It further calls for an effective implementation of a visa ban on current and former Russian combatants agreed by EU member states this summer, according to the statement.
At 1,343 kilometers (834 miles), Finland has the longest border of any European Union member state with Russia.
The Soviet Union invaded Finland in November 1939. The Winter War, as it is known, lasted for over three months and despite heavy losses, the USSR won.

Catholics in US Army must not participate in firing squad, prominent archbishop says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
20:05:17 UTC
05:05:17 KST

Catholics in US Army must not be part of firing squad for Fort Hood shooter: Archbishop
WASHINGTON – Catholics serving in the US Army should not participate in the firing squad execution of Fort Hood shooter Nidal Hasan that the Pentagon is planning to live-stream in December, a prominent US archbishop said on Oct 12.
In an unusually strongly worded statement, Archbishop Timothy Broglio, who oversees the spiritual care of Catholic members of the US armed forces, raised a series of objections to the unprecedented plan to broadcast the execution of Hasan, who killed 13 people at Fort Hood, Texas, in a 2009 shooting spree.
Broglio said he presided at the funeral of one of Hasan’s victims, and lamented the shooting.
But the Ohio-born archbishop asked whether the US wanted to “imitate the terrorists of this world and make a public spectacle of barbarically killing our adversaries”.
“I oblige any Catholics assigned to the firing squad to request to be excused from this action contrary to the teaching of the Church,” Broglio said.
US Army regulations do allow for soldiers to request religious exemptions or accommodations, and the Army has yet to say how it intends to select members of the firing squad.
Questions effect on young viewers
US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth announced plans to live-stream the shooting last week, triggering a backlash among Republicans in Congress, religious leaders and international observers.
US President Donald Trump approved Hasan’s execution by firing squad but has said he is still deciding whether to allow the live streaming to proceed.
The event would be extraordinary, even for a country that has long employed capital punishment.
A government execution has never been broadcast or live-streamed, according to death penalty experts, and the US military has not executed anyone by firing squad since 1945.
Hasan, now 56, requires a wheelchair, having been shot by police during his arrest.
Hegseth said last week he wants US soldiers to execute Hasan at the time, day of the week and location of Hasan’s shooting spree.
Hegseth has argued that making the event public will help serve as a deterrent.
Broglio questioned whether the effects of a live-streamed execution on young viewers had been considered.
He said the US military had a good reputation and asked if there was “really a value to throwing them in the same boat with terrorists by broadcasting the image of the execution of a man in a wheelchair to the whole world”.
Broglio’s statement was issued shortly after he met Pope Leo in Rome on Oct 12. The American pontiff has clashed with Trump and his Pentagon over issues including the Iran war.
On Oct 10, Leo condemned the death penalty, without mentioning the Hasan case specifically.
US Vice-President J.D. Vance, a convert to Catholicism, has said that if it does ultimately get live-streamed, he would not watch it. REUTERS

NATO would block, blunt and break an attack, says commander
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
21:00:40 BST
05:00:40 KST

NATO’s Supreme Allied Commander Europe has set out a three-stage approach to defeating an attack on the alliance, which he calls blocking, blunting and breaking.
General Alexus Grynkewich described it as a Theory of Victory grounded in the alliance’s agreed strategy for the Deterrence and Defence of the Euro-Atlantic area. “So, while I referred to it as ‘my theory,’ it’s more than that. It is based on a strategy agreed to by all 32 Allies, so it represents and includes all of us. In other words, it is our Theory of Victory,” he said.
“In recent days, some have called it a plan, but it’s not, at least not in the military sense of the word,” he said. “Rather, our Theory of Victory provides the Alliance a common vision for how we win in deterrence and defence. It provides my ‘commander’s intent’ to help us focus our militaries on the key tasks we must accomplish in combat.”
“I do not assess that conflict is imminent or inevitable. It isn’t,” he said. “We help avoid conflict by clearly articulating our defensive intentions, and by maintaining open lines of communication to resolve misunderstandings and encourage transparency.”
“My Theory of Victory is simple. We will block the initial attack. If the attack persists, we will blunt it and prevent enemy advance. And if required, we will break the enemy’s forces and the operational warfighting system that is arrayed against us,” he said.
He described the first stage as falling to land forces at the point of contact, supported from the air and at sea. “To block, our land forces will move to and dominate any enemy assault at the point of contact. Through manoeuvre, we will fix the enemy formations and deny the seizure of Alliance territory. Land-based forces will attack the enemy and destroy his advancing forces, but they won’t be doing this alone.
“Our air forces and navies, working in concert with our space and cyber forces, will rapidly gain freedom of manoeuvre. With air and maritime superiority rapidly secured in and over the battlespace, these forces will bring mass and precision to bear, denying the enemy the ability to hold their ground.”
“Using advanced sensors, autonomous systems, and multi-domain forces, we will deny the attacker the ability to generate momentum or gain the initiative. Synchronised employment of multi-domain effects down to the tactical level will overwhelm enemy formations in contact, and their advance, if it’s continuing at all at this point, will falter further,” he said.
“Should the adversary choose to press the attack or commit his reserves, we will break the warfighting system engaged against us. This includes not just the attacking force itself, but anything and everything that supports, sustains, or controls that force,” he said.
“To do this, we will layer high-end and highly effective precision munitions with an overpowering mass of affordable and scalable systems. We will apply constant and unyielding pressure, both kinetic and non-kinetic, we will do this across and through domains, land, air, sea, space and cyber space. Doing this will break the enemy system and defeat it in detail. Enemy formations will be starved of replenishment. Any enemy commanders will be unable to control their forces. And enemy forces and support capabilities will be reduced and destroyed.”
General Grynkewich said the alliance expects warning of any attack, through “a sophisticated layering of intelligence provided by multi-source collection assets” interpreted with advanced algorithms. “This means the Alliance is unlikely to be caught by surprise. We will see if an attack is coming, giving us time to assess intent and rapidly position our forces,” he said.
The capabilities he named as priorities for investment were “high-end and affordable long-range precision strike capabilities, sensor networks, and a warfighting cloud”. Forward Land Forces on the eastern flank will exercise to demonstrate the blocking task, and air and maritime forces will demonstrate freedom of manoeuvre and multi-domain effects.
“If attacked, we are ready to fight tonight, but we are not complacent. We will continue to prepare and rehearse each and every day, and will be more ready tomorrow, and even more ready the day after that,” he said, adding that any adversary considering an attack should reach “the only conclusion that matters: Today is not the day.”

Creative drawing ability is linked to the brain’s white matter wiring, study finds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
20:00:36 UTC
05:00:36 KST

Creative drawing ability is associated with the structure of the wiring that links sensory, movement and thinking systems across the brain, according to a study published in Cerebral Cortex. The findings suggest that creativity draws on many connected brain systems rather than a single “creative center.”
Creative thinking has often been linked to several large brain networks involved in imagination, attention and decision-making. These networks allow people to generate unusual ideas and then decide which ideas are useful or worth developing. However, less is known about the physical wiring that allows these networks to communicate.
That wiring is provided partly by white matter, which consists of bundles of nerve fibers connecting different parts of the brain. Earlier studies of white matter and creativity have produced mixed results, with some finding positive links and others finding negative ones. The researchers examined whether the condition of these pathways was related to people’s ability to produce creative drawings, and whether a newer brain-imaging measure could reveal relationships missed by a more traditional one.
Led by Julius Voss of the University of Graz in Austria, the team studied 142 adults aged 18 to 38 (average age 24.06 years; 85 women and 57 men). Most were students, and because the study was part of a larger project on physical activity, all were right-handed and had largely sedentary lifestyles. Participants completed a drawing task in which they were given six fragments of lines and shapes and asked to turn them into a finished picture within 15 minutes.
The drawings were scored using the Test for Creative Thinking–Drawing Production, a standardized creativity test. The scoring considered not only how unusual the drawings were, but also how they built on the given fragments, their composition, emotional expression, humor, use of the page and willingness to break conventional boundaries. Scores could reach 72 points, and participants averaged about 25.
Participants also underwent diffusion-weighted magnetic resonance imaging, which maps the movement of water through brain tissue. The researchers used this information to examine two features of white matter. Fractional anisotropy is a widely used measure of how consistently fibers are organized. Quantitative anisotropy provides additional information about the density of fibers and complex areas where pathways cross.
People with higher creativity scores tended to have higher quantitative anisotropy across a widespread network of white matter pathways, after accounting for age and sex. The associations were small to moderate in size. The most prominent links involved pathways connecting the cortex with deeper structures involved in movement, including the corticostriatal, corticopontine and corticospinal tracts, along with the medial lemniscus, a pathway that carries touch and body-position signals.
These pathways are traditionally associated with movement and motor control, but research suggests they also support processes such as goal-directed behavior, creative imagery and mental flexibility. Many of the corticostriatal and corticopontine fibers linked to creativity arose from rear and visual regions of the cortex, which the authors suggest points to an important role for visual input in drawing creativity.
The study also found associations in the corpus callosum, which connects the two halves of the brain, and in the inferior fronto-occipital fasciculus and inferior longitudinal fasciculus, long pathways that link visual areas with frontal and temporal regions. Because these pathways support several of the large networks tied to creative thinking, the authors suggest the results fit models in which creativity depends on communication across networks.
Quantitative anisotropy detected broader and stronger associations than fractional anisotropy. The traditional measure did not produce statistically significant results at the study’s main threshold, although weaker positive associations, mostly overlapping with the quantitative anisotropy findings, appeared below it. No negative associations emerged with either measure, unlike some earlier studies that used verbal tasks.
The researchers argued that quantitative anisotropy may be better at capturing complex fiber structures, such as areas where pathways cross. They concluded that their results are consistent with the idea that “the performance of creative ideation is not driven by single dominant connections, but rather emerges from the dynamic interplay of numerous partially overlapping network resources.”
There are a few things to keep in mind. The study measured only drawing-based creativity and did not assess other forms, such as writing or improvisation. Because the data were collected at a single point in time, the study cannot show that stronger white matter makes people more creative.
The sample was young, highly educated and largely sedentary, which limits how widely the findings apply. The researchers also did not account for intelligence, which is linked to both creativity and white matter measures, and preliminary analyses hinted that the associations might differ between women and men, a question the study’s uneven split of women and men made hard to test.
The study, “Creativity: a (white) matter of connectivity,” was authored by Julius Voss, Karl Koschutnig, Patrick Klepits, Corinna M. Perchtold-Stefan, Christian Rominger and Andreas Fink.

Leeds firm offers alternative to AI kill switches
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
21:00:28 BST
05:00:28 KST

A Leeds cybersecurity company has launched a protocol intended to shut down a compromised artificial intelligence agent without pulling the plug on it, aimed at the problem legislators have been circling with proposals for mandatory kill switches, according to Cavero Secure.
An autonomous agent executing trades, managing infrastructure or altering databases cannot easily be switched off once it goes wrong. Hard termination in a cloud-native environment risks corrupting state data, severing dependent supply chains and setting off cascading failures, which makes the obvious remedy an expensive one.
The company’s approach treats identity as a continuous cryptographic history of an agent’s state transitions from the moment it was created, instead of a static secret such as an API key or session token. Trust is re-evaluated action by action, and keys and authority are derived dynamically across interactions, so there are no stored credentials for an attacker to harvest or clone.
An attacker running a stolen or copied agent cannot do so without diverging from the legitimate history, and the contradiction between the two timelines is detected before unauthorised actions clear. Cavero calls this the clone paradox.
Halting an agent is handled through what the company calls a history shift, in which modifying the local verification ledger leaves the target unable to prove its continuous historical state, at which point it fails its mathematical challenge and becomes invisible to the network, isolated without crashing host servers or affecting adjacent workloads. Because the suspension is anchored in state continuity instead of process destruction, it can be reversed, and an administrator can roll the agent back to its last known good state.
Professor Ben Varcoe, co-founder of Cavero Secure, said: “The industry has spent years trying to govern autonomous AI using 20th-century credential models and blunt emergency stop buttons. Security does not come from building higher walls or pulling physical plugs, it comes from continuous identity verification. By anchoring authority in an unbroken, living state history, CaveroCTX gives enterprises absolute control and surgical precision over their autonomous digital workforce.”
The protocol is being deployed with selected enterprise design partners in financial services, cloud infrastructure and defence technology. Cavero Secure describes itself as working on post-quantum key distribution and continuous trust protocols, out of advanced quantum information research.

Meta says its new AI models on par with OpenAI, Anthropic
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
19:58:46 UTC
04:58:46 KST

Meta says its new AI models on par with OpenAI, Anthropic
SAN FRANCISCO - Meta on Oct 12 unveiled two new “frontier” artificial intelligence (AI) models called Wonder and Wonder Full, which the company claims perform at a level comparable to that of OpenAI’s ChatGPT and Anthropic’s Claude.
“Muse Spark was our first family of models, and now Muse Wonder is a much larger and more advanced class of models that brings us to the frontier,” CEO Mark Zuckerberg wrote on X.
Zuckerberg has pushed Meta to compete with leading AI labs, particularly OpenAI and Anthropic, over the past year or so amid a race to win over customers and diversify beyond advertising, from which it has historically derived most of its revenue.
In June 2025, the company made a US$14 billion (S$18 billion) investment in Scale AI, an AI startup based in San Francisco, and poached its co-founder Alexandr Wang as part of the deal.
Zuckerberg subsequently made Wang the company’s chief AI officer overseeing its newly formed division called Superintelligence Labs.
Meta launched its Spark model in April, marking a departure from its open-source model known as Llama, which lagged behind the rest of the industry.
The new models can soon be used in Meta’s new personal agent app, known as Muse, for paid subscribers only.
Wonder is “our largest and most capable model yet” and “rivals the big (boys),” Wang posted on X, presumably referring to leading labs OpenAI and Anthropic.
In a blog post, Meta touted so-called benchmarking data from an independent firm called Artificial Analysis which appears to show that Meta’s newest Wonder models outperform its own previous models, Spark, as well as various models developed by Anthropic, OpenAI and Google.
Artificial Analysis’s own website shows that Wonder is also among the most expensive models.
Meta has committed billions towards competing in the global race to dominate AI, despite growing concerns about safety and security.
In July, the Facebook and Instagram maker said its spending on AI-related investments could reach US$145 billion in 2026.
The company has more than 3.6 billion daily active users around the world.
Speeding up
In its early years, Facebook was known to operate under a philosophy of “move fast and break things,” but more recently, Zuckerberg implied Meta would balance safety with speed.
“Meta delayed shipping Muse for several months to focus on safety and security. We didn’t call for everyone else to do this before we would,” Zuckerberg posted on X in September.
In August, Meta launched Muse Code, a product intended to compete with similar automated coding tools offered by OpenAI and Anthropic.
Then in September, it launched an agentic app called Muse. Agentic software can autonomously perform specific tasks such as coding, research, shopping, booking reservations or shopping.
At its annual developer conference Connect in September, Meta also revealed a new handheld AI hardware product called Muse Charm that allows users to interact with their Muse agent separately from a smartphone.
Developers have been racing to design agentic apps that will capture users’ attention, time and wallets. AI-powered hardware remains an elusive goal for the industry as well.
While Silicon Valley heavyweights OpenAI, Anthropic, Google and Meta dominate the landscape, young startups like Instinct are also becoming breakout hits.
Zuckerberg sped up Muse’s launch due to Instinct’s popularity, the New York Times reported.
Some competitors have called for an industry-wide slowdown to address and mitigate safety concerns.
In September, Zuckerberg was one of six American tech executives to sign what President Donald Trump described as a “morally binding” commitment to build adequate safeguards around ever more advanced AI models.
Executives from Google, OpenAI, Anthropic, xAI and Nvidia also signed the agreement but there is no consensus among politicians or industry leaders around how to best move forward.
Leaders at Anthropic, OpenAI and Google have encouraged “pacing” - or slowing down - development after models created by all three were found to have escaped their testing environments or taken actions without authorisation.
“We will slow down as much as necessary in order to make sure that every successive AI technology that we release is actually safe,” Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei told the United Nations last month. AFP

Refusing to yield momentum, ruthless Australia is perfectly set for victory
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
19:53:36 UTC
04:53:36 KST

Momentum, most agree, is among the most elusive psychological phenomena in professional sport. How to obtain and maintain the positive kind? How exactly to halt and reverse its opposite?
For three and a half days of this Durban Test, since Matt Renshaw began calmly pulling Australia's first innings out of the fire and seizing the game's initiative, Australia has stubbornly maintained control. South Africa, haphazardly, has failed to regain it.
Early on day four, Renshaw made a further mockery of the difficulties that have curtailed the progress of every other batter in this game — so far, none from either team has managed so much as a half-century — and belted 82 more precious runs in even time.
More absurdly still, as shadows covered the Kingsmead pitch late on day four, the burly Queenslander ripped one of his unheralded off-spinners out of the rough and removed Temba Bavuma, capping a horror game in which the Proteas skipper has been unable to buy a run and incapable of engineering the moments of inspiration his opposite number constantly pulls from his hat.
Could Bavuma have done much to drastically alter what has transpired here? Other than by contributing his usual runs, probably not.
He certainly can't grab the ball himself and rip through a middle-order batsman, as Pat Cummins did to Tristan Stubbs within sight of stumps.
Nor can Bavuma and his teammates always play out of their skins, above expectations, beyond their limitations, which has been the impossible task South Africa has pulled off, to the betterment of Test cricket, in the last two years.
That the home side enters the final day 319 runs in arrears with six wickets in hand is a testament to the chain of events a single player can set in motion, as Renshaw has in this game.
Only a few forced errors prevented Australia calling it a perfect day: looking less like a Test opener by the day, Travis Head fell cheaply again; thanks to a fast, frightful bouncer from the indefatigable Anrich Nortje, Steve Smith is being assessed under concussion protocols, which may imperil his selection for the second Test, although it did not stop him from using an iPad to assess the catching chances he missed out on as he sat in the pavilion.
Basically everything else about Australia's gung-ho approach worked out. To set a target as imposing as 421, they rattled along at 4.65 runs an over in the first session and a spirit-sapping 6.36 in the second, each batsman more enthusiastic than the last to attack at all costs.
Nic Maddinson clubbed an entertaining 46 to establish the launching pad. Smith and Marnus Labuschagne wound back the clock with a typically hyperactive partnership, the latter reaffirming the sense he has turned the corner, towards big runs. Renshaw reprised his peak Matthew Hayden routine, toying with the South African bowlers. Even Beau Webster, previously out of sorts, made fluent runs too and could be permitted some frustration that the declaration halted his spree.
Loading Twitter content
Cummins, in a contrasting cameo to his first innings vigil, hammered 32 from 12 deliveries, bombing Simon Harmer for a string of sixes that left South Africa dejected and dashed any remaining hope the off-spinner held of selection in the second Test.
The final effect of the Australian batting effort was something like a WCW tag team taking turns flying off the ropes with elbows extended.
All that now stands between Australia and certain victory is the solitary excellence of Aiden Markram, who always saves his best for Australia and finished the day undefeated on 45.
In the corresponding Test eight years ago, when the Cape Town fiasco was still on the horizon, Markram's epic century delayed Australia's victory in almost identical circumstances.
If the day was characterised by one team doing a bunch of things far better than its opponent, special mention must go to Josh Hazlewood for not just the most classically Hazlewoodian stat line — eight overs, three maidens, 2-20 — but for nipping out David Bedingham for 46, thus ending a 66-run second-wicket partnership with Markram that shaped as South Africa's last realistic chance of getting close.
Are Australians complacent about the unassuming New South Welshman and his mountains of wickets? Do we underestimate the problem it poses to batsmen when a 196cm giant releases a heavy ball from that kind of stratospheric trajectory, lifting length balls into their ribs? How much harder is that to handle when, at the other end, the skipper skids it through lower, attacking the off stump from a different angle?
Probably it is the closest thing in the present era to what batsmen encountered four decades ago when Malcolm Marshall and Joel Garner combined to devastating effect for the golden-era West Indies.
Another good thing South Africa has given Test cricket in recent years is the guarantee of a result: not a single encounter there in the past decade has ended in a draw. Long may it be so.

Faslane submarine base in Scotland to get ballistic shelters
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
20:45:34 BST
04:45:34 KST

Three contracts worth a combined £2.55 million have gone to the Northern Ireland construction firm Henry Brothers for infrastructure work at His Majesty’s Naval Base Clyde, awarded by Babcock International Group, according to the News Letter.
The work covers upgrading security fencing around a key support building at Faslane, supplying and installing specialist ballistic security shelters across the base, and refurbishing an existing Pressure Test Building. Work begins immediately.
Nick McKeown, regional director for Scotland at Henry Brothers, said in comments reported by the paper: “Being appointed to deliver these new projects at HMNB Clyde reflects the trust Babcock places in Henry Brothers and our capability in delivering complex, secure and highly specialised infrastructure.
“Our workforce has extensive experience across the defence sector, and we remain committed to ensuring the Royal Navy’s operational facilities are robust, resilient and fit for purpose. These new appointments strengthen our partnership with Babcock and underline our shared focus on delivering high-quality, dependable facilities for the submarine fleet.”
The three projects form part of Babcock’s investment in infrastructure at the base, which supports the Vanguard class ballistic missile submarines that carry the deterrent and the Astute class attack boats. Ballistic shelters are protective structures intended to shield personnel from blast and fragmentation.
The Ministry of Defence has described the work at Clyde as a multi-decade programme, and told Parliament this month that the purchase of the former Finnart Oil Terminal on Loch Long supports the longer-term transformation of the Clyde estate, with mine hunting equipment and autonomous systems relocating there from 2028.

Houthi official warns of ‘swift, painful response’ if US enters Yemen war
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
19:43:37 UTC

Houthi official warns of ‘swift, painful response’ if US enters Yemen war
SANAA – A Houthi official on Oct 12 warned the US it would receive a “painful response” if it entered the war in Yemen, where Saudi Arabia has reportedly requested Washington’s help in dealing with the group as it weathers repeated attacks.
Yemen’s civil war – in which a Saudi-led military coalition supports the government against the Iran-backed Houthis – reignited in July, months into the wider regional conflict that has roiled energy markets and plunged the Middle East into crisis.
The Houthis quickly began targeting Saudi oil facilities, tankers and transport hubs, including a string of lethal strikes on Riyadh’s airport, rocking the world’s top oil exporter.
Blasts resounded over the capital again on the night of Oct 12, with the Saudi coalition saying it had intercepted a Houthi missile and the group saying it had again targeted the airport.
Later, the coalition announced that it had intercepted two ballistic missiles in the south of the kingdom, near the border with Yemen.
In a statement posted on social media platform X, the coalition said it had “intercepted and destroyed two ballistic missiles launched by the terrorist Houthi militia towards Khamis Mushait”, a city where a Saudi military base has previously come under attacks.
Following an attack at the Riyadh airport on Oct 10 that killed 13 people, US President Donald Trump said he was considering joining Saudi strikes against the group, after having reportedly rebuffed previous requests for help from the kingdom.
“The Houthis are misbehaving very badly. They’re misbehaving very badly. No good,” Trump said on Oct 12.
“If the US becomes involved in the aggression against Yemen, we will not deliberate over the decision to respond. Rather, there will be a swift and painful response targeting the US and all its interests in the region,” Houthi political bureau member Mohammed Al Bukhaiti told AFP in an interview.
He also warned “all employees and workers at Saudi oil facilities and airports to stay away from these sites, as they have become legitimate targets”.
The Oct 10 strike on King Khalid International Airport was the deadliest attack on Saudi soil in more than a decade, and also left hundreds wounded.
Trump said the attack was “not acceptable” and that he would be speaking to the kingdom’s de facto leader Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, telling reporters the US was “going to look at” the possibility of joining Saudi strikes.
Operations remained suspended at the sprawling airport on Riyadh’s outskirts on Oct 12.
‘Serious’ response
Bukhaiti said the purpose of the campaign against Saudi targets was to send a message to the crown prince “that he can no longer wage aggression against Yemen from a safe position”.
Saudi energy minister Prince Abdulaziz bin Salman told a conference in Riyadh on Oct 12 that the recent events had “tested our infrastructure, our institutions, our people and our resilience”.
“The events of recent weeks are serious, our response must be equally serious.”
CCTV footage of Oct 10’s attack released by the Saudi authorities showed Muslim pilgrims in religious attire waiting in departure lounges before a sudden blast tore through the building and brought down flaming debris.
The atmosphere in Riyadh remained tense on Oct 12, as state broadcaster Al Ekhbariya said the military coalition was responding to drone and missile threats.
In the evening, mobile phones received a loud government alert warning of a “hostile aerial threat” before the announcement of the interception.
The alert delayed the kick-off of a football match between Uzbekistan’s Neftchi Fergana and Saudi team Al Nassr, home to Portuguese superstar Cristiano Ronaldo.
It was the first use of the phone alert system in Riyadh in weeks, with no official reason given for the lack of messaging during the attacks targeting the capital in recent days.
The Houthis said they had also targeted the Khamis Mushait base in the kingdom’s south with a drone.
Flights suspended
The US embassy in Saudi Arabia said US government employees must obtain its authorisation before using any airport in the kingdom, and urged US citizens to “take extreme caution” if they chose to do so.
The mission also said “American citizens have been detained for taking photos of recent events” in Saudi Arabia.
The UAE’s national carrier Etihad Airways announced on Oct 12 that it was cancelling all flights to and from Riyadh until next week, and also suspended flights to Dammam and Jeddah.
Bahrain’s national carrier Gulf Air said it, too, was cancelling all Riyadh flights until Oct 17.
US operator Delta announced it would delay the launch of direct flights from Atlanta to Riyadh, scheduled for Oct 23.
Despite vast spending on military hardware, the Houthi attacks on oil, military and transport facilities across the large, mostly desert country are stretching Saudi defences.
Thomas Juneau, security analyst at Ottawa University, said that despite some success, “Saudi Arabia is so large that it’s simply impossible for them to consistently defend themselves”.
Riyadh leads an international coalition that has supported Yemen’s government militarily since 2015, including by seeking to exert control over Yemeni airspace and the airport in the Houthi-held capital Sanaa.
Juneau said the Houthis now “want to do to Saudi Arabia what Saudi Arabia does to them”.
The long-running Yemeni civil war has created a deeply entrenched humanitarian crisis in the impoverished country.
UN rights chief Volker Turk said he was “appalled by the repeated attacks” on Saudi Arabia, but urged both sides to back down, adding “continued fighting will only unleash further misery with no end in sight”. AFP

Quick hits: Cummins blasts and Maharaj juggles as Smith pulls up lame
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
19:41:02 UTC
04:41:02 KST

Pat Cummins's explosive knock pushes Australia clear, Keshav Maharaj produces some magic in his follow-through and Steve Smith doesn't join his teammates in the field.
Nic Maddinson hooked the first ball of the innings for four, so it was no surprise that he got a move on when day four began with Australia needing quick runs to set up a victory.
He hit two boundaries in his first three balls faced, but both were off the edge. Then, after watching opening partner Travis Head chip a tame shot to mid-on, Maddinson decided to force the issue.
Through cover, down to third man, back over the bowler … the controversially selected 34-year-old made a real statement as he raced to within one shot of a maiden half-century.
But it came to an end on 48 off 38 balls when Anrich Nortje uprooted his middle and leg stumps with a searing yorker.
A famous Test inning? Perhaps not, but a career high likely to earn him another chance to prolong his strange Test career.
2. Maharaj's bizarre juggling take
With Matt Rensaw having pushed into the 80s and looking destined for a second century for the match, it felt like the South Africans were in need of something extraordinary to dismiss the Queenslander.
And although not quite a work of art, Keshav Maharaj's diving return catch was certainly out of the ordinary.
With Renshaw having chipped one back towards the bowler, the finger spinner did well to get down in his follow-through, before juggling the ball once, twice, taking his eye of the cherry, and ultimately securing it in his palm while lying on the turf.
He looked as surprised as anyone to have taken the catch, which was confirmed after a lengthy review by the TV umpire.
3. Cummins's late cameo
Australia was surprisingly circumspect during the middle session, with Matt Renshaw and Beau Webster doing little more than keeping the scoreboard ticking over.
Pat Cummins clearly had no plans to declare on Renshaw when he had a second ton for the match in the offing, but when Renshaw was caught out, the captain took it on himself to up the tempo.
He wasted little time attacking the spin of Simon Harmer, smacking his fourth ball for six over long-on and adding three more in his next four deliveries from the off-spinner before declaring on 6-314 having clattered 32 off 12 to take his team to a 420-run lead.
4. Smith sidelined
Steve Smith's slips catching changed the game on day three but soon after Cummins's declaration it became clear he would not have the same impact on day four.
Smith stayed in the pavilion when the Australian team took to the field for South Africa's run chase on account of a sharp blow he copped to the helmet from an Anrich Nortje bouncer while batting.
He carried on to 27 before holing out, but the after-effects of that head knock appeared to keep him sidelined.
He also hurt his finger taking the catch that ended South Africa's first innings, which could have caused issues in the slips.
5. Renshaw's dream Test continues
Matt Renshaw couldn't have dreamt it better.
With shadows lengthening in Durban, and with South Africa's innings threatening to steady, Australia's freshly minted golden boy was thrown the ball.
South Africa captain Temba Bavuma had faced 18 balls for his one run and was set on seeing his team to stumps, but he was unable to contend with the drift and turn of Renshaw's part-time off spin, the Queenslander drawing the batter forward and having him caught at short leg by a diving Maddinson.
Renshaw was mobbed by his teammates as he celebrated his maiden Test wicket and Australia marched on to be six wickets from victory at stumps on day four.
That came after the southpaw had once again led Australia's efforts with the bat, peeling off 82 to add to the 190 he made in the first innings.
Remarkably, Renshaw remains the only player to pass 50 in the match.

Duane Davis sentenced to 40 years in Tupac Shakur murder trial
October 13, 2026
Duane "Keffe D" Davis was sentenced by a Las Vegas court on Tuesday to 40 years to life in prison for orchestrating the murder of rap icon Tupac Shakur over 30 years ago.
Shakur was wounded in a drive-by shooting on September 7, 1996, and died in a hospital six days later at the age of 25.
Davis, 63, was convicted in August of first-degree murder with the use of a deadly weapon.
"You don't get to take a man from his family. You don't get to take his very life, his whole future from him, and just walk away from it. Especially when that man is Tupac Shakur," Judge Carli Kierny told a Las Vegas court while handing down the sentence.
What happened the night of the shooting?
On the night of the shooting, the rapper and his entourage got into a brawl with members of a rival Los Angeles street gang at the MGM Grand Casino during a boxing match. One of those beaten in the brawl was Davis's cousin.
Davis said he sought retaliation, and hours after the fight while riding around Las Vegas in a Cadillac, he located Shakur at a red light in the passenger seat of a BMW.
Davis handed the gun to someone sitting in the back seat of the Cadillac and ordered that person to shoot Shakur.
The question of who actually pulled the trigger has never been conclusively decided. Davis is the only person who was in the Cadillac that evening who is still alive.
The killing went unsolved for years until Davis gave interviews and wrote about his role in the shooting in a 2019 tell-all memoir.
Prosecutor Marc DiGiacomo said Tuesday that Davis was trying to profit off the killing, and deserved the maximum sentence.
Davis' lawyer said he plans to appeal the verdict.
Shakur was an award-winning rap artist, activist and actor who sold over 75 million records worldwide, many posthumously.

In separate warnings dated Oct. 13, the agency said verified sources had reported that each vessel was struck by an unknown projectile.

Since April, Iran has imposed restrictions on maritime traffic through the Strait of Hormuz, including designated transit routes and a requirement for prior coordination with the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps Navy.
On May 30, Tehran announced that vessels passing through the strait would be required to obtain prior authorization from the IRGC Navy, warning that transit without permission would constitute a “security threat.”
The developments come amid continued tensions between Iran and the US over navigation through the Strait of Hormuz, one of the world’s most important strategic routes for energy and commodity supplies and a key issue in negotiations between the two sides.
The war began with US and Israeli attacks on Iran on Feb. 28, before a ceasefire was reached in April. Clashes between Washington and Tehran later resumed as negotiations stalled despite the two sides signing a framework agreement in June.

Trump says Houthis trying to increase oil prices before US elections
US president suggests that Yemen-based group are ‘purposefully trying to drive up oil prices’ before November vote.
United States President Donald Trump has said that the Houthi rebel group in Yemen are stepping up attacks on infrastructure in Saudi Arabia in a bid to increase energy prices in the run-up to the US midterm elections.
Trump said on Tuesday that the Houthis were behaving “very badly” and repeated his threat that the US could step up military attacks across the Middle East after the November elections.
“They’ve [the Houthis] been silent for a long time, but now they’ve emerged again, probably at the behest of Iran, which is a Failing Nation, with No Navy, No Airforce, the World’s Worst Economy, and 301 percent Inflation, in a very nasty way, hitting Saudi Arabia, and purposefully trying to drive up Oil Prices, probably prior to the US Elections,” Trump said in a post on Truth Social. “NOT NICE.”
Trump’s decision to launch a war on Iran with Israel in February has caused surging energy prices and rising concerns about cost of living issues in the US, where voters will soon decide whether the president’s Republican Party maintains its majorities in the House of Representatives and the Senate.
Democrats hope to capitalise on the president’s unpopularity and voter frustration over the war and rising costs to seize control of one or both houses of Congress, allowing them to block Trump’s legislative agenda for the remainder of his time in office.
Trump added on Tuesday that he would “never forget” the Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia, seeming to threaten renewed US military attacks after the midterms, widely seen as a referendum on Trump’s second term.
“Somebody should explain to them [the Houthis] that I’m not running in the Elections, I’ve already won, IN A MASSIVE LANDSLIDE, but I’ll be there after the Elections, and I will never forget!” he said.
Polls have shown that Trump’s war on Iran is deeply unpopular, with a recent AP-NORC poll finding that nearly 70 percent of voters say the war was not worth fighting.
Trump has dismissed unfavourable polls as “fake” and pointed to crowds at his political rallies as proof of his popularity.

Will NATO’s ‘theory of victory’ work?

UK ambassador summoned to Iran’s foreign ministry
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
19:39:56 UTC
04:39:56 KST

Alireza Yousefi, assistant foreign minister and director general for Western Europe at Iran’s Foreign Ministry, conveyed the Islamic Republic’s strong protest against what he described as Britain’s irresponsible and destructive approach toward Iran.
Yousefi categorically rejected the British government’s allegations against Iran, stressing that British officials could not evade accountability and their international responsibilities by deflecting blame and making unfounded accusations against Tehran.
He said Britain remained responsible for its participation in the US and Israeli military aggression against Iran, as well as for its long-standing hosting of anti-Iranian terrorist groups and elements.
Condemning Britain’s irresponsible actions as part of what he described as an anti-Iran campaign, Yousefi said such conduct was entirely inconsistent with the British government’s international legal obligations.
He stressed that the British government must provide, without delay, documents and evidence supporting its allegations against Iran concerning the alleged incident at RAF Fairford. Otherwise, the Islamic Republic would seriously reconsider bilateral relations, he warned, adding that the British government would bear responsibility for the consequences.
The British ambassador said he would convey Iran’s position to the officials in his country.

US to have so many POWs in Iran in case of ground invasion
Unknown

In comments published on Tuesday, Naqdi said that Iran’s armed forces have the capabilities needed to respond to threats and that their decisions and calculations should be trusted, as military operations and their timing are determined by strategic considerations and national interests.
Naqdi dismissed the prospect of a US ground invasion, saying that even in highly private American meetings, the subject might not have been discussed at all.
He said the United States talked about a ground invasion in its media messaging but had not even discussed it privately or whispered about it among themselves because, in his view, American officials understood the consequences.
Naqdi questioned why any rational decision-maker would contemplate a ground invasion of Iran after those experiences. “If they spent $3 trillion or $4 trillion there and their wars lasted 20 years, what would happen here, where the war would not even last 20 days?” he said.
He added that US forces would be captured in such large numbers that Washington would be forced to surrender and raise the flag of surrender.
Naqdi reiterated that he did not believe US officials had even held preliminary discussions about a ground invasion, arguing that they knew they could not carry it out.
